Description: THERMOSPHERIC O/N2 DENSITY AND SIGNATURES OF IMF BY ORIENTATION The dominant driver of neutral gas in the high-latitude thermosphere is momentum transfer (ion drag) from the imbedded ionosphere via E-cross-B drift, where the solar-wind-powered generator creates the externally imposed E field. Magnitude of the interaction is minimum for the IMF strongly positive, and increases as the polar angle of B increases from northward (Bz > 0) to southward (Bz < 0). As the ion convection pattern is imprinted onto the neutral flow at high latitudes, it is seen that an IMF By signature is also present in the neutral flow patterns. Thermospheric composition in the morning sector responds to increased Joule and precipitating-particle heating during geomagnetic storms and intense auroral activity; conditions favored with Bz < 0. It is expected that thermospheric neutral composition also responds to IMF By, but measurements to date have been carried out on a case-by-case basis for large geomagnetic storms and intense auroral substorm activity, so they are not numerous and never ideal. Some model work even suggests the early interpretations suffer as a result. It is proposed here to investigate this unresolved issue of thermospheric composition in a new way, by taking advantage of improved precision offered by the FUV instrument on the TIMED satellite, GUVI. This is in contrasted to work previously done with FUV imaging instruments designed with other primary mission objectives. This would entail use of the still expanding GUVI database for all levels of magnetic activity, from quiet to the most intense, but for which the largest contribution to the database of continuous observations is generally distinct from the higher levels of magnetic activity usually considered. To fulfill this science objective, it is believed necessary to first investigate with care and fully account for the several parameters not associated with geomagnetic activity that affect OIN2 latitudinal profiles: i.e., time (UT), local solar time, and season. Each can be significant and introduces complications that can greatly hamper investigations of effects more subtle within dominant heating events and the resulting compositional changes. This is in itself a distinct science objective, as it yields quantitative models for the global column density ratio of O and N2.

Description: REFLIGHT OF THE CHANGING AURORA: IN SITU AND CAMERA ANALYSIS OF DYNAMIC ELECTRON PRECIPITATION STRUCTURES This Co-I proposal (lead proposal P.I.: Kristina Lynch, Dartmouth) is submitted in response to ROSS-2006 to the Geospace Low Cost Access to Space suborbital program (NNH06ZDAOOIN-GEO/LCAS). On a scale of a few kilometers, the active aurora is spatially and temporary very complicated. The variety of motions, changes in shape and intensity are such that they cannot be defined by the measurements by three payloads alone. However, if ground-based video imagers are available the general behavior of the aurora can be defined. With this general description to serve as a context, the detailed measurements of particles and fields from the three payloads can be analyzed and related to the overall auroral behavior. We propose to provide such video data of the aurora conjugate to the Cascades-2 rocket. We will install and operate low light level, narrow-field auroral TV imagers at Kaktovik (essentially under the apogee of the rocket) and at Poker Flat Research Range (PFRR). Additionally, we will have a high-speed imager at Kaktovik. Using the Range radar track, computer programs will calculate and communicate camera-pointing information to the observing sites in real time. Only with this real-time update of the pointing information is it possible to ensure that the aurora conjugate to the payload is within the camera 20xI6 degree field of view. The real-time pointing information is even more critical to the operation of the high-speed images because of the limitations in data that this instrument can acquire. The data will be recorded on videotape and on computer disk. The GI investigators will assist in the subsequent data analysis with particular emphasis on relating the optical auroral forms to the rocket particle and field observations.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION In this NASA EPSCoR RID proposal we seek to partner with the Alaska Space Grant Program to develop core competencies in the technological development and scientific application of small satellites to observations of the Earth environment. Understanding of the near Earth environment is currently "data-starved". Constellations and/or clusters of small satellites would fill gaps in space and time and contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the Earth's geospace environment. Alaska itself would benefit from observations of constellations of small satellites in terms of understanding global warming's effect on loss of wildlife habitat, understanding space weathers affect on airplane safety for over the pole flights, and monitoring fire hazards in a state that covers an area l/Sth the size of the continental United States, to name a few. This NASA EPSCoR RID proposal focuses on development of University of Alaska (UA) faculty in support of NASA's strategic goals by establishing close connections with NASA centers and aligning faculty research to NASA's mission. This proposal seeks to address NASA's strategic goal to "Study Earth from space to advance scientific understanding to meet societal needs".

Description: INVESTIGATION OF STRAIN RATE EFFECTS ON CRACK GROWTH IN GRAPHITE EPOXY COMPOSITES WITH STIFFENERS Airframe construction using light-weight and durable composites is at the core of next generation supersonic vehicles. The structural material to be used for this task needs to be not only light-weight but also offer excellent damage tolerance, durability and thermo-mechanical performance over a broad spectrum of thermomechanical loading conditions. The loading rate dependent mechanical responses of the matrix and fibermatrix interfaces would heavily influence overall failure responses such as strength and fracture toughness. In view of these, oneneeds tackle the underlying question namely 'does inertia dominated loading produce failure responses in FRPs that are different from the ones obtained under quasi-static conditions'? This proposal hopes to address this question for graphite/epoxy composites by developing a database on strain-rate dependent behavior pertaining to mechanical failure. Understanding damage nucleation and propagation under quasistatic and dynamic loading conditions in unidirectional and multidirectional graphite-epoxy lay-ups with and without structural stiffeners is at the heart of the proposed work.

ONE OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE CAIB REPORT IS TO ESTABLISH A THERMAL PROTECTION SYSTEM (TPS) REPAIR CAPABILITY FOR THE ORBITER WHILE THE SHUTTLE IS ON-ORBIT.NASA HAS COMMITTED TO COMPLY WITH THIS RECOMMENDATION PRIOR TO THE RESUMPTION OF SPACE SHUTTLE FLIGHTS, AND FOR THE PAST THREE YEARS FOLLOWING STS-107, NASA HAS AGGRESSIVELY RESEARCHED REPAIR METHODOLOGY FOR THE SPACE SHUTTLES WING LEADING EDGE. NOAX-D IS A PASTE-LIKE, SINGLE PART, HIGHLY LOADED, PRE-CERAMIC POLYMER WHICH FUNCTIONS AS AN ENVIRONMENTAL BARRIER TO RETARD OXIDATION OF THE CARBON/CARBON SUBSTRATE WHEN EXPOSED TO THE HIGH-TEMPERATURE ENVIRONMENT OF RE-ENTRY.THIS PROCUREMENT IS FOR A FOLLOW-ON EFFORT TO SUSTAIN MONTHLY PRODUCTION OF NOAX-D, AS A RESULT OF PREVIOUS SUCCESSFUL RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES, FOR THE REMAINING SPACE SHUTTLE FLIGHTS THROUGH 2010.

Description: MAPPING HAZARDOUS CONVECTIVE WEATHER EVENTS AND THEIR ENVIRONMENTS Passive microwave imager data from the NASA TRMM and Aqua satellites can be used to diagnose storms with potential for heavy rainfall, damaging hail, or frequent lightning. Direct records of flash flood or hail events are spatially limited by the need for either stream gauges or people to observe them. Hail records in particular are biased toward populated areas and effective reporting procedures. Passive microwave ice scattering in the 37 GHz and sometimes 18 1 19 GHz channels suggests which storms do have particularly large ice hydrometeors. Strong scattering signatures, also in the 85 / 89 GHz channels, are also associated with extreme convective-scale rain rates and frequent lightning. As such, flash flood, damaging hail, and frequent lightning hazards can be inferred. Microwave-based criteria will be set to identify the storms that do pose a substantial hazard from damaging hail, heavy rainfall, or lightning. Measurements from TMI (aboard TRMM), AMSR-E (aboard Aqua), and possibly SSMII (aboard multiple DMSP satellites) will be compiled to objectively map potential hazardous convective weather events on a nearly global basis. Methods include simply identifying extremely low brightness temperatures in convective systems, and also applying a more detailed ;Virtual Radar; algorithm to retrieve radar-like properties from microwave imager data. The Virtual Radar algorithm has been developed from TRMM data and will be expanded here to apply to other microwave imagers. This will prepare for possible application to the various microwave imagers of the future Global Precipitation Mission. Environmental conditions taken from the NCAR 1 NCEP Reanalysis will be associated with each event, and with events which fail to meet the criteria for hazardous convective weather. Following the approach of previous studies that have relied upon reports of significant severe weather in the United States, environmental conditions that favor hazardous convective weather will be objectively identified. While this satellite-based study introduces uncertainty by inferring characteristics from a column-integrated measure over a relatively large (by convective standards) footprint, it allows consideration of storms in areas without effective reporting networks for hazardous weather. Ultimately, this objective identification of environmental conditions associated with hazardous convective weather can suggest whether regional climate changes should be expected to increase or decrease the hazards from flash flooding, hailstorms, or lightning.

Description: O VII Line Emission in Sersic 159-03: Whim or Galactic Orgin We propose to observe the cluster of galaxies Sersic 159-03 using a total exposure time of 50 ks to investigate the soft excess emission previously detected in the observations with ROSAT and XMM-Newton. The superior redistribution function of Suzaku will allow us to determine whether the O VII line emission detected with XMM-Newton is of local (Galactic) origin or is emitted by the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) in the vicinity of the cluster. Description: STUDY OF BOW SHOCK ENERGETIC PARTICLES We propose to investigate particle acceleration at the Earth's quasi-parallel bow shock and properties of upstream energetic ions. Main science questions to be addressed in the proposal are the following. What are the characteristic energy and energetic ion flux at the quasi-parallel shock? What is the e-folding distance for the foreshock diffuse ions? How do the bow shock ion energy spectrum and e-folding distance depend on the solar wind and IMF condition? Results of this study will be used to characterize bow shock accelerated ions. This is an important step toward the understanding of source of energetic particles inside the magnetosphere and global transport of energetic particles. We will perform data analysis for Cluster upstream events and 3-D global hybrid simulations to accomplish our goal. The array of four Cluster spacecraft provides unprecedented spatial coverage and time resolution that can easily separate the spatial and temporal structures in the foreshock and bow shock measurements that would not be possible from prior missions with a similar orbit. By comparing energetic ion flux simultaneously observed by the Cluster spacecraft, we will quantify the spatial diffusion of foreshock ions to improve estimate of bow shock energetic ion flux. In addition, upstream wave energy derived from Cluster observations will be compared with particle energy to confirm or deny predictions from shock acceleration theory. We will also examine the dependence of bow shock acceleration on solar wind parameters and IMF/bow shock geometry to derive an empirical relation. Then with this relation one would have the forecast/nowcast capability to predict bow shock energetic ions from observed foreshock ion flux and solar wind/IMF parameters. Furthermore, we will run 3-D global hybrid code to study shock acceleration and wave particle interaction in the acceleration region for a number of typical upstream events from Cluster. Simulation results (particles and waves) will be compared with Cluster observations to yield a better interpretation for upstream observations and/or for future improvement in the simulation model. To ensure the success of the project, a team of scientists who have much experience in data analysis and computer simulation with many publications in this and other related areas is assembled to carry out the proposed investigation. Since bow shock energetic ions can populate other regions in the magnetosphere and may be further accelerated to higher energy, the proposed study is an important step toward the understanding of the radiation environment within the geospace. Therefore, this study addresses NASA Strategic Goal 3B: Understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system, in particular for points 3B.l and 3B.2 described in the 2006 NASA Strategic Plan. Results ofthe study will be important for future NASA robotic and human exploration missions in space and thus the proposed investigation would be of NASA interest.

Description: REINFORCED CARBON-CARBON (RCC) REPAIR ADHESIVE: SUSTAINING PRODUCTION OF NOAX-D FOLLOW ONTHE STS-107 ACCIDENT AND SUBSEQUENT INVESTIGATION RESULTING IN THE COLUMBIA ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BOARD (CAIB) REPORT HAVE CREATED CHALLENGING TECHNICAL AND PROGRAM MANAGEMENT EFFORTS NECESSARY TO MEET THE OBJECTIVES OF RETURN TO FLIGHT (RTF).  ONE OF THE RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE CAIB REPORT IS TO ESTABLISH A THERMAL PROTECTION SYSTEM (TPS) REPAIR CAPABILITY FOR THE ORBITER WHILE THE SHUTTLE IS ON-ORBIT.NASA HAS COMMITTED TO COMPLY WITH THIS RECOMMENDATION PRIOR TO THE RESUMPTION OF SPACE SHUTTLE FLIGHTS, AND FOR THE PAST THREE YEARS FOLLOWING STS-107, NASA HAS AGGRESSIVELY RESEARCHED REPAIR METHODOLOGY FOR THE SPACE SHUTTLES WING LEADING EDGE.  MANY POTENTIAL SOLUTIONS FROM COMMERCIAL INDUSTRY, GOVERNMENT AGENCIES, AND ACADEMIA HAVE BEEN INVESTIGATED, TESTED, AND EVENTUALLY DOWN SELECTED.  OF ALL THE ORIGINAL SOLUTIONS PROPOSED, THE LIQUID SEALANT NOAX-D WAS ULTIMATELY IDENTIFIED BY THE SPACE SHUTTLE PROGRAM OFFICE AS THE MOST VIABLE TECHNICAL SOLUTION FOR ON-ORBIT REPAIR OF THE SPACE SHUTTLE WING LEADING EDGE.  NOAX-D IS A PASTE-LIKE, SINGLE PART, HIGHLY LOADED, PRE-CERAMIC POLYMER WHICH FUNCTIONS AS AN ENVIRONMENTAL BARRIER TO RETARD OXIDATION OF THE CARBON/CARBON SUBSTRATE WHEN EXPOSED TO THE HIGH-TEMPERATURE ENVIRONMENT OF RE-ENTRY.THIS PROCUREMENT IS FOR A FOLLOW-ON EFFORT TO SUSTAIN MONTHLY PRODUCTION OF NOAX-D, AS A RESULT OF PREVIOUS SUCCESSFUL RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES, FOR THE REMAINING SPACE SHUTTLE FLIGHTS THROUGH 2010.

Description: We propose to investigate the dynamics of forward and reverse shocks associated with prompt gamma-ray bursts and early afterglows observed by Swift. The newly observed, X-ray flares, early steep decay, and shallow decay are unsolved and will be examined in this project. A 3-D relativistic particle-in-cell code will be used to simulate the dynamics of forward and reverse shocks with thin and thick shells within the parameter constraints provided by present Swift observations and the present models of GRB emission. Our 3-D RPIC simulations have provided the dynamics of collisionless shocks in electron-ion and electron-positron plasmas with and without initial ambient magnetic fields and revealed the importance of "jitter radiation" with prompt and afterglow spectra due to the inhomogeneous magnetic fields generated by the Weibel instability. It is different from synchrotron radiation, which is usually assumed to be the dominant radiation process. In this project we will investigate gamma-ray burst emissions from prompt, early, and late afterglows considering microscopic processes (previously studied with ideal MHD). Based on our previous investigation of the Weibel instability for each stage of evolution of ejecta propagating in the ISM, we will incorporate the plasma conditions (relativistic jets) with the density and composition of the plasmas, the magnetic field strength ($sigma$-values (the ratio of the electromagnetic energy flux to the particle energy flux))and its direction, and the Lorentz factor for the different stages in prompt and afterglows. Systematic simulation studies of the relativistic collisionless shocks, associated particle acceleration, magnetic field generation and self-consistent radiation will provide insight into undetermined issues in prompt and afterglows observed by Swift. Self-consistently calculated lightcurves, spectra, spectral evolutions, and polarization as function of viewing angle will light a shed on recent new observations by Swift, in particular, X-ray flares, early steep decay, and shallow decay.

Description: MULTI-FREQUENCY POLARIMETRIC RADAR, PROFILER, AND SPACE-BORNE STUDIES OF PARTICLE SIZE DISTRIBUTIONS AND MIXED PHASE PROCESSES IN COLD AND WARM SEASON PRECIPITATION Overview and Objectives: Characterization of particle size distributions (PSD) and microphysics for multiple precipitation regimes is critical to accurate space-borne measurement of precipitation. To support improved microphysical representation in satellite retrieval algorithms, we propose to employ University of Alabama-Huntsville (UAH) Hazardous Weather Testbed (HWT) instrumentation to study profiles of liquid, mixed, and ice-phase microphysical processes including PSDs. These studies will be conducted over the HWT for warm and cold season regimes under TRMM satellite coverage. Currently, TRMM 3A25 and 3A12 estimates of precipitation over the HWT differ by as much as 40% and exhibit systematic warm vs. cold seasonal biases. Hence, the objectives of this research are to: 1. Conduct multi precipitation regime comparative studies of PSD microphysical profiles (liquid, mixed, ice) for assessment of discrepancy between ground and satellite-retrieved products; 2. Apply results in (1) to melting-layer and cloud microphysical models used in PMM retrieval algorithms; 3. Within the framework of (1) and (2), to further evaluate/develop PMM ground validation techniques. Methods: The observational/analysis component will leverage the UAH ARMOR (C-band) and the UAH MAX (X-band, mobile) dual-polarimetric radars, a mobile 915 MHz wind profiler, a 12-channel Radiometrics profiling radiometer, two Parsival disdrometers, and a mesoscale rain gauge network. The multi-parameter/frequency, high resolution scanning and vertically pointing capabilities of the HWT convolved with heavy/frequent precipitation, multiple regimes, and frequent TRMM, A-train and AMSU-B overpasses enable robust sampling of PSD profile microphysics for comparison to satellite retrievals. Algorithm team members will apply results to test melting-layer, satellite simulator, and cloud-resolving models. Comparative studies of ground and space-observed ice water contents will be performed using TRMM and AMSU overpass data. A bridge to global application is provided by ongoing TRMM research which cross-types precipitation structures occurring over the UAH HWT with those of other regions around the globe. Significance: Precipitation retrieval, validation and multi-satellite precipitation analysis: 1. Improved facility algorithms for precipitation retrieval via microphysical process studies in multiple regime types (cold, warm season) under mid-latitude coverage of the TRMM and A-train satellites. The research team is comprised of observational and algorithm-scientists leading to efficient transfer of results to algorithms. 2. Development of validation techniques for precipitation missions. The instruments used herein represent a significant subset of those proposed for future validation studies (e.g., GPM). This research will enable assessment of validation observational resources and methodologies. 3. Development of new global products. This research will provide a framework for producing/improving retrievals of global ice-water content. Impact on NASA'S Earth Science Strategic Objectives: Improved quantification of the global hydrologic cycle via improvements in satellite precipitation retrieval algorithms.

Description: ENVIRONMENTAL STABILITY OF FOREST CORRIDORS IN THE MESOAMERICAN BIOLOGICAL CORRIDOR REGION SUMMARY: The scale and speed of habitat loss and fragmentation in one ofthe earth's biologically richest regions has led conservationists to propose the Mesoamerican Biological Corridor (MBC), an integrated regional initiative intended to conserve biological and ecosystem diversity in a manner that also provides sustainable economic development. The MBC proposes to connect isolated parks, preserves and forest fragments with new protected areas to create a network of biological corridors within the five southern states of Mexico and the Central American countries of Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama. The intent is to provide an environment that provides better prospects for the long-term survival of species, while at the same time addressing the region;,s socioeconomic needs. The primary objective of this proposed investigation is to determine the extent of which land use change disturbances have affected and are affecting regional and local climatic conditions in ways that influence the environmental stability of protected regions and proposed corridors in the MBC. Specifically, we focus upon precipitation and temperature fields that define the various Holdridge Life Zones. The first hypothesis is that land use disturbances are large enough to alter the locations of Life Zones throughout many if not most regions within Central America. The second hypothesis is that many corridors have and are developing habitats for creatures and plants that are significantly different from the original communities as defined by the HLZs. The proposed investigation has both a satellite remote 'Sensing and a modeling component. Combining the historical precipitation database for Central America with MODIS, GOES and other satellite imagery and the GEMRAMS atmospheric modeling system, we will determine whether Central American deforestation and land use change has altered regional and local climates in ways that are likely to influence the conservation utility ofMBC core elements and corridors. Using SERVIR databases  ompiled from the Central American countries;, networks of meteorological station, and remote sensing data, we will examine historical and current spatial and temporal patterns of precipitation, comparing precipitation in deforested and forested areas within each of the region;,s Holdridge Life Zones. Paired forested and deforested simulation studies with GEMRAMS will help elucidate mechanisms underlying observed climate changes, and provide evidence of the extent to which regional climate changes may be affecting plant growth, and consequently the likelihood of the MBC preserving the original assemblage of Central American ecological communities. Description: Earth Sciences Data Services for EOSDIS Evolution  The Information Technology and Systems Center (ITSC) at the University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAB) proposes follow-on research to grant NNG04GL56A, entitled "Earth Science Data Services". This very successful project has provided a variety of robust tools to the NASA Earth science community, most notably a suite of subsetting tools for data in the BDF-EOS format. A primary focus of the new effort will be the transition of the UAB-developed BDFEOS Subsetting Appliance (HSA), which is integrated with the EOSDIS Core System (ECS) for data search and order, from the current implementation with communication via ODL messages transmitted over sockets to a more modern service-oriented architecture using XML messages transmitted over HTTP via SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol). This task, which is part of the overall EOSDIS Evolution currently underway, requires coordinated modifications to ECS, ECHO (the EOS Clearinghouse) and HSA. Over the past year, UAH has participated with the ECS and ECHO teams in planning and design activities for this transition. Migration of the HSA to a SOAP architecture is required in order to maintain the availability of subsetting as an integrated service of the EOSDIS data search and order system. This proposal also addresses other science data services that will be valuable to continued EOSDIS evolution toward a service-oriented architecture, including a stand-alone subsetting web service directly available via ECHO, and semantic search and mediation services.

Description: Research and case studies have shown that convection plays a large role in large-scale environmental circulations. Convective momentum fluxes (CMFs) have been studied for many years using in-situ and aircraft measurements, along with numerical simulations. However, despite these successes, little work has been conducted on methods that use satellite remote sending as a tool to diagnose these fluxes. Use of satellite data, especially NASA assets, have the capability to provide continuous analysis across regions void of ground based remote sensing. The objective of this study is to develop a synergistic approach to retrieving CMFs over the footprint of all NASA instruments, namely ~35 N to ~35S, for selected case events, exploiting appropriate NASA satellite platforms. The proposed study will expand on the preliminary research already7 conducted on GOES and TRMM, and will rely on data observed by CloudSat as well as on surface winds estimated by QuikScat. CloudSat will provide key storm-structure, draft profile and microphysical (e.g. raindrop size) information necessary to obtain perturbation momentum components. Flux retrievals will be performed at native sensor resolutions, and be integrated up to regional-scale momentum (flux) budgets, which in turn will be validated against high-resolution (1 km) cloud-resolving model (CMR) simulations of explicity resolved convective storms in the tropics. With sound research already conducted using GOES satellite-derived winds showing success compared to CRMs, the proposed elements of this study are viable, setting forth in the NASA Earth Sciences Division objectives for understanding the earth-atmosphere system.

Description: DEVICE REALIZATION FOR SENSOR AND HEALTH MONITORING OF SPACE TRANSPORTATION SYSTEMS Nanotechnology offers many potential benefits for the research and development of integrated sensor and health monitoring in space transportation systems for future manned and unmanned NASA missions. Realizing the full promise of nanotechnology is hindered by technical barriers to harnessing nanoproperties in a macroscopic world. Researchers from the University of Alabama in Huntsville University and Alabama A&M University seek funding from the NASA EPSCoR program to form an interdisciplinary team to bridge the gaps from nanotechnology innovation to device realization. The Nano and Micro Devices Center at The University of Alabama in Huntsville (UAH) and the Center for Irradiation of Materials at Alabama A&M University have built core research groups and facilities focused on the design, modeling, fabrication, and testing of sensors using nano & micro fabrication technologies. Researchers from the Computer Engineering Department of UAH have developed hardware and software tools to integrate sensors into networked embedded systems. This effort will merge the three capabilities to bring innovative advances in nanotechnology and MEMS to device realization in embedded sensors that address the critical needs for the sensor and health monitoring of the launch vehicle and manned environment. To achieve the goal of enabling Alabama to develop an academic research enterprise directed toward long term, self sustaining, nationally-competitive capabilities in NASA-related research, the team will align with the strategic needs for Integrated Sensor and Health Monitoring branch at NASA MSFC. Four application driven research areas have been identified in advanced sensor technologies to bridge nano-innovation to device realization. The research thrusts include; Nano and Micro Electromechanical Sensors for Hydrazine, Hydrogen Detection, Biological Detection for Water Purification System, and Energy-Efficient Wireless Sensor Platforms for Deeply Embedded Systems. The effort will also focus on providing a pool of highly educated and trained engineers and scientists for NASA's current and future employment needs.

Description: Joint Swift and GLAST Analysis of Explosive High-Energy Astrophysical Phenomena Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are short-lived bursts of gamma-ray photons lasting a few milliseconds to several minutes. Description: Preparation, execution and results reporting for a series of pressuization/electrical test on LI-Ion Cell Headers. Here is the description for the referenced PO. Li-Ion Cell Headers The test objective is to simulate an overcharge condition in order to detect arcing during CID activation. Test conditions are to replicate actual battery conditions as close as possible. Not including Pre-testing steps, at least 36 18650 cells will be modified in order to isolate the header portion of the cell container without the electrode stack. Cell types to be used are the Moli, Sony Hard Carbon and COTS High Rate cells. NASA-JSC will supply all necessary cells and electrolyte. Prior to test operations it will be required to perform this test plan on a few practice cells in order to verify test setup and validate preliminary results. Pre-testing: Overcharge 2 fully assembled cells from each type at 2.0A with 55V limit to induce CID activation. Record cell voltage and current data at 1MHz for 30s upon receiving voltage trigger at the point of CID activation. This data will be used as a confirmation of CID activation in the test samples. Remove the top portion of the cell can, containing the undisturbed header assembly, from each cell. Cell header assembly will be attached to a fixture that will allow vacuum evacuation, the introduction of a small amount of electrolyte, and gas pressurization; all while passing a 2A current through the header assembly. Pre-testing: Test 3 cell headers from each type of cell to determine the approximate pressure at which the CID activates. Evacuate the header assembly and fixture using vacuum. Insert electrolyte LPF6 in DMC into fixture cavity. Pressurize cell can to a pressure approximately 10 percent lower than the CID activation pressure determined in the Pre-testing. Continue pressurization at a very gradual rate. The pressure rate increase must be low enough 2 psi min to cause very slight movement in the CID. We believe this is the best situation to induce arcing The Test Articles will have a 2 Amp current flow simulating the charge current during overcharge. Current, voltage across the header assembly, and pressure will be recorded at 1Hz. Voltage and current detail of the CID trip will be recorded at a minimum of 1MHz. The power supply voltage limit in the first round of testing will be 55V. If arcing is induced during the 55V test, use a 25V potential for the second round, and for the final round, test at 37V if no arcing is found at 25V or 13V if arcing is found at 25V. If arcing is not present in the 55V test, 110V will be used in the second round. And a similar splitting the voltage difference iteration is to be used for the third final round. A final report detailing the methodology and the results shall be provided. Where multiple replications generate similar results, limiting the provided plots to a single typical example is acceptable, particularly, for the low speed data recordings. Pictures should be taken of test articles before and after testing, as necessary to illustrate any visual impacts from the tests. Data and plots shall be provided in a format readable by the customer. Programs available at JSC include Excel, Igor, etc. Samples will be preserved in state to allow for future DPA.

Description: Our objective Is to design and develop a simple, robust, low cost, low mass, and low power analytical instrument probe that can be attached to landers, rovers, or touch-and-go robotic spacecraft, and that can be pushed below the surface and record IR spectra as a function of depth while also recording the spectrum of the surface. Methods/techniques: The work will consist of the design of the optical train, especially at and near the windows of the probe, addressing mechanical issues such as penetration forces and window scratching, and development of spectra that validate the instrument and provide calibration. Both weakly consolidated and unconsolidated minerals, including water ice and icy soils in various combinations, will be used. Significance: OPRA will enable the analysis ofthe surface and subsurface mineralogy of a wide variety of solar system objects with a minimum of perturbations to the regolith. Thus the structure and properties of the regolith can be determined as a function of depth. Such data will be important, for example, at possible landing sites for future NASA missions to the South Pole; Aitken region ofthe Moon, a cometary nucleus, and Mars polar regions. The instrument is relevant to many high priority science issues for NASA, the martian water cycle, subsurface ice on Mars, variations in mineralogical and adsorption properties ofthe martian regolith, abundances of sulfate in the martian regolith, the composition of the lunar regolith, and water at the Moon's poles, cometary nuclei and their crusts and subsurface, organic compounds on planets, satellites, asteroids and comets.

Description: Ni-base superalloys are used in some of the most demanding NASA applications, such as gas turbines for aircraft. At elevated temperature, these materials can suffer damage from surface oxidation, creep deformation, oxidation induced grain boundary embrittlement, and microstructural evolution. These four damage processes can operate in a synergistic fashion and cause catastrophic failure of mission critical components. The interaction of oxidation and creep crack growth is not fully understood. The research project proposed will evaluate the oxidation-assisted damage mechanisms that operate in the presence of creep deformation in the crack tip region by performing controlled environment creep-fatigue experiments.

Description: NASA is committed to the journey of exploration of the solar system, with its first target, the Moon. For these long time missions to be economically and scientifically feasible, it is crucial for the resources needed for life support (oxygen, water, and energy), habitats and shielding, as well as propellants, to be produced in-situ. In order to accomplish this, innovative, robust technology and procedures must be developed for resource prospecting, extraction and benefieiation. This work focuses on the utilization of Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) technologies to identify the presence of under the surface ilmenite (FeTi03), which is considered one of the most promising minerals for the generation of oxygen and metals such as Fe and Ti. Scientists from the University of Arkansas at Little Rock (UALR), Hendrix College, NASA Kennedy Space Center, and ASRC Aerospace will work collaboratively to develop a comprehensive method for fast and accurate detection of minerals that are of interest to NASA present beneath the Moon surface. Since the distribution of minerals on Moon may not be uniform, the ability to quickly identify those areas with high concentration of the desired minerals is essential. This project is expected to generate a novel method for fast and accurate detection of various minerals, which can he used to support the life and the success of the long time manned NASA missions. The team will implement three independent schemes to study the electromagnetic signatures of a number of minerals that are of high value to NASA;s missions and goals. These schemes are: (1) synthetic modeling of GPR data for specific minerals with different concentration in the simulated lunar soils and rocks. Detection capability will be measured as a function of percentage of mineral concentration in host soil and rock; (2) lahoratoq measurement of GPR data for natural minerals and ores. The detection capability will be investigated for both percentage of mineral concentration and depth; (3) geophysical fieldwork to collect data for natural deposits of the Tokio formation in southwest Arkansas. Heavy minerals, such as ilmenite, were discovered there and mapped by the Arkansas Geological Commission (AGC) (Hanson, 1997). Raman Spectroscopy and X-Ray Diffraction will be used to determine percentages of ilmenite and other minerals in Tokio sands and their corresponding mineralogy. The measurement of the dielectric constant and other electric properties will be performed b;) the NASA collaborators at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC). Measurement of electric properties and mineral concentration for lunar samples will be conducted at UALR and KSC. Lunar samples of the Apo1lo;s missions are available to the research team. The results and analysis of the above three schemes will be integrated to develop ideal procedures for lunar prospecting and the ability to locate in a NASA Proposal Number 07-EPSCOR-00'17 short time the areas rich in the minerals of interest.

Description: IMPACT CRATERING ON MARS: HYDROTHERMAL SYSTEMS, EJ ECTA, AND RAMPARTS We will carry out high-resolution impact imulations to investigate the role of impact cratering in: 1) affecting the distribution of I subsurface water crucial for origin of life on Mars); 2) asymmetric distribution of ejecta; and 3) formation of ramparts. We will mode1 both asteroidal and cometary impacts at various impact angles and with typical impact velocities for Mars. We will continue our work on materials models, equations of state and constitutive equations, to best represent mixed targets (rock+ice/water), and their response to shocks and impact cratering flow. The entire cratering event formation, i.e., contact/compression, excavation (including material ejection), and transient crater modification will be odeled with the three-dimensional hydrocode SOVA for vertical and oblique mpacts. For testing and validation purposes, vertical impacts will be modeled up to final crater formation and ejecta deposition with the two-dimensional Eulerian code SALEB, which is optimized for crater collapse studies. The goal of task #1 is to continue our initial work to characterize the post-impact target's thermal environment (with particular attention to water/ice phase state) around impact craters. At this time we will focus on large craters, with the goal of comparing results of our study to the recent data from the MEIUMEX missions relative to the environment at Gusev crater. This study should help characterize the volatile content of the region at the time of impact. In task #2 we want to model very oblique impacts in an attempt to understand the observed asymmetries in ejecta distribution. This work will coordinate with Collaborator IIerrick's detailed study of oblique impact ejecta distribution at Martian craters (funded through MDAP). This will also allow us to characterize the distribution of shocked ejecta around crater and compare with results of previous spectral studies (e.g., work by J.R. Johnson). Finally, task #3 will focus on the formation of ramparts around craters. This is a natural extension of our recent work on modeling mixed target materials, and will address the debate on atmospheric versus target composition origin of ramparts

Description: This proposal addresses the need for a real-time Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) system to identify anomalous states in digital electronic systems used in spaceflight applications and recommend corrective actions. We identify promising host platforms for implementation of PHM and consider strategies for identifying faults at the board level. Models for each approach are developed for further study of the effectiveness in identifying faults, estimating system states, and identifying anomalous states. Each method is then ranked with respect to prognostic fault coverage (state-awareness), missed alarms, and false alarms. Finally, a strategy is developed to optimally and dynamically reconfigure or recover the digital system based on current or predicted system status given by the prognostic/reasoner approach and board topology. By responding to a need for greater health awareness in complex on-board digital systems, the technology developed in this project will improve safety and effectiveness of future spaceflight missions, and improve serviceability and availability throughout the system lifecycle.

Description: QUANTITIVE IDENTIFICATION OF PHYSICS BASED PARAMETERS GOVERNING ACTIVE SEPARATION AND CIRCULATION A series of circulation and separation control experiments using different control strategies such as steady or periodic blowing or suction, and periodic excitation (zero net mass flux) are proposed. The impact of these control schemes will be initially investigated on especially selected two-dimensional airfoils in an attempt to better understand the effects of each technique rather than produce superior airfoil performance. Special attention will be paid initially to the effects of actuation location, slot sizes, curvature and blunt trailing edges on steady circulation and separation control, to be followed by an investigation of the transient processes needed to be understood for developing closed loop control strategies. Unsteady CFD predictions will be carried out concomitantly at the Boeing Company for the purpose of code validation and optimization of experimental procedures. Such an optimization is necessary in view of the large number of parameters involved. It is suggested that the experiments carried out at the University of Arizona will be reconfirmed at a NASA facility at Langley where the parameter space could be further expanded. Preliminary data suggests that active flow control may increase the lift to drag ratio of an airfoil by a factor varying between 2 and 7, depending on the specific application. It is hoped that proper understanding of the flow physics will lead to further improvements.

Description: AN INTEGRATED VEHICLE HEALTH MANAGEMENT APPROACH TO HETEROGENEOUS STRUCTURAL SYSTEMS ABSTRACT: This proposal addresses the area of Integrated Vehicle Health Management (IVHM) with an emphasis on Detection, Diagnostics and Prognostics. Specifically, computationally efficient multiscale prognostic tools for airframe and propulsion structural components will be developed as part of an IVHM framework. This framework is significant for meeting the challenges of improving the safety of air transportation systems by reducing system or component failures, decreasing operational costs, and increasing operational readiness associated with current and next generation aircrafts. Critical to the effort is the development of technologies to determine system damage and of accurate physics based models for detection, diagnostics and prognostics. A comprehensive research program is proposed to develop a robust IVHM framework on state awareness and prognosis of heterogeneous aerospace systems. The objectives consist of efficient and accurate multiscale models, sensor placement design, damage detection and classification, prognosis and residual life estimation (RULE) to provide accurate life cycle estimates of heterogeneous aerospace structural components. A major focus will be on tracking micro/macro damage progression and its effect on the structural health of aircraft and propulsion components under varied loading conditions. The framework will have the capacity to expand to the design and analysis of smart materials. Optimal sensor placement and decision making signal processing algorithms will be integrated. A variety of benchmark laboratory experiments will be conducted to validate and calibrate the proposed procedures. The proposed tasks are: (1) multiscale modeling; (2) models for in situ interrogation and diagnosis; (3) prognosis; (4) testing, validation and application. The proposal describes approaches and advances sought in these tasks. It also explains how coordinated advances in these tasks, scaling point-information to system identification, will yield profound improvements in damage detection and classification, risk assessment and prognosis. Throughout the project, methodological developments will be steered by a closed-loop validation plan that incorporates both simulation and experimental test data. While the techniques developed are expected to be cross-cutting, validation will focus on a limited number of test problems involving complex heterogeneous airframe components with multiple load paths. Explicit outcomes from the proposed project will include (a) computationally efficient multiscale modeling techniques scaling point information from microstructural to structural level; (b)algorithms for optimal sensor set design for damage detection and quantification; (c) sensing algorithms and stochastic characterization and estimation of damage for integrated health management; (d) damage detection methodologies including novel schemes for damage classification; and (e) a systematic procedure for RULE.

Description: JUPITER'S EQUATORIAL CIRCULATIONS We propose to conduct a comprehensive theoretical investigation of Jovian equatorial dynamics, focusing on the 5-micron hot spots, equatorial plumes, and their interaction with the large-scale circulation. The investigation is crucial for several reasons. The Galileo probe, which has provided our only deep sounding of Jupiter to date, entered a 5-micron hot spot and measured extremely dry conditions and winds that increased with depth. These observations raise major questions. Is the deep troposphere widely depleted in water, or is the measured depletion confined solely to the hot spots? And does the measured wind shear represent conditions throughout the equatorial regions or only conditions local to hot spots? Furthermore, it is unclear what mechanisms are responsible for driving the hot spots and plumes and setting their dependence on latitude, longitude, and height. Finally, the existence of Jupiter's superrotating equatorial jet remains a major puzzle, because it is a local maximum of angular momentum and hence cannot result from simple zonally symmetric (e.g., Hadley) circulations. Its formation requires convergence of eddy energy, but the source of this energy remains obscure. We will address these questions with a systematic set of fully nonlinear, three-dimensional numerical simulations of atmospheric motion. Previous work has suggested that hot spots and plumes result from a large-amplitude wave that propagates near Jupiter's equator. Our new simulations will investigate this hypothesis in detail using a primitive-equation model with extreme vertical resolution and other major improvements relative to previous simulations. We will then incorporate simple parameterizations of thermodynamic forcing (e.g., moist convection and radiation) and eddy-energy fluxes into the model, which will help us determine what drives hot spots and plumes and pumps the superrotating equatorial jet. The research will use established numerical codes that the PI is experienced in using and will be groundbreaking in its ability to address the existence and spatial structure of hot spots and plumes, the implications of the measured Galileo probe winds for Jupiter as a whole, and the extent to which Jupiter's troposphere is water-rich.

Description: THE 2006 OUTBURST OF RS OPH: SWIFT OBSERVATIONS OF A RECURRENT SYMBIOTIC NOVA RS Oph is a symbiotic nova in which a white dwarf (WD) orbits a red giant star (RG) with an orbital period of 460 days. The WD accretes material supplied by the RG and explodes roughly every 20 years. The outburst mechanism for the explosion is a thermonuclear runaway in the hydrogen-rich accreted material. Its last outburst occurred in February 2006 and we observed it with Swift, XMM-Newton, and Chandra. It is now declining back to quiescence. There are more than 70 XRT observations with Swift and we propose to analyze this unparalleled data base. Recurrent novae participate in the cycle of Galactic chemical evolution by ejecting metal enriched gas into the Interstellar Medium (ISM) where the material is mixed with material from other sources and ultimately incorporated into new stars and planetary systems. It has also been suggested that RS Oph is a progenitor of Supernovae of Type Ia (SN Ia) which are important both in studies of the evolution of the universe and because they provide a major fraction of the iron-group elements in the Solar System. Therefore, the topics described in this proposal directly address NASA Strategic Goals and Outcomes. Because the WD orbits inside the RG wind, the environment in which the explosion occurs strongly affects the observations of the outburst. The material ejected from the WD produced a strong shock which moved through the wind of the RG. Then, once the extinction from the ejecta declined, the system entered a phase where the X-rays were coming from the hot, luminous, atmosphere of the WD where nuclear burning was occurring in the surface layers. We obtained a large number of Swift spectra during this stage and found large variations in the count rate plus a 35 s oscillation. Later, the continuum died away and RS Oph entered an emission line phase. We propose to analyze the spectra from these stages with a variety oftechniques. We will analyze the spectra obtained in the initial stages with a set of tools designed specifically for these data and utilize a database of spectral line emissivities constructed to analyze X-ray spectra and determine (1) the temperature structure of the shocked RG wind and explosion ejecta; (2) the chemical composition of the shocked gas; (3) the velocity profile of the expanding shell; and (4) the differential absorption over the line profiles from matter within the shocked shell. We will analyze the spectra from the hot atmosphere stage with PHOENIX, a spherical, expanding, Non-LTE, stellar atmosphere code which includes a stellar wind module. We will use this code to construct parameterized optically thick atmospheres for use in fitting the low dispersion Swift spectra. Our fits will provide estimates of temperatures, luminosities, and circumstellar extinction as a function oftime during the outburst. We will use the fits to determine which parameters of the underlying object are changing during the oscillations in count rate. We will combine new shock interaction modeling with new one-dimensional hydrodynamic calculations to better understand the early evolution ofthe shock. We will use the hydrodynamic calculations to construct simulations ofthe structure ofthe WD and test these for pulsational instability. We will also use the hydrodynamic calculations to better understand how the explosion occurs on the WD.

Description: Theory of Extrasolar Giant Planets and Brown Dwarfs With the identification of more than 180 extrasolar giant planets (EGPs) and more than 400 L and T dwarfs, the study of substellar mass objects (SMOs) is entering a particularly productive stage. The discovery and characterization of SMOs in star-forming regions, in the solar neighborhood, and in intermediate-age clusters and the identification of transiting EGPs in tight orbits, as well as the great variety of planetary systems, has excited both the astronomical community and the public at large. With the data anticipated from Spitzer, HST, WISE, Kepler, SIM, Gaia, MOST, and JWST, the maturation of astronomical interferometry via LBTI, VLTI, and KIA, the planning of coronagraphic space missions such as Eclipse and TOPS, and the many ongoing ground-based surveys for brown dwarfs, the need for better theoretical calculations of the spectra and evolution of irradiated and isolated giant planets, brown dwarfs, M dwarfs, L dwarfs, and T dwarfs is acute and growing. To respond to this need, the PI (A. Burrows), co-Is (W. Hubbard and I. Hubeny), and postdoc propose to calculate a new suite of theoretical models of both M, L, and T dwarfs and extraoslar giant planets. One major goal is to support the numerous observing campaigns now being inaugurated from the ground and from space of direct detection and characterization of extrasolar giant planets, both in wide-separation and close-in orbits. For the close-in EGP studies, we will include UV insolation and planet evaporation/mass-loss effects, and calculate the orbital phase functions and polarization as a function of wavelength and phase, as well as the potential consequences of heat redistribution to the night side. A key focus is on the implications for the atmospheres of the transiting planets HD189733b, HD209458b, TrES-1, and HD149026b of the secondary eclipse data coming and and anticipated from IRAC, MIPS, and IRS on Spitzer. Another major goal is the creation of the next generation of comprehensive models for objects with masses spanning the range from 0.05 to 250 Jupiter masses. These models will be a function of metallicity and will incorporate the latest cloud models and non-equilibrium chemistry. The product will be a state-of-the-art evolutionary, spectral, and atmospheric theory for M, L, and T dwarfs as a function of metallicity, as well as a detailed theory of the M-L and L-T transitions. Key byproducts of this investigation will be a definitive determination of the location of the edge of the main sequence as a function of silicate cloud physics and metallicity and predictions for the properties of objects cooler than the T dwarf spectroscopic class that straddle the realms of the planets and the stars and are accessible to the NASA's infrared telescopes WISE, Spitzer, and JWST. Strategic goal #3.4 of NASA's Research Program specifically identifies extrasolar planets and their physical properties as desirable science outcomes of NASA's investments. "A Renewed Spirit of Discovery: The President's Vision for United States Space Exploration (2004)'' explicitly calls for "advanced telescope searches for Earth-like planets and habitable environments around other stars" as one of the foundations of NASA's exploration goals. Extrasolar giant planets and brown dwarfs are important stepping stones to that goal. Spitzer, HST, KIA, LBTI, VLTI, Kepler, SIM, Gaia, COROT, WISE, and JWST all include as mission goals the study of planets and brown dwarfs. This proposal is in direct response to these NASA strategic objectives.

Description: Theoretical and Modeling Support of Voyager 1 and 2 Near and Beyond the Termination Shock We propose to use analytic theory together with numerical modeling and simulations to help support the interpretation of Voyager 1 and 2 observations near and beyond the heliospheric termination shock. Included in this is the modeling of anomalous and galactic cosmic rays, low-energy charged particles and magnetic fields, both in the solar wind as well as the heliosphere (or shocked solar wind). Our investigations will greatly enhance the science return of the missions, especially in view of the recent Voyager 1's crossing of the termination shock, which yielded new and surprising results, and also the forthcoming crossing of the shock by Voyager 2. Our theoretical tools and extensive library of sophisticated time-dependent, one, two and three-dimensional computer codes will combine to provide a valuable resource to NASA's Voyager missions. Our team has an extensive track record of accomplishments as interdisciplinary Scientists and Guest Investigators on spacecraft missions, as well as of having made many contributions to the fundamental theory of both magnetic field structure and the concomitant fast-particle motion in heliospheric magnetic fields. We will do both collaborative work on problems of opportunity which arise in consultation with the various experimental groups and theoretical and simulation work within our group in response to challenges from the observations. We have already written several papers interpreting some of the new Voyager 1 observations. Specifically, we propose to: (a) fully examine the effects of time dependence of the shock parameters such as speed, injection rate, etc. on the acceleration of charged particles from low-energies to ACRs and on the resulting intensity, energy spectra, and anisotropies. This includes variations arising from the motion of the shock itself, as well as fluctuations in the turbulent magnetic field and solar wind. (b) determine the importance of the spatial variation of the shock and magnetic topology in the observed properties of ACRs and GCRs. (c) continue to model the modulation of GCRs in the heliosheath. (d) perform new numerical simulations of the interaction of the termination shock with the heliospheric current sheet and energetic particles. (e) determine the influence of waves and turbulence in the heliosheath on energetic particles and magnetic fields. (f) determine the evolution of magnetic-field turbulence, magnetic structures and energetic particles both upstream and downstream of the termination shock. (g) undertake a comprehensive study of the effects of turbulence in the upstream and downstream plasma on the properties of shocks and on acceleration of charged particles. The goals of our project are clearly relevant to NASA's spacecraft mission and we expect our contribution to clarify the basic physical processes occurring both near and beyond the termination shock.

Description: MULTI WAVELENGTH STUDY OF NEARBY LATE-TYPE GALAXIES: BENCHMARKS FOR HIGH REDSHIFT STUDIES AND REIONIZATION Using the IRASIISO, Spitzer, 2MASS, HST, GALEX, and ROSATIXMMlChandra data bases, we propose to perform a synoptic study of the far-IR, near-IR, optical, UV and X-ray properties of 443 nearby galaxies selected to have existing high-quality UV+Optical images. These galaxies all have ground-based UBVRI images, and for over 150 we have unique high-resolution HSTlWFPC2 images in the mid-UV (250--300 nm) and optical (V+I), which we have already analyzed or published. Almost all objects have IRAS 12--100 micron, ZMASS JHK, GALEX 150 and 230 nm, and ROSAT 0.5--2 keV images. Some also hare ISO, Spitzer !RAC and MIPS, HST NICMOS H-band, AstroIUIT, XMM or Chandra images. This sample spans all inclinations and the entire Hubble sequence, including a rich sampling of late types, irregulars and peculiar galaxies, as well as galaxies that are undergoing or recently underwent a merger. Understanding these objects is critical for high-redshift studies, since similar objects dominate the faint galaxy counts and may have ended reionization at z - 6. We will use this unique data set as a benchmark to study star-formation and dust in the local universe. Our main science goal is to physically locate the regions in these galaxies that contain most of the dust and compare those with the regions where we detect recent or ongoing star-formation --- a fraction of which may be opticallylUV obscured --- and with regions that were actively forming stars a few Gyr ago. Specifically, we aim to: (1) Use IRASIISO to constrain their dust content using the global far-IR luminosities, and using Spitzer to get spatial information as to where the dust mainly resides, and how their dust content correlates with regions of recent star-formation as seen in the available high-resolution UV--Optical images. (2) Use 2MASS JHK and Spitzer IRAC images to locate the regions of the older stellar populations. The longer wavelength baseline will greatly help separate the effects of differences in stellar population from those of dust, and a proper (i.e., dust-corrected) estimate of the older stellar population will constrain the global mass assembly of these galaxies. (3) Use the GALEX far- and mid-UV images to measure or constrain the stellar population ages in the regions experiencing the most recent (<-I00 Myr) high-mass star-formation, for which the near-UV--near-IR data are insensitive tracers. (4) Use the ROSAT All-sky images (+ where available XMM and Chandra images) to locate weak AGN and regions of past star-formation as traced by X-ray emission from X-ray binaries and supernova remnants, and correlate the X-ray and IR source locations and fluxes with features found in the high-resolution UV--optical images. This synoptic study explicitly addresses NASA's strategic goal 3D.2: it will result in a clearer understanding of the origin, structure, evolution and destiny of galaxies --- the visible building blocks in the universe ---one of which we call home.

Description: PROBING DARK ENERGY THROUGH THE BARYON ACOUSTIC OSCILLATIONS: LAYING THE FOUNDATION FOR A ROBUST, PRECISE DISTANCE SCALE The characteristic length scale imprinted by sound waves in the early Universe into the clustering of matter offers a robust and precise route to the measurement of the cosmological distance scale and the properties of dark energy.  The standard ruler of the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) can be calibrated by CMB observations and then used to measure the anular diameter distance and Hubble parameter as a function of redshift. Because of the enormous scale and the sharp clustering signature, the method is robust to most astrophysical complications.  This virtue has drawn raised the possibility, now proposed in at least one mission concept, that the Joint Dark Energy Mission (JDEM) could be a space-based BAO experiment, surveying enough volume to reach a distance precision of about 0.1%.  The Dark Energy Task Force has found that the BAO method is less affected by astrophysical uncertainties than other methods, but that further theoretical investigations are needed for the method to reach its full potential.  This proposal is aimed at filling this need, with the goal of reaching a 0.1% accurate implementation of the method. We aim to study the theory and phenomenology of BAO so as to put the theory on a firm foundation and allow optimization of future missions.

Description: CIRCUMSTELLAR DUST AS AN INDICATOR OF PLANETARY FORMATION Dust grains in circumstellar debris disks are rapidly depleted by Poynting-Robertson drag, collisions, and radiation pressure blowout, and must be constantly renewed. The visible dust is the product of collisions between unseen parent bodies, which cannot be detected directly. Their sizes and abundances can be constrained by modeling their collisional lifetimes and the orbital evolution of their fragments, with realistic scaling of collisional outcomes and loss mechanisms. Impact velocities needed to account for the visible dust may indicate the presence of larger perturbers, i.e., planets. A multi-zone collisional code will be modified to include radiative forces; a hierarchical approach will be developed to allow explicit modeling of the collisional and orbital evolution of small grains. Self-consistent models will be constructed for debris disks around stars with a range of masses and luminosities. The production of potentially observable features, such as inner holes, gaps due to planets, and transient enhancements due to giant impacts will be evaluated. The results will clarify the relationship between observable matter (dust) in circumstellar environments and the formation of planetary bodies.

Description: The CM2 carbonaceous chondrite meteorites contain abundant organic material as diverse as kerogen-like macromolecules and simpler soluble compounds ranging from polar amino acids to non-polar hydrocarbons; a molecular diversity that points to synthetic pathways in a variety of chemical regimes. The understanding of how a-biotic organic compounds, sometimes identical to biomolecules, could have formed and survived in cosmic environments is one of the important questions posed to cosmochemical studies. The research we proposed is the outgrowth of work conducted in our laboratory that characterized L-enantiomeric excesses (ee) for Murchison and Murray amino acids and verified their indigeneity with isotopic analyses. To date, these non-racemic amino acids of meteorites provide the only natural sample of molecular asymmetry measured outside the Biosphere. Although described previously only for the 2-methyl-2-amino acids, we demonstrated recently that such asymmetry is also present in other organic material of carbonaceous chondrites, including their insoluble phase. We propose an in-depth analysis of chiral molecules in meteorites and to explore the extent of their distribution beyond current analytical constraints. Namely:  To develop new methodologies for the separation and identification of those CM2 chondrite organics that have been outside our analytical reach but are known to be present in considerable amount. Chiral analyses of the compounds so identified. It is expected that they will include higher molecular weight homologs of the known water- and solvent-soluble compounds and components of the insoluble organic material, which we recently demonstrated can be solubilized by hydrothermal treatment. The proposed study could open a lead for the understanding of cosmic processes that remain as yet unknown. Among others, the origin of molecular asymmetry, its distribution beyond the Earth, and the cosmic processes and/or locales that may have produced it. As such, they are directly relevant to the objectives of this NRA.

Description: Both observations and simulations suggest that galaxy-galaxy mergers can transform star forming, disk-dominated, gas-rich galaxies into early types. Two critical questions that remain unanswered are 1) what fraction of early types evolved from such mergers and 2) whether mergers can explain the startling connection between a galaxy's small- and large-scale physics implied by the empirical black hole-bulge mass relation. Combining UV photometry with optical spectra has the potential to answer both questions by drastically improving the constraints on when the star formation ended in a galaxy undergoing a late-to-early type transition. Here we propose to obtain UV photometry for a unique sample of 18 post-merger, post-starburst, late-to-early type transitional galaxies. With these data, we will determine the fraction of modern-day early types that might once have been post-merger, post-starburst galaxies by comparing the duration of this phase with the known number of galaxies passing through it. The narrow age constraints arising from the UV fluxes are also an exciting new test for popular theories in which nuclear feedback during mergers quickly extinguishes both star formation in the bulge and any subsequent black hole growth, leading to the black hole-bulge mass relation. This test is possible only because the UV data are particularly sensitive to stellar ages of less than a few 100 Myr, which is also the feedback timescale.

Description: THE SEASONAL HYDROLOGICAL AND METEOROLOGICAL CYCLES OF TITAN The recent dramatic images of stream networks, shorelines, and rounded pebbles on Titan's surface returned by the Huygens probe demonstrate convincingly that Titan's surface, like that on Earth, is carved by flowing fluids. Cassini radar and imaging show tantalizing examples of what appear to be fluvial features, potential lake beds, and possible shorelines. This emerging picture of an active hydrological cycle on Titan's surface lacks one critical component: Any observations of actual surface liquids. The best evidence that we currently have to suggest the presence and location of liquids on Titan is the observations of long-lived - presumably methane -- cloud systems near the south pole. However, these southern clouds and any methane rain associated with them are far removed from the locations of most of the geological evidence for flowing surface liquids. From our five years of observations of clouds, it appears likely that Titan rain is seasonal and infrequent, but torrential when it does occur. The connections between Titan's surface hydrology and active methane meteorology are not yet known, but the two are inextricably linked and dependent upon each. To explore the links between Titan's hydrology and meteorology we propose to continue and expand our successful multifaceted ground-based observing program using large telescopes (Keck and Gemini) for spatially resolved observations, medium-sized telescopes (NASA/IRTF and Lowell Perkins 1.8-m) for disk-integrated spectroscopy, and small robotic telescopes (Lowell O.8-m and a new 24" at Palomar Observatory) for nightly photometric monitoring. With the three years of observation proposed here we will cover the time period through the southern autumnal solstice and be able to answer fundamental questions surrounding Titan's seasonal meteorological cycle and when/where/how it interacts with the surface hydrology.

Description: NON-RACEMIC AMINO ACIDS IN METEORITES: A GAUGE FOR AQUEOUS PROCESSES IN EARLY SOLAR SYSTEM PLANETESIMALS. The studies of meteorites show that solar system planetesimals formed at the orbital distances of today's asteroids experienced an aqueous phase of alteration, where organic material condensed from the nebula was further modified by chemical reactions. Understanding the extent of these processes may offer insights into how abiotic organic compounds, sometimes identical to biomolecules, formed and/or survived in planetary environments. This proposal is the outgrowth of work conducted in our laboratory that characterized L-enantiomeric excesses (ee) within a subgroup of meteoritic amino acids, which provide the only case of molecular asymmetry measured outside the Biosphere. To date, these ee seem limited to the chiral 2-methyl-2-amino acids, however, it is possible that they were also present in 2-H-2-amino acids but were lost to racemization during aqueous reactions. Because racemization, the reversal and equilibration between L- and D-configurations in water, affects especially amino acids having a hydrogen attached to the second carbon, the possibility would seem hard to prove. However, acids having two chiral centers instead of one may still be able to reveal prior ee for 2-H compounds in meteorites, in spite of water exposure and racemization. Their study, would offer unique opportunities to estimate the extent of molecular asymmetry in the solar nebula upon formation of meteorite parent bodies and the physico-chemical conditions of those planetesimal aqueous processes. We propose to perform chiral analyses of Murchison and Murray diasteromeric amino and monocarboxylic acids, which are known but were never analyzed for this purpose, employing methodologies we have used previously with success. The proposed studies seek an understanding of chemical processes in the early solar system that fostered the evolution of abiotic organic molecules and of the traits they share with biomolecules. As such, they are directly relevant to the objectives of this NRA.

Description: THEORETICAL MINERALOGY OF AQUEOUS ALTERATION IN CHONDRITES The majority of chondritic meteorites reveal signs of aqueous alteration of primary reduced and anhydrous mineralogy. Description: ABSOLUTE MAGNITUDE AND ORBITAL DISTRIBUTIONS OF ASTEROIDS FROM STATISTICS OF SPACE WATCH DETECTIONS SUMMARY: We propose to assemble, debias, and analyze the detections of asteroids by the Spacewatch Project and present new determinations of the numbers and distributions of Earth Approachers (EAs), Main-Belt Asteroids, and other orbital types as functions of absolute magnitude H, semimajor axis a, eccentricity _e, and inclination _i_. The Spacewatch Survey for Hazardous Asteroids has now been funded by NASA's NEO Observation Program through mid-April 2009, which will provide a million more incidental detections of asteroids beyond what is available today. By April 2009, systematic surveying with the Spacewatch mosaic of CCDs to the limiting V magnitude of 21.7 will have been conducted for a full six years with uniform procedures, making characterizations of observational biases and selection effects straightforward. Revisiting the same cohorts of asteroids several times per lunation allows detections of asteroids to be linked across intervals as long as 16 days. Therefore, linking software developed and already in use by Larsen will yield H, _a_, _e-, and _i_ of 100,000 main belt asteroids. Simulation software developed by Larsen can then yield debiased distributions of asteroids' H values and orbital elements. They will have higher resolution in _a_than any previous large-scale debiasing of the main belt, and will add for the first time the debiased main belt distribution vs. e. For NEAs, the H distribution will be extended to at least H=26 and probably H=29, 6 mag fainter than has been determined reliably to date. By April 2009, Larsen's search for large, distant trans-Neptunian objects in Spacewatch imagery will have covered up to 20,000 square degrees ofthe sky with a unique distance range of 1000 AU. This is relevant to the hypothesis that large planetesimal(s) might still exist at great distances from the Sun. Support is requested to manage the revisiting campaign and to archive and duplicate pixel data and supporting metadata that could not otherwise be saved. Funds are also needed to characterize the efficiency, biases, and selection effects of the survey, as well as to perform the analyses and interpretations described above.

Description: EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES OF COMETARY SUBLIMATION This research will experimentally investigate a heretofore unknown yet fundamental behavior of water-ice sublimation from cometary surfaces in the inner solar system. This project will also provide important insight into the evolution of the D/H ratio in cometary comae resulting from sublimation. An experimental apparatus, the Lunar and Planetary Laboratory Cryostat, has been constructed in Professor Robert H. Brown's laboratory (Figure 1). This system is designed to study sublimaiton from icy surfaces in a vacuum resulting from surface heating by incident radiation. Using the apparatus in Professor Brown's laboratory, we have performed ten preliminary experiments, ranging in duration from 140 to 1127 hours. The initial D/H ratio of the ice, the crystal grain size (controlled by cooling rate during sample preparation), the abundance and composition of trace gas species (air, Ar, CO2) in the ice, the presence, size, and abundance of dust grains, and temperature (determined by the flux of incident radiation) have significant influence on the sublimation behavior. We will investigate all of these parameters in the proposed investigation.

Description: The Genesis mission collected solar wind and brought it back to Earth in order to provide precise knowledge of solar isotopic and elemental compositions, a cornerstone data set around which theories for materials, processes, events and time scales in the solar nebula are built, and from which theories about the evolution of planets begin. The ions in the solar wind were stopped at very shallow depths, on the order of 10 to a few hundred nanometers. Because this shallow implantation layer is critical for scientific analysis of the composition of the solar wind, it must be preserved throughout sample handling, cleaning, processing, distribution, preparation and analysis. We propose a laboratory study designed to enhance the science return from the Genesis samples. It is motivated by the need to quantitatively characterize the nanoscale contamination on the collectors in the Genesis payload. The proposed work is complementary to the work currently being done by the Genesis team. It will enable the Genesis curator to more efficiently evaluate samples for allocation, and individual laboratories to more fully understand and either eliminate or mitigate analytical interferences from the contamination, which has thus far restricted the full science return of the Genesis mission. The two types of contaminants are a molecular film now known as 'brown stain' deposited during flight, and a multitude of submicron particulates composed of pulverized spacecraft and lakebed materials and localized precipitates from brine deposited as a result of the unfortunate hard-landing of Genesis at the Utah Test and Training Range (UTTR). Both types of contamination will be quantitatively analyzed using nanoanalytical tools, Local Electrode Atom Probe (LEAP) microscopy and Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM). These analyses will give both composition and structure of the contaminants. The goals of this project address NASA Strategic Goal 3.3: To advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system, the potential for life elsewhere, and the hazards and resources present as humans explore space.

Description: IMPLANTATION OF MARTIAN ATMOSPHERE INTO METEORITES AS A FUNCTION OF TEMPERATURE Several martian meteorites contain what appear to be martian atmospheric noble gases, but the krypton to xenon ratios differ systematically among meteorite groups, suggesting fractionation of some sort. To evaluate the various mechanisms that have been proposed to explain this, we propose to do two things. First, we will do experiments on shock-implantation at Mars-analog temperatures, where fractionation by adsorption will occur, to compare with previous results at Earth-ambient temperatures. Second, we will analyze the martian meteorite data, and previously proposed mechanisms, in light of our experimental data and new spacecraft data of various sorts. As a part of this, we will evaluate the implications of these data for the ambient temperature at the time of ejection. This, in turn, can be used to evaluate proposed meteorite source craters, and whether any current model can explain all the martian meteorite data with the present climate.
