Description: William Hartmann/Planetary Science Institute CHRONOLOGY AND ANALYSIS OF RECENT AND ANCIENT MARTIAN GEOLOGICAL FEATURES AND PROCESSES This proposal continues one of the major efforts to utilize properties of crater populations to understand the gross chronology and geologic erosion/deposition processes of Mars. In terms of gross chronology our past work was notable in correctly predicting few hundred My-old volcanic regions, once disputed by others, but confirmed by basaltic Martian meteorites with ages as young as 170 My. The new work will concentrate on addressing recent issues raised in the community about use of the crater statistics, particularly the role of secondary craters and their effects on dating small geologic formations on Mars, kilometers or tens of kilometers in scale. Our technique is to count and measure the buildup of the total crater population (primaries plus distant background secondaries, but not clusters); we believe some concerns about secondaries have been overstated, and incorrectly assume that we try to count only primaries. We will refine and improve our methods as much as possible, and use the results to test the hypothesis that some forms of recent resurfacing, including mantling, fluvial features, and possible ice flow features, are tied to the timescale of major obliquity excursions, and result in climatic changes due to the obliquity cycles. We will also pursue techniques we have already published in preliminary form, to study the rates of resurfacing in the different Martian geologic eras, as a function of time. We also propose a cooperation with the Mars Express High Resolution Stereo Camera team (as requested by Dr. Gerhard Neukum) and a collaboration with Dr. Vicky Hamilton, as opportunities arise, to make crater-chronology interpretations of regions of anomalous mineralogy on Mars.

Description: GLOBAL ASSESSMENT OF GEOLOGIC PROCESSES USING THEMIS THERMAL INERTIA SUMMARY: Geologic processes, such as cratering and topographically-controlled winds, are actively modifying the Martian surface at sub-kilometer scales. THEMIS-derived thermal inertia allows the mapping of the physical nature of Mars at scales appropriate to interpret the processes that are controlling the current distribution of surface materials, and provides insight into the geologic evolution of Mars. We will create a global thermal inertia map from high-resolution Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) infrared images to permit the identification, assessment, and global correlation of surface materials, in order to better understand the processes acting on the Martian surface. Global processes will be investigated in the following tasks: 1) improve existing THEMIS-derived thermal inertia algorithms to account for the effect of topography on surface temperature; 2) derive thermal inertia values from THEMIS nighttime infrared images between 60 latitude; and 3) mosaic individual THEMIS thermal inertia images to create a global thermal inertia map. The resulting global thermal inertia mosaic will be released to the science community through the Planetary Data System. We will also investigate the global variation of local surface processes on Mars, as inferred from thermal inertia and morphology, focusing on relatively high inertia surfaces (400 to 800) and moderate thermal inertia surfaces (200 to 400). This study will allow us to infer processes affecting the Martian surface at local scales, compare these local scenarios to determine the processes that have been most active on Mars, and better understand its geologic history and climate evolution.

Description: GEOLOGIC INVESTIGATIONS OF HELLAS PLANITIA AND THE CIRCUM-HELLAS HIGHLANDS: SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL PATTERNS IN TOPOGRAPHY, CRATER MORPHOLOGY, AND LAYERED DEPOSITS SUMMARY: The objective of this research is to evaluate the perimeter and interior of Hellas basin to 1) map the distribution, examine the morphologic variability, and assess the topographic and slope characteristics of local depositional sinks, layered deposits, and topographic benches, and 2) address spatial and temporal correlations (or lack thereof) of these features within the context of basin-wide evolution. If geomorphic evidence suggests the potential for paleolake shorelines along the Hellas rim, the context of these locations will also be assessed. Using Viking Orbiter, MGS Mars Orbiter Camera, MO Thermal Emission Imaging System, and MEX High Resolution Stereo Camera images, and Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, Thermal Emission Spectrometer, Gamma Ray Spectrometer, and MEX Omega data we will: 1) Analyze morphologic, morphometric, topographic, and thermophysical characteristics of craters larger than 10 km within four major circum-Hellas highland sectors (Noachis Terra, Terra Sabaea, Tyrrhena Terra, and Promethei Terra) including, a. floor and rim deposits to locate layered outcrops and assess degradation history, b. rim height measurements looking for asymmetry (i.e., with respect to Hellas basin interior), and c. size-frequency distributions to identify i. differences in distribution with respect to distance from basin interior and elevation, and ii. variations of individual crater floor deposits. 2) Assess the distribution of layered deposits around the rim and across the floor of Hellas to, a. characterize morphology and morphometry, determine thermophysical properties, b. evaluate age variability with respect to geographic location and elevation level in Hellas Planitia, c. assess layered deposit origin(s) (lacustrine, volcanic, aeolian) and address implications, and 3) Perform statistical analyses of topographic data from local to regional scales, specifically targeting crater rim diameter and height, characteristic root mean slope variability, crater floor deposit thickness, volume, and asymmetry over elevation changes. Whether or not specific geomorphic features (shorelines, deltas, etc.) representative oflacustrine activity can be identified, a detailed examination of basin topography, including highland craters around the basin perimeter, and the distribution, age(s), and morphologic variability oflayered deposits defining circum-Hellas depositional environments will provide critical evidence for deciphering the sedimentary history of the region, including testing and refining the paleolake hypothesis. Description: VALIDATION AND BENCHMARKING OF IMPACT CODES: A BROADBASED EFFORT OF THE IMPACT CRATERING MODELING COMMUNITY This project brings together a collective expertise in numerical modeling of impact and explosion events, continuum mechanics, and numerical analysis in an unprecedented effort to uniformly compare, validate and benchmark the computer models ("hydrocodes") widely used by the impact community to model planetary scale impacts and their consequences, as well as by the defense community to model large explosions and the threat to civilization due to asteroid impact. The project identifies a two-part base of standards for comparing and validating hydrocodes. The first part consists in initially identifying sets of well-documented laboratory and field experiments that can be used as type-cases and then use them to validate code calculations over a wide range of event sizes, geological materials and problem types. The second part consists of hypothetical explosive and impact events of varying complexity that will serve as benchmarks for comparison of the numerical and physical models employed in various codes. Simulations will test a range of physical mechanisms involved in impact events. The validation tests are expected to spur new developments and improvements of code components, especially in the material models used in the codes. This effort has not been undertaken before for two reasons. First, the extensive experimental data necessary for validation of the computer models is often buried in reports that are difficult to access. Second, most modelers have specific experience with only one or two computer models. This project brings together 15 scientists from various U.S. and international universities, research institutes and national laboratories, each with extensive experience in numerical modeling of impact and explosion craters. This study will have a broad impact both from the scientific and educational point of view. By providing this information to the broad scientific and defense community this project will help prevent the incorrect and misinformed use of the codes, especially those with free distribution, thus benefiting theoretical investigations that use these codes. Identified standards, code simulations and results will be made widely available to the scientific community through the development of a website dedicated to the project. Future generations of modelers will benefit from this effort by learning from examples of the correct applications of different codes and will be provided with a set of rules and test cases to follow in order to benchmark and validate hydrocodes to come.

Numerical and to a somewhat lesser degree, due to scaling limitations, laboratory experiments are the best tools for such and undertaking. Over the past two cycles we have accumulated valuable experience in understanding the influence of target properties on the impact process by modeling the formation of specific terrestrial craters. Description: Periodic release of subsurface waters is one of the processes that would have affected chemistry and mineralogy of the martian surface. Despite exciting new data on the martian surface from in situ and orbital observations, the role of aqueous processes in chemical weathering and secondary mineralogy remains to be understood. We propose to continue our modeling of water-rock reactions in order to evaluate the chemical compositions of martian waters and precipitated solids. The model couples chemical equilibrium computations with real kinetics of mineral dissolution and also includes rates of oxidation of iron and sulfur species. For subsurface waters, the results will yield estimates of pH, oxidation states, concentrations and activities of solutes, and amounts of secondary and unaltered minerals as functions of the progress of water-rock reactions in time. Quantitative models for ground water after it appears at the martian surface will include the exchange of gases between solutions and atmosphere, oxidation of solutes by 02 and H202, interaction with minerals at the surface, evaporation and freezing of water, and precipitation of minerals. Special attention will be devoted to origin and fate of near-surface acidic solutions. Results of modeling will be interpreted in terms of secondary mineralogy and geochemistry of the martian surface.

Description: MAXIMIZING MINI-TES: REFINING THE DETAILS AND EXPANDING THE INVESTIGATION OF THE MINERALOGY OF GUSEV CRATER Gusev crater was chosen as a landing site for the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) Spirit because of geomorphic evidence observed in orbital images that suggested it may have hosted a lake sometime in its ancient past. The objective of the proposed work is to maximize the use of thermal infrared spectra (1800-380 cm-1) from the Mini-TES instrument onboard the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) Spirit to pursue knowledge of the distribution and mineralogy of rocks in Gusev crater. Our goal is to contribute to a better understanding of the geologic processes and role of water in the history of Gusev crater and more broadly, to Mars as a whole. This goal is consistent with specific goals and outcomes described in the 2006 NASA Strategic Plan (Strategic Sub-goal 3C, outcomes 3C.1-3). We will achieve the stated goal by completing a set of tasks that begins with the calibrated emissivity spectra supplied by the Mini-TES team, and through a detailed validation of the methods used to obtain mineralogy, along with the incorporation of results from other MER instruments, will end with a more complete picture of the geologic terrain through which the rover has traversed. We expect that our results will supply valuable 'ground truth' and detailed knowledge of a particular location on Mars that can be applied globally. Mini-TES data from the Spirit rover already have contributed to a range of scientific and tactical objectives during the MER mission, but most of the data have been analyzed only in a cursory fashion or not at all. Our first task will examine environmental factors at the Martian surface that have impacted Mini-TES spectra and validate the methodology used to address them. Here we will characterize fully the contributions from downwelling atmospheric radiance, temperature errors that lead to sloping emissivity spectra, variable mantles of dust on rocks, and dust that has accumulated on the Mini-TES optics. We will look at the existing solutions as well as alternative ones and for the first time quantify the uncertainty in mineralogy determination that comes from their application. With the successful completion of task 1, we can then apply the results to previously analyzed spectra and all publicly released spectra that remain to be analyzed. Tasks 2 and 3 are directed at extracting the most robust mineralogical information possible from the Mini-TES spectra of rocks and mapping the distribution of the different lithologies. Previous analyses of rocks at the Gusev site have been applied to spectral averages, yet there is clear evidence for mineralogical variations among the previously defined rock classes, which we will examine in task 2. Both tasks 2 and 3 will employ APXS and MOssbauer results where available to refine spectral deconvolutions and investigate the value of factor analysis and target transformation for identifying spectral endmembers. No significant effort has been made previously to map the distribution of the rocks observed by Mini-TES. Wherever possible, we will classify spectrally each rock and locate it in image mosaics produced from the rover cameras. This will facilitate future efforts to characterize the stratigraphy and structure of the Columbia Hills. Our final task 4 will synthesize the results from tasks 2 and 3 along with other published results into a more complete picture of the geologic processes that have shaped Gusev crater throughout its history including a more thorough evaluation of the lake hypothesis.

Description: GEOLOGIC MAPPING ALONG THE ARABIA TERRA DICHOTOMY BOUNDARY: MAWRTH VALLIS AND NILI FOSSAE, MARS The objectives of this research are to constrain the geologic evolution of Mawrth Vallis, Nili Fossae, and their immediate surroundings along the Arabia Terra Dichotomy Boundary through: 1) geologic mapping, geomorphic analyses, and chronologic studies, 2) evaluation of the distribution, stratigraphic position, and lateral continuity of compositionally distinct outcrops as seen in spectral datasets, and 3) characterization of the role and extent of volatile-driven, aeolian, volcanic, and tectonic modification and degradation processes on Mawrth Vallis and Nili Fossae. Description: TECTONICS AND EVOLUTION OF THE GALILEAN SATELLITES We propose to conduct a two-pronged theoretical investigation regarding the tectonics and evolution of the Galilean satellites.  First we will continue our investigation of the formation mechanism of grooved terrain on Ganymede.  Galileo images and theoretical modeling suggests that, in many regions, the 5-10 km-wavelength grooves visible in regional-scale images result from an extensional necking instability.  Our simulations with a visceolastic-plastic rehology have shown that necking instabilities can produce grooves under conditions relevant to Ganymede, but the topographic amplitude of the grooves is generally 5-10 times too small.  This suggests that some additional process allowing even stronger instabilities, such as strain weakening occurs on Ganymede.  Furthermore, several authors have suggested that intense tectonic formation can destroy craters and other landforms and thereby cause resurfacing, but this idea has never been tested on physical grounds.  Here we will conduct a systematic hierarchy of finite-element numerical simulations of lithospheric extension on Ganymede, valid at finite strain, to determine the conditions under which 300-400 m-tall grooves can be produced from random initial surface topography, the nature of the deformation accompanying the extension (necking instability vs. localization along "fault" planes vs. production of broad graben) and how the deformation proceeds in the presence of craters or subsurface thermal anomalies.  These simulations will be groundbreaking in their ability to address the mechanisms of groove formation and the extent to which "tectonic surfacing" can occur.  Second, we will investigate the coupled orbital and thermal evolution of Io, Europa, and Ganymede near the Laplace resonance.  Thermal models for Io, Europa, and Ganymede will be developed and coupled to a model for the evolution of the satellite orbits, including tidal heating and resonant interactions between the satellites.  The models will incorporate major improvements in the thermal-cooling, tidal disruption, and/or orbital and thermal histories than achievable with studies and hence will provide a much more faithful representation of possible orbital and thermal histories than achievable with previous models.  Goals will include investigating the existence and properties of hot and cold stable equilibrium state for Io and Europa, the possibility of coupled oscillations between hot and cold states, the effect of tidal heating on Ganymede during passage through an ancient "Laplace-like" orbital resonance, and the extent to which orbital and geophysical observables can be simultaneously explained.  In so doing, we will provide key constraints on the current interior states and geological processes operating on these fascinating models.

Description: COLLABORATOR RESEARCH: SATELLITE, AIRBORNE, AND GROUNG-BASED ASSESSMENT OF CRYOSPHERE CHANGES IN THE COOPER RIVER/CHITINA BASINS AND ADJOINING RANGES(ALASKA) FORM LATE GLACIAL MAXIMUM TO NOW The Copper River Basin-- now a region of discontinuous permafrost rimmed by glaciated mountains, which drain to the Gulf of Alaska-- was once dammed; a large, poorly studied ice-dammed lake formed, called Glacial Lake Atna (over 5,000 square kilometers). Lake Atna may or may not have undergone a period of evaporitic, hypersaline conditions, but groundwater compositions suggest that this may have been the case. We do not know whether the lake was perennially covered by lake ice or glacier ice, but this is a possibility we shall investigate. Lake Atna may serve as a now-de-iced model of lake Vostok in Antarctica and may be a useful analog of Martian lakes in glacial and permafrost environments. As the region's glaciers retreated into nearby mountains, Lake Atna drained. A series of ice-dammed lakes have formed higher in the mountains during the retreat phase, and this type of lake continues to be important in the region's hydrology. The evolution of glaciers and lakes in this region from the Late Glacial Maximum to now is a natural model of what may elapse in parts of Greenland and Antarctica. As for the future of this region of Alaska, the thawing cryosphere of the modern European Alps offers a possible analog. We shall investigate the current state of glaciers and recent glacier fluctuations in the mountains rimming the Copper River Basin and produce 3-D models of the temporal evolution of glaciers and regional hydrology from the Late Glacial Maximum to now. Tasks: (1) Satellite image and other data collection and GIS integration, manipulation, and display. (2) Land cover classification of images and integration into GIS database. (3) Field validation and GPS tracking of interannual changes. (4) 3-D glacier modeling (former Late Glacial Max up to the present). (5) Glacier and lake change assessment, including change in ice damming from the Late Glacial Maximum to the present. (6) Implications of temporal changes in glaciers for near-future evolution of glacier lakes, surging glaciers, hanging glaciers, artesian springs and mud volcanoes. The project includes separate budgets for the University of Arizona and U.S. Geological Survey, plus unfunded foreign collaborations. This project is to be conducted with the U.S. Geological Survey (Co-PI, Bruce Molnia) and his associates. Molnia has submitted a separate budget in the amount of $40,000; $21,800 and $21,800, respectively for years 1, 2, and 3.

Description: THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY LABORATORY MEASUREMENTS OF COMPLEX SURFACES AND APPLICATION TO MARS The objective of this proposal is to determine the thermal conductivity of mixtures of rocks, particulate material, duricrusts, and subsurface layering in order to aid the interpretation of orbital infrared thermal observations of complex surfaces on Mars. This objective will be addressed using a combination of laboratory measurements and theoretical models. At present, measurements of conductivity under martian conditions are available for only a limited particle size range and relatively simple mixtures. Large particle diameters, bonding between particles, and layering of particles with different grain sizes have not been investigated in detail. Conductivity measurements of these materials are needed to interpret both orbital and surface thermophysical observations, and to determine particle sizes, the presence of duricrusts, and possible subsurface layering. By placing constraints on the physical nature of surface material and improving the knowledge of the martian surface and subsurface material, this work will foster an increased understanding of geologic environments, past and modern processes modifying the martian surface, and the climate history of Mars.  This work will develop a 80 cm diameter, 60 cm tall laboratory chamber in which the temperature response to a controlled thermal impulse will be measured and modeled to derive the thermal conductivity of a suite of different samples. The results of this work will include: 1) matrices of thermal conductivity measurements for particles ranging from 900 lm to 10 em, complex mixtures of materials, duricrusts, and layered materials; 2) an analytical and theoretical model of thermal conductivity for complex surfaces; 3) an integration of these results into existing martian surface thermal models; and 4) validation of these measurements and techniques by comparing with MER surface data, allowing for the application of these results to existing data to better determine the climate and surface processes history of Mars.

Description: This proposal addresses the need for low cost, low loss, reliable phase shifters for phased array applications. A radically different approach to a basic building block component, in this case a radio frequency (RF) switch, is enabled by the use of mass transport and electrochemical processes in solid electrolyte materials. The switching element, known as a Programmable Metallization Cell (PMC), operates by electrodepositing silver at low voltage and low current on a high resistivity electrolyte between two contacts. This reversible process allows the element to switch between stable off (high resistancellow capacitance) and on (low resistancelhigh capacitance) states. The first phase of this program demonstrated the basic functionality of resistance switches at RF frequencies in the sub-6 GHz range. Phase I1 will build on this work and will include the optimization of resistance-change elements for sub-6 GHz operation as well as the development of capacitive/l.eactance-based switches for higher frequency operation. Several switch designs which best exploit the RF performance of this technology will be investigated and fabricated at Arizona State University's Center for Applied Nanoionics (CANi). Device characterization will be performed at NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). The ultimate goal of this work is the development of a state-of-the-art compact, low energy RF switch for use in communications, navigation, and surveillance applications

Description: The Argyre impact basin of Mars exhibits topography tantalizingly similar to glacial landforms on Earth. A suite of erosional landforms (cirques, aretes, horns, glacial lineations) and depositional landforms (drumlins, esker-like sinuous ridges, lobate debris aprons) are observed in this region. The glacial interpretation of these landforms is far from settled, however. In this project, we propose to use numerical modeling of 3D ice flow and bedrock erosion to test the glacial interpretation for the landforms of this region and to infer the climate conditions consistent with their formation. Model results will be compared against a suite of observations integrating MOLA laser altimetry data and imagery from the MOC, THEMIS, TES, and HiRISE cameras. Forward modeling of modern ice-cap lobes on Mars will serve as a constraint on past ice-cap rheology. Today, lobes of the northern and southern polar ice caps flow over symmetric impact craters, burying part of the crater in ice while leaving the remaining part exposed. We propose to use crater symmetry to estimate the bed topography beneath the unexposed portion of these craters and to use this data to create a "family" of ice lobes corresponding to different rheological boundary conditions. Comparison between these forward-model results and the observed ice-lobe morphology at these sites will provide fundamental constraints on ice-flow behavior on Mars. Rheological constraints inferred from forward modeling of modern ice lobes will be used as input to reconstruct the glacial geometry and flow lines of past glaciation in the southern Argyre basin (Charitum Montes). In these numerical experiments, families of possible solutions will be constructed corresponding to cold, warm, and polythermal bed conditions as well as a range of possible climates (i.e. accumulation/ablation patterns). Model results will be compared against a GIS database of landform data derived from instrumental data and imagery. Modeled and real landforms will be compared with respect to the locations of ice margins, the orientations of subglacial flow indicators, and relative magnitude of glacial scour/deposition. The integration of three separate lines of inquiry (i.e. numerical modeling, morphological analysis, and GIS analysis/image interpretation) is a novel aspect of this project. Numerical modeling will bring an objective, process-based approach to the debate concerning glaciation on Mars. If the Argyre basin was glaciated in the past, this has fundamental implications for the history of Martian climate and the search for water on Mars

Description: DURING THE NOACHIAN EPOCH (-4.5 TO 3.7 GA) THE SURFACE OF MARS APPEARS TO HAVE BEEN MODIFIED BY RATES OF SURFACE EROSION AND DEPOSITION SIMILAR TO THOSE PREVALENT ON EARTH WHICH HAVE LED MANY AUTHORS TO POSTULATE THE EXISTENCE OF "WARMER AND WETTER" EARLY MARTIAN ENVIRONMENT. ENDOGENIC HYDROLOGIC PROCESSES DURING THE HESPERIAN (-3.7 TO 3.0 GA) AND EARLY AMAZONIAN (-3.0 TO 1.7 GA) ARE THOUGHT TO HAVE RESULTED IN THE IN THE FORMATION OF THE MARTIAN OUTFLOW CHANNELS, WHICH COMPRISE SOME OF THE LARGEST KNOWN CHANNELS IN THE SOLAR SYSTEM. THE MARTIAN OUTFLOW CHANNELS HAS BEEN THE SUBJECT OF NUMEROUS STUDIES SINCE THE EARLY ACQUISITION OF ORBITAL IMAGES OF THE MARTIAN SURFACE AND THEIR ORIGIN IS TYPICALLY ATTRIBUTED TO LARGE-SCALE SURFACE FLOW AND EROSION AS PRESSURIZED SUBSURFACE FLUIDS WERE RELEASED TO THE SURFACE. THEY GENERALLY ORIGINATE FULL BORE AT DISCRETE TROUGHS, TEND TO BE SEVERAL KILOMETERS TO 10'S OF KILOMETERS ACROSS (AND EVEN WIDER) AND HUNDREDS TO THOUSANDS OF KILOMETERS LONG, HAVE FLUVIAL BEDFORMS ON THEIR FLOORS, AS WELL AS SINUOUS STREAMLINED WALLS AND TEARDROP-SHAPED 'ISLANDS'. VARIOUS MODELS HAVE BEEN PROPOSED REGARDING THE MECHANISMS THAT LED TO OUTFLOW CHANNEL FORMATION. THESE INCLUDE: OUTFLOW ACTIVITY INDUCED BY INTRUSIVE MAGMATISM, EXTENSIONAL TECTONISM, ELEVATED HYDROLOGIC HEADS INDUCED BY TOPOGRAPHIC GRADIENT BETWEEN HIGHLANDS AND LOWLANDS, AND SUPERLITHOSTATIC PRESSURES PRODUCED A THICKENING CRYOSPHERE OVER CONFINED AQUIFERS. THE OUTFLOW CHANNEL FLOODS WERE LIKELY IMPORTANT IN REDISTRIBUTING THE VOLATILE INVENTORY OF MARS, AND MAY HAVE BEEN A SIGNIFICANT DRIVER OF CLIMATE CHANGE AND OCEAN FORMATION. THE MARTIAN OUTFLOW CHANNELS ARE PRIMARILY CLUSTERED IN CIRCUM-CHRYSE, EASTERN HELLAS, AND WESTERN ELYSIUM. THE CIRCUM CHRYSE OUTFLOW CHANNELS ARE LOCATED IN THE EASTERN PORTION OF THE THARSIS TROUGH, AND THE EASTERN HELLAS AND ELYSIUM OUTFLOW CHANNELS OCCUR IN THE FLANKS OF VOLCANIC RISES. WHEREAS THIS SPATIAL CORRELATION IS SUGGESTIVE OF A CAUSAL RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE OUTFLOW AND THE FORMATION OF THARSIS AND THE ELYSIUM RISES, AS WELL AS THE VOLCANIC CENTERS IN HELLAS. NEVERTHELESS, THEIR DIVERSE MORPHOLOGIES, THEIR GLOBAL AND REGIONAL DISTRIBUTIONS AND THEIR BROAD RANGE OF AGES REMAINS POORLY UNDERSTOOD. THUS, IN ORDER TO UNDERSTAND THE GEOLOGIC CONDITIONS THAT TRIGGERED OUTFLOW CHANNEL FORMATION ON MARS AND THE DIVERSITY OF THE PROCESSES INVOLVED IN OUTFLOW CHANNEL FORMATION, WE PROPOSE A COMPARATIVE GEOMORPHOLOGIC STUDY OF THE OUTFLOW CHANNELS IN CIRCUM- CHRYSE, EASTERN HELLAS, AND WESTERN ELYSIUM, COUPLED WITH CHEMICAL AND THERMAL MODELING.

Description: With the application of larger survey telescopes, fainter candidate NEOs are being discovered. This, in turn, requires larger telescopes for astrometric follow up. Using wide-field search telescopes for targeted follow up reduces their survey efficiency, however. For example, the Mount Lemmon Survey (MLS) 15-m facility spends about 27% of its time following up objects fainter than V=20 or obtaining data for physical characterization. Although essential for confirmation, orbital arc extension, and a better understanding of the nature of NEOs, these activities reduce the capacity of this telescope for discovery. Undoubtedly, similar inefficiencies exist at other NEO search sites. We propose to upgrade an underutilized 1-m telescope adjacent to the MLS to provide a web-accessible, queue-based follow up telescope that can be used by all the NASA NEOO search programs. This will require new optics, a high performance CCD camera and filter set, computerized pointing, and facilities for data acquisition and reduction. The system will be monitored by the MLS operator, who will vet results prior to submission to the MPC. When not providing astrometric follow up, physical characterization observations, including wide band photometry and dense time-series studies can be made. Given some recent developments relating to the cost of the primary optics, we present two timeline options for completion of this project.

Description: Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun, is one of the least-studied bodies in the Solar System. The MESSENGER spacecraft, en route to Mercury now, consists of many remote sensing instruments designed to study different attributes of Mercury. In order to address many of the major scientific objectives of the MESSENGER mission, direct compositional data must be determined from the spacecraft instrumentation. Mercury close proximity to the Sun subjects it to significant alteration of the surface material , or space weathering, due collectively to micrometeoroid impact, solar wind impact, solar and cosmic ray interaction, and thermal cycling of the surface regolith. The compositional data acquired from Earth-based observations of Mercury suggests that space weathering renders analyses of the spectral reflectance acquired by the MASCS and in the MDIS filters very limited in terms of interpreting the surface mineralogy of Mercury. Data acquired by the geochemical experiments, the X-Ray Spectrometer XRS and Ray Neutron Spectrometer GNRS, will, however, probe the surface composition independent of the effects of space weathering. I propose to study (1) the extent and effects of space weathering on Mercury surface regolith, and (2) how we can decouple the surface compositional information we derive from MESSENGER instrumentation from the effects of space weathering. I plan a phased approach, including defining Si standard areas on the surface that can be used for elemental intensity ratios from the XRS and GNRS, using observations with the UVVS and VIRS spectrometers and MDIS images to search for variations in surface weathering across the surface, and using the XRS and GNRS to seek stratigraphic variations in surface composition suggesting less gardened terrain

Description: METEORITIC AMINO ACIDS AS ASYMMETRIC CATALYSTS IN PREBIOTIC CHEMISTRY SUMMARY: The non-racemic amino acids of meteorites provide the only natural sample of molecular asymmetry measured so far outside the Biosphere and it is reasonable to suggest that these compounds may have been important to the prebiotic molecular evolution of the early Earth. Much has been learned about meteoritic amino acids through extensive molecular, isotopic, and chiral analyses of the last thirty ye5ars. We know, for example, that they were formed ahiotically and that their syntheses involved several solar and pre-solar environments, with some showing high deuterium enrichments that relate them to the cold regimes of the interstellar medium. Therefore, we propose to continue the studies conducted in this laboratory during previous grant years with the following analytical tasks. i To constrain the possible origin of meteoritic amino acids by conducting computer-aided ah initio calculation of selected amino acid species. i To probe further the possible effect of abiotic ee in molecular evolution and expand the prebiotic modeling of catalytic transfer of asymmetry from di-peptides to sugars to include the syntheses of compounds that are important to extant life such as ribose and glucose. The proposed work has shown much promise in preliminary studies and will expand greatly our understanding of the prebiotic traits in chemical evolution that could foster the establishment of biomolecule precursors. As such, they are directly relevant to the study of the origin of life and the ob-jectives of this NRA.

Description: Investigating characteristic bedforms of base surge deposits: implications for cross-stratified deposits at Mars Exploration Rover (MER) landing sites and the dynamics of phreatomagmatic eruptions-(Student-Brittany Dawn Brand) The proposed work will address a portion of the broad question 'How did the Solar System evolve to its current diverse state?' by using Earth analog studies to understand specifics about the geologic history of Mars. Both Mars Exploration Rovers (MER) have observed outcrops that display cross-bedded sediments, possibly indicating a wide range of ancient environments. The suggested environments include a lake, a river, a sand-dune field, base-surge deposits associated with a violent volcanic eruption, and base-surges caused by a large meteor impact (Grotzinger et al., 2006; Arvidson et al, 2006; Knauth et al., 2005). The variety of possibilities have sparked debate over the origin of the Mars rocks and highlight the fact that no cross-specialty consensus on diagnostic bedforms exists, preventing confident interpretation of several sites on Mars. A fundamental problem with interpreting the cross-strata is that sedimentological characteristics of equivalent terrestrial rocks are not well constrained due to a lack of detailed field data (Wohletz, 1998), leaving base surge bedforms indistinguishable from other depositional environments. The dynamics of base surges are also poorly understood for both Earth and Martian conditions. Base surges can form from either impact into a wet substrate (Wohletz and Sheridan, 1983), or in eruptions where magma interacts explosively with lake or aquifer water (hydrovolcanic; Wohletz and McQueen, 1984). They are ring-shaped turbulent density currents that move radially away from the base of a vertical explosion column at 'hurricane velocities' (Moore, 1967). We propose an analog study to examine several terrestrial base-surge deposits to accomplish three primary scientific goals: (1) Characterize and quantify bedforms to determine if base-surge cross-strata can be distinguished from other depositional systems; (2) Relate bedform characteristics to flow parameters such as velocity and particle concentration; and (3) Combine data from (1) and (2) to model surge dynamics for both Earth and Mars atmospheric conditions. To accomplish this, we will complete three tasks: Task I: Identify diagnostic characteristics of volcaniclastic deposits o We will complete detailed mapping and interpretation of four mafic hydrovolcanic centers with well-exposed base-surge deposits: This includes previous work at Sinker Butte Volcano, ID (Brand and White, 2007); Narbona Pass Maar, NM (Brand et al., in prep); Table Rock, OR, and future work at Crater Elegante Maar, Sonora, Mexico (Nov 07). Our work will yield detailed measurements of sedimentology and vertical/lateral variations of base-surge deposits. With this data we expect to identify a set of cross-strata relationships that are uniquely surge- related. -Task II: Estimate vent and local dynamic conditions from surge deposits o We will combine our data from Task I with numerical models of surge flow to assess how source conditions (explosivity, melt-water ratio, local flow conditions) affect characteristics of base-surge deposits. We will then reconstruct surge emplacement conditions using estimates of initial surge velocity, particle density and size, and atmospheric conditions. Task III: Adapt new models to Martian conditions We will apply the atmospheric conditions of Mars to our models to determine the of affect surge dynamics (particle settling velocities, runout distance, etc) on deposit characteristics. This work has potential to support a more confident interpretation of the geologic history in areas near the MER landing sites. Description: Reduced Phosphorus Assemblages as Sources of Reactive P the Origin and Evolution of Early Life The proposed research will investigate the origins of phosphorylated biomolecules and the effect meteoritic phosphorus (P) had on early Earth P geochemistry. Phosphorylated biomolecules are ubiquitous in life and are the basis for cellular replication and information storage (RNA and DNA), metabolism (adenosine triphosphate, or ATP), and structure (phospholipids). A rigorous pathway leading to the formation of phosphorylated biomolecules is unknown, yet there is growing evidence that the interaction of meteoritic material with water on the early Earth may have led to their formation (Pasek and Lauretta 2005, Gorrell et al. 2006, Bryant and Kee 2006). Furthermore, recent research has shown that (Fe,Ni)3P corrosion in aqueous solution with organics produces organic P compounds including organophosphates (Pasek et al. 2007). Additionally, recent investigations of bacterial metabolic pathways (White and Metcalf 2004) and geochemistry (Pasek 2006) suggest that the inventory of P on the early Earth may have included a substantial fraction of reduced aqueous P compounds. However, the stability of these reduced P compounds is unclear and merits further investigation. We plan a two-stage experimental study of early prebiotic phosphorus geochemistry. Our goals are: 1) To understand the corrosion of schreibersite and their role in pre-biotic chemistry and the origin of life, and 2) To understand the pathways by which reduced phosphorus species degrade through a series of controlled experiments. Experiments will be prepared and analyzed at the University of Arizona. All samples will be characterized by 31P nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, a highly selective, versatile technique capable of rapid and non-destructive identification of aqueous phosphorus species. NMR will provide information of species formed, yields, and rates of reactions. Several samples will be analyzed using electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, which detects free radical species, several of which may be key precursors to biochemical compounds. Finally, several samples will be analyzed by mass spectrometric techniques, providing a rapid detection of trace compounds. The results of this work will inform chemical pathways that may have lead to the origin of life here on Earth and elsewhere, it will describe the nature of early Earth phosphorus geochemistry and the effects on early microbes, and it will aid in the development of geochemical techniques for the detection of reduced P compounds and biosignatures on other planets, like Mars.

Description: IN SEARCH OF EARLY OXYGEN: INVESTIGATION OF REDOX SENSITIVE METAL ABUNDANCES AND ISOTOPES IN NEOARCHEAN DRILL CORES SUMMARY: We propose to characterize element abundances and isotopes in two Neoarchean drill cores to investigate the oxidation state of the environment - 2.5 billion years ago. Our goal is to determine if transient or low-level quantities of 02 were present in the environment before the Great Oxidation Event (G.O.E.). The presence or absence of 02 at this time has bearing on the relationship between the timing of the evolution of oxygenic photosynthesis and the rise of atmospheric 02 i a relationship that will inform the eventual interpretation of spectra from extrasolar Earth-like planets. The proposed work builds directly on prior research on one of the two cores conducted by the PI, Co-I and others with support from the NASA Astrobiology program. In that study, summarized here, high-resolution chemostratigraphy revealed an episode of enrichment of the redox-sensitive transition metals Mo and Re in pyritic shales from the late Archean Mt. McRae Shale, Western Australia. Correlations with organic carbon and Re-Os data indicated these metals were derived from contemporaneous seawater. We proposed that Mo and Re were supplied to Archean oceans by oxidative weathering of crustal sulfide minerals and, hence, that small but significant amounts of 02 existed in the environment 50 Ma before the start of the G.O.E. We now propose to conduct similar analyses on a drill core that samples pyritic shales from the late Archean Klein Naute Formation, S. Africa, believed to be a time-correlative deposit with the Mt. McRae Shale. We also propose to conduct Fe, Mo, U and S isotope analyses and to characterize sedimentary Fe speciation in both cores. The proposed research will test key aspects of the 02 interpretation as well as alternative hypotheses, and will help determine if the event recorded in the Mt. McRae Shale was of local or global extent.

Description: EFFECTS OF LITHOLOGIES ON IMPACT CRATERING: CONTINUATION OF NUMERICAL MODELING OF KNOWN TERRESTRIAL CRATERS The study of crater populations is an important tool for understanding the geologic history of planetary surfaces. Impact cratering modifies locally and temporally the physical and Lhermal state of the target and ejects and distributes material in various physical states (melted, shocked, pulverized, etc.) over a wide region around the excavated crater. At the same time, the physical and chemical properties of target material, including porosity, volatile content and natural mixtures of diverse rocks strongly affect the cratering procas. Cn Earth craters in :2ler-saturated sediments me larger than their energy-equivalents in dry soils, which, in turn, are larger than their energy-equivalents in crystkaliine rocks. Melt production also appears to be slrongLy influenced by target lithology. A thorough understanding of the behavior and influence of material characteristics on :The impact process is crwial for using impact cratering as a tool to better understand the physical, geological and biogeochemical processes on a given planetary body. Numerical and to a somewhat lesser degree, due to scaling limitations, laboratory experiments are the best tools for such and undertaking. Over the past two cycles we have accumulated valuable experience in understanding the influence of target properties on the impact process by modeling the formation of specific terrestrial craters. In the process, we have significantly improved our numerical codes (SOVA and SALEB) and material models. Overall, current material and hydrodynamic models allow us to reproduce the main features of crater morphology versus impact size. At the same time,our results indicate that there are still limitations in the models that must be improved for an accurate reproduction of impact events. During this cycle we plan to take our investigation to the next logical step by: 1) Improve material models to reproduce simultaneously the thermodynamic properties of solid-solid transitions, melting and vaporization; 2) Model craters in complex lithologies by investigating the role of mixing materials with very different thermodynamic properties. Our investigation will involve modeling vertically layered targets, compIex targets with radial as well as vertical material variations, and intrinsically mixed targets (e.g., targets with significant pore water). 3) Investigate the role of material target complexity and impact conditions on material ejection and formation of proximal and distal ejecta. We will address these scientific objectives by modeling the formation of specific small and large terrestrial craters taking advantage of the recent progress in geological and geophysical studies of many terrestrial impact structures, to test and validate our refined models against nhservational data. Large craters cover extended targets and are thus more sensitive to spatial variations in target lithologies. Crater collapse, melt production, distal material ejection may provide clues on how target complexity affects the cratering process. On Earth large craters tend to be old, and either strongly eroded or of buried under thick sedimentary covers. Welt preserved accessible terrestrial structures are generally young and small, like Meteor Crater and Lonar. In small impact events the cratering process is simplified (limited crater collapse), yet these small craters present differences that are ultimately explained by differences in target lithologies. Furthermore,young structures tend to have a well-preserved ejecta blanket (limited erosion), which allows ns to compare the process of ejecta blanket emplacement with ground truth data.

The XMM-Newton observations are a crucial element of the COSMOS survey, because of the superb efficiency of X-ray observations in localizing and identifying active galactic nuclei (AGN) and distant clusters of galaxies. We were able to "repair" lost times of the AOS observations by appropriately scaling the A04 exposure times. Nevertheless, we still have exposure gaps. Uniformity of the flux limit across the field of view is a crucial ingredient for the study of the angular ahd spatial clustering of AGNs together with the correlation between X-ray and lensing maps. Description: Ganymede is unique amongst the icy satellites of the solar system. Voyager and Galileo images indicate that approximately two-thirds of its surface has experienced resurfacing. Furthermore, Galileo's magnetometer detected a strong (750 nT) intrinsic magnetic field at Ganymede, a feature rarely observed on solid bodies (excepting Mercury and Earth). We suggest that these unusual features result from the unique orbital history of the Galilean satellites, which may have included passage through one or more Laplace-like resonances before the system settled into its current orbital configuration. Passage through such a resonance would pump Ganymede's eccentricity, causing significant heating in both the ice shell and the silicate mantle. Heating of the ice shell may have lead to global expansion and partial melt formation, both contributing to the resurfacing of the satellite. Heating of the silicate mantle may have thermally buffered the core, delaying cooling and magnetic field generation until the current epoch. Thus, two of Ganymede's most distinctive features, its disrupted surface and its substantial magnetic field, are elegantly explained by a single event: passage through the Laplace-like resonance. Because tidal heating is weak, however, passage through the resonance does not ensure that resurfacing and magnetic field generation will occur. It is therefore essential to elucidate the conditions under which dissipation of tidal energy within Ganymede is strong enough to create its unique features. I propose to numerically model the coupled orbital and thermal evolution of Ganymede to accomplish the following objectives: 1. To determine the extent to which passage through a Laplace-like resonance could have caused the resurfacing of Ganymede. 2.To establish the conditions under which tidal dissipation within Ganymede's silicate mantle can delay cooling of the metallic core, leading to production of the observed magnetic field. In addition to addressing two major gaps in our understanding of Ganymede, this research applies to several fundamental questions regarding the solar system in general. These questions include why so few solid bodies generate intrinsic magnetic fields, and the conditions in which large-scale resurfacing can occur on icy satellites. In doing so, it will lead to a better understanding of how the solar system evolved to its current diverse state, a principal goal of NASA's Solar System Exploration Roadmap.

Description: The circum-polar sand seas potentially preserve a rich geological record of Martian paleo-climate.  Their location at the North Pole is likely to be sensitive to past variations in obliquity and orbital variations.  We proppose to use satellite data released by recent NASA and European missions to determine the characteristics and evolution of aeolian landforms in the North Polar Sand Seas (NPSS).  Specifically, we will measure dune dimensions (including length, width, height, spacing and orientation) and use this data to estimate individual and massed dune volume.  We will describe and classify dune forms and search for evidence of induration by volatiles.  We will apply 2 and 3d computational fluid dynamic modelling of flow structure across MArtian dunes associated with a variety of dune topographies.  We will use  Ergodic principals to infer dune process dyanamics and use aspects of dune form (e.g. curvature, asymetry, merging) to assess local environment conditions (e.g. relative wind speed and sediment supply).  We will apply new approaches to analyzing sand sea patterns that will enable the determination, for the first time, of the relative ages of the NPSS.  These data will also be used to establish paleo-wind directions preserved int he complex dune patterns.  We will identify sediment sources and test competing hypothesis for the evolution of the sand seas.  These combined analyses will advance our understanding of landform evolution on Mars, thereby fullfilling the guiding principle in NASA's Mars Exploration Program: to understand the planet's geology and to search for past and present life and life environments, specifically Goal III, Objective A:  To determine the nature and sequences of the various geological processes that have created and modified the Martian crust and surface.

Description: This proposal addresses the need for low cost, low loss, reliable phase shifters for phased array applications. A radically different approach to a basic building block component, in this case a radio frequency (RF) switch, is enabled by the use of mass transport and electrochemical processes in solid electrolyte materials. The switching element, known as a Programmable Metallization Cell (PMC), operates by electrodepositing silver at low voltage and low current on a high resistivity electrolyte between two contacts. This reversible process allows the element to switch between stable off (high resistancellow capacitance) and on (low resistancelhigh capacitance) states. The first phase of this program demonstrated the basic functionality of resistance switches at RF frequencies in the sub-6 GHz range. Phase I1 will build on this work and will include the optimization of resistance-change elements for sub-6 GHz operation as well as the development of capacitive/l.eactance-based switches for higher frequency operation. Several switch designs which best exploit the RF performance of this technology will be investigated and fabricated at Arizona State University's Center for Applied Nanoionics (CANi). Device characterization will be performed at NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC). The ultimate goal of this work is the development of a state-of-the-art compact, low energy RF switch for use in communications, navigation, and surveillance applications

Description: CFD-Based Aeroservoelastic Methodology for Supersonic Aircraft Flutter Suppression Gust Loads Alleviation,& Ride Quality Augmentation (NRA Proposal #06-SUP2-06-0015) **** This SOW defines the requirements for developing and demonstrating a methodology for aeroservoelastic (ASE) control law design, based on the proposed high-level CFD tool CartEuler. This methodology shall be applied to the supersonic semi-span transport (S4T) wind-tunnel model to simultaneously suppress flutter (FS), alleviate gust loads (GLA) and control ride quality (RQC) at transonic/low supersonic conditions during the conduct of ASE wind-tunnel tests in the Langley Transonic Dynamics Tunnel (TDT). To design such ASE control laws, the contractor shall follow a building-block approach as follows: (a) Generate a family of linearized plants (at various Mach numbers and dynamic pressures to cover the entire expected range of test conditions) by extracting the linearized unsteady aerodynamics from CartEuler; (b) For various Mach numbers and dynamic pressures, design classic linear controllers based on the linearized plant. The intent of these controllers is to achieve a 20% increase in flutter speed, a 20% reduction in gust loads, and a 20% increase in a measure of ride quality. (c) Based on the knowledge gained during the design of the classic linear controllers, for various Mach numbers and dynamic pressures, design robust controllers using the H and u-design techniques with the goal of achieving 20% increase in flutter speed, 20% reduction in gust loads, and a 20% increase in a measure of ride quality; (d) Based on the knowledge gained during the design of the robust controllers, for various Mach numbers and dynamic pressures, design linear parameter-varying controllers with the goal of achieving 20% increase in flutter speed, 20% reduction in gust loads, and a 20% increase in a measure of ride quality; (e) In a Simulink environment employing CartEuler aerodynamics, for various Mach numbers and dynamic pressures, conduct direct numerical simulations of each of the control laws (classic linear, robust, linear parameter-varying) to assess their stability and performance. 3.0 Technical Requirements The contractor shall attempt to meet the following target control-law performance metrics: A set of control laws of varying complexity shall be designed over a Mach number range from 0.6 to 1.2 to simultaneously: alleviate gust loads by a target of 20%; improve ride quality by reducing a representative wing aeroelastic amplitude by a target of 20%; and suppress flutter by increasing flutter speed by a target of 20%. Final control-law performance metrics shall be assessed and refined by NASA and the Contractor no later than the control law preliminary design review. The contractor shall attempt to meet the following target control-law robustness metrics: The gust load alleviation, ride quality control, and flutter suppression control laws operating one at a time and in all combinations shall have adequate gain and phase margins or other suitable measures of robustness. Final control-law robustness metrics shall be assessed and refined by NASA and the Contractor no later than the control law preliminary design review.

Description: "EXOSPHERIC SOURCES AND SURFACE CHEMISTRY TO PROBE THE FORMATION AND EVOLUTION OF MERCURY" This project is a two-part scientific investigation that determines the true sources of Mercury's exosphere using the Mercury Atmospheric and Surface Composition Spectrometer (MASCS), Energetic Particle and Plasma Spectrometer (EPPS), X-Ray Spectrometer (XRS), Mecury Dual Imaging System (MDIS), and Gamma-Ray Neutron Spectrometer (GRNS). By using data sets from instruments that probe to different depths in Mercury's surface we will discriminate between constituents that come from the Sun, interplanetary dust particles, meteorites and the crust of Mercury's surface. By determining the true sources of the exosphere we will avoid drawing flawed conclusions regarding Mercury's composition based on what may be an exosphere formed from a recycled rind of implanted meteoritic, cometary, and solar wind materials delivered to the exosphere by a variety of release mechanisms such as thermal desorption, photo-sputtering or charged particle sputtering. Specifically, we need to know if any exospheric constituent truly represents Mercury's crustal composition. A positive detection of the regional crustal source ofNa, K, and S would immediately permit discrimination between two cosmochemical classes of Mercury formation models. One uses mechanical fractionation of reduced-chondritic material and the other has high temperature loss of most silicates and all volatiles as gases. The first argues for a formation mechanism that has Mercury's starting materials form in a region of the solar nebula that is highly reducing, where small changes in the ratio of CIO in the nebula can lead to a much lower oxygen fugacity and hence much lower FeO contents. Such a model predicts higher amounts of volatile elements Na, K, and S in crustal materials. The second class of models predicts high metal fractionation in the planet and little or no volatiles. A second part of the investigation measures the chemical composition of Mercury's surface at seven especially chosen regions where there is known surface mineralogy that has been obtained through ground-based spectroscopy and imaging. The instruments of the MESSENGER payload can measure elemental abundances but can not identify specific minerals. By identifying characteristics in the MDIS, XRS, EPPS, and GRNS data sets that are associated with especially chosen regions where ortho- and clino- pyroxene and Na-rich feldspar have been identified on Mercury's surface through ground-based spectroscopy, the interpretations of the data will be enhanced. The focused studies of these regions will build on, augment, and complement the science mission already planned and described in the MESSENGER trilogy of papers describing the MESSENGER mission's scientific goals, mission implementation, and instrument payload (Solomon et a!. 2001, Santos et al. 2001, Gold et a!. 2001, respectively). Description: Searching for Aqueous Activity on Mars Through Analyses of VNIR Spectral Images. We propose to analyze OMEGA and PANCAM spectral images of Mars in order to search for evidence of sulfates and aqueous activity. Sulfates have long been associated with Martian soils and have recently been identified in the regolith as well. Recent results from the OMEGA/Mars Express instrument have shown the presence of kieserite, gypsum and other hydrated sulfates in the layered terrains in Valles Marineris and Terra Meridiani, as well as gypsum associated with the north polar dunes of Olympia Planitia. In parallel, the MER mission has identified jarosite in the bedrock at Meridiani Planum. Thus, sulfates are emerging as an important indicator for aqueous activity on Mars. Clay minerals have also been identified in some older bedrock sites in OMEGA images. We seek to better characterize the locations of these clay and sulfate deposits using new image clustering techniques and an expanded VNIR spectral library. Characterization of these alteration minerals will be used to guide our search for regions on the surface of Mars where aqueous activity is likely to have occurred through the action of liquid water, water ice, or surface-atmosphere reactions.

HOWEVER, RECENT ADVANCES IN OBSERVING SYSTEMS, COMPUTATIONAL POWER&UNDERSTANDING OF ECOSYSTEM FUNCTION OFFER CREDIBLE EVIDENT THAT THE VARIABILITY OF THE OCEAN ECOSYSTEM AND ITS IMPACT ON FISHERY YIELD CAN BE FORECAST ACCURATELY ENOUGH&WITH ENOUGH LEAD TIME TO BE USEFUL TO SOCIETY.  THE TOOLS ARE NOW IN PLACE TO PROVIDE OCEAN MANAGERS THAT CAPABILITY TO BOTH PROTECT AND WISELY USE LIVING MARINE RESOURCES.  ADVANCES IN SPACE-BASED REAL TIME SENSORS, HIGH PERFORMANCE COMPUTING, VERY HIGH-RESOLUTION PHYSICAL MODELS,&ROBUST ECOSYSTEM THEORY MAKE POSSIBLE OPERATIONAL FORECASTS OF BOTH FISH AVAILABILITY&ECOSYSTEM HEALTH. Description: This Phase I NASA SBIR Proposal seeks to demonstrate a new zero-erosion ablative thermal protection system (TPS) technology that is based upon an ultra-high temperature (UHT) ceramic fiber pre-form / organic ablative matrix composite structure. In this TPS material concept, the "char" phase is pre-engineered UHT zirconium carbide (Zr(O)C) ceramic fiber pre-forms, which have dual functions of high compressive strength of ligaments and non-recession of fiber components after matrix ablation. To increase the pre-form ligament strength and stiffness, Zr(O)C fiber reinforcements will be combined with the high-modulus carbon fibers. MG's ablative TPS are designed to retain their shape in extreme environments, thereby reducing the thickness requirement and lowering the TPS total mass, which will be crucial at high re-entry velocity. MG's new ablator slowly absorbs high levels of energy when ablated at higher temperatures. The ablative carbonaceous phase has been identified by the use of a melamine-formaldehyde and/or polyethylene polymer resin. This selection was based upon its high heat of volatilization and decomposition. At the completion of the Phase I and Phase II program, MG will have fabricated a high specific strength C-Zr(O)C / C-ablator and have demonstrated an completely integrated 5x5 size TPS with attachment features, operational at > 6000oF.

Description: UNSOLICITED RESEARCH PROPOSAL ENTITLED "A STUDY OF THE EFFECT OF BIOMASS BURNING ON THE GLOBAL UPPER TOPOSHPHERE AND LOWER STRATOSTROM" ABSTRACT FROM YEAR ONE ANNUAL REPORT: WE INVESTIGATED THE EFFECTS OF FIRE-INCLUDED PLUME-RISE ON THE PREDICTED EXPORT OF CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) OVER AFRICA DURING SAFARI 2000 USING THE NCAR COMMUNITY ATMOSPHERE MODEL (CAM) WITH CO TRACER AND PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME.  THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SIMULATES THE CONSEQUENCES OF STRONG BUOYANCY OF HOT GASES EMITTED FROM BIOMASS BURNING, INCLUDING BOTH DRY AND CLOUD-ASSOCIATED (PYROCUMULUS) LOFTING.  THE SCHEME WAS FIRST ADAPTED FROM A REGIONAL MODEL.  THE CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME INTO THE GLOBAL MODEL PROVIDES AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXAMINE THE EFFECT OF PLUME-RISE ON LONG RANGE TRANSPORT.  THE CAM SIMULATION WITH THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SHOWS A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT OF THE AGREEMENTS BETWEEN THE MODELED AND AIRCRAFT-MEASURED VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CO OVER SOUTHERN AFRICA BIOMASS BURNING.  THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM PLAYS CRUCIAL ROLE IN LOFTING BIOMASS BURNING POLLUTANTS TO THE MIDDLE TROPOSPHERE.  IN THE PRESENCE OF DEEP CONVECTION WE FOUND THAT THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM RESULTS IN A DECREASE OF CO CONCENTRATION IN THE UPPER TROPOSPHERE.  THE PLUME RISE DEPLETES THE BOUNDARY LAYER, AND THUS LEAVES LOWER CONCENTRATIONS OF CO TO BE LOFTED BY THE DEEP CONVECTION PROCESS.  THE EFFECT OF THE PLUME-RISE ON FREE TROPOSPHERE (CO) CONCENTRATION IS MORE IMPORTANT FOR THE SOURCE AREA (SHORT-DISTANCE TRANSPORT) THAN FOR REMOTE AREAS (LONG-DISTANCE TRANSPORT).  THE PLUME-RISE SCHEME ALSO INCREASES THE CO EXPORT FLUXES FROM AFRICA TO THE ATLANTIC AND INDIAN OCEANS.  THESE RESULTS FURTHER CONFIRM AND EXTENT PREVIOUS FINDINGS IN A REGIONAL MODEL STUDY. Description: VMO FOR S3C DATA: A VIRTUAL MAGNETOSPHERIC OBSERVATORY The successful management of space science measurements requires a combination of the appropriate expertise in both science and information technology. The UCLA VMO is built on decades of experience gathering space physics measurements, providing stewardship for the data and distributing them to the greater scientific community. UCLA scientists have contributed greatly to the understanding of the magnetosphere and are committed to continue those advances through this effort. The VMO creates robust links to the world js relevant data bases thus providing one-stop shopping for the magnetospheric researcher seeking data. The framework for building the VMO is based on a Representational State Transfer architecture and is implemented by using existing and widely adopted technologies. A prototype search portal for the data has been developed and can be accessed at  tp://vmo.igpp.ucla.edu. Since data are very dynamic, especially during the early phases of a mission, the VMO portal design allows frequent and asynchronous updating. Like the data, services which aid data analysis such as format translation, data sub-setting, coordinate transformation, and display are available through widely distributed sources. The VMO portal provides access to value-added sewices developed both locally and remotely. The VMO registries for both data and services are designed to make it easy for suppliers to make their resources available and update information regarding the resources. Magnetospheric data are useful long after spacecraft missions end. The VMO works with investigators to design data products that will remain scientifically useful even when the investigators are no longer involved. The financial resources available to data and service suppliers are extremely limited. Therefore the VMO requires only a small effort to get started and has minimal on-going costs. The VMO development and implementation approach is very cost effective since it unites innovative approaches with many existing resources.

Description: REMOTE SENSING METHANE EMISSIONS: FIELD VALIDATION WITH SEEPAGE FROM MARINE, URBAN, AND SUBMERGED-CITY SOURCES Although CH4 is at least 20 times more potent to greenhouse warming than CO2, its sources are poorly constrained. Remote sensing can improve atmospheric CH4 budgets by allowing measurements at multiple scales with standardized measures and repeat sampling. However, improvements in spatial resolution are necessary to validate satellite-derived CH4 measurements of sources with sub-regional scale variability. Equally important, is the lack of ground-referenced data. We propose marine hydrocarbon seeps can ground reference remote sensing CH4 data determining limitations and abilities of current and next generation remote sensing platforms. Marine hydrocarbon seeps provide an ideal natural laboratory for this validation, due to the sea surface^s relative spectral uniformity, the locality of the seeps, their clear identification (visual and sonar), the wide diversity of source strengths and Intensity, and the freedom of movement (no obstacles) on the sea surface. Total field emissions are - 100 moles s-1, thus the downwind plume should be satellite observable (e.g., SCIAMACHY, etc.). We demonstrated in a proof of concept study In the Coal Oil Point seep field that remote sensing techniques and AVIRIS sensitivity in particular could measure methane emissions. Recent studies indicate geologic CH4 is significant but poorly constrained due to a lack of data. Seeps are particularly common in oil producing basins (Gulf of Mexico, Gulf of Alaska, S. California) and interior areas (Texas, Wyoming). Also, CH4 remote sensing will aid in areas beyond climate change such as homeland defense and disaster mitigation. We propose to identify the feasibility and limitations of current (AVIRIS) and next generation, remote-sensing technology for detection and quantification of CH4 fluxes. This study uses the wide range of seep strengths and intensities in the Coal Oil Point (COP) seep field as ground-reference data. The technique will be ground-referenced in an urban aqueous seep, the La Brea Tar Pits, and then applied to AVIRIS images acquired during the flooding of New Orleans. Only remote sensing can provide continent scale methane emission data; this study provides the validation. Other benefits include quantification of natural seepage and a technique that will aid homeland defense and disaster mitigation. Disasters, natural or otherwise, can lead to massive releases of methane from natural gas pipelines, presenting a hazard to rescue workers and requiring costly repairs.

(LCROSS) NASAs Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), scheduled for launch in October 2008, will chart the lunar landscape, not only to identify obstacles and safe-to-land spots, but also sensor sweep the terrain and gauge it for usable resources.  NASA plans to launch the LRO rocket with a secondary payload, called the LCROSS, whose mission will be to determine the presence of water ice at the Moons South Pole.  After the LRO is deployed in orbit around the Moon, the LCROSS satellite will steer the launch vehicles spent Earth departure upper stage (CENTAUR) into a permanently-shadowed crater at a lunar pole. Description: Development of Advanced Algorithms and Simulations of Multi-scale/Multi-material Fluid Flow - - Solid Rocket Motor (SRM) technology has been well-established since the 1950s.  With NASA's new crew vehicle Orion which will travel back to the Moon using updated Apollo style rockets the need for accurate Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling of solid rocket motors is becoming vital.  One difficulty in simulating Solid Rocket Motor (SRM) is modeling the evolution of the burning solid propellant interface and the combusting gas.  Dr. Mohamed Hafez, Department of Mechanical and Aeronautical Engineering at UC Davis, plans to utilize the Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) methodology to efficiently and accurately model this interface evolution for more realistic solid rocket motor flow physics.  Liquid rocket propulsion will also remain important to future space exploration.  Enhanced modeling capabilities of liquid fuel injection, liquid fuel droplet combustion, and cavitation inception are necessary for designing safe cost effective liquid fueled rocket motors.  The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) method will provide proper modeling of the liquid/gas and liquid/vapor interface which is required for accurate prediction of efficiency, thrust, and power of a rocket motor.     The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) variant of the level set method is to be extended to multizone overset structured curvilinear grids and applied to multiphase compressible or   incompressible possibly chemically reacting flows.  The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) has traditionally been implemented in Cartesian coordinates, which is where our development effort will begin.  Then the Cartesian grid code will be extended to a single zone structured curvilinear coordinate grid system.  A series of test problems will then be solved to validate the code.  Finally, the single zone code will be extended to a multizone overset grid framework with hybrid MPO/OMP parallelization.  The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) multizone code will then be applied to complex propulsion problems such as liquid and solid fueled rocket motors.

Description: Next generation air traffic management systems will be based to a greater degree on predicted trajectories of aircraft. Due to the iterative nature of future air traffic management computations, the success of these systems will depend strongly on the ability to rapidly generate trajectory predictions. This proposal advances the development of a computational appliance for rapid prediction of aircraft trajectories (CARPAT) that combines the capabilities of the NASA-FACET software with the fast computing capabilities of the emerging field programmable gate array technology. By integrating the FACET software components on commercial, off-the-shelf high-speed computing technology, the proposed research will demonstrate high trajectory prediction speeds at modest cost.  Phase I research will demonstrate the feasibility of developing the trajectory prediction appliance using off-the-shelf hardware. High-speed trajectory predictions will be demonstrated under realistic traffic scenarios. A complete version of the system will be developed and provided to NASA during the Phase II work. The trajectory prediction appliance will commercialized during the Phase III work.

Description: Current and future programs of near-Earth and deep space exploration performed by NASA and Department of Defense require the development of reconfigurable, high-speed intra-satellite interconnect systems based on switching fabric active backplane architecture with high-speed serial interfaces. Electrical and/or optical transponders operating with Space Wire, Fire Wire, or Gigabit Ethernet protocols are required to support the associated data interconnects. The systems must be easily upgradeable, power-efficient, fault-tolerant, EMI-protected, and capable to operate effectively for long periods of time in harsh environmental conditions including radiation effects. To address the described needs, Advanced Science and Novel Technology Company proposes to develop a basic concept of the novel, optical, radiation-tolerant transponder, which will be implemented as a hermetically-sealed pigtailed multi-chip module with an FPGA-friendly parallel interface and will feature an improved radiation tolerance, high data rate, low power consumption, and advanced functionality. The transponder will utilize the company's patent-pending current-mode logic library of radiation-hardened-by-architecture cells. 8B10B encoding will be used to achieve data disparity equal to 0 and perform a reliable clock recovery. The encoder and decoder will utilize the company's patented half-rate architecture that improves radiation tolerance. The proposed characteristics will be achieved by utilization of an advanced SiGe BiCMOS technology.

Description: Innovative data measurement/acquisition systems are needed to support future Earth System Science measurements of the Earth's atmosphere and surface. An adequate system must employ a high-speed, extra low power, linear, analog-to-digital converter (ADC) with high input bandwidth and accuracy, followed by a digital signal processor that is usually implemented inside a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). Commercially available ADCs with input bandwidths larger than 1GHz feature high power consumption and latency, and poor linearity. With increasing ADC sampling rates, timing difficulties within the parallel interconnects between the ADC and the following FPGA become increasingly prominent. Therefore, a monolithic ADC incorporating a data converter that performs digital data demultiplexation and retiming is desired. To address these needs, the Advanced Science and Novel Technology Company proposes to develop a novel, extra low-power, extremely linear, under-sampling ADC featuring a high analog input bandwidth (>5GHz) that can easily interface to a following FPGA through a low-speed (<750Mb/s) parallel interface. To achieve this functionality, the proposed system-on-chip will utilize a proprietary sub-Nyquist front-end analog demultiplexer, a combinational ADC structure with proprietary gain-stabilization circuitry, and a digital signal processor implementing digital data demultiplexation and the company's proprietary data alignment scheme.

Description: The innovation is a Near Infrared Photon-Counting Sensor (NIRPCS), an imaging device with sufficient sensitivity to capture the spectral signatures, in the wavelength range 0.9-1.7 um from very faint extra-solar targets and events with high resolution. The NIRPCS will have near zero read noise and dark rates below the read noise to support photon counting for frame capture times as high as 10 seconds. Up to 10E5 frames can be sequentially captured and digitally averaged. Important NASA applications for the NIRPCS include spectral measurements on extra-solar planets in search of water and bio-markers and measuring the dynamics of galaxies at high redshift to better understand the formation process. The technical objectives of Phase I in the development of the NIRPCS include i) determine which sensor components from an existing NIR sensor must be optimized to achieve NIR photon counting performance of frame capture times as lone as 10 seconds; and ii) create technical specifications for a NIRPCS prototype that would be developed under a Phase II SBIR program. The Work Plan has the following tasks: i) Review of improvement in photocathode QE and dark charge reduction; (ii) photocathode dark current modeling; and iii) prototype specification.

Description: This is a Phase I proposal to develop an extremely versatile optical inspection tool for determining the optical figure of aspheric optical components, such as test objects, aspheric mirrors, segment mirrors, and optical components that are not easily inspected with conventional interferometry. Description: Hot structures fabricated from ceramic composite materials are an attractive design option for components of future high-speed aircraft, re-entry vehicles and propulsion systems to reduce weight and increase performance. One important detail in the design of such structures is that of joining and attachment. Large-area hot structures will likely be fabricated by mechanically joining smaller component sub-assemblies. Conventional metallic fasteners and fastening techniques do not provide structurally tight joints over a wide temperature range. A metallic fastener, which is snug at room temperature, will loosen at elevated temperature due to its relatively high thermal expansion. Excessive preloading at room temperature to maintain a tight joint at elevated temperature may be detrimental to the structural integrity of the joint. Ceramic composite fasteners on the other hand can be designed with near-perfect thermo-elastic compatibility with the adherends, however their prohibitively high cost to produce severely restricts their utility. The objective of this proposed program is to demonstrate the feasibility of a unique, cost-effective thermal stress-free ceramic composite mechanical fastener system suitable for assembly of high-temperature ceramic composite structures. The innovative fastener design facilitates joining load-bearing hot structural assemblies and can be produced at a cost much lower then other competing designs and methods. Ceramic composite fasteners will be produced and experimentally evaluated to determine the shear and tensile properties of the fasteners both individually and of respective lap-joined ceramic composite assemblies.
