Description: Future adaptive, smart air vehicles will continually tune themselves using sophisticated on-board health management and on-the-fly optimization of performance parameters. To support these dynamic, complex/nonlinear, and multidisciplinary optimization tasks requires novel methodologies. These new methodologies must be capable of assimilating data from disparate (heterogeneous) sources in a potentially high-dimensional parameter space, yet provide robust and updatable predictions. Recent progress in cumulative metamodel technology suggests new optimization methodologies capable of combining a priori mathematical models, numerical predictions, and noisy experimental data. The resulting representations can be constructed on-the-fly and are cumulatively enriched as more data become available. Nielsen Engineering & Research (NEAR) proposes to investigate the use of Cumulative Global Metamodels (CGM) in novel optimization techniques for conceptual design of highly integrated flight vehicle and air space concepts. The Phase I will investigate the feasibility of an orders-of-magnitude acceleration in nonlinear multidimensional design by combining existing search techniques with adaptive CGMs. A special emphasis of the work will be to capitalize on NEAR's CGM uncertainty estimation capabilities to monitor the quality of the metamodel and provide confidence estimates which can be used to guide optimization in a rational and systematic way.

Description: EMISSIONS PREDICTION AND MODELING OF SUPERSONIC VEHICLE COMBUSTION SYSTEMS Designing commercially viable propulsion systems for supersonic aircnift is a major challenge. All modern combustors nuisl balance the need for stability and performance with (he goals of efficiency and cleanliness. These competing demands, however, are exacerbated in supersonic flight, where emissions are released directly into the upper layer of the atmosphere. As such, they may more directly induce variations in the ozone level, modify the radiative balance, or influence the greenhouse effect. In short, the release of emissions, and particularly of nitrogen oxides (NOx), by supersonic aircraft may be quite harmful. This motivates placing a special significance on designing combustors for supersonic flight that run in ultra-low emission regimes. The NASA High Speed Research program has proposed and tested a scries of such strategies. They include Lean I'rcmixed I'revapori/.cd (Ll'l') combustion, Lean Direct Injection (LDI) combustion, and Kicli-Burn/Quick-Quench/Lean-Kurn (RQI.) combustion. For the exploration of such designs, computational modeling will be greatly beneficial, but most physical and chemical models that are typically used in subsonic aircraft simulations might not be applicable anymore. The added challenges for modeling advanced ultra-low NOx combustion systems include superheated evaporation, premixed and partially prcmixed burning modes, flashback, auto-ignition, combustion instabilities, and the interaction of the pilot flame with the main combustion region. For RQL, the strong production of soot in the primary region and the almost complete oxidation in the post-quenching zone, have to be described very precisely to predict the emitted soot with the desired accuracy. We have identified several pacing topics for model developments that will improve prediction of pollutant emissions from supersonic aircraft. These include several aspects of multi-phase flow modeling, development of models for premixed and partially prcmixed combustion, and several aspects in the models describing soot formation and oxidation. Validation and demonstration of new models will be performed for simplified well-characterized experiments and for full-scale engine combustors using Stanford's unstructured multi-physics LES code CDF. Description: THE LOCAL INTERSTELLAR MEDIUM LEGACY PROJECT We propose to provide a legacy database of far ultraviolet absorption spectra (912 -1100A) of 44 bright early-type B stars residing within N 250pc of the Sun. These spectra will primarily be used to map the physical and chemical characteristics of the neutral and ionized interstellar gas that lies both within and just beyond the contours of the Local Bubble region. Of particular importance will be the detection of the OVI ion, which is known to trace highly ionized, hot (N 300,000K) interstellar gas. We shall produce plots of the spatial distribution of the OVI ion with respect to the cold and dense neutral boundary to the rarefied Local Bubble cavity. This information will provide new insights into the possible production mechanisms for his ion that is widely believed to be formed at the conductive interfaces of evaporating gas clouds. Our database will also allow study of the spatial distribution of the ions of ArI, 01, Fell, CII, CIII, NI and NII, such that both diffuse neutral and ionized local gas can be probed in order to determine if photo-ionization conditions dominate within the local cavity. These data will also allow an investigation of the gas phase element abundances in the local gas, such that we will be able to compare their relative depletion patterns with both the galactic disk and halo gas. In addition to these prime science objectives these data will also provide a large database of observations of local H2 molecular absorption, as well as a large, high S/N set of early-type star spectra that can be modelled with appropriate stellar atmospheres.

Description: PROTEIN ENGINEERING OF BACTRIAL PERIPLASMIC PROTEINS The objective of this proposal is to engineer periplasmic binding proteins (PBPs) from thermophilic bacteria to develop efficient sensors in order to detect specifically a wide array of biologically relevant organic molecules such as amino acids, carbohydrates and polyamines, including their stereochemistry, without volatilization or chemical modification. These sensors based on PBPs will be similar to the sensors developed from a variety of E. coli binding proteins. The proposed research will also facilitate engineering of binding sites for D-amino acids from L-amino acid binding proteins by swapping the amino and carboxy terminal binding pockets. This approach will be validated using the latest tools in computational protein design. Similar designed changes in stereochemical specificity will be also explored in carbohydrate binding proteins.

Description: MODELS OF NEBULAR ORGANIC CHEMISTRY We propose to investigate the origin and evolution of organic compounds in planetary systems, and their delivery to young planets. We seek to better understand the organic compounds generated and destroyed in the interstellar and proto-planetary environments, through observational, theoretical, and laboratory work.  We will examine the potential for and limitations to delivery of exogenous pre-biotic organics to planets, examining factors that enhance or restrict this potential. We will, for the first time, investigate the effect of astrophysical X-rays on the evolution of exogenous organics in proto-stellar disks. We will follow these factors over time, from the natal cloud core through the end of the late heavy bombardment ( 4.1 Ga). We will evaluate the possible role of exogenous organic material in terrestrial biogenesis. The proposed research will significantly improve our understanding of the nature of organics in other planetary systems, the processes affecting them, and the potential for delivering pre-biotic organic compounds to planets. The goal of the proposed theoretical work specifically proposed here is focused on determining the chemical composition of icy bodies and establishing their potential for delivering pre-biotic organic materials and water to the young Earth and other planets. This will be addressed through detailed chemical modeling, coupled with physical evolution, of the protosolar nebula.

Description: THE EARTH MOOM MARS RADIATION EXPOSURE MODULE We are preparing to return humans to the Moon and setting the stage for exploration to Mars and beyond. However, it is unclear if long missions outside of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) can be accomplished with acceptable risk. The central objective of our project, the Earth-Moon-Mars Radiation Exposure Module (EMMREM), is to develop and validate a numerical module for completely characterizing time-dependent radiation exposure in the Earth-Moon-Mars and Interplanetary space environments. EMMREM provides the ability to predict radiation exposure anywhere on the surface or atmosphere of Earth, on the Moon, Mars, and in interplanetary space between Earth and Mars. EMMREM is designed for broad use by researchers to predict radiation exposure generated by almost any particle distribution incident from interplanetary space. EMNIREM is developed using contemporary, state-of-the-art, physics-based particle radiation models. Beyond this, it has the capability to incorporate new models, as they become available, to give continually improved estimates of radiation hazards and effects. EMMREM is comprehensively validated in the environments where risks need to be assessed, using direct and contemporaneous measurements near Earth, at the Moon and Mars to significantly reduce uncertainties in radiation exposure. EMMREM characterizes the extremes, statistics, and variations over time of radiation exposure caused by solar energetic particles and cosmic rays. The results of EMMREM will improve risk assessment models so that future human exploration missions can be adequately planned. This makes EMMREM highly relevant to NASA's Vision for Space Exploration and Living With a Star Programs. EMMREM's highly cross-disciplinary team makes the unprecedented link from particle radiation researchers to radiation biophysics researchers and risk assessment specialists. EMMREM is a powerful tool, urgently needed to reduce uncertainties in risk assessment models. EMMREM is the missing link from Space Science to Space Exploration. EMMREM's central objective is achieved through four primary activities: 1. We develop the central EMMREM module for predicting time-dependent radiation exposure (Linear-Energy-Transfer spectra and dose-related quantities) based on existing, well-established, working codes including the BRYNTRN and HZETRN code developed at NASA Langley and the HETC-HEDS Monte Carlo code developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the University of Tennessee. 2. We develop interfaces between EMMREM and energetic particle simulations using, as a test-bed, sophisticated, physics-based solar energetic particle (SEP) and cosmic ray models. Simulations and associated EMMREM radiation exposure predictions are used to characterize typical, and worst-case event scenarios, and to characterize exposure near-Earth, at the Moon, Mars and throughout the inner heliosphere over the solar cycle. 3. We develop interfaces between EMMREM and direct observations of particle radiation (SoHO, ACE, Wind, STEREO, SAMPEX, NOAA-GOES and Ulysses). The observations are used both to validate SEP and cosmic ray simulations, and as direct input to predict radiation exposure at the Earth, on the Moon, Mars and in interplanetary space environments. 4. We significantly reduce radiation exposure uncertainties through comprehensive validation in the Earth, Moon, Mars and interplanetary space environments. EMMREM is validated with previously measured LET spectra from the International Space Station (ISS) and the Space Shuttle, observations from LROICRaTER, MSL/RAD, MARIE on Mars Odyssey, and using an extensive database of Accelerator Beam Measurements.

Description: Searching for Aqueous Activity on Mars Through Analyses of VNIR Spectral Images.  We propose to analyze OMEGA and PANCAM spectral images of Mars in order to search for evidence of sulfates and aqueous activity. Sulfates have long been associated with Martian soils and have recently been identified in the regolith as well. Recent results from the OMEGA/Mars Express instrument have shown the presence of kieserite, gypsum and other hydrated sulfates in the layered terrains in Valles Marineris and Terra Meridiani, as well as gypsum associated with the north polar dunes of Olympia Planitia. In parallel, the MER mission has identified jarosite in the bedrock at Meridiani Planum. Thus, sulfates are emerging as an important indicator for aqueous activity on Mars.  Clay minerals have also been identified in some older bedrock sites in OMEGA images. We seek to better characterize the locations of these clay and sulfate deposits using new image clustering techniques and an expanded VNIR spectral library. Characterization of these alteration minerals will be used to guide our search for regions on the surface of Mars where aqueous activity is likely to have occurred through the action of liquid water, water ice, or surface-atmosphere reactions.

Description: GROUND BASED MEASUREMENTS OF VENUS NIGHTGLOW Ground-based nightglow measurements of emission from the Venus atmosphere have revealed a number of observable features in the visible and near-IR regions, including the oxygen green line at 5577 A, the 02 Herzberg I I bands at 4000-7500 A, and the 02 IR Atmospheric band at 1.27. These are interrelated entities, ultimately originating with oxygen atom recombination, and the details of their production are relevant not only to Venus, but also to Earth, Mars, and any planet with an atmosphere of C02 and/or 02. The year 2007 will bring a long-awaited opportunity to make ground-based Venus measurements in conjunction with the ESA Venus Express orbiter, supplemented by a fly-by of the planet by the Mercury-bound NASA Messenger spacecraft. This proposal describes plans to make contemporaneous ground-based measurements of the three target emissions while Venus Express and Messenger are carrying out their missions. Of particular interest is the ability to make temperature measurements from the ground, using the rotational distributions in the 02 emissions, while the spacecraft provide the altitudes at which these emissions occur. Measurements from IRTF have previously shown that the 1.27 S6;m emission can accurately measure temperature, and we plan to repeat such measurements in a series of observations pre- and post-conjunction. The SFICAV Venus Express instrument can detect this emission and make limb measurements for altitude determination. The VIRTIS instrument has already successfully detected the IR band near the Venus South Pole. Similarly, temperatures will be determined from the Herzberg I I emissions, using the APO telescope. Different combinations of observations will lead to improved understanding of the emission features, because current information is somewhat fragmentary. The green line intensity seems not to be well correlated with that of the other two emissions, and it has yet to be determined how the Herzberg II and IR Atmospheric emissions are related; the latter is much more variable in time than the former.

Description: Development of Advanced Algorithms and Simulations of Multi-scale/Multi-material Fluid Flow - - Solid Rocket Motor (SRM) technology has been well-established since the 1950s.  With NASA's new crew vehicle Orion which will travel back to the Moon using updated Apollo style rockets the need for accurate Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling of solid rocket motors is becoming vital.  One difficulty in simulating Solid Rocket Motor (SRM) is modeling the evolution of the burning solid propellant interface and the combusting gas.  Dr. Mohamed Hafez, Department of Mechanical and Aeronautical Engineering at UC Davis, plans to utilize the Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) methodology to efficiently and accurately model this interface evolution for more realistic solid rocket motor flow physics.  Liquid rocket propulsion will also remain important to future space exploration.  Enhanced modeling capabilities of liquid fuel injection, liquid fuel droplet combustion, and cavitation inception are necessary for designing safe cost effective liquid fueled rocket motors.  The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) method will provide proper modeling of the liquid/gas and liquid/vapor interface which is required for accurate prediction of efficiency, thrust, and power of a rocket motor.     The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) variant of the level set method is to be extended to multizone overset structured curvilinear grids and applied to multiphase compressible or   incompressible possibly chemically reacting flows.  The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) has traditionally been implemented in Cartesian coordinates, which is where our development effort will begin.  Then the Cartesian grid code will be extended to a single zone structured curvilinear coordinate grid system.  A series of test problems will then be solved to validate the code.  Finally, the single zone code will be extended to a multizone overset grid framework with hybrid MPO/OMP parallelization.  The Ghost Fluid Method (GFM) multizone code will then be applied to complex propulsion problems such as liquid and solid fueled rocket motors.

Description: Future adaptive, smart air vehicles will continually tune themselves using sophisticated on-board health management and on-the-fly optimization of performance parameters. To support these dynamic, complex/nonlinear, and multidisciplinary optimization tasks requires novel methodologies. These new methodologies must be capable of assimilating data from disparate (heterogeneous) sources in a potentially high-dimensional parameter space, yet provide robust and updatable predictions. Recent progress in cumulative metamodel technology suggests new optimization methodologies capable of combining a priori mathematical models, numerical predictions, and noisy experimental data. The resulting representations can be constructed on-the-fly and are cumulatively enriched as more data become available. Nielsen Engineering & Research (NEAR) proposes to investigate the use of Cumulative Global Metamodels (CGM) in novel optimization techniques for conceptual design of highly integrated flight vehicle and air space concepts. The Phase I will investigate the feasibility of an orders-of-magnitude acceleration in nonlinear multidimensional design by combining existing search techniques with adaptive CGMs. A special emphasis of the work will be to capitalize on NEAR's CGM uncertainty estimation capabilities to monitor the quality of the metamodel and provide confidence estimates which can be used to guide optimization in a rational and systematic way.

Description: Next generation air traffic management systems will be based to a greater degree on predicted trajectories of aircraft. Description: Applied Scientific Research has recently developed a Lagrangian vortex-boundary element method for the grid-free simulation of unsteady incompressible laminar-turbulent flow in/around complex geometries. The evaluation of the velocities due to vortex and boundary elements, which constitute roughly 90% of the simulation cost, are accelerated via a scalably parallel adaptive fast multipole method (FMM) for distributed computing. The objective of this proposal is to incorporate hardware acceleration into the latter using a cluster of graphical processing units (GPU). During Phase I, the direct interaction component of FMM (vortex only), which constitutes roughly half the computational cost, will be offloaded onto one GPU. Feasibility will be demonstrated by achieving order-of-magnitude GPU speedup over a CPU. Phase II activities will involve the porting of the entire FMM code (for both vortex and boundary elements) onto a cluster of GPUs. The developed grid-free flow simulation software for GPU clusters is expected to provide significant price/performance improvement over traditional CPU clusters, thereby allowing simulations for larger and more physically realistic problems.

Description: This Phase I NASA SBIR Proposal seeks to demonstrate a new zero-erosion ablative thermal protection system (TPS) technology that is based upon an ultra-high temperature (UHT) ceramic fiber pre-form / organic ablative matrix composite structure. In this TPS material concept, the "char" phase is pre-engineered UHT zirconium carbide (Zr(O)C) ceramic fiber pre-forms, which have dual functions of high compressive strength of ligaments and non-recession of fiber components after matrix ablation. To increase the pre-form ligament strength and stiffness, Zr(O)C fiber reinforcements will be combined with the high-modulus carbon fibers. MG's new ablator slowly absorbs high levels of energy when ablated at higher temperatures. The ablative carbonaceous phase has been identified by the use of a melamine-formaldehyde and/or polyethylene polymer resin. This selection was based upon its high heat of volatilization and decomposition. At the completion of the Phase I and Phase II program, MG will have fabricated a high specific strength C-Zr(O)C / C-ablator and have demonstrated an completely integrated 5x5 size TPS with attachment features, operational at > 6000oF.

Description: Hot structures fabricated from ceramic composite materials are an attractive design option for components of future high-speed aircraft, re-entry vehicles and propulsion systems to reduce weight and increase performance. One important detail in the design of such structures is that of joining and attachment. Large-area hot structures will likely be fabricated by mechanically joining smaller component sub-assemblies. Conventional metallic fasteners and fastening techniques do not provide structurally tight joints over a wide temperature range. A metallic fastener, which is snug at room temperature, will loosen at elevated temperature due to its relatively high thermal expansion. Excessive preloading at room temperature to maintain a tight joint at elevated temperature may be detrimental to the structural integrity of the joint. Ceramic composite fasteners on the other hand can be designed with near-perfect thermo-elastic compatibility with the adherends, however their prohibitively high cost to produce severely restricts their utility. The objective of this proposed program is to demonstrate the feasibility of a unique, cost-effective thermal stress-free ceramic composite mechanical fastener system suitable for assembly of high-temperature ceramic composite structures. The innovative fastener design facilitates joining load-bearing hot structural assemblies and can be produced at a cost much lower then other competing designs and methods. Ceramic composite fasteners will be produced and experimentally evaluated to determine the shear and tensile properties of the fasteners both individually and of respective lap-joined ceramic composite assemblies.

The technical objectives of Phase I in the development of the NIRPCS include i) determine which sensor components from an existing NIR sensor must be optimized to achieve NIR photon counting performance of frame capture times as lone as 10 seconds; and ii) create technical specifications for a NIRPCS prototype that would be developed under a Phase II SBIR program. Description: This is a Phase I proposal to develop an extremely versatile optical inspection tool for determining the optical figure of aspheric optical components, such as test objects, aspheric mirrors, segment mirrors, and optical components that are not easily inspected with conventional interferometry. Modern optical design and manufacturing procedures have begun using such components more and more in routine applications to improve optical system capability. Since the optical tolerances achieved in the manufacture of such components have an important bearing on the performance capabilities of the systems that employ them, instrumentation and techniques for precision metrology are vital for quality assurance. Inspection tools required for these types of optical components have lagged the capability to manufacture them. The proposed work will demonstrate a technique for full aperture precision metrology of such optical components and is anticipated to yield instrument designs that incorporate an extremely robust, reliable, and accurate wavefront sensor for precision metrology of a transmitted or reflected wavefront, together with a projection system that covers the full aperture. The proposed wavefront sensor comprises a unique combination of digital holographic interferometry, Hartmann wavefront sensing, and adaptive optics that results in an extremely flexible tool. For the Phase I study, we propose to employ an existing wavefront sensor instrument to accelerate progress towards production of useful experimental data from tests conducted on existing optical elements.

Description: To address the NASA Earth Science Division need for high-speed fiber optic multiplexers for next generation lidar systems, Luminit proposes to develop a new Fiber Optic Micromultiplexer (FOMM) based on InP/InGaAsP photonic integrated circuits (PIC) and digital optical switches (DOS). This approach makes innovative use of a modular expandable binary tree architecture for robust high-speed switching with a new application of the latest PIC and DOS technology. This approach enables us to design a lightweight (200 g), compact multiplexer that consumes only 1 A of electricity and can switch a fiber-coupled NIR laser transmitter among 16 single-mode fiber outputs in 4 ns while consuming only 5 W of electricity. In Phase I, Luminit will demonstrate the feasibility of - 20 ns switching and - 1 W laser power with a proof-of-principle 1-to-4 FOMM that has three electro-optical fiber switches, which will reduce the development risk of a Phase II 1-to-16 prototype that incorporates the PIC/DOS technology. The demonstrated results will offer NASA enhanced return signal and image resolution for lidar systems.

Description: Innovative data measurement/acquisition systems are needed to support future Earth System Science measurements of the Earth's atmosphere and surface. An adequate system must employ a high-speed, extra low power, linear, analog-to-digital converter (ADC) with high input bandwidth and accuracy, followed by a digital signal processor that is usually implemented inside a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). Commercially available ADCs with input bandwidths larger than 1GHz feature high power consumption and latency, and poor linearity. With increasing ADC sampling rates, timing difficulties within the parallel interconnects between the ADC and the following FPGA become increasingly prominent. Therefore, a monolithic ADC incorporating a data converter that performs digital data demultiplexation and retiming is desired. To address these needs, the Advanced Science and Novel Technology Company proposes to develop a novel, extra low-power, extremely linear, under-sampling ADC featuring a high analog input bandwidth (>5GHz) that can easily interface to a following FPGA through a low-speed (<750Mb/s) parallel interface. To achieve this functionality, the proposed system-on-chip will utilize a proprietary sub-Nyquist front-end analog demultiplexer, a combinational ADC structure with proprietary gain-stabilization circuitry, and a digital signal processor implementing digital data demultiplexation and the company's proprietary data alignment scheme.

Description: Current and future programs of near-Earth and deep space exploration performed by NASA and Department of Defense require the development of reconfigurable, high-speed intra-satellite interconnect systems based on switching fabric active backplane architecture with high-speed serial interfaces. Electrical and/or optical transponders operating with Space Wire, Fire Wire, or Gigabit Ethernet protocols are required to support the associated data interconnects. The systems must be easily upgradeable, power-efficient, fault-tolerant, EMI-protected, and capable to operate effectively for long periods of time in harsh environmental conditions including radiation effects. To address the described needs, Advanced Science and Novel Technology Company proposes to develop a basic concept of the novel, optical, radiation-tolerant transponder, which will be implemented as a hermetically-sealed pigtailed multi-chip module with an FPGA-friendly parallel interface and will feature an improved radiation tolerance, high data rate, low power consumption, and advanced functionality. The transponder will utilize the company's patent-pending current-mode logic library of radiation-hardened-by-architecture cells. 8B10B encoding will be used to achieve data disparity equal to 0 and perform a reliable clock recovery. The encoder and decoder will utilize the company's patented half-rate architecture that improves radiation tolerance. The proposed characteristics will be achieved by utilization of an advanced SiGe BiCMOS technology.

Description: ADVANCED GLOBAL ATMOSPHERIC GASES EXPERIMENT (AGAGE): SIO LABORATORY OPERATIONS  Advanced Global Atmospheric Gases Experiment (AGAGE) Collaborative Project Project Summary This proposal seeks four years ofzntinuing funding for the multi-national, global atmospheric measurement program entitled Advanced Global Atmospheric Gases Experimen-). The case for real-time, high-frequency measurement networks is very strong and the observations and their interpretation are recognized widely for their importance to ozone depletion and climate change studies and to verification issues arising from the M~ntrea(lo zone) and Kyoto (climate) Protocols. AGACE is distinguished by its capability to measure globally, at high-frequency, all-important species in the Montreal Protocol and all non-CO2 gases in the Kyoto Protocol. The scientific objectives of AGAGE are important in furthering understanding of global chemical and c!imatic phenomena. They are: (1) To determine optimal!y from observations the global rates of emission and/or destruction (i.e. lifetimes) of anthropogenic chlorocarbons, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), bromocarbons, hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and perfluorocarbons (PFCs) that contribute most of the reactive halogen to stratosphere and/or are strong infrared absorbers. (2) To document accurately global distributions and temporal behaviors of biogenic/anthropogenic gases important in climate change and/or ozone depletion: methane, nitrous oxide, carbon monoxide, hydrogen, methyl chloride and methyl bromide. (3) To determine optimally the average concentrations and trends of tropospheric hydroxyl radical from the rates of destruction of atmospheric methyl chloroform, HFCs and HCFCs, and estimates of their emissions. (4) To determine optimally, from atmospheric observations and estimates of their destruction rates, the magnitudes and distributions by region of surface sources/sinks of these gases. (5) To provide accurate data on the global accumulation of these trace gases, which are used to test the synoptic/regionaVglobal-scale circulations predicted by three-dimensional models. (6) To provide global and regional measurements of methane, carbon monoxide and hydrogen, and estimates of hydroxyl levels, to test primary atmospheric oxidation pathways at mid-latitudes and the tropics.

Description: SBIR 2005 Phase II Proposal Title: Dynamic Strain and Crack Monitoring Sensor. Los Gatos Research proposes to develop a new automated vehicle health monitoring sensor system capable of measuring loads and detecting crack, corrosion, and disbonding in advanced aerospace structures using a novel lock-in laser interrogation technique combined with a Bragg grating array (BGA) technology for strain and guided Lamb wave (GLW) sensing. Los Gatos Research's novel sensor instrumentation offers a number of advantages including sensor compactness (0.2mm x 0.2 mm x 10mm), lightweight (a few grams), remote data acquisition capability, low-cost, and low power consumption. The inherently reliable lock-in laser demodulation technique permit simultaneous measurements of strain, temperature, and acoustic fields with high resolution and high sensitivity. In Phase I, we have demonstrated feasibility by buildiing a prototype instrument capable of measuring static and dynamic strain, temperature, and ultrasonic waves using a lock-in laser demodulation technique and a fiber Bragg grating array sensor network. In Phase II, Los Gatos Research will deliver to NASA a rugged, compact, multi-channel instrument optimized for vehicle health monitoring studies including strain, temperature, and crack monitoring with high precision, high resolution, and high sensitivity. This dedicated prototype will include an integrated microcontroller, operate unattended, and address the power and stability requirements unique to in-flight studies. Potential NASA commercial applications could be provided through optical fiber technology which gives significant advantages for advanced aerospace platforms because they are lightweight, immune to electromagnetic wave interference, rugged, and do not produce short circuits or ground loops. Therefore the development of high sensitivity fiber optic sensors has the potential to increase reliability, enable lower cost, and facilitate more effective health monitoring and nondestructive evaluation of NASA's advanced aircraft and spacecraft components and systems. The Bragg grating array sensor deveice Los Gatos Research has demonstrated and proposed to further develop for Phase II will greatly enhance NASA efforts to develop state-of-the-art, compact, low-cost, waveform-based, quantitative strain and ultrasonic wave sensing technology for load, temperature, corrosion, and crack monitoring of advanced structures. The potential non-NASA commercial applications embrace advances in high-resolution, high sensitivity, and large dynamic range load and ultrasonic wave sensing technology has immediate applications in civil engineering for monitoring cracks, corrosion, and fatigue in steel and concrete structures such as bridges, freeways, and buildings. High frequency ultrasonic signal detection method development can be utilized in ultrasonic testing, medical imaging, and other non-destructive testing technology. Los Gatos Research's BGA technology development can readily be incorporated into current fiber optics and optical cross-connect technology for next-generation telecommunication applications.

Description: GENERAL CIRCULATION MODELING OF THE VENUS ATMOSPHERE We propose to analyze OMEGA and PANCAM spectral images of Mars in order to search for evidence of sulfates and aqueous activity. Sulfates have long been associated with Martian soils and have recently been identified in the regolith as well. Recent results from the OMEGA/Mars Express instrument have shown the presence of kieserite, gypsum and other hydrated sulfates in the layered terrains in Valles Marineris and Terra Meridiani, as well as gypsum associated with the north polar dunes of Olympia Planitia. In parallel, the MER mission has identified jarosite in the bedrock at Meridiani Planum. Thus, sulfates are emerging as an important indicator for aqueous activity on Mars. Clay minerals have also been identified in some older bedrock sites in OMEGA images. We seek to better characterize the locations of these clay and sulfate deposits using new image clustering techniques and an expanded VNIR spectral library. Characterization of these alteration minerals will be used to guide our search for regions on the surface of Mars where aqueous activity is likely to have occurred through the action of liquid water, water ice, or surface-atmosphere reactions.

Description: We propose developing a general circulation model (GCM) of Venus' atmosphere to address questions about the planet's meteorology.  The main question is what drives superrotation. Other atmospheric phenomena, polar vortex, meridional circulation, thermal tides, and planetary waves also need study. Urgency in understanding Venus' atmosphere arises from (1) confirmation by CassiniIHuygens that Titan's atmosphere also superrotates, (2) arrival of Venus Express, (3) NASA's plans to study extrasolar terrestrial planets and their habitabilitytclimate, and (4) motivation to test models of Earth's climate that predict global warming. Our work connects with (4) since our model derives from the "flagship" U.S. model for climate research. Previous models have been unable to quantitatively reproduce superrotation with input parameters that are consistent with observations. We believe the key to overcoming this difficulty involves focusing on the deep atmosphere and surface-atmosphere exchanges, together with implementing an accurate formulation of solarlinfrared radiation. Using world-class supercomputers, we will incorporate a state-of-the-art Venus solar/IR radiative transfer code into the GCM. During the first year we will simultaneously conduct extensive studies with a version of the model in which solar/IR heating rates are prescribed as input rather than computed, with emphasis on surfacetdeep atmosphere processes. Our PI'S participation in NASA missions and our formal connections with Venus Express will insure strong connections between our work and "real world" observations. Upon completion, we expect to (1) resolve the superrotation mystery, (2) make available a comprehensive Venus atmospheric circulation model to help understand continuing observations and to serve as a foundation for Venus chemistrylclimate modeling, and (3) provide a test of a standard model of terrestrial global warming. This proposal is being submitted to the NASA Planetary Atmospheres program. It will also be submitted to two programs at NSF, Climate Dynamics and Planetary Astronomy.

Description: THE ABDUNDANCES OF CARBON AND NITROGEN IN THE BE STAR NGC330-B12 IN THE SMALL MAGELLANIC CLOUD We propose FUSE observations of the Be star B12 in NGC 330 in the Small Magellanic Cloud to determine the abundances of carbon and nitrogen in its photosphere. During the past two decades there has been a consensus that the rotation rates in the Be stars are rapid but far short of their critical values (0.50<V/Ver<0.85). Just recently there has been a renewed interest in the possibility the Be stars are critical rotators (Townsend, Owocki, & Howarth 2004). Abundance studies can provide a test for the latter hypothesis, as stellar evolution modeling by Meynet & Maeder (2000) has predicted a significant enhancement in the photospheric N abundances in very rapidly rotating OB stars due to mixing of CNO-processed material from their interiors. The FUV is the best spectral region for determining CN abundances in Be stars as the strongest lines of CII, IOII, and NII, III fall in this region and the flux contribution from the disk is not important. The Be star B12 in NGC 330 is ideal for an abundance analysis as it has relatively sharp lines. A recent abundance study from optical data (Lennon et al, 2005) suggested a low N abundance, but the result was inconclusive as it was based upon only one very weak line. The low N abundance in the SMC renders it an ideal environment in which to look for altered abundances due to rotational mixing. For comparison with NGC330-B12 we propose an observation of a well-known non-emission B star in NGC 330 (B30) in order to be able to compare the CN abundances with benchmark values in this cluster.

Description: THE COSMIC INFRARED BACKGROUND EXPERIMENT: COI BUDGET REQUEST FROM UC IRVINE  The extragalactic background, based on absolute measurements reported by DIRBE/COBE and IRTS at 1.2 and 2.2 urn, exceeds the brightness derived from galaxy counts by up to a factor 5. Furthermore, both DIRBE and the IRTS report fluctuations in the near-infrared sky brightness that appear to have an extra-galactic origin, but are much larger than expected from local (z = 1-3) galaxy clustering. These observations have led to speculation that a new class of high-mass stars (PopIII) or a .first-generation of mini-quasars may dominate the Universe at high-redshifts (z -10-30), which, in order to explain the excess in the near-infrared background, must be UV luminous but produce a limited amount of metals and X-ray photons. These sources may also be responsible for reionization the Universe between redshifts 10 and 20. Regardless of the extact nature of the sources, if a significant component of the near-infrared background comes from a a redshift greater than 10 population, theoretical models generically predict a prominent near-infrared spectral feature from the redshifted Lyman-alpha line and a distinctive spatial fluctuation power spectrum of background anisotropies at these wavelengths. We propose a rocket-borne instrument to search for signatures of high redshift star formation in the cosmic near-infrared extra-galactic background. The instrument (the Cosmic Infrared Background ExpeRiment, or CIBER) consists of a wide-field two-color camera, a low-resolution absolute spectrometer, and a high-resolution Fabry-Perot spectrometer. The CIBER low-resolution spectrometer will search for the redshifted Lyman-alpha feature in the unexplored 0.8 - 1.5 urn spectral region. The CIBER Fabry-Perot spectrometer, will trace zodiacal light using the intensity of a reflected near-infrared Fraunhofer absorption feature, providing an independent measurement of the zodiacal emission and a new systematic check ofDIRBE zodiacal dust models. The combination will systematically search for the infrared excess background light reported from DIRBE/IRTS data, compared with the small excess reported by HST at optical wavelengths. The CIBER cameras will search for spatial fluctuations in the background on angular scales from 10 degrees to 10 arcsec, where a high redshift source signature is expected to peak. This range of angular scales has been poorly covered by previous experiments. CIBER will have the necessary combination of sensitivity, wide field of view, and spatial resolution to make a definitive measurement. The CIBER imager will conclusively determine if the fluctuations reported by DIRBE and IRTS are extragalactic, with sufficient resolution to remove significant point source confusion, and will accurately measure their power spectrum.

Description: We propose an investigation to determine solar wind conditions that produce specific types of geomagnetic activity. These types include substorms, magnetic storms, steady magnetospheric convection, and sawtooth injection events. Our hypothesis is that both the strength and waveform of the solar wind electric field determines which of these will occur. Thus we postulate that a moderate fluctuating field produces substorms; a steady weak field produces steady magnetospheric convection and a weak magnetic storm; a strong steady magnetic field produces sawtooth injection events and a strong storm. We will also investigate whether the magnitude of solar wind coupling to geomagnetic activity depends on the solar wind conditions such as dynamic pressure and AlfvCn Mach number. For this investigation we require I-min resolution data from solar wind monitors including IMP-8, Wind, Geotail, and ACE. In addition we need auroral images from the Image spacecraft, magnetic field and particle data from NOAA and DOE geosynchronous spacecraft, magnetic indices, and 1-sec and 1-min ground magnetometer data. The majority of these datasets are already available at UCLA or publicly available at Internet locations. Our investigation begins with the creation and acquisition of lists of solar wind features including CIRs, ICMEs, and AIfvkn wave trains. We will also generate lists of types of geomagnetic activity. These lists will then be used to construct ensemble arrays organized by significant times within solar wind structures or within types of activity. These arrays will be used to construct cumulative distribution functions and impulse response functions dependent on epoch time. These results will define the conditions that lead to each type of activity and illustrate how changes in the solar wind produce transitions to different types. The results will lead to a better understanding of the way in which the solar wind interacts with the Earthis magnetic field.

Description: A long standing problem in space plasma physics is the determination of the relative contributions of solar wind and ionospheric plasma to the Earth's magnetosphere. One of the models of solar wind plasma injection is the dual-lobe reconnection model (Song and Russell, 1992). This model describes poleward-of-the-cusp magnetic reconnection in both hemispheres during a northward interplanetary magnetic field (IMF), where magnetosheath plasma is transferred to closed field lines. During extended periods of northward IMF, this dense plasma moves anti-sunward and accumulates in the magnetotail forming the Cold Dense Plasma Sheet (CDPS). We propose to test the dual-lobe reconnection model by using a combination of FAST and Cluster data, and test particle simulations. Specifically we propose to look for continuity between the Cusp and CDPS as a signature of dual-lobe reconnection. We will also perform a detailed categorization of Velocity Dispersed Ion Signatures (VDISs, different energy ions arriving at different times) in the CDPS and compare these with dual-lobe reconnection predictions and predictions of other models. In addition, we propose to test the observed VDISs seen in the FAST and Cluster data using particle tracing through model magnetospheres simulated with northward IMF. This proposal is directly relevant to NASA's strategic goal to "understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system." In particular this proposal conforms with Strategic Objective 3B.1 by providing "progress in understanding the fundamental physical processes of the space environment from the Sun to Earth." This proposal also meets the intent of the Heliophysics Guest Investigators Program to "maximize the return from currently operating missions by providing support for research of breadth and complexity beyond those being carried out by the presently funded investigations" and by using "modeling to carry out the associated interpretative data analysis."

Description: AN INVESTIGATION OF IONOSPHERIC-TROPOSPHERIC COUPLING We propose a three-year project to thoroughly investigate the effects of atmospheric tides on the formation of the equatorial ionospheric anomaly (EU). The recent discovery of a significant global-scale disturbance of the low-latitude ionosphere by atmospheric tides propagating upward out of the troposphere and stratosphere gives impetus to this work. The major questions about these tidal effects are 1) what tidal modes are the major contributors, 2) what are the effects of longer period or large wavelength tides such as the three-day and stationary-planetary waves, and 3) how does the degree of coupling vary annually and through the solar cycle. To answer these questions we will investigate the conditions throughout the solar maximum period of 2002-2003 using TIMED-GUVI and IMAGE-FUV observations to monitor the density and morphology of the Appleton anomaly. We will also utilize lower thermospheric wind measurements from TIMED-TIDI, and mesospheric measurements from TIMED-SABER to assess the degree of upward propagating tidal energy. We will also modify the GSWM tropospheric and stratospheric inputs to characterize the variation in upward propagating tidal energy that may originate in changing weather patterns. The variations in lower-atmospheric inputs will be derived from global maps of cloud cover for the 2002-2003 period. Solar cycle dependence of the tidal influence will be determined strictly from modeling, once the shorter time-scale variability is modeled satisfactorily. The coupling of energy and momentum originating in the troposphere and stratosphere to higher altitudes is a topic that is at the forefront of aeronomy research. Recent results indicate the surprisingly clear signature of persistent tropical forcing manifesting itself in the equinoctial tropical airglow arcs. Further study is required to understand and quantify the extent to which the lower atmosphere controls the quiet-time morphology of the ionosphere, as the quiet time configuration is the initial state for sudden storm onsets. Recent findings of a preference for enhanced TEC effects over North America may also be related to the strong tropospheric forcing originating in the Amazon Basin. This study will support other investigations of the coupling of the lower atmosphere and ionosphere by the COSMIC mission and other ionospheric missions (cf. C/NOFS) This proposal directly addresses NASA Strategic Goal (3a) by proposing to "Study planet Earth from space to advance scientific understanding and meet societal needs", and by seeking to "Understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system". It also responds directly to the ROSES 2006 call "for investigations that draw extensively upon the data sets from NASA's Heliophysics spaceflight missions." It seeks to answer many scientific questions noted in the (Qrontier and (H)ome Objectives of the draft Heliophysics 2006 roadmap (February 2006), including: "What governs the coupling of neutral and ionized species at various spatial scales?" (F3.1), "How do the coupled middle and upper atmosphere respond to external drivers and each other?" (H2.3), and "What are the dynamical, chemical, and radiative processes that convert and redistribute solar energy and couple atmospheric regions" (H3.2).

Description: DETERMINATION OF RELATIVE TIMING OF SUBSTORM ASSOCIATED PHENOMENA USING MULTI-SATELLITE OBSERVATIONS ABSTRACT:Substorms are so complex that many issues related to them remain very controversial. Many models have been proposed to explain substorm activity. These models can be broadly classified into two categories depending on the cause of the expansion onset. The first invokes processes in the near-Earth region (1X1 -15 Re). The other invokes mid-tail magnetic reconnection beyond 1X1 -15 Re as a source of plasma flowing earthward. Deceleration of this earthward flowing plasma and pileup of magnetic flux close to the Earth is then the cause of near-Earth disturbances. A possible way to distinguish the cause of substorm expansion onset is to examine the relative timing of magnetotail disturbances. If the near-Earth region is the source region of substorm onset, a disturbance should be first observed in the near-Earth region and later in the midtail. Similarly, the opposite time delay should be observed if the mid-tail reconnection is the source of substorm expansion onset. Our project proposes to use magnetic data from multiple spacecraft in the tail to make a statistical examination of the relative timing of phenomena at different distances. Chance conjunctions of IMAGE, FAST, GOES, LANL, WIND, POLAR Geotail,  Cluster, INTERBALL will be used to find the statistical patterns of delay between different regions. Data from auroral imagers, world-wide ground magnetometers, Pi 2 pulsation detectors, synchronous magnetic and synchronous particle observations will be used to establish accurate onset times. This projects will also examine the statistical relationship between substorm onsets and solar wind triggers with multi-satellite observations. A major problem in previous works is the time propagation of solar wind observations. In this study, a newly proposed method for solar wind propagation [Weimer, et al., 2003] will be used and thus can help us eliminate some of the ambiguity of arrival times for solar wind perturbations.

NASA AND THE RECIPIENT MUTUALLY AGREE TO THE FOLLOWING STATEMENT OF ANTICIPATED COOPERATIVE INTERACTIONS WHICH MAY OCCUR DURING THE PERFORMANCE OF THIS EFFORT: THE INSTITUTE AND AMES' PERSONNEL WILL COLLABORATE ON THE PERFORMANCE OF THE RESEARCH AND MUTUALLY DETERMINE THE DIRECTION OF THE RESEARCH INTO UNDERSTANDING THE UPPER TROPOSPHERIC CLOUDS, WATER VAPOR, CONVECTIVE PLUMES IN CONVECTIVE SYSTEMS USING AIRCRAFT MEASUREMENTS AND CHARACTERIZE CONVECTIVELY GENERATED GRAVITY WAVES USING AIRCRAFT MEASUREMENTS. PROPOSAL:  THE FOCUS OF THIS PROPOSAL S RESEARCH IS ON THREE RESEARCH PROJECTS: 1) TO UNDERSTAND THE PROCESSES THAT FORM UPPER TROPOSPHERIC CIRRUS CLOUDS AND GOVERN THE DISTRIBUTION OF UPPER TROPOSPHERIC WATER VAPOR, 2) TO INVESTIGATE CONVECTIVE PLUMES IN CONVECTIVE SYSTEMS USING AIRCRAFT MEASUREMENTS, AND 3) TO CHARACTERIZE CONVECTIVELY GENERATED GRAVITY WAVES USING AIRCRAFT MEASUREMENTS.  IN RESEARCH PROJECT 1 THERE ARE 3 PARTS, THEY ARE: 1) EXPLORE METHODS TO IMPROVE THE CLOUD TOP ALTITUDE DISTRIBUTIONS CALCULATED FROM METEOROLOGICAL SATELLITE DATA.  THIS WILL FOCUS ON LINKING THE MICRON CHANNEL GEOSTATIONARY BRIGHTNESS TEMPERATURE, 2) EXPLORE METHODS TO DIFFERENTIATE CONVECTIVE FROM STRATIFORM CLOUDINESS, AND 3) APPLY THESE TECHNIQUES TO ANALYZE MEASUREMENTS FROM THE CR-AVE, AVE, AND TC4 MISSIONS.  THE PROJECT WILL INCLUDE NECESSARY ANCILLARY TASKS TO THE BASIC RESEARCH, INCLUDING DEVELOPING SOFTWARE TO DISPLAY THE IMAGERY AND PROCESSED TRAJECTORY DATA, AS WELL AS MANAGE THE ACQUISITION AND STORAGE OF LARGE SATELLITE DATASETS.  IN RESEARCH PROJECT 2 THERE ARE 2 PARTS, THEY ARE: 1) DEVELOP THE RAW METEOROLOGICAL SATELLITE DATA SO IT CAN BE USED TO SET THE CONTEXT FOR THE AIRCRAFT MEASUREMENTS, & 2) IF AVAILABLE, DEVELOP RADAR DATA FOR PROVIDING CONTEXT FOR AIRCRAFT DATA.  IN RESEARCH PROJECT 3 THERE ARE 2 PARTS, THEY ARE: 1) DEVELOP THE RAW METEOROLOGICAL SATELLITE AND RADAR DATA SO IT CAN BE USED TO MAP THE CONVECTION UNDERNEATH THE AIRCRAFT THAT OBSERVED THE GRAVITY WAVES, AND 2) DEVELOP STATISTICAL TECHNIQUES TO EVALUATE MOMENTUM FLUXES PRODUCED BY THESE GRAVITY WAVES. Description: MASS TRANSFER IN THE ACTIVE INTERACTING BINARY U CEPHEI Following the recent FUSE detection of a well-defined accretion hot spot in the Algol binary U Cephei (P=2.493), an active system in which the gas stream strikes the mass gainer's photosphere at a steep angle, we propose new observations to determine physical and geometrical parameters for the impact site and its apparently associated splash plasma. The capabilities of FUSE present us with an unparalleled opportunity to map a splash plasma in velocity and physical space, as many prominent shell-type absorption features are formed in this gas. Furthermore, the location, size, and temperature of the impact site can be well-determined because the flux contrast between the spot and the photosphere of the B7-8 mass gainer is large in the FUV. We propose a series of randomly spaced observations, each with a duration of 5 orbits (-10 ksec of observing time) and spanning a phase interval of 0.13 in the 60 hr period. Statistically half of the observations should fall in important phase interval 0.63-0.13 that includes totality and the transit of the hot spot through our line of sight. Based upon the results from previous FUSE observations of Algol binaries during total eclipse (Peters & Polidan 2004) we expect that the stream impact produces a high-temperature circumstellar plasma above/below the orbital plane that emits in O VI. Totality observations of U Cep would allow us to test a hypothesis that this bipolar flow is a result of an impact-produced splash of material. To increase the chance of observing the 2.3~hr total eclipse that will enable us to map the location of the expected high-temperature plasma, we request 10 visits. The physical parameters that are obtained from the observations will constrain future 3-D hydrodynamical simulations of mass flow in Algols and enable an estimate of the amount of mass lost from the system during the Algol phase of evolution.

Description: ACTIVE MESH AND MODEL REFINEMENT FOR ROTORCRAFT VEHICLES - - TO INCREASE THE WIDESPREAD USE OF COMPUTATIONAL SIMULATIONS FOR ROTORCRAFT, MUCH STILL HAS TO BE DONE TO PRODUCE ACCURATE SOLUTIONS IN AN EFFICIENT MANNER.  ALTHOUGH FIXED WING VEHICLES HAVE SEEN TREMENDOUS IMPACT FROM USE OF MODERN CFD, PROGRESS HAS BEEN MUCH SLOWER FOR ROTORCRAFT.  RELATIVE MOTION BETWEEN COMPONENTS (E.G. ROTOR/FUSELAGE) PRODUCES HIGHLY UNSTEADY FLOW ALONG WITH COMPLEX EFFECTS LIKE AEROELASTICS AND FLOW SEPARATION.  ADDITIONALLY, IT IS DESIRABLE TO ACCURATELY TRACK VORTEX WAKE CONVECTION SINCE THE INTERACTION OF TIP VORTICES FROM ONE BLADE ON ANOTHER OFTEN HAS A PROFOUND IMPACT ON THE VEHICLES AERODYNAMIC PERFORMANCE AND NOISE.  IN THE MODELING OF SUCH UNSTEADY FLOW, THE MESHES ARE INHERENTLY COMPLICATED AND MORE DENSE.  WITH THE INCREASE OF THE NUMBER OF MESH POINTS, THE COMPUTATIONAL COST SCALES AS WELL.  TO MAKE CFD A VIABLE RESOURCE TO DESIGNERS OF ROTORCRAFT VEHICLES, NEW DEVELOPMENTS MUST BE MADE TO REDUCE THE COMPUTATIONAL REQUIREMENT OF SUCH PROBLEMS.        THE OBJECTIVE OF THE PROPOSAL IS AIMED AT IMPROVING ADAPTIVE REFINEMENT TO ASSIST IN THE COMPUTATIONAL ANALYSIS OF ROTORCRAFT VEHICLES.  ADAPTIVE REFINEMENT ADJUSTS THE FIDELITY OF THE MODEL TO RESOLVE THE FLOW PHYSICS TO AN OVERALL DESIRED LEVEL OF ACCURACY.  THE CURRENT APPROACH WILL INVOLVE A TWO-PHASE PLAN.  THE FIRST PHASE WILL DEVELOP AUTOMATED ALGORITHMS TO IDENTIFY AREAS OF HIGH ERROR WITHIN THE SOLUTION.  THESE AREAS WILL BE TAGGED AND TARGETED FOR MESH REFINEMENT.  IN THE SECOND PHASE, AN ADAPTIVE SAMPLING AND DATA FUSION FRAMEWORK WILL BE CREATED.  IN GENERATING LARGE DATABASES OF DATA FOR DESIGN PURPOSES, COMPUTING COSTLY HIGH FIDELITY SOLUTIONS THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE DOMAIN IS EXTREMELY INEFFICIENT.  AN AUTOMATED PROCEDURE OF UTILIZING LOW FIDELITY SOLUTIONS WHEN POSSIBLE, WILL REDUCE DATABASE GENERATION TIME SUBSTANTIALLY.  THE GOAL IS THE SAME IN BOTH CASES; SELECTIVELY ADAPT TO ENHANCE FIDELITY ONLY WHERE NEEDED, ENABLING AN ACCURATE SIMULATION IN A FRACTION OF THE TIME OF A UNIFORMLY FINE APPROACH.

Description: UNSOLICITED RESEARCH PROPOSAL ENTITLED "A STUDY OF THE EFFECT OF BIOMASS BURNING ON THE GLOBAL UPPER TOPOSHPHERE AND LOWER STRATOSTROM" ABSTRACT FROM YEAR ONE ANNUAL REPORT: WE INVESTIGATED THE EFFECTS OF FIRE-INCLUDED PLUME-RISE ON THE PREDICTED EXPORT OF CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) OVER AFRICA DURING SAFARI 2000 USING THE NCAR COMMUNITY ATMOSPHERE MODEL (CAM) WITH CO TRACER AND PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME.  THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SIMULATES THE CONSEQUENCES OF STRONG BUOYANCY OF HOT GASES EMITTED FROM BIOMASS BURNING, INCLUDING BOTH DRY AND CLOUD-ASSOCIATED (PYROCUMULUS) LOFTING.  THE SCHEME WAS FIRST ADAPTED FROM A REGIONAL MODEL.  THE CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME INTO THE GLOBAL MODEL PROVIDES AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXAMINE THE EFFECT OF PLUME-RISE ON LONG RANGE TRANSPORT.  THE CAM SIMULATION WITH THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SHOWS A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT OF THE AGREEMENTS BETWEEN THE MODELED AND AIRCRAFT-MEASURED VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CO OVER SOUTHERN AFRICA BIOMASS BURNING.  THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM PLAYS CRUCIAL ROLE IN LOFTING BIOMASS BURNING POLLUTANTS TO THE MIDDLE TROPOSPHERE.  IN THE PRESENCE OF DEEP CONVECTION WE FOUND THAT THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM RESULTS IN A DECREASE OF CO CONCENTRATION IN THE UPPER TROPOSPHERE.  THE PLUME RISE DEPLETES THE BOUNDARY LAYER, AND THUS LEAVES LOWER CONCENTRATIONS OF CO TO BE LOFTED BY THE DEEP CONVECTION PROCESS.  THE EFFECT OF THE PLUME-RISE ON FREE TROPOSPHERE (CO) CONCENTRATION IS MORE IMPORTANT FOR THE SOURCE AREA (SHORT-DISTANCE TRANSPORT) THAN FOR REMOTE AREAS (LONG-DISTANCE TRANSPORT).  THE PLUME-RISE SCHEME ALSO INCREASES THE CO EXPORT FLUXES FROM AFRICA TO THE ATLANTIC AND INDIAN OCEANS.  THESE RESULTS FURTHER CONFIRM AND EXTENT PREVIOUS FINDINGS IN A REGIONAL MODEL STUDY.  EFFECTIVE LOFTING OF LARGE CONCENTRATION OF CO BY THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM ALSO HAS IMPLICATION FOR LOCAL AIR QUALITY FORECAST IN AREAS AFFECTED BY OTHER FIRE-RELATED POLLUTANTS.

Description: Small Business Innovative Research 2005 Phase II for Enhanced L/D and Virtual Shaping of NLF Sections. A novel and robust flow control technique for the virtual shaping of extended run Natural Laminar Flow (NLF) sections has been developed. The virtual shaping and separation control technology can be used to control the size and extent of extremely large separation bubbles to virtually shape the aft recovery region of the airfoil. The system uses a novel pressure porting technique that requires no external air source to produce a pulsed tangential jet in the separated region capable of partially or fully eliminating the presence of the separation bubble. The novel pulsed jet system was shown to produce equivalent results to continuous blowing using approximately a 42% lower jet velocity and 87% lower momentum coefficient. The virtual shaping of an extended run NLF section could offer radical performance enhancement in the form of increased lift-to-drag and maximum lift. Additionally, the system will produce a wing design enabling a hinge-less, full-span virtual shaping capability, which can be used for pilot reactive roll control, span load tailoring, and gust load alleviation. The system will provide significantly enhanced performance for the air vehicle throughout the entire flight envelope. The proposed virtual shaping and separation control technology has significant potential application in several NASA programs. The virtual shaping and flow control system could be fielded in several NASA unmanned aircraft systems, including m-UAVs, high-altitude long endurance remotely operated aircraft (HALE-ROA) for reconnaissance, and Mars exploratory aircraft. NASA designers will be eager to exploit the advantages of the current virtual shaping technology in airfoil designs and flow control systems. The technology will deliver significantly enhanced performance as compared to traditional designs in a robust package. The system will be applicable throughout NASA's high altitude unmanned and m-UAV aviation community.

Description: THE SPATIAL STRUCTURE OF THE PLASMA AND FIELDS IN EARTH'S PLASMA SHEET AND ITS VARIATIONS IN RESPONSE TO CHANGES IN THE SOLAR WIND AND IMF CONDITIONS ARE CRUCIAL TO THE FORMATION AND DYNAMIC CHANGES OF STORMS, SUBSTORMS, AND OTHER DISTURBANCES THAT AFFECT SPACECRAFT.  TO UNDERSTAND THE STRUCTURE AS A FUNCTION THE INTERPLANETARY CONDITIONS AND THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL PROCESSES OF PLASMA TRANSPORT, ENERGIZATION, LOSS, AND THEIR INTERPLAY WITH PLASMA SOURCE DISTRIBUTIONS THAT RESULT IN THE STRUCTURE, AND THUS TO INCREASE THE ABILITY TO PREDICT THESE DISTURBANCES IN SPACE WEATHER, IS THEREFORE, ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT PROBLEMS IN THE SUN-EARTH CONNECTION.  USING DATA FROM WIND, ACE, AND GEOTAIL FROM GEOSPACE MISSIONS, OUR GOAL IS TO ATTACK THIS PROBLEM BY DIRECTLY RELATING QUANTITATIVELY THIS STRUCTURE TO THE INTERPLANETARY CONDITIONS THROUGH STATISTICAL STUDY AND BY EVALUATING THE MAJOR TRANSPORT, ENERGIZATION, PARTICLE LOSS, AND SOURCE DISTRIBUTIONS THROUGH ANALYSIS AND VERIFICATION BASED ON FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL THEORY.  OUR INITIAL STUDY OF 40 MONTHS DATA HAS SHOWN VERY DIFFERENT PLASMA SHEET STRUCTURE DURING DIFFERENT IMF BZ CONDITIONS.  WE HAVE DEVELOPED ANALYSIS METHODS FOR INFERRING THE PLASMA SHEET ELECTRIC FIELDS FROM OBSERVED EQUATORIAL PLASMA AND MAGNETIC FIELD DISTRIBUTIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN PROVEN TO BE USEFUL TOOLS THAT ALLOW US TO DETERMINE QUANTITATIVELY THE LARGE-SCALE ADIABATIC TRANSPORT AND ENERGIZATION IN THE PLASMA SHEET AND QUANTIFY THE SOURCE DISTRIBUTIONS FOR THE PLASMA SHEET POPULATION UNDER DIFFERENT IMF CONDITIONS.  WE WILL USE 12 YEARS DATA TO OBTAIN STATISTICALLY THE GLOBAL DISTRIBUTIONS OF ION, ELECTRON, AND MAGNETIC FIELD IN THE PLASMA SHEET.  THESE DATA WILL BE FURTHER ANALYZED TO DETERMINE THEIR CORRELATION WITH SPECIFIC IMF AND SOLAR WIND PARAMETERS.  WE WILL EVALUATE THE ADIABATIC TRANSPORT, PARTICLE LOSS, AND SOURCE DISTRIBUTIONS FOR BOTH IONS AND ELECTRONS AND DETERMINE IF THESE PROCESSES CAN ACCOUNT FOR THE GLOBAL PLASMA SHEET STRUCTURE UNDER EACH SPECIFIC INTERPLANETARY CONDITION. Description: SBIR PHASE 2 AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED: Precision Membrane Optical (PMOS) Technology for RF/Microwave to Lightweight LIDAR Apertures Membrane Optical Shell Technology (MOST) is an innovative combination of 1) very low areal density (40 to 200g/m2) optically smooth (<290nm rms), metallic coated reflective membrane thin films, 2) advanced fabrication techniques that transform the films into self supporting shells through the introduction of permanent optically relevant double curvature, and 3) discrete active boundary control to enable rigid body alignment and maintainment of surface figure in face of environmental disturbances. Other NASA and DOD applications are expected as precision and aperture size increase. This is a crosscutting technology that has many potential spin-off applications both for NASA and other Government and commercial organizations. NASA Applications have been discussed above. Backpackable RF Comm apertures for emergency and remote location applications are possible as well. Description: LUNAR SURFACE CHARGING AND DUST TRANSPORT DURING EXTREME SPACE WEATHER EVENTS This investigation will characterize the effects of extreme space weather events on lunar surface charging, and the implications for dust charging and transport. To accomplish this task, we will utilize Lunar Prospector Magnetometer 1 Electron Reflectometer (LP MAGIER) data, supporting data from ACE and other spacecraft, and theoretical investigations and modeling. It is well understood that space weather events pose a significant hazard to exploration, primarily due to the associated radiation. However, the effects of space weather on surface charging and dust transport, also potentially a hazard, have not yet been seriously considered. The largest lunar surface charging event so far identified in the LP ER data set is a -5 kV negative potential that occurred during a solar energetic particle (SEP) event in May 1998. Negative surface potentials of a kilovolt or higher (as compared to typical potentials of < 100 V) have also been found during several other SEP events, raising the likelihood that events like these may represent a worst-case charging scenario. Potentials of this magnitude could represent a direct hazard to exploration, as could the significant dust transport likely associated with such extreme charging. We will use data analysis tools developed in previous and ongoing investigations to determine lunar surface electrostatic potentials from LP ER data. We will use supporting data from ACE, Wind and other spacecraft to identify space weather events and characterize the spectrum of incident high energy particles. We will use LP MAG data to characterize lunar magnetic topology, which partly constrains SEP access to the surface. Also, though the ER primarily measures low energy ( ~ 2k0e V) electrons, we can use it as an SEP monitor by measuring the penetrating particle background (mainly >10 MeV protons), allowing us to determine which SEP events have the greatest impact at the Moon. This analysis will provide a complete characterization of the effects of space weather events on lunar surface charging. Meanwhile, theoretical investigations and modeling, utilizing measured upstream plasma conditions and probe theory to predict surface charging, will serve both to guide the analysis and determine the implications for dust charging and transport. We will especially focus on potential hazards for exploration.

Description: INVESTIGATING DAYSIDE RECONNECTION USING CLUSTER AND DOUBLE STAR SYNOPTIC OBSERVATIONS AND GLOBAL MHD SIMULATIONS This proposal outlines a three-year investigation that will use global three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations together with ACE, Cluster and Double Star bservations to determine the large-scale topological roperties and time evolution of the regions where the hocked interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) merges with the geomagnetic field. The investigation will focus primarily on reconnection processes occurring at low and mid atitudes; it will also examine processes in regions poleward of the cusps hat promise additional insight into dayside phenomena. The effort will include a series of studies employing solar wind magnetic field and plasma parameters measured by the ACE spacecraft upstream of the bow shock as well as specified data streams to initialize the global simulations. Global configurations of the merging region will be investigated for quasi-steady conditions as well as for periods of rapid changes in the IMF and solar wind dynamic pressure. Event study imulations will be confirmed by comparing their results to Cluster and Double Star measurements as well as SuperDARN ground-based observations. The outcome of the proposed investigation will significantly enhance our understanding of the large-scale spatial configuration and time evolution of magnetic reconnection at the dayside magnetopause, and hence to many other magnetospheric processes such as the location of plasma entry into the dayside magnetosphere, the formation of structures in ion dispersions observed in the cusp, particle precipitation patterns observed in the ayside auroral region, and lobe-cell convection. In particular, results from our study will be particularly beneficial to the upcoming Magnetospheric Multi-Scale mission (MMS), the goal of which is to determine how small-scale processes dictate large-scale phenomenology.

Description: ADVANCED GLOBAL ATMOSPHERIC GASES EXPERIMENT (AGAGE) COLLABORATIVE RESEARCH PROJECT: SIO FIELD OPERA  Advanced Global Atmospheric Gases Experiment (AGAGE) Collaborative Project Project Summary This proposal seeks four years of continuing funding for the multi-national, global atmospheric measurement program entitled Advanced Global Atmospheric Gases Experiment (AGAGE). The case for real-time, high-frequency measurement networks is very strong and the observations and their interpretation are recognized widely for their importance to ozone depletion and climate change studies and to verification issues arising from the Montreal (ozone) and Kyoto (climate) Protocols. AGAGE is distinguished by its capability to measure globally, at high-frequency, all-important species in the Montreal Protocol and all non-CO2 gases in the Kyoto Protocol. The scientific objectives of AGAGE are important in furthering understanding of global chemical and climatic phenomena. They are: (1) To determine optimally from observations the global rates of emission and/or destruction (i.e. lifetimes) of anthropogenic  chlorocarbons, chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), bromocarbons, hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), hydrofluorocarbons (MFCs) and perfluorocarbons (PFCs) that contribute most of the reactive halogen to stratosphere and/or are strong infrared absorbers. (2) To document accurately global distributions and temporal behaviors of biogenic/anthropogenic gases important in climate change and/or ozone depletion: methane, nitrous oxide, carbon monoxide, hydrogen, methyl chloride and methyl bromide. (3) To determine optimally the average concentrations and trends of troposphcric hydroxyl radical from the rates of destruction of atmospheric methyl chloroform, MFCs and HCFCs, and estimates of their emissions. (4) To determine optimally, from atmospheric observations and estimates of their destruction rales, the magnitudes and distributions by region of surface sources/sinks of these gases. (5) To provide accurate data on the global accumulation of these trace gases, which are used to test the synoptic/regional/global-scale circulations predicted by three-dimensional models. (6) To provide global and regional measurements of methane, carbon monoxide and hydrogen, and estimates of hydroxyl levels, to test primary atmospheric oxidation pathways at mid-latitudes and the tropics.

Description: SNAP-L, A DEDICATED SPACE EXPERIMENT TO PROBE DARK ENERGY The key challenge for JDEM is to determine the nature of the dark energy that is driving the accelerating expansion of the Universe. The SuperNova / Acceleration Probe - Lensing (SNAP-L) employs two independent techniques, a probe of expansion using Type la supernovae (SNe), and a growth of structure probe through gravitational weak lensing (WL). SNe and WL are the methods of choice: each technique is a robust, well-understood probe of dark energy. SNe are presently the "most powerful and best proven technique" and WL's probe of the growth of structure is, "if the systematic errors are at or below the level proposed the most powerful component in a multi-technique program." Moreover, a space mission eliminates limitations on both techniques that are inherent in ground-based studies, opening up a qualitatively new approach to understanding dark energy. SNe and WL probe different aspects of the effects of dark energy on the evolution of the Universe, including testing the distinction between a new component and modification of Einstein gravity. "Combinations of the principal techniques have substantially more statistical power, much more ability to discriminate among dark energy models, and more robustness to systematic errors than any single technique." SNAP-L will carry out two imaging surveys: 1) a deep survey of 7.5 deg2 to follow over 2000 matched Type la SNe out to a redshift of 1.7, and 2) a wide survey of 1000 deg2 for WL mapping. The SNe will be observed with unprecedented detail and systematic control, resulting in a well-sampled Hubble diagram into the epoch of deceleration. The WL survey benefits from a stable, high resolution point spread function and absence of atmospheric distortions. Combined, SNAP-L will determine the dark energy density to 0.004, its equation of state to 1.4%, and the time variation to 0.07. The SNAP-L satellite will be launched into an L2 orbit by an EELV rocket. The SNAP-L 600 million pixel camera is sensitive to light from 400 to 1700 nm in nine filter bands. An integral-field unit spectrograph provides follow-up at maximum light to identify Type la SNe and provide precise redshifts. Our team has just completed three years of R&D reducing risk by enhancing readiness of all mission enabling technologies. Detector performance improvements resulting from this program enable the proposed science requirements to be met within a $600M cost cap with margin. The primary objectives of this proposal are to refine the mission design through trade studies and to strengthen our project management. The project will be thoroughly studied utilizing NASA centers and aerospace vendors, where funding is essential to increase the participation of experts in space mission construction and project management. The result of these activities will be a low-risk approach to implement the project, ready for independent assessment. Dark Energy Task Force report to the AAAC, Feb 14,2006

Description: ACTIVE MESH AND MODEL REFINEMENT FOR ROTORCRAFT VEHICLES - - TO INCREASE THE WIDESPREAD USE OF COMPUTATIONAL SIMULATIONS FOR ROTORCRAFT, MUCH STILL HAS TO BE DONE TO PRODUCE ACCURATE SOLUTIONS IN AN EFFICIENT MANNER.  ALTHOUGH FIXED WING VEHICLES HAVE SEEN TREMENDOUS IMPACT FROM USE OF MODERN CFD, PROGRESS HAS BEEN MUCH SLOWER FOR ROTORCRAFT.  RELATIVE MOTION BETWEEN COMPONENTS (E.G. ROTOR/FUSELAGE) PRODUCES HIGHLY UNSTEADY FLOW ALONG WITH COMPLEX EFFECTS LIKE AEROELASTICS AND FLOW SEPARATION.  ADDITIONALLY, IT IS DESIRABLE TO ACCURATELY TRACK VORTEX WAKE CONVECTION SINCE THE INTERACTION OF TIP VORTICES FROM ONE BLADE ON ANOTHER OFTEN HAS A PROFOUND IMPACT ON THE VEHICLES AERODYNAMIC PERFORMANCE AND NOISE.  IN THE MODELING OF SUCH UNSTEADY FLOW, THE MESHES ARE INHERENTLY COMPLICATED AND MORE DENSE.  WITH THE INCREASE OF THE NUMBER OF MESH POINTS, THE COMPUTATIONAL COST SCALES AS WELL.  TO MAKE CFD A VIABLE RESOURCE TO DESIGNERS OF ROTORCRAFT VEHICLES, NEW DEVELOPMENTS MUST BE MADE TO REDUCE THE COMPUTATIONAL REQUIREMENT OF SUCH PROBLEMS.        THE OBJECTIVE OF THE PROPOSAL IS AIMED AT IMPROVING ADAPTIVE REFINEMENT TO ASSIST IN THE COMPUTATIONAL ANALYSIS OF ROTORCRAFT VEHICLES.  ADAPTIVE REFINEMENT ADJUSTS THE FIDELITY OF THE MODEL TO RESOLVE THE FLOW PHYSICS TO AN OVERALL DESIRED LEVEL OF ACCURACY.  THE CURRENT APPROACH WILL INVOLVE A TWO-PHASE PLAN.  THE FIRST PHASE WILL DEVELOP AUTOMATED ALGORITHMS TO IDENTIFY AREAS OF HIGH ERROR WITHIN THE SOLUTION.  THESE AREAS WILL BE TAGGED AND TARGETED FOR MESH REFINEMENT.  IN THE SECOND PHASE, AN ADAPTIVE SAMPLING AND DATA FUSION FRAMEWORK WILL BE CREATED.  IN GENERATING LARGE DATABASES OF DATA FOR DESIGN PURPOSES, COMPUTING COSTLY HIGH FIDELITY SOLUTIONS THROUGHOUT THE ENTIRE DOMAIN IS EXTREMELY INEFFICIENT.  AN AUTOMATED PROCEDURE OF UTILIZING LOW FIDELITY SOLUTIONS WHEN POSSIBLE, WILL REDUCE DATABASE GENERATION TIME SUBSTANTIALLY.  THE GOAL IS THE SAME IN BOTH CASES; SELECTIVELY ADAPT TO ENHANCE FIDELITY ONLY WHERE NEEDED, ENABLING AN ACCURATE SIMULATION IN A FRACTION OF THE TIME OF A UNIFORMLY FINE APPROACH.

Description: Tropical! convection drives the climate and can he seen clearly from space yet our capacity to use this information in forecast and monitoring systems is nascent. Thus the full scientific and social benefits available from the TRMMIGPM missions remain to be unlocked. While persistence in SSTs is well studied, less analysis has been applied to the satellite rainfall record. Recent warming and changes in tropical precipitation patterns have been substantial and these variations are linked to life-sustaining terrestrial rainfall in the tropics and sub-tropics, where projections call for 2-7 billion water insecure people by 2050. Our efforts will create an integrated dataset, improve hydrologic monitoring and rainfall predictions, and increase our understanding of the links between small scale precipitation events and large scale climate variations and change. Our research will begin by developing a semi-integrated 'hydrologic monitoring system' combining 0.25O terrestrial precipitation and actual evapotranspiration fields with SSMII-derived oceanic evaporation and moisture transports. Preliminary evaluation suggests that tropical oceanic precipitation is associated with fairly predictable moisture transport anomalies at coarse reanalysis scales. We will use TRRM-TMI-SSMII data to explore and validate these relationships at higher resolutions, and discuss scaling between daily-0.25O and the seasonal-2.5O scales. We will examine persistence, linking oceanic precipitation extremes to changes in onshore moisture transports and terrestrial precipitation in Africa, Asia and Central/South America. This will improve our current NASA CAN 1-to-3 month forecast system. Our work will conclude by using model output statistics (MOS) and IPCC simulations to estimate terrestrial rainfall and AET for 2030-2050. Implications for foodlwater security will be evaluated and presented to USAID. These objectives are consistent with many key topics in the NRA. We address most of the Precipitation Variability components. We examine climatically significant variations in oceanic precipitation and link their space-time evolution to terrestrial impacts. The prognostic contribution of satellite observations will be evaluated statistically, guiding future assimilation and reanalysis efforts. We will quantify GPM in ways that elucidate variations in oceanic and terrestrial rainfall and identify new means of evaluating accelerations and changes to the hydrologic cycle. Our efforts apply to the Retrieval Algorithm topic by demonstrating new algorithms for reducing precipitation bias in areas with complex terrain. We contribute to the Applications to Hydrology component by developing a modeling methodology for large-basin ET and evaluating the agro-hydrological impacts of simulated 2xC02 satellite precipitation. The dataltechnology produced will contribute to the Education topic by enhancing the timely development and delivery of both global and regional rainfall products.
