Description: Quantifying Ring Current Losses Due to Emic Wave Scattering The overarching objective of the proposed investigation is to quantify the loss of ring current protons as a result of scattering by electromagnetic ion cyclotron (EMIC) waves. We will address this long-standing and fundamental scientific question using recently acquired data from NASA's IMAGE mission along with other observations, global kinetic ring current modeling and local hybrid simulations. Wave-particle interactions have been included the Ring Current-Atmosphere Interaction Model (RAM) and used to study the spatial and temporal evolution of EMIC wave-induced proton precipitation and to estimate the total ring current loss due to these effects. However, the uncertainty of past global loss estimates due to wave scattering is rather high due to a lack of directly comparable, global observations and also due to limitations in capturing the micro-physics of wave-particle interactions in global-scale simulations. The goal of the proposed investigation is to substantially improve the estimates of global proton loss by 1) understanding and mitigating the spatial and temporal differences between observed and predicted regions of wave-induced proton precipitation 2)improving calculations of wave growth and scattering rates by examining and parametrizing non-linear wave-particle interaction effects.

Description: Microcosm will build on the Phase I X-ray pulsar-based navigation and timing (XNAV) feasibility assessment to develop a detailed XNAV simulation capability to evaluate navigation performance for specific missions of interest, and create an XNAV flight software experiment ready to integrate on an appropriate near-term flight demonstration mission in Phase III.  Phase I demonstrated achievable XNAV accuracy, developed a preliminary source catalog, constructed an XNAV error budget, and laid out potential implementation options for XNAV, focusing on an Earth-Sun L2 lagrange point mission.  Brighter, less stable, non-traditional X-ray sources were also considered for possible XNAV application with promising initial results, especially for formation flying applications.  Taking advantage of concurrent XNAV efforts at DARPA to the maximum extent possible, Phase II will develop and validate XNAV algorithms via a simulation which will be targeted for integration with Goddard Space Flight Center's GPS Enhanced Onboard Navigation System (GEONS) software.  The error budget will be developed in more detail to support the algorithm and simulation work.  XNAV holds great potential for NASA as an enabling technology for fully autonomous interplanetary navigation and could provide a significant mission enhancement as an adjunct to the Deep Space Network (DSN) and ground based navigation. NASA's applications includes missions beyond Jupiter as an enabling technology for autonomous navigation, potentially providing improved performance over standard DSN tracking capability for very far missions.  This includes the Pioneer Anomaly mission or 500 AU mission.  XNAV provides fully autonomous interplanetary navigation capability, potentially reducing the demands on DSN for increasing tracking requirements for future missions.  XNAV can supplement DSN service and enhance DSN navigation performance.  XNAV can also provide a backup navigation capability for manned and unmanned near-Earth, lunar, and Mars missions.  Further, it can provide higher redundancy for manned missions.     This application will also provide primary and secondary navigation services for DoD and for MEO, GEO, HEO, and even cis-lunar missions where GPS has limited availability, XNAV can provide primary autonomous navigation capability, while also providing an essential backup navigation capability for missions which normally rely on GPS but have a need for continuity of operations in the event of loss or denial of GPS.

Description: Statistical Survey of Hard X-Ray Footpoints in Solar Flares Solar flares are the most energetic transients in the solar system, and are efficient particle accelerators. Yet, the details of their origin are not well understood. Powered by the coronal magnetic field, they accelerate particles, which emit Hard X-rays (HXR) at the footpoints of coronal loops. These HXR footpoints actually contain much of the quantitative information on the development of flare energy. The Ramaty High Energy Solar Spectroscopic Imagcr (RHESSI) offers unprecedented abilities to study them spatially, spectrally, and temporally. While a few individual events have been studied with RHESSI, a thorough statistical study of HXR footpoint characteristics has never been attempted. Such a study, combined with other multi-wavelength observations, would provide much-needed insight into magnetic restructuring and particle acceleration. This knowledge could be applied to other astrophysical situations where the magnetic field is important. We propose to conduct such a statistical survey of HXR footpoint characteristics (spectral index, flux, size, shape, position at different energies) and their time evolution. The reference catalog of well-observed RHESSI flares, together with other multi-wavelength (GOES/SXI, TRACE, SOHO/EIT, SOHO/MDI, HSValphaS) data products that will be generated will be made publicly available on-line. The PI designed the RHESSI imaging system, as well as the new RHESSI tool (visibilities) that will be needed to complete part of this work. The lead co-I has excellent experience in RHESSI data analysis and already maintains a database for the solar community (HEDC, Saint-Hilaire et al., 2002). He will carry out the data analysis, as well as publication and presentation of the results. The second co-I is author of, or has participated in, most of the levant single-event studies, and will provide his expertise in RHESSI and multi-wavelength data interpretation.

Description: Studying Galactic Structure and Emission With WMAP&Radio Maps We propose a plan to study large-scale diffuse Galactic emission with WMAP and other all- or nearly all-sky radio maps. This proposal is particularly timely because new all-sky radio maps, required for such work, have either been recently completed or are scheduled for completion within 1-2 years; these maps will add considerable new information relevant to studying diffuse Galactic emission structure. The all-sky maps at the various frequencies are essential to exploring spectral curvature in synchrotron emission, and a map at 10 GHz will add new information to our understanding of spinning polarized dust emission. We will extend current models of Galactic emission by adding curvature (spectral index distortion) to radio synchrotron spectra, components for superbubble structures, azimuthal structure in the Galactic magnetic field model, and diffusion of CR electrons from their sources. The overall modeling effort attempts to connect the information we have learned from small-scale observations of galactic phenomena and the ISM to much larger scales, to bring the current models up to the level of detail available in the new data, and to highlight the variety of structure and phenomena in the high-galactic latitude diffuse sky. We plan to use our new diffuse Galactic emission model for subtraction of foreground emission from WMAP and other CMB measurements, a limiting factor in accuracy of such experiments. Understanding the structure of diffuse emission in our galaxy is in accord with NASA strategic objectives for understanding the structure of our universe. The CMB foreground subtraction is in accord with NASA objectives for studying the origin of the universe. The WMAP all-sky maps, explicitly listed as a data source for this ADP, are absolutely required for this investigation, as they are the best all-sky maps at high frequency, providing rare polarization maps as well as total intensity. This proposal is for work intended to extract more galactic structure science out of WMAP data, and also improves the measurement of CMB anisotropy with these data by improving foreground component subtraction.

Description: SBIR PHASE 2 AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED:  RADIATION-TOLERANT, SPACE WIRE-COMPATIBLE SWITCHING FABRIC.  ADVR, INC WILL DEVELOP A FIBER COUPLED, HIGH POWER, ELECTRO-OPTICALLY CONTROLLED, PHASE MODULATOR FOR THE NASA LASER INTERFEROMETER SPACE ANTENNA (LISA). THE DEVICE SHOULD BE CAPABLE OF PHASE MODULATING A 1 W OR GREATER, CONTINUOUS WAVE OPTICAL SIGNAL AT MULTI-GIGAHERTZ RATES AT 1064 NM. THE KEY INNOVATION IS THE USE OF A WAVEGUIDE EMBEDDED IN A NON-LINEAR OPTICAL MATERIAL SUITABLE FOR HIGH OPTICAL POWER HANDLING. THE PHASE MODULATORS USED FOR LISA MUST BE RUGGED AND MUST PERFORM OPTIMALLY IN A RADIATION ENVIRONMENT OVER THE MISSION LIFETIME. TO ACHIEVE THIS GOAL, THE PHASE MODULATOR DEVELOPMENT WILL INCLUDE A FIBER-IN-FIBER-OUT DESIGN THAT WILL READILY LEND ITSELF TO FUTURE SPACE QUALIFICATION FOR MECHANICAL STABILITY OF THE PACKAGE AND RADIATION DAMAGE RESISTANCE OF THE NON-LINEAR OPTICAL MATERIAL.THE PHASE I EFFORT SUCCESSFULLY ESTABLISHED THE FEASIBILITY OF THE WAVEGUIDE APPROACH BY ACHIEVING HIGH POWER IN A WAVEGUIDE, MODULATING THE WAVEGUIDE, AND PERFORMING PRELIMINARY RADIATION TESTING OF THE MATERIAL. DURING THE PHASE II EFFORT, THREE ESSENTIAL ISSUES WILL BE ADDRESSED. THESE ISSUES ARE LONG TERM OPTICAL PERFORMANCE OF THE CHOSEN SUBSTRATE, TRAVELING WAVE ELECTRODE DESIGN FOR EFFICIENT MODULATION, AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF A PACKAGING PLATFORM SUITABLE FOR FUTURE SPACE QUALIFICATION.THE HIGH POWER, FIBER COUPLED PHASE MODULATOR ENABLES THE CREATION OF A DEVICE THAT IS NOT COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE. THERE ARE SEVERAL NASA APPLICATIONS THAT WILL BENEFIT FROM THIS TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT. THE MODULATOR WILL FIND USES IN HIGH POWER LASERS SYSTEMS TO PROVIDE SIDEBANDS ONTO A CARRIER SIGNAL AND LIDAR SYSTEMS WHICH UTILIZE HIGH POWER FIBER AMPLIFIERS. AN ADDITIONAL APPLICATION IS A VISIBLE LIGHT MODULATOR FOR LOCKING A LASER WAVELENGTH TO A GAS ABSORPTION REFERENCE.THE HIGH OPTICAL POWER CAPABILITY OF THE PHASE MODULATOR PROVIDES THE PRIMARY BASIS FOR ADVR TO ENTER THE COMMERCIAL MARKET WITH THIS PRODUCT. THE FIBER COUPLED PHASE MODULATOR PROVIDES AN ALTERNATIVE TO CURRENTLY AVAILABLE FREE SPACE COUPLED PHASE MODULATORS THAT CAN HANDLE SIMILAR OPTICAL POWERS, BUT ARE BULKY AND REQUIRE HIGH DRIVE VOLTAGE TO OPERATE. ADDITIONALLY, THE FIBER COUPLED MODULATOR IS CAPABLE OF HANDLING SIGNIFICANTLY HIGHER OPTICAL POWERS THAN COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE FIBER COUPLED LITHIUM NIOBATE WAVEGUIDE PHASE MODULATORS.

Funding XMM-Newton AO-5 Cycle Proposal #40105 The B Supergiant Bistability-Jump in X-ray Emission. The stellar winds of B supergiants (BSgs) to through a discontinuous jump in their terminal velocities, mass loss rates, and X-ray emission at spectral type B1 which is referred to as the bistability of BSg winds. Since wind shocks produce the X-ray emission and are highly dependent on the stellar wind parameters, BSgs provide a natural laboratory to study the relationship between the radiative force, stellar wind, and X-ray emission. Although the drop in X-ray flux appears consistent with theoretical predictions, our AO-3 XMM observations of 2 BSgs at the jump indicate severe problems with current theory. We are requesting one additional EPIC observation of J Pup (B0.5 Ib), a BSg located near the bistability jump, to determine the extent of these problems.

Description: GALAXY INTERACTIONS AND THE FORMATION AND STRUCTURE OF ELLIPTICAL GALAXIES This proposal requests funding for a project seeking to understand the formation and structure of galactic spheroids. Three students will be funded as part of the proposal. The first project studies our large suite of high-resolution simulations of galaxy mergers in order to understand analytically the key physics that determines the properties of the resulting spheroidal stellar system. This is essential both to understand the simulations and to use them as input for advanced Semi-Analytic Models (SAMs) of the entire evolving galaxy population which can be compared to the rapidly improving observations. The second project makes detailed comparisons between the structure of simulated and observed elliptical galaxies. Preliminary indications are that, although most of the observed ellipticals appear to #124;be very#124; much like the galactic remnants of our binary hydrodynamic merger simulations, an important class of giant, slowly rotating elliptical galaxies does not resemble any existing simulations. We therefore also propose to simulate a different class of merging histories in order to understand the origin of these galaxies. The third project aims to understand whether and when active galactic nuclei (AGN) are triggered during galaxy mergers, and how the resulting galaxies are affected by energy outputs from AGN. This project compares merger simulations, including dust treated by an advanced radiative-transfer code, to multiwavelength observations. The proposed research will allow detailed comparisons to observed galaxy spectra and images using new methods of measuring the morphology of highly irregular as well as normal galaxies which we are developing. These three interrelated projects focus on reaching a better understanding of the Universe in which we live. This work is important for interpreting the extensive HST imaging and Chaudra, Spitzer, and GALEX data, especially in the Extended Groth Strip (EGS) survey region of the Deep Extragalactic Evolutionary Probe 2 (DEEP2) survey.

Description: During the next 50 years, humans will begin expanding into the solar system. This exploration of extraterrestrial bodies has begun with robotic spacecraft and initial human missions to the Moon, and will continue with the re-establishment of small research outposts on the Moon and eventually the planet Mars. The use of globally diverse analog environments and high fidelity Earth-based simulations of planetary exploration can help prepare for these expensive and complex operations. The lunar experience of the 1960?s and 70?s proved that we are capable of sending humans to another planetary body and carrying out productive exploration and research on the lunar surface. The Apollo Program made extensive use of lunar analogs to train and prepare astronauts for their missions. NASA has not explored another world with astronauts since 1972 and the agency must begin to prepare the current and next generation of scientists and engineers that will design and implement its current ?Vision for Space Exploration? (VSE) goals and objectives. Within the next 15-20 years NASA is planning to return humans to the lunar surface and establish a permanent presence that will require new tools, research instrumentation, as well as EVA suits with greater mobility and life support capabilities. These new technologies will require additional development for use on Mars. Thus the need for utilizing lunar and Mars analogs on Earth is a requirement to insure mission success and reduce risk to the eventual EVA teams. As we prepare for more intense investigations of the Moon and Mars we must focus the questions to be answered and refine the tools required to address them. The study of life and ecosystems in extreme environments is a key element of Astrobiology. Astrobiology investigations of extreme environments can provide testing grounds for instrument and mission concepts for planetary exploration. These environments offer meaningful ways to develop and validate experimental hardware and software, mission operational techniques and identify and establish technical requirements applicable for future planetary exploration. It is important that science relevant to mission goals drives instrument and sensor development and also allows for the conduct of terrestrial research that in it self is relevant to the overall Astrobiology exploration goals. In an effort to develop a strategy that is part science, part operational and part programmatic, and that also seeks to bring together various ongoing and potential projects, NASA implemented the Astrobiology Science and Technology for Exploring Planets (ASTEP) Program. ASTEP is expected to lower the risks of planetary exploration through instrument/technology development aimed at or coupled with systems-level field tests in Earth?s extreme environments to obtain scientific data and develop operational capability. The real value of ASTEP will be seen when it takes the leading and guiding role for the VSE, using human explorer/scientists teamed with robotics to test technologies and procedures for future human exploration while accomplishing astrobiology science on Earth. This proposal will aid NASA in assessing the utility of current and future ASTEP and non-ASTEP projects that have bearing on VSE to support initiatives to send astronauts, scientists, engineers, and other personnel to astrobiology relevant field sites and to interact with scientists, engineers and mission personnel during the course of such field operations or expeditions. Under this proposal, the PI will participate in field activities in support of ASTEP and exploration objectives and act on behalf of the Program as a liaison between the ASTEP Program and project personnel, sponsored participants, and other field center personnel.

NASA plans to launch the LRO rocket with a secondary payload, called the LCROSS, whose mission will be to determine the presence of water ice at the Moons South Pole.  After the LRO is deployed in orbit around the Moon, the LCROSS satellite will steer the launch vehicles spent Earth departure upper stage (CENTAUR) into a permanently-shadowed crater at a lunar pole.  The impact will create a large plume of lunar ejecta that will provide a long window of observation and will excavate a large area to deeper depths than would be possible using only a robotic lunar lander. LCROSS will provide a critical ground-truth for a Lunar Prospector and LRO neutron and radar maps making it possible to assess the total lunar water inventory.

Description: The contour method is used for measuring a full cross-sectional map of residual stresses. In this method, the contour method, a part is cut in two using electric discharge machining (EDM). The contour of the resulting new surface, which will not be flat if residual stresses are relaxed by the cutting, is then measured. Finally, the original residual stresses are calculated from the measured contour using a straightforward finite element model. A 3-D model of one half of the part is constructed, the condition after it has been cut in two. The bivariate Fourier series fit to the measured contour data is evaluated at a grid corresponding to the FE nodes and then applied as x-direction displacement boundary conditions. In the 3-D case, three additional displacement constraints are applied to the model to prevent rigid body motions. The contour method for measuring residual stress has been demonstrated on several weldments including several that would have been very difficult to measure using other residual stress measurement techniques. The main advantage of the contour method is that it is relatively simple, inexpensive, and utilizes readily available equipment. In many cases, the contour method can measure a map of residual stresses on specimens where it would be very difficult to perform the measurements using any other technique.

Description: Small Business Innovative Research 2005 Phase II for Enhanced L/D and Virtual Shaping of NLF Sections. A novel and robust flow control technique for the virtual shaping of extended run Natural Laminar Flow (NLF) sections has been developed. The virtual shaping and separation control technology can be used to control the size and extent of extremely large separation bubbles to virtually shape the aft recovery region of the airfoil. The system uses a novel pressure porting technique that requires no external air source to produce a pulsed tangential jet in the separated region capable of partially or fully eliminating the presence of the separation bubble. The novel pulsed jet system was shown to produce equivalent results to continuous blowing using approximately a 42% lower jet velocity and 87% lower momentum coefficient. The virtual shaping of an extended run NLF section could offer radical performance enhancement in the form of increased lift-to-drag and maximum lift. Additionally, the system will produce a wing design enabling a hinge-less, full-span virtual shaping capability, which can be used for pilot reactive roll control, span load tailoring, and gust load alleviation. The system will provide significantly enhanced performance for the air vehicle throughout the entire flight envelope. The proposed virtual shaping and separation control technology has significant potential application in several NASA programs. The virtual shaping and flow control system could be fielded in several NASA unmanned aircraft systems, including m-UAVs, high-altitude long endurance remotely operated aircraft (HALE-ROA) for reconnaissance, and Mars exploratory aircraft. NASA designers will be eager to exploit the advantages of the current virtual shaping technology in airfoil designs and flow control systems. The technology will deliver significantly enhanced performance as compared to traditional designs in a robust package. The system will be applicable throughout NASA's high altitude unmanned and m-UAV aviation community.

Description: The Multi-Agent Architecture for Coordinated, Responsive Observations  Remote sensing missions for earth science provide a wealth of information to help us understand the dynamics of our planet. However, the current stovepipe operational model of remote sensing missions, i.e., a single spacecraft transmitting data to dedicated ground operations centers (Fig. 1), introduces untenable latencies in developing data prod-ucts that hinder model building and refine-ment as well as timely responses for hazard mitigation. Future missions will operate as part of a sensor web (Fig. 2) comprised of ^interlinked platforms with onboard information processing systems capable of orchestrat-ing real-time collaborative operations [1]. The Multi-agent Architecture for Coordi-nated, Responsive Observations (MACRO), an extension of our current work on the Adap-tive Network Architecture (ANA) is a natural technology for enabling the deployment and operation of a sensor web. The ANA software framework of multiple distributed agents provides localized autonomy on distributed sci-ence missions. The MACRO extensions will help overcome current mission limitations by facilitating real-time, reactive data acquisition, analysis, fusion and distribution which will greatly benefit society and scientific discovery/understanding. Our objective over a 3 year period is to ma-ture MACRO from TRL 2/4 to TRL 5 (Sec 2.4), by focusing on two main topics that provide significant value to NASAs earth science missions: - Incorporation of self-describing sensor, processing and measurement models (Sec. 2.2.1.1) - Collaborative observations between agents via on-board planning, scheduling, and re-source management (Sec. 2.2.1.2) - Validation on a representative hardware testbed with multiple demonstrations of a realistic earth science mission (Sec. 2.2.1.3)

Description: THE ABUNDANCES OF CARBON AND NITROGEN IN THE PHOTOSPHERES OF ACTIVE B STARS Observation of an enhanced nitrogen and reduced carbon abundance in the photosphere of a B star suggests that CNO-processed material from the starjs core has been dredged-up due to a large-scale mass motion in its interior. For several classes of active B stars, such abundance anomalies have either been theoretically predicted or serendipitously observed. We propose a two-year study using FUV spectra from the IUE, FUSE, Voyager UVS, and ORFEUS-SPAS I1 missions to test contemporary theory or confirm abnormal abundances suggested by optical data. Three classes of active 13 stars will be considered: Be stars, beta-Cephei pulsators, and mass gainers in interacting binary systems. Contrary to the consensus that has prevailed for at least two decades, there has recently been a renewed interest in the possibility that Be stars are critical rotators (Townsend, Owocki, & Howarth 2004). Abundance studies can provide a test for the latter hypothesis, as stellar evolution modeling by Meynet & Maeder (2000) has predicted a significant enhancement in the photospheric N abundances in very rapidly rotating OB stars due to meridional circulation. Several abundance analyses of sharp-lined beta Cephei stars have indicated an overabundance of nitrogen in some objects. FUV observations of the B primaries in several Algol-type systems have revealed that N-rich and C-poor material is currently being delivered to the mass gainerjs photosphere. The extent that the surface abundances have been modified is an indication of the timescale for this phase of mass transfer, the penetration depth of the impacting gas stream, or the amount of mass that is in fact lost from the system. The FUV is the best spectral region for determining CN abundances in Be stars as the strongest lines of C 11, I11 and N 11, I11 fall in this region and the flux contribution from the disk is not important. The study will provide an independent test of the critical rotation hypothesis for B stars and contemporary stellar evolution models that include stellar rotation and pulsation.

Description: INVESTIGATION OF ION PICK UP PROCESSES IN THE E-RING AND AROUND ENCELADUS Recent Cassini observations have established that the icy moon Enceladus is actively venting and ejecting water molecules, indicating strongly that it is the origin of the torus atmosphere. The interaction between the corotating plasma and neutrals is a critical process with significant implications for the evolution of both. The interaction results in plasma deflection and generation of ULF waves around Enceladus and in the torus which can be used for estimating the production rate of neutrals at Enceladus and its time variability, as well as, ionization rates throughout the torus. The proposed work has the following two objectives : (1) Use a kinetic model of plasma interaction with Enceladus and comparisons to Cassini observations to determine mass loading rates and their implications for production rates of neutrals at this icy moon. (2) Use kinetic simulations and observed properties of ULF waves by Cassini to establish average neutral cloud erosion rate in the E-ring as a function of radial distance. With Enceladus as the primary source of the torus atmosphere, our first objective enables us to establish source properties during past and future Cassini flybys and discern its time variability from encounter to encounter. Objective 2 improves current estimates of the erosion rates of neutrals due to ionization and also leads to better estimates of the production rate and energy of fast neutrals which is of direct relevance to modeling of the torus atmosphere. To achieve these objectives, we will utilize the electromagnetic hybrid simulations in which ions are treated kinetically through particle-in-cell (PIC) methods while the electrons form a charge neutralizing, fluid. Hybrid simulations have been used in the past to investigate the interaction between flowing plasmas and neutral gasses such as solar wind interaction with comets and more recently interactions in the 10 torus and plasma interactions with Titan. They are an ideal tool for pursuing the two main objectives of this proposal. The objectives of this study are in alignment with NASAs strategic goals 3.2 and 3.3, namely to understand the fundamental physical processes of the space and planetary environments and learning about the origin and evolution of planets and smaller bodies. The Cassini spacecraft is opening a new chapter in the history and our understanding of the E-ring and the role of venting by the icy moon Enceladus as the major source of neutral gasses in the torus atmosphere. The proposed work allows us to make better estimates of the gas production rates at Enceladus and the ionization and erosion rates of neutrals in the E-ring. This enhances the scientific return of the Cassini data and its implications for the complex processes involved in the E-ring and has general applicability to any planetary system where outgassing of the neutrals by a moon and interaction with the magnetospheric plasma is present such as the Io torus at Jupiter.

Description: THE COSMIC INFRARED BACKGROUND EXPERIMENT This is a Co-I proposal; PI proposal by Dr. James Bock. Light from the first generation of stars, formed from primordial gas in the early universe, has so far eluded direct detection. However, these first stars will produce characteristic signatures in the extragalactic background at near-infrared wavelengths. These distinctive features, in particular the redshifted Ly-cutoff spectral feature, and a characteristic fluctuation power spectrum, may be detectable with a specialized instrument. Recent observations of the absolute intensity and spatial fluctuations in the near-infrared background indicate a component to the background that cannot be explained by the redshift-integrated emission from known galaxy populations. This component could be due to luminous first-light high-mass stars or mini-quasars forming at high redshift (z - 10-20). However these background measurements are prone to systematic errors and first need confirmation. We propose the Cosmic Infrared Background ExpeRiment (CIBER) to search for signatures of first-light galaxy formation in the near-infrared background. The instrument consists of two wide-field cameras, a low-resolution absolute spectrometer, and a narrow-band spectrometer. The wide-field cameras will search for spatial fluctuations in the background on medium angular scales where the first-light galaxy spatial power spectrum peaks, but which has been poorly covered by previous experiments. The cameras have the necessary combination of sensitivity, wide field of view with sufficient spatial resolution, and multiple bands to make a definitive measurement. CIBER will conclusively determine if the fluctuations reported by Spitzer arise from first-light galaxies. The cameras observe in a single wide field of view, eliminating systematic errors associated with mosaicing. Two bands are chosen to maximize the first-light signal contrast, at 1.6 um near the expected spectral maximum, and at 0.8 urn, as a null test shorter than the redshifted Ly cutoff. We will jointly observe regions of the sky studied by Spitzer and ASTRO-F in order to accurately remove the contribution of local (z = 1-3) galaxies to the observed background fluctuations, and to cross correlate these independent data sets at 5 different wavelengths. The low-resolution spectrometer will search for the redshifted Lyman cutoff feature in the unexplored 0.7 - 1.8 um spectral region. The narrow-band spectrometer will trace zodiacal light using the intensity of a solar Fraunhofer line, providing an independent measurement of the zodiacal emission and a new systematic check of DIRBE zodiacal dust models. Description: SNAP-L, A DEDICATED SPACE EXPERIMENT TO PROBE DARK ENERGY The key challenge for JDEM is to determine the nature of the dark energy that is driving the accelerating expansion of the Universe. The SuperNova / Acceleration Probe - Lensing (SNAP-L) employs two independent techniques, a probe of expansion using Type la supernovae (SNe), and a growth of structure probe through gravitational weak lensing (WL). SNe and WL are the methods of choice: each technique is a robust, well-understood probe of dark energy. SNe are presently the "most powerful and best proven technique" and WL's probe of the growth of structure is, "if the systematic errors are at or below the level proposed the most powerful component in a multi-technique program." Moreover, a space mission eliminates limitations on both techniques that are inherent in ground-based studies, opening up a qualitatively new approach to understanding dark energy. SNe and WL probe different aspects of the effects of dark energy on the evolution of the Universe, including testing the distinction between a new component and modification of Einstein gravity. "Combinations of the principal techniques have substantially more statistical power, much more ability to discriminate among dark energy models, and more robustness to systematic errors than any single technique." SNAP-L will carry out two imaging surveys: 1) a deep survey of 7.5 deg2 to follow over 2000 matched Type la SNe out to a redshift of 1.7, and 2) a wide survey of 1000 deg2 for WL mapping. The SNe will be observed with unprecedented detail and systematic control, resulting in a well-sampled Hubble diagram into the epoch of deceleration. The WL survey benefits from a stable, high resolution point spread function and absence of atmospheric distortions. Combined, SNAP-L will determine the dark energy density to 0.004, its equation of state to 1.4%, and the time variation to 0.07. The SNAP-L satellite will be launched into an L2 orbit by an EELV rocket. The SNAP-L 600 million pixel camera is sensitive to light from 400 to 1700 nm in nine filter bands. An integral-field unit spectrograph provides follow-up at maximum light to identify Type la SNe and provide precise redshifts. Our team has just completed three years of R&D reducing risk by enhancing readiness of all mission enabling technologies. Detector performance improvements resulting from this program enable the proposed science requirements to be met within a $600M cost cap with margin. The primary objectives of this proposal are to refine the mission design through trade studies and to strengthen our project management. The project will be thoroughly studied utilizing NASA centers and aerospace vendors, where funding is essential to increase the participation of experts in space mission construction and project management. The result of these activities will be a low-risk approach to implement the project, ready for independent assessment. Dark Energy Task Force report to the AAAC, Feb 14,2006

Description: The origin of gas and ice giant planets is a highly active area of research with several competing scenarios for the accumulation and orbital evolution of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Each of the models requires different initial states ofthe protoplanetary disk and characteristic formation and evolution timescales for the planets. However, a common theme among them is the gross alteration of the total amount (e.g. loss of >75% ofthe initial condensed material) and spatial distribution of the solar system's mass (e.g, planetary migration, grinding down the Kuiper Belt). Indeed, several of these models suggest that the migration of the giant planets may have triggered the so-called Late Heavy Bombardment of the inner planets, long after their formation. The giant planets are the dominant perturbers in the solar system. The characteristic frequencies of their dynamical coupling and perturbation on the rest of the system are a strong function of the spacing between planet and the mass distribution of the solar system in general. Thus planet migration or any redistribution ofthe solar system's mass will tune these characteristic frequencies, resulting in the sweeping resonant perturbations from the giant planets through the solar system. We propose to study the sweeping secular resonances associated with the formation and evolution of the giant planets. We will model the evolution and migration of the giant planets under several different scenarios using analytic methods and numerical integrations and characterize the resonance sweeping that occurs. The results of this investigation may identify new dynamical signatures or additional constraints on the orbital history of the giant planets - perhaps offering tests to distinguish between models oftheir evolution. The results also have implications for those populations strongly affected by their evolution (e.g, the terrestrial planets, asteroids, KBOs, and planetary satellites).

Description: This renewal proposal will employ computational quantum chemistry calculations to predict electronic excitations in PAH ions and clusters, with the goal of making quantitative connections to laboratory measurements, and qualitative contributions to the interpretation of interstellar spectral features ranging from the infrared to the visible. These studies are aimed at aiding the interpretation of astronomical observations from various NASA missions, including present missions, Hubble Space Telescope and Spitzer, and future missions, Herschel, SOFIA, and JWST. Computational quantum chemistry calculations are capable of yielding results for electronic exitation of sufficient accuracy that the spectroscopic implications of new modes of binding can be explored in advance of laboratory measurements. This proposal follows some of the scientific opportunities that arise as a consequence of this situation. The area of particular interest to us is the mechanism by which large PAH molecules and ions condense to begin the formation of carbonaceous grains. Dimer complexes between positive ions and neutral closed shell or radical PAH's can form as a result of long-range electrostatic steering and appear to yield binding energies on the order of 0.3 eV or more. They are therefore a possible precursor to grains. Their spectroscopic properties are largely unknown at present, but it appears likely that they will exhibit intense transitions in the red or even well into the infrared. Because of their supramolecular nature, their electronic spectroscopy can be dramatically different from either of their constituents, which has unexplored interstellar implications. This first goal of this project is predicting the binding energy and electronic transitions for realistic complexes between medium to large PAH neutrals and ions to explore this fascinating issue in detail. The second goal of the project is to dovetail these investigations with an active collaboration with the NASA Ames laboratory astrophysics groups to contribute to the interpretation of electronic and infrared spectral features seen in their experiments. In this way, the outcomes of the project should be to enhance our understanding of PAN spectroscopy, and the growth modes that connect PAN molecules and ions to small particles, together with an active synergistic engagement with laboratory experimental groups that can point the way towards detailed correlations with observational data.

Description: LASER PEENING (LP) IS A RAPIDLY EXPANDING TECHNOLOGY THAT INTRODUCES A STATE OF RESIDUAL COMPRESSIVE STRESSES THAT CAN SIGNIFICANTLY INCREASE FATIGUE LIFE AND FATIGUE STRENGTH BY INHIBITING THE INITIATION AND PROPAGATION OF CRACKS. WHILE STILL IN THE DEVELOPMENT STAGE, ITS ABILITY TO DEVELOP DEEP, HIGH COMPRESSIVE STRESSES IN THE AREAS TREATED HAS BEEN DEMONSTRATED ON A NUMBER OF METALS AND ALLOYS. THE PROCESS UTILIZES HIGH ENERGY LASER PULSES FIRED AT THE SURFACE OF A METAL COATED WITH AN ABLATIVE FILM, AND COVERED WITH A TRANSPARENT LAYER (USUALLY WATER). BECAUSE VAPORIZATION RATHER THAN MELTING OF THE ALUMINUM SURFACE IS DESIRED, THE REQUIRED LASER POWER DENSITIES INCIDENT ON THE SHOCKED SURFACE TYPICALLY EXCEED 1082 W/CM AND LASER ENERGY DEPOSITION TIMES ARE LESS THAN 1 SEC.  AS THE LASER BEAM PASSES THROUGH THE TRANSPARENT LAYER AND HITS THE SURFACE OF THE MATERIAL, A THIN LAYER OF THE ABLATIVE LAYER IS VAPORIZED. THE VAPOR CONTINUES TO ABSORB THE REMAINING LASER ENERGY AND IS HEATED AND IONIZED INTO PLASMA. THE RAPIDLY EXPANDING PLASMA IS TRAPPED BETWEEN THE SAMPLE AND THE TRANSPARENT LAYER, CREATING A HIGH SURFACE PRESSURE, WHICH PROPAGATES INTO THE MATERIAL AS A SHOCK WAVE. WHEN THE PEAK PRESSURE OF THE SHOCK WAVE IS GREATER THAN THE DYNAMIC YIELD STRENGTH OF THE MATERIAL, IT PRODUCES PLASTIC DEFORMATION IN THE METAL. THE ACTUAL DEPTHS OF THE LP INDUCED STRESSES WILL VARY DEPENDING ON THE TYPE OF MATERIAL, THE LASER PEENING PROCESSING CONDITIONS CHOSEN, AND THE MATERIAL PROPERTIES. COMPRESSIVE STRESSES PRODUCED BY LASER PEENING CAN ALSO BE GENERATED DEEPER BELOW THE SURFACE BY USING SUCCESSIVE SHOCKS. PREVIOUS RESEARCH HAS SHOWN THAT THE RESIDUAL STRESS RESULTING FROM LASER PEENING CAN BE SIGNIFICANTLY HIGHER AND DEEPER THAN SHOT PEENING.  THE USE OF THE TRANSPARENT LAYERS SUCH AS WATER HAS BEEN FOUND TO INCREASE THE SHOCK WAVE PROPAGATING INTO THE METAL, AND THEREFORE THE RESIDUAL STRESS INCREASES. IF NO TRANSPARENT LAYER IS USED, THE PLASMA INDUCED BY THE LASER PEENING TENDS TO EXPAND AWAY FROM THE SURFACE OF THE SPECIMEN. THE PROCESS PROVIDES A SMOOTH SURFACE, GOOD PROCESS CONTROL, AND GOOD REPEATABILITY.

Description: Tropical! convection drives the climate and can he seen clearly from space yet our capacity to use this information in forecast and monitoring systems is nascent. Thus the full scientific and social benefits available from the TRMMIGPM missions remain to be unlocked. While persistence in SSTs is well studied, less analysis has been applied to the satellite rainfall record. Recent warming and changes in tropical precipitation patterns have been substantial and these variations are linked to life-sustaining terrestrial rainfall in the tropics and sub-tropics, where projections call for 2-7 billion water insecure people by 2050. Our efforts will create an integrated dataset, improve hydrologic monitoring and rainfall predictions, and increase our understanding of the links between small scale precipitation events and large scale climate variations and change. Our research will begin by developing a semi-integrated 'hydrologic monitoring system' combining 0.25O terrestrial precipitation and actual evapotranspiration fields with SSMII-derived oceanic evaporation and moisture transports. Preliminary evaluation suggests that tropical oceanic precipitation is associated with fairly predictable moisture transport anomalies at coarse reanalysis scales. We will use TRRM-TMI-SSMII data to explore and validate these relationships at higher resolutions, and discuss scaling between daily-0.25O and the seasonal-2.5O scales. We will examine persistence, linking oceanic precipitation extremes to changes in onshore moisture transports and terrestrial precipitation in Africa, Asia and Central/South America. This will improve our current NASA CAN 1-to-3 month forecast system. Our work will conclude by using model output statistics (MOS) and IPCC simulations to estimate terrestrial rainfall and AET for 2030-2050. Implications for foodlwater security will be evaluated and presented to USAID. These objectives are consistent with many key topics in the NRA. We address most of the Precipitation Variability components. We examine climatically significant variations in oceanic precipitation and link their space-time evolution to terrestrial impacts. The prognostic contribution of satellite observations will be evaluated statistically, guiding future assimilation and reanalysis efforts. We will quantify GPM in ways that elucidate variations in oceanic and terrestrial rainfall and identify new means of evaluating accelerations and changes to the hydrologic cycle. Our efforts apply to the Retrieval Algorithm topic by demonstrating new algorithms for reducing precipitation bias in areas with complex terrain. We contribute to the Applications to Hydrology component by developing a modeling methodology for large-basin ET and evaluating the agro-hydrological impacts of simulated 2xC02 satellite precipitation. The dataltechnology produced will contribute to the Education topic by enhancing the timely development and delivery of both global and regional rainfall products.

Description: The aim of the proposed work is to provide a definitive study of the contribution of interstellar astrochemical processes to the isotopic fractionation of 15N, 13C, 17,180, and D measured in carbonaceous meteoritic material, interplanetary dust particles (IDPs), and cometary dust samples returned by the Stardust mission. We propose a comprehensive theoretical treatment of the fractionation processes for each of these elements. This will allow us to quantify the maximum degree of stable-isotope enhancement or depletion present in the interstellar progenitors which were subsequently processed into cometary and asteroidal material. We will investigate low-temperature ion-molecule chemistry as a source of fractionation for each of these elements, and will also model the fractionation of C and 0 isotopes due to CO self-shielding in the interstellar medium. We will investigate the expected correlations between the fractionation of different elements in abundant interstellar molecules which are likely to play an important role in the subsequent chemistry of the young solar nebula. We will focus on specific molecules such as CO, HCN, NH3, and small hydrocarbons, which are likely to be the progenitors of carbonyl, nitrile, amide, and other organic functional groups. We will look at the correlations of DM with 15Nl14N in molecules formed in gas-grain processes within prestellar depletion cores, and compare these with the large, localized 15N and D enhancements found in some meteorites and IDPs. Correlations in fractionation between 13C and 17,180, as well as with D, will also be computed, both as a function of CO self-shielding and of gas temperature. We plan to undertake a detailed study of the D and 13C fractionation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons due to interstellar processes. This will allow us to identify differences in fractionation patterns that may be expected to occur between aromatic and aliphatic material. These studies will be the first to delineate the available parameter space for astronomical contributions to isotopic fractionation in primitive Solar System materials. In this way, we should also be able to exclude various astrochemical contributions and hence identify where nebular chemistry may provide the best explanation. We will seek to provide explanations of the meteoritic and IDP data and identify possible correlations that can be sought in subsequent laboratory analyses. The proposed work is therefore complementary to much previous work where the formation environments of meteoritic material have been elucidated through nucleosynthetic signatures. When completed, and the results disseminated, the results from this project should aid interpretation of the expected scientific returns from Stardust. The proposed research meshes with NASA's strategic goals, and those of the Origins of Solar Systems program Program, connected to understanding the origin of the Solar System and the evolution of its complement of planets and small solid bodies.

Description: The primary purpose of this program is to enhance our knowledge of the heliosphere through the study of the backscattered Lyman Alpha glow. The key, central objectives of this project are to study the time-dependence of the heliosphere, to estimate the very local interstellar medium (VLISM) neutral hydrogen density and to investigate the effect of the squeezing of the heliospheric interface by the interstellar magnetic field on the observed Lyman Alpha glow which would require the use of 3-d modeling of the heliosphere. The objectives will be attained using time-dependent heliospheric models with and without interstellar magnetic fields to calculate backscattered Lyman Alpha glow and compare with the post-1998 Voyager 1 Lyman Alpha data and also with the Lyman Alpha glow observed by Voyager 2 and Pioneer 10 ultraviolet detectors at different heliocentric distances and times. This project is made possible by the existence of the interplanetary Lyman Alpha background data collected by deep space spacecraft Pioneer 10/11 (P10/11) and Voyager 1/2 (V1/2) during their more than 25 years of exploration of the heliosphere. The proposed work will greatly improve our understanding of the time-dependence of the heliosphere and check the eliability of a current state of the art heliosphere models. Recently proposed time-dependent heliospheric models are the only detailed pictures of the sun-galaxy interaction available at present. The proposed work will test the accuracy of our current knowledge of the sun-galaxy interaction and is thus highly relevant to Nasa's Sun-Earth connection quest about the Sun-Galaxy interaction. The proposed work neatly fits in with a major quest posed by the Sun-Earth onnection Roadmap," How do the Sun and Galaxy interact?". The relevance of our proposed work is clearly demonstrated from the following quote from the Roadmap, "of special interest is the nature of the interface between the solar wind and the interstellar medium and the physical processes that occur there". This clearly shows that the proposed research is directly related to the NASA Sun-Earth connection Roadmap, Pioneer and Voyager interstellar programs through optimization of the future "Interstellar Probe" mission and its instrumentation. Our models and results can also be applied to the interpretation of Cassini measurements of Lyman Alpha background made during its cruise to Saturn.

Description: Lunar Crater Observation Sensing Satelite. (LCROSS) NASAs Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), scheduled for launch in October 2008, will chart the lunar landscape, not only to identify obstacles and safe-to-land spots, but also sensor sweep the terrain and gauge it for usable resources.  NASA plans to launch the LRO rocket with a secondary payload, called the LCROSS, whose mission will be to determine the presence of water ice at the Moons South Pole.  After the LRO is deployed in orbit around the Moon, the LCROSS satellite will steer the launch vehicles spent Earth departure upper stage (CENTAUR) into a permanently-shadowed crater at a lunar pole.  The impact will create a large plume of lunar ejecta that will provide a long window of observation and will excavate a large area to deeper depths than would be possible using only a robotic lunar lander. Description: We propose to continue an effort which was begun in AO-1 and continued successfully in AO-2, to perform correlative observations of bursts with the interplanetary network (IPN). The rationale is the following. 1) The BAT detects about as many bursts outside its coded field of view (which it cannot localize), as inside it. 2) Swift and other spacecraft may wish to do ToO observations of these and other IPN events if they have special properties. 3) For bursts in the BAT FOV which are also observed by other spacecraft not in low-Earth orbit (such as Konus-Wind), joint spectral analysis, which extends the energy range to 10 MeV, requires that the delays between the spacecraft be accurately known. 4) It is important to maintain as many near-Earth spacecraft in the network as possible. 5) The -200 bursts/year which are detected by the IPN and which are not localized by the BAT, serve a wide community of astronomers. The processes which govern the evolution of stars, the ways in which matter and energy are converted, and elements are formed, are all closely related to the processes at work in gamma-ray bursts. Their study is directly relevant to NASA's 2006 Strategic Plan, in particular a) "To pioneer the future in space exploration, scientific discovery,...", b) to Strategic Goal 3, "Develop a balanced overall program of science,...", and c) to the Vision for Space Exploration, "...the study of the origins, structure, evolution, and destiny of the universe".

Description: We propose to investigate the properties of Galactic F and G dwarf stars in the GALEX imaging passbands. Our objective is to determine the dependence of the GALEX UV colors and magnitudes of these stars upon basic parameters such as effective temperature, metallicity, age, and chromospheric activity. This is largely an archival program to be based on a dataset obtained by cross-correlating GALEX all-sky-survey sources with a number of large F and G dwarf catalogs. From the field star data the dependence of GALEX VV colors and absolute magnitudes, upon effective temperature (via optical colors), metallicity, Li-based ages, and various chromospheric and coronal activity indicators will be derived. In order to test more precisely for sensitivity of UV colors to stellar age, we propose GALEX imaging of the open cluster NGC 2281 (age 0.4 Gyr) for comparison with archival images of M67 (age 4 Gyr). The F and G dwarfs in these two clusters have ages that differ by a factor of 10, thus providing a wide baseline to test for any age dependence of most particularly the FUV fluxes.

Description: GRB AFTERGLOWS AS PROBES We propose to continue our on-going effort to carry out target-of-opportunity (ToO) observations of GRBs discovered with Swift. The primary objective of the proposed program is to apply the GRB afterglows as a background source of studying physical properties of intervening gas both in the local RB progenitor environment and in the foreground galaxies along the line of sight. To read the goal, we have been conducting rapid (<6 hours) spectroscopic follow-up of well-localized afterglows through various ToO programs of different ground-based facilities, including the Keck telescopes, Lick Observatory, Magellan Telescopes, and the Apache Point telescope. Over the past two years, we have demonstrated that in addition to establishing the burst redshift, these observations reveal physical properties of the interstellar medium surrounding the GRB progenitors, including: the HI column density, the metallicity and chemical abundances, the molecular fraction, and dust-to-gas ratio. While some of these properties are now known to be common in GRB host environment (such as the presence of large HI column density, excited Fe^+, and blue-shifted, high velocity absorbing components due to C^3+), they are rarely seen in other extragalactic sources. A detailed analysis of these features therefore offer important insights for understanding the nature of the burst progenitors. Furthermore, afterglow spectra offer a unique opportunity to study the stellar counterpart of strong absorbers (e.g., damped Lya systems and MgII absorbers) as z_abs<z_grb. We target these newly discovered absorbers toward the GRB sightlines for exhaustive imaging follow-up after the afterglow disappears (i.e., after a few months). Our GRAASP collaboration has demonstrated the resources , expertise, and diligence required to pursue this observing program and here we propose to continue this effort during Cycle 3 of the Swift mission.

Description: Accurate and complete knowledge of the spectral emission from the dominant heavy ions found in the solar corona, transition region, and photosphere is crucial for describing the solar EUV emission. Our understanding of this emission is, however, neither accurate nor complete. Work on understanding the EUV spectra from cool stars, such as alpha Cen, has shown that the spectral models used to describe radiation in the 20 -180 A region are very incomplete. Laboratory measurements of such ions as Fe IX, X, XI, and XII have shown that the emission below 140 A may be underestimated by existing spectral models by as much as factors of three to four. Similarly, more than half of the lines recorded in spectra available from the Sun has not yet been identified! Not knowing which elements and which ionization stages are responsible for the solar emission in this region limits our ability to understand and model the solar energy flow in this region of the electromagnetic spectrum and its effect on Earth and the space environmental conditions. By contrast, nearly complete sets of laboratory data of Ne, Mg, Al, Si, S, Ar, Ca, Fe, and Ni are now available that we can use to establish line lists and line intensities of the relevant ions found in the Sun. We are proposing to use these data in conjunction with new calculational tools to establish complete descriptions of the solar EUV radiation in the 20 - 200 A region and thus to close the glaring gap in our understanding of the electromagnetic spectrum emitted by the Sun. Very importantly, we will make a careful estimate of the multitude of weak, blended transitions that have recently been shown to form a quasi-continuum and have generally been ignored in the literature. We will apply our spectral emission data to the analysis of existing solar EUV spectra, such as those obtained from the Atmosphere Explorer-E satellite and Aerobee Rocket observations. The aim is to identify the wealth of features and lines that have been observed in this wavelength band but have never been assigned to specific ions or transitions and to assess their role in the overall energy flux in the 20 to 200 A wavelength band.

Description: A STUDY OF THE MOON'S PLASMA ENVIRONMENT  With the renewed interest in returning to the Moon, it is important to understand the detailed space plasma environment around the Moon and mini-magnetospheres near the lunar surface. To achieve this goal we propose to carry out a detailed three dimensional global kinetic simulation study of the solar wind interaction with the Moon and with lunar mini-magnetospheres formed near the surface due to crustal magnetic fields. The crustal magnetic anomolies will be modeled using Lunar Explorer data for inclusion into the simulations. We will examine the structure and dynamics of the lunar wake-tail formed by the absorption of solar wind plasma when it contacts the lunar surface, as well as the properties of the mini-magnetospheres, which include an examination of the bow shock and magnetopause locations, and particle acceleration and energization over a wide range of solar wind conditions. Surface electric fields formed by the solar wind-lunar interaction will also be examined. Simulation results will be compared with Lunar Prospector data near the lunar surface (~ 100 km altitude) and with Wind satellite data in the wake-tail region several lunar radii away from the Moon.

Description: The ambient structure of the solar corona and inner heliosphere plays a crucial role in the goals of Sun-Earth Connection science, yet both remote solar and in situ observations severely under-sample this region.  Three-dimensional, time-dependent models have recently advanced sufficiently to provide a meaningful context for interpreting and connecting these disparate observations.  We propose a strategic capability to combine the most sophisticated of these models with the latest  techniques for deriving time-dependent photospheric magnetic field data and deliver a GUI-driven model that will be of broad appeal to the solar and heliospheric scientific community.  This model will encapsulate both our current technical capabilities as well as number of important improvements that will be developed and incorporated during the course of this work. The observed photospheric magnetic field acts as the primary boundary condition to the models and we have found that the solar wind solution is strongly dependent on it.  Thus our proposed work includes detailed studies to improve the quality of this input.  Moreover, we will drive the model with time-dependent output from flux transport codes, allowing us to produce a real-time model of the solar wind, which would be delivered to the CCMC.  Ultimately, it might replace the current WSA model at the National Weather Service's Space Environment Center.  Global MHD models are, by necessity, complex.  In the past, typically only code developers were able to successfully run their code.  We propose to abstract away the unnecessary complexities by providing a uniform GUI interface with which to initiate runs.  We will also provide a set of GUI tools for post-processing, analysis, and visualization.  Much of this work has already been done as part of previous and ongoing programs.  Our team includes experts in the range of disciplines required to successfully carry out this project, including solar magnetometry, surface flux evolution modeling, coronal and solar wind modeling, and computational physics.

Description: CONSTRAINING THE REGOLITH HISTORY OF LUNAR METEORITES USING SM AND GD ISOTOPIC SHIFTS IN COMBINATION WITH COSMOGENIC NUCLIDE CONCENTRATIONS We propose to investigate the regolith history of lunar meteorites by measuring the isotopic composition of Sm and Gd. Due to extremely large cross sections for neutron capture on 149Sm and 157Gd, the 150Sm/149Sm and 158Gd/157Gd ratios are the most sensitive indicators of cosmic-ray exposure under high shielding, such as near the surface of the Moon. In conjunction with available cosmogenic radionuclide and noble gas data, the measured isotopic shifts in Sm and Gd will provide more detailed information on the duration and average depth of cosmic-ray irradiation of meteorites on the Moon. This type of information will give more insight in regolith mixing and other impact related surface processes on the Moon over the past 100 Myr -I Gyr, a period in which the lunar impact rate is believed to have increased by a factor of 2-4. Our proposed work for the next three years includes: (I) establishing the chemical separation and purification procedures of Sm and Gd from meteorite samples, (2) measuring the isotopic compositions of Sm and Gd in selected lunar meteorites using TIMS, (3) improving model calculations for the neutron capture production rates of 150Sm and 158Gd on the lunar surface, and (4) starting preliminary Sm and Gd isotopic measurements in chondrites with complex exposure histories. The described research on the regolith history of lunar meteorites on the surface of the Moon is directly relevant to some of the main goals of, NASA's Cosmochemistry program, which include increasing the understanding of the processes by which the planets and small bodies have evolved to their present states. The proposed research on surface processes on the Moon is also directly relevant to future robotic and manned missions to the Moon as well as for future human exploration, which are part of NASA's Strategic Objectives for 2005 and beyond.

Description: STRUCTURE OF THE MAGNETOTAIL DURING STEADY MAGNETOSPHERIC CONVECTION EVENTS Until recently it was thought that substorms are the only form of geomagnetic activity. However, recent work indicates that there are three major forms: substorm sequences, steady magnetospheric convection (SMC), and sawtooth injection events. SMC appear to be a consequence of balanced magnetic reconnection at day and night side x-lines since the configuration of the magnetotail is constant. It has been suggested that SMC is "impossible" theoretically because it leads to a pressure inconsistency. Flux tubes convecting up the tail build up pressure to the point they can not return to the dayside unless emptied by a substorm. However other work show SMC is possible for a special configuration of the tail magnetic field and plasma sheet involving a minimum in the vertical component of the magnetic field in the neutral sheet located 10-15 Re behind the Earth at midnight. We propose to use data from the ISEE (1978-1988) and Geotail (1992-2005) intervals to determine the statistical configuration of the tail field and plasma and the properties of the solar wind during SMC events. Geomagnetic activity will be classified using multiple types of ground and synchronous satellite data. This work should provide a conclusive demonstration of the validity of previous conjectures about the solar wind causes of SMC and the configuration of the magneto tail that are partly based on theory and partly on case histories of a few SMC events. It should reveal how SMC begin and end and when they transition to sawtooth events. The techniques for classification and the statistical results will be of particular interest to the upcoming NASA Themis mission whose expectations for resolving the substorm controversy are based on the assumption that all activity consists of substorms and that a sufficient number of "perfect substorms" can be observed in the lifetime of the mission.

Description: SIMULATIONS OF THE PHYSICS OF THE HARANG REVERSAL AND ITS RELATIONSHIP TO SUBSTORMS WITH THE RICE CONVECTION MODEL THE IMPORTANCE OF THE HARANG ELECTRIC FIELD REVERSAL TO THE LARGE-SCALE DYNAMICS OF THE MAGNETOSPHERE-IONOSPHERE AND TO SUBSTROMS HAS RECENTLY BEEN CLEARLY DEMONSTRATED OBSERVATIONALLY. THE RCM CAN APPROPRIATELY TAKE INTO ACCOUNT THE PHYSICS OF THE PLASMA DRIFT TRANSPORT WITHIN THE PLASMA SHEET AND IT SOLVES FOR THE IONOSPHERIC ELECTRIC POTENTIAL SELF-CONSISTENTLY WITH THE PLASMA SHEET DYNAMICS THROUGH THEIR COUPLING BY FIELD-ALIGNED CURRENTS. A MAGNETIC FIELD SOLVER WILL PROVIDE MAGNETIC FIELDS THAT ARE IN FORCE BALANCE WITH THE RCM PLASMA PRESSURES. WE CAN IDENTIFY FROM THE SIMULATION RESULTS THE HARANG REVERSAL REGION AND OBTAIN ASSOCIATED MEASURABLE PHYSICAL QUANTITIES, SUCH AS IONOSPHERIC FLOW SHEAR, GROUND MAGNETIC FIELD PERTURBATIONS, AND PLASMA SHEET BULK PARAMETERS, WHICH ALLOWS FOR COMPARISONS WITH OBSERVATIONS. WE WILL DETERMINE IF THE CHANGES WILL LEAD THE PLASMA SHEET AND IONOSPHERE TOWARDS INCREASINGLY RAPID CHANGES WITHIN A FEW MIN AND IF THE EVOLUTION OF THE HARANG REVERSAL IS INVOLVED IN THE TRANSITION TOWARDS INSTABILITY AS HAS BEEN RECENTLY PREDICTED BY A THEORY. Description: We propose to investigate the properties, dynamics and evolution of Saturn's faint, dusty rings, combining Cassini ISS, VIMS and CIRS data. Such rings reveal a variety of physical processes that are masked within denser rings: non-gravitational forces deflect dust grains from their Keplerian paths and can sweep grains out ofthe system, requiring embedded (and often nnseen) "parent" bodies to replenish the visible dust. Faint rings are prevalent throughout the Solar System and also serve as analogs for stages in the formation of planetary systems. Cassini data provide a unique new opportunity to understand this particular class of dynamical system. Because grains are small in size and number, modest events can trigger large visible changes. Hence, these are the most time-variable rings known. Comparison with Voyager data will reveal processes at work for the last 25 years, and Cassini data alone will show us changes in real time. Saturn has the Solar System's most diverse set offaint rings. The innermost D ring contains several narrow ringlets surrounded by broader belts. The F ring, just outside the main rings, is dominated by clumps and "braids," some of which come and go on time scales of weeks. Its surrounding strands form a spiral, suggesting that they were generated by a large impact several years ago. The E ring is outermost and broadest; it peaks at the orbit of Enceladus, but encompasses the entire region from Mimas to Dione, implying strong non-gravitational perturbations. The G ring orbits at an isolated location; it was recently found to contain a bright arc. Gaps in the main rings also contain dusty ringlets. the Encke Gap contains three, one of which shares its orbit with the moon Pan. Some clumps in this ring hve changed noticeably during the tour so far. Extracting faint ring signals from the data requires special techniques to cope with instrumental artifacts such as stray light and low signal. Detailed photometric and spectroscopic modeling will quantify the grains' properties, including composition and size distribution. This information constrains the production, transport and loss processes. For example, collisional ejecta should exhibit a broad size distribution, but Saturn's magnetic field and solar radiation pressure can selectively disperse certain grain sizes. We will also monitor longitudinal features to understand their origin and evolution. Finally, we will compare our results to existing dynamical models and will develop new models as needed. This project will enhance Cassini science by combining data from multiple instruments in a synergistic way. Faint rings can pose a significant hazard to exploration, so our results will also be useful for planning future planetary missions. FORM NRESS-300 Version 2.0 Apr-06-05

Description: APOLLO (the Apache Point Lunar Laser-ranging Operation) represents a dramatic improvement in lunar ranging capabilities, collecting more photons from the lunar reflectors in several minutes than competing stations receive in a year. APOLLO is capable of one-millimeter range precision, so that the suite of gravitational physics probed by lunar ranging (equivalence principle, time-rate-of-change of the gravitational constant, gravitomagnetism, departures from the inverse square law) may all be improved by a factor of ten or more. Lunar ranging is currently our very best probe of all these phenomena, so that APOLLO offers to enhance vastly our detailed understanding of the gravitational interaction. As physics strains under the discovery of dark energy and a nagging incompatibility between quantum mechanics and general relativity, testing gravity is a central part of the campaign to move forward in our understanding of fundamental physics. The APOLLO apparatus achieved first light in October 2005, and begins a science-quality campaign in April 2006. This proposal seeks support to carry out the bulk of this observational campaign and to extract the scientific results from the dataset. This will include software efforts for both observation and data analysis, in addition to hardware efforts for system maintenance and upgrades. Lunar laser ranging is the only active space-based test of general relativity being performed at present. The BEFS solicitation stresses that the only experimental work being supported in this year's announcement pertains to space-based tests of general relativity and fundamental physics, or to LISA technology development. This proposal clearly satisfies the former condition, and is consistent with the overall theme of the Beyond Einstein program: pushing the limits of our understanding of gravity in new and exciting ways. The APOLLO program has the added benefit of being very accessible. The fact that it utilizes reflectors left on the moon by the Apollo astronauts is highly appealing to the public. We intend to make the most of this alignment with public interest to achieve effective outreach.

Description: renewal of NASA grant number NNG04GA28G) This proposal describes work that is part of a larger NASA-sponsored effort to understand the origin of life on Earth, which will guide the search for life elsewhere in the solar system. It pertains to a form of RNA-based life that likely existed during Earth's early history. RNA-based life can be simulated, and perhaps even constructed, in the laboratory through the in vitro Darwinian evolution of RNA enzymes. The principal aim of the proposed research is to employ in vitro evolution to develop RNA-based catalytic functions that are relevant to the establishment and maintenance of RNA-based life. In addition, the operation of RNA evolution itself will be examined to gain insight into the adaptability of RNA and the behavior of Darwinian systems at the molecular level. The primary research objective research is to develop an RNA enzyme with RNA replicase activity. Two models for RNA-catalyzed RNA replication will be investigated, one involving the template-directed polymerization of activated nucleotides, and the other involving the joining of oligonucleotides by modular assembly. The secondary research objective is to develop RNA enzymes that catalyze critical steps of an RNA-based metabolism, focusing on the RNA-catalyzed condensation of glycoaldehyde and glyceraldehyde to form ribose. Finally, the proposed research will address the problem of cellular compartmentalization by examining two non-traditional approaches involving either the non-covalent association of RNA with rigid nucleic acid scaffolds, or the sequestration of evolving RNAs within small, spatially separated reaction volumes.

Description: In December 2001, the Kepler Mission became the 10th spaceprobe selected for flight by NASA's Discovery Program, and the first such mission set to achieve goals under NASA's Origins theme.  Kepler seeks to determine the prevalence of Earth-sized and larger planets orbiting solar-like stars in the solar neighborhood, and to characterize the stellar properties favoring the development of planetary systems. It achieves this goal through transit photometry by monitoring>100,000 mainsequence stars continuously and simultaneously for at least 4 years, to detect signatures of transiting planets in the flux time series of their host stars. The Kepler Mission successfully completed its Mission Critical Design Review and is entering the implementation phase. This proposal seeks to support the implementation and flight operations phases of the Kepler flight and ground segments through the characterization of the Kepler Photometer throughout the full lifecyde of the mission ending November 30, 2013. The work includes pre-flight activities: 1) monitoring and reviewing data obtained by Ball Aerospace Corporation in the test and characterization program for the Kepler photometer, 2) conducting trade studies involving simulation and analysis to enable the Kepler Project to make informed design and development decisions 3) developing a Kepler Instrument Design Handbook documenting photometer characteristics, performance and operations, as a reference document for use by the Science Office during flight operations 4) assisting the Science Operations Center with the implementation of key CSCIs capturing instrument characterization information for the purpose of calibrating/correcting Kepler Mission system data, and 5) developing a Kepler Instrument Calibration and Characterization Plan. Description: The overall goal is to understand the dynamics of giant planet atmospheres. Here we propose to expand on tasks that have led to six papers in the last few years. One specific goal is to measure the eddy momentum flux at multiple altitudes. We have measured significant differences in the zonal winds of Jupiter at two levels from UV and continuum filters (Li et al., 2006a). We have measured the eddy momentum flux in the continuum filters (Salyk et al., 2006), and we propose to repeat the measurement in the UV, which samples higher altitudes. Another goal is to use the latitude-altitude cross sections of temperature and zonal wind to define the ray paths of upward-propagating planetary waves and the surfaces where the waves are reflected or absorbed. We have started this effort for one latitude band (Li et al., 2006b). Waves are essential for understanding the velocity and shear of stratospheric jets. A third goal is to track the electrical storms on Saturn from 2004 through mid-2005. We want to see ifthe electrical activity comes from just one storm and monitor the life cycle of the storms. A fourth goal is to study the interaction of small-scale moist convection with large-scale flow. We have documented this interaction on Jupiter (Porco et al., 2003; Li et al., 2004), and we have modeled it in a quasi-geostrophic model (Li et al., 2006c). Further observational studies to define the parameters of the moist convection and extend to a 3D model are needed. The relevance to NASA's goals is that this research teaches us about processes that shape the solar system, in particular the atmospheres of the planets. It provides "ground truth" for observations about extra-solar giant planets. And it supports students and postdocs, who are the next generation of explorers.

Description: Forests of giant kelp (Macrocystis spp.), found on shallow subtidal temperate reefs throughout the world, are some of the most productive ecosystems in the world. Kelp forests have great economic value and are harvested for use in products ranging from pharmaceuticals to aquaculture feed. More importantly, giant kelp is an "ecosystem engineer" providing both food and habitat to a diverse array of biologically and commercially important species of algae, invertebrates, fish, and marine mammals while exporting large quantities of organic matter to adjacent littoral and continental shelf ecosystems. Economic analyses show revenues associated with California kelp forests of> $250 million per year. We propose to develop a predictive understanding of giant kelp forests in the nearshore waters of California using a combination of... * High-resolution remote sensing of kelp cover, biomass & its physiological state, * Metapopulation modeling of kelp patch dynamics, and * Bio-optical modeling of kelp productivity. The integration of these approaches will produce a unified assessment of kelp dynamics that can be determined using available satellite data. This proposed work takes advantage of the recent availability of high resolution, multi-spectral SPOT imagery to map kelp cover dynamics on spatial scales of 10 m at monthly time intervals (see www.spot.ucsb.edu).Using SPOT multispectral imagery, we will develop new measures of kelp canopy cover, biomass, productivity and canopy condition. These data will enable us to examine the role of disturbance and other environmental factors such as surface wave stress (using regional wave models), coastal currents (using HF radar remote sensing), sediment plumes (using MODIS & SeaWiFS ocean color imagery) and nutrient availability (using field and remote sensing proxies) on our high resolution observations of kelp canopy cover and biomass. Using these observations, metapopulation models of kelp patch dynamics as well as bio-optical models of optical kelp productivity can be implemented and coupled. Our goal is to use this bottom-up synthesis of the ecological processes driving kelp dynamics to develop a unified remote assessment of kelp dynamics for the nearshore waters off California. This work has a multitude of real-world applications including the ecological assessment of marine protected areas that have been recently designated around the Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary and other California marine protected areas including the emerging state-mandated network of marine reserves along the California coast. As such, we will collaborate with the NOAA Channel Islands National Marine Sanctuary (http://www.cinms.nos.noaa.gov/), the Santa Barbara Coastal Long Term Ecological Research project (http://sbc.lternet.edu/; NSF support), and the Coastal Data Information Project (http://cdip.ucsd.edu/; USGS & State of California support).
