Description: Comprehensive experimental investigations have been undertaken by the Eschenmoser group towards an understanding of Nature's choice of the structure type of the natural nucleic acids as the molecular basis of genetic function (Chemical Etiology of Nucleic Acid Structure). A central conclusion from these studies is the notion that Watson-Crick base-pairing is by no means unique to the ribofuranoid oligonucleotide system, but is rather widespread among potentially natural nucleic acid analogs with backbones that contain sugar units from ribofuranose. Another conclusion to be drawn from this work, one that is forcibly corroborated by the work of others in the field of medicinal antisense-oligonucleotide chemistry, is the notion of a still largely unexplored structural landscape of informational oligomer systems that may contain backbones, recognition elements and linker groups structurally quite different from those known so far. We deem this landscape to contain oligomer systems that have the generational simplicity of potentially primordial systems, primordial in the sense that, from a chemical point of view, they may have had a chance to self-assemble under the chemical and physical constraints of a prebiological geochemical environment. A structurally unconstrained experimental exploration of the landscape with focusing on such potentially primordial members would represent a continuation of the project pursued so far, yet would reach far beyond it, as the target criterion would no longer be the search for function among structural RNA alternatives of a generational complexity similar to that of RNA, but rather a search for generational simplicity among (functional) oligomers, a simplicity that justifies a given system to be deemed potentially primordial. We propose a systematic experimental study of families of such candidate systems, the structures of which are deduced by combining two conceptual strategies, first a "forward-synthetic analysis" starting from a range of elementary starting materials while obeying rather strictly defined structural constraints of prebiotic chemistry and, second, a qualitative conformational analysis that allows us, as experienced in previous studies, to predict a system's base-pairing capability with the resonable certainty. What encourages us in such an endeavour are the (unpublished) results of our (still) preliminary experimental studies of oligomers whose backbones are derived from ethylenediamine-, peptoid-, and peptide-based monomers and in which the family of the canonical nucleobases is being replaced by an alternative family of (equally primordial) heterocycles. We have found that oligomer sequences tagged with one of the members of the alternative nucleobase family are capable of cross-pairing with RNA and DNA in four different backbone series. This finding call for a comprehensive extension of these studies in a variety of directions.

Description: COMPOSITIONAL INTERPRETATION AND MAPPING OF ICY SATELLITE SURFACES Knowledge of the surface composition of icy satellites is necessary for the understanding of their formation and evolution. This information has direct bearing on models of surface and interior processes, geological and geomorphological interpretation, and planetary formation scenarios. We will investigate the surface compositions of the Saturnian and Jovian icy satellites using data returned by the Cassini Visible and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIMS) and Imaging Science Subsystem (ISS) instruments, coupled with laboratory measurements of candidate materials of interest. The objectives of this investigation will be to (1) Identify surface compounds on the icy satellites (2) Constrain the abundances and distributions of candidate surface compounds and (3) Interpret ramifications to planetary science of the occurrences (or non-occurrences) and distributions of such materials. We will primarily utilize data from the Cassini VIMS instrument but in some cases supplement with observations from ground-based telescopes or, in the case of the icy Galilean satellites, compare with Galileo data. We will apply cryogenic laboratory spectroscopy to the interpretation of spectral features observed in the Cassini VIMS measurements. This investigation will produce previously unavailable wavelength and temperature appropriate infrared reflectance spectra of candidate surface materials critical to the interpretation ofremote sensing observations of icy satellites. These reflectance spectra will be used to constrain material abundances on the icy using standard linear and intimate mixture modeling, as well as automated spectral classification methods including the USGS Tetracorder Expert System and commercially available remote sensing programs. Optical constantswill be determined through Kramers-Kronig analysis and used to derive improved quantitative abundance estimates based on nonlinear mixture modeling via a Hapke model. These results will be published, and all spectra will be made available through peer-reviewed journals with online digital supplements. We anticipate working closely with members of the Cassini VIMS Team to avoid duplication of efforts while ensuring the highest integrity and openness in our work. This investigation will enhance the scientific return of the Cassini mission and produce value-added interpretive compositional maps. We will leverage past experience and existing data from both Galileo and Cassini to improve understanding of the Galilean satellites Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. The spectral database produced by this investigation will be applicable to many Solar System objects and observations, including future results of the Cassini mission, the New Horizons mission to Pluto and the Kuiper Belt, a possible return to Saturn and Jupiter, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and other missions, as well as telescopic observations of icy objects in the outer solar system.

Description: SOLAR OSCILLATIONS INVESTIGATION - MICHELSON DOPPLER IMAGER SOHO APPROACH TO SOLAR MINIMUM NASA's long term goals require a better understanding of the Sun, solar variability on multiple scales, and the "space weather that impacts the terrestrial environment. From launch in December 1995, instruments on the SOHO spacecraft have studied the Sun over the complete 11-year duration of the Solar Cycle 23. Solar activity is predicted to reach minimum during 2007 with the transition to Solar Cycle 24 which is expected to peak in 2010 or 2011. The Solar Oscillations Investigation has a number of science goals that require MDI observations of the Sun over the rising phase of the Solar Cycle 24. The SOI-MDI program has the unique opportunity to compare observations during the minimum phase of two 11 year solar cycles using global helioseismology to measure the solar interior. This objective requires continuous observations to make accurate measurements of oscillation mode frequencies, from which the changing structure and rotation of the solar interior are determined. Other objectives require continuous observing sequences of days to months in length to study the changes near the solar surface, particularly those associated with active region and magnetic field emergence. These goals are addressed using the tools of local helioseismology which allow imaging of the motions in the interior of the star. Early progress convinced us that the developing techniques do indeed work and we will be able to watch the development of the next magnetic cycle from the inside. In addition to helioseismology observations, MDI provides observations essential for complementary views of solar processes. We have demonstrated the ability to follow the generation and evolution of magnetic fields on the granulation to global scale with a spatial and time resolution sufficient to, for the first time, follow the life-cycle of magnetic fields. MDI also provides measurements of relative brightness of active and quiet regions to enable the better understanding of the radiative flux balance. It also provides direct measurements of surface motions from meso-granulation through to global scales. These studies continued through the declining phase will provide a unique view of the processes that link interior dynamics to the phenomena that affect the Earth's space environment. Observations from the MDI instrument support research with many other missions and numerous individual researchers. In addition to fruitful collaborative efforts with the RHESSI and TRACE orbiting solar observatories, joint scientific observations with the recently launched Hinode (Solar B) and STEREO spacecraft are in development.

Description: SEARCH FOR TRACES OF LIFE IN EARTH'S OLDEST ROCKS We aim at establishing criteria for distinguishing between biogenic and inorganic carbon and to apply them to the search for remnants of life in Earth's oldest sedimentary rocks, found in the Isua Supracrustal Belt (ISB) in southern West Greenland. Our earlier work has revealed that isotopically fractionated carbon, previously thought to be the hallmark of biogenic carbon, is actually a common product of disproportionation of ferrous carbonate (siderite). Extensive beds of such graphite bearing siderite formed upon injection of hot fluids into sequences of surface related ISB rocks when they were buried deep in the crust at high temperature and pressure. Before this was realized, such isotopically light carbon in the form of crystalline graphite was commonly considered biogenic and to represent the oldest and most strongly altered carbonaceous remnants of primitive life forms. The ferrous carbonate beds in which this graphite occurs were thought to be shallow water counterparts of the sedimentary banded iron formations (BIF) that we found to be practically devoid of syngenetic carbon. In contrast a recently discovered graded bed formation in the ISB contains layers of carbonaceous shale which is clearly of sedimentary origin. This material is one of the targets of our proposed investigation. Included in our study is also a series of carbon deposits from younger Archean and Proterozoic rocks in Africa, Australia and Scandinavia that are less strongly altered, as well as fluid deposited inorganic graphite from Greenland and Spain. A promising opportunity for recognizing biogenic carbon depends on the finding that carbonaceous material of biogenic origin at the level of metamorphism found in the ISB or lower retains non-graphitic puckered layer structures formed by the incorporation of characteristic defects. In contrast, fluid-deposited inorganic carbon crystallizes as graphite. High resolution structural studies of different types of Archean carbon thus form an important part of the study. We find that the carbon isotope fractionation in all samples varies over a relatively large range from particle to particle. The sources of this variability? isotopic exchange vs. heterogeneity in the source material or in the disproportionation catalysts remain to be investigated a.o. by detailed petrographic analysis of the host rock Residual bioorganic nitrogen and hydrogen have in the past been successfully exploited as indicators of progressive organic carbon maturation. Our analyses of the content and thermal release of nitrogen in carbon samples from the ISB has shown that inorganic nitrogen, accompanied by argon, is incorporated in graphite and carbonaceous matter from crustal fluids and superposed on the organic component. Further attempts will be made to distinguish between these sources by mode and strength of bonding of these gases. The techniques developed will be applicable also to defining the origin of carbonaceous matter if found on Mars

Description: At present there are two models for the production of meteoritic oxygen Istopic anomalies. They are 1) production from the gas phase symmetry dependent chemical reaction and 2) photochemical isotopic self shielding. In the past year, we have demonstrated for the first time the ability to produce a mass independent isotopic fractionation in the synthesis of solid SiOx species as well as FeSiOx from gas phase precursors. This is a major advancement and is the first time that this has been accomplished. The next step in developing the potential applications to the solar system is to refine our mechanistic understanding of this process, In collaboration with Dr. Joe Nuth of GSFC we will propose a series of experiments to further our understanding. In the case of photochemical self shielding we have performed the only experiments that measure the short wavelength isotopic fractionation associated with CO photolysis. These experiments have been developed and performed at the Advanced Light Source at Berkeley. The key test will be to measure the isotopic fractionation at the short wavelengths where self shielding would occur. The difficulty with such experiments is that there is no window material that may be used to transmit the less than 110 nm light. To accomplish the measurements, a windowless, differentially pumped, multi chamber system is needed. We will propose to develop this capability and make the key measurements to test the photochemical self shielding models.

Description: MAGNETIC FIELD DYNAMICS AND SHOCK ACCELERATION BEYOND THE BOHM LIMIT The origin of cosmic rays (CRs) is one of the unsolved problems in astrophysics. The CR acceleration mechanisms associated with shock waves (shocks) has long been of a greatest interest, since shocks are the ultimate receptacle of an important fraction of the gravitational energy in many astrophysical environments. These include powerful Explosions (such as supernovae (SN) and gamma ray bursts) or accretion phenomena onto black holes. The accelerated charged particles (CRs) are studied observationally by both their direct detection and by measurements of associated emission such as gamma, x-ray and radio emissions and neutrinos. The observation accuracy has dramatically improved over the last years. This opens tremendous opportunities for the theoretical understanding of acceleration mechanisms. While physically appealing shock Acceleration models have long been available, they are unable to account for many detailed aspects of observations, such as diversity of the power-law indices, spectral breaks and spectral variability. One fundamental question is: can the SN remnant shocks accelerate particles to the so called "ankle" in the CR spectrum at about 10^18. eV or only to the "knee" at 10 15 eV? We propose to continue and significantly broaden our study of the shock acceleration problem based on nonlinear analytical solution of the kinetic equation for the CRs with a self-consistent shock structure along with the particle propagation and confinement at the shock. One implementation of our model already successfully explained the TeV observations of SNR RXJ 1713.7-3946 by CANGAROO and HESS telescopes. Future instruments (GLAST, VERITAS) will be able to probe regimes of broader range in energy with higher sensitivity, and thus be able to provide quantitative tests of the CR acceleration theory. Our goal is to further elucidate and describe the theory of -maximum particle energy achievable in acceleration process. This is based on our recent demonstration of the relevance of fractional (nondiffusive) particle transport in the shock precursor and the realization that scattering (to longer scales in the k-space) of magnetic fluctuation energy by stochastic density fluctuations enables the confinement and thus acceleration of higher energy CRs -particle transport and plasma heating by self generated and nonlinearly evolved compressible MHD turbulence in astrophysical shock environments -sub-shock (collisionless shock) physics, including selfconsistent determination of its strength and particle injection into acceleration process from thermal plasma Our approach is mostly analytical. We plan to quantitatively relate the micro-physics parameters such as the subshock Mach number, maximmum particle energy and injection rate to the macroscopic shock control parameters which are the sonic and Alfvenic Mach numbers along with the shock obliquity angle, so as to construct tractable models of CR acceleration, suitable for self-consistent calculation of acceleration efficiency, particle spectra and related radiation. This requires advanced methods in nonlinear plasma physics, particle kinetics and hydrodynamics with the emphasis on anomalous particle transport in self-generated turbulence. Our results will be quantitatively tested by comparison with observations and used for predictions of radiation fluxes from astrophysical objects such as SNR and AGN. They should help to understand the origin of both galactic and extragalactic CRs along with associated emission. The proposed research will help to understand observations of objects where shock acceleration is likely to take place as well as to interpret the background CR spectra. It is highly relevant to NASA missions (such as Swift and GLAST) and to the ground based facilities such as Auger Observatory

Description: EMITTING TO THE BEAT OF A DIFFERENT DRUMMER: FAR INFRARED IR SPECTROSCOPY OF POLYCYCLIC AROMATIC HYDROCARBONS (PAHs) We propose to measure, as well as theoretically calculate, the Far infrared (FIR) spectra (20 to 200 microns) of over 40 Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) and Polycyclic Aromatic Nitrogen Heterocycle (PANHs) species. The proposed research will provide a database with which to interpret FIR spectra obtained by several of the first generation SOFIA instruments as well as the HI-FI instrument on the Herschel space telescope. Given the universality of the PAH features which dominate the mid-infrared spectra of a wide variety of astronomical objects, and that the PAHs exhibit FIR vibrational modes, one would expect these new instruments will discover previously undetected PAH FIR emission features. Currently there is no applicable PAH FIR spectroscopic data available to interpret observations in this region. This proposal is aimed to remedy this situation.

Description: ALGEBRAIC CONSTRUCTIONS OF HIGH PERFORMANCE AND EFFICIENTLY ENCODABLE QUASI-CYCLIC LDPC CODES FOR SATELLITE AND SPACE COMMUNICATIONS This research project is set up to investigate several promising algebraic methods for systematic constructions of binary and q-ary , high performance and efficiently encodable, structured regular and irregular quasi-cyclic (QC) LDPC codes for satellite and space communications. Specific subjects to be investigated include: (1) a unified approach based on finite fields for constructing regular binary and q-ary QC-LDPC codes; (2) a masking technique that can be used to change the column and row weights of the parity-check matrices of the constructed codes yielding regular and irregular codes with improved performances; (3) performance of the constructed codes over the AWGN and random erasure channels; (4) construction of quasi-cyclic LDPC codes for the erasure-burst channel that yield good performance when decoded iteratively; and (5) a new simple algorithm for decoding cyclic codes, including LDPC codes, over the error-burst channel. Preliminary results are impressive and show that codes constructed by these methods perform very well with iterative decoding, either close to the Shannon limit for the AWGN channel or to the code threshold for the random erasure channel. Particularly, these codes have low error-floors. Low error-floors are important for high performance satellite and space communications where low bit or block error rates are required. Furthermore, some of these codes can correct long erasure-bursts and error-bursts using very simple decoding techniques.

Description: Recent observations from the CLUSTER mission have shown that during geomagnetically disturbed times, the 0+ number density in the plasma sheet close to the reconnection X-line in the Earth's magnetotail can become comparable to, or even higher than, the corresponding H+ number density and that the 0+ ions carry most ofthe particle pressure [Kistler et al., 2005; Wygant et al, 2005]. The presence of 0+ also has implications for transport processes at the magnetopause [e.g., Bouhram et al., 2005). However, there has been no systematic kinetic study of effects of 0+ on magnetic reconnection. Even something as basic as the linear properties of tearing mode in three-species plasma is currently lacking. This constitutes a major gap in theoretical understanding of reconnection in the magnetosphere and hampers understanding of spacecraft data. The proposed work is designed to lay the theoretical framework and address fundamental questions regarding the role of 0+ in magnetic reconnection. The proposed tasks require the unique set of tools that we have developed and used in our previous studies of reconnection. These include (i) nonlocal linear vlasov code which we have already used effectively in examining collisionless tearing and a variety of different current driven instabilities in thin current layers, (ii) our newly developed full PIC code with open boundary conditions [Daughton et al., 2006), and (iii) 2D and 3D electromagnetic hybrid code with open boundary conditions. We will use data from CLUSTER as a guide for our choice of parameters and as a way to test our predictions. The objectives of the proposed work are in tune with NASA'S aim in understanding the interaction of solar wind with the Earth and planetary magnetospheres and how solar wind controls the flow of energy and momentum throughout the system. Magnetopause reconnection is the primary mechanism for transfer of energy and momentum and is the focus of next Solar Terrestrial Probe, the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission (MMS). In fact the primary objective of MMS is the understanding of the fundamental processes of reconnection. Our study will provide insight as to the details of the reconnection process in the presence of 0+, a subject where there is almost no existing theoretical work.

Description: CONTINUED MONITORING AND TRENDS OF SELECTED TRACE GASES AT REMOTE LOCATIONS BETWEEN 71N AND 47S ABSTRACT:  We seek funds for the four-year period from June 1,2007 to May 31, 2011, to continue the ongoing global monitoring of an extensive suite of halocarbons, hydrocarbons, and alkyl nitrates. Our long-term global monitoring program is now in its 28th year, and our sampling strategy measures some 40 compounds in 70-80 whole air samples collected during a three week period each season. The measurements are made along a latitudinal transect that extends from 71N to 47S at remote surface locations of the Pacific Basin. Our research program has two main goals. The first is to monitor the latitudinal distributions and temporal trends of selected compounds that play important roles in the chemistry and physics of the atmosphere, including stratospheric ozone (03) depletion, radiative forcing, and ground-level 03 production. The prime contributors to the chlorine content of the stratosphere have been the chlorofluorocarbons (CF2CI2 or CFC-l2, CFC13 or CFC-ll, CCI2FCCIF2 or CFC-1l3), methyl chloride (CH3CI), carbon tetrachloride (CCI4), and methyl chloroform (CH3CC13). During the upcoming funding period we will continue to monitor the mixing ratios of these and other gases that are restricted under the terms of the United Nations Montreal Protocol and its amendments, including gases that have already peaked and are currently declining (CFC-ll, CFC-IB, CFC-1l4, CCI4, CH3CC13); gases that have leveled off and are expected to decline in the near future (CFC-12); and gases that are continuing to increase (CBrClF2 or H-1211).  Methane (CH4) is second in radiative forcing to carbon dioxide (C02), and its global mixing ratio is currently in the 7th year of a temporary pause. As a result, CH4 increases (predicted in IPCC 2001) of 67-111 ppbv between 2000-2010, to levels around 1850 ppbv by 2010, now appear very unlikely. On the other hand, there is significant potential for CH4 growth in the future in response to recovering economies of Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union (FSU), decreasing OH (in response to the ll-year solar cycle and stratospheric ozone recovery), and natural CH4 emissions, which may increase in response to C02 forcing. Therefore we will be continuing to closely monitor the behavior of tropospheric CH4 during the upcoming funding period. We will also monitor the seasonal and long-term trends of short-lived gases such as ethane and tetrachloroethene (C2CI4) and estimate changes in their atmospheric burden. These data will be used by research groups at the University of California, Irvine (UCI) and will be available to the atmospheric community, as described below. The second goal is to provide data to the atmospheric community to be used in applications such as climate modeling, air quality and climate related policy decisions, and the validation of satellite observations. Currently the following data have been submitted to the World Data Center for Atmospheric Trace Gases at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory: CH4 (1979-2005); CFC-11, CFC-12, CFC-IB, CCI4, C2C14, and CH3CC13 (1988-2005); H-1211, chloroform (CHC13), ethane, ethyne, propane, i-butane, n-butane, ethyl nitrate (EtON02) and iso-propyl nitrate (i-PrON02) (1996-2005); and methyl nitrate (MeON02) (2001-2005). During the upcoming funding period we will continue to regularly add to the archive as more quality controlled data (past and future) become available. In particular we are focusing on pre-1996 ethane data in order to clearly assess whether or not the global ethane mixing ratio shows a long-term decline. Our data are also routinely used in international publications such as the WMO Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion (e.g, 2003,2006) and the IPCC Climate Change Report (e.g. 1995,2001, upcoming), and our group members regularly serve as co-authors, contributors and reviewers of these international assessments...

Description: Magnetofossils: A Novel Biosignature of Ancient Ecosystems Magnetofossils, the magnetic minerals left in the rock record by a variety of magnetotactic microbes, represent a largely untapped record of paleoenvironmental conditions and microbial paleoecology. Their presence can provide a new perspective on paleobiology and, thanks to distinctive microwave and magnetic properties, they can potentially be detected and identified in rocks more easily than other microbial fossils --perhaps even by an instrument on a planetary lander. The goal of our proposal is to build the fossil record of magnetotactic bacteria so that it can be used as a tool for understanding the evolution of life and the biosphere. We will use rock magnetism, erromagnetic resonance spectroscopy (FMR), and tomographic transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to identify and characterize magnetofossils. FMR is sensitive to the presence of the chains of magnetic minerals produced by magnetotactic microbes, and tomographic TEM will enable us to construct three-dimensional images of magnetosome crystals. We have three objectives that we seek to attain in reaching this goal. We will: 1) test the limits of FMR as a screening technique for samples likely to contain magnetofossils by applying it to Cenozoic samples known to contain magnetofossils in varying concentrations, as well in control samples of magnetosomes in salts diluted with other ferromagnetic materials, 2) survey a variety of carbonate rocks with microbiallygenerated textures from throughout Earth history for magnetofossils to extend understanding of the abundance of magnetofossils throughout geologic time, and 3) examine carbonate platform sediments from across the Cretaceous-Tertiary (K-T) and Permo-Triassic (P-T) boundaries for magnetofossils to study how the K-T and P-T crises affected microbial ecology. The proposed work addresses two of the NASA strategic objectives in the domain of the Science Mission Directorate. Primarily, it will "explore the universe." In particular, it meets one of the main goals of the Astrobiology Roadmap by developing techniques for identifying a biosignature that can "reveal and characterize past or present life in ancient samples from Earth [and] extraterrestrial samples measured in situ." The application of this biosignature can address several of the goals of the Exobiology and Evolutionary Biology Program. Specifically, the magnetofossil record should be able to provide insights into aspects of the early evolution of Earth's biosphere, including the history of major biogeochemical cycles, particularly those of iron and oxygen, and the response of Earth's biosphere to mass extinction events. It should also provide insights into the evolution of biomineralization, a trait more common in "advanced" life. In addition, the FMR techniques developed in this work may potentially be applied in a robotic planetary lander mission and contribute to the strategic objective of "conduct[ing] robotic exploration of Mars to search for evidence of life."

Description: DEEP ULTRAVIOLET INSTRUMENT FOR INSTANT BIOLOAD CLASSIFICATION This proposal addresses the need for advanced methods of detection and classification of trace levels of biological and organic contamination on spacecraft and related surfaces that are more sensitive, more rapid, more cost effective, and better integrated with spacecraft assembly and mission phases than present NASA Standard Assay (NSA) methods. The primary objective of this proposed effort is to demonstrate an instrument and method to detect, enumerate, and classify both bacterial spores and cells and other biological and organic contaminants extracted from spacecraft and related surfaces using NSA swabbing techniques with a limit of detection (LOD) less than 10 spores per 2.25, by 2.25, swabbed area and with a measurement and analysis time less than 10 seconds. We call this instrument an Instantaneous Bioload Assay Sensor? or IBAS. The proposed sensor does not require germination or other alteration of extracted bacteria, dye tags, or other reagents, and leaves the samples in their original state. The proposed sensor and method is intended to eliminate present culturing steps and provide for instantaneous determination of the number and type of bacteria and other biological and organic contaminants in a sample. It is the further objective of this effort to demonstrate the ability to detect, enumerate, and classify biological particles directly on spacecraft surfaces, eliminating the need to contact the spacecraft surfaces except where biological or organic chemical contaminants are found and need to be further analyzed. The ability to detect, enumerate, and classify single spores within water samples and on surfaces in less than 1 second has been demonstrated using deep ultraviolet laser induced native fluorescence spectroscopic methods. These methods also demonstrated the ability to differentiate bacterial spores, bacterial cells, and a wide range of other biological and organic material with a low false alarm rate. Development of these methods is the outgrowth of several NASA and JPL-supported programs related to life detection as well as DOD-supported programs related to biochemical weapons sensors. These demonstrations opened the opportunity to apply these techniques to planetary protection measurement of trace levels of biological or organic chemical contamination on spacecraft or related surfaces. The proposed method would employ NSA methods for collection of samples from spacecraft as well as for extraction of contaminant materials from cotton swabs into water. The water sample containing contaminants would then be directly excited in using specific deep UV irradiation and native fluorescence spectra used to enumerate, classify, and otherwise characterize contaminants. The most immediate significance of this research is to dramatically improve the limit of detection (10 spores per sample area with a goal of 1s/sample) and speed (10 s) in determining spacecraft bioloads while maintaining the presently accepted NSA methods of microbial collection. The proposed technique is 25,000 times shorter than the present NSA requires about 72 hours for culturing. Our expected LOD is over 500 times lower and analysis time is 180 times shorter than an alternate technology presently being developed. Our instrument and method will perform the measurement with a minimum number of procedural steps, minimum manpower, and without the use of filters, reagents, or other consumables. This should dramatically reduce the labor and materials cost of identifying which samples are worthy of further analysis by culturing or molecular biological techniques. A further significance is to develop methods that are expected to enable non-contact measurement of bioloads directly on spacecraft surfaces without the need for collection or other contact with the surface. This should dramatically reduce the potential for cross-contamination with the current methods.

Description: Using Aromatic Compounds and related Molecular Species as a tracer of Carbon in the Universe and Life in the Solar System The purpose of our proposed research is to investigate aromatic compounds and related molecular species using the information gained as a tracer of Carbon in the Universe and Life in the Solar System. The ultimate goal of this project is to determine whether aromatic structures, which are prevalent in our own biochemistry, might indicate an exogenous origin of life. Since tons of organic molecules come to earth every day from space, and this mass may have been a million times more on the prebiotic Earth, such molecules might have aided in making the Earth habitable, perhaps even jump-starting life. By extension, such a delivery process may be generally applicable to habitability of the planets of other stellar systems, and thus is of fundamental interest to the SETI Institute. This program will focus on measuring the far and mid-infrared (IR) spectra of aromatic compounds under astrophysically relevant conditions; constructing a database of the measured spectra for use in interpreting astronomical observations, modeling the aromatic emissions, and utilizing the knowledge gained in the development of instrument concepts for planetary landers and probes. Since nitrogen-containing aromatics are so important to our biochemistry, particular emphasis will be placed on these compounds. However this program is not limited to solely experimental work. In addition to the proposed work, we are actively pursuing related observational and theoretical projects through collaborations with other scientists at NASA, universities, and non-profits.

Description: Microcosm will build on the Phase I X-ray pulsar-based navigation and timing (XNAV) feasibility assessment to develop a detailed XNAV simulation capability to evaluate navigation performance for specific missions of interest, and create an XNAV flight software experiment ready to integrate on an appropriate near-term flight demonstration mission in Phase III.  Phase I demonstrated achievable XNAV accuracy, developed a preliminary source catalog, constructed an XNAV error budget, and laid out potential implementation options for XNAV, focusing on an Earth-Sun L2 lagrange point mission.  Brighter, less stable, non-traditional X-ray sources were also considered for possible XNAV application with promising initial results, especially for formation flying applications.  Taking advantage of concurrent XNAV efforts at DARPA to the maximum extent possible, Phase II will develop and validate XNAV algorithms via a simulation which will be targeted for integration with Goddard Space Flight Center's GPS Enhanced Onboard Navigation System (GEONS) software.  The error budget will be developed in more detail to support the algorithm and simulation work.  XNAV holds great potential for NASA as an enabling technology for fully autonomous interplanetary navigation and could provide a significant mission enhancement as an adjunct to the Deep Space Network (DSN) and ground based navigation. NASA's applications includes missions beyond Jupiter as an enabling technology for autonomous navigation, potentially providing improved performance over standard DSN tracking capability for very far missions.  This includes the Pioneer Anomaly mission or 500 AU mission.  XNAV provides fully autonomous interplanetary navigation capability, potentially reducing the demands on DSN for increasing tracking requirements for future missions.  XNAV can supplement DSN service and enhance DSN navigation performance.  XNAV can also provide a backup navigation capability for manned and unmanned near-Earth, lunar, and Mars missions.  Further, it can provide higher redundancy for manned missions.     This application will also provide primary and secondary navigation services for DoD and for MEO, GEO, HEO, and even cis-lunar missions where GPS has limited availability, XNAV can provide primary autonomous navigation capability, while also providing an essential backup navigation capability for missions which normally rely on GPS but have a need for continuity of operations in the event of loss or denial of GPS.

Description: OBSERVING URANUS RINGS DURING RPX 2007-2008 We will conduct a detailed study of the Uranian ring system by taking high angular resolution observations when the Earth, and later the Sun, cross Uranus' ring plane. We intend to use the Keck and VLT telescopes at near-infrared wavelengths with adaptive optics techniques. The spatial resolution of these data is similar to that obtained with HST at visible wavelengths, -600--650 km at Uranus. The infrared data will be combined with HST observations to obtain a longer time baseline of ring plane crossing (RPX) data and to extend the spectral range from 0.3 up to 2.2 micron. More specifically, we intend to determine e.g., the spectrum and spatial extent (radial and vertical) of the newly discovered outer rings of Uranus, and compare these with Saturn's G and E rings. Will Uranus' outermost ring indeed be as blue as Saturn's E ring? Our data will shed light on the similarities and differences between the orbital evolution of dust ejected (geyser, impacts) off Enceladus with impact derived dust from Mab. Observations of the rings' brightness before, during and after RPX will yield accurate crossing times, with which we can refine the inclination of the ring planes, and assess the presence of vertical warping and/or clumping in the rings. Observations of the dark side of the rings will be used to search for embedded moonlets that might shephard the inner rings. These data will also enable excellent characterization of the dust sheets within and interior to the main rings, and a search for faint material outside the epsilon ring. The more open configuration in December 2007 allows characterization of longitudinal asymmetries in the rings, such as arcs. This array of observations is essential to develop theories on the dynamics and evolution of the ring system as a whole, which in turn are coupled to the more general question of planet formation in protostellar disks. This makes our research particularly relevant to NASA's Strategic Goal 3: "Develop a balanced overall program of science, exploration and aeronautics", with Sub-goal 3C: Advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the Solar System, the potential for life elsewhere, and the hazards and resources present as humans explore space. Description: MODULAR GRAVITATIONAL REFERENCE SENSOR FOR SPACE GRAVITATIONAL WAVE DETECTION Modular Gravitational Reference Sensor for Space Gravitational Wave Detection (D.6 Beyond Einstein Foundation Science) Project Summary Principal Investigator: Professor Robert L. Byer, Stanford University Project Advisor: Professor Daniel B. DeBra Co-Investigators: Dr. Saps Buchman, and Dr. Ke-Xun Sun Gravitational wave detection is one of the most compelling problems in physical sciences today. Laser Interferometric Space Antenna (LISA) and Big Bang Observatory (BBO) are highly sensitive space-borne gravitational wave detectors requiring unprecedented precision. At the heart of the LISA and BBO spacecraft is the Gravitational Reference Sensor (GRS), which houses a proof mass (PM), providing a reference at the end point of the distance measurement. Much progress has been achieved in LISA and its pilot studies, and LISA Technology Package (LTP) in various aspects such as disturbance reduction, interferometry, data analysis, and more. However, there is urgency in studying GRS architecture, which could significantly simplify LISA, but more importantly future LISA versions, such as BBO and DECIGO, and thereby enhancing the sensitivity, reliability and lowering the cost. Until recently, the baseline design for LISA GRS had been direct illumination of the PM as published in 1998. Beginning in 2003, we have revisited the GRS design with the goals of simplifying the design, reducing cross talk, and moving towards true drag free performance. We proposed the modular GRS architecture (stand-alone GRS) in 2004. This is a multi-layer proposal containing several key suggestions: 1) The laser beam from the remote spacecraft does not directly illuminate the PM, but illuminates the GRS housing surface. Therefore, the GRS is now a module providing positioning reference for external use. 2) Only one PM is used. The GRS measures PM center of mass position. 5) Multiple internal optical sensors are used to measure the gap between the proof mass and the housing. Optical sensing allows a large gap that reduces the disturbances. Of historical note, the single spherical PM has been flown in Triad and GP-B missions. Optical shadow sensing was previously used in Nova, the follow-on to the Triad. Since our presentation in 2004, the LISA and BBO baseline designs have changed substantially. The BBO has moved to a single PM. In the new LISA baseline, the laser beam from the remote spacecraft no longer directly illuminates the PM, but instead measures the separation between remote GRS housings. As such, the modular GRS architecture has been adopted partially in LISA by avoiding direct illumination and in BBO by using a single PM. In our opinion, the next step should be to use the single-proof-mass modular GRS without direct illumination of the PM. The Stanford team has made substantial progress in developing the modular GRS. The Stanford team consists of faculty, staff, and a number of graduate students pursing advanced degrees. We propose a $225K per year, three-year program to continue developing the key technologies for the modular GRS. The program will concentrate on the following aspects: 1) Investigation of key component technologies such as optical displacement and angular sensing, diffractive optics, proof mass characterization, UV LED charge management, electromagnetic modeling, and surface effects. 2) More detailed modular GRS architectural and system design. 3) Trade studies for modular GRS and other architectures. 4) Special studies as suggested by LISA and BBO research communities, such as system trade-off studies. The output of our program is a modular GRS architecture that is less susceptible to noise, simpler to implement, and perhaps less costly to engineer. Our target is not just LISA, but more importantly the next generation of gravitational wave observatories, such as BBO.

Description: THE NUCLEAR COMPTON TELESCOPE The Nuclear Compton Telescope (NCT) is a balloon-borne soft gamma-ray telescope designed to study astrophysical sources of nuclear line emission and gamma-ray polarization. It employs a novel Compton telescope design utilizing twelve 3D-GeDs with high spectral and spatial resolution, to Compton-track gamma-ray interactions for imaging the sky, measuring polarization, and reducing background. A relatively small instrument proof-of-concept instrument, NCT nevertheless achieves effective areas comparable to COMPTEL, with significantly improved sensitivity. NCT is designed as a science prototype and technology test bed for the Advanced Compton Telescope, a NASA Vision Mission. NCT underwent a test flight of a prototype 2-detector telescope from Fort Sumner, NM, on 1 June 2005, which qualified the instrument and gondola for long duration balloon flights. We are requesting 5 years of funding to fulfill the scientific mission of NCT. The first two years of funding would allow us to complete the NCT scientific instrument, and the subsequent funding would support two southern hemisphere LDBFs from Alice Springs, Australia, in December 2008 and 2010. The combination of exposure from the two flights (-800 ks/source) will realize the optimal scientific potential of NCT.

Description: QUANTUM CHEMICAL AND CHEMICAL KINETICS CALCULATIONS OF SULFUR AND SULFUR EXCHANGE REACTIONS RELATED TO MASS-INDEPENDENT FRACTIONATION OF SULFUR ISOTOPES SUMMARY: The discovery (Farquhar et al. 2000) of mass independent fractionation (MIF) in sulfur isotopes preserved in Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks has solidified our understanding of the rise of 0 2 in the ancient Earth atmosphere. Photochemical modeling has shown that a maximum concentration of 02 of 10-5 times the present atmospheric level is necessary to maintain distinct reservoirs of sulfur MIF in the Archean atmosphere. All of these conclusions have been reached without an understanding of exactly what the chemical mechanisms of sulfur MIF were in the ancient atmosphere. Elucidating these mechanisms will allow for more refined constraints on 02, and, more importantly, will yield quantitative constraints on the sulfur concentration in the ancient atmosphere. In this study we will perform high-level quantum chemical (also called ab initio) calculations of the rate coefficients for a suite of sulfur reactions and sulfur exchange reactions that are likely to be of importance in a low 02 atmosphere. In addition, we will incorporate the ab initio results into chemical kinetics models of the Archean atmosphere with the goal of determining which of several possible sulfur MIF mechanisms are most important. The proposed work is complementary to experimental investigations of MIF signatures produced during photolysis of sulfur-containing gases ongoing in the laboratory of J. Farquhar at the University of Maryland. The expected results from this study are as follows: i) an accurate determination of potential energy surfaces and rate coefficients for several important sulfur reactions and sulfur exchange reactions; ii) incorporation of these rate coefficients into a chemical kinetics model of a low 02 atmosphere, and evaluation of several possible sulfur MIF mechanisms. Ultimately, we expect to be able to constrain the atmospheric concentration of sulfur (most likely as S02) based on the sulfur MIF mechanism. The proposed study fits within the Exobiology and Evolutionary Biology program under the research area iEarly Evolution of Life and the Biospherei. By bringing some of the tools utilized in modern atmospheric chemistry (i.e., high-level quantum chemistry methods), we believe we can contribute significantly to understanding the full implications of sulfur MIF to the environment of the Archean and Paleoproterozoic Earth.

Description: The Origin of Relativistic Electrons in the Jovian Magnetosphere The middle magnetosphere of Jupiter contains intense fluxes of extremely energetic electrons (10 MeV), which provide a potential hazard to future spacecraft missions. The origin of such relativistic electrons at Jupiter is poorly understood. Resonant scattering by whistler-mode chorus emissions, has recently been established as an effective mechanism for the acceleration of electrons to relativistic energies in the Earth's outer radiation belt. Similar wave emissions have been observed in the middle magnetosphere of Jupiter, by wave instruments on the Voyager and Galileo spacecraft. A key objective of the proposed research is to understand the conditions for chorus excitation in the Jovian system, and to investigate whether such waves are capable of causing electron stochastic acceleration to highly relativistic energies. Particle and field data from the Voyager and Galileo missions will be used to evaluate path integrated gain in the Jovian magnetosphere using the HOTRAY code. The characteristics of observed chorus emission in the Jovian magnetosphere will be used to determine the rate of pitchangle and energy diffusion (using a developed PADIE diffusion code). This will allow us to evaluate timescales for precipitation loss and local stochastic acceleration to relativistic energies. Electrons above several MeV in the middle magnetosphere of Jupiter, ultimately diffuse inwards to form the synchrotron radiation belt in the inner magnetosphere. Understanding of the processes responsible for the origin of uprarelativistic electrons in the Jovian system, and their potential hazard to spacecraft, is important for the current NASA JUNO mission, and proposed missions to Europa. The proposed research is relevant to NASA strategic goals 3B.1 " Progress in understanding the fundamental physical processes of the space environment from the Sun to Earth, to other planets", and strategic goal 3B.3 "Progress in developing the capability to predict the extreme and dynamic conditions in space in order to maximize the safety and productivity of human and robotic explorers". The proposed research will "Enhance the scientific return from the Galileo, Voyager, and Pioneer missions by continuing the analysis of their respective data sets through broadened scientific participation"(OPR objective 1); and "Define the dynamical processes operating in the outer Solar System" (OPR objective 3). This proposed study involves the "Development of basic theory, and modeling relevant to the interpretation of mission data and dynamics of giant planets, their satellites" (OPR Announcement, Task 1, that support the program goals), the "Correlative analyses that combine data from outer planets missions" (OPR, Task 3); and "Research that seeks to place the results of these outer planets missions in a larger context of processes and evolution bodies in the outer Solar System" (OPR, Task 4).

Description: GAAS SEMICONDUCTOR MICRO-CHANNEL MULTIPLIER ARRAYS We propose to develop and demonstrate true, bulk-crystalline semiconductor gallium arsenide (GaAs) micro-machined MCP arrays. We argue that GaAs material properties will allow us to exceed important performance limitations of conventional glass MCPs while attaining the desired semiconductor multiplier advantages of micro-machining (e.g. manufacturing yield, collection area, small channel size, low radioactive background, and high-temperature process compatibility), and to overcome previous limitations to the fabrication of silicon semiconductor MCPs. Our pilot studies have demonstrated the fabrication of an array of 10,000 smooth 5 micron, high-aspect (60:l) through-holes in a high-quality GaAs substrate. The process appears fast and reproducible and demonstrates the successful resolution of a critical step in the making of GaAs MCPs. We intend to make GaAs arrays of micron-scale bores and to verify that the high aspect-ratio GaAs fabrication process can produce a MCP detector with operational and life characteristics that are superior to glass-pore or silicon-pore units. We propose for an initial investigation of the compatibility of GaAs MCPs with directly-deposited reduced electron affinity photo-cathodes (e.g. GaN, GaAs(Cs,O)) in order to extend MCP quantum efficiency into the near W, visible and even near-IR band passes. We also plan to analytically investigate bow photon coupling (sensitivity) and electron gain (efficiency) can benefit from the plasmon quantum phenomena in small sized GaAs pores.

Description: ULTRA VIOLET RADIATION:  THE KEY TO UNDERSTANDING EVOLUTION AND SURVIVAL OF LIFE ON EARTH AND BEYOND The overall objective of our research is to understand ultraviolet radiation (UVR) as a limiting environmental factor for life on earth and beyond. UVR is unique in that it places limits on the range of life through the destruction of biopolymers as well as acting directly on the genetic material through DNA damage and mutation. Extraterrestrial life would likely be based on organic biopolymers, and thus subject to UVR effects. Terrestrial life arose under a higher UVR flux and different spectrum than modem life endures, thus the replication of early earth UVR conditions is imperative for astrobiological applications. In the proposed work we focus on four objectives: 1. To determine the upper limits of UVR on the earth today. Specifically, areas will be targeted that are likely to have the highest levels of UVB radiation and potentially UVC. We will do broad-band measurements and complete solar spectra (200-1100 nm) in locations and during times when, based on NASA's TOMS data, the highest UVB fluxes should occur. In several of these locations, continuous monitoring stations will be deployed to  measure broad-band changes during the course of the day and over the year. 2. To determine the relative contribution of UVB and possibly UVC to DNA damage as a proxy for the hazards of these forms of radiation to living organisms. DNA dosimeters will be subjected to unfiltered and filtered solar radiation using a solar simulator, and during radiation measurements in the field, to assess several common forms of DNA damage as a proxy for severity of exposure and likely lethality and mutagenesis. 3. To assess the microbial ecosystem composition of locations with the highest levels of UV radiation. In the sites identified as being subjected to the highest levels of UVR, community composition will be assessed from morphological and sequence-based identification techniques. 4. To screen microbes collected from the ecosystems studied in objective 3 for radiation resistance for their potential to survive exposure to the space environment.

Description: The Multi-Agent Architecture for Coordinated, Responsive Observations  Remote sensing missions for earth science provide a wealth of information to help us understand the dynamics of our planet. However, the current stovepipe operational model of remote sensing missions, i.e., a single spacecraft transmitting data to dedicated ground operations centers (Fig. 1), introduces untenable latencies in developing data prod-ucts that hinder model building and refine-ment as well as timely responses for hazard mitigation. Future missions will operate as part of a sensor web (Fig. 2) comprised of ^interlinked platforms with onboard information processing systems capable of orchestrat-ing real-time collaborative operations [1]. The Multi-agent Architecture for Coordi-nated, Responsive Observations (MACRO), an extension of our current work on the Adap-tive Network Architecture (ANA) is a natural technology for enabling the deployment and operation of a sensor web. The ANA software framework of multiple distributed agents provides localized autonomy on distributed sci-ence missions. The MACRO extensions will help overcome current mission limitations by facilitating real-time, reactive data acquisition, analysis, fusion and distribution which will greatly benefit society and scientific discovery/understanding. Our objective over a 3 year period is to ma-ture MACRO from TRL 2/4 to TRL 5 (Sec 2.4), by focusing on two main topics that provide significant value to NASAs earth science missions: - Incorporation of self-describing sensor, processing and measurement models (Sec. 2.2.1.1) - Collaborative observations between agents via on-board planning, scheduling, and re-source management (Sec. 2.2.1.2) - Validation on a representative hardware testbed with multiple demonstrations of a realistic earth science mission (Sec. 2.2.1.3)

Description: NONSTATIONARY SUPERCRITICAL SHOCK FRONT: THE IMPACT OF SOLAR WIND'S FLUCTATIONS AND COMPOSITION THIS PROJECT INVESTIGATES NONSTATIONARY ASPECTS INT HE TRANSITION LAYER OF SUPERCRITICAL, PERPENDICULAR AND QUASI-PERPENDICULAR SHOCKS. PARTICULAR ATTENTION IS PAID TO (A) THE INTRINSIC NONSTATIONARITY OF SELF-REFORMING, SHOCKS, WHICH IS SEEN IN LOW-BETA SHOCK SIMULATIONS, (B) THE EFFECTS OF FLUCTUATIONS IN THE UPSTREAM PLASMA, AND (C) THE EFFECTS OF ALPHA-PARTICLES. OUR OBJECTIVES ARE: (1) TO STUDY IN DETAIL THE DYNAMICAL STURCTURE OF SELF-REFORMING SHOCKS AND UNDERSTAND HOW IT IS AFFECTED BY UPSTREAM TURBULENCE, AND (2) TO UNDERSTAND THE EFFECTS OF A POPULATION OF ALPHA-PARTICLES ON THE SPATIO-TEMPORAL SCALES OF THE REFORMING SHOCK. WE USE A 1D3V FULL PARTICLE PIC CODE THAT IS DESIGNED WITH OPEN BOUNDARIES AND HAS THE UPSTREAM PLASMA INJECTED AT ONE END OF THE SIMULATION BOX AND DOWNSTREAM PLASMA LEAVING AT THE OTHER END. THE DESIGN ALLOWS US TO WORK WITH A SHORTER SIMULATION BOX THAN THAT NEEDED BY THE OTHER SHOCK CODES, WHICH REQUIRE A BOX LONG ENOUGH TO INCLUDE A PROGAGATING SHOCK. IT ALSO ENABLES US TO MODULATE FIELD AND PARTICLE CONDITIONS AT THE UPSTREAM BOUNDARY IN ORDER TO EMULATE MAGNETOSONIC FLUCTUATIONS IN THE SOLAR WIND. FINALLY, THE CODES IMPLEMENTS THE DARWIN MODEL OF ELECTROMAGNETIC FIELD WHERE THE TRANSVERSE PART OF THE DISPLACEMENT CURRENT IS NEGLECTED. THIS ELIMINATES LIGHT WAVES FROMT HE SIMULATIONS AND ALLOWS FOR LARGER TIME STEPS, SO THAT THE SYSTEM CAN BE SIMULATED FOR A LONGER PERIOD OF TIME. COLLISIONLESS SHOCKS PLAY A KEY ROLE IN SPACE AND CERTAINLY BELONG TO THE FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL PROCESSESS OF SPACE PLASMA SYSTEMS. THEIR POSSIBLE INTRINSIC NONSTATIONARITY HAS STRONG IMPLICATIONS FOR THE HEATING AND ACCELERATION OF CHARGED PARTICLES, A FOCUS AREA OF NASA'S RESEARCH. BESIDES, OUR OWN EARTH SYSTEM INCLUDES A BOW SHOCK A T ITS FRONT STEPS, WHICH IS ACCESSED BY A FLEET OF EVER MORE SOPHISTICATED SPACECRAFT AND THUS CONSTITUTES A NATURAL LABORATORY FOR REFINING OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE STRUCTURE OF COLLISIONLESS SHOCKS. WITH THE ONGOING CLUSTER MISSION, THE PROPOSED RESEARCH IS OF MUCH CURRENT INTEREST. IT IS VERY RELEVANT FOR SUCH FUTURE POSSIBLE ENDEAVORS AS THE CROSS-SCALE MISSION.

Description: Following the Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV) Smart Buyer Design effort, the NASA Engineering and Safety Center has been performing follow-on work to determine if there are significant improvements or efficiencies that can be gained from a composite pressurized vessel design.  The team developed three different composite concepts that provided the necessary data to show that a composite pressurized vessel is achievable and comparable to the metallic designs.  Based on the results of this preliminary design work, the Associate Administrator for Exploration Systems Mission Directorate has requested that the NESC form an NASA/DoD/Industry partnership for composite spacecraft structural design to further explore and quantify these potential improvements.  The objective of this effort is to examine the efficacy of building composite crew modules for future human space systems. Objectives:   It is anticipated that future spacecraft will require inexpensive and lightweight structures to achieve mass requirements for missions to low earth orbit, the lunar surface, and beyond.  Polymeric composite materials may provide required cost and mass savings due to their higher specific strength, reduced manufacturing costs and part count, improved durability, etc.    In order to accelerate schedule and minimize risk for a new NASA led composite pressure shell application, NASA will leverage existing design and manufacturing methodologies pertaining to 3D woven pi preforms.  The relevant experience was developed on programs such as the Joint Strike Fighter (JSF) and Composite Affordability Initiative (CAI).   Description of Tasks to be Performed:  The contractor shall provide detailed information in design areas such as pi preform terminations, pi preform intersections, pi preform allowable capability, pi preform capability with overwraps.  The contractor shall also provide detailed support for manufacturing such as surface preparation methods, bagging schemes, overpress parts, gap allowances, and quality control indicators.  Finally, the contractor shall provide testing support, which shall include fixtures, test methods, and analysis correlation methods.   Subtask 1 - Participation on the On-site Composite Crew Module Team The Contractor shall participate with the NASA led team in developing recommendation for technical areas specified below.  The participation includes on-site interaction with the composite crew module team (NASA + contractors).  Co-location events will be as necessary.  The contractor shall plan on a 1-week trip every 3 months to either NASA/GSFC (Greenbelt, MD), NASA/MSFC (Huntsville, Al) or manufacture facility (TBD location) for the period of performance.  As a member of the Composite Crew Module Team, the vendor shall work with other Industrial partners who are already a part of the team.   Industrial partners now include ATK, Northrop Grumman, Swales, Collier Industries, and SDA, Inc.   Subtask 2  Pi perform Coupon Testing   The Contractor shall provide the necessary manpower and expertise to support the initial pi preform coupon testing, based on their extensive work developing design allowables for the JSF program and similar coupon testing for the CAI program.  As part of this support, the contractor shall design and deliver fixtures for coupon bonding, silicone overpress articles for curing, and pull-off and shear tests, all of which are based on heritage designs from the CAI program.  The contractor shall provide on-site support at NASA/MSFC during the coupon cobonding process and guide coupon fabrication. The contractor shall provide analysis guidance for relating composite crew module test data to flight geometry based on extensive experience with pi preform performance.  In addition, the contractor shall provide performance sensitivities to parameters such as overwrap, such that these can be incorporated into the design. Description: GIANT IMPACTS, INTERNAL STRUCTURE OF GIANT PLANETS, AND SURVIVAL OF THEIR SATELLITES RECENT OBSERVATIONS AND ANALYSIS OF GAS-GIANT PLANETS HAVE INDICATED THAT THEY HAVE DIVERSE INTERNAL STRUCTURES. FOR EXAMPLE, WHILE JUPITER HAS THREE TIMES THE TOTAL MASS OF SATURN, JUPITER'S CORE MASS IS ONE THIRD THAT OF SATURN. MOST OF THE HEAVY ELEMENTS IN JUPITER ARE CONTAINED IN THE ENVELOPE, WHEREAS IN SATURN THEY LIE PRIMARILY IN ITS CORE. IS THE INTERIOR STRUCTURE OF THE SOLAR SYSTEM'S GIANT PLANETS PRIMORDIAL IN THE SENSE THAT THEY REFLECT THE EARLIEST CONDITIONS AND MODES OF PLANET FORMATION (CORE ACCRETION, INSTABILITY, OR PAIR-WISE ACCRETION OF ICE GIANTS) OR HAVE THEIR STRUCTURES BEEN ALTERED BY SUBSEQUENT EVOLUTIONARY PROCESSES. HERE WE IDENTIFY THREE POTENTIAL PROCESSES WHICH MAY ALTER THE CORE MASS AND INTERNAL ELEMENTAL DISTRIBUTION OF GIANT PLANETS: GIANT IMPACTS, CORE EROSION, AND DIFFERENTIATION. WE PROPOSED TO EXAMINE HOW THESE PROCESSES MAY INFLUENCE THE EVOLUTION AND STRUCTURE OF GIANT PLANET INTERIORS. WE PROPOSE TO UTILIZE THREE ALREADY DEVELOPED AND WELL TESTED NUMERICAL SCHEMES TO CARRY OUT SEVERAL SERIES OF SIMULATIONS. EACH OF THESE SCHEMES HAS ITS FEATURED ADVANTAGES AND LIMITATIONS. TOGETHER THEY CAN BE APPLIED IN A COMPLEMENTARY MANNER TO ADDRESS VARIOUS RELATED AND OUTSTANDING ISSUES. WE WILL MODIFY THESE TOOLS FOR THE APPROPRIATE EQUATION OF STATE AND RADIATION TRANSFER PROCESSES. IN ADDITION TO PLANETARY STRUCTURE, OUR INVESTIGATION IS ALSO RELEVANT TO THE LONG TERM EVOLUTION OF BOTH GAS AND ICE GIANT PLANETS. THE REDISTRIBUTION OF HEAVY ELEMENTS IN THE ENVELOPE CAN INHIBIT CONVECTION, REDUCE THE COOLING RATE, AND MODIFY THE EMISSIVITY AS WELL AS THE CONTRACTION RATE OF PLANETARY RADIUS. OUR ANALYSIS CAN BE STUDY THE EMISSION DICHOTOMY BETWEEN URANUS AND NEPTUNE. GIANT IMPACTS CAN ALSO ALTER THE SPIN RATE AND TILE THE SPIN AXIS OF GIANT PLANETS SUCH AS URANUS. FINALLY, WE PLAN TO DETERMINE THE EXPANSION AND SUBSEQUENT CONTRACTION RATE OF THE GIANT PLANETS' ENVELOPE AND EXAMINE ITS IMPLICATION ON THE SURVIVAL OF CLOSE-IN SATELLITES SUCH AS IO AND EUROPA AROUND JUPITER.

Description: Comprehensive experimental investigations have been undertaken by the Eschenmoser group towards an understanding of Nature's choice of the structure type of the natural nucleic acids as the molecular basis of genetic function (Chemical Etiology of Nucleic Acid Structure). A central conclusion from these studies is the notion that Watson-Crick base-pairing is by no means unique to the ribofuranoid oligonucleotide system, but is rather widespread among potentially natural nucleic acid analogs with backbones that contain sugar units from ribofuranose. Another conclusion to be drawn from this work, one that is forcibly corroborated by the work of others in the field of medicinal antisense-oligonucleotide chemistry, is the notion of a still largely unexplored structural landscape of informational oligomer systems that may contain backbones, recognition elements and linker groups structurally quite different from those known so far. We deem this landscape to contain oligomer systems that have the generational simplicity of potentially primordial systems, primordial in the sense that, from a chemical point of view, they may have had a chance to self-assemble under the chemical and physical constraints of a prebiological geochemical environment. A structurally unconstrained experimental exploration of the landscape with focusing on such potentially primordial members would represent a continuation of the project pursued so far, yet would reach far beyond it, as the target criterion would no longer be the search for function among structural RNA alternatives of a generational complexity similar to that of RNA, but rather a search for generational simplicity among (functional) oligomers, a simplicity that justifies a given system to be deemed potentially primordial. We propose a systematic experimental study of families of such candidate systems, the structures of which are deduced by combining two conceptual strategies, first a "forward-synthetic analysis" starting from a range of elementary starting materials while obeying rather strictly defined structural constraints of prebiotic chemistry and, second, a qualitative conformational analysis that allows us, as experienced in previous studies, to predict a system's base-pairing capability with the resonable certainty. What encourages us in such an endeavour are the (unpublished) results of our (still) preliminary experimental studies of oligomers whose backbones are derived from ethylenediamine-, peptoid-, and peptide-based monomers and in which the family of the canonical nucleobases is being replaced by an alternative family of (equally primordial) heterocycles. We have found that oligomer sequences tagged with one of the members of the alternative nucleobase family are capable of cross-pairing with RNA and DNA in four different backbone series. This finding call for a comprehensive extension of these studies in a variety of directions.

Description: SELF CONSISTENT SOLAR ENERGETIC PARTICLE ACCELERATION AT EVOLVING SHOCKS ASSOCIATED WITH CORONAL MASS INJECTIONS Under the National Objective to iStudy the Earth System from space and develop new space-based and related capabilities for this purpose the proposed work is specifically concerned with the NASA objective to ;Explore the Sun-Earth System and its effects on Earth, the Solar System, and the space environmental conditions that will be experienced by human explorers. The proposal fits in with the Targeted Investigations element of the Living With A Star Targeted Research and Technology (LWST) Program under which it addresses the Focused Science Topic ishock acceleration of solar energetic particles by interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs)i. Time-dependent numerical solutions of the equations of fundamental kinetic focused transport and acceleration theory for energetic charged particles, kinetic wave excitation and transport theory, and MHD theory for CME shock evolution will be employed to achieve a fully self-consistent time-dependent model of solar energetic particle (SEP) acceleration at propagating interplanetary CME shocks from the Sun to Mars with the minimum number of simplifying assumptions. A few fully self-consistent SEP models that are based on transport and acceleration theory exist, but are either analytical, or semi-numerical such as the current C'niversity of California Riverside (UCR) model. The existing models are subject to a number of assumptions such as near-isotropic particle distributions at and downstream of the CME shock that need further investigation. The SEP model that we propose, which can be viewed as a logical extension of the current UCR model, will be used for this purpose, and for comparison of simulation resuIts with specific SEP events. Thus we expect to achieve an enhanced understanding of the significant complexities of time-dependent SEP acceleration that arises at an evolving CME shock (e.g., self-consistent wave generation by SEPs streaming away from the shock and the role of quasi-perpendicular shocks), and how this relates to the formation of radiation hazards between the Sun and Mars.

Description: SBIR PHASE III AWARD FOR THE ELECTROMAGNETICALLY CLEAN SOLAR ARRAY TECHNOLOGY READINESS DEVELOPMENT.  The objective of this program is to increase the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of the Electromagnetically Clean Solar Array concept that was developed in a NASA Phase 1 SBIR to TRL 4.  This program shall target achievement of TRL 6 prototype panel tested in relevant environments, by completing the critical design of a solar panel and testing material coupons and modular panels to a variety of simulated and combined space environments. Using the materials developed in prior research for silicone lenses, the Contractor shall perform ITO conductive coating development.  The Contractor shall fabricate coupons of the conductive integral cover/shield material, using at least two conductive coating approaches.  Conductivity requirement for the coating will be established using the MMS mission requirements based on a calculation of likely integral shield module size, maximum permissible electrical bias, and plasma environment.  Triple Junction (TJ) solar cells will be used to test cover transmittance in the spectral range of interest before and after coating.  Some coupons with successful coating adhesion and transmissivity will be subjected to thermal cycling environment to assure that required electrical sheet resistance values are maintained to the calculated requirement level. Using additional coupons fabricated from above, the Contractor shall subject the silicone and coating material to additional space environments in order to evaluate their durability.  Combined and sequential environment testing will be performed.  Coupons will be tested for their transmissivity based on solar photovoltaic response using typical Triple Junction (TJ) cells before and after each environmental exposure.  The test environments will include thermal life cycling, outgassing, UV/VUV, and radiation.  To assess the potential for self-contamination, the Contractor shall perform some UV/VUV testing on coupons that have been through the outgassing thermal bake-out test.

Description: IMPACTS ON TITAN AND THE PRODUCTION, EJECTION, AND DELIVERY OF DARK MATERIAL TO IAPETUS, HYPERION, AND RHEA We propose a novel hypothesis for the well-known and puzzling hemispheric dichotomy of Saturn ' s moon Iapetus (Cassini Regio): that the dark hemisphere is coated with a layer of organic material that has its origin in gas and solid material that was shocked by impacts into the atmosphere and surface of Titan, chemically processed, and ejected into circum-Saturnian space, where it encountered the leading face of Iapetus in its orbit. In particular, we propose that the same impact that created the 440-km diameter crater Menrva near Titan ' s apex point also supplied the material for Cassini Regio. We will test this hypothesis by means of hydrodynamic simulations, orbital integrations, and calculations of chemical processing of impact material. We will perform calculations of the impact of comets into the atmosphere and surface of Titan to assess the viability of our hypothesis. We will also determine the surface effects of airbursts leading potentially to observable traces like the so-called " dark shadows " on Venus. We will carry out integrations of test particles launched from the surface by impacts to determine the fate ejecta from the impact and material launched by the impact plume. We will assess the likelihood that material reaches Iapetus as well as the intervening moon Hyperion and how efficient the process will be. We will also calculate whether material is likely to reach the inner moons of the system such as Rhea, a crucial test of impactor material. We will use tools which have been previously developed by the PI and Co-Is (a three-dimensional hydrodynamical code, an orbit integrator, and a chemical evolution code). The codes have been extensively validated and applied to analogous environments such as the atmosphere of Venus and the Shoemaker-Levy 9 impacts. The proposed work is highly relevant to the goals of the Outer Planets research program. In particular, the proposed work involves interpretation of results from the Cassini mission, improving the understanding of the outer Solar System, and the developing basic theory for fundamental geophysical processes that have shaped prominent features on the surfaces of Saturn ' s satellites.

Description: Techniques For Single Molecule Biological Physics The ability to manipulate and detect in real-time the dynamics of single biological molecules provides direct information that remains out of reach of traditional ensemble methods. Mechanistic details such as the conformational changes of an enzyme molecule during catalysis, the dependence of applied force and torque on the efficiency of a molecular motor, the heterogeneity and sub-population classification of nominally identical molecules and the coordination of multiple events in a complex biological process, are all readily accessible to single-molecule experiments. In this Project we propose to further develop single-molecule methods for studies of biological systems. Specifically, we propose to increase the time resolution of wide-field fluorescence-resonance-energy-transfer (FRET) imaging beyond 10msec. This will allow important transient intermediates in the translation cycle of single Ribosomes to be observed for the first time. We further propose to develop two single-molecule mechanical manipulation methods. In the first one we will construct an apparatus that can apply torque to single bio-molecules with sensitivity better than 1pN. We expect this setup to allow studies of the RNA Polymerase II rotary motor. In the second we will combine Atomic-Force-microscopy with single-molecule FRET to simultaneously detect the unbinding events and the topology of cadherin molecule complexes. Finally, we propose to develop a method to detect trafficking of single molecules in living cells by photo activated fluorescent proteins. We will apply this method in identifying the presence or absence of a signaling molecule in endosomes that are actively transported during neuronal signaling.

Description: Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) Classification, Cassini Data Analysis and Particle Concentration and Aggregation by Turbulence We propose to classify and statistically analyze the near and far infrared spectra of planetary surfaces. Specifically we will investigate the stratigraphic relationship between the materials exposed by evaluating the compositional variability using spectral data obtained from orbiting spacecraft. Hogan and Roush (2006) describe an unsupervised classification scheme based on Kohonen self-organizing maps (SOMs) that automatically determines the number of clusters. In this work the SOM scheme was applied to thermal infrared spectra where spectral features are chiefly associated with vibrational transitions of molecular units. In a second paper (Roush and Hogan (2007) the SOM classifier was applied to shorter near infrared wavelengths where the spectral features are mainly due to electronic rather than vibrational transitions. The chief data to be analyzed include spectral measurements from the Thermal Emission Spectrometer of the Mars Global Surveyor, and measurements obtained by the visible and near infrared (OMEGA) spectrometer ofthe European Mars Express mission. Description: SEARCH FOR TRACES OF LIFE IN EARTH'S OLDEST ROCKS We aim at establishing criteria for distinguishing between biogenic and inorganic carbon and to apply them to the search for remnants of life in Earth's oldest sedimentary rocks, found in the Isua Supracrustal Belt (ISB) in southern West Greenland. Our earlier work has revealed that isotopically fractionated carbon, previously thought to be the hallmark of biogenic carbon, is actually a common product of disproportionation of ferrous carbonate (siderite). Extensive beds of such graphite bearing siderite formed upon injection of hot fluids into sequences of surface related ISB rocks when they were buried deep in the crust at high temperature and pressure. Before this was realized, such isotopically light carbon in the form of crystalline graphite was commonly considered biogenic and to represent the oldest and most strongly altered carbonaceous remnants of primitive life forms. The ferrous carbonate beds in which this graphite occurs were thought to be shallow water counterparts of the sedimentary banded iron formations (BIF) that we found to be practically devoid of syngenetic carbon. In contrast a recently discovered graded bed formation in the ISB contains layers of carbonaceous shale which is clearly of sedimentary origin. This material is one of the targets of our proposed investigation. Included in our study is also a series of carbon deposits from younger Archean and Proterozoic rocks in Africa, Australia and Scandinavia that are less strongly altered, as well as fluid deposited inorganic graphite from Greenland and Spain. A promising opportunity for recognizing biogenic carbon depends on the finding that carbonaceous material of biogenic origin at the level of metamorphism found in the ISB or lower retains non-graphitic puckered layer structures formed by the incorporation of characteristic defects. In contrast, fluid-deposited inorganic carbon crystallizes as graphite. High resolution structural studies of different types of Archean carbon thus form an important part of the study. We find that the carbon isotope fractionation in all samples varies over a relatively large range from particle to particle. The sources of this variability? isotopic exchange vs. heterogeneity in the source material or in the disproportionation catalysts remain to be investigated a.o. by detailed petrographic analysis of the host rock Residual bioorganic nitrogen and hydrogen have in the past been successfully exploited as indicators of progressive organic carbon maturation. Our analyses of the content and thermal release of nitrogen in carbon samples from the ISB has shown that inorganic nitrogen, accompanied by argon, is incorporated in graphite and carbonaceous matter from crustal fluids and superposed on the organic component. Further attempts will be made to distinguish between these sources by mode and strength of bonding of these gases. The techniques developed will be applicable also to defining the origin of carbonaceous matter if found on Mars
