Description: CHEMICAL CLOCKS FOR THE UPPER TROPOSPHERE AND MEASUREMENTS OF NO2, TOTAL PNs, TOTAL ANs AND HNO3 DURING TC4 Nitrogen oxides (NOy) are a central part of the engine of atmospheric chemistry and of the coupling between the atmosphere and biosphere. In the upper troposphere, the focus of this proposal, nitrogen oxides are dramatically affected by convection and lightning. Convection scrubs HNO3 and lofts NO2 from the planetary boundary layer. Convection is also associated with lightning which is one of the major sources of NOx to the troposphere. The resulting NOx is primarily deposited in the outflow of convective storms. The combined effects of convection and lightning produce extremely high ratios of NOx to HNO3 that then undergo photochemical evolution toward a steady state. This ratio provides a clock that can be used to evaluate the time an air parcel has been in the upper troposphere since it was convectively lofted. The clock also provides a clear diagnostic (by providing a uniform measure of the time of initialization by convection) for evaluating the extent of mixing of boundary layer air into the UT by storm's at least when a sufficiently broad statistical sampling of a region is obtained. We propose to 1) continue investigating the utility of this clock for understanding dynamical, radiative and chemical processes in the upper troposphere with observations from TC4 and INTEX-B, 2) to make measurements of NO2, total peroxy nitrtotal , total alkyl nitrates and HNO3 from the DC-8 during the TC4 Costa Rica experiment, and 3) continue to investigate the effects of lightning and convection on the shape of the tropospheric NO2 column for the purpose of evaluating the accuracy of OMI NO2 retrievals.

Description: SPIDER:  A LARGE ANGULAR SCALE MILLIMETER-WAVE POLARIMETER We propose SPIDER: a new long-duration balloon experiment to map the polarization ofthe CMB over more than half of the sky at 80,100,145, 225 and 275 GHz. SPIDER has 3 scientific goals: (I) precisely determine the optical depth to scattering of CMB photons since reionization, fixing the epoch of reionization (ii) characterize the polarized mm-wave emission from interstellar dust on large (1 degree) angular scales and (iii) search for the B-mode polarization signal that would be imprinted in the CMB by a Cosmic Gravitational-wave Background (CGB). SPIDER complements the frequency coverage (23,33, 41,64, 94 GHz) pf WMAP with higher sensitivity, and the relatively small sky coverage (few percent) of all currently funded sub-orbital experiments. The frequency coverage and high sensitivity provide a means to separate the polarized emission from interstellar dust from the polarization ofthe CMB. The sky coverage provides a means of measuring the large angular scale features in the polarization power spectrum associated with re-ionization, and allows the SPIDER data to be used in concert with the WMAP data to study the correlations 6f polarized synchrotron and dust emission on large angular scales. SPIDER complements both Planck and WMAP by incorporating a high-performance polarization modulator, and Planck by using highly redundant and cross-linked scan strategy, to achieve high polarimetric fldelity. SPIDER is both a scientific and technical pathfinder for a future orbital mission (CMBpol). SPIDER will help to determine the nature ofthe Galactic foregrounds which will ultimately limit the search for the signature of CGB, and will test scan strategies, polarization modulation methods, optics and detector technologies that are appropriate to CMBpol. In the absence of foregrounds, SPIDER's sky coverage and sensitivity allow detection of the CGB characterized by a tensor to scalar ratio of r = 0.04 (3 sigma).

Description: The Multi-Agent Architecture for Coordinated, Responsive Observations  Remote sensing missions for earth science provide a wealth of information to help us understand the dynamics of our planet. However, the current stovepipe operational model of remote sensing missions, i.e., a single spacecraft transmitting data to dedicated ground operations centers (Fig. 1), introduces untenable latencies in developing data prod-ucts that hinder model building and refine-ment as well as timely responses for hazard mitigation. Future missions will operate as part of a sensor web (Fig. 2) comprised of ^interlinked platforms with onboard information processing systems capable of orchestrat-ing real-time collaborative operations [1]. The Multi-agent Architecture for Coordi-nated, Responsive Observations (MACRO), an extension of our current work on the Adap-tive Network Architecture (ANA) is a natural technology for enabling the deployment and operation of a sensor web. To do this, we will incorporate detailed models of ablation, viscous heating, and radiative heating. Because many of the projectiles found in Stardust are fragmented and deposited along the cavity walls, it is important that the thermal history of the track walls be known. The proposed research will synthesize previous, but separate work, that has been done on the physics of the capture process and the physics of the impact cavity formation in aerogels. Description: Dynamics of the Solar Tachocline: The Creation and Evolution of Buoyant Magnetic Structures The current paradigm for the operation of the solar magnetic cycle relates the surface magnetic activity to the emergence of a strong toroidal magnetic field from below. It is believed that this strong toroidal field is likely generated from weak seed poloidal field by the inductive stretching action of strong localised velocity shear in the solar tachocline, a region bridging the mismatched velocity profiles of the differentially-rotating convection zone and the solid-body rotating inner radiative zone. It is further believed that the induced field somehow generates strong toroidal magnetic structures that rise by magnetic buoyancy through the solar convection zone to emerge as active regions. We propose to continue our investigations of the fully nonlinear mechanisms involved in these processes via numerical simulations of the full MHD equations and supportive analytical work. We will continue our studies of the ability of velocity shear interacting with magnetic field to create buoyant magnetic structures, both directly as "tubes'' and via instabilities of magnetic layers in the presence of shear. From earlier studies, we have already found that magnetic structures can indeed be created from seed field via shear and magnetic buoyancy mechanisms in various configurations. These structures may visually resemble our notion of an Idealised,isolated magnetic "flux tube'' but in reality are dynamically substantially different. We intend to investigate the generation and long-time evolution of such non-idealised structures further, in order to assess their relationship to idealised tubes and to categorise their intrinsic properties. We will also extend our analyses of this system's remarkable ability to operate as a dynamo complete with cyclic behaviour, polarity reversals and periods of inactivity. In particular, we will test the influence of background turbulence on the dynamo efficiency. We will subsequently examine the requirements demanded for these more realistic structures to rise successfully through a convective background to appear like active regions, or the processes involved in their destruction and possible recycling as poloidal field ("alpha-effect''-like mechanisms) both in the presence of rotation and without. We will design and extract observable characteristics, such as the strengths and geometries of the structures and especially any helical content, so that a comparison with solar observation data (such as that from SOHO, TRACE, STEREO, Ulysses and the forthcoming SDO mission) may reveal insight into the dynamics in the solar interior.

Description: SYNCHROTRON ANALYSES OF STARDUST SAMPLES The Stardust cometary particles collected in aerogel are without doubt the most technically challenging extraterrestrial samples ever returned. The captured particulate materials are buried deep in the aerogel collectors, are intimately mixed with aerogel, and are widely dispersed in long tracks that are orders of magnitude larger in scale than the particles themselves. Optical microscopy and tomography gives almost no useful information about the contents of tracks or the composition or mineralogy of individual particles. Valuable and limited TEM time is best spent on the most interesting and valuable particles. Were we propose to use multiple beamlines at the Advanced Light Source (ALS) at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, coordinated with each other and with TEM and SIMS analyses at other institutions, to conduct mineralogical and organics surveys of entire tracks in culmine (in keystones) in Stardust samples and to do detailed analyses on progressively smaller scales to characterize these samples. This will lead to quantitative mineralogical surveys of tracks, rapid identification and targeting of particularly important but apparently rare mineral phases (e.g., CAI-like materials, chondrule-like materials, fine-grained chondritic materials), identification of organic-rich tracks, quantitative surveys of minor elements and forsteritic content of olivines, and analysis of functional groups and mineral associations in organic-rich particles. These analyses will be done in coordination with TEM and SIMS analyses of the same samples by colleagues at the University of Washington and at the University of Hawaii.

THE SCHEME WAS FIRST ADAPTED FROM A REGIONAL MODEL.  THE CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME INTO THE GLOBAL MODEL PROVIDES AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXAMINE THE EFFECT OF PLUME-RISE ON LONG RANGE TRANSPORT.  THE CAM SIMULATION WITH THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SHOWS A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT OF THE AGREEMENTS BETWEEN THE MODELED AND AIRCRAFT-MEASURED VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CO OVER SOUTHERN AFRICA BIOMASS BURNING. EFFECTIVE LOFTING OF LARGE CONCENTRATION OF CO BY THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM ALSO HAS IMPLICATION FOR LOCAL AIR QUALITY FORECAST IN AREAS AFFECTED BY OTHER FIRE-RELATED POLLUTANTS.

Description: Vertical redistribution of short-lived chemicals significantly impacts the photochemistry of the middle and upper troposphere. In the tropics, this redistribution occurs primarily through convection. Massive amounts of convection occur in the period between June and September in the tropical eastern Pacific region. The Tropopause Transition Layer (TTL) is extremely cold - with the cold point occasionally reaching temperatures below 185K. Convective influence is pervasive with outflow from convection dominating the dynamical control on the chemistry; ozone concentrations in the immediate outflow are extremely low - values consistent with significant amounts of boundary layer air injected into the upper troposphere. The convective environment itself is exceedingly complex involving both multiple phase changes and physical entrainment and detrainment. Combined with the chemical boundary conditions in the entraining flows, these physical processes exert dominant control on the chemical composition of the outflow in the upper troposphere. We propose here to study this multiphase chemistry and investigate the net result of this transport mechanism on upper tropospheric chemistry. We propose to operate the Caltech Chemical Ionization Mass Spectrometers on NASA's DC8 aircraft during the TC4 campaign. The measurement of a suite of acids and hydrogen peroxides, made simultaneously with other chemicals and aerosols will allow testing of several hypotheses about the influence that short-lived chemicals have on the boundary conditions for the Tropical Tropopause Layer (TTL) and the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTILS) more generally. Because of the large variation in Henry's law coefficients, measurements of these gases in the column adjacent to a convective plume can provide constraints on entrainment and detrainment. Finally, as part of NASA's validation effort, these observations will provide profiles of trace gases for evaluation of satellite retrievals.

Each sample collected for TC4 will be assayed at our home laboratory for selected C2-C10 nonmethane hydrocarbons (NMHCs), selected C1-C2 halocarbons (including CFCs, CH3Br and CH3I), C1-C5 alkyl nitrates, DMS and OCS. Depending on the final payload and science team needs, we hope to add CH212, phosgene, and selected OVOCs such as acetaldehyde to the list, but at this point our measurements are still considered exploratory. All gases will be reported at detection limits and time resolutions that are at or better than those requested in the white paper list of flight measurement priorities. The data that we have generated as part of numerous previous NASA missions have made highly successful contributions to those projects. We have many times demonstrated the power of NMHC and halocarbon tracers to diagnose oceanic sources, urbanlcontinental, biomass burning, natural vegetative sources and air mass transport over time. This tracer capability is crucial to answering many of the fundamental TC4 science questions, such as #Does convective lofting of short lived halocarbons substantially increases the bromine content of the lowermost stratosphere? If so, are the lofted short lived bromocarbons associated more strongly with maritime convection than with continental convection?# However, with such a large suite of gases, our most interesting findings are not always ones that we have anticipated. This proposal assumes that we will collect our typical complement of 6-7 sets of 24-canisters during each DC-8 flight (i.e., up to 168 samples per flight). This equates to a sampling frequency of every 4-5 minutes on the horizontal flight legs, and every 1-2 minutes on selected vertical ascent/descents. Sample collection on board the aircraft will be coordinated with other experiments and any intercomparison activities, so as to optimize sample overlap with other groups. We also propose to provide back-up capability for the in-situ CO and CH4 measurements. The desired measurement frequency for these gases is on the order of seconds, which we cannot provide. However, if problems arise on either of the onboard COlCH4 analytical systems, as occurred during many of the INTEX-NA flights, we are prepared to assay our whole air samples for one or both of these gases, as needed. In past NASA missions we have collaborated with Professor Elliot Atlas and propose to continue that collaboration during TC4. Professor Atlas plans to propose for the high altitude airborne platform (WB-57). Our two groups will use common whole air standards and exchange approximately 5% of the samples for intercomparison.

Description: METHODS FOR SOURCE DETECTION AND PARAMETER ESTIMATION IN LISA DATA ANALYSIS This proposal concerns some LISA data challenges that have a high priority for near-term solution. The first challenge is the development ofa supermassive black hole merger (SMBH) search pipeline, as part of the upcoming Mock LISA Data Challenge. We currently plan a two-stage search pipeline. Since 5MBH mergers are chirping signals that will typically have a high signal-to-noise ratio, it should be possible to identify them, and get initial estimates of source parameters, by looking for tracks in the time-frequency plane. Using these initial estimates to narrow the search space, the second stage will employ a template-based matched filter search to confirm detection and eliminate any time-frequency tracks that turn out to be false alarms. We plan to adapt currently-existing LIGO binary-black-hole search codes for the second stage. The 5MBH search pipeline will be developed by Cutler and Vallisneri, in collaboration with CaltechlLIGO postdocs Brown and Sutton, as well as Caltech grad students Lovelace and Mandel. We also plan to resolve several issues that are closely related to the 5MBH search. First, since only post-Newtonian waveforms (not fully general relativistic ones) are likely to be available as templates, parameter estimation will suffer from systematic errors due to inaccurate templates, in addition to random errors due to detector noise. How large are the systematic errors likely to be? We plan to address this question using a linearized formalism that we have developed (closely analogous to the standard Fisher matrix estimate of the size of random errors), as well the more brute-force approach of simply simulating the parameter estimation process with slightly inaccurate templates. Another important LISA data analysis challenge is to develop a robust method for simultaneously fitting the data to a physical model containing all the different source types. We imagine that individual, stand-alone searches (one for 5MBH mergers, one for EMRIs, etc.) will provide initial lists of candidates and their parameters, but that some iterative fitting scheme will be required before one can come very close to the final source catalog. Once one has come reasonably close to the correct catalog, a plausible final sttip is to use a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm to find the best fit and the probability distribution on parameter space. We propose to implement such an MCMC "finisher" algorithm. We will generate a synthetic data set containing a realistic distribution of all sources, start off the MCMC algorithm reasonably close to the right answer, and see if the MCMC code can indeed finish the job (or, more precisely, see how close one has to start to the right answer for the MCMC algorithm to be able to finish the job). Jeff Crowder, who has considerable experience both in MCMC methods, will be joining us as a postdoc at JPL, and he will play an important role in helping develop the "finisher". A natural byproduct of this work is that we will find out quasi-empirically how parameter estimation is affected by cross-correlations between sources, in the realistic case where there are thousands of distinguishable sources of several types. In summary, we propose to develop important tools for use in LISA data analysis, thereby providing theoretical support to one of the Einstein Observatories. We will demonstrate that much of the theoretical underpinnings of LISA data analysis have reached a mature state, by producing software that works on simulated LISA data. Naturally, this exercise will also tend to uncover any problems related to LISA data analysis that have previously been overlooked. This theoretical work is therefore important for the eventual success ofthe LISA mission. FORM NRESS-

The VMO registries for both data and services are designed to make it easy for suppliers to make their resources available and update information regarding the resources. The VMO works with investigators to design data products that will remain scientifically useful even when the investigators are no longer involved. The financial resources available to data and service suppliers are extremely limited. Therefore the VMO requires only a small effort to get started and has minimal on-going costs. Description: REORIENTATION AND CONVECTION IN MID-SIZED ICY SATELLITES Two of the key objectives of the OPR program are to understand the evolution of outer Solar System satellites, and to define the dynamical processes operating. In this proposal, we intend to focus on a particular dynamical process -true polar wander - which is likely to have played an important role in determining both the evolution and the present appearance of mid-sized (radius 200-800 km) icy satellites. We will also carry out investigations of how convection (either thermal or compositional) on such satellites may lead to polar wander. In doing so, we will develop an improved theoretical understanding of both reorientation and convection as applied to icy satellites. We will also predict some likely observable consequences of reorientation, in particular crater distributions, deformation patterns and gravity anomalies. Ultimately, such predictions will allow us to place constraints on the interiors and evolutions of satellites where reorientation is thought to have occurred. Although some use will be made of Voyager images, looking for evidence of reorientation is not the emphasis of this proposal; rather, it is to develop the theoretical tools required, and to make predictions which will become testable with future observations.

Description: INVESTIGATING THE LOCALIZATION AND BIOSYNTHESIS OF 2-METHYLOPANIODS The advent of oxygenic photosynthesis was a pivotal event in the formation of the modern biosphere and the evolution of complex life. However, our constraints on the timing of this event are presently very rough. The occurrence of molecular fossils known as 2-methylhopanes in the rock record has been taken as evidence that photosynthetically-derived 02 first appeared on Earth at least 2.7 billion years ago. This assumption arises from the fact that modern cyanobacteria, organisms that engage in oxygenic photosynthesis, produce significant quantities of 2-methylbacteriohopanepolyols (2MeBHPs), progenitors of 2-methylhopanes. Nevertheless, a number of independent proxies indicate that a major global redox transition occurred roughly 400 miLLion years later (2.3 Ga). If cyanobacteria were present and engaging in oxygenic photosynthesis at 2.7 Ga, why did it take so long for the Earth to become oxygenated? Is the assumption that 2-methylhopanes are biomarkers for oxygenic photosynthesis correct, or might they reflect some other property of cyanobacteria that is decoupled from their capacity to generate 02? To date, no evidence exits that 2MeBHPs and oxygenic photosynthesis are functionally related. Based on recent evidence, we hypothesize that the presence of 2-MeBHPs may be related to the localization of a carbon-concentrating mechanism (CCM) in the membranes of cyanobacteria, rather than to oxygen production. If correct, this hypothesis implies that 2-methylhopanes record the evolution of cyanobacterial autotrophy rather than oxygenic photosynthesis per se. The specific aims outlined below will lay the groundwork for exploring the function of 2 MeBHPs in cyanobacteria. 1.) Determine where 2-MeBHPs localize within the cell. Cyanobacteria possess a relatively complex membrane arrangement, composed of an outer membrane (OM), a plasma membrane (CM), and a photosynthetically-active thylakoid membrane system (TM) derived from the CM. We will isolate these subcellular fractions and quantitatively analyze the distribution pattern of BHPs and 2-MeBHPs within two different cyanobacteria: Phormidiurn luridum and Synechocystis PCC 6803. 2.) Characterize the conditions under which 2-MeBHPs are produced. Through quantitative analysis of the production of 2-MeBHPs and measurement of carbon uptake rates by P. luridum and PCC 6803, we will test the hypothesis that conditions that affect the CCM also affect 2-MeBHP production. 2-MeBHP production will be measured under conditions where pC02, salinity and pH are independently varied. In addition, we will examine the relationship between 2-MeBHP production and mode of metabolism (photoautotrophy v. (photo)heterotrophy), as well as its relationship to growth rate and temperature. 3.) Identify the gene (or set of genes) that encodes the enzyme that methylates the C-2 atom of 2-MeBHPs. Standard techniques in bacterial genetics will be utilized to determine the gene(s) that are responsible for C-2 methylation of BHPs. One of two approaches will be used, depending on the results of the localization and regulation experiments: (i) targeted mutations in pce 6803 will be made based on microarray analyses, (ii) DNA from P.luridum will be expressed in PCC 6803 and the methylase gene will be identified by identifying the smallest gene fragment that confers the ability to make 2-MeBHPs. This collaborative effort will reveal novel aspects of biomarker biosynthesis and function, and, thus, promises to improve our ability to interpret the evolution of metabolism on Earth. Description: AFRICAN MERIDIAN B-FIELD EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH (AMBER) ARRAY This proposal seeks support to establish AMBER (African Meridian B-field Education and Research) magnetometer array in the African continent during the IHY. The AMBER array contains four magnetometers and spans across the geomagnetic equator from L of 1 to an L of 1.4. In addition to filling the largest land-based gap in global magnetometer coverage, the AMBER array will address two fundamental areas of space physics: (1) the processes governing electrodynamics of the equatorial ionosphere as a function of latitude (or L-shell), local time, longitude, magnetic activity, and season, and (2) ULF pulsation strength and its connection with equatorial electrojet strength at low/mid-latitude regions. Satellite observations show unique equatorial ionospheric structures in the African sector, though these have not been confirmed by observation from the ground due to lack of ground-based instruments in the region. In order to have a complete global understanding of equatorial ionosphere motions, deployment of ground-base magnetometers in Africa is essential. One focus of IHY will be the deployment of networks of small instruments, including the development of research infrastructure in developing nations through the United Nations Basic Space Science (UNBSS) Small Instrument Array. Therefore, we propose to deploy the AMBER magnetometer array in partnership with parallel US funded GPS receivers in Africa to study electrodynamics that governs equatorial ionosphere motions. While AMBER routinely observes the F region plasma drift mechanism (drift), the GPS stations will monitor the structure of plasma at low/mid-latitudes in the African sectors. In addition to new scientific discoveries and advancing the space science research into Africa by establishing scientific collaborations between scientists in the developing and developed nations, the program also contributes to developing the basic science of heliophysics through cross disciplinary studies of universal process. This includes the creation of sustainable research/training infrastructure within the developing nations (Africa).

GATOR-GCMOM WILL BE RUN IN GLOBAL-THROUGH-LOCAL NESTED MODE WITH HIGH-RESOLUTION GRIDS PLACED OVER ONE WORLD REGION IN WHICH STRONG SPATIAL GRADIENTS IN AEROSOL OPTICAL DEPTH ARE IDENTIFIED FROM MODTS DATA. THE TARGETED AREA WILL MOST LIKELY BE EITHER NEAR BRAZIL, CHINA, OR THE WEST COAST OF THE U.S., THE RESOLUTION OF THE FINEST NESTED GRID WILL BE 4-5 KM. SIMULATIONS WILL BE RUN FOR TWO MONTHS OF THE YEAR, TO BE DETERMINED. FOR THE SELECTED REGION, THE MODEL WILL BE RAN TWICE. THE FIRST WITH ALL AEROSOLS, AND THE SECOND WITH OTHER BIOMASS BURNING AEROSOLS (OR ANTHROPOGENIC AEROSOLS, DEPENDING ON LOCATION). AFTER THE FIRST RUN RESULTS WILL BE COMPARED WITH OBSERVATIONS TO DETERMINE WHETHER THE MODEL CORRECTLY REPRODUCES THE AEROSOL CHARACTERISTICS AS MEASURED BY SATELLITE. RESULTS WILL ALSO BE EXAMINED TO DETERMINE WHETHER THE MODEL REPRODUCES CLOUD, PRECIPITATION AND RADIATION FIELDS REASONABLY AND WHETHER IT REPRODUCES THE OBSERVED CORRELATIONS BETWEEN THESE VARIABLES. THIS IS AN IMPORTANT CHECK OF THE MODEL PHYSICS AND EMISSIONS. ASSUMING THAT THE MODEL ADEQUATELY SIMULATES THE AEROSOL-CLOUD ENVIRONMENT AS OBSERVED FROM SATELLITE, WE WILL ANALYZE THE DIFFERENCES BETWEEN RUNNING THE MODEL WITH ELEVATED AEROSOL AND RUNNING WITHOUT SUCH AEROSOLS. ONLY THE MODEL CAN UNAMBIGUOUSLY SEPARATE AEROSOL EFFECTS FROM METEOROLOGICAL EFFECTS, BUT ONLY THE OBSERVATIONS CAN HOLD THE MODEL ACCOUNTABLE TO REALITY.  DIFFERENCES BETWEEN SIMULATIONS WILL BE ANALYZED IN GRAPHICAL AND STATISTICAL FORM. RESULTS, INCLUDING A COMPARISON WITH SATELLITE DATA, WILL BE WRITTEN UP FOR PUBLICATION.

Description: THE COSMIC INFRARED BACKGROUND EXPERIMENT This is a Co-I proposal; PI proposal by Dr. James Bock. Light from the first generation of stars, formed from primordial gas in the early universe, has so far eluded direct detection. However, these first stars will produce characteristic signatures in the extragalactic background at near-infrared wavelengths. These distinctive features, in particular the redshifted Ly-cutoff spectral feature, and a characteristic fluctuation power spectrum, may be detectable with a specialized instrument. Recent observations of the absolute intensity and spatial fluctuations in the near-infrared background indicate a component to the background that cannot be explained by the redshift-integrated emission from known galaxy populations. This component could be due to luminous first-light high-mass stars or mini-quasars forming at high redshift (z - 10-20). However these background measurements are prone to systematic errors and first need confirmation. We propose the Cosmic Infrared Background ExpeRiment (CIBER) to search for signatures of first-light galaxy formation in the near-infrared background. The instrument consists of two wide-field cameras, a low-resolution absolute spectrometer, and a narrow-band spectrometer. The wide-field cameras will search for spatial fluctuations in the background on medium angular scales where the first-light galaxy spatial power spectrum peaks, but which has been poorly covered by previous experiments. The cameras have the necessary combination of sensitivity, wide field of view with sufficient spatial resolution, and multiple bands to make a definitive measurement. CIBER will conclusively determine if the fluctuations reported by Spitzer arise from first-light galaxies. The cameras observe in a single wide field of view, eliminating systematic errors associated with mosaicing. Two bands are chosen to maximize the first-light signal contrast, at 1.6 um near the expected spectral maximum, and at 0.8 urn, as a null test shorter than the redshifted Ly cutoff. We will jointly observe regions of the sky studied by Spitzer and ASTRO-F in order to accurately remove the contribution of local (z = 1-3) galaxies to the observed background fluctuations, and to cross correlate these independent data sets at 5 different wavelengths. The low-resolution spectrometer will search for the redshifted Lyman cutoff feature in the unexplored 0.7 - 1.8 um spectral region. The narrow-band spectrometer will trace zodiacal light using the intensity of a solar Fraunhofer line, providing an independent measurement of the zodiacal emission and a new systematic check of DIRBE zodiacal dust models. Description: THE COSMIC INFRARED BACKGROUND EXPERIMENT: COI BUDGET REQUEST FROM UC IRVINE  The extragalactic background, based on absolute measurements reported by DIRBE/COBE and IRTS at 1.2 and 2.2 urn, exceeds the brightness derived from galaxy counts by up to a factor 5. Furthermore, both DIRBE and the IRTS report fluctuations in the near-infrared sky brightness that appear to have an extra-galactic origin, but are much larger than expected from local (z = 1-3) galaxy clustering. These observations have led to speculation that a new class of high-mass stars (PopIII) or a .first-generation of mini-quasars may dominate the Universe at high-redshifts (z -10-30), which, in order to explain the excess in the near-infrared background, must be UV luminous but produce a limited amount of metals and X-ray photons. These sources may also be responsible for reionization the Universe between redshifts 10 and 20. Regardless of the extact nature of the sources, if a significant component of the near-infrared background comes from a a redshift greater than 10 population, theoretical models generically predict a prominent near-infrared spectral feature from the redshifted Lyman-alpha line and a distinctive spatial fluctuation power spectrum of background anisotropies at these wavelengths. We propose a rocket-borne instrument to search for signatures of high redshift star formation in the cosmic near-infrared extra-galactic background. The instrument (the Cosmic Infrared Background ExpeRiment, or CIBER) consists of a wide-field two-color camera, a low-resolution absolute spectrometer, and a high-resolution Fabry-Perot spectrometer. The CIBER low-resolution spectrometer will search for the redshifted Lyman-alpha feature in the unexplored 0.8 - 1.5 urn spectral region. The CIBER Fabry-Perot spectrometer, will trace zodiacal light using the intensity of a reflected near-infrared Fraunhofer absorption feature, providing an independent measurement of the zodiacal emission and a new systematic check ofDIRBE zodiacal dust models. The combination will systematically search for the infrared excess background light reported from DIRBE/IRTS data, compared with the small excess reported by HST at optical wavelengths. The CIBER cameras will search for spatial fluctuations in the background on angular scales from 10 degrees to 10 arcsec, where a high redshift source signature is expected to peak. This range of angular scales has been poorly covered by previous experiments. CIBER will have the necessary combination of sensitivity, wide field of view, and spatial resolution to make a definitive measurement. The CIBER imager will conclusively determine if the fluctuations reported by DIRBE and IRTS are extragalactic, with sufficient resolution to remove significant point source confusion, and will accurately measure their power spectrum.

Description: SATELLITE-BASED DYNAMICS IN TIBETAN PLATEAU IN THE CONTEXT OF GLOBAL CHANGE With a pronounced temperature rise of 0.16oC per decade, the Tibetan Plateau, sometimes called the "ROOF of the World," is one of the world is most vulnerable areas to global change. Tibetan lakes, at a density of 3.5%, serve as a sensitive indicator of global climate and water cycle variability. Tibetan lakes have shrunk greatly since the late Pleistocene, and they are currently continuing to experience changes in their distribution and inundation area. However, lake dynamics in the context of global change are not well understood due to the inaccessibility and inhospitable environment of this remote plateau. Therefore, the proposed research would quantify Tibetan lake dynamics using multi-temporal high-resolution satellite imagery and spatial information technologies. The defined study area covers approximately 1000 km by 600 km and contains thousands of lakes sensitive to global change. The proposed research is driven by three specific scientific questions, and seeks to (1) quantify both paleo (i.e., since the late Pleistocene) and recent (i.e., the past 30 years) spatial lake changes in the vast Tibetan Plateau; and (2) identify the driving mechanisms of observed lake changes. Using both high-resolution optical image data and digital elevation models, the paleo lake reconstructions will be achieved using preserved paleo lake shorelines, which are clearly visible in these datasets. Recent lake changes will be detected through data fusion of early Landsat data from the 1970 with more recent high-resolution data from Landsat and ASTER. For a subset of large lakes, modern lake dynamics will be assessed using high-temporal resolution satellite datasets as well as time series of satellite radar altimetry data to observe water level variations. The integrated GIs-based analysis of spatial patterns in lake dynamics and impact factors such as topographic, climatologic and hydrologic variables will facilitate our understanding of the driving mechanisms behind the observed changes. The proposed research would advance our knowledge about the hydroclimatology of the Tibetan Plateau and to the sensitivity. of the region to global change; and would specificaiiy address Question #3 in Water and Energy Cycle Focus Area of NASA Science Roadmap: "How are variations in water resources related to global climate variation?"

Description: MULTI CHIP MODULE MAGNETOMETER FOR PLANETARY AND LUNAR EXPLORATION SUMMARY: We propose a three-year effort to design and implement a multi chip module (MCM) state of the art vector fluxgate magnetometer. While the fluxgate magnetometer has a long history of successful space-based operations, we are not yet at the stage were many tens or even hundreds of magnetometers can be built for multi-spacecraft or multi-station (e.g lunar or Mars surface) deployment. The latest designs have achieved quite remarkable mass and power savings, but more can be achieved through the MCM design. In particular we expect to achieve a combined sensor and electronics board mass of < 150 g, with power consumption around 300 mW. Furthermore, the MCM implementation will enable us to mount the electronics near the sensor, which will enable us to reduce the cable mass to 25% of current values. In addition, the MCM lends itself to build to print implementation. The MCM magnetometer is deigned to address many questions related to planetary, lunar, and heliospheric sciences. Areas to be addressed include: identifying remanent fields on a variety of solar system bodies, such as Mars, the moon, and comets; probing the structure of moons, planets and comets through magnetic induction; deployment as part of an array of magnetoseismic stations on the moon; solar wind magnetic field measurements on flotillas of spacecraft; and measurements of remanent and induction magnetic fields on planetary rovers and balloons. Because of the low resource reuirement the MCM magnetometer is a candidate for inclusion on Discovery and New Horizons class missions, with the potential for significant enhancement of the science return for these class of missions. The MCM is also a candidate for Mars Exploration Program missions, possibly being deployed on rovers or as arrays of magnetometers deployed on the surface. The MCM has the potential for technology transfer through the demonstration of multi chip module technology for a space-based application.

Description: REMOTE SENSING OF CLIMATE CHANGE CONTROLLING PRODUCTION OF SMALL PELAGIC FISH (GRADUATE STUDENT-RYAN RYKACZEWSKI) Sardine and anchovy populations are responsible for more than 20% of global marine fish landings. Large, decadal-scale biomass fluctuations in these populations have long puzzled oceanographers and presented severe economic and social consequences to communities dependent on these fisheries. Investigation of ecosystem-based hypotheses relating climate changes to fish production has been restricted by the lack of time-series measurements of multiple environmental variables, and existing hypotheses do not provide the understanding necessary to predict how fisheries will vary under future climate conditions. Now, with the accumulation of atmospheric, hydrographic, and biologic data collected from satellites and ships, examination of more mechanistic hypotheses is possible. I propose a hypothesis relating changes in production of anchovy and sardine to variable wind stress and wind-stress curl. Coastal alongshore and equatorward wind stress results in rapid upwelling and production of large plankters. Upwelling resulting from wind-stress curl is slower, leading to production of small plankton. Anchovy feed efficiently on the large plankters produced by rapid upwelling, while sardine feed on small plankters resulting from slower upwelling. I propose to test this hypothesis by examining historical physical, chemical, biological, and fisheries relationships in the California Current Ecosystem (CCE). Data gathered from satellite scatterometers and shipboard anemometers will be used to measure changes in wind stress and wind-stress curl, and a high-resolution model will extend the time series of these measures. The hydrographic and biologic response to winds will be examined using satellite altimetry, radiometry, and ocean color. Archived cruise data will provide estimates of hydrographic conditions and concentrations of nutrients and chlorophyll. Anchovy and sardine biomasses have been estimated during various periods extending back to the 1930s. In addition to time series analyses, process studies are required to investigate the relationships between upwelling rate and plankter size. During springtime research cruises, plankter sizes will be characterized in various zones spanning the CCE. Remotely-sensed ocean color and sea-surface temperature will be used to select regions influenced by strong coastal upwelling, strong curl upwelling, and very weak or no upwelling. My dissertation research will enable prediction of how climate variability will influence economically valuable fish stocks; foster an understanding of the interactions among continents, oceans, atmosphere, and life; and serve to enhance our nation's scientific interests and food security. Given current uncertainties regarding the effects of global climate change on the world's ecosystems and the increasing exploitation of marine fish stocks, I think it is essential to make use of existing data to better understand the relationships between environmental change and fish production.

Description: Development of a Novel Modulator for CMB Polarization "B Mode" Detection (Graduate Student - Evan Bierman) Cosmic Microwave Background "B- mode" polarization is the "smoking gun" of the inflationary paradigm. However, in order to measure this signal, microwave polarization systematics and possibly a signal to noise ratio of one in a thousand must be overcome. The fully optimized polarimeter used for its detection should include a modulator to overcome these daunting challenges. Devices that use the Faraday rotation effect closely resemble a theoretically ideal modulator and are a promising answer to this need. Development of this technology, which is actively being used in other areas of research and communication, will maximize the efficiency of a CMB polarimeter.

Proved stowage and deployment techniques enable space flight application. We propose advancing 1) the basic fabrication technology and 2) the TRL level of MOST apertures for ground and space based apertures. The key resulting innovation is implementation of low areal density, compact roll stowable approaches to realize low mass, low cost reflective apertures for RF/Microwave to LIDAR. Other NASA and DOD applications are expected as precision and aperture size increase. The potential pay off of the proposed research can be summarized at the highest level as, "Less Mass, Less Cost" reflective doubly curved apertures. Once flight proven, the same basic aperture approach as well as possible microwave science applications, since all have similar or less restrictive surface figure requirements. Rather term, we see potential synergistic applications in the area of 1) very large diameter stowable/deployable diameter precision apertures to enable visible wavelength spectroscopy, and potentially imaging astronomy. Potential uses as components in solar concentrators for orbital power generation and solar thermal propulsion, and as sun shields and telescope apertures opening shields are also envisaged. This is a crosscutting technology that has many potential spin-off applications both for NASA and other Government and commercial organizations. NASA Applications have been discussed above. In the space arena, for other organizations applications for doubly curved reflective apertures exist from the RF Comm to Laser Comm and Earth Observation (both spectroscopic and imaging). Backpackable RF Comm apertures for emergency and remote location applications are possible as well. Description: CONSTRAINTS ON MARTIAN MAGNETIC HISTORY AND MAGNETIZATION FROM THE MAGNETIC SIGNATURES OF VOLCANOES AND IMPACT CRATERS ONE OF THE MOST EXCITING PLANETARY SCIENCE EVENTS IN RECENT YEARS WAS THE DISCOVERY OF STRONG MARTIAN CRUSTAL MAGNETISM [ACU    T AL., 1999]. THOUGH AN INTERNAL DYNAMO IS NO LONGER ACTIVE, MARTIAN CRUSTAL SOURCES IMPLY HUGE VOLUMES OF STRONGLY MAGNETIZED CRUSTAL MATERIALS, AND VIRTUALLY REQUIRE THE PRESENCE OF A STRONG DYNAMO FIELD AT ONE TIME. SIGNIFICANT SCIENTIFIC EFFORT HAS GONE TOWARDS CHARACTERIZING MARTIAN MAGNETISM, PARTLY BECAUSE OF ITS SHEER UNIQUENESS, BUT ALSO BECAUSE UNDERSTANDING THE MARTIAN DYNAMO IS OF FUNDAMENTAL SIGNIFICANCE IN UNDERSTANDING THE FORMATION AND EVOLUTION OF THE MARTIAN INTERIOR AND SURFACE. THE PROPERTIES OF THE CRUSTAL MAGNETIZATION PROVIDE INFORMATION ABOUT THE GEOLOGIC PROCESSES RESPONSIBLE FOR ITS FORMATION. CONSTRAINTS ON THE HISTORY OF THE DYNAMO WILL PROVIDE INFORMATION ABOUT THE THERMAL HISTORY OF THE INTERIOR, IN TURN INFORMING US ABOUT MARS' FORMATION AND GEODYNAMIC EVOLUTION. FINALLY, THE HISTORY OF THE DYNAMO MAY PROVE RELEVANT TO ATMOSPHERIC LOSS OVER TIME, WITH IMPLICATIONS FOR CLIMATE AND ASTROBIOLOGY. WE PROPOSE AN ANALYSIS USING MARS GLOBAL SURVEYOR (MGS) MAGNETOMETER AND ELECTRON REFLECTOMETER (MAG/ER) DATA TO DETERMINE CRUSTAL MAGNETIC FIELDS OVER A RANGE OF ALTITUDES, MGS MARS ORBITER LASER ALTIMETER (MOLA) DATA TO IDENTIFY VISIBLE AND BURIED IMPACT CRATERS, AND MARS EXPRESS (MEX) HIGH-RESOLUTION STEREO CAMERA (HRSC) DATA TO CONSTRAIN MAGMATIC HISTORY, WITH THE AIM OF MAGNETICALLY CHARACTERIZING THESE FEATURES, AND USING THESE OBSERVATIONS IN CONCERT WITH THERMAL AND MAGNETIC MODELING IN ORDER TO CONSTRAIN THE PROPERTIES OF MARTIAN CRUSTAL MAGNETIZATION AND THE HISTORY OF THE DYNAMO. USING THE RICH MGS DATASETS IN THIS MANNER, WITH MEX DATA, PROVIDES A UNIQUE OPPORTUNITY TO ENHANCE THE SCIENTIFIC RETURN FROM BOTH MISSIONS. WE PROPOSE A STUDY WITH THESE GOALS: GOAL 1: CHARACTERIZE THE MAGNETIC SIGNATURES OF MARTIAN VOLCANOES AND BOTH VISIBLE AND BURIED IMPACT CRATERS, AND COMPARE TO TERRESTRIAL AND LUNAR OBSERVATIONS. GOAL 2: MODEL THE MAGNETIC SIGNATURES OF VOLCANOES AND IMPACT CRATERS FOR A WIDE RANGE OF INITIAL CONDITIONS. GOAL 3: COMPARE MAGNETIC OBSERVATIONS WITH FORWARD MODELS IN ORDER TO CHARACTERIZE CURRENT MARTIAN CRUSTAL MAGNETIZATION AND PLACE CONSTRAINTS ON ITS FORMATION AND EVOLUTION. GOAL 4: DETERMINE HOW THE MAGNETIC SIGNATURES OF VOLCANOES AND IMPACT CRATERS VARY WITH AGE, IN ORDER TO PLACE CONSTRAINTS ON THE HISTORY OF THE MARTIAN DYNAMO, AND CONSIDER THE IMPLICATIONS FOR THE FORMATION AND GEOLOGIC EVOLUTION OF MARS. ACHIEVING THESE GOALS WILL LEAD TO A GREATER UNDERSTANDING OF MARS' MAGNETIC FIELDS AND THE EVOLUTION OF ITS INTERIOR, SURFACE AND ATMOSPHERE, AND THEY ARE THEREFORE HIGHLY RELEVANT TO THE NASA STRATEGIC GOALS AND OUTCOMES, INCLUDING STRATEGIC SUB-GOAL 3C: "ADVANCE SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE OF THE ORIGIN AND HISTORY OF THE SOLAR SYSTEM, THE POTENTIAL FOR LIFE ELSEWHERE, AND THE HAZARDS AND RESOURCES PRESENT AS HUMANS EXPLORE SPACE."

Description: MODELS OF NEBULAR ORGANIC CHEMISTRY We propose to investigate the origin and evolution of organic compounds in planetary systems, and their delivery to young planets. We seek to better understand the organic compounds generated and destroyed in the interstellar and proto-planetary environments, through observational, theoretical, and laboratory work.  We will examine the potential for and limitations to delivery of exogenous pre-biotic organics to planets, examining factors that enhance or restrict this potential. We will, for the first time, investigate the effect of astrophysical X-rays on the evolution of exogenous organics in proto-stellar disks. We will follow these factors over time, from the natal cloud core through the end of the late heavy bombardment ( 4.1 Ga). We will evaluate the possible role of exogenous organic material in terrestrial biogenesis. The proposed research will significantly improve our understanding of the nature of organics in other planetary systems, the processes affecting them, and the potential for delivering pre-biotic organic compounds to planets. The goal of the proposed theoretical work specifically proposed here is focused on determining the chemical composition of icy bodies and establishing their potential for delivering pre-biotic organic materials and water to the young Earth and other planets. This will be addressed through detailed chemical modeling, coupled with physical evolution, of the protosolar nebula.

Description: Current state-of-the-art climate prediction models (GCl/1s) project a ,vide range in global average surface temperature in the future. The high latitudes are the region with the largest range in projected temperature. In the high latitudes, sea ice reflects solar radiation back into space; when sea ice melts exposing the ocean, the region becomes 'warmer as more solar radiation is absorbed at the surface of the Earth. The distribution of sea ice therefore affects regional climate; in my proposal, I refer to this process as "sea ice albedo feedback" (SIAF). Current GCMs do not agree on their modeling of the climate impact of SIAF. The main reason that this occurs is that clouds are modeled differently by the GeMs. Like sea ice, clouds reflect solar radiation. If clouds are present where ice is melting, the effect of melting ice on the reflection of radiation at the surface will be reduced (solar radiation will still be reflected). The presence of clouds can therefore mask the effect of SIAF. This proposal outlines a framework for quantifying the masking effect of clouds on SIAF in satellite data and GCMs. I propose using satellite data to calculate observational values of the influence of clouds on SIAF in the Arctic and Antarctic. Observational calculations will be compared with current GCM values to quantify the influence of feedback inaccuracies in GCMs on the final modeled projections of climate change. This proposal aims to provide a framework to constrain these inaccuracies using observational data as a guide, and in so doing, constrain future climate projections. This proposal meets the Earth Science Division's goal to "Advance U.S. scientific, security, and economic interests through a robust space exploration program." The current lack of convergence between climate projection models makes it very difficult for policy makers to make informed economic and environmental policy decisions relating to climate change. This proposal aims at utilizing NASA satellite data to reduce the spread in projected Arctic and Antarctic climate change. This will directly reduce uncertainties surrounding the future climatic conditions of the high latitude regions. In the Arctic, the distribution of future sea ice is particularly tied to the strength of the SIAF. A high degree of confidence in sea ice distributions during Arctic summers would have dramatic implications for human activity in the Arctic, including navigation, global trade, and the economic development of coastal zones. More specifically, if an ice-free path opens across the Arctic Ocean during the summer, cargo ships will be able to travel between the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans without passing through the Panama Canal. In the Antarctic, knowledge of future SIAF mechanisms can be used to assess potential changes in the circumpolar current and ice sheet melting, an important region for C02 absorption and sequestration (important processes to dampen the climatic effect of this greenhouse gas).

Kelp forests provide food and shelter to countless species of marine life and are vital to the health ofthe entire channel. The structure of kelp lends itself to aerial mapping; however, very few recent studies have used satellite mapping to calculate kelp coverage and none have done this with high spatial and temporal resolution. Description: GALEX observations have largely ignored Ultraluminous Infrared Galaxies (ULIRGs). Ultraviolet light emerges from these dusty starbursts along only the least obscured sightlines, as shown by the Goldader et al. HST observations. We request new UV photometry of 37 ULIGs, to be supplemented by 4 datasets in the GALEX archive, to measure the ionization state of sodium in their galactic winds. Empirical constraints on wind velocities, mass loss rates, and solid angle are critical for identifying the physical mechanism driving these winds. The optical resonance doublet NaI 5890.96 has been employed to measure outflow velocities and column densities for many ULIRGs. However, the ionization correction for sodium likely varies by over an order of magnitude among objects, leaving the mass loss rates highly uncertain. Murray et al have recently demonstrated that the strength and spectral index of the UV continuum provide definitive constraints on the ionization state of sodium in these outflows. The proposed program would constrain variations in the ionization fraction of sodium among ULIG outflows, thereby vastly improving estimates of mass loss rates. This work will generate an important legacy of GALEX observations of nearby, dusty starbursts.

Description: A NEW APPROACH TO MODELING THREE-DIMENSIONAL NON-FORCE FREE CORONAL MAGNETIC FIELD  We propose to develop and test a new approach to deriving the three-dimensional non-force free coronal magnetic field structure from photospheric vector magnetograph measurements. The local structure in approximate magnetohydrostatic equilibrium above the photosphere is to be reconstructed, utilizing high-quality vector magnetogram which provides boundary conditions within its field-of-view. Based on the Principle of Minimum Dissipation Rate, a general non-force free magnetic field can be expressed as the superposition of two linear (constantalpha) force free field. The parameter, alpha, for each of the two linear force free field, can be determined by optimizing the requirement that the recovered transverse magnetic field components as the superposition of the corresponding components of the two linear force free field agree with the observed ones at the photospheric level. Further studies on optimizing such an agreement is proposed. Therefore, an optimal solution without the common force-free assumption is obtained by solving two linear force free extrapolation problems, in which only the normal component of the magnetic field at the lower boundary is known. The difficulties associated with such an extrapolation is well known. We will revisit these problems and propose alternative means to overcome them. The proposed research has significant impact on LWS program and Heliophysics science, since studying solar coronal magnetic field is the key element in the understanding of solar magnetic activity. It is the driving force of the space weather effect, that is a key issue to NASA's new vision for space exploration. At the present time, new high-quality and high-resolution magnetograph data from both ground-based and space-borne instrumentations are becoming available. It is imperative to develop such a tool to meet the demands for quantitative analysis of solar coronal magnetic field.

Description: RIPL: Radio Interferometric Planet Search The discovery and characterization of extra-solar planets has broad implications for our understanding of the evolution of stellar and planetary systems as well as life in the Universe. To comprehend the complete picture of planet formation, we must explore planetary systems in a variety of environments. We propose a program, the Radio Interferometric PLanet Search (RIPL), that uses long baseline radio interferometry to astrometrically detect massive planets around low mass stars. RIPL provides an important synergy with NASA goals in Solar System Origins. Our program exploits the incredible aslrometaic precision of the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) that can routinely achieve approximatety 0.1 mas accuracy in the position of a star relative to a compact background radio source. This is an order of magnitude less than the astrometric signature of a Jupiter mass planet at a radius of i AU around an M dwarf at a distance of 5 pc. We have conducted a VLA and VLBA survey to identify nearby (10 pc) M dwarfs that are sufficiently bright, compact, and strometrically stable for detection of Jupiter mass planets. Already, these results eliminate brown dwarf companions for two stars. A representative sample demonstrates that 29 nearby, active stars of stellar type M1 through MS are suitable for long-term astrometry. Simulations indicate that we can detect 50% of systems with 0.4 Jupiter mass planets at 1 AU around an 0.2 solar mass star at 5 pc. For planets detected with high SNR, RIPL will give complete determination of the mass and orbital elements. RIPL will fill an unexplored range of parameter space in extra-solar planet characterization of the most common type of star in the galaxy, M dwarfs. The results will have an important effect on our understanding of planet formation mechanisms. Radial velocity (RV) searches are most sensitive to planets at 1 AU and cannot explore active M dwarfs because of the distortion that activity causes in stellar emission lines. RV searches indicate a low fraction of planets at small radii around M dwarfs. Micro-lensing searches, on the other hand, have demonstrated a high fraction of Neptune-mass planets at larger radii, although based on a small number of detections. Unfortunately, the planets discovered through micro-lensing are at large distances from the Sun and cannot be followed-up through other imaging or spectroscopic methods. Our program is synergistic with future NASA missions including TPF and SIM. Discovery of planets at large separations from nearby stars will provide excellent candidates for imaging and spectroscopic follow-up. RIPL provides an opportunity to maximize NASA goals in the area of extra-solar planet discovery and characterization through a unique method. The project offers the promise of discovery of sub-Jupiter mass pianets at large radii around nearby M dwarfs.

Description: UV Spectroscopy of Nearby Supernovae - the Key to Understanding High-z Star/Galaxy Formation Supernova (SN) explosions play a pivotal role in triggering, driving, and (later on) inhibiting further star formation in galaxies. In fact, the combination of new observations and refined modelling shows that the little-understood and poorly constrained contribution of SNe to galaxy evolution processes (often hidden under the generic name of feedback is probably the weakest link in our understanding of structure formation in the Universe. Setting observational limits on the rate, environments, and energy output of high-redshift SNe is therefore one of the main science drivers of recent Hubble Space Telescope (HST) legacy programs, as well as of future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). However, observations of high-redshift SNe in the optical (by HST), or in the near-IR (by JWST), actually sample the rest-frame UV of these objects. Thus, proper interpretation of these observations requires knowledge about the UV properties of SNe. Such UV data are also powerful probes of the SN environment, progenitor structure and explosion mechanism. Unfortunately, UV spectroscopy of local SNe of all types, which can only be obtained from space, is scarce. Previous efforts using HST and IUE were focussed on a single SN sub-type, SNe Ia (sim10objects observed), while data for SN of all other types (core-collapse events) is almost nonexistent. We have been awarded a total of 66 GALEX orbits during cycles 1 and 2 to conduct target-of-opportunity GALEX spectroscopic observations of a single nearby, bright, core-collapse SN in each cycle. Following the successful implementation of our program, we request here similar spectroscopic observations for two additional SNe. The accumulated GALEX data on non-Ia events, combined with the results from past efforts using HST and IUE, is leading toward a full characterization of the UV spectral evolution of SNe of all types.

Description: Systematic Evaluation of the Potential Field Source Surface Model The potential field source surface (PFSS) model was developed in the 1960s to describe the coronal and heliospheric magnetic fields from photospheric measurements. It assumes that the solar corona is current-free up to an artificial spherical source surface, typically set at a heliocentric radius of 2.5 Rsun, on which the field is constrained to be radial. Simple as it is, the PFSS model forms the basis for the routine prediction of the solar wind speed and the polarity of the interplanetary magnetic field as observed near Earth. The goodness of the model is often measured in terms of how well it predicts these in-situ observations. Here we propose investigations to systematically evaluate the PFSS model using observables close to the Sun that are recorded in the available archive data. They include type 111 bursts, coronal holes, streamers, and closed loops in active regions and quiescent regions. Use of these observables is free of possible uncertainties in the magnetic field in interplanetary space. We will also assess the effect of the following on the reality of the PFSS model; variable boundary conditions (such as the photospheric magnetograms and the radius of the source surface), current carrying active regions, and the unobserved emergence of major active regions on the far side of the Sun. Using a statistical evaluation of the PFSS model on a large sample of cases, we will find out under what circumstances it most accurately represents the actual coronal field, and we will quantitatively rank the sources of error that limit its reliability. This project addresses the adequacy of the PFSS model beyond Earth's neighborhood, so it is highly relevant for NASA's Vision for Space Exploration. We will use data from SOH0 (MDI, EIT and LASCO), TRACE, Yohkoh (SXT), Wind (WAVES) and GOES (SXI), as well as ground-based data.

Description: NASA and the FAA are pursuing au ambitious plan to improve the efficiency of the national airspace system (NAS) by deployment of advanced technologies. A number of these technologies are aimed at improving the precision of 4DT trajectories, both through navigation precision and trajectory awareness. In order to estimate the effect that these improvements will have on performance measures of the airspace, fast and accurate models of the NAS are required. In this proposal, we describe our approach to building stochastic network queuing models to accomplish this task. The issues of primary concern are related to the propagation of uncertainty through the network, and how reductions in that uncertainty as a result of the above technologies will manifest themselves in improved traffic flow efficiency and operational performance. Because the NAS is such a vast and complicated network, a great deal of sophistication is required of the modeling tools to address these issues. We have proposed a succession of Progressively more advanced queuing models, including tandem and networked queues, robust scheduling, and diffusion approximations. These models are all built on sound theoretical bases and well-established methods. Significant effort is required, however, to adapt these to the problem of modeling the NAS as a queuing system. The plan requires that the theoretical formations of the models be maintained, while at the same time providing high levels of accuracy and fast execution times. The accuracy of the models will be confirmed via a thorough and robust validation effort, in which the model outputs are compared to similar statistics from empirical data, for conditions similar to those of the present, and data from detailed simulations which can represent potential future scenarios. We also propose to build an interactive visual tool that can be applied to demonstrate the relationships encompassed in the models

Description: REMOTE SENSING OF CLIMATE CHANGE CONTROLLING PRODUCTION OF SMALL PELAGIC FISH (GRADUATE STUDENT-RYAN RYKACZEWSKI)SARDINE AND ANCHOVY POPULATIONS ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR MORE THAN 20% OF GLOBAL MARINE FISH LANDINGS. LARGE, DECADAL-SCALE BIOMASS FLUCTUATIONS IN THESE POPULATIONS HAVE LONG PUZZLED OCEANOGRAPHERS AND PRESENTED SEVERE ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL CONSEQUENCES TO COMMUNITIES DEPENDENT ON THESE FISHERIES. INVESTIGATION OF ECOSYSTEM-BASED HYPOTHESES RELATING CLIMATE CHANGES TO FISH PRODUCTION HAS BEEN RESTRICTED BY THE LACK OF TIME-SERIES MEASUREMENTS OF MULTIPLE ENVIRONMENTAL VARIABLES, AND EXISTING HYPOTHESES DO NOT PROVIDE THE UNDERSTANDING NECESSARY TO PREDICT HOW FISHERIES WILL VARY UNDER FUTURE CLIMATE CONDITIONS. NOW, WITH THE ACCUMULATION OF ATMOSPHERIC, HYDROGRAPHIC, AND BIOLOGIC DATA COLLECTED FROM SATELLITES AND SHIPS, EXAMINATION OF MORE MECHANISTIC HYPOTHESES IS POSSIBLE. I PROPOSE A HYPOTHESIS RELATING CHANGES IN PRODUCTION OF ANCHOVY AND SARDINE TO VARIABLE WIND STRESS AND WIND-STRESS CURL. COASTAL ALONGSHORE AND EQUATORWARD WIND STRESS RESULTS IN RAPID UPWELLING AND PRODUCTION OF LARGE PLANKTERS. UPWELLING RESULTING FROM WIND-STRESS CURL IS SLOWER, LEADING TO PRODUCTION OF SMALL PLANKTON. ANCHOVY FEED EFFICIENTLY ON THE LARGE PLANKTERS PRODUCED BY RAPID UPWELLING, WHILE SARDINE FEED ON SMALL PLANKTERS RESULTING FROM SLOWER UPWELLING. I PROPOSE TO TEST THIS HYPOTHESIS BY EXAMINING HISTORICAL PHYSICAL, CHEMICAL, BIOLOGICAL, AND FISHERIES RELATIONSHIPS IN THE CALIFORNIA CURRENT ECOSYSTEM (CCE). DATA GATHERED FROM SATELLITE SCATTEROMETERS AND SHIPBOARD ANEMOMETERS WILL BE USED TO MEASURE CHANGES IN WIND STRESS AND WIND-STRESS CURL, AND AHIGH-RESOLUTION MODEL WILL EXTEND THE TIME SERIES OF THESE MEASURES. THE HYDROGRAPHIC AND BIOLOGIC RESPONSE TO WINDS WILL BE EXAMINED USING SATELLITE ALTIMETRY, RADIOMETRY, AND OCEAN COLOR. ARCHIVED CRUISE DATA WILL PROVIDE ESTIMATES OF HYDROGRAPHIC CONDITIONS AND CONCENTRATIONS OF NUTRIENTS AND CHLOROPHYLL. ANCHOVY AND SARDINE BIOMASSES HAVE BEEN ESTIMATED DURING VARIOUS PERIODS EXTENDING BACK TO THE 1930S. IN ADDITION TO TIME SERIES ANALYSES, PROCESS STUDIES ARE REQUIRED TO INVESTIGATE THE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN UPWELLING RATE AND PLANKTER SIZE. DURING SPRINGTIME RESEARCH CRUISES, PLANKTER SIZES WILL BE CHARACTERIZED IN VARIOUS ZONES SPANNING THE CCE. REMOTELY-SENSED OCEAN COLOR AND SEA-SURFACE TEMPERATURE WILL BE USED TO SELECT REGIONS INFLUENCED BY STRONG COASTAL UPWELLING, STRONG CURL UPWELLING, AND VERY WEAK OR NO UPWELLING. MY DISSERTATION RESEARCH WILL ENABLE PREDICTION OF HOW CLIMATE VARIABILITY WILL INFLUENCE ECONOMICALLY VALUABLE FISH STOCKS; FOSTER AN UNDERSTANDING OF THE INTERACTIONS AMONG CONTINENTS, OCEANS, ATMOSPHERE, AND LIFE; AND SERVE TO ENHANCE OUR NATION'S SCIENTIFIC INTERESTS AND FOOD SECURITY. GIVEN CURRENT UNCERTAINTIES REGARDING THE EFFECTS OF GLOBAL CLIMATECHANGE ON THE WORLD'S ECOSYSTEMS AND THE INCREASING EXPLOITATION OF MARINE FISH STOCKS, I THINK IT IS ESSENTIAL TO MAKE USE OF EXISTING DATA TO BETTER UNDERSTAND THE RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND FISH PRODUCTION.

Description: UV SPECTROSCOPY OF NEARBY SUPERNOVAE - THE KEY TO UNDERSTANDING HIGH-Z STAR / GALAXY FORMATION Supernova (SN) explosions playa pivotal role in triggering, driving, and (later on) inhibiting further star formation in galaxies. In fact, the combination of new observations and refined modelling shows that the little-understood and poorly constrained contribution of SNe to galaxy evolution processes (often hidden under the generic name of i,i,feedbackuJ is probably the weakest link in our understanding of structure formation in the Universe. Setting observational limits on the rate, environments, and energy output of high-redshift SNe is therefore one of the main science drivers of recent Hubble Space Telescope (HST) legacy programs, as well as of future missions like the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). However, observations of high-redshift SNe in the optical (by HST), or in the near-IR (by JWST), actually sample the rest-frame UV of these objects. Thus, proper interpretation of these observations requires knowledge about the UV properties of SNe. Such UV data are also powerful probes of the SN environment, progenitor structure and explosion mechanism. Unfortunately, UV spectroscopy of local SNe of all types, which can only be obtained from space, is scarce. Previous efforts using HST and IUE were focussed on a single SN sub-type, SNe Ia (simIO objects observed), while data for SN of all other types (core-collapse events) is almost non-existent. We have been awarded a total of 66 GALEX orbits during cycles 1 and 2 to conduct target-of-opportunity GALEX spectroscopic observations of a single nearby, bright, core-collapse SN in each cycle. Following the successful implementation of our program, we request here similar spectroscopic observations for two additional SNe. The accumulated GALEX data on non-Ia events, combined with the results from past efforts using HST and IUE, is leading toward a full characterization of the UV spectral evolution of SNe of all types.

Description: PLANETARY EVOLUTION AND STRUCTURE This wide-ranging theoretical study of the evolution and structure of planets and satellites has five parts: magnetohydrodynamics of giant planets, tidal dissipation in satellites, origin of the Earth-Moon system, interpretation of giant planet gravitational moments, and Titan evolution. This range of topics is highly relevant to the OSS strategic goals that concern the processes shaping the evolution and structure of planetary bodies. 1. Magnetohydrodynamics of giant planets: Unlike Jupiter, Saturn's field is almost exactly spin-axisymmetric. The difference may arise from the presence of a Saturnian zonal flow that attenuates the spin-axisymmetric part of the field. The new idea we consider is that Saturn's axisymmetric field (-0.2Gauss) is insufficient to reduce the zonal flow that provides attenuation whereas Jupiter's field (4.2Gauss) eliminates that flow. 2. Most tidal dissipation models predict a global k/Q (where k is the Love number and Q is the tidal quality factor). It is proposed to develop alternative models (mainly for 10 and Enceladus) that introduce faults and localized frictional heating. 3.The similarity of Earth and Moon in oxygen isotopes can arise through a dilution process in the hundred year epoch immediately following a giant impact when Earth and Moon have a common silicate vapor atmosphere. This hypothesis will be developed further, with particular emphasis on devising and carrying out other tests of the model. 4. The non-unique relationship between gravitational moments, the moment of inertia and gravitational energy will be examined with the goal of placing additional constraints on the possible existence of a core in Jupiter and the mode(s) of formation of Uranus and Neptune. 5. Possible evidence for cryogenic volcanism on Titan motivates examination of new models for Titan's evolution, with particular emphasis on the role of lateral heterogeneity in the crust and outer shell rather than(unpromising) global averaged models.

These applications and authoring technologies can be casily ported for use within other user communities (such as resource/regional planners and decision makers). Description: HEINZ PITSCH/ STANFORD UNIVERSITY DETAILED MODELING OF COMBUSTION NOISE USING A COMBINED LARGE-EDDY SIMULATION/COMPUTATIONAL AEROACOUSTICS MODEL The primary objective of the proposed work is to establish the foundational elements relevant to the prediction of core noise in non-premixed combustors in isolation and when coupled to the turbine. By combining the unique simulation capabilities, combustion modeling, and aeroacoustic prediction expertise developed at Stanford, a detailed and systematic study of nonpremixed combustors and their radiated sound will provide the necessary understanding to enable more advanced combustor design. We will perform an evaluation of the relative importance of direct combustion noise, i.e. the noise produced by the unsteady heat release, to indirect combustion noise, where entropy fluctuations produced by the combustor are converted into radiated noise when gassing through the turbine. The proposed work will specifically examine the relative roles the combustor and turbine play in the generation of core noise through highfidelity system-level analysis. In doing so, we will critically examine the actuator disk theory in its ability to model combustor/turbine coupling for low-frequency sound. The particular strength of this proposal is the broad coverage of the relevant issues and the consideration of fundamental aspects all the way to the application in engine simulations. Furthermore, the final product of the proposed work will be a predictive and highly efficient LES code that includes all the  aeroacoustic models developed during the project.

Description: THERMAL EMISSION ANALYSIS OF EXTINCT COMET CANDIDATES AND M-TYPE ASTEROIDS We propose thermal and compositional analysis of thermal emission spectra (5.2, 38 microns) of two groups of small bodies: Extinct comet candidates and M-type asteroids. Together, this analysis will help resolve two fundamental questions about the Solar System. The first is How many extinct comet nuclei may be hiding among the asteroids (Le. what is the ultimate fate of comets?) and what is the surface mineralogy of these nuclei? The second is How widespread was differentiation of early asteroids during accretion? The data to be analyzed were measured with the Infrared Spectrograph on the Spitzer Space Telescope. We will model the thermal flux at each ;Wavelength to derive the thermal continuum and constrain thermophysical properties of the surface (i.e. thermal inertia). The latter is a marker of both composition (e.g., metallic vs. rocky) and surface structure (e.g., particulate, blocky, bedrock). We will then divide the measured thermal flux spectra by the modeled thermal continua. The resulting emissivity spectra accentuate mineralogical signatures. Compositional analysis of the emissivity spectra will consist of comparisons to laboratory data, linear deconvolution, and advanced radiative transfer (Hapke/Mie) modeling. Together, these analyses will allow us to derive the mineralogy and surface structure ofthe observed objects. This information will in turn make it possible to distinguish extinct comet nuclei from asteroids and metallic M-types from their silicate brethren, helping to resolve the fundamental questions listed above. The continued investigation of extinct comet candidates and M-type asteroids directly addresses NASA Strategic Goals, particularly goal 3, sub-goaI3C, and Science Outcomes 3C.I, 3C.2, and 3C.4, as well as the objectives ofthe Planetary Geology and Geophysics prograM.

Description: Size, Shape, and Multiplicity in the Jupiter-Trojan Population The jovian Trojan asteroids are quite possibly the most primitive (least collisionally evolved) Solar System bodies easily accessible by observadons. We propose a multi-instrument campaign to explore the fundamental properties (size, shape, visible albedo, and intemal structure) of these objects using the capabilities ofthe Spitzer telescope, several middle size ground-based telescopes, and the high angular resolution LGS Keck AO system. Spitzer's Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) is providing the best FIR data set, which will be complemented by nearly simultaneous rotational lightcurve observations in reflected sunlight. We will then constrain the bulk properties of the asteroids using detailed thermal models , which require the combination of visible and thermal infrared data. Our study will be performed in coordination with a network of mid-sized ground-based telescopes (Lick- 3m, Lick-lm, Pic du Midi-lm, OHP-lm) in the optical to characterize the shape and visible albedo. Additionally, we have started a high angular resolution study of Trojans aimed at looking for binary systems. We are taking advantage of the spectacular high angular resolution provided by the Keck LGS AO system on faint targets (75 mas on 15-17.5th magnitude). Over this last year, we will finalize the analysis of the Trojan lightcurve recorded since 2005 and combined with the Spitzer FIR spectra when they are available. We will also initiated a spectroscopic study in the near-infrared (using OSIRIS) to better characterize the surface composidon of this interesdng small solar system bodies. By the determinadonof the physical parameters, we can constrain the intemal structure of asteroids which may only be inferred otherwise from space mission flybys. This ambitious program combines data from several facilides to obtain direct insights on the internal structure, surface properties, and formadon of Trojan asteroids, it will increase significandy our knowledge about minor bodies in the Solar System.

Description: Molecules in the Ice and Meteorites: Studying Simple and Complex Organics in Space The purpose of our proposed research is to investigate the formation and distribution of ices and organic molecules in space. (LCROSS) NASAs Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), scheduled for launch in October 2008, will chart the lunar landscape, not only to identify obstacles and safe-to-land spots, but also sensor sweep the terrain and gauge it for usable resources.  NASA plans to launch the LRO rocket with a secondary payload, called the LCROSS, whose mission will be to determine the presence of water ice at the Moons South Pole.  After the LRO is deployed in orbit around the Moon, the LCROSS satellite will steer the launch vehicles spent Earth departure upper stage (CENTAUR) into a permanently-shadowed crater at a lunar pole. LCROSS will provide a critical ground-truth for a Lunar Prospector and LRO neutron and radar maps making it possible to assess the total lunar water inventory.

Such systems will further evolve through common envolope stage to neutron star/black hole binaries which may ultimately merge to produce short gamma-ray bursts. Description: Self-Organizing Maps (SOM) Classification, Cassini Data Analysis and Particle Concentration and Aggregation by Turbulence We propose to classify and statistically analyze the near and far infrared spectra of planetary surfaces. Specifically we will investigate the stratigraphic relationship between the materials exposed by evaluating the compositional variability using spectral data obtained from orbiting spacecraft. Hogan and Roush (2006) describe an unsupervised classification scheme based on Kohonen self-organizing maps (SOMs) that automatically determines the number of clusters. In this work the SOM scheme was applied to thermal infrared spectra where spectral features are chiefly associated with vibrational transitions of molecular units. In a second paper (Roush and Hogan (2007) the SOM classifier was applied to shorter near infrared wavelengths where the spectral features are mainly due to electronic rather than vibrational transitions. Spectra data from the Brown University RELAB spectral library and the ASTER spectral library was used in this work. We also propose to use SOM classification to analyze the surface composition of Phobos in order to address its enigmatic origin. The chief data to be analyzed include spectral measurements from the Thermal Emission Spectrometer of the Mars Global Surveyor, and measurements obtained by the visible and near infrared (OMEGA) spectrometer ofthe European Mars Express mission. This work is an integral part ofthe research described in a funded proposal to NASA's Planetary Geology and Geophysics program.

Description: This proposal is to develop numerical modeling tools for the analysis of the magnetic field data collected by low-earth orbiting satellites that are suitable for studying external magnetospheric field variations and their induced counterparts in Earth.
