Description: Magnetometry is a vital aspect of much space and planetary exploration. In particular, magnetometric studies are the only way to obtain direct information about the deep interior of the Earth. Current systems for space-based magnetometers will need to be replaced by more sensitive instruments for future, more demanding missions. We propose to develop an ultrasensitive magnetometer based on an alkali atomic vapor optically pumped and read out using laser light. Potential sensitivity of I fT/Hz"(1/2)--orders of magnitude better than that provided by the instruments used in current missions--can be obtained by using an anti relaxation-coated vapor cell, allowing long atomic coherence lifetimes. The magnetometer can be made compact and with low power consumption, and a wide dynamic range is possible using a scheme based on modulated laser light. In order to design and optimize such a magnetometer, a quantitative theoretical model is required. We propose to construct such a model, using density-matrix theory, based on previous work involving related systems. This model will describe the effects of pump and probe light nonperturbatively, will track the behavior of the atoms as they move between illuminated and nonilluminated regions of the vapor cell, and will account for Doppler-broadening and velocity-changing atomic collisions. This will allow quantitative optimization of the performance of the ultrasensitive magnetometer.

Description: Aerosols in planetary atmospheres play a critical role in radiative transfer and, hence, in determining the penetration depth of UV radiation and atmospheric temperatures. For early Mars and anoxic early Earth, aerosols may have significantly influenced the stability of liquid water at the surface, climate, and habitability, yet the kinetics of particle formation and their resulting optical properties are still too poorly constrained by models and experiments to arrive at convincing conclusions. Description: SBIR 2005 Phase II Proposal Title: Dynamic Strain and Crack Monitoring Sensor. Los Gatos Research proposes to develop a new automated vehicle health monitoring sensor system capable of measuring loads and detecting crack, corrosion, and disbonding in advanced aerospace structures using a novel lock-in laser interrogation technique combined with a Bragg grating array (BGA) technology for strain and guided Lamb wave (GLW) sensing. Los Gatos Research's novel sensor instrumentation offers a number of advantages including sensor compactness (0.2mm x 0.2 mm x 10mm), lightweight (a few grams), remote data acquisition capability, low-cost, and low power consumption. The inherently reliable lock-in laser demodulation technique permit simultaneous measurements of strain, temperature, and acoustic fields with high resolution and high sensitivity. In Phase I, we have demonstrated feasibility by buildiing a prototype instrument capable of measuring static and dynamic strain, temperature, and ultrasonic waves using a lock-in laser demodulation technique and a fiber Bragg grating array sensor network. In Phase II, Los Gatos Research will deliver to NASA a rugged, compact, multi-channel instrument optimized for vehicle health monitoring studies including strain, temperature, and crack monitoring with high precision, high resolution, and high sensitivity. This dedicated prototype will include an integrated microcontroller, operate unattended, and address the power and stability requirements unique to in-flight studies. Potential NASA commercial applications could be provided through optical fiber technology which gives significant advantages for advanced aerospace platforms because they are lightweight, immune to electromagnetic wave interference, rugged, and do not produce short circuits or ground loops. Therefore the development of high sensitivity fiber optic sensors has the potential to increase reliability, enable lower cost, and facilitate more effective health monitoring and nondestructive evaluation of NASA's advanced aircraft and spacecraft components and systems. The Bragg grating array sensor deveice Los Gatos Research has demonstrated and proposed to further develop for Phase II will greatly enhance NASA efforts to develop state-of-the-art, compact, low-cost, waveform-based, quantitative strain and ultrasonic wave sensing technology for load, temperature, corrosion, and crack monitoring of advanced structures. The potential non-NASA commercial applications embrace advances in high-resolution, high sensitivity, and large dynamic range load and ultrasonic wave sensing technology has immediate applications in civil engineering for monitoring cracks, corrosion, and fatigue in steel and concrete structures such as bridges, freeways, and buildings. High frequency ultrasonic signal detection method development can be utilized in ultrasonic testing, medical imaging, and other non-destructive testing technology. Los Gatos Research's BGA technology development can readily be incorporated into current fiber optics and optical cross-connect technology for next-generation telecommunication applications.

Description: AEOLIAN SEDIMENT MOVEMENT UNDER TITAN CONDITIONS: WIND TUNNEL EXPERIMENTS AND MODELING  The objectives of this work are to conduct wind tunnel experiments and complementary modeling of Aeolian sediment transport under Titan conditions in support of interpretation of Cassini-Huygens data. We propose to conduct experiments in the Venus Wind Tunnel (VWT) at NASA Ames Research Center to assess sediment movement criteria on Titan. During year 1 of this 3-year proposal the VWT will be refurbished for equivalent Titan pressures at terrestrial temperatures (12 bar) according to the included Planetary Major Equipment proposal. We will also make theoretical calculations of saltation trajectories using previously developed models.  In year 2 we will assess the threshold for sediment movement under simulated Titan conditions. Besides determining the threshold friction wind velocity at particle lift-off we will measure lift-off angels and velocities as input into our models to estimate saltation trajectory for comparison with experimental results. During year 3 we will measure individual particle velocity and overall particle flux by grain size and we will compare the experimental results with theoretical calculations. The physical results of all experiments will also be used to investigate small-scale bedforms. This fundamental research is essential to understanding Aeolian sedimentary processes on Titan.  It will also provide information necessary to meaningfully interpret Titan features hypothesized to be the result of Aeolian sediment movement. By furthering understanding of the formation and conditions for features on Titan's surface this proposal accords with the program goals of gathering / synthesis / analysis / and comparative study of data that will improve the understanding of the extent and influence of planetary geological and geophysics processes on the bodies of the Solar System. In response to NASA Strategic sub-goal 3C this proposal will advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system.

Description: UNSOLICITED RESEARCH PROPOSAL ENTITLED "A STUDY OF THE EFFECT OF BIOMASS BURNING ON THE GLOBAL UPPER TOPOSHPHERE AND LOWER STRATOSTROM" ABSTRACT FROM YEAR ONE ANNUAL REPORT: WE INVESTIGATED THE EFFECTS OF FIRE-INCLUDED PLUME-RISE ON THE PREDICTED EXPORT OF CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) OVER AFRICA DURING SAFARI 2000 USING THE NCAR COMMUNITY ATMOSPHERE MODEL (CAM) WITH CO TRACER AND PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME.  THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SIMULATES THE CONSEQUENCES OF STRONG BUOYANCY OF HOT GASES EMITTED FROM BIOMASS BURNING, INCLUDING BOTH DRY AND CLOUD-ASSOCIATED (PYROCUMULUS) LOFTING.  THE SCHEME WAS FIRST ADAPTED FROM A REGIONAL MODEL.  THE CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME INTO THE GLOBAL MODEL PROVIDES AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXAMINE THE EFFECT OF PLUME-RISE ON LONG RANGE TRANSPORT.  THE CAM SIMULATION WITH THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SHOWS A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT OF THE AGREEMENTS BETWEEN THE MODELED AND AIRCRAFT-MEASURED VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CO OVER SOUTHERN AFRICA BIOMASS BURNING.  THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM PLAYS CRUCIAL ROLE IN LOFTING BIOMASS BURNING POLLUTANTS TO THE MIDDLE TROPOSPHERE.  IN THE PRESENCE OF DEEP CONVECTION WE FOUND THAT THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM RESULTS IN A DECREASE OF CO CONCENTRATION IN THE UPPER TROPOSPHERE.  THE PLUME RISE DEPLETES THE BOUNDARY LAYER, AND THUS LEAVES LOWER CONCENTRATIONS OF CO TO BE LOFTED BY THE DEEP CONVECTION PROCESS.  THE EFFECT OF THE PLUME-RISE ON FREE TROPOSPHERE (CO) CONCENTRATION IS MORE IMPORTANT FOR THE SOURCE AREA (SHORT-DISTANCE TRANSPORT) THAN FOR REMOTE AREAS (LONG-DISTANCE TRANSPORT).  THE PLUME-RISE SCHEME ALSO INCREASES THE CO EXPORT FLUXES FROM AFRICA TO THE ATLANTIC AND INDIAN OCEANS.  THESE RESULTS FURTHER CONFIRM AND EXTENT PREVIOUS FINDINGS IN A REGIONAL MODEL STUDY.  EFFECTIVE LOFTING OF LARGE CONCENTRATION OF CO BY THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM ALSO HAS IMPLICATION FOR LOCAL AIR QUALITY FORECAST IN AREAS AFFECTED BY OTHER FIRE-RELATED POLLUTANTS.

Description: Potentially Prebiotic Peptide Based Oligomers for Dynamic Recognition of DNA and RNA We propose to synthesize and study a chemical system that exploits the reversibel bond formation of thiolesters to create a prebiotically relevant informational oligomer capable of dynamic recognition of nucleic acids, The system employs a polycystc peptide as a dynamic backbone tether for nucleobase derivatives, Using this approach we will better understand how life could have begun and evolved to its current state on Earth, which in turn will better prepare us to search for life on other planets. A primordial genetic polymer must have had several characteristics for it to have been important in the origin of life, First, the polymer must be made up of possible prebiotic building blocks that would have existed on prebiotic Earth. Second, it must be capable of pairing with complementary stands of itself to pass on information from generation to generation, Further, the oligomer must also be able with RNA because information transfer between RNA and the pre-RNA polymer would have been necessary during the transition to the widely accepted RNA dominated world. Finally, the polymer must be capable of replication with high fidelity in the absence of enzymes, Though there are many examples of molecules that look similar to nucleic acid oligomers and can homodimerize, on oligomers have been shown to also form stable duplexes with DNA or RNA. Peptide derived polymers have been proposed by researchers to be precursors to RNA due in large part to the stability of peptides under harsh conditions, the discovery of amino acids monomers in meteorites, and numerous more or less plausible reported mechanisms for amino acid oligomerizaton. The system we propose is peptide based and is designed to undergo high fidelity information transfer with a DNA or RNA template under dynamic conditions. We will accomplish this task by using a peptide composed of a repeating cysteine-glutamic acid dimer for reversible anchoring of nucleobase monomers. To study the proposed oligomers, we will employ standard techniques of organic chemisty including HPLC, mass spectrometry, and UV and CD spectroscopy. The system and investigative process that we propose will provide insight in to the ways in which informational polymers could have formed and interacted on primordial Earth with the intent of addressing Objective 4 of the Solar System Exploration Road Map which states: Understand how life begins and evolves. The proposed studies will offer not only insights into how life might have begun and what kind of organic materials to look for on distant planets, but also the first opportunity for the characterization of a prebiotically relevant oligomer capable of dynamic self-asse and chemical evolution.

Description: Using Aromatic Compounds and related Molecular Species as a tracer of Carbon in the Universe and Life in the Solar System The purpose of our proposed research is to investigate aromatic compounds and related molecular species using the information gained as a tracer of Carbon in the Universe and Life in the Solar System. The ultimate goal of this project is to determine whether aromatic structures, which are prevalent in our own biochemistry, might indicate an exogenous origin of life. Since tons of organic molecules come to earth every day from space, and this mass may have been a million times more on the prebiotic Earth, such molecules might have aided in making the Earth habitable, perhaps even jump-starting life. By extension, such a delivery process may be generally applicable to habitability of the planets of other stellar systems, and thus is of fundamental interest to the SETI Institute. This program will focus on measuring the far and mid-infrared (IR) spectra of aromatic compounds under astrophysically relevant conditions; constructing a database of the measured spectra for use in interpreting astronomical observations, modeling the aromatic emissions, and utilizing the knowledge gained in the development of instrument concepts for planetary landers and probes. Since nitrogen-containing aromatics are so important to our biochemistry, particular emphasis will be placed on these compounds. However this program is not limited to solely experimental work. In addition to the proposed work, we are actively pursuing related observational and theoretical projects through collaborations with other scientists at NASA, universities, and non-profits.

Description: INTEGRATING THE MESSENGER GRNS EXPERIMENT INTO THE 3RD INTERPLANETARY NETWORK OF COSMIC GAMMA-RAY BURST DETECTORS We propose to add the Gamma-Ray Neutron Spectrometer experiment to the 3rd interplanetary network of cosmic gamma-ray burst detectors. Presently, the network consists of the Ulysses, Mars Odyssey, Wind, HETE, Swift, INTEGRAL, Swift, and Suzaku missions. The network operates by timing the arrival of gamma-ray bursts at these missions to derive a precise arrival direction for the bursts. To achieve good accuracy, at least two, and preferably more, long baselines are required. Presently they are provided by the interplanetary spacecraft Ulysses and Odyssey. The MESSENGER GRNS will complete the network and provide a backup for the time when these missions no longer operate. We have tested the GRNS experiment in-flight and found it to be a sensitive burst detector. We anticipate that it will observe over 500 gamma-ray bursts and over 200 soft gamma repeater bursts between 2007 and 2012.

Description: Lithospheric Stress from Plate Boundary Deformation and Surface Loads for Improved understanding of Seismic Hazard (Student-Karen Marie Luttrell) Understanding the absolute and relative magnitude of principal stress within a region is crucial to understanding the geophysical processes of that region: style of faulting, strength of faults, portion of stress relieved throughout the earthquake cycle compared to ambient geologic stresses, amount of stress transfer between brittle and ductile layers, and the role of interseismic versus coseismic deformation in determining the timing and location of the next regional rupture. Deviatoric stress within the lithosphere can he produced by tectonic forces (mostly horizontal stress) and topography on density interfaces like the free surface and Moho (mostly vertical stress). We propose to investigate the effects of various surface loads on the deviatoric stresses in the lithosphere in four ways: 1) Develop a 3-D model, constrained by geologic observations, to predict variations in Coulomb stress along the Southern San Andreas Fault in response to the transient presence of Ancient Lake Cahuilla in the Salton Trough. Variations in Coulomb stress can affect the timing of future ruptures and are thus significant for understanding Southern California seismic hazards. Much of this research has been completed [Luttrell et al., 2006,ttp://topex.ucsd.edu/kluttrelvCahuilla/LakeCahuiI1a2OO6.pd. 2) Extend the 3-D model developed in (1) to examine the long-term changes in slip rate on plate boundary faults caused by a rise in eustatic sea level over the last 25,000 years, and examine the specific effect of the catastrophic flooding of the Black Sea 7000 years ago on the nearby North Anatolian Fault. 3) Improve our 3-D stress model to include both surface loads and the buoyant restoring force of a deformed Moho. We will use SRTM topography and bathymetry data to estimate 3-D lithospheric stress both regionally and globally. 4) Compare LIDAR data from the B4 project with SRTM topography along the San Andreas Fault to understand the differences between them and predict the challenges in integrating a future global LIDAR data set with the existing topography data sets. Our results have direct relevance to understanding seismic hazard in the studied regions.

INFORMATION PROCESSING AND ACTUATION. THESE CELLS ARE SYSTEMS THAT MIMIC THE MODES OF INFORMATION PROCESSING NORMALLY ATTRIBUTED TO BIOLOGICAL CELLS.  THE APPLICATION OF NATURES STRATEGY OF DISTRIBUTED MULTILEVEL INFORMATION COLLECTION AND MANAGEMENT IS THE THREAD THAT WILL ACHIEVE A SEAMLESS LINK BETWEEN THE MOLECULAR SCALE NANOTECHNOLOGY OF SENSORS, ACTUATORS AND COMPUTATION, THE ASTRONAUTS AND THE SPACE VEHICLE.  BY MIMICKING THE COMPLEXITY OF MULTISCALE INFORMATION MANAGEMENT OF LIVING SYSTEMS COUPLED WITH THE DEVELOPMENT OF NEW NANO TECHNOLOGIES, SPACE EXPLORATION WILL ENTER A NEW ERA.  WITH THIS OUT-OF-BOX CONCEPT, UCLA PROPOSED THE INSTITUTE FOR CELL MIMETIC SPACE EXPLORATION (CMISE).  THIS INSTITUTE WILL BE DEVOTED TO THE - DEVELOPMENT OF CELL MIMETIC SYSTEMS, CONSISTING OF SENSORS, ACTUATORS AND ENERGY SOURCES.  DEVELOPMENT OF MULTI-SCALE INFORMATION PROCESSING TECHNIQUES, I.E., INFORMATICS.  DEVELOPMENT OF SCALABLE TECHNOLOGIES FOR SPACE BIOLOGICAL EXPERIMENTS, ASTRONAUT HEALTH MONITORING AND SPACESHIP RESOURCE MANAGEMENT.  DEVELOPMENT OF AN INTERDISCIPLINARY EDUCATION PROGRAM FOR EDUCATING FUTURE GENERATIONS OF YOUNG SPACE ENGINEERS AND SCIENTISTS.  CMISE ENVISIONS THAT ITS STRATEGY OF USING THE BIOLOGICAL MODEL OF HIERARCHICAL CELLULAR ORGANIZATION FOR THE APPLICATION OF NANOTECHNOLOGY AND THE MANAGEMENT OF INFORMATION WILL BE THE MODEL OF SPACE SYSTEM DESIGN THAT WILL DEFINE THE TECHNOLOGY FOR FUTURE GENERATIONS OF SPACE EXPLORERS.  THE GOAL OF THE CMISE EDUCATION PROGRAM IS TO TRAIN A CONTINUOUS STREAM OF YOUNG SPACE EXPLORERS.  THE PROGRAM WILL ENCOMPASS THE ENTIRE EDUCATIONAL SPECTRUM:  THE DEVELOPMENT OF LEARNING TOOLS FOR K-12, RESEARCH EXPERIENCES FOR UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS AND SUPPORT FOR PH.D. GRADUATE TRAINING.  SPECIAL ATTENTION WILL BE PAID TO THE RECRUITMENT OF UNDER-REPRESENTED STUDENTS.  STUDENTS OF THE CMISE PROGRAM WILL BE TRAINED IN A NEW GENERATION OF CROSS-DISCIPLINARY TECHNOLOGIES THAT ARE ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY TO SUPPORT THE NEXT GENERATION OF SPACE EXPLORERS.

Description: Simultaneous Characterization of Mass Loss and Pyrolysis Gas Species During Ablator Thermal Decomposition SRI International proposes an intensive 9-month research project to develop an experimental facility and techniques for simultaneous measurement of mass loss and pyrolysis gas species composition during thermal decomposition of candidate ablator materials. SRI International will couple a commercial thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA) to a versatile mass spectrometer (MS) system to correlate ablator mass loss during heating to the appearance of different molecular species in the gas phase. Evolved gases will be sampled into the MS system using a heated transfer line or orifice/skinner to minimize condensation. The MS system will contain both a quadupole mass analyzer with an electron impact ionization source and a time-of-flight analyzer with an ultraviolet laser ionization source, enabling simultaneous measurement of the bulk gas composition =and high-sensitivity detection and discrimination of hydrocarbon species. Quantification of species concentrations will be made by calibrating MS detection using known gas mixtures. At least one candidate ablator material supplied by NASA Ames Research Center (ARC) will be characterized by simultaneously measuring mass loss and pyrolysis gas composition as a function of heating rate, ambient pressure, and buffer gas composition. The successful completion of this project will not only generate useful data for the ablator(s) tested, but will also establish and demonstrate a highly capable experimental facility that can provide NASA valuable information about ablator decomposition and chemistry in the future.

Description: The discrimination of crustal and core sources, essential to understanding Mercury's magnetic field history, requires the identification of structure at all resolvable wavelengths. Because of the geometry of observations, and contributions from external fields, current plans for magnetic fields products and their archiving, are restricted to least-squares estimates of dipole and quadrupole terms, and a grid of deviations from these, severely limiting scientific return on the magnetic observations acquired. The work is designed to complement and extend the MESSENGER products that will be delivered by the MAG team, and to enable fundamental questions about Mercury to be addressed. The proposed tasks will: (1) characterize and assess MAG data (internal/external fields, noise, spatial resolution), (2) estimate global statistics of Mercury's internal field using flyby and early nominal mission data (enabling global inferences in the event of incomplete data return), (3) provide global maps and spectra of the static (time-invariant) part of Mercury's field, (4) identify, where discernible, temporal changes (secular variation) in Mercury's internal field during the MESSENGER mission. It is anticipated that all global field models will be delivered to the PDS, and that the results of data assessment and characterization will help in the MAG team's delivery of data. Description: MODELING THE GROWTH OF GIANT GAS PLANETS VIA CORE ACCRETION-GAS CAPTURE MODEL  The objective of this work is to obtain a better understanding of the origin and evolution of giant planets in our solar system and in extrasolar systems. The emphasis will be on the origin of the planet Jupiter. The method will involve numerical simulations in both 1 dimension and three dimensions, based on the core accretion-gas capture scenario for the origin of giant planets. In this picture small particles in a protoplanetary disk accrete to build up a solid core of a few earth masses, after which gas from the disk is gravitationally attracted to the core and builds up the envelope of the giant planet. The emphasis in this work is on the late stages, when gas is rapidly accreting and the planet is approaching its final mass. The accretion rate of gas will be determined with a three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulation that takes into account the gas flow in the disk outside the planet. The resulting rates will be fed into the one-dimensional planetary formation code to obtain mass as a function of time and to investigate the details of the process by which gas accretion is gradually cut off. These results will be significant in that they will set up initial conditions for the subsequent, possibly detectable, phase of slow contraction and cooling.

Description: SOLAR OSCILLATIONS INVESTIGATION - MICHELSON DOPPLER IMAGER SOHO APPROACH TO SOLAR MINIMUM NASA's long term goals require a better understanding of the Sun, solar variability on multiple scales, and the "space weather that impacts the terrestrial environment. From launch in December 1995, instruments on the SOHO spacecraft have studied the Sun over the complete 11-year duration of the Solar Cycle 23. Solar activity is predicted to reach minimum during 2007 with the transition to Solar Cycle 24 which is expected to peak in 2010 or 2011. The Solar Oscillations Investigation has a number of science goals that require MDI observations of the Sun over the rising phase of the Solar Cycle 24. The SOI-MDI program has the unique opportunity to compare observations during the minimum phase of two 11 year solar cycles using global helioseismology to measure the solar interior. This objective requires continuous observations to make accurate measurements of oscillation mode frequencies, from which the changing structure and rotation of the solar interior are determined. Other objectives require continuous observing sequences of days to months in length to study the changes near the solar surface, particularly those associated with active region and magnetic field emergence. These goals are addressed using the tools of local helioseismology which allow imaging of the motions in the interior of the star. Early progress convinced us that the developing techniques do indeed work and we will be able to watch the development of the next magnetic cycle from the inside. In addition to helioseismology observations, MDI provides observations essential for complementary views of solar processes. We have demonstrated the ability to follow the generation and evolution of magnetic fields on the granulation to global scale with a spatial and time resolution sufficient to, for the first time, follow the life-cycle of magnetic fields. MDI also provides measurements of relative brightness of active and quiet regions to enable the better understanding of the radiative flux balance. It also provides direct measurements of surface motions from meso-granulation through to global scales. These studies continued through the declining phase will provide a unique view of the processes that link interior dynamics to the phenomena that affect the Earth's space environment. Observations from the MDI instrument support research with many other missions and numerous individual researchers. In addition to fruitful collaborative efforts with the RHESSI and TRACE orbiting solar observatories, joint scientific observations with the recently launched Hinode (Solar B) and STEREO spacecraft are in development.

Description: THE COSMIC INFRARED BACKGROUND EXPERIMENT This is a Co-I proposal; PI proposal by Dr. James Bock. Light from the first generation of stars, formed from primordial gas in the early universe, has so far eluded direct detection. However, these first stars will produce characteristic signatures in the extragalactic background at near-infrared wavelengths. These distinctive features, in particular the redshifted Ly-cutoff spectral feature, and a characteristic fluctuation power spectrum, may be detectable with a specialized instrument. Recent observations of the absolute intensity and spatial fluctuations in the near-infrared background indicate a component to the background that cannot be explained by the redshift-integrated emission from known galaxy populations. This component could be due to luminous first-light high-mass stars or mini-quasars forming at high redshift (z - 10-20). However these background measurements are prone to systematic errors and first need confirmation. We propose the Cosmic Infrared Background ExpeRiment (CIBER) to search for signatures of first-light galaxy formation in the near-infrared background. The instrument consists of two wide-field cameras, a low-resolution absolute spectrometer, and a narrow-band spectrometer. The wide-field cameras will search for spatial fluctuations in the background on medium angular scales where the first-light galaxy spatial power spectrum peaks, but which has been poorly covered by previous experiments. The cameras have the necessary combination of sensitivity, wide field of view with sufficient spatial resolution, and multiple bands to make a definitive measurement. CIBER will conclusively determine if the fluctuations reported by Spitzer arise from first-light galaxies. The cameras observe in a single wide field of view, eliminating systematic errors associated with mosaicing. Two bands are chosen to maximize the first-light signal contrast, at 1.6 um near the expected spectral maximum, and at 0.8 urn, as a null test shorter than the redshifted Ly cutoff. We will jointly observe regions of the sky studied by Spitzer and ASTRO-F in order to accurately remove the contribution of local (z = 1-3) galaxies to the observed background fluctuations, and to cross correlate these independent data sets at 5 different wavelengths. The low-resolution spectrometer will search for the redshifted Lyman cutoff feature in the unexplored 0.7 - 1.8 um spectral region. The narrow-band spectrometer will trace zodiacal light using the intensity of a solar Fraunhofer line, providing an independent measurement of the zodiacal emission and a new systematic check of DIRBE zodiacal dust models. Description: The polar and auroral ionosphere are a signficant source of plasma for the magnetosphere. This plasma can be source for the plasmasheet and ring current, and can also affect the dynamical response of the magnetosphere through mass loading of the tail lobes and plasmasheet. Thus understanding the variability of ionospheric outflows is essential in specifying the response of the magnetosphere to changes in the solar wind drivers. We have recently derived scaling laws that specify ionospheric outflow fluxes as a function of electromagnetic and electron energy fluxes to the polar and auroral ionosphere. These scaling laws were determined from a 3-day interval of data from the Fast Auroral Snapshot Small Explorer. We will extend the scaling laws to the full solar cycle, and furhter use computer simulations such as those provided by NASA's Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CCMC) to investigate the impact of solar illumination on the flux of ionospheric plasma that flows into the magnetosphere.

Description: Under the auspices of the International Polar Year, we propose to participate in a joint oceanographic study of the carbon cycle within the Arctic Ocean. This study will entail an interdisciplinary collaboration between several French, Canadian, and U.S. institutions, with the goal of determining and understanding the sizes and transformation rates of carbon reservoirs within the Beaufort Sea. Our primary role in this collaboration will be to characterize the dynamics of the particulate organic carbon (POC) pool within the upper ocean, including the determination of geographical distributions and variability from weekly, seasonal, to interannual time scales. Our approach utilizes a combination of field measurements and satellite data. We will participate in a research cruise on the French vessel Marion Dufresne in the Beaufort Sea covering both the Mackenzie Shelf region and offshore oceanic waters in July and August 2007. A broad suite of measurements will be used to quantify the inherent and apparent optical properties of the ocean and properties of suspended particle assemblages. The analysis of field data will focus on discerning the relationships between seawater constituents, inherent optical properties, and surface spectral reflectance (ocean color). These relationships, in conjunction with radiative transfer modeling, will be used to develop and parameterize bio-optical algorithms for POC, phytoplankton pigments, and other parameters of biogeochemical significance such as total suspended matter and light absorption by dissolved organic matter. We will apply these algorithms to satellite ocean color data to derive basin scale maps of POC distributions within the upper ocean, and analyze the spatial and temporal variability of this reservoir within the context of physical forcing, biological processes, and the relationship of POC to other components of the oceanic carbon cycle. This analysis will be done for the entire operational period of SeaWiFS and MODIS ocean color satellite sensors. The results of our field and satellite studies, combined with those of our collaborators studying other aspects of carbon biogeochemistry, will provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the dynamics of carbon transformations in the Arctic Ocean, and allow the assessment of potential responses of this ecosystem to changes in climate.

Description: UNDERSTANDING MERCURY'S MAGNETOSPHERE USING MESSENGER DATA AND GLOBAL KINETIC SIMULATIONS A proposal is made to study the solar wind interaction with Mercury and its magnetic field.  Important science questions to be addressed include examining direct solar wind impact with the planetary surface, which has implications for mass recycling between the regolith, exosphere and magnetosphere; understanding mechanisms for ion and electron acceleration in the Hermean magnetosphere; examining whether substorm-like processes occur in Mercury's magetotail; and understanding the field-aligned current system within the magnetosphere.  To carry out this research, three-dimensional global kinetic simulations will be used along with measurements from the MESSENGER satellite to provide closure between theory and data.  The simulations will be carried out using the MESSENGER data as a guide to help set the solar wind and planetary conditions and to provide a global context for measurements made within the magnetosphere.  The simulation results will be output in the same format as relevant satellite data and will be provided to the Planetary Data System (PDS) for use in comparing the two in general and for event studies.  This project addresses NASA Strategic Sub-goal 3B to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system and in particular NASA Science Outcome 3B.1 to progress in understanding the fundamental physical processes of the space environment from the Sun to Earth, to other planets, and beyond to the interstallar medium.

Description: SOUNDING OF SATELLITE INTERIORS BY USING ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION Several projects to sound the interiors of the icy Galilean satellites by the use of electromag-netic induction are proposed. We would further refine the analysis of the available Galileo data on electromagnetic induc-tion from icy Galilean satellites and place better limits on the conductivity and the thicknesses of their oceans. We would develop multi-shell models to adequately represent the interior (the ocean, the mantle, and the core) and the exterior (the ionosphere) conducting layers of these moons. We would develop better models of the plasma effects to further improve the estimates of the induction signature. We would also develop better models of the external field to better char-acterize the effect of the changing primary field. We would devise new analytical and numerical techniques that could be applied to analysis of data from future orbiter and lander missions to the Galilean satellites and other solar system bodies. We would develop new techniques to invert the response of a multi-shell body to a pri-mary signal composed of multiple frequencies. We shall also develop new techniques that allow the separation of induction and primary signals at multiple frequencies from the analysis of data from a single orbiting spacecraft. New numerical simulations would be developed to model the response of an inhomogene-ous, non-spherically symmetric body to a changing homogeneous field. The new effort will address several of the current NASA roadmap and the NRC decadal sur-vey objectives. In particular by better characterizing the interiors of the icy satellites, the current proposal will help us determine those characteristics of solar system that led to the origin of life and help identify the habitable zones in the solar system. We will make the new products resulting from this study available to the community though a web page on the Internet.

Description: This proposal requests support to conduct scientific data analysis, data validation, ongoing calibration and assist the PI (Professor Henri Reme) in the operation of the Cluster Ion Spectrometry (CIS) experiment on the Cluster II spacecraft. The CIS experiment has two independent detectors that obtain full 3D distributions of ions in the magnetosphere and solar wind. Specifically, the Hot Ion Analyzer (HIA) detects 3D distributions of all ions in the energy range a few eV to ~ 40 keV/charge in one spin period of 4 seconds. In addition, the Ion Composition and Distribution Function Analyzer (CODIF) detects full 3D distribution of major ion species (H+, He+, He++ and 0+) from a few eV to -40 keV with high sensitivity and wide dynamic range. CODIF is operated in the RPA mode at perigee passes to permit measurement of 3D distributions of cold ion species from ~0 eV to ~ 40 eV (above the spacecraft potential). The primary scientific objective of CIS is to identify the solar wind and ionospheric particle sources that populate the magnetosphere and to learn about dynamics of particle transport and acceleration mechanisms of these populations. We are happy to report that significant new findings have been obtained during the last three years that are fundamentally important to space physics.

Description: THE PREVALENCE OF BRIGHT SURFACES (SNOW, GLACIERS, SEA-ICE, AND CLOUDS) MAKE THE CRYOSPHERE UNIQUELY SUSCEPTIBLE TO RADIATIVELY INDUCED EFFECTS OF BLACK CARBON (BC) SUCH AS ICE-ALBEDO FEEDBACK AMPLIFICATION. WE WILL ADVANCE CURRENT UNDERSTANDING OF CRYOSPHERIC BC CLIMATE IMPACTS BY INTEGRATING EFFECTS OF POST-DEPOSITION BC (I.E., DIRTY SNOW) WITH THE DIRECT EFFECTS OF ATMOSPHERIC BC. THIS PROJECT'S PRIMARY OBJECTIVE IS TO UNDERSTAND BC EFFECTS ON CRYOSPHERIC CLIMATE SENSITIVITY AND SURFACE HYDROLOGY. WE HAVE INTEGRATED SATELLITE-DERIVED BC EMISSIONS INTO A UNIFIED MODELING FRAMEWORK, WHERE WE WILL FORECAST AND HINDCAST CONTEMPORARY AND 21ST CENTURY CLIMATE WITH AND WITHOUT ATMOSPHERIC AND SURFACE BC EFFECTS. THESE SIMULATIONS RELY ON OUR SNOW, ICE, AND AEROSOL RADIATIVE MODEL (SNICAR) EMBEDDED IN THE COMMUNITY CLIMATE SYSTEM MODEL (CCSM) FORCED BY THE MODIS-DERIVED GLOBAL FIRE EMISSIONS DATABASE (GFED). WE ASK THREE TYPES OF QUESTIONS: FIRST, HOW DO TIMING AND LOCATION BC EMISSIONS AFFECT ARCTIC SURFACE REFLECTANCE AND ATMOSPHERIC PROCESSES? BC INCREASES ATMOSPHERIC ABSORPTANCE IN CLEAR AND CLOUDY CONDITIONS AND THIS HELPS WARM AND THUS DARKEN SNOWPACK. HOWEVER, SNOWPACK IS ALSO VERY SENSITIVE TO TEMPERATURE FEEDBACKS TRIGGERED BY THE VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF SOOT IN THE SNOWPACK ITSELF. USING ALTERNATING YEARS OF HIGH AND LOW BOREAL SOOT EMISSIONS FROM THE GFED, WE WILL TEST HOW ATMOSPHERIC AND SURFACE SOOT CONTRIBUTE TO IMPROVING MODEL AGREEMENT WITH MODIS-DERIVED SPECTRAL SURFACE REFLECTANCE. SECOND, WHAT ARE THE RELATIVE ROLES OF SURFACE AND ATMOSPHERIC BC FORCING ON ARCTIC CLIMATE SENSITIVITY INCLUDING SEA-ICE? ATMOSPHERIC BC COOLS THE SURFACE BY BACKSCATTERING AND ABSORBING INCIDENT SUNLIGHT. SNOWPACK BC HEATING COMPOUNDED BY SNOW-ALBEDO FEEDBACK CAN EXCEED ATMOSPHERIC BC SURFACE COOLING IN STRONG FIRE YEARS. WE WILL ASSESS HOW BC MIXING STATE AFFECTS TOP-OF-ATMOSPHERE ALBEDO (FROM CERES), SURFACE SPECTRAL REFLECTANCE (FROM MODIS), AND SEA-ICE EXTENT (FROM AMSR-E). THIRD, HOW DOES BC ALTER SURFACE WATER SEASONALITY SUCH AS SOIL MOISTURE, SNOWPACK DEPTH AND EXTENT, DEPTH TO PERMAFROST, AND RUNOFF TO THE ARCTIC? CONCENTRATION AND SCAVENGING OF SEASONALLY DEPOSITED BC WITHIN SNOWPACK CAN SIGNIFICANTLY ALTER PARTITIONING OF SPRING THAW PROCESSES BETWEEN SUBLIMATION TO THE ATMOSPHERE AND MELT/PERCOLATION TO SURFACE WATER. WE WILL USE IN SITU SNOWPACK BC PROFILES MEASURED DURING IPY ACTIVITIES TO IMPROVE BC SCAVENGING IN SNICAR AND CCSM. SNOW WATER EQUIVALENT, EXTENT, AND LIQUID SURFACE SOIL MOISTURE (FROM AMSR) AND SPRING DISCHARGE TO THE ARCTIC OCEAN (FROM GAUGE DATA AND GRACE) WILL TEST OUR GLOBAL SIMULATIONS. RELEVANCE TO NASA'S STRATEGIC OBJECTIVES: THE PROJECT OUTCOMES MEETS NASA STRATEGIC GOAL 3.1 ("STUDY PLANET EARTH FROM SPACE TO ADVANCE SCIENTIFIC UNDERSTANDING AND MEET SOCIETAL NEEDS") AND IDS SUBELEMENT 5 OBJECTIVES BY USING SPACE-BASED REMOTE SENSING AND GLOBAL MODELS TO IMPROVE UNDERSTANDING AND PREDICTION OF THE ROLE OF BLACK CARBON IN AFFECTING CLOUDS, PRECIPITATION, AND THE HYDROLOGIC CYCLE. OUR IMPROVED UNDERSTANDING AND PREDICTIONS OF THE CRYOSPHERIC HYDROLOGIC CYCLE WILL BE INCORPORATED VIA CCSM INTO THE IPCC AR5 REPORT TO HELP SOCIETY UNDERSTAND, PLAN FOR, AND MITIGATE BC EFFECTS ON CRYOSPHERIC CLIMATE

Description: We propose to continue to conduct small scale laboratory experiments to study impact damage and now concentrate on porous rocks and minerals, and conduct calculations so that these might be extrapolated to larger scales. We are now measuring the elastic moduli deficits via P and S wave velocities, and attenuations and inverting these using the theory of O;.Connell and Budiansky to characterize the volume density of tensile and shear cracks and their characteristic length. We expect to continue to develop damage models for planetary materials using dynamic tensile strength measurements which we are also conducting. We propose to extend our modeling into the gravity dominated regime of cratering and develop a constituted model of crack weakening Ashby-Sammis damage mechanics in a 2- and 3-dimensional shock wave code. This will provide a complete gravity rebound and oscillation model to predict the amplitude, spacing, and extent of the rings around large planetary gravity-controlled craters. We propose to continue to study and explore turbulent mixing of shock-induced iron metal and molten silicates containing various siderophiles, and examine the apparent variable pressure and temperature conditions of different elements upon metal silicate partitioning. We expect to study the scaling of these effects in the laboratory and develop a theoretical basis to extrapolate models of the accretion of planets and metal-silicate reaction occurring upon accreting planets within the Abe-Matsui magma ocean hypothesis. We expect to extend our previous measurements of shock vaporization and ionic species generation from our previous laser-induced impacts to now mechanical impacts of small explosively loaded flyer plates launched within our Caltech built time-of-flight mass spectrometer. We expect to model small scale volatilization and energetic ion production processes as these occur within mineral grains and in porous media on various scales at much lower velocities than vaporization is predicted from continuum models. We expect to develop shear band models for crystals and characteristic heating via reactant chemistry.

Description: We propose to use FUSE spectroscopy to search for evidence of outflows in the transition regions of Luminosity Class H bright giants with spectral types of late-F through early-K. The incidence of winds among such stars is of interest for a number of reasons, including: (i) these stars fall just below a region of the H-R diagram in which circumstellar Ca II is detected, and as such they may be in states of mass loss prior to, or in lieu of, the development of a cool wind, (ii) their chromospheric Mg II emission line profiles often show no evidence of outflow, thus if winds are present they must accelerate with altitude, and (iii) they may be relevant to the poorly understood mechanism by which Population II red giants with -2.7 < Mv < -1.7 lose mass prior to becoming horizontal branch stars. Emission lines from the transition region (TR) can reveal the presence of an accelerating wind. FUSE covers the crucial O VI 1032 angstrom line which arises from altitudes where the temperatures are ~3e5 K, higher and/or hotter than for TR lines typically observed by IUE and HST. Asymmetries in the profile of this line can reveal opacity associated with outflowing material. Dupree et al. (2005) found evidence for TR wind opacity in a small sample of evolved giants from FUSE O VI spectra. However, they have only one LC II giant, the binary star beta Dra (B-V = 1.0) in their sample. We propose to investigate the O VI line profile of two single LC II giants having B-V = 0.8 and 1.2 to test for a general incidence of TR outflows among such stars. The strong C III line at 977 angstroms may also be usable for this purpose depending on how much interstellar medium absorption is superimposed.

Description: This proposal requests support to conduct scientific data analysis, data validation, ongoing calibration and assist the PI (Professor Henri Reme) in the operation of the Cluster Ion Spectrometry (CIS) experiment on the Cluster II spacecraft. The CIS experiment has two independent detectors that obtain full 3D distributions of ions in the magnetosphere and solar wind. Specifically, the Hot Ion Analyzer (HIA) detects 3D distributions of all ions in the energy range a few eV to ~ 40 keV/charge in one spin period of 4 seconds. In addition, the Ion Composition and Distribution Function Analyzer (CODIF) detects full 3D distribution of major ion species (H+, He+, He++ and 0+) from a few eV to -40 keV with high sensitivity and wide dynamic range. CODIF is operated in the RPA mode at perigee passes to permit measurement of 3D distributions of cold ion species from ~0 eV to ~ 40 eV (above the spacecraft potential). The primary scientific objective of CIS is to identify the solar wind and ionospheric particle sources that populate the magnetosphere and to learn about dynamics of particle transport and acceleration mechanisms of these populations. We are happy to report that significant new findings have been obtained during the last three years that are fundamentally important to space physics.

Description: UNIFIED COMPUTATIONAL PLATFORM FOR CFD AND CSD FOR ROTORCRAFT AEROMECHANICS  We propose to perform a feasibility study of a unified computational platform for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and computational structural dynamics (CSD) with application to rotorcraft aeromechanics. The unified formulation represents a bold new direction in fluid-structure solutions, which have traditionally interfaced independent CFD and CSD codes, each using different (and sometimes incompatible) numerical techniques. The approach envisaged here is based on a common finite-volume discretization and fully implicit solution of the coupled fluid, structural and mesh motion equations. It allows full conservation of forces at the fluid-structure interface, uniform temporal and spatial accuracy of the global problem and complete coupling of the non-linear terms in the governing equations. Specific research studies will focus on algorithmic issues related to conservation, robustness, efficiency and accuracy for moving and deforming body problems, including appropriate preconditioning procedures to account for the inherent stiffness between the fluids and structural equations. To demonstrate the feasibility of the approach, a two dimensional CFD-CSD code will be developed and tested on a variety of 2D problems such as flexible beams and airfoils. It is envisaged that the unified platform will provide the foundation for a new generation of fluids-structure modeling tools with applications in rotorcraft aeromechanics as well as in the broad area of aeronautics.

Description: Lithospheric Stress from Plate Boundary Deformation and Surface Loads for Improved understanding of Seismic Hazard (Student-Karen Marie Luttrell) Understanding the absolute and relative magnitude of principal stress within a region is crucial to understanding the geophysical processes of that region: style of faulting, strength of faults, portion of stress relieved throughout the earthquake cycle compared to ambient geologic stresses, amount of stress transfer between brittle and ductile layers, and the role of interseismic versus coseismic deformation in determining the timing and location of the next regional rupture. Deviatoric stress within the lithosphere can he produced by tectonic forces (mostly horizontal stress) and topography on density interfaces like the free surface and Moho (mostly vertical stress). We propose to investigate the effects of various surface loads on the deviatoric stresses in the lithosphere in four ways: 1) Develop a 3-D model, constrained by geologic observations, to predict variations in Coulomb stress along the Southern San Andreas Fault in response to the transient presence of Ancient Lake Cahuilla in the Salton Trough. Variations in Coulomb stress can affect the timing of future ruptures and are thus significant for understanding Southern California seismic hazards. Much of this research has been completed [Luttrell et al., 2006,ttp://topex.ucsd.edu/kluttrelvCahuilla/LakeCahuiI1a2OO6.pd. 2) Extend the 3-D model developed in (1) to examine the long-term changes in slip rate on plate boundary faults caused by a rise in eustatic sea level over the last 25,000 years, and examine the specific effect of the catastrophic flooding of the Black Sea 7000 years ago on the nearby North Anatolian Fault. 3) Improve our 3-D stress model to include both surface loads and the buoyant restoring force of a deformed Moho. We will use SRTM topography and bathymetry data to estimate 3-D lithospheric stress both regionally and globally. 4) Compare LIDAR data from the B4 project with SRTM topography along the San Andreas Fault to understand the differences between them and predict the challenges in integrating a future global LIDAR data set with the existing topography data sets. Our results have direct relevance to understanding seismic hazard in the studied regions.

Description: The discrimination of crustal and core sources, essential to understanding Mercury's magnetic field history, requires the identification of structure at all resolvable wavelengths. Because of the geometry of observations, and contributions from external fields, current plans for magnetic fields products and their archiving, are restricted to least-squares estimates of dipole and quadrupole terms, and a grid of deviations from these, severely limiting scientific return on the magnetic observations acquired. Accordingly, the proposed tasks will use mature methodologies in time series analysis and inverse theory that enable the recovery of structure in the field at all resolvable wavelengths. The work is designed to complement and extend the MESSENGER products that will be delivered by the MAG team, and to enable fundamental questions about Mercury to be addressed. The proposed tasks will: (1) characterize and assess MAG data (internal/external fields, noise, spatial resolution), (2) estimate global statistics of Mercury's internal field using flyby and early nominal mission data (enabling global inferences in the event of incomplete data return), (3) provide global maps and spectra of the static (time-invariant) part of Mercury's field, (4) identify, where discernible, temporal changes (secular variation) in Mercury's internal field during the MESSENGER mission. It is anticipated that all global field models will be delivered to the PDS, and that the results of data assessment and characterization will help in the MAG team's delivery of data. The work will use MAG data explicitly, and because of the focus on internal field structure I am proposing to be a member of the geophysics team; I anticipate collaboration with the magnetosphere / atmosphere team throughout the mission.

Description: Magnetometry is a vital aspect of much space and planetary exploration. In particular, magnetometric studies are the only way to obtain direct information about the deep interior of the Earth. Current systems for space-based magnetometers will need to be replaced by more sensitive instruments for future, more demanding missions. We propose to develop an ultrasensitive magnetometer based on an alkali atomic vapor optically pumped and read out using laser light. Potential sensitivity of I fT/Hz"(1/2)--orders of magnitude better than that provided by the instruments used in current missions--can be obtained by using an anti relaxation-coated vapor cell, allowing long atomic coherence lifetimes. The magnetometer can be made compact and with low power consumption, and a wide dynamic range is possible using a scheme based on modulated laser light. In order to design and optimize such a magnetometer, a quantitative theoretical model is required. We propose to construct such a model, using density-matrix theory, based on previous work involving related systems. This model will describe the effects of pump and probe light nonperturbatively, will track the behavior of the atoms as they move between illuminated and nonilluminated regions of the vapor cell, and will account for Doppler-broadening and velocity-changing atomic collisions. This will allow quantitative optimization of the performance of the ultrasensitive magnetometer.

Description: Multiwavelength InSAR Properties of the Polar Ice Sheets Remote sensing is a critical technology for study of the Earth's polar ice sheets. Lack of accessibility, harsh environmental conditions, and the vast size of the ice sheets make microwave observation from space or aircraft especially useful for polar research. Radar methods in particular have proven very helpful in observing and constraining ice velocities, dynamics, discharge and accumulation processes. Spaceborne platforms available for polar work have mainly used the C-band (6 cm wavelength) part of the radio spectrum, as it provides a strong backscatter from the topmost 20 m of the firn, ideal for surface velocity measurements. Other radar systems have been proposed at longer and shorter wavelengths to meet objectives of other disciplines, especially solid Earth crustal deformation studies. Experimental understanding of the interaction of these other frequencies with ice is limited, as no significant and comprehensive data set exists at frequencies other than C-band. Our goal here is to acquire and analyze data at L, C, and X band (24, 6, and 3 cm) over the ice sheets and determine the mechanisms at each wavelength for microwave interaction with the ice. We will begin with a model for scattering that has been proven using C-band data, and apply it at the other wavelengths so that we may understand what physical characteristics of the surface and subsurface are reflected in the data. For example, longer L-band wavelengths will penetrate further into the ice than C-band, so that we may be sensitive to motions or structure 100s of meters deep rather than to the surface. Using both wavelengths, velocity profiles of the ice might be obtained, adding insight to the flow of glaciers and ice streams. It may also be true that some wavelengths will simply not be sensitive to parameters of interest, so that one of the outcomes of this work will be to recommend instrumentation for future space missions. Data at C and X band wavelengths are available from multiple satellite platforms, but little data is available at L-band. While the ALOS PALSAR will deliver data from the polar regions, its long repeat time and scarce scheduling time will limit its application to this problem. Therefore we propose to use the UAVSAR instrument now being developed at JPL to collect L-band data. Most of the UAVSAR project goals are highly compatible with ours, but we will have to ensure that imaging geometries and data processing return the data products we need. This may entail some changes to the nominal data processing algorithms and strategy, but we expect a sizable data set that will validate our scattering models at the longer wavelength. The concentrated activities of IPY provide a focus on this work and will result in many field experiments that will aid in verifying our modeling and analysis. Without this comprehensive set of contemporaneous in situ investigations, we would not be able to adequately validate our methods and the conclusions would only be conjectures.

Description: AN INFORMATION THEORY APPROACH TO PERSISTENT SCATTERER INSAR (GRADUATE STUDENT: PIYUSH AGRAM) We propose a new InSAR persistent scatterer (PS) selection method that uses a probabilistic approach to identify many more PS points than are found by existing algorithms. Our method for identifying PS pixels in a series of interferograms is based on comparing the phase characteristics of pixels with the theoretical distributions corresponding to assumed signal models. We first plan to develop signal models that statistically describe the radar signals from resolution elements in SAR images, and then derive their corresponding theoretical interferometric phase distributions. These distributions are then used in a Maximum Likelihood (ML) based PS selection process. Preliminary calculations (see below) show that our method finds a dense network of scatterers with stable phase characteristics in areas where conventional InSAR fails due to complete decorrelation of the majority of scatterers. These preliminary results are obtained from InSAR data acquired over the San Francisco Bay Area. With our new method, we aim to retrieve deformation time-series of regions, where lack of such data has been the major hindrance in modeling seismic processes.

Description: HYDROGEN IN THE ROCK COLUMN This proposal addresses the presence of hydrogen in the rock column. Hydrogen is an energy source for micro-organisms, especially for methanogens. The deep environment may have served as refuge for early Life in the aftermath of large impacts or during global glaciation episodes. Microbial communities in deep-seated rocks need an energy source and food. While it is well-known that hydrogen can be generated by the reduction of water through oxidation of transition metal cations, for instance Fe2 in mafic and ultramafic rocks, a much more broadly distributed hydrogen source seems to exist in the top 20-30 km of the rock column. This form of hydrogen is introduced through a solid state redox reaction taking place in the matrix of nominally anhydrous minerals that crystallized or recrystallized in water-laden magmatic or high-grade metamorphic environments. Those minerals invariably incorporate small amounts of water in form of hydroxyl, O3Si-OH. During cooling hydroxyl pairs undergo a redox reaction, in the course of which the protons rip off an electron from their oxygens. Two protons turn into hydrogen, while two oxygens change from valence 2- to 1- forming a peroxy link, O3Si-OO-SiO3. Molecular hydrogen is diffusively mobile and can enter the space between grains and dissolve in intergranular water films. It thus becomes accessible to micro-organisms. We propose a study of the presence of hydrogen in rocks. We shall measure: (i) the slow release of hydrogen after crushing rocks in inert gas using a MIS-FET detector, sensitive over the 0.5-2000 vppm range with 5-10 sec resolution. We shall analyze rocks from mid- to lower-crustal and upper mantle environments; (ii) the near-instant release of hydrogen during fracture of single crystals using a fast mass spectrometer with micro-second time resolution. Combining the two types of measurements (i) and (ii) we expect to obtain information about the amount of hydrogen contained in the rock column and, hence, its availability to deep microbial communities. This work is central to the Astrobiology Roadmap Goal 4, Objective 4.1 Earths early biosphere, to Goal 3, Objective 3.1 Sources of prebiotic materials and catalysts, and to Goal 2, Objective 2.1 Mars exploration. It will provide information about a source of molecular hydrogen that has never before been systematically investigated.

Description: INTERSTELLAR PRECURSORS OF METEORITIC ORGANICS - A THEORETICAL STUDY  It is proposed to continue theoretical studies of organic astrochemistry. The principal goals of this project are to identify interstellar molecules in the soluble organic extracts of carbonaceous meteorites, and to quantify the viability of the many interstellar organics which have been proposed as precursors of more complex meteoritic molecules formed by aqueous alteration chemistry. This will be done by chemical kinetic modeling of gas and solid phase processes, as constrained by comparison with the complex molecular inventory of meteorites and molecular clouds. Stochastic simulations will be performed to investigate pathways to molecular complexity through cold atom addition reactions on the surfaces of dust grains. The expected isotopic fractionation patterns (e.g. in D and rm 13 for the putative interstellar precursor molecules required by processes such as the Strecker synthesis will be computed and compared to the meteoritic data. The interstellar production of amino acids, in gas phase syntheses driven by ice evaporation in warm protostellar environments, will be evaluated. The isototopic fractionation patterns in large interstellar organic compounds as a function of synthesis route will also be calculated and compared to recent meteoritic analyses. The modeling effort will employ experimental data on surface processes and ion-molecule reactions provided by our collaborators. It is also proposed to undertake a modest observing program to search for new organics predicted by our theoretical work. The proposed research meshes with NASA's strategic goals, and those of the Exobiology and Evolutionary Biology Program. The results of this study will allow us to quantify the relative contribution, direct or indirect, of various interstellar chemical processes to specific classes of meteoritic organics. This will enable us to assess their general relevance for providing materials capable of initiating prebiotic chemistry in planetary systems.

Description: Mapping Sub-glacial Water Movement in Antartica with Icesat This project will build upon Pi's the recent exciting discovery of a large subglacial lake on the Whillans Ice Stream near the grounding line of the Ross Ice Shelf in repeat-track ICESat data. The elevation "draw-down" signal is large (10m over -2.5 years) and represents the most detailed dataset of sub-glacial lake drainage acquired to date, benefiting from the repeat-track orbit of ICESat and ICESat's high precision and resolution. The repeat-track ICESat elevation profiles clearly show the draw-down of the lake and the surrounding region and how it evolves over time. We have also found similar signals further south on Whillans Ice Stream at higher elevation, near Conway Ridge, where we think that complex water transport is taking place beneath the ice sheet. With this proposal, we intend to map this "sub-glacial plumbing" using ICESat data for the major ice stream systems of the Antarctic ice sheet.

Description: UNSOLICITED RESEARCH PROPOSAL ENTITLED "A STUDY OF THE EFFECT OF BIOMASS BURNING ON THE GLOBAL UPPER TOPOSHPHERE AND LOWER STRATOSTROM" ABSTRACT FROM YEAR ONE ANNUAL REPORT: WE INVESTIGATED THE EFFECTS OF FIRE-INCLUDED PLUME-RISE ON THE PREDICTED EXPORT OF CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) OVER AFRICA DURING SAFARI 2000 USING THE NCAR COMMUNITY ATMOSPHERE MODEL (CAM) WITH CO TRACER AND PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME.  THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SIMULATES THE CONSEQUENCES OF STRONG BUOYANCY OF HOT GASES EMITTED FROM BIOMASS BURNING, INCLUDING BOTH DRY AND CLOUD-ASSOCIATED (PYROCUMULUS) LOFTING.  THE SCHEME WAS FIRST ADAPTED FROM A REGIONAL MODEL.  THE CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME INTO THE GLOBAL MODEL PROVIDES AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXAMINE THE EFFECT OF PLUME-RISE ON LONG RANGE TRANSPORT.  THE CAM SIMULATION WITH THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SHOWS A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT OF THE AGREEMENTS BETWEEN THE MODELED AND AIRCRAFT-MEASURED VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CO OVER SOUTHERN AFRICA BIOMASS BURNING.  THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM PLAYS CRUCIAL ROLE IN LOFTING BIOMASS BURNING POLLUTANTS TO THE MIDDLE TROPOSPHERE.  IN THE PRESENCE OF DEEP CONVECTION WE FOUND THAT THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM RESULTS IN A DECREASE OF CO CONCENTRATION IN THE UPPER TROPOSPHERE.  THE PLUME RISE DEPLETES THE BOUNDARY LAYER, AND THUS LEAVES LOWER CONCENTRATIONS OF CO TO BE LOFTED BY THE DEEP CONVECTION PROCESS.  THE EFFECT OF THE PLUME-RISE ON FREE TROPOSPHERE (CO) CONCENTRATION IS MORE IMPORTANT FOR THE SOURCE AREA (SHORT-DISTANCE TRANSPORT) THAN FOR REMOTE AREAS (LONG-DISTANCE TRANSPORT).  THE PLUME-RISE SCHEME ALSO INCREASES THE CO EXPORT FLUXES FROM AFRICA TO THE ATLANTIC AND INDIAN OCEANS.  THESE RESULTS FURTHER CONFIRM AND EXTENT PREVIOUS FINDINGS IN A REGIONAL MODEL STUDY.  EFFECTIVE LOFTING OF LARGE CONCENTRATION OF CO BY THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM ALSO HAS IMPLICATION FOR LOCAL AIR QUALITY FORECAST IN AREAS AFFECTED BY OTHER FIRE-RELATED POLLUTANTS.

Description: IMPACTS: MARTIAN GREENHOUSES AND LONG-TERM THERMAL MODELING THIS PROPOSAL FOCUS ON TWO MAIN TASKS: 1) SIMULATION OF LARGE IMPACTS ONTO THE MARTIAN SURFACES AS POSSIBLE GENERATORS OF TRANSIENT GREENHOUSE CLIMATE REGIMES, AND 2) LONG-TERM HYDROTHERMAL MODELING OF IMPACT CRATER LAKES ON MARS. IN THE FIRST TASK, WE WILL CARRY OUT SIMULATIONS OF LARGE IMPACTS INTO THE MARTIAN SURFACE. THE RESULTING MOBILIZATION OF IMPACTOR AND CRUSTAL (SUB-SURFACE) WATER WILL BE CRITICALLY ASSESSED INPUTS FOR THE HYPOTHESIS THAT FLUIVAL FEATURES ON THE MARTIAN SURFACE WERE PRODUCED BY TRANSIENT IMPACT-DRIVEN GREENHOUSES. THE PROPOSED CALCULATIONS WILL USE THE COMPUTER CODE RAGE, DEVELOPED AT LOS ALAMOS NATIONAL LABORATORY. RAGE IS A POWERFUL AND FLEXIBLE CODE THAT SIMULATES HYDRODYNAMIC PROCESSES. IT EMPLOYS HIGH-QUALITY ALGORITHMS FOR THE BASIC DYNAMICS AND CAN MODEL IMPORTANT AND RELEVANT PHYSICS SUCH AS MATERIAL STRENGTH. IT ALSO CONTAINS AN ADAPTIVE MESH ROUTINE THAT CONCENTRATES COMPUTATIONAL RESOURCES EFFICIENTLY. IT CAN HE RUN ON COMPUTER CLUSTERS, TO WHICH THE P1 AND COL HAVE ACCESS AT LANL. THE SECOND TASK WILL FOCUS ON HYDROTHERMAL MODELING OF CRATER LAKES ON MARS. THE ENERGY BUDGET, GROWTH AND EROSION OF THE ICE-CAP LAKE COVER, AND THE THERMAL STATE AND SALINITY OF THE UNDERLYING WATER WILL CALCULATED FOR A VARIETY OF SCENARIOS, AND THE RESULTS ASSESSED IN LIGHT THEIR IMPLICATIONS FOR THE GEOLOGICAL AND CLIMATIC HISTORY OF MARS, AND ITS POTENTIAL AS AN ABODE FOR LIFE. THE HULK OF THE REQUESTED FUNDING IS FOR SUPPORT FOR GRADUATE STUDENT RESEARCHERS CATHERINE PLESKO AND CHARLES BARNHART. PLESKO HAS EXTENSIVE EXPERIENCE WITH RAGE AND HAS WORKED WITH LOS ALAMOS COLLABORATORS FOR SEVERAL YEARS. BARNHART HAS DEVELOPED INITIAL 1-DIMENSIONAL MODELS FOR THE THERMAL EVOLUTION OF CRATER LAKES, AND WILL EXTEND HIS WORK TO MULTI-DIMENSIONAL CALCULATIONS BY ADAPTING ESTABLISHED CODES DEVELOPED FOR TERRESTRIAL OTHER PLANETARY ENVIRONMENTS.

Publicly released stereo imagery from multiple spacecraft will be used to derive digital topographic maps of selected sites. Description: Small Business Innovative Research 2005 Phase II for Enhanced L/D and Virtual Shaping of NLF Sections. A novel and robust flow control technique for the virtual shaping of extended run Natural Laminar Flow (NLF) sections has been developed. The virtual shaping and separation control technology can be used to control the size and extent of extremely large separation bubbles to virtually shape the aft recovery region of the airfoil. The system uses a novel pressure porting technique that requires no external air source to produce a pulsed tangential jet in the separated region capable of partially or fully eliminating the presence of the separation bubble. The novel pulsed jet system was shown to produce equivalent results to continuous blowing using approximately a 42% lower jet velocity and 87% lower momentum coefficient. The virtual shaping of an extended run NLF section could offer radical performance enhancement in the form of increased lift-to-drag and maximum lift. Additionally, the system will produce a wing design enabling a hinge-less, full-span virtual shaping capability, which can be used for pilot reactive roll control, span load tailoring, and gust load alleviation. The system will provide significantly enhanced performance for the air vehicle throughout the entire flight envelope. The proposed virtual shaping and separation control technology has significant potential application in several NASA programs. The virtual shaping and flow control system could be fielded in several NASA unmanned aircraft systems, including m-UAVs, high-altitude long endurance remotely operated aircraft (HALE-ROA) for reconnaissance, and Mars exploratory aircraft. NASA designers will be eager to exploit the advantages of the current virtual shaping technology in airfoil designs and flow control systems. The technology will deliver significantly enhanced performance as compared to traditional designs in a robust package. The system will be applicable throughout NASA's high altitude unmanned and m-UAV aviation community.

Description: SPIDER:  A LARGE ANGULAR SCALE MILLIMETER-WAVE POLARIMETER We propose SPIDER: a new long-duration balloon experiment to map the polarization ofthe CMB over more than half of the sky at 80,100,145, 225 and 275 GHz. SPIDER has 3 scientific goals: (I) precisely determine the optical depth to scattering of CMB photons since reionization, fixing the epoch of reionization (ii) characterize the polarized mm-wave emission from interstellar dust on large (1 degree) angular scales and (iii) search for the B-mode polarization signal that would be imprinted in the CMB by a Cosmic Gravitational-wave Background (CGB). SPIDER complements the frequency coverage (23,33, 41,64, 94 GHz) pf WMAP with higher sensitivity, and the relatively small sky coverage (few percent) of all currently funded sub-orbital experiments. The frequency coverage and high sensitivity provide a means to separate the polarized emission from interstellar dust from the polarization ofthe CMB. The sky coverage provides a means of measuring the large angular scale features in the polarization power spectrum associated with re-ionization, and allows the SPIDER data to be used in concert with the WMAP data to study the correlations 6f polarized synchrotron and dust emission on large angular scales. SPIDER complements both Planck and WMAP by incorporating a high-performance polarization modulator, and Planck by using highly redundant and cross-linked scan strategy, to achieve high polarimetric fldelity. SPIDER is both a scientific and technical pathfinder for a future orbital mission (CMBpol). SPIDER will help to determine the nature ofthe Galactic foregrounds which will ultimately limit the search for the signature of CGB, and will test scan strategies, polarization modulation methods, optics and detector technologies that are appropriate to CMBpol. In the absence of foregrounds, SPIDER's sky coverage and sensitivity allow detection of the CGB characterized by a tensor to scalar ratio of r = 0.04 (3 sigma).

Description: SBIR 2005 Phase II Proposal Title: Dynamic Strain and Crack Monitoring Sensor.  Los Gatos Research proposes to develop a new automated vehicle health monitoring sensor system capable of measuring loads and detecting crack, corrosion, and disbonding in advanced aerospace structures using a novel lock-in laser interrogation technique combined with a Bragg grating array (BGA) technology for strain and guided Lamb wave (GLW) sensing.  Los Gatos Research's novel sensor instrumentation offers a number of advantages including sensor compactness (0.2mm x 0.2 mm x 10mm), lightweight (a few grams), remote data acquisition capability, low-cost, and low power consumption.  The inherently reliable lock-in laser demodulation technique permit simultaneous measurements of strain, temperature, and acoustic fields with high resolution and high sensitivity.   In Phase I, we have demonstrated feasibility by buildiing a prototype instrument capable of measuring static and dynamic strain, temperature, and ultrasonic waves using a lock-in laser demodulation technique and a fiber Bragg grating array sensor network.  In Phase II, Los Gatos Research will deliver to NASA a rugged, compact, multi-channel instrument optimized for vehicle health monitoring studies including strain, temperature, and crack monitoring with high precision, high resolution, and high sensitivity.  This dedicated prototype will include an integrated microcontroller, operate unattended, and address the power and stability requirements unique to in-flight studies. Potential NASA commercial applications could be provided through optical fiber technology which gives significant advantages for advanced aerospace platforms because they are lightweight, immune to electromagnetic wave interference, rugged, and do not produce short circuits or ground loops.  Therefore the development of high sensitivity fiber optic sensors has the potential to increase reliability, enable lower cost, and facilitate more effective health monitoring and nondestructive evaluation of NASA's advanced aircraft and spacecraft components and systems.  The Bragg grating array sensor deveice Los Gatos Research has demonstrated and proposed to further develop for Phase II will greatly enhance NASA efforts to develop state-of-the-art, compact, low-cost, waveform-based, quantitative strain and ultrasonic wave sensing technology for load, temperature, corrosion, and crack monitoring of advanced structures. The potential non-NASA commercial applications embrace advances in high-resolution, high sensitivity, and large dynamic range load and ultrasonic wave sensing technology has immediate applications in civil engineering for monitoring cracks, corrosion, and fatigue in steel and concrete structures such as bridges, freeways, and buildings.  High frequency ultrasonic signal detection method development can be utilized in ultrasonic testing, medical imaging, and other non-destructive testing technology.  Los Gatos Research's BGA technology development can readily be incorporated into current fiber optics and optical cross-connect technology for next-generation telecommunication applications.

Description: MULTI CHIP MODULE MAGNETOMETER FOR PLANETARY AND LUNAR EXPLORATION SUMMARY: We propose a three-year effort to design and implement a multi chip module (MCM) state of the art vector fluxgate magnetometer. While the fluxgate magnetometer has a long history of successful space-based operations, we are not yet at the stage were many tens or even hundreds of magnetometers can be built for multi-spacecraft or multi-station (e.g lunar or Mars surface) deployment. The latest designs have achieved quite remarkable mass and power savings, but more can be achieved through the MCM design. In particular we expect to achieve a combined sensor and electronics board mass of < 150 g, with power consumption around 300 mW. Furthermore, the MCM implementation will enable us to mount the electronics near the sensor, which will enable us to reduce the cable mass to 25% of current values. In addition, the MCM lends itself to build to print implementation. The MCM magnetometer is deigned to address many questions related to planetary, lunar, and heliospheric sciences. Areas to be addressed include: identifying remanent fields on a variety of solar system bodies, such as Mars, the moon, and comets; probing the structure of moons, planets and comets through magnetic induction; deployment as part of an array of magnetoseismic stations on the moon; solar wind magnetic field measurements on flotillas of spacecraft; and measurements of remanent and induction magnetic fields on planetary rovers and balloons. Because of the low resource reuirement the MCM magnetometer is a candidate for inclusion on Discovery and New Horizons class missions, with the potential for significant enhancement of the science return for these class of missions. The MCM is also a candidate for Mars Exploration Program missions, possibly being deployed on rovers or as arrays of magnetometers deployed on the surface. The MCM has the potential for technology transfer through the demonstration of multi chip module technology for a space-based application.

Description: ELECTRICAL PROPERTIES OF TITAN AS SEEN BY THE CASSINI RADAR SCATTEROMETER-(GRADUATE STUDENT-LAUREN C. WYE) The Cassini RADAR, a set of microwave instrumentation, is currently observing the surface of Titan at 13.78 GHz (2.18 cm wavelength) in four operational modes. These include a high-resolution imaging radar (SAR), a lower resolution scatterometer, a microwave radiometer, and a profiling altimeter. Under a contract with JPL, we have developed and calibrated a real aperture processor for the scatterometer mode data. We have also done preliminary modeling of the backscatter response to determine surface characteristics related to composition and structure. We propose here to enhance our understanding of titan; atmosphere-hidden surface with three further developments: 1) improve the resolution of the scatterometer processor using range compression and unfocused SAR techniques, 2) apply the scatterometer processor to data collected by the Cassini radar in all of its modes, thereby developing a more complete global backscatter map of Titan, and 3) develop a unified scattering and emission model that relates both the physical and chemical descriptions of the surface to the microwave observations across all RADAR datasets. We believe this will be a significant contribution to understanding this complex world that is in many ways similar to our own Earth. Its thick atmosphere, rich in Nitrogen and hydrocarbons, hides a surface that is dynamic and geologically active. With the SAR imager alone, we have discovered wind-swept sand-like dunes, fluvial channels, mountainous terrain, cyrovolcanism, and, most importantly, hydrocarbon lakes that are likely liquid. This body is eerily reminiscent of what scientists imagine early, pre-biotic Earth to have been like. Analysis of Cassini RADAR data will go along way to explaining some of the processes that take place there, and perhaps fill-in some missing pieces about the beginnings of our own planet. Scatterometry data is unique, in that it is the only active mode that has the potential to cover almost all of Titan's surface. We should exploit what this data can tell us completely.

Description: GAMMA-RAY EMISSION FROM OPTICALLY-SELECTED SUPERNOVAE The successful deployment of the Swift observatory and its ability to study the multi-wavelength properties of GRBs just minutes after the burst will undoubtedly revolutionize our physical understanding of these events. We propose here to use the sky monitoring capability of the Swift BATin complement to our wide area study of SNe and transients with SDSS-II to open new parameter space in the study of the prompt high energy emission from optical transients. During the survey, we expect to find several thousands of SNe of all types below a redshift of rv 0.4, some of which may produce y-ray emission, but are too low in flux to be triggered as GRBs. We propose to conduct an systematic archival search in the BAT data for prompt emission from optical transients. This study will target SNe of all types and, in particular, should allow us to probe the early high energy emission of core collapse SNe and the connection with hypernovae and y-ray bursts.
