Description: Newly Discovered Regions of Star Formation in Serpens and Perseus We propose XMM observations of two fields in Serpens and one in Perseus centered on newly discovered regions of recent star formation. Infrared Spitzer IRAC and MIPS maps reveal that these regions contain dense molecular gas and numerous previously unknown pre-main sequence (PMS) stars. Young stars are strong X-ray emitters throughout their PMS evolution, from embedded protostars to older PMS stars that are no longer infrared bright because accretion as ceased and circumstellar disks have dissipated. X-ray emission provides an excellent method of tracing the entire PMS population and investigating the star formation histories of these regions and the formation of stars within molecular clouds.

Description: Microcosm will build on the Phase I X-ray pulsar-based navigation and timing (XNAV) feasibility assessment to develop a detailed XNAV simulation capability to evaluate navigation performance for specific missions of interest, and create an XNAV flight software experiment ready to integrate on an appropriate near-term flight demonstration mission in Phase III.  Phase I demonstrated achievable XNAV accuracy, developed a preliminary source catalog, constructed an XNAV error budget, and laid out potential implementation options for XNAV, focusing on an Earth-Sun L2 lagrange point mission.  Brighter, less stable, non-traditional X-ray sources were also considered for possible XNAV application with promising initial results, especially for formation flying applications.  Taking advantage of concurrent XNAV efforts at DARPA to the maximum extent possible, Phase II will develop and validate XNAV algorithms via a simulation which will be targeted for integration with Goddard Space Flight Center's GPS Enhanced Onboard Navigation System (GEONS) software.  The error budget will be developed in more detail to support the algorithm and simulation work.  XNAV holds great potential for NASA as an enabling technology for fully autonomous interplanetary navigation and could provide a significant mission enhancement as an adjunct to the Deep Space Network (DSN) and ground based navigation. NASA's applications includes missions beyond Jupiter as an enabling technology for autonomous navigation, potentially providing improved performance over standard DSN tracking capability for very far missions.  This includes the Pioneer Anomaly mission or 500 AU mission.  XNAV provides fully autonomous interplanetary navigation capability, potentially reducing the demands on DSN for increasing tracking requirements for future missions.  XNAV can supplement DSN service and enhance DSN navigation performance.  XNAV can also provide a backup navigation capability for manned and unmanned near-Earth, lunar, and Mars missions.  Further, it can provide higher redundancy for manned missions.     This application will also provide primary and secondary navigation services for DoD and for MEO, GEO, HEO, and even cis-lunar missions where GPS has limited availability, XNAV can provide primary autonomous navigation capability, while also providing an essential backup navigation capability for missions which normally rely on GPS but have a need for continuity of operations in the event of loss or denial of GPS.

Description: Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental plasma process that is important in both space and laboratory. Despite more than 3 decades of observations on reconnection in space (mostly in the Earth's magnetosphere), many key questions concerning the fundamental properties of reconnection remain unanswered. The difficulty is due in part to the complex (highly varying) boundary conditions associated with magnetopause and magnetotail current sheets.  The recent discovery of reconnection exhausts in the solar wind has introduced a new, and in many ways better, laboratory where reconnection can be studied with in-situ measurements. Many solar wind current sheets are large scale (hundreds of thousand of ion skin depths), and they are nearly 1-D. Their boundary conditions tend to be stable with nearly symmetric conditions on the two sides of the current sheets. These pristine current sheets are therefore ideal for the study of the large-scale properties of reconnection without complications due to boundary conditions. We propose to address the following key unanswered questions concerning the fundamental properties of reconnection in large-scale current sheets using the best available data - the complete Wind set (and complemented by the ACE data set):   (1) Does reconnection occur commonly in a large-scale and quasi-steady manner or is the process primarily   patchy and bursty?    (2) Can reconnection occur when a significant guide (non-anti-parallel) field is present and how does the answer depend on parameters such as the plasma beta? The proposed investigations will advance our understanding of one of the most important space plasma processes. Our findings will undoubtedly spawn theoretical studies of reconnection in large current sheets. This is one of the few instances in reconnection research where observations may lead theory.

Description: The greatest limitation in current aerosol indirect effect estimates from global satellite data is the inability to separate the dynamical and aerosol impacts on cloud properties. This proposal uses state-of-the-art observations and models to test the hypothesis that aerosol-cloud correlations found in recent satellite observations are caused by aerosol indirect effects and not by a) aerosol swelling through relative humidity correlation with cloud fraction, b) cloud contamination in satellite aerosol data, and c) uncaptured changes in dynamic state that are correlated with aerosol. To test this hypothesis, satellite data alone are insufficient because several key processes that influence both clouds and aerosols occur simultaneously and cannot easily be separated (or unscrambled) in the data. Furthermore, basic information on meteorological state from data assimilation models (e.g., relative humidity, boundary layer height, advective tendencies) is inadequate due to poor boundary layer physics (parameterizations). The complexity of the problem demands that more sophisticated tools be brought to bear. The main focus of this investigation is on improving our understanding of how aerosols influence low-level clouds over ocean. The unique aspect of this investigation is that we use combined satellite observations from NASA's Terra, Aqua, CALIPSO and CloudSat missions together with high-resolution cloud resolving models (CRMs) with explicit physics to address the problem. We develop and utilize advanced dynamic state and improved aerosol assimilation data to improve the characterization of the atmosphere. CRM simulations constrained by advanced dynamic state and improved aerosol assimilation data will be performed to determine and isolate the effect of aerosol humidification and dynamic state on aerosol-cloud correlations. The CRM results will also be directly compared with the satellite observations, for the same regions and seasons, using the same analysis approach. These analyses will involve thousands of cases for each region and aerosol type to ensure the results are statistically robust. The influence of cloud contamination on aerosol-cloud property correlations will be investigated using CALIPSO and MODIS measurements. If effects a) through c) can explain all or part of the observed aerosol-cloud relationships, then the magnitude of the aerosol indirect effect estimate will be greatly reduced. This will also reduce the uncertainty in estimates of aerosol indirect effect, a key objective of the ROSES-06 Interdisciplinary Research in Earth Science (A. 14) program.

Description: THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE OF THE CENTER FOR TURBULENCE RESEARCH IS TO STIMULATE AND PRODUCE ADVANCES IN UNDERSTANDING THE PHYSICS OF TURBULENCE AND OTHER FLUID DRIVEN PHENOMENA, IN TURBULENCE MODELING AND SIMULATION, AND IN TURBULENCE CONTROL.  THE PRIMARY MEANS BY WHICH CTR SEEKS TO ACHIEVE THESE OBJECTIVES IS BY BRINGING TOGETHER GROUPS OF BRIGHT AND ACCOMPLISHED INDIVIDUALS IN SCIENTIFIC FIELDS HEARING ON MULTI-SCALE NON-LINEAR PROBLEMS, SUCH AS TURBULENCE TO ADDRESS PROBLEMS OF INTEREST TO NASA.  POSTDOCTORAL RESEARCH FELLOWSHIPS, FOR BOTH JUNIOR AND SENIOR SCIENTISTS, ARE USED TO BRING OUTSTANDING INDIVIDUALS TO CTR FACILITIES AT AMES AND STANFORD.  HERE THEY CONDUCT RESEARCH IN COLLABORATION WITH THE PERMANENT STAFF OF THE TWO HOST INSTITUTIONS, USING THE SUBSTANTIAL ARRAY OF RESEARCH FACILITIES PROVIDED BY THE AMES/STANFORD ENVIRONMENT.   IN THE FOLLOWING, THREE PROPOSED PROJECTS ARE DESCRIBED THAT ARE OF MUTUAL INTEREST TO NASA/AMES AND STANFORD:   HYPERSONICS FUNDAMENTALS - THIS WORK ADDRESSES THE MODELING OF THE CONVECTIVE AND RADIATIVE HEAT FLUXES FOR THE MANNED EXPEDITION TO THE MOON AND MARS, AND FOR THE RELATED MISSIONS OF DEMONSTRATION OF TECHNOLOGY.  THE DESIGN OF THE HEAT SHIELD USED TO PROTECT SPACECRAFT DURING THEIR ENTRY PHASE INTO A PLANETARY ATMOSPHERE IS BASED ON THE ESTIMATION OF THE HEAT FLUXES TO THE VEHICLE SURFACE.  CFD PREDICTIONS OF THESE QUANTITIES STRONGLY RELY UPON THE ACCURACY OF THE MODEL TO DESCRIBE NON-EQUILIBRIUM PHENOMENA IN THE FLOW.  DURING THE ENTRY OF THE SPACECRAFT, THE TRANSLATIONAL ENERGY OF THE FLUID PARTICLES DRASTICALLY INCREASES AS THEY PASS THROUGH A SHOCK WAVE.  IT IS PROPOSED TO INVESTIGATE TWO CRITICAL ISSUES ENCOUNTERED AT THESE ELEVATED ENERGIES:  1) THE TRANSPORT OF MASS, MOMENTUM, AND TRANSLATIONAL ENERGY IN AN IONIZED FLOW, AND 2) THE MODELING OF RADIATION PHENOMENON.   KINETIC THEORY OF PLASMAS - KINETIC THEORY CAN BE USED TO OBTAIN THE MACROSCOPIC EQUATIONS GOVERNING IONIZED REENTRY FLOWS AND THE EXPRESSIONS OF THE TRANSPORT FLUXES (DIFFUSION OF CHEMICAL SPECIES, HEAT, AND MOMENTUM). Description: Neutral gas density measurements are a vital tool in characterizing the detailed structure and dynamics of the Martian thermosphere (above -80 km). This characterization is crucial for successful planning of spacecraft aerobraking, aerocapture, and descent maneuvers, as well as for understanding the fundamental processes that drive variations in the present Martian climate and affect atmospheric loss to space. Understanding the relationship between the observable energy inputs into, and the often complex response of, the upper atmosphere requires correlating density measurements with these inputs, which vary on quite different time scales: diurnal (e.g. rotation in/out of sunlight), seasonal (e.g. heliocentric distance, solar declination), inter annual (e.g. ll-year solar EUV cycle, yearly dust activity) and transient, from hours/days (e.g. solar flares, solar energetic particle (SEP) events, coronal mass ejections to weeks/months (e.g. lower atmospheric dust storms). Thus it is clear that a multi-year density data set, well sampled both spatially and temporally, is required to investigate the effect of these inputs on the upper atmosphere. Recently a new technique was developed to use MGS Magnetometer/ Electron Reflectometer (MAGIER) pitch angle distributions to extract upper thermospheric densities [Lillis et al., 2005] in regions of Mars with very strong crustal magnetism of the planet) by measuring atmospheric absorption of magnetically reflecting solar wind electrons. We propose to expand this technique, extending it to -70% of the surface and gaining a 100-fold increase in the volume of reliable density measurements. Using this dramatically expanded data set, we will characterize, for the first time, the behavior of the night side Martian upper thermosphere from 170 km to 250 km continuously over 4 Martian years, both alone and in concert with the coupled MichiganlNASA Ames Mars Global Circulation Model (MGCM-MTGCM, see Bougher-Michigan MDAP proposal 2006). We propose 4 specific objectives: Objective 1: Construct a database of -3 million neutral mass density measurements at 2 a.m. local time from 170 km to 250 km altitude, continuously over four complete Martian years over -70% of the planet at all latitudes, using MGS MAGIER data. Objective 2: Using this database, characterize the upper thermosphere;,s geographic, seasonal, and inter-annual variability and correlate with observable inputs: seasonal solar insolation, dust activity and solar EUV conditions. Objective 3 : Compare/integrate database with predictions from the coupled MGCM-MTGCM over 4 Martian years, for validation of seasonal & geographic variation and particularly to understand how dust and solar EUV conditions drive inter-annual variability. Objective 4: Determine the effect of extreme space weather events (solar flares, SEPs, CMEs) on the upper atmosphere, particularly in the context of atmospheric loss to space.

Description: Searching for Aqueous Activity on Mars Through Analyses of VNIR Spectral Images.  We propose to analyze OMEGA and PANCAM spectral images of Mars in order to search for evidence of sulfates and aqueous activity. Sulfates have long been associated with Martian soils and have recently been identified in the regolith as well. Recent results from the OMEGA/Mars Express instrument have shown the presence of kieserite, gypsum and other hydrated sulfates in the layered terrains in Valles Marineris and Terra Meridiani, as well as gypsum associated with the north polar dunes of Olympia Planitia. In parallel, the MER mission has identified jarosite in the bedrock at Meridiani Planum. Thus, sulfates are emerging as an important indicator for aqueous activity on Mars.  Clay minerals have also been identified in some older bedrock sites in OMEGA images. We seek to better characterize the locations of these clay and sulfate deposits using new image clustering techniques and an expanded VNIR spectral library. Characterization of these alteration minerals will be used to guide our search for regions on the surface of Mars where aqueous activity is likely to have occurred through the action of liquid water, water ice, or surface-atmosphere reactions.

Description: The objective of the proposed research is to develop system architecture and algorithms to generate optimized solutions for super-density surface traffic in the presence of uncertainties and under multiple constraints for NGATS ATM: Airportal Project, Subtask 2: Surface Traffic Optimization in the Presence of Uncertainties. The literature covering previous efforts on surface optimization has several shortcomings that indicate a need for work in this area. The major shortcomings include: (a) little work on dealing effectively and explicitly with uncertainty, (b) focusing only on optimization of specific surface sub-problems (e.g., aircraft sequencing at the runway, taxi trajectories, gate allocation) without considering the context of surface-wide optimization and interactions among these sub-problems, and (c) proposing overall surface operations at a concept of operations view without proposing any particular optimization algorithms or techniques. Description: The objective of this 3-year proposal is to develop an understanding of the raised curvilinear features (RCFs), in the western Medusae Fossae Formation (MFF). This proposed work will be accomplished in four progressive parts: 1) mapping the features 2) characterizing them, 3) estimating their aqueous discharges, and 4) assesing their implications and origins. Mapping the features will be accomplished with THemal Emission Imaging Spectrometer (THEMIS) and Mars Orbiter Camera (MOC) imagery. Then we will characterize them dimensionally and contextually using this imagery and co-registered Mars Orbiter Laser Alimeter data points. Volumetric discharges will be estimated from the dimensional measurements with a) a suite of empirical terrestrial techniques scaled for Martian gravity and b) a theoretical technique derived to address fluid flow on Mars and Titan. Finally, we will use the features characterization and discharge estimates to test the previously published hypotheses for their origin (s) and to address their geologic, hyrdologic, abd climatic implications. Our publication of substaintiated hypotheses will include an electronic version of all the characterization data and discharge estimates in order to fully substantiate our conclusions, enable comparison with similar discoveries elswhere on Mars, and facilitate testing of our conclusions by independent researchers. The previously published hypothese for the features origin(s) include i) inverted fluvial, ii) eskers, iii)fluidized impact ejecta, and iv) glacier crevasse fill. These hypothese all involve water. Thus, by investigating and assessing the origin (s) of these features, this work is directly relevant to Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG 2004) Goal I, Objective A, Investigation 1, Determine the geologic history of water on Mars, and Goal III, Objective A, Investigate 2, Evaluate fluvial, subaqueous, and subaerial sedimentary processes and their evolution and distribution technique.

Description: UV-Visible spatial heterodyne spectroscopy (SHS) is a promising technology that combines high spectral resolution and etendue (effective area x field of view) in an instrument compact enough for use on remote solar system probes. Spectrally resolving neutral and ion emission/absorption features is an important tool for remote sensing of the atmospheres and space environments of planets, their satellites, and comets. Such measurements provide access to a vast amount of diagnostic information including velocity, energy, thermal/non-thermal characteristics, radiative transfer effects, isotopic ratios, and the separation of distinct populations (coronal vs. atmosphere) along a single line of sight. However, despite the obvious value of such measurements to the study of the solar system, the substantial limitations on size and etendue imposed by traditional grating spectrographs renders high-resolution impractical for small spacecraft. By contrast SHS is ideally suited to such a platform, because its design naturally provides the compact size and large etendue of grating spectrographs on modern remote probes, but with a 100+ fold increase in spectral resolving power. The caveat to this is that current implementations of SHS are limited to a single narrow bandpass that is suitable for the study of only one spectral feature. The purpose of our program is to continue development of a new format of SHS, one that is able to access very large bandpasses, thereby providing the capability for remote probes to perform detailed study of spectral features from the FUV through the visible with a single instrument. To date we have explored one avenue for achieving this, the tunable SHS (TSHS), which has a narrow (~5 nm) bandpass that can be set to an arbitrary tuning wavelength over a bandpass exceeding 300nm. Our results have validated this basic concept and we propose here to develop and validate field-testable instrument suitable for further development as a space flight instrument. In addition, we will develop a prototype for a second broadband design, the `echelle mode SHS (ESHS). ESHS instruments use the principle of overlapping orders to enable simultaneous study of a bandpass comparable to the TSHS without having to re-tune between observations. Finally we will compare the relative sensitivity, stability, complexity, and overall performance of TSHS and ESHS designs with the aim of identifying niche applications for both.

Description: UNSOLICITED RESEARCH PROPOSAL ENTITLED "A STUDY OF THE EFFECT OF BIOMASS BURNING ON THE GLOBAL UPPER TOPOSHPHERE AND LOWER STRATOSTROM" ABSTRACT FROM YEAR ONE ANNUAL REPORT: WE INVESTIGATED THE EFFECTS OF FIRE-INCLUDED PLUME-RISE ON THE PREDICTED EXPORT OF CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) OVER AFRICA DURING SAFARI 2000 USING THE NCAR COMMUNITY ATMOSPHERE MODEL (CAM) WITH CO TRACER AND PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME.  THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SIMULATES THE CONSEQUENCES OF STRONG BUOYANCY OF HOT GASES EMITTED FROM BIOMASS BURNING, INCLUDING BOTH DRY AND CLOUD-ASSOCIATED (PYROCUMULUS) LOFTING.  THE SCHEME WAS FIRST ADAPTED FROM A REGIONAL MODEL.  THE CURRENT IMPLEMENTATION OF THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME INTO THE GLOBAL MODEL PROVIDES AN OPPORTUNITY TO EXAMINE THE EFFECT OF PLUME-RISE ON LONG RANGE TRANSPORT.  THE CAM SIMULATION WITH THE PLUME-RISE PARAMETERIZATION SCHEME SHOWS A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT OF THE AGREEMENTS BETWEEN THE MODELED AND AIRCRAFT-MEASURED VERTICAL DISTRIBUTION OF CO OVER SOUTHERN AFRICA BIOMASS BURNING.  THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM PLAYS CRUCIAL ROLE IN LOFTING BIOMASS BURNING POLLUTANTS TO THE MIDDLE TROPOSPHERE.  IN THE PRESENCE OF DEEP CONVECTION WE FOUND THAT THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM RESULTS IN A DECREASE OF CO CONCENTRATION IN THE UPPER TROPOSPHERE.  THE PLUME RISE DEPLETES THE BOUNDARY LAYER, AND THUS LEAVES LOWER CONCENTRATIONS OF CO TO BE LOFTED BY THE DEEP CONVECTION PROCESS.  THE EFFECT OF THE PLUME-RISE ON FREE TROPOSPHERE (CO) CONCENTRATION IS MORE IMPORTANT FOR THE SOURCE AREA (SHORT-DISTANCE TRANSPORT) THAN FOR REMOTE AREAS (LONG-DISTANCE TRANSPORT).  THE PLUME-RISE SCHEME ALSO INCREASES THE CO EXPORT FLUXES FROM AFRICA TO THE ATLANTIC AND INDIAN OCEANS.  THESE RESULTS FURTHER CONFIRM AND EXTENT PREVIOUS FINDINGS IN A REGIONAL MODEL STUDY.  EFFECTIVE LOFTING OF LARGE CONCENTRATION OF CO BY THE PLUME-RISE MECHANISM ALSO HAS IMPLICATION FOR LOCAL AIR QUALITY FORECAST IN AREAS AFFECTED BY OTHER FIRE-RELATED POLLUTANTS.

Description: THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE OF THE CENTER FOR TURBULENCE RESEARCH IS TO STIMULATE AND PRODUCE ADVANCES IN UNDERSTANDING THE PHYSICS OF TURBULENCE AND OTHER FLUID DRIVEN PHENOMENA, IN TURBULENCE MODELING AND SIMULATION, AND IN TURBULENCE CONTROL.  THE PRIMARY MEANS BY WHICH CTR SEEKS TO ACHIEVE THESE OBJECTIVES IS BY BRINGING TOGETHER GROUPS OF BRIGHT AND ACCOMPLISHED INDIVIDUALS IN SCIENTIFIC FIELDS HEARING ON MULTI-SCALE NON-LINEAR PROBLEMS, SUCH AS TURBULENCE TO ADDRESS PROBLEMS OF INTEREST TO NASA.  POSTDOCTORAL RESEARCH FELLOWSHIPS, FOR BOTH JUNIOR AND SENIOR SCIENTISTS, ARE USED TO BRING OUTSTANDING INDIVIDUALS TO CTR FACILITIES AT AMES AND STANFORD.  HERE THEY CONDUCT RESEARCH IN COLLABORATION WITH THE PERMANENT STAFF OF THE TWO HOST INSTITUTIONS, USING THE SUBSTANTIAL ARRAY OF RESEARCH FACILITIES PROVIDED BY THE AMES/STANFORD ENVIRONMENT.   IN THE FOLLOWING, THREE PROPOSED PROJECTS ARE DESCRIBED THAT ARE OF MUTUAL INTEREST TO NASA/AMES AND STANFORD:   HYPERSONICS FUNDAMENTALS - THIS WORK ADDRESSES THE MODELING OF THE CONVECTIVE AND RADIATIVE HEAT FLUXES FOR THE MANNED EXPEDITION TO THE MOON AND MARS, AND FOR THE RELATED MISSIONS OF DEMONSTRATION OF TECHNOLOGY.  THE DESIGN OF THE HEAT SHIELD USED TO PROTECT SPACECRAFT DURING THEIR ENTRY PHASE INTO A PLANETARY ATMOSPHERE IS BASED ON THE ESTIMATION OF THE HEAT FLUXES TO THE VEHICLE SURFACE.  CFD PREDICTIONS OF THESE QUANTITIES STRONGLY RELY UPON THE ACCURACY OF THE MODEL TO DESCRIBE NON-EQUILIBRIUM PHENOMENA IN THE FLOW.  DURING THE ENTRY OF THE SPACECRAFT, THE TRANSLATIONAL ENERGY OF THE FLUID PARTICLES DRASTICALLY INCREASES AS THEY PASS THROUGH A SHOCK WAVE.  IT IS PROPOSED TO INVESTIGATE TWO CRITICAL ISSUES ENCOUNTERED AT THESE ELEVATED ENERGIES:  1) THE TRANSPORT OF MASS, MOMENTUM, AND TRANSLATIONAL ENERGY IN AN IONIZED FLOW, AND 2) THE MODELING OF RADIATION PHENOMENON.   KINETIC THEORY OF PLASMAS - KINETIC THEORY CAN BE USED TO OBTAIN THE MACROSCOPIC EQUATIONS GOVERNING IONIZED REENTRY FLOWS AND THE EXPRESSIONS OF THE TRANSPORT FLUXES (DIFFUSION OF CHEMICAL SPECIES, HEAT, AND MOMENTUM).  CLOSURE OF THE MACROSCOPIC CONSERVATION EQUATIONS IS REALIZED AT THE MICROSCOPIC LEVEL BY EITHER DETERMINING THE INTERACTION POTENTIALS OR THE CROSS-SECTIONS FROM EXPERIMENTAL MEASUREMENTS.  MODELING OF IONIZED REACTIVE GAS MIXTURES IN FLIGHTS AT VELOCITIES HIGHER THAN 10 KM/S IS STILL BEING DEBATED IN THE SCIENTIFIC COMMUNITY.  PLASMAS ARE IONIZED GASES COMPOSED OF ELECTRONS AND HEAVY PARTICLES (ATOMAS, MOLECULES, AND IONS).  THE RATIO OF THE ELECTRON MASS TO A CHARACTERISTIC MASS OF HEAVY PARTICLES IS SMALL.  HENCE, THE TRANSFER OF ENERGY BETWEEN UNLIKE PARTICLES IS NOT EFFICIENT.  IT IS PROPOSED TO DERIVE THE KINETIC THEORY OF PLASMAS FOCUSING ON TWO ASPECTS:  1) THERMAL NON-EQUILIBRIUM BETWEEN THE TRANSLATIONAL POPULATIONS OF ELECTRONS AND HEAVY PARTICLES.  2) THE TREATMENT OF REACTIVE COLLISIONS.  COLLISIONAL-RADIATIVE MODEL FOR SHOCK-TUBE FLOW SIMULATIONS - IT IS PROPOSED TO DEVELOP A COLLISIONAL-RADIATIVE (CR) MODEL OF AIR TO PREDICT THE RADIATIVE HEAT-FLUXES ON THE THERMAL SHIELD OF A SPACECRAFT.  THE MODEL WILL BE ASSESSED BY MEANS OF EXPERIMENTS REPRESENTATIVE OF MOON AND MARS RETURNS.  RADIATIVE HEAT FLUXES PREDICTED BY OUR MODEL WILL BE COMPARED WITH THE ONES MEASURED DURING EXPERIMENTS CARRIED OUT IN THE EAST SHOCK-TUBE FACILITY OF NASA AMES RESEARCH CENTER.  RESULTS WILL ALSO BE COMPARED WITH THE ONES OBTAINED BY MEANS OF THE CR MODEL OF PARK CURRENTLY IMPLEMENTED INTO THE NEQAIR CODE.

Description: We propose research to assess whether Mg-isotope geochenlistry can be used to detect the signal of photosynthesis, which addresses goals in the Astrobiology program to identify the signals for early life. We recently discovered that biosynthesis of chlorophyll-a in Synechococcus elongatus, a unicellular cyanobacterium, induces a distinct Mg-isotope fractionation. Magnesium extracted from chlorophyll-a is depleted in the heavier isotopes, relative to magnesium in the culture media. This fractionation may be common to all photosynthetic organisms, and, thus, global in extent. We propose a series of tasks to establish this fact. The research is guided by two hypotheses. First, is the Mg-isotope fractionation occuring during the insertion of Mg(I1) into the Protoporphyrin IX molecule, which is a tetrapyrrole that is common to the synthetic pathways for both chlorophyll and heme? To test this hypothesis, we propose to show that Mg-isotopic fractionation is insensitive to the taxonomy of the organism in a series of lab and field measurements where the pigments are separated and the Mg-isotopic compositions compared. We are also examining whether the recycling of Mg in photo-damaged chlorophyll allows for isotopic equilibrium to be established. Our second hypothesis is that the pool of metal for pigment synthesis is recycled in magnesium-poor environments. The record of Mg-isotopes in chlorophyll in such an environment would then reflect Rayleigh distillation of the bioavailable magnesium isotopes, since chlorophyll biosynthesis favors lighter isotopes over heavy isotopes of magnesium. If so, then we expect to see different Mg-isotope values, and ranges of values, in environments that differ only in magnesium bioavailability. Photosynthesis accounts for -100 gigatons of carbon per year on Earth, which is fundamental to all geochemical cycles. Magnesium is the metal center in the chlorophyll molecule and thus is central to the history and geochemistry of life on the planet, and perhaps others.

Description: SNAP-L, A DEDICATED SPACE EXPERIMENT TO PROBE DARK ENERGY The key challenge for JDEM is to determine the nature of the dark energy that is driving the accelerating expansion of the Universe. The SuperNova / Acceleration Probe - Lensing (SNAP-L) employs two independent techniques, a probe of expansion using Type la supernovae (SNe), and a growth of structure probe through gravitational weak lensing (WL). SNe and WL are the methods of choice: each technique is a robust, well-understood probe of dark energy. SNe are presently the "most powerful and best proven technique" and WL's probe of the growth of structure is, "if the systematic errors are at or below the level proposed the most powerful component in a multi-technique program." Moreover, a space mission eliminates limitations on both techniques that are inherent in ground-based studies, opening up a qualitatively new approach to understanding dark energy. SNe and WL probe different aspects of the effects of dark energy on the evolution of the Universe, including testing the distinction between a new component and modification of Einstein gravity. "Combinations of the principal techniques have substantially more statistical power, much more ability to discriminate among dark energy models, and more robustness to systematic errors than any single technique." SNAP-L will carry out two imaging surveys: 1) a deep survey of 7.5 deg2 to follow over 2000 matched Type la SNe out to a redshift of 1.7, and 2) a wide survey of 1000 deg2 for WL mapping. The SNe will be observed with unprecedented detail and systematic control, resulting in a well-sampled Hubble diagram into the epoch of deceleration. The WL survey benefits from a stable, high resolution point spread function and absence of atmospheric distortions. Combined, SNAP-L will determine the dark energy density to 0.004, its equation of state to 1.4%, and the time variation to 0.07. The SNAP-L satellite will be launched into an L2 orbit by an EELV rocket. The SNAP-L 600 million pixel camera is sensitive to light from 400 to 1700 nm in nine filter bands. An integral-field unit spectrograph provides follow-up at maximum light to identify Type la SNe and provide precise redshifts. Our team has just completed three years of R&D reducing risk by enhancing readiness of all mission enabling technologies. Detector performance improvements resulting from this program enable the proposed science requirements to be met within a $600M cost cap with margin. The primary objectives of this proposal are to refine the mission design through trade studies and to strengthen our project management. The project will be thoroughly studied utilizing NASA centers and aerospace vendors, where funding is essential to increase the participation of experts in space mission construction and project management. The result of these activities will be a low-risk approach to implement the project, ready for independent assessment. Dark Energy Task Force report to the AAAC, Feb 14,2006

Description: Pratt and Whitney Rocketdyne (PWR) proposes to demonstrate a small attitude control thruster that is regeneratively cooled with both gaseous oxygen and gaseous methane. The advantages of regenerative cooling of gas-thrusters as compared to other potential approaches (e.g. ablative or film cooling) is that it assures propellants are in the gaseous state when they reach the injector without the need for any external thermal conditioning. The advantage of the fully gaseous propellants at the injector enables a simpler thruster design as compared to one that would need to be designed fir saturated gas or liquid injection. The sub-scale test thruster will be appropriate for application to a reaction control system of the type being envisioned for the Crew Exploration Vehicle or the lunar lander /ascent vehicle. The thruster hardware proposed fit thus activity is a modification of existing equipment originally developed be PWR for a previous Space Station application. The use of existing hardware assets significantly reduces the cost of this activity. In addition to the thruster itself, PWR proposes to include a self-ignition system based on a piezo resonance process. The advantages of this ignition process over other potential approaches (e.g. spark igniter/exciter) is the elimination of high voltage cables (an EMI concern) and separate exciter electronics (a significant mass savings). This unique ignition approach has been demonstrated by PWR with oxygen and methane propellants at the element level. This proposed activity would demonstrate end to end performance of this unique ignition system with a complete thruster. The work plan proposed by PWR includes all of the necessary elements for an advanced development activity of this type, including design, fabrication, and subscale testing at PWR. Testing of the full scale thruster will be performed at the NASA facility (either NASA/GRC or WSTF) under separate funding. PWR includes work elements and cost associated with test support and post-test data analysis and reporting. The proposed program schedule is reasonable and well structured, providing timely results for the identified tasks. The proposed management approach is well structured and should provide the necessary controls and insight into contract performance, including earned value and a formal risk management process. An IPT approach us proposed, which has been demonstrated to be effective past programs. The leadership project and principle investigator are highly qualified and have a wealth of experience in rocket engine development and previous advanced development activities of this type. Facilities and equipment at PWR are extensive and should provide all necessary elements for completing the work proposed, including manufacturing (machining and welding) and sub-scale testing. Overall, this is an excellent proposal. The results of this activity will provide a significant body of knowledge on the applicability of dual regenerative cooling for gas-gas RCS-class thrusters.

Description: The Multi-Agent Architecture for Coordinated, Responsive Observations  Remote sensing missions for earth science provide a wealth of information to help us understand the dynamics of our planet. However, the current stovepipe operational model of remote sensing missions, i.e., a single spacecraft transmitting data to dedicated ground operations centers (Fig. 1), introduces untenable latencies in developing data prod-ucts that hinder model building and refine-ment as well as timely responses for hazard mitigation. Future missions will operate as part of a sensor web (Fig. 2) comprised of ^interlinked platforms with onboard information processing systems capable of orchestrat-ing real-time collaborative operations [1]. The Multi-agent Architecture for Coordi-nated, Responsive Observations (MACRO), an extension of our current work on the Adap-tive Network Architecture (ANA) is a natural technology for enabling the deployment and operation of a sensor web. Description: We will analyze Mars Express (MEx) High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) color data for the regions containing the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) Spirit and Opportunity landing sites. We will combine the HRSC data with the MEx OMEGA spectrometer and MER Pancam multispectral imager data. These broader spectral/compositional unit maps will be interpreted in the context of the MER geology and mineralogy results and place them in a regional geological context. In the process, the HRSC radiometric calibration will be checked and improved to benefit the entire HRSC data set and those using it. This is a team effort, combining the expertise and capabilities of scientists experienced with not only HRSC color data, but also with OMEGA and MER-Pancam spectrophotometry. Phase I is a 1-year base period, and Phase II is a 2-year Option period. The purpose of this effort is to develop and validate predictive capabilities for the design and performance of Cruise Efficient, Short Take-Off and Landing (CESTOL) subsonic aircraft, and to validate predictive capabilities for an estimate of CESTOL aircraft noise during takeoff and landing. For Phase I (i.e., Year 1 Base Period), these methodologies will be then be used to achieve the final objective of year 1, which is to select and further refine one CESTOL concept and then to complete a preliminary design of a large scale wind tunnel model and test. For Phase II (i.e., Years 2 and 3 Option Period), the wind tunnel design and construction is to be completed in year 2, and a large scale wind tunnel test is to be completed in year 3. The final objective of Phase II is the development verification of predictive codes for these advanced powered-lift concepts and the generation of an open collection of wind tunnel data that can be used by modelers to improve the capability of modeling these complex flows. It is intended that the Phase I and Phase II (if option is exercised) effort will address the following topics: Low-speed aerodynamic characteristics up to and beyond maximum lift via a combination of computational and experimental efforts in order to obtain a more complete picture of the flow physics. Acoustic characteristics of a low-noise hybrid wing-body system via experimental efforts and noise signature modeling to analyze not just the noise generated by the vehicle, but also to analyze the noise footprint around the airport during takeoff and landing. 2.0 Scope of Work Phase I will conduct a preliminary design study to determine the hybrid wing-body design to be analyzed in Phase II, including powered lift aerodynamic studies, both computational and experimental, to better understand of the flow physics associated with using the propulsion system to improve the aircraft lifting capability. Phase II will expand the understanding of the physics of the flow field associated with powered lift configurations. The design determined from Phase I will be the focus of both the experimental and computational efforts. The propulsion modeling will be focused on methods of improving the aerodynamic predictive capabilities. The large scale wind tunnel model effort in Year 2 will focus on finalizing the wind tunnel model, assembling the test plan, and scheduling the experiment in the chosen facility. Year 3 for the large scale wind tunnel model effort will focus on performing the experiments, analyzing the results, and preparing the results for release. Description: This program has direct relevance to future NASA programs and interests, specifically, the objectives described in NRA Subtopic A.2.4.3, Materials & Structures for Wing Components and Non-Circular Fuselage.  It focuses on a new structural concept that integrates skin, stringers, and frame elements into a single cocured unitized panel assembly. The resulting structure is a novel solution for addressing the demanding fuselage loading requirements inherent in a pressurized shaped vehicle like the Hybrid Wing or Blended Wing Body (BWB) concept.The Pultruded Rod Stitched Efficient Unitized Structure (PRSEUS) design approach represents a bold vision in composite design theory and manufacturing methods. It is a conscious progression away from conventional laminated and bonded assemblies toward larger one-piece cocured panel designs with seamless transitions and damage-arrest interfaces. The PRSEUS structural concept is an evolution of the stitched-composite technologies first introduced under the NASA Advanced Composites Technology (ACT) Wing Program. The proposed program described in this document builds upon, extends, and tailors these structural technologies in order to meet the demanding challenges intrinsic in shaped-vehicle designs.The primary thrust of Phase I (Base Period) will be to quantify by analysis the benefits of a PRSEUS fuselage concept in the complex loading environment found on the BWB. To minimize development costs, an existing Boeing BWB finite element model (FEM) will be adapted for vehicle sizing, weight statement development, and internal loads generation for the test program. The weights statement will be used to establish structural metrics which will be used to quantitatively assess the success of the PRSEUS test program, as well as to appraise the competitiveness relative to alternate concepts and technologies. During Phase II (Option I) more complex aspects of pressurized flat-panel designs will be investigated analytically and tested. Secondary bending affects will be assessed using a pressure-box subcomponent and thin-gauge skin damage-arrestment concerns with multi-stringer tension specimens.

Description: Title of Effort: Acoustic Prediction Methodology and Test Validation for an Efficient Low-Noise Hybrid Wing Body Subsonic Transport. (Reference: NASA AMRD NRA NNH06ZEA001N Amendment 4, Appendix A.2, Topic A.2.4 Hybrid Wing/Body Technologies). The new technologies for this effort are directed primarily towards meeting the reduced noise goal. While the SAX-40 based geometry being proposed offers substantially improved fuel burn, the fuel burn goal is somewhat secondary in that the focus of the changes to the geometry are to meet the noise goal. Thus, the plan is to determine the fuel burn advantages of the configuration including impacts of potential changes to reduce noise. Since LTO NOx emissions are from the engine, emissions technology development needs to be done as an engine discipline. Therefore, this effort is to enable development of prediction methods with wind tunnel test validations using a fuel-efficient hybrid wing body configuration based on the non-proprietary CMI SAX-40 geometry. The NASA long-term goal is to develop high-fidelity physics-based prediction methods. Most of the very low flyover noise potential of the hybrid wing body derives from noise shielding for which validated fundamental prediction methods are still in an early state of development. Thus, a non-proprietary 3D definition representative of a flyable efficient transport suitable for wind tunnel testing needs to be created in Phase 1. A major portion of the following Phase 2 proposed effort is to design and build a wind tunnel model with test configuration requirements guided by development of the predictive methods. Advancing prediction methodologies for noise shielding will initially start with empiricism to identify the needs. As investigations continue into years 2 and 3, increasing fidelity refinements will be incorporated. The wind tunnel model will be designed and wind tunnel tested for low-speed aerodynamic and noise data in Phase 2 (year 2 and year 3 respectively).

Description: Geospace-Related Missions of Opportunity Phase A and Bridge Phase Option--MORE Investigation - AO Award The Robotic Lunar ExplorationLunar Precursor Robotic Program (RLEPLPRP) consists of a series of robotic lunar exploration missions to prepare for and to support future human exploration activities. The primary purpose of the robotic preparation is to reduce risk, enhance mission success, and reduce the cost of future human missions. The LRO payload used to accomplish the mission objectives consists of the following six Instruments: 1. Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) Measurement Investigation shall determine the global topography of the lunar surface at high resolution, measure landing site slopes and search for polar ices in shadowed regions; 2. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) shall acquire targeted images of the lunar surface capable of resolving small-scale features that could be landing site hazards, as well as wide-angle images at multiple wavelengths of the lunar poles to document changing illumination conditions and potential resources; 3. Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND) shall map the flux of neutrons from the lunar surface to search for evidence of water ice and provide measurements of the space radiation environment which can be useful for future human exploration; 4. Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment (DLRE) shall map the temperature of the entire lunar surface at 300 meter horizontal scales to identify cold-traps and potential ice deposits; 5. Lyman-Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) shall observe the entire lunar surface in the far ultraviolet to search for surface ices and frosts in the polar regions and to provide images of permanently shadowed regions illuminated only by starlight; 6. Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) shall investigate the effect of galactic cosmic rays on tissue-equivalent plastics as a constraint on models of biological response to background space radiation. Each Instrument will be managed by a Principal Investigator (PI), who will be responsible for delivering the flight Instrument to the LRO project, as well as producing the Instrument's data products and delivering them to the Planetary Data System (PDS) in accordance with their data product specification document.

Description: A DATA ANALYSIS AND MODELING STUDY OF SECULAR CHANGE IN THERMOSPHERIC DENSITY We propose a data analysis and modeling study of long-term changes that have occurred in the upper atmosphere over the recent several decades. Interest in these trends has been stimulated by the classical modeling study of Roble and Dickinson (1989), who predicted a dramatic response to a hypothetical future increase of greenhouse gases: the upper atmosphere is expected to cool down by tens of degrees in response to the standard doubled-C02 scenario. The search for signs of global change in upper-atmospheric and ionospheric historical data records has been inconclusive. While some parameters clearly reveal long-term trends in general agreement with the model predictions, other estimates have produced inconsistent and even contradictory results due, in part, to the scarcity of sufficiently long uniform observational records. Our ability to detect trends is also confounded by the enormous variability of the upper atmosphere driven primarily by solar and geomagnetic activity on various temporal and spatial scales. The "greenhouse cooling" is expected to result in a substantial thermospheric density decline that depends on the level of solar activity. Existing analyses of neutral density trends based on satellite drag data over the last 2 to 3 decades have provided perhaps the most robust evidence of global change in the upper atmosphere to date. These results inherently provide a global view and qualitatively agree with each other and with theoretical model predictions. More work is required to improve our confidence in the trend estimates, to delineate the contributions of solar activity and other parameters, to better understand the physical mechanisms, and to quantify their contributions to the observed changes. The science goal of this project is to advance our understanding of the mechanisms driving the long-term global changes in the upper atmosphere and the near-Earth space environment. Our approach is unique in that it synergistically combines two key components: (1) we will extend, in time and altitude coverage and in number of observations per year, our comprehensive analysis of the global satellite-drag database to delineate the contributions of solar activity and other sources of natural variation, and to detect anthropogenic and possible natural long-term trends; (2) we will use an updated global upper-atmospheric numerical model to study the natural and anthropogenic variability using the records of greenhouse gas concentrations and solar activity over the same period of time. A direct comparison of the results of theoretical modeling with the analysis of accurately determined trends in the upper atmosphere will be carried out for the first time. This will provide insights into the key physical mechanisms and their possible interactions and feedbacks, and will facilitate the attribution of the observed trends. A clearer understanding of the thermospheric "greenhouse cooling" will lead to development of meaningful long-term forecasting capabilities. This work is immediately relevant to the science goals of the NASA Living With a Star program and, in particular, to its Targeted Research science topic T3e. The ability to understand and predict the long-term density variability in the near-Earth space environment is also of enormous practical significance to any spacecraft operators, including the NASA's programs and missions.

Description: The Stratospheric Deployment Parafoil is a proposed technology that will be designed and tested to provide a greatly superior parachute precision delivery system under thin atmosphere conditions, including Mars entry. Current systems incorporate a parachute which lacks the controllability necessary for precision landing. The non-controllable parachutes act only as a delivery system but afford no way to direct the parachute descent. The new technology will eliminate the uncontrollable system and, rather than using a round parachute variant, will have a high L/D parafoil capable of precision control and landing. This controllable parafoil will have a multistage deployment sequence which will accomplish high speed, even supersonic parachute deployment with the parachute in a reefed condition. The first stage of the deployment will approximate a conical ribbon parachute which will slow the system to subsonic speeds. Once the system has slowed sufficiently, subsequent stages of the deployment will transition the non-controllable parachute to a fully controllable, precision-landing parafoil.

Description: We propose to build and evaluate NDIR Analyzers that can observe eddy covariance flux of CO2 from unmanned airborne platforms. For both phases, a total of four analyzers are to be evaluated for their nose (ppb rms, Dry Mole Fraction) and susceptibility to artifacts on platform. We present original framework for their evaluation. It consists of expressions for their potential noises, artifacts and the functionality of their electro-optical processors on platform. Phase I begins with the construction of two innovative NDIR analyzers, one close- and the other open-path. Each is based on the industry-standard airborne analyzer made by the proposing corporation. It is solid-state, runs at 8 Hz and has negligible sensitivity to motion. We propose existing technologies to increase the electro-optical modulation frequency to 100 Hz. The rms sensitivity (ppb), the level of drying and frequency response to air will be documented. The goal is a technology having the air sampling frequency of 100 Hz, rms sensitivity of 100 ppb and negligible artifacts, the target specifications of NASA's Southern Ocean Initiative. The plan for Phase II will be to evaluate the analyzers by observations of eddy covariance flux made from unmanned and piloted aircraft above terrestrial and marine ecosystems.

Description: The Stratospheric Deployment Parafoil is a proposed technology that will be designed and tested to provide a greatly superior parachute precision delivery system under thin atmosphere conditions, including Mars entry. Current systems incorporate a parachute which lacks the controllability necessary for precision landing. The non-controllable parachutes act only as a delivery system but afford no way to direct the parachute descent. The new technology will eliminate the uncontrollable system and, rather than using a round parachute variant, will have a high L/D parafoil capable of precision control and landing. This controllable parafoil will have a multistage deployment sequence which will accomplish high speed, even supersonic parachute deployment with the parachute in a reefed condition. The first stage of the deployment will approximate a conical ribbon parachute which will slow the system to subsonic speeds. Once the system has slowed sufficiently, subsequent stages of the deployment will transition the non-controllable parachute to a fully controllable, precision-landing parafoil.

Description: We propose to build and evaluate NDIR Analyzers that can observe eddy covariance flux of CO2 from unmanned airborne platforms. Description: Chemistry-Climate Studies Using General Circulation Models ABSTRACT:  Goal of this research is to understand the impact of dynamical and chemical processes that interact in the model. We will carry out a systemic analysis of the tropospheric and stratospheric climate responses and relate these responses to changes in the tropospherestratosphere coupling, and to changes in lower boundary conditions and stratospheric radiative properties. For each model configuration, we will examine, the difference between the time slice experiments and do analysis of the 150 year transient runs. We are especially interested in the response of sea level pressure temperature and precipitation and will investigate the changes in the mid-tropospheric flow (variability of low and high frequencies, teleconnections). We will determine both changes in the stratospheric basic states and the impact on the occurrence of major warmings. In order to determine the changes in extreme events, we will examine the probability density function of leading variability modes of tropospheric and stratospheric  circulation. In addition, we investigate in features of the dynamic troposphere-stratosphere coupling on daily to interannual time scale and changes in these features. We will determine the structure of planetary waves, and analyze the vertical propagation using cross-coherence analysis, and time-lagged singular values decomposition analysis. We will relate the changes in the vertical and meridional propagation of planetary waves to changes in reflective properties of the stratospheric basic state, and to changes in the downward progression zonal mean anomalies. The climate responses and the changes in the coupling between the troposphere and stratosphere will depend both on the changes of the lower boundary conditions and changes in radiative properties of the stratosphere. We will analyze the climate responses and the fcatures of dynamical troposphere-stratosphere coupling for 30 year overlapping periods of the transient runs and relate the results to parameters like tropical SST change, meridional temperature gradient, high latitude temperature change, stratospheric temperature decrease. This will allow us to investigate the relative roles of stratospheric and tropospheric driving mechanisms of chemistry-climate interactions.

Description: SOLAR TERRESTRIAL RELATIONS OBSERVATORY (STEREO) WAVES PHASE E Data on hourly or 3-hourly precipitation over the globe has recently become available from TRMM and other satellite measurements. This new data allows analyses of precipitation frequency, intensity and diurnal variations on a global scale and more detailed evaluation of model precipitation. We propose to study the precipitation characteristics and apply the results to evaluate climate models by analyzing several high-resolution precipitation products from TRMM (e.g., 3B42) and other satellite-based products such as the PERSIANN from UC, Irvine and CMORPH from NCEPICPC. The satellite observations will be compared with surface rain gauge and radar hourly measurements over the U.S. and rain gauge daily precipitation (including bias-corrected data) over land and 3-hourly weather reports of precipitation frequency over the globe. We will focus our analysis on (1) differences between satellite precipitation products with and without blending with infrared (IR) observations; (2) precipitation frequency and intensity derived from daily, 3-hourly, and hourly precipitation; and (3) the diurnal timing and amplitude in the hourly or 3-hourly products. Our goal is to quantify (a) whether the inclusion of the IR measurements improves the estimates of precipitation frequency, intensity and diurnal variations compared with microwave-only products; (b) what the strength and weakness of the various high-resolution products are; and (c) whether and how these relatively-new products can improve our knowledge about the spatial and temporal variations in precipitation frequency, intensity and diurnal cycle. The satellite data will then be applied to evaluate precipitation characteristics from coupled climate models with data archived at PCMDI. Significant results from this proposal are expected to help evaluate TRMM and other satellite precipitation products, help design future precipitation missions, improve our knowledge about the various precipitation characteristics, and evaluate climate models. The project will also produce global monthly climatology of precipitation characteristics for community use. lTRMM=Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission 2PERSIANN=Precipitation Estimation from Remotely Sensed Information using Artificial Neural Networks 3CMORPH= Climate Prediction Center (CPC) morphing method.

Description: PHYSICS OF GRAVITATIONAL INSTABILITY IN ACCRETION DISKS PROPOSAL TITLE: PHYSICS OF GRAVITATIONAL INSTABILITY IN ACCRETION DISKS ABSTRACT:We propose a theoretical study of the structure and evolution of gravitationally unstable accretion disks around young stars and supermassive black holes. Gravitationally unstable disks are those that are massive enough that their own self-gravity is dynamically important. We will use local hydrodynamic and magnetohydrodynamic simulations, in shearing box geometry, to address three related questions. First, where in the disk is the accretion energy deposited? This bears directly on the question of whether protoplanetary disks can fragment to form substellar objects. Second, how does self-gravity interact with the magnetorotational instability, in disks that are sufficiently well-ionized that the two instabilities can coexist? Third, what role, if any, does gravitational instability play in the concentration and growth of solids within protoplanetary disks. The proposed work addresses NASA's goal of 'Advancing scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system.

Description: INVESTIGATIONS OF GLOBAL ULF STRUCTURE IN EARTH'S MAGNETOSPHERE SUMMARY: Ultra Low Frequency waves, electric and magnetic variations at mHz time scales, play an important role in the transport and acceleration of energetic particles in the magnetosphere. However, not all sources and types of ULF energy in the magnetosphere may equally affect trapped particle dynamics. For example, mode structure, propagation direction, and azimuthal occurrence of ULF waves are all important factors in determining the degree to which a source of ULF waves will affect magnetospheric particles. These factors may depend on elements of the instantaneous state of the global magnetosphere, which may not be possible to extract from the few measurements typically available via in situ observations. Event studies have shown that the spatiotemporal structure and generation of these waves is well suited to study by global-scale magnetospheric simulations. While event studies provide an important validation of the approach, the complicated structure of real solar wind observations make it very challenging to isolate the physical factors controlling the generation of magnetospheric ULF waves. In this study, we propose to use global, 3d MHD simulations ofthe magnetosphere driven by idealized solar wind conditions to study the effects of external driving of ULF waves within the magnetosphere. This study will isolate the most important conditions in determining relevant characteristics of magnetospheric ULF waves. Wherever possible, results will be verified through comparison to Polar and geosynchronous in situ measurements.Understanding the relevant conditions pertaining to the transmission of energy from the solar wind into Earth's magnetosphere will be of vital importance to understanding the environmental conditions to which human technologies will be subject in near-Earth space.The results of this study will be relevant to NASA strategic goal 3B, to Explore the Sun-Earth system to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system.

Description: A DATA ANALYSIS AND MODELING STUDY OF SECULAR CHANGE IN THERMOSPHERIC DENSITY We propose a data analysis and modeling study of long-term changes that have occurred in the upper atmosphere over the recent several decades. Interest in these trends has been stimulated by the classical modeling study of Roble and Dickinson (1989), who predicted a dramatic response to a hypothetical future increase of greenhouse gases: the upper atmosphere is expected to cool down by tens of degrees in response to the standard doubled-C02 scenario. The search for signs of global change in upper-atmospheric and ionospheric historical data records has been inconclusive. While some parameters clearly reveal long-term trends in general agreement with the model predictions, other estimates have produced inconsistent and even contradictory results due, in part, to the scarcity of sufficiently long uniform observational records. Our ability to detect trends is also confounded by the enormous variability of the upper atmosphere driven primarily by solar and geomagnetic activity on various temporal and spatial scales. The "greenhouse cooling" is expected to result in a substantial thermospheric density decline that depends on the level of solar activity. Existing analyses of neutral density trends based on satellite drag data over the last 2 to 3 decades have provided perhaps the most robust evidence of global change in the upper atmosphere to date. These results inherently provide a global view and qualitatively agree with each other and with theoretical model predictions. More work is required to improve our confidence in the trend estimates, to delineate the contributions of solar activity and other parameters, to better understand the physical mechanisms, and to quantify their contributions to the observed changes. The science goal of this project is to advance our understanding of the mechanisms driving the long-term global changes in the upper atmosphere and the near-Earth space environment. Our approach is unique in that it synergistically combines two key components: (1) we will extend, in time and altitude coverage and in number of observations per year, our comprehensive analysis of the global satellite-drag database to delineate the contributions of solar activity and other sources of natural variation, and to detect anthropogenic and possible natural long-term trends; (2) we will use an updated global upper-atmospheric numerical model to study the natural and anthropogenic variability using the records of greenhouse gas concentrations and solar activity over the same period of time. A direct comparison of the results of theoretical modeling with the analysis of accurately determined trends in the upper atmosphere will be carried out for the first time. This will provide insights into the key physical mechanisms and their possible interactions and feedbacks, and will facilitate the attribution of the observed trends. A clearer understanding of the thermospheric "greenhouse cooling" will lead to development of meaningful long-term forecasting capabilities. This work is immediately relevant to the science goals of the NASA Living With a Star program and, in particular, to its Targeted Research science topic T3e. The ability to understand and predict the long-term density variability in the near-Earth space environment is also of enormous practical significance to any spacecraft operators, including the NASA's programs and missions.

Description: OPTICAL PROPERTIES OF PLANETARY HAZES The most visible aspect of Titan is the organic haze layer that completely covers this moon of Saturn. While much less optically thick, stratospheric hazes are also known to exist in the atmospheres of Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune. Planetary hazes have also been proposed to be an important component of the early Earthjs atmosphere. While there have been many attempts to model the atmospheric hazes in these different environments, significant uncertainties remain in the chemical, physical and optical properties. On Titan, the haze has a dominant effect on the propagation of solar radiation in the atmosphere and thereby significantly effects the temperature structure of the atmosphere and the surface temperature. The haze has an "anti-greenhouse" effect due to strong absorption in solar wavelengths combined with low opacity in thermal wavelengths. The optical properties of the haze material are essential to determining its effect on the thermal structure. In other settings (early Earth, extrasolar planets, Jupiter and Saturn) the haze optical properties would vary and the resulting effect on the thermal structure would vary as well. Thus to understand and accurately model the temperature structure of planetary atmospheres that contain haze material the optical properties of that material must be determined. Accurate optical constants are also needed to retrieve the properties of planetary haze particles. While optical constants have been previously measured for Titan-like organic haze, there are several outstanding issues. First the haze optical constants determined by several groups vary by up to two orders of magnitude at visible wavelengths. The cause of the variability could be due to the different gas mixtures, different excitation sources or another unknown variable. In addition to differences between various laboratory measurements, there is also an offset between the laboratory measurements and the refractive indices needed to match the observations of Titan haze. Finally all of the optical constants have been measured for particles impacted on a plate over long time periods. This leads to uncertainty in the analysis because the particles are treated as films, and can also lead to significant sample contamination. We propose to use state-of-the-art instrumentation to measure the optical constants of freely floating haze particles. We will use the recently developed technique of aerosol cavity ring down (CRD) spectroscopy to determine the optical properties of single-sized organic haze particles. We are currently in the process of building a laboratory CRI) spectrometer. Here, we propose to use the CRD spectrometer for measurements of planetary haze particles. We will generate haze particles in the laboratory and measure their chemical composition using a novel aerosol mass spectrometer. We will then use the CRD spectrometer system to determine the single scattering albedo of the haze monomers. Neither technique requires collecting the particles so contamination will be minimized. Our overarching goal is to correlate the optical properties of the haze monomers with their chemical properties. These studies will be performed as a function of excitation source, gas composition, total pressure and temperature to cover a wide range of planetary hazes. The data provided by this work will be directly applicable to retrievals of aerosol physical properties on planets and moons in our solar system. By providing a correlation between optical and chemical signatures, current retrievals may also be extended to include information on haze chemical properties and provide insight into chemistry in planetary atmospheres. Finally, the improved information on aerosol optical properties will be relevant to understanding and modeling the temperature structure of planetary atmospheres containing an organic haze.

These field data have also been valuable for improving explicit numerical models of convection. In the proposed research, we will continue to interleave TRMM data, field campaign, and model data towards further validating the numerical models. We will develop a more formal, statistically based methodology for comparing model and observational data. We will also continue research using the extensive PF database from T Wto s tudy climatic variability of tropical convection and identify improvements to the retrieval algorithms needed to account for this variability. Description: SOLAR TERRESTRIAL RELATIONS OBSERVATORY (STEREO) WAVES PHASE E Data on hourly or 3-hourly precipitation over the globe has recently become available from TRMM and other satellite measurements. This new data allows analyses of precipitation frequency, intensity and diurnal variations on a global scale and more detailed evaluation of model precipitation. We propose to study the precipitation characteristics and apply the results to evaluate climate models by analyzing several high-resolution precipitation products from TRMM (e.g., 3B42) and other satellite-based products such as the PERSIANN from UC, Irvine and CMORPH from NCEPICPC. The satellite observations will be compared with surface rain gauge and radar hourly measurements over the U.S. and rain gauge daily precipitation (including bias-corrected data) over land and 3-hourly weather reports of precipitation frequency over the globe. We will focus our analysis on (1) differences between satellite precipitation products with and without blending with infrared (IR) observations; (2) precipitation frequency and intensity derived from daily, 3-hourly, and hourly precipitation; and (3) the diurnal timing and amplitude in the hourly or 3-hourly products. Our goal is to quantify (a) whether the inclusion of the IR measurements improves the estimates of precipitation frequency, intensity and diurnal variations compared with microwave-only products; (b) what the strength and weakness of the various high-resolution products are; and (c) whether and how these relatively-new products can improve our knowledge about the spatial and temporal variations in precipitation frequency, intensity and diurnal cycle. The satellite data will then be applied to evaluate precipitation characteristics from coupled climate models with data archived at PCMDI. Significant results from this proposal are expected to help evaluate TRMM and other satellite precipitation products, help design future precipitation missions, improve our knowledge about the various precipitation characteristics, and evaluate climate models. The project will also produce global monthly climatology of precipitation characteristics for community use. lTRMM=Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission 2PERSIANN=Precipitation Estimation from Remotely Sensed Information using Artificial Neural Networks 3CMORPH= Climate Prediction Center (CPC) morphing method.

Description: SBIR PHASE 2 AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED: Modular, Plug and Play, Distributive Avionics. The objective of this SBIR Phase II effort is to prove the viability of an Ethernet version of the MicroSat Systems, Inc. (MSI) modular, plug and play (PnP) spacecraft avionics architecture. This revolutionary architecture provides a near-term solution to modular plug and play avionics while distributing power and data management functions on a single circuit allowing rapid interfacing to other satellite avionics such as the GSFC Space Cube. By integrating the MSI protocol converter technology with the ABET Technologies Digital Current System, MSI can provide a network with standardized attachment nodes that carries data and power on an Intelligent Power/Data Ring (IPDR). The IPDR network, which can host a variety of data protocals, currently implements a high speed SPA-S (SpaceWire) core to support the AFRL PnP efforts. It enables full PnP Modularity reducing spacecraft integration and test to a few days. Since the system is implemented with a common set of nodes for every interface instead of custom cards in a card cage, the hardware costs are dramatically lower as well, only 40-60% of comparable centralized systems. Using commercial Ethernet parts integrated into the existing IPDR node processor and interface boards successful proof of concept testing was performed during Phase I. The transfer of Ethernet data frames was demonstrated into the IPDR ring via a peripheral Ethernet device, from one IPDR node to another, and finally back out of the ring to the external Ethernet device. Although this testing verified the fundamental functionality of Ethernet communication on the IPDR ring avionics, there is significant effort remaining to mature this into a flight worthy avionics architecture. The Phase II will investigate flight parts selection for the nodes, firmware development required to improve bandwidth, and flight qualification and delivery of an Ethernet version of an IPDR node.

Description: Helioseismic Mapping of Subsurface Flows Near Solar Filaments. Solar filaments are beautiful and enigmatic solar features that, despite years of study, still pose questions as to their formation and evolution. There are competing theories as to whether they are formed by the emergence through the photosphere of fully mature magnetic structures or built in situ by strong shearing or converging flows acting on ambient fields. It is still unknown why certain filaments persist for many solar rotations while otfaers rapidly erupt as coronal mass ejections (CMEs). The existence and energetic eruption of solar filaments depend on magnetic fields anchored in the photosphere and possibly deeper, so flows existing within the convection zone probably play an important role in tbeir formation and evolution. Flows can advert field lines---twisting, shearing, and braiding the footpoints within the photosphere from which the coronal field emerges. To study these persistent flows at different depths, we propose to refine our new helioseismic high-resolution ring-analysis (HRRA) procedure. This includes using new tracking, remapping, and fitting strategies; achieving a horizen'al resolution of about 10 Mm (1 degree); and finding optimal averaging strategies to minimize the effects of supergranulatim. We will use this HRRA procedure to analyze subsurface flows underlying a large number of solar filaments using Dynamics Program data from the Michelson Doppler Imager (MDI) instrument aboard SOHO, searching for convergent andlor shearing flows near the magnetic neutral line of these filaments. The MDI Dynamics data set, spanning 10 years, is a treasure trove of information an the interaction of subsurface flows and magnetic fields that we can now mine in new ways with the development of our HRRA procedure. The  characterization of flows near filaments will put important constraints on theories of filament formation and evolution, prsssoting a better understanding of the differences between quiescent and active filaments

Description: Beyond the Cool Cores in Galaxy Clusters: Testing a Hierarchical Model with X-ray Observations and AMR Simulations We propose to rigorously test and evolve a new model for the formation of cool core (CC) clusters of galaxies using a unique combination of archival X-ray data from ROSAT, Chandra, and XMM-Newton with unprecedented spatial dynamic range from kiloparsec to Megaparsec scales. Clusters with cool cores have central regions with high levels of X-ray emission and gas that are 30% cooler than average for the cluster. Our cosmological numerical simulations show that there are evolutionary differences between CC clusters and their non-cool core (NCC) counterparts. Many of the numerical CC clusters at the present epoch accreted mass more slowly over time and grew enhanced cool cores via hierarchical mergers; when late major mergers occurred, the CCs survived the collisions. By contrast, NCC clusters of similar mass experienced major mergers early in their evolution that destroyed embryonic cool cores and produced conditions that prevent CC re-formation. This model is in stark contrast to previous simple models where CC clusters were believed to be stable, uniform, and in dynamical equilibrium. The observational validation of this hierarchical formation model is important if galaxy clusters are to be used as precision mass probes for cosmology including the parameterization of dark energy. Our computer simulations make concrete predictions that CC clusters differ from NCC clusters beyond the core regions out to the peripheries of the clusters. In this proposed research, we will comparelcontrast the X-ray surface brightness profiles, the distributions of spectral temperatures, the X-ray scaling relations (e.g., cluster mass versus temperature), and the effects of cluster mass on the formation of cool cores. This powerful combination of extensive X-ray observations and state-of-the-art numerical simulations will allow us for the first time to understand the formation of cool core clusters within a proper cosmological context.

Description: In situ plasma and magnetic field observations have provided direct evidence that magnetic reconnection commonly occurs in the solar wind from 0.3 to 5.4 AU. Thus far, events have been recorded at the Helios, ACE, WIND, Cluster, and Ulysses sic. The proposed investigation will focus on data analyses of plasma and magnetic field observations of solar wind reconnection and comparisons with hybrid (kinetic ions and fluid electrons) simulations to answer the following questions: Can Hall current generation alone explain the observed asymmetric field rotations at the bifurcated current sheets bounding the exhausts? Is the ion-ion two-stream instability (due to observed counter-streaming ion beams) related to the observed enhanced power of compressional magnetic field fluctuations within the exhausts? Why is the magnetic field non-zero within exhausts? The analysis will utilize data for a large number of reconnection events that cover the inner and the outer heliosphere from the two Helios sic (0.3-1.0 AU), ACE (1 AU), Ulysses (1.4-5.4 AU), and the STEREO sic, respectively, to explore the 3-D geometry and extent of reconnection exhausts and their X-lines within the solar wind environment. The proposed research is directly relevant to the NASA dual-spacecraft STEREO mission which is expected to be launched in 2006 and the objectives as stated in two Priority Research Focus Areas (RFA) of the 2005 Sun-Solar System Connection Roadmap that supports the NASA strategic goals and objectives: (1) RFA F.1 to "understand magnetic reconnection in the very different regimes where it occurs"; (2) RFA F.2.3 to "understand how the solar wind evolves".
