Description: Localized electrostatic structures such as double layers and phase-space holes have now been found in numerous space environments. It has been established observationally by satellites such as FAST and Polar, with support from numerical simulations, that double layers and electron and ion holes play an important role in the particle-acceleration process in different regions of Earth's auroral current system. Both observations and simulations suggest that double layers vary in the direction perpendicular to Earth's magnetic field. This nonuniformity can influence the spatial distribution of accelerated field-aligned electron populations. It can also influence the perpendicular acceleration of ions, which can contribute to observed ion outflows. The proposed research effort will employ a suite of open-boundary kinetic Vlasov simulation codes to study the nonlinear evolution of localized electrostatic structures throughout Earth's auroral ionosphere. Emphasis will be placed on the interplay between these structures -- especially their variations in the direction perpendicular to B -- and the acceleration of electrons and ions. Many of these simulation algorithms, which are designed to efficiently treat different particle magnetization regimes, have already been developed and tested. The proposed research will extend the simulations to include both ion magnetization and true kinetic evolution of the perpendicular ion distribution. The coupling of small-scale and fast electrostatic processes with large-scale and slow electromagnetic processes will also be incorporated into the simulations. The simulation studies will be guided by and employed in the interpretation of recent and ongoing auroral-altitude satellite missions such as FAST. This research program will address Sub-goal 3B of NASA's 2006 Strategic Plan to "understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system" in that the acceleration of particles in the auroral zone is a primary manifestation of solar-wind driving of the magnetosphere. Understanding the spatial structure of particle acceleration can play an influential role in modeling the accelerated distributions that couple to the collisional ionosphere at lower altitudes -- to be studied in situ by the proposed GEC mission. This research will also be relevant to the upcoming MMS mission, which will probe regions of the magnetosphere associated with reconnection, where electron holes have previously been observed by multiple satellites. In addition, localized fields have been observed in the solar wind, making the proposed investigation relevant to the analysis of wave and particle measurements by the forthcoming STEREO mission. The simulation methods to be developed here can be employed to study these more weakly magnetized domains as well.

Description: A DATA ANALYSIS AND MODELING STUDY OF SECULAR CHANGE IN THERMOSPHERIC DENSITY We propose a data analysis and modeling study of long-term changes that have occurred in the upper atmosphere over the recent several decades. Interest in these trends has been stimulated by the classical modeling study of Roble and Dickinson (1989), who predicted a dramatic response to a hypothetical future increase of greenhouse gases: the upper atmosphere is expected to cool down by tens of degrees in response to the standard doubled-C02 scenario. The search for signs of global change in upper-atmospheric and ionospheric historical data records has been inconclusive. While some parameters clearly reveal long-term trends in general agreement with the model predictions, other estimates have produced inconsistent and even contradictory results due, in part, to the scarcity of sufficiently long uniform observational records. Our ability to detect trends is also confounded by the enormous variability of the upper atmosphere driven primarily by solar and geomagnetic activity on various temporal and spatial scales. The "greenhouse cooling" is expected to result in a substantial thermospheric density decline that depends on the level of solar activity. Existing analyses of neutral density trends based on satellite drag data over the last 2 to 3 decades have provided perhaps the most robust evidence of global change in the upper atmosphere to date. These results inherently provide a global view and qualitatively agree with each other and with theoretical model predictions. More work is required to improve our confidence in the trend estimates, to delineate the contributions of solar activity and other parameters, to better understand the physical mechanisms, and to quantify their contributions to the observed changes. The science goal of this project is to advance our understanding of the mechanisms driving the long-term global changes in the upper atmosphere and the near-Earth space environment. Our approach is unique in that it synergistically combines two key components: (1) we will extend, in time and altitude coverage and in number of observations per year, our comprehensive analysis of the global satellite-drag database to delineate the contributions of solar activity and other sources of natural variation, and to detect anthropogenic and possible natural long-term trends; (2) we will use an updated global upper-atmospheric numerical model to study the natural and anthropogenic variability using the records of greenhouse gas concentrations and solar activity over the same period of time. A direct comparison of the results of theoretical modeling with the analysis of accurately determined trends in the upper atmosphere will be carried out for the first time. This will provide insights into the key physical mechanisms and their possible interactions and feedbacks, and will facilitate the attribution of the observed trends. A clearer understanding of the thermospheric "greenhouse cooling" will lead to development of meaningful long-term forecasting capabilities. This work is immediately relevant to the science goals of the NASA Living With a Star program and, in particular, to its Targeted Research science topic T3e. The ability to understand and predict the long-term density variability in the near-Earth space environment is also of enormous practical significance to any spacecraft operators, including the NASA's programs and missions.

Description: Retrieval of Ice Cloud Properties from CoSSIR During TC4 Evaluation and improvement of the representation of tropical convective clouds in cloud resolving models and large scale climate models requires improvements in remote sensing of ice clouds and upper tropospheric water vapor profiles. Traditional remote sensing methods cannot accurately retrieve the vertically integrated ice mass (ice water path or IWP) over the full range of IWP in tropical convective anvils. submillimeter-wave radiometry is a promising new method for measuring swath-wide IWP, mean mass weighted ice particle diameter (Dme), and water vapor profiles in ice clouds. The NASA Goddard Space Flight Center has been developing the Compact Scanning Submillimeter-wave Imaging Radiometer (CoSSIR) which has flown on board the NASA ER-2 and WB-57 aircraft. Under a separate proposal, collaborator Dr. James Wang offers to deploy the upgraded CoSSIR on the ER-2 in the Tropical Composition, Cloud, and Climate Coupling Experiment (TC4) field campaign in Costa Rica during July 2007. The objectives of the proposed research are to further develop the emerging technique of submillimeter-wave remote sensing of ice clouds, to provide needed remote sensing products for the TC4 experiment, and to provide information for validating CloudSat ice cloud retrievals. The research proposed will retrieve ice cloud IWP, Dme, and water vapor profiles from CoSSIR data (and any available infrared radiometer data) acquired during TC4. The retrievals will be performed with an existing Bayesian algorithm that includes available prior information on ice cloud and atmospheric profiles and outputs products with realistic error bars. The ice cloud and water vapor retrievals will be evaluated using other remote sensing data from the ER-2 and in situ measurements from other aircraft. The CoSSIR polarized brightness temperatures will be analyzed and the Bayesian method extended to retrieve ice particle shape and orientation information. CloudSat IWP retrievals will be evaluated using CoSSIR retrievals, mainly by using CloudSat algorithms on data from the Cloud Radar System flying on the ER-2. The proposed research will provide ice cloud and water vapor remote sensing products that will be important for TC4 objectives, such as improving cloud resolving models and hence the understanding of tropical cirrus anvils. Continued development of the submillimeter-wave ice cloud remote sensing method will eventually lead to improvements in NASA's capabilities for global cloud sensing and thence to NASA's goal of improving the prediction of climate evolution.

Description: INVESTIGATIONS OF GLOBAL ULF STRUCTURE IN EARTH'S MAGNETOSPHERE SUMMARY: Ultra Low Frequency waves, electric and magnetic variations at mHz time scales, play an important role in the transport and acceleration of energetic particles in the magnetosphere. However, not all sources and types of ULF energy in the magnetosphere may equally affect trapped particle dynamics. For example, mode structure, propagation direction, and azimuthal occurrence of ULF waves are all important factors in determining the degree to which a source of ULF waves will affect magnetospheric particles. These factors may depend on elements of the instantaneous state of the global magnetosphere, which may not be possible to extract from the few measurements typically available via in situ observations. Event studies have shown that the spatiotemporal structure and generation of these waves is well suited to study by global-scale magnetospheric simulations. While event studies provide an important validation of the approach, the complicated structure of real solar wind observations make it very challenging to isolate the physical factors controlling the generation of magnetospheric ULF waves. In this study, we propose to use global, 3d MHD simulations ofthe magnetosphere driven by idealized solar wind conditions to study the effects of external driving of ULF waves within the magnetosphere. This study will isolate the most important conditions in determining relevant characteristics of magnetospheric ULF waves. Wherever possible, results will be verified through comparison to Polar and geosynchronous in situ measurements.Understanding the relevant conditions pertaining to the transmission of energy from the solar wind into Earth's magnetosphere will be of vital importance to understanding the environmental conditions to which human technologies will be subject in near-Earth space.The results of this study will be relevant to NASA strategic goal 3B, to Explore the Sun-Earth system to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system.

Description: JET STRUCTURES AND PHOTOSPHERE PROPERTIES OF GRBS ABSTRACT: GRB jet models predict that the photosphere lies outside the acceleration zone, at radii here the flow is coasting with nearly constant Lorentz factor. Some form of internal dissipation such as internal shocks must then be invoked to reconvert kinetic energy to radiation. Such a reconversion process would be unnecessary if the photosphere were close to or inside the acceleration zone. The prompt RB emission could then consist mainly of the degraded and Lorentz boosted relic radiation of the central engine essentially a distorted black body. We propose to study a set of promising mechanisms for moving the photospheres of GRB jets inward, without compromising their principal energetic and kinematic properties. In magnetized jets, both Parker instabilities and photon bubble instabilities could lead to the development of a two-phase structure, in which most of the jet matter is compressed into narrow, optically thick filaments. Radiation passes between the filaments. Radiation passes between the filaments, escaping from smaller radii. We will analyze the conditions under which such instabilities are likely to grow inside accelerating GRB jets, characterize the nature of the resulting two-phase structure (adapting existing analytic and numerical models for the nonlinear outcomes of these instabilities), and compute the resulting spectral and temporal signatures. The results of this investigation could help in understanding the characteristic peak energies and slopes of GRB spectra.

Description: This proposal requests funding to install a suite of state-of-the-art and new microphysical instruments on the NASA WB-57F and the UND DC-8 for the upcoming TC4 project. Funding is also requested in the first year for participation in the TC4 field campaign, quality control and processing of the collected data that will be placed in the NASA data archives. The proposal also includes funding for data analysis for years two and three, because as stated in the solicitation, SPEC is not currently funded for data analysis under the NASA Radiation Sciences Program (RSP). However, SPEC does have a pending proposal to RSP to analyze data from the CRYSTAL-FACE and MidCiX projects, and if this proposal is awarded, it is understood that the second and third year funding requested here will likely be modified. For TC4, SPEC proposes to install cloud particle imagers (CPIs) and 2D-S (Stereo) probes on both the WB-57F and DC-8 aircraft. Both probes have previously been installed on these aircraft for NASA field projects (i.e., C-F, MidCiX, CR-AVE and the upcoming NAMMA-06 projects) and therefore have heritage on NASA research aircraft. The CPI recently recorded the first highquality digital images of subvisible cirrus near Costa Rica (CR-AVE). Data from the 2D-S collected during CR-AVE shows that it is the only imaging probe capable of reliably measuring the particle size distribution between 30 and 150 microns. The 2D-S produces stereo images of particles in the middle of the viewing volume, and also makes two independent measurements of particles in the size range from 10 to 1280 microns, providing a redundancy check on particle size distribution measurements. In addition to the CPI and 2D-S probes, SPEC is partnering with Alexei Korolev and Walter Strapp of Environment Canada (EC) to also install a new high-output total water content evaporator (that fits into a PMS canister), and a flight-tested transmissometer that directly measures extinction coefficient. These instruments, along with all expenses except travel and per diem for Korolev and Strapp, will be contributed by EC. Data collected by the microphysical instruments proposed here will provide critical information needed to answer several of the key scientific questions addressed by TC4. In particular, we anticipate using the collected data to provide closure on uncertainties surrounding measurements of extinction and ice water content in maritime anvils and cirrus, document the differences in particle shape, size and concentration in tropical anvils and in situ cirrus compared with their continental counterparts, and provide insights into the formation, evolution and radiative properties of tropical clouds. We also anticipate that additional measurements in subvisible cirrus will extend the data set collected during CRAVE, revealing any seasonal differences that may be present, and furthering our understanding of the formation, evolution and radiative characteristics of subvisible cirrus.

Description: MICROPHYSICAL MEASUREMENTS AND ANALYSIS IN SUPPORT OF THE TROPICAL COMPOSITION, CLOUD, AND CLIMATE COUPLING EXPERIMENT This proposal seeks to investigate and characterize the microphysical properties of tropical convection and cirrus clouds and their interactions with the environment by making measurements from the DC-8 aircraft during the Tropical Composition, Cloud, and Climate Coupling Experiment (TC4) experiment in July of 2007. Our research group comprises experts in the areas of aerosol, cloud and precipitation physics, cloud dynamics, and cloud radiative properties. Our expertise spans the areas of airborne instrumentation, data processing and analysis, and theory. Group members have worked together over many years and can work as a team to meet key TC4 measurement needs and scientific objectives. We propose to make a comprehensive set of measurements of hydrometeor properties, including cloud particle sizes, shapes and liquid and ice water contents, from instruments mounted on the NASA DC8 research aircraft. A major thrust of the effort of this group will involve a characterization of tropical cloud microphysical properties in convective clouds and anvil cirrus over Central America, the tropical eastern Pacific and Gulf of Mexico. Our TC4 data will also be archived to be available for other scientific investigations. Our data collection and analysis activities will address several topics identified in the Roses A.9 Request for Proposals. 1) We are thrilled by the opportunity to study the effects of aerosols on convective cloud microphysical properties, formation and precipitation, and the resulting effects on particles carried from convection into anvils. A key component of our effort will be to evaluate the importance and impact of homogeneous vs. heterogeneous ice nucleation processes and their dependence on temperature and aerosol properties. 2) We have given considerable thought as to how to evaluate/validate satellite remote sensing measurements, primarily from active sensors. The complement of instruments we propose to provide for the DC-8 are almost ideal for evaluating active and passive satellite and aircraft remote sensors. 3) As part of a recent field campaign in the area near Darwin Australia, we believe that we have detected aircraft icing and high concentrations of haze particles in and around convection at temperatures well below 40C, which is approximately the temperature for homogeneous nucleation of activated cloud droplets. If this observation applies for widespread areas of the tropics, it would have significant implications for anvil radiative properties and satellite-borne remote sensing retrievals. With an instrument we propose as an option on the DC-8 together with other microphysical probes and water vapor measurements, we believe that we can make significant contributions for identifying and understanding new crystal generation in anvil cloud regions.

Description: Measurements of NO and NOy on the WB57F During TC4 The Tropical Composition, Cloud and Climate Coupling Experiment (TC4) will investigate the structure, properties, and processes in the tropopause transition layer (TTL) over Central America, the tropical eastern Pacific, and Gulf of Mexico. Additionally, in support of the AURA Validation Experiment (AVE), aircraft measurements will be used for validation of satellite data products. We propose to fly a 2-channel chemiluminescence instrument on the WB57F for the in situ measurement of NO and NOy. These measurements will contribute to some of the major questions to be addressed by TC4, as well as to satellite validation. While TC4 has a strong focus on the control of cirrus particles and water vapor in the TTL, chemical observations are important for addressing questions that are among those posed for TC4, in particular those having to do with the control of O3 in the TTL, and the role in this of NOx, especially that from lightning. NO and NOy will also contribute to the chemical characterization of the air in the TTL, which is the chemical boundary condition for the lower stratosphere. Since reactive nitrogen (NOx = NO + NO2) is critical to O3 production chemistry, the measurement of NO is central to addressing the TC4 questions about processes which control O3 in the TTL. NOx is expected to be predominantly NO in the TTL, given the temperatures and O3 mixing ratios there. NO2 amounts will be calculated assuming steady state and using measurements of O3 (proposed by NOAA -- Fahey/Gao) and measurements of actinic fluxes (proposed by NCAR/CU -- Shetter/Hall/Petropavlovskikh, Collaborators on this proposal). In cirrus clouds associated with convective outflows, NOx levels are expected to be greatly elevated due to lightning [Ridley et al., 2004] and therefore likely to significantly enhance downstream O3 production. Additionally NOx can also be convected upward from a polluted boundary layer and into cirrus outflows. The impact of convective outflows, with an emphasis on NOx from lightning, is the subject of modeling work by K. Pickering (NASA Goddard, Collaborator on this proposal) using the TC4 data set. It is hypothesized that NOx production for the tropical TTL is dominated by lightning. From measurements in convective outflow cirrus clouds, and by contrasting those due to convection over land versus those well out over the ocean, it will be possible to shed light on the role of lightning as a source of NOx to this region (and so its role in O3 production), as well as to determine differences in the impacts of maritime versus continental convection on both NOx and O3. These measurements will also provide a useful tracer of convective outflow as well as information on the age of the air mass. The presence of elevated NOx indicates a lightning and therefore recent convective influence. The measurements will contribute to analysis of the partitioning of total reactive nitrogen, especially if the NOAA HNO3 CIMS is also aboard the WB57F. For the AVE objectives, we propose for the WB57F to fly vertical profiles for the determination of NO2 (calculated from measured NO, O3, j-NO2, estimated RO2) for comparison with AURA/OMI NO2 column measurements, with some of these profiles flown above cloud. This will be done in close collaboration with Pickering's existing project to validate OMI NO2 in regions dominated by lightning-generated NOx. It is proposed to fly on the WB57F a newly built and laboratory-tested twochannel NO-NOy instrument. Minor modifications are required for flight at high altitude in an unpressurized environment. This includes the design and construction of 3 pressure vessels (computer vessel from CRYSTAL-FACE will be re-used) and flow controller modifications. A significant effort will go into design, fabrication, and structural analysis of the mechanical structure for mounting instrument components into the WB57F pallet. The inlet from CRYSTAL-FACE will be re-used.

Description: CORPORATION FOR ATMOSPHERIC RESEARCH ACTINIC FLUX MEASUREMENTS ON THE NASA WB-57 FOR THE TC-4 MISSION IN SUPPORT OF AURA INSTRUMENT VALIDATION The primary objective of this proposed research is to support AURA validation activities by deploying solar radiation measurement instrumentation from the NASA WB-57 for the determination of ozone column abundance. Description: In Situ Measurements of Cloud Ice Water Content During TC4 in Support of Satellite Validation We propose to make fast-response in situ measurements of cloud ice water content (IWC) using a tunable diode laser hygrometer coupled to a subisokinetic inlet from the NASA WB-57F in support of the Tropical Composition, Cloud and Climate Coupling Experiment (TC4). IWC is a common prognostic variable in modern general circulation models from which cloud effective radius is determined; effective radius is a fundamental parameter used to estimate a cloud's radiative impact. Direct measurements of IWC are critical not only for validation of cloud properties remotely sensed by satellite instruments, but also for improving the treatment of clouds in climate models. The University of Colorado closed-path laser hygrometer (CLH) has flown on several airborne campaigns to provide observations of IWC primarily in cirrus clouds and high altitude rocket exhaust plumes. High temporal resolution data are available from SOLVE (1999/00, DC-8, Arctic); CRYSTAL-FACE (2002, WB-57F, sub-tropical); and MidCiX (2004, WB-57F, mid-latitude) in a variety of cirrus cloud types. We propose to extend this measurement database with observations of tropical and subtropical cirrus obtained during the July 2007 TC4 campaign. CLH is a compact, lightweight (less than 35 lbs), power-efficient instrument that provides rapid (minimum of 2 Hz) measurements of "total water" with an accuracy of better than 20% (2-sigma). In combination with a simultaneous measurement of water vapor, typically obtained from JPL's JLH instrument, ice water content can be calculated. Data analysis activities after TC4 will focus on quantification of the variability of IWC in different cloud types and the impact of horizontal and vertical variability on the accurate retrieval of cloud properties from remote sensors. We will work with satellite instrument teams, especially the AIRS team at JPL, to validate cirrus retrieval algorithms and to assess the importance of the variability of cloud properties on the accuracy of those retrievals.

Description: THE SECULAR EVOLUTION OF CLOSE RING-SATELLITE SYSTEMS The proposed research will examine the secular gravitational interactions exerted between a satellite and a nearby planetary ring. We use a model to show that a satellite orbiting in a narrow gap in a planetary ring launches very long-wavelength spiral waves at the ring edge. Those waves are excited by the satellite's secular perturbations, and the model shows that the excitation of these waves results in vigorous damping of the satellite's eccentricity and inclination. In the following, we will determine analytically the rate of the satellite's orbital evolution, as well as the waves' properties (wavelength, amplitilde, etc.). These waves may be quite imporiant, since their excitation may play a key rale in stabilizing the eccentricity and inclination of a satellite iahabiting a gap in a ring. An application of these results will be in the Encke gap, a narrow gap in Saturn's main A ring maintained by the satellite Pan. Faint ringlets have also been observed here, which suggests other small unseen moonlets are also present, maintaining those ringlets (Porco et. al. 2005). However, Nbody simulations show that Pan's gravity quickly clears the Encke gap of any moonlets. We will re-examine this, to see if the excitation of waves at the gap edge can damp the moonlets eccentricities sufficiently to stabilize their orbits inside gap. These results will be significant, since they will lead to a better understanding of an important process that appears to play a key role in stabilizing the orbits of satellites orbiting in/near a planetary ring. This research is also relevant to NASA's strategic goal: to better understand the workings of the Solar System. These results are also relevant to the Outer Planets Research program, since they will lead to improved understanding of an important process thought operate in the ring/satellite systems of the giant planets.

Description: TECHNICAL ABSTRACT ( Limit 2000 characters, approximately 200 words) T3RSS is the system engineer's tool that allows a systematic approach to ensuring that even if one or more failures occur in a single component or subsystem, then the subsystem will continue to function and most, if not all, mission objectives can still be achieved. T3RSS does this by using a Configuration Manager for a Dynamically Reconfigurable System (CMDRS). This piece of logic employs a Mission Survivability Assurance Algorithm (MSAA) for the subsystem. Should radiation, manufacturing or even launch damage render a particular region of the FPGA temporarily or permanently unusable while on orbit, then the MSAA can shift the critical logic to a new region, or even to a new FPGA altogether. The shifting logic uses a network of components to maintain the ability of each logic block to communicate with the required memory and hardware. Ensuring that needed logic is always available ensures that the satellite can maintain 100% mission survivability even during failures. POTENTIAL NASA COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS ( Limit 1500 characters, approximately 150 words) Mr. Clint Patrick is the Reconfigurable Computing point of contact for NASA at Marshall Space Flight Center. He currently leads two programs that may benefit from the research that Redefine Technologies is doing with T3RSS. He has expressed his full support of our research in an attached letter. The first program, Fault Tolerant Avionics, is researching the feasibility of including a single, reconfigurable FPGA as a 'common spare'. This spare would be a backup for the other avionics boards on the aircraft: if one goes down, the functionality of that system would be passed to the spare to take over in real-time. The T3RSS concept is directly applicable to this program because the same goals are being investigated. The second program is in support of Radiation-Hardened Electronics for Space Exploration (RHESE). Their self-training, autonomous, neural network is currently configured to run on powerful CPUs. The speed and power savings of moving this processing to logic would mean better performance out of the network, however, the size of each neuron implies that a 'shifting' or 'time-multiplexing' of logic within each FPGA would be needed. The on-demand and priority-driven algorithms developed for T3RSS to ensure the modules are where they're needed, when they're needed, could be the enabling technology for the redesign of this system. Description: Our primary goal is to quantify the contribution of North American summer-time convective transport to the distribution of ozone (O3) and carbon monoxide (CO) in the upper troposphere. Understanding convective transport of pollutants initially residing in the boundary layer is critical to the characterization of upper tropospheric pollutant pathways. In addition we will assess the ability of a state-of-the-art convective-system-resolving convective transport model and of convective parameterizations to accurately predict the convective contribution to the distribution and evolution of trace gases in the upper troposphere. These objectives will be achieved by comparing vertically resolved profiles of CO and O3 from the Aura Tropospheric Emission Spectrometer (TES) to model fields produced by the Weather Research Forecast coupled with chemistry (WRF-Chem) model. The WRF-Chem model will be integrated at two horizontal resolutions for the eastern 2/3 of the United States. The coarse-grid simulation, which parameterizes convection, is run daily as part of the WRF-Chem operations. A high-resolution WRF-Chem simulation, which explicitly simulates convection, will be integrated for a one-month summertime period to model convection in the U.S. Comparison between the model output and TES observations will characterize the processes, such as convection, global transport, or in-situ chemistry that contribute to the distribution of O3 and CO in the upper troposphere. We will employ the TES special observation mode, which measures O3 and CO every 20 km along orbit tracks, in order to assess the convective transport capability of WRF-Chem for specific case studies. This assessment will provide new understanding and quantification of the role of convective transport in controlling the regional and global scale distribution of trace gases. Furthermore, the study naturally leads to identification of shortcomings in existing convective parameterizations and motivates improvements in the schemes in WRF: a task which is critical for improving numerical weather forecasting and is a necessary step towards chemical forecasting.

Description: AIR QUALITY MEASUREMENTS FROM SPACE: DEFINING AN OPTIMUM OBSERVING STRATEGY Pollutants are those compounds that serve to dirty or contaminate the atmosphere and which may be directly harmful to human, animal, and plant health, or result in adverse changes in the natural enviroument that lead to a reduction in the quality and sustainability of life. There is a need for measuring, monitoring and understanding the processes which pollute the atmosphere, to determine the effects of local and regional air pollution on the global atmosphere, and also the effects of global pollution on regional air quality. As part of an integrated measurement system, satellite observations provide the context for localized observations, and extend local measurements to regional and global scales. Chemical transport models help integrate these diverse measurements with the aim of providing a unified understanding. Ideally, a space mission could provide the spatial and temporal measurement sampling required to match the anticipated tropospheric chemistry model resolutions of the near future, and support the air quality research, forecasting, and assessment mandates of government agencies. A study is proposed to define the key parameters and measurement characteristics that are required for the successful use of satellite remote sensing in measuring enviroumentally significant pollutant trace gases from space. We plan to motivate this work with an examination of the current satellite measurements and their appropriateness for air quality studies. To this end, we will use a suite of chemical transport models, measurement simulation codes, and surface air quality data in conjunction with the satellite observations. We then propose to address three inter-related objectives: to assess the degree to which current satellite measurements are useful for air quality studies; to determine the important spatial and temporal scales for air quality processes; and to assess the implications for near-term air quality satellite missions.

Description: VERTICAL STRUCTURE OF PRECIPITATION RETRIEVED FROM MULTI-FREQUENCY PROFILING RADARS FOR VALIDATING SATELLITE-BASED PRECIPITATION PRODUCTS Analysis of vertically-pointing profiler and polarimetric scanning radar observations is proposed to quantify the vertical and spatial structure of raindrop size distributions (DSDs) in precipitating cloud systems and will address NASA's request for (i) improving current precipitation algorithms from satellite observations, (ii) developing, testing and validating future dual-frequency precipitation radar (DPR) algorithms, and (iii) developing statistical validation techniques that include improving ground-based comparison products. The DSD is a fundamental precipitation property from which nearly all other precipitation products, such as rainfall rate, can be derived. Vertically-pointing profilers retrieve the ESE from near the surface to just below the melting layer in precipitating cloud systems that advect directly overhead. Scanning polarimetric radars use polarization diversity to estimate the DSD parameters throughout the precipitating cloud system. These unique instruments provide valuable information on the DSD that is not available in conventional scanning weather radars (e.g. WSR-88D) and not available from spaceborne radars. The proposed research is divided into three themes. The first theme deals with the retrieval of raindrop size distributions from profilers and from scanning polarimetric X-band radars. The first task in this theme will retrieve and analyze DSDs from multiple years of profiler observations producing tens-of-thousands of DSD profiles in different rain regimes that will lead to physically based DSD parameterizations needed to reduce the errors in current and future precipitation satellite algorithms. The second DSD retrieval task will use a polarimetric X-band radar in combination with profilers to analyze the spatial and temporal variability of DSD parameters to develop and improve ground-based comparison products needed for ground validation facilities supporting the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. The second theme of the proposed research focuses on the attenuation at Ku- and Ka-bands through precipitation. The first task will use profiler observations to statistically determine the errors in the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) Ku-band Precipitation Radar (PR) attenuation correction algorithm. Profiler and TRMM PR reflectivity distributions above the brightband agree very well. In contrast, there is a 5 dBZ disagreement in the reflectivity distributions below the brightband suggesting errors in the attenuation correction algorithm through the brightband. The proposed analysis will isolate these errors in the current PR algorithms providing feedback from ground observations to improve TRMM PR precipitation algorithms. The second attenuation task will exploit the fact that the attenuation at Ka-band is linearly proportional to the rain rate in the attenuation path. The proposed analysis will convert zenith-looking ground-based attenuation-based algorithms estimating rain rate to the nadir geometry for use with the GPM Ka-band radar to provide independent rain rate estimates to supplement DPR algorithms. The third theme continues collaborations with North Carolina State University, University of Alabama in Huntsville, and North Dakota University by analyzing profiler observations collected in support of their respective NASA Precipitation Measurement Mission (PMM) proposals. These collaborations will focus on retrieving ice particle size distributions above the freezing ivied complementing tie DSD work proposed here.

THIS REGION DOES NOT YET HAVE THE DENSE NETWORK OF GROUND-BASED GPS RECEIVERS NECESSARY TO PERFORM A COMPLEMENTARY STUDY, NOR DOES IT HAVE SUFFICIENT MAGNETOMETER CHAINS TO MONITOR THE ELECTRODYNAMICS. THIS IHY-IN-AFRICA CONSORTIUM IS EXPLORING WAYS TO INCREASE THE OBSERVATIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE IN THE AFRICAN SECTOR AND LEVERAGE ACTIVITIES IN OTHER DISCIPLINES, IN ORDER TO ADDRESS COMPELLING SCIENCE QUESTIONS UNDER THE IHY UMBRELLA. IN ADDITION TO ADDRESSING COMPELLING SCIENCE QUESTIONS, THE NEW OBSERVATIONAL INFRASTRUCTURE AND RESEARCH WILL FACILITATE SCIENTIFIC COLLABORATION AND THE STUDY OF SPACE WEATHER IN AFRICAN UNIVERSITIES, WILL SPARK INTEREST IN THE LOCAL SCHOOLS, AND ENCOURAGE THE NEXT GENERATION TO BECOME INSPIRED BY THE SPACE SCIENCES. THE WORKSHOP WILL PROVIDE AN IDEAL OPPORTUNITY TO DEVELOP A STRONG INTERACTION BETWEEN THE INTERNATIONAL SPACE SCIENCE COMMUNITY AND SCIENTISTS IN AFRICA. THE PROPOSED LOCATION OF THE MEETINGS IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA IS A REGION OF PARTICULAR GEOGRAPHIC AND GEOMAGNETIC INTEREST FOR UNDERSTANDING SPACE WEATHER PHENOMENA. THE IHY-IN-AFRICA GROUP OF SCIENTISTS INCLUDES REPRESENTATIVES FROM NORTH AMERICA, EUROPE, AND SEVERAL SUB-SAHARAN AND OTHER AFRICAN COUNTRIES, DEMONSTRATING THE INTERNATIONAL INTEREST GENERALLY AND COMMITMENT TO AFRICA IN PARTICULAR. THE PROPOSAL ADDRESSES SEVERAL IHY GOALS INCLUDING FOSTERING INTERNATIONAL SCIENTIFIC COOPERATION; UNDERSTANDING THE RESPONSE OFTHE PHYSICAL SYSTEM THROUGH ANALYSIS OF UNIVERSAL PROCESSES; COMMUNICATION OF IHY RESULTS TO THE SCIENTIFIC COMMUNITY; AND ESTABLISHING A LEGACY FOR FUTURE SPACE SCIENCE ACTIVITIES IN AFRICA.

Description: OBSERVATIONS OF AEROSOL INDIRECT EFFECTS THROUGH MULTI-SENSOR ESTIMATES OF CLOUD LIQUID WATER PATH FROM THE A-TRAIN(GRADUATE STUDENT: MATTHEW D. LEBSOCK) The intent of the proposed research is to investigate aerosol indirect effects on cloud properties while paying particular attention to the liquid water budget of clouds. The study will utilize the unique multisensor observing capabilities of the A-Train constellation of satellites. Observation of aerosol indirect effects requires accurate observations of cloud liquid water path (LWP) yet analysis shows disagreement between microwave and visible derived LWP as well as between different algorithms using the same sensor. Therefore, an improved multi-sensor cloud retrieval will be developed that merges shortwave (MODIS) and microwave (AMSR-E) observations in a physically consistent manner. This retrieval will be analyzed in concert with co-located observations of geophysical parameters such as aerosol optical depth from PARASOL/CALIPSO and precipitation rates derived from CloudSat along with large-scale meteorological information from model reanalysis in an effort to identify the environmental parameters that govern the susceptibility of clouds to aerosol indirect effects.

Description: SPECTROSCOPY AND PHOTOCHEMISTRY OF ATMOSPHERIC ORGANIC HYDRATES RELEVANT IN AEROSOL NUCLEATION AND CLIMATE (GRADUATE STUDENT: MEGHAN DUNN) The proposed research will investigate atmospheric organic hydrates in order to understand their role in aerosol nucleation and effects on climate. Organics comprise a significant portion of aerosols. In this research, we seek to understand how organics are processed by solar radiation in the atmosphere and what spectral changes occur as they bind to water in order to reveal the effect organics have on the Earth's temperature, radiative transfer and climate. One of NASA's objectives in the NESSF program, to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth,' is a central theme to this research, as the reactions we propose to study are initiated by light in the solar wavelength range that is abundant at the Earth's surface, the low energy visible red. In addition, this research addresses NASA's goal to predict the consequences of human-induced change in the atmosphere. By studying anthropogenic as well as biogenic organic acids and alcohols, we can understand the atmospheric fate and processing of these organics and predict their role in the broader scope of climate change while comparing the natural and human sources. Three of the six focuses of the NASA Earth Science Division to be addressed are climate variability and change, atmospheric composition and the carbon cycle. Climate variability and change is the major implication of our research. I will research organics in aerosols through spectroscopy to reveal shifts in spectra and subsequently the ability of aerosols to scatter and absorb light, as well as their effects on temperature, radiative transfer and climate. Thermodynamic data will be obtained in order to evaluate the abundance of compounds and the energy (wavelength of light) required to initiate a reaction that processes these organics in an aqueous environment. Atmospheric photo-processing of organic hydrates will be evaluated through thermodynamic data obtained by the proposed spectroscopic and theoretical work. The carbon cycle is inherently involved in the study of organic environmental targets. Through collaboration with atmospheric modeling, the national priorities of NASA's Applied Science Program will be advanced in the field of ecological forecasting. My research will be able to provide new inputs for modeling through a better understanding of the fundamental chemistry involved in atmospheric modeling of aerosols. The experimental approach is spectroscopic, using Fourier Transform IR spectrometers and a cavity ring down spectrometer to find the spectra of organic acids and alcohols and their hydrates, using a range of energies relevant in photochemical reactions. We will determine how the inclusion of organics in aerosols affects the scattering and absorption of radiation in the atmosphere, thus how it affects climate, through comparing the observed spectra of organics to their hydrates. The results of these experiments will provide insight into the processing of organics in the atmosphere, aerosol nucleation and cloud formation.

Description: The global hydrological cycle has a profound influence on life on earth, and understanding its effects is a major scientific pursuit. Tropical rainfall comprises more than two-thirds of global rainfall and is the primary distributor of heat through the circulation of the atmosphere. Understanding rainfall and its variability and surface impact is crucial to understanding our dynamic planet, especially when tropical storms evolve into cyclones. Spaceborne precipitation radars, such as the one on the Tropical Rainfall Measurement Mission (TRMM) can provide valuable information for this purpose. Current methods of estimating rainfall use a surface reference which is more complex over land. Surface backscatter characteristics and changes can be studied using high resolution synthetic aperture radars (SARs). The proposed research will investigate the synergy between a spaceborne precipitation radar and SAR observations, with particular interest in times when cyclonic events are observed over land and how ground backscatter changes with precipitation. Ultimately, this could also aid in determining surface change resulting from the storm, providing more information for disaster management. This research will utilize a number of methods to achieve the research objectives. Surface backscatter is characterized by its statistical properties in terms of received power at the radar and is both a function of radar parameters and how the surface scatters the radar wave and is referred to as the radar cross section of an area. For SAR data collected, standard statistical methods will be used to describe the signal and how it changes with time and precipitation. When there is spatial overlap with TRMM comparisons will be made at the same spatial resolution, which requires averaging the SAR data. When the data are from fully polarimetric SARs, the covariance matrix provides a more detailed description of the scattering mechanisms, and this has a known probability distribution. We will use existing land classification and polarimetric change detection algorithms which take advantage of the multiple polarizations. In addition, new algorithms, and potentially new filtering techniques, will be employed. By using the known relationship between normalized radar cross section (NRCS) and radar parameters such as incidence angle and wavelength, we can use probabilistic optimization techniques to derive an estimate of the NRCS for TRMM. For the change detection aspect, optical images can be used to verify significant changes and evaluate the false alarm rate. With this research, a deeper understanding of the effects of precipitation on land NRCS can be achieved. This will help with the surface reference technique used to estimate the rainfall with the TRMM radar, which is not as well defined over the complex structure ofland. As a result, the future Global Precipitation Mission can benefit. This research can also benefit SAR algorithms, which are sometimes adversely affected by precipitation, especially at higher frequencies such as X-band. If the SAR signal is attenuated through a storm, and knowledge about that attenuation is known from a system like TRMM, then it can be mitigated. Ultimately, though, this research can demonstrate the potential to detect land surface damage and flooding caused by tropical cyclones in a timely fashion, prior to assessing damage with optical sensors that must wait for clouds to dissipate. This can provide more information to disaster management organizations so they can better execute a plan.

Description: Snow cover plays a tremendous role in our planet's water and energy cycles. Yet, measurement and estimation of snow pack remain critical challenges. In the Western US, where the water balance is dominated by snowmelt, scenarios offuture climate forecast a drier, more variable system, especially in the Colorado River Basin. Compounded with increasing demand from a growing population, we currently lack the tools and knowledge base necessary to meet anticipated water management challenges. Development of such tools is considered vital to our national security and prosperity in the coming decades. Furthermore, approximately 40% ofthe world's population looks to snowmelt for it's primary water source. While our project is pertinent to several areas of the NASA ESD, our approach directly address the long-term goals ofthe NASA ESD Water and Energy Cycle Roadmap through a combination of observation, modeling, and prediction of a variable which is is integral to both water and energy cycles, including phenomena at regional scales and extreme events such as drought and floods. We develop a methodology for producing spatially-distributed probabilistic estimates of temporally evolving snow pack with the ability to target and assimilate data in order to reduce uncertainty in estimates. Our estimates will permit a fresh evaluation of other currently available estimates such as satellite products and point measurements which go largely unused in water management due their highly uncertain ability to properly represent snow pack at meaningful hydrological scales. Our methodology also guides sampling design of snow cover which will facilitate efficient in-situ validation of remotely sensed products with reduced uncertainty in future campaigns. We formulate static estimates and uncertainty of spatially distributed snow cover and the propagation of these in time; we examine uncertainty arising from both initial and boundary conditions. To formulate ensembles of initial and boundary conditions we employ parallel tracks of 'best' and 'limited' data. This amounts to a data degradation experiment comparing complementary formulations of ensembles which represent uncertainty in the estimates. We hold the 'best' approach as truth and the 'limited' case simulates what we would do with out extensive data. In the case of static or initial condition estimation, we guide ensemble selection of generally applicable regression models by the explicit distributed uncertainty offered by a Bayesian hierarchical interpolation of an extensive data set. This is a novel application of Bayesian modeling to understand ensemble regression modeling. In formulating ensembles of boundary conditions, we guide derivation of local forcings from regional models by ensemble forcing sets drawn from local weather station Observations. Here we employ previously existing methods for disaggregation in both cases while aiming to maintain consistency and proper uncertainty (ensemble spread). We combine the initial and boundary condition ensembles within just one physical model, as we do not consider uncertainty arising from model formulation in this project. Uncertainty is propagated in time within the physical model and we introduce data assimilation and ensemble error statistic analysis to target and assimilate observations. We aim to reduce uncertainty and improve estimates in our limited knowledge case. We assess our ability to formulate probabilistic estimates from limited knowledge against our estimates from best knowledge in all three areas: static estimation, boundary condition estimation, and combined estimation. Improvements from data assimilation are also judged against our best knowledge estimates. We will explore applications of our expected results to a variety of available products from the Cold Lands Process field eXperiment (CLPX), including both air- and space-borne measurements, and to designing sampling for FMCW radar to improve hydrological surveys. Description: Uranus reaches equinox in 2007 (the last equinox was in 1965, the next is 2049). Pre-equinox images from Keck and HST show significant change on the planet: wavelength-dependent latitudinal structure, the presence of numerous atmospheric features in the northern hemisphere, the first detection of a global-scale equatorial wave, and the first detection of localized short-term convective activity in the southern hemisphere. We propose to observe the atmosphere of Uranus during and through equinox using: mid-IR spectroscopy at moderate resolution using BASS at NASA's Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) and at high resolution using the Michelle spectrograph on Gemini North; adaptive optics imaging and spectroscopy with NIRC2 at the Keck 10-m; near-IR spectroscopy with Spex at the IRTF, and other observations. The observations proposed here build on our pre-equinox programs at the IRTF, Keck, Gemini, and HST. We propose to analyze the observations with radiative transfer and photochemical modeling. By integrating our analyses with those of other Uranus specialists, we will establish new observational constraints on the behavior ofthe troposphere and stratosphere ofthe equinoctial Uranus. In addition, the PI proposes to coordinate and facilitate world-wide Uranus observational and analytic efforts, using meetings, email, and the IOPW website. The proposed project will address a number of unresolved questions. Is the asymmetry of the Uranian atmosphere time-variable? How do the planet's northern and southern hemispheres differ in vertical aerosol structure? How is Uranus' southern hemispheric haze abundance varying? To address these questions, we will work with the community to obtain critical observations and to develop a self-consistent model ofthe time-dependent vertical and horizontal distribution of aerosols in the Uranian atmosphere. A more comprehensive understanding of the ice giants in our own solar system will be invaluable as we begin to probe the atmospheres of ice giants orbiting other stars.

Description: X-RAY EVOLUTION OF CLASSICAL NOVAE: TIMESCALES FOR THE SSS PHASE The outbursts of novae are driven by a thermonuclear runaway at the base of an accreted shell. Soft X-ray emission resulting from high surface temperatures on the WD after outburst are expected, but seldom observed (SSS phase). Some novae enter the SSS phase within the first year after outburst, and quickly turn off thereafter (the very fast ONeMg novae). Others (e.g., slow novae) are delayed years after outburst before entering the SSS stage, which then lasts many years. ROSAT detected only 3 novae in their SSS state; XMM has observed 5, 3 which have SSS spectrums. Insight into the diversity and evolution of novae can be gained by determining when (or if) the SSS stage begins, when turnoff occurs, and how this relates to composition and the WD mass from XMM-EPIC and OM data analysis.

Description: An Independent Assessment of the Contribution of Ice Melt to Sea Level Change The greatest uncertainty in current estimates of sea level change, and for predictions of future sea level change, is the contribution of melting ice and subsequent runoff from the continents. The melting of mountain glaciers appears to have accelerated, with recent contributions as large as 1 mm/year. The contributions of ice melt from Greenland and Antarctica, hoviever, are much more uncertain.  This is important because the potential sea level contribution of Greenland (-7 m) and Antarctica (- 60 m) have far more potential for catastrophic outcomes that the contributions from mountain glaciers (- 1 m) or thermal expansion (- 1 m). Direct satellite measurements of the ice sheets have provided conflicting results, with some suggesting the polar ice sheets are roughly in balance, while others pointing towards large sea level contributions of 0.5 mm/year from each of the ice sheets. These satellite measurements are each affected by a unique set of errors that makes it difficult to arrive at a single conclusion that satisfies all the observational constraints. There is, however, another place we can look for the effects of the melting ice - in the oceans. In many ways, observing the changes in the oceans caused by the melting ice is an easier problem than measuring the changes in the ice mass on the continents. But we can still answer the basic question of sea level change research - how much do the ice sheets contribute to sea level change? We propose to measure the contributions of ice melt to sea level change using a suite of satellite altimeter measurements, satellite gravity measurements, ocean temperature measurements, and tide gauge measurements. Each member of our team possesses expertise in one or more of these measurement techniques. This gives our investigation an excellent chance at success. Satellite altimeter measurements from TOPEX/Poseidon (T/P) and Jason-I provide an estimate of total sea level change thermal expansion plus water mass from the continents) since 1992. By analyzing ocean temperature measurements for the same time period, we can remove the thermal contribution from the altimeter data to get a time series of mass contributions to sea level change since 1992. This payload is being developed first because it is the technically simpler payload, and can be brought to launch on shorter time scale. No previous or planned instrumentation has ever performed imaging in this waveband. The payload will observe nearby galaxies, and image their star forming regions and structures in the galaxy. Not only does this provide significant insight into the most recent star formation history of the galaxy, it also provides a critical calibration of the total bolometric flux from star forming regions. This is essential to the understanding of highly obscured, highly red shifted sub-mm galaxies, in which all of the stellar output in the UV and optical is converted to the far infrared by dust. Description: ATOMIC LAYER DEPOSITION OF Ti02, Zn0, Hf02, TiN FILMS ON PARTICLES FOR IMPROVED WEAR AND OXIDATION RESISTANCE AND RADIATIVE AND THERMAL BARRIER PROPERTIES OF MATERIALS Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a proven mechanism to modify the surface properties of primary ultrafine particles, including nanoparticles, while maintaining bulk properties of the substrate particles. This technique provides an opportunity to deposit conformal nanothick films on particles or surfaces of varying geometries to enhance the structural, electrical and/or temperature resistant properties of the substrate. The four films to be deposited in this work are titanium dioxide (TiO2), Zinc Oxide (ZnO), hafnium dioxide (HfO2) and titanium nitride (TiN). The first two coating materials have been successfully deposited on particles using an ALD Fluidized Bed Reactor (FBR). TiN-based materials are known for their superior tribological, or wear-resistant properties. A TiN thin film, being oxygen deficient, is suspected to perform very well on metal nanopowders, as both an oxidation barrier and a sintering prevention agent. Nanothick alumina (AI2O3) films have successfully and significantly increased the oxidation temperature of metals such as iron, cobalt, copper and nickel in oxygen-laden environments. Hafnium dioxide, or hafnia, is very stable at high temperatures and its coatings provide additional thermal protection to materials designed to operate in extreme environments. Wide band-gap semiconductors have the intrinsic ability to absorb solar irradiation at and below the energy associated with the band gap. For instance, the typical band gap of ZnO is about 3.3 eV, which corresponds to a wavelength (X.) of 370-380nm, in the UVA range. ZnO and TiO2 are efficient sunblock materials for use on the Earth's surface, because the atmosphere filters out UVC wavelengths and below (X. < 290nm).  Large band gap semiconductor-based films will be deposited on nano- and ultrafine particles (e.g. silicon carbide, nickel, titania-alumina composites) to be used as additives in transparent spacecraft materials, in order to enhance irradiation protecting properties, while not sacrificing the thermal and tribological properties of these light-weight materials. Progress in this front is critical to further current efforts to decrease spacecraft weight while increasing the protective nature and structural integrity of materials.

Description: The two tasks of this study address important problems in icy satellite geology, especially as relevant to Europa. 1) We will advance our technique of Computer Assisted Stratigraphic Sorting (CASS) as a quantitative means of addressing the evolution and dynamics of planetary surfaces, most notably the complex tectonic deformation of Europa. We will develop and refine an algorithmic approach for disentangling the rich information inherent in the abundant cross-cutting relationships among the moonjs enormous number of lineaments. This involves converting information discerned from spacecraft images into a data structure known as a jdirected graph, which can be topologically sorted to quantitatively constrain the order of events in a region, even in complexly deformed regions where reactivation has occurred. The innovative computer techniques proposed here can be applied to sets of complexly intersecting structures to constrain the order of events, and thus to elucidate the preserved geological history of Europa or other icy satellites, in ways infeasible for any stratigrapher to discern manually. 2) Borup Fiord Pass in the High Canadian Arctic may be the best analog to near-term Europa exploration that exists on Earth. There, sulfur-rich springs discharge onto the surface of glacial ice, forming deposits of native sulfur, gypsum, and calcite that are also home to microbes. We will utilize this unique terrestrial analog to test methods of remote sensing of sulfurous compounds on ice, while simultaneously surveying this sitejs promise as a fruitful analog to near-future Europa exploration. Specifically, we will investigate how the sitejs biologically mediated geochemistry may he identified and characterized by remote sensing observations. This will be achieved by correlation of field-acquired samples of precipitates and microbes to satellite, aerial, and field spectroscopy. The results will be correlated in a Geographical Information Systems (GIs) database and used to interpret spectral signatures as related to the geomicrobiology of the site. Implications for remote sensing of Europa's ruddy non-ice materials will be considered. The objectives and expected results of this two-pronged study are directly applicable to NASA's Vision for Space Exploration, NASAjs Strategic Goals and Outcomes, and the Planetary Geology and Geophysics Program

Description: The first millimeter-wavelength (W-band) radar in space will provide global cloud information that was previously unavailable from other spaceborne instruments. Although the modest sensitivity (~ ?28dBZ) and vertical resolution (~500 m with a 240 m sampling) of this radar will hamper retrievals of very thin cirrus and non-drizzling thin stratus clouds, it will effectively fill some gaps in atmospheric hydrometeor property profiling. Vertical information on optically thin clouds was previously available from spaceborne lidars and precipitation retrievals have been available from longer wavelength radars (such as a TRMM radar). Vertically-resolved information about multi-layer clouds and optically thick clouds that are associated with precipitating systems is not readily and unambiguously available from other sensors and such information will be the most unique part of the information available from CloudSat. This proposal seeks funding to extend CloudSat standard retrieval algorithms and develop and apply new product retrieval techniques for the optically thick clouds that often constitute a part of precipitating systems. The studies will include (i) the development and application of microphysical retrieval techniques that are specifically tailored for thick ice clouds (snow) which are melting and producing precipitation; (ii) the development and application of techniques for estimating cloud extinction profiles and optical thickness for thick ice clouds as an experimental CloudSat product; (iii) the assessment, analysis and correction of biases in the CloudSat standard retrieval products due to sensitivity and resolution limitations of the spaceborne W-band radar; (iv) studies of interactions between the cloud content above the melting level and rain characteristics in precipitating systems. Although this proposal is mostly focused on the CloudSat data, measurements from other A-train sensors will be used for combined retrievals when appropriate (e.g., single layer clouds that are not opaque) and compared with the CloudSat radar-based retrievals. It will help to better estimate uncertainties of retrievals

Description: As part of the NOAA/NASA Pathfinder Program in the 1990's, NASA provided funding for the AVHRR Polar Pathfinder (APP) data products. These products included gridded and geolocated AVHRR channel radiances, clear-sky albedo and temperature, scan and solar angles, a cloud mask and surface type data at 5-km resolution, twice per day, for both the Arctic and the Antarctic. The original funding was to cover the period from fall of 1981 through 1997. Subsequent NASA funding allowed the dataset to be extended through 2000. Description: Joint distributions of tropical ice cloud mass and precipitation from CloudSat, MODIS, and AMSR-E for GCM evaluation The objective of the proposed work is to evaluate parameterizations in global climate models (GCMs) in a novel way using joint distributions of vertically integrated ice cloud mass and precipitation from instruments on the A-train. In the tropics cloud ice mass (or ice water path, IWP) and precipitation are two observable outputs from the convective cloud process. Therefore, the joint distribution of IWP and precipitation will be a strong constraint on both the convective parameterization, which determines most of the rainfall and the injection of cloud ice into the upper troposphere, and on the cloud microphysical parameterization, which determines the residence time of ice cloud particles. This work will help to improve climate models and hence climate prediction. The proposed work will: 1) Develop a statistical procedure to use CloudSat IWP retrievals to correct MODIS IWP retrievals over a broad swath outside the CloudSat radar path. The CloudSat IWP retrievals and uncertainty estimates will be evaluated with an existing Monte Carlo Bayesian ice cloud retrieval methodology. 2) Produce joint distributions of cloud IWP and precipitation at spatial scales from 10 km to 300 km for selected tropical oceanic regions and seasons. The cloud IWP will be obtained from the CloudSat-trained corrected MODIS retrievals, and the rain rate from AMSR-E GPROF retrievals. A part of producing these joint distributions will be to assign uncertainties due to the satellite retrieval and sampling errors. 3) Compare the measured joint distributions at the appropriate spatial scales with those from the NCAR CAM GCM, the GFDL AM2 GCM, and the NASA GMAO GEOS-5 model. The cloud IWP and precipitation fields from the GCM will be sampled at the local time corresponding to the A-train overpass time. The differences between the measured and modeled joint distributions of IWP and precipitation will be interpreted using GCM runs having adjusted parameterization values, in order to indicate what aspects of the cloud parameterizations might need refinement.

Description: SEA ICE ROUGHNESS AS AN INDICATOR OF FUNDAMENTAL CHANGES IN THE ARCTIC ICE COVER: OBSERVATIONS, MONITORING, AND RELATIONSHIPS TO ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS Sea Ice Roughness as an Indicator of Fundamental Changes in the Arctic Ice Cover: Observations, Monitoring, and Relationships to Environmental Factors Since the macro-scale (meters to 10's of meters) roughness characteristics of sea ice are a function of a combination of dynamical and thermodynamical processes and conditions, observations and monitoring of ice roughness could provide new insights into such basic issues as the magnitude and distribution of ice thinning, changes in the nature and amount of ice of different ages, and modifications of the ice cover in ways that might enhance or reduce the effects of rising air temperatures. On a larger scale, sampled via aircraft or satellite, monitoring of the distributions of ridged and rubbled ice would help address questions such as the degree to which changes in Arctic ice mass reflect melting or less growth versus redistribution of mass into regions such as areas north of the Canadian Archipelago. The proposed research combines the use of a variety of remote sensing methods, including satellite observations and uninhabited aerial vehicles, to provide fundamental new insights into ice roughness on the scale of meters to 10's of meters in the context of larger-scale environmental forcings. Our intent is to be able to relate scattering and emission properties to surface roughness and hence to geophysical properties that are difficult or impossible to observe directly. Fine scale and in situ observations are essential to understanding physical processes at work, but it is necessary to know how processes aggregate over the scale of the types of spaceborne observations that we must rely upon for regional and hemispheric-scale monitoring. In keeping with this, the proposed work has three main goals: - Determine the degree to which ice-roughness monitoring via remote sensing can detect basic changes in ice conditions such as ice thickness and ice age; - Investigate relationships between ice roughness and factors affecting the loss or maintenance of the perennial ice cover; - Determine how roughness varies as a function of different kinematic conditions and ice properties. As part of IPY, the proposed work would provide fundamental new insights into important but difficult-to-observe aspects of the ice cover and would complement other planned and proposed IPY projects. The nature of the proposed research would further the contribution of satellites as tools for long-term monitoring and observations, and thus help solidify the role of spaceborne remote sensing as a key element of IPY.

Description: A MULTISENSOR ANALYSIS OF LIGHT PRECIPITATION REGIMES Establishing closure of the global hydrologic cycle is a fundamental goal in advancing our understanding of the global climate system that requires accurate assessment of the regional and temporal distribution of precipitation. While significant progress has been made in satellite-based precipitation measurement, light precipitation is poorly sampled by current instruments but may represent a significant component of total precipitation particularly at latitudes poleward of 30 degrees. By virtue of its sensitivity, the CloudSat Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR) offers a unique opportunity to perform a global survey of light rainfall and quantify its contribution to the global water cycle. The proposed research will exploit CPR observations in conjunction with data from other A-Train sensors to (a) generate a global light rainfall dataset, (b) characterize statistically the spatial distribution of global light rainfall, (c) quantify the fraction of global light rainfall that is missed by current precipitation sensors, (d) assess the fidelity of current rainfall products in light of observing system limitations, (e) advance our understanding of the role of aerosols in modifying light rainfall in turbid air masses, and (f) examine drizzle regimes in pristine air masses and their relationship to the accompanying cloud top particle size. The products of this research will complete the rain rate histogram in a regime that current sensors have the most difficulty in identifying. Scientific outcomes from this effort will help improve our understanding of the importance of light precipitation regimes within the global hydrological cycle in the context of climate change and mankind's role within it.

Description: Impact of Soil Freeze/Thaw Dynamics on the North American Carbon Cycle.  Changes in frozen ground have great impacts on environment and engineering construction.  There is an increasing need for the general public to understand these impacts and potential consequences under global warming scenarios.  To educate the general public and transfer knowledge of frozen ground to the next generation, the overall objective of this proposal is to assist K-12 students/teachers and the public to understand frozen ground, its relation to climate system and its impact on engineering in cold regions.  The objective will be accomplished through the development and thorough evaluation of an online resource for the education and public audiences. Impacts of Soil FrcezelThaw Dynamics on the North American Carbon Cycle PIs: Tingjun Zhang, Lixin Lu, Kevin Schaefer, and A. Scott Denning We will integrate remote sensing data sets, ground-based measurements, and numerical modeling to quantify the effects of soil temperature, soil freeze-thaw dynamics, and snow cover on seasonal to inter-annual variability in the North American terrestrial carbon cycle. Our overall goal is to understand the role of freeze-thaw processes in determining seasonal and inter-annual variability in terrestrial biomass, photosynthesis, respiration, and net C02 fluxes over continental North America. Using remote sensing products, in situ observations, and a soil thermodynamic model, we will estimate soil temperatures and snow cover over North America at 25-km resolution for North America from 1981-2003 (23 years). We will feed these estimated soil temperatures and snow cover, along with additional remote sensing data, into an ecosystem model to estimate biomass and net carbon fluxes. Both models will use the North American Regional Reanalysis, so the resulting estimates of soil thermodynamic properties, biomass, and carbon ,fluxes will be optimally consistent with each other and with actual weather conditions in North America. We will statistically analyze these optimal carbon fluxes to understand the environmental drivers and biophysical responses regulating the spatial patterns and temporal variability in the North American terrestrial carbon cycle. Using standard Monte Carlo techniques, we will quantify uncertainty in our estimated carbon fluxes. Lastly, we will perturb our input data to assess the sensitivity of our estimated fluxes to long-term climate change. Our research addresses the North American Carbon Program (NACP) goals of reducing uncertainty about the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere and the dynamics of the carbon cycle. Specifically, we address the NACP goal~ of I) quantifying the magnitudes and distributions of terrestrial carbon sources and sinks within North America; 2) understanding the processes controlling carbon source and sink dynamics; and 3) producing consistent analyses of the carbon budget of North America, explaining regional contributions and year-to-year variability. We will archive data products generated by this investigation at the National Snow and Ice Data Center;,s Frozen Ground Data Center for access by other NACP investigators and for general use by the scientific community.

Description: STELLAR ACTIVITY ON STARS IN THE 7 MYR OLD ETA CHA CLUSTER AND ITS INFLUENCE ON THEIR PROTOPLANETARY DISK The young (7 Myr), nearby (97 pc), sparse Eta Cha cluster provides a very special opportunity to understand the processes controlling protoplanetary system evolution. MANY STUDIES HAVE BEEN CONDUCTED IN AN ATTEMPT TO UNDERSTAND THESE FEATURES, BUT NONE HAVE USED THE FULL NUMBER OF KNOWN CRATERS NOR MODERN DATA SETS. THE MOST COMPREHENSIVE SURVEYS (BARLOW, 1990; BARLOW, 1994) USED VIKING-ERA DATA, BEFORE HIGHER RESOLUTION SETS WERE AVAILABLE. RECENT LOBED CRATER STUDIES HAVE RELIED ON SMALL SAMPLES IN ISOLATED LOCATIONS (E.G., BARATOUX ET AL., 2003; MERESSE ET AL, 2005). NO MODERN, COMPREHENSIVE, CROSS-DATA SET STUDY EXISTS FOR THE LOBATE EJECTA BLANKETS ON MARS, AND THIS LIMITS ANY CONCLUSIONS THAT CAN BE DRAWN AS TO THEIR FORMATION AND MODIFICATION, AND ANY INFORMATION ABOUT THE SUBSURFACE THAT THEY MAY REVEAL. THIS PROPOSAL IS TO USE ALL KNOWN LOBED CRATERS IN A COMPREHENSIVE CROSS-DATA SET ANALYSIS TO FUNDAMENTALLY INCREASE OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THESE UNIQUE FEATURES. MOLA DATA WILL BE USED PRIMARILY TO DERIVE RAW FEATURES OF EACH CRATER: DEPTH, DIAMETER, VOLUME, RIM HEIGHT ABOVE SURFACE, LOBE AREA AND VOLUME, LOBE PERIMETER, AND LOBATENESS (RATIO OF LOBE PERIMETER TO PERIMETER OF A CIRCLE WITH THE SAME AREA). THESE RESULTS WILL BE CORRELATED WITH OTHER DATA SETS - INCLUDING THEMIS TO DETERMINE THE SIZE AND SORTING OF EJECTA AND GRS TO DETERMINE THE AMOUNT OF SUB-SURFACE WATER - TO DETERMINE WHICH FORMATION MECHANISM IS MORE LIKELY (FOLLOWING BARLOW AND PEREZ (2003)) - AN IMPACT INTO VOLATILE-RICH MATERIAL THAT PRODUCES FLUIDIZED EJECTA, OR AN IMPACT THAT CREATES INTENSE ATMOSPHERIC VORTES THAT CREATE THE LOBES AND DO NOT NEED SUBSURFACE VOLATILES. IF THE FORMER FORMATION HYPOTHESIS IS CONFIRMED, THE IMPLICATIONS FOR HUMAN EXPLORATION OF MARS ARE SIGNIFICANT. WITH NASA'S CURRENT "FOLLOW THE WATER" APPROACH TO MARTIAN EXPLORATION, THESE LOBED CRATERS COULD BE USED AS AN INDICATOR OF WHERE SUB-SURFACE WATER AND OTHER VOLATILES LIE AND BE USED FOR AN EXTENDED HUMAN PRESENCE ON THE PLANET. THEY WILL ALSO HAVE IMPLICATIONS FOR THE HISTORICAL LOCATION OF WATER ON MARS AND PALEOCLIMATE SINCE CRATERS TODAY ARE NOT ZERO-AGE.

Description: IDENTIFICATION OF ATMOSPHERE-INTERACTION MECHANISMS DURING ARTIC SEA-ICE FREEZEUP USING NASA EOS AND AIRBORNE OBSERVATIONS The dramatic shrinking of Arctic sea ice cover during the past few decades has enormous consequences for polar and global climate, as well as for human commercial activities. An observed increase in the Arctic melt season has been suggested as a major reason for the decrease in spatial extent and mass of Arctic pack ice. By forcing large, transitory changes in the surface energy budget (SEB) over the Arctic Ocean, late summer tropospheric synoptic and mesoscale disturbances may trigger the end of the melt season through positive feedbacks associated with these large transitory changes, suggesting the importance of these events for determining the length of the melt season. Satellite-based sensors are incapable of providing both accurate observations of Arctic sea ice cover and type along with meteorological measurements of the mesoscale processes, which are necessary to understand the dynamics of this ice-atmosphere interaction process under these disturbance-driven conditions. A complete study of the ice-atmosphere interaction process thus requires satellite-based data augmented by regional-scale in situ data that can only be provided by airborne and ship-based sampling. We therefore propose to integrate a ship-based meteorological campaign occurring during IPY on the Swedish ice breaker Oden with an airborne campaign using the NASA P-3B aircraft. The P-3 measurements will include high resolution microwave imagery of sea ice using te Polarimetric Scanning Radiometer (PSR) system, discrimination of fresh water meltponds using the SLFMR L-band imaging radiometer, and direct sampling of thermodynamic, kinematic, and cloud variables over wide areas using in situ cloud probes, dropsondes, and radiometric profiling. The observations will occur during August-September 2008. The uniqueness of this campaign will be to provide the first observations of late-summer Arctic sea ice and atmospheric state variables with high enough spatial resolution and three-dimensional specificity to elucidate in detail the ice-atmosphere interaction processes that occur during freezeup. The observations are required to understand the impact of mesoscale and turbulent atmospheric processes on surface-energy transition-to-freezeup conditions, along with providing critical data required to improve the AMSR-E sea ice algorithm during late-summer Arctic conditions. The simultaneous occurrence of the Oden IPY campaign and this proposed one represents a rare opportunity to combine extensive surface-based point measurements with spatial airborne measurements to validate and improve the capabilities of satellite remote sensing instruments and to address questions important for understanding recent changes in Arctic pack ice.
