Description: CALIPSO STUDIES OF PSC'S, TSC'S AND AEROSOLS MODELING AND LABORATORY SUPPORT  We propose to join the CALIPSO science team. We request funding to perform four tasks. First, we will use CALIPSO data to identify the location of polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs), and to categorize them. We will compare these data with POAM, HIRDLS and other data. We will then use this data to test and develop a numerical model for PSCs that we are constructing using the NCAR WACCM model. Our simulations use analyzed winds, so we will make one-to-one comparisons with the actual data for the time period of the observations, rather than doing climatologically comparisons. This work will help us make more realistic PSC models for use in ozone chemistry codes. It will help us test algorithms that distinguish PSC types. It will aid in three-dimensional visualization of the PSC fields and stratospheric aerosols. Our second task will be to use CALIPSO data to identify nitric acid particles in tropical stratospheric clouds (TSCs). These clouds can be separated from sub-visible cirrus by particle size (wavelength dependent backscatter).  This work will help us identify where these clouds form and improve our models of them. We will explore the importance of nitric acid condensation to the nitric acid fields in the stratosphere. lJld upper troposphere in the tropics using Aura data on nitric acid coupled with CALIPSO data on clouds. We will model the waysin which clouds alter the nitric acid abundance. Using a three-dimensional model of tropical cirrus clouds, we will simulate the nitric acid abundance in the tropical tropopause transition layer (TTL) and explore where nitric acid should be impacted by clouds and how this relates to water vapor transport. Our third task will be to use lidar data to characterize the properties of tropospheric aerosols. The lidar data should provide unprecedented insight into the heights of aerosol layers, and constrain aerosol opacity over wide areas. We will use CALIPSO data to constrain the altitudes of smoke clouds from fires. The injection altitudes are poorly known, but greatly influence the long-range transport of smoke. Our goal will be to develop a database, from which we can develop a physical model of the plume rise. We expect the plume rise to depend on fire intensity, and on meteorological parameters that determine the heights of cumulus. We will use the CALIPSO data to constrain our modeling of the global scale transport of aerosols, especially smoke, and their impact on climate. Finally, we will perform laboratory studies to support CALIPSO. One goal is to better understand the backscatter from ice clouds. The backscatter from large ice crystals should be wavelength independent. CALIPSO plans to use the neutral scattering by clouds for its calibration. However, lidar data from field campaigns indicate the near infrared backscatter can be only 80% of its value in the visible. Possibly this data indicates small particles are present at cloud top. Perhaps it indicates that non-spherical ice particles have surprising optical behavior. We propose to measure both the extinction and backscatter from ice crystals in the lab to determine if there is unexpected wavelength dependent scattering and what causes it. We will also measure the scattering properties of NAT and NAD, which cannot be calculated, so that PSC properties may be retrieved from CALIPSO data. Our second laboratory project is to determine how solid PSCs and TSCs form. This is a critical unresolved issue for denitrification. CALIPSO is likely to shed light on when and where solid PSC particles occur. We will make laboratory measurements to confirm how nucleation occurs.

Description: IMAGING AND SPECTROSCOPY IN THE FAR ULTRAVIOLENT This is a proposal for a five-year sounding rocket investigation. During this time, two separate payloads will be built and launched, one imaging payload and one spectroscopy payload. Both of these concepts address capability gaps in the current NASA mission suite, and will perform exceptional science in their own right. The first payload, the Far ultraviolet Imaging Rocket Experiment: FIRE, is an imager in the 900-1150 Aband. This payload is being developed first because it is the technically simpler payload, and can be brought to launch on shorter time scale. No previous or planned instrumentation has ever performed imaging in this waveband. The payload will observe nearby galaxies, and image their star forming regions and structures in the galaxy. Not only does this provide significant insight into the most recent star formation history of the galaxy, it also provides a critical calibration of the total bolometric flux from star forming regions. This is essential to the understanding of highly obscured, highly red shifted sub-mm galaxies, in which all of the stellar output in the UV and optical is converted to the far infrared by dust. Currently, the total IR/sub-mm flux is used to compute a star formation rate. But without calibrating the flux in the sub Lyman alpha band, this extrapolation is open to question. The second payload, the High Resolution FUV payload (HRF), will perform high resolution(R - 60,000) spectroscopy over a limited region in the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) band (900-1200 A). This will be accomplished by the use of new holographic recording techniques that allow the correction of additional aberration terms beyond the Type I solutions utilized in FUSE and COS. The design will serve as a prototype for future MIDEX class FUV spectroscopy missions, allowing more credible proposals utilizing this technology. In concept, this is similar to the technology employed on FUSE and on HS COS (gratings/detectors) all of which were prototyped and flight proven in the University of Colorado Ultraviolet sounding rocke rogram. The high resolution of the payload will allow it to address scientific questions, originally intended to be answered by but which were not, due to the fact that the FUSE mission did not achieve its design spectral resolution. On its first flight, i ine the ratio of COIH2 in a translucent cloud, a measurement that has been need for more than a decade, to provide rom radio measurements of CO to H2 to galactic mass. The CO/H2 ratio is only calibrated in low column density events, where the effects of UV dissociation can only be estimated. Anchoring the CO/H2 measurement along higher density lines of sight is essential to the reliability of the mass estimate of distant galaxies from radio CO observations.

Description: ATOMIC LAYER DEPOSITION OF Ti02, Zn0, Hf02, TiN FILMS ON PARTICLES FOR IMPROVED WEAR AND OXIDATION RESISTANCE AND RADIATIVE AND THERMAL BARRIER PROPERTIES OF MATERIALS Atomic Layer Deposition (ALD) is a proven mechanism to modify the surface properties of primary ultrafine particles, including nanoparticles, while maintaining bulk properties of the substrate particles. This technique provides an opportunity to deposit conformal nanothick films on particles or surfaces of varying geometries to enhance the structural, electrical and/or temperature resistant properties of the substrate. The four films to be deposited in this work are titanium dioxide (TiO2), Zinc Oxide (ZnO), hafnium dioxide (HfO2) and titanium nitride (TiN). The first two coating materials have been successfully deposited on particles using an ALD Fluidized Bed Reactor (FBR). TiN-based materials are known for their superior tribological, or wear-resistant properties. A TiN thin film, being oxygen deficient, is suspected to perform very well on metal nanopowders, as both an oxidation barrier and a sintering prevention agent. Nanothick alumina (AI2O3) films have successfully and significantly increased the oxidation temperature of metals such as iron, cobalt, copper and nickel in oxygen-laden environments. Hafnium dioxide, or hafnia, is very stable at high temperatures and its coatings provide additional thermal protection to materials designed to operate in extreme environments. Wide band-gap semiconductors have the intrinsic ability to absorb solar irradiation at and below the energy associated with the band gap. For instance, the typical band gap of ZnO is about 3.3 eV, which corresponds to a wavelength (X.) of 370-380nm, in the UVA range. ZnO and TiO2 are efficient sunblock materials for use on the Earth's surface, because the atmosphere filters out UVC wavelengths and below (X. < 290nm).  Large band gap semiconductor-based films will be deposited on nano- and ultrafine particles (e.g. silicon carbide, nickel, titania-alumina composites) to be used as additives in transparent spacecraft materials, in order to enhance irradiation protecting properties, while not sacrificing the thermal and tribological properties of these light-weight materials. Progress in this front is critical to further current efforts to decrease spacecraft weight while increasing the protective nature and structural integrity of materials.

Description: HELIOSEISMICK PROBING OF THE NEAR SURFACE SHEAR LAYER USING REFINED TIME DISTANCE APPROACHES-NICHOLAS FEATHERSON  I propose to develop new time-distance helioseismology procedures designed to explicitly resolve the role of giant cells and supergranulation in the dynamics of the solar near-surface shear layer. Description: Photochemistry in the atmosphere of the early Earth may have led to the formation of complex organic molecules, similar to those observed on Saturnjs moon Titan. Previous work in our laboratory has used a novel aerosol mass spectrometer (AMS) to probe aerosols formed in a likely post-biotic early Earth atmosphere. We found a myriad of aerosol organic products were produced with complex functional groups beyond simple hydrocarbons. Thus photochemistry in the early Earth atmosphere might have provided complex organics for the sustenance of early life. Here we propose to extend our previous studies of post-biotic haze formation to conditions more representative of early Earth before the development of life. Little is known about the composition of the early Earth atmosphere so we will consider a range of possible compositions including CH4, N2, H2, S02, NH3 and H20. A state-of-the-art high resolution AMS will be used for part of this study. One main aspect of this work will be to determine if an early Earth haze could supply life-building organics to the surface of the Earth. In addition to studies of aerosol chemical composition, we will also examine how early Earth haze particles might directly and indirectly influence the ancient climate. We will use a novel aerosol cavity ring down spectrometer system to probe how early Earth particles take up water and grow to sizes that efficiently scatter incoming solar light. We will also use this technique to evaluate the potential role of early Earth haze particles as nuclei for cloud condensation. As is the case on current Earth, the direct and indirect effect of aerosols on climate could be very large. Thus our measurements will provide key data needed for improving climate models of the early Earth

Description: The light toned bedrock that has been observed at the Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity landing site is an upper layer in a sequence >500 m thick in places. These outcrops contain mineral and textural signatures that require interaction of, and possibly formation from, water. Many distinct layers are visible in the remote sensing data and no work has ever characterized the full set of these materials that cover an area >3 x 10A5 kmA2 spanning 20" of longitude. Thus, whatever water-related process(es?)altered, and possibly formed, the rocks at the Opportunity landing site extended over a vast region of Mars. Yet many questions remain to be answered, such as: (1) in what capacity did water form and alter the deposits?, (2) what are the temporal and spatial relations with other major events known from ancient Mars?, and (3) would this type of environment have been conducive to the development of life? To address these questions we propose to complete a detailed geologic, stratigraphic, and thermophysical properties study of this widespread terrain. Specifically, we are proposing to draft a 1:2M-scale geological map covering the full extent of these water-related deposits. In tandem with the mapping, we will conduct a thorough stratigraphic analysis of the stack of materials. Finally, we will study the thermophysical properties of the varied layers to derive possible compositional information of the materials. These tasks serve several purposes including gaining an understanding of the complex nature of these materials, their potential sources region@), and their timing of emplacement. All of these efforts are necessary to place the observations by the Opportunity Rover in a broader context and prepare for potential future landed missions to the region. Understanding the large-scale paleohydrology of Mars is central to NASA's goals and vital for determining if life ever arose on the planet.

Description: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This environment should provide an excellent platform from which to improve the understanding of factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off and extinction and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The goals of the research will be the generation of modified kinetic mechanisms for hydrocarbon fuels that are able to model effectively diffusion flame structure under a larger parameter range than existing mechanisms and the development of submodels for soot formation that are capable of predicting both high and low soot loading levels in hydrocarbon flames of various fuels.

Description: DISTANT ACTIVE GALAXIES: INSIGHTS FROM THE LOCAL POPULATION A substantial fraction of the distant absorbed AGNs detected in the Cbandra Deep Fields (CDFs) lack optical evidence of nuclear activity in ground-based observations. Spectra of these X-ray-luminous objects are dominated by starlight, rather than the strong Seyfert 2-like emission tines that characterize absorbed AGNs in the local universe. However, it remains unclear whether these differences are real or largely apparent in nature. Samples of nearby and distant objects are assembled in very different ways, which affects the portions of the luminosity functions they represent. Moreover, the data normally acquired for nearby and distant objects differ greatly. For example, emission from the nucleus can be (and almost always is) isolated for nearby objects, whereas only the integrated emission of distant galaxies can be obtained at most wavelengths. Thus, comparisons of local and redshifted samples of absorbed AGNs must be carried out with extreme care. Observational differences between nearby and distant populations of AGNs -- or a lack thereof - have important implications for the cosmic evolution of supermassive black holes and their environments. The goal of the science described in this proposal is to characterize the multiwavelength properties of nearby absorbed AGNs and their host galaxies in a way that will facilitate a meaningful direct comparison to the absorbed AGNs detected in the Chandra Deep Fields. To accomplished this, we will use 6 NASA-supported data archives to assemble the spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of the *integrated* emission of a large, unbiased sample of nearby Seyfert 2 galaxies. We will examine the SEDs of the local objects for correlations in their overall shape that might be driven by the contrast between the nucelus and host galaxy in the integrated light, and we will derive the median values and effective I-sigma ranges of their luminosities at all frequencies. Comparisons of the SEDs of individual absorbed AGNs from well-defined portions of the CDF surveys to our local sample will properly account for redshift effects and the way the intrinsic luminosity function is sampled in deep pencil-beam surveys. This approach, and the leverage afforded by the multiwavelength perspective, will provide a very sensitive test for the cosmic evolution of the absorbed AGN population. Our results will also allow us to investigate important related issues: the differences between the nuclear and integrated SEDs of local Seyfert 2s, and the absorbed AGN contribution to the cosmic infrared background.

Description: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This environment should provide an excellent platform from which to improve the understanding of factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off and extinction and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The goals of the research will be the generation of modified kinetic mechanisms for hydrocarbon fuels that are able to model effectively diffusion flame structure under a larger parameter range than existing mechanisms and the development of submodels for soot formation that are capable of predicting both high and low soot loading levels in hydrocarbon flames of various fuels.

Description: EXPLORATION OF SEQUENCE SPACE AND THE EVOLUTION OF THE GENETIC CODE Proteins consist of linear sequences of amino acids. These sequences can be thought of as inhabiting a space consisting of the set of all possible protein sequences given the 20 amino acids used in the genetic code. Similar sequences are closer to each other in this protein space; evolution can be thought of as an exploratory walk connecting neighboring sequences. Current protein space is so large that no imaginable process can even approach exploring it thoroughly. Did an earlier, simpler genetic code allow a more thorough exploration of protein space? What was the nature of this primitive genetic code, and how did it expand to the modern schema? We propose two approaches to investigate the mechanism and importance of the expansion of the genetic code during early evolution. Our first approach is a novel methodology called Compositional Stratigraphy. We will analyze existing proteins to illuminate the order in which amino acids were added to the genetic code. Amino acid positions that came and remained under purifying selection early in the evolution of life will be conserved in all or most homologous versions of the protein: clearly, if tryptophan is a late addition to the genetic code, it could not have been under purifying selection in a given sequence position before it was present. Our analysis will focus on genes that evolved early in evolution and show a high amount of sequence conservation. One group of proteins selected for study is ribosomal proteins. Arguably, these were among the first proteins to evolve. The cenancesteral ribosome (i.e., the common ancestor of all extant ribosomes) existed after the code was already fully developed. However, the cenancestral ribosome spent a larger part of its purifying selection under a still-evolving, simpler genetic code, in contrast to the ribosome ancestral to specific domains of life. The fraction of early amino acids among positions conserved from the cenancestral ribosome is therefore expected to be higher than in positions that came under purifying selection more recently. Using ancient paralogous sets of genes, we can reach back even further to a time before the most recent common ancestor. The identity of conserved residues in these ancient proteins provides an untapped window into the history of the expansion of the genetic code. Second, we will attempt to explore the distribution of proteins in sequence space. Existing protein folds are too divergent for standard alignments to reveal their common ancestry, thereby making it difficult to study relationships between them in deep evolutionary history. The use of random oligopeptide sequence motifs as dimensions of protein space addresses this problem by expanding the concept of sequence space to sequences that cannot be reliably aligned. This approach allows us to investigate the global organization of protein sequence space in such a way that the impact of the expansion of the genetic code can be potentially detected and analyzed.

Description: COLLABORATIVE:  A LARGE-SCALE MULTI-COLOR PHOTOMETRIC SURVEY OF TRANS-NEPTUNIAN OBJECTS, IRREGULAR SATELLITES, AND TROJAN ASTEROIDS OBJECTIVES: We will survey 30 bodies from three populations - trans-Neptunian objects, irregular satellites and Trojan asteroids -- with nightly multicolor photometry over their entire apparitions. Our unique well-sampled light curves and solar phase curves will provide tracers for their physical structure and dynamical evolution. Detailed tasks are: (1) Discover correlations between the phase curve properties and physical/orbital parameters relating to the three populations' origins. (2) Test the recent idea that the Jupiter Trojans are captured bodies that formed closer to Neptune and were later scattered inward by measuring whether their photometric properties are like those of Centaurs or main-belt asteroids. (3) Investigate the rarely-observed phenomena of extremely narrow opposition surges at phase angles 0.01-0.2 deg. (4) Test if the neutral color together with a weak opposition surge which we find characteristic of Pluto-sized bodies occurs only for large bodies. (5) Seek serendipitous discoveries such as long rotation periods, eclipsing light curves, and secular changes. METHOD: We will take advantage of the service-mode observing of the SMARTS 1.3-m telescope on Cerro Tololo to make nightly observations of each target covering the entire range of phase angles visible from Earth. We will measure the V- and I-band light curves, and also the B-band for all but the faintest targets. RELEVANCE: Our observations will add to our understanding of the physical properties and evolution of the Kuiper Belt and the outer solar system. This is central to the goals of NASA's planetary astronomy program to understand the general properties and evolution of the solar system. Our effort also has direct relevance to the New Horizons mission to Pluto since a major goal is to explore the Pluto-like objects. NOTE: This is a Collaborative proposal between LSU and Yale, wherein both institutions submit identical proposals but with separate budgets.

Description: Two of the goals of NASA's Vision for Space Exploration (Vision) plan is to develop an initiative to return humans to the moon by 2020 leading into landings on Mars and other destinations and to develop the innovative technologies, knowledge, and infrastructures both to explore and to support decisions about the destinations for human exploration. Human research missions to extraterrestrial locations depend on development of techniques to mitigate hazards, advances in capabilities for sustainable exploration, and available resources. A large part of this initiative depends on developing a spacesuit and tools that will enable an astronaut to perform optimally in Extra-Vehicular Activities (EVA) and under extraterrestrial conditions. As a part of the Vision initiative, a collaborative effort between the Anthropometry and Biomechanics Facility (ABF) part of the Habitability and Human Factors Office (SF3) within the Habitability and Environmental Factors Office (SF) of NASA and the Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, TX and the Biodynamics Laboratory at the University of Connecticut Health Center is investigating ways to make the future generations of the spacesuits and tools more biomechanically efficient to improve performance. Recently, a year-long project, that involves working with the Autonomous Motion Tracking System Development (AMTSD) Team in the ABF at JSC, was identified and is briefly described. In brief, the AMTSD Team has been developing a ways to model the human-device interface between the astronaut and spacesuit. One part of this investigation is an attempt to track astronaut motion within a pressurized suit and compare the results to the externally and simultaneously tracked motion of the suit itself. Measuring movement inside a space suit introduces many limitations that are not typical human movement tracking, such as the space between the astronaut and the suit, the operation of electronics within the suit, and the maintenance of suit pressure. The Biodynamics Laboratory will assist the ABF by attempting to identify and verify the optimal motion tracking modality to complete this portion of the spacesuit analysis, beginning with an assessment of the current systems that the AMTSD has chosen to track motion within the spacesuit.

Description: The MK-III space suit technology demonstrator was developed in the 1980s as a prototype to serve as a test bed to investigate different types of suit joint mobility systems that can be used in the design of future planetary exploration space suits. The hardware on the space suit was- and still is- fabricated and designed by Air-Lock, Inc.; the soft goods were a product of ILC Dover. Over the past 20 years, the uses for the MK-III space suit technology demonstrator have been quite varied. Most recently the suit has been serving in comparative space suit testing with other styles of prototype space suits and current flight program space suit configurations. The comparative analysis allows engineers to put quantitative values to the subjective data that has been collected with respect to suit mobility. Test data is being used by the Exploration Program to develop requirements for lunar surface extra vehicular activity tasks. Functional mobility range of motion testing has included the following activities: walking, crawling, kneeling, ascending and descending a ladder, translating up and down an inclined surface, shoveling, hammering, ingressing and egressing seats, and the operation of multiple hatch actuation concepts. Further the MK-III, has been utilized on the reduced gravity aircraft for interface feasibility testing with the Constellation Program Orion vehicle side hatch, the low impact docking system tunnel, and micro-gravity space suit don and doff testing. The MK-III space suit technology demonstrator also serves as the primary suit for the Desert Research and Technology Studies conducted each year in Arizona. The Desert Research and Technology Studies activities center around the development and testing of hardware and mission operations anticipated for future planetary exploration programs. Most notably, the MK-III space suit technology demonstrator has be used to study the interfaces between a suited subject and the Science, Crew, Operations and Utility Test bed (SCOUT), which is a combination planetary roving vehicle and robotic assistant. The interfaces studied include the suit to seat interface, the suit to displays interface, and the suit to controls interface.

Description: Diffusion flames are the flame type of most practical combustion devices. The ability to predict the coupled effects of complex transport phenomena with detailed chemical kinetics in such systems is critical in the modeling of turbulent reacting flows and in understanding the processes by which extinction, soot formation and radiative transfer take place. Turbulent diffusion flames are generally nonbuoyant due to the large flow velocities. In addition, in practical devices combustor configuration and flow field patterns may produce flames with sharp edges. Extinction along these edges can result from incomplete combustion. In other regions combustion generated soot particulates may be formed. To understand better the factors that affect flame extinction and particulate formation, we propose to focus this study on flame phenomena at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, namely dilute flames near extinction and pure-fuel (sooting) flames. Previous work has shown that existing computational models are unable to predict accurately the behavior of these systems. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will enable the stabilization of flames with increased levels of dilution and will help generate flames that have increased soot residence times compared to normal gravity facilities. This environment should provide an excellent platform from which to improve the understanding of factors that affect diffusion flame lift-off and extinction and it should also provide an excellent test-bed to determine the roles of inception, surface growth and oxidation processes in soot formation models. The goals of the research will be the generation of modified kinetic mechanisms for hydrocarbon fuels that are able to model effectively diffusion flame structure under a larger parameter range than existing mechanisms and the development of submodels for soot formation that are capable of predicting both high and low soot loading levels in hydrocarbon flames of various fuels.

Description: A FAR UV SEARCH FOR GAMMA CAS ANALOGS IN THE SMALL MAGELLANIC CLOUD Through the decades of robotic space exploration, heliospheric physics missions have accumulated vast amoimts of data from just about all comers of tbe interplanetary medium. However, the different data sets, collected by different spacecraft, were not designed to be mined as a single system. Tbe resulting various data products are archived and distributed in widely different formats using radically different services requiring a considerable level of expertise from the end users. With the implementation of the Living With a Star (LWS) program, an even larger influx of data is expected from sources that will include foreign partners and planetary missions for which interplanetary observations will be only a secondary objective increasing the complexity and variety of the available data products. At the same time, new multi-soiu-ce investigations cutting across discipline boimdaries require simple, reliable and rapid access to all of the collected data. Making the various data sets easily accessible is not sufficient by itself to facilitate scientific research. Software tools for data ingest, visualization, and analysis are necessary. Therefore, the development of a heliospheric data environment standard, leading to a imified heliospheric software library, is essential to increase the effective use of heliospheric data. Here we propose that a Virtual Heliospheric Observatory (VHO) be developed that has the following key features: - A fully distributed system where individual data nodes can range from data centers to individual instrument sites of current and future heliospheric missions. A common interface to access all participating heliospheric data either through a web browser or through an application programming interface (API). The ability to query participating data sources based on industry-standard protocols. - The ability to exchange queries with other VxOs. A standard heliospheric data enviromnent for software tools that access and use the data. Standards for services that allow access to value-added functionalities. The primary objective of the VHO is to enable scientists to search for, locate and efficiently use distributed heliospheric data sets. This can be accomplished with a middleware architecture that will accept user queries and redirect the user to the corresponding data products combined with the establishment of commimity standards for data environment and services. Our design philosophy is to build only the minimum necessary fimctionality as part of this proposed work, and to focus on establishing community accepted standards that will allow later seamless extension of the system. We also seek to mvolve the largest possible set of data providers to maximize the early utility of the VHO.

Description: SPACE WEATHER AND AIRCRAFT SAFETY:OPPORTUNITIES FOR SPACE WEATHER AND CLIMATE RESEARCH  Space weather affects a wide variety of technological activities on Earth, including satellite operations, energy transmission, the accuracy of GPS signals, and air travel. Space weather resulting from very strong solar storms can severely damage some of these systems. Nevertheless, better space weather information, improved modeling and forecasts, and a variety of decision support tools can sharply improve the ability of system operators to protect against or mitigate the most devastating effects. For aircraft, flight safety is critical. Aircraft cruising at the high altitudes characteristic of long distance routes are particularly vulnerable to space weather effects.  Space weather may increase radiation levels for passengers and crew, interrupt or totally disrupt HF communications, and potentially interfere with operation of the delicate avionics circuitry. Polar routes flown routinely by U.S. and European carriers are especially at risk (for example, polar flights were delayed or rerouted following the January 20, 2005 large solar storm). Business jets and military aircraft that routinely fly above commercial airline routes are also at risk, even at lower latitudes.  The process for reducing aviation operational sensitivities to terrestrial weather impacts is now well established and integrated into the flight planning processes of all aircraft operations. However, the processes of coping with space weather effects have not been well developed and incorporated fully into aircraft operations. Of more immediate concern, the health and economic effects of space weather on aircraft operations are not well understood. We need to improve our state of knowledge regarding space weather effects on the health of airline crew and pilots, HF communications, and avionics.

Description: Solar Radio Emissions in the 3D Heliosphere Observed by Stereo, Wind and Ulysses: The overall focus of this proposed research program is to achieve a more complete picture of these solar and heliospheric energetic phenomena in three dimensions. This will be accomplished primarily by analyzing the radio data from the complete suite of radio and plasma wave instruments on the STEREO spacecraft to locate and track solar and heliospheric radio sources, as well as to analyze their intensity and frequency characteristics. The STEREO mission, which was launched on Oct. 25, 2006, will provide the first dedicated stereoscopic observations of remotely generated solar radio emissions. The unique perspective, made possible by the two STEREO spacecraft, will enable new and unprecedented methods for locating and tracking radio sources through interplanetary space. Analyses of these radio data, together with the complementary observational data from other experiments on STEREO, will provide the first complete 3D picture of the evolution of transient phenomena in the solar corona and heliosphere. Description: Dynamics of Solar Transient Phenomena Based on High Time Resolution EUV Spectra An existing, extensive database of rapid cadence (9.8 sec) spatially resolved EUV slit spectra of solar transient phenomena (including flares, nanoflares, and blinkers) obtained with CDS during the past six years of SOH0 operations will be analyzed and interpreted, along with coordinated observations from other NASA instruments. This unique database represents a nearly untapped resource for analyzing and understanding solar transients. Observed EUV emission lines cover a wide range of temperature from the chromosphere (He I) through the transition region (He 11, 0 111, 0 IV, 0 V, Ne VI, Ca X) to the corona (Mg X, A1 XI, Si MI), and include hot flare emission (Fe XIX). Profile fits to emission lines in the slit spectra yield the integrated intensity, centroid wavelength, and width, from which E Wli ght curves, relative Doppler velocities, and nonthermal turbulent velocities will be calculated, all in high time resolution. This reveals the time dependent response of the solar atmosphere (over a wide temperature range) to the observed transient phenomena, and provides new insight into physical processes that occur during solar transients. For example, the measurement of simultaneous, cospatial mass flows in lines formed at different temperatures will provide new information regarding momentum balance during chromospheric evaporation. Light curves and velocity histories of nanoflares will reveal if nanoflares are miniature versions of regular flares. Time-dependent transition region densities within the various transient phenomena will be derived from the density sensitive ratio of 0 IV lines, and time-dependent temperature distributions of emitting plasma (the differential emission measure DEM) will be constructed for selected events. Two-dimensional imagery associated with each transient event observed with CDS will be obtained with SOHO's EIT. These will be used to fine-tune the CDS pointing coordinates, and establish the context within which the CDS spectra were obtained. Associated two-dimensional imagery obtained with TRACE will be used for cases in which more rapid cadence context imagery is available. Magnetograms from SOHO's MDI will be used to not only associate the EUV transients with specific magnetic features, but also to establish whether the transients are associated with changes in those magnetic features. Images from RHESSI will reveal the locations of hard X-ray sources relative to observed EUV transients. Hard X-ray spectra and light curves will be examined at the locations of EUV transients. Relative timings between the onsets and peaks of the thermal and nonthermal hard X-ray emission, combined with the onsets and peaks of the (thermal) E W emission, will provide information on the dominant mechanism(s) by which flare (and nanoflare) energy is transported to the chromosphere (e.g., particle beam, thermal conduction). Coordinated hard X-ray observations from Yohkoh will be employed for older events. This investigation addresses the fifth National Objective of NASA's Strategic Objectives, namely, to "Study the Earth system from space and develop new space-based and related capabilities for this purpose." It will focus primarily on the second NASA Objective of this fifth National Objective by exploring the "Sun-Earth system to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth, the Solar System, and the space environmental conditions that will be experienced by human explorers."

OUR MAIN SCIENTIFIC GOALS ARE: 1) DETERMINE THE MICROSCALE DISTRIBUTION OF ISOTOPIC RATIOS IN ORGANICS (H, C, N, 0, S) FROM A RANGE OF METEORITE CLASSES, BOTH IN SITU AND IN WELL-CHARACTERIZED INSOLUBLE ORGANIC RESIDUES. Description: BOARD ON EARTH SCIENCES AND RESOURCES AND ITS ACTIVITIES The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Earth Science Division) is requested to provide partial support for the Board on Earth Sciences and Resources and its activities for the two-year period from May 1, 2006 through April 30, 2008 in the amount of $165,000 ($80,000 in year 1 and $85,000 in year 2). Support is being requested from the Department of Energy (Office of Basic Energy Sciences), Department of Interior (U.S. Geological Survey), National Science Foundation (Geoscience Directorate), as well as the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Earth Science Division). The Board on Earth Sciences and Resources provides the focal point for National Research Council activities related to the earth sciences. Through its activities, it provides independent advice in the national interest on a wide range of earth science issues, including those involving basic and applied research, the environment, natural hazards, resources, data (from acquisition and archiving to dissemination and management), and education. It also provides guidance on U.S. participation in international earth science programs. The Board, its committees, and staff recognize that one of the great tasks in the years ahead is to take advantage of the increased importance of the earth sciences by contributing more strongly than ever to the broad concerns of science and society. Board membership is constituted to provide the breadth and depth of expertise necessary to address the strategic earth science issues facing the nation, ranging from identifying the frontiers of basic and applied research and improving use of scientific data to assessing resources, understanding environmental change and human interactions with the earth, and evaluating breakthrough technologies. The Board has six standing committees, whose role is to act as the specific focus points for their particular specialist areas. The Board recognizes the need to continually reassess its activities and procedures to ensure that it is has established the mechanisms and guidance to enable the optimum provision of advice to agencies in accordance with its strategic objectives. The core funding by NASA and the other major earth science agencies provides the essential support for this mission. The Board's strategic planning process has resulted in an increased emphasis on collaboration with other NRC boards to ensure that issues that span the boundaries between one or more boards are addressed in the most effective manner possible. Collaboration with other boards occurs in both structured (e.g., joint studies) and less formal (e.g., requests for committee and reviewer nominations) modes. The Board recognizes that many of the issues that will arise in the next few years will be cross-disciplinary, or beyond the range of 'normal' activities addressed by the Board in the past. Description: This main objectives of this proposal are (i) to determine the conditions in a protoplanetary disk necessary for giant planets to form and survive planetary migration, (ii) to determine what conditions can give rise to planetary systems with architectures similar to the Solar System, and (iii) to establish the variety of possible planetary systems and compare these with observed extrasolar systems. This will be achieved using N-body simulations of the oligarchic growth of planetary embryos embedded in a disk of planetesimals. Simulations will include accretion of gaseous envelopes to form gas-giant planets, as well as inward planetary migration due to torques exerted by the protoplanetary disk. Unlike most previous studies, this proposal will consider the rapid migration rates predicted by analytical models and numerical simulations. This work will help determine whether current models for planet formation and migration are compatible with the ubiquity of planetary systems. In addition, the work will help establish the range of conditions under which Earth-like planets can form and provide pointers as to where we might find them.

Description: Correlated ion microprobe, multicollector ICP-MS, and petrologic studies of calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions (CAIs) will be undertaken on a new collection of large CAIs sampled from 4 CV3 meteorites (Vigarano, Leoville, Efremovka, and Allende). Description: Solar Radio Emissions in the 3D Heliosphere Observed by Stereo, Wind and Ulysses: The overall focus of this proposed research program is to achieve a more complete picture of these solar and heliospheric energetic phenomena in three dimensions. This will be accomplished primarily by analyzing the radio data from the complete suite of radio and plasma wave instruments on the STEREO spacecraft to locate and track solar and heliospheric radio sources, as well as to analyze their intensity and frequency characteristics. The STEREO mission, which was launched on Oct. 25, 2006, will provide the first dedicated stereoscopic observations of remotely generated solar radio emissions. The unique perspective, made possible by the two STEREO spacecraft, will enable new and unprecedented methods for locating and tracking radio sources through interplanetary space. Description: BOARD ON EARTH SCIENCES AND RESOURCES AND ITS ACTIVITIES The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Earth Science Division) is requested to provide partial support for the Board on Earth Sciences and Resources and its activities for the two-year period from May 1, 2006 through April 30, 2008 in the amount of $165,000 ($80,000 in year 1 and $85,000 in year 2). Support is being requested from the Department of Energy (Office of Basic Energy Sciences), Department of Interior (U.S. Geological Survey), National Science Foundation (Geoscience Directorate), as well as the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Earth Science Division). The Board on Earth Sciences and Resources provides the focal point for National Research Council activities related to the earth sciences. Through its activities, it provides independent advice in the national interest on a wide range of earth science issues, including those involving basic and applied research, the environment, natural hazards, resources, data (from acquisition and archiving to dissemination and management), and education. It also provides guidance on U.S. participation in international earth science programs. The Board, its committees, and staff recognize that one of the great tasks in the years ahead is to take advantage of the increased importance of the earth sciences by contributing more strongly than ever to the broad concerns of science and society. Board membership is constituted to provide the breadth and depth of expertise necessary to address the strategic earth science issues facing the nation, ranging from identifying the frontiers of basic and applied research and improving use of scientific data to assessing resources, understanding environmental change and human interactions with the earth, and evaluating breakthrough technologies. The Board has six standing committees, whose role is to act as the specific focus points for their particular specialist areas. The Board recognizes the need to continually reassess its activities and procedures to ensure that it is has established the mechanisms and guidance to enable the optimum provision of advice to agencies in accordance with its strategic objectives. The core funding by NASA and the other major earth science agencies provides the essential support for this mission. The Board's strategic planning process has resulted in an increased emphasis on collaboration with other NRC boards to ensure that issues that span the boundaries between one or more boards are addressed in the most effective manner possible. Collaboration with other boards occurs in both structured (e.g., joint studies) and less formal (e.g., requests for committee and reviewer nominations) modes. Description: The properties of the low solar corona with million degree and accelerating plasma continue to intrigue the scientists in understanding the underlying physical properties that cause these observations. As a natural consequence for modeling it is very important to measure the plasma temperature and its flow speed in the low solar corona. We have developed Multi Aperture Coronal Spectrograph (MACS) that allows for the simultaneous and global measurements of both the electron temperature and its flow speed, which is a very important constituent of the coronal plasma. MACS comprises of fiber optics that simultaneously observes multitude of positions, both in latitude and altitude, in the low solar corona to produce the K-coronal spectra in the visible wavelength region. The shape of the K-coronal spectrum from each fiber is then a measure of both the electron temperature and its bulk flow speed. The low solar corona extending from the solar limb can only be observed during a total solar eclipse and thus MACS will be operated in conjunction with a total solar eclipse. In addition to the electron temperature and its bulk flow speed one other important parameter that is required in modeling the shape of the K-coronal spectrum is the location of any streamers that might cross the line of sight. At these locations the electron density in enhanced above the ambient and depending on whether cross the line of sight in front or behind the plane of the solar limb the shape of the resulting K-coronal spectrum is affected differently. Now with the launch of the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) it is now possible to create three dimensional images of the low solar corona with the CORl (coronagraph) instrument and better understand the coronal structures such as streamers and coronal mass ejections and identify its locations and enhancement above the ambient. This information we believe will greatly enhance our modeling capabilities of the K-coronal spectrum for a given line of sight and enable us to make more accurate measurements of the electron temperature and its bulk flow speed.

Description: A census of the galaxy population as a function of time is needed in order to help us better understand how galaxies acquired their present morphology. However, only recently there are enough data available covering large areas with sufficient depth and resolution needed for a detailed analysis of the galaxy population since redshifts < 5. In this project we will use a combination of data taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and NICMOS as part of the Ultra Deep Field (UDF) champaign as well as part of the Great Observatories Origins Deep Survey (GOODS). We will also add data taken with the Sptizer satellite to our database in order to increase the wavelength coverage of our analysis. Large multiwavelength coverage is particularly important when analyzing high-redshift galaxies since the optical/uv is shifted towards the infrared. Moreover, galaxies morphology can be wrongly classified if seen in only one wavelength since the radiation from the stellar population peaks at different wavelengths as a function of age. The effects of dust and the contribution of active galactic nuclei to the radiation can also be underestimated without large multiwavelength coverage. In this three-year project we will acquire all data from the observatories archives, generate catalogs identifying all objects, test the matches between the catalogs, estimate photometric redshifts, classify galaxies morphologies, and ultimately estimate the epoch of the formation of the Hubble classification sequence.

Description: AN EXPERIMENTAL STUDY OF HIGH PRSESURE MINERAL AND MELT PHASE QUILIBRIA IN TERRESTRIAL PLANETARY INTERIORS-PHASE II ABSTRACT: The goal of our experimental study is to provide the fundamental high-pressure data necessary to explore the structure and evolution of the interiors of terrestrial planets with emphasis on Mars, Mercury, and Venus. Space missions to Mars and Mercury have provided important constraints on the physics and chemistry, of the interior including density distribution, physical state of the core, the nature of magnetic field, and chemistry of the surface rocks. A full explanation of the observations from space missions ultimately requires knowledge on the fundamental properties of the planetary cores, including density, temperature, composition, and physical state. Building on the success of our previous research program that integrates geochemical models and laboratory experimental data with geophysical observations, we will focus this proposal on the thermal and physical states of the cores of Mars, Mercury, and Venus, and their implications for magnetic field generation and thermal evolution of the planets. We propose a series of melting experiments in the Fe-NiiS system up to 40 GPa, a pressure corresponding to the center of Mars and Mercury, using both multi-anvil apparatus and laser-heating diamond anvil cell. The experimental data will be used to establish a thermodynamic model that will extend the applications to the Earth and Venus cores. We will also obtain experimental data on structure and density of Fe-S liquids with applications to liquid cores of Mars and Mercury. Finally, we will continue our experiments on potassium (K), uranium (U), and thorium (Th) partitioning between liquid metal and liquid silicate to quantify the amount of radioactive elements in planetary cores. These data will provide critical constraints on thermal evolution and dynamo models.

Description: STUDY OF MINOR ATMOSPHERIC CONSTITUENTS ON MARS AND VENUS SUMMARY: Our current PAST program which ends in March 2007 has been rather successful. It resulted in the first detection of CH4 on Mars. We studied possible sources and sinks of methane and concluded that the extant biosphere is plausible. We established a very low upper limit to S02 on Mars which strongly restricts seepage of gases from the interior. Our first detection of NO in the lower atmosphere of Venus is a convincing proof oflightning and very important for Venus photochemistry. We continued our mapping observations of the 02 dayglow at 1.27 mu and made them at three seasonal points near Mars' perihelion. This dayglow is a sensitive tracer of Mars photochemistry and its diurnal, latitudinal, and seasonal variations. We continued observations of the discovered north-south asymmetry in the CO mixing ratio that appears because of the condensation and sublimation of C02 on and from the polar regions. This phenomenon refers to all incondensable species (N2, Ar, 02, CO, H2) and was later confirmed by the Mars Odyssey observations of Ar, Our programs resulted in 5 of 12 IRTF-based refereed publications on the composition of Mars' atmosphere. We propose to solve five observational tasks in the next three-year period. Task 1: Continued mapping ofthe 02 dayglow at 1.27 mu using IRTF/CSHELL to cover all seasons on Mars and study interannual variability of Mars photochemistry. Some observations will be made almost simultaneously with the infrared heterodyne observations of ozone to make some conclusions on the vertical profile of ozone. The measured dayglow intensities will be compared with the predictions of photochemical models and photochemical GCMs. Task 2: Continued mapping ofthe CO mixing ratio on Mars using IRTF/CSHELL to cover all seasons on Mars and study interannual variability of the polar processes. Our final goal is a detailed seasonal-latitudinal map of CO that will improve understanding of the atmospheric dynamics and the polar processes and may be used to test GCMs. Task 3: Study of the isotope ratios in H20 on Mars using the CELESTE and TEXES high-resolution spectrographs at NASA IRTF, observations of DIH variations on Mars and comparison with the GCM predictions. Task 4: Search for ethane on Mars using IRTF/CSHELL. Although the expected result is an upper limit of -0.5 ppb, it may be helpful for the problem of origin of methane on Mars. Task 5: Search for 02 on Venus. The current upper limit was established 25 years ago and looks puzzling because of a significant disagreement with the predictions of photochemical models. Our search will be made at 762 nm using the high-resolution (resolving power up to 400,000) coude spectrometer at the 2.7 m Harlan Smith telescope at the McDonald Observatory. Detection of 02 or a further improvement of the current upper limit would be of great importance for Venus photochemistry.

Description: CHARACTERIZATION OF PRESOLAR MATERIALS IN METEORITES AND INTERPLANETARY DUST - PHASE II SUMMARY: We propose to identify and characterize presolar material in meteorites and interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) using a wide range of microanalytical techniques (primarily SIMS and TEM). The studies will provide fundamentally important information about stellar and galactic evolution, dust formation in stars, interstellar chemistry, and processes in the early solar system and are directly relevant to NASA's goals of understanding the origin of the solar system and other stars. The research will take advantage of an advanced new ion probe, the NanoSIMS 50L, recently installed at the Carnegie Institution. The major goals of the proposed research are to: (1) Create large, unbiased multi-isotope databases of single presolar SiC, Si3N4, oxide and silicate grains to better understand their origins, (2) Investigate the range of presolar silicate minerals and their isotopic compositions. (3) Investigate the relative abundances of presolar grains (mainly silicates and SiC) in different meteorite classes and IDPs to better understand how they are affected by early solar system and parent body processes. (4) Investigate the microstructures of presolar grains to better understand dust formation and processing, (5) Characterize on a sub-micron scale the carriers of isotopically anomalous H and N in IDPs and to search for correlations between H and N anomalies and presolar circumstellar grains, (6) Search for isotopically anomalous O, C, Si, S, Mg and Fe in IDPs, (7) Chemically, mineralogically and structurally characterize isotopically anomalous material in IDPs using correlated microanalytical techniques on the same particles analyzed by ion probe. These techniques include analytical electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), scanning transmission x-ray microscopy [STXM], laser Raman microscopy and fluorescence microscopy. (8) Compare isotopic compositions of IDPs collected by NASA at different times to investigate whether IDP collections include samples from specific earth-crossing comets. (9) Compare IDP data with complementary data obtained by us and others on comet Wild-2 samples returned by NASA's Stardust spacecraft.

Description: AN EXPERIMENTAL STUDY OF HIGH PRSESURE MINERAL AND MELT PHASE QUILIBRIA IN TERRESTRIAL PLANETARY INTERIORS-PHASE II ABSTRACT: The goal of our experimental study is to provide the fundamental high-pressure data necessary to explore the structure and evolution of the interiors of terrestrial planets with emphasis on Mars, Mercury, and Venus. Space missions to Mars and Mercury have provided important constraints on the physics and chemistry, of the interior including density distribution, physical state of the core, the nature of magnetic field, and chemistry of the surface rocks. A full explanation of the observations from space missions ultimately requires knowledge on the fundamental properties of the planetary cores, including density, temperature, composition, and physical state. Building on the success of our previous research program that integrates geochemical models and laboratory experimental data with geophysical observations, we will focus this proposal on the thermal and physical states of the cores of Mars, Mercury, and Venus, and their implications for magnetic field generation and thermal evolution of the planets. We propose a series of melting experiments in the Fe-NiiS system up to 40 GPa, a pressure corresponding to the center of Mars and Mercury, using both multi-anvil apparatus and laser-heating diamond anvil cell. The experimental data will be used to establish a thermodynamic model that will extend the applications to the Earth and Venus cores. We will also obtain experimental data on structure and density of Fe-S liquids with applications to liquid cores of Mars and Mercury. Finally, we will continue our experiments on potassium (K), uranium (U), and thorium (Th) partitioning between liquid metal and liquid silicate to quantify the amount of radioactive elements in planetary cores. These data will provide critical constraints on thermal evolution and dynamo models.

Description: Measurements of Metal Ion/Neutral Total Content in the Earths Ionospheres/Atmosphere Using GOME on the ERS-2 Satellite This is a proposal to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration under the cooperative agreement between the Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America. The proposal seeks funding to investigate the interaction between interplanetary dust particles and the Earth's atmosphere and ionosphere, using satellite observations. The GOME satellite on the European ERS-2 satellite is utilized to determine the total atmospheric content of meteoric metals as determined by their solar radiation-induced resonant radiations in the 240 to 300 run spectral region. Species that are measurable include Mg+, Mg, Fe+, Fe, Na+, and possibly Si. The global total content will be compared against a one-dimensional model that includes computation of the deposition rate of incoming meteoric material. In addition to being published the results from this study will be used as the basis for a doctoral thesis at the Catholic University of America. Anticipated results include the response of the metal content to meteor showers, seasonal variations, and latitudinal changes. The data set comprises the time period 1996 to 2002. It may be possible to observe a possible solar cycle dependence. If resources permit comparison will be made with total metal content being obtained with the SCIAMACHY instrument on the ERS-3 satellite. This data set begins in 2002 and runs at least through 2007 allowing observations ofthe variation of metal content over a complete solar cycle.

Description: THE NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY NEW ATLAS OF THE OCEAN AND TEACHER'S GUIDE In 2008 The National Geographic Society (NGS) will re-release the highly popular Atlas of the Ocean. Published in 2001, the original Atlas of the Ocean was the first ocean atlas to provide full, detailed maps of the ocean floor, and to be easily accessed by popular readers and oceanographers alike. Its accompanying Teacher's Guide received an excellent rating from NASA's education review panel, and saw distribution to thousands of teachers and students across the nation. The advent of ocean-observing satellites has launched a new era of marine discovery. In this new era NGS seeks to capitalize on NASA's unique capability to understand the Earth system and apply Earth system science to improve predictions of Earth system change. NGS and NASA will partner to create the New Atlas and Teacher's Guide, creating a unique opportunity to build student, educator, and public awareness of the ocean's role in the Earth system. The 2008 New Atlas of the Ocean will build upon the success of the previous Atlas and Teacher's Guide. The New Atlas will host at least 100 new maps and diagrams; more background content, including the latest advances in technology and policy; and an increased emphasis on education and outreach. The New Atlas revisions and updates will include adding comprehensive indexing to the existing maps, and updating the 75 diagrams. The resulting Atlas will be an unprecedented reference of the Earth's ocean for the 21" century. The proposed outline of the New Atlas will feature three prominent sections. Part one will provide a glimpse of the world ocean, such as ocean basics, ocean life, and oceans past. Section two will feature geographic ocean regions, such as the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, The Indian Ocean, The Southern Ocean, and the Arctic Ocean. Finally, part three of the Atlas will host two chapters dedicated to ocean technologies and the future of the ocean.

Description: Marc Fries/Carnegie Institution of Washington Characterization of Carbonaceous Matter in Cometary Material by Raman Imaging The proposed work will focus on the characterization of the carbonaceous material found in 81P/Wild-2 cometary particles captured and returned by the Stardust spacecraft using Raman spectroscopic imaging. The carbonaceous component of cometary bodies in general is of special scientific interest since cometary organics are believed to have played an important role in prebiotic chemistry on the early Earth. This material likely constitutes a major component of the carbonaceous material found on planetary bodies throughout the solar system. Additionally, understanding the structure and chemical composition of carbonaceous materials will help to constrain the formation and metamorphic history of the 81P/Wild-2 comet and so help us understand the conditions present during the formation of comets in the early solar system. The Raman spectroscopic imaging technique proposed here is especially well suited to the study of carbonaceous material due a combination of high detection sensitivity and ability to characterize all carbon polymorphs in fine structural and spatial detail. This proposed effort will follow four primary courses of investigation, namely 1.) characterization of macromolecular carbon (MMC) to include spatial, microstructural and modal abundance analyses, 2) similar analyses for the aliphatic component observed during the preliminary examination (PE), 3) measure the degree of shock/thermal processing experienced by carbonaceous material in Stardust particles, 4) assessment of the origin of both carbonaceous phases to include general physiochemical constraints,taking into account the possibility of contamination and 5) analysis of any targets of opportunity that may arise, as successful Raman analysis of silicate and other phases in Stardust material has proven to be elusive. This effort will be of sufficient scope to cover a statistically meaningful number of analyses are performed to draw conclusions about the form and prevalence of 81P/Wild-2 carbonaceous matter, and every effort will be made to collect a statistically meaningful number of measurements for each particle capture track investigated. After each analysis, the particles examined will be made available to others in the Washington Area Sample Consortium (WASC) in order to build a complementary data set using a variety of analytical methods, applied in a predetermined order such that subsequent analyses are not affected by preceding measurements. This effort has the added bonus that it minimizes sample disruption due to shipping as well as reducing the curatorial workload that would be required for repeated, individual sample requisitions. Collected data will be presented in appropriate conferences and publications, as well as compiled for Stardust curators for inclusion in their sample database. Summer intern students will also be encouraged to participate in this proposal through the Carnegie Institution's annual Summer Intern Program in Geoscience.

Description: Eta Carinae has long been suspected to be a massive binary system, but the hot companion has eluded detection until now. Our FUSE Cycle 4 observations have revealed the hot companion of eta Car for the first time. FUV spectra show that the companion is consistent with a late O or WR star, possibly nitrogen rich. FUSE observations of eta Car now span one complete binary orbit (5.54 years). Future FUSE spectra will allow us to begin to separate cyclical binary orbit variability from long-term secular changes. We propose two Cycle 7 observations about six months apart to place further constraints on the hot companion, perhaps obtaining spectral classification and radial velocity measurements which could lead to direct mass estimates for the system. These objectives are supported by spectral analysis of STIS observations from 1998.0 -2004.5 that are yielding radial velocity curves for the wind-wind interaction in the binary system.

Description: FUSE observations of the star, rJ Car, and its surrounding stellar ejecta present a unique opportunity to study the FUV properties of recently ejected material from a very massive stellar system and to identify the hot secondary companion. We propose to 1) use the MDRS to obtain rj Car's polar stellar spectrum scattered from the SE lobe, which should provide spectral signature of the mysterious companion star, 2) use the HIRS and MDRS to disentangle the 'stellar' spectrum from the dust-scattered, nebular emission, and 3) obtain the nebular spectrum of the S-condensation, where recent, fast moving ejecta are colliding with previously-ejected, nitrogen-enriched material. This proposal builds on multiple observing programs using FUSE, HST/STIS, RXTE, CHANDRA, VLT/UVES and other ground-based instruments that have followed 77 Car over the recent 5.54-year cycle. These proposed observations, along with improved modeling of this very complex system, will provide new insight on the nature of massive (binary) stars in their last stages of stellar evolution and on how they interact with, and enrich, the ISM. Since very massive. Population III stars are thought to be the source of heavy elements and dust in the early Universe, we need a complete description of how stars of extreme mass, such as 77 Car, deposit nucleosynthesis products into the ISM, and how they form dust

Description: The Mars community is poised to come together to develop a fuller understanding of the Mars' space environment and its interaction with the solar wind. A number of significant advances have been made recently in the arenas of modeling and spacecraft measurement. For example, several modeling groups have achieved high enough resolution and  completeness that the entire system, from the solar wind down to the atmosphere, can be included in a single model. Further, these models have advanced to the point where they could and should be compared with each other, and with in situ measurements. At the same time, the Mars Express spacecraft has increased the number of instruments currently making relevant measurements of the Martian plasma environment, and is for the first time enabling simultaneous measurements of different parts of the interaction region by different spacecraft. These advances have been made by a diverse group of investigators, both geographically and in terms of their expertise and experience. In order to stimulate discussions between the variety of scientists interested in the Martian solar wind interaction, we propose to organize and execute a topical conference on the solar wind interaction with Mars. The conference will cover the following topics: 1) What are the underlying physical processes that occur at each of the plasma boundaries? 2) In what ways do crystal magnetic fields affect the global solar wind interaction? 3) How does the interaction between the solar wind and Mars affect the upper atmospheric structure and atmospheric loss rate? 4) Which physical processes are important in modeling the interaction (and where and under what conditions)? 5) What are the similarities and differences between the plasma environments at Mars and other bodies such as Venus, comets, and Titan? The meeting format will include presentations and posters. Session chairs will present a synthesis of results, especially as they apply to the science questions in this proposal. Authors will be strongly encouraged to submit papers from the conference to a refereed proceedings volume such as a Geophysical Monograph or a special section of a journal. participation in the conference will be open to anyone. Description: SOLAR NEBULA EVOLUTION   This proposal is to continue a program of numerical studies of the formation and dynamical evolution of circumstellar disks, and the possible formation of giant planets by gravitational instability. The work would use numerical modeling of gas hydrodynamics with self-gravity and radiative transport. 2D models of collapse of rotating prestellar clouds will be used to derive surface density and thermal profiles of the resulting disks. Modeling of marginally gravitationally unstable disks in 3D will be extended to lower disk masses and more massive stars. Models of the solar nebula will be computed to smaller heliocentric distances to assess production of shocks and processing of solids. Orbital evolution will be computed for planetary cores embedded in a marginally unstable disk. Work will be started to determine the suitability of an adaptive mesh code for investigations of these problems. Calculations will be made to compare with those of another group's code to identify reasons for differences between their results.

Description: MESSENGER INVESTIGATIONS OF THE GEOCHEMISTRY OF MERCURY Mercury is the least explored and least understood of the terrestrial planets, yet as the smallest, densest and closest terrestrial planet to the Sun, it may hold the keys to understanding the origin and early evolution of the inner solar system. NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft was launched August 3,2004 and will orbit Mercury for one year beginning in March 2011. The PI proposes to be formally added to the IESSENGER Science Team as a Participating Scientist, specifically as a member of the Geochemistry discipline group. His experience in both laboratory analysis of extraterrestrial materials and planetary remote geochemical sensing will provide needed expertise to the Science Team in both developing techniques to improve the geochemical data products from MESSENGER and in interpreting the actual data that will be obtained during the orbital phase of the mission. Among the lIESSENGER science payload are 3 instruments that will provide geochemical information of the planet's surface: the x-ray spectrometer (XRS), the gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer (GRNS), and the Mercury Atmospheric and Surface Composition Spectrometer MASCS, which includes both a visible/infrared spectrometer (VIRS) and UltraViolet-Visible Spectrometer (UVVS). Specific goals of the proposed research are to: (1) Modify and improve x-ray fluorescence models developed by the PI for the NEAR mission to include improved solar x-ray spectral models, characteristics of the lIESSENGER XRS instrument, and improved physics (e.g., secondary fluorescence effects). (2) In collaboration with Dr. Lucy Lim (GSFC), explore Monte Carlo radiation transport models of x-ray production in planetary surfaces to investigate surface topography effects and compare with results of analytical models. (3) Perform laboratory x-ray fluorescence experiments to validate and refine models. (4) Explore more realistic range of possible Mercury surface compositions in modeling both XRS and GRNS spectra than has been done thus far in preparation for the orbital phase of the MESSENGER mission. (5) Once geochemical data are available for Mercury, aid in extracting elemental abundance data from XRS spectra and generate abundance maps. (6) Use elemental abundance data from XRS and GRNS to explore fundamental questions of Mercury's origin and history, including whether the planet is extremely depleted in volatiles, whether it is related to any other known planetary materials (e.g. enstatite chondrites, angrites), and whether the radar-bright materials in polar craters are indeed water ice or elemental sulfur. (7) Correlate spatially resolved abundance data with data from VIRS to identify surface rock types and aid in reconstructing the geological history of Mercury. Correlate spatially resolved abundance data with data from the UVVS to identify possible sources and sinks of the volatile elements observed in Mercury's exosphere.

Description: GEOPHYSICAL EVOLUTION OF THE TERRESTRIAL PLANETS This proposal requests support to continue our work on the geophysical evolution of the terrestrial planets, currently funded by a three-year grant (NNG04164G) from the NASA Planetary Geology and Geophysics Program. The central objective of our research continues to be a deeper understanding of the comparative tectonic, volcanic, and thermal histories of the terrestrial planets. Emphasis for the coming three years will be on targeted aspects of the evolution of Mars, Mercury, and Venus. Specifically, we shall: (1) Investigate the process of core formation in terrestrial planets and large asteroids and satellites by the percolation of molten iron-rich liquids through a deforming silicate matrix; (2) Assess the effect of water on the thermal evolution of the Martian mantle and crust as a means to constrain the history of interior and outgassed water on that planet; (3) Develop models for the deformation near and within major impact basins on Mercury to assess the relative contributions of basin-scale processes and global contraction to the planet ' s tectonic history; and (4) Assess the influence of climate change on the tectonic and magmatic history of Venus-with a particular focus on crustal plateaus, shield fields, and regional plains-with the aim of exploring whether global climate change might contribute to a `directional ' geological history on that planet.

MY SPECIFIC CONTRIBUTION TO THIS EFFORT WILL BE DEVELOPMENT OF ANALYSIS TOOLS FOR THE XRS EXPERIMENT, MODELING OF PARTICLE TRANSPORT IN THE PLANET S SURFACE, AND MODELING OF DETECTOR RESPONSE FUNCTIONS. Description: SOLAR NEBULA EVOLUTION   This proposal is to continue a program of numerical studies of the formation and dynamical evolution of circumstellar disks, and the possible formation of giant planets by gravitational instability.
