Description: The geologic history of Mercury - from planetary accretion through to space weathering - is so poorly constrained that a wide variety of models can be accommodated by available data.  MESSENGER will provide global geology, geochemistry, spectroscopy, imaging and gravity necessary to constrain this history.  A key component in this is unraveling the oxidation state of the material that formed Mercury, including the FeO concentration in silicates accreted to form the planet, the current FeO concentration in the mantle and the influence of space weathering and production of nanophase iron.  I propose to serve on the Geochemistry subgroup with the aim of integrating the geochemical and spectral data to constrain the mineralogy of regions for which both data sets exist.  This integration can be accomplished using integrative mathematical techniques (normalized element ratios, matrix deconvolution) developed by the PI for the NEAR mission, combined with synthetic spectra generated from the constrained mineralogies.  I anticipate that the mineralogy of 200 distinct regions can be constrained by data provided by the gamma-ray, neutron, and X-ray spectrometers, when combined with visible spectra out to 1.45 micrometers provided by MASCS.  These will be used to produce broad-scale mineralogical maps that will be useful to the geochemistry, geology and geophysics group, as well as the broader scientific community.  They will also be used to address why the FeO concentration of the Mercurian crust is so low and whether this reflects formation from FeO precursors and supports a radial gradient for FeO during formation of the inner Solar System.

Description: A NEXT GENERATION PRECISION DOPPLER SURVEY Nearly two hundred extrasolar planets have been discovered over the past decade.  Discoveries made during just the last 18 months include the first three Neptune-mass planets, the first terrestrial mass planet, and the second and third transiting planets orbiting nearby stars.  With the cancellation of TPF and Keck-I, and SIM moved to the edge of the budgetary horizon, precision Doppler surveys will continue to dominate the discovery of planets orbiting nearby stars for at least the next two decades.  Nearly everything that has emerged from precision Doppler surveys contradicts existing theory.  Among the discoveries not anticipated by theory are "Hot Jupiters" with orbital periods of a few days to a few weeks, and planets in eccentric orbits.  These two classes account for roughly 95% of known planets.  Though massive companions are the easiest to detect, only a few companions with mass greater than 10 Jupiter-masses have been found.  The planet mass function begins steeply climbing at less than 5 Jupiter-masses, and continues to rise down to a Saturn-mass, where incompleteness becomes a serious issue for the current generation of surveys.  Our immediate goal is to improve long term Doppler precision from 3 to 1 m/s.  With 1 m/s precision we can attack a number of outstanding questions, including: 1) Does the planet mass function continue to rise in the SATERN to Neptune-mass range, 2) Are multiple planet systems common, 3) Are solar system analogs common, 4) Are terrestrial mass planets common?  Reaching 1 m/s precision is both an enormous technical challenge, and a photon collection challenge.  1 m/s is 3 ten-thousandths of a pixel on a high resolution spectrometer, about 20 silicon atoms on the CCD substrate.  In addition to controlling all systematic errors at this level, reaching 1 m/s requires exposure times a factor of nine longer than for 3 m/s.  Carrying out a 1 m/s survey on more than handful of the brightest stars requires a 6.5 to 10-m telescope.  We are currently building a new "planet hunting" spectrometer for Magellan specifically designed to reach 1 m/s precision.  This spectrometer will be ready for operation in one year.  We request NASA/OSS funding to carry out the Magellan 1 m/s Doppler survey, and the complementary 1 milli-mag photometric survey, of nearby southern hemisphere stars.

Description: Waterfalls and springs are both known to undercut the base of valley headscarps on Earth, facilitating mass wasting and extending theater-headed fluvial valleys into layered rock. As many theater-headed valleys occur on Mars, these end-member hypotheses have motivated considerable attention and debate within the planetary community, but they have never been subjected to quantitative field testing on the Earth, either individually or in combination. The relative importance of runoff is still numerically unconstrained, despite the facts that rainfall is nearly ubiquitous, flash floods are common in canyons, and discharge is a measurable variable with a well established and quantifiable geomorphic effect. A lithological and hydrological model has been devised whereby seepage processes could dominate erosion of a valley, but it remains unknown whether features of this model apply universally or are even common in theater-headed valleys, as few of them have been studied in detail. The goal of this project is to determine whether overland flow plays a significant or even dominant role in forming theater-headed valleys in several regions of the United States, or if direct runoff is essentially negligible in some areas, leaving a groundwater sapping origin as a unique interpretation. Our first objective is to examine the diversity of lithology, stratigraphy, structure, hydrology, weathering environments, and base-level control in theater-headed valleys, in order to establish the controlling variables on valley morphology. Objective 2 is to constrain the dominant discharge, which is responsible for channel dimensions and much of the sediment transport in fluvial channels, using well established paleoflow techniques. Objective 3 seeks to determine the weathering processes and rates in these valleys, to evaluate whether overland flow or groundwater sapping could reasonably be responsible for producing most of the mobile sediment. These three objectives will provide the first quantitative constraints on erosion processes in theater-headed valleys, which are a well established analog to Martian valley networks. This project is well suited to the MFRP guidelines of (i) theoretical and experimental studies, including laboratory studies of analog materials, to investigate the coupled atmospheric and geological systems on Mars; and (ii) quantitative terrestrial field experiments that improve understanding of the in situ measurements that have been or that will be made on Mars. The project will address the NASA research goal expressed in the MEPAG 2004 document: GOAL 111: DETERMINE THE EVOLUTION OF THE SURFACE AND INTERIOR OF MARS; Objective A: Determine the nature and evolution of the geologic processes that have created and modified the Martian crust and surface; Investigation 2: Evaluate fluvial, subaqueous, pyroclastic, subaerial, and other sedimentary processes and their evolution and distribution through time, up to and including the present.

Description: THE NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC SOCIETY NEW ATLAS OF THE OCEAN AND TEACHER'S GUIDE In 2008 The National Geographic Society (NGS) will re-release the highly popular Atlas of the Ocean. Published in 2001, the original Atlas of the Ocean was the first ocean atlas to provide full, detailed maps of the ocean floor, and to be easily accessed by popular readers and oceanographers alike. Its accompanying Teacher's Guide received an excellent rating from NASA's education review panel, and saw distribution to thousands of teachers and students across the nation. The advent of ocean-observing satellites has launched a new era of marine discovery. In this new era NGS seeks to capitalize on NASA's unique capability to understand the Earth system and apply Earth system science to improve predictions of Earth system change. NGS and NASA will partner to create the New Atlas and Teacher's Guide, creating a unique opportunity to build student, educator, and public awareness of the ocean's role in the Earth system. The 2008 New Atlas of the Ocean will build upon the success of the previous Atlas and Teacher's Guide. The New Atlas will host at least 100 new maps and diagrams; more background content, including the latest advances in technology and policy; and an increased emphasis on education and outreach. The New Atlas revisions and updates will include adding comprehensive indexing to the existing maps, and updating the 75 diagrams. The resulting Atlas will be an unprecedented reference of the Earth's ocean for the 21" century. The proposed outline of the New Atlas will feature three prominent sections. Part one will provide a glimpse of the world ocean, such as ocean basics, ocean life, and oceans past. Section two will feature geographic ocean regions, such as the Atlantic Ocean, the Pacific Ocean, The Indian Ocean, The Southern Ocean, and the Arctic Ocean. Finally, part three of the Atlas will host two chapters dedicated to ocean technologies and the future of the ocean.

Description: ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION OF VOYAGER 1 AND 2 MAG DATA The Principal Investigator of this proposal is an Adjunct Professor at CUA and will continue to use his experience and familiarity with the study of the weak magnetic fields in interplanetary space, as measured by spacecraft, to analyze and interpret the science data from the twin Voyager spacecraft, each launched in 1977. These may be of solar or extra-solar origin. These combined data sets will be studied to identify variations caused by time variable solar sources as well as interactions of this non-steady solar wind and energetic particles from solar eruptions such as flares or coronal mass ejections as these disturbances propagate outward through the heliosphere. On day of year 334, November 30,2006, the V2 SIC sent a spurious, i.e., unrequested and unneeded, command to the MAG-Outboard Low Field Magnetometer (OBLFM) which caused it to activate its flipper mechanism. Description: The recent performance increases in graphics processing units (GPUs) have made graphics cards an attractive platform for implementing computationally intense applications. With their numerous parallel computational pipelines and SIMD architecture, modern GPUs can outperform high-end microprocessors by one to three orders of magnitude, depending on the problem. Description: SOLAR MODULATION OF COSMIC PROTONS, ANTIPROTONS, AND ELECTRONS  Solar modulation of cosmic rays is the process by which the Sun, via the solar wind, alters the intensity and energy spectrum of high-energy charged particles that continually bombard the heliosphere from outside. This project aims to gain a solid understanding of solar modulation from first principles (ab initio), by developing a modulation model in which the properties of turbulence throughout the heliosphere are specified from modern turbulence transport theory, and the cosmic ray diffusion tensor is computed from fundamental particle transport theory based upon the derived properties of the turbulence. The work will serve both to improve the performance of modulation codes, and to serve 'as ii demanding observational test of turbulence transport theory and particle transport theory. The ab initio modulation model will be validated by comparing model predictions to spacecraft (Ulysses, Voyager, IMP 8) and balloon observations of cosmic protons,' antiprotons, and electrons in various phases of the solar activity (11 year) and solar magnetic (22 year) cycles. This project directly addresses NASA's strategic goals, in particular Strategic Sub-goal 3B: "Understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system" and Science Outcome 3B.1: "Progress in understanding the fundamental physical processes of the space environment from the Sun to Earth, to other planets, and beyond to the interstellar medium."

Description: The overall objective this group proposes to achieve through this proposal is to design, construct, and test a proof of concept inflatable structure, focusing on its deployment characteristics and durability in a representative harsh environment-the Antarctic. The design will begin from recent work carried out by several NASA centers (i.e., JSC, LaRC, and MSFC) with all three organizations contributing to the requirements development for the proof of concept. If, at the end of this requirements phase, all three organizations are satisfied with the overall concept and the data it will generate in a deployment phase, ILC/Dover will construct the primary pressure vessel and portions of the interior outfitting. NASA will develop the data system that will monitor and transmit performance data during the deployment phase. The NSF will transport the entire system to the Antarctic and assist with the deployment at a suitable location. The NSF will also provide on-site monitoring and support during the deployment and post-deployment test phase. All three organizations will have access to the performance data generated during the deployment. The uniqueness of this approach is embedded within the partnership between the NSF, NASA, and ILC, Dover. While there has been work in the area of inflatable habitat design (within NASA and outside of NASA), most relevant technology research and demonstrations have targeted zero-g operations in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). The requirements for inflatable habitats for the lunar and Mars surface will have to address structural design differences, environmental differences and operational differences that are design drivers if they are to be utilized for surface applications. Inflatable pressure vessel experience must be gained over time through thorough habitatability assessments, test/modeling, design iteration, and LEO DTO in order to have sufficient confidence in inflatables for extended stays. Recently, a lunar habitat mockup optimized for horizontal surface area per volume has been commissioned for dimensional evaluations in a shirt-sleeve environment. Current inflatable spacecraft activities in industry do not include evaluation of inflatabled surface habitats and have limited on-orbit instrumentation. It must be kept in mind though, that inflatable technology has been successfully applied in cases such as the JPL Mars Exploration Rover Mission Airbag Landing System (prime contractor was proposed partner ILC Dover). NASA has limited experience (TransHab) certifying inflatable pressure vessels, materials and thermal models for human habitation in a space environment. Therefore, the technical merit of this proposal is based on gaining experience in building, outfitting, and living in an inflatable pressure vessel under the unique extreme environment conditions of Antarctica.

Description: "AIR-ICE SURFACE ENERGY EXCHANGE AND SEA ICE-MASS REDISTRIBUTION IN THE ARCTIC" SUMMARY: MEASUREMENTS OF THE ARCTIC SEA ICE COVER FROM BUOYS, SUBMARINES, AND SATELLITES INDICATE THE THICKNESS AND THE TEMPORAL AND SPATIAL DISTRIBUTION OF THE ICE HAVE CHANGED OVER THE LAST 30 YEARS.  THESE CHANGES IN THE ARCTIC ICE APPEAR TO BE DRIVEN BY CHANGES IN BOTH THERMODYNAMIC AND DYNAMIC FORCING, AND NUMERICAL MODELING STUDIES HAVE PROVIDED A RANGE OF EXPLANATIONS WHICH DEPEND ON EACH MODEL S SENSITIVITY TO SIMILAR ATMOSPHERIC FORCING.  CHANGES IN ICE MASS ARE CLOSELY LINKED TO THE DYNAMIC RESPONSE TO ATMOSPHERIC FORCING THROUGH THE PROCESSES OF ICE DEFORMATION, LEAD OPENING, AND NEW ICE GROWTH.  HIGH-QUALITY OBSERVATIONAL DATA ON AIR-ICE SURFACE FLUXES AND THE STRESS/STRAIN RELATIONSHIP IN SEA ICE HAVE BECOME AVAILABLE, AND CAN BE USED TO CONSTRAIN THE FORMULATIONS OF AIR-ICE TURBULENT TRANSFER AND ICE RHEOLOGY.  THE SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY ARE: (I) TO ANALYZE RECENT STRESS/STRAIN AND SURFACE FLUX DATA FOR THE PURPOSE OF DEVELOPING PARAMETERIZATIONS FOR ICE AND CLIMATE MODELS, (II) TO SIMULATE THE ARCTIC SEA ICE COVER OVER RECENT DECADES AND COMPARE THE IMPACT OF CONSTRAINING THE PARAMETERIZATIONS WITH OBSERVATIONS, AND (III) COMPARE MODEL SIMULATIONS WITH ICE THICKNESS OBSERVATIONS AND DETERMINE THE CONTRIBUTIONS OF DYNAMICS AND THERMODYNAMICS TO THE OBSERVED CHANGES.  THE ICE MODEL USED FOR THE STUDY WILL BE THE COMMUNITY CLIMATE SYSTEM MODEL (CCSM) SEA ICE MODEL VERSION 4 (CSIM 4), WHICH IS USED IN CLIMATE AND GLOBAL CHANGE SIMULATIONS.  THE FINAL GOAL IS TO COORDINATE WITH THE CCSM DEVELOPMENT COMMUNITY TO INTEGRATE NEW PARAMETERIZATIONS IN THE MODEL.  WE WILL USE ATMOSPHERIC BOUNDARY LAYER DATA FROM SHEBA TO IMPROVE THE PRESENTLY USED AIR-ICE TRANSFER PARAMETERIZATIONS OVER SNOW-COVERED AND BARE SEA ICE, AND UNDER VARYING STABILITY CONDITIONS.  ICE STRESS, MOTION AND DEFORMATION DATA FROM A SERIES OF ICE-BUOY DYNAMIC STUDIES IN THE ARCTIC WILL BE USED TO CONSTRAIN THE VALUES OF ICE STRENGTH AND DEFORMATION IN THE ELASTIC-VISCOUS-PLASTIC ICE MODEL.  THE ICE MODELING WILL USE AN ENSEMBLE APPROACH, WHICH WILL USE MONTE CARLO SIMULATIONS WITH RANDOMIZED YEARS OF FORCING TO DETERMINE WHETHER THE CHANGES IN THE BASELINE SIMULATION AND THE MODELING IN THIS STUDY WILL CONTRIBUTE TO A GREATER UNDERSTANDING OF THE DRAMATIC CHANGES OCCURRING IN THE ARCTIC.

Description: DETERMINING THE PROPERTIES OF THE ETA-CARINAE SYSTEM VIA HYDRODYNAMICAL MODELS OF SPACE-BASED OBSERVATIONS (GRADUATE STUDENT - THOMAS MADURA) Abstract: I propose to use the immense collection of NASA observations of Eta-Carinae to better understand non-spherical stellar winds, wind-wind collisions, and the binarity of this system. X-ray modeling will place constraints on the wind and stellar parameters of the primary and secondary star, while hydrodynamical simulations will place constraints on the parameters of the binary orbit. GOLD Instrument - AO Award The Robotic Lunar ExplorationLunar Precursor Robotic Program (RLEPLPRP) consists of a series of robotic lunar exploration missions to prepare for and to support future human exploration activities. The primary purpose of the robotic preparation is to reduce risk, enhance mission success, and reduce the cost of future human missions. The LRO payload used to accomplish the mission objectives consists of the following six Instruments: 1. Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) Measurement Investigation shall determine the global topography of the lunar surface at high resolution, measure landing site slopes and search for polar ices in shadowed regions; 2. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) shall acquire targeted images of the lunar surface capable of resolving small-scale features that could be landing site hazards, as well as wide-angle images at multiple wavelengths of the lunar poles to document changing illumination conditions and potential resources; 3. Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND) shall map the flux of neutrons from the lunar surface to search for evidence of water ice and provide measurements of the space radiation environment which can be useful for future human exploration; 4. Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment (DLRE) shall map the temperature of the entire lunar surface at 300 meter horizontal scales to identify cold-traps and potential ice deposits; 5. Lyman-Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) shall observe the entire lunar surface in the far ultraviolet to search for surface ices and frosts in the polar regions and to provide images of permanently shadowed regions illuminated only by starlight; 6. Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) shall investigate the effect of galactic cosmic rays on tissue-equivalent plastics as a constraint on models of biological response to background space radiation. Each Instrument will be managed by a Principal Investigator (PI), who will be responsible for delivering the flight Instrument to the LRO project, as well as producing the Instrument's data products and delivering them to the Planetary Data System (PDS) in accordance with their data product specification document.

Description: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDE/REFRACTORY CARBIDE CER-CER FUELS.  IN THIS PROPOSAL, A NEW CARBIDE-BASED FUEL IS INTRODUCED WITH OUTSTANDING POTENTIAL TO ELIMINATE THE LOSS OF URANIUM, MINIMIZES THE LOSS OF URANIUM AND RETAINS FISSION PRODUCTS FOR MANY HOURS OF OPERATION IN HYDROGEN ENVIRONMENT AT TEMPERATURES IN EXCESS OF 3,200K.  THE PROPOSED FUEL IS A CERAMIC-CERAMIC (CERCER) COMPOSITE OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS (U,ZR)C OR (U,ZR,NB)C IN A MATRIX OF REFRACTORY CARBIDES THAT MOSTLY INCLUDE TRANSITION METAL CARBIDES SUCH AS ZRC, NBC, TAC AND HFC.  DUE TO ITS LOW NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION, ZRC IS THE PRIMARY REFRACTORY CARBIDE OF CHOICE.  REPLACING ZRC WITH HIGHER TEMPERATURE REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS TAC AND HFC COULD FURTHER IMPROVE THE HIGH TEMPERATURE PERFORMANCE OF CERCER FUELS.  HOWEVER, HIGHER NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION PENALTY FOR A TA AND HF COULD POTENTIALLY OFFSET THE PERFORMANCE ENHANCEMENT GAIN.  DUE TO COMPLETE CONTAINMENT AND ENCAPSULATION OF MIXED URANIUM CARBIDE IN ZIRCONIUM CARBIDE MATRIX, THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL COULD BE CONVENIENTLY FABRICATED TO DIFFERENT GEOMETRIAL SHAPES SUCH AS SOLID BLOCK PRISMATIC, TWISTED RIBBON, PEBBLES, WAFER OR SQUARE LATTICE HONEYCOMB.  CONSIDERING THE OPERATIONAL PARAMETERS FOR THE NT/BP SYSTEMS, IT IS REASONABLE TO ARGUE THAT THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL CONCEPT COULD SET THE PROPER MATERIAL PERFORMANCE LIMITS WHILE PROVIDING MORE FLEXIBILITY IN THE GEOMETRICAL DESIGN OF THE FUEL.

Description: SHEAR-STRESS SENSOR ARRAY MEASUREMENT TECHNOLOGY FOR THE SUPPORT OF TURBULENCE MODE FOR FLOW SEPARATION The University of Florida (UF) proposes a four-year study to develop wall shear-stress sensor array measurement technology to provide benchmark three-dimensional, time-resolved, fluctuating skin friction data to aid turbulence model development for flow separation. Specifically, these sensors will be developed to facilitate the synthesis of #turbulence models applicable to flow separation on high-speed cruise wings through and beyond buffet onset, low-speed high-lift systems up to and beyond maximum lift, and/or empennages across the speed range, or in highly loaded compressors and turbines# as discussed in Subtopic A.2.3.2 of NASA NRA NNH06ZNHOOl. Therefore, the ultimate goal of this research is to develop an advanced measurement tool that will enable the realization of LlIL2 Milestone #SFW.l.l1.05 Experimental data for low speed separation onset and control# by providing a method to capture three-dimensional, time-resolved, fluctuating shear-stress data in complex flow fields. To achieve this goal, micromachining technologies will be used to create passive (batteryless), wireless shear-stress sensors. Arrays of these low-profile sensors will be inlayed in thin, flexible substrates that will conformably adhere to the curved surface of an airframe. Using an antenna embedded in the substrate, the time-resolved shear-stress from all the sensors will be interrogated simultaneously. This approach requires only one cable connection from the antenna to an external data acquisition and signal processing system, thus reducing cabling requirements. Rigorous characterization in UF wind tunnel facilities will be used to validate the system as a quantitative, instrumentation-grade turbulence measurement tool. Finally, benchmark shear-stress data will be obtained in several attached and separated turbulent flows.

Description: Current and upcoming NASA space links require both highly reliable low-rate communications links supporting critical TT&C, ranging and voice services and highly efficient high-data rate links supporting Mission or Payload Data return. Both are important to the success of a mission and for many ongoing missions rely on aging ground element equipment. Investing in re-usable elements, such as Programmable Communications Radios, for ground and flight data handling that are capable of receiving both highly-reliable low-rate links and highly-efficient high-rate links would address current Communication and Navigation needs without foregoing future capabilities. Current receiver designs typically address either high-rate or low-rate requirements but not both. NASA has requested a high-rate receiver capable of receiving coded and un-coded highly efficient modulation schemes supporting data throughput greater than 300Mbps. The proposed Phase I effort by Summation Research, Inc. (SRI) will develop, load, characterize and optimize these high-efficiency CCSDS and related modulations on a modern, high speed digital processing platform that can also support lower rate TTC and related links. Phase II work would then implement an analog IF front-end, develop deployable digital hardware to replace the evaluation boards used in Phase I, and combine the elements in an innovative Programmable High-rate Multi-mission Receiver (PHMR).

Description: Mainstream is proposing a methodology to reduce the development time and cost, and improve the reliability of future thermal control systems for the next decade of deep space missions by utilizing a Plug-and-Play (PnP) thermal control strategy. A unique modular thermal control approach is described in the proposal as well as discussions why such an approach is ideally suited to reducing the development time and cost of deep space satellite thermal control systems as well as power conversion systems. Phase I will experimentally demonstrate that the proposed PnP approach can be configured to provide design flexibility, long life and extremely high reliability. In this Phase I effort, Mainstream will demonstrate a unique PnP Tool-Box approach where the thermal control system is easily built-up into a complete integrated system, as well as being integrated into the power conversion components. Highly integrated systems will reduce cost, reduce system size, improve reliability, and tighten the thermal control.

Description: We propose to develop novel FPGA-based algorithmic technology that will enable unprecedented computational power for the solution of large sparse linear equation systems. In Phase I, we will develop a prototype of a non-von-Neumann linear equation solver equipped with our technology, and demonstrate an intermediate milestone for its operational speedup and performance gains using at least two of the CFD problems in the NAS benchmark. Phase I will also deliver a clear technology roadmap in terms of algorithmic and architectural innovations needed to bring the project to success by the end of Phase II.  Four mission-critical areas to the success of an FPGA-based non-von-Neuman system within a von-Neumann-based supercomputing environment are identified, namely (1) portability; (2) ease of use; (3) algorithmic speed balance between von-Neumann and non-von-Neumann components; and (4) communication speed. Innovative architectural and algorithmic methods aimed at boosting system effectiveness through each one of the four areas are proposed. In particular, we propose the use of portability wrappers to enable wide portability at both hardware and software levels, software drivers in the form of an API for ease of use from a C and/or Fortran environment, innovative reconfigurable computing algorithms and bit structure optimizations suited to the LU factorization problem for speed, and a novel algorithmic technique within the reconfigurable computing paradigm that effectively eliminates the communication bottleneck, typical of multi-system distributed algorithms, for the LU factorization problem. The performance attainable with a single FPGA will be comparable to that of a 1,000-node commodity cluster, while exhibiting reductions of one to two orders of magnitude in both cost and power consumption.

IN THIS PROPOSAL, A NEW CARBIDE-BASED FUEL IS INTRODUCED WITH OUTSTANDING POTENTIAL TO ELIMINATE THE LOSS OF URANIUM, MINIMIZES THE LOSS OF URANIUM AND RETAINS FISSION PRODUCTS FOR MANY HOURS OF OPERATION IN HYDROGEN ENVIRONMENT AT TEMPERATURES IN EXCESS OF 3,200K.  THE PROPOSED FUEL IS A CERAMIC-CERAMIC (CERCER) COMPOSITE OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS (U,ZR)C OR (U,ZR,NB)C IN A MATRIX OF REFRACTORY CARBIDES THAT MOSTLY INCLUDE TRANSITION METAL CARBIDES SUCH AS ZRC, NBC, TAC AND HFC.  DUE TO ITS LOW NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION, ZRC IS THE PRIMARY REFRACTORY CARBIDE OF CHOICE.  REPLACING ZRC WITH HIGHER TEMPERATURE REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS TAC AND HFC COULD FURTHER IMPROVE THE HIGH TEMPERATURE PERFORMANCE OF CERCER FUELS.  HOWEVER, HIGHER NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION PENALTY FOR A TA AND HF COULD POTENTIALLY OFFSET THE PERFORMANCE ENHANCEMENT GAIN.  DUE TO COMPLETE CONTAINMENT AND ENCAPSULATION OF MIXED URANIUM CARBIDE IN ZIRCONIUM CARBIDE MATRIX, THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL COULD BE CONVENIENTLY FABRICATED TO DIFFERENT GEOMETRIAL SHAPES SUCH AS SOLID BLOCK PRISMATIC, TWISTED RIBBON, PEBBLES, WAFER OR SQUARE LATTICE HONEYCOMB. Description: The proposed research is in the area "mesoscale precipitation initialization" for improving hurricane and monsoon (heavy rain) forecasts. This entails the development of physical initialization (for nowcasting of rain rates using TRMM datasets) and using Newtonian relaxation and variational data assimilation methods already being developed at FSU. A comparison of these methods and studies of impacts of the initialization for high resolution short range (2-3 days) forecast will be an additional goal. Furthermore, an application of these findings will be incorporated into high resolution state-of-the-art mesoscale models to construct a multimodel mesoscale superensemble to enhance the prediction of hurricane intensity and precipitation. We propose to do the following: Assimilation of brightness temperatures by ECMWF and total precipitable water by NCEPEMC for improving precipitation initialization has limitations. If those products are validated against the NASA TRiiM (2A12 or 3B42) we find rather large errors in nowcasting of rain. The Newtonian relaxation appears to directly nudge TRMM rainfall products much more effectively. (Note: In our current TRMM research, we note that the correlation of model rain versus those from TRMM estimates are of the order 0.90 for the Newtonian relaxation where those values were as low as 0.30 for the variational data assimilation.) These differences between variational data assimilations based precipitation initialization and those based on FSUs Newtonian relaxation will be examined. These results extend to short range forecasts. The major proposed research will be on mesoscale modeling (including physical initialization of rain rates) for studies of hurricane and heavy rain related floods over the monsoon region. This will utilize the FSU Global Spectral Model at a horizontal resolution of T255 with a grid separation of - 50 km. Two regional mesoscale models WRF and HWRF (also subject to physical initialization) will be run at horizontal resolutions less than 5 km and will be driven by global model forecasts. Specifically we will address sensitivities for improving mesoscale forecasts from satellite based datasets (precipitation, moisture profiling, QuikSCAT winds and high resolution SSTs), data assimilation and model physics (especially related to precipitation processes). The final component of the proposed work will deal with the study of interaction among the diurnal wave and synoptic scale waves to improve the diurnal modulation of precipitation within heavy rainfall monsoon events, tropical disturbances and hurricanes. These results would help us to better forecast hurricane intensity. The proposed research addresses NASA objectives under the PMM in the category ;precipitation variability and its relationship to climate diagnostics and change; with emphasis on development of new data analysis and modeling techniques for detecting acceleration in water cycling through the atmosphere and the Earth's surface.

Description: We propose to develop novel FPGA-based algorithmic technology that will enable unprecedented computational power for the solution of large sparse linear equation systems. In Phase I, we will develop a prototype of a non-von-Neumann linear equation solver equipped with our technology, and demonstrate an intermediate milestone for its operational speedup and performance gains using at least two of the CFD problems in the NAS benchmark. Phase I will also deliver a clear technology roadmap in terms of algorithmic and architectural innovations needed to bring the project to success by the end of Phase II.  Four mission-critical areas to the success of an FPGA-based non-von-Neuman system within a von-Neumann-based supercomputing environment are identified, namely (1) portability; (2) ease of use; (3) algorithmic speed balance between von-Neumann and non-von-Neumann components; and (4) communication speed. Innovative architectural and algorithmic methods aimed at boosting system effectiveness through each one of the four areas are proposed. In particular, we propose the use of portability wrappers to enable wide portability at both hardware and software levels, software drivers in the form of an API for ease of use from a C and/or Fortran environment, innovative reconfigurable computing algorithms and bit structure optimizations suited to the LU factorization problem for speed, and a novel algorithmic technique within the reconfigurable computing paradigm that effectively eliminates the communication bottleneck, typical of multi-system distributed algorithms, for the LU factorization problem. The performance attainable with a single FPGA will be comparable to that of a 1,000-node commodity cluster, while exhibiting reductions of one to two orders of magnitude in both cost and power consumption.

Description: Current and upcoming NASA space links require both highly reliable low-rate communications links supporting critical TT&C, ranging and voice services and highly efficient high-data rate links supporting Mission or Payload Data return. Both are important to the success of a mission and for many ongoing missions rely on aging ground element equipment. Investing in re-usable elements, such as Programmable Communications Radios, for ground and flight data handling that are capable of receiving both highly-reliable low-rate links and highly-efficient high-rate links would address current Communication and Navigation needs without foregoing future capabilities. Current receiver designs typically address either high-rate or low-rate requirements but not both. NASA has requested a high-rate receiver capable of receiving coded and un-coded highly efficient modulation schemes supporting data throughput greater than 300Mbps. The proposed Phase I effort by Summation Research, Inc. (SRI) will develop, load, characterize and optimize these high-efficiency CCSDS and related modulations on a modern, high speed digital processing platform that can also support lower rate TTC and related links. Phase II work would then implement an analog IF front-end, develop deployable digital hardware to replace the evaluation boards used in Phase I, and combine the elements in an innovative Programmable High-rate Multi-mission Receiver (PHMR).

Description: THE IMPACT OF ATMOSPHERIC WAVES ON THE IONOSPHERIC STRUCTURE AND THE H3+ EMISSION OF JUPITER AND SAT We model the effects of atmospheric gravity waves on the structure of the ionosphere of Jupiter and Saturn and develop a radiative transfer model to predict wave signatures in the mid- and low-latitude H3+ emission of both planets. We argue that the system of layers of enhanced electron density observed in the lower ionosphere of Saturn is driven by atmospheric gravity waves. This project is based on our experience with modeling the lower ionosphere of Jupiter, which exhibits a similar structure. We propose to further develop our ZD, fully non-linear model of a gravity wave interactions with the ionospheric plasma to include equatorial and high latitude geometries, presence of variable wind in the neutral atmosphere, as well as a more realistic treatment of the wave dissipation processes. The model describes the dynamical, the thermal, and the chemical interaction between the neutral atmosphere and the ionized gas and simulates wave-induced variations in the electron density and the vertical distribution of the H3+ ions. The output is used in a radiative transfer scheme to predict observable wave-driven variations in the intensity of the H3+ emission of Jupiter and Saturn. We will analyze spectral maps of Jupiter's non-auroral H3+ emission, as well as limb observations of the North Polar region to search for wave activity in the Jovian ionosphere. This analysis will provide information on the spectral characteristics of the present wave modes, their amplitude, and direction of propagation. It will help us understand the structure and the dynamics of the ionospheres of giant planets and will provide input information for current Global Circulation Models of the upper atmosphere of Jupiter and Saturn. The outcome of this project can lead to the design and the proposal of innovative techniques to study the aeronomy of Solar system planets from ground and space.

Description: A MULTI-YEAR DATA SET OF THE DIURNAL CYCLE OF SEA SURFACE TEMPERATURE VARIABILITY AND IMPACTS ON SURFACE FLUXES The goal of the proposed research is to produce increased understanding of the diurnal cycle of sea surface temperature, including its temporal and spatial variability, and its effect on surface fluxes. The scientific objectives we anticipate completing include: - Creation of a global field of SST at a fine temporal (3-hourly) and spatial resolution from mid-1987 through the present. These fields will resolve the diurnal cycle of SST with minimum bias and consistent error characteristics. The final data set will then be compared globally with previous long-term data sets (principally the Reynolds data set) for differences in daytime and nighttime values and daily mean values throughout the time period covered. We will also compare the daily and longer timescale means from this data set and previously developed satellite SST fields with in situ data in expectation that the higher temporal resolution will improve mean temperature fields. Analysis of the temporal and spatial variability of diurnal warming throughout the global oceans. A short time series analysis has already indicated substantial temporal and spatial variability in the diurnal warming, with possible connections to such large-scale changes as ENSO and smaller-scale variability such as the Madden-Julian Oscillation. These types of analyses will be greatly enhanced by both the expanded length of the data series and also the increased spatial domain. The use of additional statistical techniques will allow for increased understanding of the scales of variability in the diurnal warming, and connections to synoptic to interannual events. - Evaluation of effect of higher temporal resolution on surface fluxes. A comparison of the completed data set with previously-derived data sets and the effect on surface fluxes at all spatial and temporal scales will be performed. Comparisons with in situ data will indicate the extent to which the higher resolution sea surface temperatures impact and improve the representation of the fluxes. Reducing error in SST analyses is one aspect of the Climate Variability and Change roadmap. This improved data set can be used for evaluating or forcing climate or ocean models, and for continued improvement in our conceptual understanding of the mechanisms by which the ocean and atmosphere affect each other. The SST impacts the water cycle through the latent heat flux, thus the improved data set and an understanding of the variability of the diurnal warming and its effect on fluxes will contain information for understanding how the global water cycle is changing. The Climate Variability and Change program foci such as forcing and feedback assessment, data assimilation as the models reproduce the diurnal variability, and improved water cycle estimates, will find the data set useful, and this data is in direct support of researchers addressing the global ocean circulation variability on shorter to climatic time scales.

Description: IMPROVED SATELLITE SST RETRIEVALS  Objectives: To characterize error sources in SST retrievals with particular focus on areas where retrievals are compromised by complexities of the intervening atmosphere or upper ocean properties, e.g. high and low latitudes, coastal upwelling areas and aerosol-perturbed environments. Background This proposal responds to the need for reduced error budget in sea surface temperaasre and proper eherseterization of current sensors for future instrumentation development, as outlined in the NASA ROSES "Remote Sensing Science for Carbon and Climate" announcement of opportunity. The measurement of SST by satellite-based infrared radiometry is a relatively mature subject and current uncertainties in the retrievals (bias errors of <0.2K with a scatter of 0.3-0.5K)approach those that are required for climate research. However, these estimates of accuracy are specified on a global basis and result from the application of globally-optimized atmospheric correction algorithms. There is evidence that the accuracy of the retrievals could be markedly improved by developing such algorithms with regional and temporal optimization, especially in situations whicb are known to introduce larger errors into the current retrievals. These include areas of heavy atmospheric aerosol burden such as the Saharan Dust OuMow (which is frequently accompanied by an anomalous distribution of water vapor in the very dry Saharan Air Layer in the middle troposphere which in itself also introduces a pathological situation for the infrared atmospheric correction algorithm), areas of coastal upwelling where anomalous$ large air-sea temperahre diltfferences can be found, areas of dry, high-latitude atmospheres where the atmospheric effects that require correction are not dominated by water vapor, and Equatorial areas where the confluence of atmospheric water vapor and enhanced local evaporation lead to high water vapor burdens, relatively low infrared transmissions and situations where the infrared radiance measured at the satellite height is dominated by atmospheric, rather than surface, emission. One of the criteria required of sateuite-derived variables for climate research is traceability to a national reference standard, so that confidence can be built in the quantitative retrievals that originate from several satellite sensors. In terms sf SST, this is achieved by compr~isonb etween the satellite-derived fields and collocated, contemporaneous measurements from ship-board spectro-radiometers with NIST traceable calibration. The premier instrument is the MarineAtmospheric Emitted Radiance Interferometer (M-AERI) that was developed for the validation of the SSTs derived from MODIS measurements. The three M-AERIs are very stable, extremely-well calibrated Fourier-Transform Infrared interferometers that have an excellent track record of providing high-quality measurements of the ocean skin SST from a wide range of ships. With funding from the NOPP, we are developing a robust biameter, tte iiifrared Scanning Autonomous Radiometer 0w,hich will also have NIST-traceability by virtue of the MST-characterized infrared calibration facilities at the University of Miami. Work Plan: We propose to install the M-AERls (3) and ISARs (2) on research vessels and ships of the Voluntary Observing Fleet in areas of greatest SST retrieval uncertainties. This builds on, and is complementary to, the NASA-funded work on MODIS SST algorithm maintenance and AIRS SST validation. This proposal extends the activities currently underway for MODIS to other sensors, including AVHRR, AASTR, and AMSR-E. It exploits the capital investment already made by NASA in the development of the M-AERIs and ISARs, the refinements of the measurement and analyses protocols and procedures, and in providing NIST-traceabaity to the measurements, both from ships and from satellites.

Description: RADIOMETRIC CONSISTENCY FOR MULTI-SATELLITE CONSTELLATIONS This proposal is to develop analytical cross-calibration techniques for cooperative satellites within a multi-satellite Global Precipitation Mission (GPM) constellation. Fur GPM, the data from multiple satellite instruments are to be merged into a self-consistent precipitation product, therefore this research is necessary to assure that the instrument radiometric calibrations are likewise made self-consistent. Under the previous Precipitation Measurements Mission science team activities, we have developed a template-based algorithm to search efficiently for coincidences between any pair of satellites with any given time difference. However, when two satellites simultaneously view the same point, generally they have similar, but not identical, observation parameters such as frequency, polarization and view angle. To accommodate these difrerences, we have developed several candidate algorithms, which predict the ocean brightness temperature observations from one satellite based on the observations of another. Comparison between observed and predicted radiances between two systems can establish cross-calibration consistency. This proposal is to extend the previous results by conducting comprehensive inter-satellite radiometric comparisons between the existing passive microwave imagers TMI, SSM, SSMIS, AMSR and WindSat. Based upon these studies, we propose to evaluate and refine the current candidate algorithms. Further, we will extend our algorithms to include other natural targets such as tropical rain forest, sea ice and glaciers. Finally, we will investigate the effects of radiometric calibration errors on merged precipitation products.

Description: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDE/REFRACTORY CARBIDE CER-CER FUELS.  IN THIS PROPOSAL, A NEW CARBIDE-BASED FUEL IS INTRODUCED WITH OUTSTANDING POTENTIAL TO ELIMINATE THE LOSS OF URANIUM, MINIMIZES THE LOSS OF URANIUM AND RETAINS FISSION PRODUCTS FOR MANY HOURS OF OPERATION IN HYDROGEN ENVIRONMENT AT TEMPERATURES IN EXCESS OF 3,200K.  THE PROPOSED FUEL IS A CERAMIC-CERAMIC (CERCER) COMPOSITE OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS (U,ZR)C OR (U,ZR,NB)C IN A MATRIX OF REFRACTORY CARBIDES THAT MOSTLY INCLUDE TRANSITION METAL CARBIDES SUCH AS ZRC, NBC, TAC AND HFC.  DUE TO ITS LOW NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION, ZRC IS THE PRIMARY REFRACTORY CARBIDE OF CHOICE.  REPLACING ZRC WITH HIGHER TEMPERATURE REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS TAC AND HFC COULD FURTHER IMPROVE THE HIGH TEMPERATURE PERFORMANCE OF CERCER FUELS.  HOWEVER, HIGHER NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION PENALTY FOR A TA AND HF COULD POTENTIALLY OFFSET THE PERFORMANCE ENHANCEMENT GAIN.  DUE TO COMPLETE CONTAINMENT AND ENCAPSULATION OF MIXED URANIUM CARBIDE IN ZIRCONIUM CARBIDE MATRIX, THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL COULD BE CONVENIENTLY FABRICATED TO DIFFERENT GEOMETRIAL SHAPES SUCH AS SOLID BLOCK PRISMATIC, TWISTED RIBBON, PEBBLES, WAFER OR SQUARE LATTICE HONEYCOMB.  CONSIDERING THE OPERATIONAL PARAMETERS FOR THE NT/BP SYSTEMS, IT IS REASONABLE TO ARGUE THAT THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL CONCEPT COULD SET THE PROPER MATERIAL PERFORMANCE LIMITS WHILE PROVIDING MORE FLEXIBILITY IN THE GEOMETRICAL DESIGN OF THE FUEL.

Description: We propose a three-year study to develop advanced zero-net mass-flux (ZNMF) actuators and validated design tools for active flow control applications. Active flow control is the foundation of future innovative aerodynamic concepts for improved vehicle efficiency. However, the active flow control community generally lacks efficient, powerful actuators and, more importantly, corresponding validated design methodologies capable of demonstrating potential benefits at realistic vehicle flight Mach numbers and Reynolds numbers. This proposal brings together a multidisciplinary team with expertise in electromechanical transducers, lumped element modeling, CFD, and experimental fluid dynamics to model, design, fabricate, and test advanced ZNMF actuators that use different transduction schemes: including piezoelectric and electrodynamic. The outcome of this research is a validated constrained design optimization tool that enables a class of robust ZNMF actuators for deployment on a larger scale.

Description: Understanding the Spectrum and Anisotropy of Termination Shock Particles Observed by Voyagers We propose to make model calculation of low-energy termination shock particles (TSP) and anomalous cosmic rays (ACR), in hope to maximize science return from Voyager observations in the heliosheath. Our goal is to understand how energetic particles are accelerated and how they propagate near the termination shock including the foreshock region and heliosheath. With these understandings we can more effectively use energetic particles to probe the heliosheath. These issues are central to the Voyager mission exploring the final frontier of the solar system and the outcome will benefit other Sun-Earth connection programs, because NASA wants to know the space environment where Earth and its magnetosphere reside. Our goal will be achieved by simulating particle propagation using a stochastic differential equation of particle transport, which includes pitch-angle diffusion and particle acceleration. The simulation permits us to get the exactly solution to the full particle transport equation. We will calculate particle distribution function, energy spectrum and anisotropy. The calculation results will be compared with Voyager observations to gain understanding of the physics of heliosheath. Specific tasks that will lead us to the goal are: i Develop computational codes to solve 3-d particle transport equation with pitch-angle diffusion and particle acceleration. Test the codes with special cases. i Build and run models for particle acceleration and propagation near the termination shock. The models include some of popular ideas put forward by the community, e.g., (1) non spherical shock with upstream field lines intersecting the shock at one or both ends, (2) dynamic termination shock under the influence of GMIR, and (3) particle transport through the current sheet. i Compare the calculation results with observations, such as the particle spectrum and anisotropy, to figure out the physics related to particle acceleration and termination shock. Description: Our central objective relates to genesis of tropical storms/hurricanes from African waves. The three major tools for this study are i) NAMMA's special observations, ii) data assimilation both regional and global and iii) very high resolution mesoscale models. The specialized NAMMA observations include those from NASA's DC-8, ER2 and satellites: TRMM, AIRS/AQUA, AMSRIE, MODIS, DMSP/SSMI. This provides a rich database (temperature, moisture and winds) for the assimilation of African waves. The FSU Global Spectral Model at a high resolution carries a variational data assimilation component. The mesoscale model is NCAR's WRF which includes a 4D variational data assimilation component. Mesoscale resolution approaching a kilometer will be used in these proposed studies. The goal is to cover the entire field phase period of NAMMA and follow disturbances from their incipient stage over Africa to their genesis stage over the Atlantic Ocean. In effect the mesoscale domain will move following these disturbances. The understanding of storms will require us to implement a state-of-the-art diagnostics in order to follow the storm's life cycle. The superdiagnostics carries a suite of model output interrogation algorithms. These include i) role of diabatic PV components on the spin-up of storm relative vorticity during genesis, ii) depletion of outer angular momentum by torques (such as cloud torques) during genesis, iii) the evolution of the organization of convection as the genesis is encountered (this manifests in the growth of low wave numbers along the azimuthal coordinate, iv) possible contributions to the destruction of organization of convection by the incursion of dust aerosols into the passing disturbance. (This will also require radiative transfer computations with aerosol effects), v) effect of dry air intrusion, vi) effect of encountering warm/cold pockets of SST anomalies along the pathways of the African wave, vii) the standard question on the effects of vertical shear of the horizontal wind and viii) model sensitivity to the inclusion of newer datasets (This component addresses data assimilation for NAMMA observational platforms). Our study is designed to address the following specific NAMMA-06 objectives: i) characterization of precipitation processes in the West African region and adjacent eastern Atlantic, with specific focus on the transition of convective systems from continental to maritime and ii) tropical cyclogenesis in the eastern and central Atlantic. Funding is requested in years two and three only.

Description: Debris disks are composed of dust particles that are not primordial but are continually replenished by the erosion of their planetesimal populations. These dust particles may be produced by the collisional destruction of planetesimals or by cometary activity. Debris disks therefore provide a natural laboratory for studying the combined dynamical and collisional behavior of dust particles. The solar system's debris disk, better known as the zodiacal cloud, is just an example of a debris disk that is much older than those that are typically observed around stars other than the Sun. Surprisingly, several basic questions regarding the provenance and evolution of the solar system's debris disk have still not been resolved: (1) Is the bulk of the zodiacal cloud asteroidal or cometary in origin, or a mixture of both? (2) Is the asteroidal contribution to the zodiacal cloud produced by the gradual collisional grinding down of asteroids over time or by violent stochastic events? (3) How does the cross-sectional area of material in the zodiacal cloud vary with time? The goal of this proposal is to develop answers to these 3 basic questions and the key to unraveling these answers lies in first understanding the origin and structure of the solar system dust bands. The solar system dust bands were discovered by the IRAS and their asteroidal origin quickly established. The dust bands are of fundamental importance because they represent the "tip of the iceberg" of the total contribution of asteroidal dust to the zodiacal cloud, and hence provide a direct source of information on the origin of particles in the cloud. A more complete understanding of the solar system dust bands is therefore not only of intrinsic value, but also of wider value in investigating the zodiacal cloud as whole. An exciting recent development in this area has been the discovery of several young asteroid clusters, less than 10 million years old, some of which have now been identified as potential sources of the IRAS dust bands. Our approach to building detailed models of the zodiacal cloud is to utilize the results from numerical simulations of the dynamical and collisional behavior of its constituent dust particles. This proposal focuses on building models of the zodiacal cloud using this numerical simulation data. This requires determining the three-dimensional spatial distribution of the cross-sectional area of material produced by the size and orbital element distributions of the dust particles. The flux from this spatial distribution of material is then visualized, taking into account the thermal and optical properties of the particles and their variation with particle size, composition and structure. Using this tool, which has already been developed, various viewing geometries can be specified, allowing images and flux profiles to be created that can be compared with observations. A wealth of archival data is available that we are challenged to reproduce and explain using these models. In this work, we aim to exploit the IRAS, COBE, and MSX datasets, which together provide a comprehensive and complementary database of information. We will also incorporate Spitzer data as it becomes available. These observations provide information on the global structure of the zodiacal cloud as well as details of fine structure, such as the dust bands, that we extract using a well established Fourier analysis technique. The specific objective of this research is to better understand the origin, structure, and evolution of the zodiacal cloud. Models produced as a result of this work will be made available to the research community. This research also has broader application to the study of other mature debris disks. Developing a better understanding of the zodiacal cloud, and building models of a debris disk that is well constrained by observational data, is an excellent starting point for developing a deeper understanding of exozodiacal clouds around other stars.

Description: The proposed research is in the area "mesoscale precipitation initialization" for improving hurricane and monsoon (heavy rain) forecasts. This entails the development of physical initialization (for nowcasting of rain rates using TRMM datasets) and using Newtonian relaxation and variational data assimilation methods already being developed at FSU. A comparison of these methods and studies of impacts of the initialization for high resolution short range (2-3 days) forecast will be an additional goal. Furthermore, an application of these findings will be incorporated into high resolution state-of-the-art mesoscale models to construct a multimodel mesoscale superensemble to enhance the prediction of hurricane intensity and precipitation. We propose to do the following: Assimilation of brightness temperatures by ECMWF and total precipitable water by NCEPEMC for improving precipitation initialization has limitations. If those products are validated against the NASA TRiiM (2A12 or 3B42) we find rather large errors in nowcasting of rain. The Newtonian relaxation appears to directly nudge TRMM rainfall products much more effectively. (Note: In our current TRMM research, we note that the correlation of model rain versus those from TRMM estimates are of the order 0.90 for the Newtonian relaxation where those values were as low as 0.30 for the variational data assimilation.) These differences between variational data assimilations based precipitation initialization and those based on FSUs Newtonian relaxation will be examined. These results extend to short range forecasts. The major proposed research will be on mesoscale modeling (including physical initialization of rain rates) for studies of hurricane and heavy rain related floods over the monsoon region. This will utilize the FSU Global Spectral Model at a horizontal resolution of T255 with a grid separation of - 50 km. Two regional mesoscale models WRF and HWRF (also subject to physical initialization) will be run at horizontal resolutions less than 5 km and will be driven by global model forecasts. Specifically we will address sensitivities for improving mesoscale forecasts from satellite based datasets (precipitation, moisture profiling, QuikSCAT winds and high resolution SSTs), data assimilation and model physics (especially related to precipitation processes). The final component of the proposed work will deal with the study of interaction among the diurnal wave and synoptic scale waves to improve the diurnal modulation of precipitation within heavy rainfall monsoon events, tropical disturbances and hurricanes. These results would help us to better forecast hurricane intensity. The proposed research addresses NASA objectives under the PMM in the category ;precipitation variability and its relationship to climate diagnostics and change; with emphasis on development of new data analysis and modeling techniques for detecting acceleration in water cycling through the atmosphere and the Earth's surface.

Description: Our central objective relates to genesis of tropical storms/hurricanes from African waves. The three major tools for this study are i) NAMMA's special observations, ii) data assimilation both regional and global and iii) very high resolution mesoscale models. The specialized NAMMA observations include those from NASA's DC-8, ER2 and satellites: TRMM, AIRS/AQUA, AMSRIE, MODIS, DMSP/SSMI. This provides a rich database (temperature, moisture and winds) for the assimilation of African waves. The FSU Global Spectral Model at a high resolution carries a variational data assimilation component. The mesoscale model is NCAR's WRF which includes a 4D variational data assimilation component. Mesoscale resolution approaching a kilometer will be used in these proposed studies. The goal is to cover the entire field phase period of NAMMA and follow disturbances from their incipient stage over Africa to their genesis stage over the Atlantic Ocean. In effect the mesoscale domain will move following these disturbances. The understanding of storms will require us to implement a state-of-the-art diagnostics in order to follow the storm's life cycle. The superdiagnostics carries a suite of model output interrogation algorithms. These include i) role of diabatic PV components on the spin-up of storm relative vorticity during genesis, ii) depletion of outer angular momentum by torques (such as cloud torques) during genesis, iii) the evolution of the organization of convection as the genesis is encountered (this manifests in the growth of low wave numbers along the azimuthal coordinate, iv) possible contributions to the destruction of organization of convection by the incursion of dust aerosols into the passing disturbance. (This will also require radiative transfer computations with aerosol effects), v) effect of dry air intrusion, vi) effect of encountering warm/cold pockets of SST anomalies along the pathways of the African wave, vii) the standard question on the effects of vertical shear of the horizontal wind and viii) model sensitivity to the inclusion of newer datasets (This component addresses data assimilation for NAMMA observational platforms). Our study is designed to address the following specific NAMMA-06 objectives: i) characterization of precipitation processes in the West African region and adjacent eastern Atlantic, with specific focus on the transition of convective systems from continental to maritime and ii) tropical cyclogenesis in the eastern and central Atlantic. Funding is requested in years two and three only.

Description: PROBING THE BASIC PHYSICS OF ECTRAGALACTIC JETS Relativistic jets appear to be a ubiquitous result of accretion onto compact objects. The jets of active galactic nuclei (AGN) axe enormously powerful, transporting energy from the sub-parsec scale regions surrounding the central black hole to radio lobes many times larger than the host galaxy. Their total bolometric power output is often comparable to or greater than that from the host galaxy, and the kinetic energy flux can be comparable to the AGN's bolometric luminosity (Rawlings & Saunders 1991). Interactions between jets and the interstellar medium through which they propagate can profoundly influence the jets themselves as well as the host galaxy's appearance and structure. Their most extreme properties, seen in blazars, are variability (Ulrich, Maraschi & Urry 1997) and apparently superluminally moving components (Vermeulen & Cohen 1994; Biretta, Sparks Sz Macchetto 1999). Due to the high polarizations observed in the radio and optical, the jet emission in those bands is interpreted as synchrotron radiation (e.g. Roser & Meisenheimer 1991). Until the last decade, almost all progi-ess towards understanding the physics of jets had come either from numerical modeling or multi-frequency radio mapping. However, the pace of discovery has accelerated greatly in the past decade with HST and Chandra observations. The very first observation by Chandra is a perfect illustration: the target, PKS 0637-752, was a bright radio-loud quasai-. It was believed that this source would be unresolved in the X-rays, and therefore ideally suited to focus the telescope. Instead, we saw a beautiful X-ray jet well over 10 arcseconds long (Chartas et al. 2000, Schwartz et al. 2000), with morphology quite similar to that seen in the radio. Indeed, since the launch of the two Great Observatories, the number of jets known to emit in the optical and X-rays has increased about ten-fold, from less than 5 to more than three dozen, including members of every luminosity and morphological class of radio-loud AGN. This explosion in the number of known optical and X-ray jets has been accompanied by a large increase in our knowledge about these objects. Even though the presence of relativistic particles in the jets is implied by their radio emission alone, meaningful constraints on physical parameters - e.g., kinematics, structure, orientation and composition - can be gained only through multiwaveband observations, which break the degeneracy that can result from interpreting singleband observations. For example, because of the long radiative lifetimes (10 years) of radio synchrotron emitting electrons, radio emission responds only to an integral of particle acceleration in the upstream jet. Optical synchrotron emitters are much shorter-lived (hundreds of years) and thus can only ai'ise close to particle acceleration regions. The X-ray emission can either be synchrotron (with even shorter radiative lifetimes) or inverse-Compton. In either case, X-ray emissions give a third, independent set of constraints, because they represent either the most dynamic component of the jet, or an entirely separate spectral component, which still must be linked to the radio emission.

Description: Atmospheric Sciences/University of Miami Whole Air Sampling and Analysis During the Tropical Composition, Cloud, and Climate-Coupling (TC4) Experiment We propose to investigate the sources, distributions, and relationships of chemical species in the upper troposphere/lower stratosphere during the TC4 mission by measurement of multiple trace gases from whole air samples collected on the WB-57 aircraft. Up to 50 whole air samples will be collected either in predetermined sequence or on command to study the chemical environment associated with convection, cirrus formation and related processes, and aerosol composition. A large range of trace gases of different chemical lifetimes and that have either natural and anthropogenic emissions will be used to evaluate source regions, air mass transport, and chemical gradients in the upper troposphere and across the tropical tropopause region. The measurements provide needed information on the role of short-lived halogen compounds to the chemistry of the UT/LS. Further, the measurement of hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) with significant tropospheric trends will help define the age spectrum of air in the TTL region. The samples will be analyzed for methane and non-methane hydrocarbons, halocarbons, organic nitrates, CO, N2O, and other relevant trace gases using a combination of instruments based on gas chromatography with mass spectrometric and other detection systems.

Description: WILL SLOWING OF THE MOC WARM OR COOL EUROPE? SUMMARY: This is a high-risk, high pay-off mini proposal for exploratory research of the atmospheric response to a (potential) slow down of the meridional overturning cell (MOC). Our recent analyticalcalculations suggest that, in contrast to what the global numerical climate models redict, a slow down of the MOC will cause Europe to warm, not cool. As in the numerical models, the analytically modeled slow down is accompanied by a reduced heat flux to the atmosphere. However, thisreduced amount of heat is applied to a significantly smaller amount of air. We hypothesize that the strong horizontal diffusion that is unavoidably employed by the numerical simulations camouflages the local warming by mixing the negative heat flux anomaly around making it appear as if there is merely a broad cooling.  We propose to spend up to one year exploring this new and unconventional hypothesis. This will be done in three stages. First, in line with the (admittedly controversial) suggestion made recently by Bryden et al. (2005) that the MOC has slowed down during the last 50 years, we will push our preliminary analytical efforts to the point where the most realistic, yet still clear, answers are provided. Second, we will examine the records of atmospheric temperatures in various European stations downstream of the convection sites. This will enable us to see whether these regions warmed or cooled during the last 50 years. (According to conventional wisdom, Europe didn't cool during the last 50 years.) Third, we will analytically model the atmospheric diffusion to see whether the numerical diffusion is indeed large enough to spread a negative heat anomaly around to the extent that a local warming is wiped out. Should the results of this exploratory work prove useful, a full regular proposal will be submitted within a year.

Description: SCUBA SCOUTS USA OF TAMPA BAY: EDUCTION THROUGH EXPERIENCE FOR THE NEXT GENERATION OF EARTH EXPLORERS American students have decreasing interest in science, math and technology professions. The Scuba Scouts USA program was established to increase the attraction to science and technology careers in today's youth. Scuba Scouts USA of Tampa Bay, a non-profit 501(c)3 organization formed in 2001, consists of a diverse group of young men and women (ages 12-18) mentored by federal, state and academic research scientists in an informal education environment. The program's mission is to expand and promote opportunities for young and emerging explorers by involving them in the marine sciences through underwater exploration and research activities, such as special environmental and undersea conservation projects that educate, promote active citizenship, and develop effective leadership skills. This proposal seeks to secure funding for the Scuba Scouts USA of Tampa Bay to support their education and outreach goals, which includes providing research-quality data to meet the needs of ocean scientists, and maintaining direct interaction between the two groups. Specifically, the Scuba Scouts will be collecting optical data to monitor water column and benthic community health on a monthly basis for Tampa Bay and the nearby Gulf of Mexico, in addition to summer expeditions to create and validate benthic habitat maps of coral reef environments produced from remote sensing imagery. The scuba scouts are tasked with sharing their experiences to raise the environmental awareness of a larger audience by providing education outreach in formal and informal venues. Finally, the lessons learned here will be shared with interested parties wishing to begin their own Scuba Scout entity, accomplished by an openly available manual of Standard Operating Procedures. The overarching goal of the Scuba Scouts is to provide a diverse group of young men and women the wisdom and tools to become the next generation of explorers.

Description: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDE/REFRACTORY CARBIDE CER-CER FUELS.  IN THIS PROPOSAL, A NEW CARBIDE-BASED FUEL IS INTRODUCED WITH OUTSTANDING POTENTIAL TO ELIMINATE THE LOSS OF URANIUM, MINIMIZES THE LOSS OF URANIUM AND RETAINS FISSION PRODUCTS FOR MANY HOURS OF OPERATION IN HYDROGEN ENVIRONMENT AT TEMPERATURES IN EXCESS OF 3,200K.  THE PROPOSED FUEL IS A CERAMIC-CERAMIC (CERCER) COMPOSITE OF MIXED URANIUM-REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS (U,ZR)C OR (U,ZR,NB)C IN A MATRIX OF REFRACTORY CARBIDES THAT MOSTLY INCLUDE TRANSITION METAL CARBIDES SUCH AS ZRC, NBC, TAC AND HFC.  DUE TO ITS LOW NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION, ZRC IS THE PRIMARY REFRACTORY CARBIDE OF CHOICE.  REPLACING ZRC WITH HIGHER TEMPERATURE REFRACTORY CARBIDES SUCH AS TAC AND HFC COULD FURTHER IMPROVE THE HIGH TEMPERATURE PERFORMANCE OF CERCER FUELS.  HOWEVER, HIGHER NEUTRON ABSORPTION CROSS-SECTION PENALTY FOR A TA AND HF COULD POTENTIALLY OFFSET THE PERFORMANCE ENHANCEMENT GAIN.  DUE TO COMPLETE CONTAINMENT AND ENCAPSULATION OF MIXED URANIUM CARBIDE IN ZIRCONIUM CARBIDE MATRIX, THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL COULD BE CONVENIENTLY FABRICATED TO DIFFERENT GEOMETRIAL SHAPES SUCH AS SOLID BLOCK PRISMATIC, TWISTED RIBBON, PEBBLES, WAFER OR SQUARE LATTICE HONEYCOMB.  CONSIDERING THE OPERATIONAL PARAMETERS FOR THE NT/BP SYSTEMS, IT IS REASONABLE TO ARGUE THAT THE PROPOSED CERCER FUEL CONCEPT COULD SET THE PROPER MATERIAL PERFORMANCE LIMITS WHILE PROVIDING MORE FLEXIBILITY IN THE GEOMETRICAL DESIGN OF THE FUEL.

Description: The Pacific-North American (Pa-NA) plate boundary zone is a complex, multipart system having dynamic interactions with surrounding areas. To better describe and understand the intricacies of this boundary it is necessary to divide it into discrete regions and analyze their interaction. This is an oblique transform boundary, with mainly strike slip motion coupled with extension. Two areas of interest to me are Northern Baja California, Mexico and the Sierra Nevada Block (SNB). Northern Baja California is defined by a complex fault system positioned west of the Pa-NA plate boundary; intimately associated with the spreading center within the Gulf of California as well as the southern extension of the San Andreas Fault (SAF). In a preliminary study I focus on the normal faulting components of the region. I analyzed 7 years of campaign GPS data from a network of stations located throughout the area to characterize the kinematic motion of the San Pedro Martir fault, a normal fault on the East coast of the peninsula. I calculated the expected isostatic uplift magnitude and distribution in response to unloading that occurs along a normal fault due to crustal thinning. We obtained our solution using a two stage calculation procedure, the first of which was an elastic half space model, which allowed me to define the spreading rate and locking depth of the fault. The second stage of calculations applied the calculated mass removal and uplift magnitude from purely kinematic means, to an elastic plate bending model. The results indicate a misfit of data to model at the fault axis. This mismatch indicates an additional unmodeled uplift process, most likely with a deeper, mantle source. I propose that with new GPS data and a more sophisticated, multi-fault Finite Element Model it may be possible to define the strain partitioning within this region as well as to identify the uplift source (eg small scale convection or delamination) and quantify a more precise magnitude. The SNB is a long, narrow block, bounded on the west by the SAF, on the east by a complex fault system comprising the Eastern California Shear Zone and the Walker Lane Belt, and on the south by the Garlock fault. The northern extent of the block is not well defined. Also, previously published estimates for the motion of SNB include clockwise, counter-clockwise and no rotation relative to stable North America; new velocity data may also help to resolve this discrepancy. I present a new surface velocity field for California and Nevada and use it to solve for a new angular velocity for the rigid SNB. We use all publicly available GPS data for this region, from both continuous and episodic sites. I propose that new data and a strain accumulation algorithm may help to define the northern boundary as well as to characterize a more accurate Euler Vector for the block. This may give us better insight into the dynamics of the Pa-NA system and the role of the SNB within it.

Description: High velocity outflows are ubiquitous in quasars and an important part of SMBH evolution. They might even be necessary to carry away angular momentum and facilitate disk accretion. Studies of broad absorption line (BAL) quasars have revealed large X-ray absorbing columns and some tentative UV-X-ray correlations consistent with radiative acceleration in accretion disk winds. But BALs are only part of the story - sampling a narrow range of flow types or viewing angles. We propose XMM observations of quasars with high-velocity mini-BALs and weak/borderline BALs to extend the range of measured outflow parameters, test the BAL correlations/physical models, and solidify constraints on the global wind geometry, orientation, acceleration, mass loss rates, launch radii, etc.

Description: DEVELOPING A SNOW CLOUD DATABASE USING CLOUDSAT AND OTHER A-TRAIN DATA FOR GLOBAL SNOWFALL RETRIEVALS In the high latitudes during cold seasons, a substantial portion of precipitation falls in the form of snow. Measuring snow precipitation has many applications such as forecasting hazardous weather, understanding hydrological water budget and evaluating the cooling and freshening effects of snow onto ocean surface. However, unlike rainfall, snowfall measurement is extremely limited due to technical difflculties. Over ocean and in the uninhabited polar regions, perhaps there is no snowfall observation of any kind. The CloudSat Cloud Profiling Radar (CPR) is the first spaceborne radar orbiting the high latitudes and has the sensitivity to detect snowfall. The CloudSat mission thus provides a great opportunity to measure snowfall from space. First, the radar reflectivity can be used to retrieve snowfall. Second, the snow profile statistics derived from CPR can be used to build a snow cloud database that can be used to develop snowfall retrieval algorithms for other remote sensors, such as high frequency microwave  radiometers available on current and future satellites. Given the fact that CPR only observes a 1.S km width strip with each orbit, the second application seems to be more important for global snowfall measurement. We have been developing a snowfall retrieval algorithm using high frequency (8S GHz) microwave data from aircraft and satellite for the past several years. Based on the experience gained from the above exercise, we propose to develop a snow cloud database using CloudSat and other A-train data over a global (excluding areas where it never snows) scale. This database will benefit all precipitation retrieval and modeling community. The proposed research consists of the following components: (1) Develop a radar reflectivity (Z) - snowfall rate (S) relation for CloudSat CPR based on backscattering of nonsphcrical snowflakes calculated using DDA modeling. (2) Derive snowfall rate profiles from the Z-S relation. By combing AMSR-E retrievals and numerical model analysis, we build a database of snow cloud profiles with snow and liquid cloud layers. (3) Perform radiative transfer modeling at high microwave frequencies, in which the nonsphericity of snowflakes is accounted. The snow cloud profiles and corresponding brightness temperatures constitute a priori database for further snowfall retrieval algorithm development using available satellite sensors, sucli as HSB (AQUA), SSMIS, and AMSU-B. It is noted that snowfall rate is not a standard product of CloudSat. Through this project, we provide not only CPR-based snowfall retrievals, but also an obscrvational-data-based database that can be used for developing snowfall retrieval algorithms. The PI has been working in the area of satellite remote sensing of cloud and precipitation for about 20 years. If selected, he is willing to serve as a member of the CloudSat science team
