Description: We propose to address the oceanic sink of carbon dioxide in the Arctic Ocean as parlof the International Polar Year (IPY). The North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans are believed to represent the largest ocean sink for atmospheric carbon dioxide in the Northern Hemisphere, yet the variability in oceanic uptake is poorly constrained. The Arctic is undergoing rapid change. The fate of vast stores of carbon previously frozen in the permafrost is a big unknown in future models. If released as carbon dioxide, will they be taken up locally? How will decreased ice cover impact the Arctic sink of atmospheric carbon dioxide? Here we propose to obtain improved fields of air-sea gas exchange in the Arctic basin. We will use QuikSCAT estimates of the Normalized Radar Cross-section (NRCS) to obtain ;,elds of gas transfer velocity at around 10 km daily resolution. These fields will be used to quantify seasonal and interannual variability in air-sea fluxes of C02 in the ice-free Arctic waters. We base our approach on the role of capillary waves in mediating gas transfer for intermediate wind speeds. The short capillary-gravity component, corresponding to roughly 2 cm surface waves of the wave field, usually dominates the Ku-band measurement made by QuikSCAT. In past work we have used air-sea transfer of carbon dioxide measured in situ during GasEx2001 and concurrent upwind NRCS (via the Geophysical NRCS-to-Wind Transfer Model Function) to obtain a NRCS-based transfer velocity. We found that the transfer velocity obtained from NRCS and that based on standard wind parameterizations were similar in mean and variance over the study area, indicating that they represent the same quantity. However, since the QuikSCAT upwind NRCS values are not averaged within a cell, they are obtained on a finer grid than the wind speed values. This enables us to carry out studies over shorter time scales and at finer spatial resolution than using wind, although the broad satellite coverage is conserved. Furthermore, the dynamic range of the NRCS-based transfer velocity is greater than in the wind-based estimates, indicating greater sensitivity to near-surface turbulence dynamics. In this project we will use data from two upcoming experiments with proposed involvement by the PIs (Drennan): the 2007 Canadian SOLAS Arctic program to the Arctic Archipelago and the 2008 Finnish IPY cruise to Svalbard. The C02 flux and ancillary data will be used to (1) fine tune our algorithm and apply it to turbulent conditions and (2) to provide an estimation of air-sea exchange in Arctic basins. The expanded database will lead to a novel estimate of gas transfer based on NRCS that is uniquely applicable to conditions in the Arctic or to comparable conditions. We will validate and compare our algorithm with independent in situ measurements as well as with standard wind based parameterizations.

Description: THREE DIMENSIONAL NUMERICAL AND EXPERIMENTAL INVESTIGATION OF ELASTIC-PLASTIC GROWTH AND DUCTILE TEARING MODELS FOR METALLIC ALLOYS In 2010 NASA plans to retire the Space Shuttle and employ the new Ares I crew launch vehicle. The propulsion systems for the Ares I, such as the 3-2X upper stage engine and the Reusable Solid Rocket Motor (RSRM), are of particular research Interest. In order to push the envelope of design, continued advancement in damage tolerance analysis and testing will be essential. Pressurized structures on the first and upper stages of the Ares I launch vehicle, such as the RSRM case, will be the focus of the proposed research. The reliability and reusability of these critical aerospace structures will rest substantially upon the ability to model the crack growth. Many models have been used for this application but have proved to be limited in versatility. The basis for this research is the evaluation of three dimensional numerical analysis methods of elastic-plastic crack growth and ductile tearing for the systematic development of an imminent failure/simulated- service proof test methodology for materials of interest to NASA.

Description: UNSTEADY CIRCULATION CONTROL FOR HIGH-PERFORMANCE, LOW-NOISE AIRCRAFT We propose to rigorously investigate the aerodynamic and aeroacoustic characteristics of unsteady circulation control (CC) configurations via wind tunnel tests incorporating fluid dynamic and phased microphone array measurements, numerical simulations, and acoustic analogy-based integral methods. A conventional CC airfoil uses steady trailing-edge momentum injection via the Coanda effect to achieve extremely high lift performance independent of aircraft speed. Here, we propose an extension to unsteady injection to reduce system mass flow requirements while maintaining low-noise aerodynamic performance. In particular, we will characterize the aeroacoustic behavior of the system, which has never been studied, and optimize the unsteady waveform shape for low-noise, high-lift performance. In Year 1 we will focus our attention on (1) a demonstration of the capability of unsteady circulation control on an existing elliptic airfoil and (2) initial prediction tool development. The ultimate goal of this research is to develop an advanced low-noise, high-lift system that will achieve NASAs long-term aircraft noise reduction goals. The unsteady CC airfoil accomplishes this by eliminating the noise sources associated with conventional high-lift flap/slat systems and, via high lift at low approach speeds, enabling an increase in the takeoff and approach angles, thereby substantially increasing the distance between the aircraft and the ground. If successful in Year 1, we will study a suitable blended wing body configuration in Years 2-3. In terms of tools, novel microphone array processing methods applicable to coherent and incoherent, point and distributed noise sources will be used and/or developed and rigorously compared. Hybrid LES/RANS schemes will be used to simulate and analyze the detailed unsteady flow behavior and acoustic noise source characteristics. Acoustic-analogy based integral methods will also be developed and validated to provide a prediction tool suitable for future design optimization.

Description: WIRELESS SHEAR-STRESS SENSOR ARRAY (STUDENT: JEREMY SELLS) Abstract: The proposed project for this fellowship involves design, fabrication and testing of wireless shear-stress sensors. The design and fabrication of individual sensors will be done in the first year. From there, testing of individual sensors and arrays of sensors will follow pending renewal of the fellowship. Each sensor is a Micro- Electromechanical system (MEMS) device comprising a floating element with interdigitated comb fingers at one end. Shear- stresses move the floating element causing a change in capacitance of the comb. Coupling with an embedded inductor will enable wireless detection. The change in capacitance, and thus the change in stress, is detected by tracking the resonant frequency of the LC tank. An array is realized through fabricating sensors with different inductors giving each individual sensor a unique starting resonance. Efforts will focus on the MEMS sensor design as well as the RF interrogation and signal processing strategies. Once achieved, this array will provide a method of capturing time-resolved, fluctuating shear- stress data in complex flow fields. The size of the device and the freedom from wires will allow them to be inlayed in thin, flexible substrates that will conformably adhere to the curved surface of an airframe.

Description: UNDERSTANDING THE PROCESSES WHICH CONTROL THE DISTRIBUTION AND RADIATIVE PROPERTIES OF CLOUDS IS ESSENTIAL FOR THE SUCCESSFUL MODELING OF EARTH'S CLIMATE. THE FEEDBACKS ASSOCIATED WITH TROPICAL CONVECTIVE AND BOUNDARY LAYER CLOUDS ARE PARTICULARLY IMPORTANT IN THIS REGARD AS THEY ARE BELIEVED TO PLAY A KEY ROLE IN DETERMINING THE RESPONSE OF THE CLIMATE SYSTEM TO AN INCREASE IN GREENHOUSE GASES. THE PREMISE OFTHIS PROPOSAL IS THAT THE BASIC PHYSICAL PROCESSES CONTROLLING THE DISTRIBUTION AND LIFECYCLE OF TROPICAL CLOUD SYSTEMS MUST BE LUIOWN BEFORE THEIR FEEDBACK ON CLIMATE CAN BE RELIABLY PREDICTED IN GCMS. TO ADDRESS THIS, WE PROPOSE AN INNOVATIVE METHOD OF COMBINING CLOUDSAT/CALIPSO MEASUREMENTS WITH LAGRANGIAN CLOUD TRAJECTORIES FROM GEOSTATIONARY SATELLITES AND MID-TROPOSPHERIC VERTICAL VELOCITY FROM OPERATIONAL ANALYSES TO EXAMINE THE LIFECYCLE OF TROPICAL CLOUD SYSTEMS, THEIR DEPENDENCE UPON DYNAMICAL REGIMES, AND THEIR IMPACTS ON THE RADIATIVE AND HYDROLOGIC BUDGETS. THE RESULTING DATA SETS WILL THEN BE USED TO ASSESS THE REPRESENTATION OF THESE PROCESSES IN THE GLOBAL CLIMATE MODELS (GCMS). BY INTEGRATING LAGRANGIAN CLOUD TRAJECTORIES AND DYNAMICAL COMPOSITING TECHNIQUES WITH 3-DIMENSIONAL CLOUD FIELDS FROM CLOUDSAT AND CALIPSO WE INTEND TO TEST AND ULTIMATELY IMPROVE THE REPRESENTATION OF TROPICAL CLOUDS IN THESE MODELS AND, IN SO DOING, REDUCE UNCERTAINTY IN THEIR SIMULATION OF CLOUD FEEDBACK. THE PRIMARY TASKS TO BE ACCOMPLISHED ARE: (1) COMPUTE THE FORWARD / BACKWARD TRAJECTORIES AND RELATED LAGRANGIAN DIAGNOSTICS FOR TROPICAL CONVECTIVE CLOUD SYSTEMS OBSERVED BY THE CLOUDSAT AND CALIPSO INSTRUMENTS. (2) USE LAGRANGIAN-BASED COMPOSITES TO: (A) CHARACTERIZE THE RADIATIVE, MACROPHYSICAL, AND MICROPHYSICAL EVOLUTION OF TROPICAL CLOUD SYSTEMS AND (B) ASSESS THE DEPENDENCE OF THE DETRAINED CIRRUS CLOUD PROPERTIES UPON THE CONVECTIVE SOURCES WHICH GENERATE THEM. (3) DIAGNOSE THE LOCAL ENVIRONMENTAL DEPENDENCES OF TROPICAL BOUNDARY LAYER CLOUD SYSTEMS OBSERVED BY CLOUDSAT / CALIPSO USING THE METHOD OF BONY ET AL. (2004). (4) EVALUATE THE ABILITY OF GCMS TO SIMULATE THE LIFECYCLE AND ENVIRONMENTAL DEPENDENCES OF TROPICAL CLOUD SYSTEMS, AND THEIR HYDROLOGIC AND RADIATIVE IMPACTS.

Description: METHANE HAS BEEN RECENTLY DETECTED IN THE MARTIAN ATMOSPHERE AT HETEROGENEOUSLY DISTRIBUTED LOCATIONS BUT AVERAGING APPROXIMATELY 10 PPB. HOWEVER, THE LIFETIME OF METHANE IN THE ATMOSPHERE OF MARS HAS BEEN ESTIMATED TO BE APPROXIMATELY ONLY 340 YEARS, AND, THUS, IT IS ARGUED THAT THE METHANE MUST BE CONSTANTLY REPLENISHED TO BE DETECTED. SEVERAL MECHANISMS FOR THE ONGOING PRODUCTION/RELEASE OF METHANE ON MARS HAVE BEEN PROPOSED, AND INCLUDE: ABIOGENIC PRODUCTION FROM HYDRATED OLIVINE IN THE MARTIAN REGOLITH, PHOTOLYSIS OF H20 IN THE PRESENCE OF CO, OUTGASSING OF MAGMATIC OR HYDROTHERMAL FEATURES, COMETARY IMPACTS, OUTGASSING OF CH4 FROM THE DEEP LITHOSPHERE, LOW-TEMPERATURE ALTERATION OF BASALTIC CRUST BY CARBON-BEARING HYDROTHERMAL FLUID, AND BIOGENIC METHANOGENESIS. SINCE THE DETECTION OF METHANE ON MARS IN 2004, NO REPORTS IN THE RECENT LITERATURE HAVE BEEN FOUND THAT PROPOSE THE W DEGRADATION OF ORGANIC MATERIALS ON MARS AS A SOURCE OF METHANE. THUS, WE WILL PROPOSE EXPERIMENTS TO TEST THE HYPOTHESIS THAT METHANE COULD BE PRODUCED ON MARS FROM THE UV DEGRADATION OF CARBONACEOUS MATERIALS INCLUDING CARBONATES, CARBONACEOUS METEORITES, AND INTERPLANETARY DUST PARTICLES (IDP). THESE EXPERIMENTS WILL BE CARRIED OUT IN A FULLY OPERATIONAL MARS CHAMBER AT THE KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, FI, (SCHUERGER LAB) THAT IS CAPABLE OF SIMULATING FIVE KEY COMPONENTS OF THE MARS SURFACE ENVIRONMENT INCLUDING: (A) PRESSURES DOWN TO 0.1 MH, (B) UVC, UVB, AND UVA IRRADIATION FROM 190 TO 400 NM, (C) DUST LOADING IN THE ATMOSPHERE FROM OPTICAL DEPTHS OF 0.1 (DUST-FREE SKY) TO 3.5 (GLOHAL DUST STORM), (D) TEMPERATURES FROM -100 TO +30 OC, AND (E) GAS COMPOSITION THAT SIMULATES THE TOP FIVE GASES IN THE MARTIAN ATMOSPHERE [C02 (95.3%), N2 (2.7%), AR (1.6%), 02 (0.2%) AND H20 (0.03%)]. THE MARS CHAMBER IS ALSO FITTED WITH A RESIDUAL GAS ANALYZER (RGA) CAPABLE OF DETECTING<0.5 PPM EACH OF A WIDE DIVERSITY OF VOLATILE UV BREAKDOWN PRODUCTS FROM 1 TO 200 AMU. THUS, WE WILL BE ABLE TO TRACK IN REAL-TIME THE VOLATILE EMISSIONS OF VARIOUS CARBONACEOUS MATERIALS RELEASED BY UV-IRRADIATION UNDER A DIVERSITY OF MARTIAN ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS. THE EXPERIMENTS WILL BE DESIGNED TO (I) TO CHARACTERIZE THE PRODUCTION OF CH4 FROM W-IRRADIATED ORGANICS MIXED INTO MARS ANALOG SOILS AND EXPOSED TO ROBUSTLY SIMULATED MARTIAN CONDITIONS: (2) DETERMINE THE EFFECTS OF MARS SURFACE ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS ON CH4 EVOLUTION INCLUDING HIGH UV IRRADIATION, LOW PRESSURE (7 TO 100 MB), LOW TEMPERATURE (-85 TO +20 C), AND MARS GAS COMPOSITION [C02 (95.3%), N2 (2.7%), AR (1.6%), 0 2 (0.13%) AND H20 (0.03%)]; (3) DETERMINE THE CHEMICAL BREAKDOWN PRODUCTS OF UV IRRADIATION OF ORGANICS TO ASSIST IN FUTURE ORGANIC DETECTION EXPERIMENTS ON MARS, (4) DETERMINE THE EFFECTS THAT REGOLITH COMPOSITION MIGHT HAVE ON THE UV-PHOTOCHEMICAL REACTIONS ON ORGANICS UNDER MARTIAN CONDITIONS, AND (5) CHARACTERIZE THE SPECTRAL CHANGES IN ORGANIC MATERIALS UNDER MARTIAN CONDITIONS OF HIGH UV AND LOW PRESSURE TO ASSIST IN THE ANALYSIS OF REMOTE SENSING DATA FROM MARS ORBITERS, LANDERS, AND ROVERS. RESULTS WILL MAKE IMMEDIATE AND RECT CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE PHOENIX AND MSL MISSIONS, AND SUPPORT SEVERAL KEY OBJECTIVES OF THE MARS EXPLORATION PROGRAM.

Description: METHANE HAS BEEN RECENTLY DETECTED IN THE MARTIAN ATMOSPHERE AT HETEROGENEOUSLY DISTRIBUTED LOCATIONS BUT AVERAGING APPROXIMATELY 10 PPB. HOWEVER, THE LIFETIME OF METHANE IN THE ATMOSPHERE OF MARS HAS BEEN ESTIMATED TO BE APPROXIMATELY ONLY 340 YEARS, AND, THUS, IT IS ARGUED THAT THE METHANE MUST BE CONSTANTLY REPLENISHED TO BE DETECTED. SEVERAL MECHANISMS FOR THE ONGOING PRODUCTION/RELEASE OF METHANE ON MARS HAVE BEEN PROPOSED, AND INCLUDE: ABIOGENIC PRODUCTION FROM HYDRATED OLIVINE IN THE MARTIAN REGOLITH, PHOTOLYSIS OF H20 IN THE PRESENCE OF CO, OUTGASSING OF MAGMATIC OR HYDROTHERMAL FEATURES, COMETARY IMPACTS, OUTGASSING OF CH4 FROM THE DEEP LITHOSPHERE, LOW-TEMPERATURE ALTERATION OF BASALTIC CRUST BY CARBON-BEARING HYDROTHERMAL FLUID, AND BIOGENIC METHANOGENESIS. SINCE THE DETECTION OF METHANE ON MARS IN 2004, NO REPORTS IN THE RECENT LITERATURE HAVE BEEN FOUND THAT PROPOSE THE W DEGRADATION OF ORGANIC MATERIALS ON MARS AS A SOURCE OF METHANE. THUS, WE WILL PROPOSE EXPERIMENTS TO TEST THE HYPOTHESIS THAT METHANE COULD BE PRODUCED ON MARS FROM THE UV DEGRADATION OF CARBONACEOUS MATERIALS INCLUDING CARBONATES, CARBONACEOUS METEORITES, AND INTERPLANETARY DUST PARTICLES (IDP). THESE EXPERIMENTS WILL BE CARRIED OUT IN A FULLY OPERATIONAL MARS CHAMBER AT THE KENNEDY SPACE CENTER, FI, (SCHUERGER LAB) THAT IS CAPABLE OF SIMULATING FIVE KEY COMPONENTS OF THE MARS SURFACE ENVIRONMENT INCLUDING: (A) PRESSURES DOWN TO 0.1 MH, (B) UVC, UVB, AND UVA IRRADIATION FROM 190 TO 400 NM, (C) DUST LOADING IN THE ATMOSPHERE FROM OPTICAL DEPTHS OF 0.1 (DUST-FREE SKY) TO 3.5 (GLOHAL DUST STORM), (D) TEMPERATURES FROM -100 TO +30 OC, AND (E) GAS COMPOSITION THAT SIMULATES THE TOP FIVE GASES IN THE MARTIAN ATMOSPHERE [C02 (95.3%), N2 (2.7%), AR (1.6%), 02 (0.2%) AND H20 (0.03%)]. THE MARS CHAMBER IS ALSO FITTED WITH A RESIDUAL GAS ANALYZER (RGA) CAPABLE OF DETECTING < 0.5 PPM EACH OF A WIDE DIVERSITY OF VOLATILE UV BREAKDOWN PRODUCTS FROM 1 TO 200 AMU. THUS, WE WILL BE ABLE TO TRACK IN REAL-TIME THE VOLATILE EMISSIONS OF VARIOUS CARBONACEOUS MATERIALS RELEASED BY UV-IRRADIATION UNDER A DIVERSITY OF MARTIAN ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS. THE EXPERIMENTS WILL BE DESIGNED TO (I) TO CHARACTERIZE THE PRODUCTION OF CH4 FROM W-IRRADIATED ORGANICS MIXED INTO MARS ANALOG SOILS AND EXPOSED TO ROBUSTLY SIMULATED MARTIAN CONDITIONS: (2) DETERMINE THE EFFECTS OF MARS SURFACE ENVIRONMENTAL CONDITIONS ON CH4 EVOLUTION INCLUDING HIGH UV IRRADIATION, LOW PRESSURE (7 TO 100 MB), LOW TEMPERATURE (-85 TO +20 C), AND MARS GAS COMPOSITION [C02 (95.3%), N2 (2.7%), AR (1.6%), 0 2 (0.13%) AND H20 (0.03%)]; (3) DETERMINE THE CHEMICAL BREAKDOWN PRODUCTS OF UV IRRADIATION OF ORGANICS TO ASSIST IN FUTURE ORGANIC DETECTION EXPERIMENTS ON MARS, (4) DETERMINE THE EFFECTS THAT REGOLITH COMPOSITION MIGHT HAVE ON THE UV-PHOTOCHEMICAL REACTIONS ON ORGANICS UNDER MARTIAN CONDITIONS, AND (5) CHARACTERIZE THE SPECTRAL CHANGES IN ORGANIC MATERIALS UNDER MARTIAN CONDITIONS OF HIGH UV AND LOW PRESSURE TO ASSIST IN THE ANALYSIS OF REMOTE SENSING DATA FROM MARS ORBITERS, LANDERS, AND ROVERS. RESULTS WILL MAKE IMMEDIATE AND RECT CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE PHOENIX AND MSL MISSIONS, AND SUPPORT SEVERAL KEY OBJECTIVES OF THE MARS EXPLORATION PROGRAM.

Description: We propose to observe four radio quasars with unusually high X-ray/radio core flux ratios. Such high values point to a synchrotron origin of their X-rays and this we wish to confirm. So far only low-power blazars, the BL Lacs, were known to have jets with synchrotron emission reaching energies as high as X-rays. Description: SUZAKU XIS OBSERVATIONS OF THE GALACTIC HALO AND LOCAL BUBBLE We propose Suzaku XIS observations of the hot gas in the Galactic halo and Local Bubble. The spectra's bright emission lines and complexes will reveal the plasma's ionization history and thus its origins. The Local Bubble's spectrum will be garnered from an observation of a nearby opaque cloud. The halo's spectrum will be found by subtracting the Local Bubble spectrum from that of an adjacent off-cloud observation. Description: DETECTION AND CONTROL OF INSTABILITIES AND BLOWOFF FOR LOW EMISSIONS COMBUSTORS This research program will provide fundamental knowledge and technology development that will enable supersonic jet aircraft to produce the lowest emissions possible. Our goal is to use nonintrasive sensors and a multi-tiered, smart control system to operate an ultra low emissions combustor while simultaneously ensuring that the engine; combustor operates safely. One of the major concerns for future supersonic aircraft is tow pollirtant emissions, during takeoff, climb and supersonic cruise. Most approaches currently envisioned for producing low emissions involve tight restrictions on the fuel-air distribution in the combustor. The idea is to make sure the fuel always burns in regions of excess air to prevent hot spots that lead to high NOx emissions. However, these lean low-emissions combstoarrse prone to various instability problems, incltdingle an blowout and dangerous presslire flitctuations caused by coupling between the heat release and the combustor acoustics. Thus, operation of future clean engines requires a tradeoff between low emissions operation, and engine reliability and safety. The optimal approach to manage this tradeoff over the wide range of conditions that an aeroengine experiences is an active control system. Much of the proposed approach can be characterized by the axiom; simple sensing, smart processing. We will develop the ftndamentanl nderstanding necessary to convert the sensor signals to quantities that measure stability margin and that are necessary for active control. We will also be developing an overall stability control system that will incorporate three lower level control systems that share the same fuel actuators. One system will provide Active Static Stability Control (ASSC) through relatively low bandwidth spatial fitel redistribution. Two systems will provide dynamic stability control. The first, Active Instability Margin Management (AIMM) control, is a new approach designed to slowly adjust the combustor conditions (fuel distribution) in order to prevent conditions conducive to dynamic instability. The second, Active Instability Control (AIC), would suppress the pressure fluctuations through medium bandwidth fuel modllations hould the combustor be forced into an unstable operating condition by rapid changes beyond the capability of the AIMM controller. While various AIC have been previously demonstrated, the proposed work focuses on providing the fundamental knowledge needed to predict the effectiveness of active control under varying operating conditions. This will provide the anderstanding needed to determine the appropriate active control algorithms to employ under different conditions. Finally, this effort will lead to an algorithm for combining all three stability control systems into a unitied architecture.

Description: USING OCEAN COLOR TO QUANTIFY THE SIGNIFICANCE OF MARINE PHOTOCHEMISTRY TO CO AND CARBON CYCLING IN THE SOUTH ATLANTIC BRIGHT To quantify the significance of solar-induced photochemical reactions on carbon cycles, CO2 and CO exchange in the South Atlantic Bight (SAB) using ocean color data. Background: Coastal waters have been viewed as net sinks for atmospheric CO2. New data on the SAB, however, show it to be a net source for atmospheric CO2 (Cai & Dai, 2004 Science, 306:1477). The overall role of coastal oceans in CO2 exchange is uncertain and may vary with latitude. The fate of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) in coastal waters is controlled by bacterial and photochemical processes, both resulting in CO2 production. Exposure of colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM) to sunlight directly produces CO, CO2 and a myriad of small organic compounds that can alter microbial production. This complex situation is difficult to quantify as to the overall significance of photochemical reactions on large-scale carbon cycles. Preliminary calculations using SeaWiFS data and limited photochemical data estimate that in the SAB -1/3 of the CO2 flux and up to 40% of DOC turnover may depend on photochemistry. Methods: We will combine satellite and photochemical data to assess the significance of carbon-related photochemical reactions in North American coastal waters, concentrating on the SAB. Our new optical model (SeaUV; Ocean Optics XVII, 2004) uses principal component analysis of ocean color data (aircraft, SeaWiFS/MODIS) to estimate in situ spectral UV downwelling attenuation (Kd) and UV absorbance by CDOM, the driver for virtually all marine photochemistry. Our algorithms were developed using a wide range of water-types, were verified using both Hydrolight modeling and SeaWiFS match-up analysis (SeaBASS archive), and significantly improve remote estimates for UV light fields in seawater. Using spectral UV irradiance fields and aCDOM from SeaUV (MODIS/SeaWiFS) we will construct depth-resolved surface ocean maps for CO/CO2 photoproduction and photoinduced changes in biologically labile products (BLPs) using spectral quantum yield (QY) and satellite optical data. Regional scale coastal calculations are severely limited by the lack of photochemical QY data reflecting spatiotemporal variability. Credible QY data are available for CO, rare for CO2, and from one study for BLPs. We will use multispectral laboratory irradiations of samples from seasonal transects and shore stations to quantify QY variations in the SAB. These new data will provide greatly improved estimates of carbon fluxes in the SAB. We will also expand estimates using SAB QY data to available in situ data from other North American coastal systems to examine the general validity of this approach. Significance: This project supports the NACP and OCCC goals of developing "quantitative scientific knowledge, robust observations, and models to determine the emissions and uptake" of CO2 and CO in ocean basins adjacent to North America. CO & CO2 dynamics will be addressed together using ocean color and in situ studies.

Description: LABORATORY MEASUREMENTS OF RATE CONSTANTS AND PRODUCT DISTRIBUTION FOR MODELING THE IONIZED TITAN AT There is heightened interest in Titan after the insertion of Cassini into the Saturnian system in July 2004. Using the INMS on Cassini, information is being obtained on the ion and neutral composition of this ionosphere. This is being modeled by several workers using literature data (rate constants and product distributions) for ion-molecule reactions and electron-ion recombination. These data are inadequate; ion-molecule studies were only at 300K, and not at the temperatures of the Titan atmosphere, and recombination studies, apart from our previous studies with temperature (100-SoOK), are generally only at 300K. We will study the critical reactions in the models as a function of temperature to obtain kinetic data at Titan temperatures. I will give these data to the modelers so that the models can be upgraded and perhaps suggest other species to look for in the 1-99 amu range of INMS. Data enable accurate chemical models to be produced, which couple the in-situ measurements of ion and neutral compositions of the atmosphere. Differences between the observed and modeled abundances will indicate inadequacy in models, which can be corrected. This is important given the limited resolution of the INMS and the mass overlaps that could occur (e.g., EIZCN+, C2H4+, N2+, CO+) and the possibility of different isomers, e.g., the higher hydrocarbons. Our laboratory studies will be made using Selected Ion Flow Tubes and Flowing Afterglows that we have developed. In these, ions are injected into, or generated in, flowing helium and flow to a downstream mass spectrometer/counting system for identifying and quantitating signals andlor an axially movable electrostatic probe for determining ionization density and electron temperature. Controlled and accurate flows of reactant gases are added to the helium to create and react with the ions. The data obtained will be in a web accessible database which will contain Literature data post 2003, the date of the most recent compilation. Collected data will be evaluated and best values given with the accuracy. For all reactions, rate constants will be determined at appropriate temperatures andlor versus temperature, allowing extrapolation. Ion product distributions will be determined for ion-molecule reactions; the determination of neutral products for recombination is much more difficult. Some determinations of excited state products will be possible; we have not yet fully developed the techniques for ground state products. The studies are directly relevant to the Planetary Atmospheres program, comets and extrasolar planetary atmospheres. Parts of this study also have relevance to the NASA programs, APRA, Outer Planet Research, Cosmochemistry, and Astrobiology and the prebiotic Earth. They are significant to Stardust and Deep Impact.

Description: IMPACT OF HUMANS ON PRECIPITATION VARIABILITY, CLIMATE, AND THE WATER CYCLE Knowledge of how urban environments impact precipitation will have implications for how urban areas are represented in future generations of weather and climate models; how urban planners and water resource managers plan cities; how agricultural activities carried out; and numerous other societal benefit applications. Algorithm development, ground validation, and modeling are vital research areas, but it is increasingly important that the NASA Precipitation Science Team represent research tracks addressing applications and implications of precipitation variability to weather, climate, and hydrology. In a recent report to the National Academy of Sciences and Senior Review Panel at NASA (TRMM, 2005), the need for extended TRMM observations (and future GPM observations) were placed in the context of current and emerging science questions. The role of human activities (e.g. aerosols and urbanization) in precipitation-related processes was prominently highlighted in the report. Our proposed research program is consistent with the Academy report recommendations, addresses NASA Precipitation Science program elements and enables us to leverage the extended dataset of TRMM while preparing for the GPM era. Here, we describe our science objectives and their linkages to the objectives (for example, objective 1.1 and 1.3) listed in the NASA Research Announcement. Precipitation Variability and its Relationship to Climate Diagnostics and Change: Objective 1: We will analyze 3-hourly TRMM daily and merged product data cross-referenced with rain gauge rainfall measurements for a cross-section of U.S. and global cities to perform a national and global climate assessment of urban effects on precipitation. This effort will focus on identifying influencing factors(geography, aerosols, climate, terrain, coastal effects, etc.) and establishing the presence of an jurban climate signalj in precipitation variability Objective 2:We will use TRMM, MODIS, and emerging cloud satellite data to investigate the relative role of urban aerosol-microphysics and urban-induced dynamics on precipitation variability and regional climates and then test our hypotheses using a newly introduced aerosol parameterizations in a climate version of the WKF regional model (with advanced urban parameterization). Objective 3: Using projected urban growth scenarios for selected urban areas; we will assess the impact of future urban land use and aerosol loads on regional climates, in terms of precipitation variability and surface hydrologic response (e.g., runoff, evapotranspiration). Applications to Hydrology and Oceanography: Objective 4: We will continue to develop a regional-to-urban scale distributed hydrologic model. We will develop a technique to link TRMM-based merged 3-hour and 1-hour rainfall observations to the multi-scale model and define the pathway for similar applications using GPM data. A downscaling approach will be developed to correctly scale the TRMM-based Merged Products to the spatial resolution necessary to drive a regional distributed hydrologic model and an urban flood prediction model. Objective 5: We will use space-based precipitation dataqets to assess urban water sustainahility. First, an approach integrating remote sensing and ancillary geospatial datasets will be developed to define the spatial extent (including imported water sources) of the urban hydrologic influence, which we will term the urban hydrologic footprint. We will then quantify the fluxes of water to and from the hydrologic footprint, determine the stores as residuals, and estimate residence times from flux time series. The study will uniquely incorporate remote sensing precipitation and land surface observation datasets into short-term urban water planning and reduce the uncertainty associated with spatial distribution of estimates of precipitation fluxes and consumptive uses at the urban water budget scale.

Description: HAZARD ANALYSIS FOR A FORWARD-LOOKING INTERFEROMETER The Forward-Looking Interferometer (FLI) is a new instrument concept for obtaining the measurements required to alert flight crews to potential weather hazards to safe flight. To meet the needs of the commercial fleet, such a sensor should address multiple hazards to warrant the costs of development, certification, installation, training, and maintenance. The FLI concept is based on high-resolution Infrared Fourier Transform Spectrometry (FTS) technologies that have been developed for satellite remote sensing. These technologies have also been applied to the detection of aerosols and gases for other purposes. The FLI concept is being evaluated for its potential to address multiple hazards including clear air turbulence (CAT), volcanic ash, wake vortices, low slant range visibility, dry wind shear, and icing, during all phases of flight (takeoff, cruise, and landing). Several project team members formerly investigated the physical basis for radiometric detection of the six hazards listed above. The ability of the FLI to provide estimates of the range to hazards was also investigated, with the result that both detection and ranging are enabled by the high spectral resolution provided by the FTS. A sufficient infrared spectral signature appears to be associated with the hazards to enable detection and/or mitigation of all of them, although detection of CAT at relevant ranges may also require that the FLI have high temperature resolution (low noise). The combination of high spectral and temperature resolutions in an imaging instrument is expected to enable sophisticated algorithms with high detection rates and low false alarm rates. The FLI will also function as an infrared imager, providing a real-time video display with night vision capability and enhanced vision in obscured conditions. This project has three major elements: further sensitivity studies and applications of a satellite remote sensing technique known as EOF Regression; development of algorithms to estimate the hazard severity; and field measurements to provide an empirical demonstration of the FLI aviation hazard detection and display capability. These theoretical and experimental studies will lead to a specification for a prototype airborne FLI instrument for use in future in-flight validation. The project supports NASA work objectives under the Integrated Intelligent Flight Deck Technologies Research Program as described in scope item (d) "development of a comprehensive surveillance system design that enables robust detection of external hazards with sufficient time-to-alarm for safe maneuvering to avoid the hazards." The research team includes the Georgia Tech Research Institute, Hampton University, the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research, the Air Force Institute of Technology, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The project will be conducted cooperatively with personnel at the NASA Langley Research Center.

Description: ENERGETIC PROCESSING AND STIMULATED CHEMISTRY OF PRE-COMETARY ICES AND PRIMORDIAL SURFACES OF COMET NUCLEI Comets are frequently considered time capsules which hold important clues regarding the formation and early evolution of the outer planets 4 to 4.5 billion years ago. This is a time when the presolar dense molecular cloud was condensing to form the protoplanetary disk. Consequently there has been much interest in the chemical transformations that may skew any extrapolation backward to this time. An important, but often-overlooked process is radiation-induced isotope enrichment. In our studies of electron-beam induced processing of ice surfaces, we have measured large isotope effects leading to enrichment of deuterium in the condensed phase. This effect can be enhanced due to pores and the presence of co-adsorbed species. These phenomena may be potentially relevant to understanding the deuteriumhydrogen ratios observed in comets Halley, Hyakutake and Hale-Bopp (and in future comets). Since comets are related to early planet formation models, we plan to study the radiation processing, reactions and release of gas from mixed ices as surrogates of comet cores. Specifically, we will address the following issues regarding radiation processing of both long and short-period comets: What is the role of pores, interfaces, grain boundaries and energy transport in the stimulated reactions within ice and ice-coated grains reminiscent of comet cores? These heterogeneous interactions can play a major role in isotopic fractionation as well as ortholpara spin conversion, thus altering estimates of thermal history. What is the relative importance of pore collapse and grain boundaries on the release of gases such as 82, CO, C02 and 02? Products of irradiation of mixed ices can be trapped and released at a later time during thermal cycling and pore collapse. Observed depletions of H2 and 02 in comet outgassing suggest that they have experienced a degree of thermal cycling in the past. We have observed an important link between the physical morphology of ice and the yields of direct and delayed release of molecular fragments from ice that may have direct consequence to cometary studies. Laboratory studies will be conducted on cometary ice analogs at low temperatures under ultrahigh vacuum using a wide range of excitation energies. Studies using high energy ion irradiation utilizing the beam line facility at the Radiation Physics Laboratory at the University of Notre Dame, by Prof. Jay Laverne, while experiments using low energy electrons, and VW photons will be conducted at Georgia Institute of Technology under the provisions of Prof. Orlando and Dr. Grieves.

Description: OMI/MLS DERIVED TROPOSPHERIC OZONE COLUMNS An objective of the OMI experiment is to produce global maps of tropospheric ozone columns. These maps would play an important role in analyzing continental outflows of pollutants, long term trends in those outflows, and their potential role in climate change. The challenge is to provide accurate maps which represent as short a time scale as possible - a stated NASA objective is daily maps. This proposal addresses this objective by subtracting Aura MLS ozone prorde measurements from OMI total columns measured in clear sky conditions. In addition it is proposed that a PV mapping approach be used to fdl in the cross track regions between measured MLS, and perhaps HIRDLS, profdes. In principle this would result in tropospheric column maps globally on a spatial scale of approximately 100 km and on the synoptic, or better, time scale. This proposal focuses on evaluating the accuracy and precisions of the derived tropospheric ozone columns starting with a detailed evaluation of the MLS (and HIRDLS) profiles in the lower stratosphere and of the total stratospheric columns. The resulting tropospheric columns will be compared against ozonesonde measurements and against results from other techniques including those which also use the OMI total ozone column measurements. A  complementary objective is to evaluate the meteorological conditions under which the tropospheric ozone columns are the most reliable.

Description: DESIGNING HUMAN-AUTOMATION INTERACTION THROUGH COMPUTATIONAL MODELING OF COGNITION AND THE DYNAMIC FLIGHT ENVIRONMENT Introduction of highly automated systems within the dynamic flight environment has led to an increased precision and efficiency of operations but has created new forms of errors. Thus, rigorously, broadly-applicable and easy-to-apply methods and tools are needed to carefully assess several issues early during automation design: 1. The automation may be unobservable by its human operator, i.e., the pilot may not be able to accurately identify the automation's current state and behavior. 2. The automation may be too complex for the operator to reliably understand and predict the current and near-term behaviors of the automation, and to effectively identify which automated behaviors should be commanded. 3. The automation may be contextually inappropriate for the immediate situation and the pilot's needs. This work will develop conceptual and computational models of the flight deck environment and pilot cognitive performance to address sources of error in human-automation interaction early in design. These models address many sources of human-automation interaction error, including human perceptual and cognitive factors, the complexity of the automation, and from its use in a dynamic flight envelope. The models capture the demands of the task, human cognitive performance, and the broader physical and procedural environment. The resulting models can be examined computationally for human-automation errors. The work will then seek to validate these methods and models through an examination of new IIFD automated systems in an important Next Gen air traffic operations scenario and extend them into a tool with broad applicability and suitable for use by the automation design community. The proposed research seeks to establish robust, broadly-applicable and easy-to-apply methods and tools in order to systematically assess automation complexity, observability and contextual appropriateness early during automation design. Being able to understand and evaluate such human-automation interaction issues through an examination of foundational is critical to advanced concepts for integrated intelligent flight deck technologies, which are in turn needed for a safe and higher capacity air transportation system. The proposed research is thus relevant to NASA's higher-level Strategic Goal 3 and to Strategic Sub-goal 3E, directly supports Milestone 1.8.6, and provides insight towards Milestones 1.8.2, 1.8.3, 1.8.4, 1.8.5, 1.8.6, 1.7.1, 1.5.11, 2.2.6, 2.2.10. and 2.2.

Description: COLLISIONAL EXCITATION AND OPACITIES FOR EXTRASOLAR GIANT AND TERRESTRIAL PLANETS: TOWARDS ACCURATE COMPARATIVE EXOPLANETOLOGY Over the past decade more than 160 exoplanets have been discovered, mostly through precision radial velocity measurements of their central star's motion with the vast majority of these being gas giants, or extrasolar giant planets (EGPs). Of all the EGPs, only the transiting planets, HD 209458b, TrES-l, and HD 149026b, have been observed directly either through IR photometry or transit spectra. Recently, a number of exoplanets have been detected with masses as small as 7.5 times that of the Earth. The direct spectroscopic investigation of EGPs and these so-called terrestrial planets (TPs), including observations in the visible to far infrared, is the next step in understanding and characterizing exoplanets, their evolution, and their host systems. However, exoplanet atmospheric models require extensive amounts of molecular data including opacities and, for non-equilibrium situations, collisional excitation rate coefficients and photochemistry. For many species relevant to exoplanets, there is a general lack of complete and accurate molecular opacity data including line positions, oscillator strengths, and continuum cross sections. Comprehensive collisional excitation data are even more rare. In an effort to improve this situation, we propose to compute molecular opacity and collisional data relevant to TFs and EGPs, in particular for the so-called hot Jupiters. Because this proposal is an extension of our previous and current work, we propose here to compute i) rotational-vibrational (RV) excitation rate coefficients for VO, C02, and NH3 due to collisions with H, He, and H2 and C02, 03, and NH3 due to collisions with 0 and 02; ii) RV photodissociation cross sections of C02, 03, NH3, and CH4; and iii) RV line wavelengths and transition probabilities of 03. The calculations will be performed using quantum-mechanical techniques with an emphasis on obtaining complete sets of data for nearly all RV levels. The data will then be tested using model atmospheres calculated with the PHOENIX code and used to predict spectra of EGPs and TPs. This work will help to guide future missions and interpret observations from the next generations of space- and ground-based telescopes. All data will be made available on the WWW to the planetary and astronomical community.

Description: We propose a 3-year project to analyze OMI HCHO measurements using a global chemical transport model GEOS-CHEM and to evaluate the constraints by OMI HCHO on global emissions of isoprene and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Biogenic VOC emissions (particularly those of isoprene) strongly affect regional air quality, global oxidizing power of the atmosphere, and climate (in part through secondary organic aerosol formation). There are large uncertainties in the estimates of these emissions. HCHO is produced with high yields during VOC oxidation and hence can be used as a proxy for VOC emissions. Over remote continental regions, biogenic isoprene is often the major precursor of HCHO. This work is motivated by our previous work on the Bayesian inversion of global isoprene emissions based on GOME HCHO measurements. In this project, we will implement a newly developed Model of Emissions of Gases and Aerosols from Nature (MEGAN) by Guenther et al. [2005] into GEOS-CHEM. MEGAN incorporates in situ enclosure and flux measurements in the past decade, particularly over the tropics and considers additional factors affecting biogenic emissions such as low-frequency meteorological variations and leaf age. The bottom-up estimates are expected to be much better than the widely used GEIA inventory by Guenther et al. [1995]. In situ eddy flux measurements are very limited in their geographical coverage. Only satellite measurements have the potential to provide the evaluations of these bottom-up inventories on a global scale. The OMI instrument onboard NASA Aura satellite vastly improves the previous GOME instrument in spatial (13x24(m2) and temporal (global coverage in 1 day) resolutions. Preliminary analysis indicates that the OMI instrument is producing measurements that conform to its design specifications. The retrieval process is expected to improve further and OMI HCHO product is expected to be available on January 1, 2006. We will analyze 2-year OMI measurements for 2005 and 2006. Bayesian inversion using GEOS-CHEM as the forward model will be conducted using 2006 measurements because of 3 planned aircraft field missions by NASA, NSF, and NOAA in that year. We will use aircraft in situ measurements to evaluate the OMI measurements and modeling (CTM and inversion) results. The research objectives are: (1) improve the operational retrievals of OMI HCHO vertical columns by using model simulated HCHO vertical profiles in the air mass factor (AMF) calculation; (2) map the global isoprene emissions using Bayesian inversion with MEGAN-derived a priori biogenic emissions and OMI HCHO measurements; (3) evaluate the critical levels of sensitivity and resolution of satellite observations necessary for improving the global mapping of isoprene emissions; and (4) assess the effects of isoprene emissions on regional air quality and the oxidizing power of the atmosphere. Our research objectives are in lint; with the first principal area of support of this NRA. Specially they address the area of "map(ping) emissions and export of trace gases and aerosols important to air quality and climate".

Description: The attractive combination of light weight and high stiffness of Al-Li alloys has made them important candidate materials for aerospace applications. These aluminum alloys however, are considered difficult to weld by conventional fusion welding due to the dentritic structure typical of a fusion weld. The dentretic structure can seriously weaken and degrade the welded joint mechanical properties deeming the weld ineffective for structural applications. Friction stir welding (FSW) was developed recently as a promising solid state process with encouraging results. This welding technique has potential significant application in different industrial applications, and has resulted in welded joints being used in critical load bearing structures, and structurally demanding applications. This welding process transforms the metal into a plastic state at a temperature below the melting temperature of the material, and then mechanically stirs the material together under pressure to form a welded joint. The FSW consists of a wed nugget, a thermo-mechanical affected zone (TMAZ), and a heat affected zone (HAZ). FSW takes place at temperature below the melting temperature; therefore, residual stresses may be considerably less than those in fusion welds. Nevertheless, residual stresses that develop during the FSW process can reach values up to 75% of the yield stress. These residual stresses can have a significant effect on the service performance of the welded material. Residual tension stresses in the weld can also result in stress corrosion cracking (SCC). Aluminum alloys may fail by cracking along grain boundaries when simultaneously exposed to certain environments and stresses of sufficient magnitude. The stresses capable of crack initiation and crack growth can be far below the stresses required for yielding. Inspection and maintenance of the weldments continues to be extremely important for proper detection and repair of stress corrosion cracks. However, sometimes it may be difficult to inspect the welds due to access restraints. Therefore, laser shock peening was investigated as a mean of moderating the tensile residual welding stresses. Laser shock peening is a process in which a laser beam is pulsed upon a metallic surface, producing a planar shockwave that travels through the workpiece and introduces compressive residual stresses in the material. Laser peening has been proven to be capable of enhancing the fatigue and mechanical properties of a number of metallic materials. The laser peening technique generates a compressive residual stress at the surface that can be significantly higher and deeper than for conventional shot peening. In this study, shot peening, and a variety of laser peening intensities were used to introduce compressive residual stresses into FSW AA 2195. The influence of the different peening techniques on stress corrosion cracking for FSW specimens were characterized and assessed by slow strain load testing. The benefits from the various peening techniques were assessed and documented.

Description: INNOVATIVE STRATEGIES FOR ROTARY-WING COUPLED AEROELASTIC SIMULATIONS The Georgia Institute of Technology (GIT) proposes this research in response to NASA's Research Announcement NNH06ZEA001N-SSRW2, subtopic SRW.1.03.09, advanced coupling methods. Description: DESIGNING HUMAN-AUTOMATION INTERACTION THROUGH COMPUTATIONAL MODELING OF COGNITION AND THE DYNAMIC FLIGHT ENVIRONMENT Introduction of highly automated systems within the dynamic flight environment has led to an increased precision and efficiency of operations but has created new forms of errors. Thus, rigorously, broadly-applicable and easy-to-apply methods and tools are needed to carefully assess several issues early during automation design: 1. The automation may be unobservable by its human operator, i.e., the pilot may not be able to accurately identify the automation's current state and behavior. 2. The automation may be too complex for the operator to reliably understand and predict the current and near-term behaviors of the automation, and to effectively identify which automated behaviors should be commanded. 3. The automation may be contextually inappropriate for the immediate situation and the pilot's needs. This work will develop conceptual and computational models of the flight deck environment and pilot cognitive performance to address sources of error in human-automation interaction early in design. These models address many sources of human-automation interaction error, including human perceptual and cognitive factors, the complexity of the automation, and from its use in a dynamic flight envelope. The models capture the demands of the task, human cognitive performance, and the broader physical and procedural environment. The resulting models can be examined computationally for human-automation errors. The work will then seek to validate these methods and models through an examination of new IIFD automated systems in an important Next Gen air traffic operations scenario and extend them into a tool with broad applicability and suitable for use by the automation design community. The proposed research seeks to establish robust, broadly-applicable and easy-to-apply methods and tools in order to systematically assess automation complexity, observability and contextual appropriateness early during automation design. Being able to understand and evaluate such human-automation interaction issues through an examination of foundational is critical to advanced concepts for integrated intelligent flight deck technologies, which are in turn needed for a safe and higher capacity air transportation system. The proposed research is thus relevant to NASA's higher-level Strategic Goal 3 and to Strategic Sub-goal 3E, directly supports Milestone 1.8.6, and provides insight towards Milestones 1.8.2, 1.8.3, 1.8.4, 1.8.5, 1.8.6, 1.7.1, 1.5.11, 2.2.6, 2.2.10. and 2.2.

Description: IMPACT OF AEROSOLS ON THE ARCTIC HYDROLOGICAL CYCLE  Variations in atmospheric aerosolcharacteristics have the potential to modulate the Arctic cryosphere through their impact on precipitation, radiation fluxes, and surface albedo. Atmospheric aerosols influence the nucleation of cloud particles, which affects directly the cloud cover and precipitation processes. Aerosols (particularly  carbonaceous and dust) can directly influence surface albedo of snowlice. Aerosols also affect the surface radiative fluxes through direct and indirect radiative forcing. Biomass burning in the northern forests, pollution aerosol, biogenic aerosol, and desert dust have been proposed as significant sources of Arctic aerosol. The overarching science question addressed by this proposal is: What are the effects of variations in aerosol characteristics in the Arctic on cloud properties, the surface radiation budget, precipitation, and surface snow cover? The PIS have submitted an interdisciplinary IPY proposal to the WMOIICSU entitled iHydrologic Impacts of Arctic Aerosol (H1AA)i that has been endorsed by the International IPY Planning Group. This large project is part of an international effort to coordinate atmospheric aerosol science associated with clouds, radiation, surface hydrology and cryospheric research efforts, including co-location of field measurements. In coordination with the WMOIICSU HIAA project, the goal of the proposed project is to develop an understanding and predictive capability of the interactions and feedbacks associated with aerosol forcing of the arctic hydrological cycle. This goal is accomplished through a synthesis of surface-based and suborbital observations and regional modeling activities being undertaken during the IPY in conjunction with A-Train observations. Specific objectives of the proposed research are: i Evaluation of A-Train data products associated with aerosols, clouds, precipitation, and surface energy balance using ground based, aircraft and UAV measurements near Barrow, AK, Prudhoe Bay, AK and other sites in Canada, Europe and Russia; i Integrated analysis of the relevant A-Train data with surface-based and suborbital data to address the overarching science question targeted by this proposal; i Evaluation of the regional modeling capability being developed under the PIis NASA MAP project for the different regions in the Arctic and for different conditions of aerosol forcing; i Conduct sensitivity studies by perturbing aerosol characteristics for the different regions being studied to develop an improved understanding of the effects of variations in aerosol characteristics on arctic hydrological cycle and the cryosphere. We also propose to deploy the Aerosonde UAVs. The main period of field investigations is targeted for 2008, and we anticipate requesting resources from the Suborbital Program to deploy the Aerosonde during Spring 2008 in the Barrow/Prudhoe region.

Description: Improving Prediction of Climate Radiative Forcing of Atmospheric Mineral Dust Using the CALIPSO Space Lidar Data in Conjunction with Passive Remote Sensing and Modeling Large uncertainties in the effects of changing atmospheric aerosols are among the major factors currently limiting our understanding of and ability to predict global climate changes. Among major aerosol types, mineral dust is of special interest because it causes diverse impacts on the Earth's environment and climate that remain poorly quantified. The recent IPCC (2001) report revealed that the magnitude and even the sign of the top-of-the atmosphere direct radiative forcing caused by dust remain uncertain, whereas dust-cloud interactions were completely overlooked in the assessment of indirect radiative forcing. The urgent need to improve predictions of direct and indirect radiative forcing of atmospheric dust provides motivation for this proposal. The main goal is to gain a better understanding of the properties and spatio-temporal distribution of atmospheric dust required for improved predictions of dust radiative forcing on climate by capitalizing on the new data to be provided by the CALIPSO, CloudSat, and solar and IR passive satellite sensors of the A-Train mission. Our strategy is to perform an in-depth sensitivity study to explore the potential of the CALIPSO lidar and infrared imager in characterizing atmospheric dust and to develop a novel capability for integrating passive and active remote sensing observations of the A-Train mission in the dust-laden conditions enabling studies of dust radiative impacts as well as dust-cloud interactions. To address the goal of this proposal, we will conduct the following: i) Develop new regional dust models by incorporating recent data on the morphology (shape) and size-resolved composition (especially the new data on the iron oxide content obtained in our group) into optical modeling based on the Discrete Dipole Approximation, T-Matrix, and Mie theory approaches. A new type of regional dust models that will predict dust optical properties at both the solar and IR wavelength in a consistent fashion will be constructed. ii) Perform extensive forward modeling to investigate the effects of dust particles on the scattering phase function, aerosol extinction-to-backscattering ratio, and lidar depolarization at the 532 and 1064 nm CALIPSO lidar wavelengths. Incorporate the regional dust models into the CALIPSO research retrieval algorithm and assist in the development and testing of the CALIPSO operational algorithm in the dust-laden atmospheric conditions; iii) Develop a methodological framework for merging the CALIPSO lidar and infrared imager data for discrimination of dust from clouds and retrieval of the effective dust particle size; begin the analysis of dust-cloud-precipitation interactions by using CALIPSO and CloudSat observations; iv) Investigate how the distinct regional properties and vertical distribution of atmospheric dust affect its radiative impacts (such as top-of-the-atmosphere and surface radiative forcing, and radiative heating and cooling rates in cloud-free and cloudy atmospheric conditions) by analyzing CALIPSO lidar and infrared imager observations in conjunction with the MM5 model coupled with the dust module, DuMo, and selected data provided by the A-Train sensors. The study will be focused on analyzing and contrasting Asian vs. Saharan dust. Overall, our proposed research will provide deeper insights into links between the dust properties and related radiative effects and dust-cloud interaction that are critical to both remote sensing applications and climate change studies. Our research directly addresses the goals identified by the NASA NRA (ROSES NRA NNH05ZDA001N-CCST). Furthermore, our proposal contributes to the overall goals of NASA and its vision on To understand and protect our home planet.

This proposal focuses on evaluating the accuracy and precisions of the derived tropospheric ozone columns starting with a detailed evaluation of the MLS (and HIRDLS) profiles in the lower stratosphere and of the total stratospheric columns. The resulting tropospheric columns will be compared against ozonesonde measurements and against results from other techniques including those which also use the OMI total ozone column measurements. A  complementary objective is to evaluate the meteorological conditions under which the tropospheric ozone columns are the most reliable.

Description: FLIGHT MECHANICS AND CONTROL ORIENTED MODELING OF NEXT GENERATION ON-BLADE CONTROL CONCEPTS  Individual Blade Control (IBC) and On-Blade Control (OBC) concepts offer tremendous potential for expanding the design space for tailoring control input signals for desired individual blade responses to simultaneously address the flight control issues and the rotor control issues. The implications of higher-bandwidth arising from IBC and OBC concepts are currently only amenable to CFD plus CSD analyses. Further, the state-of-the-art CFD plus CSD analyses tools are computationally expensive and are not suitable for controller synthesis, analysis and simulations needed in the design cycle. Hence, reduced-order models that capture the essential physics of OBC control concepts for fast and real-time simulations and linearized models in a linear time invariant (LTI) form that retain the important coupled rotor/body dynamics with various IBC and OBC concepts are needed for handling qualities assessment and integrated flight/rotor control development. The proposed 2-year research program to be conducted by a team of researchers from the Georgia Institute of Technology, the Washington University, Advanced Rotorcraft Technology, Inc., and the Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation is aimed at addressing these two important issues towards a successful development of next generation civilian rotorcraft. The objectives of our proposed research are to develop physics based reduced order models of next generation OBC concepts suitable for fast and real time simulations and to develop a computationally efficient framework and algorithms for extraction of time-invariant linearized models suitable for handling qualities assessment and integrated flight and rotor control design and analyses. Our approach for reduced order model development will exploit the experience gained by the Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation with analyses and wind tunnel test data of a variety of OBC concepts and the enhanced CFD and CSD tools from the DARPA Quieting Program. The prediction accuracy of the developed reduced-order models will be evaluated through comparisons with high fidelity CFD predictions and available test data. The developed reduced order models will be integrated into the modular architecture of FLIGHTLAB simulation model for fast and real time demonstrations. Description: DESIGNING HUMAN-AUTOMATION INTERACTION THROUGH COMPUTATIONAL MODELING OF COGNITION AND THE DYNAMIC FLIGHT ENVIRONMENT Introduction of highly automated systems within the dynamic flight environment has led to an increased precision and efficiency of operations but has created new forms of errors. Thus, rigorously, broadly-applicable and easy-to-apply methods and tools are needed to carefully assess several issues early during automation design: 1. The automation may be unobservable by its human operator, i.e., the pilot may not be able to accurately identify the automation's current state and behavior. 2. The automation may be too complex for the operator to reliably understand and predict the current and near-term behaviors of the automation, and to effectively identify which automated behaviors should be commanded. 3. The automation may be contextually inappropriate for the immediate situation and the pilot's needs. This work will develop conceptual and computational models of the flight deck environment and pilot cognitive performance to address sources of error in human-automation interaction early in design. These models address many sources of human-automation interaction error, including human perceptual and cognitive factors, the complexity of the automation, and from its use in a dynamic flight envelope. The models capture the demands of the task, human cognitive performance, and the broader physical and procedural environment. The resulting models can be examined computationally for human-automation errors. The work will then seek to validate these methods and models through an examination of new IIFD automated systems in an important Next Gen air traffic operations scenario and extend them into a tool with broad applicability and suitable for use by the automation design community. The proposed research seeks to establish robust, broadly-applicable and easy-to-apply methods and tools in order to systematically assess automation complexity, observability and contextual appropriateness early during automation design. Being able to understand and evaluate such human-automation interaction issues through an examination of foundational is critical to advanced concepts for integrated intelligent flight deck technologies, which are in turn needed for a safe and higher capacity air transportation system. The proposed research is thus relevant to NASA's higher-level Strategic Goal 3 and to Strategic Sub-goal 3E, directly supports Milestone 1.8.6, and provides insight towards Milestones 1.8.2, 1.8.3, 1.8.4, 1.8.5, 1.8.6, 1.7.1, 1.5.11, 2.2.6, 2.2.10. and 2.2.

Description: HAZARD ANALYSIS FOR A FORWARD-LOOKING INTERFEROMETER The Forward-Looking Interferometer (FLI) is a new instrument concept for obtaining the measurements required to alert flight crews to potential weather hazards to safe flight. To meet the needs of the commercial fleet, such a sensor should address multiple hazards to warrant the costs of development, certification, installation, training, and maintenance. The FLI concept is based on high-resolution Infrared Fourier Transform Spectrometry (FTS) technologies that have been developed for satellite remote sensing. These technologies have also been applied to the detection of aerosols and gases for other purposes. The FLI concept is being evaluated for its potential to address multiple hazards including clear air turbulence (CAT), volcanic ash, wake vortices, low slant range visibility, dry wind shear, and icing, during all phases of flight (takeoff, cruise, and landing). Several project team members formerly investigated the physical basis for radiometric detection of the six hazards listed above. The ability of the FLI to provide estimates of the range to hazards was also investigated, with the result that both detection and ranging are enabled by the high spectral resolution provided by the FTS. A sufficient infrared spectral signature appears to be associated with the hazards to enable detection and/or mitigation of all of them, although detection of CAT at relevant ranges may also require that the FLI have high temperature resolution (low noise). The combination of high spectral and temperature resolutions in an imaging instrument is expected to enable sophisticated algorithms with high detection rates and low false alarm rates. The FLI will also function as an infrared imager, providing a real-time video display with night vision capability and enhanced vision in obscured conditions. This project has three major elements: further sensitivity studies and applications of a satellite remote sensing technique known as EOF Regression; development of algorithms to estimate the hazard severity; and field measurements to provide an empirical demonstration of the FLI aviation hazard detection and display capability. These theoretical and experimental studies will lead to a specification for a prototype airborne FLI instrument for use in future in-flight validation. The project supports NASA work objectives under the Integrated Intelligent Flight Deck Technologies Research Program as described in scope item (d) "development of a comprehensive surveillance system design that enables robust detection of external hazards with sufficient time-to-alarm for safe maneuvering to avoid the hazards." The research team includes the Georgia Tech Research Institute, Hampton University, the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research, the Air Force Institute of Technology, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The project will be conducted cooperatively with personnel at the NASA Langley Research Center.

Description: FLIGHT MECHANICS AND CONTROL ORIENTED MODELING OF NEXT GENERATION ON-BLADE CONTROL CONCEPTS  Individual Blade Control (IBC) and On-Blade Control (OBC) concepts offer tremendous potential for expanding the design space for tailoring control input signals for desired individual blade responses to simultaneously address the flight control issues and the rotor control issues. Description: Surface Traffic Optimization in the Presence of Uucertainties A portal is an entity through which we transition between domains (or states). Given this definition, an airportal may be thought of as the entity through which aircraft transition between the state where they are parked at the gate (i.e. motionless on the ground) and the state where they are at cruise. Thus, the control volume around an airportal would enclose all the airside elements of an airport and the terminal area around the airport. The flow of traffic through an airportal may be controlled in at least four ways. First, the number of aircraft entering the airportal (crossing the boundary of the control volume) can be regulated. Second, the planned trajectory (4-D) of each aircraft within the control volume of can be customized. Third, aircraft may be buffered at various locations within the control volume ifthere is congestion downstream of the aircraft. Fourth, the trajectory of each aircraft can be adjusted (re-planned) in response to changing environmental conditions or unpredicted changes in the behavior of other aircraft. The first two ways of controlling the flow of traffic -- regulating the entry of aircraft and planning their trajectories -- may be thought of as strategic control actions as the related decisions are made before the aircraft enter the control volume and when there are uncertainties as to the actual operating conditions within the control volume. The second two ways of controlling the flow of traffic -buffering aircraft and re-planning their trajectories -- may be thought of as tactical control actions as the related decisions are made after the aircraft enter the control volume and at a time when one of these actions must be taken to prevent conflicts. We propose to develop the algorithms and techniques to optimize the application of these other novel strategies and tactics such that efficiency is enhanced in the presence of uncertainties.

Description: A SELF CONSISTENT INVESTIGATION OF SEP PRODUCTION IN GRADUAL EVENTS BASED ON REALISTIC MODELS OF TURBULENCE AND IFM We propose to study the shock acceleration of solar energetic particles (SEPs), and their transport, coupled to the dynamics of CME-driven turbulent shock waves in the heliosphere. Our goal is to develop a selfconsistent model, which integrates the best theories developed for every aspect of the SEP production and transport problem. This will include a realistic model of turbulence near the shock front and effects of SEP spectrum anisotropy. The new SEP-turbulence model will be coupled with a realistic model of CME volution to enable the LWS community to tackle important problems related to the shock acceleration of SEPs by CME shocks. A comparison between the two data sets does not yield a one-to-one correlation as expected for instruments that acquire direct measurements of titanium. Thus, our objective is to thoroughly examine the GRS and NS calibration techniques and identify potential sources of error in order to improve their correlation. We will use Apollo/Luna ground-truth and a Ti02 distribution map created using fast neutron data to provide independent corrections to these uncovered errors. We will use these data products to advance scientific knowledge of the geologic processes needed to produce the observe distribution of Ti02, and to explain the breakdown in the correlation between Clementine UVVIS continuum and Ti02. In addition, accurate maps of ilmenite and Hydrogen abundance will provide critical information for targeting future lunar settlements. Our findings will further understanding of the geologic evolution of the Moon and will provide an assessment of lunar resources needed to enable human presence in space. These results will aid NASA in achieving the strategic goals and outcomes of the Science Mission Directorate.

Description: In collaboration with Drs. G. Huss, K. Nagashima, and H. Yurimoto (SIMS+SCAPS), I. Hutcheon (NanoSIMS), J. Lyons and F. Ciesla (astrophysical modeling of oxygen isotopic evolution and radial mixing of solids in the protoplanetary disk), M. Petaev (thermodynamic modeling), J. Nuth and G. Libourel (evaporation-condensation experiments), and A. Toppani (FIB+TEM), we propose to study mineralogy, chemistry, and isotope chemistry (oxygen, Mg, Ca, Ti) of solar-system corundum and corundum-hihonite grains in matrices in situ and in acid-resistant residues of the CI, CM, CR, CV, CO, CH, enstatite and ordinary chondrites, and in several corundum-bearing CAIs from Murray, Murchison, and the ungrouped carbonaceous chondrites Acfer 094 and Adelaide. Corundum and corundum-hibonite grains in primitive chondrite matrices probably represent gas-solid condensates, which have been largely unsampled by refractory inclusions; some of the grains may be evaporative residues. Formation of these refractory grains could have started prior to CAI formation and lasted over the entire life of the protoplanetary disk in the hot nebular region near the Sun or during high-temperature transient heating events, such as shock waves at different radial distances from the Sun. As a result, such refractory grains may be more representative samples of evaporation-condensation processes in the early Solar System than CAIs. The combined study of mineralogy, chemistry, and isotopic compositions of the corundum and corundum-hibonite condensates will provide important constraints on (1) the origin and evolution of oxygen isotopic composition of the inner solar nebula, (2) the distribution of short-lived radionuclides among the most refractory condensates, (3) the kinetics of gas-solid reactions and the residence time of corundum-bearing grains in the high-temperature nebular regions, and (4) the role of radial mixing of high temperature condensates in the protoplanetary disk.

Description: The past decade has witnessed major advances in space-borne remote sensing that have revolutionized our ability to observe and study oceans, atmosphere and Earth climate system. At the same time ocean-atmospheric modeling has advanced to a point that for the first time, global models have achieved resolutions approaching those of satellite observations, enabling them to take full advantage of satellite's high resolution both as forcing and for validation. Under its current NASA support, the International Pacific Research Center (IPRC), as a climate diagnostic and modeling center, has developed strength in climate research that explicitly takes advantage of NASA products. IPRC's innovative use of NASA satellite data has led to a number of important discoveries, including the world's longest island wake west of Hawaii, spatial organization of monsoon convection by narrow mountains of Asia, and ubiquitous oceanic influence on the atmosphere near major currents in the world ocean. Based on satellite and insitu observations, IPRC scientists have developed a mean sea surface height dataset, a major achievement in oceanography, and have used it to confirm, for the first time, the ubiquitous existence of narrow zonal jets in the deep ocean, a phenomenon first suggested from numerical modeling. We propose to continue to explore satellite data, uncover new phenomena, and then study the physical mechanisms at work in them through complementary in-situ measurements and modeling. The interdisciplinary nature of our research in air-sea interaction and climate fosters integration (synergy) of data from a variety of sensors and satellites, in situ observations, and numerical modeling. The proposed research is organized into four broad Themes: multi-scale interaction, climate processes and variability, modeling, and experimental data assimilation.  Each Theme includes a set of Projects, and if its scope is sufficiently broad, a Project is also subdivided into specific Tasks. We expect Themes to remain unmodified throughout the duration of this grant, but individual Projects and Tasks will change as they are completed and replaced by new ones. The proposed research will further our ability to characterize, understand, and predict climate variability, thereby contributing to NASA's objective to "explore the dynamic Earth system to understand and predict change." It will also contribute to major international programs such as Climate Variability and Predictability (CLIVAR) and Global Energy and Water Cycle Experiment (GEWEX).

Description: PRIMORDIAL SOLAR SYSTEM ICES 1. Description of Key Research Objectives The distant Kuiper Belt Objects (KBOs) harbor some of the most primitive material in the solar system. Volatile ices can be found on these distant objects which are absent from inner solar system objects such as asteroids due to prior heating. Of particular interest are water ice and methane ice, the primary goals of our study. Understanding the water ice distribution in the solar system is of the utmost importance because water ice is one of the key ingredients of comets, potential suppliers of water to earth, a required ingredient for life. Methane ice is scientifically interesting as an indicator of prior heating --- it is lost quickly from warm bodies. To date, methane and water ices have been seen on the a few of the largest KBOs (2005 FY9 and "the tenth planet" 2003 UB313,2003 EL61 and PlutoICharon). Due to lack of other comparison objects the processes creating these surface types. The key goals of our survey are: (1) classify the KBOs to determine which have fundamental ices; (2) once identified, target the ice-rich KBOs for follow-up to determine their solid state configuration and detect possible trace ices; (3) use these results to draw parallels between the KBOs and well-studied system members. 2. Methods to Accomplish Research Objectives Our key method will be a telescopic survey of a large sample (about 100) of KBOs utilizing a custom narrow band filter set designed to detect water ice and methane ice. The PI and Co-I have institutional access to four of the largest U.S. operated telescopes in the world: the twin Gemini 8 m telescopes (Hawaii and Chile) and the twin Magellan 6.5 meter telescopes (Chile). Such large telescopes are needed for all phases of our study due to the faintness of the KBOs. We will first use our custom filter photometric survey to identify KBOs with interesting surface ices (years 1-2). After this we will target the bodies of greatest interest using the more telescope intensive spectroscopic methods to determine the state and abundance of ices, and place limits on possible trace ices such as ammonia, methanol, and nitrogen (years 2-3). The use of our custom filter set in the first phase of our study allows us to save precious telescope time by identifying interesting objects before the more detailed spectroscopic studies. No other investigators have ever used special filter sets to catalog KBO ices. 3. Significance to NASA Interests and Programs. Our proposed work seeks to catalog the distribution of volatile ices in the Kuiper Belt, the most primitive regions of the solar system. We will be able to find correlations between ices and dynamical factors, which may be an indication of their formation and evolution. We will address the first three science objectives of NASA's Mission to the Solar System, which focus on the origins of the minor bodies, their diversity and the link to life

Such interactions have been shown to produce intense ultra-sharp radio pulses in ice.
