Description: Comets are least altered remnants of planetary accretion, thus measurements of their physical and chemical properties can place constraints on our understanding of the processes which shaped the formation and evolution of our solar system. We are proposing to continue our investigation of the primordial properties of comets in three focused and related research areas which relate the understanding of the nucleus characteristics to the mechanisms of activity and ultimately to better understand the comet formation process in the early solar system. ({it i}) {it Mechanisms for Distant Comet Activity} -- Many comets exhibit activity, or dust production, at extremely large distances from the sun, where sublimation from water-ice is not important. We are continuing an observing program combined with dust dynamical and thermal modeling and laboratory work, to understand the physical and chemical processes in these comets. ({it ii}) {it Comet Nucleus Sizes}-- The sizes of small icy bodies reflect the processes of growth and accretion in the nebula, as well as the dynamics of scattering and collisions as these planetary building blocks were accumulating. We will be obtaining optical measurements of nucleus fluxes to obtain albedos of comet nuclei to be observed in a companion Spitzer Space Telescope program that has been awarded time to measure the Jupiter Family comet nucleus size distribution. We will extend these nucleus size measurements to long-period and Oort comet nuclei, which formed at different disk locations (and thus have different chemistries) and which have experienced different collisional histories. ({it iii}) {it Support for Selected Comet Space Missions}-- The Deep Impact spacecraft is fully functional and the OJ team is proposing to execute an extended mission to flyby comet 85P/Boethin in December 2008. This Jupiter-family comet has been observed only at two previous apparitions. We propose an observing campaign to recover the comet, refine it's orbital information and characterize the nucleus properties prior to encounter to maximize the results from an extended mission. A second Discovery mission has been proposed to repeat the Deep Impact experiment at comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko at the time of the Rosetta encounter, and we propose a modest pre-encounter observing campaign to help characterize this nucleus. Understanding the primordial composition of comets will help us to understand the process of planetary formation. This is a key element of the NASA vision, and comets, as the possible carriers of organics and volatiles to the terrestrial planets also potentially played a key role in establishing habitability for Earth. Description: INTEGRATING MESSENGER DATA TO INVESTIGATE THE ORIGIN OF MERCURY'S INTERCRATER AND SMOOTH PLAIN DEPOSITS Two commonly held models for the formation of the intercrater and smooth plains on Mercury are: 1) volcanic resurfacing, or 2) basin-ejecta material. Although Mariner 10 images have provided limited compositional and morphologic information of these plains materials, their origin materials remains ambiguous. We propose to investigate the origin of the intercrater plains by integrating data from MESSENGER's X-ray spectrometer (XRS), Gamma-ray and Neutron spectrometer (GRNS), Mercury Atmospheric and Surface Composition Spectrometer (MASCS), and the Mercury Dual Imaging System (MDIS). The intercrater and smooth plains are analogous to the lunar light-plains deposits (e.g., Cayley Formation) and cryptomare deposits (e.g., Schillar-Schickard ancient mare deposits). Using Lunar Prospector gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer data, Apollo X-ray and gamma-ray data, and Clementine UVVIS reflectance measurements we will devise tests and establish quantifiable criteria using the lunar light plains, cryptomare, lunar plains volcanism deposits and highlands as analogs to the intercrater plains, before MESSENGER arrives at Mercury. These tests and criteria will be adjusted to the known compositional, space-weathering environment at Mercury, and specifics of the individual sensors.After orbit insertion, I will use these metrics to examine the origins of the intercrater plains. In addition to conducting scientific research, I will utilize my intermediary position between instrument teams to promote and facilitate date synergy. Description: The overarching goal of the proposed work is to better understand Mars' volatile inventory through analysis of the distribution and formation of fields of small volcanic cones observed in the Mars data sets. In our previous work we have identified numerous candidate rootless cone fields, which are interpreted to form by explosive interactions between lava flows and ice-rich substrates. The positive identification of rootless cones, and quantitative modeling of their formation, yields information on the amount and spatial distribution of water in the martian regolith at the time of cone formation. It has become apparent from our previous work that several aspects of this work require further investigation, including development of techniques to automatically and unequivocally identify rootless cones in the data sets. Furthermore, the ongoing return of data from Mars Global Surveyor and Mars Odyssey means that our global inventory of cone groups is incomplete. A recent I-year MDAP grant allowed us to develop automated data search and statistical analysis tools that set the stage for further efforts. We therefore propose a suite of data analysis tasks aimed at identifying and characterizing martian cone fields. Specifically, we will (i) further develop and apply our preliminary automated detection algorithms to identify MOC and THEMIS images containing candidate volcanic cones; (ii) further develop and apply a suite of statistical tools (including nearest neighbor and linear alignment analyses) to distinguish volcanic from nun-volcanic features (e.g., pingos, pedestal craters, secondary impact crater clusters), as well as rootless cones from primary cones (e.g., cinder cones formed over volcanic conduit), and to characterize the inter- and intra-group spatial distribution of cones; (iii) make morphometric measurements on volcanic cones; and (iv) determine the implications of cone spatial distribution and dimensions for the locations and amounts of ice involved in the rootless cone-forming explosions. In this way we will directly address NASA and Mars Exploration Program goals of etermining the distribution of regolith water stores through time, the implications for climatic conditions, and locations favorable for biogenic development.

Description: The concentrations of elements on Mars shed light on understanding the bulk composition of the planet, the evolution of its crust, and the extent to which aqueous processes have operated. I propose to use data from the Mars Odyssey Gamma Ray Spectrometer (GRS), existing geologic maps of Mars, TES, magnetic, and imaging data, and compositional data from Viking, Pathfinder, MER, and martian meteorites to unravel the evolution of the Martian crust. The contributions to crustal evolution made by the  formation of the primary crust, subsequent volcanism, impact processes, and aqueous processes will be investigated. The central data product will be global petrologic maps, using smoothed 5 x 5 degree GRS data for H, Cl, Fe, Si, Al, Ca, K, and Th. These maps will be used to identify conspicuous compositional regions on Mars by using multivariate cluster analysis. The maps will form the basis for detailed geologic studies of each identified map unit. An important part of the geochemical mapping will be trying to deconvolve the compositional effect of overlying dust from that of the underlying bedrock. This project will address several fundamental questions about the history of Mars: (1) What is the source of water in Mars? What is the total inventory of water in Mars? (2) What processes operated during the initial differentiation of Mars and what are the chemical characteristics of the mantle reservoirs produced? (3) What was the effect of the late heavy bombardment on the Martian crust? (4) What is the full range in composition of Martian volcanic deposits? (5) What is the origin of the pervasive  on the martian surface? This project will address NASA goals: increase our scientific understanding of the Solar System, the objects in it, and the processes by which planets and small bodies have evolved, lead to new interpretations of data from NASA missions, and help plan future missions by characterizing major geologic regions on Mars. It will also address one of the major goals of the Mars Exploration Program, unraveling the formation and evolution of the crust. Specifically, this project will help understand the distribution of water on Mars, the nature of sedimentary processes, Martian igneous history, and the structure and composition of the crust.

Description: Importance of the Project: The laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) investigation (Chemcam, R. Wiens, PI) recently selected to be on the payload of Mars Science Laboratory is the first application of LIBS to planetary science. Many fundamental practical issues relating to the use of this type of spectroscopy for the study of rocks on Mars must be resolved. In particular, LIBS has not yet been extensively tested on altered and volatile-bearing minerals and rocks that will provide the key data for the understanding of the ancient climate and habitability of Mars. We propose a comprehensive plan to bring the LIBS technique in general to a fully calibrated, matrix-corrected state capable of acquiring rapid, complete chemical characterizations of altered and volatile-bearing minerals and rocks with well-quantified precision and accuracy. It should be emphasized that the investigation goals of Chemcam (the LIBS instrument on MSL) can be met with the current understanding of the LIBS technique. However, the application of LIBS to detailed understanding of volatile bearing material is currently poorly understood and is not in the instrument budget itself.  Objectives: The objective of this proposal is to obtain LIBS spectra of alteration and volatile bearing minerals shown to be important to the Martian conditions, including sulfates, phyllosilicates, and select halides, and the effects of adding these minerals to well-characterized basaltic rock compositions. We will carefully evaluate the matrix effect on the LIBS spectra of these minerals and sulfur, in particular. The goal of the work is to enable the extraction of quantitative mineralogy from LIBS spectra of alteration and volatile materials. We will develop calibration curves and compositional matrix corrections using existing volatile-bearing sulfate minerals from Rio Tinto (Spain), well-characterized mineral and rock samples from Roger Clark's collection at US Geological Survey, and in-house rock samples characterized by onsite analytical equipment. The University of Hawaii and Los Alamos teams will work cooperatively on this entire endeavor.

Description: NEW PARADIGM FOR STATISTICAL VALIDATION OF SATELLITE PRECIPITATION ESTIMATES FOR HYDROLOGIC APPLICATIONS ABSTRACT: We propose a new approach to statistical validation of maps of precipitation that are derived from satellite remote sensing observations. This approach requires availability of ground-based reference data and we plan to use NEXHAD observations. Our approach will answer the following question: #Given radar and satellite rainfall maps, what is the probability that the true rainfall amount exceeds tbe satellite rainfall estimate over an arbitrary region on the map? Posing the validation problem in a probabilistic context standardizes the notion of what is #good# or #bad# as there is a common scale (from 0 to 1) that is easy to interpret. Answering this question wilt greatly enhance the use of satellite data in flood forecasting and in operating water resources systems. Validation activities for GPM should directly assess the utility of rainfall estimates from the perspective of the drainage basin and at basin scales that are reievant to flood hazard problems that can be addressed by GPM rainfall products. Our focus in hydrologic studies will be on rainfall estimation for extreme floods at basin scales ranging from approximately 100 km2 to 100,000 km2. Hydrologic validation perspective requires use of a probabilistic model of the reference data uncertainty. We have developed such a model for hourly rainfall accumulation based on radar-rainfall estimates. It is known as Probabilistic Quantitative Precipitation Estimations. The model accounts for seasonal, scale, and range dependence of radar-rainfall uncertainties. The parameterization we have developed using a large set of empirical data addresses the multiplicative errors conditional on the estimated radar-rainfall amount. To address the validation issues from the perspective of flood hazards, we will perform hydrologic studies of the scale-dependent properties of flood-produeing rainfall in the Potomac River basin and the Texas-Gulf drainage basins. These studies will center on analyses of more than 50 flood events in each of the study regions. The proposal addresses several topics of the NNRO6ZDAOOlN-PMM, including (i) Development and application of statistical validation techniques; (ii) Developlnent of metrics and methodologies for assessing satellite precipitation produets in hydrological modeling; and (iii) Impact of future precipitation data sets on hydrological prediction, including methods for quantifying and using estimates of systematic and random precipitation measurement errors.

Description: The general understanding of the physical processes involved in auroral electrodynamics has been accepted for many years, however the details of the geometry of auroral arc current systems and their relation to the electrodynamics within an arc is at best only theoretically modeled and lacks experimental confirmation. Though numerous measurements have been made in auroral structures through either satellite, rocket or ground measurements; a multi-dimensional geometric picture of the aurora electrodynamics still requires reliance on multiple developed models that lack solid experimental confirmation. The single point measurement in a large-scale system and spatial/temporal limitations of satellites can only provide a glimpse of a piece of the auroral electrodynamics. Even modern multi-spacecraft missions and near conjunctions of satellites cannot provide sufficient resolution of these geometries due to their "randomness" in conjunction in both space and time relative to each other and the arc system. Furthermore, no current satellite project provides measurements at important altitudes (~120km) of the aurora current closure. To investigate the geometry and electrodynamics of a complete auroral arc current system requires a controlled placement of the appropriate instrumentation in the correct locations within an arc structure. We propose here two appropriately instrumented sounding rocket payloads with specific trajectories to place them at key position, simultaneously, within an auroral arc structure to provide confirmation of models and theories related to auroral arc structure and electrodynamics. To address the structure of an auroral arc, appropriate measurements must be made at multiple points. The ACES experiment will utilize two suitably instrumented rockets at two key altitudes within the arc. One payload will be above the ionospheric F peak to measure the imposed fields and energy input into the arc, the second payload will be at a lower altitude slicing through the classic current closure region (~120km). Both payloads will be in fight simultaneously to minimize any temporal variation between the measurements. Both payloads will be instrumented to measure DC Electric and Magnetic Fields, supra-thermal to energetic electron and ion distributions, cold plasma density and temperature. This mission will address some of the questions that are key to understanding the near Earth plasma environment and in particular Ionospheric-Magnetospheric coupling as well as Ionospheric-Thermospheric coupling. In fact many of the issues to be investigated here are identified as topics to be addresed in the GEC roadmap mission. The results obtained by this experiment would be instrumental in helping shape any future GEC type mission.

Description: Magnetic reconnection is widely accepted as the main solar wind entry into the Earth's magnetosphere. Our goal is to use our newly developed full particle simulations with open boundary conditions to address one of the fundamental questions regarding reconnection:  Why does reconnection appear to be quasi-steady at times and time-dependent at others times? The answer to this fundamental question will not only address some of the key basic physics questions regarding magnetic reconnection process, but it will have an immediate impact on understanding the observables of reconnection at the Earth's magnetopause where both quasi-steady and intermittent reconnection (so-called flux transfer events) have been observed. Determining the conditions under which flux transfer events occur remains one of the major goals of space physics. One of the main obstacles to using full PIC to examine these questions has been the lack of realistic inflow-outflow boundary conditions. The vast majority of full PIC calculations in recent years have employed periodic boundary conditions for the particles and the fields. This causes the reconnection jets to collide which leads to the rapid saturation of the island. Although this is also an issue with fluid calculations, the problem is even more severe in full PIC due the intense electron flows that are generated along the separatrices. These flow velocities can easily exceed the electron thermal speed and are thus rapidly re-circulated along the separatrices back to the diffusion region and "pollute" the solution long before saturation of reconnection. In this proposal, we plan to use our newly developed full particle code and diagnostics with open boundary conditions to address this issue with unprecedented realism. The objectives of the proposed work are in tune with NASA's aim in understanding the interaction of solar wind with the Earth and planetary magnetospheres and how solar wind controls the flow of energy and momentum throughout the system. Magnetopause reconnection is the primary mechanism for transfer of energy and momentum and is the focus of next Solar Terrestrial Probe, the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission (MMS). In fact the primary objective of MMS is the understanding of the fundamental processes of reconnection. The results of our work have a direct bearing on planning of MMS.  Already our work [Daughton et al., 2006] indicates that the length of the electron diffusion is much larger than previously thought. The GEM challenge studies [Birn et al., 2001] had predicted the electron diffusion region to have a width along the inflow of a few electron skin depth and a length along the accelerated outflow of only 1-2 ion inertial length. We have reported [Daughton et al. 2006], using our newly developed open boundary conditions that the electron diffusion region does not remain microscopic along the outflow axis, but can extend to ~ 30 ion skin depths and even larger with the exact value depending on the parameters. Its width along the inflow, however, stays much thinner at several electron skin depths. Our study will provide insight as to the details of the reconnection process and its temporal behavior, which will help in planning for MMS observations and analysis and enable a closer connection with observation.

Description: DYNAMICAL SELECTION OF THREE-DIMENSIONAL INTERFACIAL PATTERNS IN DIRECTIONAL SOLIDIFICATION The project on the Dynamical Selection of Three-Dimensional Interface Pattern will be carried out with a focus on the fundamental understanding of cellular interface pattern formation during the directional solidification of alloys. The instability of the interface and its reorganization into an ordered pattern is central to the microstructure formation that controls the properties of a material. This highly nonlinear pattern formation is significantly influenced by gravitational effects on ground-based experiments which precludes the understanding of fundamental physics that govern the dynamics of pattern formation. The project win be carried out in close collaboration with Prof. Bernard Billia, who is the principal investigator of the flight experiment to be carried out by the French Space Agency, CNES. Significant experimental studies are planned to be carried out in the Laboratory Module of DECLIC that is in Dr. Billia's laboratory in Marseille France. The goal of the project is to develop quantitative understanding of the correlation between the processing conditions and complex microstructures that governs the properties and reliability of materials. The specific goal is to design and to carry out experiments on the complex dynamics of three-dimensional pattern evolution during the solidification of a model transparent alloy, and to develop a realistic theoretical model with predictive capabilities.

Description: BASIL PRODUCTION IN LONG-TERM MISSION FACILITIES: A HIGHER QUALITY DIET FOR ASTRONAUTS (GRADUATE STUDENT: ANGELA BEAMAN) We have determined that Genovese Compact Improved sweet basil is not a suitable cultivar for production in a nutrient film technique system because it did not produce as much biomass as Aroma 2, Genovese, Italian Large Leaf, and Nufar. Therefore, continued research is being done to determine the top two cultivars for biomass production in a nutrient film technique system. Currently, experiments are being done to evaluate the general growth response of basil subjected to four different irradiance levels (200, 300, 400, and 500 umol/m2/sec). We hope the results of these experiments will enhance the biomass production in future experiments using the nutrient film technique. We will determine the total nitrogen requirement, optimum NHA N.N03 - N ratio, and whether recycled urine can be used in the nutrient solution used for rapid, hydroponic basil production during long-term space missions. We also believe synthetic urine, and later, astronaut urine, will be usable in the nutrient solution.

Description: DYNAMICAL SELECTION OF THREE-DIMENSIONAL INTERFACIAL PATTERNS IN DIRECTIONAL SOLIDIFICATION The project on the Dynamical Selection of Three-Dimensional Interface Pattern will be carried out with a focus on the fundamental understanding of cellular interface pattern formation during the directional solidification of alloys. The instability of the interface and its reorganization into an ordered pattern is central to the microstructure formation that controls the properties of a material. This highly nonlinear pattern formation is significantly influenced by gravitational effects on ground-based experiments which precludes the understanding of fundamental physics that govern the dynamics of pattern formation. The project win be carried out in close collaboration with Prof. Bernard Billia, who is the principal investigator of the flight experiment to be carried out by the French Space Agency, CNES. Significant experimental studies are planned to be carried out in the Laboratory Module of DECLIC that is in Dr. Billia's laboratory in Marseille France. The goal of the project is to develop quantitative understanding of the correlation between the processing conditions and complex microstructures that governs the properties and reliability of materials. The specific goal is to design and to carry out experiments on the complex dynamics of three-dimensional pattern evolution during the solidification of a model transparent alloy, and to develop a realistic theoretical model with predictive capabilities.

Description: The purpose of this proposed work is to develop fundamental relationships between dielectric material properties and the degradation processes at work in air- and spacecraft wire insulation, in order to support the development of effective nondestructive methods # both ultrasonic and electromagnetic # for evaluating wire health. In atldition, a capacitive nondestructive method for measuring the permittivity and hence characterizing damage in wire insulation material will be developed. Theoretical models will be developed that describe the relationship between changes in permittivity, elastic constants, mass density, development of micro-cracks and material loss of electrical wire insulation (PI, PTFE and ETFE), and processes which occur during aging such as heat exposure, humidity exposure, chafing and mechanical stress. Measurements will be made both on pure samples of the insulation materials and on coated wires. Measurements of the storage and loss moduli as a function of frequency and temperature will be made using dynamic mechanical analysis. These measurements will allow us to investigate the influence of chemical structure, material aging, and heat and humidity exposure on the viscoelastic response of the polymers. Mass density of bulk samples will be deduced from measurements of mass and, more specifically, mass loss. The change in volume with temperature will be evaluated using thermogravimetric analysis, through the onset of material decomposition. The presence and extent of micro-cracking will be estimated by sectioning of bulk samples and optical microscopy. The permittivity of wire insulation will be measured as a function of temperature, humidity conditioning and applied tensile stress, and after cyclic loading for increasing periods of time. A kinetic model for the changes in mass density due to heat and humidity exposure in PI, PTFE, ETFE will be based on dynamic and isothermal thermogravimetric and thermomechanical analyisis data. These models for the mass/density loss (or gain) as a function of time and temperature will be based upon the co-PIs previous experience on kinetic analysis of thermal measurements using multivariate non-linear regression. First principles models of micro-cracking in response to applied stress will be developed based on prior work in which a rate dependent theory of fracture for polymers is developed. This work will be extended to model relationships between permittivity and fracture. A model-based, nondestructive, capacitive method will also be developed, to measure the permittivity of a dielectric material that coats a central conductor in a cylindrical configuration, by clipping capacitor plates to the exterior of the dielectric. The fundamental relationships between material properties and degradation processes will be used to guide optimization of the capacitive nondestructive evaluation (NDE) technique in terms of capacitor plate size, shape, arrangement and frequency of operation etc, and to predict the sensitivity of the method for detecting damage due to the processes under investigation. In addition, the successful development of material parameter response models will underpin the development of electromagnetic and ultrasonic wire diagnostics techniques which are already being reported in the literature. It is envisaged that the capacitive NDE method will be particularly applicable for detailed secondary testing of insulation zones that are suspected of being defective. Complementary initial large-scale testing of wire bundles may be performed by lamb-wave ultrasound, or electromagnetic wave propagation in transmission-line mode, for example, and is not the subject of this proposal. The work is directed towards prevention of loss of function of air- and spacecraft electrical systems due to catastrophic failure of wire insulation. It has widespread application in reducing both monetary and human cost of lost air- and spacecraft.

Description: The proposers will develop a computer language compiler to enable inexpensive, low-power, integer-only processors to carry our mathematically-intensive comptutations at high speed, with excellent computational accuracy. This will enable space systems designers to select from a wide range of radiation-hard processors for math-intensive command and data handling applications such as spacecraft attitude control, advanced sensing, instrument data processing and calibration, and autonomous operation. Integer-only processors are capable of accurate math-intensive computing if properly programmed using a fixed point computational model. This presents a major challenge to the program designer. Software tools are available to help the programmer analyze fixed point implementations, but not to create them. This kind of trial-and-error design cycle can be expensive, time-consuming and error-prone. Our compiler will analyze system specifications, such as input data ranges and formats, architectural constraints, and a description of the computational algorithm. It will insert data scaling operations into the integer instruction stream to make the most effective use of the internal data representation. The resulting code will be an order of magnitude faster and more compact than a software floating point implementation, with very competitive computational accuracy. This technology will be available for NASA programs immediately after Phase 2.

Description: IDAHO NASA EPSCOR RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT The NASA Idaho Space Grant Consortium (ISGC), in cooperation with the Idaho EPSCoR program, has prepared this proposal in response to the NASA solicitation for an Experimental Program to Stimulate Competitive Research RID project announcement. The Project Plan provides an overview of the proposed NASA Idaho EPSCoR program, the goals, objectives and priorities of the Idaho program, and planned program elements. The ISGC was established in 1991 at the University of Idaho, and has since grown to comprise twenty-two organizations, including nine institutions of higher education in the state of Idaho. Individuals from higher education, state and federal government, nonprofit organizations, and industry serve as ISGC representatives within this state network. This group of contacts assists with setting the vision and goals for the ISGC and has been instrumental in disseminating information about the ISGC. Under the NASA Idaho EPSCoR 2000 program, the ISGC was responsible for selecting research teams for funding, identifying graduate students to participate in the research efforts, monitoring the progress of the teams, and directing the writing of the NASA Idaho EPSCoR proposal. The ISGC Director, Jean Teasdale, and Idaho Technical Advisory Committee assisted the research teams with preparation of their research proposals through review and editing of the documents. As a commitment to the objectives of the NASA EPSCoR program, the ISGC revised the guidelines for its Research Initiation Grant program to strengthen collaborations between Idaho researchers and NASA personnel. This revision also aligned the research efforts of the ISGC more closely with the research efforts of the NASA Idaho EPSCoR program. This change greatly enhanced the  elationship between NASA personnel and Idaho researchers, and helped identify several areas of strategic importance to NASA. Under the NASA Idaho EPSCoR RID grant, the ISGC will continue to improve the programs developed under the NASA EPSCoR 2000 grant by supporting collaborative research efforts between Idaho researchers and NASA scientists and engineers, providing funding for graduate research assistants to work with faculty, and offering general administrative support for the program.

Description: ESTIMATION OF SEASONAL SNOW COVER, GLACIAL AND LAKE AREA CHANGES AT THE OB/YENISEY RIVER HEADS DURING THE LAST 40 YEARS USING NASA ESE PRODUCTS AND IN SITU DATA The Altai-Sayan mountains geographically define the southern periphery of the Asian Arctic Basin.  The Ob and Yenisey rivers account for 40% of the total river inflow into the Arctic Ocean.  The 2340 Altai-Sayans glaciers are receding since the middle of the 19th century.  There has not been any precise estimation on the glacial and seasonal snow-covered area changes and the consequent changes in water resources.  Our main objective is to estimate changes in snow-glacial- and lake-covered areas and glacier volume in the head of Ob/Yenisey river basin over forty  years, and to simulate and forecast consequent snow and glacial runoff variability.  Research approaches: (1) Collect and process in-situ data and NASA data products; (2) Simulate snow-glacier- and lake cover area and volume changes through developing a model; (3) Implement the snow/glacial runoff model parameters; (4) Characterize the annual to decadal variations in river runoff component and assess the climate-driven impact on future snow/glacial water resources.  Methods: (1) We will check data for homogeneity and repsentativeness.  Topographic and photo-grammetric measurements will be geo-referenced to a common coordinate system;  (2) Glacial area distribution will be evaluated by Landsat and Terra ASTER data, and satellite products (IKONOS and CORONA) will be used for validation.  Sub-pixel techniques using MODIS and AVHRR data will be used for snow mapping, and snow-covered areas will be validated using Landsat and ASTER image data.  Aerial photographs and Corona photographs and ASTER, SPOT, and IKONOS images will be used for subsequent lake area changes.  (3) Snow/glacier melt Runoff Model will simulate the annual mean runoff through a snow distribution, snow/glacier ablation and quantifying the precipitation partitioning; Snow/glacier melt runoff models will be assimilated with MODIS Evapotranspiration products, MODI Snow Cover, and MODIS Land Cover Science Data Product (MOD12Q1).  (4) Forecast of glacier retreat will be based on the Equilibrium Line Altitude, which is determined through mean summer air temperatures and annual precipitation.  Hypothetical climate-change scenarios will be imposed as an annual progression of changes in temperature and precipitation.  Value:  Proposed project addresses an important unifying component of the NASA IPY Program, particularly with respect to the terrestrial components of the cryosphere in the Cold Land Regions of the Northern Hemisphere.  Modeling and predicting glacier and snow cover changes is an important unifying component of the U.S. Global Change Research Program and the World Climate Research Program, and will contribute to the International Climate and Cryosphere Program, the Climate Variability and Predictability Research, and the North Eurasia Earth Science Partnership Initiative.

Description: We propose to investigate the reliability, including radiation resistance and failure mechanisms, of a novel, potentially multi-state, phase-change memory technology using test arrays and sensing circuitry. This potentially multi-state memory, based on a layered chalcogenide structure, would significantly increase the memory density by allowing more than one data state per bit, resulting in the much needed larger, denser memories for future space applications. Phase-change memory technology is aligned to become the next generation of non-volatile memory, with the potential to replace Flash memory and hard-drive storage, and is ideal for space applications due to its radiation resistance, large number of cycles, and lower power operation. While much research is currently underway both in industry and in academia to build phase-change memory devices, there are little data available that can describe or guarantee how these types of memory arrays will perform under the conditions they will experience in a space application. In addition, these currently studied phase-change memories do not have the potential multi-state memory capabilities like our proposed materials do. Our proposal comprises three main research areas: (1) design and fabricate a test chip for chalcogenide-based memory devices which use the multi-state memory material stack structures that we have previously explored under NASA EPSCoR grant NCC5-577, and are further researching under a DEPSCoR grant with the Air Force Office of Scientific Research; (2) design and perform reliability (including radiation tests) experiments on our test chip and, if it becomes available, on a commercial chip for a comparison study; and (3) determine failure mechanisms for these electronic devices and explore methods of yield enhancement. Reliability and radiation testing methods for phase-change materials, especially our potentially multi-state memories, need to be developed since they offer challenges that are unique to chalcogenide amorphous and crystalline materials.

Description: NASA's next generation of x-ray observation missions require x-ray calorimeters with superior energy resolution. Semimetallic HgTe has already proven itself as an excellent soft x-ray absorber material due to its low heat capacity. The alloy Hg0.834Cd0.166Te is predicted to also have zero energy gap at T=0 K and a heat capacity even less that that of HgTe due to: (i) a greater Debye temperature (resulting in a lower lattice heat capacity), and (ii) a smaller electron effective mass (resulting in a lower electronic heat capacity). Thus Hg0.834Cd0.166Te-based microcalorimeter arrays are expected to have an energy resolution superior to that of HgTe-based ones. We propose the growth of single crystal Hg0.834Cd0.166Te layers by molecular beam epitaxy on Si substrates. Mercury vacancies will be filled after growth to reduce the possibility of them acting as acceptors and introducing a significant electronic heat capacity. The Hg0.834Cd0.166Te layers will be characterized by x-ray diffraction to asses their structural quality and crystallinity, FTIR mapping to confirm the uniformity of their energy gaps and alloy compositions, Hall measurements to assess their electrical transport properties, etch pit density  counts to determine dislocation densities, transmission electron microscopy to determine microscopic structural information, and heat capacity measurements at mK temperatures to test their promise as high energy resolution quantum calorimeters.

Description: "MASSIVE BLACK HOLE BINARIES WITH EXTREME MASS RATIOS" The existence of black holes with a range of masses that covers many orders of magnitude is now well established: the centers of many galaxies contain ?supermassive black holes? with masses of millions to billions of solar masses; ordinary massive stars end their lives in supernova explosions that leave behind ?stellar-mass black holes? of a few to a few tens of solar masses.  Recently, a new class of ?intermediate-mass black holes,? with masses between a few hundreds and a few tens of thousands of solar masses have been identified by astronomers.  These appear to be associated with dense clusters of stars where they might have indeed formed through dynamical interaction processes, such as physical collisions between stars.  In dense cluster centers, non-degenerate stars dwelling in the cluster centers can be captured by the intermediate-mass black hole at close enough orbits, so mass transfer onto the black hole can be initiated.  Such binaries could be responsible for the ultra-luminous X-ray sources discovered in abundance in nearby galaxies with young populations using the NASA X-ray satellite Chandra.  When dense star clusters form close enough to galactic centers, they can spiral in and deposit stars and stellar-mass black holes on their way to the center.  The intermediate-mass black hole at the cluster center, gradually peeled of its stellar envelope, eventually in spirals into the galaxy central supermassive black hole, its orbit decaying by emission of gravitational waves.  Our work aims at finding observational signatures of the interactions between black holes of different masses and non-degenerate stars.  Detection of X-rays and gravitational waves offer the most promising channels for constraining the evolution of black hole binaries with extreme mass ratios in dense stellar environments.

Description: Rotating and Binary Stars in General Relativity The existence of binary and rotating neutron stars is beyond dispute. However, the two-body problem remains the most important unsolved problem in classical general relativity (GR) and has enormous consequences for the detection of gravitational waves. Binary neutron stars (NSNSs) and binary black-hole neutron stars (BHNSs) may also hold the keys for resolving other astrophysical puzzles, such as the origin of short-hard gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and planets around pulsars. Likewise, the stability of rotating neutron stars is not fully understood in GR, and the final fate of unstable stars is not known, especially in the presence of a magnetic field. Differential rotation, which is likely to characterize a NSNS or core collapse remnant, has not been fully explored in GR. Resolving these issues is crucial to determining the maximum mass and spin of a neutron star, as well as the aftermath of NSNS coalescence, particularly the question of immediate versus delayed collapse. The collapse of a very massive, rotating, magnetized star, including a supermassive star and a Pop 111 star, to a black hole has not been well-studied in GR, yet massive star collapse is a likely progenitor of a long-soft GRB and may provide the seed for the growth of a supermassive black hole. The collapse of a massive star generates gravitational wave bursts, possibly detectable by LIGO or LISA. In addition, quasiperiodic waves may arise from the growth of bars or other nonaxisymmetric modes during rotating collapse, or in the massive disk that forms outside the nascent hole. Treating all of these pheonomena requires the same computational machinery: a fully relativistic code that simultaneously solves Einstein's equations for the gravitational field, Maxwell's equations for the electromagnetic field and the equations of relativistic magnetohydrodynamics for the matter, all in three spatial dimensions plus time. Recent advances we have made in constructing such a code make it possible for us to solve these fundamental, closely related computational problems, essentially for the first time. - - - -

Description: LOCK AND KEY CHEMICAL SENSORS USING NANOSTRUCTURES AND LASER TWEEZERS This work represents the initial exploration of deposition and individual manipulation of nanostructures, in particular CNT material, and its application in the design, fabrication, and applications of chemical sensing. The importance of purification, positioning and manipulation, functionalization, and measurement of CNT properties simultaneous with exposures to target gases is being addressed in the creation of new sensors. Singular CNTs have been deposited onto substrates and cut. Several technical challenges are currently being addressed to enhance the possibilities for fabrication of practical sensor systems using CNTs. Since standard methods of synthesizing SWCNT generally have significant contamination by amorphous carbon, purification of SWCNT powders by solubilization and centrifugation as reported herein dramatically diminishes the amount of amorphous carbon. A second technical challenge addressed herein is the need for the precise manipulation of a CNT within a microstructure. While AFM has shown by many groups to be a powerful to imager for CNT materials, here AFM was demonstrated to both image and cleave/move the CNT. These molecular scale manipulations by AFM will become increasingly important in both the study and fabrication of selective and sensitive chem./bio sensors using nanoscale materials.

Description: SUMMARY: In collaboration with scientists at NASA-Goddard, the Northwestern Universityinfrared group has developed the first polarimeter for infrared/radio astronomy that uses VPMs (Variable-delay Polarization Modulators). The VPM is a novel device forpolarization modulation that is being considered by NASA scientists as a possible key component of future space-based cosmology experiments. Our new polarimeter, that we call HertzIVPM, was tested successfully at the University of Arizona's SMTO (SubMillimeter Telescope Observatory) in April 2006. In order to more fully understand the characteristics of this new device, we propose to return the polarimeter to the Northwestern University infrared laboratory for a series of tests designed to fully characterize the systematic errors of this device, including instrumental polarization and polarimetric transfer function. Due to limited observing time, it is not possible to fully characterize these errors at SMTO. In addition to this work with Hertz-VPM, we propose to develop new techniques for fabricating large polarizing grids, which will be needed for eventual use of VPMs for space cosmology. The fabrication method will be an extension of one previously developed by the Principal Investigator and another member of the Northwestern team when they both worked at University of Chicago and collaborated on on an airborne astronomy experiment during the 1980s.

Description: Gamma Ray Bursts (GRBs) represent some of the most energetic explosions in the universe. However, in spite of several years of observations, we are still unsure of the progenitors of these objects. The recent association of supernovae with GRBs suggests that their progenitors are massive stars, and in particular Wolf-Rayet stars. The latter are compact massive stars that have mostly lost their H and He envelopes via high-mass-loss stellar winds. Mass lost from these stars accumulates in the surrounding medium, forming complicated wind-blown bubbles. The relativistic blast-wave from the GRB will expand in this medium, and the delayed emission, or 'afterglow', will result from the interaction of the blast wave with this medium. Absorption of the afterglow by the surrounding medium can help to unveil the physical characteristics of this medium. In this project we aim to make high-resolution numerical simulations ofthe medium surrounding Wolf-Rayet stars. Using the results from the latest available stellar evolution models for single and binary stars at various metallicities as input conditions to our computations, we will simulate the evolution of the circumstellar medium during the stellar lifetime. This will be followed by a computation of the X-ray, optical and radio afterglows from the expansion of a relativistic jet within this medium. Comparison of our results with observed gamma-ray burst afterglows, and the results of absorption-line spectroscopy, will allow us to limit the available parameter space, and produce a viable set of models suitable for GRBs. The results will be used to place further constraints on GRB progenitor stars. The project will enhance our understanding of GRB progenitors as well as the ambient medium in which the progenitors are born. Therefore it will increase our understanding of the interstellar medium (ISM) in GRB host galaxies, thereby also allowing us to unveil the characteristic properties of the ISM in very high-redshift galaxies.

Description: COORDINATED XMM-NEWTON AND HST MONITORING OF SGR A We propose to carry out further monitoring of the central supermassive black hole in Sgr A in X-rays and the near-IR with simultaneous XMM-Newton and HST observations. Our goals is to determine the physical mechanisms governing the accretion onto a supermassive black hole when the accretion luminosity is at an extremely low level. X-ray flares are very likely to be produced within 10 Schwarzschild radii and hence probe the environment very close to the black hole. Description: CREATION AND ANALYSIS OF C3VP SYNTHISIS DATASETS The Canadian Calipso-CloudSat Validation Project (C3VP) Intensive Observing Period(lOP)3 was conducted during January 2007 at the Center for Atmospheric Research Experiments (CARE) near Barrie, Ontario, Canada.  During C3VP, many new, unique, and complimentary datasets useful for Global Precipitation Mission (GPM) algorithm development and ground validation were collected. In particular, the lOP saw the collection of several cases during a variety of winter precipitation scenarios, which will be valuable in developing and testing new algorithms for the GPM core (radar and passive microwave) and constellation (passive microwave) satellites. This proposal represents analysis of datasets collected during lOP 3 for improving the construction and assumptions contained within developed and future GPM algorithms in cold season precipitation regimes. The overarching goal of this project is to facilitate the use of the detailed observations collected in C3VP for use by the GPM algorithm developers such that GPM algorithms may be improved.

Description: MOLECULAR FOSSILS IN ARCHEAN AND PROTEROZOIC SEDIMENTS AND METASEDIMENTS: MULTIDIMENSIONAL GAS CHROMATOGRAPHY, HIGH PRESSURE CATALYTIC HYDROGENATION AND SYNTHESES OF BUTYLOID STANDARDS This project will analyze the molecular fossils extracted and released by high pressure catalytic hydrogenation from Archean and Proterozoic sediments and metasediments (1.45 to 3.3 billion years) for paleobiological purposes. The molecular fossils recovered from these sediments often form unresolved complex mixtures (UCMs). We have demonstrated that comprehensive 2-dimensional gas chromatography (GCxGC) can resolve these UCMs and provide inestimable paleobiological information, including the first direct evidence for the presence of Archaea in the late Archean (2.705 billion years). We propose to investigate the unresolved complex mixtures of extractable organic matter from an array of Proterozoic and Archean sediments using GCxGC technology. Lipids released during high pressure catalytic hydrogenation will also be analyzed by GCxGC, providing further constraints for paleobiological reconstruction. Additionally we propose to synthesize three authentic standards of novel butyloid compounds (containing 4 to 10 quaternary carbon atoms) identified in 2.705 billion year old metasediments. This research proposal includes an addendum for the Planetary Major Equipment program for the acquisition of Investigator Facility Instruments, GCxGC.Flame ionization detection and GCxGC-time of flight mass spectrometer.

Description: THEORETICAL STUDIES OF THE EXTRATERRESTRIAL CHEMISTRY OF BIOGENIC ELEMENTS AND COMPOUNDS We propose to continue to use theoretical quantum chemistry to study reactions occurring on or within ices that lead to the formation of compounds relevant to Astrobiology, providing insight into processes that can operate in protostellar nebulae and form prebiotic molecules or their precursors. Icy grain mantles consist of water, ammonia, and simple carbon-bearing species such CO, CO2, CH30H, and HCN. There are various ways in which chemistry can occur even at very cold temperatures to produce more complex species. For example, these and other species may encounter radicals deposited from the gas phase or produced by photolysis in the ice itself and may include H, OH, CN, NH2, or others. Alternatively, photoionization may generate charged species and these may exhibit different chemical behavior than the neutrals. Under some circumstances, charge transfer processes may occur, such as proton transfer between an acid and a base. We propose to employ quantum chemistry to evaluate chemical pathways and to make predictions of corresponding spectroscopic properties. To achieve this, we will use density functional cluster calculations, supported as necessary with continuum solvation or ONIOM hydrid calculations. We will also develop an extended model that incorporates a mineral substrate, forsterite (Mg2Si04), which may be a component of interstellar dust and was observed in Comet Hale-Bopp. In the next three-year funding cycle, we propose to continue to focus on potential pathways occurring within icy grain mantles leading to the formation of critical biochemical precursor species, including amino acids or their precursors and nitrogen-containing heterocyclic compounds or their precursors. We will examine paths involving both neutral radicals formed through photolysis and charged intermediates generated via photoionization. We will characterize radical intermediates and estimate the fractions that do not go to product or revert to reactants. Specific reactions will include CN, NH2, and OH generated by photolysis of HCN, NH3, and H20, respectively, reacting with CO, C02, HCN, C2H2, CH3C2H, and HC3N. We will also characterize cyanide ion (CN-) formed in astrophysical ices via proton transfer from HCN and HNC. These studies will contribute to meeting the Astrobiology programs goal to chararacterize ". .. the formation of complex molecules in space ..."

Description: "MASSIVE BLACK HOLE BINARIES WITH EXTREME MASS RATIOS" The existence of black holes with a range of masses that covers many orders of magnitude is now well established: the centers of many galaxies contain ?supermassive black holes? with masses of millions to billions of solar masses; ordinary massive stars end their lives in supernova explosions that leave behind ?stellar-mass black holes? of a few to a few tens of solar masses.  Recently, a new class of ?intermediate-mass black holes,? with masses between a few hundreds and a few tens of thousands of solar masses have been identified by astronomers.  These appear to be associated with dense clusters of stars where they might have indeed formed through dynamical interaction processes, such as physical collisions between stars.  In dense cluster centers, non-degenerate stars dwelling in the cluster centers can be captured by the intermediate-mass black hole at close enough orbits, so mass transfer onto the black hole can be initiated.  Such binaries could be responsible for the ultra-luminous X-ray sources discovered in abundance in nearby galaxies with young populations using the NASA X-ray satellite Chandra.  When dense star clusters form close enough to galactic centers, they can spiral in and deposit stars and stellar-mass black holes on their way to the center.  The intermediate-mass black hole at the cluster center, gradually peeled of its stellar envelope, eventually in spirals into the galaxy central supermassive black hole, its orbit decaying by emission of gravitational waves.  Our work aims at finding observational signatures of the interactions between black holes of different masses and non-degenerate stars.  Detection of X-rays and gravitational waves offer the most promising channels for constraining the evolution of black hole binaries with extreme mass ratios in dense stellar environments.

Description: THE EVOLVED YET OXYGEN-RICH SNR CTB 1:SN EJECTA CLUMPING AND HARD X-RAY EMISSION Based on prior ROSAT observations, the supernova remnant (SNR) CTB 1 features X-ray center-filled emission within well-defined radio shell, characteristic of "mixed-morphology" SNRs. Our ASCA and Chandra observations revealed that CTB 1 is an oxygen-rich SNR with enhanced abundances of O and Ne despite its evolved state. We also found a hard component to the X-ray emission, and our chandra images suggest that the hard emission may be localized within a few arcmin scale clumps. The scientific goals of our proposed XMM-Newton observations of CTB 1 are i) to examine clumping structures of SN ejecta, where the ejecta are still dominant at an old age, ii) to determine if the hard emission has a non-thermal origin and is truly localized, and iii) to resolve the hard point-like source.

Description: In the coming year three new, major experiments are opening a new survey window to the Universe through the first surveys for galaxy clusters using the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (SZE). These efforts have also been marked as one of the four most promising routes to tackle the problem of Dark Energy observationally. To fully understand the results to be obtained and for their use for first cosmological applications, a maximum of information on the clusters to be detected is needed (at least in an initial test field). Therefore the leaders of three major SZ experiments, SPT, APEX and ACT have agreed to put an early focus of their efforts into a common test region in the sky that is being surveyed by deep optical observations. To gain a very precise understanding of the SZ-cluster survey selection function and to secure the best information on global structural parameters of the clusters we also need X-ray observations, which still provide the best understood way of surveying for clusters. We propose to combine the SZ and optical survey efforts with X-ray data in a minimal test area of 12.5 deg2. XMM-Newton is the only instrument which can effectively provide such a survey and it would be a pity if the XMM mission would miss this unique chance to help opening a new window to our Universe. Therefore we propose XMM-Newton observations providing a typical exposure of ~ 12 ksec in a 12.5 deg2 test field of a combined SZ- and optical survey, requiring a total exposure time (including overhead) of 972 ksec. From this survey first cosmological results will be obtained. In this context the survey will provide a very important complement to the 9 deg-2 field of the XMM-LSS, since both surveys are not large enough by themselves to overcome the problem of cosmic variance. Thus important checks, uncertainty estimates and corrections will become possible by their combination.

Description: LARGE DATASETS ARE BEING PRODUCED AT A VERY FAST PACE IN A VARIETY OF FIELDS FROM ASTRONOMY PHYSICS, BIOLOGY, MEDICINE, AND AMNY OTHERS.  AS A PROCESSING CYCLES BECOME CHEAPER AND DATA SETS DOUBLE IN SIZE EVERY YEAR, THE MAIN CHALLENGE FOR RAPID TURNAROUND INT HE ANALYSIS OF LARGE FATASETS IS THE LOCATION OF THE DATA RELATIVE TO THE AVAILABLE COMPUTATIONAL RESOURCES.  MANY ANALYSES OF ALRGE DATASETS FOLLOW A SPLIT/MERGE METHODLOGY, WHICH INCLUDES AN ANALYSIS QUERY TO BE ANSWERED, THE SPLITTING DOWN INTO INDEPENDENT TASKS TO BE COMPUTED, AND THE MERGING OF ALL THE INDEPENDENT RESULTS BACK INTO A SINGLE AGGREGATED RESULT.  THE HYPOTHESIS IS THAT SIGNIFCANT PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENTS CAN BE OBTAINED IN THE ANALYSIS OF THE LARGE DATASET BY LEVERGING INFORMATION ABOUT THE DATA ANALYSIS WORKLOADS RATHER THAN INDIVIDUAL DATA ANALYSIS TASKS.  WE BELIEVE IT IS FEASIBLE TO ALLOCATE COMPUTE RESOURCES AND CACHING STORAGE RESOURCE THAT ARE ANALYSIS TASKS.  WE BELUIEVE IT IS FEASIBLE TO ALLOCATE COMPUTER RESOURCES AND CACHING STORAGE RESEARCH THAT ARE RELATIVELY REMOTE FROM THE ORIGINAL DATA LOCATION. CO-SCHEDULED TOGETHER TO OPTIMIZE THE PERFORMANCE OF ENTIRE DATA ANALYSIS WORKLOADS. BASED ON THE SPLIT/MERGE METHODOLOGY, WE PROPOSE AMDASK, AN ABSTRACT MODEL FOR DATA-CENTRIC TASK FARMS, WHICH DEFINES THE ABSTRACT MODEL THAT ALLOWS US TO STUDY THE STATED HYPOTHESIS.  A DATA-CENTRIC TASK IS DEFINED AS A COMMON PARALLEL PATTERN WHICH DRIVES THE INDEPENDENT COMPUTATIONAL TASKS TAKING INTO CONSIDERATION THE DATA LOCALITY IN ORDER TO OPTIMIZE THE PERFORMACE OF THE ANALYSIS OF LARGE DATASETS.  WE INTEND TO VALIDATE THE AMDASK MODEL THROUGH SIMULATIONS.  WE EXPECT THE DISCRETE EVENT SIMULATIONS TO SHOW THE AMDASK MODEL IS BOTH EFFICIENT AND SCALABLE GIVEN A WIDE RANGE OF SIMULATION PARAMETERS.  ONCE THE MODEL IS VALIDATED, WE WILL IMPLEMENT SEVERAL APPLICATIONS ON TOP OF AMDASK IN ORDER TO SHOW THE MODEL'S EFFICIENCY, EFFECTIVENESS, SCALABILITY, AND FLEXIBILITY IN PRACTICE.  IN ORDER TO STREAMLINE THE IMPLEMENTATION OF VARIOUS APPLICATIONS, WE HAVE DEFINED FOUR COMPONENTS WHICH WILL BE THE BASIC BUILDING BLOCKS FOR ANY APPLICATION USING AMDASK MODEL.  THE FOUR MAIN COMPONENTS ARE: COMPUTE RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (DRP: DYNAMIC RESOURCE PROVISIONING), DATA RESOURCE MANAGEMENT (3D CACHE GRID: DYNAMIC DISTRIBUTED DATA CACHE FOR GRID APPLICATIONS), SCHEDULING (COMPUSTORE: A DATA AWARE TASK SCHEDULER), AND DISTRIBUTED EXECUTION ENVIRONMENTS (DEEF: DISTRIBUTED EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT FRAMEWORK).  ALL THESE FOUR COMPONENTS ARE INTEGRATED TOGETHER TO IMPLEMENT THE AMDASK ABSTRACT MODEL AND TO PROVIDE THE FOUNDATION NEEDED TO IMPLEMENT APPLICATIONS THAT CAN STAND TO BENEFIT FROM THE DATA-CENTRIC TASK FARM MODEL.  THE SUCCESSFUL IMPLEMENTATION OF THESE BASIC COMPONENTS WILL ALLOW US TO VALIDATE SOME OF OUR SIMULATION RESULTS, AS WELL AS GIVING US INSIGHT INTO BOTH THE EFFICIENCTY AND THE SCALABILITY OF OUR IMPLEMENTATION OF THE AMDASK MODEL IN  PRATICE.  FINALLY, WE EXPECT TO INVESTIGAE A DATA ANALYSIS APPLICATION NAMED THE "ASTROPORTAL" FROM THE ASTRONOMY DOMAIN TO SHOW THE EFFECTIVENESS ND FLEXIBILITY OF THE MODEL IN PRACTICE ON LARGE DATASETS, VARIOUS WORKLOADS, AND ANALYSIS CODES.  WE BELIEVE AMDASK IS AN IMPORTANT MODEL THAT GENERALIZES TOO MANY DOMAINS AND APPLICATIONS, AND COULD OFFER SYSTEM BUILT AROUND IT SIGNIFCANT PERFORMANCE IMPROVEMENTS WITH REDUCED RESOURCE CONSUMPTION.

Description: NEW SEARCH FOR SUBDWARF B STARS FROM THE GALEX We propose to carry out medium-resolution spectroscopic follow-up (1) for the identification of bona fide subdwarf B (sdB) stars from the new set of sdB star candidates chosen from the GALEX photometry in the GR2, in combination with other optical and near IR photometry, and (2) for the radial velocity variability monitoring for sdB stars identified from our previous and current efforts in order to determine the binary fraction of sdB stars. The UV bright, hot sdB stars are considered to be core helium-burning stars of 0.5 MQ with very thin hydrogen envelopes of Menv < 0.02M0, and immediate progenitors of white dwarfs. Although their current and post evolutionary status is relatively well understood, very little physics behind their formation/evolution is known. For instance, it is not clear whether such objects are born as single stars or can form only in binary systems. The number ratio of sdB stars in each Galactic stellar population (i.e., thin disk, thick disk, and halo) may give a clue to answer whether major formation mechanism can be explained by binary scenario or RGB peel-off scheme (Altmann et al. 2004, A&A, 414, 181). This approach was hampered by lack of identified sdB stars belonging to the thin disk and halo. Thus, of primary importance is new detection of sdB stars with faint magnitudes (halo) and at lower Galactic latitudes (thin disk). The huge data set of GALEX sdB stars, which reach the entire UV visible Milky Way, will eventually answer most of the remaining questions associated with their formation and evolution mechanism, and Galactic structure.

Description: NEW SEARCH FOR VERY METAL POOR STARS WITH [Fe/H]<-2.0 FROM THE GALEX The old, and most metal-poor stars in the halo and thick disk of the Galaxy provide vital clues for unraveling the structure, kinematics, and chemical composition of the early Milky Way. There have been a few successful anaylses of chemical abundances and dynamical motions of such stars, but the spatial scales have mostly been limited to include only a few kpc from the Sun since most of them are dwarfs and sub-giants near the main-sequence turnoff. Metal-deficient red giant stars are ideal probes of both the inner and outer halo, since they are intrinsically luminous, and thus more distant. We propose to carry out (1) medium-resolution spectroscopic follow-up for the identificaiton of bona fide very metal-poor (VMP) red giant stars with [Fe/H] < -2.0 from the new set of VMP star candidates chosen from the GALEX photometry in the GR2, in combination with other optical and near IR photometry, and (2) subsequent high-resolution spectroscopic follow-up of comprehensive abundance analyses for the VMP red giant stars identified from previous step. From this effort, we expect to newly reveal a few thousand bona fide VMP stars over a range of depths and sky-coverages. Indeed, this huge data set of GALEX VMP stars will help unravel the early nucleosynthesis, stellar dynamics, and substructure of the Galaxy.

Description: TOWARD UNDERSTANDING SPECTRAL ENERGY DISTRIBUTION OF MICROQUASARS We propose to expand an on-going effort on systematically studying the spectral energy distribution (SED) of MIcroquasars. As a first step, we plan to begin the process of establishing a database on broadband SEDs, which will provide critical data for understanding microquasars that are severely lacking at present. For instance, such data will facilitate a more accurate characterization or the spectral properties of microquasars - a valuable lesson from the studies of active galactic nuclei or gamma-ray bursts. The proposed work will not only involve reducing and analyzing a large amount of data from the archival databases but also compiling results from the literatures. The key scientific objectives include: 1) assessing the roles of jets and accretion flows in microquasars; 2) systematically re-examining the concepts of spectral states, state transitions, and spectral hysteresis, which have become increasingly confusing; 3) disentangling variabilities associated with the jets and accretion flows and thus quantifying the coupling between the two; and (4) identifying promising candidates for a new generation of gamma-ray experiments, such as GLAST and VERITAS, as we enter a golden era of astronomy at very high (GeV--TeV) energies. The proposed research will address some of the most fundamental issues under NASA's Strategic Sub-goal 3D, by probing important physical processes in the immediate vicinity of black holes.

Description: High-Velocity Clouds in the Galactic Environment:  A Numerical Study Motivated by Observations The high-velocity clouds OfVCs) are massive clouds (up to 10 million solar masses) of rapidly moving material in the outskirts of the Milky Way. Originally identified as neutral clouds at velocities inconsistent with Galactic rotation, observational breakthroughs using FUSE and HST demonstrate many HVCs are low metallicity objects (-0.1 to 0.3 times the solar abundance) falling onto the Milky Way from large distances (>I0 kpc). HVCs represent the gaseous building blocks of the on-going process of galaxy assembly. In addition, ground- and space-based observations of H alpha emission and high ionization absorption (e.g., from 0 VI, C IV) in HVCs demonstrate they are multiphase  entities, containing strongly ionized plasmas in addition to neutral matter. The properties of the HVC plasmas hint at a previously unidentified component of the Milky Way (or Local Group) - an extended hot, massive corona stretching to>SO kpc from the Sun. HVCs thus serve as probes of the Galactic environment and its on-going evolution. Although an active field of research, models for the interpretation of new HVC data rely on incomplete physics, especially for the ionized component of the clouds. We propose to perform 3D adaptive mesh magnetohydrodynamic simulations of idealized HVCs falling through a hot corona. Our models will be a significant advance over earlier work in that they will include (a) a realistic treatment of magnetic fields, including anisotropic thermal conduction; and (b) nonequilibrium cooling and ionization tracking, important for interpreting the 0 VI, C IV, and other ions. We will derive diagnostics from our simulations that can be directly compared with the FUSE and HST observations of the plasmas about the HVCs. Our proposed work will allow us to (1) probe the physics of the HVC plasmas; (2) constrain the evolution of HVCs; (3) explore the use of HVCs for probing the properties of a putative Galactic corona; and (4) understand the importance of HVCs to the on-going evolution of the Milky Way. Among the questions we will probe are: Do interactions between a neutral HVC and a corona produce the observed column densities of highly ionized gas? Are the velocity profiles of the ionized gas tracers observed by HST and FUSE consistent with this? How much of Halpha is produced in shock-induced ionization vs. photoionization? Can the low metallicity HVCs survive passage through a corona to be incorporated into the Galactic disk? or will they fragment and be incorporated into the corona? How important are magnetic fields to HVCs? Our confrontation of model diagnostics with observational results will help better our understanding of both.

Description: Blue Compact Dwarf galaxies (BCDs) are extreme examples of star-forming dwarf galaxies. They exhibit the highest specific star-formation rates (star-formation rates per unit mass) of any class of galaxy in the local universe. Description: Proposal Tille: TC4: Ground-based Validation for Aura and CALIPSO with NATIVE and Sondes SECTION VII - Project Summary The TC4 (Tropical Composition, Clouds and Climate Coupling) Field Experiment, scheduled for July 2007, focuses on two objectives: (1) elucidation of processes in which chemistry, clouds, temperature and dynamics interact in the tropical tropopause layer; (2) validation of CALIPSO aerosol and of Aura ozone and other gases. Both elements are addressed in this proposal. First, tropical Kelvin and convectively-generated gravity waves are identified in ozone and temperature data from Costa Rican sondes using the lamina-labeling approach of Pierce and Grant [1998] as adapted for analysis of INTEX Intercontinental Chemical Transport Experiment) and SHADOZ (Southern Hemisphere Additional Ozonesondes) data [Thompson et al., 2006a,b]. A wider sub-tropical perspective will be provided by analysis ofINTEX-B/Milagro IONS-06 sondes at Mexico City and Houston. Second, the NATIVE (Nittany Atmospheric Trailer and Integrated Validation Experiment) mobile facility will be deployed to Costa Rica or Panama in TC4 to provide (1) continuous surface ozone, CO, NO, and NOy data and aerosol size distribution; (2) column uv, aerosol extinction and ozone from shadowband radiometry and aerosol extinction from sunphotometry; (3) 532-nm aerosollidar measurements throughout the troposphere and UT/LS; (4) ozone and P-T-U profiles from sonde launches. A unique synergism between the observational and analytical research provides tropospheric ozone budgets determined from soundings, trajectories, satellite data and meteorological fields. We compute ozone amounts in the troposphere from four sources: regional convection and lightning (RCL), advection of pollution (AD), stratospheric injection (ST) and local boundary-layer (BL) convection. Expected outcomes of our research are (1) tropospheric ozone budgets from TC4 to be delivered to the data archive for comparison with models; (2) improved discrimination between stratosphere and troposphere for more accurate derivations of tropospheric ozone from Aura instruments. Components of the proposed research are provided by the PI with Valparaiso and by PSU and BAERI collaborators. The one-year budgets for PSU and Valparaiso, submitted separately, are for deployment costs only. Description: POWER AND BANDWIDTH-EFFICIENT CODING TECHNIQUES FOR SPACE AND SATELLITE COMMUNICATIONS The goals of the coding and modulation research effort at Notre Dame are to provide more bits, faster bits, and better bits in support of NASA's space and satellite digital communication systems. More bits imply higher spectral efficiencies. The proposed research will focus on the design and analysis of binary codes for binary-input channels. While increased bandwidth efficiency - i.e., "flattening the bit pipe" - requires non-binary signaling, there is an emerging consensus within the digital communications community that this is best carried out (in terms of performance and complexity) through bit-interleaved coded modulation (BICM). In BICM, binary codewords are interleaved and then Gray-mapped onto a non-binary signal space, with little loss in capacity. Thus, the results obtained for binary codes carryover to applications at higher spectral efficiencies. Faster bits imply higher decoding speeds. We propose to focus on the design of low-density parity check convolutional codes with an innovative pipelined decoding strategy well suited for high speed iterative message-passing decoding. In this phase of the proposed research, we will continue our collaboration with the research group of Dr. Stephen Bates at the University of Alberta, Canada on very high speed FPGA and ASIC decoder implementations for these codes. Better bits imply higher reliability. The proposed research investigates low-density parity check convolutional coding schemes capable of achieving very low bit and frame error rates at signal-to-noise ratios near the Shannon limit. Our goal is to improve the reliability of these schemes while maintaining near capacity performance. In addition, we propose methods of achieving this goal that result in reduced decoding latency. We will focus our research effort on the additive white Gaussian noise channel model most commonly seen in space and satellite communication.

Description: NONLINEAR AEROSERVOELASTICITY OF HIGH SPEED CRUISE VEHICLE This research supports NASA's development of the high speed cruise vehicle concept with a particular interest in developing an in-situ filter capable of detecting the onset of dynamic instability. The development of high speed cruise capabilities has mandated the need for an expanded flight envelope to meet the needs of increasing varieties of flight objectives. The linear and nonlinear dynamic response characteristics of a model aircraft structure are examined in this research. To identify the linear modal characteristics (mode shape, modal frequency, modal scaling), impact testing was conducted and the nominal frequency response functions were constructed. A model aircraft with reconfigurable pre-stressed components has been constructed as a test bed for developing the algorithms to be used in future semispan model wing tunnel tests. Local effects of nonlinearities in a model aircraft structure result in the appearance of multiple linear modal frequencies and shapes when different reference measurements are used in the modal analysis of frequency response function data. Despite the broadband spectral nature of a modal impact excitation, frequency response data collected using modal impacts have shown promise for identifying linear modes and characterizing local nonlinearities using input- output coherence functions. Swept sine testing with dynamic shakers has also been used to identify higher-order frequency response functions and restoring forces for characterizing structural nonlinearities. The characteristics identified using modal impact and swept sine testing have been utilized to simulate the effects of nonlinearities on individual modes and modal coupling in the modal space. This approach will be compared with a reduced-order physical model to determine the advantaqes and disadvantaqes of these two approaches.

Description: Discovery of A Lyman Limit System @ Z=0.20258: The IBM/Galaxy Connection In contrast with high redshift studies of the IGM, observations of low z absorption systems provide the opportunity to examine the IGM/galaxy connection in great detail. From STIS E140M/E230M observations, we have detected 4 metal systems toward the quasar PKS 0312-77 (z=0.223). One of them is a Lyman limit system (LLS; log N (H I) > 17.3) at z=0.20258, which shows one of the strongest O VI system ever detected and several elements in different ionization stages, implying a multiphase structure of the gas. This LLS is therefore well suited for a study of the atomic abundances and ionization state. It also provides the rare chance to compare the metallicity in the LLS and in the galaxy that we suspect gives rise to the LLS. The H I column density remains, however, largely unknown from the STIS spectrum. We therefore request a FUSE spectrum of PKS 0312-77 with good signal-to-noise (S/N 14) in order to have access to the whole Lyman series H I from Ly down to the Lyman limit. The FUSE spectrum will also provide the S VI, C III, and O I lines for the LLS. combining FUSE and STIS observations will provide the unique opportunity to derive the overall metallicity of the LSS, the fractions and kinematics of ionized gas, and to compare the abundances of the associated galaxy with the LLS. Our proposed observations will also complete O VI surveys at low z to 20 mA.

The L-GIP will include a seismometer, a heat flow probe, and a magnetometer. These instruments have been chosen because their individual data sets will address several unanswered scientific questions regarding the lunar interior and lunar evolution, as well as provide valuable data for exploration. Each dataset will enhance the other, as using combined data types together in cooperative inversion approaches can be effective in limiting the number of acceptable interpretations. The seismic models resolve horizontal layers well, while magnetic approaches resolve lateral variations or vertical interfaces in subsurface magnetic susceptibility (and density if gravity data are available). Heat flow data can provide additional lateral and sometimes (coarse) vertical property constraints, but also provide key model constraints for seismic (velocity) and density models. So, by combining these instruments in the L-GIP the datasets thus generated will dramatically lessen ambiguities in our understanding of the lunar interior. Each instrument considered in this proposal is relatively mature and is a payload on past, current or future planetary missions. However, the modifications to these (required for integrating into one deployable unit), along with the required architecture, are what form the basis for this proposal. Therefore, this project encompasses a number of trade studies for each instrument and the L-GIP architecture in order to arrive at a robust, deployable design. Significant trade studies include how to operate in an adverse thermal regime (transition between lunar night/day), long-lived power supply options, networking of different L-GIPs, defining the best design of heat flow probe to achieve the sciences goals (i.e., designs from Apollo, Lunar-A penetrator, and Rosetta missions), inclusion (or not) of a solar wind detector for the magnetic studies, and deployment strategies. The spectra are expected to provide a severe test of the inverse-Compton origin of X-rays from such sources, as expected from accretion-based models.
