Description: THERMAL DIFFUSIVITY AND CONDUCTIVITY TPS ABLATOR TESTING DESCRIPTION With the recent improvements in rapid data acquisition and laboratory equipment, transient measurement techniques have gained markedly in popularity. The flash method, has been used to measure materials whole diffusivities range from 0.001 to 10 (a range of 10 over 4) over a temperature range from 80 to 2500K (-315 to 4050 F). The method uses small easy to fabricate samples and results can be obtained within seconds. The flash method was first described in 1960 by Parker, Butler, Jenkins, and Abbott of the U.S. Navy Radiological Defense Laboratory. In this method the front face of a small disk-shaped sample (often about the size of a small coin), is subjected to a very short burst of radiant energy. The source of the radiant energy is usually a laser or a xenon flash lamp and irradiation times are of one millisecond or less. The resulting temperature rise of the rear surface of the sample is measured and thermal diffusivity values are computed from the temperature rise versus time data. Often times of less than one second are involved. The ambient temperature may be controlled by a small furnace tube or chiller. NASA has a requirement to provide the thermal conductivity, a measurement of the capability of a material to transfer heat, for 7 different formulas of a research ablator material. The Thermophysical Properties Research Lab requires the conductivity measurements at three temperatures (Room Temperature, 250 degrees F, and 500 degrees F) and at two pressures (0.01 atm and 1.0 atm). The measurements will be made by measuring the thermal diffusivity of the material through a technique knows as the flash laser diffusivity method. Small samples, approximately 0.5 inch in diameter, are flashed with a short pulse laser. The temperature on the opposite side of the sample is measured as a function of time. The diffusivity is the resultant value. Two more properties are necessary in order to determine the conductivity of the specimen: density and specific heat. The density of the specimen is readily determined through the weight and volume of the specimen. The specific heat is measured in a Differential Scanning Calorimeter, in which the amount of energy needed to increase the temperature of the specimen a certain increment is measured. Once the diffusivity, density and specific heat of the specimen are determined, the conductivity can be determined through the use of the equation: k = a x Cp x p Where k = thermal conductivity a = thermal diffusivity Cp = specific heat p = density

Description: The internal structure of a planet has profound implications for its tectonic history and thermal evolution. The MGS Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topography and gravity data sets are powerful tools that hold information on the internal structure of the planet. Gravity inversions for density are non-unique, and it is quite likely that mantle density structure is being mapped into crustal structure models at the longest wavelengths in current models. I propose a combination of 3D spherical convection models, using ensemble averaging to eliminate uncertainties resulting from initial conditions, core radius and Rayleigh number. I will use the probability distribution from the geoid and topography harmonics of the convection calculations to weight the uncertainty in the isostatic geoid inversion for crustal structure. I will compare the crustal structure from this new inversion with an inversion that does not include the effects of mantle density to estimate how much mantle structure is mapped into current crustal structure models. By comparing whole mantle and layered calculations, I will be able to extract the mantle density signal from the geoid and topography, providing insight into the current mantle structure.

Description: Discovery of A Lyman Limit System @ Z=0.20258: The IBM/Galaxy Connection In contrast with high redshift studies of the IGM, observations of low z absorption systems provide the opportunity to examine the IGM/galaxy connection in great detail. From STIS E140M/E230M observations, we have detected 4 metal systems toward the quasar PKS 0312-77 (z=0.223). One of them is a Lyman limit system (LLS; log N (H I) > 17.3) at z=0.20258, which shows one of the strongest O VI system ever detected and several elements in different ionization stages, implying a multiphase structure of the gas. This LLS is therefore well suited for a study of the atomic abundances and ionization state. It also provides the rare chance to compare the metallicity in the LLS and in the galaxy that we suspect gives rise to the LLS. The H I column density remains, however, largely unknown from the STIS spectrum. We therefore request a FUSE spectrum of PKS 0312-77 with good signal-to-noise (S/N 14) in order to have access to the whole Lyman series H I from Ly down to the Lyman limit. The FUSE spectrum will also provide the S VI, C III, and O I lines for the LLS. combining FUSE and STIS observations will provide the unique opportunity to derive the overall metallicity of the LSS, the fractions and kinematics of ionized gas, and to compare the abundances of the associated galaxy with the LLS. Our proposed observations will also complete O VI surveys at low z to 20 mA.

Description: The Effect of Gravitational Instabilities on Particle Growth and Migration in the Solar Nebula (Student-Scott A. Michael)  I propose to conduct three dimensional radiative hydrodynamics simulations including particles to study the effects of gravitational instabilities (GIs) on the growth and migration of rocky bodies in protoplanetary disks. The main theories behind gas giant formation are core accretion and disk instability. Each theory has unresolved issues, which make gas giant planet formation by either mechanism alone seem unlikely. However, the hybrid theory of gas giant planet formation combines aspects form each of these theories to resolve these issues. Basically, the hybrid theory posits that GIs can act to accelerate core accretion, solving the timescale problem for core accretion and the problem of directly forming gas giants via disk instability. My work will model the effect of GIs on small rocky bodies in a protoplanetary disk in an effort to see if GIs can indeed accelerate core accretion. Since our research group has one of the most sophisticated schemes for treating the gas physics of a protoplantary disk, we are uniquely suited to bridge the gap between pure gas disks and the accretion of rocky bodies. This work will make significant progress in understanding the interplay of GIs and solids and may confirm that planets can form via the hybrid theory of gas giant planet formation.

Another area of emphasis will be the Jovian x-ray aurora and the aeronomy associated with this aurora. Description: SPECTRA AND LIGHTCURVES OF GRB'S IN THE JITTER EMISSION PARADIGM SUMMARY: In a standard model of GRBs, the observed emission is produced at shocks, which generate strong magnetic fields and accelerate relativistic electrons, which produce radiation via synchrotron mechanism. To account for the very small-scale structure of the shock-generated fields, an alternative -- jitter mechanism of emission -- has been proposed and it has been shown to provide a more accurate (than synchrotron) description of prompt GRB spectra. With the new high-quality data being delivered by Swift, it is highly important to carefully study the available emission models. We propose to develop a theory of shock based on the jitter mechanism of emission and compare it with the existing synchrotron model. Together with our collaborators at U. Colorado, Boulder, we plan to implement the results of this proposal and make comparisons with observational data. In the course of our investigation, we will (i) develop a theory of jitter self-absorption and (ii) calculation of afterglow light curves in the jitter paradigm. We also plan to start a pilot project in modeling of prompt and X-ray flare emission.

Description: UNDERSTANDING THE DIFFUSE X-RAY BACKGROUND: THE EXTRAGALACTIC TO SOLAR SYSTEM ENVIRONMENT Soft X-ray emission exhibits substantially more structure on the sky than its higher energy counterpart. With the greater complexity also comes greater controversy concerning its source components. Until recently, the standard view held that the soft X-ray sky had three primary contributors, all farther than a parsec. Proceeding from the most distant, these are (1) the residual flux from the extragalactic power law, (2) a lumpy distribution of 10 6 K plasma in the lower halo of the Milky Way and (3) a 10 6 K plasma filling a cavity surrounding the Sun in the Galactic disk, the local bubble. However, recently another component originating within about 10-3 parsecs has been discovered, solar wind charge exchange emission from the heliospheric termination shock, the interplanetary medium, and the magnetosheath surrounding the Earth. This emission contributes significantly to the soft X-ray sky with a magnitude comparable at times to all the other components together. We will mine the X-ray data archive to quantify the extent to which solar wind charge exchange emission contributes to the diffuse X-ray emission. We will compare temporal and spatial variations of the observed diffuse emission in archived data from ROSAT, XMM-Newton, Chandra, ASCA and Beppo-SAX to predicted X-ray spatial and temporal intensity profiles using the Fahr and other models for the heliospheric neutral H and He distributions, Hodges results along with more recent data for the distribution of exospheric hydrogen, and the Spreiter and MHD BATSRUS models for the near-Earth plasma. By varying the model input parameters for solar wind density, velocity, temperature and heavy ion composition along with interstellar hydrogen and helium and exospheric hydrogen densities to the degree allowed by observational constraints and incorporating soft X-ray efficiency factors that are a function of solar wind composition, we will obtain the best agreement possible between the modeled and observed light curves. We will provide this modeling capability to the X-ray community. Our research will answer the following science questions: (1) Is the local hot bubble dead? That is, can we account for all observed diffuse emission within a few hundred parsecs previously identified as local hot bubble with the solar wind charge exchange mechanism? (2) How can we predict the strength of the solar wind charge exchange using geometric information from the X-ray observatory, solar wind observations and simulations? The research will produce an optimized capability to model solar wind charge exchange emission for use in (a) analyzing data from past observations (b) planning upcoming observations to minimize potential contamination and (c) evaluating the potential loss of data due to solar wind charge exchange on future X-ray missions.

Description: KENTUCKY EPSCOR: EFFICACY OF COUNTERMEASURES TO CARDIOVASCULAR DECONDITIONING IN MEN AND WOMEN DURING SIMULATED MOON EXPLORATIONS The central objective of the proposal is to develop an easily administered countermeasure that would mitigate human cardiovascular risks (primarily fainting upon re-exposure to gravity) associated with physiological adaptations to microgravity during extended duration missions to the moon and eventually Mars. This objective will be accomplished, in collaboration with JSC and Ames investigators, by testing, a human (both men and women) model of space flight-induced cardiovascular deconditioning (hypovolemia protocol), in conjunction with 1) a countermeasure to cardiovascular deconditioning (compression stockings with spatially distributed, or cyclically applied, pressure), 2) a model of the first day of lunar activity (Altcr-G lunar simulator) and 3) a model of g profiles experienced in a lunar mission (using NASA Ames 20G Centrifuge). Methods: This study will determine deconditioned men and womens: 1) orthostatic tolerance limits (ability to maintain consciousness in a gravity environment), and 2) any reasons related to change in the limits, including: a) the relative distribution of fluid volume changes in four body segments (thoracic, splanchnic, thigh and calf), and intra/extravascular plasma volume shifts b) changes in responsiveness of heart rate, heart rate control sensitivity, cardiac output, continuous arterial pressure, total peripheral resistance, c) contributions from neurohormones. 3) Effectiveness of compression garments (either to prevent development of orthostatic intolerance Significance: This research is important to NASA because diminished orthostatic tolerance of astronauts continues to be a problem that may only become worse with long duration lunar explorations. The current countermeasures are insufficient to prevent orthostatic intolerance in 30% of astronauts returning from short duration Shuttle missions and in 83% returning from missions that are longer than six months. Also, the decreased size of the proposed Crew Exploration Vehicle for moon missions compared to the current Shuttle dictates that the countermeasure be small and efficient. Therefore, testing of countermeasures in simulations of lunar explorations is a necessary component of upcoming NASA related research. The goal of developing optimally designed compression stocking has the potential to meet these requirements. It is also important to note that the cost of cardiovascular deconditioning studies using conventional bed rest is extremely expensive and time consuming for NASA. The use of the proposed hypovolumia model to simulate space flight and extraterrestrial cardiovascular deconditioning could decrease time and cost significantly. Likewise, blood pooling results from the proposed lunar mission G profile on the Ames centrifuge could serve as a good estimate for matching with existing tilt and LBNP data in order to use these devices as substitutes for expensive centrifuge experiments for testing countermeasures for lunar and other space missions. In addition, some musculoskeletal activity in extraterrestrial G environments and associated fluid volume shifts, could be approximated using the Alter -G device described in this proposal. Any one of these possibilities could significantly increase NASAs research productivity and decrease cost. Lastly, the educational component of the proposed research involves support for two graduate students per year and a continuation of our outreach program for undergraduate and high school students with special emphasis on the recruitment of women and minorities.

Description: This joint LSU-Southern NASA EPSCoR project addresses adhesively bonded joints which have been widely used in aircraft, space shuttles, and other structures due to their ease offabricating both large and integrated structures. It is well known that, for almost all the structures in-use, joints cannot be avoided and they are the weakest structural component and control the overall load carrying capacity of the structure. Unfortunately, joint-failure induced structural disintegration has been a challenging, on-going problem; as evidenced by many fatal incidents related to inadequate bonding in recent flight history. In this project, we plan to develop a 'smart' joint by integrating piezoelectric particle/fiber reinforced layers into the adherents and utilizing a functionally graded carbon nanotube reinforced shape memory polymer adhesive. The research objectives are to (i) dramatically and self-adaptively reduce the peel stress and shear stress concentration at the adhesive bondline, (ii) self-monitor, self-control, and self-heal the composite joint system in-situ, and (iii) extend the service life of aged/aging aircraft. The educational/workforce objective is to develop a 'research-oriented approach' designed to attract and retain a greater number of high quality students, including minority students, in STEM disciplines. Four tasks have been identified as essential: (1) analytical modeling and optimization; (2) raw materials selection and characterization; (3) fabrication technology; and (4) testing and validation. Our multi-institutional team will address each of these in consultation with NASA engineers. Several NASA field-centers (KSC, MSFC, GRC, Dryden) have expressed interest in this research since its applications span from aircraft to space systems to Lunar/Mars outposts. Moreover, applications in industry are potentially huge, thereby supporting Louisiana economic development. We are optimistic that this project will enhance NASA related composite materials and structures research in Louisiana as well as nationally.

Description: The GLAST (Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope) satellite mission is scheduled for launch in January 2008. GLAST will perform a sensitive survey of the sky at energies from approximately 10 keV to 200 GeV. Its target sources will include galactic black holes, active galactic nuclei, gamma ray bursts, and other sources of high energy photons. Energetic gamma rays are typically produced in non thermal processes associated with the acceleration of energetic particles. In order to understand the mechanisms producing the high energy radiation and the processes driving the sources of the particles and gamma rays, it would be extremely useful to be able to do correlated measurements of the additional components of radiation produced in the sources: the X-rays produced in conjunction with the gamma rays by the synchrotron-Compton process, optical and radio fluxes from the sources, the very high energy cosmic rays produced by shock wave acceleration in sources such as active galactic nuclei observed by GLAST in gamma rays, and the neutrinos possibly produced by energetic particle interactions or in coincidence with gamma ray bursts. This proposed EPSCOR program will make such multiwavelength and multimessenger observations through a collaboration between Louisiana State University and Southern University-Baton Rouge which will allow Louisiana scientists to participate in the multiwavelength observing campaign and analysis program of the GLAST mission. The GLAST astrophysics will enhance faculty and postdoctoral training and will motivate and train students for STEM careers. The project involves collaborations with MSFC, GSFC and JPL, the IceCube neutrino detector, the Auger cosmic ray experiment, and ground-based optical and radio telescopes.

Description: "SENSOR WEB DYNAMIC REPLANNING" We will propose to extend the dynamic replanning capability of Draper's Earth Phenomena Observing System (EPOS), which has successfully demonstrated the capability to dynamically replan the activities of NASA space-based sensor assets to maximize the return of useful science measurements (e.g., ensure cloud free targeting). We will propose to enhance and extend EPOS to include the replanning of sensors on UAVs (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles) and USVs (Unmanned Surface Vessels) being fielded by NASA over the next few years. The new dynamic replanning capability will utilize complementary and cooperative suites of heterogeneous sensor assets that can be triggered by observation data and/or predictive models to adaptively respond to significant events and provide enhanced understanding of temporal Earth phenomena. An event-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to observation-triggered cues for phenomenon, such as harmful algal bloom outbreaks. A model-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to significant increases in meteorological forecast model error growth due to model sensitivities within specific atmospheric regions. The events and phenomena that present the largest potential payoff to the proposed replanning capability are characterized by being localized and transient and also capable of causing damage to both human life and property, e.g., weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, etc.), harmful algal blooms, volcanic eruptions, ice shelf break-up, seismic activities, oil spilis, and search and rescue. Description: EARTH MOOM MARS RADIATION EXPOSURE MODULE (EMMREM) We are preparing to return humans to the Moon and setting the stage for exploration to Mars and beyond. However, it is unclear if long missions outside of Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) can be accomplished with acceptable risk. The central objective of our project, the Earth-Moon-Mars Radiation Exposure Module (EMMREM), is to develop and validate a numerical module for completely characterizing time-dependent radiation exposure in the Earth-Moon-Mars and Interplanetary space environments. EMMREM provides the ability to predict radiation exposure anywhere on the surface or atmosphere of Earth, on the Moon, Mars, and in interplanetary space between Earth and Mars. EMMREM is designed for broad use by researchers to predict radiation exposure generated by almost any particle distribution incident from interplanetary space. EMMREM is developed using contemporary, state-of-the-art, physics-based particle radiation models. Beyond this, it has the capability to incorporate new models, as they become available, to give continually improved estimates of radiation hazards and effects. EMMREM is comprehensively validated in the environments where risks need to be assessed, using direct and contemporaneous measurements near Earth, at the Moon and Mars to significantly reduce uncertainties in radiation exposure. EMMREM characterizes the extremes, statistics, and variations over time of radiation exposure caused by solar energetic particles and cosmic rays. The results of EMMREM will improve risk assessment models so that future human exploration missions can be adequately planned. This makes EMMREM highly relevant to NASA's Vision for Space Exploration and Living With a Star Programs. EMMREM's highly cross-disciplinary team makes the unprecedented link from particle radiation researchers to radiation biophysics researchers and risk assessment specialists. EMMREM is a powerful tool, urgently needed to reduce uncertainties in risk assessment models. EMMREM is the missing link from Space Science to Space Exploration. EMMREM's central objective is achieved through four primary activities: 1. We develop the central EMMREM module for predicting time-dependent radiation exposure (Linear-Energy-Transfer spectra and dose-related quantities) based on existing, well-established, working codes including the BRYNTRN and HZETRN code developed at NASA Langley and the HETC-HEDS Monte Carlo code developed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the University of Tennessee. 2. We develop interfaces between EMMREM and energetic particle simulations using, as a test-bed, sophisticated, physics-based solar energetic particle (SEP) and cosmic ray models. Simulations and associated EMMREM radiation exposure predictions are used to characterize typical, and worst-case event scenarios, and to characterize exposure near-Earth, at the Moon, Mars and throughout the inner heliosphere over the solar cycle. 3. We develop interfaces between EMMREM and direct observations of particle radiation (SoHO, ACE, Wind, STEREO, SAMPEX, NOAA-GOES and Ulysses). The observations are used both to validate SEP and cosmic ray simulations, and as direct input to predict radiation exposure at the Earth, on the Moon, Mars and in interplanetary space environments. 4. We significantly reduce radiation exposure uncertainties through comprehensive validation in the Earth, Moon, Mars and interplanetary space environments. EMMREM is validated with previously measured LET spectra from the International Space Station (ISS) and the Space Shuttle, observations from LRO/CRaTER, MSL/RAD, MARIE on Mars Odyssey, and using an extensive database of Accelerator Beam Measurements.

Description: Sources and Sinks of Carbon from Land-Use Change, Management, and Disturbance in the U.S.:  Steps Toward a Synthesis SOURCES AND SINKS OF CARBON FROM LAND-USE CHANGE, MANAGEMENT, AND DISTURBANCE IN THE U.S.: STEPS TOWARDS A SYNTHESIS ABSTRACT: A previous analysis by the principal investigator estimated the annual flux of carbon for the U.S. with census-based data on changes in land use, forestry, and fire management. The estimated sink in forests was low compared with studies based on data from forest inventories, but there were a number of processes omitted from the historical analysis. A reanalysis is warranted. The conterminous U.S. is a particularly good region for a detailed historical reconstruction because of the unusually rich assortment of historical data available. Landsat data on disturbance, available since 1972 offer a second data set, independent of census-based reconstructions of land-use change, for calculating sources and sinks of carbon during recent decades. These Landsat data are currently being compiled under on-going NACP projects. This proposal seeks support (1) to update the historical analysis based on census data and (2) to use the recent data compiled from the NACP Landsat analyses (3) to calculate two independent estimates of carbon flux for the conterminous U.S. over the period 1972-2000. Differences in the estimates of carbon flux (census-based versus Landsat-based) will reveal strengths and weakness of the two approaches and will be used to construct a harmonized estimate of carbon flux more accurate than possible from either approach by itself. For example, changes in land use obtained from the Landsat record miss disturbances before 1972 and thus underestimate both the area of recovering forests and the carbon accumulating in them. On the other hand, changes in land use based on census data (agricultural and forestry statistics) miss important processes affecting carbon storage (for example, natural disturbances). The overall objective of the proposed research is to determine the annual net flux of carbon for terrestrial ecosystems of the conterminous U.S. The emphasis will be on forests and will include the effects of forest conversion to agricultural land, abandonment of agricultural land, harvest of forests, other forms of forest management, wildfires, other disturbances, and forest growth. The approach will use an improved carbon model with two independent data sets of land-use/cover change: one, historical census data; the second, recent Landsat data. Model results will be tested against SRTM-derived estimates of aboveground biomass (from another on-going NACP project). The results of the proposed research are expected to contribute significantly to NASALS goals in at least two respects. First, the research will produce a new estimate of carbon flux for the conterminous U.S. The estimate will be spatially specific, based on a harmonization of historical, census data and Landsat data. The results will include an evaluation of the error of the estimated flux, including the effect of spatial resolution on error. Second, the research will produce a spatial/historical (1700-2005) data set of land-use change for the forests of the U.S.

Description: We propose to improve productivity of high performance computing for applications on multicore computers and clusters. These machines built from one or more chips that may have from two to hundreds of cores on a chip or socket, are notoriously hard to program. Interactive Supercomputing's Star-P platform has been designed to meet this need but requires more components to fully deliver the dream of high performance computing. We will work with NASA to develop the ability to reuse existing MPI and serial codes. Software writers can then move forward by working in high productivity interactive languages such as Mathworks MATLAB. Star-P already has this general capability, but what is further needed are functional transformations from the language as it appears on the desktop. In this work we will identify those transformations that will benefit NASA codes, and apply them first as a prototype in Phase I. In Phase II we will complete the prototype fully automating what might be thought of as semi-automatic transformations. We will in addition widen the scope of NASA codes that will benefit from such productivity enhancement. As a synergistic activity, visits to NASA sites including workshops are envisioned so that the work has maximum impact.

Description: Helium plays several critical rolls in spacecraft propulsion. High pressure helium is commonly used to pressurize propellant fuel tanks. Helium cryocoolers can be used to sub-cool and thereby densify cryogenic propellants such as liquid hydrogen (LH2) and liquid oxygen (LO2). The use of densified cryogenic propellants can reduce the gross payload weight of a launch vehicle by up to 20%, or increase payload capability. Helium compressors are critical components for cryogenic propellant storage and distribution systems, whether used in cryocoolers for densification or to compress gaseous helium for propellant pressurization. Regenerative compressor technology can serve high head, low flow helium pressurization applications in a compact form with high reliability. Pressure ratios on the order of 3:1 per impeller-stage are commercially available. Non-lubricated gas-bearing supported prototypes have been successfully demonstrated. However, even state-of-the-art prototype regenerative compressors are limited to efficiencies of about 55%. This was achieved using aerodynamic rotor blades rather than the straight radial blades previously used. Commercially available regenerative compressors with straight vaned rotors operate at much lower efficiency. An innovation is proposed that promises to improve the efficiency of regenerative compressors well beyond the current state of the art.

Description: Axis Engineering Technologies proposes a revolutionary new technology that can provide performance levels, in terms of output power, bandwidth and mass, previously unmet in current commercially available actuation platforms. The approach features a new hybrid pump, which is powered by active material stacks, and produces fluidic power to directly power hydraulic actuators. The compact, sealed unit eliminates external hydraulic components, such as accumulators, reservoirs, and, especially, long hydraulic tubing runs. By increasing system efficiency, reducing system mass and exploiting the unique characteristics of active materials, we expect to get a significant performance improvement in representative applications. This is in contrast with many commercially available actuation systems, composed of either traditional hydraulic or electromechanical mechanisms. Each of these systems is limited due to either excessive mass or limited bandwidth, or both. And yet these technologies have been adopted across a wide spectrum of applications, including Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), high performance fighter aircraft, active automotive suspension systems and mobile robotic systems. Each of these applications would benefit greatly from the introduction of an actuation system that can provide mass-savings and bandwidth improvements, simultaneously.

Description: Research Support Instruments, Inc. (RSI) proposes to develop the Retroreflector Array for Test Environments (RATE), an innovative technology that will non-intrusively measure pressure on aerodynamic surfaces in NASA ground test facilities with high sensitivity and bandwidth. The signal from RATE units will change locally due to pressure changes. Description: PREDICTING LANDSLIDES USING MEASUREMENTS OF PRECIPITAION FROM SPACE The key to advancing the prediction and predictability of many landslides is the transient response of the subsurface moisture to spatio-temporal patterns of precipitation that satellite platforms such as the TRMM and the future GPM provide. These precipitation data, however, are only useful for landslide hazard forecasting if physically-based hydrology models that are capable of capturing these transient dynamics are used to interpret the spatially complex precipitation. Using models to forecast landslides over large regions in reasonable detail requires knowledge of topography, vegetationiland cover, and rainfall at resolutions of at least large hillslopes. NASA data have facilitated the necessary terrain assessment by deploying a network of sensors to observe topography (SRTM) and vegetationlland cover and its change (MODIS, LANDSAT) over large regions with sufficient spatial resolution and adequate revisit intervals. This proof-of-concept study will test the following hypotheses: 1. Because TRMMIGPM data capture complex spatial patterns in precipitation and provide frequent observations, they can be used with a distributed hydrology model to capture the spatio-temporal distribution of soil moisture at resolutions consistent with relevant slope stability indices. 2. Detailed process modeling of spatiotemporal patterns of infiltration and lateral moisture redistribution using TRMMJGPM precipitation input as forcing significantly improves the skill of predictions of landslide timing, location and spatial extent. The proponents will focus on small tropical montane watersheds of the Luqnillo Experimental Forest (LEF) in northeast Puerto Rico. This site is rich in data and its landslides have been extensively studied. It is well sampled by TRMM observations and precipitation ground truth is available from raingages and meteorological radar. Satellite precipitation will be used to drive an advanced distributed model of hydrology and vegetation (tRIBS-VEGGIE) in order to predict regions of high landslide risk and the potential impact. Predictions will be verified against observations.

Description: DIURNAL SALT ENRICHED LAYER UNDER EVAPORATION: EFFECT ON SKIN-BULK SALINITIES AND IMPLICATIONS FOR THE AQARIUS SALINITY MEASUREMENTS The upcoming Aquarius/SAC-I) mission, with a promise of providing global sea surface salinity (SSS) maps at a monthly 100 km resolution and 0.2psu accuracy for three years, holds great potential for augmenting a global salinity database and for improving global climate monitoring and predictions. However, the Aquarius mission will not operate as stand alone i it depends on in situ sampled bulk SSS to provide ground-truth, to ensure instrument stability, and to reduce measurement noise. It is, therefore, important to obtain a good knowledge of the differences between the radiometric skin SSS and in situ bulk SSS made at sub-skin depths. Much has been studied about skin-bulk SSS differences during episodic rainfall events, but little is known of the effect of persistent evaporation on skin-bulk salinities. Buoy measurements obtained at three distinct locations reveal for the first time that, in absence of rainfall, the near surface experiences salt enrichment on diurnal timescales. This salt layer is located at a depth similar to that of the diurnal warm layer, but has a peak occurring slightly ahead of the diurnal warming and shows a dependence of evaporation. The salinity diurnal cycle anomalies at ~lm depth are usually about 0.1-0.2psu, but can reach O.Spsu in case of strong evaporation. The proposed research focuses on the investigation of the diurnal salt layer under evaporation and its effect on skin-bulk SSS differences using data analysis combined with a mixed-layer model study. The specific objectives include: (i) characterizing the formation of the diurnal salt enriched layer under evaporation, its forcing mechanisms, and its relationship to the surface temperature diurnal cycle; (ii) improving the ability of the Price-Weller-Pinker (PVVP) mixed-layer model in simulating the diurnal near-surface haline processes; and (iii) developing skin-bulk salinity parameterization based on Saunders (1967) skin SSS treatment and PWP bulk SSS simulation and studying its potential application to near-real time Aquarius global SSS processing.

Description: Small Business Innovative Research Phase II - Aircraft Sensor-Logger with Power Replenishment Capabilities. Traditional instrumentation of an aircraft is a complex and time-consuming chore. Once the sensors are installed, long wires for power and data must be routed through to a central data collection location where several large off-the-shelf electronic components reside, adding weight, cost and increasing the probably of introducing noise or faults into the testing system. All of this necessary infrastructure leads to prohibit the use of some types of sensors and limit the total number of sensors used so save on time, cost, complexity and resources. During the course of this Phase II SBIR research, Metis Design Corporation (MDC) proposes to develop a standardized data acquisition hub for aircraft testing sensors dubbed a sensor-logger. The sensor-logger would essentially serve as a durable sensor infrastructure node capable of autonomously facilitating local testing for multiple sensors of various types. Controlled wirelessly by PC or PDA, data could be displayed in real-time, or logged internally for up to 40 hours. The second half of the proposed research would then tie together the sensor-logger with the Phase I research, developing a power-replenishment device to attach to the sensor-logger to extend its operating capabilities. Finally both devices will be flight tested in true aircraft environments. Potential commercial applications extend to factors such as device marketability including but not limited to its versatility. The ability not only to be integrated into new applications, but also retrofitted into existing systems. There are several areas of potential NASA applicability. The first is for experimental aircraft programs. This device will give the ability to collect more data , with less complexity cost and risk to the testing program. Another important aerospace market would be for expendable launch vehicles (ELV) to help facilitate launch/no launch decisions. Of probably greatest importance, this device could be a key technology for reusable launch vehicle (RLV) for quick turn around times, to avoid lengthy manual tear down inspections.

Description: Do intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) exist? The discovery of ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs), with typical luminosities larger than the Eddington luminosity for a 10 solar mass object has suggested the existence of black holes iwth masses larager than those of typical sstellar remnants but smaller than those of supermassive black holes in the centers of galaxies. If MBHs exist, most would be expected to emit at sub-Eddington luminosity for their mass, due to limited material availability for accretion and to exhibit softer spectra than stellar BHs because of their larger Schwarzchild radii. It is a challenge to theory to understand their genesis, and a challenge to observations to find them near enough tto us that dynamical studies can accurately determine their masses. The class of Quasisoft Sources (QSSs) is a promising set of sources to search for IMBHs. We have discovered hundreds of QSSs in external galaxies as distant as the Virgo cluster. Only a fraction of QSSs may be IMBHs, however, because of the presence of other systems that could have similar spectral characteristics. The primary goal of this proposal is to identify, using NASA archival data, a population of nearby QSSs large enought that one or more of them is likely to be an IMBH. Identification of a nearby QSS with an IMBH would allow the first dynamical mass measurement of an IMBH. QSSs that are not IMBHs are interesting in their own right, because they represent poorly understood systems. Because cooling or lightly accreting neutron stars have spectra in the QSS range, our proposed work will also constitute a search for an interesting sub-class of neurton stars.

Description: Multi-wavelength studies of galaxy groups and clusters provide strong constraints on models of galaxy evolution and on heating and chemical enrichment of the surrounding (IGM) gas. Signatures of gasdynamical and gravitational processes responsible for galaxy and IGM evolution are imprinted on hot gas in the form of surface brightness edges, wakes, tails, and outflow cavities. We propose to use XMM-Newton and Chandra data to study the frequency of these features in nearby galaxy groups and cool clusters, and identify an X-ray selected sample of galaxies associated with these features to study ram pressure, turbulent viscous and tidal gas stripping, and nuclear outflows. We will analyze XMM-Newton and ROSAT data to measure the temperature, metallicity, density, pressure and entropy of the IGM to characterize its dynamical and chemical state, and measure the thermodynamic properties of the X-ray edges, wakes and tails using XMM-Newton and Chandra data. Combining these results, we will determine the 3-dimensional motion of the galaxies through the IGM, identify high velocity interactions unlikely to be found any other way, and probe the dominant physical processes acting on these systems. We will use 2MASS redshift data to determine whether high velocity galaxy motions are correlated with flows along filaments, signalling structure formation on larger scales. We will use 2MASS and Spitzer data to identify asymmetries in the stellar and dust distributions to distinguish between tidal and gasdynamical interactions, and will correlate observed temperature, abundance and pressure gradients with HST, Spitzer, IRAS and radio measures of recent star formation and nuclear activity to explore how these interactions affect the complex cycle regulating star formation, nuclear activity, and feedback into the IGM.

Description: SBIR PHASE 2 AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED: Fast Readout for Large Area Photon-Counting Infrared Detectors. Many NASA Space and Earth programs in the infrared range 1060 a?? 1550 nm are limited by the detector performance that require long exposure time due to their low sensitivity and/or high noise. Large format infrared photon counting arrays with ranging capability would provide a valuable tool to many space missions. Current state-of-the-art fabrication of photon counting infrared detector arrays on non-silicon semiconductors is not mature enough to monolithically integrate complex readout circuitry at pixel level and large format array multiplexing. APEAK will develop novel, fast readout, integrated circuits (ROIC) to be integrated with large photon-counting infrared detector arrays into 3D imaging cameras with photon-counting sensitivity. These new cameras will support NASA missions in applications such as space docking, landing, remote mapping, and robotic vision. The goal of this project is to develop smart-pixel ROIC arrays in silicon with enhanced radiation tolerance and ready for hybrid integration with large infrared photon-counting avalanche photodiode arrays that will enable large-area detectors with short integration time, sub-nanosecond timing resolution, and on-pixel logic. The simulation, implementation and validation of all the blocks of a ROIC array specifically developed for operation with infrared photon-counting arrays In Phase II, APEAK will improve, fabricate and qualify ROIC arrays with integrated timing functions at pixel level and capable of integration in flip-chip technology with large infrared photon counting detector arrays. The potential NASA commercial applications are the following: free space optical communications, LADAR, LIDAR, planetary mapping, obstacle detection, 3D remote robotics, and docking. There are also potential non-NASA commercial applications. ROIC arrays could enhance the performance of hyperspectral imaging in medical and defense applications when interconnected to a large format detector arrays covering different spectral ranges. Specific biomedical applications include positron emission tomography (PET), laser correlation spectroscopy (LCS), single molecule detection and fast DNA sequencing. Military and security applications would include generic 3D imaging, hyperspectral imaging, laser ranging, night vision, surveillance, anti-collision devices, underwater imaging, and cargo imaging. In High-Energy and Nuclear Physics, these ROIC arrays could be used for high-resolution tracking and experiments using time-of-flight methods.

Description: AN ANALYSIS OF POLAR CAP POTENTIAL SATURATION  The objective of this proposal is to investigate why the polar cap potential saturates, at what values does the polar cap potential saturate, and Ghat parameters influence and determine the saturation value. We intend to examine these questions through a cornbiiiecl data analysis and MIiO modeling investigation. DMSP observations of the polar cap potential will be used to identify saturation events in combination with solar wind observations from ACE or WIND to characterize the driving parameters that determine how and when saturation occurs. In parallel to ihe data analysis we will perform a parameter study of polar cap potential satmation using the Megrted Space Weather Model (ISM) MHD model. From the simulation results we will identify the processes responsible for potential saturation. Those aspects of the polar cap potential saturation process that can be discriminated in the simulations will be tested with the available observations. Unique aspects of this study include: (1) using data from a whole solar cycle from which to select saturation events to ensure a wide range of all critical parameters; (2) sub-grouping events into categories that emphasize a particular parameter; (3) combining data analysis and MHD simulation to separate the responses to different parameters. Understanding solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling during extreme conditions such as when the polar cap potential saturates is a critical part of understanding and predicting the magnetospheric response over the full range of solar wind stimuli.

Traditional instrumentation of an aircraft is a complex and time-consuming chore. Once the sensors are installed, long wires for power and data must be routed through to a central data collection location where several large off-the-shelf electronic components reside, adding weight, cost and increasing the probably of introducing noise or faults into the testing system. Potential commercial applications extend to factors such as device marketability including but not limited to its versatility. The objectives of this proposed project are to test a hypothesis on the climatological impact of BC aerosols on clouds and precipitation in the tropics, to quantify the magnitude of this impact, and to identify the dominant dynamic and physical mechanisms that govern this impact. Based on our previous work, we hypothesize that owing to its absorption of sunlight, heating of the atmosphere, and cooling of the surface, BC causes a significant change in the distribution of tropical precipitation primarily through forced changes to the large-scale circulation, and secondarily through direct local impact. Description: "SENSOR WEB DYNAMIC REPLANNING" We will propose to extend the dynamic replanning capability of Draper's Earth Phenomena Observing System (EPOS), which has successfully demonstrated the capability to dynamically replan the activities of NASA space-based sensor assets to maximize the return of useful science measurements (e.g., ensure cloud free targeting). We will propose to enhance and extend EPOS to include the replanning of sensors on UAVs (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles) and USVs (Unmanned Surface Vessels) being fielded by NASA over the next few years. The new dynamic replanning capability will utilize complementary and cooperative suites of heterogeneous sensor assets that can be triggered by observation data and/or predictive models to adaptively respond to significant events and provide enhanced understanding of temporal Earth phenomena. An event-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to observation-triggered cues for phenomenon, such as harmful algal bloom outbreaks. A model-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to significant increases in meteorological forecast model error growth due to model sensitivities within specific atmospheric regions. The events and phenomena that present the largest potential payoff to the proposed replanning capability are characterized by being localized and transient and also capable of causing damage to both human life and property, e.g., weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, etc.), harmful algal blooms, volcanic eruptions, ice shelf break-up, seismic activities, oil spilis, and search and rescue. Description: Spectral Modeling of the Far Infrared Molecular Components of Luminous Galaxies We propose a thorough study of the warm, far-IR emitting molecular component of luminous galaxies by uniformly re-reducing, analyzing, and modeling with our radiative transfer codes the full IS0 archival dataset of far-infrared spectra of galaxies. There are 18 such galaxies taken with full-grating-scan (IS0 "L01") moderate-to-high SNR spectra showing molecular features including OH (six lines have been detected), H20 (five line), CH, and some others, as well as atomic features. We have published results on three of these already (Arp 220, NGC 1068, and M82). Strikingly, the objects analyzed so far show that the warm far-infrared molecular component is clearly distinct among them, and provides direct clues to the nature and evolution of their warm molecular clouds (sizes, densities, temperatures, metallicities). The remaining 13 LO1 LIRGs have good quality spectra with clear molecular features, and will yield a wealth of new information. Our analysis of lines of molecules such as OH, H20, NH3, NH, and CH, together with the models of the far-infrared continua, will yield the physical conditions such as: variation of far-infrared grain temperature, molecular abundances and excitation, and gas density in the galactic ionized and photodissociation regions that produce both the observed continuum emission and molecular absorption and emission spectra. We will carry out this analysis for the full set of galactic molecular spectra in the archive as we have done for the prototypical ultraluminous galaxy Arp 220 and the Seyfert 2 galactic nucleus in NGC 1068 (Gonziilez-Alfonzo et al. 2004; Spinoglio et al. 2005). By comparing line intensities to predictions in the photodissociation regions lines such as [C 111158 microns and 10 I] 63,145 microns, we can ascertain whether the observed molecules are in fact located in the photodissociation regions and determine whether the OH and H20 maser emission is pumped within the same regions that produce the far-infrared molecular lines, as we did for Arp 220 (Skinner et at. 1997). This work is critical if we are to understand the nature of such systems, and is very timely in that it will provide a local-universe benchmark against which galaxy evolution, soon to be traced to moderate redshifts with the Herschel Space Observatory, can be assessed. By investigating the structure and origins of molecular clouds in infrared galaxies, along with star formation and black hole activity, this proposal directly advances NASA Strategic Goal3 via snbgoals 3D and outcomes 3D.1 and 3D.2: NASA Science Outcomes 3D.1 Progress in understanding the origin and destiny of the universe, phenomena near black holes, and the nature of gravity. NASA Science Outcomes 3D.2 Progress in understanding how the first stars and galaxies formed, and how they changed over time into the objects recognized in the present universe.

Description: The NRC Space Studies Board has pre-released a NASA- and NOAA-sponsored report titled Earth Science and Applications from Space: National Imperatives for the Next Decade and Beyond. This decadal study is the first of its kind for the Earth science community and underscores the importance of developing a comprehensive, integrated plan for Earth science observations over the next decade. The report recommends a specific set of missions to be implemented over the next 10-15 years and recognizes the need for interagency communication and cooperation, consideration of socio-economic issues, and a robust end-to-end system design that incorporates the needs of all relevant stakeholders. Achieving the goals set forth in the decadal study will require NASA to embark on a comprehensive multi-mission planning strategy that significantly differs from the single mission design approach used in the past. By exploiting the benefits of modularity, extensibility, and commonality across multiple missions, NASA can realize significant long-term savings in cost, reduction in risk, and greater functionality than could be achieved through the single-mission approach. It is our goal to support NASA Goddard. in this endeavor through the development of a system architecting methodology and toolset that will be applied to a suite of missions in response to the NRC report. To support this, we have developed a comprehensive system architecting framework that covers the early system design process from stakeholder analysis through architecture analysis to conceptual design and commonality analysis. These tools will supplement the current capability of Goddard's Integrated Design Capability system engineering studies. We will carry out our analysis in two phases. The first phase will involve knowledge capture, stakeholder analysis, and benchmarking. Here, we will review previous earth observation system architectures as well as prior NRC, NASA, and NOAA studies. We will identify and incorporate relevant stakeholders and their needs into a formal model, and we will define performance metrics for the overall system. During the second phase we will fully explore the system architecture space. We will identify and characterize architecture components, enumerate and evaluate all architecture options, identify a set of "good" architectures for more in-depth analysis, and recommend a small number of architecture options for further analysis by NASA Goddard.

Description: We propose to build and test an exciting new instrument - a type of Rotational Shearing Interferometer (RSI) capable of achieving the extreme nulling contrasts required to image an extra-solar planet --- lOA6:1 for the closest planets; lOAIO:l for more numerous systems. Our design will improve on the current state of the art in nulling interferometer by reducing the optical elements to a single monolithic prism. This will result in a system which is much more robust than previous designs and holds huge promise of reducing both overall mission cost and risk for future NASA missions ranging from Small Explorers to TPF or its equivalent. Our design features two crucial new concepts: coherent wavefront sensing, and optical monolithic construction. This design path recapitulates the design path see in interferometric spectrometers such as those developed at BU. The first spectral system were large multi-optic system which were quite capable but which suffered from the inherent difficulties in operating with a large number of optics such as alignment, contamination and so forth. The succeeding generation of SHS has reduced the optical system to a highly robust compact prism. This proposal seeks a similar advance in the state of the art interferometric nulling system.

Description: THE EXTENSIONAL VISCOSITY IS A FUNDAMENTAL PHYSICAL PROPERTY OF ALL NON-NEWTONIAN MATERIALS, AND CANNOT BE DETERMINED FROM SIMPLE VISCOMETRIC SHEAR FLOW EXPERIMENTS. CONSTITUTIVE EQUATIONS FOR VISCOELASTIC FLUIDS SUCH AS DILUTE POLYMER SOLUTIONS PREDICT LARGE CHANGES IN THE EXTENSIONAL VISCOSITY AS THE ELONGATION RATE IS INCREASED; HOWEVER, THE VALIDITY OF THESE THEORIES HAS ONLY RECENTLY BEEN CONFIRMED DUE TO PAUCITY OF EXPERIMENTAL DATA THAT WAS AVAILABLE IN EXTENSIONAL FLOWS. TO DATE, MOST QUANTITATIVERHEOLOGICAL MEASUREMENTS IN SHEAR-FREE FLOWS HAVE ONLY BEEN POSSIBLE FOR HIGHLY ELASTIC OR "STIFF' MATERIALS SUCH AS POLYMER MELTS WHICH CAN EASILY BE ELONGATED WITHOUT SAGGING UNDER A GRAVITATIONAL BODY FORCE. IN A REVIEW FOR THE NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL ON THE FUTURE OF FLUID DYNAMICS RESEARCH, DENN (1993) REMARKED THAT "...THERE ARE TWO MAJOR OUTSTANDING PROBLEMS IN RHEOLOGICAL MEASUREMENTS. ONE ISTHE MEASUREMENT OF EXTENSIONAL STRESSES OF MOBILE FLUIDS SUCH AS POLYMER SOLUTIONS." PREVIOUS RESEARCH ONFILAMENT STRETCHING RHEOMETRY SUPPORTED BY NASA IN THE P.L'S LAB HAS GONE AT LEAST SOME WAY TO ADDRESSING THIS SITUATION. THE PERTURBATIVE EFFECTS OF GRAVITY AND/OR CONTAINER BOUNDARIES THAT HAVE INTERFERED WITH ALMOST ALL PREVIOUS STUDIES OF EXTENSIONAL RHEOLOGY IN MOBILE FLUIDS HAVE BEEN ADDRESSED IN TWO WAYS; (I) BY MINIATURIZING THE APPARATUS OR USING NEUTRAL BUOYANCY TANKS TO MINIMIZE BODY FORCES, OR (II) BY PERFORMING SIMILAR EXPERIMENTS IN AN EXTENDED MICROGRAVITY ENVIRONMENT. USING THE INSTRUMENTATION DEVELOPED IT HAS BECOME POSSIBLE TO OBTAIN ACCURATE MEASUREMENTS OF THE EXTENSIONAL VISCOSITY FOR MORE 'MOBILE' FLUIDS SUCH AS DILUTE AND CONCENTRATED POLYMER SOLUTIONS, GELS, SUSPENSIONS AND LIQUID CRYSTALLINE MATERIALS. THIS RHEOLOGICAL DATA IS IMPORTANT IN VALIDATING OR EXTENDING CONSTITUTIVE MODELS THAT AIM TO DESCRIBE THE RESPONSE OF COMPLEX FLUIDS IN ARBITRARY DEFORMATION FIELDS. SUCH MODELS WILL ULTIMATELY ALLOW DESIGNERS OF BOTH SPACE- AND GROUND-BASED MATERIAL PROCESSES TO USE NUMERICALSIMULATIONS FOR A PRIORI PREDICTIONS OF THE PROPERTIES OF NEW MATERIALS THAT INVOLVE COMPLEX TWO- AND THREE-DIMENSIONAL FLUID FLOWS.IN A SIMPLE STRETCHING FLOW, FLUIDS SUCH AS WATER OR SYRUP EXHIBIT A RESISTANCE TO STRETCHING THAT IS EXACTLY THREE TIMES THE VALUE OF THEIR NEWTONIAN VISCOSITY. THIS RESISTANCE IS USUALLY TERMED THE "EXTENSIONAL VISCOSITY" OF THE MATERIAL. HOWEVER, FOR FLUIDS CONTAINING LONG MACROMOLECULES (E.G., SYNTHETIC POLYMERS, LIQUID CRYSTALS, OR DNA) OR OTHER MICROSTRUCTURAL ELEMENTS (SUCH AS MICELLES, OR OTHER PHYSICALLY-INTERACTING NETWORKS/GELS) IT IS PREDICTED THAT THE EXTENSIONAL VISCOSITY CAN BE ANYWHERE FROM 100 TO 10000 TIMES GREATER THAN THE NORMAL SHEAR VISCOSITY OF THE FLUID. IN THE NEAR FUTURE, NASA PLANS TODEVELOP "CONTAINERLESS PROCESSING" OPERATIONS UNDER MICROGRAVITY AND A DETAILED UNDERSTANDING OF EXTENSIONAL PROPERTIES IN FLUIDS WILL BE ABSOLUTELY CRITICAL -- SINCE, IN THE ABSENCE OF CONTAINER WALLS, THE ONLY WAY TO MIX, POUR, AND SHAPE FLUIDS WILL BE THROUGH PURE STRETCHING MOTIONS. KNOWLEDGE OF SUCH NONLINEAR MATERIAL FUNCTIONS IS FUNDAMENTAL TO THE DEVELOPMENT AND VERIFICATION OF RELATIVELY CHEAP GROUND-BASED COMPUTATIONAL MODELING TECHNIQUES WHICH CAN BE USED EFFECTIVELY IN THE "A PRIORI" DESIGN OF ADVANCED MICROGRAVITY MATERIAL PROCESSES - THEREBY ALLEVIATING THE NEED FOR COSTLY IN-FLIGHT PILOTEXPERIMENTS. FINALLY, IN ADDITION TO THEIR SIGNIFICANCE IN MANY INDUSTRIAL PROCESSES SUCH AS FIBER-SPINNING AND FILM COATING OPERATIONS, STRETCHING FLOWS OF NON-NEWTONIAN FLUIDS ARE OF FUNDAMENTAL SCIENTIFIC IMPORTANCE TO A NUMBER OF COMPLEX FLUID DYNAMICS PHENOMENA, INCLUDING THE STABILITY AND BREAKUP OF JETS, ENHANCED OIL RECOVERY AND TURBULENT DRAG REDUCTION FOR ADVANCED AIRCRAFT, BOATS, AND SUBMARINES.1.1 OBJECTIVESTHE OBJECTIVES OF THE PROPOSED RESEARCH ARE TO (I) ADAPT AN EXISTING FILAMENT STRETCHING DEVICE DEVELOPED AT MIT IN ORDER TO ENABLE EXTENSIONAL MEASUREMENTS OF A WIDER RANGE

Description: The Vision for Space Exploration (VSE) announced in January, 2004 has provided NASA with a new direction for human spaceflight and exploration. The Vision outlines a long-term plan for the robotic and human exploration of the Solar System including the development of a new crew CPIS spaceflight capability by 2014. robotic precursor missions to the Moon and Mars, and a return of humans to the Moon by 2020. The Vision emphasizes a "stepping stone" approach with human missions to the moon as preparation for future human missions to Mars. Meeting the goals of the Vision, NASA's Exploration Systems Mission Directorate requires the acquisition and operation of a number of new complex space systems such as the CEV, human-rated launch vehicles for crew and cargo transportion, in-space propulsion stages, habitats, and others. To conduct a program of this magnitude in a sustainable fashion represents a formidable challenge from both a management and technical perspective. It is our goal to provide NASA with an independent analysis and design capability, and to supply methods and tools for use in NASA's systems architect and design processes with focus on sustainability of the exploration enterprise. To that end we developed a comprehensive system architect framework that covers the early system design process fro stakcholder- analysis through architecture analysis to conceptual design and commuonality analysis. Specifically, we will carry out a systematic assessment of coinrnoiialily options for human Moon and Mars exploration with a focus on lunar surface systems.The analysis will include the enumeration and evalilation of lunar surface system and human Mars mission architectures, commonality screening on the architectural level. and a detailed quantitarives assessment of individual commonality options. In addition and analysis of methods and heuristics  for succissfully implementing commonalith options in organizations and management will be performed. The study will produce a set of architetures and preferred strategies which will inform the ESMD lunar architecure and Mars mission design activities.

Description: Terahertz frequency range (1-10 THz) is rich in spectral lines that are important for astrophysics. However, this frequency range also happens to be in the so-called "THz gap" between conventional semiconductor electronic devices and photonic devices. As a result, the development of suitabie iocai oscillators for several current NASkiESA missions such as Iierschei and SOFIA has been a major challenge, and it is likely to be so for future mission concepts such as SAFIR and STO. Fortunately, a breakthrough in the field could change the lsndscape significantly and overcome this major hurdle. A compact solid-state laser device based on intersabband transitions in quantum-well structures (quantum-cascade lasers, QCL) was developed at 4.4 TBz in 2001. Since then, rapid progress has been made. To date, the PI'S group has achieved many performance records in THz quantum-cascade lasers. Theses include but not limited to: the highest pulsed operating temperature of 164 K, the highest CW operating temperature of 117 K, and the longest wavelength of 162 pm (1.86 THz). Just as important, our collaborators at SRON have pumped a superconducting NEB mixer with a QCL at 2.8 THz and achieved a receiver noise temperature as low as 1400 K. Furthermore, our collaborators at University of Colorado have frequency locked a QCL at 3.0 THz over an indefinite period of time, and measured the FWHM linewidth as narrow as 65 kHz. These developments have clearly demonstrated the suitability of THz quantum-cascade lasers in local-oscillator applications. In this proposed three-year (1115107-1/14/10) project, we plan to extend our recent success and further develop the THz QCLs for future missions, especially for a SMEXIMIDEX or a LDB program. Specifically, by end of the three-year project, we will develop THz QCLs with single-mode frequencies within -10 GHz from several target spectral lines, namely the CII line at 1.901 THz, the HD line at 2.675 THz, and the 0 1 line at 4.745 THz. These devices will operate at -80 K and provide CW power levels of >I mW. This operating temperature can be achieved in a near-earth orbit by passive radiative cooling, and can be conveniently achieved in a LDB program or in laboratory testing using liquid nitrogen. In order to achieve this objective, two major tasks will be pursued. The first one is to develop robust THz gain medium at high temperatures. This will be accomplished by iterative designs and investigation of suitable quantum-cascade structures. The second major task is to develop surface-emitting QCLs using second-order DFB gratings (period = wavelength), which have several important advantages compared to the currently used edge-emitting lasers. The power levels will he higher, the emission spectra can be made single-mode, and the beam pattern will be much more symmetric and convergent. This proposed project mainly addresses NASA's Strategic Goal 3.4. It also addresses NASA's Strategic Goal 3.1 and Goal 3.3.

Many NASA Space and Earth programs in the infrared range 1060 a?? 1550 nm are limited by the detector performance that require long exposure time due to their low sensitivity and/or high noise. Large format infrared photon counting arrays with ranging capability would provide a valuable tool to many space missions. Current state-of-the-art fabrication of photon counting infrared detector arrays on non-silicon semiconductors is not mature enough to monolithically integrate complex readout circuitry at pixel level and large format array multiplexing. Description: In space, astronauts are exposed to a complex and unique radiation environment that includes energetic protons and heavy charged particles. During long-duration missions outside the earth's protective magnetic field, the cumulative radiation doses from these particles could be appreciable, but the individual particle traversals though the cells of an astronaut's body would be well separated in time and location. Under these low tluence conditions, effects such as bystander responses could be important. Bystander responses are biological changes that occur in unirradiated cells "neighboring" the cells actually traversed by the ionizing particles. These responses result from signals sent by the "hit" cells to the unirradiated cells; the exact nature of the signals is still unclear. In recent experiments at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Lab, we have demonstrated that bystander responses occur in several types of normal human cells exposed to high energy protons and iron ions, two of the prominent types of radiations found in space. Hence, we hypothesize that at the low, chronic fluences of charged particles to which astronauts are exposed in space, a significant fraction of the cellular damage may be due to bystander effects, in addition to damage from direct radiation traversals of cells. We propose to test this hypothesis by assessing bystander effects at low, fractionated, doses of the various components of space radiation. Furthermore, we will investigate molecular mechanisms underlying the effect, including assessing the role of DNA damage and repair in the process, evaluating the signaling mechanisms between various cell types, and assessing chemical countermeasures to ameliorate the effect. Such studies should shed light on the mechanisms of cancer induction and late tissue damage that are risks to astronauts from space radiation and provide insight into ways to prevent such deltterious effects.

Description: Numerical simulations suggest that the metal-poor stars that formed first in the Universe were probably massive, and so they could have served as progenitors for long-duration Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). The early afterglow of GRBs is as bright as quasars, and can be used to probe the conditions in the intergalactic medium during the epoch of reionization. The recently launched Swift satellite offers a unique opportunity to probe the first (Pop-III) stars, one star at a time. We propose to investigate a key theoretical question related to this emerging frontier in observational cosmology, namely: What are the unique signatures of a GRB that originated from a Pop-III progenitor compared to a high-redshift GRB from normal Pop I/II stars? We will use 3D cosmological numerical simulations to examine the likely environments in which the first GRBs form within the first metal-poor condensations in the Universe. The simulations of the formation sites of the first stars will also include their radiative feedback on the surrounding gas. We will focus on the differences between the afterglows expected in these early environments and those characteristic of lower-redshift galaxies. Any such differences will have direct implications with respect to the capabilities of Swift to detect the earliest GRBs and their afterglows.  The formation of the first stars, as probed by the highest redshift GRBs, occurred at the end of the cosmic dark ages, an epoch which we can only now begin to explore. The work proposed here therefore aims at closing a crucial gap in the longstanding goal of tracing the entire history of star formation in the universe.

Description: ISOTOPIC STUDIES OF SOLAR SYSTEM ORIGINS The main objective of this proposal is to investigate processes leading to the formation of the Solar System as well as the earliest stages of planetary formation by measurement of isotopic variations and trace element abundance ratios in meteorites. To achieve our objectives we will analyze a series of meteorites for isotopic compositions of Mg, Ca, Ti, Ni, Nd, Ba, and Pt using our new very high precision MC-TIMS and MC-ICPMS techniques. The proposed study focuses on two major themes related to one another: (1) isotopic anomalies in bulk samples of primitive meteorites and their major components such as CAIs, chondrules and matrix, and (2) fossil isochron relationships for 26AI-26Mg and 60Fe-60Ni in the same primitive and differentiated meteoritic materials. Upon completion of the proposed measurements we will be in a position to better answer several major questions pertinent to the origin and evolution of the Solar System such as (1) How many nucleosynthetic components have contributed to the Solar System and how well were they mixed together? (2) What was the nature of those components? Do they represent a supernova ejection(s) close to the time of the Solar System formation or reflect isotopic heterogeneities in the interstellar medium? (3) Are there any correlations between the isotopic anomalies in heavy elements and the initial 26AI/27AI and 60Fe/56Fe ratios in the same materials? (4) Are there unique initial 26AI/27Al and 60Fe/56Fe ratios for the Solar System? If so, what are their values? (5) How precise are the" most precise" 26AI-26Mg fossil isochrons? Can they be further improved by refining the fractionation correction laws? (6) What do new isotopic constraints tell us about the processes responsible for mixing of nucleosynthetic components in the early solar nebula? Which nebular models, if any, are the most compatible with these new constraints? The isotopic constraints on the formation of stars and planets constitute observational benchmarks that can guide astrophysical models of the nebula, directly supporting a goal of the NASA 2006 Strategic Plan (3D.3 "Progress in understanding how individual stars form and how those processes ultimately affect the formation of planetary systems" which is part of Strategic Sub-goal 3D "Discover the origin, structure, evolution, and destiny of the universe, and search for Earth-like planets ").

Description: REPLICATING VESICLES AND THE EMERGENCE OF LIFE The goal of the proposed research is to improve our understanding of the origin of life on earth, and of the potential for life to arise on other planets. This proposal is focused on the role of membranes as replicating cellular compartment boundaries. It is a continuation of work currently funded by the NASA Exobiology Program. Our specific goals are: 1. To explore prebiotically realistic pathways for the ormation, growth and division of membrane vesicles. 2. To study the permeability properties of model protocell membranes, and the potential roles of pH gradients in energy storage and transformation in early cells. 3. To demonstrate both spontaneous and catalyzed nucleic acid synthesis inside model protocell vesicles. We will approach these goals using a wide range of methods, beginning with the chemical synthesis of simple lipids. Vesicles prepared with mixtures of fatty acids and their derivatives will be characterized by a variety of biophysical techniques, including light scattering, fluorescence methods and microscopy. Permeability and pH gradient studies will make use primarily of methods based on fluorescent dyes that exhibit ligand or pH sensitive fluorescence. Studies of nucleic acid synthesis will use standard molecular biology methods such as gel electrophoresis to follow the course of the reactions, complemented by mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF) for product characterization. The significance of the proposed work lies in its potential to discover surprising and unanticipated phenomena related to the origin of life. For example, our currently funded work led to the finding that clay particles can act to bring together nucleic acids and membrane vesicles, and also led to the discovery of a simple mechanism by which nucleic acid replication could directly influence the growth of the membrane boundary of a primitive cell. The present proposal could go even further in identifying plausible pathways from molecules to cells. A better understanding of the origin of life is central to the stated goals of the Astrobiology and Exobiology Programs of NASA. Moreover, an improved understanding of the conditions under which life could emerge, and of the possible nature of early living systems, will facilitate the search for life (or signs of extinct life) in other solar system environments such as Mars and Europa.

Description: Small Business Innovative Research Phase II - Aircraft Sensor-Logger with Power Replenishment Capabilities. Traditional instrumentation of an aircraft is a complex and time-consuming chore. Once the sensors are installed, long wires for power and data must be routed through to a central data collection location where several large off-the-shelf electronic components reside, adding weight, cost and increasing the probably of introducing noise or faults into the testing system. All of this necessary infrastructure leads to prohibit the use of some types of sensors and limit the total number of sensors used so save on time, cost, complexity and resources. During the course of this Phase II SBIR research, Metis Design Corporation (MDC) proposes to develop a standardized data acquisition hub for aircraft testing sensors dubbed a sensor-logger. The sensor-logger would essentially serve as a durable sensor infrastructure node capable of autonomously facilitating local testing for multiple sensors of various types. Controlled wirelessly by PC or PDA, data could be displayed in real-time, or logged internally for up to 40 hours. The second half of the proposed research would then tie together the sensor-logger with the Phase I research, developing a power-replenishment device to attach to the sensor-logger to extend its operating capabilities. Finally both devices will be flight tested in true aircraft environments. Potential commercial applications extend to factors such as device marketability including but not limited to its versatility. The ability not only to be integrated into new applications, but also retrofitted into existing systems. There are several areas of potential NASA applicability. The first is for experimental aircraft programs. This device will give the ability to collect more data , with less complexity cost and risk to the testing program. Another important aerospace market would be for expendable launch vehicles (ELV) to help facilitate launch/no launch decisions. Of probably greatest importance, this device could be a key technology for reusable launch vehicle (RLV) for quick turn around times, to avoid lengthy manual tear down inspections.

Description: Exploring the Outer Solar System with Stellar Occultations: Instrumentation Knowledge of the physical characteristics of bodies in the outer solar system plays an important role in our understanding of the formation and early evolution of that region. These objects are most sensitively probed from Earth by the technique of stellar occultations, which can provide size information and atmospheric temperature and pressure profiles at a spatial resolution of a few kilometers. For example, recent observations of an occultation by Charon constrained its radius to within a few kilometers and placed an upper limit on a possible atmosphere. Occultation observations show that Pluto's atmosphere has been expanding, Triton's atmospheric pressure has been increasing, and that the shape of both atmospheres may deviate from the expected spherical figure. Our research program involves identifying occultation candidates for bodies in the outer solar system, predicting and observing occultations, analyzing data, and synthesizing the results. Here we propose to construct an instrument optimized for observing occultations, for use on the IRTF (NASA InfraRed Telescope Facility) in Hawaii. This system would consist of a frame-transfer, back-illuminated CCD with low read noise, a GPS receiver for accurate timing, and a computer system capable of sustained fast frame rates. Hawaii is uniquely positioned for occultation observations over a range of longitudes from which there are no other fixed observatories. This instrument would benefit the parent proposal by (i) enabling us to obtain high-quality data from Hawaii (it would be the only science instrument on Mauna Kea with the required capabilities, and it would allow multi-wavelength observations) and (ii) increasing the total number of occultations we can observe. We anticipate employing the proposed instrument to observe 10 events per year, of which two or more should yield successful results. This research directly supports NASA's Strategic Goal 3C and would help prepare for the New Horizons mission.
