Description: Palynology, the study of structurally preserved microscopic organic matter, provides a very useful method for the study of ancient ecosystems because this method can recover abundant direct remains of once-living organisms. Spores and cysts of both algal and embryophyte (true land plants) origin can directly trace the history of surface-dwelling subaerial and freshwater aquatic organisms. The proposed research will compare palynomorphs from terrestrial (an near-shore) rocks of Precambrian age with their counterparts from non-marine facies from lower Paleozoic rocks. This study will identify and characterize those components of lower Paleozoic (about 0.5 billion years ago) terrestrial ecosystems that were in existence around 1 billion years ago. This information will be crucial in resolving questions about the evolution of morphological characters leading up to the origin of land plants. There are no records of (macroscopic) plant axes from rocks older than middle Silurian. Yet, the spore record indicates that land plants (embryophytes) originated much earlier by middle Cambrian time, or perhaps earlier. By examining entire assemblages of diverse populations of spores and associated remains from non-marine sediments that clearly predate the origin of land plants, I hope to distinguish those components of the ancient subaerial and terrestrial aquatic flora that are more algal in character from those related to the evolving charophyte to embryophyte lineage. This will be the first study to examine in a comprehensive and comparative way, the nature of the evolving terrestrial (=subaerial and freshwater aquatic) landscape based on a direct microfossil proxy. The proposed work involves field collection and chemical maceration of rock samples. The extracted microfossils will be characterized using transmitted light microscopy, scanning electron microscopy and transmitted electron microscopy. An assessment of the development of non-marine ecosystems can help constrain geochemical (and other) models of planetary development that include atmosphere-organism interactions. In helping to document the water to land transition within the course of plant evolution on Earth, this proposal is relevant to the study of universal evolutionary processes that may apply to the evolution of life on planets in general. Research on Precambrian paleobiology is based largely on microfossils and geochemistry from marine sources rocks. This proposal represents an opportunity to add studies of microfossils that inhabited the Precambrian terrestrial landscape.

The new dynamic replanning capability will utilize complementary and cooperative suites of heterogeneous sensor assets that can be triggered by observation data and/or predictive models to adaptively respond to significant events and provide enhanced understanding of temporal Earth phenomena. An event-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to observation-triggered cues for phenomenon, such as harmful algal bloom outbreaks. A model-driven use of a sensor web would be to task sensor resources in response to significant increases in meteorological forecast model error growth due to model sensitivities within specific atmospheric regions. The events and phenomena that present the largest potential payoff to the proposed replanning capability are characterized by being localized and transient and also capable of causing damage to both human life and property, e.g., weather (tornadoes, hurricanes, etc.), harmful algal blooms, volcanic eruptions, ice shelf break-up, seismic activities, oil spilis, and search and rescue. Description: Sedimentary rocks deposited during the later Neoproterozoic Era (ca. 800-542 million years ago) record the first unambiguous signs of animal life, multiple glaciations of global dimensions, and the oxidation of the deep ocean. Despite recognition that Earth and life 1 changed fundamentally during this interval, much remains to be understood about the interrelationships of and feedbacks between Neoproterozoic biological and physical events. Here we propose to couple detailed chemostratigraphic analyses of paleobiologically informative Neoproterozoic sedimentary successions with geobiological experiments designed to provide empirical calibration of temporal changes in seawater sulfate. The microbiological experiments will employ a novel, continuous flow bioreactor system that will provide quantitative constraints on the relationships among seawater sulfate concentration, microbial activity (and diversity), and sulfur isotope fractionation. Many biochemical reactions discriminate against minor isotopes, resulting in end products that are isotopically distinct relative to the substrate pool. Therefore, all isotopes of sulfur [32S, 33S, 34S, 36S] will be measured in substrates and products. Complementary geochemical analyses will focus on fossiliferous Neoproterozoic successions that record physiologically distinct events in early animal (and algal)evolution; detailed profiles of carbon isotopes (to facilitate correlation with other localities) and iron-speciation chemistry (which provides a proxy for redox conditions in waters overlying the seafloor) will be joined with easurements of the total isotopic composition of sulfur. The proposed research will, thus, marry high resolution chemostratigraphic data and microbial experiments to test hypotheses about the relationship between evolution and environmental history on the one planet where life is known to exist. The sulfur isotopic data will also provide a baseline for interpreting total sulfur isotopic abundances in sedimentary surface minerals collected during sample return missions to Mars.

Description: A variety of intriguing prebiotic scenarios involve systems that are difficult to study by conventional methods. Here we identify several well known systems for which NMR, particularly solid state NMR, can provide unique probes capable of answering unresolved questions. We propose carrying out definitive studies of two systems for which we have interesting preliminary results. Both involve the spontaneous polymerization of small molecules that would have been ubiquitous in prebiotic environments. In the first case, the question is whether a proposed direct pathway to polypeptides exists. In the second case, we seek to determine what kinds of chemical activity could occur inside the microspherules that are formed. Both of these investigations require probes of amorphous polymers. We also propose undertaking feasibility and demonstration studies for systems in which minerals have been shown to perform enzyme-like functions. Here we seek to understand how catalytic mineral surfaces interact with and modify bound reactants and products. These studies require probes of immobilized and exchanging substrates. The insights obtained will contribute directly to the goal of the NASA Astrobiology Program "to understand the pathways and processes leading from the origin of planetary bodies to the origin of life", focusing particularly on "determining what chemical systems could have served as precursors of metabolic and replicating systems on Earth and elsewhere". This information is important to inform the pursuit ofthe NASA objectives to "advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system [and) the potential for life elsewhere" and "to discover the origin, structure, evolution and destiny of the universe". In particular, our studies should allow the prebiotic significance of specific molecular processes to be better assessed and could thereby influence what molecules we look for as signs of the habitability of other parts of the universe.

Description: 2005 SBIR PHASE II - WIRELESS IN-SITU NONDESTRUCTIVE INSPECTION OF ENGINE ROTOR DISKS WITH ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVES.  THE STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY OF JET ENGINE TURBINE OR FAN ROTOR DISKS IS VITAL FOR AVIATION SAFETY.  CUMULATIVE CRACKS AT CRITICAL LOADING AND HIGH STRESS AREAS, IF NOT DETECTED AND REPAIRED IN TIME, MAY LEAD TO CATASTROPHIC FAILURE.  TRADITIONAL METHODS, SUCH AS FLUORESCENT PENETRANT INSPECTION (FPI) AND EDDY CURRENT ARE LIMITED TO POINT-BY-POINT MEASUREMENTS AND ARE VERY TIME CONSUMING. DISASSEMBLY OF THE ENGINE IS REQUIRED FOR EACH INSPECTION, WHICH IN TURN MAY CAUSE MAINTENANCE INDUCED PROBLEMS.  WE PROPOSE A WIRELESS IN-SITU ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE HEALTH MONITORING APPROACH.  IT APPLIES LIGHT, THIN, HIGH TEMPERATURE LEAVE-IN-PLACE ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE CIRCUMFERENTIAL PATCH TRANSDUCERS AOUND THE ROOT OF THE DISK, AND A PAIR OG INNOVATIVE TUBE ANTENNAE THAT WIRELESSLY COUPLE THE TRANSDUCERS TO THE INSPECTION INSTRUMENTS.  GUIDED WAVES TRAVEL IN THE DISK FOR CRACK INSPECTION, AND THE INSPECTION COULD BE DONE EVEN WHEN THE DISK IS ROTATING.  PHASE I RESULTS CLEARLY DEMONSTRATE THAT THE GUIDED WAVE IS VERY SENSITIVE TO TINY CRACKS ON A ROTATING ALUMINUM DISK, AND THE TUBE ANTENAE WORKED WELL.  THE ENVISIONED SYSTEM CAN INSPECT A RELATIVELY LARGE AREA, HAS MINIMAL EFFECT ON THE ROTOR PERFORMANCE, INSTANTANEOUSLY PROVIDES RELIABLE AND QUANTITATIVE DATA SUCH AS CRACK LOCATION AND SEVERITY LEVEL, AND MINIMIZE AND EVENTUALLY ELIMINATE THE NEED FOR STRUCTURAL DISASSEMBLY.

Description: PROBING SMALL SCALE ISM VARIATIONS WITH MULTI EPOCHF FUSE OBSERVATIONS The existence of small scale structures in the interstellar medium (ISM) has now been verified using a variety of techniques, including optical, radio, and ultraviolet instruments. They have been observed on scales ranging from tens of AU to parsecs. One of the best ways to probe the smallest scales is with multi-epoch observations, in which one discerns spectral changes arising from material between an observer and a background source. The number of such observations in dominant species in the ISM, as revealed by absorption lime studies in the ultraviolet, is very small. In addition, the physics of these structures, including their confinement mechanisms, lifetimes, pressures, and composition, is not well-understood. We propose a survey program to re-observe 18 stars already observed witb FUSE more than 3 years earlier to search for time dependent changes in their spectra. We will do profile fitting, curve-of-growth, and apparent optical depth analyses to search for changes in N2 and a variety of other species, such as CI, FeII, PII, ClI, and ClII. These will allow estimates of electron temperatures, volume densities, and depletions. The stars were selected on the basis of early spectral type, and existing high S/N FCSE spectra obtained in TTAG mode, which will allow the best opportunity to detect subtle changes in the spectral features. The newly obtained data will he useful for a variety of investigations beyond those described here, by providing a dataset of multi-epoch, high S f i spectra of early-type stars.

Description: FINAL ATIC LDB FLIGHT AND ANALYSIS A final flight of the advanced Thin Ionization Caloriment (ATIC) payload --ATIC 3b-- is proposed as a replacment for the ATIC-3a flight which suffered a balloon failure upon launch. Description: 2005 SBIR PHASE II - WIRELESS IN-SITU NONDESTRUCTIVE INSPECTION OF ENGINE ROTOR DISKS WITH ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVES.  THE STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY OF JET ENGINE TURBINE OR FAN ROTOR DISKS IS VITAL FOR AVIATION SAFETY.  CUMULATIVE CRACKS AT CRITICAL LOADING AND HIGH STRESS AREAS, IF NOT DETECTED AND REPAIRED IN TIME, MAY LEAD TO CATASTROPHIC FAILURE.  TRADITIONAL METHODS, SUCH AS FLUORESCENT PENETRANT INSPECTION (FPI) AND EDDY CURRENT ARE LIMITED TO POINT-BY-POINT MEASUREMENTS AND ARE VERY TIME CONSUMING. DISASSEMBLY OF THE ENGINE IS REQUIRED FOR EACH INSPECTION, WHICH IN TURN MAY CAUSE MAINTENANCE INDUCED PROBLEMS.  WE PROPOSE A WIRELESS IN-SITU ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE HEALTH MONITORING APPROACH.  IT APPLIES LIGHT, THIN, HIGH TEMPERATURE LEAVE-IN-PLACE ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE CIRCUMFERENTIAL PATCH TRANSDUCERS AOUND THE ROOT OF THE DISK, AND A PAIR OG INNOVATIVE TUBE ANTENNAE THAT WIRELESSLY COUPLE THE TRANSDUCERS TO THE INSPECTION INSTRUMENTS.  GUIDED WAVES TRAVEL IN THE DISK FOR CRACK INSPECTION, AND THE INSPECTION COULD BE DONE EVEN WHEN THE DISK IS ROTATING.  PHASE I RESULTS CLEARLY DEMONSTRATE THAT THE GUIDED WAVE IS VERY SENSITIVE TO TINY CRACKS ON A ROTATING ALUMINUM DISK, AND THE TUBE ANTENAE WORKED WELL.  THE ENVISIONED SYSTEM CAN INSPECT A RELATIVELY LARGE AREA, HAS MINIMAL EFFECT ON THE ROTOR PERFORMANCE, INSTANTANEOUSLY PROVIDES RELIABLE AND QUANTITATIVE DATA SUCH AS CRACK LOCATION AND SEVERITY LEVEL, AND MINIMIZE AND EVENTUALLY ELIMINATE THE NEED FOR STRUCTURAL DISASSEMBLY.

Measurements of ionospheric electric fields are crucial to providing a full accounting for the energy budget or'&e lower thermosphere. Unfortunately, the TIMED spacecraft does not include instrumentation for this purpose. In addition, the SuperDARN radars provide the TIMEDICEDAR community measurements of meteor winds near the mesopause through the use of the meteor scatter technique. Description: ELECTRON MICORSCOPY, SPECTROSCOPY, AND CHEMICAL ANALYSIS OF AIRCRAFT ENGINE PARTICULATE (SOLID AND VOLATILE) FOR COMPLETE PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CHARACTERIZATION This proposal addresses the environmental challenges imposed by subsonic fixed wing aircraft. Soot produced within the upper troposphere has significant consequences for atmospheric chemistry. Although black carbon is hydrophobic, chemical and physical changes occurring at its surface can create functional groups that attract and retain water, thereby causing it to become hydrophilic. Such changes determine whether soot acts as cloud condensation nuclei, its susceptibility to washout and participation in atmospheric heterogeneous reactions, thereby significantly impacting the atmospheric radiative balance. Such chemical changes and subsequent interactions depend upon the soot surface chemistry. To ultimately control soot emissions requires detailed modeling based on experimental results. Alternatively analysis of soot nanostructure could be used as a tracer of the combustion conditions leading to its formation. Such an experimental record could guide models of soot nucleation and growth. In addition to nanostructure soot aggregate size, characterization of aggregates by the number of primary particles could guide modeling of the aerosol dynamics. Our approach will use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) to reveal soot nanostructure and to provide images for statistical analysis of aggregate size and morphology. X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) will be used to measure heteroelements, surface oxygen functional groups such as phenolic, carbonyl and carboxylic and graphitic/non-graphitic carbon. A database will be developed with these results. Experimental evidence of soot nucleation and growth stages as recorded in the nanostructure will provide feedback to combustor models of soot. Soot aggregate size and structure will guide atmospheric modeling calculations of soot contribution to atmospheric radiative forcing, and the radiative balance between the ground and upper atmosphere. Gaps in knowledge with respect to NOx-soot, SOx and ozone-soot interactions may be addressed. Confirmation of soot role as condensation nuclei will be substantiated while the mechanism (involving polar oxygen functional groups versus adsorbed sulfur species) will be differentiated.

Description: We propose to develop electronics for operation at temperatures that range from -230oC to +130oC. This new technology will minimize the requirements for external heat sources that are currently necessary for operation of low-temperature electronics. Such technology would significantly improve reliability, performance, lifetime of electronics that are used for space applications, including satellites and space travel. This will be achieved through the development of unique circuits that are derived from novel physics based device and circuit modeling techniques and verified by experiment. Statistical methods will be employed to connect the resistive heating caused by individual devices to heating of the entire integrated circuit. Special algorithms will be further developed which allow for determination of operating conditions where the intrinsic operation of the circuit will allow for sufficient heat generation to eliminate carrier freeze-out and efficient operation of integrated circuits in environments ranging from -230oC to +130oC. Description: The Stellar Imager, an ultraviolet, sparse-aperture telescope, was one of the fifteen Vision Missions chosen for a study completed last year. Stellar Imager will enable very high angular resolution images of stellar surfaces. The baselined design is a Fizeau beam combiner with 20 to 30 separated (free-flying) elements. This proposal is for funding to develop and test an alternative beam combiner design for the Stellar Imager Mission. We designate this new combiner the Spatial Frequency Remapper (SFR). In the SFR, the large field-of-view of the Fizeau design is sacrificed in favor of simultaneous observations at multiple wavelengths. Also, depending on the details of the design of the rest of the telescope, the SFR should either produce better images or relax the very tight stability requirements. Since the large field of view of the Fizeau combiner is not needed for the mission, the SFR, if it works, is clearly the better design; it's only expense is the addition of one or perhaps two extra reflections, needed to incorporate the spectral dispersion. The work that will be accomplished, including Phase 2, will include A) completing the analysis of the design as it pertains to Stellar Imager, B) performing a laboratory test at longer wavelengths to verify the soundness of that design and C) developing a more rigorous test of its imaging capabilities to be performed on a large, ground-based telescope. Description: To be used naturally in design optimization, parametric study and achieve quick total time-to-solution, simulation must naturally and personally be available to the scientist/engineer, as easily as email or word-processing. Environments such as Matlab/IDL allow ease of use, but unless simulations are extremely fast, they cannot be used naturally. Many large-scale numerical calculations require storage and computation that grow as the square/cube of the number of variables, including such linear algebra operations as solving dense linear systems, computing eigen-values/vectors, and others. The use of fast algorithms such as the fast multipole method (FMM) coupled with iterative methods allows many problems of interest to be solved in near linear time and memory. We have taken a leadership role in applying and extending the FMM to various problems in acoustics, fluid flow, electromagnetics, function fitting and machine learning. Graphical Processing Units (GPUs) are now ubiquitous in game consoles, in workstations and other devices and are special purpose processors for graphics, that are predicted to shortly achieve performance in the hundreds of gigaflop range for specialized calculations (much faster than COTS PCs) at low price points. It is conceivable now to equip personal workstations with several CPUs and GPUs, and solve problems with millions or billions of variables quickly using fast algorithms. We will take an important algorithm with wide applicability: the FMM, and implement it on the widely available heterogeneous CPU/GPU architecture, and prove the feasibility of accelerating it tremendously. A fundamental reconsideration of the algorithm that maps appropriate pieces on to the correct part of the architecture forms the basis of our approach. Developed software will be tested, and benchmark problems solved. A library of software that will support the porting of the FMM and other scientific computing to the CPU/GPU architecture will be developed.

Description: ADVANCED DARK ENERGY PHYSICS TELESCOPE (ADEPT) We propose to conduct a study of a space mission to determine the nature of the mysterious dark energy that is driving the accelerated expansion of the universe. The objective of the proposed study is to determine the most powerful but cost-effective detailed mission concept The best approach is a mission optimized to measure baryon acoustic oscillations, but one that can also survey type la supernovae with no additional hardware or operating modes. The baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler that can be compared to the scale of the cosmic microwave background anistropy at very high redshift, while supernovae provide a relative luminosity distance with respect to local supernovae. Both methods have been proven by ground-based observations. Space-based observations would provide the high redshift leverage for constraints on the variability of the dark energy. The ADEPT team combines scientific and technical expertise from all of the major methods to measure dark energy, in addition to space-flight experience, to achieve both breadth and depth. The team is organized around specific tasks, including the task to build computer mission simulation tools to evaluate the effectiveness of various hardware approaches, and the task to conduct cosmological simulations to evaluate effectiveness and potential systematic measurement errors. The organization of the study is designed to create two-way interaction between the development of science requirements and the evaluation of the simplest and most robust engineering implementations. The proposed work is directly responsive to the specific NRA call for JDEM mission concept proposals. JDEM research fits NASALS objectives. Description: TECHNICAL ABSTRACT  LARGE-SCALE AGENT SYSTEMS HAVE BECOME A KEY PART OF IN MODELING AND SIMULATION TOOLS SUCH AS NASA'S AIRSPACE CONCEPT EVALUATION SYSTEM (ACES), AN AGENT-BASED SIMULATION OF THE NATIONAL AIRSPACE SYSTEM (NAS). AS DISTRIBUTED REAL-WORLD SYSTEMS COMPRISED OF MANY AUTONOMOUS DECISION-MAKING ENTITIES BECOME MORE COMPLEX, SO DO THEIR CORRESPONDING INDIVIDUAL MODELS AND SIMULATION SYSTEMS. HOWEVER, EXISTING TOOLS FOR LOW-LEVEL SINGLE HOST DEBUGGING, DATA AND EVENT COLLECTION AND LOCAL ANALYSIS DO NOT ADEQUATELY ADDRESS THE PROBLEM OF UNDERSTANDING LARGE DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS CONSISTING OF THOUSANDS OF AUTONOMOUSLY EXECUTING AGENTS. IN THIS PHASE II EFFORT, WE PROPOSE TO CREATE A COMPREHENSIVE SEMANTIC DEBUGGING AND KNOWLEDGE DISCOVERY AND ANALYSIS SYSTEM FOR AGENT-BASED SIMULATIONS CALLED INTELLITRACE. THE KEY INNOVATION BEHIND SEMANTIC AND MODEL DRIVEN SYSTEM ANALYSIS IS THAT IT WILL BRIDGE THE GAP BETWEEN THE SEMANTICS OF MODEL EXECUTION AND THE RESULTANT IMPLEMENTATION BEHAVIOR REALIZED WITHIN A SOFTWARE SYSTEM. WE WILL USE THESES TOOLS AND CAPABILITIES TO DEVELOP AND DEMONSTRATE A METHODOLOGY AND APPROACH FOR APPLICATION-LEVEL ANALYSIS, KNOWLEDGE AND DISCOVERY AND DATA MINING AND ANALYSIS.  POTENTIAL NASA COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS  ONGOING ACES DEVELOPMENT, ACES CONCEPT DEVELOPMENT, AND THE RELATED ACES WITH COMMUNICATIONS NAVIGATION AND SURVEILLANCE (AWCNS) PROJECT AND FOLLOW ON WILL BOTH IMMEDIATE BENEFIT FROM THE INTELLITRACE TOOL. THE PROPOSED CAPABILITY AND TOOLS HAVE IMMEDIATE USEFULNESS TO THE ACES AND AWCNS DEVELOPMENT TEAMS. Description: 2005 SBIR PHASE II - WIRELESS IN-SITU NONDESTRUCTIVE INSPECTION OF ENGINE ROTOR DISKS WITH ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVES.  THE STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY OF JET ENGINE TURBINE OR FAN ROTOR DISKS IS VITAL FOR AVIATION SAFETY.  CUMULATIVE CRACKS AT CRITICAL LOADING AND HIGH STRESS AREAS, IF NOT DETECTED AND REPAIRED IN TIME, MAY LEAD TO CATASTROPHIC FAILURE.  TRADITIONAL METHODS, SUCH AS FLUORESCENT PENETRANT INSPECTION (FPI) AND EDDY CURRENT ARE LIMITED TO POINT-BY-POINT MEASUREMENTS AND ARE VERY TIME CONSUMING. DISASSEMBLY OF THE ENGINE IS REQUIRED FOR EACH INSPECTION, WHICH IN TURN MAY CAUSE MAINTENANCE INDUCED PROBLEMS.  WE PROPOSE A WIRELESS IN-SITU ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE HEALTH MONITORING APPROACH.  IT APPLIES LIGHT, THIN, HIGH TEMPERATURE LEAVE-IN-PLACE ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE CIRCUMFERENTIAL PATCH TRANSDUCERS AOUND THE ROOT OF THE DISK, AND A PAIR OG INNOVATIVE TUBE ANTENNAE THAT WIRELESSLY COUPLE THE TRANSDUCERS TO THE INSPECTION INSTRUMENTS.  GUIDED WAVES TRAVEL IN THE DISK FOR CRACK INSPECTION, AND THE INSPECTION COULD BE DONE EVEN WHEN THE DISK IS ROTATING.  PHASE I RESULTS CLEARLY DEMONSTRATE THAT THE GUIDED WAVE IS VERY SENSITIVE TO TINY CRACKS ON A ROTATING ALUMINUM DISK, AND THE TUBE ANTENAE WORKED WELL.  THE ENVISIONED SYSTEM CAN INSPECT A RELATIVELY LARGE AREA, HAS MINIMAL EFFECT ON THE ROTOR PERFORMANCE, INSTANTANEOUSLY PROVIDES RELIABLE AND QUANTITATIVE DATA SUCH AS CRACK LOCATION AND SEVERITY LEVEL, AND MINIMIZE AND EVENTUALLY ELIMINATE THE NEED FOR STRUCTURAL DISASSEMBLY.

Description: RADID DEVELOPEMENT OF A FOCUSED VIRTUAL MAGNETOSPHERIC OBSERVATORY AND ITS INTEGRATION WITH VXOS FOR S3C DATA We propose the rapid development of a focused Virtual Magnetospheric Observatory (VMO) that will facilitate query-based discovery and access of data from past, current and future NASA magnetospheric missions. This VMO's intelligent magnetospheric search capability is highly relevant to NASA programs and interests because it will decrease data discovery efforts and, thus, improve the efficiency of magnetospheric research and enable many faster (and cheaper) complex multi-spacecraft studies. Ultimately, the VMO has the potential to become a distributed data and service environment with Google-like context search capabilities. As a demonstration of the VMO's utility, we will focus on plasma and magnetic field measurements from widely used and harder to access databases. The selection of initial data providers was driven by the need to demonstrate the distributed nature of the VMO, to develop and document standards for data providers, and to give the proposed VMO a scientific focal point, namely "Multispacecraft correlative studies of the dayside magnetospheric interactions and substorms". The core VMO part called Middleware will be responsible for composing queries, sending them to data and service providers, interpreting query results and returning them to the VMO users. An extended SPASE-based data model will be created to describe participating data sets which will not only provide metadata necessary for performing data queries, it will also represent a unified layer between the various data sets and users. The VMO will also take advantage of an existing data mining service RemoteMiner, that will be used to create event lists such as magnetopause crossings or FTEs, to enable more intelligent searches as, for example, "When were FTEs observed at the dayside magnetopause while other spacecraft were gathering data nearby?". The VMO team will collaborate with other VxOs towards a standard for inter-VxO queries and, in particular, we will demonstrate such inter-VxO queries by providing the VMO users information about relevant solar wind/IMF conditions obtained by sending queries between the VMO and VHO Middleware. It is expected that the VMO will become an important part of the VxO environment enabling intelligent access to ever increasing number of data products and services. The modular architecture of the MO environment will assure high flexibility and extensibility of the functionality to satisfy the space physics community's evolving needs. We perceive the VMO as an extremely important data discovery tool that is highly relevant to the U.S. National Goal "Study the Earth system from space and develop new space-based and related capabilities for this purpose" and to the NASA's Strategic Objectives as specified in Table of 1 in the Summary of Solicitation of this NRA because the VMO is a new technology and tool that will improve scientific understanding of the space environment and conditions experienced by human explorers near Earth.

Description: To be used naturally in design optimization, parametric study and achieve quick total time-to-solution, simulation must naturally and personally be available to the scientist/engineer, as easily as email or word-processing. Environments such as Matlab/IDL allow ease of use, but unless simulations are extremely fast, they cannot be used naturally. Many large-scale numerical calculations require storage and computation that grow as the square/cube of the number of variables, including such linear algebra operations as solving dense linear systems, computing eigen-values/vectors, and others. The use of fast algorithms such as the fast multipole method (FMM) coupled with iterative methods allows many problems of interest to be solved in near linear time and memory. We have taken a leadership role in applying and extending the FMM to various problems in acoustics, fluid flow, electromagnetics, function fitting and machine learning. Graphical Processing Units (GPUs) are now ubiquitous in game consoles, in workstations and other devices and are special purpose processors for graphics, that are predicted to shortly achieve performance in the hundreds of gigaflop range for specialized calculations (much faster than COTS PCs) at low price points. It is conceivable now to equip personal workstations with several CPUs and GPUs, and solve problems with millions or billions of variables quickly using fast algorithms. We will take an important algorithm with wide applicability: the FMM, and implement it on the widely available heterogeneous CPU/GPU architecture, and prove the feasibility of accelerating it tremendously. A fundamental reconsideration of the algorithm that maps appropriate pieces on to the correct part of the architecture forms the basis of our approach. Developed software will be tested, and benchmark problems solved. A library of software that will support the porting of the FMM and other scientific computing to the CPU/GPU architecture will be developed.

Description: The Stellar Imager, an ultraviolet, sparse-aperture telescope, was one of the fifteen Vision Missions chosen for a study completed last year. Stellar Imager will enable very high angular resolution images of stellar surfaces. The baselined design is a Fizeau beam combiner with 20 to 30 separated (free-flying) elements. This proposal is for funding to develop and test an alternative beam combiner design for the Stellar Imager Mission. We designate this new combiner the Spatial Frequency Remapper (SFR). In the SFR, the large field-of-view of the Fizeau design is sacrificed in favor of simultaneous observations at multiple wavelengths. Also, depending on the details of the design of the rest of the telescope, the SFR should either produce better images or relax the very tight stability requirements. Since the large field of view of the Fizeau combiner is not needed for the mission, the SFR, if it works, is clearly the better design; it's only expense is the addition of one or perhaps two extra reflections, needed to incorporate the spectral dispersion. The work that will be accomplished, including Phase 2, will include A) completing the analysis of the design as it pertains to Stellar Imager, B) performing a laboratory test at longer wavelengths to verify the soundness of that design and C) developing a more rigorous test of its imaging capabilities to be performed on a large, ground-based telescope. This final item will be the main component of the commercialization plan.

Description: We propose to develop electronics for operation at temperatures that range from -230oC to +130oC. This new technology will minimize the requirements for external heat sources that are currently necessary for operation of low-temperature electronics. Such technology would significantly improve reliability, performance, lifetime of electronics that are used for space applications, including satellites and space travel. This will be achieved through the development of unique circuits that are derived from novel physics based device and circuit modeling techniques and verified by experiment. Statistical methods will be employed to connect the resistive heating caused by individual devices to heating of the entire integrated circuit. Special algorithms will be further developed which allow for determination of operating conditions where the intrinsic operation of the circuit will allow for sufficient heat generation to eliminate carrier freeze-out and efficient operation of integrated circuits in environments ranging from -230oC to +130oC. For situations where intrinsic circuit resistive heating at cryogenic temperatures is insufficient to overcome carrier freeze out, we will design on-chip micro-heaters to provide direct heating to chips at the submicron device level. Thermal modeling of packaging will also be performed. With the intrinsic temperature control established, we will design specific single electron latchup immune circuits for application extreme environments.

Description: DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUATION OF A GENERALIZED FRAMEWORK TO ASIMILATE OBSERVED MICROWAVE RADIANCES EMERGING FROM RAINING AREAS INTO A GLOBAL CIRCULATION MODEL ABSTRACT:The objectives of this proposal are the development and the evaluation of a generalized framework to assimilate observed microwave radiances emerging from raining areas into a global circulation model. Current systems for assimilating microwave radiances into numerical weather prediction models are suboptimal because of deficiencies in representing microphysical processes in the prediction models. These deficiencies are caused by the models' inability to numerically resolve small-scale processes at global scales, but also by limited knowledge of these processes. On the other hand, precipitation assimilation schemes are robust and less sensitive to the above-mentioned deficiencies in global numerical models, However, there might be information in the global models that can improve the satellite precipitation estimation if considered simultaneously with the global numerical modeling. In this project, we propose the incorporation of information from a high-resolution, high-quality precipitation-microwave radiance database used in precipitation retrievals into a microwave radiance assimilation framework. The framework will generalize existing radiance and precipitation assimilation schemes by allowing the estimation of precipitation variables at scales not resolved by the model in agreement with the model variables, and observed and predicted radiances. Its implementation will be based on a forward radiative transfer model and its adjoint used currently for precipitation estimation and the variation framework for precipitation assimilation used in an existing global circulation model. The framework's impact on global atmospheric analyses and forecasts will be tested using data from the TRMM Tropical Imager (TMI) and other satellite instruments. Specifically, the proposed research consists of the following elements: (1) Development of a variational assimilation framework to incorporate radiance information from passive microwave sensors into a numerical weather prediction model. The radiances will be assimilated into a one-dimensional (ID) nonlinear column model with tendencies prescribed by the 3D full model integration. The analyzed variables from the ID assimilation will be incorporated into the full model either as tendency correction or retrieved state variables. Additional information derived from the precipitation-radiation databases currently used in precipitation retrievals will be considered in the time-dependent 1D assimilation framework to account for deficiencies in the column model. (2) Comparisons of results from the new assimilation technique with results from existing formulations. (3) Application and further evaluation of the newly developed assimilation framework. This research is directly responsive to one of NASA's strategic goals, i.e. the advancement of precipitation assimilation techniques for the benefit of global atmospheric analyses and forecasts.

Description: SBIR PHASE II AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED:  THERMAL CONTROL FOR INSTRUMENTS - MINIATURE LOOP HEAT PIPE (LHP) WITH MULTIPLE EVAPORATORS AND MULTIPLE CONDENSERS.  LHP IS A HIGH-PERFORMANCE HEAT TRANSPORTATION DEVICE USING CAPILLARY FORCES TO CIRCULATE THE WORKING FLUID IN A CLOSED LOOP.  CONVENTIONAL LHP'S USUALLY HAVE ONE CAPILLARY PUMP (EVAPORATOR) TO ACQUIRE WASTE HEAT FROM A HEAT SOURCE.  RECENT EFFORTS HAVE FOCUSED THE DEVELOPMENT OF LHP'S THAT CONTAIN TWO OR MORE EVAPORATORS.  EVEN THOUGH TWO- EVAPORATOR LHP'S PERFORMED VERY WELL, THE VOLUME OF EACH COMPENSATION CHAMBER (CC) BECAME MUCH LARGER THAN THAT OF THE SINGLE-EVAPORATOR COUNTERPART.  THE REASON WAS THAT ALL BUT ONE CC WOULD BE LIQUID-FILLED DURING NORMAL OPERATION.  THE ONE THAT WAS NOT LIQUID-FILLED HAD TO LARGE ENOUGH TO ACCOMMODATE THE SYSTEM LIQUID EXPANSION AT MAXIMUM TEMPERATURE.  AS A RESULT, LHP'S WITH MORE THAN 3 EVAPORATORS WERE NOT FEASIBLE FOR PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS SIMPLY BECAUSE THE CC'S BECAME PROHIBITIVELY LARGE.  IN THE CURRENT RESEARCH, THE CC'S OF A MULTIPLE-EVAPORATOR LHP WERE CAPILLARY-LINKED.  IN OTHER WORDS, THE CC'S ALWAYS CONTAINED A MIXTURE OF LIQUID AND VAPOR (TWO- PHASE), ALLOWING THE LOOP TO OPERATE WITH A MUCH SMALLER FLUID CHARGE.  CONSEQUENTLY, THE REQUIRED CC VOLUME WAS ALSO REDUCED.

Description: STUDIES OF THE NEAR-NUCLEUS DUST JETS AND COMA MORPHOLOGY IN COMETS 9P/TEMPEL 1, 81P/WILD2 AND 19P/BORRELLY In this proposal, we are requesting NASA support to study the spatial and temporal morphology of the comae of comets 9PlTempel1, 81Pn-lild 2 and 19P/Borrelly, to determine the sources of the jets and relate them to surface properties of the nucleus. The ultimate goal of this work is to investigate the conditions under which cometary activity occurs, to constrain the mechanisms that act to produce it, and to evaluate potential evolutionary processes that act on the nucleus. Isolated jets are visible in the comae of all three comets, and we will use a number of techniques to project them back to the nucleus to determine where they originate. We will then explore the physical properties of these source regions and will use the nucleus shape models to examine the illumination circumstances that are present during the onset and cessation of the activity. We will also explore some of the special cases of jets, including jets that appear to originate from regions of the nucleus that are unilluminated and jets that are clearly connected to the surface of comet Tempe1 1. The requested funds will be used for analysis of the jet structures, for applying minor modifications to existing software that can be applied to the current problems, and for interpretation of the results.

Description: OUTBURSTS BY COMET TEMPEL 1 ABSTRACT: One of the many surprises from the approach of Deep Impact to comet Tempel 1 was the realization that spontaneous outbursts are far more common than expected, at least one per week. They are correlated, although not perfectly, with the rotational phase of the nucleus, thus ruling out exogenic models for their cause. Our goal is to investigate the driving mechanism for these outbursts. The release of material from the nucleus is very fast, in some cases being completed in a matter of minutes. Some of the outbursts were also observed from Earth, such as the June 14 outburst that was seen at Calar Alto and with HST. We also have spectroscopic observations before and after some outbursts. Due to the difficult nature of the dark subtraction in the IR spectra from Deep Impact, these data require extensive effort to derive reliable spectra. We will examine the imagery from Deep Impact and from other sources, such as the HST, to determine the geometry and speed of the ejection. We will use a shape model of the comet to locate sources on the surface. We will examine the spectra to determine the chemical changes during the outbursts. The combination of chemical changes and tying to the surface should allow important constraints to be place on the driving mechanisms for the outbursts. Understanding the outburst mechanism is important for interpreting the behavior of all comets that exhibit outbursts and in particular it is important to understand the extent to which the localization of outbursts is related to the primordial accretion of disparate cometesimals and thus to our models of planetary origins.

Description: The EOS A-train will allow tightly constrained cross-validation of AURA-TES radiances using the well validated AQUA-AIRS radiances. Very extensive validation of AIRS over the last 2 years, using multiple independent data sources, indicates that AIRS radiometric calibration is better than 0.5%, well below the stated requirement for TES radiometric accuracy of 1 %. The validation of TES radiances using AIRS, and simulated radiances computed from ECMWF model data, is the main activity proposed here. Since AIRS and TES observations will only be separated by several minutes, the atmospheric state will be almost identical under clear conditions, especially averaged over many observations. Our overall methodology will be to use AIRS and MODIS data to determine which AIRS/TES observations are clear, and intercompare AIRS and TES radiances in these cases. Degradation of the TES radiances to AIRS spectral resolution will allow detailed intercomparisons of the TES radiometric accuracy over a wide range of wavelengths and radiometric signal levels. We will also compare clear TES radiances to radiances computed from ECMWF model fields. These comparison will be performed at both full TES spectral resolution, and with TES radiances degraded to AIRS spectral resolution. The biases between AIRS measured radiances and radiances computed from ECWMF fields have been very well-characterized by our group, and will allow a quick check-out of the TES radiometry and the performance of the LI b algorithm. These comparisons will allow us to ascribe any observed bias errors to the various possible sources, such as forward model errors, Lib algorithm problems, radiometric errors, and validation data inaccuracies. This information can then be fed back into the TES forward model and L2 retrieval. Lower-priority tasks proposed here include providing the TES Science Team with (1) accurate surface emissivities for a subset of "important" TES observations derived from multiple observations by AIRS of the same nominal field-of-view, and (2) infrared dust aerosol spectral models, derived from AIRS observations that will help TES understand and mitigate uncertainties in these parameters in their minor gas retrieval algorithms. We also plan to carefully intercompare the UMBC "line-by-line" radiative transfer algorithm used to generate the AIRS forward model (kCARTA) to the line-by-line algorithm LBLRTM used to generate the TES fast radiative transfer algorithm using both the AIRS and TES observations. This work is already partially funded (NPP Science Team).

Description: CHARGE MOBILITY OF THE IRRADIATED REGOLITH MICROATMOSPHERES AND MICROIONOSPHERES OF THE ICY BODIES IN THE SOLAR SYSTEM ABSTRACT: THE UNIVERSITY OF MARYLAND, IN CONJUNCTION WITH CO-INVESTIGATORS FROM THE UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA, AND NASA GODDARD SPACE FLIGHT CENTER, PROPOSES TO STUDY IN THE LABORATORY, AND THROUGH MODELING, THE MANIFESTATION OF CHARGE SEPARATION (SEPARATION OF IONS AND ELECTRONS) AND CHARGE MOBILITY IN WATER-RICH ICES ON THE HEAVILY IRRADIATED SURFACES OF ICY BODIES IN THE OUTER SOLAR SYSTEM. CHARGE PRODUCTION, SEPARATION, AND MOBILITY MAY OCCUR WITHIN GAS AND SOLID PHASES OF THE POROUS ICE REGOLITH ON THESE BODIES. THIS INVESTIGATION FOCUSES ON THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THE PRODUCTION OF RADIATION-INDUCED TRAPPED GAS AND THE MOBILITY OF ELECTRONS AND HOLES BOTH THERMALLY AND UNDER PHOTO-ACTIVATION AT TEMPERATURES (30 K - 150 K) RELEVANT TO ICY MOONS OF THE GIANT PLANETS AND WITH FURTHER POTENTIAL APPLICATIONS TO CENTAURS, THE PLUTO/CHARON SYSTEM, AND THE KUIPER BELT. STUDIES PROPOSED HERE ARE BASED ON THE PRINCIPAL INVESTIGATOR S RECENT LABORATORY FINDINGS THAT ORGANIC IMPURITIES IN AN ICE MATRIX ARE VERY EFFICIENTLY (E.G., 80%) IONIZED.  THERE ARE SEVERAL IMPLICATIONS OF THESE FINDINGS, INCLUDING THE STORAGE OF ENERGY, COLORATION OF ICES, SEPARATION OF POSITIVELY CHARGED IMPURITY IONS AND ELECTRONS, AND PHOTO-INDUCED MOBILITY OF ELECTRONS AND HOLES LEADING TO MICRO-IONOSPHERES. THESE PROCESSES CAN IN PRINCIPAL GREATLY AFFECT THE MAGNETOSPHERE-MOON INTERACTIONS. THAT IS, THE CHARGE SEPARATION PRODUCED BY THE INCIDENT RADIATION CAN CREATE LOCAL IONOSPHERES THAT AFFECT ELECTRIC AND MAGNETIC FIELD INTERACTIONS BETWEEN THE MOONS AND THEIR MAGNETOSPHERIC ENVIRONMENTS.  CHARGING EFFECTS (E.G., ICE LIGHTNING) COULD ALSO BE IMPORTANT ENERGY SOURCES FOR RADIOLYTIC EVOLUTION OF MOLECULAR CHEMISTRY, INCLUDING PREBIOTIC ORGANIC PRODUCTION, IN IRRADIATED PLANETARY ICES. IT IS OUR AIM TO UNDERSTAND THE IONIZATION PROCESSES IN ICES, INCLUDING THE TRAPPING AND MOBILITY OF ELECTRONS IN ICES, THEIR CONNECTION WITH THE PRODUCTION OF GASES FOR SATELLITE ATMOSPHERES, AND INTERACTIONS OF THE RESULTANT MICROIONOSPHERIC CHARGES AND CURRENTS WITH THE MAGNETIC FIELD ENVIRONMENT. IN PARTICULAR WE WILL ADDRESS THE FOLLOWING QUESTIONS. 1. WHAT IS THE EFFICIENCY OF IONIZING RADIATION FOR PRODUCING TRAPPED ELECTRONS OR IONS (HOLES) IN AN ICE CONTAINING IMPURITIES.  2, HOW LARGE ARE THE PHOTOCURRENTS IN IRRADIATED WATER-ICES CONTAINING IMPURITIES, INCLUDING THE ELECTRON AND HOLE MOBILITY UNDER THERMAL AND PHOTO-STIMULATION? 3. DO THE PRODUCTION AND MOBILITY OF CHARGE CARRIERS INFLUENCE THE FORMATION OF GASEOUS MOLECULES TRAPPED IN VACANCY AGGREGATES CALLED BUBBLES OR MICROATMOSPHERES? 4. DO ELECTRONS AND HOLES GET TRAPPED PREFERENTIALLY IN THE MICROATMOSPHERES? 5. HOW DO THE ENERGIES AND NUMBER DENSITIES OF THE TRAPPED CHARGED SPECIES IN ICES VARY BASED THE DENSITY AND TYPE OF CONTAMINANT AND ON THE INCIDENT RADIATION AND PENETRATION DEPTH? 6. WHAT FRACTIONS, IF NOT L00%, OF THE MEASURED INDUCED MAGNETIC FIELDS ON THE ICY GALILEAN MOONS ARE CONTRIBUTED BY MICROIONOSPHERIC CURRENTS? ENERGETIC IONS AND ELECTRONS IN THE MAGNETOSPHERES OF JUPITER AND SATURN BOMBARD THE SURFACES OF ICY MOONS WITHIN THESE GIANT PLANET SYSTEMS AND DELIVER LARGE RADIATION DOSAGES TO THE METERS-THICK ICY REGOLITHS. MANIFESTATIONS OF THESE INTERACTIONS INCLUDE THE SPUTTERED O2 ATMOSPHERE AT EUROPA, PREDICTED IN 1982 BASED ON LABORATORY DATA AND LATER DETECTED VIA AIRGLOW EMISSIONS BY HUBBLE SPACE TELESCOPE (HST) OBSERVATIONS, THE FORMATION OF SOLID-LIKE O2 TRAPPED IN ICE INCLUSIONS WITHIN THE SURFACES OF GANYMEDE AND EUROPA, AND TRAPPED O3 ON GANYMEDE, DIONE AND RHEA. WE PROPOSE TO EXPERIMENTALLY AND COMPUTATIONALLY INVESTIGATE THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN THESE RADIATION EFFECTS AND THE CHARGE SEPARATION PRODUCED BY THE INCIDENT RADIATION AS A POTENTIALLY CRITICAL RELATIONSHIP THAT HAS NOT BEEN EXAMINED TO DATE.

Description: KEIFER, WALTER/LUNAR PROSPECTOR GRAVITY OBSERVATIONS AS CONSTRAINTS ON LUNAR VOLCANIC PROCESSES Lunar Prospector observations have dramatically improved our knowledge of the lunar gravity field and currently provide our best global constraint on the crustal structure of the Moon. Previous lunar gravity modeling has mostly focused on impact structures but has not previously been used to constrain the Moon's volcanic history. I will use a combination of spectral domain and spatial domain gravity modeling methods to model gravity anomalies associated with several classes of volcanic structures on the Moon. Specific targets of study include (1) the Marius Hills, which is the most extensive volcanic dome field on the Moon, (2) the Aristarchus Plateau, which contains numerous sinuous rilles and is also the site of the largest pyroclastic eruption known on the Moon, and (3) concentrations of dark halo craters in the Schiller-Schickard region, which are thought to expose an ancient episode of mare volcanism (prior to the Orientale impact, > 3.8 Ga). The primary goal of the study is to constrain the nature of subsurface mass anomalies (e.g. dikes, sills) found in these regions and to quantify the dimensions of these bodies (horizontal size, minimum vertical thickness, total mass anomaly). A secondary objective is to provide new constraints on the elastic lithospheric thickness in these regions and thus to improve our overall knowledge of the Moon's thermal evolution. The overall outcome will be a better understanding of the Moon's volcanic history. The proposed work builds on a series of successful studies using similar methods to examine large highland volcanos and the hemispheric dichotomy on Mars (Kiefer, Earth Planet. Sci. Lett., 2004; Geophys. Res. Lett., 2005).

Description: ANALYSIS OF THE IRTF CSHELL COMET C/1996 B2 HYAKUTAKE TEAM DATA The primary scientific objective of this work is to analyze and interpret the comet C11996 B2 (Hyakutake) Team Data acquired with the Cryogenic Echelle Spectrometer (CSHELL) at the NASA Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) in April and May 1996. Ground-based high-resolution IR spectroscopy is a relatively new but powerful technique for probing the abundances of parent molecules in cometary comae. The apparition of C/Hyakutake in March 1996 offered the first significant opportunity to characterize the chemistry of a comet in this way. High-resolution infrared spectroscopy provided many insights into the chemistry of C/Hyakutake over a few dates near its closest approach to Earth during scheduled Principal Investigator (PI) observing time, however, additional data obtained on 13 dates from April 16 - May 25,1996 by the Hyakutake Team have yet to be fully analyzed, interpreted and published. Analysis of the IRTF CSHELL Hyakutake Team Data is important for two reasons: 1) These data provide more extensive heliocentric coverage of production rates, rotational temperatures and spatial distributions of volatile species detected in C/Hyakutake, placing the published infrared PI data in a broader context. These data also complement and enhance the studies of volatile release at all wavelengths. For example, spectroscopic monitoring of molecular production rates versus heliocentric distance was done for C/Hyakutake at radio wavelengths, so production rates derived from our proposed study would provide independent measurements of species detectable at radio wavelengths (e.g. CO, HCN, CH30H, and H2CO), and unique measurements of species detectable only at infrared wavelengths (e.g. CH4, C2H6, and C2H2). 2) These data provide significant wavelength coverage between 3.01- 3.61 microns. Although CSHELL is not generally well-suited for conducting broad spectral surveys, these data dedicate 62 grating settings to this task. Spectral surveys using more powerful cross-dispersed spectrometers are now much more efficient, and data obtained from this work can be compared to existing high-resolution comet surveys. The proposed work (duration Mar. 1,2007 - Feb. 28,2010) consists of two primary tasks. 1) Determine production rates, and when possible, rotational temperatures, and spatial distributions of all detected species in the Hyakutake Team Data. 2) Analyze, interpret and publish a high-resolution infrared survey of Hyakutake and compare detected spectral emissions to those seen in other comets. Results obtained from this dataset provide both supplementary and unique information about the volatile chemistry of C/Hyakutake. This research is relevant to NASA's Vision and Mission. Comets likely preserve primordial information from the time of the formation of the Solar System. Comets have also bombarded the Earth throughout its history, and provided some of the raw materials necessary for the genesis of life. Therefore, understanding the chemistry of comets addresses two of NASA's strategic goals and outcomes: 1) Advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system, the potential for life elsewhere, and the hazards and resources present as humans explore space; and 2) Discover the origin, structure, evolution, and destiny of the universe and search for Earth-like planets. This work is also highly relevant to the Planetary Atmospheres Program: (a) PAT supports scientific investigations that contribute to the understanding of the origins and evolution of the atmospheres of planets and their satellites, and of comets. (B) The broad objectives of PATM include the determination of compositions, dynamics, energetics, and chemical behaviors of planetary atmospheres including comets. This investigation is also relevant to the PATM program since a valuable dataset will be analyzed that was obtained during a campaign at a NASA-sponsored telescope facility.

Description: Measuring Particles, Antiparticles, and Isotopes in the Cosmic Radiation Cosmic rays propagate through the Galaxy by scattering off magnetic irregularities in a process described as diffusion. The particles reaching Earth from their distant sources are modified by interactions with interstellar matter as they are guided through the interstellar gas/plasma by the galactic magnetic fields. The interactions produce secondary particles whose abundance relative to the primary particles is a measure of the amount of material traversed. This relative abundance and the secondary particle energy distributions are keys to understanding the nature and distribution of sources. In addition to known astronomical objects, possible exotic sources would include antimatter, dark matter, primordial black holes, etc. The goal Otis proposal is to study the sensitivity of searching for dark matter in the cosmic-ray antiparticle channels, with a focus on positrons. One major objective is to develop an optimal measurement strategy for positrons, including reduction of the signal. selection uncertainties. Our previous studies have demonstrated that systematic uncertainties present a serious challenge to precision measurements of these rare particles, which may be key to one of the fundamental questions in the 2003 National Academy of Science, Board on Physics and Astronomy report "Connecting Quarks with the Cosmos: Eleven Science Questions for the New Century", specifically "What is Dark Matter?" Previous investigations with balloon-borne magnetic spectrometers indicate that the positron fraction has an excess in the 7 - lOGeV range that continues to higher energies. A new balloon-borne instrument optimized to measure 1 - 50 GeV positrons and electrons with sensitivity much better than that of the previous experiments could discriminate between these possibilities with a 30-day balloon flight around Antarctica. Description: UNIVERSAL RECONFIGURABLE TRANSLATOR MODULE Currently, printed circuit boards (PCBs) are designed and built to a specific standard interface. These PCBs are not easily re-usable with other standard interfaces. Usually, a unique one-time-use adaptor is designed and built or the PCB is re-designed and built. Either approach costs time and money. A solution to this problem would be important to the interoperability of reconfigurable computing resources for manned exploration, as well as realize a cost savings from reusability and reduced spares for computing/communications designs. The proposed URTM implements a Reconfigurable Protocol Translation Module (RPTM) and Physical Interface Modules (PIM) to provide a reconfigurable solution targeted for various standard serial links (MIL-STD-1553B, SpaceWire, and FireWire). The PIM simply plugs into the RPTM and the internal implementation of the RPTM automatically configures with appropriate computing cores for the attached PIMs to achieve the desired serial link. Study the feasibility of a configurable URTM to translate serial link data and resolve technical issues, and of using the concept for a universal serial interface to space computer and/or communication boards. Based on the results, design, develop, document, and deliver engineering prototype model of the URTM with a path to spaceflight. The specific objectives of the URTM are: Design and develop an engineering prototype of an universal serial link translator Adapt any two point-to-point data links logically, electrically, and mechanically Support popular data links for space applications Automatic reconfiguration with plug-and-play Simply connect the Physical Interface Modules (PIM) on either end of the RPTM The RPTM then self configures via a library of interface translation functions Thus allowing the two data links to communicate seamlessly SCOPE OF WORK: Work areas include research and trade studies, procurement, hardware development and build, VHDL development, test development, prototype test and deliver, modeling, documentation and design delivery, and reviews.

Description: We propose to develop a hard X-ray photoelectric polarimeter for prompt gamma-ray burst (GRB) emission in the 15-80 keV energy band. Linear polarization measurements would provide unique and important constraints on theories of GRB production mechanisms. The photoelectric polarimeter is based on a large-volume micropattern time-projection chamber that can determine, on a photon-by-photon basis, the angle of emission of the photoelectron resulting from an X-ray interaction. The photoelectron emission direction is correlated with the X-ray electric field vector and thus provides polarization information. This polarimetry technique combines high sensitivity with broad bandpass and is potentially the most powerful method below about 80 keV, where the photoelectric effect is the dominant interaction process. The proposed effort includes the development and testing of both detector hardware and simulation and analysis tools. It is expected that this effort would lead to a follow-on proposal for either a long duration balloon flight or other mission of opportunity.

Description: DIPOLARIZATION AND PLASMA INJECTION IN THE INNER MAGNETOSPHERE.  This project seeks to investigate substorm-related features inside geosynchronous orbit. Although dipolarization and particle injection are fundamental features of tail substorm dynamics, their characteristics in the inner magnetosphere remain to be understood. However, a detailed study of substorm processes in the inner magnetosphere is compelling because (a) it will cast new light on the cause of dipolarization and particle injection and (b) dipolarization and particle injection can play an important role in the intensification of the ring current during magnetospheric storms. The present project will examine the occurrence frequency of dipolarization/injection inside geosynchronous orbit in terms of the location and geomagnetic activity. The project will also examine whether the local plasma and magnetic field need to be preconditioned. For example, the depression of the equatorial magnetic field during magnetospheric storms may he favorable for the occurrence of dipolarization/injection. It is also possible that dipolarization/injection takes place preferably in association with a specific type of geomagnetic activity such as sawtooth injections. By testing these ideas the project will address favorable conditions for dipolarization/injection in the inner magnetosphere. The project will also address the intensification of the storm-time ring current by comparing in situ measurements with global ENA images. An emphasis will be placed on nergization of oxygen ions. Magnetic field and particle data from the Cluster, Polar, AMPTEICCE and CRRES satellites will be used as primary data sets. Although the orbits of these satellites are not necessarily favorable for investigating the inner magnetosphere, accumulated data over their mission periods make the proposed statistical study feasible. Data from the Cluster constellation will also be used for examining the spatial propagation of dipolarization/injection signatures. The project will use ENA images taken by the IMAGE satellite, and for case studies it will use data from various magnetospheric missions of the NASA's Great Observatory.

Description: Multi-Satellite Observations of Flux Transfer Events FTE durations and inter-arrival times provide important information concerning the generation mechanism and dynamics of reconnection on the magnetopause. We will survey the characteristics multiple FTEs observed in three data sets. First, we will examine Interball-1 observations during the period from 1995 to 1999. Interball-1 observations allow us to study quasi-periodic FTEs at higher dayside latitudes and greater downstream distances than those accessible to previous statistical surveys. We will compare the characteristics of FTEs in these locations to those previously reported on the dayside magnetopause. In particular, we will explore the relationship between the energy within individual FTEs and the accumulated free energy since the last event. We want to determine whether or not there are special conditions in the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field that favor the generation of multiple FTEs. Second, we will survey FTE data sets from Geotail. Geotail observations permit us to study ion and electron velocity distribution functions within FTEs, enabling determination of connectivity to the magnetopause through a survey of particle streaming. Finally, we will examine observations by NASA's forthcoming THEMIS mission (launch in February 2007). Observations from the five near-equatorial satellites in this mission can also be used to determine the dimensions of FTEs on the magnetopause.

Description: ADVANCED DARK ENERGY PHYSICS TELESCOPE (ADEPT) We propose to conduct a study of a space mission to determine the nature of the mysterious dark energy that is driving the accelerated expansion of the universe. The objective of the proposed study is to determine the most powerful but cost-effective detailed mission concept The best approach is a mission optimized to measure baryon acoustic oscillations, but one that can also survey type la supernovae with no additional hardware or operating modes. The baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler that can be compared to the scale of the cosmic microwave background anistropy at very high redshift, while supernovae provide a relative luminosity distance with respect to local supernovae. Both methods have been proven by ground-based observations. Space-based observations would provide the high redshift leverage for constraints on the variability of the dark energy. The ADEPT team combines scientific and technical expertise from all of the major methods to measure dark energy, in addition to space-flight experience, to achieve both breadth and depth. The team is organized around specific tasks, including the task to build computer mission simulation tools to evaluate the effectiveness of various hardware approaches, and the task to conduct cosmological simulations to evaluate effectiveness and potential systematic measurement errors. The organization of the study is designed to create two-way interaction between the development of science requirements and the evaluation of the simplest and most robust engineering implementations. The proposed work is directly responsive to the specific NRA call for JDEM mission concept proposals. JDEM research fits NASALS objectives. In response to the national objective to, Implement a sustained and affordable human and robotic program to explore the Solar System and beyond, NASA has developed the specific objective: Explore the universe to understand its origin, structure, evolution, and destiny. Also, in response to the national objective to, Develop innovative technologies, knowledge, and infrastructures both to explore and to support decisions about the destinations for human exploration, NASA has a specific objective to, ;Use NASA missions and other activities to inspire and motivate the nation's students and teachers, to engage and educate the public, and to advance the scientific and technological capabilities of the nation.

Description: 2005 SBIR PHASE II - WIRELESS IN-SITU NONDESTRUCTIVE INSPECTION OF ENGINE ROTOR DISKS WITH ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVES.  THE STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY OF JET ENGINE TURBINE OR FAN ROTOR DISKS IS VITAL FOR AVIATION SAFETY.  CUMULATIVE CRACKS AT CRITICAL LOADING AND HIGH STRESS AREAS, IF NOT DETECTED AND REPAIRED IN TIME, MAY LEAD TO CATASTROPHIC FAILURE.  TRADITIONAL METHODS, SUCH AS FLUORESCENT PENETRANT INSPECTION (FPI) AND EDDY CURRENT ARE LIMITED TO POINT-BY-POINT MEASUREMENTS AND ARE VERY TIME CONSUMING. DISASSEMBLY OF THE ENGINE IS REQUIRED FOR EACH INSPECTION, WHICH IN TURN MAY CAUSE MAINTENANCE INDUCED PROBLEMS.  WE PROPOSE A WIRELESS IN-SITU ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE HEALTH MONITORING APPROACH.  IT APPLIES LIGHT, THIN, HIGH TEMPERATURE LEAVE-IN-PLACE ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE CIRCUMFERENTIAL PATCH TRANSDUCERS AOUND THE ROOT OF THE DISK, AND A PAIR OG INNOVATIVE TUBE ANTENNAE THAT WIRELESSLY COUPLE THE TRANSDUCERS TO THE INSPECTION INSTRUMENTS.  GUIDED WAVES TRAVEL IN THE DISK FOR CRACK INSPECTION, AND THE INSPECTION COULD BE DONE EVEN WHEN THE DISK IS ROTATING.  PHASE I RESULTS CLEARLY DEMONSTRATE THAT THE GUIDED WAVE IS VERY SENSITIVE TO TINY CRACKS ON A ROTATING ALUMINUM DISK, AND THE TUBE ANTENAE WORKED WELL.  THE ENVISIONED SYSTEM CAN INSPECT A RELATIVELY LARGE AREA, HAS MINIMAL EFFECT ON THE ROTOR PERFORMANCE, INSTANTANEOUSLY PROVIDES RELIABLE AND QUANTITATIVE DATA SUCH AS CRACK LOCATION AND SEVERITY LEVEL, AND MINIMIZE AND EVENTUALLY ELIMINATE THE NEED FOR STRUCTURAL DISASSEMBLY.

Description: Solar Gamma-Ray Line Observations with RHESSI We propose to continue our program in gamma-ray spectroscopy of solar flares detected by RHESSI. This effort has resulted in a new understanding of the solar atmosphere during intense flaring activity based on observations of the electron-positron annihilation line. The gamma-ray observations together with particle measurements in space offer the opportunity for understanding the relationship between the processes accelerating particles impacting the Sun and those escaping to interplanetary space. Our recent work on the 2005 January 20 flare has revealed what appears to be a second very hard particle component. We plan on completing the spectroscopic studies of the twenty nuclear line flares observed since launch. With the upcoming rise in solar activity and RHESSI's continued nominal performance we plan to study emissions from the tens of nuclear-line flares expected. Description: FAST: SELF-CONSISTENT INVESTIGATION OF POLAR IONOSPHERIC PRECIPITATION AND CONVECTION, AND EFFECTS ON THE THERMOSPHERE  It is proposed here to formulate an self-consistent empirical model of both particle precipitation and convection in the polar ionosphere, using observations from the FAST spacecraft. Simultaneous observations of the convection electric field and particle precipitation will enter the modeling process together, tagged by the same model control parameters. Thus the representations of convection and precipitation will be consistent with each other. The observations will be separated into bins spatially and by activity. The energy spectra of electrons and ions, ion species fraction, and electron acceleration frequency will then be calculated for each bin. Importantly, from the point of view of thermospheric impact, ionospheric convection will be realistically aligned with auroral conductivity enhancements. One version will be set in an MLAT-MLT spatial grid, the other will organize the observations latitudinally relative to auroral boundaries. The model will be controlled by Interplanetary Magnetic FieldJSolar Wind (IMFISW) parameters. Both versions will be integrated into the TIE-GCM in order to asses their impact on the Ionosphere-Thermosphere (IT) system. By incorporating precipitation and convection together self-consistently, the relationship between the two will be realistically portrayed, properly specifying this aspect of IT coupling to the magnetosphere and solar wind.

Description: INVESTIGATION OF RING CURRENT DYNAMICS THROUGH OBSERVATIONS AND SIMULATIONS OF ENERGETIC NEUTRAL ATOM EMISSIONS The ring current plays a pivotal role in the dynamics of the inner magnetosphere, magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling, and plasmaspheric interaction with hot plasmas. Oservations and simulations of energetic neutral atom (ENA) emissions have provided important progress in understanding the global dynamics of the ring current. Quantitative analysis requires inversion of the line-of-sight ENA emissions to 3D spatial distribution of energetic ions. Two unresolved features arise from ENA investigations: (1) the local time asymmetry of ENA intensity frequently showing higher values in the post-midnight sector in contrast to the general perceived notion of the partial ring current having highest intensity in the pre-midnight sector, and (2) simultaneous RNA observations from two vantage points showing an order of magnitude difference in intensity. These unsolved features constitute a stumbling block to utilize the global ENA emissions confidently for quantitative investigations of ring current dynamics. Objectives: We propose to resolve the two unsolved issues discussed above (local time asymmetry and intensity mismatch from two vantage points) by examining the ring current pressure and its anisotropy as well as magnetic field distortion from dipole values through a synergistic combination of data analyses and numerical modeling of ENA emissions. Methodology: (1) statistical and case studies of ring current pressure and its anisotropy using Cluster and CCEmeasurements, elucidating their dependence on local time, radial distance, and storm phase, (2)comparison of in-situ ring current ion (proton and oxygen) fluxes from Cluster with the corresponding inverted ion fluxes from IMAGE, directly evaluating the accuracy of the inversion procedure, and (3) numerical modeling of the line-of-sight ENA intensities from two vantage points as represented by IMAGE and Geotail using the Comprehensive Ring Current Model (CRCM) that includes realistic ionospheric conductivity based on IMAGEIFUV data. Importance: At the completion of the proposed program, the ring current pressure and its anisotropy will be better known, the inversion procedure of ENA images will be validated or caveats on the energetic ion intensity from the inversion will be ascertained, and the CRCM will be improved to examine ring current dynamics. Relevance to NASA: The proposed program is relevant to the NASA strategic objectives 3B: ;,Explore the Sun;,Earth system to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth, the solar system, and the space environmental conditions that will be experienced by human explorers, and demonstrate echnologies that can improve future operational systems.; The ring current is a vital component of space weather forecasting that has impacts on human explorers, assets in space, as well as operational systems on Earth for societal function. The results will help to better define scientific objectives of the planned NASA RBSP mission.

Description: TRACKING PLAGIOCLASE AND HIGH-CA PYROXENE AS INDICATORS OF THE PETROGENESIS OF ASTEROID 433 EROS Despite more than five years of study and by far the best characterization of any asteroid to date, the meteoritic analog and, more importantly, the geologic/petrogenetic history of 433 Eros remain unresolved. The major goal of this proposal is to further our knowledge of that geologic history by providing an essential tool to resolve the discrepancy between data sets. Specifically, we aim to define a method to extract the plagioclase and high-Ca pyroxene abundances of 433 Eros. These minerals are concentrated in early silicate partial melts and their enrichment or depletion relative to ordinary chondrites is a strong indicator of partial melting. This proposal centers on three main tasks: the preparation of an array of appropriate mineral powder mixtures, measurement and analysis of these spectra, and the application of these results to the interpretation of meteorite spectra and the spectra from the NEAR mission to asteroid 433 Eros.

Description: INFRARED STUDIES OF THE MATERIAL EXCAVATED BY THE DEEP IMPACT EXPERIMENT  We propose an in-depth analysis of the amount and composition of volatile and non-volatile material released by the Deep Impact Experiment. To do this, we will compare data obtained in-situ by the Deep Impact HRI and MRI instruments to complementary remote space-based (Hubble, Spitzer), and ground-based (Keck, Subaru, IRTF and KPNO) measurements. Our proposed program consists of: (1) Measuring absolute line intensities and applying molecular fluorescence models to the high-resolution Keck NIRSPEC data to assess the volatile gas-phase contribution to the excess HRI-IR emissions while quantifying the non-volatile contribution to the ejecta using the mid-IR Spitzer composition model propagated to the 1-5 um HRI-IR passband. (2) Understanding the amount, kind, and spatial distribution of the dust ejected by DI by using remote imaging of the ejecta over 10 days, in comparison with the short time scale but high resolution in situ DI imagery, to create a 3-dimensional dynamical model of the dust ejection and outflow. (3) Performing laboratory infrared studies of mineral groups seen in the mid-IR Spitzer spectrum to help verify and refine those identifications and to determine the contribution of these species at shorter wavelengths covered by HRI-IR. In so doing, we will extract the maximal amount of information from the Deep Impact dataset on the gas and dust composition of the excavated material, allowing us to explore the relationship between Tempe1 1 and other comets, as well as the processes important for the formation of the comet from the proto-solar nebula and the subsequent effects of cometary evolution.

Description: We propose to analyze archival Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE) data of central stars of planetary nebulae (CSPN) as an extension of our several FUSE programs dedicated to studying CSPN in environments of differing metallicities. In our FUSE programs we have attained FUSE spectra of Galactic and Megallanic Cloud (MC) CSPN and modeled them in conjunction with archival UV spectra to determine the stellar and wind parameters using stellar atmospheres codes. From this, we have gained much insight into the evolution and structure of planetary nebulae systems. One goal of this work is to study the influence of metallicity on the evolution of lowfintermediate mass stars. During post-asymptotic giant branch (AGB) evolution, metallicity is believed to affect a star's evolution mainly through the stellar wind, due to a more efficient transfer of radiation to wind momentum with increasing opacity. This affects the mass-loss rate, and hence, how quickly the star evolves. Although the majority of stars from our MC sample have winds, few from our Galactic sample do, hindering our ability to assess the influence of metallicity on the winds of CSPN. Here we propose to perform a similar analysis on archival spectra of Galactic CSPN with winds observed with FUSE not part of our original programs, for which detailed stellar atmosphere models have not been developed and high-resolution IUE data exist. This additional analysis will significantly expand our original Galactic sample and allow for a direct comparison with our MC sample, from which the influence of metallicity on wind parameters and post-AGB evolution will be determined. This work will facilitate the understanding of CSPN evolution and their influence on the evolution of their host galaxies, which directly applies toward NASA's objective to "Discover the origin, structure, evolution, and destiny of the universe".

Description: SUPERDARN OBSERVATIONS IN SUPPORT OF TIMED/CEDAR The Super Dual Auroral Radar Network (SuperDARNl is one of the original ground-based experiments selected to support the NASA TIMED mission. SuperDARN is an international network of HF radars that provides continuous measurements of high-latitude electric fields 29d plasma convection on a global scale. Measurements of ionospheric electric fields are crucial to providing a full accounting for the energy budget or'&e lower thermosphere. Unfortunately, the TIMED spacecraft does not include instrumentation for this purpose. The SuperDARN radars provide grlrounci-based measrrremeiiis that can be used to fulfill this i~riporiansi cience need. This research will use SuperDARN data in conjunction with TIMED GUVI to measure high-latitude Joule heating; TIMED GUVI column O m ratios calculated from dayglow measurements will then be examined to see if there is any response in the lower thermosphere. In addition, the SuperDARN radars provide the TIMEDICEDAR community measurements of meteor winds near the mesopause through the use of the meteor scatter technique. These data will be used in conjunction with TIMED SABER to study the longitudinal structure of planetary waves. The SuperDARN mesospheric wind measurements provide instantaneous distributed longitudinal information about the atmospheric state that is not available from the TIMED spacecraft. To maximize the potential for collaborative efforts between TIMEDICEDAR scientists the SuperDARN community has maintained separate databases of electric field and meteor wind measurements, which reside at the Johns Hopkins University and the British Antarctic Survey, respectively. We propose to continue maintaining these databases in support of TIMEDICEDAR science and proceed with our investigations of planetary waves and the thermospheric impacts of high latitude auroral heating. We have also added an exciting new mid-latitude component to the northern hemisphere SuperDARN network that enables us to study electric fields at middle latitudes during major geomagnetic storms. We propose to use this new capability to support TIMED investigations of the effects of geomagnetic storms on the ionosphere and upper atmosphere. The activities outlined in this ~roposalw ill enhance TMED science by providing data products that are complementary to & instruments on the spacecraft. In particular, the correlative analysis of GUVI and SuperDARN data will significantly enhance the science return from CWI because SuperD provides the additional measurements of ionospheric electric field that allow a complete characterizztion of the energy input to the thermosphere in the form of Joule heating. This proposal is also aligned with the NASA Sun-Earth Connection science objectives because it is focused on obtaining an hproved quantitative understanding of variability in the flow of energy between the components of the coupled magnetosphereionosphere- e-themosphere system.
