Description: SBIR PHASE II AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED:  THERMAL CONTROL FOR INSTRUMENTS - MINIATURE LOOP HEAT PIPE (LHP) WITH MULTIPLE EVAPORATORS AND MULTIPLE CONDENSERS.  LHP IS A HIGH-PERFORMANCE HEAT TRANSPORTATION DEVICE USING CAPILLARY FORCES TO CIRCULATE THE WORKING FLUID IN A CLOSED LOOP.  CONVENTIONAL LHP'S USUALLY HAVE ONE CAPILLARY PUMP (EVAPORATOR) TO ACQUIRE WASTE HEAT FROM A HEAT SOURCE.  RECENT EFFORTS HAVE FOCUSED THE DEVELOPMENT OF LHP'S THAT CONTAIN TWO OR MORE EVAPORATORS.  EVEN THOUGH TWO- EVAPORATOR LHP'S PERFORMED VERY WELL, THE VOLUME OF EACH COMPENSATION CHAMBER (CC) BECAME MUCH LARGER THAN THAT OF THE SINGLE-EVAPORATOR COUNTERPART.  THE REASON WAS THAT ALL BUT ONE CC WOULD BE LIQUID-FILLED DURING NORMAL OPERATION.  THE ONE THAT WAS NOT LIQUID-FILLED HAD TO LARGE ENOUGH TO ACCOMMODATE THE SYSTEM LIQUID EXPANSION AT MAXIMUM TEMPERATURE.  AS A RESULT, LHP'S WITH MORE THAN 3 EVAPORATORS WERE NOT FEASIBLE FOR PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS SIMPLY BECAUSE THE CC'S BECAME PROHIBITIVELY LARGE.  IN THE CURRENT RESEARCH, THE CC'S OF A MULTIPLE-EVAPORATOR LHP WERE CAPILLARY-LINKED.  IN OTHER WORDS, THE CC'S ALWAYS CONTAINED A MIXTURE OF LIQUID AND VAPOR (TWO- PHASE), ALLOWING THE LOOP TO OPERATE WITH A MUCH SMALLER FLUID CHARGE.  CONSEQUENTLY, THE REQUIRED CC VOLUME WAS ALSO REDUCED.

Description: As the world's leading space science and exploration institution, NASA has a unique capacity to capture the attention and imagination of the nation's youth. Recognizing this capacity, NASA views the mandate to inspire and educate the next generation of explorers as one of its key missions. The main goal of this proposal is to support and enhance the effectiveness of NASA's education mission. This effort will be focused around three central objectives: First, using the latest insights from science education research to inform existing education programs at NASA and to institute new ones. In recent years, the science education research community has uncovered critical weaknesses in traditional modes of science instruction and has developed innovative methods that are more effective. However, there continues to be a gap between science education research and the scientific community delivering educational content, with NASA being no exception. We propose to apply the expertise of the Physics Education Research group at the University of Maryland, which has been a leader in the field, to bridge this gap. The second objective is to assess the role of women in science at NASA and to identify concrete measures to correct the under-representation of women in science at NASA. The status of women in academia has been studied in depth by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and science societies. But to date, a thorough study of women scientists at federal laboratories is lacking. The final objective is twofold: first, to build enduring relationships with secondary and post-secondary institutions to enhance diversity in NASA Goddard's education programs; and secondly, to build productive partnerships with other federal agencies such as NSF.

Description: In the current grant cycle we upgraded the code HYDROTHERM so that it is suitable for modeling impact-generated hydrothermal systems. HYDROTHERMAL is a finite difference code from the United States Geological Survey that simulates multiphase fluid flow and heat transport in systems from 0 to 1200 A0 c. We modified the code for the geometry and topography of impact craters, the higher temperatures that may be associated with impact melt sheets, and the permeability of impact-fractured crust. We tested the modified code by modeling the Sudbury impact crater on Earth, which has known geologic constraints. Following that successful test, we applied the code to three generic impact craters produced on early Mars, with diameters of 30,100, and 180 km, and further tested the effects of crustal permeability, presence or absence of crater lakes, and the relative cooling times of purely conductive cooling sytems and more complex convective cooling systems. We propose to continue this investigation by using HYDROTHERM to calculate the thermal evolution of additional (primarily larger) craters on Mars, integrate the effects of these hydrothermal systems on , early Mars when the impact rate was higher than it is today, evaluate the thermal evolution of younger craters during periods of dryer and colder ambient conditions, model specific impact craters that are potential landing sites for future spacecraft missions, and begin to explore the chemical and mineralogical consequences of the hydrothermal activity. Products of the investigation will include the thermal lifetimes of hydrothermal systems, the subsurface evolution of those systems and likely locations of surficial vent deposits, the volume of hydrothermally-heated water, volume suitable for thermophillic and hyperthermophillic life, and predictions about the mineral assemblages associated with these systems. The goals of this project are central to NASA's goal for understanding liquid water environments on Mars, potential sites of biologic activity, and the signatures of those environments that might be measured by spacecraft instrumentation.

Description: The Earth Sciences Directorate of the NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center and the College of Computer, Mathematical, and Physical Sciences, University of Maryland at College Park, share common research goals in the areas of meteorology, oceanography, terrestrial physics, climate research, chemistry of the earth's atmosphere, and satellite research. A cooperative agreement was signed by both parties in 1993 to establish a Joint Center for Earth System Science that serves as a center for multi-disciplinary research in Earth System Science. In 1999 the Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center (ESSIC) by a cooperative agreement that superseded the original. ESSIC serves as a means to increase the effectiveness of research and teaching through close collaboration by both parties, and serve as a means to train personnel for research in Earth System Science. This proposal requests funding to enable the UMCP and GSFC researchers to conduct new research through the collaborative research program within the ESSIC frame of reference for the next four years. The scientific objectives of this proposal encompass four major research areas: climate variability and change; atmospheric composition and processes; the global carbon cycle (including terrestrial and marine ecosystems/land use/cover change), and the global water cycle. Research is conducted through in situ and remotely sensed observations, together with component and coupled ocean-atmosphere-land modeling. This multi-pronged approach provides a foundation for understanding and forecasting changes in the global environment and regional implications. Data assimilation and regional downscaling are used to link the observations and models, enabling us to study the interactions between the physical climate system and biogeochemical cycles from global to regional scales.

Description: AURORA CURRENT AND ELECTRODYNAMIC STRUCTURE SOUNDING ROCKET EXPERIMENT MAGNETOMETERS: ACES-MAG SUMMARY: The primary objective of the Aurora Current and Electrodynamic Structure (ACES) dual sounding rocket experiment is the determination of the intensity and structure of electric currents associated with auroral arcs. By flying two rockets, ACES-High at 400 km maximum altitude and ACES-Low at 120 km maximum altitude through the same arc simultaneously the experiment will provide the observations necessary to characterize the structure of electric fields and currents in auroral arcs. To determine the structure of the currents, ACES includes a high performance magnetometer (MAG) on each payload. This proposal is for the magnetometer instrumentation and science support to the ACES sounding rocket proposal (proposal number N6-LCAS06-0006). The ACES-MAG instruments consist of two identical high performance tri-axial fluxgate magnetometers, one on ACES-High and one on ACES-Low. Description: DYNAMICS OF PLANET-DISK INTERACTIONS  WE PROPOSE TO INVESTIGATE SOME THEORETICAL ISSUES CONCERNING PLANET MIGRATION AND ECCENTRICITY EVOLUTION THROUGH PLANET-DISK INTERACTIONS. THE ISSUES INVOLVE POSSIBLE FAST PLANET MIGRATION, THE EFFECTS OF OOROTATIONAL RESONANCES ON MIGRATION, MIGRATION IN DECRETION DISKS, THE EFFECTS OF ORBITAL ECCENTRICITY ON MIGRATION, AND THE EVOLUTION OF PLANET ECCENTRICITY. THE INVESTIGATIONS UTILIZE NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS AND ANALYTIC MODELING WHICH LARGELY BUILD ON OUR RECENT RESULTS SUPPORTED BY THIS PROGRAM. THE PROPOSED STUDIES WILL PROVIDE AN INCREASED UNDERSTANDING OF THE EVOLUTION AND OBSERVED PROPERTIES OF PLANETARY SYSTEMS. THE PROJECTS ARE ENUMERATED BELOW. 1) OUR RECENT MIGRATION SIMULATIONS OF A SATURN MASS PLANET EMBEDDED IN A RELAXED DISK (DISK WHOSE GAP IS CLEARED TO A STEADY STATE GAP BEFORE PLANET RELEASE) DID NOT REVEAL FAST MIGRATION. WE PROPOSE TO EXTEND THESE CALCULATIONS BY INCLUDING THE EFFECTS OF MASS ACCRETION ON THE PLANET MASS, STARTING WITH A SMALL MASS PLANET. WE WILL DETERMINE WHETHER FAST MIGRATION SETS IN DURING THE EVOLUTION. 2) OUR RECENT MIGRATION SIMULATIONS OF A SATURN MASS PLANET EMBEDDED IN AN UN RELAXED DISK (DISK WHOSE GAP IS NOT CLEARED TO A STEADY STATE GAP BEFORE PLANET RELEASE) DID SOMETIMES REVEAL FAST MIGRATION. WE WILL EXPLORE THE NATURE OF THE DISK FLOW AND DETERMINE THE ORIGIN OF THE STRONG TORQUE ON THE PLANET. 3) WE RECENTLY DEVELOPED AN ANALYTIC THEORY OF NONCOORBITAL COROTATIONAL RESONANCES FOR A MOVING PLANET. WE PROPOSE TO TEST OUR THEORY BY MEANS OF NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS AND EXAMINE REGIMES THAT ARE NOT TREATED BY THE THEORY. 4) WE RECENTLY DEVELOPED AN ANALYTIC MODEL OF THE COORBITAL REGION FOR A MOVING PLANET. WE WILL TEST THE MODEL AND DETERMINE BY MEANS OF NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS WHETHER IT DESCRIBES FAST MIGRATION. 5) WE HAVE BEGUN SIMULATING PLANET MIGRATION IN DECRETION DISKS WHICH CAN CAUSE OUTWARD MIGRATION. WE PROPOSE TO EXPLORE THE SITUATIONS IN WHICH OUTWARD MIGRATION OF A PLANET CAN OCCUR WHERE A CENTRAL TORQUE IS PROVIDED BY A BINARY STAR SYSTEM OR A STAR-INNER PLANET SYSTEM. 6) OUR RECENT SIMULATIONS SHOW THAT THE RATE OF PLANET MIGRATION IS SENSITIVE TO ITS ORBITAL ECCENTRICITY AND CAN REVERSE (BE DIRECTED OUTWARD) IF THE ECCENTRICITY IS GREATER THAN A FEW TENTHS. WE AIM TO DETERMINE THE NATURE OF THE TORQUE BY NUMERICAL AND ANALYTIC MEANS. 7) OUR RECENT SIMULATIONS SHOW THAT PLANETS OF A JUPITER MASS AND GREATER CAN ACQUIRE AN ECCENTRICITY OF ABOUT 0.1 IN A FEW THOUSAND ORBITS, AS A RESULT OF DISK INTERACTIONS. WE WILL EXPLORE PARAMETER SPACE MORE BROADLY AND DETERMINE WHETHER ECCENTRICITIES AS LARGE AS 0.4 (FREQUENTLY FOUND BSERVATIONALLY) CAN OCCUR IN LONGER SIMULATIONS.

Description: NASA-LEND-SPS SCHOLARS PROGRAM The Society of Physics (SPS), a member organization of the American Institute of Physics (AIP), proposes a 2.5-year collaboration between physics departments, SPS, NASA Minority University-SPace Interdisciplinary Network (MU-SPIN), and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center's Solar System Exploration Division, for students and faculty. The collaboration is a facet of the Education and Public Outreach (EPO) efforts associated with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Mission and the Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND) experiment. The program provides a set of internships for students and fellowships for faculty, sustained over the timeline of the LEND project, with the goal of producing active research groups in the field of space science at the selected campuses. Undergraduates (to be known as NASA/LEND Scholars) at participating institutions will engage in summer internships at GSFC for the duration of the LEND project (2006-09), while their faculty mentors (to be known as LEND Fellows) will visit GSFC for several weeks to famiUarize them with the project and data. One institution selected to participate will also be part of MU-SPIN's Network Resource and Training Site program (NRTS). The students and faculty will work directly with NASA scientists active in the LEND project in the summer, and continue the project when the summer is over. The program is sustained during the academic year by a variety of mechanisms which may include: funding for student research stipends, a new course (or courses) or seminar series in tmdergraduate research developed by the faculty mentor, and travel to appropriate conferences and launch events by student and faculty. As the faculty member gains familiarity and expertise with the science of the mission, she/he then will take on a larger role in the mentorship process, which is another critical ingredient to sustaining the benefits of the program beyond a mere summer internship. The intent is to involve the LEND scholars in the research endeavor until they graduate, and to engage the institution, the SPS chapter and the LEND Fellows in the research process until the mission is completed in 2009.

Description: A HIGH-TEMPORAL RESOLUTION SUPRATHERMAL ION SPECTROMETER CONCEPT FOR FUTURE HELIOSPHERIC (STISH) MISSIONS Recent studies have revealed the importance of low-energy suprathermal particles (~lOs of keV/q) in the heliosphere. They are found to contribute significantly as seed particles accelerated either close to the Sun during a solar energetic particle event, or locally at 1 AU during an energetic storm particle event. Traditionally these particles are measured using energy-per-charge (E/Q) and time-of-flight by energy (TOFxE) techniques. However, a spherical E/Q analyzer has the inherent difficulty in duty cycle; hence, high time resolution measurements of the suprathermal particles have never been made. Together with Southwest Research Institute, we propose to develop a new suprathermal ion spectrograph that measures energetic ions from 3 to 150 keV/q. This proposal fulfills one of the S3C strategic objectives: by designing, building, and validating the next generation of S3C instrumentation.

Description: This work will model the supply of ions to the Hermean magnetosphere in response to the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field (IMF), including the transport and loss of magnetospheric ions. Of particular interest to this study will be six CME events detected by the Helios spacecraft within Mercury's orbital range. Previously published modeling runs have tested exploratory or extreme cases for the solar wind at Mercury and tell us nothing about how often these configurations occur. We reanalyzed Helios particle and field data for Mercury's heliocentric distances and computed kernel density estimates (probability of specific solar wind and IMF configurations). Using these proper boundary conditions for Mercury's magnetosphere and providing associated probabilities, we will compute the long-term temporal and spatial variability of the solar wind ion flux that precipitates into Mercury's magnetosphere (aphelion to perihelion) in a systematic way. Likewise, we will simulate the transport and loss of magnetospheric ions that are likely present in Mercury's weak ionosphere (Na+, K+, O+) for various solar wind and IMF conditions. While CME transport is expected to be briefer through Mercury that through the Earth's neighborhood, at least one detected event lasted 32 hours. We will use statistical pattern recognition techniques (clustering, dendrograms) to classify these events; then we will run them through magnetosphere models. In this way we will predict the variability of the precipitating ion flux both due to the ambient solar wind and during specific CME events. Among planetary magnetospheres, Mercury's is a special case not only because it is subjected to the strongest gradients of density, velocity and field magnitude between aphelion and perihelion, but also because its small size and short ion residence times make analytical and global MHD modeling computationally feasible for a statistically significant sample of solar wind conditions. We are investigating the structure and dynamics of a weak magnetosphere in a strong solar wind environment. This work is relevant to the Messenger mission both for predicting likely conditions the spacecraft will encounter during the three flybys (all close to perihelion) and the magnetospheric response to these conditions.

Description: Cassini data have confirmed the presence of a distribution of neutral gas surrounding Saturn and have put constraints on its size and density. Unlike other magnetospheres, such as Jupiter's, the neutral to plasma densities at Saturn have been found to be very high. This means the flow of momentum and energy through the system is unique. For example, the presence of a dense gas cloud limits the intensity of the ion radiation belts. This in turn protects the icy surfaces of the inner satellites and rings from some weathering processes. In this project, we plan to make more quantitative what the consequences of this cloud are on energetic charged particle radiation. To do this, we will analyze and integrate data from the three sensors of the Cassini Magnetospheric Imaging Instrument (MIMI). Taken together, these sensors measure charged particles from a few keV to many MeV and neutrals from a few to hundreds of keV. Since energetic charged particles are believed to be transported inward, it is interesting to consider which particles penetrate the cloud. There is evidence in the published MIMI data that energetic electrons coexist with the gas cloud. Very energetic electrons begin to increase in intensity inward of Enceladus. Ions in the keV range are heavily lost at the periphery of the cloud between approximately 6 and 8 Saturn radii, but at some energies, ion fluxes return inward of Enceladus's orbit. The high ion losses near the cloud edge and its variations during the early Cassini orbits will be quantified to estimate the energetic neutral atom source strength and to infer the gas density there. Furthermore, we will investigate the source of the inner population of ions considering competing mechanisms. And lastly, we will calculate the energy input to the neutral material to study surface processes.

Description: UNDERSTANDING TITAL'S GLOBAL GEOLOGY FROM CO-ANALYSIS OF CASSINI ISS, VIMS AND RADAR DATA The Cassini spacecraft has had several close encounters with Saturn's satellite Titan and has returned a wealth of data about its surface. Cassini's Imaging Science Subsystem (ISS), RADAR, and Visual and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIMS) have revealed an intriguing surface that is at once familiar and alien. Although water-ice and liquid hydrocarbons play the roles that rock and water play on Earth, the surface appears to have been worked by a wide variety of processes resulting in a seemingly Earth-like balance of fluvial, aeolian, and volcanic features, with relatively few impact craters (e.g., Porco et al., 2005; Elachi et al., 2005; Sotln et al., 2005; Barnes et al., 2005). There seem to be at least two classes of surface material: dark areas (at visible-Iff wavelengths) that are spectrally consistent with contaminated water ice, and brighter areas of unknown composition that show greater variations. The expected bodies of liquids have yet to be definitively identified; however, circumstantial evidence for liquids having acted upon the surface in Titan's past is abundant, primarily in the form of channels, and possible ponds or lakes, which have been observed by multiple instruments.  Other features suggest that wind redistributes some surface materials, most likely the detritus of the complex atmospheric chemistry, creating diffuse IR-bright deposits and long, narrow, radar-dark (2.2-cm) stripes, all of which trend generally east-west. Only two impact structures have been identified to date, although several other suspiciously circular features have been documented. A number of the morphologies observed bear strong resemblances to volcanic structures. Other features still remain mysterious. Careful co-analysis of these data sets is needed to fully understand the nature of Titan's surface, the albedo variations observed at different wavelengths, and the processes that have acted upon it (and may continue to). We propose to analyze observations of Titan's surface acquired by the complementary suite of instruments on board Cassini-Huygens, the combination of which is proving essential to interpreting Titan's geology. Specifically, we plan to coregister ISS, VIMS, and RADAR data available via the Planetary Data System (PDS). We will then map the surface features and use correlations between the data sets documented in places where they overlap to extrapolate to the global view. In this way we will work toward an understanding of Titan's geology at both the global and local scales.  We plan to make the data products we create available to the community via the PDS.

Description: INVESTIGATING CO2 IN THE SURFACES OF THE ICY SATURNIAN AND OUTER GALILEAN SATELLITES Better understanding the compositions of the surfaces of the icy Saturnian satellites, the outer Galilean satellites, and the processes which occur there will help us determine how the satellites have evolved to their current states and to better understand the reasons behind their similarities and differences. Carbon dioxide is a significant component in the surfaces of these objects and has been detected by infrared mapping spectrometers on the Cassini and Galileo spacecraft. It is the next most abundant volatile to water in the surfaces of the outer two Galilean satellites: Ganymede and Callisto, and exists at similar abundances on the Saturnian satellites Iapetus, and Phoebe. It has also been identified in the surfaces of Hyperion and Enceladus. We propose to analyze the Cassini spacecraft Visual and Infrared Mapping Spectrometer (VIMS) and the Imaging SubSystem (ISS) data more precisely and in more detail than has so far been done. We will combine results from the analyses of both datasets to leverage each instrument's strengths for investigating C02 on these surfaces. Our improved analyses will enable us to precisely characterize the spectral nature of the C02 for both the Saturnian and Jovian satellites and to map abundance distributions on the Saturnian satellites. We will relate the results of our analysis to previous results obtained for C02 on the Galilean satellites from our similar prior analyses of data from Galileos Near Infrared Mapping Spectrometer and to results from our and others attempts to simulate various forms of bound C02 in the laboratory. The goal of this research is to identify origin(s), physical states, host materials (if any), and to identify any commonality between the C02 in Saturnian and Jovian systems. Specific questions we will address include: 1) What are the precise spectral characteristic(s) of the C02 on the icy Saturnian and Galilean satellites? 2) What is the pixel-by-pixel distribution of C02 abundance and its physical state on the icy Saturnian satellites? 3) Are there variations in C02 abundance or absorption band shape that are related to surface geology on the icy Saturnian satellites and are these patterns similar or different from what has been reported for the Galilean satellites? 4) Are there longitudinal variations in either spectral structure of abundance on the Saturnian satellites? 5) Are there variations related to local time of day? 6) What is the host material(s), or is the C02 segregated? Description: PERIODICITIES IN SATURN'S MAGNETOSPHERE The Saturnian magnetosphere exhibits periodicities in radio emissions, total magnetic field strength, and energetic charged and neutral particle fluxes. Periodicities in these phenomena all occur at nearly the 10 hour 46 minute period thought to be associated with the rotation of the "core" of the planet. However, the close alignment of the magnetic and spin axes of Saturn makes the source of such periodicities highly problematic, since little azimuth asymmetry such as "tilt" exists. Subtle variations in the period have appeared over the years between encounters of several spacecraft with the planet, which is inconsistent with periodicity locked to the angular momentum of the planet. We propose a systematic investigation combining the results from several data sets observing the periodicities by using data from charged and neutral particles, radio emissions, and magnetic fields. The investigation focuses on three central questions: 1. What are the periodicities of the Saturnian magnetosphere observed in each of these datasets? We use several analysis techniques to determine Characteristics ofthe periodic signals. 2. How do the periodicities compare in duration, phase, strength, and location? We explore physical relationships between observed characteristics by bringing together experience from outer planets and terrestrial magnetospheric research. 3. Which models are compatible with the observed periodicities? We critically assess current hypotheses and models by testing against the observed characteristics and physical relationships. The investigation Involves several Cassini datasets including two Magnetospheric Imaging Instrument (MIMI) sensors: the Low Energy Magnetospheric Measurement System (LEMMS) and the Ion Neutral Camera (INCA); the magnetometer instrument (MAG), the Radio and Plasma Wave Science (RPWS) instrument, and the Cassini Plasma Spectrometer (CAPS). Data from these instruments is publicly available through the Planetary Data System (PDS). We believe our history of Energetic Neutral Atom (ENA) data analysis of the terrestrial magnetosphere enhances the scientific participation in the Cassini data analysis, a key objective of this program as stated in the announcement of opportunity. The proposed research is relevant to both the Cassini Data Analysis Program (CDAP) and to NASA's long-term strategic goals. In accordance with CDAP, the proposed research "enhances the scientific return of the Cassini mission by broadening the scientific participation in analysis and interpretation of the data returned by the mission" (NASA, 2006). The research clearly addresses the NASA strategic goals "to develop a balanced overall program of science, exploration" (SG-3) and "to progress in understanding fundamental physical processes of the space environment from the Sun to other planets" (SG3.2). The Solar System Exploration Roadmap (NASA, 2003) further amplifies these themes and adds the objective of "learning what our solar system can tell us about extrasolar planets [by studying] in detail the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn..."

Description: Multi-Satellite Observations of Flux Transfer Events FTE durations and inter-arrival times provide important information concerning the generation mechanism and dynamics of reconnection on the magnetopause. We will survey the characteristics multiple FTEs observed in three data sets. First, we will examine Interball-1 observations during the period from 1995 to 1999. Interball-1 observations allow us to study quasi-periodic FTEs at higher dayside latitudes and greater downstream distances than those accessible to previous statistical surveys. We will compare the characteristics of FTEs in these locations to those previously reported on the dayside magnetopause. In particular, we will explore the relationship between the energy within individual FTEs and the accumulated free energy since the last event. We want to determine whether or not there are special conditions in the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field that favor the generation of multiple FTEs. Second, we will survey FTE data sets from Geotail. Geotail observations permit us to study ion and electron velocity distribution functions within FTEs, enabling determination of connectivity to the magnetopause through a survey of particle streaming. Finally, we will examine observations by NASA's forthcoming THEMIS mission (launch in February 2007). Observations from the five near-equatorial satellites in this mission can also be used to determine the dimensions of FTEs on the magnetopause.

Description: A Water and Energy Cycle EOS Clearing House Client Water has long been known to be essential to human activity. Both plants and animals upon which humans depend, require water to survive. The ability to monitor and to study the amount and location of water is critical for the management of earth's resources. To this end, metadata in NASA's EOS Clearing House (ECHO) is an essential information resource for connecting water users to the best available data. In response to the NASAROSES A.19 Advancing Collaborative Connections for Earth System Science (ACCESS) call to enhance and improve existing components of the data and information systems infrastructure supporting NASA's Earth science research communities, we propose to develop a new Water and Energy Cycle (WEC) EOS Clearing HOuse (ECHO) client (WECHO). The purpose of this client is to use ECHO middleware technology to provide access to and discovery of data resources related to the NASA Global Water and Energy Cycle Focus Area (one of 6 such NASA research focus areas). Science and technology professionals will be able to access NASA data and services via a web-based tool tightly integrated with ECHO Application Program Interfaces (APIs) to combine and then display via the client web browser data sets and subsets within the realm of ECHOs'holdings. Our objective is to establish practical applications that benefit the research of the community of known science users and extend those benefits to society at-large. Interfacing with the ECHO API, the users of this new ACCESS client will be able to browse NASA's water and energy cycle related holdings and then display characteristics of the data set(s). This new portal will incorporate statistical and quantitative graphical displays allowing the user to apply educated human insight and analysis in the formulation of new hypothesis and the validation of current theories. The portal will be based upon industry standards for performing web-based computing. The proposed portal will also offer some command-line based functionality for use in automating general tasks.

Description: STUDY OF THE EFFECTS OF DUST RADIATIVE AND MICROPHYSICAL PROPERTIES ON PRECIPITATION AND ENERGY BUDGET USING A-TRAIN SATELLITE MEASUREMENTS AND CLOUD-RESOLVING MODEL Active summertime easterly waves over northern Africa and Atlantic Ocean are clearly seen from satellite images. Tropical depressions, subsequently developing into tropical storms and hurricanes, are frequently formed as a result of wave breaking and cyclogenesis. Under the prevailing easterlies, dust outbreaks from the Sahara Desert have been a strong seasonal phenomenon, coinciding with hurricane developing region of the northern Atlantic Ocean. Several studies revealed that enhanced convection is shown along the Saharan air layer (SAL) western and southern boundaries but prohibited in its interior due to the combination of dry stable air and strong easterly wind shear. Tropical cyclone Erin in 2001 was shown to be a case that rapidly developed into a strong hurricane when emerging from the SAL influence (Dunion and Velden, 2004). Most model studies, however, are focused on storm intensity change with simplified aerosol parameterization schemes without feedback, or simply without considering impacts due to aerosols. Thus, the effects of dust microphysical properties and radiative properties on cloud formation (or suppression) and precipitation, especially their effects on easterly wave structure and intensification, are not well understood. This study is focused on the year-2 and -3 data analysis of NAMMA-06. In this research, we will use MM5 and NASA GMAO GEOS assimilated meteorological data, as well as those from field campaign airborne (e.g., NASA DC-8), shipborne (e.g., NOAA R/V Ronald Brown) and surface-based atmospheric profile measurements (e.g., radiosonde), as inputs to the 2-D Goddard Cumulus Ensemble (GCE) model. Dust layer height estimated from MODIS and AIRS dust retrievals could shed some light on the vertical extent of the SAL in entire satellite swaths, in addition to MODIS-derived dust loading and effective radius (size). The OMI aerosol index, less subject to clouds, would be useful to define the horizontal boundary of the SAL. MODIS and AIRS onboard the Aqua satellite and OMI onboard Aura are parts of the NASA A-Train constellation with overpass times less than 10 minutes apart, which minimizes temporal inconsistency of the measurements. The spatial swaths of these three sensors are also wide enough to provide a daily global coverage. Thus, with all these satellite and field data, the GCE model with bin microphysical scheme should be able to simulate the evolution of clouds, precipitation, and energy budgets under the ambient dusty condition. As demonstrated in previous field campaign, GCE model derived precipitation will be compared with TRMM rainfall retrievals for validation. The NASA DC-8 onboard instruments would provide quasi-Lagrangian measurements, which enables comparison with model simulations. In addition, the DC-8 in-situ measurements, if available, could also shed some light on the microphysical properties (e.g., size and hygroscopicity) of the elevated dust layer and provide validation/verification to satellite-derived products. We expect the results of this proposal can significantly improve our understanding of dust effects on precipitation and energy budget in both the near source and downwind regions.

Description: We propose to perform a novel field study of terrestrial dust devils in Arizona using initially an array, evolving into an intelligent network, of smart sensor platforms. Dust devils are a dynamic feature of the Martian environment, playing an important part in climate via dust loading, and can significantly affect surface operations by sweeping dust off solar panels as well as possible electrostatic discharge effects. Even on Earth, dust devils are implicated in ~100 light aviation accidents in the last 15 years and thus can be considered a genuine hazard. A systematic study, which without the application of intelligent systems would be a labor-intensive effort, is therefore suggested. An array of rapid-sampling sensor platforms can generate datasets on the formation, structure and evolution of dust devils that can be compared with mesoscale numerical models. After initial data acquisition, algorithms will be developed by which the field network can autonomously identify the presence of dust devils and generate reports. Intelligent sensing yields orders of magnitude reduction in data volume.

Description: THIN CURRENT SHEETS AND MAGNETIC RECONNECTION: MULTISCALE PROCESSES AND CROSS - SCALE COUPLING Thin current sheets are essentially kinetic structures with thicknesses as small as the ion gyro radius, and during magnetic reconnection the physical processes have scale sizes ranging from the electron gyro radius to a few earth radii. These processes are in turn connected to the macroscale processes in the magnetosphere. Recent data from Cluster spacecraft have stimulated the study of many new features such as bifurcated sheets, transient and meso-scale processes and their interconnections. Four main approaches will be used to study the kinetic physics of thin current sheets and reconnection. The first is the Vlasov theory of equilibria which is based on the constants of motion. The second is the forced current sheets based on quasi-adiabatic orbits of the particles. The third is the kinetic simulations using PIC codes. The fourth is the generalized stability analysis which is capable of yielding eigenvalues for complicated orbits and geometries. These will be used to study the structures, their evolution and coupling to other phenomena. Comparison with multi-spacecraft data, e. g., Cluster and its conjunction with THEMIS, will be used to the refine the models, and prepare for the finer scale measurements by MMS mission.

Description: Combined RadarlRadiometer Estimates of Precipitation and Latent Heating Profiles for Training Spaceborne Passive Microwave Radiometer Algorithms Precipitation estimates from satellite passive microwave radiometry have proven useful in a variety of applications, including numerical weather prediction, atmospheric general circulation modeling, and climate analysis. Since the mid-1990's, the Goddard Profiling (GPROF) algorithm has been used successfully to provide estimates of surface rain rate based upon satellite microwave radiance data; it is currently the TRMM facility algorithm. As major contributors to GPROF, the Principal Investigator and his colleagues helped to improve the physical basis of the algorithm and exploited methods to characterize the error in algorithm estimates of precipitation and latent heating. The GPROF algorithm is currently supported by a set of cloud/radiative model simulations that establish the physical relationships between sensor-observed radiances and the precipitation/latent heating profiles that are estimated. Systematic errors in these modeled relationships, as well as other factors that make the relationships non-representative, have led to biases in GPROF estimates, particularly in precipitation vertical structure. As an alternative, the supporting data for passive microwave algorithms have recently been derived "empirically", based upon high-resolution spaceborne radar observations from the Precipitation Radar (PR) in combination with collocated microwave radiometer data from the TRMM Microwave Imager (TMI). In these studies, physical models of precipitation vertical profiles are fit to combined PRITMI observations, and the best-fit vertical profile models can then be used to simulate upwelling microwave radiances at any specified Frequencies/polarizations, thereby establishing the relationships between precipitation vertical profiles and upwelling radiances applicable to any satellite microwave radiometer. The investigators ofthis proposal recently developed a combined PRITMI method for estimating precipitation vertical profiles over ocean regions, calculated the upwelling microwave radiances associated with these profiles, and then incorporated the profiles/radiances in a TMI-only algorithm for estimating precipitation and latent heating. The new TMI-only method yielded precipitation estimates with less bias than the current GPROF algorithm; however, the combined PRITMI method did not make full use ofthe higher-frequency TMI data due to uncertainties in the modeling of ice- and mix ed-phase particles, and it was otherwise sub-optimal for calculating radiances at microwave frequencies other than those of the TMI. The objectives of the proposed study are, therefore, (1) to improve the physical description of ice- and mixed-phase precipitation in the vertical profile model of the combined method, evaluating the resulting model using available field campaign observations, (2) to generalize the combined method to estimate the environmental parameters needed to calculate radiances at other radiometer frequencies, and (3) to evaluate the resulting combined method using TMI data, alternative radiometer data, and ground validation radar observations. The proposed investigation will contribute to the development of combined radar/radiometer methods that will yield estimated profiles of precipitation over ocean surfaces with reduced bias. Using these profiles as supporting data for radiometer-only algorithms, the resulting algorithms should also yield precipitation profiles with less bias. The reduction of biases in precipitation/latent heating estimates is critical for numerical weather prediction model and general circulation model data assimilation applications, as well as for climate analysis applications. Description: JOHNS HOPKINS UNIVERSITY HI, DI AND OTHER ABUNDANCES ALONG THREE EXTENDED SIGHTLINES Measurements of the DIH and DIO ratios have been shown to be remarkably constant up to logN(H) -19.2, which corresponds roughly to the limits of the Local Bubble. Between 19.2 < 10gN(H) < 20.6, these ratios present a large scatter, while for logN(H) > 20.6 DIH and DIO seem to be constant again. albeit with values roughly half that of the Local Bubble. Although several mechanisms have been proposed to explain these variations, a global consistent picture of these abundance patterns is still missing. The low yield of high column density sightlines suitable for accurate DIH measurements has bun a major barrier to progress in this area. This derives from the extreme difficulty of finding suitable targets at these high column densities, both in terms of DI not being obscured by either HI or H2 absorption and having data available to determine reliable HI column densities from Lya. This proposal requests additional observing time to obtain signal-to-noise ratios adequate for determining the column densities of DI, NI, 01, and Fell, along three high N(H) sightlines that have been previously observed by FUSE. Preliminary analyses of the current datasets show that these sightlines are suitable for DI measurements. Existing high resolution HST/STIS data for the three sightlines will be used to determine N(Hl) along two of the sightlines (N(Hl) has been published for the other one) as well as to model the velocity structure along the sightlines.  These datasets will also allow us to determine the abundances of species that do not have unsaturated transitions in the FUSE bandpass (SI, Ni11, etc.). Description: COMPARISONS OF TRMM AND GPM PRODUCTS TO GROUND-BASED MEASUREMENTS: AN APPROACH TO IMPROVE THE VALIDATION OF SATELLITE PRECIPITATION PRODUCTS Validation of precipitation measurements and estimates from satellite active and passive sensors is essential for the success of the TRMM and GPM missions. One of the critical steps of validation is to accurately resample data from space-borne and ground-based instruments to a common grid. Because of differences in the scattering geometries of space-borne and ground-based observations, accurate registration of data is a challenging problem. This problem is further complicated if there are offsets in time among the measurements. As a result, one or more ofthe data sets may require translation, rotation, or scaling to ensure reliable comparisons among them. In our proposed study, we will establish data coordinate transformation system (DCTS) that would be used to accurately register the data acquired by multiple sensors from space- and ground-based platforms followed by instantaneous and statistical comparisons of the satellite products such as rain rate and radar reflectivity factor derived from TRMM TMI and PR (or GPM GMI and DPR) to the same products obtained from the ground-based observations. Comparisons of PR and DPR to ground radars (such as WSR-88D) provide a means to examine the radar calibrations and attenuation correction procedures adopted in the satellite radar algorithms. The microphysical properties of hydrometeors derived from the DPR can also be verified through the results obtained from the polarimetric ground-based radar systems. A strategy for an assessment of multiple scattering effects at the DPR Ka-band is also described. In addition, because the spatial (sample) resolution of the ground-based weather surveillance radar varies as a function of radar range (while the satellite radar yields nearly uniformly spatial sampling), uniform gridding over the overlap area of satellite and ground radar observations might lead to biases or ambiguities particularly because of variability of the precipitation in space.  These uncertainties will be estimated by means of radar simulations using cloud resolving models (CRM), TRMM PR data sets and ground-based radar measurements. To improve the degree of agreement between the PR and ground-based radar, non-uniform gridding, where the grid spacing at a particular location depends on the inherent resolutions of the radars, will be considered.

Description: Multi-Satellite Observations of Flux Transfer Events FTE durations and inter-arrival times provide important information concerning the generation mechanism and dynamics of reconnection on the magnetopause. We will survey the characteristics multiple FTEs observed in three data sets. First, we will examine Interball-1 observations during the period from 1995 to 1999. Interball-1 observations allow us to study quasi-periodic FTEs at higher dayside latitudes and greater downstream distances than those accessible to previous statistical surveys. We will compare the characteristics of FTEs in these locations to those previously reported on the dayside magnetopause. In particular, we will explore the relationship between the energy within individual FTEs and the accumulated free energy since the last event. We want to determine whether or not there are special conditions in the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field that favor the generation of multiple FTEs. Second, we will survey FTE data sets from Geotail. Geotail observations permit us to study ion and electron velocity distribution functions within FTEs, enabling determination of connectivity to the magnetopause through a survey of particle streaming. Finally, we will examine observations by NASA's forthcoming THEMIS mission (launch in February 2007). Observations from the five near-equatorial satellites in this mission can also be used to determine the dimensions of FTEs on the magnetopause.

Description: We propose FUSE observations of a sample of hot subdwarf B stars (sdB) in order to carry out an abundance analysis of heavy elements and see how their abundance patterns emerge from the observations. It is a well known fact that the atmospheres of these extreme horizontal branch stars exhibit abundance anomalies. Diffusion processes such as gravitational settling, radiative levitation, weak stellar winds, and accretion have been proposed to explain the abundance anomalies. Our goal is to identify which mechanisms operate in the atmospheres of these stars, study their interactions, understand the abundance patterns, and ultimately, constrain the structure of the atmospheres of sdB stars. With this proposal we want to pursue the goal of our FUSE proposal El52 by doubling the number of stars in our sample. To study and interpret the abundance patterns in sdB stars, we need a large sample of stars with atmospheric parameters that cover the whole effective temperature and gravity domains for this type of stars (20,000 K < Teff < 40,000 K ; 5.0 < log g < 6.5). To achieve a thoroughly abundance analysis we need FUSE observations, because many resonance lines of elements such as phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, and many iron peak elements are only visible in the FUV range for the effective temperatures of interest. This study will not only provide new insights to the stellar atmosphere structure of sdB stars, but also to the evolution of galaxies since these stars are the most important candidates for the source of the UV excess in elliptical galaxies and early-type spiral bulges.

Description: UNDERSTANDING THE DIFFUSE X-RAY BACKGROUND: THE EXTRAGALATIC TO SOLAR SYSTEM ENVIRONMENT Soft X-ray emission exhibits substantially more structure on the sky than its higher energy counterpart. With the greater complexity also comes greater controversy concerning its source components. Until recently, the standard view held that the soft X-ray sky had three primary contributors, all farther than a parsec. Proceeding from the most distant, these are (1) the residual flux from the extragalatic power law, (2) a lumpy distribution of 106 K plasma in the lower halo of the Milky Way and (3) a 106 K plasma filling a cavity surrounding the Sun in the Galactic disk, the local bubble. However, recently another component originating within about 10-3 parsecs has been discovered, solar wind charge exchange emission from the heliospheric termination shock, the interplanetary medium, and the magnetosheath surrounding the Earth. This emission contributes significantly to the soft X-ray sky with a magnitude comparable at times to all the other components together. We will mine the X-ray data archive to quantify the extent to which solar wind charge exchange emission contributes to the diffuse X-ray emission. We will compare temporal and spatial variations of the observed diffuse emission in archived data from ROSAT, XMM-Newton, Chandra, ASCA and Beppo-SAX to predicted X-ray spatial and temporal intensity profiles using the Fahr and other models for the heliospheric neutral H and He distributions, Hodges' results along with more recent data for the distribution of exospheric hydrogen, and the Spreiter and MHD BATSRUS models for the near-Earth plasma. By varying the model input parameters for solar wind density, velocity, temperature and heavy ion composition along with interstellar hydrogen and helium and exospheric hydrogen densities to the degree allowed by observational constraints and incorporating soft X-ray efficiency factors that are a function of solar wind composition, we will obtain the best agreement possible between the modeled and observed light curves. We will provide this modeling capability to the X-ray community. Our research will answer the following science questions: (1) Is the local hot bubble dead? That is, can we account for all observed diffuse emission within a few hundred parsecs previously identified as local hot bubble with the solar wind charge exchange mechanism? (2) How can we predict the strength of the solar wind charge exchange using geometric information from the X-ray observatory, solar wind observations and simulations? The research will produce and optimized capability to model solar wind charge exchange emission for use in (a) analyzing data from past observations (b) planning upcoming observations to minimize potential contamination and (c) evaluating the potential loss of data due to solar wind charge exchange on future X-ray missions.

Description: CONSTRAINING ALBEDOS OF NEAR EARTH OBJECTS USING NEAR IRSPECTROSCOPY Determining the albedo of an object is the critical piece in turning a brightness into a size. Observations in the thermal infrared typically are performed in order to measure an asteroidi,s albedo. However, near-Earth objects (NEOs) are significantly warmer than main-belt objects, and exhibit measurable thermal flux at much shorter wavelengths. Over the past several years, this fact has been used on several objects, including by Abell et al. (2002) and Rivkin et al. (2004) to constrain their albedos. Rivl,in et al. Description: VITMO: A VXO FOR S3C DATA FOR THE IONOSPHERE MESOS PHERE THERMOSPHERE COMMUNITY The ionosphere, thermosphere, and mesosphere (ITM) community studies an area of the atmosphere that is a transition region between the atmosphere and space, where many important physical and chemical processes change dramatically temporally and spatially. As a result, the areas of studies within the ITM community span a wide spectrum of scientific subjects in geophysics and space physics. The relevant data for the community collected during the past few decades consequently come from a variety of sources including ground and space-based instruments as well as from modeling and data assimilation. As the different sub-fields mature, a system-oriented approach to understand the ITM as a whole and its relationship to the sun and the surrounding geospace environment is critical. This approach requires a data system with efficient access to all data sets (present and historical) relevant to disciplines across agencies, including NASA, NSF, NOAA and others. We present a Virtual ITM Observatory (VITMO) implementation for such a data system that leverages current resources. The design incorporates a modular framework that accepts distributed data and services from across the community and encourages widespread participation. Data can be added as both new missions and historical holdings become available, and services added or replaced as technologies and standards evolve. The core VITMO system is based upon a set of services: centralized browse and query/retrieval of distributed resources, access to data reader software and other tools, and integration of current data with data from previous missions and long-term data sets. The VITMO will specifically tie together data from TIMED, AIM, C/NOFS, SuperDARN, and services such as CDAWeb, SSCWeb, and ModelWeb. The VITMO will have vastly improved data search and location capabilities allowing multidisciplinary and multisatellite studies to be performed. The VITMO approach is easily extensible to future data sets and will be able to tie into other VxO as either a peer node or a service.

Description: Isotopic and Geochemical Investigation of Meteorites Established chemical purification techniques will be combined with high-precision thermal and inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry to pursue 4 major tasks: (i) Core Separation-Crystallization. Isotope dilution concentration measurements of the highly siderophile elements (HSE=Re, Os, Pt, Pd, Ir, Ru), and the long-lived 187Re-187Os and 190Pt-186Os isotope systems, will be used to study crystal-liquid fractionation processes and chemical closure ages of metal present in iron meteorites and pallasites. (ii) Abundances and Evolution of HSE in the Lunar and Martian Interiors. The 187Re-187Os system and HSE abundances of lunar basalts and SNC meteorites will be examined in order to constrain the Os isotopic evolution and relative abundances of the HSE in the lunar and Martian mantles. The ultimate objective of this work is to constrain the timing and proportions of lunar and Martian late accretion. (iii) 187Re-187Os and HSE Systematics of Chondrites. The 187Re-187Os isotopic system and HSE abundances of chondrite components will be applied to constrain the timing of HSE distribution in chondrites with particular emphasis placed on chondrite components. (iv) Search for Siting and Magnitude of Nucleosynthetic Anomalies in Meteorites. Osmium, Ru, Pt and Mo isotopes will be examined in bulk irons and chondrites, and in the insoluble residues of primitive meteorites. The goal of this work will be to identify carriers and isotopic compositions of contributors to previously reported nucleosynthetic heterogeneities. All aspects of this study are directed to the understanding of early solar system processes leading to planetary accretion, differentiation and subsequent planetary growth.

Description: FUSE Observations of Hot Subdwarf B Stars We propose FUSE observations of a sample of hot subdwarf B stars (sdB) in order to carry out an abundance analysis of heavy elements and see how their abundance patterns emerge from the observations. It is a well known fact that the atmospheres of these extreme horizontal branch stars exhibit abundance anomalies. Diffusion processes such as gravitational settling, radiative levitation, weak stellar winds, and accretion have been proposed to explain the abundance anomalies. Our goal is to identify which mechanisms operate in the atmospheres of these stars, study their interactions, understand the abundance patterns, and ultimately, constrain the structure of the atmospheres of sdB stars. With this proposal we want to complete our FUSE proposal El52 and F909 with targets that are feasible with the new FUSE. Only four targets out of forty have been already observed within these two programs, and only three more targets are still feasible. This is why we propose to observe a new sample of sdB stars that are observable with the new FUSE. To study and interpret the abundance patterns in sdB stars, we need a large sample of stars with atmospheric paremeters that cover the whole effective temperature and gravity domains (20,000 K < Teff c 40,000 K; 5.0 < log g < 6.5). To achieve a thorough abundance analysis we need FUSE observations, because many resonance lines of elements such as phosphorus, sulfur, chlorine, iron peak elements, and elements beyond the iron group are only visible in the FUV range for the effective temperatures of interest. This study will not only provide new insights into the stellar atmosphere structure of sdB stars, but also to the evolution of galaxies since these stars are the most important candidates for the source of the UV excess in elliptical galaxies and early-type spiral bulges.

Description: ADVANCED DARK ENERGY PHYSICS TELESCOPE (ADEPT) We propose to conduct a study of a space mission to determine the nature of the mysterious dark energy that is driving the accelerated expansion of the universe. The objective of the proposed study is to determine the most powerful but cost-effective detailed mission concept The best approach is a mission optimized to measure baryon acoustic oscillations, but one that can also survey type la supernovae with no additional hardware or operating modes. The baryon acoustic oscillations provide a standard ruler that can be compared to the scale of the cosmic microwave background anistropy at very high redshift, while supernovae provide a relative luminosity distance with respect to local supernovae. Both methods have been proven by ground-based observations. Space-based observations would provide the high redshift leverage for constraints on the variability of the dark energy. The ADEPT team combines scientific and technical expertise from all of the major methods to measure dark energy, in addition to space-flight experience, to achieve both breadth and depth. The team is organized around specific tasks, including the task to build computer mission simulation tools to evaluate the effectiveness of various hardware approaches, and the task to conduct cosmological simulations to evaluate effectiveness and potential systematic measurement errors. The organization of the study is designed to create two-way interaction between the development of science requirements and the evaluation of the simplest and most robust engineering implementations. The proposed work is directly responsive to the specific NRA call for JDEM mission concept proposals. JDEM research fits NASALS objectives. In response to the national objective to, Implement a sustained and affordable human and robotic program to explore the Solar System and beyond, NASA has developed the specific objective: Explore the universe to understand its origin, structure, evolution, and destiny. Description: SULFUR TRIPLE ISOTOPE STRATIGRAPHY OF ARCHEAN DRILL CORE MATERIAL This project will focus on collecting and interpreting the multiple-sulfur data for the NASA Astrobiology Drilling Program (ADP) Hammersley-Fortescue core. A funded NSF investigation involving the collaborators of this proposal (but not the PI) supports collection of general lithological characterization, cm-scale logging, thin section microscopy, micropaleontology, and sedimentary petrology of all rock types as well as biomarker analysis, inorganic redox proxies, elemental and isotopic characterization (but not multiple-sulfur isotopes) of all major lithologies. The funds requested here will support efforts by the PI to join with these efforts by bringing a new tool and expertise to bear on this research. Multiple-sulfur isotope analyses will be undertaken using two analytical techniques available at the University of Maryland  -  a new rapid technique for obtaining D33S and d34S using EA combustion followed by continuous - flow IRMS of SO, and an established technique for obtaining high precision and accuracy determinations of D33S and D36S using fluorination and gas chromatography followed by dual inlet IRMS of SF6. The rapid determination of D33S and d34S by EA-IRMS of SO provides an opportunity to survey the multiple-sulfur isotope record in the Hammersley-Fortescue ADP core at a meter scale allowing us to select targets for the high precision D33S and D36S by dual inlet IRMS analysis of SF6.  The goals of this project include: (1) establishing a record D33S and d34S for the Hammersley-Fortescue ADP core that can be used to evaluate systematic variations of D33S and d34S between this and other cores (e.g., ongoing work by S. Ono at the Geophysical Laboratory for Agouron-Griqualand Paleoproterozoic Drilling Project (AGPDP)  drill cores from the Transvaal supergroup), (2) establishing the relationship between D33S and D36S (D36S/D33S) for different parts of Hammersley-Fortescue ADP core (Work undertaken at UMCP an the Geophysical Laboratory over the past year and a half has led to the observation that D36S/D33S varies for different formations, and can vary as a function of the stratigraphic position of samples within a single formation. It has not been established whether these variations are consistent for the same stratigraphic position of samples within a single formation. It has not been established whether these variations are consistent for the same stratigraphic levels in different cores.), and (3) evaluating the significance of the D33S, D36S, and d34S record that we observe in the Hammersley-Fortescue ADP core in the context of the lithological, geochemical, and isotopic characterization of the core material that being undertaken by the collaborators to this proposal. The combination of high throughput and high precision analytical capabilities for measuring d34S, D33S and D36S at the University of Maryland and the expertise of the PI (Farquhar) and of the collaborators for collecting and interpreting data for the Hammersley-Fortescue ADP core presents a unique opportunity to study the evolution and cycling of sulfur during the middle and late Archean.

Description: AN INTERCOMPARISON OF TROPOSPHERIC CARBON MONOXIDE MEASUREMENTS FROM THE PAST AND CURRENT SATELLITE INSTRUMENTS:  USING A UNIFORM RETRIEVAL ALGORITHM Tropospheric CO has been measured from space since the 1980s, with recent emphases on spatial and temporal coverage from EOS satellites. To establish a CO climate record and study the global decadal and annual variabilities, a thorough comparison of the measurement accuracy between each instrument is crucial. Although each instrument team has carried out quality validations, they are localized both in time and geographic regions. A major challenge to intercomparing satellite global datasets is to ensure that the information being compared is from the same vertical layer ofthe atmosphere. This requires that a similar retrieval algorithm and the same apriori information be used. The retrieval algorithm for both EOS/Terra/MOPITT and EOS/Aura/TES are based on Roger's Optimum Likely-hood Method. We will develop a new, and off-line, retrieval algorithm for EOS/Aqua/AIRS CO for this study that uses Roger's technique and similar apriori information as used by MOPITT. The same approach will be taken to reprocess MAPS data from the shuttle flights taken 10 to 20 years ago to extend CO time series. Trace gas measurements in the thermal region from a satellite have limited information in the lower atmosphere. The quality ofthe trace gas retrievals largely depends on how apriori or first ;uess information is treated in the retrieval algorithm. By developing this off-line Optimum Likely-hood retrieval algorithm for AIRS and MAPS, we can evaluate the differences, using the same datasets, between the algorithms that have been used in the past for trace gas retrievals. The development of this off-line algorithm also provides foundations to study other trace gases from AIRS measurements and measurements from future instruments. A study to compare AIRS and MOPITT CO has been carried out by the PI and colleagues, and the preliminary results are shown in section 5. This study is based on current AIRS operational physical algorithm and is compared with Rogers optimum likely-hood method that MOPITT uses. Although the CO mixing ratios from the same vertical regions are compared between the two instruments and they agree within 20ppbv, detailed understanding of these differences requires the comparisons based on the same algorithm so that the similar averaging kernels can be used to explain the source of vertical information. The UMBC investigators (Dr. Strow, McMillan, and Warner) with collaborator Dr. Barnet (NOAA/NESDIS) have experience and capability to collect and process AIRS retrievals as demonstrated by their involvement in the INTEX'A field campaign and by the AIRS trace gas validation work led by Dr. McMillan. The UMBC investigators are also working collaboratively with the TES i:eam in an effort to validate TES CO retrievals against AIRS CO, which offers the opportunity for these investigators to access TES products before public release. Although MOPITT and MAPS data are available to the public from NASA, we are continuing working with collaborators from each team to ensure high quality of this study.

Description: THE NEBULAR SHELL AROUND THE ULTRALUMINOUS X-RAY SOURCE HO IX X - 1: SUPERSHELL OR HYPERNOVA We propose FUSE observations of a large shell associated with the ultraluminous X-ray source Holmberg IX X-1 (a.k.a. M81 X-9). The optical spectrum of the shell shows a classic 'shock' spectrum, with strong [SII] relative to Halpha. The X-ray emission derives primarily from an embedded ultraluminous (le40 ergs/s) X-ray source (ULX). The source is pointlike and may be an accreting intermediate mass (100-1000 solar mass) black hole. Its relationship to the nebular shell is poorly understood. The shell may be a supershell blown by multiple stellar winds and SNe, or it may be the remnant of a single highly energetic (E le53 ergs) explosion (i.e., hypernova). Understanding the kinematics of the shell will provide a critical clue to the origin of the X-ray source Ho IX X-1. We will search for C III and/or O VI and other FUV line emission from the shell and use the line ratios to constrain the shock speed. As a bonus, we also plan to search for emission from the compact photoionization nebula around the ULX itself. The detection of O VI from this source would provide valuable information such as the absorbing column in the immediate vicinity of the compact object and the shape of the Ionizing spectrum. The Ho IX X-1 shell is likely the only ULX with low enough extinction to be observable in the FUV, and is well-matched to the diffuse source capabilities of FUSE.

Description: INVESTIGATING GALILEAN ICY SATELLITE EVOLUTION USING IMPACT CRATER AND BASIN MORPHOLOGY Ganymede's ancient dark terrain preserves the record of several early impact events that formed giant sets of tectonic structures known as furrows. Portions of the furrows and dark terrain were later modified and possibly translated by the formation of bright grooved terrain, leaving isolated segments of impact basins. Understanding the sequence of events by which this occurred will help to constrain Ganymede's divergent evolutionary path from that of its neighbors, Europa and Callisto. The first task of the proposed work is a continuation from a previous award, in which we used portions of Ganymede's giant impact basins as strain markers, to investigate the magnitude and method of disruption during grooved terrain formation. We now wish to compare putative shear zones along sections of grooved terrain to our previous results to further constrain the history and evolution of the surface at that tumultuous time. The second task will focus on the formation mechanism for the furrow systems. Although much is known about impact cratering processes, the exact mode of formation of rings around impact basins is still not well understood. One area of debate is whether there is a characteristic spacing between rings around terrestrial impact basins, and if so, what this spacing (or lack thereof) implies for the mechanics of the cratering process. Thus far, only a cursory survey of ring spacing around icy satellite basins has been performed, using low resolution Voyager data, and with a sample too small to draw any statistically significant conclusions. We plan to revisit this issue using our existing GIS database of furrows on Ganymede, and will create similar databases of furrows on Callisto and of two impact craters on Europa, to examine this issue utilizing the higher resolution and increased spatial coverage afforded by Galileo. We will compare our results among the different icy moons, and among the terrestrial planets. Our third task involves revisiting the issue of dome-floored craters on Ganymede. Voyager data suggested that many craters in Ganymede's dark terrain had domed floors, and the doming has been proposed to result from relatively viscous cryovolcanic flows. We wish to study these craters using Galileo data, to determine the origin of their domed floors, and how they relate to other crater morphological types. In particular, we will revisit the issue that they may result from viscous relaxation, or may have formed as floor-fractured craters of the type documented on the Earth's moon. This work meets several of NASA's research objectives, as it uses existing spacecraft data to study processes including impact cratering and volcanism that are ubiquitous across the solar system, and were fundamental during its formation and evolution. The proposed work is expected to enhance our understanding of how impact processes differ between terrestrial and icy bodies, how impact craters evolve over time, and what this can tell us about the surface evolution of the Galilean moons. This work will also lay the foundation for future detailed studies of the Saturnian satellites, which are now being imaged by the Cassini spacecraft.

Description: D, O, AND OTHER ABUNDANCES BEYOND THE LOCAL BUBBLE The D/H and D/0 abundance ratios have been found to be uniform within the Local Bubble, for lines of sight typically shorter than 100 parsecs. At distances of 100 pc to 1000pc measurements of D/H show considerable scatter, and at greater distances the values are well below that of the Local Bubble. FUSE measurements of D/0 exhibit a trend of decreasing values with increasing distance beyond 100 pc. A consistent framework encompassing the behavior of D/H and D/0 has proven elusive. Measurements of D/H, D/0, and other elemental abundances in different environments are essential for improving our understanding of chemical evolution within the Galaxy. It has been suggested that some of the seemingly contradictory abundance patterns may be the result of differential depletion of D and H onto dust grains. Unfortunately, relatively few lines of sight beyond the Local Bubble have a velocity structure that is simple enough for reliable measurements to be made, so the present sampling of different Galactic environments is insufficient to disentagle the possible contributing processes. Existing FUSE spectra for the three stars in this program (distances ranging from 400 to 1000 pc) reveal isolated DI lines. Preliminary analyses indicate that log N(DI) 15, hence N(HI) should be high enough to be determined from the Ly damping profile. This proposal requests additional observing time to obtain signal-to-noise ratios adequate for measuring column densities of HI, DI, 0I, NI, and FeII. N(HI) will also be determined from archival IUE, GHRS, or STIS data for 2 of the 3 stars, and compared to that derived from the FUSE Lyman profiles.

Description: ANALYSIS AND SIMULATION OF THE INFLUENCE OF THE SAHARAN AIR LAYER ON TROPICAL CYCLOGENESIS USING DATA FROM NAMMA-06 AND A-TRAIN SATELLITES The 2005 hurricane season was the busiest on record with 27 tropical cyclones forming in the Atlantic basin and Hurricane Katrina(2005) is believed to be the costliest hurricane in U. S. history. There are growing concerns regarding the increasing tropical cyclone impacts on the United States, including whether this is a result ofthe ongoing global warming or just a natural oscillation. Addressing this issue requires knowledge on the crucial physics involved in the tropical cyclogenesis process, which is still poorly understood. Moreover, the Saharan Air Layer (SAL), an elevated mixed layer of warm and dry air that extends from Africa to the tropical Atlantic and contains a substantial amount of mineral dust, complicates the tropical cyclogenesis in the Atlantic basin. So far the impact of the SAL on the tropical cyclogenesis is uncertain. Advancing our understanding of the physical mechanisms of tropical cyclogenesis and the associated role of the SAL strongly depends on obtaining better observations over the data-sparse ocean areas. The NASA African Monsoon Multidisciplinary Activities 2006 (NAMMA-06), which is specifically designed to understand tropical cyclogenesis in the eastern and central Atlantic, will provide a unique dataset for study of both tropical cyclogenesis and the SAL. We propose a two-year research plan, which will extend our current study on tropical cyclogenesis and the associated roles of the SAL. The goal of this proposed study is to use the data from the NAMMA-06 field campaign, the 'A-Train' satellites (Aqua, CloudSat and CALIPSO), and the TRMM satellite to further investigate the physical mechanisms associated with tropical cyclogenesis and the impact of the SAL on tropical cyclone development. The proposed research will combine observational analysis with high-resolution numerical simulation using the WRF and MM5 models. We believe that the combination of these unprecedented datasets and the state-of-the-art mesoscale numerical models can greatly improve our understanding in this field. The primary goals of this proposed study are: 1) to examine the evolution and structure of the SAL; 2) to explore the interaction between tropical cyclones and the SAL; 3) to understand the roles of various physical processes such as African Easterly Waves (AEWs) and Mesoscale Convective Systems (MCSs) in tropical cyclogenesis.

Description: IMPACTS OF CONFLICT ON LAND COVER, FIRE DYNAMICS, AND BIODIVERSITY POTENTIAL IN THE IMATONG MOUNTAINS OF SOUTHERN SUDAN (GRADUATE STUDENT - VIRGINIA GORSEVSKI) This project will provide insight into the consequences of conflict and post-conflict population migration on land coverlIand use, fire dynamics, and biodiversity. In the Imatong Mountains of southern Sudan, the end of hostilities associated with the civil war has caused significant demographic change, resulting in heightened tensions between competing groups as well as increased pressure on the environment. For this study, multi-scale remote sensing data will be analyzed with information on human factors within a modeling framework to understand how changes in human population pressure are modifying the local fire regime, land cover, and future levels of biodiversity. Specifically, the first phase of the project will map forest cover in 1987 (TM), 2001 (ETM+ and ASTER) and 2005 (ASTER) to determine change during the conflict period when the region was largely depopulated. Forest cover will then be mapped for the post-conflict period to show the impact of returning populations in 2007 and 2009 (ASTER). Phase two will compare changes in the fire regime during the two periods by detecting burned areas using daily MODIS surface reflectance data at a spatial resolution of 250m for years 2000 - 2008. The resulting near-daily burned area maps will be used to construct a detailed fire chronology to separate out different ignitions. Observed changes in forest cover and fire regime will be linked to people by developing robust, spatially explicit layers of key indicators of human activity using ASTER 15m data to create layers of villages, roads and fields - three different indicators of human pressure during and after the conflict. Phase three will combine species data with the land cover outputs in the IDRISI Andes Land Change Modeler (LCM) to predict the course of habitat change and assess implications for biodiversity. This proposed study will support NASA's Applied Science Program in the areas of ecological forecasting by using Earth observation data and dynamic models to predict how observed changes in land cover due to shifting demographics could impact forest habitat and biodiversity over the long term. The project will also contribute to NASA's disaster management objectives by providing decision-makers with the information they need to monitor both natural (fire) and man-made (conflict) disasters in this strategically important area of the world. In addition, this project builds on previous studies that attempt to 'link people and pixels' across themes and spatial scales, through the theoretical development and a technical demonstration of how rapid and significant demographic changes due to conflict impact land cover, fire dynamics and biodiversity. Finally, this research will contribute to practical conservation efforts currently underway in southern Sudan.

Description: UNIVERSITY OF MARYLAND, BALTIMORE Global Sea Level in a Changing Climate: Reference Frames, Data Analysis, and Interpretation This proposal addresses the key sea level problem. How much water is going where? We will exploit NASA's primary contributions to this problem: satellite altimetry (Topex/Poseidon, Jason-1, and Jason-2), gravimetry (GRACE), and the critical underlying terrestrial reference system. Tide gauge records are also emphasized because they provide critical calibration data and lend further insight into the causes of sea level variation. Our previous investigation (PI: B. Chao) improved the geodetic and measurement consistencies of the satellite datasets and created the necessary infrastructure for the present proposal. We now have the capability to provide truly integrated terrestrial reference frames from rigorous combination of VLBI, Doris, SLR, and GPS tracking data. Our ongoing work with reference frames has demonstrated their importance to sea-level determination; this affects the interpretation of sea level measurements, including "fingerprint" and EOF analyses, and related aspects such as determination of vertical crustal motions from combined tide-gauge and altimeter analyses. We propose to derive new terrestrial reference frames from a consistent and comprehensive analysis of space-geodetic data, emphasizing geodetic stations important to tracking of T/P, Jason-1, and Jason-2. Emphasis is also given to stations near tide gauges, which will improve altimeter calibrations. We propose to derive new global estimates of sea level from T/P and Jason altimetry, based on our refined reference frames, new precise orbits, and calibrations. This work will include "cal/val" activities for Jason- 2 and other reprocessing necessary for a seamless transition between successive altimeter missions. A consistent interpretation of sea level from altimetry and historical tide gauge measurements requires further study of the origin of low-frequency variations. We propose to use a combination of ancillary data as well as ocean model outputs to address this critical issue. We intend to revisit some issues regarding fingerprint analyses, which bear on the contribution of melting ice to sea-level rise. However, the most direct route to determining the contribution of ice sheets is obtained with satellite gravimetry. We propose to build on our technique of localized inversions of GRACE range-rate measurements, which we have shown are capable of placing firm error bounds on the contribution to sea level rise from Greenland and Antarctic ice melting. This proposal responds to NASA's Strategic Goal 3A, studying the Earth to advance scientific understanding and to meet societal needs.
