Description: ENSEMBLE KALMAN FILTER DATA ASSIMILATION FOR MARTIAN WEATHER ANALYSIS AND FORECASTING Temperature and dust opacity data retrieved from the Thermal Emission Spectrometer (TES) spectra will be analyzed using a data assimilation system (DAS) that will generate synoptic maps of the thermal, wind, and cloud distributions. A direct assimilation of the TES radiances is also planned. The DAS to be used in the proposed analysis is based on the Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) approach developed at the University of Maryland, with the mapped products generated by applying the LETKF to optimally combine TES observations with the short-range atmospheric forecasts from the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory Mars general circulation model. The LETKF is the tool of choice for Mars data assimilation because it is able to extract maximum information from sparse data and provide limits of confidence for the analysis, as shown with real atmospheric observations for the Earth. Validation and radiance assimilation will be carried out using radiative transfer tools developed at the Atmospheric and Environmental Research, Inc. The scientific expertise of the proposing team in terrestrial and Mars data assimilation, modeling, and remote sensing, and the optimal characteristics of the proposed DAS, will assure timeliness and maximum scientific return from the proposed analysis. The proposed analysis will provide a coherent view of the Mars atmosphere that is critical to the answering of key scientific questions about Mars meteorology, in particular the predictability in the Mars weather system and the mechanisms responsible for the generation and propagation of global dust storms. By making this product available to the Mars community, we aim to duplicate the success and benefit for both research and society at large of the terrestrial NCEP 40-year reanalysis effort. Furthermore, the application of the DAS to the analysis of TES data will serve as a testbed for a prototype Mars weather forecasting system that could be used for the planning and execution of future missions, both robotic and human.

Description: This study proposes to examine the impact of the oceanic intraseasonal oscillations (OISOs) in the southern Indian Ocean (IO) on the Madden-Julian Oscillations (MJOs) in the atmosphere. It is assumed that MJOs and OISOs interact with each other in the coupled ocean-atmosphere system. MJOs propagate eastward and force OISOs in the southeastern Indian Ocean (SEIO). The forced OISOs propagate westward as baroclinic Rossby waves, leading to the OISOs in the southwestern Indian Ocean (SWIO). Then the OISOs in SWIO influence the genesis and evolution of MJOs. This coupling cycle may enhance both the MJOs and the OISOs. There concepts lead to the two driving hypotheses: 1) The OISOs in the SWIO significantly affect the MJOs. 2) The MJOs and the OISOs strengthen each other due to the ocean-atmosphere coupling. Method/Technique: This study will rely on satellite data and reanalysis products to identify interactions between OISOs and MJOs. The indices for MJOs and ISOs will be established, indicating their strength. Lag-correlations between the indices for ISOs in SSTs and the MJO index will be calculated to delineate cause and effect and to estimate the response time of the MJOs. The correlations between different ISO indices will be calculated to indicate the effective communication-channel between the OISOs and the MJOs. An analytical coupled model will be solved to verify whether MJOs and OISOs can feedback to each other in the coupled system. Finally, the impact of MJOs on OISOs and the feedback of OISOs on MJOs will be tested in an OGCM and an atmosphere model (SPEEDY model) separately. If the OISOs are enhanced by MJOs and MJOs are enhanced by OISOs in both models, they will indicate that the OISOs and MJOs will strengthen each other in the coupled ocean-atmosphere system. Significance/Relevance to NASA ESS Fellowship Program: This study will contribute to the understanding of the MJOs over IO and further our understanding of the ocean-atmosphere interactions in the southern IO. A better understanding of the coupling mechanism between MJOs and OISOs will have consequences for forecasting of extreme weather over the IO rim countries. Furthermore, when the ISOs are enhanced, they will interact with oscillations with longer time periods, such as ENSO and the Indian Ocean Zonal Mode, carrying their influences to global scales. The outcome of this study is of direct relevance to NASA interests in subseasonal climate forecasting and the use of NASA data products for extending predictive understanding of subseasonal climate. The proposed study directly contributes to two focus areas for the NASA ESS Fellowship Program: 1) Climate variability and change, because MJOs have a global influence on the global climate; 2) Weather, because MJOs and OISOs usually cause extreme weather events and the predictability of the tropic intraseasonal variability is still very limited.

Description: Observations of the gravity and topography of Mars made by Mars Global Surveyor and Mars Odyssey currently provide our best constraints on the subsurface structure of Mars. Quantitative modeling of the gravity field can produce an improved understanding of the processes that have sculpted the martian surface, including tectonism, volcanism, impacts, erosion, and deposition. I will use a combination of spectral domain and spatial domain gravity modeling methods to model gravity anomalies in parts of Tharsis and of the hemispheric dichotomy, which are the two largest geologic provinces on Mars. I will model gravity anomalies in several ancient tectonic units on the periphery of Tharsis, including Tempe Terra, Claritas Fossae, Thaumasia and the Coprates Rise. These studies will improve our knowledge of the early evolution of the Tharsis region. I will also model gravity anomalies along the hemispheric dichotomy in Arabia Terra and will compare the results with previous studies of the hemispheric dichotomy in eastern Mars. The results will improve our understanding of possible segmentation along the hemispheric dichotomy and thus will serve as important clues to the processes that formed and modified the dichotomy. One ofthe primary goals ofthese studies is to quantitatively constrain the nature of subsurface mass anomalies in these regions (e.g., dikes, magma chambers). The second goal is to constrain regional variations in lithospheric properties on Mars. The proposed work builds on several successful gravity modeling studies using similar methods to examine large highland volcanos such as Syrtis Major (Kiefer, Earth Planet. Sci. Lett., 2004) and the hemispheric dichotomy in eastern Mars (Kiefer, Geophys. Res. Lett. 2005). The results of these studies will contribute to our understanding of Mars in several ways: (1) Knowledge ofthe shape, amplitude, and distribution of subsurface mass anomalies associated with circum-Tharsis tectonic units will provide new constraints on the processes that formed these provinces, improving our knowledge of the early stages of Tharsis history. (2) Knowledge of the shape, amplitude, and spatial distribution of subsurface mass anomalies in the Arabia Terra portion of the hemispheric dichotomy and comparison with previous results for the hemispheric dichotomy in eastern Mars will permit a more detailed assessment of possible segmentation of the dichotomy boundary and thus will place new constraints on the processes that formed and modified this global scale structure. Description: Biomass burning is recognized as a significant source of atmospheric perturbing trace gas and particulate matter emissions and has received attention from the scientific community over the past several decades as an important contributor to total climatic radiative forcing, atmospheric chemistry, and human health impacts (Innes, 2000; Levine, 1991; Andreae, 1991). The current uncertainty surrounding the impact of aerosol forcing is "one of the largest unknown factors in climate research", in large part due to poor estimates of the contribution from biomass burning (lPCC, 2001). Earth observing satellites have made a significant contribution to biomass burning detection, monitoring, and characterization (Giglio, Kendall, & Tucker, 2000). Estimates have raditionally been based on calculating the biomass consumed from estimates of fuel loads, burned area, and combustion completeness. The biomass consumed is then multiplied by an emission factor to calculate emissions (van der Werf et al., 2006; Seiler & Crutzen, 1980). However, this bottom-up method has a great deal of uncertainty (Korontzi et al., 2004; Robinson, 1989), perhaps as much as 50% (Andreae & Merlet, 2001). An approach to estimate biomass burning emissions using fire radiative power (FRP) has emerged from remote sensing science (Kaufman et aI., 1998). Field and laboratory validation has successfully confirmed the effectiveness of this approach, but to date it has not been applied at a broad, global scale (Wooster et aI., 2005). Through investigation of the relationship between MODIS FRP and a new MODIS derived biomass burning aerosol emissions product (OC-BCem) I propose to develop a methodology to generate emission estimates at a global scale. I will produce monthly global emission estimates for 2000-2006 and compare the results against current estimates (e.g. van der Werf et al., 2006). I will investigate sources of variability in the FRP- OC-BCem relationship and parameterize emissions to account for variation in landcover, fire intensity temporal cycle, and emission factors. Using both MODIS sensor's retrieved FRP (aboard Terra and Aqua satellites), I will examine the fire intensity temporal cycle and empirically derive the total fire radiative energy (FRE). FRE is currently unavailable from MODIS due to limited temporal sampling inherent with polar orbiting satellites. Accuracy assessment of the FRE derived in this study will be based on comparison with geostationary data. Geostationary satellites offer frequent temporal sampling of FRP retrievals (e.g. 15-30min. vs. 4hr. for MODIS), and therefore can be integrated to calculate FRE (Wooster et aI., 2005), thus providing a metric to assess this study's derived FRE. Emission factors derived in this project will be compared with published values to examine consistency. Finally, uncertainty analysis and accuracy assessment will be performed and lead to refinement in the application of FRP to generate improved estimates of biomass burning emissions. The proposed project has direct relevance to NASA's Carbon Cycle and Ecosystems Roadmap, particularly to "reduce uncertainties and improve quantitative information concerning atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases". The estimates calculated in this research will also help fulfill the goal of quantifying carbon fluxes while providing data for improving climate change predictions. The proposed efforts leverage LPIs successful Explore! Program. The objectives of the project include: 1) Development of an IPY educational package appropriate for childrens and youth programs that primarily utilizes existing NASA IPY-related Earth and space educational products and resources. The trained facilitators will provide IPY educational experiences through their childrens and youth programs, reaching an estimated minimum of 25,000 children annually in 16 states nationwide. 3) Ongoing support of the program providers as they implement the programs in their own communities. Support includes assisting them in collaborating with local NASA scientists and Polar Palooza efforts, and providing information about NASAs IPY projects and related research and missions, resources, and educational opportunities. The proposed efforts will connect children and families with NASAs goal of understanding our home planet, specifically how NASA studies Earth from space to advance scientific understanding and meet societal needs. The efforts will share current understanding of the role of oceans, atmosphere, and ice in the climate system and in improving predictive capability for its future evolution. In addition, the project will promote public literacy in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines and strengthen and build relationships between NASA and the informal educational learning environments of libraries and after-school programs. The proposal objectives align with NASAs IPY objectives of engaging, informing, and inspiring diverse public audiences by sharing knowledge about polar science and its global connections during IPY, and by communicating NASAs unique contributions to recent advances in Arctic and Antarctic research and climate science. They extend the spirit of polar exploration and discovery to the poles of the Moon, Mars, and other planets and moons of our solar system and to help attract and educate the next generation of scientists and engineers through programming in informal learning environments of libraries and after-school programs.

NASA has the opportunity to contribute to the GEOSS societal benefit goals, through the integration ofNASA satellite capabilities to support global agricultural monitoring and the development of sustainable agriculture strategies. Since the 1970's NASA and the USDA, have gained significant experience in agricultural monitoring through integration of satellite data, data products, and climate model outputs into the USDA's agriculture monitoring systems. NASA and the USDA currently run several successful joint proj ects that integrate new NASA data and modeling capabilities into the global and domestic production and yield forecasting mandates ofthe USDA. The expertise gained from these collaborative projects, the US federal agencies' charge to support GEO, and the GEOSS need for help in coordinating international agriculture-monitoring efforts, all would suggest that NASA's Agriculture Efficiency program is in a strong position to help USGEO and GEOSS achieve their key tasks of: designing an agricultural monitoring system, and developing a long term strategy for agricultural monitoring. Building on the success of the IGOL International Workshop in 2005, the near-term priority is to coordinate a set of follow-on international coordination workshops. The goal of these workshops is to formulate the GEOSS short and long tenn strategies for an enhanced agriculture monitoring system. Taking a lead role in these workshops is a natural progression ofthe NASA-USDA recent collaborative projects that will extend the jointly developed capabilities from the national to the international level.

Description: STRUCTURE AND DYNAMICS OF MAGNETIC ISLANDS DURING RECONNECTION (GRADUATE STUDENT:  RAYMOND FERMO)ABSTRACT: THE FAST DISSIPATION OF ENERGY CONTAINED IN MAGNETIC FIELDS DRIVES EXPLOSIVE PHENOMENA IN SUCH DISPARATE MEDIA AS THE SOLAR CORONA, THE TERRESTRIAL MAGNETOSPHERE, AND LABORATORY FUSION DEVICES. IN EACH CASE THE UNDERLYING PROCESS IS THOUGHT TO BE MAGNETIC RECONNECTION IN WHICH OPPOSITELY DIRECTED COMPONENTS OF THE MAGNETIC FIELD CROSS-LINK, FORMING WHAT IS CALLED AN X-LINE. THE CHANGE IN TOPOLOGY, WHICH HAPPENS AT SMALL SCALES, LEADS TO LARGE-SCALE TRANSFERS OF ENERGY BETWEEN THE MAGNETIC FIELD AND THE SURROUNDING PLASMA. MAGNETIC ISLANDS (OR FLUX ROPES), SELF-CONTAINED REGIONS OF MAGNETIC FLUX, ARE COMMONLY OBSERVED IN ASSOCIATION WITH RECONNECTION SITES AS, FOR EXAMPLE, IN WHAT ARE KNOWN AS FLUX TRANSFER EVENTS (FTES) AT THE MAGNETOPAUSE. NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS OF RECONNECTION PRODUCE SIMILAR STRUCTURES AND HAVE LED TO A PROPOSED LINKAGE OF ISLANDS TO THE ENERGIZATION OF ELECTRONS IN BOTH THE MAGNETOTAIL AND THE SOLAR CORONA. WE PROPOSE TO CONTINUE THESE RECENT STUDIES OF MAGNETIC ISLANDS BOTH THROUGH LARGE-SCALE NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS OF RECONNECTION AND BY FORMULATING AN ANALYTIC DESCRIPTION OF THE STATISTICS OF MAGNETIC ISLAND BEHAVIOR. FOR THE NUMERICAL SIMULATIONS WE WILL USE P3D, A MASSIVELY PARALLEL PARTICLE-IN-CELL CODE THAT HAS BEEN USED FOR A NUMBER OF PREVIOUS RECONNECTION SIMULATIONS. THE ANALYTIC STUDY IS EXPECTED TO PRODUCE AN INTEGRO-DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION GOVERNING THE EVOLUTION OF THE DISTRIBUTION OF ISLANDS. WE WILL WRITE A CODE TO EXPLORE THE PROPERTIES OF THESE SOLUTIONS. MAGNETIC RECONNECTION IS AN ACTIVE FIELD OF STUDY FOR SEVERAL OF NASA'S HELIOPHYSICS MISSIONS AND THE PRIMARY SCIENCE OBJECTIVE FOR THE UPCOMING MAGNETOSPHERIC MULTISCALE MISSION. WORK IN THIS AREA WILL DIRECTLY CONTRIBUTE TO NASA'S INTERESTS.

Description: Measuring Particles, Antiparticles, and Isotopes in the Cosmic Radiation Cosmic rays propagate through the Galaxy by scattering off magnetic irregularities in a process described as diffusion. The particles reaching Earth from their distant sources are modified by interactions with interstellar matter as they are guided through the interstellar gas/plasma by the galactic magnetic fields. The interactions produce secondary particles whose abundance relative to the primary particles is a measure of the amount of material traversed. This relative abundance and the secondary particle energy distributions are keys to understanding the nature and distribution of sources. In addition to known astronomical objects, possible exotic sources would include antimatter, dark matter, primordial black holes, etc. The goal Otis proposal is to study the sensitivity of searching for dark matter in the cosmic-ray antiparticle channels, with a focus on positrons. One major objective is to develop an optimal measurement strategy for positrons, including reduction of the signal. selection uncertainties. Our previous studies have demonstrated that systematic uncertainties present a serious challenge to precision measurements of these rare particles, which may be key to one of the fundamental questions in the 2003 National Academy of Science, Board on Physics and Astronomy report "Connecting Quarks with the Cosmos: Eleven Science Questions for the New Century", specifically "What is Dark Matter?" Previous investigations with balloon-borne magnetic spectrometers indicate that the positron fraction has an excess in the 7 - lOGeV range that continues to higher energies. This could be a "smoking gun" for the dark matter signature from the annihilation of neutralinos, but it might also be an artifact of systematical uncertainty in measurements dominated by a cosmic-ray background. A new balloon-borne instrument optimized to measure 1 - 50 GeV positrons and electrons with sensitivity much better than that of the previous experiments could discriminate between these possibilities with a 30-day balloon flight around Antarctica. Our study plan includes modeling a magnetic spectrometer with an optimal combination of acceptance, maximum detectable rigidity, and particle identification capability for measuring the cosmic-ray positron/electron ratio with a high degree of confidence. We believe this objective could be realized with the relatively inexpensive technique of a warm permanent magnet and a high resolution tracking system. Description: We propose to develop and interpret the best-ever model of the lunar magnetic field environment utilizing magnetic and electron reflectometer measurements collected from the Lunar Prospector mission.  This time-variable model will be used to better understand the space environment, and will be utilized, with supporting geological, chemical, mineralogical, and petrologic data, to better characterize the surface and sub-surface sources of the magnetic field.  We will address such scientific issues as the evolution of the lunar magnetic field and the existance and size of a lunar core, the role of crater and basin impacts in producing and exposing anomalies, and where appropriate, crustal structure and thickness, the level of contamination of the crust by dikes, and transport of magma to the surface.  Unlike all previous models, our model will parameterize and coestimate the magnetic fields associated with the major current sources in near-lunar space.  We have previously developed such comprehensive models for near-Earth space as part of a joint effort between U.S. and European researchers.  Models developed from these efforts stand out from their peers in low S/N regimes, such as the Earth and Moon.  Magnetic field mapping is a geologic tool in the terrestrial environment, and researchers have developed a suite of mathematical tools that can be used to facilitate interpretation.  We have adapted several of these tools to the lunar environment, and show that dike-like features in the vicinity of the South Pole-Aitken basin region are at mid-crustal depths.  Our team is composed of experts in comprehensive modeling of the earth's magnetic field and petrophysics, and in lunar geology and space physics.  This new approach will extract the most information possible from the available Lunar Prospector data sets by integrating field directions and magnitudes from the magnetic field instrument with estimates of the surface magnetic field made using the electron reflectometer.  The result of this approach will be a magnetization model.  We will make our comprehensive magnetic field model available as an interactive web application, and we will be working with collaborators who will utilize the magnetic field model to better understand the physics of the lunar mini-magnetospheres.

Description: COMPARISON OF ACCELERATED PARTICLE POPULATIONS AT 1 AU AND AT THE SUN We propose to study the flare-accelerated particle population at the Sun using gamma-ray observations from RHESSI, Yohkoh, CGRO, and SMM. These can be compared to particle-acceleration models and to particle measurements in space and at Earth. This is a key element in determining the contribution of flare-accelerated particles to large gradual SEP events, a goal of the LWS-TR&T in preparing for the Sentinels Mission. As an example of this study we discuss a recent RHESI analysis of the 2005 January 20 event that revealed two distinct accelerated-particle components at the Sun: 1) an impulsive release lasting 10 minutes with a power-law index of 3 observed in a compact region on the Sun and 2) an associated release of much higher energy particles with index 2.3 interacting at the Sun for about two hours. The spectrum of the latter component is consistent with that measured in space. A similar study can be performed in any of over fifty jointly observed gamma-ray flares and SEP events. We suggest that emphasis be placed on the most energetic of these events, those that produce Ground Level Events (GLE).

Description: The Earth Sciences Directorate of the NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center and the College of Computer, Mathematical, and Physical Sciences, University of Maryland at College Park, share common research goals in the areas of meteorology, oceanography, terrestrial physics, climate research, chemistry of the earth's atmosphere, and satellite research. A cooperative agreement was signed by both parties in 1993 to establish a Joint Center for Earth System Science that serves as a center for multi-disciplinary research in Earth System Science. In 1999 the Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center (ESSIC) by a cooperative agreement that superseded the original. ESSIC serves as a means to increase the effectiveness of research and teaching through close collaboration by both parties, and serve as a means to train personnel for research in Earth System Science. This proposal requests funding to enable the UMCP and GSFC researchers to conduct new research through the collaborative research program within the ESSIC frame of reference for the next four years. The scientific objectives of this proposal encompass four major research areas: climate variability and change; atmospheric composition and processes; the global carbon cycle (including terrestrial and marine ecosystems/land use/cover change), and the global water cycle. Research is conducted through in situ and remotely sensed observations, together with component and coupled ocean-atmosphere-land modeling. This multi-pronged approach provides a foundation for understanding and forecasting changes in the global environment and regional implications. Data assimilation and regional downscaling are used to link the observations and models, enabling us to study the interactions between the physical climate system and biogeochemical cycles from global to regional scales.

Description: ELECTRON MICORSCOPY, SPECTROSCOPY, AND CHEMICAL ANALYSIS OF AIRCRAFT ENGINE PARTICULATE (SOLID AND VOLATILE) FOR COMPLETE PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL CHARACTERIZATION This proposal addresses the environmental challenges imposed by subsonic fixed wing aircraft. Soot produced within the upper troposphere has significant consequences for atmospheric chemistry. Although black carbon is hydrophobic, chemical and physical changes occurring at its surface can create functional groups that attract and retain water, thereby causing it to become hydrophilic. Such changes determine whether soot acts as cloud condensation nuclei, its susceptibility to washout and participation in atmospheric heterogeneous reactions, thereby significantly impacting the atmospheric radiative balance. Such chemical changes and subsequent interactions depend upon the soot surface chemistry. To ultimately control soot emissions requires detailed modeling based on experimental results. Alternatively analysis of soot nanostructure could be used as a tracer of the combustion conditions leading to its formation. Such an experimental record could guide models of soot nucleation and growth. In addition to nanostructure soot aggregate size, characterization of aggregates by the number of primary particles could guide modeling of the aerosol dynamics. Our approach will use high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) to reveal soot nanostructure and to provide images for statistical analysis of aggregate size and morphology. X-Ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) will be used to measure heteroelements, surface oxygen functional groups such as phenolic, carbonyl and carboxylic and graphitic/non-graphitic carbon. A database will be developed with these results. Experimental evidence of soot nucleation and growth stages as recorded in the nanostructure will provide feedback to combustor models of soot. Soot aggregate size and structure will guide atmospheric modeling calculations of soot contribution to atmospheric radiative forcing, and the radiative balance between the ground and upper atmosphere. Gaps in knowledge with respect to NOx-soot, SOx and ozone-soot interactions may be addressed. Confirmation of soot role as condensation nuclei will be substantiated while the mechanism (involving polar oxygen functional groups versus adsorbed sulfur species) will be differentiated.

Description: CONTROL-ORIENTED MODELING OF FREE VORTEX WAKES  Several advanced methods to control the dynamics of helicopter rotor blades have been proposed in the last several years. Most of these methods rely on devices placed on the blade or inside it, which create localized but important aerodynamic effects. An accurate description of these aerodynamic effects requires a model of the vortex wake generated by the rotor. The design of the control systems for these devices require mathematical models entirely formulated in state-space form, that is, in the form of systems of ordinary differential equations (ODE). Currently, the only rotor wake models formulated in this way contain simplifying assumptions that severely limit their applicability. Therefore, the objective of the proposed research is to develop a rotor wake model that does not suffer from these limitations, and that is entirely in state-space form. The starting point for the new wake model is an existing "free wake" model, currently formulated as a system of partial differential equations (PDE). In this wake, the PDE are transformed into a system of algebraic equations using a finite difference method both in space and in time. The proposed approach consists of a semidiscretization of the PDE, that is, of using finite differences only to approximate the evolution in space. The result of the semidiscretization is the desired system of ODE. This method is known in the numerical analysis community as the "method of lines". The new wake model will be incorporated in a complete flight dynamic simulation model, and used to study four representative problems that cannot be rigorously solved with current wake models. These are: (i) the evaluation of the aeroelastic stability of a helicopter in steep descending turns; (ii) the aeromechanic stability of a helicopter with and active rotor control system turned on (closed loop stability); (iii) the frequency response to pilot inputs and the flight stability of a helicopter in a very steep descent (near the so called "vortex-ring state"); and (iv) the design of a flight control system for a helicopter with a coaxial twin rotor. An accurate free wake model in state-space form is a critical missing ingredient for the design of helicopter with the newest types of advanced flight controls. The proposed wake model will help fill this gap, and therefore contribute to a more accurate and reliable design of flight control systems in all flight conditions and for all types of rotor configurations.

Description: 2PI-STERADIAN ENERGETIC ION SENSOR Increasingly, and particularly in the Planetary Program where low launch frequency demands multiple science goal payloads, energetic ion sensors fly on 3-axis stabilized spacecraft (eg, MESSENGER EPS, New Horizons (Pluto) PEPPSI, Cassini MIMI). While 3-axis stabilization serves imaging science well, it hampers the goal of obtaining 4pi steradian ion measurements. In some cases, articulation mechanisms have been added to provide an additional degree of freedom, but this is expensive in mass and power, and increases risk (eg, the Cassini MIMI/LEMMS turntable, which failed after one year in Saturn Tour). Compelling science requirements have driven the inclusion of energetic ion sensors on most past planetary missions (including all of those to magnetized planets), and will likely continue to do so in the future. The magnetospheres of the planets both trap and energize ions and electrons, whose sources are various: planetary atmospheres/ionospheres (Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune), active moons (Io and probably Europa at Jupiter, Enceladus at Saturn), moon atmospheres (Titan at Saturn, Triton at Neptune), sputtering of the surfaces of inert moons and rings (Saturn, Jupiter, Neptune, Uranus), and the solar wind. These energetic particles further serve to modify the surfaces of moons and ring particles, influence the transport of material through charge exchange and sputtering, provide energy for atmospheric chemistry, and generate aurorae and synchrotron radiation. The pitch angle distribution (PAD) of energetic particles is especially important in interpreting the measurements. Evolution of the PAD over time or location in a planetary magnetosphere is critical to unfolding particle sources and sinks, interactions with moons and rings, as well as acceleration and transport processes. Therefore, we are proposing to develop an energetic ion sensor that measures ion energy and composition, and covers 2pi steradians without an articulation mechanism (the best that may reasonably be achieved from a body-mounted sensor). The sensor will measure the angular distribution of ions with roughly 22.5 degree resolution, and with sufficient ion mass resolution to separately characterize hydrogen, helium, CNO, neon, argon, and iron over an energy range of 30 keV to 2 MeV for protons, 70 keV to > 10 MeV for oxygen, as well as separating He3 and He4 over a reduced energy range (80 keV to 2 MeV). Separation of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen from one another should be possible between about 0.3 and 10 MeV. There are no new technology development issues in this design--the timing requirements are high, but no more stringent than others we have built to even as long ago as AMPTE. However, the design is mechanically somewhat complex, and requires development to a high precision breadboard level with ion beam test results so that a convincing flight proposal may be based on it. Based on its shape, we refer to this design as the Mushroom.

Description: VOLVANIC PLUMES ON MARS AND VENUS This proposal comprises three tasks to continue ongoing research to study explosive volcanic eruption plumes on Mars and Venus. Over the last 30 years, there have been numerous models for explosive volcanic eruption columns based on the basic ideas for convecting plumes presented by Morton et al. |1956|. Our prior efforts [Glaze and Baloga, 2002), however, indicated that these accepted plume models are not valid for most plausible conditions on Mars, and that basic model assumptions were not strictly valid on Earth or Venus. Under current PGG funding, we have developed a new approach to buoyant plume modeling that addresses the fundamental assumptions of pressure balance [Glaze and Baloga, 2005). We propose to build on the success that we have had in developing this new plume model in an effort to revise thinking as regards explosive volcanic eruption column dynamics. The primary objectives of the three proposed tasks are to 1) develop a robust model, based on the new Glaze and Baloga [2005] approach, that Is fully time dependent describing plumes with gas, liquid and solid components, and with the ability for solids to be transported at a different velocity, 2) modify the basic model developed under Task 1 in order to explore the importance of linear vent sources (i.e., fissures and flood volcanism), and 3) incorporate new constraints on the boundary conditions for the central and linear vent models developed in Tasks 1 and 2 based on recent terrestrial experience.

Description: THE ORIGIN OF CAL 83 X-RAY OFF-STATES The close binary supersoft X-ray source CAL 83 is a most promising candidate of SN IA progenitors. Our XMM-Newton and Chandra observations show a massive white dwarf, exhibit large amplitude short-term variations of the X-ray flux, and establish definitively its recurrent nature. We propose now to conduct a campaign with EPIC and OM on XMM-Newton to substantiate the correlation between X-ray and optical variations on a short, medium, and long-term basis. This campaign will trace the physical relation between the accretion disk and the white dwarf, and will discriminate between several models explaining the origin of CAL 83 off-states. XMM-Newton data will offer unique and timely insights into accretion and unstable nuclear burning during the last evolution stages of SN Ia progenitors.

Description: Understanding the Evolution and Impacts of Storm-Enhanced Electric Fields in the Mid-Latitude Ionosphere The proposal is directed to the NASA LWS TR&T Targeted Invesigation program element and addresses the Focused Science Topic, 'Storm effects on the global electrodynamics and the middle and low latitude ionosphere, which is identified by program descriptor T3d. We seek a deeper understanding of the penetration of nominally high-latitude ionospheric electric fields into the mid and low-latitude ionosphere and accordingly into the inner magnetosphere. Electric fields and plasma convection are of high importance for both scientific understanding and operations; in the inner magnetosphere they contribute to the circulation of energetic particles, the energization of plasma, the creation of plasma pressure gradients and the generation of fieldaligned currents; in the ionosphere they redistribute plasma, generate ionospheric structure, and populate the medium with irregularities through processes of plasma instability. During quiet periods the electric field is largely confined to the high-latitude zone and is highly variable in both time and space. During geomagnetic storms the electric field penetrates into the inner magnetosphere where it produces significant changes in magnetosphere-ionosphere coupling and major changes in the subauroral ionosphere. The ionospheric effects adversely impact modern technological systems including communications, surveillance, and global positioning. Two of the major goals of LWS science are to understand the processes that lead to these disturbances and to predict when they will occur. Reaching these goals requires a significantly improved understanding of the spatial and temporal evolution of both ionospheric and magnetospheric electric fields during storms.

Description: SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT - THE OBJECTIVE OF THIS PROCUREMENT IS TO PROCURE A SOFTWARE PROGRAM THAT WILL BE USED TO DEMONSTRATE VIRTUAL INSPECTION CAPABILITY USING ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVES AS APPLIED TO A VARIETY OF EXPLORATION HARDWARE AT NASA.   BACKGROUND: A CHARTER ESTABLISHED THE COMPUTATIONAL NONDESTRUCTIVE EVALUATION (NDE) TEAM WITHIN THE NASA ENGINEERING AND SAFETY CENTER (NESC).  THE FOCUS OF THIS TEAM IS TO ADDRESS THE CRITICAL NEED FOR COMPUTATIONAL NDE METHODOLOGIES TO ENABLE NDE CONSIDERATIONS TO BE INCORPORATED AS PART OF THE DESIGN PROCESS FOR FRACTURE CRITICAL STRUCTURES IN THE CONSTELLATION PROGRAM DEVELOPMENT.  NDE TECHNIQUES TO DETECT FLAWS AND DAMAGE IN FRACTURE CRITICAL STRUCTURES ARE SPECIFIED IN NASA STANDARDS SUCH AS NASA-STD-5007 GENERAL FRACTURE CONTROL REQUIREMENTS FOR MANNED SPACEFLIGHT SYSTEMS AND NASA-STD-5009 NONDESTRUCTIVE EVALUATION REQUIREMENTS FOR FRACTURE CRITICAL METALLIC COMPONENTS.  TO MOST EFFECTIVELY USE SUCH NDE TECHNIQUES, IT IS IMPERATIVE TO INCLUDE THE CONSIDERATION OF INSPECTION REQUIREMENTS AS PART OF THE DESIGN PROCESS, AND IN FACT, THIS WAS SPECIFIED IN THE SPACE SHUTTLE ORBITER FRACTURE CONTROL PLAN.  OTHERWISE, IT IS OFTEN THE CASE THAT THE CRITICAL COMPONENT, AS OPTIMIZED FOR PERFORMANCE, PROVES DIFFICULT, IF NOT IMPOSSIBLE, TO INSPECT DUE TO THE COMPLEXITY OF STRUCTURAL DESIGN OR THE INCORPORATION OF NEW AND ADVANCED COMPOSITE MATERIALS.  SUBSTANTIAL BUDGET EXPENDITURES AND SCHEDULE DELAYS ARE OFTEN THEN REQUIRED TO DEVELOP AND DEMONSTRATE EFFECTIVE NDE TECHNIQUES FOR CRITICAL COMPONENTS NOT DESIGNED FOR INSPECTION.  TO AVOID SUCH PROBLEMS AS NASA MOVES FORWARD IN THE CONSTELLATION PROGRAM TO DEVELOP THE CREW EXPLORATION VEHICLE, CREW LAUNCH VEHICLE, AND FOLLOW-ON SPACECRAFT AND HABITAT STRUCTURES, IT IS ESSENTIAL TO PROVIDE DESIGN TOOLS THAT WILL ENABLE RAPID ASSESSMENT OF THE FEASIBILITY OF NDE METHODS AS PART OF THE DESIGN PROCESS FOR CRITICAL SYSTEM COMPONENTS (THERMAL PROTECTION SYSTEMS, PRESSURE SYSTEMS, COMPOSITE STRUCTURES, ETC.).  COMPUTATIONAL NDE METHODOLOGIES ARE REQUIRED TO PREDICT THE RESPONSE FOR A VARIETY OF NDE METHODS (ULTRASONIC, RADIOGRAPHIC, THERMOGRAPHIC, ELECTROMAGNETIC, OPTICAL, ETC.) IN COMPLEX AEROSPACE STRUCTURES.  IT IS CRITICAL TO FOCUS RESOURCES IN THIS AREA DUE TO THE ELEVATED IMPORTANCE OF INSPECTION FOR ASSURING SAFE DEVELOPMENT OF CONSTELLATION PROGRAM COMPONENTS. NASA INTENDS TO UTILIZE A SOFTWARE PROGRAM PURCHASED UNDER THIS ORDER TO CONDUCT VIRTUAL INSPECTION TO PREDICT WHETHER THE GUIDED WAVE METHOD IS ACTUALLY A GOOD METHOD TO CHOOSE FOR INSPECTION FOR A VARIETY OF EXPLORATION HARDWARE.  BY DEVELOPING VIRTUAL INSPECTION TOOLS, WE MAY BE ABLE TO COMPUTATIONALLY MODEL INSPECTIONS TO DETERMINE THEIR FEASIBILITY PRIOR TO ACTUALLY OBTAINING SPECIMENS AND PERFORMING INSPECTIONS.  THIS EFFORT CAN THUS RESULT IN SIGNIFICANT TIME AND COST SAVINGS.  THERE IS CURRENTLY NO KNOWN COMMERCIALLY-AVAILABLE COMPUTATIONAL MODELING VIRTUAL INSPECTION SOFTWARE PACKAGE SPECIFIC TO ULTRASONIC GUIDED WAVE INSPECTION.

Description: The self-adaptive Earth Predictive System (SEPS) concept combines Earth System Models (ESM) and Earth Observations (EO) into one system. EO measures the Earth system state while ESM predicts the evolution of the state. A feedback mechanism processes EO measurements and feeds them into ESM during model runs or as initial conditions. A feed-forward mechanism analyzes the ESM predictions against science goals for scheduling optimized/targeted observations. The SEPS framework automates the Feedback and Feed-forward mechanisms (theFF-loop). Scientists from GMU, GSFC, and UBMC will collaborate to 1) develop a general SEPS framework for dynamic, interoperable coupling between ESMs and EO, based on open, consensus-based standards; 2) inplement and deploy the the framework and plug in diverse sensors and data systems to demonstrate the plug-in-EO-and-play capability; and 3) prototype a Bird- Migration-Model-to-aid-avian-influenza-prediction SEPS and an atmospheric chemistry composition SEPS using this framework, to demonstrate the frameworks' plug-in-ESM-and-play capability and its applicability as a common infrastructure for supporting the focus areas of NASA research. This project will significantly advance 1) dynamic, interoperable and live coupling of ESM with the sensor web; 2) the sensor web from concept to peration with existing sensors and data sources; and 3) the use of service-oriented architecture in modeling and integration. The project will improve the accuracy and timeliness of monitoring and predicting rapidly changing Earch phenomena, suca as sever weather and air pollution. The 3-year project will start in October 2006. The entry TRL is 4 ad the exit TRL is 7.

Description: The Earth Sciences Directorate of the NASA/Goddard Space Flight Center and the College of Computer, Mathematical, and Physical Sciences, University of Maryland at College Park, share common research goals in the areas of meteorology, oceanography, terrestrial physics, climate research, chemistry of the earth's atmosphere, and satellite research. A cooperative agreement was signed by both parties in 1993 to establish a Joint Center for Earth System Science that serves as a center for multi-disciplinary research in Earth System Science. In 1999 the Earth System Science Interdisciplinary Center (ESSIC) by a cooperative agreement that superseded the original. ESSIC serves as a means to increase the effectiveness of research and teaching through close collaboration by both parties, and serve as a means to train personnel for research in Earth System Science. This proposal requests funding to enable the UMCP and GSFC researchers to conduct new research through the collaborative research program within the ESSIC frame of reference for the next four years. The scientific objectives of this proposal encompass four major research areas: climate variability and change; atmospheric composition and processes; the global carbon cycle (including terrestrial and marine ecosystems/land use/cover change), and the global water cycle. Research is conducted through in situ and remotely sensed observations, together with component and coupled ocean-atmosphere-land modeling. This multi-pronged approach provides a foundation for understanding and forecasting changes in the global environment and regional implications. Data assimilation and regional downscaling are used to link the observations and models, enabling us to study the interactions between the physical climate system and biogeochemical cycles from global to regional scales.

Description: Multi-Satellite Observations of Flux Transfer Events FTE durations and inter-arrival times provide important information concerning the generation mechanism and dynamics of reconnection on the magnetopause. We will survey the characteristics multiple FTEs observed in three data sets. First, we will examine Interball-1 observations during the period from 1995 to 1999. In particular, we will explore the relationship between the energy within individual FTEs and the accumulated free energy since the last event. We want to determine whether or not there are special conditions in the solar wind and interplanetary magnetic field that favor the generation of multiple FTEs. Second, we will survey FTE data sets from Geotail. Geotail observations permit us to study ion and electron velocity distribution functions within FTEs, enabling determination of connectivity to the magnetopause through a survey of particle streaming. Finally, we will examine observations by NASA's forthcoming THEMIS mission (launch in February 2007). Observations from the five near-equatorial satellites in this mission can also be used to determine the dimensions of FTEs on the magnetopause.

Description: MERCURY'S EXOSPHERE-COMPOSITION, VARIABILITY AND SOLAR WIND INTERACTION I propose to obtain MESSENGER MASCS data, and to use it, along with available data from other instruments onboard MESSENGER and ground-based observations, to uncover the relationship between the extreme surface of Mercury, its exosphere, and the external environment and the magnetic fields. The composition and distribution of exospheric species about Mercury provides insight into both surface composition and responses to external processes. The spatial anisotropies of the exosphere may reflect variations in the surface composition, short-term depletion or enhancement of volatiles, external forcing, or recycling patterns. Short term volatile redistribution will be distinguished from the underlying crustal composition by using the UV measurements to deduce the exospheric composition and distribution as a function of time, while using the visual and infrared channels on MASCS to determine the underlying mineral composition also as a function of time. Temporal variations in the exosphere can reflect changes in external influences on the planetary surface, such as particle sputtering, thermal or photon effects, and micrometeoroid bombardment. In order to distinguish the source processes, we will use a current atmosphere model which is coupled with a magnetosphere model, and we will complete and refine a Monte Carlo model. We will compute photon scattering coefficients (g-values) as needed. Working closely with the magnetospheres team, we will be able to identify source and loss processes for volatiles and for those refractory species. As part of an established observing program, we will obtain ground-based data that will show a larger context within which to plan and interpret MESSENGER MASCS observations. We will establish and maintain an educational website that will make physics phun in the context of Mercury science. Mariner 10 established that Mercury is very different than it was previously believed to be, and now thirty years later we still have not been able to explain why Mercury is so different. NASA 's strategic goal, to learn how the Sun's family of planets and minor bodies originated and evolved, will not be achieved until we understand the strange little planet nearest to the Sun. Mercury's weak magnetic field and its interaction with the strong solar wind is part of this puzzle, and the tenuous exosphere is part of this dance. Redistribution and loss rates of volatiles and refractories alike can be established by this program. The ionization and acceleration of atoms that make up the exosphere also give us a window into the space environment near Mercury, a potentially hazardous environment to humans. The continuous loss of Mercury's exosphere to space also adds heavy species to the space environment, and these are entrained in the solar wind and convected outward. Thus an understanding of this small exosphere/magnetosphere lends progress in exploration of the space environment.

Description: Measuring Particles, Antiparticles, and Isotopes in the Cosmic Radiation Cosmic rays propagate through the Galaxy by scattering off magnetic irregularities in a process described as diffusion. The particles reaching Earth from their distant sources are modified by interactions with interstellar matter as they are guided through the interstellar gas/plasma by the galactic magnetic fields. The interactions produce secondary particles whose abundance relative to the primary particles is a measure of the amount of material traversed. This relative abundance and the secondary particle energy distributions are keys to understanding the nature and distribution of sources. In addition to known astronomical objects, possible exotic sources would include antimatter, dark matter, primordial black holes, etc. The goal Otis proposal is to study the sensitivity of searching for dark matter in the cosmic-ray antiparticle channels, with a focus on positrons. One major objective is to develop an optimal measurement strategy for positrons, including reduction of the signal. selection uncertainties. Our previous studies have demonstrated that systematic uncertainties present a serious challenge to precision measurements of these rare particles, which may be key to one of the fundamental questions in the 2003 National Academy of Science, Board on Physics and Astronomy report "Connecting Quarks with the Cosmos: Eleven Science Questions for the New Century", specifically "What is Dark Matter?" Previous investigations with balloon-borne magnetic spectrometers indicate that the positron fraction has an excess in the 7 - lOGeV range that continues to higher energies. This could be a "smoking gun" for the dark matter signature from the annihilation of neutralinos, but it might also be an artifact of systematical uncertainty in measurements dominated by a cosmic-ray background. A new balloon-borne instrument optimized to measure 1 - 50 GeV positrons and electrons with sensitivity much better than that of the previous experiments could discriminate between these possibilities with a 30-day balloon flight around Antarctica. Our study plan includes modeling a magnetic spectrometer with an optimal combination of acceptance, maximum detectable rigidity, and particle identification capability for measuring the cosmic-ray positron/electron ratio with a high degree of confidence. Description: Advanced MHD modeling of the magntosphere of Mercnry to snpport the Messenger mission Mercury is one of the most interesting planets in the field of comparative magnetospheric physics. Our knowledge of the composition and the dynamics of its enigmatic magnetosphere is limited to what we learned from two of the three Mariner 10 flybys in 1974 and 1975, and from a limited number of optical earth-based observations. The Messenger mission, designed to flyby and orbit Mercury starting from 2007 to 2010 (Solomon et at, 2001), comes as a unique opportunity to improve our understanding of this complex magnetospheric system and the extent of its interaction with the solar wind. The objective of this investigation is to support Messenger's science operations by conducting a detailed study of the interaction processes taking place between the solar wind and the Hermean magnetosphere and by characterizing the resulting magnetospheric structures. More specifically, this research aims to: a)provide a reliable theoretical model that combines dynamics and basic chemistry analysis to serve as a tool of expertise during the implementation of the mission science operations and to help interpret accurately the magnetospheric data that will be returned by Messenger's magnetometer (MAG) and plasma spectrometer (EPPS); b) investigate the mechanisms of mass and energy transfer between the solar wind, the magnetosphere, the exosphere and the surface of Mercury, and characterize the induced electric currents that connect different regions of Mercury's magnetospheric system; and c) study in detail the variability of the Hermean magnetosphere and its response to transient or permanent changes in the solar wind conditions and assess the implication of such variability to the mission science operations as they are planned. Our investigation will use the capabilities of the time-dependant multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model that we developed during the past few years to study the interaction of the solar wind with tenuous atmospheres/exospheres. The use of this approach will bring a substantial improvement to the description of the mechanisms responsible for shaping the Hermean magnetosphere. We will initially constrain and validate our model using data from Mariner 10 and Messenger's flybys of Mercury, which later will allow us to provide an analysis tool that will serve during the Messenger orbital phase. Then, this model will be refined and improved during the orbital phase of the mission to quickly assimilate the data returned by the magnetospheric instruments onboard of the spacecraft and to provide analysis that will in return help optimize the science operations.

Description: Decision Support Through Earth Science Results The purpose of this NASA Applications Division and SSAI effort is to support an applications project conducted by FEWS NET collaborators Molly Brown, James Verdin and Malaria expert Stephen Connor. The Global Inventory Monitoring and Modeling Studies (GIMMS) group of the Goddard Space Flight Center will conduct interdisciplinary applied research and data acquisition, analysis, and distribution to support famine and malaria early warning. Two new products will be developed using NASA data, and will be integrated into the FEWS DSS to enhance its functioning: 1) coarse resolution climate information for advance prediction of climate-driven food security hazards, and 2) a malaria transmission index based on biophysical variables. This activity would produce and distribute five operational indices based on global NASA data products: a standardized NDVI index (SNI), a standardized precipitation index (SPI), a standardized relative humidity index (SRI), and a standardized total precipitable water index (SQI). Standardization and broadening of the already used NDVI and precipitation to include humidity and precipitable water will significantly improve the FEWS NET DSS's ability to detect and quantify reductions in food production due to drought and flooding. Short-lag projections of indicators will enable decision makers to look one to four months into the future. Satellite observations will play a strong role in making these projections.

Description: Understanding Propagation Characteristics of Heavy Ions to Assess the Contribution of Solar Flares to Large SEP Events Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) events are the most powerful explosions in the solar system, able to create high radiation levels at Earth with little warning. In the large events, particles are known to be accelerated both in the solar flare itself and by the shock driven by the associated Coronal Mass-Ejection (CME). The flare SEPs are known to have a distinct compositional signature including enhancements in electrons, the rare isotope 3He, and the relative abundance of Fe compared to O. Recent observations have shown that these energetic particle signatures of flare particles are often present in events with powerful CMEs along with shock-accelerated particles. This raises the question what are the basic mechanisms responsible for the most intense SEP events? For example: are the SEPs from the flare directly? or are they pre-accelerated at the flare and further energized by the shock? or are remnant suprathermals from previous flares supplying a critical component of the seed population? The investigation proposed here probes these questions using the heavy ion signature of flare material, namely enhanced Fe/O ratios and their variation with time and energy. We have recently found new evidence that interplanetary scattering plays a critical role in a majority of large western hemisphere SEP events. We describe how to use these observations to provide an observational basis for developing our theoretical understanding of the important role played by particle scattering during large SEP events. Specifically, the observations along with detailed modeling will enable us to place limits on the contributions of particle transport processes to the observed timing and composition in large SEP events. Our proposed study will therefore provide a sound framework for other modelers and TR&T teams to better understand the primary causes ofthe variability and the temporal evolution ofthe heavy ion abundances, such as the Fe/O ratio. This, in turn, will allow us to assess the relative contributions of flare particles (either indirectly in the form of seed particles or directly in the form of high-energy particles) to large gradual SEP events observed at 1 AU.

Description: Towards an Archeology of Elliptical Galaxies Despite significant progress, our understanding of the formation of giant elliptical galaxies is far from complete. While the fundamental role of hierarchical merging and early (z>2) establishment of the stellar population are clear, the nature of the protogalactic fragments, the timing and details of star formation, and the role of dissipation and feedback are unresolved. Many of these puzzles connect to complex gasdymanical processes that are not directly observable, but that leave clues in the form of the level and pattern of heavy element enrichment of stars and hot interstellar plasma. XMM-Newton RGS observations represent the state-of-the-art for high resolution spectroscopy of high central X-ray surface brightness elliptical galaxies for the foreseeable future. In concert with XMM-Newton EPIC and/or Suzaku XIS data, we will utilize archival RGS data (1) to unambiguously constrain the elemental abundances of N, O, Ne, Mg, Si, S, and Fe. Simultaneously, we will (2) investigate the degree of temperature homogeneity, and evaluate and quantify the effects of (3) turbulence and (4) resonant scattering. Our primary goals are to derive hot ISM abundances as completely and accurately as is currently possible, and apply detailed astrophysical phenomenological models that we have specifically constructed to interpret these results. In this way we utilize X-ray spectroscopy to help deconstruct how elliptical galaxies, and the stellar populations that compose them, form and evolve.

Description: TELESCOPE SCIENCE INSTITUTE A GENERAL TOOL FOR ASTROPHYSICAL DATA ANALYSIS SUMMARY: We propose to develop a powerful, integrated tool for astrophysics data analysis deployed as a web service to significantly simplify the process of comparing calibrated astrophysical data with theoretical stellar population models. Tools to do this exist today but only as many separate packages and mastering their use can be challenging, leading different users to obtain inconsistent results. Building upon our extensive experience with Synphot (a synthetic photometry algorithm) and Chorizos (a Bayesian multi-parametric chi-squared fitting package), we will construct an integrated analysis tool that will allow users to easily and reliably compute a variety of fundamental observables including synthetic photometry from theoretical spectral energy distributions (SEDs), color corrections, and bandpass transformations. The tool will also readily support the cross-calibration of photometry from different archives, SED model fitting, statistical analyses of Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagrams, and self-consistent prediction of astronomical instrument performance. As part of this project, we will assemble and maintain a comprehensive and updatable repository of throughputs of astronomical instruments and filters, stellar and synthetic spectra, and evolutionary models. The web service and user interface will be able to ingest photometric and spectroscopic data directly from observatory archives, while allowing users to input their own tables and models, run batch processes, see results in graphic format, and produce output in Virtual Observatory compatible formats. Our proposed tool will enhance the scientific productivity of NASAlS astronomy missions by greatly facilitating the analysis of calibrated data extracted from multiple archives. This proposal requests funding to produce a robust, working system (beyond the prototype phase) that will be ready for widespread community use at the completion of the proposed project. We will seek additional funds from the Space Telescope Science Institute for long-term support of the system.

Description: I propose a comprehensive investigation of the Mercurian exosphere that is focused on answering several open science questions in the literature. To accomplish this, four objectives are proposed that span the range of science issues: 1) adapt an existing Monte Carlo model for use as an investigative tool; 2) map the exospheric composition and structure; 3) determine the spatial and temporal variability of the exosphere; and 4) identify the exospheric source and loss processes. The conclusions of this investigation bear directly on two of the primary science questions of the MESSENGER mission: 1) "What volatiles are important at Mercury?" and 2) "What are the unusual materials at Mercury's poles?" To carry out the proposed objectives, I will work closely with the MASCS instrument team. MASCS is the primary workhorse instrument for the study of the Mercurian exosphere, and the proposed objectives mesh well with its defined role. I will also collaborate with the other MESSENGER instrument teams to ensure that the supporting observations needed for this study are obtained. The proposed investigation combines an active role in observation planning with targeted science goals to meet the objectives. The development of modeling and analysis tools, detailed data products, a rigorous archival plan, and interactive EIPO activities are integrated with the primary science activities to provide a comprehensive MESSENGER Participating Scientist investigation.

Description: Those brave individuals traveling in space are exposed to a variety of radiations. It is known that exposure to ionizing radiation can lead to a greater risk for developing cancer later. Since there is currently no way to protect astronauts from space radiations, it is important that the biological consequences of exposures to these radiations are understood. Using proton and iron ion radiations we will investigate the delayed effects of radiation exposure based on the type of radiation and the rate at which the radiation dose is delivered. Specifically, we will investigate those deleterious effects observed in the progeny of irradiated cells multiple cell generations after the initial exposure. These deleterious effects are grouped under the term of radiation-induced genomic instability and are thought to be an early step in the carcinogenic process. We will also compare these delayed effects of direct irradiation with the effects observed in cells that were not directly ?hit?, but were bystanders at the time of irradiation. The primary objective of this proposal is to evaluate the differences in dose rate effects and radiation quality among protons and mixed proton/heavy ions in the induction of delayed genomic instability and bystander effects. We will accomplish this by measuring cell survival, gene mutations/deletions and rearrangements, and other forms of chromosome damage. Further this project will explore the possible molecular mechanisms underlying this biological process

Description: International Workshop on Global Dimming/Brightening: Trends in Solar Radiation at the Surface, their Causes, and Environmental Impacts Ground-based measurements indicate that the amount of solar radiation reaching the surface of the Earth decreased significantly during the three decades from 1960 to 1990 (Stanhill and Cohen, 2001). The term Global Dimming was coined to describe this phenomenon. More recent surface observations as well as satellite observations suggest that this trend has reversed since 1990 (Global Brightening). The reasons for these variations are not clear, but must be linked to changes in atmospheric properties - clouds, aerosols, gases - and not the Sun, since solar irradiance variations are small compared to the observed dimming/brightening. Such trends in solar radiation could have profound effects on climate and biogeochemistry, on both global and regional scales. For example, dimming would reduce greenhouse warming rates, while brightening would amplify greenhouse effects. It is of critical importance to review the observational basis for these trends, the factors controlling them, and their environmental impacts.

Description: THE FINE STRUCTURE OF ACTIVE REGIONS AND WEAK MAGNETIC FIELDS FROM MDI IMAGES In response to NASA Roses 2006 B.7 - Living With a Star Targeted Research and Technology Program (NNH06ZDA001N-LWS), we submit this proposal entitled "The Fine Structure of Active Regions and Weak Magnetic Fields from MDI Images" under the Focused Science Topic: "Solar Origins of Irradiance Variations". The goal of the proposed research is to carry out a detailed study of solar spectral irradiance variations from UV to the infrared wavelengths and to compare the measured spectral irradiance changes to the observed variations in total solar and spectral irradiances. The proposed investigation will focus on the following three major science questions: (1) How does the formation and evolution of sunspots and active regions influence spectral irradiance variations; (2) what is the energy budget of solar active regions; and (3) how to detect and characterize the weak magnetic fields outside of active regions? The proposed research will directly address one of the Focused Science Topics: namely, our research will study in detail the magnetic topology of active regions and their role in irradiance changes to better understand the physical processes by which solar magnetic activity causes these variations. To achieve our goals, we will use the full disk and high resolution MDI images. Solar spectral irradiance to be used in this study will come from the SORCE/SIM experiment and also from the UARS/SUSIM and SOLSTICE experiments at UV wavelengths. Description: INNOVATIVE PARALLEL FRAMEWORK FOR COUPLING ADVANCED ROTORCRAFT AEROMECHANIC SIMULATIONS SUMMARY: The main objectives of this proposed research are to extend the capabilities of the CHIMPS (Coupler for High-performance Multi-Physics Simulations) infrastructure by the addition of: (1) an innovative time-accurate and energy preserving tight structural/fluid coupling methodology, and (2) a hole-cutting algorithm for dynamic adaptive unstructured overset mesh connectivity. Specifically, the fluid/structural coupling framework will include the following capabilities: (1) ensure conservation of virtual work when CFD loads are mapped onto CSD, (2) ensure accuracy of interpolation when CSD deformations are mapped onto CFD, (3) preserve the orders of accuracy of CFD and CSD solvers during time integration, (4) incorporate a mechanism to determine trim control angles based on flight dynamic targets, (5) support efficient parallel implementations of CFD and CSD, and (6) ensure a modular and generalized interface whereby the individual CSD and CFD codes can be replaced with different codes of similar functionality. The parallel unstructured overset grid connectivity framework will include the following capabilities: (I) determination of hole and fringe points and establishing domain connectivity information, (2) be scalable for unstructured parallel computing, (3) work on dynamic moving body problems, (4) incorporate the ability for the addition and/or removal of specified mesh points to facilitate adaptive meshes, (5) support high-order interpolation, and (6) work in stand alone mode as a preprocessor and exist as callable libraries to be directly callable by other simulation codes. It is expected that the validated frameworks resulting from this research will significantly advance the state-of-the-art in physics-based computational techniques for rotary wing applications in the area of efficient coupling strategies for domain-hybridization. The proposed overset grid library will be the first such scalable library for unstructured parallel computing. The proposed tight-coupled CFDICSD approach will iteratively become equivalent to strong-coupling at each time step, and along with the loose-coupled flight dynamics capabilities will enable first-principles (no ad hoc coupling) based simulation of maneuvers and provide a detailed physical understanding of the rotor aerodynamics and structural dynamics in such maneuvers. The resulting frameworks will result in rotorcraft simulation capabilities that are time-accurate, efficient, parallel and tight-coupled; furthermore, various CFD and CSD modules will be interchanged, with the results compared to each other as well as validated against existing flight test data in steady level-flight as well as transient maneuvers. Such a physics-based simulation capability will form the basis for next generation flight mechanics and multi-disciplinary design-analysis-optimization analyses.

Description: Decision Support Through Earth Science Results The purpose of this NASA Applications Division and SSAI effort is to support an applications project conducted by FEWS NET collaborators Molly Brown, James Verdin and Malaria expert Stephen Connor. The Global Inventory Monitoring and Modeling Studies (GIMMS) group of the Goddard Space Flight Center will conduct interdisciplinary applied research and data acquisition, analysis, and distribution to support famine and malaria early warning. Two new products will be developed using NASA data, and will be integrated into the FEWS DSS to enhance its functioning: 1) coarse resolution climate information for advance prediction of climate-driven food security hazards, and 2) a malaria transmission index based on biophysical variables. This activity would produce and distribute five operational indices based on global NASA data products: a standardized NDVI index (SNI), a standardized precipitation index (SPI), a standardized relative humidity index (SRI), and a standardized total precipitable water index (SQI). Standardization and broadening of the already used NDVI and precipitation to include humidity and precipitable water will significantly improve the FEWS NET DSS's ability to detect and quantify reductions in food production due to drought and flooding. Short-lag projections of indicators will enable decision makers to look one to four months into the future. Satellite observations will play a strong role in making these projections.

Description: INVESTIGATION OF AEROSOL SPECTRAL ABSORPTION PROPERTIES FOR UV TO NIR SUMMARY: Knowledge of aerosol spectral absorption is critically important to develop methods of aerosol remote sensing and to understand the effect of aerosols on climate. Many assumptions are involved in the remote sensing of aerosols: the MODIS aerosol algorithms assume a particular aerosol single scattering albedo for each wavelength; the TOMS aerosol algorithm assumes that the aerosol imaginary index does not change between the two UV channels; and similar set of assumptions is used for OMI. The present algorithms to invert satellite data for aerosols do not include the real complexities of the aerosol spectral properties and must rely on many assumptions. Presently, there is not enough data to clearly formulate and evaluate these assumptions. Our present knowledge of the spectral single scattering albedo of aerosols, for the entire atmospheric column, is derived mainly from AERONET data for a limited spectral range of 0.44 to 1.03pm. Field experiments commonly report values of the single scattering albedo of aerosol layers but restrict their measurements for the center of the visible spectrum, or very limited spectral range. In this proposal we will generate and make available a systematic database of UV-NIR spectral properties of aerosols from different locations worldwide (USA, Brazil, Africa, China, etc) to be used in the design of proper satellite algorithms and model simulations. We have recently developed an in situ method (Martins et al., 2005) to measure the aerosol spectral absorption efficiency across the solar spectrum from 0.35pm to 2.5pm. In this work we will extend this method to 0.25pm and measure the wide spectral absorption properties of organics and other complex aerosols. Recent analysis shows that aerosol produced from high temperature combustion (car engines) have spectral absorption inversely proportional to the wavelength, as expected from spectrally neutral refractive index. However aerosol produced in tow combustion temperatures, e.g. biomass burning has an elevated absorption in the UV above the inverse wavelength dependence. Urban pollution aerosols often show enhanced UV absorption that can be several times larger than the absorption by black carbon itself. Absorption by dust aerosols from different locations also shows particular spectral dependence features. This knowledge is critical to develop better methods to invert aerosol properties from the A-train data (e.g. OM1 + MODIS) and to better model the aerosol effect on climate. In addition to improve satellite retrievals, the correct interpretation of the wide spectral absorption efficiency data can also characterize the aerosol composition allowing the discrimination between black carbon, certain organic materials, dust, and its combinations. These measurements produce also additional information on internal or external mixtures and the relative size of the aerosol absorbers, all critical parameters to model the effect of aerosols on the Earth system.

Description: This project uses computational modeling tools to explore how the motions of the particles that comprise the rings of Saturn tell us what they are made of - and perhaps even how they came to evolve to their current state. Specifically, we will model the gravitational effects of small moonlets near the edges of gaps in the rings, and study the perturbations caused by those moonlets on the ring material. Understanding how this material responds to these disturbances is key to understanding how this system evolves a" a whole. We use an N-body computer code to model the motions of tens of thousands to millions of ring particles as they interact by self-gravity and hard-sphere collisions. The simulations focus on small patches of the rings: tens to thousands of kilometers in scale. These small patches include a perturbing moonlet, a few kilometers in scale, which gravitationally dominates the ring particles. The code uses a tree-based algorithm to reduce the computational burden of gravity calculations, and is optimized for parallel processors to increase throughput. Simulation results will be applicable to any dense debris system interacting gravitationally with nearby perturbers including Saturn's Keeler and Encke gaps - as well as providing insight into the dynamics of protoplanets embedded in gaseous and/or planetesimal disks. These gaps have been studied recently by the Cassini spacecraft, and our simulations have reproduced observed persistent ring/gap dynamical features, such as downstream edge waves. Further comparison with Cassini data will allow our simulations to reveal elusive data; for example: the mass and eccentricity of embedded moons; and spin parameters, thermal properties, collisional characteristics, and surface composition of the particles. Knowledge of these data provides clues to the origin of the material, and perhaps even the rings themselves. The research proposed here is relevant to NASA's objectives, and those of the Planetary Science Research Program, as it is enabled by the current robotic exploration of the outer solar system (specifically, by the Cassini spacecraft), and addresses two of the fundamental science questions the Planetary Science Division asks: "How did the Sun's family of planets and minor bodies originate?" and "How did the Solar System evolve to its current diverse state?" The ring particles, and the embedded moonlets, are "small bodies," and this research seeks to find new information on these bodies in order to better understand their origin and evolution. For this work, we have access to both local Beowulf Linux clusters and supercomputers. Code development and testing, along with preliminary investigations, will be achieved using the Dept. of Astronomy's cluster "Borg," and the High Performance Computing Cluster's "Deepthought." Large science runs will be performed on supercomputers, with 175,000 SUs (CPU-hours) already awarded on the nationwide TeraGrid system for this project

Description: Observations with ROSAT, ASCA, and recently Chandra have demonstrated the existence of Vela-like pulsar + wind-nebula X-ray emission from deep within the unusual radio nebula DA 495, which has a poorly understood annular morphology. The available evidence suggests that DA 495 is a rare, and therefore valuable, example of an aging "plerionic" supernova remnant (SNR). Direct constraints on the system's age, e.g., from the spin-down timescale of the putative central pulsar, have not been achievable-because of short exposure times and the soft spectrum of the unresolved source, none of the past observations has been capable of detecting pulsations. For the same reason, the energetics of the engine driving the X-ray and radio nebulosities are poorly constrained. We propose a 50 ksec XMM observation of DA 495 to search for pulsations and obtain high-quality spectra of both the point-like and diffuse emission components, to better understand this object and the observationally unexplored aging process for plerionic SNRs.

Description: We analyzed FUSE, HST/IUE and optical spectra of O-type stars in the Milky Way and found Teff and luminosities significantly lower (about 10 to 20percent for Teff) than previous determinations for our sample stars, and than values assigned to their spectral types from previous compilations. This result has relevant implications for our understanding of massive stars' evolution, and of the energy balance of HII regions. Although modeling of optical lines with line-blanketed atmospheres also indicates lower effective temperatures than classical calibrations, the hitherto still quantitatively discrepant (between optical and UV diagnostics) results on Teff and especially mass loss rates could be reconciled with a revised inclusion of X-rays from shocks and clumping in the wind modeling. These effects can only be constrained by lines in the FUSE range (e.g. Bianchi, Herald, and Garcia 2006). Such analysis for a representative number of stars covering the early spectral types, will ultimately provide a refined calibration of the temperature scale versus spectral type and luminosity class, as well as other important parameters such as mass loss rate. We propose to observe a final sample of four Milky Way stars, to remedy remaining gaps in the coverage of early spectral types in the list of FUSE observed or approved Galactic stars. By contrast, a very good coverage of spectral types for Magellanic Cloud stars is already available in the FUSE archive. A similar sampling of the early spectral types in the Milky Way will provide a unique opportunity to compare massive stars' parameters among the three galaxies with very different metallicities (MW, LMC, SMC). The data will have additional value as an archival resource for population synthesis work, and ISM studies.
