Description: We will implement a scalable, modular, extensible, ensemble-based Mars data assimilation system (Mars-DAS) by coupling an existing Local Ensemble Transform Kalman Filter (LETKF) algorithm with the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory GFDL Mars GCM. We will use this system to carry out predictability experiments for the Martian atmosphere. The proposed research is expected to lead to (i) the development of a new practical tool, a state-of-the-art DAS to assimilate Martian weather observations collected in the past and future (ii) a thorough assessment of the potential value of different observing strategies and (iii) new theoretical results on the predictability of the Martian circulation. The LETKF, developed at the University of Maryland, will provide estimates of the state of the Martian atmosphere by optimally combining observations with short-range atmospheric forecasts from the GFDL Mars general circulation model. The LETKF is the tool of choice for Mars data assimilation because it is able to extract maximum information from sparse, asynchronous observations. In addition to an estimate of the atmospheric state, the LETKF DAS will also provide an ensemble of perturbed initial states that represent the uncertainty in the state estimate. These initial ensemble perturbations will have realistic magnitude and structure in the sense that they will correctly reflect the effects of the deployment of the observational resources and the effects of the observational errors on the initial uncertainties. The realistic magnitude and structure of the perturbation will ensure that the estimated forecast error growth rates will also be realistic. This approach will lead to a coherent view of the limits of predictability in the Mars atmosphere. Such knowledge is critical to answering key scientific questions about Marsi meteorology, such as the role of the different quasi-permanent and transient components of the Martian circulation in limiting predictability and the effects of the different observing strategies on predictability. The scientific expertise of the proposing team in data assimilation, ensemble forecasting, predictability research, numerical modeling of the Mars atmosphere and Martian weather observations ensures that the aforementioned objectives will be achieved with high probability. We propose to create and make available to the community a data assimilation tool, providing researchers easy access to a state-of-the-art data assimilation system to generate self-consistent and comprehensive four-dimensional analyses based on observed data. It is expected that this will accelerate the advancement of research in Mars. In summary, a successful analysis/forecast system coupling the LETKF with the Mars GCM will provide a powerful tool to investigate key science questions and support future robotic and human missions.

Description: The amended work plan contained herein describes activities we propose to carry out during the last 19 months of support, for an award that is in "progress," with a total of 36 monhts of support. The award was for a proposal entitled "Measurements, Modeling, and Analyses in Support of Aura and other NASA Satellite Observations of Earth's Atmosphere (Aura Validation)," submitted to NASA NRA NNH04ZYS004-N. It was originally awarded when we were employed at the jet propulsion laborartoy, California Institute of Technolgy. On 1 September 2007, R. Salawitch and T. Canty will join the faculty of the University of Maryland, College Park. This statement describes the activities we propose to carry out during the final 19 months of support of this award, at the University of Maryland (UMd). We include a summary of the accomplishments during the initial period of support (Section 1.1), an amended work statement (Section 1.2), and a budget prepared by Umd (section4). The orginal proposal is included as an Appendix to this document. Our original proposal sought to quantify the factors that regulate stratospheric ozone using a variety of photochemical models tied to observations from Aura and many of the balloon and aircraft observations to be obtained by field campaigns outlined in the NRA. The orginally proposed research was use of a variety of esxisting models to tie together observations from Aura and measurements from field campaigns, to assist in the validation of observations from Aura and to enhance the scientific return from these missions. Description: Spatial searches over the celestial sphere represent the most frequent queries on astrophysics data sets. The AISRP program funded the original Hierarchical Triangular Mesh library which produced a very fast C++ search engine now used at more than 20 institutions over the world, also in various Earth Sciences applications. With the recent advances in the worldwide Virtual Observatory effort, we have now a standard XML data model for space-time data. The community is now ready to deploy sophisticated spatial search engines, but this requires an API with multiple language bindings and interfaces to multiple database platforms. We seek funding to rewrite, extend and refine our existing lihrary, make it fully compliant with the VO interface standards, and enhance its functionality and performance. The new implementation will consist of four layers: a kernel library with all the spatial algorithms, the code for the hierarchical tree representation of the regions, an extensible interface to describe the spherical regions, and a flexible and east interface to relational databases. We will add several new algorithms to the core of the existing library, develop a new VO-compliant API, and build several new language implementations that others can integrate with their own archives. We will develop a Web Services implementation of the library, accessible through remote calls. We will integrate our toolkit with the OpenSkyQuery framework for cross-matching large astronomical catalogs. We will provide a framework for critical analysis of the HTM toolkit, including built-in unit testing modules. We will build Java, C++ and C# implementations of the library. We will also build a web-service based visualization toolkit to display the spherical regions specified in a selection. All our code from our three year proposal is public domain Open Source (FreeBSD) and made available to the public on-line.

Description: DESIGN, IMPLEMENTATION, AND ARCHIVING OF VERY LARGE SKY SURVEYS PLAY A CRITICAL ROLE IN TODAY'S ASTRONOMY RESEARCH. HOWEVER, ASTRONOMERS WILL BE UNABLE TO TAP THE RICHES OF THIS COLLECTION OF GIGABYTE, TERABYTE, AND (EVENTUALLY) PETABYTE CATALOGS WITHOUT A COMPUTATIONAL BACKBONE THAT INCLUDES SUPPORT FOR QUERIES AND DATA MINING ACROSS DISTRIBUTED VIRTUAL TABLES OF DC-CENTRALIZED, JOINED, AND INTEGRATED SKY SURVEY CATALOGS. MOREOVER, USE OF LOCAL DATA MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS SUCH AS MYDB, MYSPACE IN ASTROGRID, AND GRID BRICKS FOR STORING AND MANAGING USER'S LOCAL DATA IS BECOMING INCREASINGLY POPULAR. THIS IS OPENING UP THE POSSIBILITY OF CONSTRUCTING A PEER-TO-PEER (P2P) NETWORK FOR DATA SHARING AND MINING. THIS DOCUMENT PROPOSES RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT FOR A NEW GENERATION OF SCALABLE DATA ANALYTIC SERVICES FOR THE NVO BASED ON ADVANCED DISTRIBUTED AND P2P DATA MINING CAPABILITIES ACROSS MULTIPLE DATA REPOSITORIES. THIS RESEARCH WILL DEVELOP TECHNOLOGY FOR SUPPORTING WEB SERVICES WITHIN THE NVO THAT WILL ALLOW ASTRONOMY RESEARCHERS TO ANALYZE DATA FROM MULTIPLE SURVEYS USING FUNDAMENTALLY DISTRIBUTED ALGORITHMS. IT WILL ALSO DEVELOP SEVERAL DISTRIBUTED DATA MINING ALGORITHMS FOR ANALYSIS OF DISTRIBUTED ASTRONOMY CATALOGS WITHOUT REQUIRING THE DATA TO BE DOWNLOADED AND CENTRALIZED. SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES INCLUDE THE FOLLOWING ITEMS: (1) THE PROJECT WILL DESIGN AND IMPLEMENT DISTRIBUTED ALGORITHMS FOR COMPUTING STATISTICAL PRIMITIVES, PRINCIPAL COMPONENT ANALYSIS, AND OUTLIER DETECTION FROM DISTRIBUTED ASTRONOMY CATALOGS AND THEIR PARTIAL IMAGES STORED IN USERS' LOCAL DATA MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS. THESE ALGORITHMS WILL BE ABLE TO ANALYZE DATA WITHOUT REQUIRING SOURCE CATALOGS TO BE DOWNLOADED AND CENTRALIZED. (2) THE PROJECT WILL DEVELOP A PROTOTYPE SYSTEM WHICH WILL OFFER A RICH COLLECTION OF WEB-SERVICES BASED ON VARIOUS DDM ALGORITHMS. THIS SERVICE OFFERS A NOVEL AUGMENTATION TO THE EXISTING NVO ENVIRONMENT AND IT WILL SUPPORT A RICH VARIETY OF DATA MINING TASKS THAT WILL WORK IN A DISTRIBUTED FASHION. (3) THE DEVELOPED SYSTEM WILL BE TESTED USING SPECIFIC ASTRONOMICAL RESEARCH PROBLEMS. IN PARTICULAR, WE WILL EXPLORE THE MULTI-DIMENSIONAL MULTI-WAVELENGTH PARAMETER SPACE OF ASTROPHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF STARBURSTING GALAXIES. WE WILL SEARCH FOR UNUSUAL CORRELATIONS, OUTLIERS, SUB-CLUSTERS, AND FUNDAMENTAL PLANES WITHIN THE MULTI-DIMENSIONAL PARAMETER SPACE PRESENTED BY SEVERAL LARGE SURVEYS. TO CARRY OUT THIS RESEARCH WE WILL SET UP A SIMULATED DISTRIBUTED ASTRONOMY CATALOG ENVIRONMENT IN THE LAB USING DATA FROM PUBLICLY AVAILABLE SOURCE CATALOGS. OUR SYSTEM WILL BE BENCHMARKED ACCORDING TO SPEED, COMMUNICATION COST, AND ACCURACY. ACCURACY WILL BE VALIDATED WITHIN THE CONTEXT OF THE ASTRONOMY PROBLEM DESCRIBED ABOVE. THIS RESEARCH IS DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE ALSR PROGRAM FOR SEVERAL REASONS. FIRST, IT ENABLES INCREASED PRODUCTIVITY OF NASA'S SCIENCE MISSION DIRECTORATE (SMD) RESEARCH ENDEAVORS THROUGH RAPID MULTI-MISSION CORRELATIVE ANALYSIS, SUCH AS DISTRIBUTED AND P2P MINING OF THE LARGE SURVEY CATALOGS FROM GALEX, SPITZER, ZMASS, AND EVENTUALLY WISE. SECOND, THIS RESEARCH INVOLVES AN INTERDISCIPLINARY TEAM OF RESEARCHERS IN ASTROPHYSICS (BORNE), DATABASE TECHNOLOGIES(KARGUPTA, GIANNELLA), DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS (KARGUPTA), AND DISTRIBUTED DATA MINING (ALL). DR. BORNE IS A SENIOR MEMBER OF THE NVO PROJECT. WE ALSO HAVE STRONG SUPPORT FROM NASA'S SPACE SCIENCE DATA OPERATIONS OFFICE (SEE ATTACHED SUPPORTING LETTER) REGARDING THIS PROPOSED COLLABORATIVE PROJECT AND ITS TRANSITION TO THE PRACTICE. FINALLY, THIS PROJECT EXPLICITLY DEMONSTRATES THE RELEVANCE, APPLICABILITY, AND POTENTIAL IMPACT OF EMERGING INFORMATION TECHNOLOGIES TO SMD MISSIONS AND PROGRAMS. A TOTAL OF $722,543 IS REQUESTED FOR SUPPORTING THIS RESEARCH OVER THREE YEARS.

Description: MULTI-OBJECTIVE OPTIMAL SCHEDULING FOR SPACE SCIENCE APPLICATIONS We propose to develop and assess a new multi-objective multi-participant optimization application for scheduling space-based observatories. Our approach will address how to optimize scheduling given a set of competing global objectives for a mission as well as a large set of operational and scientific constraints. We will initially focus on James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) as it is under development and is representative of a broad class of science scheduling problems. We will also consider the requirements of the Space Interferometry Mission (SIM) to ensure and validate the generality of our approach. Multi-objective means retaining and exploiting information about multiple, often competing objectives, during schedule optimization. This is in contrast to optimization techniques that require the consolidation of all objectives into a single quantity to be optimized. Consolidation necessarily implies committing in advance to the relative importance of different objectives, and hides information that can be used to make scheduling more effective. Multi-participant means arcbitecting and designing the system to allow multiple users to work with the system at one time, generally in collaborative ways, but possibly independently. This is in contrast to approaches based on a single central scheduling process. By incorporating both of these capabilities into a single framework we gain more than we would from either one separately. This is because it is frequently the case that competing objectives arise directly from the various participants, and balancing these objectives requires the participants to cooperate and compromise. This work will advance the state of the art for observatory scheduling in three ways: (I) by providing simulation and trade study capabilities that will facilitate key early design choices; (2) by scheduling more responsively in reaction to interesting events or system capability changes, and (3) by optimizing competing objectives of the mission so that the overall science schedule is more efficient, and robust. The key elements of our approach are: a) a model-based representation of objectives, constraints, and preferences, which will provide a basis for schedule optimization and for flexible modification as the mission progresses b) an architecture to support multi-participant scheduling with both global and per-participant objectives c) multi-objective optimization algorithms to find and characterize Pareto-optimal solutions d) an experiment plan to systematically investigate and document our results e) the application of our approach to two distinct observatory missions, as a demonstration of its generality and applicability. Our approach will leverage our experience and familiarity with science planning and scheduling in past missions, including HST, Spitzer, Chandra, EUVE, FUSE, etc. from both operational and software perspectives. Description: IMPROVING REMOTE SENSED DATA PRODUCTS USING BAYESIAN METHODOLOGY FOR THE ANALYSIS OF COMPUTER MODEL OUTPUT The NASA Science Directorate supports an array of Earth Observing satellites which provide global coverage, whose observations are used to produce a wide array of data products, from sea surface temperature, to polar ice coverage, to plant type and growth rates. These are used in a wide variety of further scientific studies, and also as inputs to important policy decisions, especially those concerning the impact of human activity on the biosphere. Many of the studies of human impact concern changes over time. To accurately characterize changes it is vitally important that the uncertainties in the estimates of the quantities being observed are known, so that the uncertainty in the estimated changes can be accurately determined -- making scientific or policy decisions based on estimates with large, or worse, unknown or poorly determined errors, is poor science and poor policy. Many of the data products (eg Leaf Area Index (LAI), Photosynthetically Active Radiation (WAR) from MODIS) are produced by inverting a Radiative Transfer Model (RTM), which simulates the upwelling radiation at the top of the atmosphere (and so observed by the satellite) as a function of the biospheric parameters (e.g. land cover type; available water; leaf chemistry; etc.). These RTMs are implemented as complex computer codes, and the analysis and inversion of these codes is a challenging task. In the last several years the area of Bayesian Methods for the Analysis of Computer Model Output has made great progress, and is coming to a point where its wider application will show significant utility in application domains. These methods are well developed in the statistics literature, but are almost unknown in the GeoscienceiRemote Sensing domain (apart from Kriging). Applied to an RTM, these methods will allow the determination of: a) the uncertainty in the RTM output; b) the main effects, ie, which of the inputs is mainly responsible for the output uncertainty; c) validation using field data; d) rapid approximation of the RTM for use when computing the inverse; e) a direct model for the inverse incorporating uncertainty. Advances in these areas will improve the accuracy and utility of the data products. The RTM in operational use for estimating LA1 and WAR is the MOD15 algorithm. We will initially apply the methodology to the LCM (leaf-canopy model) RTM, a similar model to which we have more direct access. The methods and code developed will be readily applicable to MOD15 and other RTMs -- treated as a "black boxes" by the methodology. We will use a number of Bayesian nonparametric methods to approximate the LCM, including Gaussian Processes, and Dirichlet Process Mixtures, to study the robustness of the analysis to different models. The models will be built using runs of the LCM. First we will perform a sensitivity analysis to determine which inputs have most effect on the variability of the output, and so determine where more information is required about the distributions of the inputs. We will use the approximate model to enable practical inversion of the LCM, to determine the distribution over LA1 given measured reflectances. We will incorporate field data, and build a model of the bias between the LCM and the field data. This will result in a fully calibrated inversion procedure. A successful conclusion of the work in this proposal would demonstrate the utility of the methodology in an important application domain, with significant scientific and policymaking consequences, and would significantly advance the state-of-the-practice in remote sensing science.

Description: CLIMATE CHANGE AND ITS IMPACT ON THE ECOSYSTEM OF THE ARABIAN SEA The recent trend of declining winter and spring snow cover over Eurasia is causing a land-ocean thermal gradient that is particularly favorable to stronger southwest (summer) monsoonal winds (Goes et al., 2005). Since 1997, sea surface winds have been strengthening in the western Arabian Sea. This escalation in the intensity of summer monsoonal winds accompanied by enhanced upwelling along the coasts of Somalia and Oman, and a 350% increase in average summer time phytoplankton biomass in the western Arabian Sea, raises the intriguing possibility that the current warming trend in the Northern Hemisphere could make the Arabian Sea more productive. This three-year data (ship and satellite) analysis, data assimilation and regional modeling effort is aimed at probing remote and local controls on regional circulation and phytoplankton productivity and marine living resources in the Arabian Sea as they relate to climate change. In order to achieve our goals, we have put together an international research team consisting of oceanographers (physical, chemical and biological), atmospheric and fisheries scientists who will work together to: (1) Examine the dominant scales of coupling between atmospheric forcing (snow cover, land and sea radiation budgets, wind fields) and biological oceanographic responses (ocean circulation, mixed layer physics and stratification evolution, phytoplankton blooms). (2) Determine how large-scale climatic events (IOD, El-Nino) contribute to interannual and decadal variability in biological productivity. (3) Develop a coupled physical-biological model capable of simulating climate mediated changes in the circulation of the Arabian Sea and predicting the response of the Arabian Sea ecosystem and its living marine resources to climate change on seasonal, interannual and decadal time scales. Our activities fall under NASA's Earth Science Research Program which emphasizes inter-disciplinary research and the development of new scientific knowledge that address natural and man-made changes in our environment on various time scales which affect the habitability of our planet. The two focus areas that are sought to be covered under this proposal are: i) Climate Variability and Change and ii) Carbon Cycle and Ecosystems. By integrating NASA's observational capabilities with innovative modeling, it aims to provide answers to the following: (1) How is the global ocean circulation varying on interannual, decadal and longer time scales? (2) How can predictions of climate variability and change be improved?  1. Goes, J. I., T.G. Prasad, H. do R. Gomes, J. T. Description: SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL VARIABILITY IN CHLOROPHYLL, PRIMARY PRODUCTION AND CARBON EXPORT IN THE BERING SEA LINKED TO CLIMATE CHANGE The wintertime sea-ice sheet in the Bering Sea plays a pivotal role in heat and biogeochemical transport into the Arctic Ocean. Its formation and retreat have a major influence on the baroclinic structure of the Bering Sea and in addition the timing, the intensity and the fate of its spring phytoplankton bloom. Several studies have shown that the sea ice sheet is sensitive to climate change. Over the past decade, large parts of the Bering Sea have been witnessing a year-on-year absence of sea-ice due to the steady rise in winter to summer temperatures being experienced over the entire Arctic. What do these changes portend for the Bering Sea ecosystem? These and other questions remain largely unresolved because of difficulties in making measurements of biological productivity by traditional shipboard means. The absence of biological datasets that match those available for atmospheric and oceanographic properties continues to remain a major impediment to understanding the potential consequences of climate change on the Bering Sea ecosystem. Satellites present us with an unprecedented opportunity to resolve this problem. While satellite images have helped reveal general trends in phytoplankton biomass and productivity in the Bering Sea, discrepancies still persist between satellite and field estimates that urgently need to be resolved to accurately assess the consequences of climate change on the Bering Sea ecosystem. In the coastal domain in particular, which sustains a large part of the spring bloom, ocean color signals continue to be confounded by riverine material, bottom reflection and sediment resuspension. These uncertainties in the satellite ocean color estimates in the Bering Sea suggest the need for more field bio-optical studies to improve assessments of sea-water constituents especially coccolithophores, which in recent years have been responsible for exceptionally large, anomalous phytoplankton blooms in the region. In this collaborative study between US and Japanese researchers we plan to collect bio-optical data in conjunction with measurements of phytoplankton chlorophyll and productivity, eDaM, suspended matter, coccolithophore counts and calcium carbonate in support ofNASA's efforts to develop robust ocean color empirical and semi-analytic algorithms for the Bering Sea. We have been offered ship time aboard the Japanese ship TIS Oshoro Maru which will be conducting field activities as part of the Japanese contribution to the IPY program. Nutrient data collected during the field program will be utilized to fine-tune our existing algorithms for estimating sea surface nitrate and nitrate based export production. These measurements will be utilized together with other satellite derived products such as sea-ice cover, sea surface winds, sea surface temperature and sea-surface height anomaly etc. to study seasonal and long-term trends in response to climate change.

Description: Heat shield technology is a critical component of manned spaceflight. In particular, the new Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV) requires thermal protection systems (TPS) beyond the current state of the art. While new TPS shields are under development, a key difficulty is the ability to diagnose TPS performance. Technology demonstrator missions are being planned, but designing instrumentation capable of surviving the reentry environment is a non-trivial challenge. We propose the development of a low intrusive fiber optic plug insert for TPS materials that will enable spectrographic measurements of the reentry environment surrounding an ablating TPS. This would provide benchmark data for fundamental flow, radiation, and materials modeling as well as provide operational correlations between vehicle reentry drag and radiation if implemented in a TPS flight test. In addition to spectrographic data, the proposed technology will also intrinsically provide a highly reliable measurement of TPS ablation rates. These fiber-optic plug inserts provide an enabling capability for reentry spacecraft development. The program proposed here will take the concept, originally encouraged at the request of researchers at NASA Ames, from concept to demonstration, through prototype, to a technology readiness level suitable for inclusion in the design of an ablation shield flight demonstrator mission.

Description: A versatile class of high-performance structural joints is proposed where massive interatomic bonds over the large surface areas of nanostructured surfaces constitutes the primary joining mechanism. The new nano-engineered joints embody nanomaterials which are self-assembled and anchored onto the joining surfaces. Compatible functionalization of nanomaterials on opposite surfaces creates favorable energetic conditions for their effective engagement and joining via massive primary (chemical) bond formation. Complementary self-assembly techniques will be used for rapid, low-cost, energy-efficient and environmentally friendly processing and anchorage of nanomaterials upon substrate surfaces. Various nanomaterials and anchorage conditions can be used for different substrates (ceramics, metals, polymers, composites) and service requirements. The length of nanomateials would be selected to compensate for the surface roughness. The proposed joints can be engineered to provide broad ranges of mechanical performance, accommodate various material incompatibilities (e.g., thermal expansion mismatch), and different functionalities (e.g., thermal/thermal conductivity, or reversibility). The proposed Phase I research will establish the theoretical potential of the proposed nano-engineered joints, and will develop and characterize a precursor joint system embodying the proposed joining principles in order to verify the technical merits of the technology and its commercial potential.

Description: MODELING THE VACUUM ASSISTED RESIN TRANSFER MOLDING PROCESS FOR FABRICATION OF FIBER/METAL HYBRID LAMINATES THE VACUUM ASSISTED RESIN TRANSFER MOLDING (VARTM) PROCESS HAS BEEN DEVELOPED AS A LOW COST METHOD FOR THE MANUFACTURE OF COMPOSITE STRUCTURES. VARTM HAS BEEN USED TO SUCCESSFULLY FABRICATE COMPOSITES FOR BOTH MILITARY AND COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS AND STRUCTURAL LAMINATES FOR GROUND COMBAT VEHICLES. RECENT ADVANCES IN VARTM PROCESS TECHNOLOGY HAVE DEMONSTRATED THE POTENTIAL TO FABRICATE AIRCRAFT-QUALITY COMPOSITE STRUCTURES WITH FIBER VOLUME FRACTIONS APPROACHING 60%. THE VARTM PROCESS FOR NEW MATERIALS AND APPLICATIONS IS COMMONLY DESIGNED EMPIRICALLY BY TRIAL-AND-ERROR METHODS. THIS APPROACH TO PROCESS DEVELOPMENT IS TIMECONSUMING AND EXPENSIVE. IN ADDITION, WITH AN EMPIRICAL APPROACH IT IS IMPOSSIBLE TO EVALUATE ALL THE RESIN AND PREFORM MATERIAL PROPERTIES THAT MUST BE KNOWN FOR SUCCESSFUL COMPLETION OF THE PROCESS. THE OBJECTIVE OF THE PROPOSAL WILL BE TO DEVELOP AND VERIFY A SCIENCE BASED SIMULATION MODEL OF THE VARTM PROCESS FOR FABRICATION OF FIBER/METAL HYBRID LAMINATES. THE MODEL FORMULATION WILL INCLUDE SUBMODELS THAT DESCRIBE, FLOW OF THE INFILTRATING RESIN INTO THE REINFORCEMENT PREFORM, COMPACTION AND PERMEABILITY OF THE FIBER/METAL HYBRID PREFORM, AND THE RESIN CURE KINETICS. THE KINETICS MODEL WILL USED TO PREDICT THE CURE RATE, DEGREE OF CURE, AND VISCOSITY OF THE RESIN REQUIRED FOR SOLUTION OF THE RESIN FLOW PROBLEM. FOR A SPECIFIED SET OF PROCESSING CONDITIONS, THE MODEL WILL BE USED TO PREDICT THE FOLLOWING PARAMETERS DURING INFILTRATION AND CURE: A) THE FLOW FRONT POSITION AND TOTAL INFILTRATION TIME; B) THE PREFORM DEFORMATIONS AND PERMEABILITIES; C) THE VISCOSITY AND DEGREE OF CURE OF THE RESIN; AND D) FIBER/RESIN VOLUME FRACTIONS. THE APPROACH WILL BE TO MODIFY AND EXTEND AN EXISTING COMPUTER PROGRAM THAT WAS DEVELOPED FOR VARTM OF LOW TEMPERATURE COMPOSITES. THIS WILL REQUIRE CHARACTERIZATION OF NEW REINFORCEMENT MATERIALS AND RESIN SYSTEMS THAT ARE REQUIRED FOR FABRICATION OF METAL/FIBER HYBRID LAMINATES. THE CHARACTERIZATIONS INCLUDE THE FLOW AND COMPACTION PROPERTIE S OF THE FIBER/METAL HYBRID PREFORMS AND CURE REACTION KINETICS AND RHEOLOGICAL PROPERTIES OF THE RESIN SYSTEMS. THE TEST FIXTURES AND PROCEDURES REQUIRED TO PERFORM THE CHARACTERIZATION EXPERIMENTS WILL BE DEVELOPED. IN ADDITION TO THE NEW MATERIAL CHARACTERIZATIONS, A SIGNIFICANT EFFORT WILL BE MADE TO IMPROVE THE ACCURACY AND COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY OF THE PROGRAM TO PERMIT SIMULATION OF LARGE AIRFRAME STRUCTURAL COMPONENTS. THE OUTCOME OF THIS INVESTIGATION WILL BE A COMPUTATIONAL TOOL THAT CAN BE USED FOR MANUFACTURING PROCESS DEVELOPMENT OF FIBER/METAL HYBRID LAMINATES WITH IMPROVED PROPERTIES. THE COMPUTER CODE WILL BE USEFUL IN MODELING COMPLEX SHAPE AIRCRAFT STRUCTURES, DEVELOPING NEW INNOVATIVE TOOLING CONCEPTS, AND EXAMINING NEW APPROACHES TO PREFORM COMPACTION FOR IMPROVED FIBER VOLUME FRACTION. THE VARTM MANUFACTURING PROCESS WILL POTENTIALLY REDUCE THE FABRICATION COST OF NEW LIGHTWEIGHT, DURABLE MATERIALS FOR SUPERSONIC AIRFRAME APPLICATIONS.

OUR GOALS ARE TO FULLY EXPLOIT THE DATA BASE OF IN SITU SPACECRAFT AND REMOTE OBSERVATIONS OF THESE SYSTEMS IN ORDER TO UNDERSTAND IN A SELF-CONSISTENT MANNER, (1) THE GENERATION OF THE TENUOUS NEUTRAL ATMOSPHERE ITSELF, (2) THE LOCAL PLASMA ENVIRONMENT IN THE CIRCUM-SATELLITE REGIONS, AND (3) THEIR INTERACTIONS WITH THE JOVIAN MAGNETOSPHERIC PLASMA. THESESYSTEMS ARE INEXORABLY COUPLED WITH ONE ANOTHER. WHAT DISTINGUISHES THIS INVESTIGATION IS THAT PAST EFFORTS HAVE WEIGHED HEAVILY ON EITHER THE NEUTRAL OR PLASMA SIDE WHILE WE PLAN TO ADDRESS BOTH PARTS TOGETHER. AT THE CORE OF OUR PROGRAM ARE STATE-OF-THE-ART NUMERICAL MODELS, WHICH WE HAVE DEVELOPED AND USED EXTENSIVELY FOR THIS AND SIMILAR PURPOSES. THE FIRST IS A THREE-DIMENSIONAL PARALLELIZED MAGNETOHYDRODYNAMICS CODE, BATS-R-US, WHICH STANDS FOR BLOCK-ADAPTIVE-TREE SOLAR-WIND ROE-TYPE UPWIND SCHEME.OUR EXTENDED GROUP HAS USED THIS AND PREVIOUS VERSIONS OF THE CODE TO MODEL THE INTERACTION OF THE SOLAR WIND WITH THE EARTH, MARS, VENUS, MERCURY, JUPITER, SATURN AND COMETS, AS WELL AS THE INTERACTION OF PLANETARY MAGNETOSPHERIC PLASMA WITH LO, EUROPA AND TITAN. THE SECOND IS A PARALLELIZED KINETIC NEUTRAL-GAS DIRECT SIMULATION MONTE CARLO CODE, WHICH HAS BEEN APPLIED FIRST TO THE EXPANDING NEUTRAL GAS ATMOSPHERE, OR COMA, OF COMETS, BUT WHICH IS COMPLETELY GENERAL AND CAN ALSO BE APPLIED TO STUDY THE STRUCTURE OF THE TENUOUS NON-EQUILIBRIUM NEUTRAL ATMOSPHERES OF THE ICY SATELLITES. THE GOALS OF THIS RESEARCH ARE SPECIFICALLY APPLICABLE TO THE GOALS OF THE NASA PLANETARY ATMOSPHERES PROGRAM AS THEY CONTRIBUTE TO THE UNDERSTANDING OF THE ORIGINS AND EVOLUTION OF THE ATMOSPHERES OF PLANETARY SATELLITES. IT DEALS DIRECTLY WITH BROAD PLANETARY ATMOSPHERES THEMES SUCH AS DETERMINATION OF COMPOSITION, DYNAMICS AND ENERGETICS IN SATELLITE ATMOSPHERES AS WELL AS DYNAMICAL PROCESSES AND MECHANISMS OF DEPOSITION OF ENERGY AND THE EFFECTS OF MAGNETIC FIELDS BOTH PERMANENT AND INDUCED. THE WORK IS ALSO EXTREMELY RELEVANT TO FULLY EXPLOITING DATA RETURNED FROM PAST MISSIONS SUCH AS GALILEO, AS WELL AS PLANNING FOR FUTURE MISSIONS TO THE JUPITER SYSTEM.

Description: INTERCALIBRATING OF GLOBAL PRECIPITATION CONSTELLATION OF RADIOMETERS Overview of Project - We propose to develop and implement a comprehensive Level 2 inter-calibration procedure between all spaceborne microwave radiometers that could reasonably be included in the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) Constellation. Our approach will be to adapt the vicarious calibration techniques that we have developed for previous spaceborne radiometers (SSMtI, TOPEX, GEOSAT Follow-On, Jason and WindSat) and apply them to the suite of adiometers expected to comprise the GPM constellation (SSMtI, AMSR, WindSat, CMIS and others). The vicarious calibration technique provides a means to transfer main beam brightness temperature calibration standards between spaceborne radiometers that operate at different frequencies, incidence angles, polarizations andlor orbit geometries. Using the technique, absolute calibration of the sensors has been demonstrated at the - 1K level. Relative calibration between sensors, as well as stabilization of a sensorjs calibration over time periods of ten years or more, has been demonstrated at the - 0.3 K level. In summary, the vicarious calibration technique consists of three principle steps. First, calibration algorithms are coded up for each sensor. These algorithms convert raw (Level 0) radiometer digital counts into Level 1 radiometric antenna temperatures - by correcting for on board calibration and other instrumental effects - and then into Level 2 min beam averaged brightness temperatures - by correcting for antenna pattern and spacecraft attitude effects. The algorithms will at first be based on the Algorithm Theoretical Basis Documents (ATBDs) that were developed by the cognizant instrument developers and will be adapted and corrected as needed. Step 2 involves the assembly of external, vicarious calibration measurements. This process is explained in detail below. To summarize, certain statistical properties of the brightness temperature measurements made over specific classes of radiometrically cold ocean and warm land regions can be predicted with high accuracy and extremely high precision. The vicarious calibration data allows for the identification of errors in sensor calibration. The third step involves characterization of the calibration errors, typically by appropriate sorting and binning of the results of Step 2, followed by an iterative refinement of the Level 1 and Level 2 algorithms to remove the errors. Adequate characterization of the errors is critical in order to determine which part(s) of the algorithms should be adjusted.

Description: SBIR PHASE II AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED: ROBUST CCSD IMAGE DATA TO JPEG2K TRANSCODING. Images from space satellites are often compressed in a lossy manner to ease transmission requirements such as power, error-rate, and data stream size. These requirements differ from standard computer image processing requirements since storage space, processing speed, and power constraints differ between PCs and satellites. To facilitate use of satellite images in applications such as image analysis, dissemination, storage and retrieval, etc., a method is needed to convert images to a widely supported format. Since lossy formats lose information, too many transcodings, poorly performed transcodings, or transcodings between poorly chosen formats will degrade image quality, sometimes making them useless. Images such as military photos and deep space objects require high quality, so it is desirable to avoid or minimize loss during transcodings. NASA has requested software transcoding from the CSSDS Image Data Compression recommendation to JPEG2000 (J2K) with minimal image degradation. In Phase I Cybernet demonstrated mathematically that the wavelets used in the CCSDS format can easily, quickly, and accurately be transformed to the JPEG2000 format. This mathematical proof was implemented in a GUI software tool. For this Phase II proposal, Cybernet Systems Corporation will create a robust, end-to-end solution for transcoding CCSDS images to widely supported formats for dissemination, using mathematical techniques developed during the Phase I. This will be done in four stages. First the contractor will evaluate or implement production level CCSDS, in order to provide users with an easy to integrate, small, fast implementation of this image compression standard. Second, the contractor will create a toolset for optimal conversion to other image formats, including J2K, minimizing transcoding error. Thirdly, since J2K allows a lot of choice for encoding, the contractor will create an optimal J2K encoder tailored for CCSDS images. Finally, they will integrate these toolsets into existing systems as needed.

Description: IMPROVED SIMULATIONS OF ASTROPHYSICAL PLASMAS: COMPUTATION OF NEW ATOMIC DATA We propose to continue our existing research program which is designed to improve the current understanding of the ionization balance and line emission of cosmic plasmas. With the support of NASA's SARA and APRA programs, over the past four years we have made substantial progress in this work. Our work has focused on calculations of 1) ielectronic recombination (DR), 2) fluorescence and Auger yields due to a Is vacancy, and 3) inner-shell photoabsorption. DR is the dominant electron-ion recombination for most ions in cosmic plasmas. Recently our group has completed calculations of DR for the H-like through Na-like isoelectronic series for elements up through Zn, Our theoretical calculations are in good agreement with existing high-resolution storage ring measurements for Fe ions. Accurate fluorescence yield and Auger yield data due to Is vacancies are needed for modeling shocked gas in supernova remnants and X-ray photoionized plasmas. We have completed calculations for the entire second row of isoelectronic series for elements up through Zn, Our results have revealed large errors in the fluorescence/Auger database currently being used by the astrophysicists, and we have elucidated the higher-order effects that are necessary for the proper description of these atomic processes. Accurate photoabsorption cross sections are also required to model properly X-ray photoionizaed plasmas. We have completed calculations for the the photoabsorption of all oxygen and neon ions and have included these data into the modeling of abundances in the ISM and opacities in accretion disks. Unlike existing independent-particle data, our method is ideally suited for modeling the observed X-ray absorption features by also including resonance excitation, Auger broadening, and relaxation effects. We propose to continue our DR, fluorescence, and photoabsorption work. We will extend our DR work to calculate rate coefficients for isoelectronic sequences of the more complicated third row elements. We will also continue calculating new Auger/fluorescence data. In specific, we will investigate lsuelectronic sequences for which multiple electrons and/or photons can be emitted. We will continue research along the lines of inner shell photoabsorption for all ions of carbon, magnesium, silicon and sulfur, working in close collaboration with X-ray modeler colleagues. All of our new atomic data will be made publicly available and will be used by us in the non-equilibrium plasma simulation code CLOUDY to enable more accurate interpretations of ionized mission/absorption line gas. Our work will be relevant to the interpretation of spectroscopic data from a range of past, present, and future satellite observatories including WE, HST, EUVE, ISO, HUT, ORFEUS, Einstein, EXOSAT, ROSAT, ASCA, FUSE, GALEX, NGST, Chandra, XMM, JWST, SIRTF, ASTRO-E2, and Constellation-X.

Description: Cassini's arrival at Saturn has yielded several exciting new discoveries about the behaviour of the Kronian magnetosphere, yet work remains in order to understand the details and implications of these phenomena. The data analysis program which we propose will combine Cassini data from the CAPS, MAG, RPWS and MIMI instruments with high performance MHD models to perform the following studies. Intrinsic to understanding Saturn's magnetosphere is the need to know the upstream solar wind conditions.  However, there is no upstream monitor at Saturn and therefore when Cassini is in the magnetosphere there are no measurements of the solar wind. All studies of the magnetosphere, even those not examining the solar wind driving, would benefit from knowing the upstream conditions. Therefore, as an integral part of this study, we intend to provide solar wind conditions upstream of Saturn to the entire community using both a 1 and a 3 dimensional MHD model of the solar wind. These include the apparent shift in the Saturn Kilometric Radiation (SKR) period and its possible dependence on the mass loading rate or on solar wind modulation; the apparent periodic variability that is associated with either changes in the solar wind conditions or is internally driven either by the intrinsic magnetic field, variation in the mass loading rate or an ionospheric conductance anomaly; and finally, we intend to investigate the apparent lack of magnetospheric nitrogen in the magnetosphere which we attribute simply to configuration and dynamics. Our data analysis program and global MHD model are uniquely suited to perform these studies: *Using Cassini data to validate both 3D and 1D model, we intend to provide solar wind condition to the community for use in magnetospheric studies. *Does the SKR period depend on the ion mass loading rate, the solar wind characteristics or both? *Does the periodic variability of the magnetosphere result from large scale processes and does the response depend on ionospheric conductance, mass loading, solar wind driving or a combination? *Can the lack of nitrogen in the magnetosphere be simply atttributed to convective loss to magnetospheric configuration?

Description: Soft X-ray emission exhibits substantially more structure on the sky than its higher energy counterpart. With the greater complexity also comes greater controversy concerning its source components. Until recently, the standard view held that the soft X-ray sky had three primary contributors, all farther than a parsec. Proceeding from the most distant, these are (1) the residual flux from the extragalactic power law, (2) a lumpy distribution of 10^6 K plasma in the lower halo of the Milky Way and (3) a 10^6 K plasma filling a cavity surrounding the Sun in the Galactic disk, the local bubble. However, recently another component originating within about 10^3 parsecs has been discovered, solar wind charge exchange emission from the heliospheric termination shock, the interplanetary medium, and the magnetosheath surrounding the Earth. This emission contributes significantly to the soft X-ray sky with a magnitude comparable at times to all the other components together. We will mine the X-ray data archive to quantify the extent to which solar wind charge exchange emission contributes to the diffuse X-ray emission. We will compare temporal and spatial variations of the observed diffuse emission in archived data from ROSAT, XMM-Newton, Chandra, ASCA and Beppo-SAX to predicted X-ray spatial and temporal intensity profiles using the Fahr and other models for the heliospheric neutral H and He distributions, Hodges' results along with more recent data for the distribution of exospheric hydrogen, and the Spreiter and MHD BATSRUS models for the near-Earth plasma. By varying the model input parameters for solar wind density, velocity, temperature and heavy ion composition along with interstellar hydrogen and helium and exospheric hydrogen densities to the degree allowed by observational constraints and incorporating soft X-ray efficiency factors that are a function of solar wind composition, we will obtain the best agreement possible between the modeled and observed light curves. We will provide this modeling capability to the X-ray community. Our research will answer the following science questions: (1) Is the local hot bubble dead? That is, can we account for all observed diffuse emission within a few hundred parsecs previously identified as local hot bubble with the solar wind charge exchange mechanism? (2) How can we predict the strength of the solar wind charge exchange using geometric information from the X-ray observatory, solar wind observations and simulations? The research will produce an optimized capability to model solar wind charge exchange emission for use in (a) analyzing data from past observations (b) planning upcoming observation to minimize potential contamination and (c) evaluating the potential loss of data due to solar wind charge exchange on future X-ray missions.

Description: SBIR PHASE II AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED: ROBUST CCSD IMAGE DATA TO JPEG2K TRANSCODING. Images from space satellites are often compressed in a lossy manner to ease transmission requirements such as power, error-rate, and data stream size. These requirements differ from standard computer image processing requirements since storage space, processing speed, and power constraints differ between PCs and satellites. To facilitate use of satellite images in applications such as image analysis, dissemination, storage and retrieval, etc., a method is needed to convert images to a widely supported format. Since lossy formats lose information, too many transcodings, poorly performed transcodings, or transcodings between poorly chosen formats will degrade image quality, sometimes making them useless. Images such as military photos and deep space objects require high quality, so it is desirable to avoid or minimize loss during transcodings. NASA has requested software transcoding from the CSSDS Image Data Compression recommendation to JPEG2000 (J2K) with minimal image degradation. In Phase I Cybernet demonstrated mathematically that the wavelets used in the CCSDS format can easily, quickly, and accurately be transformed to the JPEG2000 format. This mathematical proof was implemented in a GUI software tool. For this Phase II proposal, Cybernet Systems Corporation will create a robust, end-to-end solution for transcoding CCSDS images to widely supported formats for dissemination, using mathematical techniques developed during the Phase I. This will be done in four stages. First the contractor will evaluate or implement production level CCSDS, in order to provide users with an easy to integrate, small, fast implementation of this image compression standard. Second, the contractor will create a toolset for optimal conversion to other image formats, including J2K, minimizing transcoding error. Thirdly, since J2K allows a lot of choice for encoding, the contractor will create an optimal J2K encoder tailored for CCSDS images. Finally, they will integrate these toolsets into existing systems as needed.

Description: A MINIATURIZED SENSOR FOR ELECTRICAL FIELD MEASUREMENTS IN DUSTY ENVIRONMENTS  Dusty phenomena such as regular wind-blown dust, dust storms, and dust devils are the most important, currently active, geological processes on Mars. Electric fields larger than 100kV/m have been measured in terrestrial dusty phenomena (Stow, 1969; Schmidt et al., 1998; Qu et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2004), and theoretical calculations predict that the bulk electric fields in martian dusty phenomena are limited by a large (when compared to that on the terrestrial atmosphere) leakage current and the breakdown of the thin martian air at about 20kV/m (Melnik and Parrot, 1998; Farrell et al., 2003; Renno et al., 2004). Renno et al. (2003) showed theoretical and observational evidence that martian dusty phenomena are electrically active. This might have important implications for dust lifting and for atmospheric chemistry. The large electric fields produced by dusty phenomena can substantially reduce the critical windspeed necessary to produce saltation, a process by which sand particles are moved by the wind and bounce on the surface, ejecting the smaller, harder to lift, dust particles into the air, and even directly lift dust particles from the surface (Kok and Renno, 2006). Thus, electric fields might facilitate saltation and dust lifting on Earth, Mars and elsewhere. Moreover, on Mars electrochemical processes driven by these electric fields probably dissociate water vapor and produce large quantities of hydrogen peroxide, a powerful oxidant that can make the surface inhospitable to life, as we know it (Atreya et al., 2006; DeLory et al., 2006). Electric field sensors are usually grounded. Grounded sensors distort the electric fields in their vicinity, and usually produce large errors when subject to ion currents or impacts from clouds of charged particles. In addition, grounded instruments are incapable of providing information about the direction of the electric field, an important parameter for a vector quantity. Finally, typical sensors with more than 10 em of diameter are not able to measure electric fields at distances as small as 1 cm from the surface. Measurements this close to the surface are necessary for the understating of the effects of electric fields on dust lifting (Kok and Renno, 2006). To solve these  shortcomings, we have been developing a small isolated electric-field sensor (E-Field sensor) for in-situ measurements in dusty environments. To the best of our knowledge, our sensor is the first capable of making accurate measurements of electric fields in the presence of large ion-currents and clouds of charged dust particles. We describe our technique in detail below, and propose to design and breadboard a flight-qualifiable, low-power, miniaturized version of our E-Field sensor. In addition, we propose to test the breadboard sensor in the laboratory and identify potential components for future flight models. The main goals ofthe proposed sensor are: 1. To make in-situ measurements of electric fields in dusty phenomena to study their electrification; 2. To measure electric fields at distances as close as 1 cm from the surface and study their role on dust lifting; 3. To study the role of electric fields on ion-chemistry in planetary atmospheres. The proposed low-power, miniaturized E-Field sensor has the potential to shed light on dust lifting, saltation, and the effects of electro chemistry on the habitability of Mars. Moreover, it could also be used to make in-situ measurements on lunar and other planetary atmospheres in which blowing dust or snow might produce electrification such as those of Venus and Titan. Finally, the proposed E-Field sensor could be used to measure electric fields near the surface of the Moon and shed light on the processes responsible for the levitation of lunar dust discovered by the Apollo astronauts (Rennilson and Criswell, 1974; McCoy, 1976).

Description: Population Studies of Simulated Galaxy Clusters Powerful searches for galaxy clusters, the largest bound cosmic structures, are underway using detection methods in X-ray, optical and radio wavelengths. We have the capability to identify, within the next decade, all clusters as large as Coma that exist in our universe, along with tens of thousands of smaller systems. This population will be mined for clues to dark matter and dark energy, but accurate conclusions will emerge only if astrophysical issues that pose limiting systematic uncertainties are properly addressed and understood. We propose a computational project that will improve our understanding of clusters as mUlti-component, dynamically active systems. Using state-of-the-art simulations with a range of astrophysical treatments, we will characterize how the intrinsic, visible content of clusters relates to total mass and epoch. We will study multiple characteristics simultaneously, and provide the first estimates of covariance between important, independent observable properties, such as X-ray temperature and luminosity, optical richness and total gas thermal energy. Mock sky maps from the same simulations will be used to test and improve cluster detection methods. Although our studies will be guided by specific surveys - South Pole Telescope and Dark Energy Survey, in particular - we will naturally explore a number of generic issues, such as projected source confusion and transient effects during mergers. We will seek to convene a Spring KITP workshop on clusters that will bring together observers, computational modellers and theorists in an effort to develop a consensus view of clusters as an astrophysical population.

Description: ANALYSIS OF MGS AND MEX ELECTRON OBSERVATIONS TO QUANTIFY THE SOLAR WIND IONOSPHERE INTERACTION AND ATMOSPHERE It is proposed to unravel the physical processes that contribute to the observed electron distributions at Mars and to use these discoveries to learn about the solar wind interaction with Mars' upper atmosphere, with a focus on atmospheric escape. A detailed examination of data from the Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) Magnetometer and Electron Reflectometer (MAG/ER) instrument as well as the Mars Express (MEX) ASPERA-3 electron spectrometer (ELS) instrument will be conducted with the aid of three models. The first computational code is a kinetic transport model that resolves the electron velocity space distribution along a magnetic field line, taking into account B-field variations along the field line. This will be the main tool used in the analysis of the MGS and MEX electron data. Parameters within the code will be varied to obtain a best-fit match to the data, thereby quantifying what physical mechanisms dominate the formation and dynamics of the measured electron distributions. The second numerical tool to be employed is a multispecies magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) model that simulates the global interaction of the solar wind with Mars. Specific field lines will be extracted from the results of this code for use in the kinetic model. The third code to be used is the Mars Thermosphere General Circulation Model (MTGCM), from which altitude profiles of the upper atmospheric and ionospheric density structure will be extracted for use in the kinetic model. The governing processes acting on the electrons for three types of field lines will be investigated: (1) crustal field loops that are #closed# at both ends; (2) #open# crustal field lines that are connected to the interplanetary magnetic field (IMF); and (3) #draped# IMF field lines (in the magnetic pileup region (MPR) and in the ionosphere). The MGS MAG data will be used to constrain the MHD results, when possible. As part of our present MDAP grant, photoelectron escape from the dayside ionosphere along open or draped field lines has been examined. In addition, a very preliminary study of auroral electron precipitation has been conducted, particularly looking at the magnetic topology leading to their formation. It is the goal of this proposed effort to methodically assess the response of low- and high-altitude electrons (auroral and photoelectrons), as seen by MGS and MEX, to various influencing terms to rigorously quantify the dominant physical processes acting on them. This will yield information about the solar wind interaction with the Mars space environment, with a particular emphasis on how these electrons are tracers or instigators of atmospheric escape.

Description: The primary objective of the research outlined in this proposal is to augment limited Mars upper atmosphere sampling with new MGS derived data products (Electron Reflectometer neutral densities, Accelerometer zonal winds) based upon archived measurements. These new data products will be combined with available MGS and Odyssey Accelerometer datasets to enhance the characterization of the Mars upper atmosphere and its response to coupling from below. All datasets will be compared with state-of-the-art three dimensional (3-D) modeling simulations (coupled NASA Ames MGCM and Michigan MTGCM) yielding improved understanding of the underlying coupling processes. Model simulations and validation will be conducted over solar cycle, seasonal, and inter-annual time scales and for two specific dust storm events. The ultimate outcome of these data/model activities will be the improvement of these same global atmospheric models for the forecasting of Mars conditions that impact spacecraft aerobraking/aerocapture and entry. A second objective of this proposed research is to support MGS Electron Reflectometer data analysis and interpretation [see companion MDAP proposal of Lin et al., 2006]. The construction of a 4-Martian year density dataset (Berkeley team) will be complemented by detailed model interpretation (Michigan team) resulting in an integrated analysis. The coupling of atmospheric regions also extends to atmosphere-surface exchange processes. The final objective of this proposed research is to advance our understanding of equatorial water equivalent hydrogen (WEH) regions as measured by the Odyssey Neutron Spectrometer. The NASA Ames MGCM will be exercised to determine if water ice deposition, driven by the daily water cycle, can produce the WEH region observed in Arabia through the hydration of certain minerals. The outcome will be a further validation of the MGCM synergistic water-dust cycles, and incorporated surface-atmosphere exchange processes. This validation will also lend confidence to MGCM dust driven thermal and dynamical forcing processes impacting the upper atmosphere

I will use a systems approach to integrate all components, and use a landscape perspective to evaluate spatial patterns and human-environment interactions. The results will begin to explicate the linkages between social and environmental systems in trans-boundary contexts. As the first attempt to evaluate NAFTAs impact on land cover and primary productivity in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands, this proposed project will have significant implications for coupled human-environment systems theory, method, and application. The systems model will facilitate scaling up from this study area to other trans-boundary contexts (e.g., the 1-69 corridor).

Description: PLANET MIGRATION: ECCENTRICITY DAMPING AND/OR EXCITATION BY CIRCUMSTELLAR DISKS SUMMARY: Within the currently observed sample, extrasolar planets are found to have unexpected orbital elements. More specifically, most planets detected so far possess larger eccentricities and smaller semi-major axes than similarly sized planets in our own solar system. Although it is generally agreed that interactions between planets and circumstellar disks can drive planets inward to these small radii, the effect of the same disks on the orbital eccentricity is currently the subject of much controversy. Numerical simulations generally indicate that circumstellar disks damp eccentricity, whereas recent analytic calculations suggest that eccentricity can be excited. This project will address this controversy using a quasi-analytic approach, drawing on previous analytic treatments. This project will refine the current description of eccentricity evolution due to interactions of planets with circumstellar disks. In particular, we will investigate the extent to which the surface density profile in the vicinity of the planet influences eccentricity evolution.

Description: IMPROVED SIMULATIONS OF ASTROPHYSICAL PLASMAS: COMPUTATION OF NEW ATOMIC DATA We propose to continue our existing research program which is designed to improve the current understanding of the ionization balance and line emission of cosmic plasmas. With the support of NASA's SARA and APRA programs, over the past four years we have made substantial progress in this work. Our work has focused on calculations of 1) ielectronic recombination (DR), 2) fluorescence and Auger yields due to a Is vacancy, and 3) inner-shell photoabsorption. DR is the dominant electron-ion recombination for most ions in cosmic plasmas. Recently our group has completed calculations of DR for the H-like through Na-like isoelectronic series for elements up through Zn, Our theoretical calculations are in good agreement with existing high-resolution storage ring measurements for Fe ions. Accurate fluorescence yield and Auger yield data due to Is vacancies are needed for modeling shocked gas in supernova remnants and X-ray photoionized plasmas. We have completed calculations for the entire second row of isoelectronic series for elements up through Zn, Our results have revealed large errors in the fluorescence/Auger database currently being used by the astrophysicists, and we have elucidated the higher-order effects that are necessary for the proper description of these atomic processes. Accurate photoabsorption cross sections are also required to model properly X-ray photoionizaed plasmas. We have completed calculations for the the photoabsorption of all oxygen and neon ions and have included these data into the modeling of abundances in the ISM and opacities in accretion disks. Unlike existing independent-particle data, our method is ideally suited for modeling the observed X-ray absorption features by also including resonance excitation, Auger broadening, and relaxation effects. We propose to continue our DR, fluorescence, and photoabsorption work. We will extend our DR work to calculate rate coefficients for isoelectronic sequences of the more complicated third row elements. We will also continue calculating new Auger/fluorescence data. In specific, we will investigate lsuelectronic sequences for which multiple electrons and/or photons can be emitted. We will continue research along the lines of inner shell photoabsorption for all ions of carbon, magnesium, silicon and sulfur, working in close collaboration with X-ray modeler colleagues. All of our new atomic data will be made publicly available and will be used by us in the non-equilibrium plasma simulation code CLOUDY to enable more accurate interpretations of ionized mission/absorption line gas. Our work will be relevant to the interpretation of spectroscopic data from a range of past, present, and future satellite observatories including WE, HST, EUVE, ISO, HUT, ORFEUS, Einstein, EXOSAT, ROSAT, ASCA, FUSE, GALEX, NGST, Chandra, XMM, JWST, SIRTF, ASTRO-E2, and Constellation-X.

Description: The existence of cold fronts in the galaxy clusters is an intruiging but currently unexplained phenomenon. In some instances, the observational evidence supports the idea that the cold core is the remnant of a subcluster merger with the main cluster. However, this seems unlikely in cases where the cluster contains multiple cold fronts or looks veryn relaxed, in which case the oscillation of the cluster core in its potential well might better explain the cold front. Description: Particle Precipitation into and Particle Escape from the Mars Thermosphere and Exosphere It is proposed to apply two Monte Carlo particle transport models to study the effects of ion and neutral bombardment of and escape from the upper atmosphere of Mars. A 3-D particle tracking code has been developed and successfully applied to ion precipitation into the Earth's mesosphere, lower thermosphere, and ionosphere, which will be readily converted for use at Mars. A Mars pick-up ion transport model already exists to allow for particle acceleration exerted by the convection electric field. These two codes will be used in conjunction with existing model results from the Mars Thermosphere General Circulation Model (MTGCM) and the BATS-R-US global MHD model to assess the influence of pick-up ion escape and hot ion precipitatin on the thermosphere and exosphere of Mars. The loss of exospheric neutrals through ionization, in which they become pick-ups ions in the solar wind, will be calculated to examine the relative contribution of the various ionization processes. Solar wind protons as well as pick-up ions from the planetary exosphere routinely enter and alter the upper atmosphere. In addition, the influence of the Martian renmant crustal fields on particle entry and escape will be examined. A study of the pick-up ion escape, sputtering, ionization, excitation, and energy deposition will be conducted. The result will be a robust examination of the influence of energetic ion transport on the Mars upper atmosphere. It is highly relevant to the definition and scientific return for any future Mars aeronomy mission.

Description: TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY A STUDY OF BIOMASS-BURNING AND ANTHROPOGENIC IMPACTS ON ARCTIC TROPOSPHERIC CHEMISTRY USING MEASUREMENTS AT SUMMIT, GREENLAND AS PART OF THE POLARCAT INTERNATIONAL POLAR YEAR PROJECT Although it is a remote region, the Arctic is impacted by boreal biomass-burning and anthropogenic emissions that significantly alter tropospheric composition, affecting levels of ozone and ozone precursors and causing radiative and air quality impacts. These impacts have large seasonal and interannual variability and are expected to respond to climate change, as a result of dependencies on boreal wildfire emissions and the state of the North Atlantic Oscillation. However, continuous in-situ high-altitude measurements are required for this purpose and are not available at any arctic station. We propose to make continuous year-round measurements of total reactive nitrogen oxides, PAN, NOx, and NMHC at the high-altitude (3208 m) GEO-Summit station in Greenland, for a period of 2 years. These measurements will be analyzed in conjunction with FLEXPART transport modeling and simultaneous observations of CO, ozone, and black carbon to identify sources and impacts of both anthropogenic and biomass-burning emissions, with a focus on impacts on arctic tropospheric ozone, ozone precursors, and OH levels and consideration of potential feedbacks upon snowpack photochemistry. This proposal responds to the ROSES-2006 A.16 (International Polar Year) solicitation for individual US investigator participation in multinational field activities carried out as part of IPY. The proposed research is part of the multinational IPY POLARCAT study. Integration with POLARCAT will make available FLEXPART and other modeling and satellite products that will increase the value of the proposed measurements, and the Summit observations will provide seasonal and interannual context for intensive measurements associated with POLARCAT. The results will contribute to multiple NASA strategic science goals involving understanding and predicting current and future atmospheric composition as it relates to climate forcing and air quality.

Description: A STUDY OF COMETARY ACTIVITY USING MEASUREMENTS BY  THE SOLAR WIND ANISOTROPIES (SWAN) INSTRUMENT ON SOHO Atomic hydrogen is the most abundant species in the atmopshere (or coma) of a comet.  Most hydogren is produced in a photodissociation chain originating with water, and water is the most abundant volatile species in a comet's nucleus.  Measurement of the abundance and distribution of hydrogen in the coma, when appopriately modeled, can provide a reliable time history measure of the water production rate in comets.  Virtually all compositional information is compared to water, making water the most important for obtainning accurate production rates.  Variations in production rates with time generally, and with heliocentric distance in particular, provide information about the composition and structure of the nucleus.  Determining the activity of Oort cloud comets, which are likely composed of the most pristine material in the solar system, and Jupiter Family Comets which are pieces of Kuiper Belt Objects and the targets of past and upcoming missions to comets are both critical for both similar and highly complementary reasons.  the objectives of this program address the analysis of observations of the LYman-alpha comae of a number of comets that have been observed by the Swan instrument on the SOHO spacecraft.  We have developed significant model analysis tools for extracting detailed daily-averages of water production rates from sequences of images of the H Lyman-alpha coma.  While the SWAN instrument continues to operate and observe new comets, a considerable archive of observations of over 50 comets already exists since the first observatrions of comet Hyakutake in 1996.  Our specific science goals are (1) to analyze a statistically significant sample of comets, of various taxnomic types and and over as wide range of heliocentric distance as possible, (2) to study their production rate variations with time, covering both long time scales (heliocentric distance dependence) as well as short times scales to investigate outbursts, fragmentation and splitting which can provide valuable information about cometary nuclei, (3) to perform a particular study of Deep Space 1 target comet 19P/Borrelly, and (4) to study the variation of hydrogen lifetime and water photochemistry over solar cycle.

Description: Proactive System Design and Evaluation: Supporting Pilot-Automation Through Empirical and Modeling Analyses The NGATS (Next Generation Air Transportation System) program projects a major increase in flight deck and ground-based automation technology, designed to increase the productivity of the airspace by moving from tactical separation of aircraft to the strategic management of traffic flow, without sacrificing air travel safety. A wide range of new automation technologies are proposed to support the key capabilities of the NGATS system: network-enabled information access, performance-based services, weather assimilation into decision making, layered adaptive security, broad area precision navigation, trajectory-based operations, equivalent visual operations, and super-density operations. The history of airspace automation suggests that, while safety and efficiency have gradually improved with the introduction of automation systems, such as the FMS (Flight Management System), GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System), or TCAS (Traffic alert and collision avoidance system), these improvements are sometimes associated with temporary dips in system performance or, in some cases, longer-term unexpected problems with human-automation interaction (HAI). For example, difficulties with monitoring the status and behavior of the Flight Management System due to poor feedback and inadequate training were observed early on and continue to present a challenge to pilots on modern flight decks. These problems with the FMS have contributed to a number of aircraft incidents and accidents. A major overall objective of the current project is to provide tools to help flight deck designers introduce new systems in a way that can mitigate these unwanted transients to the overall curve of maintaining or further increasing safety. In terms of specific goals to meet this overall objective, we will: (1) Provide a valid tool to assist designers in understanding and anticipating the impact of new automation tools on PSI, with particular emphasis on the classification of systems according to their level of autonomy and the cognitive functions they support, and on assessing the impact of parameters of that system on pilot-mediated influences on aviation system safety. (2) Provide systematic guidelines for PSI problem mitigation strategies. The distinction between (1) parameters that influence safety and (2) strategies that mitigate PSI problems is important. Parameters of the situation in which automation may be applied, such as airspace complexity or density, or meteorological visibility, are properties over which the designer may have little control but that can increase or decrease the likelihood of PSI breakdowns. In contrast, a mitigation strategy is a particular action that can be taken to lower risk or prevent/minimize consequences of a PSI breakdown. While this may include adjustment of a design parameter, it can also include actions such as implementing training, integration with other displays, or recommendations for limiting the conditions of implementing the automation tool. (3) Develop computational models of pilot-automation interaction. To do this, the automation systems, the PSI-breakdowns, and the mitigating strategies will all be represented in matrices, to be described in part B below. The key objective to our approach, which will be essential to assure its validity, is to develop and refine a series of computational models of Human-Automation Interaction (HAI), based upon empirical data from pilot-in-the-loop simulations, which will show how different automation systems may invite qualitatively and/or quantitatively predictable increases in PSI-breakdowns.

The project has 5 specific and interrelated objectives: 1) evaluate how NAFTA impacted sustainability (e.g., primary productivity and land cover), 2) identify publicly perceived threats to environmental sustainability, 3) determine attributes of individuals who have constraints (e.g., low education, low income) against participation in environmental decision making (e.g., land use planning) but still participate, 4) compare environmental world views of groups living in degraded environments and healthier environments, and 5) model and simulate spatio-temporal dynamics of human-environment relationships under different policy scenarios. Further, remotely sensed data will allow evaluation of land use and primary productivity change in Mexican areas of the border region where fine scale (below state) social data is not available. I will use a systems approach to integrate all components, and use a landscape perspective to evaluate spatial patterns and human-environment interactions. The results will begin to explicate the linkages between social and environmental systems in trans-boundary contexts. As the first attempt to evaluate NAFTAs impact on land cover and primary productivity in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands, this proposed project will have significant implications for coupled human-environment systems theory, method, and application. The systems model will facilitate scaling up from this study area to other trans-boundary contexts (e.g., the 1-69 corridor).

Description: Graphite fiber/epoxy composites are one of the primary structural materials used in the modern civilian and military aircraft.  Their excellent specific-stiffness and specific-strength properties are due to a sophisticated microstructure of constituent materials.  However, the presence of the complex microstructure leads to several possible failure modes, including the formation of craze zones in the polymer matrix and the degradation of the polymer/fiber interface.  Furthermore, the potential for mechanical failure of these materials increases significantly when they are exposed to elevated temperatures and possible moisture for long periods of time (aging).  An improved understanding of the failure modes of aged composites at the atomic level can lead to improvements in the development and durability of the graphite/epoxy materials used in many aircraft structures.  The proposed research will develop a multiscale modeling approach that relates physical, chemical, hydrothermal aging mechanisms on the molecular level with mechanical behavior of graphite/epoxy on the structural level.  Specifically, the modeling approach will predict the onset of crazing in the cross lined epoxy resin, the elastic properties of the epoxy resin, and the stiffness and strength properties of the fiber-matrix interface in graphite giber/epoxy composite as a function of the aging level and type.  The results of this research can be used directly in current NASA damage models to assist the agency and the Aging Aircraft and Durability Project in understanding and predicting the effects of aging on current and future civilian and military aircraft.  The proposed research will support a graduate student who will spend one month in residence at the National Institute of Aerospace (NIA).  The student's residence at NIA will provide opportunities for collaboration and information dissemination, as well as provide a means to receive feedback form NASA researchers regarding the research,  In this manner, NASA will be directly involved with the proposed research conducted At Michigan Technological University.

It is motivated by a sensor-web measurement scenario including spaceborne and in-situ assets. The objective of the technology proposed is to enable a guided/adaptive sampling strategy for the in-situ sensor network to meet the measurement validation objectives of the spaceborne sensors with respect to resolution and accuracy. The sensor nodes are guided to perform as a macro-instrument measuring processes at the scale of the satellite footprint, hence meeting the requirements for the difficult problem of validation of satellite measurements. Satellies allows global mapping but with coarse footprints. The total variability is impractical . Our hypothesis is that a sparser but smarter network can provde the validation estimates by operating in a guided fashion with guidance form its own sparse measurements. The feedback and control take place in the context of a data assimilation system. The design and demonstration of the smart sensor web including the control architecture, assimilation framework, and logic actuation are the goals of this project. Description: Our overarching goal is to develop a powerful, flexible, general use simulation tool applicable to a large variety of space science problems.  Over the last decade our group at the University of Michigan has developed a highly parallelized adaptive mesh refinement scheme for solving the equations of ideal and resistive magnetohydrodynamics.  The BATS-R-US code makes use of robust high-resolution upwind finite-volume schemes and explicit and/or fully implicit time stepping to solve the time-dependent 3D MHD equations in conservation form.  A flexible block-based hierarchical tree data structure is used to facilitate automatic solution adaptation on a logically Cartesian grid.  With the support of a previous AISRP grant the proposing team has added the capability of solving the Hall-MHD equations that enables a more realistic modeling of space science phenomena, such as magnetic reconnection.  Modern global simulation tools are now widely used to address a variety of space science problems.  However, there are some extremely important physics and performance limitations to our simulation capabilities.  We plan to remove some of these limitations to extend the physical validity and efficiency of space plasma simulation codes.  Specifically: * We propose to develop a multi-fluid Hall MHD code with anisotropic pressure.  This ambitious goal will be approached through intermediate stages: multi-fluid MHD, single-fluid MHD with anisotropic pressure, multi-fluid Hall MHD with isotropic pressure, and finally multi-fluid Hall MHD with anistropic pressure. * We propose to implement a new phenomeological resistivity model to efficiently model reconnection.  * In order to mitigate the computational cost we propose implement various subcycling algorithms into our code.  The algorithmic improvement will benefit many space physics applications that require high resolution in a small fraction of the computational domain.  The BATS-R-US code is already available to the space science community.  The new algorithms will also be freely available to maximize the potential benefits.

Description: This SBIR project will achieve trusted, reconfigurable, intelligent autonomy through system-level validation. The goal is to design and develop a representation and reasoning system for system-level verification and validation (V&V) of high-level autonomous control for complex systems operating in dynamic environments. Starting from component-level behavioral guarantees, the System-Level Autonomy Trust Enabler (SLATE) will reason about composition, abstraction, and embedding of system components, resulting in high-confidence guarantees of behavior for high-level autonomous control systems relevant to a wide range of NASA applications, including manned and unmanned spacecraft, rovers, and habitats. Description: Advanced Aerothermodynamics Simulation Tools for HMMES Design and Optimization Future High Mass Mars Entry Systems (HMMES) will require accurate predictions of the aerothermal environment during entry into the Mars atmosphere. Current computational fluid dynamics simulations can reliably predict convective heat transfer rates to the forebody of capsule-like shapes similar to the Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) vehicle. However, current state-of-the-art NASA afterbody heat transfer rate predictions are very uncertain, leading to mission risk and conservative thermal protection system designs. The presence of reaction control system (RCS) thrusters that may operate during the entry further complicate the prediction of afterbody heating. Thus, even on heritage lowmass systems, the design of the afterbody TPS remains an unsolved problem.
