Description: THE ROLE OF GPM FOR LANDSLIDE HAZARD ASSESSMENT Landslides in the US and around the world constitute a serious hazard that causes substantial human and financial loss. In the US alone, the estimated loss averages 25 to 50 deaths and approximately $1 billion to $3 billion per year (NRC, 2004). As a result of a Congressional directive, a National Landslide Hazards Strategy, coordinated by the USGS, has been established which calls for focused activities, ranging from basic research to improved policy measures. The future GPM products offer a tremendous opportunity to: (a) advance our understanding of rainfall-induced landslide hazards, (b) develop and test predictive models that incorporate uncertainty and risk, and (c) deploy effective operational forecasting and warning systems over large areas. Specifically, the goal of the proposed research is to evaluate the potential of the GPM products to advance fundamental understanding and enhance our operational ability to predict rainfall-induced landslides. The specific objectives are: (I) develop quantitative understanding of the statistical multiscale properties of space-time rainfall in complex terrain; (2) develop and test multiscale/multisensor merging techniques and a space-time downscaling model to disaggregate rainfall from the GPM scale of 4 km, 3 hrs to scales commensurate with those needed for landslide prediction (-0.1-0.5km; -0.5-1.0 hrs); (3) build, based on accepted slope stability and hillslope hydrology theories, a process based mode1 for predicting shallow landslides, acknowledging the uncertainty in the rainfall products and in model parameters; and (4) apply the model in an operation context and for enhancing our understanding of the factors that control the spatio-temporal pattern of landslides. The proposed research aims to bridge the TRlMMiGPM remote sensing community with the hydro-geomorphology, earth-surface hazards communities for the purpose of improved prediction of rainfall-induced hazards using GPM precipitation products in mountainous regions. Although this proposal does not directly address flood prediction, the proposed physical-statistical downscaling model for orographic precipitation will contribute to the wider use of GPM products for hydrologic applications.

Description: Sources of Solar total Irradiance Variations Solar cycle variations in Total Solar Irradiance (TSI) have implications for both solar physics and for one of the most challenging long term environmental issues facing humanity, global warming. If we are to fully understand and predict the climatic effects of human modification of the terrestrial atmosphere and surface, we must fully understand the natural drivers of climate change. The most important of these is solar variability and the most widely accepted solar driver is variability of TSI. To fully understand and ultimately predict past and future variations in TSI, we need to improve our understanding of the sources of these variations. The proposed investigation uses measurements of photospheric intensities and magnetic fields obtained by the MDI instrument on SOHO to study the contribution of various types of solar features to variations of TSI. Also used are data from the VIRGO and SORCE total solar irradiance monitors and data from the LOI component of VIRGO. The goal is to determine the role of different solar features in generating variations of TSI over time scales of days to years and to improve our understanding of the cause(s) of the solar cycle variation of TSI. The investigation builds on results and techniques reported by Withbroe (Paper I, 2006, Solar Phys., in press). Paper I demonstrates that MDI data can be used to derive values of the mean irradiance from the solar disk whose temporal variations are in good agreement with corresponding precise measurements of TSI from VIRGO. Paper I provides evidence that the quiet sun (regions with magnetic fields less than 10 gauss as measured by MDI) is a major contributor to the solar cycle variation of TSI. Many questions remain including: What feature or features cause(s) the solar cycle variation of the quiet sun irradiance? Is it the network? Is the global migration of elements from active region faculae the source of the quiet sun irradiance variations? Can we confirm with other data Paper I's finding that the irradiance from solar polar regions is brighter at solar maximum by 0.05% or more than at solar minimum? Do active region (sunspots and faculae) contributions to TSI cancel or nearly cancel on average over several solar rotations or less resulting in variations in the quiet sun irradiance being the primary source of longer term variations of TSI?

Description: MICROPHYSICS OF INTERPLANETARY SHOCKS The role of microphysical processes in the structure and dynamics of collisionless shocks has long been of interest, in space and astrophysical plasmas and in basic plasma physics. Interplanetary shocks play an important role in modulating the structure and dynamics of the heliosphere and are associated with acceleration of energetic particles, including gradual SEP events. Near 1 AU, most interplanetary shocks are associated with coronal mass ejections (CMEs). Because of their role in energization of particles and in modulating transport, a detailed understanding of the microphysics of shocks is critical to characterizing and, ultimately, predicting the; space environmental conditions that will be experienced by human [and robotic] explorers; (NASA Sun-Solar System 2005 Roadmap) in the heliosphere. The shock ramp region contains strong currents, and often other sources of free energy such as ion and/or electron beams. Wave growth due to these free energy sources often leads to very large amplitudes, and nonlinear electric field structures are observed. Recent PIC simulations of magnetosonic shocks have shown that electron phase space holes develop in the ramp region and result in electron scattering and energization, as well as modification of the ion distributions. Understanding this type of nonlinear structure requires time-domain measurements of the electric field waveform as are provided by the Wind Waves TDS. However, to our knowledge, there have been no studies oftime domain waveform capture data to reveal in detail the microphysics of interplanetary shocks near 1 AU. Our pilot study, described below, has revealed a rich and highly variable phenomenology. We propose to use an existing database of interplanetary shocks observed by Wind to perform a statistical study of detailed study of the microphysics of shocks and waves upstream and downstream of the shocks. In addition, the data sets from the magnetometer and several plasma instruments will be utilized. The proposed work will help to provide the fundamental physics understanding of interplanetary shocks that will be required to ultimately obtain a predictive capability for interplanetary shock evolution and dynamics and the associated particle energization. The WindlWaves TDS provides a unique data set for the study of microphysics of interplanetary shocks. The primary goal of the proposed research is to perform an in-depth observational study to characterize the waves and micro-scale structures associated with fast mode interplanetary shocks observed by the Wind satellite and to compare the satellite observations to simulations that address the role of microphysics in the dynamics of shocks and energization of particles. This research is enabled by developments in both satellite instrumentation (high time resolution; burst mode;, electric field measurements with large dynamic range) and in computers, allowing particle-in-cell simulations to follow electron dynamics and structures on electron scales (rather than just hybrid or MHD simulations) of these physical processes. Our team has the experience in analysis of shocks, time-domain electric field and wave data and in comparisons of observations and simulations to obtain closure on the proposed questions.

Description: Previous work in the University of Minnesota laboratory has shown that a few interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) from several stratospheric dust collectors contain abundances of helium-3 substantially above the levels expected for implantation of solar wind radiation during their residence in space. A model developed at Minnesota, of the plausible free-space or regolith burial lifetimes of IDPs from either asteroidal or Kuiper Belt sources, demonstrates that it is difficult to attribute these He-3 excesses to cosmic-ray spallation reactions unless the particles were buried for long periods of time in the regoliths of Kuiper Belt objects and were subsequently delivered to the inner solar system by short-period comets originating in the Belt. IDPs that may have originated from comets are therefore of considerable interest, particularly since data from particles collected from comet Wild-2 and returned to Earth by the Stardust Mission are now becoming available for comparison with possible cometary IDPs. Recent research at Minnesota has concentrated on a suite of IDPs collected in the stratosphere at a time coinciding with Earth's passage through the dust of comet Grigg-Skjellerup. Analyses of helium, neon, and argon in several of these particles by high precision, high sensitivity mass spectrometry revealed anomalous elemental ratios, isotopic compositions, and helium release profiles of a type rarely if ever seen in previous IDP measurements; interestingly, excess He-3 was not observed. A second suite of these particles has been allocated for continuation of efforts to identify and decipher clues to their provenances and histories. The key objectives of the proposed studies are to confirm the noble gas anomalies seen in the first suite, and additionally to obtain chemical, isotopic, and physical data through Micro-Raman, TEM, and NanoSIMS measurements carried out by collaborators on the same particles subsequently analyzed for noble gas characteristics. The collaborators are actively involved in analyses of the Wild-2 comet samples, and so cross-comparisons with their IDP results will be immediate and centrally important. We also propose to attempt measurements of light noble gases in Stardust materials. Success in this part of the project is problematic: the question is whether highly volatile elements would be retained in particles subject to flash heating during their deceleration in the aerogel. It is highly likely that particles from many comets are included in the IDP collection. Description: Quantitative Evaluation and Analysis Path Planning Algorithms for Autonomous Unmanned Rotorcraft A key challenge in deploying autonomous aerial vehicles is guiding and controlling them through complex 3D environments and challenging flight conditions. Historically much of the research on motion planning has been performed for wheeled robots and robot manipulators. Many such planning algorithms are based on heuristic techniques and provide practical advantages over more formal, optimal control theoretic approaches. The latter provide a more rigorous framework for dynamic systems but have been difficult to implement due to computational cost and rigidity of mathematical fonnalism. So far these heuristic techniques have mainly been demonstrated on vehicles with much simpler dynamics than those of aerial vehicles like rotorcraft. Two popular robot motion planning algorithms have recently been proposed for unmanned rotorcraft. A roadmap based Voronoi algorithm and a incremental search based Rapidly expanding Randomized Tree (RRT) algorithm. We propose to study the performance characteristics of these algorithms in their application to aerial vehicles. For this task, during the first year, we plan to develop and implement a 3D Reactive Navigation System based on RRT. We will then evaluate its performance using a framework developed by the Army Aeroflightdynamic Directorate (APOD) and then subsequently compare the RRT algorithm with AFDD Voronoi graph-based Reactive Navigation System from. This comparison will help better understand the effects of heuristics used in the algorithms and provide a basis for future work aimed at developing improved algorithms. Long term activities will include determining the factors influencing performance; generating benchmark that can provide realistic performance bounds for aerial vehicle; guidelines on how to best combine heuristics with more formal techniques based on optimality principles.

Description: THEOLOGICAL BEHAVIOR OF THE LITHOSPHERES OF TERRESTRIAL PLANETS   Our research focuses on an experimental investigation of the viscosity of upper mantle minerals and rocks under the relatively low-temperature, high-stress conditions characteristic of the lithospheres of the terrestrial planets. While an extensive literature exists on the rheological properties of mantle rocks at high temperatures and low differential stresses typical of the asthenosphere of a terrestrial planet, relatively little is known about the deformation behavior at lithospheric conditions, where flow occurs by mechanisms not sampled in high-temperature experiments. Flow laws describing deformation under lower temperature, higher stress conditions are currently based either on the micro-indentation experiments of Evans and Goetze (1979; see also Goetze, 1978; Goetze and Evans, 1979) or the D-DIA experiments of Raterron et al. (2004); the uncertainties in both are large. We propose bridging the high-resolution results obtained at high temperatures and low stresses in a gas-medium apparatus and those obtained at lower temperatures and higher stresses in low-resolution indentation and D-DIA experiments, thus producing a reliable flow law describing deformation under lithospheric conditions. To do so, we will carry out experiments on olivine single crystals in a high-resolution gas-medium apparatus at temperatures between 5000 and 12000C and a confining pressure of 300 to 500 MPa. By using single crystals, it is possible to deform samples at differential stresses that substantially exceed the confining pressure while remaining fully within the plastic flow field (i.e., without microfracturing and cracking samples), as is necessary to obtain robust deformation data and a flow law appropriate for the lithospheric mantle of a terrestrial planet. Such a constitutive equation provides an essential constraint for modeling the thermomechanical properties and deformation behavior based on satellite images of tectonic structures combined with topography and gravity data.

Description: Effect of Iron and Water Content on the Martian Mantle We propose an experimental investigation of the effect of iron and water content on the viscosity of Fe-Mg olivine to provide a basis for developing convection models for mantle of Mars, which has more Fe-rich mantle than Earth.  Our study builds on four experimental observations: (i)At a given temperature, the viscosity of San Carlos olivine,  Fo90 ((Fe0.1 Mg0.9)2 SiO4), is significantly higher than that of fayalite, Fo0, (ii) the viscosity of Fo90 increases with decreasing oxygen fugacity, with viscosity proportional to fO2-1/5 (iii) the viscosity of Fo90 decreases with increasing water concentration, and (iv) the solubility of water in olivine increases with increasing iron concentration.  Deformation experiments will be carried out on polycrystalline samples of olivine with Fe contents between Fo60 and F080 over a range of wxygen fugacity from nickel-nickel oxide (NNO) to iron-wustite(IW).  Deformation-produced microstructures will be analyzed using optical and electron microscopy techniques, including EBSD (electron backscattered diffraction)to quantify the LPO (lattice preferred orientation) and thus the mechanism(s)of deformation.  Under both anhydrous and hydrous conditions, as iron content increases from Fo90 to Fo60, the viscosity is expected to decrease.  The viscosity of a sample of a specific Fe:Mg ratio deformed under hydrous conditions is anticipated to be lower than its counterpart deformed under anhydrous conditions.  Therfore, at the same thermodynamic conditions (e.g., P, T, fO2, water fugacity (fH2O)), the viscosity of the more Fe-rich (18 wt% FeO) mantle of Mars will be lower than the mantle of Earth (8 wt% FeO).  A theoreticalframework will be developed and scaling laws will be formulated to permit extrapolation of our constitutive equation from laboratory to martian mantle conditions. The results will tehn be incorporated into a new generation of convection models used to explore the geodynamic evolution of Mars.

Interplanetary (IP) shocks, typically created by interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs), play an important role in particle energization in the heliosphere. The particles associated with IP shocks can excite waves in space plasmas which can be studied in situ by spacecraft currently in the solar wind. Waves occurring within IP shocks are thought to be an energy dissipation mechanism and can give us clues to understanding IP shock wave evolution. Understanding the evolution of IP shocks is crucial to characterizing and ultimately predicting the 'space environment conditions that will be experienced by human (and robotics) explorers' in the heliosphere. The work we propose will strongly support the strategic objectives of NASA and Heliophysics (Sun-Solar System Connection) division: to `Explore the Sun-Earth system to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth, the Solar System, and the space environmental conditions that will be experienced by human explorers,??The central objectives of this study are: 1. Identify the wave modes that occur in the upstream, downstream, and ramp region of IP shocks utilizing Time Domain Sampler (TDS) data (waveform captures) from the STEREO and Wind spacecraft. 2. Determine whether a correlation exists between the amplitude of the waves generated by IP shocks and various shock parameters like Mach number, shock normal angle, or shock strength. 3. Examine particle distribution data to look for particle reflection for comparison to theoretical critical Mach numbers as well as to examine possible free energy sources for these waves. 4. Compare our experimental results to theoretical and simulation studies of Collisionless shocks. We propose to achieve these goals in the following manner: 1. Determine the time corresponding to the ramp region using 3 second magnetic field data. 2. Collect all the TDS data for a two hour window around the shock arrival time and separate by region (upstream, ramp, downstream). 3. Identify the various waveforms (using frequency and polarization) in the TDS data and record their electric field amplitudes. 4. Determine the relevant shock parameters using the Rankine-Hugoniot conservation equations. 5. Compare wave amplitudes with shock parameters (Mach number, shock normal angle, shock strength, etc.) and look for correlations. 6. Examine particle distributions for particle beams supercritical shock speeds. 8. Compare experimental results to theory and simulations. A fundamental understanding of the microphysics involved in IP shock evolution is critical to enable predictive capabilities. The resulting energetic particles can be dangerous to humans in space and spacecraft longevity. Their role in particle acceleration and geomagnetic storms make IP shock microphysics and important subject which strongly supports the strategic goals NASA has set forth to explore'...the space environmental conditions that will be experienced by human explorers...'

Description: Quantitative Evaluation and Analysis Path Planning Algorithms for Autonomous Unmanned Rotorcraft A key challenge in deploying autonomous aerial vehicles is guiding and controlling them through complex 3D environments and challenging flight conditions. Historically much of the research on motion planning has been performed for wheeled robots and robot manipulators. Many such planning algorithms are based on heuristic techniques and provide practical advantages over more formal, optimal control theoretic approaches. The latter provide a more rigorous framework for dynamic systems but have been difficult to implement due to computational cost and rigidity of mathematical fonnalism. So far these heuristic techniques have mainly been demonstrated on vehicles with much simpler dynamics than those of aerial vehicles like rotorcraft. Two popular robot motion planning algorithms have recently been proposed for unmanned rotorcraft. A roadmap based Voronoi algorithm and a incremental search based Rapidly expanding Randomized Tree (RRT) algorithm. We propose to study the performance characteristics of these algorithms in their application to aerial vehicles. For this task, during the first year, we plan to develop and implement a 3D Reactive Navigation System based on RRT. We will then evaluate its performance using a framework developed by the Army Aeroflightdynamic Directorate (APOD) and then subsequently compare the RRT algorithm with AFDD Voronoi graph-based Reactive Navigation System from. This comparison will help better understand the effects of heuristics used in the algorithms and provide a basis for future work aimed at developing improved algorithms. Long term activities will include determining the factors influencing performance; generating benchmark that can provide realistic performance bounds for aerial vehicle; guidelines on how to best combine heuristics with more formal techniques based on optimality principles.

Description: Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) is a wide bandgap II-VI semiconductor used in the detection of X-rays and gamma-rays in the keV-MeV energy range. Owing to the excellent spatial (sub-nun) and energy (l%-2% FWHM at 662 keV) resolutions achieved with CZT and the fact that it can be operated at room temperature, CZT plays an important role for space-borne X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes. During the last two years, our group has been funded for the fabrication and testing of 0.5 cm x 2 cm x 2 cm CZT detectors with pixels on a pitch of 2.5 mm based on low-cost substrates grown with the Modified Horizontal Bridgman (MHB) process. Here we propose to continue our work and to expand it in several ways: (i) fabricate and test detectors with higher spatial resolution (1.25 mm pixel pitch) as required for an EXIST-type Black Hole Finder Probe (BHFP), (ii) develop thicker CZT detectors between 0.75 cm and 2 cm thicknesses based on MHB CZT, (iii) optimize the finely pixelated thick detectors with the help of detailed detector simulations. Owing to the moderate cost of MHB CZT substrates and the in-house contacting and mounting of the detectors, we will be able to carry through a large-scale fabrication and testing program at moderate costs. Each year, we will purchase a set of 10 CZT substrates and characterize the substrates with infrared transmission microscopy, photoluminescence zinc mapping, and surface and bulk resistivity measurements. We will then fabricate the detectors, and evaluate their spectroscopic performance with flood illumination and collimutetl X-ray beams. Furthermore, we will study the correlation of the substrate properties with the spectroscopic performance of the detectors, and model all available data with a detector simulation code. Our systematic study will make it possible to optimize the thickness of CZT detectors used on missions like the BHFP and the Advanced Compton Telescope.

Description: This study combines analyses of the global tectonic patterns on Saturns midsized icy satellites, determined from Cassini imaging, as well as advances in numerical modeling of processes such as solid-state convection and tidal dissipation to understand which processes drive tectonic and cryovolcanic resurfacing on these bodies. In Task 1, we propose to map the global tectonic pattern on Mimas, Enceladus, Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, and compare each to calculated stress patterns due to tidal retreat, diurnal tidal flexing, despinning, nonsynchronous rotation, forced libration, and other sources to determine the forces that drive tectonics on each satellite. In Task 2, we will determine whether solid-state convection can occur within each satellite, either now or in the past, using state-of-the-art numerical techniques and recent laboratory results regarding the rheologies of planetary ices. We will calculate the thermal evolution of each satellites interior, including modern relationships for convective heat transfer (if convection occurs in the satellite), to address the evolution of the interior and potential for thermally-driven tectonics and cryovolcanic resurfacing. In Task 3, we will model dissipation in a multi-layered viscoelastic Enceladus to address what its observed heat flux can tell us about its internal structure. The work described here will substantially advance our knowledge of the processes that shape the surfaces and interiors of the midsized saturnian satellites, and icy satellites in general.

Description: The principal objectives of our research are to further the understanding of three geologic processes that occur on Earth's moon: (1) formation of the crust, (2) basaltic volcanism, and (3) modification of the crust and redistribution of material by meteoroid impacts.  We also seek to decipher information recorded on the Moon about the early impact history of the inner solar system. Our work mainly involves the compositional and petrographic study of samples of the Moon by a variety of analytical techniques followed by quantitative modeling of the data. We will analyze and study lunar samples using neutron activation, optical petrography, electron microprobe analysis, secondary ion mass spectrometry. We will integrate compositional, petrologic, and isotopic data obtained on Apollo and Luna samples, and lunar meteorites with compositional and mineralogical data obtained from orbit by the Clementine and Lunar Prospector missions. Using a variety of data, we will characterize the materials and their distribution on the Moon and model geological processes that formed them. Our proposed work focuses on the following specific tasks. (1) We will use lunar meteorites as a scientific resource, obtain new compositional and petrographic data on lunar meteorites, and integrate those data with data from Apollo samples and orbital missions. (2) We will explore the possibility that certain feldspathic breccias from the Apollo 16 site with low concentrations of incompatible elements are crystallized impact melt from the Nectaris basin and that the basin may, consequently, be older (4.1 Gyr or more) than generally assumed on the basis of ages (3.9 Gyr) determined on more mafic breccias with high concentrations of incompatible elements that likely were not formed in the Nectaris region. (3) We will complete a study of regolith samples (2-4-mm rock fragments) from the Apollo 11 mission that addresses key questions about the distribution of basin ejecta and mare volcanism in surrounding regions and recorded in the Apollo 11 regolith. The proposed work addresses a portion of NASA Strategic Sub-goal 3C ("Advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system ...") and, less directly, Strategic Goal 6  (" Establish a lunar return program having the maximum possible utility for later missions to Mars and other destinations ") by providing new information about lunar geochemistry and geology. We perceive our work to be significant because our analytical results are of high quality, we have a large database of comparative data, we have considerable experience with and a large knowledge base of lunar materials, lunar geochemistry, and lunar geology, we strive to synthesize and integrate our results with those of others, and we report our results in a manner that will be useful to future researchers.

Description: HISTORY OF PRESOLAR GRAINS The broad goal of the work proposed herein is an understanding of the history of presolar grains, from their origins in stellar outflows through their residence in the interstellar medium (ISM), introduction into the Solar Nebula, incorporation into solid bodies, and finally their participation in parent body regolith processes. The proposed work consists of: I) A wide variety of coordinated TEM/SIMS microanalyses of presolar SiC and graphite, to establish their stellar sources, and to determine their mineralogies, morphologies, microstructures, internal grains, and chemical compositions; 2) Thermochemical modeling of the mineral phase composition and formation sequence revealed by TEM observations, particularly of presolar graphite, SiC grains, and the sub-grains in each, to infer the physico-chemical conditions in the grain formation environments; 3) Detailed studies of the surfaces of presolar SiC grains previously isolated in their "pristine" state (i.e., as they exist in primitive meteorites), using coordinated AES/FIB/NanoSIMS/TEM techniques to determine the isotopic and chemical composition and physical characteristics of the grain surfaces, as indicators of grain histories from their formation through residence in the ISM and final incorporation into meteorite parent bodies; 4) Coordinated TEM/SIMS studies of ultrathin sections of presolar graphites from separates of the Orgueil (CI) chondrite newly prepared in our laboratory using the detailed University of Chicago chemical dissolution procedures, and the determination of their microchemical and microstructural properties, in order to extend systematic presolar grain studies beyond those of the much-studied Murchison CM2 meteorite. The proposed work is highly relevant to several of NASA's goals and research focus areas, as discussed in The 2006 NASA Strategic Plan, specifically Strategic Sub-goals 3C.I (Progress in learning how the Sun's family of planets and minor bodies originated and evolved) and 3D.3 (Progress in understanding how individual stars form and how those processes ultimately affect the formation of planetary systems).

Description: STUDIES OF NUCLEATION AND GROWTH, SPECIFIC HEAT AND VISCOSITY OF UNDERCOOLED MELTS OF QUASICRYSTALS AND POLYTETRAHEDRAL-PHASE-FORMING ALLOYS Under previous NASA funding we developed a new technique, Beamline Electrostatic Levitation (BESL), for x-ray structural studies of supercooled liquids. Our initial BESL studies demonstrated the tendency for some supercooled metal alloy liquids to develop an icosahedral short range order that decreased the nucleation barrier for the icosahedral quasicrystal, providing the first experimental proof of a half-century-old hypothesis.  We also demonstrated that in conflict with theoretical predictions and previous experimental studies, there is no measurable change in the coordination number of liquid silicon with supercooling, ruling out a possible liquid-liquid phase transition. Our structural, specific heat, density and surface tension measurements, however, did suggest the presence of a new type of metastable liquid-liquid phase transition in Ti-Zr-Ni supercooled liquids that correlates with the increasing icosahedral order and couples to the nucleation barrier. This is a new type of nucleation process. With this NASA support for ground-based studies, we will make ESL measurements of the specific heat, viscosity, density and surface tension and BESL structural studies of supercooled metallic liquid alloys (at the Advanced Photon Source). The results of these studies will (1) confirm or refute the suggested liquid-liquid phase transition in Ti-Zr-Ni liquids and its coupling with the nucleation barrier, (2) further determine a trend from our initial studies indicating a competition between close packing and the angular character of transition metal bonding in determining the short range order in supercooled metallic liquids, and (3) identify the mechanism by which oxygen stabilizes icosahedral order in Ti-Fe-Si-O liquids.  These investigations will increase our understanding of the structures of liquids and their relations to thermo-physical properties, and deepen our knowledge of the phase transitions that occur in liquids. They will also provide valuable new data for possible future experimental studies in a microgravity environment.

Description: RIBOZYME EVOLUTION BY TRANSACTIVATION Objectives: The RNA world model for prebiotic evolution posits the existence of a random library of RNAs that were selected for catalytic and other properties. The model requires (1) the population complexity of the RNA library must be sufficiently large to contain enough distinct species for selection of rare catalytic RNAs (2) Structural complexity so that individual RNA molecules are large enough for active catalysis. While relatively short RNAs can achieve population complexity, structural complexity is more problematic in short RNAs. De novo synthesis of structurally complex RNAs requires a highly processive polymerization mechanism, which has not been demonstrated in the RNA world. Recombination of smaller RNAs could make larger RNAs, a process termed accretion. This is a three-step process of encounter, recombination and selection. The goal of this program is to determine the likelihood of the accretion mechanism under environmental conditions that are compatible with RNA structure and function. This termination requires kinetic and statistical descriptions of RNA encounter, recombination, and mutation in vitro. Previous work showed that the first step is surprisingly likely. The current proposal is to (1) determine the likelihood of in vitro recombination between interacting RNAs (2) determine the frequency by which already recombined RNAs can be evolved into functional domains in composite RNAs. Methods: The system for study is the ribozyme RNase P RNA, for which the domain structure and enzymatic properties are well-known. Methods include RNA biochemical analysis and statistical analyses of the frequency of RNA events capable of carrying out the steps in accretion. Significance to NASA goals: This program directly relates to the goal ofthe Exobiology and Evolutionary Biology Program because it evaluates the ability of the RNA world "to serve as a precursor of metabolic and replicating systems on Earth and elsewhere." Establishing likelihood parameters for the emergence of the RNA world will allow evaluation of other possible alternatives to Earth's extant RNA-DNA-protein biochemical system. This will support the NASA objective of "exploring the Universe to understand its origin and structure" in support of the national goal to "explore the solar system and beyond."

Description: EFFECTS OF SAHARAN AIR LAYER WATER VAPOR AND AEROSOL CONTENT OF TROPICAL CYCLOGENESIS USING NAMMA DC-8 DATA (GRADUATE STUDENT: MICHAEL FOLMER) Every hurricane season, about 100 low- pressure weather disturbances whirl westward out of West Africa and over the Atlantic Ocean, but less than one-fifth of them become tropical depressions, storms or hurricanes. One of the most difficult questions to answer is how do we tell the difference between weather disturbances that are going to develop into tropical depressions, storms or hurricanes, and those that do not? Part of the answer to this question lies in the West African Monsoon. During the monsoon, the contrast between hot Sahara air and cooler air to the south gives rise to the African easterly jet stream, which blows from east to west. When this jet forms, disturbances associated with the jet rapidly move into the Atlantic. Approximately half of the major hurricanes that hit the United States have their origin in these disturbances. In order to better understand how these African Easterly Waves becomes hurricanes, NASA conducted the NASA African Monsoon Multidisciplinary Analyses (NAMMA) field campaign from the Cape Verde Islands, in August 2006. The evolution and structure of African Easterly Waves (AEWs) were studied via an extensive surface observation network, aircraft and orbiting satellites (including Aqua, TRMM, and the recently-launched Cloudsat/CALIPSO. Major goals of the project were to: (1) identify and characterize African Easterly Waves (AEWs) and Mesoscale Convective Systems; (2) examine the formation and evolution of tropical hurricanes from African Easterly Waves in the eastern and central Atlantic and their impact on the U.S. east coast; and (3) determine the composition and structure of the Saharan Air Layer, and whether aerosols affect cloud precipitation and influence cyclone development. The data collected during the NAMMA DC-8 flights should provide significant insight into the role that the SAL plays in regulating tropical cyclone genesis. Dunion and Veldon (2004) suggest that the SAL might suppress Tropical Cyclone (TC) activity in the North Atlantic and document its suppressing characteristics for a number of specific TC SAL interactions that have occurred during several recent Atlantic hurricane seasons. I propose to incorporate the dropsonde data. MODIS, Calipso, and LARGE instrument data collected during the field phase of the NAMMA mission into both the WRF-Chem model and the MM5/HYSPLIT_4 MODEL (Pasken and Pietrowica;2005) used at Saint Louis University to hope to gain a better understanding of how the aerosols and dry air interact with the TCs. An advantage of using the WRF-Chem model is that the chemistry package allows the user to manipulate the concentrations and type of aerosol in a given area. The first run of the WRF-Chem for each case will be a clean run without any aerosol injection to set a control case. Each successive run will be with various degrees of aerosol and dry air concentrations to see how the interaction with TCs and/or AEWs affects organization and strength. I will also examine the effect of varying particle concentrations and microphysical properties on TC formation or dissipation.

Description: Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) is a wide bandgap II-VI semiconductor used in the detection of X-rays and gamma-rays in the keV-MeV energy range. Owing to the excellent spatial (sub-nun) and energy (l%-2% FWHM at 662 keV) resolutions achieved with CZT and the fact that it can be operated at room temperature, CZT plays an important role for space-borne X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes. During the last two years, our group has been funded for the fabrication and testing of 0.5 cm x 2 cm x 2 cm CZT detectors with pixels on a pitch of 2.5 mm based on low-cost substrates grown with the Modified Horizontal Bridgman (MHB) process. Here we propose to continue our work and to expand it in several ways: (i) fabricate and test detectors with higher spatial resolution (1.25 mm pixel pitch) as required for an EXIST-type Black Hole Finder Probe (BHFP), (ii) develop thicker CZT detectors between 0.75 cm and 2 cm thicknesses based on MHB CZT, (iii) optimize the finely pixelated thick detectors with the help of detailed detector simulations. Owing to the moderate cost of MHB CZT substrates and the in-house contacting and mounting of the detectors, we will be able to carry through a large-scale fabrication and testing program at moderate costs. Each year, we will purchase a set of 10 CZT substrates and characterize the substrates with infrared transmission microscopy, photoluminescence zinc mapping, and surface and bulk resistivity measurements. We will then fabricate the detectors, and evaluate their spectroscopic performance with flood illumination and collimutetl X-ray beams. Furthermore, we will study the correlation of the substrate properties with the spectroscopic performance of the detectors, and model all available data with a detector simulation code. Our systematic study will make it possible to optimize the thickness of CZT detectors used on missions like the BHFP and the Advanced Compton Telescope.

Description: NOBLE GASES IN RETURNED STARDUST SAMPLES Noble gas components in Stardust samples can be delineated into two spatial categories: volume-correlated and surface correlated. Volume-correlated include such indigenous components as i.planetary(' or Q-gases, possible extra-solar components and in-situ produced components from radioactive decay and cosmic-ray interactions, while the surface-correlated are largely solar wind. We are in a unique position to address both of these components, and each has a significantly different story to tell. Although several laboratories have the capabilities of measuring volume-correlated noble gases, and preliminary results are already available, the small sizes of track-producing particles severely constrain the quantity of noble gases, severely limiting precision of reported results [Marty et al., 2006]. Our laboratory, with high sensitivity multiple multiplier instruments, developed during the course of our Genesis work, is uniquely equipped to provide valuable results. The study of surface-correlated noble gases would appear to be even more difficult, but we are precisely suited for this effort and the particle-size distributions reported by Horz, et al. (2006) are very encouraging. For use with the Genesis samples, we developed a unique computer-controlled raster extraction technique using short-pulsed UV lasers which is directly applicable to Stardust aerogel and the study of surface-correlated components. Micron and sub-micron particles have much greater surface-to-volume ratios than the larger Stardust grains and provide ideal samples for the study of surface-correlated noble gases, whose likely source is the ancient solar wind. We propose to request samples of exposed aerogel which contain very small or no visible tracks, but large numbers of sub-micron particles (Horz, et al., 2006), degassed in our laboratory by laser rasters of the aerogel. If originally accreted into an icy matrix as discrete particles or small clusters, these particles record surface implanted noble gases. Moreover, particles that stop near the surface without leaving major tracks or undergoing significant heating during deceleration will preserve these components. How far out the solar wind is dominant depends upon when the solar outflow becomes sub-sonic (termination shock). Earlier estimates that place this at less than 10 AU have proved to be wrong. Voyager detected this shock, and subsequent drop in solar wind flux, at nearly 100 AU, so the surface component of Wild 2 grains may represent an ancient solar wind sequestered for perhaps 4.6 Ga. Studies of individual olivine grains from CM chondrites [Caffee et ai, 1987; Hohenberg et al, 1990] show preserved records of an early naked T-Tauri sun with energetic particle activities enhanced by >10,000. It would be exciting to study the ancient solar wind, even if it were after termination of a T-Tauri phase, as it would sample an ancient solar wind billions of year prior to Genesis.

Description: MICROCHARACTERIZATION OF COMETARY MATTER The cometary samples returned by NASA's Stardust Discovery mission are heterogeneous on the smallest scales and contain both solar system and presolar matter. A comprehensive analytical approach is mandatory to identify individual components and to determine their mineralogical, elemental and isotopic compositions. We propose to build on the experience gained during the Preliminary Examination by studying cometary samples with field emission scanning electron microscopy, secondary ion mass spectrometry, Auger spectroscopy and focused ion beam extracted sample analysis by transmission electron microscopy. One focus will be the search for additional circumstellar grains, their detailed characterization and a comparison with circumstellar grains found in other types of extraterrestrial materials, such as primitive meteorites, interplanetary dust particles, and Antarctic micrometeorites. We will also work on the identification of the carrier phases of other isotopic anomalies that were observed in Wild 2 samples and perform isotopic measurements beyond the elements that were studied during the Preliminary Examination. This research will provide important clues about the makeup of the comet and about the origin of its components. This research is thus highly relevant to the Strategic Goals of the 2006 NASA Strategic Plan as outlined in Table 1 of the ROSES-2006 NRA, especially to Strategic Goal3/Sub-Goal 3C "Advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system...", and NASA Science Outcome 3C.1 "Progress in learning how the Sun's family of planets and minor bodies originated and evolved".

Description: Martian evolution: From magma oceans to present day mantle dynamics Initial conditions play a significant role in Martian evolution. This is suggested by the rapid occurence of several global scale events early in Mars history including crust-mantle-core differentiation, generation of a transient dynamo, early development of large scale crustal structure including the hemispherical dichotomy and Tharsis, and production of long-lived geochemical resevoirs, One planetary formation process that strongly influences the initial thermal and compositional state of Mars is giant impacts which are capable of forming large, intact, locali~edm elt regions, i.e. local magma oceans. The new results will lead to a better understanding of the role of local magma oceans production during planetary formation for subsequent mantle processes and Martian evolution.

Description: EFFECTS OF RHEOLOGY ON THE DYNAMICS AND EVOLUTION OF PLANETARY INTERIORS The objective of this proposal is to understand the nature of the fundamental differences between the planets using observational data as well as improved physical models of mantle processes. Our studies have shown that the rheology of rocks has a major effect on mantle dynamics and evolution. In particular, we found that it is highly unlikely for plate tectonics to begin after a planet has completely crystallized. On small planets, such as Mars and Mercury, not only plate tectonics but any type of mantle convection seems to be problematic. In the past we could only study mantle dynamics with realistic rheologies in two dimensions. With the rapid growth of computing power it has become possible to systematically investigate mantle dynamics in fully three-dimensional spherical shell geometry. The realistic rheology of rocks and three dimensional geometry are two computationally challenging factors. Putting them together will be a major step forward. We will be able to model the whole planet over its entire evolution as opposed to regional modeling in a narrow time window. This will allow us to use a substantially larger set of observational data to constrain planetary evolution. This will help us to better understand the mechanisms of global resurfacing of Venus around 750 million years ago and the formation of different types of upwellings on this planet. We will explore the origin of different global patterns of mantle convection on the terrestrial planets such as a long-lived single plume in the Martian mantle versus multi-plume structure on Venus. We will also develop new models of crystallization of the Mercurian core, which are based on new experimental constraints on the phase diagram of iron and which can help to explain the small change in planetary radius during secular cooling of this planet. In addition, we will continue the fluid dynamical investigation of convection-induced stresses to understand the observed patterns of crustal deformation on planetary bodies and will address the question of applicability of the sluggish lid regime of temperature-dependent viscosity convection to the dynamics of planetary interiors. Our three-dimensional modeling will be guided and complemented by theoretical analysis, parameterized convection calculations and two-dimensional models.

Description: SPECTROSCOPIC AND EXPERIMENTAL STUDIES OF SULFATE MINERALOGY AND FORMATION PROCESSES ON MARS The overarching goal of the proposed work is to better understand and interpret data from the surface of Mars in terms of important material properties such as mineral stability and water content. An emerging paradigm from recent surface and orbital exploration missions is that a major past geologic surface environment was associated with drying and perhaps freezing. Evaporation of surface water produced vast deposits of evaporite minerals. Depending on conditions that prevailed during their formation and since then, the evaporite minerals may retain significant quantities of water, or they may exist in desiccated or anhydrous forms. Materials at the surface that are exposed to the atmosphere may experience dehydration and rehydration during diurnal, seasonal, and long-term cycling. Knowledge of the mineralogy and water content of Mars' surface and near-surface materials are thus key to understanding martian hydrology past and present, as well as potential habitability and resource potential. The primary objectives of our work are to determine the stability relationships among the sulfate minerals, specifically the magnesium and iron sulfate hydrates whose presence on Mars is indicated by mission results, under a range of conditions relevant to the martian environments in which they likely formed, and in present-day martian surface environments. The proposed work includes experimental synthesis of sulfate minerals and mineral mixtures, and reactions in response to varying conditions. It will also include analysis of mixtures of sulfates with basaltic minerals and glass. We seek to determine the hydrous phases that have the potential to exist on Mars today as well as the environmental (and historical) conditions that led to their formation. The proposed work will lead to a better understanding of orbital remote sensing results that identify sulfate signatures and the potential for sulfate hydration as a significant host of near-surface water, as well as the implications for sulfate occurrence and potential hydration states at Viking, Pathfinder, MER, and future landing sites.

Description: Studies of chemical processes leading to the origin of life are aided by geochemical models that involve reactions of aqueous organic mixtures. In turn, these models require accurate values of the thermodynamic properties of these compounds as a function of temperature and pressure. Currently, these model calculations depend largely on extrapolated or estimated values of the thermodynamic properties from a sparse experimental database, mostly at low temperatures. Model calculations also illustrate the biochemical pathways used by microorganisms that live at conditions on the Earth that are considered extreme. These environmental conditions include elevated temperatures and pressures, very low (or high) values of pH, and metabolism of unusual chemical compounds. The presence of these organisms has led many to speculate that similar organisms may exist or have existed on extraterrestrial objects such as Mars or Europa. We propose to determine experimentally the thermodynamic properties of aqueous organic compounds at elevated temperatures and pressures. Specifically, we will measure the partial molal heat capacities of aqueous organic compounds as a function of temperature. Our initial efforts will be directed at a number of simple organic compounds that may be considered as precursors to biomolecules (in particular, thiols and organic sulfides) and several important biomolecules (coenzyme M, cysteine, ATP, adenosine). These data will provide direct tests of the estimation methods currently used in theoretical geochemistry to estimate thermodynamic properties. The data will also aid in developing new methods to predict thermodynamic properties for aqueous organic mixtures and help to refine the equations used to calculate reaction properties away from the standard state conditions of and 1 bar. Lastly, these data are necessary for realistic geochemical models of extreme environments on the Earth, the early Earth and solar system bodies such as Mars and Europa.

Description: COASTAL DISASTER INVENTORY ASSESSMENT: THE IMPACTS OF KATRINA AND PREVIOUS HURRICANES ON BARRIER ISLAND VEGETATION, HABITATS AND GEOMORPHOLOGY IN THE NORTHERN GULF OF MEXICOABSTRACT:BARRIER ISLANDS, EARTHS YOUNGEST AND ARGUABLY MOST DYNAMIC MAJOR LANDFORMS, ARE BEING EXPOSED TO AN INCREASING FREQUENCY AND SEVERITY OF TROPICAL CYCLONES THAT HAVE BEEN ATTRIBUTED TO INCREASING SEA SURFACE TEMPERATURES. A GREATER STORM FREQUENCY AND INTENSITY COMBINED WITH SEA LEVEL RISE, DIRECT ANTHROPOGENIC INFLUENCES ON SAND SUPPLIES AVAILABLE FOR NATURAL REBUILDING PROCESSES FOLLOWING STORMS, AND INCREASING HUMAN POPULATIONS IN COASTAL ENVIRONMENTS ARE LIKELY TO NEGATIVELY AFFECT BARRIER ISLANDS DURING THE 21ST CENTURY. THE IMPORTANCE AND INTELLECTUAL MERIT OF THE PROPOSED STUDY WILL BE IN USING NASA ASSETS TO DEVELOP A MORE COMPREHENSIVE UNDERSTANDING OF STORM IMPACTS ON BARRIER ISLAND VEGETATION, HABITAT DIVERSITY AND GEOMORPHOLOGICAL FEATURES AND THEIR POTENTIAL RESPONSES TO SEA LEVEL RISE AND INCREASING STORM SEVERITY. THE ALABAMA-MISSISSIPPI-LOUISIANA BARRIER CHAIN IS IDEAL IN REPRESENTING DELTAIC AS WELL AS COASTAL PLAIN ORIGINS AND A DIVERSITY IN ISLAND SIZE AND DOMINANT PLANT COMMUNITY TYPES. OBJECTIVES AND METHODS WILL BE TO 1) ACQUIRE HISTORICAL HURRICANE DATA, MAPS (ACCURATE SINCE CA. 1850), AERIAL PHOTOS (SINCE CA. 1940), DIGITAL MULTISPECTRAL (SINCE CA. 1975) AND SATELLITE IMAGERY OF THE ISLANDS, EMPHASIZING PERIODS IMMEDIATELY BEFORE AND AFTER HURRICANES; 2) QUANTIFY HISTORICAL AND PRESENT-DAY AERIAL COVERAGES OF TERRESTRIAL VEGETATION, HABITAT-TYPES AND SEAGRASSES ALONG WITH LAND AREA AND ELEVATION; 3) QUANTIFY SHORT-TERM (DAYS TO YEARS) AND LONG-TERM (DECADES TO CENTURIES) PATTERNS OF IMPACT AND RECOVERY FROM HURRICANES; 4) DETERMINE THE EFFICACY OF NASA, NASA-LEGACY AND COMMERCIAL ORBITAL SENSORS IN POST-HURRICANE ASSESSMENTS OF VEGETATION COVER, HABITAT-TYPE AND GEOMORPHOLOGY, AND 5) COMPARE NASAGLAS/ICESAT LASER ALTIMETRY WITH AIRBORNE LIDAR FOR MAPPING BARRIER ISLAND ELEVATIONS AND POST-HURRICANE ELEVATIONAL CHANGES. HYPOTHESES TO BE TESTED INCLUDE: 1) LOSS IN VEGETATIVE COVER DURING HURRICANES IS A FUNCTION OF PRE-STORM ISLAND LAND AREA, DISTANCE FROM STORM CENTER AND STORM INTENSITY; 2) INITIAL RATES OF ISLAND RE-FORMATION AND RE-VEGETATION FOLLOWING HURRICANE KATRINA WILL BE SIMILAR TO THOSE WHICH OCCURRED AFTER PREVIOUS HURRICANES, AND 3) RELATIVE COVERAGE BY MARSH AND SWALE HABITATS HAS INCREASED, POTENTIALLY AS A RESULT OF SEA-LEVEL RISE (APPROX. 30 CM SINCE 1850). Description: MAGNOLIA-1 SMALL SATELLITE PROGRAM The US space industry and requirements communities have come under severe scrutiny for failing to develop and execute critical national programs in an affordable way. While there are numerous factors contributing to this condition, innovative technologies and processes are available and can be readily leveraged into the genesis of a national campaign to address this problem. Mississippi State University (MSU) and its team members, BAE Systems (BAE) and Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd. (SSTL), propose to collaborate with NASA through its Stennis Space Center (SSC) to begin this process. By providing US access to one of the worlds premier small satellite companies, we propose to accomplish the following goals: 1) Create a new US paradigm for more affordable and responsive spacecraft design, manufacture, and operation by taking advantage of the scale economies realized through small spacecraft mass production. 2) Develop an academic curriculum aimed at educating and training the next generation of US scientists and engineers in this revolutionary approach. 3) Create a US-resident capability in small satellite solutions constructed on the highly successful SSTL model through a program of international cooperation. This team has the unique ability to make this goal a reality. 4) Set the stage for significant UK participation in the Vision for Space Exploration as a potential partner. This proposal offers NASA a unique opportunity to evaluate proven, proprietary technology along with a complete transfer of the knowledge base compiled from 26 fully successful small spacecraft missions. The program proposed details a thorough know how training and transfer program (KHTT) that will be accomplished by designing, building, and operating a pathfinding lunar navigation and communications mission. The program provides NASA with an opportunity to work with the technology in a hands-on, educational context from development through system integration, launch and operations. We believe the successful completion of the program detailed in this proposal will lead to a revolutionary US approach to space exploration.

Description: THIOESTERS PLAY ESSENTIAL ROLES IN METABOLISM OF MODERN ORGANISMS. IT HAS BEEN SUGGESTED THAT THE IMPORTANCE OF THIOESTERS COULD HAVE BEEN TRACED BACK TO THE EARLY STAGES OF EVOLUTION, E.G., THE RNA WORLD. SUPPORTED BY NASA'S EXOBIOLOGY PROGRAM, WE HAVE SUCCESSFULLY ISOLATED A NUMBER OF RIBOZYMES THAT CAN CATALYZE THE SYNTHESES OF COA, THIOESTERS, AND AMINOACYLATED RNA FROM COA THIOESTERS. IN THIS PROPOSAL RESEARCH, I PLAN TO CONSTRUCT AN EXTENSIVE RIBOZYME-BASED METABOLIC SYSTEM THAT WILL HAVE MANY OF THE SALIENT FEATURES OF CONTEMPORARY METABOLIC PATHWAYS. THE PROPOSED RIBO-METABOLIC SYSTEM WILL HAVE THIOESTERS AT ITS CENTER AND LINK DIFFERENT BIOLOGICAL SUBSTRATES AND PRODUCTS (SUCH AS PEPTIDES AND LIPIDS) VIA CATALYTIC ACTIVITIES OF RIBOZYMES. PROPOSED RIBOZYME ACTIVITIES WILL CATALYZE THE SYNTHESES OF PEPTIDES AND PRECURSORS TO FATTY ACIDS AND PHOSPHOLIPIDS FROM THIOESTER BUILDING BLOCKS. IN ADDITION, REGULATION OF THE RIBO-METABOLIC SYSTEM WILL BE ACHIEVED THROUGH INHIBITION OR ACTIVATION OF RIBOZYME ACTIVITIES BY SUBSTRATES, PRODUCTS, AND/OR OTHER METABOLIC STATE INDICATORS (SUCH AS ATP). IN VITRO SELECTION TECHNIQUES AND SYNTHETIC CHEMISTRY WILL BE EMPLOYED TO ACHIEVE THE OBJECTIVES. RESULTS FROM THIS PROJECT WILL DEMONSTRATE THAT IT IS PLAUSIBLE NOT ONLY TO EVOLVE RIBOZYME-BASED METABOLIC SYSTEMS BUT SUCH SYSTEMS ARE ALSO CAPABLE OF ADAPTING TO CHANGES IN THEIR ENVIRONMENTS AND METABOLIC STATES. THE WORK MAY HELP DEFINE THE PROBABILITY OF EXISTENCE OF RIBO-ORGANISMS IN A PRE-PROTEIN ERA ON EARTH OR ELSEWHERE IN THE UNIVERSE AND GAIN UNDERSTANDING ON THE METABOLIC COMPLEXITY OF SUCH ORGANISMS. THE PROPOSED RESEARCH THEREFORE FITS WELL WITHIN NASA'S SECOND MISSION - TO EXPLORE THE UNIVERSE AND SEARCH FOR LIFE.

BECAUSE OF THE PAUCITY OF INFORMATION AND THE AGGREGATION OF CATCH DATA,OFTEN SINGLE-SPECIES ASSESSMENT CANNOT BE DONE. ADDITIONALLY,SINGLE-SPECIES APPLIED TO SPECIES COMPLEXES MAY IGNORE IMPORTANT EXOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS. TYPICAL EXAMPLES OF THES PHENOMENA IN THE GULF OF MEXICO INCLUDE THE SNAPPER COMPLEX, THE GROUPER COMPLEX AND THE AGGREGATES OF LARGE AND SMALL COASTAL SHARKS. FISHERIES ON INDIVIDUAL SPECIES WITHIN THESE GROUPS ARE NOT VERY SIGNIFICANT EITHER IN TERMS OF BIOMASS OR OF FISHERIES PRODUCTION. HOWEVER THE AGGREGAE OF THESE SPECIES GROUPS ARE IMPORTANT, BOTH EXOLOGICALLY AND ECONOMICALLY AND FORM A SIGNIFICANT MANAGEMENT ISSUE OF THE GULF OF MEXICO FISHERY MANAGEMENT COUNCIL AND OTHER MANAGEMENT BODIES.THE RESEARCH SHALL BUILD UPON PREVIOUSLY EFFORTS OF THE PI TO QUANTIFY EXOSYSTEM IMPACTS OF FISHING AND DEVELOP FISHERY MANAGEMENT CRITERIA FOR MODEL ECOSYSTEMS. AGE-STRUCTURED PRODUCTION MODELS AND BAYESIAN APPLICATIONS TO BOTH SHALL ALSO BE EXPLORED. THE MODELINGH APPROACH SHALL BE TO UTILIZE DATA ON COMMUNITY/COMPLEX STRUCTURE WITHIN THE ESTIMATION PROCESS. THE RESULTS SHALL BE TESTED AGAINST LARGE SCALE SIMULATIONS SUCH AS LOTKA-VOLETERRA SYSTEMS OR ECOPATH/ECOIM APPLICATIONS TO THE GULF OF MEXICO. THE PERIOD OF PERFORMANCE SHALL BE ONE YEAR.

THESE PROJECTS WILL BUILD ON THE CURRENT STRENGTHS OF INDIVIDUAL MEMBERS OF THE CONSORTIUM, BUT FOCUS THESE ON ISSUES OF PARTICULAR RELEVANCE TO NASA. THESE SERVICES INCLUDE DISCOVERING HIGH-VALUE NOAA AND NON-NOAA DATASETS,DEVELOPING METADATA, AND PROVIDING DATA ACCESS. IN ORDER TO PROVIDE BOUNDS ON THIS EXTENSIVE DATA MANAGEMENT PROBLEM,THE INITIAL FOCUS OF THE EDAC WILL BE BASED ON THE FIVE THEMES IDENTIFIED AS IMPORTANT PROBLEM AREAS BY GULF OF MEXICO STATE GOVENORS THROUGH THE GULF ALLIANCE. THESE ARE:WATER QUALITY,COASTAL WETLAND/ESTUARINE RESTORATION & CONSERVATION,POLLUTION & NUTRIENT LOAD REDUCTION,GULF HABITATS IDENTIFICATION & CHARATERIZATION AND EXPANSION OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION. A COMMOM THREAD CONNECTING THESE THEMES IS THAT ALL HAVE A DIRECT BEARING ON THE TIMELY SOCIAL,CULTURAL AND EXONOMIC QUESTIONS CONFRONTING THE GULF STATES. RESEARCH THAT APPLIES TO THESE THEMES MAY THEREFORE BE EXPECTED TO TRANSLATE TO APPLICATIONS THAT HELP ENABLE MORE EFFECTIVE GOVERANCE AND POLICY DEVELOPMENT. THE EDAC IN ORDER TO MAXIMIZE THE UTILITY OF THE DATA IT MANAGES AND PROVIDE THE MOST COST-EFFECTIVE SERVICE TO ITS CONSTITUENCY,WOULD BENEFIT GREATLY FROM THOUGHTFUL GUIDANCE FROM THE STATES IN DEVELOPING AND MAINING ITS DATA OFFERINGS. AS A MEANS OF OBTAINING THIS GUIDANCE, THIS EFFORT WILL FUND A STATE GOVERNMENT AGENCY AND/OR STATE UNIVERSITY AND/OR CONTRACTOR TO CONDUCT A SURVEY THAT RANKS CRITICAL STATE NEEDS FOR ENVRIRONMENTAL DATA AND MATCHES THOUSE NEEDS AGAINST THE DIRECT SOCIOECONOMIC AND CULTURAL BENEFITS THAT CAN BE ACCRUED THROUGH THE NORTH GULF INSTITUE, A NOAA OAR COOPERATIVE INSTITUTE AND THE EDAC. THE RESULTS WILL BE AN ANALYSIS OF CRITICAL DATA GAPS THAT NEED TO BE ADDRESSED BOTH BY THE EDAC THROUGH ITS CHOICES OF WHICH DATASETS TO TARGET FOR DEVELOPMENT AND THE RESEARCH COMMUNITY IN PLANNING FOR AND CONDUCTING FUTURE FIELD RESEARCH AN DMONITORING IN THE NORTHERN GULF OF MEXICO REGION. THE TASK AND DELIVERABLES ARE AS FOLLOWS: 1. IDENTIFY TARGET DATA SETS-ANALYZE DATA GAPS THAT NEED TO BE ADDRESSED USING PRIORTIZED CRITICAL STATE NEEDS FOR ENVIRONMENTAL DATA MATCHED AGAINST THE DIRECT SOCIOECONOMIC AND CULTURAL BENEFITS THAT CAN BE ACCRUED. PROVIDE A LIST OF TARGET DATA SETS FOR REVIEW.2. DEVELOP AN ECONOMIC DATA DATABASE-USING THE IDENTIFIED TARGET DATA SETS, GATHER ALL ECONOMIC DATA RELEVANT TO NOAA'S MISSIONS AND THE NEEDS OF REGIONAL STAKEHOLDERS(FELERAL,STATE,AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT,ACADEMIA,NGO'S EX) CONSULT WITH NCDDC ON THE SELECTION OF DATABASE FORMAT. CONSTRUCT A DATABASE THAT CAN EASILY BE ACCESSED. DATASETS SHALL INCLUDE DATA FROM THE BUREAU OF LABOR STATISTICS COUNTY BUSINESS PATTERNS ANNUAL SERIES. 3. PREPARE A FINAL REPORT-BASED ON THE ANALYSIS OF DATA GATS AND FROM THE DEVELOPMENT OF ECONOMIC DATA BASE PREPARE A FINAL REPORT SUMMARIZING ANALYSIS ACTIONS,FINDING,RECOMMENDED GUIDANCE AS WELL AS OVERALL PROGRAM RECOMMENDATION. THE PERIOD OF PERFORMANCE SHALL BE FROM THE DATE OF THIS ORDER AND CONTINUE THROUGH EIGHT MONTHS.

Description: This Small Business Innovation Research Phase I project will demonstrate the feasibility of fabricating waveguides in stoichiometric lithium tantalite (SLT) for highly efficient, quasi-phase matched (QPM) frequency conversion of continuous wave and high peak-power, quasi-continuous laser sources used in lidar-based remote sensing and ranging applications. The key innovation in this effort is the use of large diameter, optical quality, z-cut SLT, which has only recently become commercially available, as the waveguide substrate material. Relative to the standard congruently grown lithium tantalate wafers, stoichiometric lithium tantalate wafers have significantly higher optical damage thresholds, stronger nonlinear and electro-optic response, an expanded transparency window and significantly reduced poling field. Furthermore, because the stoichiometric materials are not lithium deficient, the fabricated waveguides are expected to be optically stable. During the Phase I effort the feasibility of fabricating waveguides in z-cut SLT wafers using annealed proton exchange will be determined, and the impact that variations in processing conditions have on the optical properties will be measured. In the Phase II effort, the waveguide fabrication and poling technology will be refined and grating structures suitable for specific NASA applications requiring wavelength conversion.

Description: There is a growing need to develop improved technologies for precise airborne measurements of carbon dioxide, CO2. CO2 measurements are of great importance to many areas of research, including climate change, global carbon budgets, and geological research in relation to volcanic activity. At the same time, we are entering a period of time in which Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) are becoming more widely used for atmospheric research. UAS platforms have already proven themselves as a uniquely capable means for making measurements in remote areas and over oceans. However, existing CO2 measurement technologies are difficult to adapt to or use in the UAS world. This proposal describes a simple and inexpensive sensor for the precise determination of atmospheric CO2 that will be small enough for flight on small UAS platforms and sounding balloons. Phase I will include the fabrication of a proof-of-concept sensor system, laboratory characterization of the sensor, and culminate in a demonstration of the sensor on a UAS. Phase II will emphasize improving the basic manufacturability of the design, as well as much more extensive laboratory and UAS testing.

Description: Probing the sources of the high-speed solar wind with the Multi-Order Solar EUV Spectrograph We propose to explore solar wind outflows in the upper transition region of the sun using simultaneous imaging spectroscopy. MOSES Observations of intensity, doppler shift and line width will allow the first spatially-resolved observations of the atmospheric dynamics generating waves that are believed to accelerate the high speed solar wind. Description: EVOLUTION OF GENOME ARCHITECTURE IN DE NOVO YEAST SPECIES SUMMARY: INTELLECTUAL MERIT. Large-scale chromosomal alterations occur during formation of hybrids, either between two different species or between diverging subtypes within a species. How these alterations are utilized or accommodated after the initial hybridization event determines genome architecture in the new lineage. Although this phenomenon has been most extensively studied in higher plants, evidence for polyploidy, aneuploidy, and other genome rearrangements arising from hybrid formation has also been observed in the ancestral lineages of Animals and Fungi. However, because most studies of hybrid genomes have been performed using species that either hybridized millions of years ago, are impractical to breed in the laboratory, and/or have no genome sequence available, there has been little opportunity to follow genomic changes as they occur during speciation and adaptive evolution. We propose an innovative experimental approach to address this problem that integrates genomics and experimental evolutionary biology, and utilizes two tractable model organisms, Bakers yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and its fully-sequenced congener, Saccharomyces bayanus. These species and their hybrid Fl and F2 progeny will be evolved under long-term resource-limiting and resource-variable conditions. In each evolving lineage, we will assay physiological performance, competitive ability and changes in genome architecture, the last using pulsed field gel electrophoresis in conjunction with newly developed two-species DNA microarrays. Thereby we will be able to link specific large-scale genome rearrangements to changes in physiology and fitness, thereby establishing the degree to which adaptation is guided by genome architectural changes. We will also be able to identify the suite of evolutionary trajectories that are possible or forbidden when newly hybridized genomes stabilize. Our investigation will constitute the first systematic, genome-wide assessment of the extent and types of genome rearrangements that occur in hybrid organisms during real-time evolution. The ability to generate interspecific hybrid yeasts in the laboratory, coupled with the ability to follow and recisely characterize genome rearrangements during adaptive growth, offers an attractive and attainable experimental program almost certain to yield new insights nto hybrid and polyploid genome evolution. We expect our data to yield fundamentally new insight into the role that genome plasticity plays in adaptive evolution and speciation, and to have broad impact on the study of fundamental processes in higher eukaryotic systems, including the progression of cancer. RELEVANCE to the NASA Mission. GoalS of The Astrobiology Roadmap[http://astrobiology.arc.nasa.gov/roadmap/gS.html) is to Understand the evolutionary mechanisms and environmental limits of life. The research project we propose specifically addresses all four elements of the GoalS, Objective 1 research agenda, namely to (a) experimentally investigate and observe the evolution of genes, metabolic pathways, genomes and microbial species; (b) experimentally investigate the forces and mechanisms that shape the structure organization, and plasticity of microbial genomes; (c) examine how these forces control the genotype to phenotype relationship; and (d) conduct environmental perturbation experiments on single microbial species to observe and quantify adaptive evolution. Indeed, a succinct description of our project is that which NASA uses to describe an exemplary GoalS, Objective 1 investigation: to "examine microbial genome rearrangements, including gene deletion and acquisition processes, in response to nutrient change and physical-chemical stress." Description: I propose to apply a suite of satellite optical and microwave remote sensing, and biophysical models to quantify spatio-temporalpatterns and interactions among major boreal-arctic ecosystem processes, including vegetation structure and productivity, freeze-thaw state, evapotranspiration and fire disturbance, and their response to climate variability. The MOD17 Production Efficiency Model(PEM) will be used with a new integrated long-term AVHRR-MODIS time series and corrected reanalysis meteorology to quantify temporal trends and annual anomalies in vegetation productivity for the pan-Arctic basin and Alaska. Regional wildfire effects will be determined from SPOT and MODIS fire products and will be integrated within the PEM to determine the effects of fire disturbance on satellite based productivity calculations. Recent changes in the timing and length of seasonal growing seasons will be derived from SSM/I and AMSR-E multi-frequency brightness temperature based freeze-thaw classifications. A new satellite based ET algorithm will be developed under this investigation using MODIS vegetation information and AMSR-E derived soil temperature and soil moisture. The impacts of large-scale atmospheric and ocean circulation patterns (i.e. teleconnections) on ecosystems of the domain will be assessed by analyzing the linkages between the major oscillation indices and atellite based productivity, freeze-thaw and ET anomalies across the region. I will address the following science questions; (1) How is northern vegetation productivity changing under a warming climate? and (2) What are the primary environmental drivers of these changes and the consequences for land-atmosphere C02, water and latent energy exchanges? The proposed study will produce consistent, validated long-term records of northern vegetation productivity (NPP and GPP, 1982 onward) that incorporate the effects of boreal wildfires and freeze-thaw dynamics. This research will also establish a novel satellite-based ET algorithm for independent assessment and monitoring of regional land-atmosphere water and energy exchanges. These unique data sets effectively encompass major elements of the regional terrestrial carbon, water and energy cycles and will be applied with regional biophysical station networks and stand-level ecosystem process modeling to quantify the regional patterns, temporal trajectories, interactions and associated environmental drivers of these variables. The results of this investigation will produce new understanding and Earth System Data Records for northern latitudes that address NASA objectives for Carbon Cycle and Ecosystems and Water and Energy Cycle focus areas. Description: MAGNETIC ORIGINS OF SOLAR IRRADIANCE VARIATIONS We propose to explore the magnetic origins of solar spectral and total irradiance variations, through observations, data analysis and modeling approaches to directly address NASA-LWS TR&T Program's Focused Science Topic "d) Solar Origins of Irradiance Variations" as stated in this NRA. Changes in the spectrally integrated total solar irradiance (TSI) affect global climate directly, since TSI is the primary source of radiative energy input to the Earth system. Indirect climate influences include the solar radiative output at different wavelengths (spectral irradiance), which affect specific components of Earth's atmosphere in diverse ways. Exploring the nature and physical basis of this solar radiative forcing is vital towards understanding and predicting its effect on life and society, and for clearly distinguishing the natural and anthropogenic causes of global climate change. Solar spectral and total irradiance variability is governed by the changing magnetism of the Sun. Specifically, the appearance, evolution and associated dynamics of solar active region magnetic fields and its overlying coronal loops, directly contribute to irradiance variations - the latter is clearly magnetic in origin. In this proposal we plan to explore the magnetic origins of solar irradiance variations by: I) Establishing the relationship between important active region magnetic parameters (such as field strength, flux, loop length, measures of non-potentiality) derived from magnetograms and the observed solar spectral and total irradiance, II) Studying the connection between active region evolution and irradiance variations through the usage of a magnetogram partitioning algorithm that can follow the fragmentation of a decaying active region and the consequent redistribution of flux between the main spot and fragmented regions, III) Modeling the observed  dependence through analytic and numerical techniques to develop predictive capabilities for solar irradiance variations. Through specific examples, we demonstrate that the proposed data analysis and modeling are feasible and the probability of success in the proposed research is high. The research experience of the proposal team encompasses solar vector magnetic field analysis, coronal imaging, and data analysis and modeling of spectral irradiance variations. This proposal is highly relevant for the LWS TR&T program's focused research topic "d) Solar origins of Irradiance variations" as stated in this NRA. Our proposal also addresses the LWS program's general objective to understand the solar origins of Space Weather and Climate and develop predictive capabilities to mitigate their adverse effects on life and society. In the larger context, our proposal supports NASA Science Mission Directorate's strategic sub-goal 3-B - "Understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system".

Description: The presence of intrinsic defects and non-controlled impurities in materials for lasers and sensors can be one of the sources of possible failure and/or performance degradation of space system devices. Replacement of these devices is very expensive and even impossible for many spacecrafts. The study of non-controlled impurities and intrinsic defects and their correlation with definite physical properties allows us to characterize the quality of samples before use.  Most of these atomic size defects are paramagnetic or can be recharged to a paramagnetic state. Due to very high sensitivity and resolution the magnetic resonance methods  -  Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) and Electron Nuclear Double Resonance (ENDOR) are the most suitable methods for the study of such point defects. We propose to carry out the study of intrinsic defects and non-controlled impurities in nonlinear optical crystals, comparison and characterization of materials from different vendors. Together with scientific results, this research will give necessary background data for a reliable selection of laser and sensor crystals suitable for use in a space environment and for possible improvement of these materials

Description: Reaction wheel disturbances are some of the largest sources of noise on sensitive telescopes. Such wheel-induced mechanical noises are not well characterized. Disturbances can be amplified by wheel and other structural dynamics (for example, isolator modes), that are coupled to gyroscopic effects and therefore are wheel speed dependent. Tonal disturbances and wheel structural modes thus sweep across a frequency band. When one or more tones crosses the frequency of an observatory mode, a large jitter response will result. These higher harmonic effects have not been very significant in the past, for larger spacecraft having looser pointing requirements. However, many current and planned missions have much tighter pointing requirements than past missions. The higher harmonic wheel disturbances are being found to interact with structural modes to cause jitter exceedances. The lack of knowledge of higher harmonic wheel disturbance behavior forces engineers to carry more conservatism in the observatory design, resulting in potentially higher costs. The proposed innovation is a modeling tool that will create a hybrid physical/empirical wheel disturbance model from reaction wheel Induced Vibration data, suitable for high-confidence on-orbit jitter prediction.

Description: Reaction wheel disturbances are some of the largest sources of noise on sensitive telescopes. Such wheel-induced mechanical noises are not well characterized. Disturbances can be amplified by wheel and other structural dynamics (for example, isolator modes), that are coupled to gyroscopic effects and therefore are wheel speed dependent. Tonal disturbances and wheel structural modes thus sweep across a frequency band. When one or more tones crosses the frequency of an observatory mode, a large jitter response will result. These higher harmonic effects have not been very significant in the past, for larger spacecraft having looser pointing requirements. However, many current and planned missions have much tighter pointing requirements than past missions. The higher harmonic wheel disturbances are being found to interact with structural modes to cause jitter exceedances. The lack of knowledge of higher harmonic wheel disturbance behavior forces engineers to carry more conservatism in the observatory design, resulting in potentially higher costs. The proposed innovation is a modeling tool that will create a hybrid physical/empirical wheel disturbance model from reaction wheel Induced Vibration data, suitable for high-confidence on-orbit jitter prediction.
