Description: Convincing evidence exists from space and ground-based observations of young supernova remnants that magnetic fields in some remnants are many times larger than ambient fields in the interstellar medium. While it is likely that these fields are produced by diffusive shock acceleration, the same mechanism believed responsible for accelerating particles to cosmic-ray energies, no fully self-consistent theory coupling the efficient production of energetic particles with strong magnetic field amplification exists. We propose to develop such a theory and to apply it to observations of supernova remnants, radio jets, gamma-ray bursts and other objects. Such a theory will aid the interpretation of data from a number of NASA missions including Chandra, XMM-Newton, INTEGRAL, SWIFT, and GLAST by forming a sound physical connection between the observed radiation, the underlying particle populations accelerated by strong shocks, and the hydrodynamics of the shock system.

Description: The primary goal of CLASIC is to collect a dataset that can be used to improve parameterizations of cumulus convection and associated parameterizations of land surface processes. An important part of the experiment will be to decipher the respective roles of local and regional forcing on the served cloud structure. Thus, the spatial and temporal observation of turbulent fluxes in the atmospheric boundary layer(ABL) is essential for the overall success of this experiment. The Duke University Helicopter Observation Platform (HOP) is the best platform available nowadays to perform this type of observations. This is because it can measure turbulent fluxes at a slower airspeed and lower to the ground than other aircraft, thus increasing the resolution of observations and measuring where it greatly matters, namely in the atmospheric surface layer near the ground surface. The main objective of the project proposed here is to observe the spatial and temporal variation of fluxes of momentum, heat, moisture and carbon dioxide in the ABL over the different types of land cover found at the experimental site where CLASIC will be carried out, under the different meteorological conditions that will be encountered during the intensive observation period (IOP) in June 2007. We plan to perform a total of 100 flight-hours during the IOP. Well coordinated with properly-located towers and soundings, the information collected with the HOP will provide the crucial dataset needed to link and integrate the land-surface forcing into the overall observation system necessary for this experiment to be successful. Using a triangular flight pattern at three different altitudes in the ABL (near the ground surface, near the middle, and near the top of the ABL), the data collected will allow to study the balance of heat, moisture, and carbon dioxide at three sites where clusters of ground observations will be operated (i.e., the Little Washita River basin, the ARM/CART "Central" site, and Okmulgee - a forested site located in the eastern part of Oklahoma).

Description: INVESTIGATION OF COASTAL PHYTOPLANKTON DYNAMICS BY ADJOINT DATA ASSIMILATION OF SATELLITE OCEAN COLOR DATA Our underlying scientific objective is to determine the mechanism that control variations in phytoplankton biomass inferred from satellite-derived ocean color imagery. We hypothesize that the observed distributions result from the interaction of the ecosystem dynamics with the physical circulation. The problem is posed mathematically as an advection-diffusion-reaction equation for a scalar variable representing phytoplankton concentration. Given an initial distribution of phytoplankton, we seek to invert for the ecosystem dynamics such that integration of the forward model will result in predictions that minimize the sum of squares of differences with observed concentrations at some later time. An adjoint data assimilation technique has been designed for these purposes. We propose to use this general approach in a retrospective analysis of SeaWiFS and MODIS ocean color imagery in the highly productive United States (US.) northeast coastal ocean. We have the capability to generate hindcasts of the flow field for time periods in which ocean color images are available. Thus, we are poised to achieve optimal solution of a coupled physical-biological problem: given two synoptic snapshots of phytoplankton distribution and the associated flow field, we will invert for the phytoplankton dynamics that must be occurring during the intervening period. The resulting representations of the physical and biological properties will then be used for term-by-term diagnosis of the mechanisms controlling these extremely complex coupled systems. In particular, we will analyze the modulation of growth rates through both light and nutrient effects and various physically-controlled contributions to fluctuations in phytoplankton biomass.  The proposed project will support research-based education programs for graduate student and undergraduate interns to perform intensive "hands on" research and analysis on satellite remote sensing data, and data assimilative numerical modeling. Public education and outreach efforts will consist of public presentations, writings, and collaborations with educators and coastal managers. The approach will capitalize on the intriguing aspects of local coastal science and unique satellite technologies to educate general public about satellite observed ocean color, temperature, surface heights, sea-winds and to demonstrate important processes in costal ecosystem, including phytoplankton biomass, circulation, nutrient supply, and their interactions.

Description: Satellite data shows a strong spatial gradient in aerosol concentrations along the Himalayan range separating the Indo-Gangetic Plains from the relatively pristine atmosphere of the Indian Plateau, which is consistent with landform and regional orographic precipitation patterns. Description: IMPACTS OF LAND-COVER/LAND-USE CHANGE ON TERRESTRI AL ECOSYSTEMS CARBON BUDGET Human activities have changed land-covernand-use (LCLU) on earth surface tremendously. Among the most prominent changes are deforestation, urban sprawl and fragmentation of terrestrial ecosystems. The potential consequences of these land-coverAand-use changes (LCLUC) include, but not limited to, regional water and air quality, biodiversity, infectious diseases, and climate change. LCLUC has become a global phenomenon, and threatens the very goods and services that terrestrial ecosystems provide to sustain human society and other ecosystenls. It is highly unlikely that the trend in LCLUC will slow down in the foreseeable future, but to intensify. There is an urgent societal need to accurately estimate the potential impacts of LCLUC on terrestrial ecosystem functions so that timely measures can be taken to resolve or mitigate serious environmental consequences. There are many unknowns to the environmental impacts of LCLUC, and a thorough understanding requires coordinated investigations by scientists across multiple disciplines around the world. The goal of this project is to estimate the impacts of LCLUC on net primary productions (NPP) from the European settlement to the most recent urban expansion in the Triangle area of North Carolina with an emphasis on the most recent episode of LCLUC. The project will use multiple sources of remotely sensed data to characterize terrestrial ecosystem structure, particularly integrating the use of both spectral and spatial information of recently available images at meterlsubmeter spatial resolutions. The project emphasizes the link between ecosystem structure and functions in understanding the impacts of LCLUC on the environment. The detailed terrestrial ecosystem structure mapped with high resolution remotely sensed imagery will be integrated into models simulating ecosystem processes. The modeling results will he evaluated with ground measurements at various spatial and temporal scales. The Triangle area of North Carolina has been one of the most rapid growing regions in the US in the past two decades, and it has experienced rapid LCLUC. The Triangle area is also a unique place to enhance education for Geography. Among the Big Four universities (Duke, UNC Chapel Hiil, NCSU and Wake Forest), only UNC Chapel Hill has a Department of Geography. Through this project, I plan to develop a School Program for 8th-12th grade students in collaboration with the Morehead Planetarium and Science Center. The goal is to help them understand LCLUC with remote sensing and geographic information systems and foster career interests in Geography. In the meantime, I will integrate this project with my existing courses and develop a new course on LCLUC to attract undergraduate and graduate students in the Triangle area. I wish to build a solid scientific foundation for a life-long career in understanding impacts of LCLUC on terrestrial ecosystem functions through this project.

Description: PHYSICAL AND COMPOSITIONAL CHARACTERIZATIONS OF NEAR-EARTH OBJECTS The NEO search programs have generated a large number of discoveries and continue to do so at a significant rate. However detailed physical characterizations of these objects have lagged far behind the discovery rate. While it is not feasible to obtain detailed characterizations of a11 NEOs, it is important to characterize a representative sample of the NEO population in order to better understand the hazard potential of different segments of this population. Ongoing radar studies are providing an increasing body of information on NEO configurations, sizes and - in some cases - masses and densities. NEO albedos and sizes can be independently determined for a subset of NEOs from near-IR spectra using a technique that we pioneered. However, knowledge remains scanty about the detailed compositions and appropriate meteorite analogues of the NEO population. Most spectral studies of NEOs have focused on taxonomy and have provided only broad hints concerning NEO compositions. The research proposed here would continue our program of utilizing proven observational strategies and interpretive methodologies to derive detailed compositional characterizations of a sample of the NEO population. Existing density and lightcurve data, theoretical formation models, and our previous work suggest that: (a) binary NEOs - which are an important component of the PHA (potentially hazardous asteroids) population - are generally be loosely bound rubble piles irrespective of composition, and (b) NEOs smaller than -100-250 meters are predominately coherent solid bodies ("monoliths"). The proposed work would address the issue of the physical strength and integrity of NEOs as a function of composition and body size. This work should contribute to a better understanding of the physical properties of entire NEO population. These results would allow a more accurate evaluation of the implications of their physical properties on the potential hazards that arise from presence of objects in near-Earth space. This work will also continue to set a high standard for expectations of future compositional characterization efforts seeking funding in this program.

Description: NORTH DAKOTA NASA EPSCOR RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT As an upper Midwestern state, North Dakota faces a variety of challenges in nurturing and expanding an incipient science and technology competency. Its relatively small population and the dominance of agriculture as a source of employment and income have inhibited North Dakota's ability to compete for, and obtain, a proportionate share of federal science and technology dollars. If North Dakota, and other traditionally agricultural states, are to succeed in diversifying and growing their economies, then it will be necessary to train its workforce in science and technology occupations that will be of value to academia, the federal government, and industry - as well as contributing to the general scientific and technical literacy of its population. After accounting for population, North Dakota ranks 24th in the number of doctoral scientists per 1000 citizens, 42nd in the number of doctoral engineers per 1000 citizens, and 12th in the number of science and engineering doctoral degrees awarded per 1000 citizens in 2002.1 These statistics suggest that North Dakota maintains a modest science and technology workforce. A major goal is to develop an in-state science and technology industry that will employ North Dakota's graduates and employ a high-tech, high-value workforce that will diversify the state's economy and promote higher standards of living. Enhancing North Dakota's relevance to NASA requires continuing commitments to develop faculty research expertise and to produce students with science, engineering, and technology degrees that will both assist NASA in accomplishing its future science and spaceflight agendas while also developing an indigenous technical industry and workforce. Enhancing North Dakota's contribution to NASA's goals requires continuation of the North Dakota NASA EPSCoR program, which has begun the process of nurturing research efforts complementary to NASA's current and future goals.

Description: THE OPTICAL DATING RESPONSE OF MARS SEDIMENT ANALOGS INCLUDING GEOLOGIC SALTS TO SIMULTANEOUS UV/VIS IRRADIATION One of the greatest challenges to our understanding of Mars, whether we are "following the waler" or preparing the way for manned missions, is the need for geochronology. Numeric (or absolute) age-dating will help us understanda aronlet on the surface of Mars, (ii) the climate history of Mars that is recorded in the polar regions and other glaciated areas, and (iii) the frequency and intensity of dust and sand storms that could threaten the safety of human explorers. Optical dating, the subject of this proposal, is well suited to address these questions. Optical dating, also h.nown as Optically Stimulated Luminescence (OSL) dating, is based on principles of solid-state physics, and therefore, does not rely on atom counting or resolving isotopes of trace elements. The primary objective of this research is to expand the fundamental research base that will be needed to adapt this technique for in-situ robotic age-dating on Mars and to aid in deployable instrument design. The work has three specific objectives: cataloging the fundamental optical dating properties of geologic salts, evaluating the effects of simultaneous ultraviolet and visible light (IWNIS) irradiation on the optical dating properties of silicate and geologic salt analogs of Martian surface materials, and examining in detail the optically stimulated luminescence signal stability of silicate and salt analogs. The goals of this research are well aligned with four research foci within two major objective categories of NASA's Solar System E.xp1oration Roadmap. The significance of this project is in its potential to contribute to a more detailed chronology (than could be obtau11:d by sample-return) for Mars geologic and climatic history. This history is recorded in sedimentary deposits and geomorpholo@c surface features. Optical dating is uniquely suited among all current dating techniques to unravel depositional chronologies.

Description: MINERALOGICAL CHARACTERIZATIONS OF ASTEROIDS SUMMARY: The proposed research would focus in two general areas: quantitative mineralogical analysis of asteroid spectra and improvement of the quantitative methodologies and calibrations for analyzing asteroid-type reflectance spectra. The first effort will continue a long running productive program which remains the leading mineralogical characterization effort for asteroids. The second effort will address issues of the effects of space weathering on asteroid mineralogical characterizations, of limited wavelength coverage in asteroid spectra data, and of the presence of additional mineral on the widely used bi-mineralogic spectral calibrations. This research will support the NASA science goals to better understand small solar system bodies and what they tell us about the origin and early evolution of the solar system. This research will also support the planning and operation of asteroid spacecraft missions and the interpretation of the data returned by such missions.

Description: POLARMETRIC RADAR AND RAIN GAUGE MEASUREMENTS OF M ESOSCALE CONVECTIVE SYSTEMS DURING NAMMA The variability and characteristics of precipitation over West Africa are regulated by an interplay among African Easterly waves (AEWs), mesoscale convective systems, and Saharan dust outbreaks. For example mesoscale convective systems (MeSs) produce most of the rainfall over West Africa and are generated by among other things lower tropospheric shear associated with the Afr-ican Easterly Jet (AEJ), which is found between 700 and 600 mb. The AEW's which have lifetimes of 2-4 days, are not only important for rainfall over West Africa but also serve as precursors for Atlantic tropical cyclones. Each year approximately 80-100 AEWs emerge from the West African coast, with approximately 10% of these waves becoming named tropical systems. Despite the importance of these systems to rainfall over West Africa and Atlantic tropical cyclone activity understanding of their underlying properties and how they evolve, and vary remain lacking. A team of scientist and students from Howard University, University of Virginia, University of North Dakota, and NASA have been supported through NASA's Precipitation Measurement Mission (PMM) to obtain precipitation and supporting meteorological measurements in the vicinity of Dakar, Senegal during AMMA SOP-3 that could more precisely define the precipitation regime over the Atlantic coast of West Africa. The measurement systems that will be deployed include the NASA Polerametric radar (NPOL), upper air soundings, and surface-based networks of rain gauges, flux sites. For this proposal the team seeks support: for supplemental efforts to collect, quality control and archive the data, particularly making data available during NAMMA for operational activities; and to carryout data analysis and modeling studies. Through data analysis and modeling the team will investigate the following research questions and issues: - What are rain characteristics over this region? - Intensity, type, duration and microphysical characterization - Examination of precipitation systems in transition between land and ocean areas - What are antecedent conditions (thermodynamic and dynamic) of the atmosphere associated with precipitating systems? - What are the links between Saharan dust outbreaks and precipitating systems over the region? - Define the uncertainty of rainfall estimates from the precipitation radar and radiometers onboard TRMM.

Description: A STUDY OF ARCTIC RADIATION BUDGET USING CERES/MODIS SATELLITE AND ARM NSA SURFACE OBERVATIONS AND NASA GISS MODEL This proposed research is in response to the announcement of NASA ROSE-2005 NRA, in particular for NASA Energy and Water Cycle Study (NEWS), using three data sets: satellite, surface, and model over Arctic regions. We propose to develop a long-term merged aerosol-cloud-radiation vertical distribution product and use it to evaluate climate model simulations of the atmospheric structure. We plan to use DOE Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) surface observations, the NASA Clouds and the Earth's Radiant Energy System (CERES) on Terra and Aqua flux measurements and coincident Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) cloud and aerosol products, cloud and radiation flux products from GOES-10 to fill in gaps, and the NASA GISS Single Column Model (SCM) at the ARM Northern Slope Alaska (NSA, 71' 19' N, 156' 37' W) site during 2000-2006 period. Based on 6-yr dataset, we propose: Objective 1: Developing a long-term merged aerosol-cloud-radiation vertical distribution product. In this objective, we will develop the vertical profiles using two differently subsetted EOS datasets and a pseudo-EOS dataset based on GOES data. NASA CERES SW and LW fluxes and MODIS cloud and aerosol properties will be averaged in a 1' box centered on the ARM NSA site. Also, data from all CERES FOVs that include the site will be averaged for a given overpass. The GOES data are currently being analyzed at NASA LaRC and will be converted to CERES-like data using site specific narrowband-broadband conversion functions. A radiative transfer model will be used as input, the vertical distributions of cloud properties determined from the ARM ground-based radar-lidar-radiometer data, surface fluxes, and temperature and humidity profiles to compute the vertical distribution of radiative divergence. The satellite flux, cloud, and aerosol measurements wifl be used to constrain the calculations. Since large uncertainties are possible in the cloud and aerosol properties, they will be adjusted to ensure consistency between the TOA and surface fluxes. We wifl then study the seasonal and diurnal variations of surface, TOA and atmosphere SW and LW radiation budgets using the 6 years of surface-satellite data. Finally we will investigate the impacts of clouds on the surface/TOA/atmosphere radiation budgets in duration and strength and study the relationships between the radiation budget and the cloud vertical distributions for both multi-layered and single-laycred cloud systems. Objective 2: Evaluation of SCM simulations using the surface-satellite data. It is critical to link the model activities with the observations because the data cannot provide detailed physical processes and insight information. However, the models are frequently of little use in explaining the past or present, let along for predicting the future without the observations as constraints. In this objective, we will compare both surface and satellite results with the model simulations, understand the physical processes associated with cloud formation, maintenance, and dissipation, and modify the existing cloud-radiation parameterizations if necessary. From the comparison, we want to know if correct cloud-radiation properties produce agreement between observed and modeled values and if not, what the reasons for any discrepancies are. This proposed research is designed to address some key scientific issues and to help bridge the gaps in understanding that currently exist between Arctic clouds, surfacelTOAlatmosphere radiation budgets, and their interactions using three datasets. This proposed research will leverage current NASA instruments and resolirces and the proposed objectives apply to all four categories of the amended NEWS announcement. This project; research team is unique because we bring to bear documented expertise in the proposed research areas: satellite remote sensing

Description: Geospace-Related Missions of Opportunity Phase A and Bridge Phase Option - AO award The Robotic Lunar ExplorationLunar Precursor Robotic Program (RLEPLPRP) consists of a series of robotic lunar exploration missions to prepare for and to support future human exploration activities. The primary purpose of the robotic preparation is to reduce risk, enhance mission success, and reduce the cost of future human missions. The LRO payload used to accomplish the mission objectives consists of the following six Instruments: 1. Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) Measurement Investigation shall determine the global topography of the lunar surface at high resolution, measure landing site slopes and search for polar ices in shadowed regions; 2. Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) shall acquire targeted images of the lunar surface capable of resolving small-scale features that could be landing site hazards, as well as wide-angle images at multiple wavelengths of the lunar poles to document changing illumination conditions and potential resources; 3. Lunar Exploration Neutron Detector (LEND) shall map the flux of neutrons from the lunar surface to search for evidence of water ice and provide measurements of the space radiation environment which can be useful for future human exploration; 4. Diviner Lunar Radiometer Experiment (DLRE) shall map the temperature of the entire lunar surface at 300 meter horizontal scales to identify cold-traps and potential ice deposits; 5. Lyman-Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) shall observe the entire lunar surface in the far ultraviolet to search for surface ices and frosts in the polar regions and to provide images of permanently shadowed regions illuminated only by starlight; 6. Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) shall investigate the effect of galactic cosmic rays on tissue-equivalent plastics as a constraint on models of biological response to background space radiation. Each Instrument will be managed by a Principal Investigator (PI), who will be responsible for delivering the flight Instrument to the LRO project, as well as producing the Instrument's data products and delivering them to the Planetary Data System (PDS) in accordance with their data product specification document.

Description: NASA's future missions to investigate the structure and evolution of the universe require highly-efficient, very low temperature coolers for low-noise detector systems. We propose to develop a highly-efficient, lightweight, space magnetic cooler that can continuously provide remote/distributed cooling at temperatures in the range of 1 K with a heat sink at about 30 K. The proposed magnetic cooler uses an innovative cryogenic circulator that enables a lightweight magnetic cooler to achieve a large cooling capacity over a large temperature span. The circulator also enables the magnetic cooler to provide remote/distributed cooling and reduces the mass of the magnetic shields. The circulator has heritage in Creare's space-proven micro-turbomachine technology which has demonstrated long-life (>10 years) with no-discernable emitted vibrations. The proposed system will be much lighter than current multistage magnetic coolers. In Phase I, we will prove the feasibility of the magnetic cooler by producing designs for the magnetic cooler and the circulator that will demonstrate the mass and performance benefits of the approach. A magnetic cooler design will be delivered to NASA for future mission studies at the end of Phase I. In Phase II, we will design, build, and demonstrate the operation of a complete prototype circulator that will be delivered to NASA for integration into a magnetic cooler.

Description: NASA's future missions to investigate the structure and evolution of the universe require highly-efficient, very low temperature coolers for low-noise detector systems. We propose to develop a highly-efficient, lightweight, space magnetic cooler that can continuously provide remote/distributed cooling at temperatures in the range of 1 K with a heat sink at about 30 K. The proposed magnetic cooler uses an innovative cryogenic circulator that enables a lightweight magnetic cooler to achieve a large cooling capacity over a large temperature span. The circulator has heritage in Creare's space-proven micro-turbomachine technology which has demonstrated long-life (>10 years) with no-discernable emitted vibrations. The proposed system will be much lighter than current multistage magnetic coolers. In Phase I, we will prove the feasibility of the magnetic cooler by producing designs for the magnetic cooler and the circulator that will demonstrate the mass and performance benefits of the approach. A magnetic cooler design will be delivered to NASA for future mission studies at the end of Phase I. In Phase II, we will design, build, and demonstrate the operation of a complete prototype circulator that will be delivered to NASA for integration into a magnetic cooler.

Description: The goal of this work is to use CLUSTER/CIS data to determine the role of ionospheric ions in the plasma sheet in geomagnetic storm development. It is only during storm-times that O+ is a major constituent of the plasma sheet. The O+ density is highest during storm main phase, and is reduced during the storm recovery phase. This is consistent with observations in the inner magnetosphere during storms. Thus there is a good indication that the plasma sheet is the direct feeder for the storm-time plasma sheet, and that the inner magnetospheric composition reflects this source. Earlier work has also shown evidence for two sources for the O+ n the tail: the nightside aurora and the dayside cleft. Whic of these sources is dominant is not known. In the first four years of the CLUSTER mission, we have identified 38 storms where CLUSTEr has extended coverage of the magnetotial. In this study we will examine these individual storms in order to answer the follwoing questions: when does the increase in O+ in the plasma sheet occur, relative to changes in solar wind parameters and changes in Dst? Does the amount of O+ in the plasma sheet correlate with the minimum Dst of the storm? Which source contributes the most O+ to the plasma sheet? What is the role of substorms in the storm-time plasma sheet? Detailed analysis of these events will clarify the role that ionospheric input to the plasma sheet plays in forming the ring current. This goal is at the heart of the NASA strategic goal to understand the sun and its effects on Earth and solar systems. This proposal will lead to both progress in "understanding the physical processes of the space environment," and in "developing the capability to predict the extreme and dynamic conditions in space."

Description: DETECTION AND ANALYSIS OF MHD WAVES GENERATED BY INTERSTELLER PICKUP PROTONS The MHD waves generated by the isotropization of newly ionized interstellar pickup protons are a dominant source of fluctuation energy in all but the innermost region of the heliosphere, and are responsible for the heating of the thermal plasma in the outer solar wind. Continual spectral enhancements from this process were predicted by Lee&Ip (1987), but analysis of almost two years of Ulysses data uncovered only a limited number of short-lived events. These events are sporadic and apparently confined to the heliospheric equatorial region. Further observational work has not been reported. In the meantime, theoretical modeling of the interactions responsible for these waves has advanced well beyond the original Lee&Ip picture. However, this theoretical work proceeds in the absence of ongoing comparisons with observations, and the various predictions of this further work have not been tested against observational constraints. Understanding the detailed processes that determine the generation of these waves is important to correctly model the wave-particle interactions which operate throughout most of the heliosphere. Whether they produce observable spectral features or not, these waves are the primary driver for MHD turbulence in the outer heliosphere. As such, they govern the transport of cosmic rays and other energetic particles into the interplanetary region. Studies of their generation may also resolve puzzles that have arisen about the long mean-free-paths of low rigidity energetic particles. We propose a coordinated observational and theoretical program to investigatp where and how these waves can be generated, and to explain their sporadic nature. Our data analysis and theoretical efforts will support and guide each other to fully explore these questions. We propose to: Complete the analysis of the Ulysses data set up to the present. We will compile the spectral enhancement events, tabulating their properties and the solar wind conditions in which they are found. Expand this effort to analyze the available data from Pioneer and Voyager spacecraft and from the Cassini cruise data to obtain additional events. These new data sets will extend our observational capabilities to earlier solar cycles, larger radial positions, and a full range of heliospheric angular positions with respect to the interstellar gas inflow direction. i Compare these observational results with theoretical models to determine the necessary conditions for observable wave enhancements, and to understand the effects of competing processes such as turbulent spectral transport or wave dispersion. This proposal will meet the objectives of the Heliophysics Guest Investigator program by utilizing magnetometer and plasma data from several NASA spacecraft. These projects will further the NASA Strategic Objective 38.1 and, with regard to the applications to energetic particle propagation, Objective 3B.3. FORM NRESS-300 Version 2.0 Apr-06-05

Description: Numerical simulations of the turbulent cascade in the solar wind at kinetic scales This project is aimed at understanding and describing quantitatively the dissipation of the turbulent fluctuations in the solar wind and the resulting ion heating. To this end, two contradictory pieces of evidence need to be reconciled. On the one hand, ions are observed to be heated across the magnetic field, which is usually a signature of the cyclotron damping of the turbulent fluctuations. On the other hand, MHD turbulent cascades are expected to produce fluctuations that are mostly low-frequency and highly oblique to the magnetic field, so that they cannot be cyclotron-resonant with the ions. To address this problem, the project team proposes a series of hybrid (fluid electrons and particle ions) numerical simulations of the turbulent cascade at the kinetic scales of frequencies and wavenumbers. At these scales, the cascade mechanism is likely to be modified. The investigators' preliminary analysis indicates that the ion cyclotron-resonant fluctuations can be generated in the kinetic range, in contrast with the MHD regime. The goal of the proposal is to verify this hypothesis, guided by a variety of data. The turbulence spectra and ion heating rates resulting from the simulations will be tested against observations from the Wind, ACE, and Helios spacecraft. The proposers have access to over 800 one-hour spectra reduced from ACE and Wind data. They have also extracted a typical perpendicular ion heating rate as a function of solar wind speed from the published Helios data, which will verify the numerical heating rates. The ion kinetics presumably plays a leading role in the cascade mechanism. Nevertheless, the heating of the electrons can extract a significant portion of the turbulent cascade energy. Therefore, the Landau damping of the turbulent fluctuations on the electrons has to be taken into account. Since that cannot be done in a hybrid code directly, a less detailed fluid description of the Landau damping will be employed. This approach will be sufficient for the purposes of this study because the details of the electron (unlike the ion) distribution functions in the solar wind will not be investigated. The obtained theoretical results will guide and enhance the observational capabilities of any present and future NASA missions designed to investigate the physical processes in the solar wind plasma, such as STEREO or Solar Orbiter. The solar wind is the conduit connecting the geospace and the solar active phenomena. It significantly affects the propagation of energetic particles and strong disturbances from the Sun to the Earth. Therefore, knowing the properties of the solar wind helps prevent the potential exposure of humans to harmful effects of the solar activity in the outer space. Thus, this work is important for the success of the future space exploration mapped out in the new national program of prolonged human activity on the Moon and on the roundtrip to Mars and supports the National Objective to extend the human presence across the Solar System. This proposal is centrally connected to ongoing efforts of the Theory Group at the University of New Hampshire. The group is led by eminent scientists and educators with a wide sphere of influence in the scientific community and the public at large. The interactions with the group members will help to engage and educate the public thus advancing the scientific and technological capabilities of the nation. By guiding and enhancing the observational capabilities of the space missions, this research will provide the information for policy formulation of federal agencies coordinating the national program of space exploration. Therefore, it will help to meet the National Objective to develop innovative technologies, knowledge, and infrastructures both to explore and to support decisions about the destinations for human exploration.

Description: Advancing Our Understanding of the Earth System Through Coupled Carbon-Climate Modeling and observations Accurate predictions of the future of the Earth system rely upon our ability to simulate the many complex interactions between ecosystems, the hydrosphere, and the atmosphere. These simulations must also account for changes in forcing related to human and natural perturbations. This proposal is focused on the continued development and application of the Earth System Model at GFDL. The new land component of this model has been developed through a collaboration between NOAA GFDL and NASA with previous IDS support (NRA-03-OES-03) and is based on an integrated set of submodels developed at NOAAJGFDL, Princeton, and the University of New Hampshire. It consists of a new dynamic global vegetation model that is able to simulate ecosystem dynamics and exchanges of water, energy, and C02 and other gases with the atmosphere, accounting for the effects of climate variability, atmosphere, and land-use changes. The model includes state-of-the-art tracking of secondary (recovering) lands that have resulted from prior land-use and logging activities-- now 10-44 million km2 worldwide and the dominant net carbon sink in at least some regions. This proposal will build on this collaboration and specifically address Subelement 4: Coupled Carbon-Climate Modeling of the Interdisciplinary Research in Earth Science Program as part of NASA ROSES 2006. Our project will focus on model development and global model validation using NASA remote sensing. We will address research Goals 1-5 of the of U.S. Climate Change Science Program is Strategic Plan, and NASA Earth science questions: How does the carbon cycle respond to and affect global environmental change? How can predictions of climate variability and change be improved?

Description: The general understanding of the physical processes involved in auroral electrodynamics has been accepted for many years, however the details of the geometry of auroral arc current systems and their relation to the electrodynamics within an arc is at best only theoretically modeled and lacks experimental confirmation. Though numerous measurements have been made in auroral structures through either satellite, rocket or ground measurements; a multi-dimensional geometric picture of the aurora electrodynamics still requires reliance on multiple developed models that lack solid experimental confirmation. The single point measurement in a large-scale system and spatial/temporal limitations of satellites can only provide a glimpse of a piece of the auroral electrodynamics. Even modern multi-spacecraft missions and near conjunctions of satellites cannot provide sufficient resolution of these geometries due to their "randomness" in conjunction in both space and time relative to each other and the arc system. Furthermore, no current satellite project provides measurements at important altitudes (~120km) of the aurora current closure. To investigate the geometry and electrodynamics of a complete auroral arc current system requires a controlled placement of the appropriate instrumentation in the correct locations within an arc structure. We propose here two appropriately instrumented sounding rocket payloads with specific trajectories to place them at key position, simultaneously, within an auroral arc structure to provide confirmation of models and theories related to auroral arc structure and electrodynamics. To address the structure of an auroral arc, appropriate measurements must be made at multiple points. The ACES experiment will utilize two suitably instrumented rockets at two key altitudes within the arc. One payload will be above the ionospheric F peak to measure the imposed fields and energy input into the arc, the second payload will be at a lower altitude slicing through the classic current closure region (~120km). Both payloads will be in fight simultaneously to minimize any temporal variation between the measurements. Both payloads will be instrumented to measure DC Electric and Magnetic Fields, supra-thermal to energetic electron and ion distributions, cold plasma density and temperature. This mission will address some of the questions that are key to understanding the near Earth plasma environment and in particular Ionospheric-Magnetospheric coupling as well as Ionospheric-Thermospheric coupling. In fact many of the issues to be investigated here are identified as topics to be addresed in the GEC roadmap mission. The results obtained by this experiment would be instrumental in helping shape any future GEC type mission.

Description: This co-investigator proposal represents a collaborative effort supporting the Auroral Currents and Electrodynamic Structure (ACES) rocket experiment (NOI #N6-LCAS06-0006) proposal being submitted by Dr. Scott Bounds of University of Iowa. The ACES-LO is of particular interest in this regard, since Kelley and Earle (1988) reported HF emissions at E-region altitudes, possible evidence of a bump on tail instability involving suprathermal electrons, which could have wider implications even beyond the auroral ionosphere if confirmed. The instrument consists of two spherical probes mounted on a fiberglass axial boom, connected to a receiver which directly modulates a dedicated analog telemetry link, providing a measurement with approximately 5 MHz bandwidth. Similar instruments have flown successfully on RACE, HIBAR, and PHAZE-II among other previous experiments.

Description: NITRIC ACID AND FINE AEROSOL SULFATE MEASUREMENTS ONBOARD THE DC-8 AS PART OF THE TROPICAL COMPOSITION, CLOUD, AND CLIMATE COUPLING EXPERIMENT (TC4-COSTA RICA) The proposed investigation will provide measurements of nitric acid (HN03) and fine (1 um) aerosol sulfate (fine S04=) from the DC-8 with approximately 90 second resolution during TC4 - Costa Rica. Our measurement technique is based on collection by mist chamber samplers with analysis by on board ion chromatography. We are able to report near final mixing ratios of HN03 and fine S04= during flight after a chromatographic runtime delay of approximately 5 minutes. Field data is generally submitted within 24 hours of each flight, and in all recent campaigns our final data products have been virtually identical to the initial submission. Our HN03 technique is well established and it has been employed by our group for all GTE campaigns beginning with ABLE 2A in 1985 through the final GTE campaign (TRACE P) in 2001. We also participated in INTEX phase A in July - August, 2004, PAVE in January - February, 2005, and INTEX phase B during February - May, 2006. In addition, the system flew on the DC-8 for the SASS SONEX campaign in 1997, on the NCAR C-130 during TOPSE in 2000, and a second system flew on the NASA P3 for PEM Tropics B (coincident with operations on the DC-8 during this campaign). The majority of airborne data on HN03 mixing ratios in the troposphere have been collected by us with this technique. We added the capability to quantify fine S04= during the PEM TROPICS B campaign and have included this in all subsequent missions. Nitric acid remains a high priority measurement for AURA validation. It is our understanding that the TES team views correlative HN03 measurements above 500 mbar as priority 1, while the MLS and HIRDLS teams both list HN03 measurements in the UT/LS as priority 2 in their ongoing validation programs. Our technique has an unmatched heritage, and our DC-8 system has logged approximately 1800 hours on that platform already. Our sample integration time may be inadequate to address some questions about fast photochemistry, or to characterize plumes, but it translates into better than 10 mile horizontal and 1000 - 2000 foot vertical resolution, which should make a valuable contribution to AURA validation efforts. In addition, measurements of HN03 are central to several of the TC4 scientific objectives, e.g., defining the chemical boundary condition for the stratosphere, understanding ozone chemistry in the TTL, and interaction between short-lived soluble gases and ice crystals in cirrus. Similarly, fast measurements of fine S04= will contribute to better understanding of the factors controlling cirrus in the TTL, and the impact that different aerosols have on the number and size of crystals in cirrus in this region.

Description: Further Tests on a Modeling Framework to Detect and Analyze Changes in Land-to-Coastal Fluxes of Freshwater and Constituents Recent estimates made possible by improvements in remote sensing, GIS, data assimilation, and synthesis show that many of the changes unfolding across inland and coastal ecosystems are today detectable over continental-to-global domains. In this proposal we extend ongoing work to develop an integrated framework for analyzing the new system states. Three major advancements are targeted here, to: (i) establish within-basin geographies for multiple and interactive bioactive constituents; (ii) produce consistent time-varying (7-10 day composite) fluxes; and, (iii) explore the feasibility of an integrated inland-water / coastal zone surveillance system based on remote sensing from NASA and other agency satellites. We first focus on a set of Test Basins, emblematic of the major forces at work transforming modern river basin-coastal zone complexes. We then extend the work to the fully global domain in order to develop a geography of change to the major horizontal linkages joining land and ocean. Our principal technical goal is to develop a surveillance system that employs multiple platform, multi-resolution sensors. We have worked consistently toward this end, having developed models and data processing systems to analyze regional-to-global scale hydrology, suspended sediment transport, and fluvial delivery of bioactive nutrients to the coastal zone. Members of the study team are also pioneering remote sensing techniques to operationally monitor inland and coastal zone water quality. This proposal unites and enhances these resources into the Framework for Aquatic Modeling of the Earth System (FrAMES). We will consider fluxes of freshwater, suspended sediment, organic carbon and major nutrients and corresponding water-leaving radiances and derived products (chlorophyll, CDOM, optical density). We will document seasonal-tointerannual variability as well as episodic events coincident with recent multiple platform ocean color sensors (1997 present). We also plan to create a lessons-learned document to support future NASA mission planning in this arena.

Cascades2 is composed of five separated payloads that will make multipoint measurements of the auroral plasma at scale lengths of up to a several km and that will resolve spatial and temporal ambiguities. Cascades2 will address the following questions: (1) Do substorm aurora have proper motions? And what are the implications of this proper motion for magnetosphere/ionosphere coupling? (2) What is the absolute magnitude of ExB shears and current shears? And what are the implications for theories of wave particle interactions and instabilities? (3) Are the parallel and oblique motions of Alfvenic structures significant for magnetosphere/ionosphere coupling? And do direct observations of these motions validate theories and models? A winter 2009 launch from PFRR is requested. The Cascades2 science questions directly support the Themis mission, and the technology goals have direct ties to Themis, MMS, and MagCon through the development of "sensorcraft", the development of data analysis techniques for multiple point observations, and the training of students competent to continue developing the these techniques. Description: Natural disturbances across the Amazon landscape range in size from single tree fall gaps (- meters) to large blow-downs (kilometers). Quantitative studies of natural disturbances in the Amazon are rare. I intend to study natural disturbances and their effects on forest dynamics and carbon cycling in tropical forests using remote sensing (RS) approaches at two overlapping scales of natural disturbances. A primary goal of this work is to link disturbances to their proximal causes such as severe weather and to quantify the disturbance effects on biomass accumulation oftropical forests. The proposed study will provide regional constraints on present rates of disturbance for understanding the regional carbon cycle and for development of improved ecosystem models. The study will complement existing studies in permanent sample plots and will allow me to assess whether disturbance (mortality) rates measured in small plots are representative of regional patterns of disturbance. Existing forest inventory plots in old-growth neotropical forest are few in number, limited in size, and do not document spatial dependencies of vegetation elements across the landscape. Most permanent plots in tropical forest were designed for floristic analysis rather than for the study of carbon budgets. My proposed research combines (i) use of remote sensing to observe terrestrial ecosystems changes; and (ii) field measurements of carbon components (including coarse woody debris) to calibrate and test remote sensing approaches. The proposed work will help to answer one of the key questions for NASA Earth Science research, How is the Earth system changing, and what are the consequences for life on Earth? The proposed study responds to questions in the NASA focus area of Carbon Cycle, Ecosystems and Biogeochemistry: What are the magnitudes of terrestrial carbon changes caused by natural processes when compared with human activities?

Description: VARIATIONS IN SEP ACCESS TO EARTH DURING GEOMAGNETIC STORMS  The development and validation of a numerical model of solar energetic particle (SEP) access and trapping in the magnetosphere is proposed, to improve predictive capability of SEP fluxes and our understanding of magnetospheric dynamics responsible for variations in SEP fluxes during geomagnetic storms. During severe storms sudden changes in SEP access to Earth are caused both by cutoff variations due to changes in the geomagnetic field configuration and by the transport and heating of ions due to the storm sudden commencement (SSC) inductive electric electric field pulse associated with the impact of an interplanetary shock on the magnetosphere. An accounting for both of these effects is needed to model energetic particle fluxes in the geospace environment. A numerical model that predicts SEP fluxes in the magnetosphere from a given solar wind energetic particle distribution will be developed. The distribution is modeled by following Lorentz and guiding center test particle trajectories in time-dependent fields from a global MHD magnetospheric model, driven at its sunward boundary by measured solar wind parameters. Points in phase space are sampled using test particles weighted by an observed solar wind SEP distribution and retain their weight along particle trajectories.  Fluxes predicted by the model will be compared with SAMPEX and HEO spacecraft measurements. The model will be used to improve our understanding of the mechanism(s) responsible for SEP access to low L-shells during storms. The proposed work is submitted under 1.2.2 Independent Investigations in the ROSES 2006 Solicited Research Programs Appendix B, and addresses the NASA LWS TR&T goal of developing "the knowledge needed to provide advance warning space environment predictions along the path of robotic and human exploration." and to characterize "those aspects ofthe Earth's dynamic environment needed to design reliable electronic subsystems for use in air and space transportation systems."

Description: STOCHASTIC PARTICLE ACCELERATIONIN SOLAR FLARES  The acceleration of particles to energies exceeding 50 MeV in solar flares is a long-standing problem and one of the Focused Science Topics of NASA's 2006 Living-With-a-Star (LWS) program. This proposal addresses one of the leading theories for particle energization in flares, namely stochastic particle acceleration. In this theory, turbulent waves are excited in the flaring region by magnetic reconnection and the ideal fluid motions that arise as the magnetic field relaxes to a new configuration. The energy in these waves undergoes a turbulent cascade to small scales, resulting in high-frequency waves that accelerate particles to high energies through resonant wave-particle interactions. If the power spectra of these waves have the right properties, stochastic acceleration can explain many of the observed features of flares, including the acceleration time scales, the energy spectra of different particle species, and the highly enhanced abundance of helium-3 relative to helium-4 in the accelerated particle population. However, there is still no predictive theory for the turbulent power spectra of waves on the Alfven/ion-cyclotron and fast-magnetosonic/whistler branches of the dispersion relation in flaring regions. The determination of these power spectra is the most important unsolved problem for the stochastic-acceleration model, and is the focus of this proposal. Building on previous work by the PI and co-I, we will carry out weak turbulence calculations and direct numerical simulations to determine the power spectra of the above-mentioned waves for solar-flare conditions. A notable feature of this turbulence research is its extensive use of analytic theory in addition to numerical simulations, which will lead to highly detailed quantitative results, a theoretical framework that can be applied by other investigators, and a clear physical picture of the energy cascade mechanisms. We will use these power spectra to determine the acceleration times and energy spectra of different particle species as a function of the overall turbulence amplitude (i.e., the rms velocity at the largest scales) using quasilinear theory to treat the particle-acceleration process. We will then compare our results to x-ray, gamma-ray, and in-situ particle measurements. By determining the power spectra of the different wave modes in solar-flare conditions, our work will provide key missing information that is essential for assessing the importance of stochastic acceleration in solar flares, and for determining the contribution of flare-accelerated particles to large solar-energetic-particle (SEP) events observed at Earth.

Description: The Coupled Magnetosphere-Ionosphere-Thermosphere (CMIT) global simulation model will be used to determine how stormtime ionospheric outflows influence 1) the convective transport of ionospheric plasma at auroral and polar latitudes, 2) the distribution and intensity of field-aligned currents at the ionosphere, and 3) the distribution and dynamics of the ionospheric conductivity and Joule dissipation. CMIT integrates the Lyon-Fedder-Mobarry (LFM) global magnetospheric model with the NCAR Thermosphere-Ionosphere Nested Grid (TING) model. This project takes an important step in modeling the magnetospheric and ionospheric-thermospheric regions as a single connected system by including both electrodynamic and inertial couplings between the regions. To this end, we will utilize and advance a recently implemented, multifluid version of the LFM component of CMIT. Proposed extensions to the CMIT model also include causally driven cusp-region, auroral/polar-cap boundary-region, and polar-wind outflows at LFM's ionospheric boundary, regulated by TING's dynamic specification of the ionosphere. This investigation is directly aligned with the goals of LWS TR&T Focused Science Topic b) Effects oflonospheric-Magnetospheric Plasma Redistribution on Storms. The results will provide a useful touchstone for interpreting measurements, especially mass composition measurements, from existing NASA satellite missions such as Polar and Cluster, and it anticipates future needs to interpret distributed measurements of ionospheric and magnetospheric dynamics from the imminent THEMIS and TWINS missions, the LWS Radiation Belt and IT Storm Probes, and the GEC and MMS satellites.

The project uses both optical images (Landsat, MODIS) and synthetic aperture radar images (ALOS/PALSAR, L-band, HH and HV polarizations, 7.5-m spatial resolution) to generate improved geospatial datasets tbat would help improve our understanding of ecolog}' and risk factors of infectious diseases. Tills project also has an interdisciplinary education and training component, including graduate student fellowships. This EPSCoR project will make substantial contributions to the public health, one of 12 national priorities identiiied by NASA. Description: CHARACTERIZATION OF SI:LI DONOR FOR QUANTUM COMPUTING ERS - ABSTRACT OF PROPOSAL OBJECTIVES:  IT HAS RECENTLY BEEN PROPOSED THAT TWO STATES OF A LI DONOR IN STRAINED SI CAN BE USED AS A QUBIT FOR QUANTUM INFORMATION PROCESSING.  IT HAS BEEN PREDICTED THAT THESE TWO STATES WILL HAVE LONG RELAXATION AND COHERENCE TIMES.  THE TWO ELECTRON STATES HAVE DIFFERENT AMPLITUDES AT THE DONOR NUCLEUS AND THUS THE HYPERFINE INTERACTION WITH THE NUCLEAR SPIN IS  DIFFERENT.  HERE IT IS PROPOSED TO USE PULSED ELECTRON SPIN RESONANCE (ESR) TO TIME RESOLVE THE EVOLUTION OF THE HYPERFINE LINES AND THUS PROBE THE RELAXATION PROCESSES.  TECHNIQUES WILL BE DEVELOPED TO APPLY UNIAXIAL STRESS TO THE SI IN THE PULSED-ESR CAVITY AT TEMPERATURE DOWN TO 300MK.      A PARTICULARLY INTERESTING ASPECT OF THE DONOR STATES FOR SI:LI IS THE COUPLING BETWEEN THEM AND THE SPIN OF THE ELECTRON BOUND TO THE DONOR.  IN THE GROUND STATE (WHEN STRESS IS APPLIED) THERE IS NO HYPERFINE INTERACTION BETWEEN THE ELECTRON AND THE SPIN OF THE LI NUCLEUS SINCE THE VALLEY STATE IS ANTISYMMETRIC.  HOWEVER, IN THE EXCITED STATE (WITH STRESS) THE VALLEY COMBINATION IS NOT ANTISYMMETRIC, AND THERE IS A NON-ZERO HYPERFINE INTERACTION, AS SEEN BY WATKINS AND HAM, [5] IN CW-ESR EXPERIMENTS.  THUS THERE IS A NONTRIVIAL COUPLING BETWEEN THE SPIN AND SPATIAL STATES, BUT THE SPIN DYNAMICS (PULSED-ESR) HAS NOT BEEN STUDIED IN THIS SYSTEM. THE CHANGE IN THE HYPERFINE INTERACTION BETWEEN THE TWO LOWEST STATES MEANS THAT PULSED-ESR CAN PROVIDE A WAY TO MEASURE THE RELAXATION RATES FROM THE 1> TO 0> DONOR STATES.  FIRST, THE SI:LI WOULD BE EXCITED BY EITHER IR OR ABOVE-GAP LIGHT TO IONIZE THE DONORS.  ABOVE-GAP EXCITATION LEADS TO THE FORMATION OF BOUND EXCITONS AT THESE TEMPERATURES, WHICH DECAY THROUGH AN AUGER PROCESS.  THE RECAPTURE OF THE ELECTRONS PRODUCES COMPARABLE POPULATIONS OF THE 1> AND 0> STATES, WITH THE 1> THEN DECAYING WITH A TIME.  T, TO THE GROUND STATE.  THIS DECAY CAN BE MONITORED WITH A PULSED-ESR SPECTROMETER THROUGH THE TIME DEPENDENCE OF THE POPULATION OF 1> AND ITS UNIQUE ELECTRON SPIN RESONANCE (ESR) SIGNATURE.

Description: The need for higher performance fiber optic telecommunications receivers has provided the impetus for substantial progress during the last decade in the understanding and performance of InP-based linear mode avalanche photodiodes (APDs) for the wavelength range from 1.0 to 1.7 um. However, these advances have not been paralleled in the performance and availability of single photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) based on similar design and materials platforms. Moreover, the limited work that has been done to date has been focused on optimizing devices for telecommunications wavelengths in the vicinity of 1550 nm, and there has been even less effort towards devices for use at 1064 nm. Description: THE STAR FORMATION RATE IN A NERBY DAMPED LYMAN-ALPHA ABSORBER We wish to obtain deep GALEX images of the intervening Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxy SBS 1543+593 (z=0.009) which lies in front of the background QSO HS 1543+5921 (z=0.807). A detailed analysis of the CII* absorption line from the LSB galaxy in the background QSO spectrum has enabled us to calculate the star formation rate (SFR) along the sightline. To validate our results, we wish to use GALEX to measure directly the SFR in the galaxy. This is an important test, since CII* absorption lines are currently being used to quantify the SFRs in the population of high-redshift Damped Lyman-alpha (DLA) absorbers. Although this method is likely to be an important diagnostic of the physical conditions in these systems, the high-z of the DLAs makes it extremely difficult to test whether the absorption line data is giving the correct answer for the SFRs. We know, however, that SBS 1543+593 is itself a DLA, and its low-z means that the SFR can be measured directly with GALEX, allowing us to compare the real SFR with our inferred value. The LSB is also interesting in its own right: the optical emission is embedded in an HI disk with a radius -10 times that defined by the starlight. GALEX data would enable us to search for low rates of star formation in these outer regions, as well as isolated stellar complexes, offering important insights into the star formation history of the galaxy. SBS 1543+593 also appears to be part of a galaxy group, which raises the problem of how the large HI disk has managed to survive in such a potentially destructive environment. Since CALEX is adept at revealing low surface brightness features such as tidal tails, our data would allow us to search for clues as to how the LSB galaxy is interacting with its environment.

Description: High Cadence, High Resolution Studies of Solar Flares Under the support of our expiring Guest Investigator grant, we have made significant progress in studies of solar flares jointly observed by Big Bear Solar Observatory and RHESSI. Some unique instruments have been developed such as flare imaging systems with a cadence down to lOms and a resolution down to 0.3" in Haipha, visible and near infrared (NIR) continuum, and a new NIR imaging vector magnetograph system. New techniques have been implemented to analyze high cadence RHESSI data. We have also obtained some breakthrough results in understanding the observational signatures of flares. The most notable ones are the discoveries of rapid changes of magnetic fields associated with flares and the inward motion of footpoints in the early impulsive stage of flares before they start to separate. Building on these achievements, we propose to advance our studies in the next three years by carrying out research in the following three related areas: (1) We will investigate the nature of sub-second time scale elementary bursts. These observations will provide details of flare energy precipitation on small temporal and spatial scales. By combining high cadence optical imaging with hard X-ray imagingllight curves from RHESSI, as well as high resolution vector magnetograms, we expect to obtain a more detailed picture of how the individual sub-second peaks in the hard X-ray time profiles correspond to the rapid precipitation along various flux loops. (2) We will study a large number of events with high cadence, high resolution, to characterize the footpoint motion in the impulsive phase of flares. In particular, we will find if contracting motion of footpoints always occurs in early stage of flares, and the relationship between the extend of the contraction and the energy release of the flares. Multi-wavelength observations will be compared with a few models, in particular the possible "implosion1' suggested by Hudson (2000). (3) We propose to study the structure and evolution of magnetic fields in flaring active regions with advanced vector magnetograms. We will investigate: (a) Can we obtain 3-D coronal structure change corresponding to the beforelafter changes of photospheric magnetic fields? (b) What is the role of the evolution of the photospheric magnetic field in triggering solar flares? (c) Can the observed field evolution add information in understanding the flare footpoint contraction in the early stage of flares? The proposed research will mainly fit the core scientific objectives of RHESSI, secondarily, TRACE and SOHO, as well as the future mission Solar-B.

Although 02 is considered a biosignature gas in its own right, and can be sensed remotely, the presence of 02 and N20 would be compelling evidence of non-equilibrium metabolic reactions that are related to life as we presently know it. Description: OCEAN COLOR, CARBON AND CIRCULATION: STUDIES WITH AN EARTH SYSTEM MODEL This proposal examines links between ocean circulation and biogeochemical cycling using coupled climate models. It builds on three recent results in our group. The first shows that tropical ocean color can act as a positive feedback on climate change and variability. Removing ocean color from the near-equatorial zones can actually result in warming the equator and reducing the magnitude of vertical exchange in this region. The second result shows that the tropical circulation in the ocean and atmosphere of appears to be slowing down under climate change in a manner consistent with anthropogenic climate change. The third result is that the efficiency of the oceanic biological pump, which plays an important role in regulating atmospheric carbon dioxide, is determined by the circulation of the Southern Ocean. Changes in the preformed nutrient content can greatly alter the biological pump, and simulations with ideal age tracers indicate that the processes that ventilate the deep Southern Ocean with high preformed nutrients are very sensitive to climate and the numerical representation of ocean circulation. We propose to build on these results by 1. Performing studies which seek to better understand the mechanisms and processes determining shortwave absorption. This will involve analyzing satellite and insitu estimates of ocean color and chlorophyll (revisiting the bio-optical approximation), performing sensitivity studies where the impacts of colored dissolved organic matter and chlorophyll are separately considered, and developing prognostic models of ocean color. 2. Including prognostic biogeochemical models in a coupled model built around GFDL's isopycnal ocean model. This model (which was used to do the simulations in which ocean color was removed) has a much more realistic representation of oceanic overflows than previously run level-coordinate models. This model will be used to build prognostic models of ocean color and run under changed and changing climates. The work will involve a close collaboration between researchers at Princeton/GFDL developing state-of-the-art coupled models, and researchers at UCSB who have worked over the past decade to characterize shortwave absorption in the deep ocean. It will advance IDS objectives by quantifying the impact of ocean color on climate and by identifying key feedbacks and processes that needs to be modeled to simulate the entire earth system.

Description: Early in 2006, the Stardust spacecraft returned to Earth, carrying particles that it captured when it passed through the coma of Comet P81/Wild 2. The recovery ofthe particle collector has created the opportunity to analyze documented cometary material for carbon and nitrogen. We describe experiments aimed at determining, non-destructively, the abundances of C and N in a set of Wild 2 fragments and at making related measurements that will set the results for C and N in context and allow their generalization. In particular, we propose to study a representative suite of Stardust fragments through measurements of: 1. The numbers of atoms of C, N, Si, and O by nuclear reaction analysis; 2. Particle shapes, petrography, and composition by combining observations made using an optical microscope and a scanning electron microscope; 3. The types of organic compounds present by using infrared spectroscopy; 4. The numbers of atoms of Fe and other elements by observing x-ray fluorescence generated by synchrotron x-radiation. Concurrently, we will attempt to develop methods for analyzing the Stardust fragments without extracting them from the aerogel capture cells. The measurement of cometary carbon and nitrogen is relevant to NASA^s strategic goal of advancing scientific knowledge ofthe origin and history ofthe solar system, the potential for life elsewhere, and the hazards and resources present as humans explore space. Carbon and nitrogen are of interest for many reasons. They are the principal components of the ^organic^ phase(s) known from remote observations in many comets. The absolute and/or relative abundances of C and N may help in classifying different types of comets.

Description: FROM THE SUN TO THE STARS: THE NEW SCIENCE OF HELIOPHYSICS "FROM THE SUN TO THE STARS: the New Science of Heliophysics" is a one hour High Definition Video documentary on the first five decades of the Space Age, beginning with IGY (1957) and America's Explorer 1 satellite, and ending - during IHY - with the twin Voyager spacecraft at the very edge of the heliosphere. The television special will be enhanced and extended "beyond broadcast" by the production of shorter, edited versions adapted to multiple additional audiences and different media formats, from streaming video to podcasts. Every component of the project is intended to inform and excite young people (middle school and above) and public audiences about the new science of heliophysics by presenting dramatic examples of Sun-Earth-solar system connections, from "space weather" impacting our planet, to the universal processes that also shape galaxies and the Universe at large. From Van Allen's epochal discovery of the radiation belts that bear his name, to exploring the region where our solar system tails off into inter-stellar space, we've come to realize that magnetism shapes our planet's - and life's - origin and evolution. The program shows how space weather affects important aspects of our modern global civilization, and why learning to explore the Moon, Mars and beyond requires space-faring nations discovering how to keep human voyagers safe from radiation. One location segment shows how the United Nations Basic Space Science program and IHY collaborators are distributing low-cost space weather monitors to youngsters around Earth, to motivate developing nations' involvement in earth and space science. FROM THE SUN TO THE STARS will appear on NASA-TV, and will be offered to PBS and other networks. An experienced Advisory Board will guide the science content of the program, which will be produced in 1080i HDV, and also Standard Definition. A detailed Management and Staffing Plan, and Production timetable, are proposed. SUN TO STARS will be made accessible through the NASA portal, and other podcast aggregators such as iTunes, Google, YouTube, etc. HDV segments will be offered to science centers and museums for hosting on kiosks and other venues. Effective education and outreach collaborators have already been identified (such as Sun-Earth Day 2008.) If funded as proposed, 10,000 DVDs will be provided to NASA CORE. IHY provides a uniquely "teachable moment" to raise the visibility of the fundamental new science of the Sun-Earth-Solar System connection, vividly demonstrating its relevance and application to life on Earth and to future human exploration of the solar system. FROM THE SUN TO THE STARS provides a state-of-the-research broadcast documentary in a classic one hour format, together with an extensive suite of innovative new media formats, making 2007-2008 a unique opportunity to engage young people and public audiences with some of the key themes of NASA's heliophysics program. Description: ASSESSMENT OF THE PREDICTIVE SKILL OF GPM-ERA PRECIPITATION ESTIMATES FOR HYDROLOGIC APPLICATIONS It is expected that spaceborne precipitation estimates during the era of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission (available at a resolution of approximately three hours in time and ten kilometers in space) will be useful for a wide range of hydrological applications. This expectation is particularly high for regions where traditional hydrometeorological networks are sparse, such as in Africa and much of Asia. The extent to which GPM-era precipitation estimates will be skillful and useful, however, is unresolved, and a better determination thereof is the primary focus of this research project. Secondary objectives include a refinement of the error characterization of spaceborne precipitation estimates and exploration of ways to improve the predictive skills of spaceborne precipitation estimates by means of integrating them with other remotely sensed information like surface soil moisture and surface temperature. A framework for systematic evaluation of the predictive skill of GPM-era precipitation estimates will be developed and applied to hydrologic applications ranging from event-based river flow forecasting for basins of approximately 10,000 km2 and larger to regional-to-continental scale water cycle variables such as soil moisture and water budget studies. The predictive skill of a variety of precipitation products for forecasts of streamflow and soil moisture content will be objectively assessed relative to a reference standard. Use will be made of available precipitation records based on surface rain gauge and radar data, and infrared, passive and active microwave information observations from spaceborne sensors. This project will yield a quantitative assessment of the predictive skill of GPM-era precipitation estimates and how that may vary with geographical region, seasons, and space and time scales of the hydrologic application. The outcome of this research is not only central to NASA's GPM mission, but also of great interest to the broader hydrometeorology and climate research and operational communities.

Description: PI- V. RAMASWAMY PRINCETON UNIVERSITY EMISSION, TRANSPORT, AND DEPOSITION OF MINERAL DUST IN THE SOUTHERN OCEANS AND ANTARCTICA AN  INTEGRATED APPROACH USING GCM AND SATELLITE OBSERVATIONS  (GRADUATE STUDENT: FUYU LI)  EMISSION, TRANSPORT AND DEPOSITION OF MINERAL DUST IN THE SOUTHERN OCEANS AND ANTARCTICA: AN INTEGRATED APPROACH USING GCM AND SATELLITE OBSERVATIONS THE GOAL OF THE PROPOSED INVESTIGATION IS TO QUANTIFY THE EMISSION, TRANSPORT AND DEPOSITION OF MINERAL DUST IN THE SOUTHERN OCEANS (SO) AND ANTARCTICA, PARTICULARLY FOCUSING ON THE SENSITIVITY OF THESE PROCESSES TO THE SURFACE CHARACTERISTICS OVER THE SOURCE AREAS. DUST IS OF PARTICULAR INTEREST IN THE SO AND ANTARCTICA AS AN INDICATOR OF CLIMATIC CONDITIONS, A FERTILIZING AGENT FOR OCEAN PHYTOPLANKTON, AND AN IMPORTANT SCATTERER AND ABSORBER OF SOLAR RADIATION. HOWEVER, OUR CURRENT KNOWLEDGE OF THE DUST CYCLE IN THIS REGION IS FAR FROM BEING COMPLETE AND QUANTITATIVE, AND DISCREPANCIES EXIST BETWEEN MODEL RESULTS AND OBSERVATIONS. WE WILL INVESTIGATE THE VARIABILITY OF CYCLE, AND ITS SENSITIVITY RELATIVE TO THE SURFACE CHARACTERISTICS BY INCORPORATING SATELLITE OBSERVED VEGETATION IN THE ATMOSPHERIC MODEL. WE WILL ALSO ASSESS HOW FAR DUST EMISSION AND TRANSPORT CAN BE CONSTRAINED BY SATELLITE AEROSOL PRODUCTS AND HOW INDICATIVE IN-SITU DATA ARE IN THE EVALUATION OF UNCERTAINTIES IN DUST DISTRIBUTION COMPARED TO SATELLITE DATA. THE CONTRIBUTION OF EACH MAJOR DUST SOURCE TO DUST DEPOSITION IN ANTARCTICA WILL BE QUANTIFIED AND SENSITIVITY STUDIES WILL BE PERFORMED TO UNDERSTAND HOW SENSITIVE DUST DEPOSITION IN ANTARCTICA IS RELATIVE TO VEGETATION COVER IN SOURCE AREAS AS WELL AS OTHER FACTORS SUCH AS THE WIND SPEED AND PRECIPITATION. THESE OBJECTIVES WILL BE ACHIEVED BY USING AN INTEGRATED APPROACH, TAKING ADVANTAGE OF THE STATE-OF-THE-ART GFDL ATMOSPHERE MODEL AND SIX SATELLITE INSTRUMENTS INCLUDING MODIS ON 2 PLATFORMS, MISR, AVHRR, TOMS, AND OMI. IN THE INVESTIGATION, THE LEAF AREA INDEX (LAI) WILL BE USED AS THE MAIN INDICATOR OF SURFACE CHARACTERISTICS NEAR DUST SOURCES. THE DUST DISTRIBUTION WILL BE SIMULATED OVER THE 1980-2003 PERIOD BY CONSTRAINING THE MODEL HORIZONTAL WINDS WITH RE-ANALYSIS. DETAILED ANALYSIS OF SOME CASE STUDIES WILL BE PERFORMED BY FOLLOWING THE SIMULATED AND OBSERVED LONG-RANGE TRANSPORT OF DUST PLUMES. THE INTER-ANNUAL VARIABILITY WILL BE ASSESSED BY COMBINING THE MODEL RESULTS WITH LONG TERM RECORDS (~ 25 YEARS) OF SATELLITE DATA AND IN-SITU MEASUREMENTS. THESE QUESTIONS PRIMARILY SUPPORT THE NASA SCIENCE FOCUS AREA OF ATMOSPHERIC COMPOSITION, WHICH SEEKS TO DEVELOP THE UNDERSTANDING OF THE EVOLUTION OF AEROSOLS AND THEIR IMPACTS ON CLIMATE, AND THE RESPONSE OF ATMOSPHERIC TRACE CONSTITUENTS TO GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE AND THE SUBSEQUENT EFFECTS ON GLOBAL CLIMATE. THEY WILL ALSO PROVIDE USEFUL INFORMATION FOR (1) RESPONSE OF THE DUST CYCLE TO VARIATIONS AND CHANGES IN LAND COVER, AND (2) THE PREDICTIONS OF CLIMATE VARIABILITY AND CHANGE    BY IMPROVING OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE CLIMATE VARIABILITY IN THE PAST UTILIZING LONG TERM DUST RECORD IN PALEO-ARCHIVES AS AN INDICATOR OF CLIMATE. THESE TWO ASPECTS ARE DESCRIBED IN THE NASA SCIENCE FOCUS AREAS OF CARBON CYCLE & ECOSYSTEMS AND CLIMATE VARIABILITY AND CHANGE, RESPECTIVELY.

Description: The need for higher performance fiber optic telecommunications receivers has provided the impetus for substantial progress during the last decade in the understanding and performance of InP-based linear mode avalanche photodiodes (APDs) for the wavelength range from 1.0 to 1.7 um. However, these advances have not been paralleled in the performance and availability of single photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) based on similar design and materials platforms. Moreover, the limited work that has been done to date has been focused on optimizing devices for telecommunications wavelengths in the vicinity of 1550 nm, and there has been even less effort towards devices for use at 1064 nm. For this SBIR program, we propose to apply innovative design concepts for the development of high performance SPADs optimized for 1064 nm applications. In particular, we will implement a novel bandgap engineering approach to tailor the SPAD avalanche gain properties to realize higher single photon detection efficiency while maintaining the very low dark count rates that are made possible by optimizing the absorption region design for the detection of 1064 nm photons. We will also apply design concepts that we have innovated during the course of developing state-of-the-art 1550 nm SPADs that involve optimization of the device electric profile for photon counting as well as epitaxial layer compositions that provide lower dark count rates through defect density reduction. These efforts will culminate in 1064 nm large area detectors (with active area diameters on the order of 200 - 500 um) that demonstrate feasibility in meeting SPAD performance targets including 50% detection efficiency, bandwidth of 500 MHz, saturation levels of 50 Mcounts/s, and non-gated operation. We will also use the detectors developed to deliver linear SPAD arrays for use as photon-counting line-scan imagers. These detectors will benefit general lidar applications including systems for measuring atmospheric properties such as wind and weather patterns, air pollution, and general trace gas analysis.
