Description: Plasma Actuators for Turbomachinery Flow Control, 06-SSFW-06-0105 The proposed effort is to create a CFD and theoretical model development and validation team that will work together with NASA to explore high authority flow control by dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasmas. The team research effort will develop further understanding of the physics behind the mechanisms that cause the DBD discharge to generate surface flow, will develop computational models that incorporate that physics, and through the use of those models, will design configurations that are optimized for particular applications. This team will build on preliminary theory, modeling and experimental work at Princeton that indicates that dielectric barrier discharges driven by high repetition rate (hundreds of kilohertz), ultra-short (several nanosecond) high voltage pulses together with a DC voltage bias have the potential of generating high authority control. This preliminary model suggests that breakthrough performance, at least 1 order of magnitude better than previously demonstrated DBD plasma actuators, can be achieved through the use of the high voltage pulses and a DC bias. The proposed effort is to build more complete computational models and validate by experiments the model projections. The primary goal is to develop and validate a powerful physically-based computational design tool that will be transferred to NASA and used for evaluating the utility of this technology. The secondary goal is to demonstrate a high authority DBD configuration that will be useful for the control of turbomachinery. Work will also address the issue of DBD plasma actuator operation in an atmosphere other than air (combustion gases), at elevated temperatures and at the high pressures characteristic of internal conditions in turbo machinery. The experimental work will include studies of the possibility of reducing leakage losses and controlling separation under conditions appropriate for turbo machinery. The proposed effort will be a cooperative work with researchers and engineers at nasa glenn

Description: GALEX Survey of the Atacama Cosmology Telescope Strip We propose imaging of the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) strip with GALEX. In conjunction with the ACT collaboration optical follow up program, GALEX observations will enable us to achieve accurate photometric redshifts for galaxies lensed by the ACT clusters in the redshift range 0.6 1.2. In addition to the mm observations provided by ACT, we have obtained optical (griz) observations from the Blanco Cosmology Survey. The ACT collaboration will construct a weak lensing map offield galaxies by clusters in the ACT strip. Accurate photometric redshifts of the lensed field galaxies are needed in order to obtain accurate (to within 10%) mass estimates for the dark matter of clusters. Most galaxies lensed by clusters at z > 0.5 are blue and therefore their photometric redshifts are difficult to measure with bands that only sample the 4000 AA, break. By obtaining GALEX photometry we will be able to sample the Lyman-alpha break, as well, a feature which is more pronounced in blue galaxies. We will thus be able to increase the accuracy in the photometric redshift to 0.06 rms. One of the main goals of ACT is to measure the equation of state of dark energy with high accuracy (a few %) by obtaining masses for ACT clusters through weak lensing; this accuracy will not be possible without the proposed GALEX observations. Additionally, a welcome by-product of these observations will be a measurement of star formation in the galaxies in ACT clusters for z 0.5. The ACT strip is unique in the sense that it will contain optical and mm observations of clusters selected by the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect, i.e. a mass selection. The addition of GALEX observations to the ACT strip will provide a Legacy set of observations for the astronomical community.

Description: DISTRIBUTION AND DYNAMICS OF THE SOLAR MAGNETIC FLUX IN THE PHOTOSPHERE AND HELIOSPHERE This proposal is being written in response to a request by the TRT focus team on "Solar and Heliospheric Magnetic Field" led by T.H. Zurbuchen, University of Michigan. The team, and especially its lead, has been encouraged to propose for a third year of funding to allow a successful completion of the focus team work. The need for this proposal arises from two reasons: First, our initial proposal extended only over two years. We are well on the way to achieving the statements of work (SOW) for this initially proposed research. Second, in response to team-objectives, we have adjusted our SOW to be of maximum help to the focus team and our work is now well connected to other parts of the team-work. During the first year of our collaboration we have analyzed dynamics of emergence of new dipoles inside coronal holes and in adjacent quiet-Sun areas. We have shown for the first time that the dipole emergence rate of the magnetic flux inside coronal holes is suppressed as compared to the quiet sun areas. This finding agrees with the idea that coronal holes are formed at locations where the dipole emergence rate is low, and therefore, open magnetic flux can be accumulated at these places (theory of the coronal holes formation and solar wind acceleration, Fisk 2005). This theory suggests that reconnection between open magnetic flux and closed-magnetic loops is an essential diffusion mechanism for open filed lines. We are currently improving and modifying our existing algorithms and numerical codes to calculate power spectra of magnetic field fluctuations (both spatial and temporal) as well as high statistical structure functions, which would allow us to derive flatness functions and filling factor, and estimate intermittency of the magnetic field both in the photosphere and in the solar wind. This analysis will then be compared to the results of other team members (both observational and theoretical). Our funding is likely to run out before the completion of this collaboration, which is an important part of the work by the focus team. During the third year, we will study magnetic flux distribution in the photosphere both inside and outside of coronal holes. We intend to apply our techniques to photospheric and solar wind measurements. Conclusions and parameters obtained from the study will be used as input date and/or constrain the models of coronal hole formation and solar wind acceleration developed by our focus team.

Description: STUDIES OF NET AND GROSS PRODUCTION IN THE SOUTHERN OCEAN: CONTROLS AND SCALING Studies of the biogeochemistry of the Southern Ocean are of great interest for several reasons. Upwelling of deep water supplies nutrients to the surface, causing summertime production to be high. The nutrient flux to the surface, as well as the character of regional ecosystems, may change as stratification and upwelling respond to global warming. Net production in the Southern Ocean removes nutrients from the upper waters. This process therefore determines the nutrient burden of Subantarctic Mode Waters, which supply nutrients to much of the extrapolar ocean (Sarmiento et al., 2004). The Southern Ocean is the world's largest high nutrient - low chlorophyll region. Because biogeochemical processes in HNLC waters from different regions share some common attributes, the Southern Ocean can serve as a model region for studying distributed phenomena. Finally, the cause of glacial-interglacial CO2 differences remains unresolved, but changes in Southern Ocean biogeochemistry remain a primary option for explaining these variations.

Description: COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF INTERACTING VORTICES SPANNING JUPITER'S SOUTHERN MIDLATITUDES ALL THE MAJOR VORTICES IN JUPITER RESIDE IN THE SOUTHERN MID-LATITUDES, AND A GREAT WEALTH OF INFORMATION, DERIVED FROM REMOTE SENSING OBSERVATIONS, EXISTS ON THE PROPERTIES OF THESE FEATURES AND REGIONS AT AND ABOVE THE CLOUD COVER LEVEL. HOWEVER, IT IS STILL UNCLEAR WHAT IS THE STRUCTURE OF THE ATMOSPHERE BELOW THAT LEVEL. BY APPLYING FORWARD-MODELLING TECHNIQUES TO REPRODUCE THREE DISTINCT AND UNIQUE DYNAMICAL EVENTS THAT INVOLVE THE INTERACTION BETWEEN SOME OF THE MAJOR VORTICES IN THE PLANET LOCATED IN THREE ADJACENT LATITUDINAL DOMAINS, CENTERED APPROXIMATELY AT 23, 33, AND 40 DEGREES SOUTH RESPECTIVELY, WE EXPECT TO GAIN NEW INSIGHTS INTO THE PATTERNS GOVERNING JUPITER'S GLOBAL CIRCULATIONS, AND TO DRAW A COHERENT PICTURE OF THE VERTICAL STRUCTURE OF THE ATMOSPHERE FOR THE WHOLE SOUTHERN MID-LATITUDINAL REGIONS OF JUPITER. WE WILL USE WELL-ESTABLISHED FORWARD-MODELLING TECHNIQUES TO STUDY THE OBSERVED DYNAMICS OF THE THREE DIFFERENT EVENTS UNDER CONSIDERATION. THESE TECHNIQUES ARE EXTENSIONS OF STRATEGIES USED RECENTLY TO ACCURATELY REPRODUCE IN DETAIL SIMILAR DYNAMICAL EVENTS IN JUPITER'S ATMOSPHERE. THE GENERAL CIRCULATION MODEL USED WILL BE THE EXPLICIT PLANETARY ISENTROPIC CODE (EPIC V3.8 AND V4.0) DEVELOPED UNDER THE DIRECTION OF PROJECT COLLABORATOR PROF. TIMOTHY DOWLING AT THE UNIVERSITY OF LOUISVILLE.  THE PI, MORALES-JUBERIAS, HAS WIDE FAMILIARITY WITH THE MODEL ITSELF AND WITH ITS APPLICABILITY ON FORWARD-MODELLING PROBLEMS. THIS PROPOSAL IS PARTICULARLY RESPONSIVE TO NASA'S PLANETARY ATMOSPHERES PROGRAM BECAUSE IT ADDRESSES THE CHARACTERIZATION AND UNDERSTANDING OF DYNAMICAL PROCESSES AND CIRCULATIONS, BOTH GLOBAL AND LOCAL, OF THE ATMOSPHERE OF JUPITER. IT ALSO ADDRESSES THE EXAMINATION OF CURRENTLY PROPOSED THEORIES REGARDING THE VERTICAL STRUCTURE OF THE ATMOSPHERE AND IT INVOLVES THE ANALYSIS OF ATMOSPHERIC DATA FROM NASA SPACE SCIENCE MISSIONS ARCHIVED IN THE PUBLIC DOMAIN ON THE PLANETARY DATA SYSTEM. THE RESEARCH IS ALSO RELEVANT TO NASA'S STRATEGIC SUBGOAL 3C ADVANCE SCIENTIFIC KNOWLEDGE OF THE ORIGIN AND HISTORY OF THE SOLAR SYSTEM, THE POTENTIAL FOR LIFE ELSEWHERE, AND THE HAZARDS AND RESOURCES PRESENT AS HUMANS EXPLORE SPACE, OUTCOME 1 PROGRESS IN LEARNING HOW THE SUN'S FAMILY OF PLANETS AND MINOR BODIES ORIGINATED AND EVOLVED.

Description: HRTEM PETROLOGY OF COMET WILD 2 DUST CAPTURED IN THE STARDUST SILICA AEROGELTHE RECENT NASA STARDUST MISSION TO THE JUPITER-FAMILY COMET WILD2 COLLECTED, THOUGH REGRETFULLY NOT INTACT, SOME OF THE EJECTED DUST. THE DUST INCLUDED A SURPRISINGLY LARGE AMOUNT OF CRYSTALLINE SILICATES, MOSTLY MG,FE-OLIVINE AND PYROXENES [MG/(MG+FE) 0.5], A DIVERSE SET OF REFRACTORY SILICATES AND OXIDES, AND FE(NI)-SULFIDES. THESE MINERALS ARE MOSTLY FOUND IN TERMINAL PARTICLES (2-10 MICRONS). THE MINERAL SPECIES ALSO OCCUR SCATTERED WITHIN THE AEROGEL CAPTURE WHERE THEY TEN TO BE SUB-MICRON IN SIZE DOWN TO A FEW NANOMETERS. WILD 2 DUST APPEARS TO BE WEAKLY CONSTRUCTED MIXTURES OF SUCH NM-SCALE GRAINS WITH OCCASIONAL LARGER GRAINS (ZOLENSKY ET AL., 2006). MANY CRYSTALLINE GRAINS ARE FOUND PARTIALLY ENCAPSULATED IN MASSIVE AEROGEL THAT APPEARS TO HAVE ACQUIRED SOME OF THE MINERAL CHEMISTRY IN A PROCESS YET UNCLEAR, THE (SOLID-STATE DIFFUSION; MELTING?) WHILE AEROGEL WITH EMBEDDED COMET MATERIAL ARE OFTEN MASSIVE COHERENT (MELTED?) ENTITIES 5 TO 20 MICRONS IN DIAMETER. I WILL USE HIGH-RESOLUTION TRANSMISSION ELECTRON MICROSCOPY WITH ANALYTICAL CAPABILITY FOR THE PETROLOGICAL AND MINERALOGICAL CHARACTERIZATION OF WILD 2 DUST EXTRACTED FROM SELECTED TRACKS TO DETERMINE THE PETROLOGICAL PROPERTIES OF THE COMET DUST, THE EXTENT OF ITS THERMAL MODIFICATION, AND ITS INTERACTIONS WITH AEROGEL. THESE PROPOSED LABORATORY ANALYSES WILL BE RELEVANT TO DETERMINE THE ORIGINAL NATURE OF THE WILD2 DUST, TO UNDERSTANDING NEBULAR CHEMISTRY AND DYNAMICS AS THEY CONTROLLED TO DUST SUPPLY IN THE KUIPER BELT AND IT WILL SUPPORT OBSERVATIONAL ASTRONOMERS AND MODELERS OF COMET DUST FORMATION AND EVOLUTION IN THE TO EARLY SOLAR NEBULA. REFERENCE: ZOLENSKY M. ET AL. (2006) SCIENCE, 314, 1735-1739

Description: INTEGRATED MINERALOGICAL AND ISOTOPIC STUDIES OF STARDUST COMETARY PARTICLESIN JANUARY 2006, THE STARDUST MISSION SUCCESSFULLY RETURNED MYRIAD SAMPLES OF DUST EJECTED FROM COMET WILD 2. THE STARDUST COMETARY PARTICLES REPRESENT AN IMPORTANT NEW SOURCE OF EXTRATERRESTRIAL MATERIALS WHICH HAS THE POTENTIAL TO PROVIDE SIGNIFICANT NEW INSIGHTS INTO THE NATURE OF EARLY SOLAR SYSTEM MATERIALS AND PROCESSES. IN THIS PROPOSAL, WE WILL CARRY OUT COMBINED MINERALOGICAL AND ISOTOPIC STUDIES OF STARDUST PARTICLES IN AN EFFORT TO CONSTRAIN THE ORIGINS AND THERMAL HISTORIES OF THESE MATERIALS AND ESTABLISH THEIR RELATIONSHIPS TO KNOWN SAMPLES OF FINE-GRAINED EXTRATERRESTRIAL MATERIALS SUCH AS CARBONACEOUS CHONDRITES AND INTERPLANETARY DUST. THESE STUDIES WILL BUILD ON THE SUBSTANTIAL KNOWLEDGE BASE GENERATED DURING THE SUCCESSFUL PET INVESTIGATIONS. WE PROPOSE TO USE STATE-OF-THE-ART TRANSMISSION ELECTRON MICROSCOPE TECHNIQUES TO FULLY CHARACTERIZE A RANGE OF PARTICLES INCLUDING TERMINAL PARTICLES AS WELL AS PARTICLES COLLECTED AT DIFFERENT DISTANCES ALONG TRACKS. THESE STUDIES WILL PROVIDE COMPLETE MINERALOGICAL AND CRYSTALLOGRAPHIC CHARACTERIZATION OF INDIVIDUAL PARTICLES INCLUDING THE DISTRIBUTION OF SOLID CARBON-BEARING PHASES. FOLLOWING TEM STUDIES, SUITABLE PARTICLES WILL BE STUDIED USING ION MICROPROBE TECHNIQUES TO DETERMINE THE ISOTOPIC COMPOSITIONS OF INDIVIDUAL PHASES AS WELL AS THE ELEMENTAL DISTRIBUTIONS OF MINOR AND TRACE ELEMENTS WITHIN THE PARTICLES. THESE STUDIES WILL INCLUDE OXYGEN ISOTOPIC STUDIES IN COLLABORATION WITH GARY HUSS AT UNIVERSITY OF HAWAII AND YUNBIN GUAN AT CALTECH. WE ARE PARTICULARLY INTEREST IN FINDING PARTICLES IN WHICH THE FINEST GRAINED COMPONENT OF THE COMETARY MATERIAL HAS BEEN CAPTURED WITH MINIMAL PROCESSING DURING THE CAPTURE PROCESS.

Description: Aerospace structural systems experience a broad spectrum of environmental and operational loads. Severe and/or prolonged load exposures may trigger the damage accumulation process even recently deployed structures. The process of implementing a strategy of damage detection for engineering structures is referred to as structural health monitoring{SHM). Three important new issues/approaches impacting SHM methodology are addressed in this proposal. The first is to treat SHM as a comprehensive, multi-scale phenomenon in which damage detection maybe needed over a spectrum of length scales from the microscopic to the macroscopic. The second issue is attributing to damage in joints and connections an importance commensurate with fracture and fatigue damage that develops in the structural material. Our third new approach is to develop material self-healing systems (SHS) capable of repairing material damage while maintaining structural integrity. The strategies proposed will be intended for many aerospace structures, including aircraft, launch vehicles, space vehicles, permanent structures placed on the moon or Mars, and robotic devices that patrol these structures for SHM. The lines of attack that will be followed in pursuit of the new SHM and SHS methodologies include new methods for use of nonlinear vibration data, novel use of electrical conductivity measurements for SHM, and embedded nonlinear ultrasonic methods for local damage detection. In addition, development of the theory and technology for self-healing systems (SHS) in metals, alloys and composites could lead to significantly improved safety of aerospace vehicles and structures. These approaches will be integrated to develop a comprehensive SHM/SHS strategy that will be of significant value to NASA during coming decades. The proposed research enables development of research infrastructure in New Mexico in areas of strategic importance to NASA's mission and will enhance the capability of New Mexico to obtain space, aerospace, and related research support from sources outside the NASA EPSCoR program by I)developing new, approaches for SHM/SHS of aerospace structures and systems of importance to NASA, 2)developing research collaborations between NASA and New Mexico research groups, and 3)developing research credibility and national competitiveness in SHM/SHS through research publication and graduate student education. These objectives address NASA EPSCoR Goals 1,2,3 and 4 respectively. The research team has a long term relationship with New Mexico Space Grant Consortium (NMSGC) and their statewide partners and the team will work to increase interest in aerospace and other STEM disciplines among New Mexico's students, especially women and minorities in fulfillment of Goal #5. A key element of this proposal is development of a collaboration among NASA Marshall and Glenn Centers, the other New Mexico research institutions, and Los Alamos and Sandia National Labs. This collaboration and the future funding generated by it will significantly enhance New Mexico is overall research infrastructure, including development of the graduate aerospace engineering programs in the state and attraction of aerospace entities to New Mexico.

Description: Although methane is the third most abundant component in the atmosphere of Uranus and it is the principal absorber at visible and near-infrared wavelengths, its precise abundance is not well known. Baines et al. (1995, Icarus 114,328) determined the tropospheric mixing ratio for methane to be between 1.1 and 2.3 percent, but the findings of Sromovsky and Fry (2006, BAAS, 38,3, #05.07) suggest that the methane content is lower. Since Uranus' 98-degree axial tilt results in extreme seasonal variations, its methane abundance is likely influenced by the seasonal variations in insolation. It is vital to take advantage of the time period around Uranus' December 2007 equinox for studies of seasonal variation, as the next equinox will not occur until 2049. Determining the methane content will further our understanding of the structure, thermodynamics, and photochemistry in Uranus' atmosphere, and will elucidate similarities and differences between Uranus and other giant planets. This project also has applications to the field of extrasolar planets, as Uranus- and Neptune-sized planets around other stars are now being discovered (Butler et al. 2004, ApJ, 617,580). Determining the abundance of methane in Uranus' atmosphere will assist in modeling the formation and evolution of our own solar system and will place these recently discovered extrasolar planets into context. The issue of the methane distribution in Uranus' atmosphere will be addressed using near-infrared spectra obtained at NASA's Infrared Telescope Facility in 2006. These spectra will be compared to the synthetic spectra resulting from various model atmospheres. These atmospheres will consist of an opaque cloud layer located beneath an optically thin methane cloud layer and a scattering haze layer. The free parameters of these model atmospheres will be varied to determine which vertical profiles of methane best replicate the observed spectra. Spectra from multiple latitudes on Uranus will be employed in order to investigate any possible latitudinal variation in the methane distribution. The near-infrared spectra of Fink and Larson (1979, ApJ, 233,1021-1040), taken when Uranus was about halfway between equinox and solstice, will be similarly analyzed to search for seasonal variations in the methane abundanee. This project will answer the following three questions: -What is the methane abundance in Uranus' atmosphere at equinox? -Does the methane distribution vary with latitude or longitude? - Is there evidence for seasonal changes in the methane abundance? An improved understanding of the composition of Uranus' atmosphere will help constrain the parameters of the circumsolar disk from which the planets formed, as welt Uranus' own evolutionary history. By addressing these subjects, this project fulfills two goals established in the Solar System Exploration Roadmap for NASA's Science Mission Directorate (2006). FORM NRESS-300 Version 2 0 AD^-06-05

Description: TRACTICAL ROVER-BASED MARTIAN GEOLOGIC MAPPING Current state-of-practice techniques for location refinement of planetary surface rovers are too time-consuming to conduct during the tactical science process of surface operations. As a result, uncertainty in the location of a rover during the tactical decision-making process detracts from the quality of science planning. By expanding existing tactical software to "harvest" the inputs of team member targeting of surrounding features during the normal course of science analysis, we have learned that it is possible to perform location refinement quickly enough to inform the tactical science process. This improved knowledge will lead directly to the planning and execution of superior geologic mapping observations. Enabling rover operators to perform location refinement during the tactical planning process will enhance productivity in many ways, including: -increased data return and time available for execution of science by using previously transmitted images for targeting and avoiding wasting time and bandwidth by retransmitting images of terrain already on the ground to compensate for inadequate localization knowledge. -increased accuracy and quality of targeted science observations -improved collaboration between science investigators, particularly those who are geographically distributed: We will present an accurate geologic context to each scientist from within the science planning tool that he or she uses to analyze science data and to collaborate with the group in planning new science observations. -support for integrating geologic mapping information from rover science on a planetary scale by geographical information systems (GIs) integration jopening additional avenues for cross-domain collaboration and sharing of knowledge between science investigators This study directly addresses the specific goals of the ASlR program by (I) adapting existing tactical processes to solve an important issue (positioning and data location within that position) for rover science operations, (2) demonstrating that, through use of relatively simple improvements in existing data acquisition methodologies the pace of mission accomplishments can be increased, (3) build on the interdisciplinary interaction of spacecraft information specialists and cud-users (scientists) to further refine operational methods, and (4) fostering increased science return through methods that ;stitch; site to site remote observations in a geologic framework supported by accurate position data.

These techniques will also be used to provide a virtual experience of the Mars Exploration Rover (MER) landing sites. This program combines existing strengths of NSHE researchers in the fields of geomorphology, geology, biology, remote sensing and computer visualization. Remote sensing data from the Mojave Desert and Lunar Crater Volcanic Field analog sites will be coupled with new, cutting edge experiments on surface processes at these sites. The resulting 'virtual field labs' will be used to train a new generation of investigators in terrestrial geosciences, the interpretation of image and other data from NASA planetary missions, and mission planning and operations for future manned and robotic surface exploration ofthe Moon and Mars. We will integrate existing airborne and spacebome imagery with new high-resolution digital elevation data. The visualization approach will include the development of software which will immerse the viewer into the terrain and allow creation of landform and compositional maps. Experiments conducted at the analog sites will emphasize understanding the links between microbiology, mineralogy and oxidation in a dry, desert environment. In addition, studies of controls on sediment transport and implications for rover rafiicability will be undertaken. Our proposal directly supports integration and synthesis of data on multiple scales, and from differing perspectives, in order to maximize future return from present and future robotic probes and train students and future mission teams in the interpretation of data on various scales to make informed decisions on navigation or understand landscape evolution. The proposed activities support NASA Strategic Goals and specific objectives outlined for both the Mars Exploration Program and Lunar Exploration Program as documented by MEPAG and LEAG.

Description: INVESTIGATION LARGE SCALE TROPICAL ATMOSPHERIC DYNAMICS USING TRMM DATE We propose to use TRiMM precipitation radar (PR) data to study the dynamics of synoptic-scale weather variability over the tropical oceans. Large rain events over the tropical oceans are often associated with convectively-coupled wave disturbances of specific types, such as Mixed Rossby-Gravity waves, Kelvin waves, etc. Different wave types have different dynamical characteristics, so their interaction with deep convection may be different, and preliminary work with surface radar data from Kwajalein Atoll shows that this is the case. The proposed work will generalize and broaden these preliminary results using the PR data. An understanding of the differences in precipitation structure between wave types may lead to new insights into the mechanisms by which convection is modulated on large scales over tropical oceans. In simple terms, we will use the PR data to understand how weather disturbances which have different fluid dynamics on the large scale induce different dynamics in the precipitation systems on smaller scales. Meteorological analyses and satellite observations will be used to identify and classify wave events, and then PR data will be used to characterize the convective systems associated with different wave types. The convectively coupled waves will be identified and classified using spectral analysis following Wheeler and Kiladis. PR data will then be composited by wave type, and the composites compared. Contoured frequency by altitude diagrams (CFADs) will be used to characterize the PR data in a compact way. Radiosonde data will then be composited as well, to investigate the dynamical reasons for differences seen in the CFADs. Description: ESTIMATION ENTROPY WITH ERROR BARS: COMPUTING INFORMATION- THEORETIC MEASURES OF CAUSALITY We naturally describe the "Earth's system" as 2 collection of interacting subsystems whose interactions are commonly described as forcing and feedback. Changes in one subsystem will cause or force responses in other subsystems. These responses then in turn feed back to force other subsystems, and so on. The Earth's system can be described as an enormous multivariate nonlinear dynamical system. As such, it is self-reactive in the sense that climate can change and evolve without human-induced forcing. To understand such a system is a formidable task, since there do not yet exist general techniques for analyzing such complex dynamical systems. The first and most important step is to identify the relevant variables, their primary feedbacks, and to determine the magnitudes and time scales of their causal interactions. While many important feedbacks have long been known, the details of their causal interactions remain unknown.  The focus of our long-term efforts is centered on developing a suite of data mining tools that would allow the estimation of causal interactions among climate variables from data in large databases. These techniques will rely on the estimation of entropy-based quantities, such as mutual information and transfer entropy. While this is a critical goal, we have identified rapid and accurate entropy estimation from data as a significant bottleneck in the technological development process. The specific aims of this project are to develop novel computational techniques that accurately estimate entropy from multi-dimensional data sets. These methods must be accurate, relatively fast, and must quantify all uncertainties. Our efforts will focus on applying a recent stochastic integration method called Nested Sampling to a variety of density models such as Mixtures of Gaussians, Spline-Based Models and Voronoi Cell models. We will make these computational techniques publicly available as tools to allow researchers to compute entropies and higher-order information theoretic quantities from data in large datasets of their choosing.

Description: A Very Low Noise CMOS Detector Design for National Aeronautics and Space Administration We propose to design, fabricate, develop, and test a novel new detector for NASA space missions. These missions reply on low noise array detectors that must operate in the harsh radiation environment of space. Most current missions use CCDs for their optical detectors. White these devices have low noise (2 few electrons) at the beginning of mission life, they are gradually degraded by radiation damage. The design we propose will address this, and several other problems. Our device will deliver lower noise, lower power consumption, much larger dynamic range, and greater radiation immunity than presently available CCD and CMOS detectors. In addition, it will allow much greater operational flexibility. All of these benefits will lead to lower mission cost and greater scientific productivity. Our design efforts will produce 2 new multiplexor having application over a large wavelength range, spanning from UV to mid-infrared, via hybridization to a variety of light-sensitive materials, i.e. silicon, HgCdTe, InSb, InGaAs, %:As, and Ge:As. The new device will also have applications for Homeland Safety, i.e. in surveillance in low light conditions on our nation's borders and in battlefield platforms on UAVs. The design uses low power CMOS circuits that are arranged in high density packaging within individual pixels. The low noise readout is achieved by sampling the signal using a sigma-delta analog-to-digital (AID) circuit with a feedback path that restores charge to the charge collection node. The keys to the lower noise readout are the close proximity of the conversion circuit to the photogenerated charge, oversampling nature, and noise-shaping property of the in-pixel sigma-delta AID converter. These properties allow our design to highly attenuate the photodetector reset noise, DC offset related fixed-pattern noise, and readout transistor thermal and Ilf noise. Since the design is insensitive to threshold voltage variations of the readout transistor, we believe that our design will be less susceptible to radiation transients and long-term damage that can cause shifts in the readout transistor performance parameters. We have fabricated early prototypes of our design and the measured performance is promising. We estimate single read noise of approximately 0.3 electrons, consistent with our model predictions. In addition, we have demonstrated power consumption of 0.88 nW per pixel, or three orders of magnitude less than in the most advanced CCDs and more than one order of magnitude less than presently available CMOS detectors. In addition, our design shows inherent linear response to the incident photon flux (i.e., the design is insensitive to non-linear capacitance of the photodetectors). This feature allows further reduction in power supply voltage (i.e., photodetectors do not require high biasing voltages to stay in their linear regime), which in turn reduces junction and gate leakage currents of the readout transistors and improves low-light response.

Description: Observations from the AMMA SOP (September 2006) along with satellite observations will be used to improve our ability to predict tropical yclogenesis in the eastern and central Atlantic by improving our (1) prediction of African wave disturbances (AWDs) entering the Atlantic basin and (2) understanding of the physical processes involved in the transition of AWDs into tropical Atlantic cyclones. The focus will be on examining the relationship between tropical Atlantic cyclones and surface and atmospheric conditions over West Africa to see if the inclusion of more detailed information can improve our ability to simulate and understand tropical cyclogenesis. This includes paying close attention to land surface characteristics including soil moisture distributions to see if they offer any value for extended range prediction of AWDs and tropical Atlantic cyclones. The physical analysis will focus on mechanisms that influence the transition of AWDs into tropical cyclonic systems. These objectives will be addressed through the application of current (MM5) and next-generation (WRF) mesoscale atmospheric models. Observational and reanalysis data, including the NASA QuikSCAT Sea Winds surface winds, TRMM precipitation, EOS-class Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer (AMSR-E) land data products, NCEP/NCAR reanalysis, and AMMA SOP surface and aircraft observations, will be used to specify surface and lateral boundary conditions in the models. Model resolution will be on the order of 30 km (depending on the application), with nests down to resolutions of the order of 10 km to better resolve AWDs and tropical cyclones. Such relatively high resolution is also needed to accurately capture the strong meridional gradients in land surface conditions that are important to the development and maintenance of African precipitation system. Bringing the model resolution close to that of the higher resolution or highly localized observations facilitates model validation. Description: The regional climate model of GISS/CCSR (RM3) has achieved a documented and rather unique success in simulating the important mesoscale and synoptic features of the West African monsoon, including daily precipitation rates that are highly correlated in time and place with TRMM daily estimates. The research will create a mesoscale four-dimensional data set of evolving climate variables over West Africa for the AMMA Special Observing Period-3 (SOP-3) for September 2006 from a continuous RM3 climate simulation. Lateral boundary conditions (LBC) to drive RM3 simulations will come from NCEP or ECMWF global analyses. As a first step, several adjustable RM3 components will be optimized for best agreement between sample simulations versus SOP-3 ground and aircraft measurements and observational evidence culled from TRMM, QuickSCAT, AMSR-E, AIRS, MODIS and SSM/I data. The optimal configuration of the following will be determined by testing and validation: horizontal and vertical resolution; moisture convergence; terrain relief. Resolution will be tested at 0.3 and 0.5 horizontal grid spacing and up to 28 vertical levels. The 4-D data set will be transmitted to the designated NASA data archive center for general access. Observational data collected during the SOP-3, supplemented by available meteorological observations from satellite platforms, will be used as validation to document the 4-D data set's quality, i.e., its strengths and weaknesses. Satellite and rain gauge observations of precipitation rates during SOP-3 will validate precipitation rates from simulations. The sensitivity of forecasts to the quality of the initial data specification will also be evaluated. LBC for forecast experiments will come from global model (GCM) forecasts. The research will make an important contribution to the AMMA effort by providing data sets that can be used to investigate the characteristics of precipitation processes in the West African region and the adjacent eastern Atlantic, with focus on the transition between continental and maritime convective systems and eastern Atlantic cyclogenesis. Description: Some interplanetary dust particles (IDPs) are the most primitive (i.e., least altered by thermal or aqueous processing) samples of the dust that condensed as our Solar System formed that are currently available for laboratory analyses. Many primitive IDPs even preserve interstellar material, as demonstrated by non-Solar D, 15N, and 16O contents (detected by Dr. S. Messenger, NASA Johnson Space Center and others). This project has three major objectives: 1) determine the types and abundances of organic matter delivered to the Earth, Mars, and other planets and moons by the IDPs and assess its importance as a source of pre-biotic organic matter for the origin of life (a possibility suggested by Anders, Nature, 1989), 2) compare the organic matter in the most primitive anhydrous IDPs with that in hydrated IDPs and hydrated meteorites to determine the changes in this pre-biotic organic matter brought about by aqueous alteration, and, 3) characterize the organic matter in the most primitive IDPs to understand and constrain the conditions and infer the mechanisms for the production of organic matter in the early Solar System, and, in the case of organic matter exhibiting non-Solar D or 15N, the production of organic matter in the interstellar medium or around other stars. The IDPs are small, typically ~10 microns in size, and are dominated by silicate minerals. Thus we require instruments of high-sensitivity to detect and characterize their organic matter. We determine the amount and types of organic matter in these particles using two high-sensitivity, synchrotron-based instruments: 1) a Scanning Transmission X-ray Microscope with a resolution ~35 nanometers to determine the C , N and O abundances and to characterize the organic functional groups by X-ray Absorption Near-Edge Structure spectroscopy, and, 2) a microscope-based Fourier Transform InfraRed spectrometer with a spatial resolution of ~3 to 5 micrometers to determine the organic functional groups.

Description: CORRECTIONS TO SCATTEROMETER WIND VECTORS: MEASUREMENTS OF ERRORS CAUSED BY RAIN-INDUCED SURFACE ROUGHNESS USING HIGH RESOLUTION NEXRAD RADAR MEASUREMENTS The primary mission of the orbiting QuikSCAT satellite scatterometer is to measure wind speeds and directions on the sea surface. An important source of error is rain in the atmosphere and its impact on the sea surface.  The satellite radar performs measurements of the reflections from the sea surface (the normalized radar cross section). One of the rain-induced error sources is the rain-impact (splash) at the surface which modifies the radar cross section.  These modifications cause errors in the sea surface wind speed and direction derived from the affected data, the magnitude of which depends on the true surface relative wind speed and the rain intensity. This project is developing a method that can partially correct the errors caused by the rain-impacts on the surface. This project will continue the development of high resolution three-dimensional measurements of the precipitation structure within a QSCAT cell using the NEXRAD radar. These measurements are being used to correct the measured NRCS by removing the attenuation, volume scattering and rain-impact ("splash") on the surface. This results in an estimate of the sea surface NRCS that would exist, for the local wind speed, if rain were not present. The efficacy of this approach depends on the wind speed and rainrate. This new work will bring two benefits to the utilization of scatterometer wind vectors  when they are affected by rain. By developing a model for the rain-impact NRCS, it will be possible to make confident estimates about when the total rain contribution to the Level 2A NRCS can be ignored, even though measurable, but low intensity, rain is falling, and the Level 2B rain flags indicate a "rain contamination". The limitation these rain flags currently have is that while they can detect the presence of rain, there is currently insufficient knowledge about whether or not this rain (including splash) changes the total NRCS significantly. By using the high resolution NEXRAD radar collocated with the QuikSCAT cells, all the electromagnetic properties of the  rain column can be measured and used to determine the effect on the L2A data, and subsequently the wind vectors, L2B data. The other benefit exist when the rain is sufficiently intense so that it appreciable changes the total NRCS. The new results expected here for the relative rain-impact NRCS, when combined with the atmospheric corrections, will complete the model needed to remove all rain effects. It will permit estimation of the "wind driven" sea surface NRCS.

Our specific objectives are 1) to estimate the fraction of bodies that are in a binary configuration; 2) to measure the physical properties of the small bodies (including mass, size, and density), to constrain their mechanical properties and to probe their interior structure; 3) to characterize the formation mechanisms of binaries and subsequent evolutionary processes; 4) to infer constraints on the compositional and thermal characteristics of the early solar system, and the current distribution of volatiles. The proposed investigation addresses a number of NASA strategic goals: learning how the Sun's family of planets and minor bodies originated and evolved, exploring the space environment to discover potential hazards to humans, and understanding the processes that determine the history and future of habitability in the solar system.

Description: STUDIES OF GEOMORPHIC EVOLUTION IN SOUTHEASTERN MARGARITIFER SINUS, MARS This study will characterize geomorphic relationships among valley networks and impact craters/basins within portions of southeastern Margaritifer Sinus in order to evaluate hypotheses on details of the evolution of valley networks. Description: MOIST PHYSICS DEVELOPMENT FOR GEOS-5 USING COLUMN MODELS WITH PARAMETERIZED DYNAMICS AGCMs exhibit a number of major, long-standing deficiencies which are at partly caused by inadequacies in their moist physics parameterization schemes. These deficiencies include an inability to correctly simulate most aspects of the tropical subseasonal oscillation in precipitation - the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), and an inability to correctly simulate the seasonal means of tropical precipitation. The second problem is usually manifested by the existence of a so-called "double ITCZ" bias, which refers to the presence of an excessively ,strong Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) in the southern hemisphere. This bias exists in most current AGCMs (Meehl and Arblaster, 1998). In addition to these clearly manifested errors, AGCMs also exhibit a bewildering variety of sensitivities to parameters and to external orcings. A criticai area of uncertainty is in the response of the climate system to increases in C02 and other greenhouse gases. The major part of this uncertainty can be traced to the behavior of simulated clouds in AGCMs. Even AGCMs with similar net senstitivites to imposed ichanges in C02 can arrive at this sensitivity through very different combinations of cloud responses. This project will support on-going moist physics development for the GEOS-5 AGCM. Ultimately it aims to understand and alleviate biases in GEOS-5 due to problems in moist process parameterization. As part of this of this effort we plan to develop a Single Column Model (SCM) framework with parameterizes large-scal dyamics (SMC/PD).

Description: AERSOL REMOTE SENSING As part of NASA Goddard's Space Flight Center's New York City Research Initiative (NYCRI http://education.gsfc.nasa.gov/nvcri), LaGuardia Community College will mentor a team consisting of one high school student (paid by NASA INSPIRE program) and LaGuardia Community College undergraduate (paid by a stipend), who will conduct research on: Aerosol Remote Sensing. Backgrouttd Aerosols are solid or liquid particles suspended in the atmosphere. They are produced from both anthropogenic and natural sources. In order to truly understand global warming, it is crucial that we evaluate the role aerosols play in climate change. Aerosols are highly varied in size, composition, and lifetime and this makes it extremely hard to quantify their cooling effect, which is comparable in magnitude to the warming effect of greenhouse gases. Various remote sensing instruments, like the polarimeter and sunphotometer retrieve information about aerosol properties-their refractive index (composition), radius (size), and tau (optical depth, concentration). Project This project involves the use of a hand-held polarimeter, a rotating shadowband radiometer, and a CIMEL sunphotometer. By analyzing the data from all three ground instruments accurate values for the optical depth, the size and refractive index of the aerosols can be obtained. Such information will be used by scientists to develop better computer models which make predictions about future climate change. Concltisions Both the data from the LaGuardia Community College MFR and the hand-held polarimeter seem to confirm the data from the CIMEL at CCNY, since all instruments measured a tau near .30. On July 17, as shown by the CIMEL radius plot, most of the aerosols were comprised of either two sizes:. 1 (fine) or 5 (coarse) microns. Since the polarimeter cannot account for these coarse aerosols due to its being monomodal, variations existed in the data for each of the color wavelengths. This is also why an exact refractive index could not be obtained but instead approximated at a range of 1.35-1.45.

Description: TISSUE'S RESPONSE TO MECHANICAL STIMULITHE NATIONAL RESEARCH COUNCIL'S SPACE STUDIES BOARD HAS STATED THAT A PRINCIPAL PHYSIOLOGIC HURDLE TO MAN'S EXTENDED PRESENCE IN SPACE IS THE OSTEOPENIA AND SARCOPENIA WHICH PARALLELS REDUCED GRAVITY. THE EXTENT OF THE LOSS IS EXTREMELY HIGH, APPROACHING A DECREASE IN BONE MINERAL DENSITY (BMD) IN THE LOWER APPENDICULAR SKELETON AT A RATE OF 2% PER MONTH AND REDUCING MAXIMAL VOLUNTARY CONTRACTIONS OF SOME MUSCLE GROUPS AT A RATE OF 5% PER MONTH. INTERESTINGLY, THE AMOUNT OF BONE (AND MUSCLE) LOSS BETWEEN INDIVIDUAL ASTRONAUTS IS HIGHLY VARIABLE WITH SOME ASTRONAUTS LOSING LARGE AMOUNTS OF TISSUE WHILE OTHERS ARE LARGELY UNAFFECTED. THIS LARGE INDIVIDUAL VARIABILITY, WHICHHAS ALSO BEEN OBSERVED DURING BEDREST AND IMMOBILIZATION STUDIES ON EARTH, MAY BE ACCOUNTED FOR, AT LEAST TO A LARGE EXTENT, BY GENETIC VARIATIONS WHICH MAY GIVE RISE TO A DIFFERENTIAL MECHANOSENSITIVITY OF THE MUSCULOSKELETON. WE HAVE COLLECTED DATA DEMONSTRATING THAT GENETICALLY DISTINCT INBRED STRAINS OF MICE ALSO DEMONSTRATE A DISTINCT SENSITIVITY TO CONDITIONS OF SIMULATED WEIGHTLESSNESS; WHILE AS MUCH AS 60% OF TRABECULAR BONE IS LOST IN THE HINDLIMBS OF ONE SPECIFIC STRAIN OF MICE WITHIN 3 WEEKS OF DISUSE, THE SAME CONDITIONS LEAVE TRABECULAR BONE QUANTITY AND QUALITY NEARLY UNCHANGED IN ANOTHER GENETIC STRAIN OF MICE. IN THIS PROJECT, WE ARE ELUCIDATING THIS GENETIC BASIS OF THE SENSITIVITY OF THE MUSCULO-SKELETON TO THE LOSS OF APPROPRIATE MECHANICAL SIGNALS BY IDENTIFYING THE QUANTITATIVE TRAIT LOCI (QTL) RESPONSIBLE FOR THE DIFFERENCE EXHIBITED BETWEEN THESE TWO STRAINS OF INBRED MICE. THE IDENTIFICATION OF QTL (AND ULTIMATELY THE RESPONSIBLE GENES) MAY BE USED AS BOTH A CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC SENSOR FOR THE IDENTIFICATION OF ASTRONAUTS THAT ARE IN GREATEST NEED OF PHARMACOLOGIC AND/OR BIOMECHANICAL COUNTERMEASURES IN SPACE AND AS A DISCOVERY TOOL OF NOVEL DRUG TARGETS AGAINST THE LOSS OF MUSCULO-SKELETAL TISSUE.

Description: Cascades-2: Reflight of "Cascades: The Changing Aurora: In Situ and Camera Analysis of Dynamic Electron Precipitation Structures" This co-I proposal (lead proposal P.I.: Kristina Lynch, Dartmouth) is submitted in response to ROSS-2006 to the Geospace Low Cost Access to Space suborbital program (NNH06ZDA001N GEO/LCAS). The CASCADES-2 experiment will investigate the spatial and temporal structures within electron precipitation and low-frequency electric field activity in the topside ionosphere during a winter 2009 launch from the Poker Flat Research Range. A single Black Brant XII vehicle will carry the multiple science payloads to an altitude of 600 km above the premidnight aurora. Cornell University will provide two free-flying subpayloads with wire-boom electric field instrumentation and GPS position and timing to complement two free-flying particle detectors with GPS position and timing information and instrumentation on the main payload. This fleet will make multipoint measurements of the auroral plasma at scale lengths of up to several kilometers. An onboard, field-aligned camera will provide auroral context for the in situ plasma measurements. CASCADES-2 will address the questions of local vs. distant origins of motion and convective (static mapping) vs. propagation (wave mapping) of electrodynamics from the acceleration region through the topside ionosphere to the conducting ionosphere below. Specific science questions to be investigated include: 1. Do the local electric field and plasma flow correctly represent the auroral motions or do the auroral motions originate from flows above a "fractured" region of the geomagnetic field? 2. Are there narrow scale propagating or standing wave electrodynamic structures associated with auroral structures that have scale lengths less than the skin depth? 3. Are there small magnitude, parallel electric fields that can be measured by a change in the perpendicular electric field along the geomagnetic field? In addition, CASCADES-2 will be the first attempt at measuring electric field and magnetic field gradients or shears along a magnetic field line on dimensions of several to 8 km.

Description: ROLE OF MINERALS IN PREBIOTIC CHEMISTRY Minerals may have promoted both prebiotic synthesis and degradation or decomposition reactions. The proposed effort, which will support one graduate student, builds on earlier work and is organized in three tasks. The objective of task one, Mineral-promoted Dinitrogen Reduction, is to determine the kinetics of the reduction of dinitrogen to ammonium in the presence of NiFe alloys. NiFe alloys, such as the mineral awaruite, are formed during serpentinization and would have been present on the prebiotic Earth. Flow-through and batch experiments with a suite of synthetic alloys with compositions ranging from pure Fe to pure Ni will be conducted over a temperature ranging from 80 to 150C. Experiments will be conducted with and without dissolved CO2 to evaluate the effect of this electron acceptor on the efficiency of the N2-reduction process. The objective of the second task, modeling water-rock interaction on the Hadean Earth, is to determine the conditions necessary for the formation of secondary minerals with catalytic potential. Thermodynamic data for NiFe alloys, such as awaruite, will be added to the data base. Reaction-path modeling will explore a range of conditions for both komatiite and tonalite, two starting materials representing ultramafic and more felsic components of the Hadean Earth surface. The objective of task 3, Mineral-promoted degradation of biomolecules, is to evaluate if minerals can promote the degradation or decomposition of biomolecules through radical reactions. This work builds on our earlier work in which we showed that pyrite can spontaneously produce radicals and decompose RNA. Radical reactions lead to fragmentation of large biomolecules. These fragments may recombine to form a suite of new organic molecules (so called cross coupling reactions). Batch experiments will be conducted in which the fate of model compounds in a mono-mineralic slurry of relevant minerals is studied. Besides the loss of the model compound, we will also analyze the composition of the products, using Electrospray Ionization Mass Spectrometry. The results of the first two task will deepen our understanding of the role minerals may have played in prebiotic chemistry and which minerals may have been present on the prebiotic earth. The results of the third task may have implications for the interpretation of fossil biomolecules. Biomolecules may be transformed and complex molecules may form abiotically through cross coupling reactions.

Description: IDENTIFICATION AND CHARACTERIZATION OF CARBONATES, METAL-OXIDES, NITRIDES AND OTHER UNUSUAL MINERALS IN WILD 2 SAMPLES COLLECTED BY STARDUST We propose a multi-disciplinary approach to identify exotic, unexpected minerals, including carbonates, metal-oxides, and nitrides, in ultramicrotome sections of grains collected from Wild 2, and then to determine their elemental and isotopic compositions and their structures. The abundance, chemical and isotopic compositions of these mineral phases can help to constrain a variety of processes in the early Solar System including: the amount of mixing from the inner to the outer Solar System, the fraction of surviving interstellar grains, the extent of collisional metamorphism of Kuiper Belt comets, etc. We propose to employ a Scanning Transmission X-ray Microscope (STXM) using X-ray Absorption Near-edge Structure (XANES) spectroscopy to quickly locate potential exotic minerals, and to follow-up on the identification of candidate grains in the ulramicrotome sections in a sequenced approach. We will: 1) use C-, N-, and O-XANES to identify rare, exotic C-, N-, or O-bearing minerals down to 100 nanometers in size, 2) perform Fourier Transform InfraRed (FTIR) spectroscopy on those grains large enough to be identified by this technique, 3) employ Analytical Transmission Electron Microscopy (ATEM) to obtain major element compositions and determine the structure by electron diffraction, 4) determine the trace element contents of selected minerals and perform heavy element XANES characterization using a nanoscale X-Ray Microprobe (XRM), and, 5) determine important isotopic ratios of selected grains using a nano-Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometer (nano-SIMS).

Description: Superactive-Active-Passive (SAP) Shipboard/Airborne/Satellite Analysis of Phytoplankton Pigment, Group, and Physiological Variability in Coastal Ocean To summarize this brief overview, we have already acquired significant amount of unique airborne and shipboard observations of phytoplankton pigment and physiological variability in coastal and estuarine areas. Instead, our approach is based on shipboard and airborne surveys of real phytoplankton communities in a range of bio-environmental variability observed in selected coastal areas. We will support extensive laser fluorescence measurements with underway collection of water samples to provide assessments with well-established methods, such as HPLC pigment analysis and optical microscopy. Description: CRUST-MANTLE EVOLUTION ON MARS: INTEGRATING THE MISSION DATA The proposed research is part of a long-term program, currently funded under MDAP, to better understand the composition and compositional evolution of the Martian crust-mantle system by integrating chemical and mineralogical data from a variety of orbital and landed missions and Martian (SNC) meteorites. Description: Radiation Tolerant Detector for NASA Planetary Missions SECTION We propose to design, fabricate, develop, and test a novel detector that promises to revolutionize future NASA planetary space missions in the area of radiation tolerance, low noise, low power, and low mass. These missions rely on low noise array detectors that must operate in the harsh radiation environment of space. Most current missions use CCDs for their optical detectors. While these devices have low noise (a few electrons) at the beginning of mission life, they are gradually degraded by radiation damage. Our device will deliver lower noise, lower power consumption, much larger dynamic range, greater short wavelength sensitivity, and greater radiation immunity than presently available CCD and CMOS detectors. In addition, it will allow much greater operational flexibility. All of these benents will lead to lower mission cost and greater scientiflc productivity. Our design efforts will enable a broad range of applications, including demanding hyper-spectral imaging in the most severe radiation environments in the Solar system. They will help NASA to achieve science objectives for future planetary missions now being considered by the Discovery, Mars Exploration, and New Frontiers programs. Our design uses low power CMOS circuits that are arranged in high density packaging within individual pixels. The low noise readout is achieved by sampling the signal using a sigma-delta analog-to-digital (A/D) circuit with a feedback path that restores charge to the charge collection node. The keys to its performance are the close proximity of tlie conversion circuit to the photogenerated charge, oversampling nature, and noise-shaping property ofthe in-pixel sigma-delta A/D converter. These properties allow our design to highly attenuate the photodetector reset noise, DC offset related fixed-pattern noise, and readout transistor thermal and 1/f noise. Since the design is insensitive to threshold voltage variations of the readout transistor, we believe that our design will be less susceptible to radiation transients and long-term damage that can cause shifts in the readout transistor performance parmeters. We have fabricated early prototypes of our design, and the measured performance is promising. We estimate single read noise of approximately 0.3 electrons, consistent with our model predictions, and power consumption of 0.88 nW per pixel, or three orders of magnitude less than in the most advanced CCDs and more than one order of magnitude less than presently available CMOS detectors. Furthermore, our design shows inherent linear response to the incident photon flux (i.e., the design is insensitive to non-linear capacitance ofthe photodetectors). This feature allows reduction in power supply voltage (i.e., photodetectors do not require high biasing voltages to stay in their linear regime), which in turn reduces junction and gate leakage currents ofthe readout transistors and improves low-light response. Finally, the detector design uses proven thinning and delta-doping techniques to achieve enhanced short wavelength quantum efflciency.

Description: A variety of observations from recent Mars missions, including MER, Mars Odyssey and Mars Express, point to surficial alteration processes being strongly influenced by low pH aqueous conditions and to the importance of evaporative processes throughout much of the geological history of Mars. The unique conditions under which surface alteration and evaporation took place, including low pH, Fe(II and III)-rich brines, high S/Cl brines, and fluid provenance dominated by interaction with basalt, limit the use of terrestrial analogs.  We propose to evaluate these processes on Mars using an experimental approach to basalt alteration and fluid evaporation. Our laboratory has successfully carried out research into low pH alteration processes under Mars-like conditions for the past six years and has recently built and validated an experimental evaporation vessel. The research, proposed here, will evaluate the role of trace element mobility during low pH alteration of Marslike basaltic rocks and trace element behavior during evaporation of Mars-like brines under a variety of pH conditions. The trace elements that we will focus on are those for which there are remote sensing or in situ measurements on Mars and will include: Th, Cr, Ni, Zn and Br. Studies of basalt alteration will focus on two questions: (1) what role could phosphatic minerals play in controlling the behavior of Th during surficial processes on Mars? (2) How do Cr and Ni behave during low pH alteration of synthesized martian basalts and how does this behavior differ for compositions that are olivine-bearing versus olivine-absent and that are glassy versus crystalline? Studies of evaporative processes will similarly focus on two major questions: (1) How do Cr, Ni and Zn behave during evaporation of sulfate-rich fluids derived from basaltic weathering and into what evaporite minerals do they partition? (2) Do Cl and Br behave conservatively during evaporation of sulfate-rich fluids derived from basalt weathering and if not, do they fractionate from each other during precipitation of sulfate minerals (e.g., Ca-, Mg-, Fe-sulfates)? Implications of the results from such experiments will be further evaluated by comparison to available chemical, mineralogical and spectroscopic data available from Mars by orbital missions (e.g., global GRS data) and landed missions (e.g., martian soils, altered rock surfaces and Meridiani outcrops).

Description: A Very Low Noise CMOS Detector Design for National Aeronautics and Space Administration We propose to design, fabricate, develop, and test a novel new detector for NASA space missions. These missions reply on low noise array detectors that must operate in the harsh radiation environment of space. Most current missions use CCDs for their optical detectors. White these devices have low noise (2 few electrons) at the beginning of mission life, they are gradually degraded by radiation damage. The design we propose will address this, and several other problems. Our device will deliver lower noise, lower power consumption, much larger dynamic range, and greater radiation immunity than presently available CCD and CMOS detectors. In addition, it will allow much greater operational flexibility. All of these benefits will lead to lower mission cost and greater scientific productivity. Our design efforts will produce 2 new multiplexor having application over a large wavelength range, spanning from UV to mid-infrared, via hybridization to a variety of light-sensitive materials, i.e. silicon, HgCdTe, InSb, InGaAs, %:As, and Ge:As. The new device will also have applications for Homeland Safety, i.e. in surveillance in low light conditions on our nation's borders and in battlefield platforms on UAVs. The design uses low power CMOS circuits that are arranged in high density packaging within individual pixels. The low noise readout is achieved by sampling the signal using a sigma-delta analog-to-digital (AID) circuit with a feedback path that restores charge to the charge collection node. The keys to the lower noise readout are the close proximity of the conversion circuit to the photogenerated charge, oversampling nature, and noise-shaping property of the in-pixel sigma-delta AID converter. These properties allow our design to highly attenuate the photodetector reset noise, DC offset related fixed-pattern noise, and readout transistor thermal and Ilf noise. Since the design is insensitive to threshold voltage variations of the readout transistor, we believe that our design will be less susceptible to radiation transients and long-term damage that can cause shifts in the readout transistor performance parameters. We have fabricated early prototypes of our design and the measured performance is promising. We estimate single read noise of approximately 0.3 electrons, consistent with our model predictions. In addition, we have demonstrated power consumption of 0.88 nW per pixel, or three orders of magnitude less than in the most advanced CCDs and more than one order of magnitude less than presently available CMOS detectors. In addition, our design shows inherent linear response to the incident photon flux (i.e., the design is insensitive to non-linear capacitance of the photodetectors). This feature allows further reduction in power supply voltage (i.e., photodetectors do not require high biasing voltages to stay in their linear regime), which in turn reduces junction and gate leakage currents of the readout transistors and improves low-light response.

Description: ESTIMATION ENTROPY WITH ERROR BARS: COMPUTING INFORMATION- THEORETIC MEASURES OF CAUSALITY We naturally describe the "Earth's system" as 2 collection of interacting subsystems whose interactions are commonly described as forcing and feedback. Changes in one subsystem will cause or force responses in other subsystems. These responses then in turn feed back to force other subsystems, and so on. The Earth's system can be described as an enormous multivariate nonlinear dynamical system. As such, it is self-reactive in the sense that climate can change and evolve without human-induced forcing. To understand such a system is a formidable task, since there do not yet exist general techniques for analyzing such complex dynamical systems. The first and most important step is to identify the relevant variables, their primary feedbacks, and to determine the magnitudes and time scales of their causal interactions. While many important feedbacks have long been known, the details of their causal interactions remain unknown.  The focus of our long-term efforts is centered on developing a suite of data mining tools that would allow the estimation of causal interactions among climate variables from data in large databases. These techniques will rely on the estimation of entropy-based quantities, such as mutual information and transfer entropy. While this is a critical goal, we have identified rapid and accurate entropy estimation from data as a significant bottleneck in the technological development process. The specific aims of this project are to develop novel computational techniques that accurately estimate entropy from multi-dimensional data sets. These methods must be accurate, relatively fast, and must quantify all uncertainties. Our efforts will focus on applying a recent stochastic integration method called Nested Sampling to a variety of density models such as Mixtures of Gaussians, Spline-Based Models and Voronoi Cell models. We will make these computational techniques publicly available as tools to allow researchers to compute entropies and higher-order information theoretic quantities from data in large datasets of their choosing.

The porosity of unweathered ordinary chondrite meteorites has been measured to range from 5% to 20% while the porosity of unweathered carbonaceous chondrites ranges from 10% to 30%. The matrix of the chondritic meteorites is dominated by either fine-grained anhydrous phases (e.g., the CV and CO carbonaceous chondrites and the ordinary chondrites) or clay minerals (e.g., the CI and CM carbonaceous chondrites). We plan to study the disruption of a asteroids and the production of interplanetary dust by disrupting anhydrous and hydrous meteorites, including 4 hydrous CM2 chondrites, at the NASA Ames Vertical Gun Range to determine the mass-frequency distribution of the fragments, the composition of the dust fragments as a function of fragment size, and the 'threshold collisional specific energy' (QD), which is a parameter used frequently in disruption modeling.

Description: Superactive-Active-Passive (SAP) Shipboard/Airborne/Satellite Analysis of Phytoplankton Pigment, Group, and Physiological Variability in Coastal Ocean To summarize this brief overview, we have already acquired significant amount of unique airborne and shipboard observations of phytoplankton pigment and physiological variability in coastal and estuarine areas. Description: HD 109962: THE MOST MASSIVE DWARF NOVA? HD 109962, a bright F2 star and an ellipsoidal variable, is a recently-recognized erupting variable star. Fairly regular outbursts over the past 5 years suggest it is a dwarf nova. Spectra during the January 2006 outburst revealed strong He II 4686 emission, and the residual spectrum (outburst - post outburst) is that of an accretion disk. The large mass function (f(m)=0.17) suggests a total system mass of about 2.3 M_O, making this one of the most massive dwarf novae known. The radial velocity curve of the primary suggests either an eccentric orbit or shadowing by an asymmetric disk. Both possibilities are interesting. We will observe the system for one binary orbit (80 ksec) to study the quiescent X-ray emission, and the orbital modulation of the X-ray flux, and look for an X-ray eclipse.

Description: For the majority of red giant stars the basic mass-loss processes at work are unknown. Indeed, for stars of spectral types between KO III and M5-M6 III, much remains unknown about the regions above the visible photosphere and the transportation of the processed material outwards to the ISM. Theories and models are in need of observational constraint, and in particular it is vital to derive spatially resolved information throughout the wind acceleration region within a few giant radii of the star's photosphere. Eclipsing symbiotic binary systems, consisting of an evolved giant in orbit with a white dwarf, provide an opportunity to take advantage of the finite size of the hot component to probe different levels of the chromosphere and wind acceleration region in absorption. This provides spatially resolved thermal, ionization and dynamic information on the wind which can then be compared against predictions of hydrodynamical stellar atmosphere codes. We propose FUSE observations of2 eclipsing symbiotic systems, utilizing the 60 day periodicity inherent in FUSE scheduling to phase space the observations. Results will be compared to PHOENIX wind models and also to a successful analysis of other eclips ing systems (EG And and BF Cyg with FUSE) with different binary and giant parameters, with a view towards constraining th e wind acceleration and chromospheric models.

Description: Although most symbiotic stars produce only soft X-ray emission, hard X-ray emission greater than --50 keV has recently been detected with INTEGRAL and Swift from several exceptional symbiotic stars. These objects are members of a subclass of symbiotics characterized by rapid optical flickering. This flickering subclass may also contain high-mass white dwarfs (WDs) headed toward supernova Type Ia explosion. However, the basic underlying properties that make these these accreting WDs different from those in other symbiotics are not known. Very little observational data in the UV range exist for this new class of objects. Since the far-ultraviolet regime gives the best view of the hot WDs in symbiotic stars and their immediate environs, FUSE observations will help us determine the nature ofthese objects -- i.e., whether the WDs are indeed massive, whether they are magnetic (as is the case for hard X-ray emitting cataclysmic variables), whether they are jet-producing, or whether they have some other feature that distinguishes them from other symbiotic stars. We propose to perform FUSE observations of the hard X-ray symbiotics RT Cru, CD-573057, and CH Cyg. The properties of these hard X-ray symbiotics may hold the key to the signatures of magnetism in symbiotic stars, how the WDs in some symbiotics can grow to large masses, and the nature of jets and jet production in accreting WDs.

Description: The proposed work will result in the continuation of the Stratospheric Processes and Their Role in Climate (SPARC) Data Center (SPARC-DC). The important roles of the SPARC-DC are to provide links to SPARC-related data sites where they exist; to provide central data access for special SPARC data collections that either have been used or are being used by SPARC projects; and to provide open access to all the data holdings where allowed. The SPARC-DC has been operational at the State University of New York at Stony Brook (now called Stony Brook University) since July 1999. In addition to making data publicly available to the research community, SPARC-DC reformats and converts data from various sources into common readable and portable formats. This postprocessing includes automatically detecting and assigning of measurement errors, if necessary. As SPARC activities are evolving, it becomes clear that upgrades will be required for the SPARC-DC to continue to provide the needed services. One such example requiring upgrades will be SPARC activities contributing to the International Polar Year (IPY) 2007-2008. Another is SPARC'S new emphasis on chemical-climate modeling. In addition to archiving and distributing data, the proposed SPARC-DC activities include implementations for online plotting software, strengthened internet security measures. In order to accomplish these goals, this proposal includes a request for hardware and software updates. SPARC-DC staff members are also actively involved in research projects utilizing the archived data. Data analysis and data interpretation are performed for the SPARC research group, especially the reference climatology project. This proposal includes a study of the impact that large-scale temperature changes at the tropopause due to the Quasi-Biennial Oscillation have on dynamics of the tropical troposphere. We want to see to what extend the intraseasonal signals, which are a common phenomenon in the upper tropical troposphere, are influenced by changes in tropopause properties (e. g. temperature and pressure). One area where stratospheric processes have a role in climate appears to be in modulating deep convection through modulating the tropical tropopause and also possibly affecting upper tropospheric wind shears. Little research has been done on this topic.

Description: We propose to observe a range of CTTSs with FUSE to understand the structure of the accretion shock, estimate its contribution to disk photoevaporation, and analyze wind heating mechanisms. Description: Dose-rate effects of protons on the induction of genomic instability in vivo Protons are the most abundant component of solar particle events in space. Information on biological effects of protons delivered at low dose rates is limited. This study is designed to determine the dose-rate effects of protons on in vivo induction of genomic instability (expressed as delayed chromosomal damage). This approach is highly relevant for assessing cancer risks; however, it has not been applied with proton exposure. We will characterize the type, the frequency, and the distribution of initial and subsequent chromosome aberrations, and the expression of genomic instability induced in vivo in bone marrow cells after exposure of mice to IGeV/amu protons at the dose and dose rates encountered in space. A novel genome-wide multicolor fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) of mouse chromosomes will be used to detect and characterize chromosome aberrations in metaphase cells prepared from bone marrow cells of exposed mice collected at different times (up to 6 months) post-irradiation. To increase the reliability of risk assessments, a much improved understanding of the molecular basis for dose-rate effects of protons is essential. In this study, levels of activated nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-kB) (a highly important transcription factor) and expression of selected NF-kB target proteins will be measured in bone marrow cells collected at early times after irradiation. This will be coupled with the quantitation of kinase activity of the DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PK) and ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) protein kinase. We anticipate that these two kinases will be crucial for NF-kB activation after irradiation, leading to the activation of proteins involved in inflammatory response and cell survival. Thus, activation of NF-kB may playa pivotal role in the maintenance of cells carrying genomic instability. To provide unique information directly related to the NASA mission, experiments describing the differences in dose-rate effects of protons and gamma rays will be conducted. Groups of mice will be exposcd to 137Cs gamma rays at selected doses and dose rates that are comparable to those of protons. The same endpoints assessed for protons will be used. These results will help determine whether dose-rate effects of protons differ from those of gamma rays. Our research will be the first to use integrative in vivo endpoints (both cellular and molecular) for evaluating dose-rate effects of protons. Our results will deliver information that is of high priority for NASA. Our data will not only contribute to reducing the uncertainties in the assessment of cancer risk from exposure to protons during space flights but will also improve the understanding of the molecular basis for dose-rate dependencies of proton-induced genomic instability. These studies are important becausc it has been widely suggested that elevation of genomic instability also elevates cancer risk.

Description: We propose to develop time dependent thermal and dynamic models that explain the faulting on Mars. We consider the complete set of forces that act on the lithosphere, including membrane and flexural strains from surface and internal loading of the lithosphere, lateral variations in gravitational potential energy (GPE), and tractions associated with mantle flow (both radial and tangential). The lithospheric loading is constrained, in part, from MOLA topography and MGS gravity. We model the thermal evolution of the Martian lithosphere (3-D) to investigate time dependent effects such as the thickening of the elastic layer as the planet cools in conjunction with localized variations in elastic thickness associated with periods of magmatic activity and periods of faulting. Since the crustal structure on Mars was established early in Martian history, the present-day crustal structure can be used in this modeling as a constraint on lateral heterogeneity of initial thermal input. Our thin shell method accounts for lateral variations in elastic layer thickness, which likely has profound effects on the style and distribution of deviatoric stresses in the brittle elastic layer. Moreover, we apply three-dimensional finite element models of lithosphere loading to quantify flexural stresses and strains. We score the success of our time dependent dynamic models through quantitative comparison of model deviatoric stress field with fault data inferred from Viking, MOLA, MOC, and THEMIS IR images. The proposed research falls under Strategic Goal 11, OSS Theme Solar System Exploration. In particular, our research is relevant to l(b): "Study the processes that determine the characteristics of bodies in our Solar System and how these processes operate and interact". The stress field, and associated strains, has had a large influence on the evolution of the morphology of surface features on the planet. Moreover, our research will delineate the relative contribution of various driving mechanisms for Mars lithosphere deformation. Our research also falls under l(c):"Understand why the terrestrial planets are so 8 different from one another". We expect to compare dynamic results for Mars with those for Earth. Finally our proposed work falls under 4(d): "Determine the characteristics and dynamics of the interior of Mars".

Description: Geomorphotogical evidence has shown that water has shaped the martian surface in prominent outflow channels and tributary networks, but the final fate of this water is unresolved. There has been analysis, discussion, and speculation that water responsible for carving channels eventually accumulated in relatively large bodies of open or ice-covered water (ponds, lakes, oceans) early in martian geologic history. However, the evidence for standing bodies of water on Mars has been circumstantial and controversial. One of the key components of the debate has been whether ancient shoreline erosion features are still evident. Unrecognized in the debate is the following question: Is the expectation of shoreline erosional features a physically reasonable concept, given likely scenarios of martian atmospheric pressure, gravity, local wind strength and fetch, and other conditions influencing wave height and power? Under what comhination of these environmental circumstances-different from our terrestrial experience-would shoreline erosional features be likely or unlikely to form? We propose to answer these questions, informing the long-standing debate over whether bodies of open or ice-covered water ever existed on Mars. We intend to examine the results of a martian General Circulation Model capable of estimating conditions for various past climatic scenarios. Using these results, we intend to consider the observable shoreline effects hese modeled wind stresses would have had on the ice surface of a freezing ancient martian sea. We will also consider the scenario where the surface of the ancient martian sea had an open surface.
