Description: MIRNA PROFILING OF RADIATION RESPONSE: A SYSTEMS BIOLOGY APPROACH TO UNDERSTANDING REGULATION OF PROTON AND HEAVY ION DOSE EFFECTS miRNA has recently emerged as an important regulator of gene expression, possibly regulation as many as one-third of all human genes.  Despite this progress, the characterization of miRNA-related mechanisms is still in its intial stage.  There is almost no data on the involvement of miRNAs in stress or radiation response.  In preliminary work for this grant proposal we have shown that signifcant change, involving almost 24% of cellular miRNA, occurs after irradiation of normal human cells.  Moreover, transfection of purified miRNA from non-irradiated and irradiated ells in non-irradiated cells, showed that several categories of known stress-related pathways were uprefulated (p0.04) in cells transfected with miRNA from irradiated cells but not in cells transfected with miRNA from non-irradiated cells.  These differences assign important regulatory functions for miRNA expressed in radiated cells.  The main hypothesis of the present study is that miRNA expression will bery specifically reflect the type and dose of radiation, and that the combination of miRNA and gene expression profiling will characterize radiation responses even beeter.  This is the first comprehensive study of miRNA regulation of radiation response.  The confirmed ability of miRNA to precisely classify tumors leads naturally to the idea of developing miRNA expression as a biomarker.  If miRNA profiling is as exact in the estimation of radiation response as it is in the classification of tumors, we wil have a unique system for monitoring radiation effects.  The integration on miRNA and gene expression analysis will definitely increase our understanding of the mechanisms involoved in the response to stress.  The propses studies, which build from cell models to mouse models to whole human blood, represent a comprehensive set of experiments that will allow us to build on results from each stage.  The integrated interperatation of these reults is intended to accelerate our understanding of the signaling mechanisms invloved in the response to ionizing radiation in general, and to the protons and HZE particles specifically, and to facilitate discovery of new biomarkers for biodosimetry in space.

Description: NASA AERONAUTICAL MISSIONS NEED HIGH-TEMPERATURE ELECTRONICS AND SENSORS FOR REAL TIME HEALTH MONITORING OF AERONAUTIC ENGINES TO IMPROVE AVIATION SAFETY (SUBTOPIC IVHM-2.1) AND IN SITU COMBUSTION DIAGNOSE (SUBTOPIC A.4.4.2) OF THE NEXT GENERATION OF AERONAUTIC ENGINES FOR SUPERSONIC AIRCRAFTS TO STUDY AND REDUCE HIGH ALTITUDE EMISSIONS (NASA OUTCOME 3E.1).  HIGH TEMPERATURE ELECTRONICS AND SENSORS ARE ALSO NEEDED FOR PROBING THE INNER SOLAR PLANETS (SUB-GOAL3C OF STRATEGIC GOALS).  VARIOUS HIGH-TEMPERATURE OPERABLE ELECTRONICS AND SENSORS HAVE BEEN DEMONSTRATED AT 500 C, ONLY IN THE LAB ENVIRONMENT PARTIALLY BECAUSE SYSTEMATIC PACKAGING TECHNOLOGY FOR SUPPORTING THESE DEVICES OF 500 C AND BEYOND WAS NOT AVAILABLE.  OAI COLLABORATED WITH NASA GRC IN DEVELOPING PACKAGING TECHNOLOGIES FOR 500 C ELECTRONICS AND SENSORS, AND SUCCESSFULLY DEMONSTRATED PROTOTYPE CERAMIC CHIP-LEVEL PACKAGE AND PRINTED CIRCUIT BOARD (PCB) TECHNOLOGIES FOR HIGH-TEMPERATURE SIC DEVISES DESIGNED AND FABRICATED AT NASA GRC.  BASED ON THESE PACKAGING COMPONENTS, A SIC TRANSISTOR WAS SUCCESSFULLY TESTED IN 500 C OXIDIZING AIR AMBIENT FOR OVER 500 HRS IN 2004, AND MORE RECENTLY A LOW FREQUENCY VOLTAGE AMPLIFIER BASED ON SIC TRANSISTOR AND CERAMIC PACKAGING TECHNOLOGY HAS BEEN DEMONSTRATED IN 500 C AIR AMBIENT FOR STABLE OPERATION FOR OVER 1100 HRS.  AUBURN UNIVERSITY AND OAI HAVE ALSO DEMONSTRATED WIRE BOND RELIABILITY FOR 1000 HRS AT 500 C WITH AND WITHOUT DC BIAS.  IN ORDER TO ESTABLISH A COMPLETE 500 C PACKAGING SYSTEM AND UTILIZE THESE PACKAGING COMPONENTS A PCB-EDGE-CONNECTOR IS NECESSARY.  IN ADDITION, MATERIALS FOR ATTACHING SIC DEVICE CHIPS (WITH VARIOUS METALLIZATION) TO CERAMIC PACKAGES ARE ALSO ESSENTIAL TO MAKE THE PACKAGING SYSTEM MORE APPLICABLE AND VERSATILE.  WE PROPOSE TO DEVELOP PCB CONNECTOR TECHNOLOGY COMPATIBLE TO THE CURRENT CERAMIC PACKAGES AND PCBS ESTABLISHING A 500 C PACKAGING SYSTEM FOR SYSTEM-LEVEL APPLICATIONS, AND A DIE=ATTACH MATERIAL WITH LOW PROCESSING TEMPERATURE AND HIGH THERMAL CONDUCTIVITY TO MAKE THE PACKAGING SYSTEM BE MORE RELIABLE AND VERSATILE.  CERAMIC SUBSTRATES AND THIN/THICK FILM METALLIZATION MATERIALS WILL BE USED FOR DEVELOPMENT OF PCB CONNECTOR.  TWO KEY ISSUES TO ADDRESS IN THE DIE ATTACH MATERIAL ARE THE COEFFICIENT OF THERMAL EXPANSION MISMATCH BETWEEN THE DIE ATTACH MATERIAL, THE DIE AND CERAMIC SUBSTRATE, AND THE ADHESIONS AT THESE MATERIAL INTERFACES.  IN ORDER TO IMPROVE DIE-ATTACH RELIABILITY, LOW TEMPERATURE TRANSIENT LIQUID PHASE BONDING MATERIALS GENERATED FROM MULTI-LAYER METAL ALLOYS AND/OR NANO-MATERIALS WILL BE DEVELOPED FOR DIE-ATTACH APPLICATION. ADVANCED HIGH TEMPERATURE PACKAGING TECHNOLOGIES WILL BE FURTHER DEVELOPED AND USED TO PACKAGE NASA HIGH TEMPERATURE SENSORS AND DEVICES/CIRCUITS TO MEET NASA S GOALS.  LOW TEMPERATURE CO-FIRE MULTI-LAYER PACKAGING MATERIAL SYSTEMS WILL BE EXPERIMENTALLY EXAMINED FOR POSSIBLE HIGH TEMPERATURE APPLICATIONS.

Description: STRAIN TOLERANT SELF SENSING ENVIRONMENTAL BARRIER COATING FOR SIC/SIC CERAMIC MATRIX COMPOSITES AND SI3N4 CERAMICS Silicon-based ceramics, such as SiCISiC composites and monolithic Si3N4 ceramics, are leading candidate materials for next generation gas turbine engine hot section structural components. However, they suffer from rapid surface recession in gas turbine combustion environments due to the volatilization of the silica scale by water vapor. Their use in gas turbine engine applications is not possible without the availability of effective environmental barrier coatings (EBC). Current state of the art plasma-sprayed EBCs developed for SiC/SiC composites under the NASA-EPM program based on BSAS (BaO or Sr0-A1203-2Si02) provide adequate protection only up to about 1300AC. Plasma spraying is a line-of-sight process, and is not suitable for a complex-shaped component. Current plasma-spray EBC process requires that EBC be sprayed onto a sample kept in a high temperature furnace, fkther limiting the process flexibility. Plasma-sprayed EBC degrades the fracture strength of the Si3N4 substrates (50-70 percent debit in the room temperature strength!). EBCs are required that not only protect the Si-based ceramics against saltIwater vapor damage at elevated temperatures, they also must not degrade the fracture tolerance of the substrates. This proposal has two main objectives: development of non-line-of-sinht solution-based EBC processes and incorporation of built-in microstructural textures to eliminate the room temperature strength debit. Slurry-based coating processes will be developed to create a nano/micro-porous bond coat that provides excellent crack-deflection as well as process flexibilitv. The outer coatings, based on rare earth silicates, will provide a water vaporresistant, high insulating surface laver. The coatinn technique proposed under this research offers a very attractive potential to incorporate a self-sensing mechanism, based on the detection of the atomic emission from tracer dopants located at the substrate-bond coatinterface. This will allow an online, in-situ, nondestructive testing of coating failure without having to stop the engine for visual inspection.

Description: SUPERSONIC JET NOISE SUPPRESSION USING PLASMA ACTUATORS: COUPLED EXPERIMENTS, LES AND ADJOINT BASED OPTIMIZATION  One of the four main NASA's ARMD research and development projects is the Supersonics Project. It is established to maintain intellectual stewardship of aeronautical core competencies for the U.S. in supersonic flight. One of the two major areas of the Project deals with the challenges associated with the fficiency, environmental concerns, and performance of practical supersonic cruise vehicles. These issues are intimately coupled, and the challenge is to address one or more of the issues, without adversely affecting the others. This proposal will deal with the environmental concerns, speciJica1ly with airport noise suppression at takeoffand landing. We have assembled a multidisciplinary team of experts with unique capabilities for the primary objective of utilizing localized arc filament plasma actuators to suppress supersonic jet noise. The tremendous capabilities of these actuators for high-speed, high-Reynolds-number jet control for mixing enhancement and noise suppression have been demonstrated at OSU. Their scalability has also been demonstrated recently at NASA Glenn Research Center. Recent work at UIUC has demonstrated the potential of adjoint-based control optimization for noise suppression in simple flows in a direct numerical simulation framework. This control optimization approach will be integrated with a jet noise large-eddy simulation capability recently developed at Stanford, enabling us to couple the optimization technology directly with the experimental efforts at OSU to suppress supersonic jet noise. Guided by our understanding of jet noise mechanisms and the role of instabilities, we will undertake an extensive parametric study for noise mitigation using plasma actuators. At the same time we will use the adjoint-based control optimization in a simulation framework to automatically find optimal configurations, implementing in the experiments the best new configurations to demonstrate their capabilities for noise suppression. The best actuator arrangements will be implemented and tested at NATR, if the facility and funding for it are available.

Description: Residual Stress Modeling. RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION ASSESSMENT OF THE FLANGE TO SKIN WELD FOR THE ARES I-1 UPPER STAGE. THE CONTRACTOR WILL PERFORM SIX FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS OF WELDING RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION. THESE WILL BE USED TO PROVIDE A DESCRIPTION OF THE RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION STATE OF THE AREA OF THE SKIN-TO-FLANGE WELD OF THE UPPER STAGE OF THE ARES I-1 PROGRAM. THE SIX FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS WILL BE COMPLETED FOR TWO WELDING PROCEDURES USING THE FOLLOWING THREE MODELS: A TWO-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITH ROTATION PREVENTED (BY GUSSET) BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE, A THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITHOUT STIFFENERS OF THE WELD BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE, AND A FULL THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITH STIFFENERS OF THE WELD BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE. IT SHOULD BE NOTED THAT THE SECTOR OF AXI-SYMMETRY BETWEEN GUSSETS IS 10 DEGREES PER DRAWING PROVIDED BY NASA. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE TEMPERATURE-DEPENDENT THERMAL, PHYSICAL, AND MECHANICAL PROPOERTIES APPROPRIATE TO THE MATERIAL BEING WELDED. THESE PROPERTIES WILL BE COMMUNICATED TO NASA FOR CONFIRMATION. THE FIRST THREE FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS (FIRST WELDING PROCEDURE) ARE INTENDED TO DESCRIBE THE NASA GRC PATHFINDER 1 SEGMENT WHERE THE FLANGE IS NON-NORMALIZED ASTM A516 GRADE 70 STEEL AND THE SKIN IS NON-NORMALIZED ASTM A36 STEEL. THE LAST THREE FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS (SECOND WELDING PROCEDURE) ARE INTENDED TO DESCRIBE THE NASA GRC PATHFINDER 2 SEGMENT WHERE NOTH THE FLANGE AND THE SKIN MATERIAL WILL BE NORMALIZED ASTM A516 GRADE 70 STEEL. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE TWO MODELS OF WELDING PROCEDURES RESPRESENTATIVE OF THE PROCEDURES FOR THE FLANGE-TO-SKIN WELDING. THICKNESSES AND WELD SIZES WILL BE PROVIDED BY NASA. NASA WILL ALSO PROVIDE INFORMATION ON THE CHOSEN WELD PROCEDURE, SUCH AS THE JOINT SHAPE SPECIFICS, NUMBER AND POSITION OF WELD PASSES AND PARAMETERS SUCH AS HEAT INPUT. A BEST ESTIMATE FOR THE WELDING INFORMATION MAY BE SUFFICIENT. NASA WILL PROVIDE ONE PROCEDURE REPRESENTATIVE OF THE PLAN FOR FLIGHT HARDWARE AND ONE PROCEDURE REPRESENTATIVE OF THE EXISTING PATHFINDER EXAMPLE. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE THERMAL AND THERMOMECHANICAL ANALYSIS METHODS THAT CAN HANDLE MELTING AND RE-MELTING IN THE WELD AREA. THE CONTRACTOR WILL PROVIDE DESCRIPTIONS OF THE ANALYSIS AND FIGURES SHOWING THE EXTENT OF DISTORTION AND THE MAGNITUDES AND DIRECTIONS OF RESIDUAL STRESSES IN THE WELD AREA. INFORMATION WILL BE PROVIDED ON RESIDUAL STRESSES IN THE AXIAL, RADIAL AND ALONG-THE-WELD DIRECTIONS. A MID-TERM PROGRESS REPORT (POWERPOINT FORMAT) SHOULD BE DELIVERED AFTER 5 WEEKS WITH A DRAFT REPORT (POWERPOINT FORMAT THAT WILL BE REVIEWED BY NASA) DUE WITHIN NINE WEEKS OF PROJECT INITIATION. THE FINAL REPORT (WORD DOCUMENT FORMAT) WILL BE COMPLETED WITHIN AN ADDITIONAL ONE MONTH.

Description: NESC requirement for modification to BASS code software. . The NASA Engineering and Safety Centers (NESC) has approved the Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions as a discipline enhancing initiative. This discipline enhancing initiative was proposed by the Flight Sciences Super Problem Resolution Team (SPRT). The scope of the investigation of the Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions pro-active proposal is focused on the development and validation of a high-accuracy coupled fluid-structures interaction solver. The investigation covers the initial development of the coupled solution method and acquisition of experimental data for validation. The BASS code accounts for the fluid response to a known excitation, such as moving boundary. Structural dynamic finite element codes predict the vibratory response for a known set of loads. The proposed work will couple the two types of analytical tools to predict the response of both media to a variety of excitations. An important aspect of such a merger is accounting for the fact that vibration of the structure represents a moving boundary for the fluid flow, and that the fluid loading on the structure drives this movement. In other words, it is necessary to develop a fully coupled analytical capability. At the end of the first phase of this work, a decision point is reached where the team can either disengage or continue to improve the speed and applicability of the fluid-structures interaction solver. Fluid-structures interactions cause persistent technical issues with aerospace vehicles. Redesigning these structural components for safety is problematic due to the lack of accurate computational prediction tools. Existing linearized flow acoustic prediction tools are not accurate when applied to the high-amplitude nonlinear acoustic waves present in the complex launch or re-entry environment. The scope of the proposed work is to develop and validate a computational tool to directly predict nonlinear fluid-structures interaction. Experiments will be performed in parallel to provide accurate validation data for the computational code.

Description: Our theory for the origin of cosmic structure, inflation, correctly predicts that the universe is homogeneous with only small fluctuations. These are sound waves from the early universe that later collapsed under the gravity to form galaxies, clusters,...Inflation also predicts that all the "notes" should have nearly the same volume. Statistically these fluctuations should be isotropic--they should not line up with each other. By examining the cosmic microwave backbground (CMB)--remnant light of the early universe--researchers test these predictions. Using the technique of multipole vector analysis, developed by Starkman and collaborators, they have shown that the lowest notes--the largest angle fluctuations--are not only too quiet, but aligned with each other and with the geometry of the solar system. These alignments suggest that even the low notes we detect may be from the solar system. The true cosmic low notes may be still quieter. This demands contrived interactions of the particle that drives inflation. We must get to the bottom of this issue. There are a number of avenues to be pursued. So far, we have looked in detail mostly at the very lowest modes (1=2&3). Higher modes hint at discrepancies, but we must improve our statistical approach to them. To better understand what we are seeing we must examine more than just maps of CMB intensity. First we will look at applying multipole vectors to polarization maps. Polarization may be a good diagnostic of new foregrounds--polarization due to local foregrounds will be uncorrelated to distant structures. The expected relation between different types of polarization would likely be spoiled by foregrounds. CMB polarization has been detected, but current map quality is too poor to study isotropy. Hopefully, maps from planned (Planck) and envisioned (CMBPol) space missions will be better. Another avenue to explore is the CMB spectrum. Foreground sources have different spectra than the CMB. We use this to filter known forwgrounds from CMB maps. Better spectral information, from future CMB experiments, could allow us to remove an unexpected fourth foreground signal. A third avenue is to look for changes in the CMB. If some of the CMB is from within the solar system, then it could vary with time either because the source is chaning or because or perspective changes as we orbit the sun. Finally ther are other large scale probes of the universe. Astronomers survey the sky for galazies, quasars, supernovae...at many wavelengths. These surveys are improving rapidly. Survey data presents different challenges than the CMB, but promises to give us a 3-D view of the universe. Our plan is to explore the origin and pehnomenology of the large scale universe that deviates so mysteriously from our otherwise successful standard model of cosmology.

Description: Calibrating for Dark Energy with ROSAT and 2MASS One primary objective of NASA is to discover the origin and destiny of the Universe, a question that is intimately related to the properties of the dark energy that increasingly drives the expansion of the universe. One means of measuring the properties of dark energy is to measure the galaxy cluster mass function locally and at higher redshifts because the mass function and its evolution depend on the expansion history. Many future attempts to apply this method will use optically-selected cluster catalogs which must then calibrate the relationship between optical richness and mass in order to have a cosmological test. The principal objective of this proposal is to use ROSAT All-Sky Survey X-ray data to study and calibrate the average relationship between richness and mass in recent optical cluster surveys including the 2MASS, DPOSS, 2dF and SDSS surveys. Rather than relying on detections of individual clusters, we will stack (average) the X-ray data for clusters as a function of richness and redshift. Completed results from the local 2MASS cluster survey and initial applications to the SDSS survey demonstrate the power of the approach. The secondary objective is to better understand the consequences of statistical fluctuations in the numbers of galaxies residing in a cluster halo of a given mass for determinations of the cluster mass function. The effects of such fluctuations were easily detected in the analysis of the 2MASS cluster survey and clearly lead to Malmquist-like biases in richness-mass relations that will be significant for cosmological tests. We will quantify these effects further in the analysis of the mean X-ray properties of the DPOSS, 2dF and SDSS cluster samples and explore means of better quantifying them or reducing them in the local 2MASS cluster sample. Tertiary objectives will be to publicly release the well-calibrated 2MASS cluster sample, accurately measure the infra-red luminosity function of cluster galaxies, and measure the halo occupation distribution of the clusters.

Description: This proposal specifically addresses subtopic A.2.3.1 of the NASA NRA titled Research Opportunities in Aeronautics # 2006: #Develop flow control concepts that work on the principles of plasma, fluidics, and/or flow recirculation. The purpose is to delay the onset of flow separation and boundary layer growth on the blades and/or endwalls in highly loaded compressors, turbines, inlets and annular ducts to improve the aerodynamic efficiency and operability.# Aerodynamic losses in gas turbines result from flow separation and secondary flows. Secondary flows are generated at the blade endwalls, while flow separation is primarily associated with the nominally two-dimensional flow region of the span away from the endwalls. Discrete jet blowing has been demonstrated in the laboratory to dramatically reduce the 2-D flow separation of low pressure turbine (LPT) blades, thus allowing more aggressive (higher loading) blade designs. However, jet blowing requires massflow, which is a precious commodity in turbines. At the same time, LPT hlade aspect ratios are small enough that endwall losses represent a substantial portion of stage inefficiency. The horseshoe vortex generated where the endwall boundary layer confronts the blade leading edge is one of the well-documented secondary flow structures responsible for passage tosses. This proposal will explore the application of suction at the blade root (and vane tip) to eliminate the source of the horseshoe vortex. Massflow removed from the endwall region will be used for blown-jet flow control at midspan, thus creating a zero-net mass flux flow control system. This novel design strategy will be implemented on a new-generation highly-loaded LPT profile in a low-speed linear cascade facility, with and without impinging wakes. Both steady and unsteady (pulsed) implementations will be explored, synchronizing the pulsing with the oncoming wakes. Though this flow control methodology will be demonstrated on a turbine profile, it may also be implemented for compressor blading. Test results to date suggest that the integration of active flow control into LPT blading could revolutionize blade design. Ultra-aggressive blade profiles could be used that are inherently unstable, relying on flow control to insure efficient flow turning and reduced secondary flow losses. With broad engine integration, flow control blading could be used to (1) obtain the same blade loading with reduced axial chord, (2) increase blade loading at constant chord and solidity, or (3) decrease solidity at constant blade loading. As such, the liberal use of flow control in blade design could potentially pave the way to savings in engine weight and/or part count without a loss in stage efficiency. Thus, engine thrust/weight could be increased allowing longer range missions and/or larger payloads. In addition, reduced part count would decrease operating and maintenance costs over the life-cycle of the engine.

Description: DEVELOPMENT AND CHARACTERIZATION OF HIGH TEMPERATURE SHAPE AND MEMORY ALLOY ACTUATORSABSTRACT:  WORK IS BEING DONE AT THE GLENN RESEARCH CENTER (GRC) UNDER THE NEW FUNDAMENTAL AERONAUTICS PROGRAM TO ADVANCE THE CURRENT STATE OF THE ART (SOA) IN ACTIVE STRUCTURES AND HIGH TEMPERATURE SHAPE MEMORY ALLOYS (HTSMAS). COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE SMAS OFFER STRAIN OUTPUTS THAT ARE ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE LARGER THAN OTHER 'SMART" MATERIALS SUCH AS PIEZOELECTRIC TRANSDUCERS (PZTS). SMAS ALSO PROVIDE ACTUATION SOLUTIONS THAT ARE MUCH LIGHTER, SMALLER, AND SIMPLER THAN TRADITIONAL HYDRAULIC AND PNEUMATIC ACTUATION SYSTEMS. GENERALLY, SMAS ARE ACTIVATED BY HEATING THE MATERIAL TO A CHARACTERISTIC TRANSITION TEMPERATURE AND OPERATED WITHIN A CERTAIN TEMPERATURE RANGE ABOVE THAT LEVEL. HOWEVER, DEVICES BASED ON CONVENTIONAL SMA TECHNOLOGIES HAVE VERY LIMITED USE IN HIGH-TEMPERATURE APPLICATIONS (SUCH AS TURBOMACHINERY) AS THEIR TRANSITION TEMPERATURE OCCURS BETWEEN 7Q C AND L10 C, DEPENDING ON THE ALLOY, CURRENTLY SOME NEW HTSMAS ARE BEING CREATED AT GRC WHICH TRANSITION AT TEMPERATURES OF 300 C AND ABOVE (UP TO 800 C). THE RESEARCH BEING DONE TO CHARACTERIZE THE BEHAVIOR OF THESE MATERIALS HAS BEEN LIMITED TO PURE AXIAL LOADING OF RODS AND WIRES. IT IS FOUND THAT IN PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS, THESE AXIAL ACTUATOR FORMS OFTEN TAKE UP MORE ROOM THAN DESIRED AND PROVIDE AN EXCESSIVE AMOUNT OF WORK OUTPUT CAPABILITY. THE WORK BEING DONE UNDER GSRP GRANT #NNC06HA1H IS AIMED AT PROVING THE FUNCTIONALITY OF OTHER MORE COMPACT FORMS OF HTSMA ACTUATORS, NAMELY SPRINGS. IT IS THE HOPE THAT THE ACTUATORS BASED ON THESE COMPACT FORMS WILL PROVIDE GREATER STROKES AND MORE PROPORTIONATE WORK OUTPUT WHILE TAKING UP SMALLER VOLUMES AND WEIGHING MUCH LESS THAN CURRENT ACTUATION METHODS. IN ORDER TO PROVE THIS, A MODEL RELATING THE WORK OUTPUT TO THE GEOMETRY AND TEMPERATURE OF THE ACTUATORS WILL BE DEVELOPED AND VERIFIED USING EXPERIMENTAL DATA COLLECTED IN THE SMART LAB LOCATED IN THE BASEMENT OF BUILDING 49 AT GRC. DEMONSTRATION OF THE FUNCTIONALITY OF THESE ACTUATORS WILL ENABLE THE GROUP DEVELOPING ACTIVE TURBOMACHINERY STRUCTURES TO INCORPORATE GRC'S WORLD LEADING HTSMA TECHNOLOGY INTO THEIR SYSTEMS, GREATLY ADVANCING THE CURRENT SOA. THIS WORK WILL ALSO SERVE TO FURTHER THE UNDERSTANDING AND CHARACTERIZATION OF THE HTSMAS AS BEHAVIORS UNDER TORSIONAL LOADS AND COMBINED AXIAL AND TORSIONAL LOADING WILL BE OBSERVED.

Description: Support for the "Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions" in accordance with the attached Statement of Work (SOW) and Terms and Conditions. BACKGROUND: The NASA Engineering and Safety Centers (NESC) has approved the Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions as a discipline enhancing initiative. This discipline enhancing initiative was proposed by the Flight Sciences Super Problem Resolution Team (SPRT). OBJECTIVE/SCOPE: The scope of the investigation of the Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions pro-active proposal is focused on the development and validation of a high-accuracy coupled fluid-structures interaction solver. The investigation covers the initial development of the coupled solution method and acquisition of experimental data for validation. The BASS code accounts for the fluid response to a known excitation, such as moving boundary. Structural dynamic finite element codes predict the vibratory response for a known set of loads. The proposed work will couple the two types of analytical tools to predict the response of both media to a variety of excitations. An important aspect of such a merger is accounting for the fact that vibration of the structure represents a moving boundary for the fluid flow, and that the fluid loading on the structure drives this movement. In other words, it is necessary to develop a fully coupled analytical capability. At the end of the first phase of this work, a decision point is reached where the team can either disengage or continue to improve the speed and applicability of the fluid-structures interaction solver. Fluid-structures interactions cause persistent technical issues with aerospace vehicles. Redesigning these structural components for safety is problematic due to the lack of accurate computational prediction tools. Existing linearized flow acoustic prediction tools are not accurate when applied to the high-amplitude nonlinear acoustic waves present in the complex launch or re-entry environment. The scope of the proposed work is to develop and validate a computational tool to directly predict nonlinear fluid-structures interaction. Experiments will be performed in parallel to provide accurate validation data for the computational code.

Description: DEVELOPMENT AND CHARACTERIZATION OF HIGH TEMPERATURE SHAPE AND MEMORY ALLOY ACTUATORSABSTRACT:  WORK IS BEING DONE AT THE GLENN RESEARCH CENTER (GRC) UNDER THE NEW FUNDAMENTAL AERONAUTICS PROGRAM TO ADVANCE THE CURRENT STATE OF THE ART (SOA) IN ACTIVE STRUCTURES AND HIGH TEMPERATURE SHAPE MEMORY ALLOYS (HTSMAS). COMMERCIALLY AVAILABLE SMAS OFFER STRAIN OUTPUTS THAT ARE ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE LARGER THAN OTHER 'SMART" MATERIALS SUCH AS PIEZOELECTRIC TRANSDUCERS (PZTS). SMAS ALSO PROVIDE ACTUATION SOLUTIONS THAT ARE MUCH LIGHTER, SMALLER, AND SIMPLER THAN TRADITIONAL HYDRAULIC AND PNEUMATIC ACTUATION SYSTEMS. GENERALLY, SMAS ARE ACTIVATED BY HEATING THE MATERIAL TO A CHARACTERISTIC TRANSITION TEMPERATURE AND OPERATED WITHIN A CERTAIN TEMPERATURE RANGE ABOVE THAT LEVEL. HOWEVER, DEVICES BASED ON CONVENTIONAL SMA TECHNOLOGIES HAVE VERY LIMITED USE IN HIGH-TEMPERATURE APPLICATIONS (SUCH AS TURBOMACHINERY) AS THEIR TRANSITION TEMPERATURE OCCURS BETWEEN 7Q C AND L10 C, DEPENDING ON THE ALLOY, CURRENTLY SOME NEW HTSMAS ARE BEING CREATED AT GRC WHICH TRANSITION AT TEMPERATURES OF 300 C AND ABOVE (UP TO 800 C). THE RESEARCH BEING DONE TO CHARACTERIZE THE BEHAVIOR OF THESE MATERIALS HAS BEEN LIMITED TO PURE AXIAL LOADING OF RODS AND WIRES. IT IS FOUND THAT IN PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS, THESE AXIAL ACTUATOR FORMS OFTEN TAKE UP MORE ROOM THAN DESIRED AND PROVIDE AN EXCESSIVE AMOUNT OF WORK OUTPUT CAPABILITY. THE WORK BEING DONE UNDER GSRP GRANT #NNC06HA1H IS AIMED AT PROVING THE FUNCTIONALITY OF OTHER MORE COMPACT FORMS OF HTSMA ACTUATORS, NAMELY SPRINGS. IT IS THE HOPE THAT THE ACTUATORS BASED ON THESE COMPACT FORMS WILL PROVIDE GREATER STROKES AND MORE PROPORTIONATE WORK OUTPUT WHILE TAKING UP SMALLER VOLUMES AND WEIGHING MUCH LESS THAN CURRENT ACTUATION METHODS. IN ORDER TO PROVE THIS, A MODEL RELATING THE WORK OUTPUT TO THE GEOMETRY AND TEMPERATURE OF THE ACTUATORS WILL BE DEVELOPED AND VERIFIED USING EXPERIMENTAL DATA COLLECTED IN THE SMART LAB LOCATED IN THE BASEMENT OF BUILDING 49 AT GRC. DEMONSTRATION OF THE FUNCTIONALITY OF THESE ACTUATORS WILL ENABLE THE GROUP DEVELOPING ACTIVE TURBOMACHINERY STRUCTURES TO INCORPORATE GRC'S WORLD LEADING HTSMA TECHNOLOGY INTO THEIR SYSTEMS, GREATLY ADVANCING THE CURRENT SOA. THIS WORK WILL ALSO SERVE TO FURTHER THE UNDERSTANDING AND CHARACTERIZATION OF THE HTSMAS AS BEHAVIORS UNDER TORSIONAL LOADS AND COMBINED AXIAL AND TORSIONAL LOADING WILL BE OBSERVED.

Description: Residual Stress Modeling. RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION ASSESSMENT OF THE FLANGE TO SKIN WELD FOR THE ARES I-1 UPPER STAGE. THE CONTRACTOR WILL PERFORM SIX FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS OF WELDING RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION. THESE WILL BE USED TO PROVIDE A DESCRIPTION OF THE RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION STATE OF THE AREA OF THE SKIN-TO-FLANGE WELD OF THE UPPER STAGE OF THE ARES I-1 PROGRAM. THE SIX FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS WILL BE COMPLETED FOR TWO WELDING PROCEDURES USING THE FOLLOWING THREE MODELS: A TWO-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITH ROTATION PREVENTED (BY GUSSET) BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE, A THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITHOUT STIFFENERS OF THE WELD BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE, AND A FULL THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITH STIFFENERS OF THE WELD BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE. IT SHOULD BE NOTED THAT THE SECTOR OF AXI-SYMMETRY BETWEEN GUSSETS IS 10 DEGREES PER DRAWING PROVIDED BY NASA. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE TEMPERATURE-DEPENDENT THERMAL, PHYSICAL, AND MECHANICAL PROPOERTIES APPROPRIATE TO THE MATERIAL BEING WELDED. THESE PROPERTIES WILL BE COMMUNICATED TO NASA FOR CONFIRMATION. THE FIRST THREE FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS (FIRST WELDING PROCEDURE) ARE INTENDED TO DESCRIBE THE NASA GRC PATHFINDER 1 SEGMENT WHERE THE FLANGE IS NON-NORMALIZED ASTM A516 GRADE 70 STEEL AND THE SKIN IS NON-NORMALIZED ASTM A36 STEEL. THE LAST THREE FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS (SECOND WELDING PROCEDURE) ARE INTENDED TO DESCRIBE THE NASA GRC PATHFINDER 2 SEGMENT WHERE NOTH THE FLANGE AND THE SKIN MATERIAL WILL BE NORMALIZED ASTM A516 GRADE 70 STEEL. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE TWO MODELS OF WELDING PROCEDURES RESPRESENTATIVE OF THE PROCEDURES FOR THE FLANGE-TO-SKIN WELDING. THICKNESSES AND WELD SIZES WILL BE PROVIDED BY NASA. NASA WILL ALSO PROVIDE INFORMATION ON THE CHOSEN WELD PROCEDURE, SUCH AS THE JOINT SHAPE SPECIFICS, NUMBER AND POSITION OF WELD PASSES AND PARAMETERS SUCH AS HEAT INPUT. A BEST ESTIMATE FOR THE WELDING INFORMATION MAY BE SUFFICIENT. NASA WILL PROVIDE ONE PROCEDURE REPRESENTATIVE OF THE PLAN FOR FLIGHT HARDWARE AND ONE PROCEDURE REPRESENTATIVE OF THE EXISTING PATHFINDER EXAMPLE. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE THERMAL AND THERMOMECHANICAL ANALYSIS METHODS THAT CAN HANDLE MELTING AND RE-MELTING IN THE WELD AREA. THE CONTRACTOR WILL PROVIDE DESCRIPTIONS OF THE ANALYSIS AND FIGURES SHOWING THE EXTENT OF DISTORTION AND THE MAGNITUDES AND DIRECTIONS OF RESIDUAL STRESSES IN THE WELD AREA. INFORMATION WILL BE PROVIDED ON RESIDUAL STRESSES IN THE AXIAL, RADIAL AND ALONG-THE-WELD DIRECTIONS. A MID-TERM PROGRESS REPORT (POWERPOINT FORMAT) SHOULD BE DELIVERED AFTER 5 WEEKS WITH A DRAFT REPORT (POWERPOINT FORMAT THAT WILL BE REVIEWED BY NASA) DUE WITHIN NINE WEEKS OF PROJECT INITIATION. THE FINAL REPORT (WORD DOCUMENT FORMAT) WILL BE COMPLETED WITHIN AN ADDITIONAL ONE MONTH.

THESE WILL BE USED TO PROVIDE A DESCRIPTION OF THE RESIDUAL STRESS AND DISTORTION STATE OF THE AREA OF THE SKIN-TO-FLANGE WELD OF THE UPPER STAGE OF THE ARES I-1 PROGRAM. THE SIX FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS WILL BE COMPLETED FOR TWO WELDING PROCEDURES USING THE FOLLOWING THREE MODELS: A TWO-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITH ROTATION PREVENTED (BY GUSSET) BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE, A THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITHOUT STIFFENERS OF THE WELD BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE, AND A FULL THREE-DIMENSIONAL MODEL WITH STIFFENERS OF THE WELD BETWEEN THE SKIN AND THE FLANGE. IT SHOULD BE NOTED THAT THE SECTOR OF AXI-SYMMETRY BETWEEN GUSSETS IS 10 DEGREES PER DRAWING PROVIDED BY NASA. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE TEMPERATURE-DEPENDENT THERMAL, PHYSICAL, AND MECHANICAL PROPOERTIES APPROPRIATE TO THE MATERIAL BEING WELDED. THESE PROPERTIES WILL BE COMMUNICATED TO NASA FOR CONFIRMATION. THE FIRST THREE FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS (FIRST WELDING PROCEDURE) ARE INTENDED TO DESCRIBE THE NASA GRC PATHFINDER 1 SEGMENT WHERE THE FLANGE IS NON-NORMALIZED ASTM A516 GRADE 70 STEEL AND THE SKIN IS NON-NORMALIZED ASTM A36 STEEL. THE LAST THREE FINITE ELEMENT ASSESSMENTS (SECOND WELDING PROCEDURE) ARE INTENDED TO DESCRIBE THE NASA GRC PATHFINDER 2 SEGMENT WHERE NOTH THE FLANGE AND THE SKIN MATERIAL WILL BE NORMALIZED ASTM A516 GRADE 70 STEEL. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE TWO MODELS OF WELDING PROCEDURES RESPRESENTATIVE OF THE PROCEDURES FOR THE FLANGE-TO-SKIN WELDING. THICKNESSES AND WELD SIZES WILL BE PROVIDED BY NASA. NASA WILL ALSO PROVIDE INFORMATION ON THE CHOSEN WELD PROCEDURE, SUCH AS THE JOINT SHAPE SPECIFICS, NUMBER AND POSITION OF WELD PASSES AND PARAMETERS SUCH AS HEAT INPUT. A BEST ESTIMATE FOR THE WELDING INFORMATION MAY BE SUFFICIENT. NASA WILL PROVIDE ONE PROCEDURE REPRESENTATIVE OF THE PLAN FOR FLIGHT HARDWARE AND ONE PROCEDURE REPRESENTATIVE OF THE EXISTING PATHFINDER EXAMPLE. THE CONTRACTOR WILL USE THERMAL AND THERMOMECHANICAL ANALYSIS METHODS THAT CAN HANDLE MELTING AND RE-MELTING IN THE WELD AREA. THE CONTRACTOR WILL PROVIDE DESCRIPTIONS OF THE ANALYSIS AND FIGURES SHOWING THE EXTENT OF DISTORTION AND THE MAGNITUDES AND DIRECTIONS OF RESIDUAL STRESSES IN THE WELD AREA. INFORMATION WILL BE PROVIDED ON RESIDUAL STRESSES IN THE AXIAL, RADIAL AND ALONG-THE-WELD DIRECTIONS. A MID-TERM PROGRESS REPORT (POWERPOINT FORMAT) SHOULD BE DELIVERED AFTER 5 WEEKS WITH A DRAFT REPORT (POWERPOINT FORMAT THAT WILL BE REVIEWED BY NASA) DUE WITHIN NINE WEEKS OF PROJECT INITIATION. THE FINAL REPORT (WORD DOCUMENT FORMAT) WILL BE COMPLETED WITHIN AN ADDITIONAL ONE MONTH.

Description: SENSOR TECHNOLOGY MODEL DEVELOPMENT AND EVALUTUATION FOR AN INTEGRATED FLIGHT DECK (IIFD) EXTERNAL HAZARD MONITORTHIS PROPOSAL COVERS THE DEVELOPMENT OF SENSOR MODELS REQUIRED TO EVALUATE VARIOUS INTEGRATED INTELLIGENT FLIGHT DECK (IIFD) EXTERNAL HAZARD MONITOR ARCHITECTURES. HENCE, THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE OF THE PROPOSED RESEARCH WILL BE THE IDENTIFICATION AND CHARACTERIZATION OF HAZARDS, THE CHARACTERIZATION OF POTENTIAL SENSORS THAT CAN BE USED TO DETECT THESE HAZARDS AND THE DEVELOPMENT OF MODELS THAT CAN BE USED TO EVALUATE VARIOUS EXTERNAL HAZARD MONITORS. THIS PROPOSAL WILL FOCUS ON SENSORS THAT CAN BE USED FOR AUTOMATIC DETECTION OF OBJECTS ON OR NEAR THE RUNWAY DURING NON-PRECISION AND PRECISION APPROACH FLIGHT PROCEDURES UNDER VARIOUS ADVERSE WEATHER CONDITIONS. INTEGRATION OF EXTERNAL HAZARD MONITORS IN THE IIFD HAS A HIGH POTENTIAL OF REDUCING THE ACCIDENT RATE DUE TO CONTROLLED-FLIGHT-INTO-OBJECTS DURING APPROACH AND LANDING PHASES OF FLIGHT.. TO DETECT OBJECTS ON OR NEAR THE AIRPORT RUNWAYS THE AIRCRAFT WILL BE EQUIPPED WITH A MONITOR SYSTEM THAT INTERFACES TO ONE OR MORE AIRBORNE REMOTE SENSORS AND IS CAPABLE OF DETECTION, CLASSIFICATION, AND TRACKING OF VARIOUS-SIZE OBJECTS IN VARYING WEATHER CONDITIONS. UPON DETECTION OF OBJECTS ON OR NEAR THE RUNWAY, THE CLASSIFICATION AND TRACKING RESULTS WILL BE USED TO ASSESS THE HAZARD LEVEL ASSOCIATED WITH THE OBJECTS IN TERMS OF SEVERITY AND RISK USING STATISTICAL METHODS BASED ON THE MEASUREMENT/DETECTION CAPABILITIES OF THE SENSORS. TO INCREASE BOTH THE PROBABILITY OF DETECTION AND THE LEVEL OF CONFIDENCE IN THE HAZARD ASSESSMENT, THE DISSIMILAR CHARACTER WILL BE EXPLOITED BY INTEGRATING/FUSING THE AIRBORNE REMOTE SENSOROUTPUTS. TO FURTHER INCREASE ROBUSTNESS THE DETECTED OBJECTS WILL BE CROSS-CHECKED WITH THE OBSTACLE AND TERRAIN DATABASES AVAILABLE IN THE IIFD DECK DATA SERVERS AND OTHER SOURCES SUCH AS COMMUNICATIONS FROM THE GROUND SURFACE RADAR AND AUTOMATIC DEPENDENT SURVEILLANCE I BROADCAST (ADS-B). SENSORS THAT WILL BE CONSIDERED ARE FORWARD-LOOKING AIRBORNE LASER RANGE SCANNERS,THREE-DIMENSIONAL (3D) IMAGING SENSORS, FORWARD-LOOKING INFRARED (FLIR) CAMERAS, FORWARD-LOOKING VISIBLE LIGHT CAMERAS,MILLIMETER-WAVE RADAR AND X-BAND RADAR. RESEARCH TASKS WILL FOCUS ON IDENTIFICATION AND CHARACTERIZATION OF HAZARDS, CHARACTERIZATION AND MODELING OF THE VARIOUS SENSOR CANDIDATES, ESTABLISHING ALGORITHMS TO EXTRACT FEATURES FROM THE SENSOR IMAGERY, CLASSIFLCATION OF THESE FEATURES AS PART OF OBJECTS AND MOTION ANALYSIS OF THE THESE OBJECTS. THE SENSOR HARACTERIZATION EFFORT WILI CONSIDER FACTORS SUCH AS UPDATE RATE, RANGE/ANGULAR RESOLUTION, ACCURACY, PRECISION AND SENSITIVITY TO VARIOUS WEATHER CONDITIONS. FLIGHT SENSOR DATA AVAILABLE ATBOTH OHIO UNIVERSITY AND NASA WILL BE USED FOR MODEL VALIDATION PURPOSES. BASED ON THE DISSIMILAR CHARACTER OF THESE SENSORS, SENSOR INTEGRATION/FUSION METHODS WILL BE INVESTIGATED TO INCREASE BOTH THE PROBABILITY OF DETECTION AND THE LEVEL OF CONFIDENCE THAT AN OBJECT IS PRESENT. THE PROPOSED RESEARCH WILL BUILD ON THE EXPERIENCE PRESENT WITHIN THE OHIO UNIVERSITY AEC IN THE AREAS OF DATABASE INTEGRITY MONITORING, AIRBORNE LASER SCANNER (ALS) BASED TERRAIN REFERENCED NAVIGATION AND FEATURE EXTRACTION, INTEGRATION OF NAVIGATION AND REMOTE SENSORS AND ALS-BASED OBSTACLE DETECTION. THE PROPOSED WORK WILL SIGNIFICANTLY CONTRIBUTE TO THE NASA INTERESTS AND TO AVIATION IN GENERAL. THE PROPOSED EXTERNAL HAZARD MONITOR CONSTITUTES A TECHNOLOGY THAT ADVANCES AIRCRAFT SAFETY BY MAKING THE PILOT AWARE OF OBJECT AND OBSTACLES ON AND IN THE VICINITY OF THE RUNWAY WHILE HE/SHE CAN STILL ABORT THE FLIGHT PROCEDURE. THE PROPOSED RESEARCH FURTHERMORE ADVANCES THE FUNDAMENTAL DISCIPLINES OF AERONAUTICS BY INVESTIGATING ADVANCED TECHNIQUES TO PERFORM AIRBORNEREMOTE SENSOR CHARACTERIZATION, MODELING AND INTEGRATION.

Description: Submillimeter-wave Laboratory Spectroscopic investigations We propose to continue our highly successful laboratory program into the submillimeter-wave spectra of known and likely interstellar molecules. Determination of laboratory spectra in this wavelength region is critical for the success of NASA's missions such as Herschel, which will operate at frequencies as high as 1.9 THz, since spectra from space cannot be analyzed without supporting laboratory data. Moreover, such spectra normally arise from star- and planet-forming regions of the interstellar medium, so our program fits closely with NASA's strategic goals 3.3 and 3.4, which concern the origins and history of the solar system and the origin, structure, evolution, and destiny of the universe. We propose to study a variety of molecular species, including denterated isotopologues of known interstellar molecules, molecules in excited torsional states, and molecules of astro-biological interest. The deuterated isotopologues are of great importance in understanding the early stages of low-mass star formation, where deuterium fractionation can occur quite dramatically depending on the physical conditions. Molecules in torsionally excited states are excellent probes of warm conditions in star-forming regions. We also propose to study molecules at THz frequencies to a greater extent than in the past, so that there will be at least some laboratory data available when Herschel is launched. Finally, a radically new proposal to eliminate the "weeds" from astronomical spectra in hot cores based on spectrum simulation will be presented.

Description: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center shall utilize the contractors Polysonic Wind Tunnel (PSWT) to support the Ares project.  To support the assessment of the Ares DAC 2 1st stage element, the data to develop the aerodynamic database is required over the descent Mach range.  A wind tunnel model has been built to test at NASA MSFCs Aerodynamic Research Facility, for the Mach range 0.5 - 4.96.  A larger facility with a similar Mach range capability is needed to test the existing model and thus reduce or eliminate the effects of the tunnel walls. The primary Mach range of concern is between 0.5 and 1.46.  The PSWT covers the Mach range of M = 0.45 to 1.6 and will thus provide the needed data for the reentry phase for Ares I 1st stage flight and assess the effects of wall interference. The contractor shall provide hardware requirements for testing in the Polysonic Wind Tunnel. The contractor shall provide the wind tunnel facility and personnel to install the model hardware and perform the test matrix and shall provide all data reduction set-up, transmittals, data files and verification.  The contractor shall perform check-loadings and angle-of-attack verification, wind off zeros, and weight tare procedures.  Based on the test matrix, the contractor shall provide flow angularity evaluations. The contractor shall provide preliminary test data to MSFC on-site engineers for review during the test. Final data shall be provided three (3) weeks after completion of the test matrix to MSFC. The contractor shall disassemble the model, box, and ship the model to MSFC upon completion of the test.

Description: NORTH ATLANTIC LAND-ICE SURFACE MASS BUDGET The North Atlantic region land ice masses volume fluctuations significantly affect global sea level and regional climate. Land ice response to climate is amplified by the ice-albedo feedback. Recent climate warming has framed the Greenland ice sheet a driver of global sea level change. We beginning our final year of a NASA IDS-2003 grant to determine surface mass budgets for the Greenland ice sheet over the past 24 years. We have thus far determined and published several analyses of ice sheet surface mass balance spatial distributions and temporal variability, including mass budget sensitivity functions. We aim to expand this work spatially and temporally. Specifically, our objectives are: 1) to apply a refined atmospheric data assimilation model over land ice masses in the North Atlantic region to determine the spatiaUtemporal patterns of ice surface mass budget variability over the past 50-years and relate them to climate forcing; 2) apply downscaling techniques to determine the time-variation of surface mass budget components over individual ice masses, their drainage basins, and different glaciological zones at fine spatial resolution (-lkm); and 3) use information contained in past variability to construct empirical sensitivity functions to determine the mass budget changes in the coming century, given state of the art IPCC 2007 global climate forecast time-series available through the National Center for Atmospheric Research. 4) Surface mass balance variability information combined with thickness changes derived from satellite and airborne altimetry (ATMIICESat)facilitates partitioning of land ice mass balance into its ice dynamic flow and surface melt components, and to evaluate their apparent interplay. Similarly, GRACE surveys have and will continue to facilitate backing out ice dynamical mass fluxes given surface melt water runoff rates from this work. Important model boundary conditions and validation data sets come from satellite and airborne remote sensing. Specifically, daily surface albedo grids from the MODIS and AVHRR densors have been critical in defining the driver for melting, absorbed solar radiation. MODIS-derived surface temperature and emjssivity facilitate gauging model skill for this key parameter in melt modeling. Microwave remote sensing of a) snow melt frequency (SMMR and SSMII) and b) melt intensity (NASA and other Scatterometers) are necessary sources of validation data. Further, we propose to test the hypothesis that a significant link exists between the interannual variability in North Atlantic land ice mass barance and global sea level, as recorded by TOPEXmoseidon and Jason satellite altimeters. The proposed work is a collaborative endeavor between the J.E. Box (PI), D.H. Bromwich (Co-PI), and graduate and honors program undergraduate students at Byrd Polar Research Center (The Ohio State University); and collaborators W. Abdalati at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center; E. Rignot at NASA JPL; M. Dyurgerov at University of Colorado/Stockholm University; J.-0. Hagen at the Universityof Oslo; H. Bjornsson at the University of Iceland; M. Sharp at the University of Alberta; S. Marshall at the University of Calgary, Canada; L. Smith at University of California, Los Angeles; and R. Forster at the University of Utah. We propose a 3-year-,dudy with an annual budget of -$230K.

Description: INTERFACIAL AREA TRANSPORT EQUATION IN MICROGRAVITY CONDITION (PHASE II) The objective of this proposed research is to continue an awarded project (Award Number: NNC06GA09G) to collaborate with Dr. M. Ishii at Purdue University to develop an interfacial area transport equation applicable for micro gravity conditions. The interfacial area transport equation will be evaluated based on experimental data acquired from both small diameter (25.4 mm) and large diameter (305 mm) flow channels. This new interfacial area transport model can make a leapfrog improvement by furnishing dynamic constitutive relations for the interfacial interaction terms in the two-fluid model. This revolutionary approach can eliminate the non-physical system behavior caused by the traditional flow-regime dependent approach. Under the microgravity condition, the traditional approach presents evident problems because the two-phase flow structures may not reach an equilibrium configuration in the microgravity condition; whereas the interfacial area transport equation dynamically models the changes of the interfacial structures, which have dominant effects on the overall transport processes.

Description: Support for the "Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions" in accordance with the attached Statement of Work (SOW) and Terms and Conditions. BACKGROUND: The NASA Engineering and Safety Centers (NESC) has approved the Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions as a discipline enhancing initiative. This discipline enhancing initiative was proposed by the Flight Sciences Super Problem Resolution Team (SPRT). OBJECTIVE/SCOPE: The scope of the investigation of the Extension of NASA Broadband Aeronautics Stator Simulation (BASS) Code for the Accurate Prediction of Nonlinear Fluid-Structures Interactions pro-active proposal is focused on the development and validation of a high-accuracy coupled fluid-structures interaction solver. The investigation covers the initial development of the coupled solution method and acquisition of experimental data for validation. The BASS code accounts for the fluid response to a known excitation, such as moving boundary. Structural dynamic finite element codes predict the vibratory response for a known set of loads. The proposed work will couple the two types of analytical tools to predict the response of both media to a variety of excitations. An important aspect of such a merger is accounting for the fact that vibration of the structure represents a moving boundary for the fluid flow, and that the fluid loading on the structure drives this movement. In other words, it is necessary to develop a fully coupled analytical capability. At the end of the first phase of this work, a decision point is reached where the team can either disengage or continue to improve the speed and applicability of the fluid-structures interaction solver. Fluid-structures interactions cause persistent technical issues with aerospace vehicles. Redesigning these structural components for safety is problematic due to the lack of accurate computational prediction tools. Existing linearized flow acoustic prediction tools are not accurate when applied to the high-amplitude nonlinear acoustic waves present in the complex launch or re-entry environment. The scope of the proposed work is to develop and validate a computational tool to directly predict nonlinear fluid-structures interaction. Experiments will be performed in parallel to provide accurate validation data for the computational code.

Description: SIMULATION BASED ASSESSMENT OF SPINAL INJURY RISK DURING IMPACT LANDING WITH A NOVEL SPACE SUIT A new design of the space suit involves firm rings at various joints and at the trunk level. These may have the potential to cause injury during impact landing, particularly at the spine due to the placement of the trunk ring relative to this body segment. It is critical to evaluate spinal injury risk to identify safety issues associated with the use of this suit and to address design changes to reduce the risk. Our goal is to provide a simplified yet effective approach for spinal injury assessment of the new space suit through computational modeling. A planar finite element model of the spine, soft tissue, suit and seating will be developed incorporating deformation characteristics of all under loading. Impact loads will simulate different landing scenarios and spinal loading and deformation will be extracted and compared against failure loads of the spine. The simulations will evaluate current design in terms of its safe use during landing. In addition, the completion of the project will provide a computational platform for prospective testing of suit design parameters (e.g. ring placement and shape) and seating choices.

Description: A Feasibility Study on Development of Dust Abrasion Resistant Gear Concepts for Lunar Vehicle Gearboxes This research project proposes a feasibility study on development of dust abrasion resistant gear concepts for future lunar vehicle gearboxes. Conventional gearbox design practices, lubrication methods and gear materials are not suitable for this application due to presence of fine lunar dust that is extremely abrasive and wide ranges of operating temperatures. Operating lunar gearboxes in a marginally lubricated environment containing lunar dust under extreme temperatures short gear lives due to excessive tooth surface wear. In contrast to past missions where limited life cycles were expected from lunar gearboxes, long life cycle requirements for future lunar vehicles necessitates an investigation into novel design methods as well as material and manufacturing techniques in order to develop gears having require wear resistance. This is the main goal of this research project. With abrasive wear as the main concern, the feasibility of the use of steel and ceramic gears as well as hybrid gear designs that combine both materials for lunar gearbox applications will be investigated, Best gear tooth and gear wheel design practices, stress limits and manufacturing accuracy requirements for of each gear concept will be determined. Test specimens representing these gear concepts and design practices will be designed and fabricated. Highly abrasive test conditions will be used to demonstrate the feasibility of these concepts under realistic operating conditions.

Description: SOIL MECHANICS STUDIES FOR IN-SITU RESOURCE UTILIZATION  -  PHASE TWO One of the most important issues related to in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) is to understand the mechanical behavior of lunar soils. As the design of excavation, transportation, and processing equipment for lunar regolith depends critically on the measurement of mechanical properties of lunar soils and accurate numerical simulation of these operations, it is very important to develop a protocol to investigate the mechanical behavior of lunar soils and to simulate the operations on the moon numerically. However, since only a small quantity of lunar soils was ever brought back from the moon in past lunar missions, it is imperative to produce a soil on the Earth that can simulate the most critical mechanical properties of lunar soils and can be produced in large quantity at a reasonable cost. At present, the lunar stimulant JSC-la is the only stimulant that is officially available. Extensive laboratory testing is needed to determine the mechanical properties of JSC-la under conditions that are expected on the moon. In addition, protocols must be developed to prepare soil bins that will be used to test different tools to be used on the lunar surface for ISRU operations.

Description: NORTH ATLANTIC LAND-ICE SURFACE MASS BUDGET The North Atlantic region land ice masses volume fluctuations significantly affect global sea level and regional climate. Land ice response to climate is amplified by the ice-albedo feedback. Recent climate warming has framed the Greenland ice sheet a driver of global sea level change. We beginning our final year of a NASA IDS-2003 grant to determine surface mass budgets for the Greenland ice sheet over the past 24 years. We have thus far determined and published several analyses of ice sheet surface mass balance spatial distributions and temporal variability, including mass budget sensitivity functions. We aim to expand this work spatially and temporally. Specifically, our objectives are: 1) to apply a refined atmospheric data assimilation model over land ice masses in the North Atlantic region to determine the spatiaUtemporal patterns of ice surface mass budget variability over the past 50-years and relate them to climate forcing; 2) apply downscaling techniques to determine the time-variation of surface mass budget components over individual ice masses, their drainage basins, and different glaciological zones at fine spatial resolution (-lkm); and 3) use information contained in past variability to construct empirical sensitivity functions to determine the mass budget changes in the coming century, given state of the art IPCC 2007 global climate forecast time-series available through the National Center for Atmospheric Research. 4) Surface mass balance variability information combined with thickness changes derived from satellite and airborne altimetry (ATMIICESat)facilitates partitioning of land ice mass balance into its ice dynamic flow and surface melt components, and to evaluate their apparent interplay. Similarly, GRACE surveys have and will continue to facilitate backing out ice dynamical mass fluxes given surface melt water runoff rates from this work. Important model boundary conditions and validation data sets come from satellite and airborne remote sensing. Specifically, daily surface albedo grids from the MODIS and AVHRR densors have been critical in defining the driver for melting, absorbed solar radiation. MODIS-derived surface temperature and emjssivity facilitate gauging model skill for this key parameter in melt modeling. Microwave remote sensing of a) snow melt frequency (SMMR and SSMII) and b) melt intensity (NASA and other Scatterometers) are necessary sources of validation data. Further, we propose to test the hypothesis that a significant link exists between the interannual variability in North Atlantic land ice mass barance and global sea level, as recorded by TOPEXmoseidon and Jason satellite altimeters. Bjornsson at the University of Iceland; M. Sharp at the University of Alberta; S. Marshall at the University of Calgary, Canada; L. Smith at University of California, Los Angeles; and R. Forster at the University of Utah. We propose a 3-year-,dudy with an annual budget of -$230K.

Description: THE MAIN PURPOSE OF THIS PROPOSAL IS TO STUDY VARIOUS ADVANCED TECHNIQUES FOR STRUCTURAL HEALTH MONITORING OF HIGH ENERGY, ROTATING AEROSPACE PROPULSION COMPONENTS.  TO ACHIEVE THIS GOAL, A UNIQUE EXPERIMENTAL TEST FACILITY IS BEING DESIGNED, ASSEMBLED AND PERIODICALLY UPDATED.  THIS FACILITY CONTAINS TWO TABLE TOP SPIN RIGS.  EACH SPIN RIG IS BASED ON A HORIZONTAL SHAFT SUPPORTED BY TWO BEARINGS WITH ONE OR MORE SUBSCALE DISKS TO MIMIC THE DISKS OF A TURBINE ENGINE.  THE TWO SYSTEMS DIFFER CONCERNING PRECISION, MAXIMUM ROTATIONAL SPEED, AND ELEVATED TEMPERATURE CAPABILITY.  TESTS ARE CONDUCTED WITH BOTH HEALTHY AND DAMAGED DISKS AND SHAFTS.  MULTIPLE TYPES OF SENSORS ARE UTILIZED DURING THE TESTS.  RADIAL AND TRANSVERSE DISPLACEMENT SENSORS ARE USED TO MONITOR THE VIBRATION RESPONSE OF THE ROTOR AS WELL AS OBSERVING ANY DISTORTIONS IN THE DISK DUE TO INTERNAL DAMAGE.  ALSO, ULTRASONIC TECHNIQUES USING PIEZOELECTRIC PATCHES (E.G., PZT) ARE APPLIED DURING THE SPIN TESTS.  THESE INCLUDE ACTIVE GUIDED WAVE ULTRASONICS AND PASSIVE ACOUSTICS EMISSIONS, UTILIZED WITH EITHER A CONVENTIONAL SLIP RING CONNECTION OR AN INNOVATIVE BROADBAND WIRELESS TELEMETRY SYSTEM.  IN ADDITION TO THE ROTOR TESTING, MATERIAL CHARACTERIZATION STUDIES ARE CONDUCTED ON ADVANCED METALS AS WELL AS COMPOSITES.  DURING THESE TESTS THE MECHANICAL BEHAVIOR IS STUDIED BY IMPLEMENTING VARIOUS NONDESTRUCTIVE EVALUATION (NDE) TECHNIQUES TO HELP IN GRADING THE DAMAGE LEVEL WITHIN THE MATERIAL SYSTEMS.  THE RESULTS OF THIS ACTIVITY CONTRIBUTE MAINLY TO THE NASA'S INTEGRATED VEHICLE HEALTH MANAGEMENT (IVHM) PROGRAM ALTHOUGH THE RESULTS ARE ALSO VERY RELEVANT TO VARIOUS OTHER AERONATUICS AND SPACE EXPLORATION PROGRAMS INTERESTED IN IMPROVING THE HEALTH MONITORING OF STRUCTURAL COMPONENTS AND THE ABILITIES OF NDE FOR ADVANCED MATERIAL CHARACTERIZATION.

Description: SIMULATION AND PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS FOR CNS PHASE IIRESEARCH FOR THE NEXT PHASE OF FUNDING WILL CONTINUE THE PREVIOUS WORK PERFORMED BY CLEVELAND STATE UNIVERSITY. THE FOCUS WILL BE ON EXPANDING AND ENHANCING COMMUNICATIONS, NAVIGATION, AND SURVEILLANCE SIMULATION MODELS AND USING THESE MODELS TO ESTIMATE THE POTENTIAL IMPACT OF THESE SYSTEMS ON THE NATIONAL AIRSPACE SYSTEM (NAS). THE PRIMARY COMMUNICATIONS SYSTEM EXPLORED TO DATE BY OUR RESEARCH IS VHF DIGITAL LINK (VDL) MODES 2, 3, AND 4. VDL MODE 2 IS THE LEADING NEAR-TERM SOLUTION FOR COMMUNICATIONS IN THE NAS, ENABLING DIGITAL APPLICATIONS AND INFORMATION TO BE EXCHANGED THAT CANNOT BE SUPPORTED BY THE CURRENT ANALOG VOICE TECHNOLOGY. AS SUCH, IT IS IMPORTANT TO ACCURATELY UNDERSTAND THE PERFORMANCE OF THIS SYSTEM IN FUTURE SCENARIOS. FOR THIS REASON, ENHANCEMENTS TO THE SIMULATIONS ARE REQUIRED. PREVIOUS RESEARCH HAS FOCUSED MAINLY ON THE COMMUNICATIONS ASPECTS OF THE NAS. NAVIGATION AND SURVEILLANCE ARE EQUALLY IMPORTANT IN THE OVERALL SYSTEM, AS THE ACCURACY OF THESE SYSTEMS WILL DETERMINE THE MINIMUM SPACING BETWEEN AIRCRAFT THAT CAN SAFELY BE IMPLEMENTED. THESE SYSTEMS WILL BE RESEARCHED TO IDENTIFY THE ONES THAT WILL BE VALUABLE TO MODEL. IN PARTICULAR, WE PROPOSE THE MODELING, SIMULATION AND ANALYSIS OF AN AIRPORT SURFACE FADING MODEL, SUBNETWORK COMPRESSION SCHEMES, VDL MODE 2 ENHANCEMENTS AND NAVIGATION AND SURVEILLANCE MODELS SUCH AS VHF OMNIDIRECTIONAL RANGING (VOR), DISTANCE MEASURING EQUIPMENT (DME), AND GLOBAL POSITIONING SYSTEM (GPS) AND AIRCRAFT DEPENDENT SURVEILLANCE-BROADCAST (ADS-B). THIS RESEARCH WILL BE CONDUCTED AT NASA GLENN RESEARCH CENTER.

Description: ANALYSIS AND MODELING OF MARTIAN ELECTRON DENSITY PROFILES RETURNED FROM SPACECRAFT We propose to address several objectives relating to the data on electron density profiles returned from the MGS radio science experiment the MEX MaRS and MARSIS instruments. The project also relates to ion outflows measured by the MEX ASPERA instrument. We propose the following. 1. We will investigate the occurrence of a sharp E region peak by carrying out case studies, in which we build a given electron density profile by adding and scaling different portions of the EUV and soft xrays  spectrum to a model until it mimics the data. 2. We will investigate the "grazing incidence" ionosphere by modeling profiles in the very near-terminator and beyond. We will determine whether the profiles can be explained by absorption of sunlight or if transterminator ion-transport is required. We will also determine whether the observed peaks, which may be above the photochemical region, are subject to transport by dynamical processes, as they are in the outer planets. 3. We will compare the features of experimental and model electron density profiles to determine their solar zenith angle and F10.7 dependence and the average densities of the peaks. This will allow us to evaluate the quality of the neutral models from the MTGCM of collaborator Bougher and our input parameters, such as cross sections and rate coefficients. It will also provide a better understanding of the near-terminator ionosphere/thermosphere. We will also compare the experimental and model electron density scale heights above the PCE region. These scale heights are indicative of the rate of ion outflow. An upward velocity boundary condition on the ions in the model produces upward fluxes of the ions. The rate of outflow indicated by the scale heights should be consistent with that obtained by the ASPERA instrument. 4. Finally, we will carry out a small study of the effect of different solar flux models on the ionosphere of Mars. It appears that the use of the model that best fits the terrestrial ionosphere predicts too small electron densities at Mars. These studies are highly relevant to the NASA MDAP program, which seeks to maximize the science return from the Mars missions. They will provide a better understanding of the near-terminator ionosphere/thermosphere region, which is crucial to aerobraking and aerocapture. Data and models of this region of the ionosphere are rare. The ion escape studies are important for studies of the evolution of the Martian atmosphere, which is included in the overall goals of NASA, although not the MDAP program specifically.

Description: CONTRIBUTIONS TO MESSENGER AND THE GEOPHYSICAL STRUCTURE AND EVOLUTION OF MERCURY We propose a comprehensive set of contributions to the MESSENGER mission to broadly enhance the scientific return and provide operational assistance and expertise in the collection and validation of geophysical datasets. Our investigation will focus on leveraging MESSENGER data in order to quantify the geophysical structure of Mercury, the internal evolution of the planet, and the long-wavelength tectonic character and behavior of the lithosphere. These contributions will primarily benefit three of the MESSENGER mission's driving science questions: (1) What planetary formational processes led to the high metal/silicate ratio in Mercury? (2) What are the structure and composition of Mercury's core? (3) What are the nature and origin of Mercury's magnetic field? (4) What is the geological history of Mercury? Specifically, this investigation will leverage the PI's experience to address: (i)the structure and composition of the planet and especially the core, (ii) existence and amount of any long-wavelength, low-amplitude folds that may record regional or global contraction as well as characterization of large scale variations in the lithosphere, and (iii) constraints on the internal evolution of Mercury from surface tectonics, source of the magnetic field, and global structure and composition.

The results of this study will not only affect the NLSl paradigm, but also our understanding of formation and evolution of AGNs in general.

Description: The Ohio Aerospace Institute requests funds to implement the Students and Teachers Exploring Local Landscapes to Interpret the Earth from Space (SATELLITES) Program focusing on the International Polar Year (IPY) for 50 teachers and their students from Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania and West Virginia. We will work with middle and high school teachers to link the study of the polar regions, geospatial technology (the third fastest growing field in the United States according to the Department of Labor) to Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) content. Teachers will attend a week-long SATELLITES institute in Morgantown, West Virginia, have their students participate in a field campaign and implement an inquiry-based application project in the spring of 2008 and 2009 based on IPY. The institute will focus on how Global Positioning Systems (GPS), Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and remote sensing are applied in polar regions to understand some of the radical changes that are occurring in polar regions. IPY scientists and their research from the Byrd Polar Research Center at Ohio State University and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center will highlighted. During the field campaign, students will take observations using GLOBE protocols (observations could include snow depth and water equivalent, air temperature, surface temperature, cloud type and cover, and land cover) that will help students link their local environment to global issues. Students will then complete inquiry-based research projects utilizing data from around the world and their own data from the GLOBE database. Education research shows that students learn best when they do hands-on activities tied to inquiry-based projects. Students will communicate with scientists via videoconferencing technology about their inquiry-based projects to receive feedback. The finished projects will be entered into a competition and awards will be made to the winning teams via a videoconference. Each activity of the SATELLITES Program has been mapped to the Ohio academic standards addressing Earth and Space Science, Technology, Mathematics and English Language Arts and will be mapped to Maryland, Pennsylvania, West Virginia and federal standards. Scientists from Ohio, West Virginia, Pennsylvania and Maryland will team together to offer the program to 6-7 teachers per year per state. A pilot for SATELLITES-IPY is currently being conducted in Ohio through a grant from the state#s Board of Regents. The goal is to develop a group of Master Teachers who will be able to bring the program back to each state and implement it on a broader level. The significance of this program is that it will bring together Polar research sponsored by NASA with the NASA sponsored GLOBE program to students in a real way. Description: Three-dimensional Defect Engineering of GE/SIGE/SI substrates for the Growth of High Efficiency Solar Cells There is a tremendous need to create a space photovoltaics technology that can generate electric power with high efficiency and at a light weight, so that maximum power with minimum mass can be provided to space vehicles. The solution to this need is very complex, and involves basic materials science such that high efficiency and low mass density can be provided by a single technology. This project addresses this need through the investigation of integrating lattice-mismatched 111-V semiconductors that generate high solar conversion efficiency, with light weight substrates, such as Si. Specifically, the objective of this project is to utilize various approaches encompassed by substrate engineering to mitigate material defects that are created by virtue of this integration scheme. These approaches include compositional lattice grading of substrates to achieve an ideal virtual substrate lattice constant upon which an ideal solar cell may be grown, as well as "3-d" engineering of the substrate that effectively filters defects in other dimensions. A long term goal is to in fact combine both lattice grading and substrate patterning, a process that can lead to optimized arrays of both optoelectronic and photovoltaic devices on a variety of substrate platfoms. Of particular focus on this project are (I) the use of anion and cation based 111-V graded buffers to generate ideal virtual substrate lattice constants, (2) the direct epitaxy of 111-V materials on SiGe virtual substrates on Si where the SiGe lattice constant itself is ideal, and (3) to perform materials science studies regarding defect control; strain introcliiction, s-m-face conditions, etc., that lead toward a greater understanding of how these approaches may be optimized for device applications. Once solved, the inclusion of patterned substrates provides the final dimension for complete defect control. Ultimately, the knowledge gained from this research will advance the goal of achieving a defect engineering methodology that will guide development of lightweight and high efficiency 111-VISi space photovoltaics and a range of other advanced device technologies that can exploit the wide range of properties made available by using lattice-mismatched semiconductor heterostructures.

We will model these FUV data, along with ancillary optical spectra, UV spectra, and optical polarimetry, to probe the temperature, density, velocity structure, and geometry of B[e] disks. Additionally, we will probe the role metallicity may play in the formation and evolution ofthe B[e] phenomenon.

Description: NASA's Aircraft Aging and Durability (AAD) project is part of the Aviation Safety Program. This program has two key themes which our work will address: (a) Detection - locate and characterize fully damage or degradation of materials and structures and (b) Prediction - life and strength predictions accounting for accumulated damage associated with long-term exposure to thermal/mechanical/environmental loads. We will respond to NASA's needs and expectations to develop additional multi-scale modeling and testing methodologies. These will address predictability of both the local behavior of fan blade impact on aged/degraded fan case structures as well as the global behavior of fan case engine system structural dynamics. These will occur via development of material models and its implementation into LSDYNA code allowing a consistent and integrated computational framework. We will also focus on testing methodologies for generating material characterization and model validation data of aged/degraded composites static and dynamic behavior. The proposed research program will address the following: I. Effects of cyclic environmental conditions (temperature, moisture, etc.) and nominal loading conditions on the static and dynamic/impact response of advanced composite materials/structures. Typical jet engine cyclic temperature/humidity exposure will be imposed on the resins & composites for generating aged samples. 2. The composite materials used in this research will be those of mutual interest to NASA and aerospace industry. In particular, we will focus on tri-axial braid with large unit cell and ribbon like strands. 3. Numerical models will be extended to predict the impact behavior of both hard-wall and soft-wall, composite jet engine containment structures. 4. Material models will be able to capture complex deformation, damage, and failure progression mechanisms during dynamic/impact loading events. This will be accomplished primarily through introduction of interface strength and aging evolution of the interface. Existing NASA test data on un-aged composites will be reviewed and integrated into the proposed program. NASA facilities will be required with graduate students co-located at NASA GRC. The products of this research will be: new mechanical and impact test data for various aged resin and composites; validated material model incorporating interface strength, aging, and strain rate effects; and developed FE models of test coupons, impacted plates, and jet engine containment. This approach will allow predicting blade-out process in the most cost effective way while allowing better understanding of physics behind the failure of braided composites under impact conditions.

Description: THE AVETEC RESEARCH TEAM PROPOSES TO DEVELOP A NEW TURBOMACHINERY DESIGN SYSTEM INCORPORATING MULTI-FIDELITY MODELS AND UTILIZING MULTI-DISCIPLINARY ANALYSIS AND OPTIMIZATION (MDAO) TO CREATE BOTH COMPONENT AND ENGINE SYSTEM OR MISSION OPTIMUS.   TRADITIONALLY, INDIVIDUAL ENGINE COMPONENTS ARE DESIGNED SEPARATELY AND THEN MADE TO WORK TOGETHER THROUGH A TIME-CONSUMING, ITERATIVE PROCESS.  THE PO=ROPOSED DESIGN SYSTEM WILL ALLOW ENGINE COMPONENT DESIGNERS TO OPTIMIZE HIGH-FIDELITY, 3D AERODYNAMIC AND STRUSTURAL COMPONENT DESIGNS BY COUPLING THEM TO LOWER-FIDELITY (0- AND 1D) ENGHINE SYSTEM DESIGN MODELS.  THIS APPROACH WILL ALLOW DESIGNERS TO ESTIMATE COMPONENT EFFECTS ON THE ENGINE SYSTEM AND TAILOR THEIR DESIGNS SO THAT THEY BETTER NATCH THE OPERATION OF THE OTHER ENGINE COMPONENTS.  THIS LEADS TO BETTER DESIGNS IN LESS TIME.  THE PROPOSED SYSTENM WILL UTILIZE CAD SOFTWARE (T-AXI, BLADE GEOMETRY MODELER, CAPRI AND TGS) TO GENERATE CFD MESH FROM COLD-PART GEOMETRY.  THREE-DIMENSIONAL CFD TURBOMACHINERY FLOW SOLVERS SUCH AS APNASA, TURBO AND SUmb, WILL BE USED TO SOLVE THE NAVIER-STOKES FLUID FLOW EQUATIONS ON THE MESH.  FROM THOSE SOLUTIONS, THE PRESSURE-INDUCED DEFLECTIONS TO THE GEOMETRY ARE USED TO DETERMINE HOT-PART GEOMETRY.  A HIGH-FIEDLITY OPTIMIZER IS USED TO IMPROVE COMPONENT DESIGN.  FLOW SOLUTIONS ARE ALSO AVERAGED TO PROVIDE INPUT TO ONE-DIMENSIONAL COMPONENT MODELS, CONSTRUCTED IN NPSS, WHICH WILL BE USED WITH AN NPSS ENGINE CYCLE MODEL.  THE ENGINE CYCLE IS RUN FOR THE ENGINE MISSION TO PROVIDE COMPONENT SENSITIVITIES AND RELATIVE WEIGHT, WHICH DEFINE THE OBJECTIVE FUNCTION THAT WILL DRIVE A SECOND OVERALL OPTIMIZER.  ALTHOUGH SOME OF THE PIECES OF THE SYSTEM ARE READY OR NEARLY READY FOR USE, KEY ADDITIONS WILL BE MADE TO MAKE A SEAMLESS SYSTEM THAT ALSO ADDRESSES MANY ISSUES THAT ARE REQUIRED FOR A DESIGN SYSTEM.

Description: INVESTIGATIONS OF DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS - TO DATE, MANNED SPACE FLIGHT HAS BEEN CONDUCTED UNDER CLOSE SUPERVISION FROM MISSION CONTROL.  ASTRONAUTS HAVE BEEN PROVIDED WITH EXTENSIVE REPETITIVE PRACTICE FOR HIGHLY SCRIPTED MISSIONS.  WHENEVER UNEXPECTED SITUATIONS WERE ENCOUNTERED, THEY HAVE RELIED ON MISSION-CONTROL AND GROUND RESOURCES FOR DECISION SUPPORT.  HOWEVER, IN THE FUTURE, MISSIONS MAY LAST MUCH LONGER AND MAY INVOLVE SUBSTANTIAL PERIODS WHEN THE CREW WILL BE OUT OF SYNCHRONOUS COMMUNICATION WITH EARTH-BASED RESOURCES.  DURING THESE PERIODS, THE CREW WILL NEED TO MAKE DECISIONS AUTONOMOUSLY.  AUTOMATED DECISION SUPPORT TOOLS MAY PROVIDE ONE MEANS OF SUPPORT FOR CREWS DURING THESE TIMES.  TOOLS COULD BE DEVELOPED THAT WOULD COMPENSATE FOR HUMAN INFORMATION PROCESSING CONSTRAINTS AND DECISION BIASES.  HOWEVER, IT IS NOT CLEAR HOW THESE TOOLS SHOULD BE STRUCTURED.  IN PARTICULAR, IT IS NOT CLEAR WHETHER IT IS POSSIBLE TO DEVELOP USEFUL GENERAL PURPOSE DECISION SUPPORT TOOLS OR WHETHER ANY TOOLS THAT ARE DEVELOPED WILL NEED TO BE HIGHLY TASK SPECIFIC AND THEREFORE OF MORE LIMITED VALUE.  IN THIS PROJECT, WE PROPOSE TO REVIEW THE STATE OF THE ART OF DECISION SUPPORT SYSTEMS AND BEGIN RESEARCH TO DETERMINE WHETHER TOOLS CAN BE DEVELOPED THAT CAN PROVIDE GENERAL DECISION SUPPORT BY COMPENSATING FOR HUMAN CONSTRAINTS AND DECISION-MAKING BIASES WITHOUT CAUSING NEW PROBLEMS.     HUMANS SUFFER FROM A VARIETY OF INFORMATION PROCESSING CONSTRAINTS AND DECISION BIASES THAT INTERFERE WITH OUR ABILITY TO MAKE OPTIMAL CHOICES IN MAY SITUATIONS.  DECISION SUPPORT TOOLS OFFER ONE MEANS OF ATTEMPTING TO COMPENSATE FOR SOME OF THESE CONSTRAINTS AND BIASES.  AS MANNED SPACEFLIGHT PROGRESSES BEYOND THE EARTH-MOON SYSTEM, IT WILL BECOME INCREASINGLY IMPORTANT FOR CREWS TO BE ABLE TO ACT AUTONOMOUSLY IN IDENTIFYING PROBLEMS, DEVELOPING SOLUTIONS, AND MAKING DECISIONS.  DECISION SUPPORT TOOLS COULD BE DEVELOPED TO SUPPORT THESE MISSIONS.  HOWEVER, IT IS NOT CLEAR THAT THESE TOOLS ARE CAPABLE OF PROVIDING THE TYPE AND DEGREE OF ASSISTANCE THAT WOULD PROVE USEFUL TO AN AUTONOMOUS CREW. TO BE USEFUL UNDER THESE CONDITIONS, A DECISION SUPPORT TOOL WOULD NEED TO BE ABLE HANDLE A WIDE VARIETY OF PROBLEMS, SOME OF WHICH MIGHT NOT HAVE BEEN ANTICIPATED DURING ITS DEVELOPMENT.  THE TOOLS WOULD NEED TO BE ABLE TO COMPENSATE FOR KNOWN HUMAN CONSTRAINTS (E.G., LIMITED SHORT TERM AND LONG TERM MEMORY) AND DECISION BIASES (E.G., FRAMING EFFECTS, RELIANCE OF SUB-OPTIMAL HEURISTICS) WITHOUT CAUSING NEW PROBLEMS.  IN PARTICULAR, IT SHOULD NOT INTERFERE WITH THE CREW ABILITY TO IDENTIFY AND SOLVE PROBLEMS THAT THE SYSTEM CANNOT HANDLE PROPERLY.  IT SHOULD ALSO NOT BE SO INTRUSIVE AND CUMBERSOME THAT IT IS ABANDONED.

Description: A linear mode HgCdT electron-initiated avalanche photodiode (EAPD) capable of 1570nm photon detection efficiency (PDE) at >10 MHz will be developed. The Phase I design, is based on vertical-charge-transport HgCdTe EAPDs recently fabricated using a 3.8-micron wavelength cutoff HgCdTe alloys, which showed excellent 1570nm response, nearly noiseless gain, >650, and GHz bandwidth operation at thermoelectric temperatures. During Phase I, we will perform tradeoff analysis to determine the optimal HgCdTe alloy composition for the application. As example, shortening the cutoff wavelength (e.g. 2-microns) will result in a HgCdTe alloy with reduce dark current and/or higher temperature operation, but will result in a concomitant gain reduction and thereby compromise PDE. In Phase I, we will develop the optimal HgCdTe LPE alloy and we will also modifying our low noise amplifiers (LNA) to match the higher capacitance of the HgCdTe APD, so optimal PDE is achieved. We will deliver at least one packaged part to NASA. During Phase II, we will further optimize the detector, integrate it with the LNA, and deliver a fully-functional, single photon counting module to NASA.
