Description: It has been suggested that aerosols entrained by deep convection might lead to smaller cirrus particles which would in turn affect the radiation and water vapor budget of the tropical tropopause. We propose to investigate this proposed mechanism using observations from MLS (Aura) carbon monoxide to identify polluted convective events and MODIS (Aqua) aerosol property and cloud ice particle size data to differentiate the anvils of polluted convection and non-polluted cumulonimbus complexes. Both the MLS and MODIS instruments are part of the A-Train and hence the observations are taken within a few minutes of each other. We will extend the study with availability of CALIPSO lidar and CloudSat cloud radar data in 2007 and HIRDLS cloud data when available - these data sets will improve the estimates of the cloud and aerosol layer heights and our screening process. This proposal also includes an important cloud, cirrus and aerosol modeling component. We intend to use the Goddard cloud, cirrus, and aerosol models to guide the data analysis and simulate aerosol-cloud impact mechanisms. We propose to also use appropriate field campaign data from Aura validation experiments in '06 and '08 to validate our data analysis and model studies.

Description: DIRK IWATA-REUYL / PORTLAND STATE UNIVERSITY MOLECULAR AND GENETIC INVESTIGATIONS OF RNA STABILITY IN HYPERTHERMOPHILIC ARCHAEA RNA OCCUPIES A CENTRAL ROLE IN THE METABOLISM OF EXTANT ORGANISMS, AS WELL AS BEING IMPLICATED AS THE ORIGINAL GENETIC AND CATALYTIC MACROMOLECULE AS FORMALIZED IN THE RNA WORLD HYPOTHESIS. HOWEVER, RNA IS BOTH STRUCTURALLY AND CHEMICALLY UNSTABLE, READILY DENATURING AT HIGH TEMPERATURES. IN SPITE OF THIS INHERENT INSTABILITY, THE EXISTENCE OF HYPERTHERMOPHILIC ORGANISMS DEMONSTRATES THAT SOLUTIONS TO THE RNA STABILITY PROBLEM HAVE BEEN FOUND. INDEED, IN CONTRAST TO THE TRANSFER RNA (TRNA) FROM MESOPHILIC MICROORGANISMS, TRNA FROM THERMOPHILIC ORGANISMS POSSESS REMARKABLE THERMAL STABILITY, A PROPERTY HYPOTHESIZED TO BE A CONSEQUENCE PRINCIPALLY OF CHEMICAL MODIFICATION AT SPECIFIC POSITIONS IN THE RNA. BECAUSE TRNA REQUIRES A WELL-DEFINED STRUCTURE FOR ITS BIOLOGICAL ACTIVITY, IT PRESENTS AN IDEAL SYSTEM IN WHICH TO EXPLORE CONTEMPORARY SOLUTIONS TO THE PROBLEM OF RNA STABILITY, AND TO TEST MECHANISMS OF IMPARTING THERMAL STABILITY POTENTIALLY AVAILABLE TO PRIMITIVE ORGANISMS OR PRIMORDIAL RNA. THE OBJECTIVE OF OUR PROPOSED RESEARCH IS TO TEST THE HYPOTHESIS THAT ARCHAEOSINE, A HYPERMODIFIED NUCLEOSIDE UBIQUITOUS TO THE TRNA OF THE ARCHAEA, IS ESSENTIAL TO THE STRUCTURAL STABILITY OF TRNA IN EXTANT ARCHAEAL HYPERTHERMOPHILES. SPECIFICALLY WE PLAN: 1) TO DETERMINE IF ARCHAEOSINE IMPARTS SIGNIFICANT STRUCTURAL STABILITY TO OTHERWISE THERMALLY UNSTABLE TRNA, 2) TO DETERMINE IF STRUCTURAL ANALOGS OF ARCHAEOSINE KNOWN TO BE SYNTHESIZED UNDER PUTATIVE PREBIOTIC CONDITIONS ARE CAPABLE OF IMPARTING THERMAL STABILITY TO OTHERWISE THERMALLY UNSTABLE TRNA, AND 3) TO INVESTIGATE THE ROLE OF ARCHAEOSINE IN VIVO IN SULFOLOBUS SOLFATARICUS, A HYPERTHERMOPHILIC ARCHAEON. THE GOALS OF THIS COLLABORATIVE PROPOSAL BUILD ON THE COMPLEMENTARY STRENGTHS OF THE PI (A CHEMIST/BIOCHEMIST) AND CO-PI (A MOLECULAR BIOLOGIST/VIROLOGIST). THE PROPOSED WORK DIRECTLY ADDRESSES NASA S INTEREST IN UNDERSTANDING THE ORIGIN AND EVOLUTION OF LIFE IN THE UNIVERSE. IN PARTICULAR, OUR WORK ADDRESSES ISSUES RELATING TO THE NATURE OF THE MOST PRIMITIVE ORGANISMS AND THE ENVIRONMENT IN WHICH THEY EVOLVED. WHETHER THE ENVIRONMENT OF THE EARLY EARTH WAS HOT OR ORGANISMS MOVED INTO HOT ENVIRONMENTS AS A CONSEQUENCE OF NICHE EXPANSION, ELUCIDATING THE FACTORS RESPONSIBLE FOR RNA STABILITY OF EXTANT ORGANISMS INHABITING HYDROTHERMAL ENVIRONMENTS IS CENTRAL TO UNDERSTANDING THE STRUCTURAL REQUIREMENTS FACED BY PRIMITIVE ORGANISMS IN THE EARLY HISTORY OF THE EARTH, AS WELL AS THE REPLICATING SYSTEMS THAT PREDATED THE EMERGENCE OF LIFE ON EARTH IN THE PUTATIVE RNA WORLD.

Description: Oceanic biophysical provinces provide a remarkably useful platform to describe physical and biochemical processes; their objective establishment is critical for comparative analyses of ecosystem dynamics and for understanding biotic resiliency of different regions to global climate change. By utilizing a suite of available satellite products, we will establish dynamic biophysical provinces in the North Pacific using novel methodology that is especially appropriate for objective mapping of potentially non-linear interactions between processes. By validating these provinces with alternative methods and in situ data, we will provide the scientific community with a means of improved monitoring of oceanographic biophysical dynamics, a more precise understanding of the sources of ecological resiliency and therefore improved understanding of the biotic component of carbon cycling, and an objective, quantitative basis by which to spatially extrapolate data from local experiments and long-term time series.

Description: Antarctic Peninsula ice shelves are changing rapidly through a combination of iceberg calving and basal melt. The loss of complete ice shelves such as Larsen-A (1995) and Larsen-B (2002) has been accompanied by dramatic acceleration of the ice streams feeding these embayments, providing a contribution to global sea level change. These are other nearby rapidly changing shelves provide an environment for testing modeis of ocean impact on the evolution of the greater Antarctic ice sheet, in particular in the west Antarctic sector. This research will improve our understanding of the ocean-ice system and will enhance our ability to predict ice shelf changes; consequently, it will help broaden NASA's commitment to the International Polar Year (2007-2009) as well as contribute to NASA's directives for improving understanding and predictability of the Earthgs cryosphere.

Description: SELECTION IN VITRO OF A RIBONUCLEOTIDE REDUCTASE RIBOZYME The RNA World hypothesis describes a time when RNA served as both the catalytic and genomic molecules for primitive organisms. As extant organisms contain three classes of informational macromolecules (DNA, RNA, and protein), the question of which came next, DNA or protein, remains. This research proposed here attempts to find a ribonucleotide reductase ribozyme (RRR or R3), which would be analogous to known protein ribonucleotide reductase enzymes, by in vitro selection. An initial population of random molecules will be incubated under reducing conditions. This population will then be subjected to a nucleotide-by-nucleotide search using site-specific RNase H cleavage to check for the presence of reduced nucleotides at multiple sites within each molecule in the RNA population. Once a subclass of active R3 molecules has been identified, conventional in vitro selection techniques will be nsed to isolate the fastest and most active variants. This selection methodology allows for a very rigorous and thorough search for R3s. If RNA is capable of catalyzing the reduction of RNA to DNA, this selection should find it. However, if the selection fails to identify a successful R3, it argues strongly that proteins preceded DNA in the course of evolving from an RNA-only system to one containing DNA, RNA and proteins. In either case, the results of this work will vastly improve our understanding of the pathway of the evolution of life on the Earth.

Description: INVESTIGATIONS OF AEROSOL-CLOUD INTERACTIONS FROM CALIPSO AND A-TRAIN OBSERVATIONS STRATEGIES USED TO EMPIRICALLY DERIVE THE AEROSOL INDIRECT RADIATIVE FORCING FROM SPACE-HOME OBSERVATIONS INVARIABLY SEEK REGIONAL SCALE CORRELATIONS BETWEEN RETRIEVED AEROSOL AND CLOUD PROPERTIES TO DETERMINE THE RESPONSE OF CLOUDS TO CHANGES IN AEROSOL BURDENS. THROUGH SUCH CORRELATIONS SEVERAL STUDIES HAVE SHOWN THAT DROPLET RADII DECREASE AND CLOUD VISIBLE OPTICAL DEPTHS AND CLOUD COVER INCREASE AS AEROSOL OPTICAL DEPTHS INCREASE. THESE TRENDS ARE CONSISTENT WITH THOSE EXPECTED FOR THE AEROSOL INDIRECT RADIATIVE FORCING. SUCH TRENDS, HOWEVER, MAY BE DUE IN PART TO PHYSICAL PROCESSES THAT HAVE NO RELATIONSHIP TO THE EFFECTS OF AEROSOLS ON CLOUDS AND IN PART TO BIASES IN THE CLOUD PROPERTIES DERIVED USING THRESHOLD METHODS. FOR EXAMPLE, THE ENHANCEMENT IN AEROSOL BURDEN IN CLOUDY REGIONS COULD BE DUE TO 1) INCREASES IN THE CLOUD CONTAMINATION OF AEROSOL RETRIEVALS PERFORMED IN THE VICINITY OF CLOUDS, 2) ENHANCEMENTS IN THE APPARENT REFLECTIVITIES OF CLOUD-FREE COLUMNS THAT ARISE FROM THE SCATTERING OF SUNLIGHT THAT WAS REFLECTED BY NEARBY CLOUDS, AND 3) THE GROWTH OF AEROSOL PARTICLES IN THE HUMID CLOUD  ENVIRONMENT OR BY CLOUD PROCESSING WHICH INCREASES THE MASS OF THE RESIDUAL PARTICLES WHEN DROPLETS EVAPORATE. HERE CALIPSO AND A-TRAIN OBSERVATIONS, PRIMARILY MODIS RADIANCE, AEROSOL, AND CLOUD PRODUCTS, WILL BE USED TO INVESTIGATE DIFFERENCES IN THE MODIS AND CALIPSO AEROSOL PROPERTIES IN THE VICINITY OF THE CLOUDS. DIFFERENCES IN DETECTION STRATEGIES AND SENSITIVITIES OF THE PASSIVE (MODIS) AND ACTIVE (CALIOP) SENSORS, SHOULD PROVIDE INSIGHT INTO THE DIFFERENT ROLES PLAYED BY CLOUD CONTAMINATION, ENHANCED ILLUMINATION, AND THE RESPONSE OF PARTICLES TO THE CLOUD ENVIRONMENT. IN ADDITION, A PARTLY CLOUDY IMAGER PIXEL RETRIEVAL WILL BE USED TO STUDY THE RESPONSE OF CLOUDS TO CHANGES IN AEROSOL LOADING. THE PARTLY CLOUDY IMAGER PIXEL RETRIEVALS REDUCE THE POTENTIAL FOR BIASES THAT ARE POSSIBLE IN THE MODIS MOD06 CLOUD PRODUCT WHICH PRODUCE TRENDS IN CLOUD OPTICAL DEPTHS AND DROPLET EFFECTIVE RADII THAT COUPLED WITH THE RISE IN AEROSOL OPTICAL DEPTH WITH INCREASING CLOUD COVER COULD, ON THEIR OWN, BE MISTAKEN FOR THE INDIRECT EFFECT OF AEROSOLS.

Description: The origins of life required the advent of biological information. Such information could exist in a pool of short linear polymers, such as RNA oligomers synthesized abiotically. We propose to demonstrate that self-replicating RNA molecules can emerge spontaneously via the aggregation of a collectively autocatalytic set found within a pool of random RNA oligomers, each 40 nucleotides or less in length. This would be an empirical demonstration of the ideas proposed by Stuart Kauffman regarding emergence of order from chaos. Our approach is to exploit the intrinsic ability of some RNAs to recombine other RNAs to produce new combinations of sequences. In publications and preliminary data we have demonstrated that the Azoarcus ribozyme, 198 nucleotides in length, can be fragmented into four pieces that can spontaneously self-assemble into a covalently-contiguous molecule through recombination reactions. These assemblages can self-replicate because they can autocatalytically catalyze further self-assembly reactions. In the current proposal we will extend this methodology by exploring whether smaller and more random fragments in a pool of oligomers can accomplish the same task. We propose three sets experiments to achieve this goal. The first is to break the current Azoarcus RNA system into five or more fragments, such that the average fragment length drops below 40 nucleotides. The second is to select for a shorter version of the Azoarcus ribozyme by deleting large sections of the molecule, targeting a recombinase that is less than 140 nucleotides. The third is to use a novel type of in vitro selection, termed autocatalytic enrichment selection, to bring a pool of RNA oligomers which does not demonstrate detectable self-assembly back across a complexity threshold to the point where it does self-assemble and self-replicate. We can accomplish these experiments inexpensively with graduate and undergraduate students at Portland State University in three years time

Description: EXGKS: EXTRAGALACTIC KNOWLEDGE SYSTEM This is a modest project to explore techniques and tools to enhance the final stages of data analysis prior to publication. There is a growing gap between the size of ever increasing data archives and the capability of individual researchers to absorb and compare these datasets. Our goal is to begin the development of a knowledge framework through a three prong program; 1) establish a data system that allows for flexible use, in our case we will be adopting an XML format that introduces several unique features when combined with the Python interpretive language, 2) develop a system of network data retrieval that is independent of the features of the data archive (e.g. ranging from password protected websites to simple sftp areas) and 3) present these new features and techniques in a flexible, yet sophisticated GUI framework that the researcher can easily define and expand to meet their own needs. Our plans are novel, but realistic. We will propose some innovative ideas, and applied them to concrete tools as both a proof of concept to our ideas and as examples for other developers. This project has the larger goal of enhancing the development of tools to exploit the data in NASA archives. The framework, as it develops, will enable Virtual Observatory capability to existing applications, provide new techniques to combining data and literature searches and offer a flexible, user designed GUI system in which to explore these new ideas. Our immediate goal is to provide the community with three testbed tools to outline our XkIL procedures, script browsing and GC'I construction. These prototypes enable inclusion of VO-like power to data reduction and final analysis, new types of viewers to expand individual resources and allow wider science goals from our space mission datasets.

Description: A COMPREHENSIVE MODEL FOR THE PREDICTION OF SUPERSONIC JET NOISE This proposal addresses two specific areas of interest in the Noise Prediction and Modeling Objective (A.4.3.1) NASA Supersonics Project. These are the extension of the capability of existing CFD-based analysis tools to include the prediction of noise from supersonic jets and the development of statistical broadband shock-associated noise models to use RANS-based CFD input to predict broadband shock noise from generic, non-axisymmetric, hot and dual-stream jet plumes. The focus is a stochastic prediction scheme for broadband shock-associated noise. The addition of simulations of turbulent mixing noise will result in the development of a comprehensive supersonic jet noise prediction model. The broadband shock-associated noise prediction scheme will require only the nozzle geometry and jet operating conditions to be specified and is applicable to non-axisymmetric, dual-stream, heated supersonic jets. The average properties of the jet flow will be predicted using a RANS-CFD code. The Wind US code has been selected because of its previous extensive use in the prediction of jet flows from nozzles for which both flow and acoustic experiments have been conducted. The code will provide the time average velocity and temperature distribution, including the shock structure for jets operating at off-design conditions. In addition, the local characteristic velocity, length and time scales of the turbulence can be computed. This information will be used in a new model for broadband shock-associated noise. In preliminary analysis it can be shown how the broadband shock-associated noise is related to an integral of the product of the turbulent velocity fluctuations and the perturbations in pressure associated with the jets shock cell structure. The integral involves local regions of the flow in the jet shear layer where this product exceeds a value that will be determined in the research. The radiated noise also depends on the correlation of the turbulent fluctuations between the locations where the shock cells intersect the jet shear layer and the convection velocity of the turbulence. These properties will be modeled on the basis of turbulence measurements, which are a key part of the experimental component of the research program. The turbulent mixing noise will be predicted based on an acoustic analogy using the same RANS-CFD simulations. This will provide the fine-scale turbulent mixing noise. The same approach cannot predict the large-scale turbulent mixing noise which radiates in directions close to the jet downstream axis, which also includes the peak noise radiation direction. An existing LES-based noise prediction code will be used in selected cases to provide this noise component. The turbulence measurements will be made in small scale jets using an Optical Deflectometer. This instrument measures the instantaneous fluctuations in the density gradient. It can measure two point space-time cross correlations of the turbulent fluctuations. These measurements will provide the first extensive measurements of turbulence statistics in supersonic shock-containing flows and they will be the basis for the models of these properties required in the noise prediction scheme. In addition, the average flow properties will be measured to provide a validation database for the RANS-CFD simulations. Noise measurements will be made at moderate scale in the Boeing Low Speed Aeroacoustic Facility. These data, which will establish a high quality noise database in their own right, will be used to validate the noise predictions. A technique for separating the shock-associated noise from the jet mixing noise will be used to validate the separate predictions of the noise radiation by these different sources. The outcome of the proposed research will be a validated comprehensive noise prediction method for supersonic jets based on a RANS-CFD simulation of the jet flow field.

Description: Spacecraft System Design Using Grid Computing and Evolvable Systems Technology NASA has a multitude of difficult design and optimization problems that challenge conventional approaches. These cutting-edge space applications continue to require ever-better performance, new capabilities, and reduced costs, all while the design complexity and difficulty are skyrocketing. The current generation of automated design tools is vital in managing the complexity explosion however they fall short when it comes to finding creative and new types of solutions that can solve design problems more effectively than solutions constrained by traditional methods. Evolutionary Design methods hold great promise that they can cope with both the complexity and creativity issues needed to future NASA applications. In this proposal, we show an example of Evolutionary Design successfully solving very challenging NASA antenna design problems, with a focus on SELGA, an S-band evolved low-gain antenna. We posit that such a demonstration is just the very beginning of a research breakthrough that will revolutionaize optimization and design in the future. Because these techniques require vast amounts of computer processing, we intend to use a grid-computing system to enable the widespread use of powerful Evolvable Systems methods across NASA applications.

Description: An important measurable property of the Universe is its dust content. The amount and distribution of dust not only reveal the details of dominant astrophysical processes and galactic evolution, but also impact many measurements in observational cosmology, since dust attenuates background sources. The cosmological effects of dust are clearly observed, but quantitative measurements of it could be improved significantly. Observations indicate that the dust resides in regions which contain large amounts of neutral hydrogen gas. We have developed a method to identify cosmological sightlines which intercept large columns of neutral hydrogen gas using SDSS quasar absorption spectra. So far we have analyzed -41,400 quasar sightlines and found -14,200 MgII absorption-line systems along -10,800 sightlines. A subset of these MgII absorption-line systems trace large columns of neutral hydrogen gas. A substantial fraction of these quasars are detected by GALEX and 2MASS. We propose to use these detections to construct UV to IR composite spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of quasars with and without absorption. Our analysis of the composite SEDs, derived for different subsamples, will provide cosmological measurements of the amount and distribution of dust in the Universe over the redshift interval 0.4 < z < 2.2.

Description: Measuring the Ultrahard X-Ray Emission of a Local Population of Seyfert 2S The majority of accretion onto supermassive black holes in the local Universe occurs in obscured Seyferts. At moderate redshifts, the optical narrow emission-lines used to identify Seyfert 2s become difficult to isolate from the host galaxy's emission, resulting in an underestimate of the numbers of Seyfert 2s. Description: Simulation technology plays an important role in rocket engine test facility design and development by assessing risks, identifying failure modes and predicting anomalous behavior of critical systems. Advanced numerical tools assume greater significance in supporting testing and design of high altitude testing facilities because of the greater inter-dependence and synergy in the functioning of the different sub-systems. This is especially true for J2-X testing because of a challenging operating envelope linked to variable throttle conditions at relatively low chamber pressures. Facility designs require a complex network of diffuser ducts, steam ejector trains, fast operating valves, spray nozzles and flow diverters that need to be characterized for steady state performance. More importantly, integrated facility designs will also have to be evaluated for startup/shutdown transients that can trigger engine unstart modes leading to catastrophic failure. The proposed innovation expands on the multi-element unstructured CFD which has been validated for complex valve/feed systems and high pressure propellant delivery systems used in engine and component test stands at NASA SSC. The focus here will be on extending this capability to include advanced models for supersonic diffuser design, steam ejector performance, spray nozzle cooling efficiency, plume aspiration dynamics and isolation valve operation.

Description: Designing multi-color imaging surveys for precision cosmology A number of multi-color imaging surveys have been planned with space and ground-based telescopes to measure the properties of the dark energy. The use of photometric redshifts in weak lensing, baryon oscillations and other cosmological measurements is a key component of these dark energy missions. However there is no systematic study that propagates realistic photo-z errors to cosmological measurements, and uses the results to optimize imaging survey parameters. We propose to conduct a set of investigations into the theory and applications of photometric redshift techniques which will enable JDEM and precursor ground-based missions to constrain dark energy via weak lensing and baryon oscillation measurements. These will be based on a Monte-Carlo framework for photo-z's and Fisher matrix calculations for cosmology, and will account for the full probability distribution of the photo-z's including scatter and the fraction of catastrophic errors. We will carry out trade-off studies of filters, exposure time and sky coverage to optimize the design of imaging surveys. Particular attention will be paid to the unique capabilities of space-based imaging due to the use of infra-red filters, and to the identification of redshift ranges and galaxy types that are promising for cosmology. Our software will be made available for survey design and other applications.

Description: ADVANCED STATISTICAL TECHNIQUES FOR STUDYING THE CMB TEMPERATURE AND POLARIZATION FIELDS WITH WMAP DATA Observations of the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) have provided a wealth of information about the origin and evolution of our universe. Analysis of WMAP data is a complex task that typically involves the parametric modeling of the CME and non-CMB effects (such as instrumental characteristics and foregrounds). Determining the sensitivity of statistical inferences to changes in these models is critical; for instance, the WMAP temperature sky maps exhibit anomalies that may indicate that standard inflationary cosmology is insufficient. But these anomalies might only signal the misspecification of nun-CMB effects. It is critical to distinguish between these alternatives, but the sheer amount of data and complexity of the models makes this difficult with traditional techniques. To attack this problem, we will develop and apply new, computationally efficient methods of nonparametric statistical analysis. Nonparametric methods are well established in the statistical literature and have the flexibility and accuracy to capture expected and unexpected model effects with reduced bias compared to parametric analyses. In this project, we will achieve the following three objectives. First, we will use nonparametric methods to study instrument characteristics (e.g., the autocovariance structure of the detector noise). We will make CMB sky maps from the WMAP three-year time-ordered data using software we developed to analyze the first-year data (Freeman et al. 2006, ApJ, 638,l). Second, we will estimate foreground emission (e.g., by simultaneously inferring the spatial distribution of emission and the cosmological parameters), which needs to be separated from the CMB for proper inferences to be made. Third, we will analyze the CMB to determine, e.g., the impact of possible non-Gaussianities and to generate statistical inferences for the temperature and polarization fields. We will apply our techniques to WMAP data, but our methods will be broadly applicable throughout astrophysics.

Description: PROBING SUPERMASSIVE BLACKHOLE FEEDING THROUGH AGN LUMINOSITY FUNCTION AND CLUSTERING PROPERTIES This investigation consists of two lines of analysis of the astrophysical archival data on the active galactic nucleus (AGN) activities, which is a probe of the accretion onto supermassive blackholes (SMBHs). As the first line, we plan to improve the determination on the luminosity function and its evolution of mainly X-ray selected active galactic nuclei (AGNs). This includes a critical comparisons of luminosity functions of soft X-ray, hard X-ray, nearby soft gamma-ray, optical and infrared selected AGNs. The correlations and selection effects of the surveys will be critically investigated. The second line is to investigate the clustering properties of the AGNs. The purpose is to investigate the environments of the AGN activity. The clustering investigations include auto-correlation function of AGNs as well as cross-correlation function of X-ray AGNs with optical and infrared selected galaxies. By this investigation, we aim to find the bias parameter, which is the contrast enhancement factor in the AGN clustering with respect to that of underlying mass. We plan to probe the typical mass of the "dark matter halo", in cold dark matter structure formation scenario, in which AGNs with various luminosities/types/redshifts reside and the typical lifetime of the AGN activity in these objects. The data we plan to use include X-ray sources in XMM-COSMOS (A03) correlated with large galaxy catalog from the COSMOS consortium and ROSAT All Sky-survey based AGN catalogs correlated with the Sion Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) catalogs.

Description: THE BIG BLUE BUMP IN ACTIVE GALACTIC NUCLEI It is a known fact that (almost) all galaxies harbor a supermassive black hole in their center. While most galaxies appear to be inactive, about l0% show activity in their center. Powered by accretion of surrounding matter onto the central black hole these Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are one of the must luminous sources in the Universe. There are several question that we want to answer with this proposal: 1) How do black holes in Active Galactic Nuclei evolve? 2) Are there different phases in the evolution of an AGN? How long does the AGN activity last? How do measurements of the low-redshift Universe relate to high-redshift quasars at the early phases of the Universe? In order to answer these fundamental questions the knowledge of the bolometric luminosity is the key parameter. The most energetic part of the spectral energy distribution (SED) of AGN is the Big-Blue-Bump emission (BBB) which stretches from the optical/UV part of the spectrum to the soft X-ray regime. In this part of the SED in AGN most of the bolometric luminosity is deposited . The knowledge of the bolometric luminosity is therefore critical for estimating the Eddington ratio $L/L-{ m Edd}$ which seems to he the parameter that drives most observed properties in AGN (e.g. Sulentic et al. 2000, Boroson 2002, Grupe 2004). Unfortunately most of this BBB emission, especially where the BBB peaks in the extreme W, is unobservable to us because of interstellar absorption in our Galaxy. Due to their strong variability, in the past studies of the BBB of AGN were hampered by the lack of simultaneity between the optical/UV and X-ray observations. However, which the launch of the multi-wavelengths observatories XMM and Swift we have the tools now to approach this research. The plan of this proposal is to make use our ongoing AGN observing program with swift and of already existing data from the XMM public archive. Once we have enough low redshift source to have good statistics to reliably measure the relations between the strength of the BBB, meaning the bolometric luminosity, and the W and X-ray spectral slopes, we can apply this knowledge to high redshift quasars where we can only measure the W slope, but not the soft X-ray spectral slope because this part of the spectrum is due to their redshifts shifted out of the observable window. The key objects in our study are Narrow Line Seyfert 1 galaxies which are a subclass of Seyfert 1s that exhibit extreme optical and X-ray properties. They are also objects in the local Universe in which we can still observe rapidly growing black holes. How black holes in AGN evolve depends strongly on their accretion rate. This accretion rate is a function of the Eddington ratio L/Ledd, one of the parameters we intend to measure. The Eddington ratio represents also different stages of the development of an AGN. Description: Astrophysics of Dense Stellar Systems Physical interactions and collisions in dense stellar systems, such as galactic nuclei and compact star clusters, may significantly alter the properties of the stars, binary systems, and compact objects these systems contain. We propose to study the structure and evolution of dense stellar systems and the role played by stellar interactions in making these extreme environments efficient factories for the creation of "exotic" astrophysical objects--X-ray sources, millisecond pulsars, ultracompact binaries, supermassive stars, and intermediate-mass black holes. We will perform realistic, high-resolution N-body simulations of the dynamics and evolution of these systems, combining direct integration of all stars in the cluster with self-consistent treatments of external tidal fields and dynamical friction. In addition, the evolution of stars and binaries will be followed in detail and fully integrated into the simulations. The central computational challenge in support of our astrophysical goals will be the design and inplementation of modular software tools, combining many independent physics modules, that run efficiently on parallel platforms accelerated by special-purpose hardware. Initial conditions for our simulations will be chosen to model specific systems of interest, including the central parsec of our Galaxy, and the Arches and Quintuplet clusters within a few tens of parsecs of the Galactic center. Special emphasis will be placed on studies of the initial mass function and mass segregation, the population of primordial binaries and multiples, the formation of white-dwarf binaries and X-ray sources, the inward transport of stellar remnants and merger products to the Galactic center and, for the first time, self-consistent treatment of intracluster gas. The results of our simulation will be compared directly with optical, infrared, and X-ray observations of real clusters. Specific astrophysical problems to be addressed include: dynamics of single and binary black holes in galactic nuclei; collisional formation of supermassive stars and intermediate-mass black holes; effects of environment on the properties of compact binaries and the progenitors of gamma-ray bursts and type Ia supernovae; and the likely properties of gravitational radiation sources in these regions.

Description: The proposed research addresses the issues of real-time fault detection&isolation (FDI) and degradation monitoring in aircraft propulsion systems. The objective is to enhance aircraft safety and performance and significantly reduce the risk of engine failures. The challenge is to detect and identify the incipient faults in critical components, which are not directly observable from the available sensor data. The research efforts will focus on development of algorithms and real-time software for engine health assessment in the discrete-event setting. The decision algorithms will follow a two-tier hierarchical structure for risk reduction and will be based on the information derived from analytical models of engine dynamics and time series data of available sensors. Engine FDI algorithms, based on Symbolic Dynamic Filtering (SDF), will be executed at the lower tier. The propulsion system at the upper tier will assess the health status, perform load reconfiguration of individual engines, and interface with the flight system. The algorithms and software will be validated on a test bed that has been constructed in the laboratories of Penn State under research grants from NASA GRC. The test bed is built upon the NASA MAPSS model and a real-time model of a generic turbofan engine with similar complexity and details. The test bed is capable of real-time anomaly detection, event discrimination, and health management of the engine systems under different operational scenarios. A multi-engine propulsion system model will be integrated with the AIAA flight model for health monitoring under dynamically varying flight conditions, including asymmetric health states for engines and differential thrust situations. Anticipated outcomes of the proposed research include model -based and data-driven algorithms and validated real-time software for: (i) engine component FDI and engine health status assessment, and (ii) propulsion level decision-making for engine load reconfiguration.

Description: PERFORMANCE STUDIES OF THE EJECTOR MODE OF AN UNSTEADY PULSE DETONATION RBCC ENGINE A benchmark study is proposed to demonstrate and understand the increased propulsive performance for the ejector mode of a pulse detonation rocket-based combined cycle engine (PD-RBCC). The proposed study responds to the Propulsion Topic of the Hypersonics Project in the Fundamental Aeronautics Program and addresses this program#s goal of conducting foundational research to further our fundamental understanding of the underlying physics and our ability to model that physics. The foundational experimental database that results can then be leveraged by NASA and industry to develop technologies and analytical tools focused on discipline-based-solutions. RBCC engines involve four stages: 1) an ejector mode in which a rocket engine, in the present case a pulse detonation rocket engine (PDRE), induces the air flow for the combustor up to a Mach number of approximately three; 2) the ejector mode is followed by a ramjet mode in which the PDRE is shut off; 3) the ramjet mode is followed by a scramjet mode to a Mach number between 10 and 12; and, finally, 4) the air inlet is closed and an all rocket mode is used to achieve orbit. The RBBC ejector mode is selected for study because RBCC cycle analysis has shown it to be the most critical mode in terms of achieving overall high engine performance. These proposed studies will be conducted using the existing RBCC engine previously developed under NASA support. This facility allows measurements of the thrust, and pressure and wall heat flux profiles as a function of axial position. A direct connect air supply is available for testing up to approximately Mach 3. Experiments will be conducted over a range of inlet Mach number conditions, O/F ratios and will also examine sea level static conditions to assess the ejector performance under free jet conditions.

Description: WHERE IS THE TURBOPAUSE? INSTABILITIES, GENERATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF TURBULENCE IN THE 100-KM REGION This is a Co-I proposal under a lead proposal submitted by Gerald Lehmacher (PI, Clemson University). In the mesosphere and lower thermosphere, energy and momentum propagating from below are deposited via wave breaking, instabilities, and turbulence. The turbopause is the level where turbulence becomes less efficient than molecular diffusion. In the 90-110 km region, large-scale instabilities, overturning of density contours, wind shears, and adiabatic temperature gradients are common, but their relationship to turbulence is not clear. This investigation addresses the lifecycle of these instabilities: how they form, generate turbulence, and decay. The proposed work will consist of a series of four rockets launched from Poker Flat, Alaska, to study the evolution of an instability event in the 90-110 km region. The rockets are equipped with experiments that measure turbulence either by a chemical release or by instrumentation. In situ and ionization gauges and electron probes measure small-scale fluctuations in neutral and electron densities, which are also tracers for turbulence. When an upward-propagating gravity wave becomes large enough for the altitude temperature gradient to exceed the adiabatic lapse rate, the wave "breaks," and energy transfers through a cascade of spatial scales to eventually heat the region through viscous damping. This cascade of fluctuation scales can be seen in both neutral density and charged species variations, which serve as passive tracers of the neutral motion. The data analysis procedure involves spectral analysis to identify the transition between the inertial and viscous subranges, from which the energy dissipation rate can be determined. Technical support will be provided for the experimental investigations involving the two rocket systems with active electronics. This effort involves refining the design of the probes, building the data sections of the instrumented payloads, payload integration and preflight testing, conducting the field experiments, and reduction and analysis of the probe data.

Description: UV OBSERVATIONS OF NEARBY STAR-FORMING GALAXIES Understanding the star-formation history of the universe is key to our understanding of the formation and evolution of galaxies. Studying the star-formation of galaxies out to large redshifts is currently the focus of several large-scale programs using multiple NASA facilities, including GALEX. Interpreting the results of such efforts, however, requires a detailed understanding of the nature of star forming galaxies in the local universe. We propose an archival study based on a ground-based sample of H-alpha emission-line galaxies at z < 0.1 combined with existing ground-based optical and near-IR imaging (NOAO) and archival GALEX data centered on the NOAO Deep Wide-field Survey (NDWFS) Bootes field. This field also has archival radio, x-ray (Chandra), and mid and far-IR (Spitzer) observations. Combining the optical (H-alpha, and multiband photometry) data with FUV and NUV photometry from GALEX will allow us to better understand the nature of dust extinction in nearby star forming galaxies and improve estimates of star-formation rates in the high-redshift universe.

Description: THE UV DEPENDENCE OF THE PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF QUASARS We propose to determine how the physical characteristics of quasars, e.g, black hole mass, accretion rate, luminosity, and line strength, are related to their UV properties. Description: CONTROLS ON PALEOZOIC RATES OF TAXONOMIC EVOLUTION: ECOLOGY, ENVIRONMENT AND PRESERVATION Changes in global diversity through time are ultimately driven by variations in taxonomic origination and extinction rates. Because the origin and diversification of major taxonomic groups tends to be concentrated in certain intervals of time, such as those following mass extinctions, knowing how and why taxonomic rates vary can point to important factors leading to the evolution of advanced life.  As one example, there is growing evidence to suggest that the dynamics of origination and extinction have undergone secular changes over the course of the Phanerozoic. Extinction rates during the Paleozoic tend to be more diversity-dependent compared to origination rates, whereas in the post-Paleozoic origination and extinction rates tend to be equally diversity-dependent. Also, origination cohorts following mass extinctions in the post-Paleozoic tend to be longer lived than other cohorts; this intriguing pattern is not observed in the Paleozoic. Progress in understanding the relative roles of ecology, environment, and preservation in determining variation in taxonomic rates of evolution during the Phanerozoic is hampered by a lack of detailed comparative studies that apply the same analytical methods to multiple events. Without these uniform comparative studies, statements about similarities and differences in diversity trends and evolutionary rates among biotic events are not based on truly comparable data and methods and are difficult to interpret. We propose to investigate controls on Paleozoic taxonomic rates of origination and extinction in order to search for common patterns and causes. This new proposal will extend previously funded research on the Late Ordovician mass extinction to include two additional Paleozoic mass extinctions: the Late Devonian and the Middle Carboniferous. We will use the same methods developed in our previous work on the Late Ordovician mass extinction and recovery interval so that we can make robust comparisons of diversity patterns and taxonomic rates among all three events. We will use data from the Paleobiology Database for our analyses, which we will supplement with additional data from the literature. Much of our effort will go into vetting the data for taxonomic assignments, stratigraphic resolution, and paleoenvironmental determination. We will perform sample-standardized analyses of diversity and taxonomic rates at both regional and global scales for the Late Devonian and Middle Carboniferous events. Finally, through our comparative approach, we will determine shared patterns and inferred evolutionary processes among these three Paleozoic biotic events as well as identify unique characters of each. Our results will bear on the most important processes that govern diversity and variation in taxonomic rates for the Paleozoic, and more generally, for the Phanerozoic.

Description: TC4: GROUND BASED VALIDATION OF AURA AND CALIPSO WITH NATIVE AND SONDES The TC4 (Tropical Composition, Clouds and Climate Coupling) Field Experiment, scheduled for July 2007, focuses on two objectives:(1) elucidation of processes in which chemistry, clouds, temperature and dynamics interact in the tropical tropopause layer;(2)validation of CALIPSO aerosol and of Aura columns of ozone, among other gases. Expected outcomes of our research are (1) tropospheric ozone budgets from TC4 to be delivered to the Data Archive for comparison with models; (2) improved discrimination between stratosphere and troposphere for more accurate derivations of tropospheric ozone from Aura instruments. Description: BIOTIC RECOVERY AFTER MASS EXTINCTION: ECOLOGICAL RESPONSE TO THE CRETACEOUS/PALEOGENE BOUNDARY EVENT SUMMARY: Periods of recovery from mass extinctions provide a means to discover how complex ecosystems and biogeochemical systems are assembled. Many mass extinctions are followed by an "initial recovery phase" dominated by a few species, and characterized by drastically reduced productivity, reduced grazing and unusual biogeochemical conditions. This "boom-bust" community is succeeded by an "intermediate recovery phase" in which species dominance is reduced and productivity proxies such as surface-to-deep carbon isotope gradients are restored. A "final full recovery phase" may follow much later when species diversity is restored to pre-extinction levels, often long after basic ecosystem services and chemical cycling seem to have fully recovered. Major mass extinctions seem to 'reset' the global ecosystem back to a "Precambrian-like" microbially-dominated state which subsequently recovers by a combination of physical environmental change and re-evolution of extinguished ecologies. Consequentially, extinctions give us a window into the structural development of complex ecosystems. The dynamics of recovery events has received only cursory, and mostly descriptive, study except from a theoretical stand point. How does the interplay of extinction selectivity, species richness, the re-evolution of key ecological strategies, and restoration of coupling between plankton and benthos contribute to these stages of recovery? Here, we propose an integrated study to test the role of biological and environmental variables in the structure of the recovery from the Cretaceous-Paleogene mass extinction. Our project will be a detailed investigation of community structure during the Cretaceous/Paleogene boundary mass extinction and the subsequent recovery focusing on fossil groups that represent three different trophic levels, planktonic primary producers (calcareous nannoplankton), planktonic consumers (planktonic foraminifera), and benthic consumers (bivalves). Our investigations will reconstruct population structure for all three groups using detailed assemblage counts and analyses of evenness and diversity, as well as geochemical and biological proxies for biogeochemical evolution of oceanic ecosystems. We will compare the timing and rates of recovery of the different groups and major changes in population structure in an attempt to determine the environmental and ecological controls on speciation. Previous studies have focused largely on the 200-300 kyr interval on either side of the boundary, whereas our study will encompass the interval from just before the extinction to about 4 million years after the extinction, the time period in which most of the major structural features of marine ecosystems appear to stabilize. We will investigate sections across a spectrum of environments, ranging from the open ocean to the shelf, and we will use geochemical proxies for biological production to reconstruct the re-assembly of oceanic biogeochemical pathways and environmental structure. Our goal is to provide a unique, ecosystem-wide assessment of the Cretaceous/Paleocene boundary mass extinction and the subsequent recovery that should have broad relevance to the study of other major mass extinctions. We expect that the dynamics of the KIP recovery may also bear on the late Precambrian development of complex communities of multicellular organisms and the consequent stabilization of global climate and carbon cycle fluctuations.

Description: LOW BOOM SONIC BOOM COUPLED DIFRACTION AROUND AND TRANSMISSION THROUGH INDIVIDUAL AND AGGREGATED BUILDING STRUCTURES  Although many are coming to believe that outdoor acceptability is likely for new low-boom designs of small supersonic jets, It is completely unclear if overaii acceprabiiiry wiii occur because of indoor sonic boom. Hence, an essentiai technicai hurdie for overiand sonic boom acceptability is an understanding of indoor noise and vibration impact. The loading of sonic booms on buildings is NOT spatially or temporally uniform, and this loading must be determined before accurate indoor sonic boom models can be trusted. The purpose of this acoustical physics project is to fundamentally address the noise impact of low-boom sonic booms on building structures via time domain computational simulation. As a cooperative agreement with NASA the simulations will be coordinated with existing NASA experimental data sets and future field measurements. Description: Thermal Effects in Gas Lubricated Foil Journal Bearing Performance Gas lubricated foil journal bearings are a critical component technology for high speed, high performance rotor systems for which alternate bearing technologies such as rigid surface bearings or rolling element bearings are not suitable. With gas as the lubricant and a compliant foil structure, these bearings eliminate the need for oil based lubrication and operate at temperatures where oil will not function. Furthermore, the high rotor speeds and low friction that are possible with foil bearings allow for the design of compact systems with high power densities. Typical applications include oil free gas-turbine engines, turbo-chargers, and cryogenic turbo=compressors. The abilit"'j to understand and predict thermal effects in these bearings is critical to the design process. The efforts proposed here will produce analysis approaches and computer codes that will facilitate the design and development of high temperature gas lubricated foil journal bearings. These codes will be used to predict: (i) steady operating conditions such as load, pressures, gas film thickness, temperature distributions, and thermal dissipation, and (Ii) rotordynamic coefficients. A fully coupled thermal-fluid-structural model will be developed for high speed gas foil journal bearings. The top-foil will be treated as a three-dimensional shell. The sub-foil will be treated as a continuous structure. The Reynolds equation will be used to predict the gas film pressure distributions. The effects of viscous dissipation and pressure work will be included in a thermal transport analysis of the complete gas film. Thermal fluxes through the foil and into the journal will be included as will the effects of gas flow on thermal transport at the inlet, outlet, and sides of the gas film. Rotordynamic coefficients will be predicted by analytically perturbing the governing equations. The effects of Coulomb friction in the foil structure will be modeled as equivalent viscous friction.

Description: SWIFT OBSERVATIONS TO PROBE TYPE Ia SUPERNOVAE AS STANDARD CANDLES IN THE UV SUMMARY: We propose to observe young (pre-maximum luminosity), local (50 Mpc), Type Ia Supernovae with the Swift Ultra-Violet/Optical Telescope to determine whether they are standard candles in the UV portion of the spectrum. Swift's rapid response to targets-of-opportunity, such as supernovae, and capability to perform multi-fdter UV observations make it an ideal platform to perform such a study. An investigation of the UV brightness and colors of local Type Ia Supernovae will greatly enhance the astronomical community's ability to classify and understand high redshift supernovae observed in optical bands. This will allow the useable redshift range of supernovae to be expanded. In addition, understanding the intrinsic W colors better constrains the line of sight extinction as well as the shape of the UV extinction curve of host galaxies. To determine if Type Ia Supernovae are standard candles in the UV, the absolute magnitude in each UV filter will be calibrated by applying established optical standard candle relations and reddening indicators to the optical data obtained from the UVOT andfor ground based observatories This will permit us to compare the dispersion of the absolute magnitudes in the different UV bands and to search for correlations between the luminosity and the light curve shape. The work proposed will significantly expand our understanding of Type Ia Supernovae and increase our knowledge of cosmology. This work meets the criteria established in the solicitation of "rapid, time-critical muttiwavelength follow-up observations on unique astrophysical targets-of-opportunity." Description: PERFORMANCE STUDIES OF THE EJECTOR MODE OF AN UNSTEADY PULSE DETONATION RBCC ENGINE A benchmark study is proposed to demonstrate and understand the increased propulsive performance for the ejector mode of a pulse detonation rocket-based combined cycle engine (PD-RBCC). The proposed study responds to the Propulsion Topic of the Hypersonics Project in the Fundamental Aeronautics Program and addresses this program#s goal of conducting foundational research to further our fundamental understanding of the underlying physics and our ability to model that physics. The foundational experimental database that results can then be leveraged by NASA and industry to develop technologies and analytical tools focused on discipline-based-solutions. RBCC engines involve four stages: 1) an ejector mode in which a rocket engine, in the present case a pulse detonation rocket engine (PDRE), induces the air flow for the combustor up to a Mach number of approximately three; 2) the ejector mode is followed by a ramjet mode in which the PDRE is shut off; 3) the ramjet mode is followed by a scramjet mode to a Mach number between 10 and 12; and, finally, 4) the air inlet is closed and an all rocket mode is used to achieve orbit. The RBBC ejector mode is selected for study because RBCC cycle analysis has shown it to be the most critical mode in terms of achieving overall high engine performance. These proposed studies will be conducted using the existing RBCC engine previously developed under NASA support. This facility allows measurements of the thrust, and pressure and wall heat flux profiles as a function of axial position. A direct connect air supply is available for testing up to approximately Mach 3. Experiments will be conducted over a range of inlet Mach number conditions, O/F ratios and will also examine sea level static conditions to assess the ejector performance under free jet conditions.

Description: NASA's goal for the Southern Ocean (SO) Carbon Program is to resolve uncertainties in the size, dynamics, and global significance of the SO as a carbon sink as well as processes controlling this sink. The field component of this program (the GASEX-III cruise) aims to improve models of air-sea C02 flux and related remotely sensed data. Accurate measurement of photosynthesis from space can contribute to modeling sea-air flux of C02 at the basin scale because photosynthesis influences near-surface pC02. Photosynthesis rates have been modeled using phytoplankton pigment concentration (chlorophyll) but results have been spatially and temporally variable and the SO has often been treated as a special case. An alternative hypothesis proposed by Marra et al.(2007) suggests that photosynthesis is better modeled from phytoplankton absorption than from chlorophyll concentration. To test this hypothesis we propose to make coordinated measurements of phytoplankton spectral absorption and photosynthesis rates together while collecting in situ and satellite optical and bio-optical data during the GASEX-III cruise. Because all methods for measuring phytoplankton absorption used to date have limitations, the approach for this cruise is to compare multiple methods via separate proposals (from Marra, Subramaniam, Vaillancourt, Lee, and Hargreaves). The best combination of in situ measurements will then be used to estimate phytoplankton absorption for modeling photosynthesis rates from satellite data. The specific objectives of this proposal (Hargreaves) are to; I. Measure spectral absorption of phytoplankton in samples collected during the GASEX-III cruise using a Filter Pad Technique that incorporates both Transmittance and Reflectance (FPT-TR); 2. Develop and test (through rigorous on-site and laboratory calibrations) a universal equation for the Beta function that is required to interpret FPT data; 3. Compare two FPT-compatible methods for separating absorption into pigment and non-pigment components (bleaching versus alcohol extraction); 4. Improve detection of protective pigments that influence photosynthesis models by using the broad spectral response (225-800 nm) and rapid processing features of a new portable instrument (pFPT-TR) to analyze freshly Altered samples; 5. Improve estimates of the package effect in phytoplankton that suppresses absorption by pigments in living cells. One outcome of the proposed research is the rigorous comparison of methods for measuring phytoplankton spectral absorption that should improve future in situ and satellite Studies of phytoplankton ecology. A direct product of this study will be a unique data set of optical and bio-optical properties and phytoplankton photosynthesis rates for the Southern Ocean, providing an important test of a general model of phytoplankton productivity based on absorbance, and for the role of photosynthesis as a modulator of air-sea carbon flux.

Description: Planetary exploration has entered a new era in which our data-gathering capahility has outpaced our capacity for timely analysis. A combination of high-resolution instruments, spacecraft autonomy and mobility, and extended lifetimes is adding to a vast library of image and spectral data. The Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter is the latest following this trend, with HiRISE and MARC1 images providing unprecedented resolution of surface features. The catalog of images will continue to grow. The amount of resources devoted to analysis remains mostly static, so we require automated methods to improve image analysts' productivity. We address the analysis bottleneck in data analysis by creating methods to automatically generate maps from image and spectral data. Our method exploits recent advances in machine learning and object recognition. The system will learn to infer mapping rules statistically from "training" data in the form of existing geologic maps and registered orbital images. This is a natural application of existing learning-based methods of image segmentation and boundary detection. We will extend these methods to the orbital mapping domain with geologically-relevant descriptors like texture, spectral signatures, and surface features like boulders, craters, and dunes. The result is a system that uses features to predict the locations of geologic units and their boundaries. Automating geologic mapping will yield immediate benefits for the science community. It will dramatically improve the speed of image analysis which is limited by manual feature labeling. Maps offer fast summaries of gigapixel images that may include hundreds of thousands of features. These "draft" maps can be refined by human experts in less time than it would take to construct an entire map from scratch. Our mapping system will also permit new classes of spatial data mining. Exhaustive statistical analysis of image libraries can quantify trends and discover hidden correlations and anomalies. The system will yield summary statistics that improve geologists' ability to understand large datasets rapidly. Automated mapping can also improve the quality of data analysis: it can quickly examine thousands of images, perfectly, consistently and without fatigue. This reduces the need for redundant analysis for quality assurance. Automated mapmaking is not intended to replace human expertise; both human and automated image analysis play to different strengths. The human can offer expert geologic insight and authoritative segmentations of geologic units. The information system can examine many images quickly, quantify features with accuracy and consistency, and perform exhaustive statistical analysis to search for unexpected patterns and anomalies. In this sense the roles of the geologist and the automated mapping system are strongly complementary. The mapping system automates some of geologists' more arduous tasks, freeing them to focus on interpretation.

Description: Laser remote sensing and optical communication are two important technology areas with great potentials in improving human lives and impacting the global economy. While these two fields are distinct in their application areas and market place, they share many common technology elements such as lasers, detectors, modulators, and other photonic and semiconductor devices. Laser remote sensing finds major applications in areas as diverse as atmospheric studies and climate research, marine ecology, weather forecasting, space studies, air travel safety and efficiency, military target identification and countermeasure, to name a few, thus addressing significant societal needs. However, widespread utilization oflaser remote sensing systems (LIDARS) calls for more robust, efficient, and reliable systems, thus needing a multidisciplinary and concerted approach involving solid-state technology, materials science, electronic engineering, and photonics. The recent advances in optoelectronics made possible by unprecedented investment in optical communication can greatly benefit the laser remote sensing field. Optical or fiber-optic communication systems are revolutionizing the telecommunications and data transmission industries and playa major role in the advent ofthe Information Age. The need of high data rate transmissions continues to increase as the demand for the internet and cellular phones expands daily. This symposium provides a forum for gathering technologists from different technical backgrounds as well as scientists, system developers, and end-users representing both laser remote sensing and communication communities in order to facilitate new interactions and collaborations leading to advancement of both fields. This symposium will allow for identifying critical remote sensing and communication needs, reporting on latest progress in relevant advanced materials and devices, and discussing the application of modern optoelectronic technologies.

Description: SUPPORT OF THE 2007 GORDON RESEARCH CONFERENCE ON POLAR MARINE SCIENCE Grant support is requested as a contribution toward support of travel and registration costs for participants in the Sixth Gordon Research Conference on Polar Marine Science. The conference, scheduled to take place on 20-25 March 2007, will address the topic of An Interdisciplinary Look at Processes Over Multiple Scales of Variability. The conference will explore in detail the physical, chemical, and biological processes that dominate temporal and spatial scales ranging from the microscale to the global scale and from seconds to eons. For example, the session titled "Zooming in: Processes at the limits of detection" will include a talk on microscale physics (e.g. thin layer formation), another on microscale chemistry and biology of the sea ice, and a final talk on microbial diversity and its impact on ecology. Each of the other sessions will include the relevant physics, chemistry, and biology for a particular scale of variability. This new format is exciting because it allows us look at each scale from a variety of different vantage points and to better understand how the fundamental physical, biological, and chemical processes of that scale interact to produce the phenomena we measure. It also avoids the more typical mode of starting a meeting with physical oceanography, moving on to the biology and chemistry, and then ending with the charismatic megafauna or global modeling.  Gordon Research Conferences are unusual in that attendees are expected to attend all sessions and to actively participate in the discussions, which play a crucial role. A second unusual aspect of this conference is a bilateral treatment of the northern and southern high latitude oceans. The Arctic and the Antarctic are frequently treated in separate sessions at meetings. It has been our observation that many of the processes, interactions and impacts with which we are concerned are common to both polar regions. A bipolar focus helps lead us to new insights into these processes. Given the anticipated number of participants, the requested level of funding would allow us to cover more than 25% of the expenses for qualified participants who would otherwise be unable to attend, including young scientists, graduate students, and scientists from developing countries.

Description: Volatile elements appear to have played an important role in the generation of the most primitive lavas erupted on the Moon's surface. The association of a fire-fountain mechanism of eruption with condensation and enrichment of volatile elements on the surface of the lunar picritic volcanic glasses suggest the existence of a deep mantle source comparatively enriched in volatiles. The implication that follows this view is that, contrary to prevailing ideas, the bulk Moon is not uniformly depleted in highly volatile elements. Furthermore, the isotopic compositions of the picritic glasses and their correlated surface elements point to the existence of a reservoir that is not only volatile enriched, but also undifferentiated with trace element ratios close to chondritic values. The origin of such geochemical signatures has been a matter of debate, and solutions to these fundamental questions have important implications for the formation and evolution of the Moon. The composition and sources of lunar volatiles is one of the most important unsolved questions regarding the formation of the Moon, and the research described in this proposal aims at solving it. We propose to quantify the dissolved volatile contents (C02, H20, F, S and CI) in the picritic volcanic glasses by taking advantage of major advances in SIMS analytical techniques, which have improved the detection limits for H20, C, F, S and CI by more than 2 orders of magnitude compared with electron probe and earlier SIMS instrumentation (Hauri et al, 2002; Koga et al., 2003, Aubaud et al., 2004; Hauri et al., 2006). The final goal of this proposal is to estimate the abundance of these volatile species in the Moon mantle and their role during mantle melting, melt transport and eruption, while simultaneously filling holes in the geochemical data sets for lunar picritic glasses. The specific objectives are to: 1) establish whether or not there is any correlation between the volatile content and the major and trace element contents as well as the isotopic composition of the distinct varieties volcanic picritic glasses; 2) determine the extent of degassing and the variation in volatile content with the size of the glass beads, with radius within individual glass spherules, and with the depth in the sample cores; 3) use the obtained information to evaluate thermo-chemical models for in-situ redox reactions experienced by these picritic melts; 4) evaluate the proposed mechanism that triggered the fire-fountain eruptions; and 5) distinguish volcanic eruption in an extra-lunar vacuum from eruption in a volatile rich cloud, which will help us understand the dynamics of the eruption and post-depositional adsorption of volatiles on glass surfaces.

Description: CONFERENCE ON ATMOSPHERIC CHEMISTRY The Gordon Research Conference on Atmospheric Chemistry is held every two years, the next one being August 26-31, 2007 in Big Sky, Montana. This conference brings together academic, govemment and industrial scientists from around the world to discuss current problems in atmospheric chemistry. The planned program covers the breadth of topics in atmospheric chemistry, from the lower to the upper atmosphere, and polluted to remote regions. This year the Conference Chair is Dr. Douglas R. Worsnop (Aerodyne Research, Inc.) and the Vice-Chair is Prof Paul O. Wennberg (California Institute of Technology). The Vice-Chair will become the Chair for the 2009 conference and a new Vice-Chair will be elected by the attendees ofthe 2007 conference. We anticipate that the number of participants will be 150, a limit set by the Gordon Research Conference in order to promote the vigorous discussion and close interchange of ideas that is the hallmark of these conferences. Recent Atmospheric Chemistry Gordon Research conferences have been fully or over-subscribed and we expect the 2007 conference to be no exception. Ofthe 150 participants, 25 are recent Ph.D.'s who attend the ACCESS meeting held in the three days preceding the Gordon Conference. The fimds provided by the Gordon Research Conference are insufficient for the planned program; this is a request to supplement those funds as has been done for past GRC on Atmospheric Chemistry. The intellectual merit ofthe requested support will be significant. First, this research conference brings together a large number of atmospheric scientists who specialize in diverse research topics and who represent research in universities, govemment laboratories, and private research institutes. The formal presentations, the off-the-record exchanges from the floor, the discussions at the poster sessions, and the casual interactions outside the meeting room constitute a substantial exchange of information and ideas on topics of contemporary interest in atmospheric science. The collective features of this intellectual exchange are unique to the Gordon Research Conference format. The broader impact of this support will occur at a number of levels. The focused discussions and presentations on new thoughts and results in atmospheric science invariably influence the course of research for many individuals in the years following the conference. This influence within the scientific community reinforces or changes research directions, speeds the progress of research, and increases its efficiency; and, hence, creates a broad impact on the community.

Description: Reshaping Computer Engineering and Training for the Information Era While rapid advances in computer and networking technologies have dramatically changed the way of our life, the high education in our country has not fully exploited such technology advances in delivering high quality education and training. The limitations are reflected mainly in two aspects. First of all, traditional computer engineering (CE) curricula in most of universities in the country are CPU-centric (central processing unit) as it has been for the past few decades, ignoring the desperate need in the real world for computer engineers who have in depth knowledge of data communication and data storage technologies. Secondly, our engineering curriculum is still delivered in the traditional way in classrooms physically located on university campuses although high performance and low cost computers and the Internet are readily available. This is particularly true in computer engineering education and training where hands-on laboratory experiments and design projects are essential components of a CE curriculum. We propose here two innovative educational approaches to reshape the computer engineering education for the new information era.

Description: THE ROLE OF WATER IN THE EARLY FORMATION OF MARS: WET MAGMA OCEAN CRYSTALIZATION, THE GROWTH OF A WATER ATMOSPHERE, AND RETENTION OF WATER IN THE MANTLE Introduction: On Mars crater densities indicate that crust in both hemispheres dates from the early Noachian (e.g., Solomon et al., 1990; Frey et al., 2003)). Magnetized crustal provinces are further evidence for very ancient crustal formation (Acuna et al., 1999, Connerney et al., 1999). For Mars, our previous research indicates that the process of magma ocean fractional crystallization and subsequent mantle overturn is consistent with the formation of ancient crustal regions. On the Moon, magma ocean processes are thought to be responsible for the formation of the anorthitic highlands (Warren, 1985). If both the Martian and lunar earliest crusts were created by magma ocean processes, why does Mars lack a conspicuous plagioclase element? The Moon has likely been a completely dry body from its formation from heated material following the giant impact with the Earth (Hartman and David, 1975). Its shallow pressure range and dry composition both encourage plagioclase formation. Mars is known to have been a wetter planet in its past, and its high mantle iron content indicates more oxidizing initial conditions than were present on the Moon or Earth. Water in silicate melt suppresses plagioclase formation, and the higher pressure range of the Martian interior further limits its stability field. Water, then, may be one of the dominant variables in determining the outcomes of magma ocean crystallization and subsequent evolution of the terrestrial planets. Primary research areas: We propose to extend our magma ocean solidification and subsequent planetary evolution to the study of a wet magma ocean and its implications for creating an early steam atmosphere on Mars as well as a heterogeneously hydrous mantle with present-day implications for mantle viscosity, convective vigor, and magmatic source regions. These models make predications about the age and composition of the oldest Martian crust, about the compositions and ages of mantle reservoirs, and about the volumes and locations of water on the planet today. The proposed work should form an important link between theoretical modeling of early planetary formation and mission data from the planet today. Objectives: This proposal seeks funding for a three-year period, allowing work toward understanding the role of water in early planetary evolution that builds on the strong progress we have made to date (Elkins-Tanton et al., 2003; Elkins-Tanton and Parmentier, 2004). The three major proposed research areas are: 1. Applying models for magma ocean crystallization and overturn to a hydrous mantle composition, 2. Continuing work on the physics of crystallization of the magma ocean, and 3. Comparing predictions with surface and remote sensing data for Mars; and comparing predictions for Mars with those for other terrestrial planets, in particular, with the Earth and Moon.

Description: GEOLOGICAL MAPPING OF VENUS:  EARTH ARCHEAN COMPARISONS Venus and the Earth's Archean share many similarities in terms of geological features, structures, thermal conditions, and interpreted processes. To bring fresh insight to both fields, we have gathered a team of experts to undertake a synergistic examination of two key adjacent Venus quadrangles. Archean experts bring direct field mapping, structural, and sample analysis to the study of Venus; Venus experts bring knowledge of the global areal distribution of uneroded and contiguous units and structures, a perspective poorly preserved in the Archean record. The team identified the following key questions common to both the Archean and Venus: I) Crustal Thickening Environments and Processes: Over what range of environments does crustal thickening occur on Venus; what insight does this provide for the Archean? 2) Role of Diapirism: What are similarities/differences between coronae and diapiric structures on Venus and Archean basement-cored domes? 3) Nature and Origin of Deformation Belts: What is the geologic setting of Venus linear deformation belts; how do they compare to the Archean? 4) Origin and Context of Regional Plains: Do Archean komatiitic plains deposits bear similarities to the regional plains on Venus in terms of emplacement style and relationships? 5) Geodynamic Evolution: a) Archean-Venus: What insight does the Earth's Archean record provide to the nature and understanding of features, units and sequences on Venus? b) Venus-Archean: What insight does the local, regional and global geology of Venus provide into selecting among the geodynamic processes thought to have operated during Earth's Archean (e.g, vertical or lateral crustal accretion, mantle/crustal overturn, diapirism, flood basalts, crustal thickening)? We propose to address these questions through geologic mapping of Snegurochka Planitia (V-I) and Fortuna Tessera (V-2); the project will be accompanied by specific process studies and a synthesis describing key similarities, differences and insights in Venus/Archean comparisons for future use by both communities.

Description: INTEGRATED SPECTROSCOPY OF SYNTHETIC PYROXENES: TOOLS TO CHARACTERIZE IGNEOUS PROCESSES ON THE INNER PLANETS Pyroxene is one of the most common minerals in both evolved and undifferentiated solid bodies of the solar system, and has been observed remotely by telescopic and orbital measurements of the Moon, Mars, and several classes of asteroids. Laboratory studies of pyroxene spectra have shown that absorption features diagnostic of pyroxene in the visible, near- and mid-infrared are composition dependent. A challenge for remote analyses has been to rigorously quantify absorption properties in a manner that is directly linked to mineral chemistry and physics. We propose an integrated spectroscopic analysis of a set of well-characterized synthetic Ca-Fe-Mg pyroxenes from the visible through near-infrared to address the fundamental constraints of crystal structure on absorption properties. Our overall goal is to develop a quantitative understanding of how diagnostic absorptions of pyroxene spectra vary with chemical composition, site ordering, and exsolution. We propose to characterize the diagnostic electronic crystal field absorptions for high purity synthetic pyroxenes and quantitatively track their variations as a function of octahedral cation chemistry (Ca, Mg, Fe). Diagnostic spin-forbidden and spin-allowed crystal field absorption bands will be measured and quantitatively characterized using the Modified Gaussian Model, then combined with the results of the chemical analyses to produce a rigorous understanding of how diagnostic absorptions in pyroxene spectra vary with crystal structure, major element chemistry, and site occupancy. We will integrate MOssbauer spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements with observed spectral features to characterize the effects of exsolution; we will characterize the scale of cation site preference on absorption spectra. We will also document exsolution in the pyroxene series. For pyroxenes with substantial exsolution, we will characterize the scale of exsolution and relate it to the effects on diagnostic absorption bands. Lastly, we will integrate the above quantitative results into models for deconvolving pyroxene spectra of materials with unknown chemistries (remote sensing applications). These results will allow significantly tighter bounds on spectral interpretations. The improved capability will be particularly valuable for interpretations of new spectroscopic data soon to be collected for the Moon, Mars and Vesta by hyperspectral mapping missions such as the Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3), CRISM, and Dawn. Our proposal is directly relevant to the exploration goals of NASA emphasizing the character and composition of the terrestrial planets. The results are specifically valuable to the PG&G program as they feed into the synthesis, analysis and comparative study of planetary geological processes on the bodies of the Solar System.
