Description: HYDRATION AND MINERAL ABUNDANCE FROM REFLECTANCE SPECTROSCOPY Our recent work resulted is a first-order quantitative understanding of water in geologic materials using visible-near infrared reflectance (VNIR) spectroscopy, leading to the conciiision that reflectance spectroscopy is capable of providing estimates of absolute water content with uncertainties of I. Nevertheless, a number of critical issues remain before our methods can be applied confidently as a general approach. Recent observations of Mars by the OMEGA experiment on Mars Express showed that Fe-rich smectite clays constitute an important hydrated constituent of the Martian surface and also show that sulfates are perhaps the most dominant hydrated mineral phase on Mars. Yet VNIR databases of reflectance spectra, which are necessary to interpret and analyze these remotely acquired data, are not sufficient, particularly with regards to Fe-rich smectite clays and ferric-ferrous sulfate minerals. Thus a portion of the proposed research will complete the study of hydration in geologic materials by investigating natural materials, mixtures, sample texture, and Fe-rich smectite and sulfate minerals under dehydrating conditions. The second major thrust of the proposed research seeks to advance methodologies in quantifying mineral abundance from VNIR reflectance spectra, a first-order capability needed to characterize the composition of planetary surfaces. While linear deconvolution has been shown to be a useful technique in the thermal IR (TIR) for estimating mineral abundances, the picture is less clear in the VNIR. Techniques for mineral identification are reasonably robust but mineral abundance has only reliably been demonstrated in limited cases (e.g. binary or ternary mixtures under laboratory conditions). Both the hydration and modal mineralogy research objectives will be addressed through laboratory spectroscopic measurements of diverse, well characterized samples. These data will be analyzed with spectroscopic modeling approaches to quantify modal mineralogy and hydration characteristics. Quantification of surface composition and hydration from VNIR data has broad application to NASA's exploration of the So!sr System. Surface composition is fundamental to understanding the planetary processes and evolution. A rich array of VNIR data sets have been or will be collected of diverse planetary bodies in the next decade. Water is an important component of many processes on planets and small bodies in the solar system. Igneous processes, such as the temperature of melting, fractionation of melts, and effusive characteristics of volcanic eruptions are all affected to some degree by the presence of water. Aqueous alteration of certain classes of meteorites has been studied, and asteroids exhibit spectroscopic signatures indicative of hydrated phases. Radar data have been interpreted to indicate the presence of water on Mercury and the Moon. For Mars, water bas clearly played an important role in the evolution of its surface.

Description: WITHIN THE LAST DECADE, A NEW CREEP MECHANISM FOR ICE, SO-CALLED SUPERPLASTIC FLOW, HAS BEEN DISCOVERED. ICE MAY OFTEN IF NOT MOST COMMONLY BE ALLOYED WITH DISPERSED HARD INCLUSIONS (E.G., SILICATES), OR EXIST, FOR EXAMPLE, IN BINARY SYSTEMS WITH OTHER COMPOUNDS. HARD INCLUSIONS CAN DRAMATICALLY AFFECT MATERIAL STRENGTH IN THE SUPERPLASTIC FLOW AND DIFFUSION CREEP REGIMES, DEPENDING ON THE AMOUNT, SIZES, AND DISTRIBUTIONS OF INCLUSIONS.  THE EFFECTS OF HARD INCLUSIONS ON SUPERPLASTIC FLOW OF ICE ARE UNKNOWN. PARTIAL MELTING OF A MATERIAL CAN CAUSE DRAMATIC REDUCTIONS IN ITS STRENGTH DEPENDING ON THE WETTING PROPERTIES OF THE MELT AND THE MELT FRACTION. ABOVE A RHEOLOGICALLY CRITICAL MELT FRACTION, A PARTIALLY MOLTEN MATERIAL LOSES NEARLY ALL OF ITS STRENGTH. PARTIAL MELTING OF TWO-PHASE BINARY AGGREGATES IN THE H20-NH3 AND H20-H2S04 SYSTEMS MAY MOBILIZE THESE MATERIALS AT CONDITIONS FOR WHICH WATER ICE WOULD BE COMPARATIVELY IMMOBILE, RENDERING THEM EFFECTIVE PLANETARY RESURFACING AGENTS. WHILE LIMITED RHEOLOGICAL DATA ARE AVAILABLE FOR PARTIALLY MOLTEN H20-NH3 ICES, LITERALLY NOTHING IS KNOWN ABOUT THE RHEOLOGY OF ICES IN THE H20-H2S04 SYSTEM. A CONTINUING EXPERIMENTAL INVESTIGATION OF THE RHEOLOGY OF INCLUSION-BEARING WATER ICE, AND A NEW INVESTIGATION OF THE RHEOLOGICAL BEHAVIOR OF PARTIALLY MOLTEN H20-NH3 AND H20-H2S04 ICES, IS THEREFORE PROPOSED. EXPERIMENTS WILL BE CONDUCTED OVER A WIDE RANGE OF TEMPERATURES OF PLANETARY INTEREST AT BOTH AMBIENT AND ELEVATED CONFINING PRESSURES, TECHNIQUES FOR PREPARING ICE + PARTICULATE SAMPLES ALLOW THE SIZE, VOLUME FRACTION AND DISTRIBUTION OF PARTICLES TO BE SYSTEMATICALLY VARIED WITHIN SAMPLES OF VARYING ICE GRAIN SIZE, ALLOWING THE RELATIVE CONTRIBUTIONS OF SEVERAL STRENGTHENING MECHANISMS TO BE ASSESSED. NEW METHODS FOR FABRICATING H20-NH3 AND H20-H2S04 ICE SAMPLES WILL ALLOW FOR THE MAINTENANCE OF TEXTURAL EQUILIBRIUM DURING DEFORMATION, PARTIAL MELTING EXPERIMENTS WILL EXPLORE THE FUNCTIONAL RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN STRAIN RATE AND MELT FRACTION. IN ADDITION TO PROVIDING FUNDAMENTAL KNOWLEDGE OF THESE IMPURE ICE RHEOLOGIES, WE WILL CONTINUE OUR QUEST TO LOCATE AND EXPLORE THE DIFFUSION CREEP REGIME. THE DISCOVERY OF DIFFUSION CREEP FOR ICE WOULD BE A MAJOR ADVANCE IN OUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE PHYSICS OF ICE FLOW, AND WOULD ALLOW THE PLANETARY COMMUNITY TO ASSESS THE DEGREE TO WHICH THIS NEWTONIAN CREEP MECHANISM CONTROLS THE FLOW OF ICE ON MARS AND WITHIN THE ICY SATELLITES.

Description: PHYSICS-BASED MULTISCALE MODELING OF MULTIFUNCTIONAL NANOCERAMIC COMPOSITES FOR SUBSONIC ENGINE COMPONENTS Next-generation engine components require new materials possessing high strength and toughness, good thermal conductivity, and stability and erosion resistance at moderately elevated temperatures. Such multifunctionality requires well-engineered materials and underlying physics-based, multiscale models to guide the design of such materials. Here, we propose to create a suite of multiscale modeling tools to predict the macroscopic performance of nanotubes-and nanofiber-reinforced ceramic composites based on atomistic, mesoscale, and continuum features of the material deformation, and to perform key validating experimental studies on new nanocomposite materials. This effort builds on our world-leading expertise in composite modeling and fabrication at both nano and micron scales, and will culminate in a powerful, validated, materials design strategy for high strength and toughness, as well as enhanced thermal conductivity, erosion resistance, and possibly both acoustic damping and self-damage-detection, in this class of materials system. The modeling work will use three sets of tools in a multiscale framework: molecular statics/dynamics, mesoscale micromechanics models, and analytic models. Atomistic models will address key issues relating deformation in nanofibers to composite toughness: internal inter-wall coupling in Carbon nanotubes, use of nanotubes vs. nanofibers including SiC, and nanofiber/matrix interface bonding and roughness. Mesoscale crack-bridging models will import the key physics from the atomistic models and predict toughness versus material parameters for cracks bridged by aligned and/or random nanofibers, and will be used to deduce nanoscale constitutive behavior from experimental measurements on new materials. Parametric analytic models for macroscopic performance will be developed, based on state-of-the-art models by the PI. Nanotubes and nanofibers also provide excellent opportunities for multifunctionality. Erosion resistance will be evaluated via predicting toughness versus crack size and is expected to be enhanced when nanoscale toughening mechanisms exist. Mechanical damping will be investigated in carbon nanotubes systems through both inter-wall sliding tuned by interwall coupling and through matrix/fiber interface sliding. Complementing the modeling of mechanical performance, we will also use and/or develop models for thermal conductivity and electrical resistivity, the latter for potential in-situ damage detection. The suite of modeling tools could also be applied to predict the performance of hybrid nano/micro composites. Critical parallel experimental work on the fabrication and testing of new nanotubes and nanofiber composites will be carried out. These studies will assess the role of nanotubes/nanofiber structure, fiber/matrix interface structure, and processing methods on the toughness and strength of these materials. Having previously demonstrated toughening mechanisms in Alumina/Carbon-nanotube systems, we will continue working on nanocomposites composed of Si3N4 matrices reinforced with carbon nanotubes and SiC nanofibers, some of which have already being fabricated and tested at Brown. Our success in the in-situ conversion of carbon to SiC to create highly refractory nanocomposites will be pushed further to fabricate and test improved SiC-based composite systems. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons between modeling and experiment on a variety of properties will be made to validate and improve the models and to directly observe mechanisms of damage tolerance and multifunctionality in nanoceramic composites.

Description: GEOLOGICAL MAPPING OF VENUS:  EARTH ARCHEAN COMPARISONS Venus and the Earth's Archean share many similarities in terms of geological features, structures, thermal conditions, and interpreted processes. To bring fresh insight to both fields, we have gathered a team of experts to undertake a synergistic examination of two key adjacent Venus quadrangles. Archean experts bring direct field mapping, structural, and sample analysis to the study of Venus; Venus experts bring knowledge of the global areal distribution of uneroded and contiguous units and structures, a perspective poorly preserved in the Archean record. The team identified the following key questions common to both the Archean and Venus: I) Crustal Thickening Environments and Processes: Over what range of environments does crustal thickening occur on Venus; what insight does this provide for the Archean? 2) Role of Diapirism: What are similarities/differences between coronae and diapiric structures on Venus and Archean basement-cored domes? 3) Nature and Origin of Deformation Belts: What is the geologic setting of Venus linear deformation belts; how do they compare to the Archean? 4) Origin and Context of Regional Plains: Do Archean komatiitic plains deposits bear similarities to the regional plains on Venus in terms of emplacement style and relationships? 5) Geodynamic Evolution: a) Archean-Venus: What insight does the Earth's Archean record provide to the nature and understanding of features, units and sequences on Venus? b) Venus-Archean: What insight does the local, regional and global geology of Venus provide into selecting among the geodynamic processes thought to have operated during Earth's Archean (e.g, vertical or lateral crustal accretion, mantle/crustal overturn, diapirism, flood basalts, crustal thickening)? We propose to address these questions through geologic mapping of Snegurochka Planitia (V-I) and Fortuna Tessera (V-2); the project will be accompanied by specific process studies and a synthesis describing key similarities, differences and insights in Venus/Archean comparisons for future use by both communities.

Description: We propose to develop a multiscale design tool to predict short-term and long-term fracture in, and to guide the microstructural design of, structural metals. The work emphasizes prediction of the nano- and micro-scale evolution of dislocations, cracks, and chemistry interactions that drive fracture under monotonic and fatigue loadings. These phenomena at sub-continuum scales will be used to deduce physically-based cohesive zone models for incorporation into the finite-element simulations of fracture in polycrystalline microstructures. This work is aligned with the Aging Aircraft and Durability thrusts on foundational research in physics-based modeling of durability of metallic airframe components [CP-01; Topics AAD-10 and AAD-3]. Predicting fracture in metallic materials is challenging due to its intrinsic multiscale nature. Fracture is fundamentally the breaking of bonds and thus quantum-mechanical. However, the local stresses driving that atomic-scale process are determined by behavior occurring at much larger scales due to dislocations, grain-boundaries, and microstructure, physical phenomena not directly contained in standard continuum constitutive modeling. To capture the physics of interactions among material defects at short range (atomistic/chemical effects), long-range (dislocation structuring) requires a truly multiscale model. Here, we propose to apply and extend our innovative ^Coupled Atomistic/ Discrete-Dislocation^ (CADD) model to predict critical non-continuum fracture phenomena at sub-micron scales. The CADD model can represent crack tips and grain boundaries with full atomistic resolution while handling dislocation plasticity at both atomistic and continuum scales simultaneously, and is the only multiscale tool existing today with such a capability. We will apply it to the fracture of selected Al, Ni, and Fe-based structural materials, including fracture along and near grain boundaries (Topic AAD-10). To incorporate chemistry effects, we will use first-principles quantum mechanics methods to predict the fundamental decohesion energetics of hydroxylated alumina/metal interfaces. This work will guide CADD modeling to predict mechanisms by which nano-oxide layers influence dislocation/crack interactions at the nanoscale and thereby influence macroscopic fracture (Topic AAD-3). These methods will be used to simulate fatigue crack growth, which is most important for durability of airframe systems. Microstructure at larger scales is also important in macroscopic fracture, and so methods to pass the nanoscale physics to microstructural scales are essential. We will develop continuum cohesive zone models in which the small-scale material separation behavior uncovered in CADD and quantum modeling is embedded. The cohesive zone models can then be used in standard finite-element models to predict nucleation and propagation of cracks in microstructures, enhancing traditional modeling of crack growth in metallic components.

Description: TIMOTHY GIBLIN/THE COLLEGE OF CHARLESTONTHE TRANSITION FROM GAMMA-RAY BURST TO AFTERGLOWTHE TRANSIENT NATURE OF GAMMA-RAY BURSTS (GRBS) AND THE LIMITATIONS ENCOUNTERED IN DETECTING THEIR AFTERGLOWS HAVE MADE OBSERVATIONS OF THE TRANSITION FROM GRB TO AFTERGLOW ELUSIVE. HOWEVER, IN THE PAST DECADE, OBSERVATIONS OF BEPPOSSAX BURSTS AS WELL AS ARCHIVAL STUDIES OF BATSE DATA INDICATE A VARIETY OF POSSIBLE AFTERGLOW ONSET TIMES. IN SOME CASES THIS DELAY TIME IS SHORT (ON THE ORDER OF SECONDS), RESULTING IN CONTEMPORANEOUS PROMPT AND AFTERGLOW EMISSION, WHILE IN OTHER CASES THE DELAY TIME EXCEEDS THE BURST DURATION AND IS THEREFORE TEMPORALLY DECOUPLED FROM THE PROMPT BURST EMISSION. GIVEN THE SENSITIVITY OF SWIFT'S BAT AND XRT AT ENERGIES < 100 KEY, AFTERGLOW EMISSION MAY BE PREVELANT IN BURSTS AT THESE HIGH ENERGIES. THIS PROPOSAL AIMS TO UTILIZE THE BAT (AND XRT) DATA TO SEARCH FOR DISTINCT AND/OR ABRUPT SPECTRAL CHANGES DURING THE BURST THAT MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO A SEPARATE UNDERLYING ORDELAYED EMISSION PHASE. IN THE INTERNAL/EXTERNAL SHOCK(ISIES) MODEL WE EXPECT AN EARLY TRANSITION FROM FAST TO SLOW COOLING, AS THE BREAK ENERGY (I.E. THE SYNCHROTRON SPECTRAL BREAK) PASSES THROUGH THE X-RAY BAND. ANALYSIS TOOLS INCLUDE TIME-DEPENDENT COLOR-COLOR DIAGRAMS TO PROBE SPECTRAL EVOLUTION PATTERNS. HARDNESS RATIOS WILL BE GENERATED BY BINNING THE BAT DATA TO PRODUCE HARD AND SOFTCOLOR INDICES. FURTHER, WE WILL FOLD THE REDSHIFTED AFTERGLOW SPECTRUM PREDICTED FROM THE EXTERNAL SHOCK THROUGH THE DETECTOR RESPONSE TO PREDICT THE EVOLUTION OF THE OBSERVED HARD AND SOFT COLORS. ONCE THE EMISSION COMPONENT IS IDENTIFIED, THE DELAY TIME WITH RESPECT TOTHE PROMPT EMISSION CAN BE DETERMINED. Description: A COMPREHENSIVE FUSE SURVEY OF THE ROTATION RATES OF VERY MASSIVE STARS IN THE SMALL AND LARGE MAGELLANIC CLOUDS Stellar interior models are critical tools used in all branches of astronomy from chemical evolution and population synthesis studies to the determination of evolutionary masses. Until recently the effects of rotation were not included in these codes. The new models show that rotation induces interior mixing that produces some drastic external changes for massive stars while they are still core-hydrogen burning. While the inclusion of rotation was expected to explain the enhanced surface abundances seen in some stars, the prediction that massive stars have luminosities that are rotation dependent was not expected. This last prediction creates a serious scatter in the mass-luminosity relationship and makes the determination of an evolutionary mass essentially impossible. These new models must be tested to determine if their treatment of angular momentum is correct. A straightforward method is to determine if massive stars rotation rates match those predicted by the new models. At solar or Galactic metallicity (Z = 0.020), massive stars are expected to quickly slow their rotation speeds while on the main sequence (MS). Stars at lower metallicity (Z) experience reduced mass loss rates and subsequently retain more of their angular momentum during the MS. The FUSE archive at the Multimission Archive at Space Telescope (MAST) contains spectra of 140 LMC (Z= 0.007) and SMC (Z = 0.004) O-type stars. The targets are 87 evolved (luminosity classes I, II,&III) and 53 unevolved (IV&V classes) in these low Z environments. In addition MAST contains spectra of 115 Galactic O-type stars, 59 evolved, 56 unevolved. This is an extremely large sample of O-type spectra, all observed with the same instrument. It contains both cluster and field stars. These stars represent a completely uniform, unbiased sample for evaluating the predictions from the new stellar interior models. Projected rotation velocities for all 255 stars will be obtained through a cross-correlation methodology that we have used successfully in the past with both IUE and HST/STIS spectra. Comparisons of the rotation rates of unevolved (close to ZAMS) stars at low Z to those of the same classes at higher Z will determine if the initial rotation rates of massive stars are metallicity dependent. Comparisons of the rotation rates of evolved (close to TAMS) massive stars to the unevolved stars in the same metallicity environment will determine the extent of angular momentum (and hence mass) loss during the core hydrogen burning. The proposed survey represents a critical and needed test of the treatment of angular momentum in the new stellar models and the accuracy of the models predictions.

Description: The PI proposes to carry out theoretical research in and cimputer modeling of 1) general nucleosynthesis, 2) stellar evolution and grain formation, and 3) chemical evolution. The goal of this research will be to understand isotopic effects in presolar grains, calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions, and bulk meteorites. The results from this work will provide insights into the birth of the Solar System and the formation of planetary bodies. The work will be carried out by the PI and a graduate student. In addition to presenting their work in publications, the PI and student will make all computer codes they develop during this research available for use by the scientific community and by the general public over the internet. Under the topic of general nucleosynthes, the PI will use the Clemson nucleosynthesis code to seek to understand how the r-process and p-process isotopes of molybdenum and ruthenium are made and what the consequences are for isotopic anomalies in presolar grains and bulk meterites. The PI will also study the nuclear dynamics of and reaction rate uncertainties in the neutrom burst in the helium shell of massive stars that is putatively responsible for production of the short-lived radioactivities 60Fe 1291, and 182Hf in the early solar system. Under the topic of stellar evolution and grain formation, the PI will study stellar evolution models run at Clemson to explore how uncertainties in these models affect the yields of neutron-burst nucleosynthesis in helium shells. The PI will also extend his chemical kinetic networks to further explore growth of carbonaceous dust in supernova debris. Under the topis of chemical evolution, the PI and his graduate student will perform calculation of admixtures of stellar debris with both solar composition and with proxy compositions determined from chemical evolution models. The goal is to predict the possible anomalies in stable isotopes that would accompany injection of short-lived radioactivities into the early proto-solar nebula or disk and the uncertainties in those predictions. The PI and student will also follow dust cycling in the interstellar medium to understand chemical-memory effects in calcium-aluminum-rich inclusions and in bulk meteorites. This research will be highly relevant to the Cosmochemistry Program's goal of understanding exterrestrial samples and Solar System formation. Work on nucleosynthesis and chemical kinetics will shed light on presolar grain formation and isotopic effects. Work on stellar evolution and admixing of stellar yields and proxy Solar System compositions will provide insights into the circumstances of the Sun's birth and the formation of primitive minerals. Work on siting of isotopes in dust will provide constraints on the basic building blocks of the Solar System. This research will also further NASA's strategic goal to advance scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the Solar System.

Description: Lead proposal: In the mesosphere and lower thermosphere (MLT), energy and momentum propagating from below are deposited via wave breaking, instabilities, and turbulence. The turbopause is the level where turbulence becomes less efficient than molecular diffusion. In the region 90-110 km, large-scale instabilities, overturning of density contours, wind shears, and adiabatic temperature gradients are common, but the relationship to turbulence is not clear. Our investigation addresses the lifecycle of these instabilities; how they form, do they generate turbulence, how they decay. We also ask: Does turbulence exist above 100 km, and what contributes to the eddy diffusion at those heights? We propose a series offour rockets from Poker Flat, Alaska, in January 2009 to study the evolution of an instability event in the 90-110 km region. Observation of wave overturning by sodium lidar will initiate the salvo. We prefer aurorally quiet conditions to focus on forcing from the neutral atmosphere. The rockets are equipped with experiments that measure turbulence by different techniques. Trimethyl aluminum (TMA) chemiluminescence delivers winds and is a tracer for turbulent diffusion. Electron probes and ionization gauges measure electron and neutral densities and small-scale fluctuations, also tracers for turbulence. In the case of electron enhancements by sporadic layers, the new AMISR radar may provide additional input. We also expect that our measurements will resolve the apparent discrepancy in turbulence results from TMA and fluctuation techniques, which have never been directly compared. The work is part of the Geospace Science Program and addresses NASAs Strategic Goal 3B: Understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system. The results will be relevant to two of NASAs future missions: GEC and AIM. It supports investigations of the physics of the mesosphere, thermosphere, ionosphere of the Earth, including the coupling of these phenomena to the lower atmosphere

Description: THE ROLES OF GRAVITY WAVES IN THE POLAR ATMOSPHERE  Flow over topography, latent heating associated with polar fronts, and jetstream fluctuations can generate gravity waves (GWs) that propagate into the stratosphere. While the coupling processes between near-surface disturbances and those in the middle atmosphere are still unclear, GWs are thought to playa key role in interacting with planetary-scale flows and distributing energy at different parts of the atmosphere. Damping of GW can significantly alter the stratospheric circulation, distorting the polar vortex and the underlying planetary-scale disturbances. Anomalous changes in the polar vortex have been suggested to bias near-surface climate conditions.  Perturbed polar dynamics on mesoscale and planetary scales can have significant implications in the formation of polar stratospheric clouds (PSCs) which could facilitate stratospheric ozone destruction. The goal ofthis study is to investigate the roles of GWs in coupling the polar troposphere to the stratospheric evolution. The study aims to better understand the dynamical connection between GWs and planetary waves, to access GW forcing on the polar vortex, and to examine the role of GWs in PSCs formation. As such, our objectives are (1) to characterize the sources/properties of GWs in the polar region and their propagation into the stratosphere, (2) to assess the interactions between GWs and planetary-scale disturbances in the polar region, and causes of wave intensification, and (3) to estimate impacts of GW perturbations on the formation of PSCs in the lower stratosphere. Methods: To achieve these objectives, GW simulations will be performed using the ARPS weather model (extended up to the mesosphere) to explicitly resolve GWs of horizontal scales greater than 50 krn. Focus will be placed on events in which synoptic disturbances significantly raise the tropopause. These cases are often associated with enhanced cloudiness (in the troposphere and the stratosphere) and strong GW generation. Model results will be compared with satellite observations like NASA AIRS radiance to elucidate wave properties and their sources. Gravity wave forcing of the polar stratosphere in relation to planetary waves will be analyzed using model results and reanalyses data from GEOS-4. Description: Biodiversity threats are not solely from deforestation. Human land use fragments remaining forests into smaller and smaller pieces. Forest fragments are altered habitats that change community composition and structure. It has not generally been understood that an equal or greater percentage of standing Amazonian forests have been degraded by fire, selective logging and fragmentation than have been deforested. Biodiversity implications of ongoing forest degradation and its relation to human landuse have not been quantified or placed in the spatial context necessary for predicting future landcover and hence biodiversity dynamics. The fundamental hypothesis underlying this proposal is that biodiversity levels of Amazonian forests are strongly related to two competing factors: forest disturbance and time since last disturbance. We will use Landsat and MODIS satellite imagery and derived products to create a 10 year spatial database (2000-2009) of all major forest disturbances (selective logging, fire, fragmentation and deforestation) across the Brazilian Amazon. Integration of Landsat based analyses of forest disturbance with MODIS-derived burned area products will enable us to accurately separate fires into their 3 main types; (1) deforestation fires, where slash is burned, creating relatively hot fires that burn for several hours; 2) maintenance fires, which rapidly burn as narrow fire lines through grass and early second growth; 3) forest fires, escaped fires in standing forests which vary from extremely low intensity in previously undisturbed forests to high intensity in previously burned or logged forests. We will use this database to stratify and interpret extensive field studies designed to investigate the response of 4 major indicator taxa (understorey birds, dung beetles, trees and euglossine bees) as a function of disturbance history and time since last disturbance.

Description: Land Cover Dynamics, Regional Hydrometeorology, and the Vulnerability of Rain-Fed Agriculture to Climate Change under Scenarios of Extensive Cultivation of Biofuel Feedstocks Land cover dynamics remains one of the continuing critical issues for weather and climate modeling. It is difficult to find the appropriate coupling ofthe slower land surface processes that can be highly heterogeneous at finer spatial scales with the much faster tempo of boundary layer processes that exhibit heterogeneity only at much coarser spatial scales. VegET, a novel model for estimation of evapotranspiration in non-irrigated croplands and grasslands has recently been developed for operational use in the Famine Early Warning System Network. This approach blends concepts from irrigation engineering with a remote sensing datastream to estimate actual ET quickly at low computational and data cost with a surprising degree of accuracy. A key piece of information for VegET is the land surface phenology (LSP), which describes the seasonal progression of vegetation growth and development at locations of interest. The LSP can be observed by spaceborne sensors, modeled by an empirical climatology, or modeled using simple functional forms linking vegetation growth to temperature and/or precipitation. We propose to refine, validate, and apply VegET to explore the consequences of land cover change and variability on seasonal water use in rain-fed croplands. We will evaluate altemative MODIS datastreams and vegetation indices for VegET (it currently uses AVHRR NDVI). We will explore synergies with daily passive microwave products from AMSR-E. We will compare VegET predictions against a complex mesoscale model WRF/CLM. We will validate VegET with data from in-situ and flux tower networks and in corn, soybean, wheat, and switchgrass fields in South Dakota and western Minnesota. The focal application of VegET will be to assess the vulnerability of rain-fed agriculture in the Northern Great Plains (ND, SD, NE, western MN and LA) under scenarios of extensive cultivation of biofuel feedstocks and the regional climate projections of the IPCC AR4. We will investigate how the LSPs associated with biofuel feedstocks may affect the regional liydrometeorology by changing the amount of ET and shifting peak seasonal latent heat fluxes. We will explore the impact of these changes on risk of drought and other forms of extreme weather and on wildfire risk.

Description: NON WOVEN BASED COMPOSITES FROM POLYETHYLENE/PROPYLENE FOR SPACE APPLICATIONS The purpose of this research is to use the proven polyethylene fibers to produce useful materials using the nonwoven based processing techniques. Polymeric materials such as polyethylene (PE) containing higher percentage of hydrogen have been found to be very effective radiation shield materials. Polypropylene (PP) also as a high hydrogen content as it has only carbon and hydrogen in the structure. In addition, these are light weight, with specific gravity less than one, and the strongest known fiber, spectraB is produced from Polyethylene. With the combination of super strong spectra fiber and appropriately chosen PPIPE binder fibers, it will be possible to produce excellent webs and composite panels. For this, nonwoven processes will be used to form fleeces from appropriate combination of fibers. Staple fibers will be blended and then carded to form webs of different' area density. These webs will be consolidated to form dense webs for insulation purposes or molded into composites for structural applications. Using the Nonwoven based approach will provide a unique opportunity to engineer the properties by suitably changing the structure. Nonwoven based approach also allows the fabrication of products in different shapes with fair amount of ease. The webs and composites produced from these compositions will be evaluated for their structure and physical properties. Also, samples will be provided to NASA for further evaluation of radiation performance.

Description: EARTH-MOON-MARS RADIATION EXPOSURE MODULE(EMMREM) WE ARE PREPARING TO RETURN HUMANS TO THE MOON AND SETTING THE STAGE FOR EXPLORATION TO MARS AND BEYOND. HOWEVER, IT IS UNCLEAR IF LONG MISSIONS OUTSIDE OF LOW-EARTH ORBIT (LEO) CAN BE ACCOMPLISHED WITH ACCEPTABLE RISK. THE CENTRAL OBJECTIVE OF OUR PROJECT, THE EARTH-MOON-MARS RADIATION EXPOSURE MODULE (EMMREM), IS TO DEVELOP AND VALIDATE A NUMERICAL MODULE FOR COMPLETELY CHARACTERIZING TIME-DEPENDENT RADIATION EXPOSURE IN THE EARTH-MOON-MARS AND INTERPLANETARY SPACE ENVIRONMENTS. EMMREM PROVIDES THE ABILITY TO PREDICT RADIATION EXPOSURE ANYWHERE ON THE SURFACE OR ATMOSPHERE OF EARTH, ON THE MOON, MARS, AND IN INTERPLANETARY SPACE BETWEEN EARTH AND MARS. EMMREM IS DESIGNED FOR BROAD USE BY RESEARCHERS TO PREDICT RADIATION EXPOSURE GENERATED BY ALMOST ANY PARTICLE DISTRIBUTION INCIDENT FROM INTERPLANETARY SPACE. EMMREM IS DEVELOPED USING CONTEMPORARY, STATE-OF-THE-ART, PHYSICS-BASED PARTICLE RADIATION MODELS. BEYOND THIS, IT HAS THE CAPABILITY TO INCORPORATE NEW MODELS, AS THEY BECOME AVAILABLE, TO GIVE CONTINUALLY IMPROVED ESTIMATES OF RADIATION HAZARDS AND EFFECTS. EMMREM IS COMPREHENSIVELY VALIDATED IN THE ENVIRONMENTS WHERE RISKS NEED TO BE ASSESSED, USING DIRECT AND CONTEMPORANEOUS MEASUREMENTS NEAR EARTH, AT THE MOON AND MARS TO SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCE UNCERTAINTIES IN RADIATION EXPOSURE. EMMREM CHARACTERIZES THE EXTREMES, STATISTICS, AND VARIATIONS OVER TIME OF RADIATION EXPOSURE CAUSED BY SOLAR ENERGETIC PARTICLES AND COSMIC RAYS. THE RESULTS OF EMMREM WILL IMPROVE RISK ASSESSMENT MODELS SO THAT FUTURE HUMAN EXPLORATION MISSIONS CAN BE ADEQUATELY PLANNED. THIS MAKES EMMREM HIGHLY RELEVANT TO NASA'S VISION FOR SPACE EXPLORATION AND LIVING WITH A STAR PROGRAMS. EMMREM'S HIGHLY CROSS-DISCIPLINARY TEAM MAKES THE UNPRECEDENTED LINK FROM PARTICLE RADIATION RESEARCHERS TO RADIATION BIOPHYSICS RESEARCHERS AND RISK ASSESSMENT SPECIALISTS. EMMREM IS A POWERFUL TOOL, URGENTLY NEEDED TO REDUCE UNCERTAINTIES IN RISK ASSESSMENT MODELS. EMMREM IS THE MISSING LINK FROM SPACE SCIENCE TO SPACE EXPLORATION. EMMREM'S CENTRAL OBJECTIVE IS ACHIEVED THROUGH FOUR PRIMARY ACTIVITIES: 1. WE DEVELOP THE CENTRAL EMMREM MODULE FOR PREDICTING TIME-DEPENDENT RADIATION EXPOSURE (LINEAR-ENERGY-TRANSFER SPECTRA AND DOSE-RELATED QUANTITIES) BASED ON EXISTING, WELL-ESTABLISHED, WORKING CODES INCLUDING THE BRYNTRN AND HZETRN CODE DEVELOPED AT NASA LANGLEY AND THE HETC-HEDS MONTE CARLO CODE DEVELOPED AT OAK RIDGE NATIONAL LABORATORY AND THE UNIVERSITY OF TENNESSEE. 2. WE DEVELOP INTERFACES BETWEEN EMMREM AND ENERGETIC PARTICLE SIMULATIONS USING, AS A TEST-BED, SOPHISTICATED, PHYSICS-BASED SOLAR ENERGETIC PARTICLE (SEP) AND COSMIC RAY MODELS. SIMULATIONS AND ASSOCIATED EMMREM RADIATION EXPOSURE PREDICTIONS ARE USED TO CHARACTERIZE TYPICAL, AND WORST-CASE EVENT SCENARIOS, AND TO CHARACTERIZE EXPOSURE NEAR-EARTH, AT THE MOON, MARS AND THROUGHOUT THE INNER HELIOSPHERE OVER THE SOLAR CYCLE. 3. WE DEVELOP INTERFACES BETWEEN EMMREM AND DIRECT OBSERVATIONS OF PARTICLE RADIATION (SOHO, ACE, WIND, STEREO, SAMPEX, NOAA-GOES AND ULYSSES). THE OBSERVATIONS ARE USED BOTH TO VALIDATE SEP AND COSMIC RAY SIMULATIONS, AND AS DIRECT INPUT TO PREDICT RADIATION EXPOSURE AT THE EARTH, ON THE MOON, MARS AND IN INTERPLANETARY SPACE ENVIRONMENTS. 4. WE SIGNIFICANTLY REDUCE RADIATION EXPOSURE UNCERTAINTIES THROUGH COMPREHENSIVE VALIDATION IN THE EARTH, MOON, MARS AND INTERPLANETARY SPACE ENVIRONMENTS. EMMREM IS VALIDATED WITH PREVIOUSLY MEASURED LET SPECTRA FROM THE INTERNATIONAL SPACE STATION (ISS) AND THE SPACE SHUTTLE, OBSERVATIONS FROM LRO/CRATER, MSL/RAD, MARIE ON MARS ODYSSEY, AND USING AN EXTENSIVE DATABASE OF ACCELERATOR BEAM MEASUREMENTS.

Description: REAL TIME METHODS TO REDUCE INFLIGHT ICING HAZARDS  The University of Tennessee Space Institute (UTSI) in partnership with Bihrle Applied Research (BAR) proposes to conduct a three year research program in response to the NASA Research Announcement (NRA) NNH06ZEA001N under Appendix B, Aviation Safety Program. This partnership will address the objectives defined under the Integrated Vehicle Health Management (IVHM) Project, topic IVHM 3.1, Environmental Hazards, which are caused by the Effects of Icing on Aircraft State. UTSI and BAR propose to conduct a three year research program, which is expected to begin in March, 2007. The major purpose of the program is to develop and validate the integration of real time methodologies for assessing aircraft state in an icing environment. The objective is to develop a means for providing pilots with real time aircraft state and icing environment information for early detection of impending aircraft handling problems and avoidance of an upset condition. Pilot displays which provide envelope protection cues, real time or near real time icing weather information are an essential aspect of this research. To that end, this program will demonstrate how the fusion of these technologies when integrated with intuitive cockpit displays, improve pilot situational awareness and decision making capability. The result is safer aircraft operation, improved management and use of ice protection systems, and mitigation of the hazards of an icing encounter. UTSI and BAR are uniquely qualified to perform this  research. The UTSI Principal Investigator (PI) is a former NASA research pilot and has over 16 years experience in performing icing flight research including the first tail stall upset investigations. He has authored and co-authored several technical publications on this research. The PI was also a flight test manager and senior experimental test pilot with Bombardier Aerospace for approximately five years and conducted icing development and certification for intercontinental business and large regional jet aircraft. BAR, a highly experienced aeronautical research company specializing in flight model development, data analysis, and flight dynamics, developed the NASA Ice Contamination Effects Training Device (ICEFTD) under a NASA Glenn Research Center contract, and continues to provide technical support for its use. UTSI currently utilizes the ICEFTD for pilot training in icing short courses offered by the Department of Continuing Education. This unique simulator uses an experimentally derived aerodynamic data base from wind tunnel and flight to provide a highly realistic simulation of icing effects on flight characteristics. Aside from its utility as a training device, it is also an excellent facility for conducting engineering evaluations. Because its data base represents the Twin Otter aircraft, engineering evaluations are facilitated by flight test validation, which is essential to the conduct of this proposed research program.

Description: NON WOVEN BASED COMPOSITES FROM POLYETHYLENE/PROPYLENE FOR SPACE APPLICATIONS The purpose of this research is to use the proven polyethylene fibers to produce useful materials using the nonwoven based processing techniques. Polymeric materials such as polyethylene (PE) containing higher percentage of hydrogen have been found to be very effective radiation shield materials. Polypropylene (PP) also as a high hydrogen content as it has only carbon and hydrogen in the structure. In addition, these are light weight, with specific gravity less than one, and the strongest known fiber, spectraB is produced from Polyethylene. With the combination of super strong spectra fiber and appropriately chosen PPIPE binder fibers, it will be possible to produce excellent webs and composite panels. For this, nonwoven processes will be used to form fleeces from appropriate combination of fibers. Staple fibers will be blended and then carded to form webs of different' area density. These webs will be consolidated to form dense webs for insulation purposes or molded into composites for structural applications. Using the Nonwoven based approach will provide a unique opportunity to engineer the properties by suitably changing the structure. Nonwoven based approach also allows the fabrication of products in different shapes with fair amount of ease. The webs and composites produced from these compositions will be evaluated for their structure and physical properties. Also, samples will be provided to NASA for further evaluation of radiation performance.

Description: The objective of this research is to develop and evaluate innovative, physics-based, validated computational prediction tools to support design and pre-flight development of new configuration concepts for hybrid wing/body vehicles with highly integrated airframe and propulsion systems. These new concepts are motivated by efficient high-speed cruise with low takeoff and landing noise, and with adequate stability and control characteristics throughout the flight envelope. The proposed computational capabilities will provide aerodynamic flow prediction and computational design enhancement for design/testing of integrated embedded propulsion systems, at flight-relevant conditions and with confidence sufficient to support development of new vehicles. The effect of inlet flow distortion and airframe boundary-layer ingestion on fan performance is a key design issue and will be the subject of the Phase I study. Inlet induced flow distortion can cause fan and engine stall, surge, and reduced operating envelope, which are critical design constraints. The proposed study will provide a validated capability for aerodynamic analysis of single (isolated) or multiple integrated components (for example inlets, fans and their interactions), for the purpose of prediction, sensitivity analysis, and design enhancement. The proposed work will utilize the SimCenter's recently developed state-of-the-art unstructured grid, flow simulation, and sensitivity analysis software (Tenasi codes). Key computational technologies to be applied are a) simulations using unstructured viscous grids with grid motion and embedded rotating components, and b) complex-variable sensitivity analysis to generate computationally enhanced aerodynamic designs. These software tools will provide design-team support for computationally enhanced integrated aerodynamic design of wing/body airframe, engine inlet(s), fan duct(s), core engine(s), and exhaust nozzle(s). This technology will enable future pre-flight predictions supporting multiple concept vehicle designs, including detailed design, fabrication and testing phases of promising concept vehicles. NASA collaboration is envisioned for system-level planning, selection of configurations, validation experiments, aerodynamic design integration, and technology transfer and exchange.

Description: Proof testing is a well known and accepted procedure for finding flaws in a material or product before the product is put to use. As a vital part of the design process, proof testing involves loading the est specimen with a load greater than what will be seen in service. The idea is that if the specimen is able to withstand this extra load, it can safely be assumed that the specimen will not fail under normal operating conditions. Proof testing is a necessity when Non-destructive Evaluation (NDE) is not possible, but the optimal situation is for proof testing and NDEto work hand in hand. NASA has several standards or fracture control in order to ensure safety. With the Constellation program in full swing, proof testing will once again be utilized in order to meet those standards. Each piece of the new flight hardware for the Reusable Solid Rocket Motor V (RSRMV) used on the new fleet of launch vehicles will need to be tested. I propose to validate and refine the proof test methodology for the new hardware by using Elastic-Plastic Fracture Mechanics and studying the effects of plastic constraint. The result will be a better understanding of constraint arameters and a more accurate NASGRO elastic- lastic crack growth model.

Description: THERMOMECHANICAL PROCESSING AND MODELING OF HIGH TEMPERATURE SMA'S FOR MULTIFUNCTIONAL ENGINE COMPONENTS Project Description We propose to fabricate Ti49.2Pt20Ni30.8 and Ti49.2Pd30Ni20.8 HTSMAs and process them by at least two different processing techniques, which include Equal Channel Angular Extrusion (ECAE) and rolling/drawing. Superior material behavior can be obtained by varying the percentage of reduction and the temperature of rolling. ECAE is a severe plastic deformation (SPD) technique and can permit application of a large amount of uniform strain without reducing the cross section of the material.  This processing technique combined with post processing techniques such as marforming, aging and other thermomechanical treatment techniques have been shown to provide superior thermomechanical response in SMAs. The proposed processing techniques will be aimed at improving the thermomechanical performance of the material specifically focusing on (1) texturing and texture strengthening using ECAE, (2) minimizing high temperature creep effects by grain refinement/strengthening by deformation twinning in austenite/compound twinning in martensite (3) eliminating large precipitates and, by using Nirich compositions for smaller precipitates, induce precipitation hardening for suppressing plastic deformation and grain growth. Calorimetric effects, microstructure and thermomechanical response will be initially analyzed. The phase diagram ofthe material will be generated by a series of tension and compression tests. The material will also be tested under fixed temperature 'and stress to document the visco-plastic behavior of the material. The visco-plastic behavior of the material due to microstructural thermally activated dislocation motion, atomic diffusion, grain sliding and grain growth may be captured in terms of macroscopic parameters of stress, strain, temperature and time. The need to develop a rate dependent model is motivated by experimental evidence suggesting the presence of significant rate/time effects observed in moderate to high composition palladium and platinum based alloys. The existing phenomenological SMA model capable of predicting complex loading paths will be extended to incorporate the time dependent behavior observed in high temperature SMAs.  Viscosity coefficient and strain rate will be input parameters coupled with the transformation temperatures, maximum transformation strain and the stress influence coefficients to effectively capture the visco-plastic behavior in the material. In summary, the objectives of the proposed research are to, (1) investigate the effect processing techniques on the visco-plastic behavior of High Temperature Shape Memory Alloys (HTSMAs) (2) develop a constitutive SMA model incorporating visco-plasticity to capture the high temperature creep behavior (3) use the model predictions to the effectively predict the thermomechanical response of the HTSMA fabricated by different processing techniques. The key outcomes from the proposed research are identified as, (1) developing a deeper understanding on the effects of different processing techniques on the visco-plastie behavior and the overall thermomechanical behavior of HTSMAs, (2) developing the first thermomechanical constitutive SMA model capturing the high temperature creep effects to predict the HTSMA behavior, (3) implementing the model in a 3-D environment for FEA of smart structures with HTSMAs. (4) strengthening the partnership between NASA and Texas A&M University. The proposed phenomenological SMA model is designed with the purposes of developing an improved prediction tools for obtaining accurate predictions capturing the unique behavior observed in high temperature SMAs and thereby aid in the development of smart structures incorporating HTSMAs for various aerospace applications.

Description: TEXAS ENGINEERING EXPERIMENT STATION RANS AND VARIABLE-RESOLUTION PANS MODELS FOR SEPARATED FLOWS The complexity of the separation problem and its crucial role in aeronautics applications dictates a two-tier research approach. For applications involving steady separation, a sophisticated Reynolds averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) model may be adequate. For applications with unsteady separation - e.g., high-lift airfoils operating close to the boundaries of the flight envelope -- a higher fidelity approach will be necessary. Our proposal is to develop a physics-based integrated closure model suite that provides the best possible closure at any level of scale resolution from RANS to direct numerical simulations (DNS). The proposed approach similar to hybrid methods -- is based on accuracy-on-demand paradigm. It is called the partiallyaveraged Navier-Stokes (PANS) method and presents the user the option of choosing a computational effort level that is in commensurate with the flow physics and desired accuracy. The starting point ofthe research is the RANS stress transport equation (STE) model as it is the lowest level of closure at which the key physical effects can be introduced in a scientifically rigorous manner. RANS algebraic stress model (RANS-ASM) and PANS-ASM closures will then be formally extracted from RANS-STE closures leading to an integrated model. suite. For research planning and execution, the proposed work is divided into six tasks: (l) RANS-STE model development; (2) RANS-ASM closure extraction; (3) RANS validation and testing; (4) PANS-ASM development; (4) PANS improvement to minimize commutation error; and (6) , PANS-ASM testing and validation. Each task represents an important piece of progress in the proposed research. Apart from the PI, two full-time graduate students and one full-time postdoctoral fellow will be involved. The proposed work will directly support NASA research in the sub-topic area A.2.3.2. Other sub-areas that will benefit from the proposed research are highfidelity numerical simulations for unsteady flow fields (A.2.U), physics-based flow modeling for turbulence-chemistry interactions (A.2.2.1) and noise prediction tools (A,2.1.3). The PI has worked routinely with NASA researchers and many ofthe turbulence models developed by him have been incorporated in NASA codes (pAB3D and CFUD). All efforts will again be made for timely transition oftechnology to NASA

Description: Spacecraft generate huge amounts of data. A significant challenge for both human operators and autonomous control systems is ensuring that the right data (and combinations of data) are available at the right time for control and decision-making and ensuring that the data is at the right abstraction level. A key part of this process is data abstraction -- that is converting low-level analog or digital signals into higher-level data. We are proposing a data abstraction architecture that provides a provides a tool-box of components, connections and development environment that allow engineers to build  and maintain data abstraction systems. In addition, having a  well-defined data abstraction architecture allows data displays to be automatically generated and updated as the architecture develops. Thus, a data abstraction architecture can support both human decision-making as well as providing data services to autonomous control systems. We are also proposing to build an integrated development environment in which designers or operators can graphically build data abstraction architectures from standard components to accomplish their data tasks. Description: EXPERIMENTAL MEASUREMENTS AND COMPUTATIONAL PREDICTIONS OF CONJUGATE HEAT TRANSFER IN STATIONARY COOLED TURBINE VANE This proposal addresses the NASA ROA-2006 Topic A.4.2 - Lightweight, Durable Airframes and Engines for Supersonic Cruise Temperatures. One of the objectives within this topic is to develop and validate the conjugate heat transfer computational prediction of cooled turbine airfoils. The basis for this objective is the need to develop improved life-prediction and thermal analysis tools required for designs to operate at the sustained high temperatures encountered by supersonic cruise propulsion systems. Current design practice relies on separate analyses of the external and internal cooling of turbine airfoils. An iterative process is involved between the external and internal boundary conditions to arrive at the airfoil body temperature. It is, however, well known that the internal and external flows are coupled. A need exists to account for this coupling that would eliminate the iterations. A conjugate heat transfer analysis that combines external and internal heat transfer with computation of the conduction heat transfer within the solid body is required. Our proposed research addresses this need for a conjugate heat transfer analysis of turbine airfoils with a combined experimental and computational effort. The experimental effort involves use of a unique conducting model of a typical turbine vane to obtain detailed velocity and thermal field information that is critical for development and validation of computational simulation of the conjugate heat transfer mechanisms. This model will be designed to match the thermal characteristics of actual turbine vanes by matching the Biot number (ratio of conduction thermal resistance to convection thermal resistance) of the test model to that of the actual turbine airfoil. Currently, experimental data for such a matched Biot number model is non-existent, which is a tremendous hindrance to the development and validation of computational predictions of the conjugate heat transfer that is inherent in turbine airfoil cooling. For the proposed research, measurements using the matched Biot number model will include internal and external temperature distributions, heat flux measurements at selected locations, and thermal and velocity boundary layer measurements. The parallel computational effort for our proposed research will include development of improved computational techniques specifically tuned to conjugate heat transfer analyses. These computational techniques will be validated using predictions of the experimental matched Biot number model. This validated code will then be used to examine effects for the higher Mach number flows encountered at engine conditions.

Description: EFFECTS OF MICROGRAVITY UPON YEAST SUSCEPTIBILITY TO ANTIFUNGAL DRUGS: COUNTERMEASURE DEVELOPMENT ABSTRACT: The PharmaSat experiment and flight system are designed to measure the influence of microgravity upon yeast resistance to the antifungal agent posaconazole. Microgravity and modeled microgravity data suggest that resistance to azoles is increased, which can have an important effect upon management of fungal infections during space habitation. Owing to its excellent stability and broad spectrum of activity, posaconazole is being evaluated in vitro as a potential antifungal countermeasure. The experimental design is based upon an internationally recognized in-vitro laboratory testing method; in addition to determining the effect of the antifungal agent on yeast growth, cell viability will be monitored using bioluminescence, fluorescence, and colorimetry. The PharmaSat flight hardware will strongly leverage the recent technology demonstration of GeneSat (Ricco et a/., 2005), the first fully autonomous free-flyer system for multiwell cell culture and genetic analysis. To meet schedule and budget constraints, science experimental design will include cognizance of feasible development pathways using GeneSat as the hardware starting point.  The test yeast will be genetically engineered to express luciferase to confer bioluminescence, a green fluorescent protein reporter, or similar approach.  The selection of the yeast is between Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Candida albicans. Saccharomyces cerevisiae has been used in our previous modeled microgravity studies, and we are familiar with its genetics and morphology in modeled microgravity; however, it is a rare opportunistic pathogen in humans. Candida albicans is a potential candidate because it is used as a quality-control strain in the Clinical and Laboratories Standards institute ii/i27-2A standardized method for evaluating antifungal drugs, it is normal human flora; and it is the most common yeast that causes infection in humans. Statistical analysis of the data will be based upon the methods used to analyze longitudinal data, a more robust methodology than traditional end-point based analysis. Statistically relevant measurements will be supported by PharmaSatis 48-well capability, enabling the study of two different concentrations of the test yeast against 3 different concentrations of posaconazole. Data from this experiment will address the underlying hypothesis that "Yeasts growing in microgravity have an altered resistance to azole antifungal agents", a hypothesis with important implications for the prevention and management of fungal infections that may occur during space exploration

Description: TIMED CEDAR COLLABORATION STUDIES: ENERGENITICS AND DYNAMICS OF THE MLT The goal of this investigation is to enhance our understanding of the global energetics of the atmosphere, and its effect on the structure of the lower thermosphere. The energy budget is not well understood at this time because of the difficulty of measuring all the relevant parameters on both the local and global scales. For example, an accurate knowledge of Joule heating is important because it contributes >lo percent of the global thennospheric energy budget, and is a major factor in determining the global latitudinal gradients of temperature, wind, composition and hence the F-region electron density. In principle the global specification of conductivities .and Joule heating is currently possible using global coupled thermosphere/ionosphere models such as the TIMF,GCM, and also by using the AMIE technique. We have recently begun to validate these techniques, and show their usefulness. we have also begun to validate the GUVI conductance estimates by combining global estimates of electron density fiooj assimilation techniques with neutral densities fiom the TIMEGCM. This is another step towards global estimates of Joule heating.

Description: Coronal Dimming Regions as Proxies for Coronal Mass Ejections and Geomagnetic Storms Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are the most powerful geoeffective solar phenomena observed. Unfortunately, research has shown not all Earth-directed CMEs capable of observation by a coronagraph (Davey et al. 2004, Yashiro et a!. 2005). However, there is evidence that these missing CMEs do appear in the Kp index as geomagnetic storms (St. Cyr et al. 2000), giving us reason to believe that knowledge of the origins and properties of such CMEs might impact our predictive capabilities, and hence, their geoeffectiveness. We propose to use coronal dimming regions as proxies for CMEs and geomagnetic storms. Since coronal dimming regions are the origins of CMEs (Thompson et al. 1998, Harra & Sterling 2001), some statistical relationship must exist between these events. Using automated methods, we will determine physical and dynamic properties of coronal dimming regions and CMEs and establish levels of statistical correlation. We will also correlate the geomagnetic Kp index with properties of coronal dimming regions. By developing such proxies, we can better understand the physical relationship between coronal dimming regions and CMEs/geomagnetic storms, expanding the breadth and knowledge of the field. We will also provide in statistically significant quantities important physical parameters hitherto considered mainly on small scales. Additionally, such proxies give us some level of predictive capability for otherwise unobservable geoeffective CMEs, impacting our lives and technology. By considering this problem, we address the following NASA strategic goals: We improve our understand[ing] of the Sun and its effects on Earth (Strategic Sub-goal 3b), and advance scientific knowledge of the hazards present as humans explore space (Strategic Sub-goal 3c). Through this study, we improve our observational capabilities, our physical understanding, and our predictive abilities.

Description: EXPLORING THE DYNAMICS OF FLUX-EMERGENCE IN MAGNETICALLY-COMPLEX SOLAR ACTIVE REGIONS The dynamical evolution of active region magnetic fields provides insight into the processes of flux emergence and it relationship to sub-photospheric fluxtube dynamics. Moreover, an understanding of these processes allows us to explore the generation of free energy in the corona required to drive eruptive phenomena such as flares and CMEs. Active regions and sunspots are generally thought to form via the emergence of an -shaped fluxtube rising through the convection zone into the photosphere. Photospheric observations show that the most energetically productive active regions possess complex morphologies. Such complexity is evidenced, for example, by strong asymmetries between leading and following polarities where, typically, the flux of the leading polarity tends to be concentrated in large well-formed sunspots, whereas the following polarity flux tends to be more dispersed and fragmented. In addition, the axis connecting the leading and following polarities is tilted to the solar equator, and the tilted direction is very different for active regions which follow the Hale-Nicholson polarity law and those that dont. Observations of sunspot rotation and measurements of active region twist point to both a hemispheric and leading/following division with the rotation and twist being stronger in the leading polarity. The observed relationships between the twist and writhe of magnetic fields in Hale and non-Hale regions are important signatures of the interior processes influencing the dynamics and evolution of the buoyant -shaped fluxtubes responsible for active region formation. Furthermore, the relationship between observed sunspot rotation and the emergence of already-twisted fluxtubes and how sunspot and sunspot-group rotation drive helicity production and injection into the solar corona are key to divining the fundamental physics behind active region formation, evolution and activity. We propose to combine data analysis of a large amount of active regions from SOHO/MDI, BBSO, TRACE and YOHKOH and upcoming Solar-B, STEREO, and SDO/HMI, with improved sub-photospheric fluxtube models to explore the process of magnetic flux emergence and the generation of active region dynamics. Such a study is both crucial and necessary if we are to understand the links between the observed magnetic activities at the surface, the dynamo-generated magnetic fields in the interior, and solar transient phenomena.

Description: Prominences have long been associated with coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and provide an important component in our understanding of the Sun-Earth system as a whole. Although some prominences are long-lived and others erupt or disappear on short time scales, all types of prominences are dynamical and many show mass loss in observations through draining. There are several different potential mechanisms involved in causing such mass loss. The proposed work, motivated by the close connection between prominences and coronal mass ejections (CMEs), offers a detailed study of the variation in mass of various types of prominences by addressing four mechanisms involved in mass loss: draining along field lines, reconnection, cross-field diffusion, and MHD instabilities. The prominences in this study will range from those that lift and settle (sometimes called a failed or frustrated eruption), to those that exhibit a partial prominence eruption, to those that have a complete prominence eruption. Included in this study of prominence flows and concomitant mass variations will be a range of CMEs that exhibit the various types of eruptive prominence behavior. A search for a relationship between the nature of a prominence eruption and the pre-eruption flow patterns will be conducted as well as an examination of the basic CME properties (e.g., speed, mass, and energy) that are associated with the different types of prominence eruption.

Description: The leading theory for lunar origin is the giant impact hypothesis, which links what was perhaps the largest impact experienced by the Earth during its accretion to the formation of our Moon. The impact theory is favored for its potential to explain key properties of the Earth-Moon system such as its high angular momentum, the low lunar iron content, and lunar volatile depletion. Models of the Moon's formation from an impact with the Earth provide important details about the "starting conditions" for our particular Earth-Moon system. The wealth of dynamical, compositional, and geophysical knowledge about the Earth and Moon provides an abundance of constraints with which to compare (and challenge) modeling results, making the Earth-Moon system perhaps the best test case for developing an understanding of giant impacts. Such an understanding is helping to reveal that multiple other satellites in our solar system Likely also originated from such events. Large impacts are believed to be common during late stage solid planet formation, and because they yield extremely hot planets and debris disks, might provide an observable signature of planet formation in extrasolar systems (e.g. Stern 1994, Kenyon & Bromley 2005). This proposal requests renewed support of a program focusing on the impact-generation of terrestrial planet satellites. Task 1 addresses the origin of the Moon from a giant impact, using a variety of numerical and analytical techniques, while Task 2 involves impact simulations of a potential impact origin for the satellites of Mars. Task 3 explores whether there is an upper limit to planet size for which collisions will produce large satellites, and whether, e.g., extrasolar "super earths" containing - 5 to 10 Earth masses could harbor potentially habitable Earth-sized satellites.

Description: We propose to use our Mars brines and evaporites facility to perform experiments that simulate the conditions on Mars under which sulfates and other evaporites are formed. In this way, it will be possible to identify observed salt mineralogies and sequences on Mars as either alterations of an original direct precipitate, or as products of processes fundamentally different from direct precipitation from water. The proposed work is divided into two tasks: Task 1. The first produces evaporites from simulated Mars conditions, past and present, and Task 2. The second produces brines and basaltic alteration products under a variety of Mars-like conditions. In both tasks, special emphasis will be placed on the observed mineralogy of salts at Meridiani and elsewhere, and on the potential role of sulfuric acid. The mineralogy of evaporites will be determined using X-ray diffraction spectroscopy and TEM and microprobe anaysis. Brine cation and anion abundances will be determined using Ion Chromotography and Atomic Emission Sectroscopy. Salts, predominently sulfates, are widespread on Mars, in a variety of geologic settings. Determining whether more clement climate conditions produced them, and whether these conditions were local or global, transient or long-lived, will require a more complete knowledge of mineral species present and their geologic context (Bibring et at. 2005). With the significant new knowledge from the MER rovers and the Mars Express mission of salts on Mars, now is the time for the fundamental laboratory data that connects the physical and chemical conditions on early Mars to what is observed in the sediments at the surface. Description: MODELING THE IMPACT OF STORMTIME ELECTRODYNAMICS ON THE MID AND LOW LATITUDE IONOSPHERE The goal of this research is to determine the circumstances leading to the massive restructuring of the mid and low latitude ionosphere and the development of large-scale bite-outs of electron density at low latitudes during geomagnetic storms. Good examples of these features occurred during the Halloween storm in October 2003. Maps of total electron content (TEC) showed a factor of four increase at mid latitudes, and measurements of electron density by the DMSP satellite at 850 km indicated the ionosphere had virtually disappeared over a wide latitude swath at low latitudes. The depleted region, or "bite-out," was ccompanied by smaller scale ionospheric irregularities, or bubbles, on its flanks. It is expected that the dramatic gradients were created by exceptionally large upward ExB plasma drifts, raising the ionosphere to higher altitudes, transporting plasma poleward, and driving the huge depletions at low latitude. This study will investigate the interaction and feedback between the two main sources of the plasma drift -- the prompt penetration (PP) and disturbance dynamo (DD) electric fields, and determine the cause of the massive restructuring of plasma at mid and low latitudes during storms. This project is a "linked" proposal between research teams at University of Colorado (PI Tim Fuller-Rowell) and Rice University (PI Stan Sazykin). The success of the project relies on the self-consistent coupling between physical processes in the thermosphere, ionosphere, and plasmasphere (as captured in the CTIPe model) and the inner magnetosphere (as captured in the RCM). Combining these two models includes both dynamo and penetration electrodynamics, and consistently handle the feedback between the two regimes. This study is therefore unique in its ability to couple the various domains and address the science questions in a rigorous mathematical approach. This study will: 1) Determine the physical processes leading to the large vertical plasma drifts and the interaction and feedback between the penetration and dynamo electric fields, 2. Determine the impact on the mid and low latitude ionosphere including the cause of the massive restructuring of plasma density, and 3) Investigate the possible causes of the strong longitude dependence in the storm-time response. The first phase of the study will perform the comprehensive coupling of the CTlPe and RCM models where the polar cap boundary, the neutral wind driven dynamo currents, and the field-aligned magnetospheric currents are consistent between the two codes. The effects of under and over shielding in the inner magnetosphere will be implicitly included in the field-aligned currents and the potential solver. Numerical experiment will be performed with a goal of understanding the complex interaction between the geophysical domains including the electrodynamic feedback between PP and DD. For validation, the coupled model will be used to simulate the recent storms targeted by the recent CDAW workshop. The chosen storms have good global and regional coverage for TEC, have reasonable measurement of the electric fields, and have well developed experimental/observational databases. The potential benefit of this study for space weather is clear. Large-scale changes in the ionosphere impact GPS navigation signals and alter the propagation of HF radio-wave communication. The large-scale ionospheric changes are also associated with the generation of small scale ionospheric irregularities responsible for scintillations on satellite communication signals. Understanding the physical processes will lead to the possibility of improvement in predicting and forecasting the storm-time plasma redistribution and the creation of irregularities. This proposal targets the specific research topic of the LWS TR&T Focused Science Topic"Storm effects on the electrodynamics and the middle and low latitude ionosphere" .

Description: TRANSPORT AND LOSS OF THERMAL PLASMA FROM THE INNER MAGNETOSPHERE The goal of this proposal is to resolve a long-standing controversy as to the ultimate fate of plasmaspheric thermal plasma by using multi-spacecraft and ground-based observations coupled with operational MHD, convection, and circulation models. During storm times thermal plasma from the inner magnetosphere in plasmaspheric plumes may flow into one or several locations such as into the magnetopause boundary layer, out into the magnetosheath through the reconnection site, into the polar cusp, or convect over the polar cap and into the tail. Correlative observations from IMAGE, Cluster, Polar and LANL satellites, simulations, and model results will show the latitudinal and longitudinal time structure of plasmaspheric plumes and how these structures evolve as the thermal plasma, that is contained in the plumes, is lost from the inner magnetosphere. Our proposal is for conducting research with respect to NASA Goal 3.2: Understanding the Sun and its effects on the Earth and the solar system. Specifically we seek to make progress in understanding a fundamental physical process of the space environment, a main NASA strategic science outcome.

Description: THE FORMATION OF PROTOPLANETARY DISKS FROM INFALLING ENVELOPS SUMMARY: The initial mass and other properties of the proto-planetary disks are established during the phase of infall from the molecular envelope. While there have been many studies of disks in later stages, it has been difficult to study them during the early stages. With the combination of the Spitzer data and extensive observations at longer wavelengths that we have obtained, we can now attack this problem. We will compare the large data base to models ofthe evolution during the infall phases. Based on evolutionary models developed during the current project, we can already see that the data show a much larger range of luminosity at a given evolutionary stage than predicted by simple models. One solution, suggested by our discovery of very low luminosity objects, is that accretion onto the central object is episodic. We will produce new evolutionary models that include this effect and use the large data base becoming available to constrain the nature of this episodic accretion. In this picture, the properties of the disk at the end of infall may be set by the timing of the episodic accretion. Thus this work will provide important insight into the preconditions for planet formation.

Description: Fredericksburg High School's Aeroscience Program (FHSAP) has been challenged by three factors which limit its potential for replication and dissemination - nozzle and fuel grain fabrication and the availability of a portable launch tower. A JSC grant (number NNJ04VC15G) awarded in April 2004 has allowed research towards alternative fuel grain and nozzle materials for educational application. Six preliminary static tests were conducted in 2004; the data collected reflected a low oxidizer mass flow rate throughout the system. After reviewing the data and system, it was concluded that the multiple orifices on the feed system were not providing the necessary mass flow rate. Also, the diameter differences throughout the oxidizer feed system caused cavitations, resulting in insufficient oxidizer flow. To correct the problem, new tanks and valves were purchased and hoses became uniform in diameter. Testing is still underway to complete the proposed research. By the end of the research period, FHSAP will have completed 24 tests encompassing four alternative fuels and five alternative nozzle materials. This grant renewal is requesting funding to complete the research phase to find affordable and effective materials that can be utilized safely in a public education environment. Specifically, this grant renewal is for a launch tower and to cover the launch support fee at White Sands Missile Range (WSMR). Six tests were performed to analyze the performance of various nozzle/fuel grain combinations. These tests revealed critical information regarding the oxidizer flow system hardware and its performance. During the tests, a "dirty burn" was noticed and a low oxidizer flow rate was suspected. Upon investigation, calculations were reviewed, cold-flow tests were performed, and it was found that the inner diameter of the oxidizer feed hoses were not consistent. This caused pressure differences and cavitations resulting in the confirmation of a low oxidizer flow. A new oxidizer tank, new hoses, a new solenoid, and some simple modifications were applied to fix the mass flow rate problem. The solenoid, a 1-inch piloted solenoid donated by Moog, was sufficient for the proper oxidizer mass flow rate. Description: INVESTIGATIONS INTO IOS SO2 LIFE CYCLE  ABSTRACT:   IO's S02 dominated atmosphere is supplied by tidally-driven volcanism, and the sublimation ofthe highly volatile S02 surface frost.  Yet, whether sublimation or volcanism is the dominant atmospheric support mechanism on 10 is unknown. We plan to obtain spatially resolved 4-micron spectroscopy of 10 to detect S02 gas on 10 at a density of 1016 cm-2 or more. These observations will provide the first simultaneous measurement of the dayside S02 gas and frost distribution within lo's thermally inactive regions at high (300 km) spatial resolution; and the first simultaneous measurement of the S02 gas and magma temperatures of lo's thermally active regions.  From these measurements the atmospheric response to diurnal (day-to-night) variations in insolation (surface temperature) will be documented. Since a volcanic atmosphere would have no response to diurnal variations these observations will clarify the relative importance of sublimation and volcanism in the support of lo's atmosphere. Additionally, we will define the amount of re-surfacing on 10 occurring due to the condensation of volcanically released S02 gas. We plan to obtain the ground-based observations during the New Horizons (NH) spacecraft flyby of Jupiter. NH will monitor lo's dusty plume activity, but has no means for obtaining spatially resolved observations of lo's dayside atmosphere and measurement of the gas abundances of lo's thermally active regions is limited to hot (1000 K) volcanically active regions producing abundances of several times 1019 cm-2 or more. Therefore, the ground-based observing campaign complements the planned NH observations of the Jovian system, and fulfills NASAs goals of developing a balanced overall program of science, exploration, and aeronautics consistent with the redirection of the human spaceflight program to focus on exploration; advancing scientific knowledge of the origin and history of the solar system; making progress in learning how the Sun's family of planets and bodies evolve.
