Description: Physical Observations of Very Young Dynamical Families of Asteoroids  We propose to make a suite of observations of the youngest asteroids known. We will continue our current program of observing young dynamical families by following up on a staggering new development: we now have precise dates for asteroids only hundreds of thousands of years old, after being created by catastrophic inter-asteroidal collisions. Such collisions create fragments of the original body, a few of which may become satellites of each other, but most of which go into similar, independent heliocentric orbits forming asteroid families. New theoreticallnumericai investigations have determined precise ages of 7 young, compact familieslclusters. For instance the Karin cluster within the Koronis family formed 5.75 +/- 0.05 My ago while the Datura cluster formed just 450 +/- 50 thousand years ago. These are the first non-radiometric determinations of ages of events in the asteroid belt. We exploit these advances to study the rates of fundamental asteroidal processes (including space weathering of asteroid surfaces by solar wind and micrometeoroid bombardment, loss of volatiles, early evolution of just-formed asteroid satellites, and the Yarkovsky Effect) by observing the properties of just-formed family members before they have had time to suffer further collisions, dynamical dispersal, or surface modifications.  We are making astronomical observations (low- and medium-resolution spectroscopy, adaptive optics imaging, thermal radiometry, and lightcurve photometry) of members -- spanning a range of sizes -- of the Karin, Iannini, and Veritas familieslclusters (just millions of years old) and propose to extend our observations to four even younger clusters (just hundreds of thousands of years old). We use Keck, VLT, IRTF, and Gemini (and smaller telescopes) to obtain data comparable with published data on non-family or older asteroids. The theoretical advances that have permitted precise age determinations of families present an extraordinary opportunity to quantitatively address many of the central puzzles in asteroid research.

Description: Observatory Toward Discovery Of Short-Periodic Terrestrial Planets And Rare Jovian-Class Companions To M Dwarf Stars We propose to expand our search efforts to detect extrasolar planets around M dwarf stars (stars with half a solar mass or less) using highly precise velocity measurements. Low mass stars like M dwarfs hold the promise to find planets with smaller masses than currently possible for solar-type stars. For some of our targets we have already pushed the detection limit down to a few Earth masses inside the habitable zone close to the parent star. We aim to extend our planet search programs using the Hobby-Eberly Telescope (HET) at McDonald Observatory and the Very Large Telescope (VLT) at the European Southern Observatory in Chile. We will employ the iodine absorption cell technique to measure the stellar radial velocities of 150-200 M dwarfs with a precision level to detect companions with masses ranging from a few Earths to Neptunes and gas giants more similar to Jupiter. Searching for M dwarf planets is a critical test for planet formation models and can offer a first glimpse at the frequency of Earth-like worlds in our galaxy. Our results will be important for future NASA missions with the goal to find and characterize extrasolar planets (e.g. KEPLER, SIM, JWST).

Description: TRANSPORT AND LOSS OF THERMAL PLASMA FROM THE INNER MAGNETOSPHERE The goal of this proposal is to resolve a long-standing controversy as to the ultimate fate of plasmaspheric thermal plasma by using multi-spacecraft and ground-based observations coupled with operational MHD, convection, and circulation models. During storm times thermal plasma from the inner magnetosphere in plasmaspheric plumes may flow into one or several locations such as into the magnetopause boundary layer, out into the magnetosheath through the reconnection site, into the polar cusp, or convect over the polar cap and into the tail. Correlative observations from IMAGE, Cluster, Polar and LANL satellites, simulations, and model results will show the latitudinal and longitudinal time structure of plasmaspheric plumes and how these structures evolve as the thermal plasma, that is contained in the plumes, is lost from the inner magnetosphere. Description: Using Satellite Data and Fully Coulpled Regional Hydrologic, Ecological and Atmospheric Models to Study Complex Coastal Environmental Processes This proposal seeks to improve our understanding of how linked upland and estuarine ecosystems respond to combined changes in the hydrological and nutrient cycles that result from changes in climate and land use/ land cover (LULC). Within this broad framework we will focus on five specific questions. 1) What is the relationship between global climate forcing and seasonal-to-interan nual climate variability and extreme storm events over the Gulf Coast region? 2) What are the spatial patterns in LULC as defined by satellite data in the Gulf Coast region? 3) How does riverine nutrient export to Gulf Coast estuaries vary with LULC patterns and hydrologic conditions? 4) What is the relationship between the frequency of extreme events in the hydrologic and nutrient cycles and the mean productivity and the resiliency of productivity in Gulf Coast estuaries? 5) Can we use the answers to the questions above to predict the response of Gulf Coast estuaries to future climate perturbations? Extreme weather events are given particular attention in this study because of their dominant influence on hydrological and nutrient dynamics within the Gulf Coast region, and also because such events are typically not well represented in regional scale modeling efforts. Our group brings together research expertise from a diversity of fields that includes climate modeling, remote sensing analysis, biogeochemical cycling in watersheds, surface hydrology and estuary ecology. To address the above questions we will develop a nested regional atmospheric modeling system augmented with satellite remote sensing data to predict high-resolution spatial and temporal hydrometeorological variables for the Gulf Coast region. At the highest detail level, we will characterize two biologically distinct watersheds in the semi-arid region of Central and South Central Texas, the Nueces River watershed and the San Antonio / Guadalupe watershed using modeling data, existing satellite observations, existing water quality data and new fieldwork. A key consideration in each component of the project will also be an assessment of the uncertainties related to data products and modeling in order to derive confidence values for the model's predictive capabilities. Precipitation in the south central United States is highly variable and thus resource availability in Gulf Coast estuaries is highly dependent on the frequency and distribution of extreme hydrological events. This type of climate pattern creates a watershed/estuary dynamic that is different from the terrigenous nutrient driven systems typical of the eastern coast of the US and also different from the ocean dominated systems that typify much of the west coast. In addition to representing a significant portion of the Gulf Coast and other semi-arid coastlines around the world, these types of highly variable systems may be a good model for imminent changes to coastal systems in response to climate change. Global climate model (GCM) predictions suggest that as climate warms, the Earth will experience an increase in the frequency and intensity of flooding and drought, changes in their spatial occurrence, and a redistribution of water availability on land. Nearly all of these predictions have been carried out on global scale models that have very poor resolution at the regional scale. The frequency and intensity of extreme streamflow events in semi-arid watersheds is also highly influenced by changes in LULC and water management methods such as impoundments and controlled water releases.

Description: TEXAS ENGINEERING EXPERIMENT STATION RANS AND VARIABLE-RESOLUTION PANS MODELS FOR SEPARATED FLOWS The complexity of the separation problem and its crucial role in aeronautics applications dictates a two-tier research approach. For applications involving steady separation, a sophisticated Reynolds averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) model may be adequate. For applications with unsteady separation - e.g., high-lift airfoils operating close to the boundaries of the flight envelope -- a higher fidelity approach will be necessary. Our proposal is to develop a physics-based integrated closure model suite that provides the best possible closure at any level of scale resolution from RANS to direct numerical simulations (DNS). The proposed approach similar to hybrid methods -- is based on accuracy-on-demand paradigm. It is called the partiallyaveraged Navier-Stokes (PANS) method and presents the user the option of choosing a computational effort level that is in commensurate with the flow physics and desired accuracy. The starting point ofthe research is the RANS stress transport equation (STE) model as it is the lowest level of closure at which the key physical effects can be introduced in a scientifically rigorous manner. RANS algebraic stress model (RANS-ASM) and PANS-ASM closures will then be formally extracted from RANS-STE closures leading to an integrated model. suite. For research planning and execution, the proposed work is divided into six tasks: (l) RANS-STE model development; (2) RANS-ASM closure extraction; (3) RANS validation and testing; (4) PANS-ASM development; (4) PANS improvement to minimize commutation error; and (6) , PANS-ASM testing and validation. Each task represents an important piece of progress in the proposed research. Apart from the PI, two full-time graduate students and one full-time postdoctoral fellow will be involved. The proposed work will directly support NASA research in the sub-topic area A.2.3.2. Other sub-areas that will benefit from the proposed research are highfidelity numerical simulations for unsteady flow fields (A.2.U), physics-based flow modeling for turbulence-chemistry interactions (A.2.2.1) and noise prediction tools (A,2.1.3). The PI has worked routinely with NASA researchers and many ofthe turbulence models developed by him have been incorporated in NASA codes (pAB3D and CFUD). All efforts will again be made for timely transition oftechnology to NASA

Description: Title - "The Effect of Spaceflight Analog Conditions on Genotypic and Phenotypic Characteristics of Staphylococcus Aureus:  An Evaluation toward Improved Microbial Risk Assessment"/Graduate Student Stipend for Sarah Castro Abstract: The assessment of risk associated with infectious disease during spaceflight has historically been based on medical experience and expert opinion ofthe crew exposure to microorganisms that were expected during the mission. Within the last few years, the use of quantitative models has permitted a systematic approach to determining infectious disease risk in given environments. These models have provided an approach to understanding and communicating risk while simultaneously determining knowledge gaps which lead to uncertainty in the risk assessment. During the development of such a model at the Johnson Space Center, the uncertainty in behavior of microorganisms in response to spaceflight conditions, specifically microgravity, was indicated as a key knowledge gap in the assessment. While some research has been successfully completed using Gram negative organisms, such as Salmonella typhimurium, an absence of information was available for Gram positive organisms. One such organism. Staphylococcus aureus, is a ubiquitous opportunistic pathogen that is commonly found in spacecraft. S. aureus can be the causative agent of food poisoning, pneumonia, and dermal infections. While normally not infectious through the environment to a healthy individual, slight changes in its genetic or physical properties could increase the risk of this organism to the crew. As such, understanding the effect of spaceflight on Gram positive, opportunistic pathogens, such as S. aureus, is very important to decrease uncertainty in the risk assessment modeling process. As this modeling project is currently underway, rapid collection of data on microbial characteristics during flight is necessary to provide information within a useftil timeline.

Description: Using Satellite Observations and a Fully Coupled Land-Atmosphere-Chemistry Model to Study the Coupling between Vegetation and the Hydrologic Cycle through Biogenic Emissions Pathways Vegetation plays a key role in modulating the Earth's hydrologic cycle and climate. Vegetation not only affects precipitation by changing heat fluxes near the surface, but it also influences climate and the hydrologic cycle by indirectly altering the concentration of atmospheric aerosols. Biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) emitted by vegetation play an important role in the formation of secondary organic aerosols (SOA), which influence the formation of clouds and which may redistribute the pattern of precipitation. The objectives of the proposed research are to: 1) Quantify the contribution of BVOCs to atmospheric aerosol concentration and cloud formation with the aid of in-situ observations, satellite data, and a coupled numerical model; 2) Assess the effects of SOA produced by the oxidation of BVOCs on precipitation by using satellite-derived aerosol and cloud data; 3) Examine the strength of the coupling between vegetation and the hydrologic cycle through biogenic emissions pathways. To achieve the goals, I will combine satellite data, ground-based observations and modeling together as a means to investigate this coupling. The interaction between vegetation and SOA is given particular attention in this study because vegetation is controlling the emissions of biogenic compounds. Assessment of the uncertainties related to satellite data products and modeling is also a key consideration for the research. This research will make significant contributions to our current understanding of the links between biogenic emissions, SOA, and the hydrologic cycle. The proposed research is related to NASA's strategic plan to develop a scientific understanding of Earth's system and its response to natural or human-induced changes and to improve prediction of climate, weather, and natural hazards. It is also relevant to the Earth Science Division focus areas including ecosystems, biogeochemistry, and water cycle.

Description: "OPTIMUM BAND SELECTION TECHNIQUES UNDER HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGE ANALYSIS FOR MATERIAL IDENTIFICATION AND CLASSIFICATION"THE COMPLEXITY INVOLVED IN COLLECTING, STORING, ANALYSIS AND PROCESSING OF VOLUMINOUS REMOTE SENSING MULTI-DIMENSIONAL DATA FOR AN ARRAY OF "EARTH SYSTEM SCIENCE" APPLICATIONS IS A WELL KNOWN PROBLEM TO NASA. THE RECENT HYPERSPECTRAL IMAGING (HSI) TECHNOLOGY HAVE EVOLVED FROM ITS EARLIER VERSION OF MULTISPECTRAL IMAGING (MSI). IN HSI, IMAGES ARE ACQUIRED USING HUNDREDS OF SPECTRAL CHANNELS WHEN COMPARED TO FEWER CHANNELS IN MSI. HOWEVER, OVER THE YEARS THERE HAS NOT BEEN MUCH SIGNIFICANT DEVELOPMENT OF PROCESSING ALGORITHMS FOR THESE EVER GROWING (IN THE SPECTRAL DIRECTION) ELECTRO-OPTICAL DATA SETS. THE NEED TO COME UP WITH INTELLIGENT BAND SELECTION TECHNIQUES IS EVEN STRONGER SINCE WE ARE MOVING IN TO THE ERA OF ULTRASPECTRAL IMAGING (USI). THE USI TECHNOLOGY USUALLY CONSISTS OF MEASUREMENTS TAKEN IN THOUSANDS OF SPECTRAL CHANNELS. IN ALL THREE IMAGING TECHNOLOGIES, EACH SPATIAL PIXEL IS TREATED AS A COLUMN VECTOR THAT CONTAINS SPECTRAL INFORMATION FROM EACH CHANNEL. DUE TO THE EVER GROWING HIGHER SPECTRAL DIMENSIONALITY OF THE REMOTE SENSING DATA, EACH IMAGE PIXEL VECTOR POSSESSES MORE INFORMATION THAN EVER BEFORE. HOWEVER, DUE TO NOISE AND OTHER UNAVOIDABLE ATMOSPHERIC INTERFERENCE, A PURE SIGNATURE FOR A CLASS KNOWN AS THE END-MEMBER MAY BE REPRESENTED BY A MIXTURE OR COMBINATION OF SPECTRAL SIGNATURE FROM NEIGHBORING PIXELS. TO ENCAPSULATE THE UNCERTAINTY CREATED BY A PIXEL VECTOR DUE TO NOISE AND OTHER INTERFERENCE DEMANDS A STOCHASTIC TREATMENT. THIS PROPOSAL FOCUSES ON DERIVING CLASSIFICATION AND TARGET DETECTION METHODS BASED ON NON-TRANSFORMED DATA. THE INTENT IS THAT WITHOUT THE COST OF THE DECORRELATING TRANSFORM, THAT THE DERIVED CLASSIFICATION ALGORITHMS WILL HAVE SUITABLE COMPLEXITY FOR USE IN PRACTICAL CLASSIFICATION SYSTEMS. EARLIER RESEARCH HAS INVESTIGATED USING A REDUCED COLOR SPACE FOR IMPLEMENTING MATERIAL CLASSIFICATION OFHSI DATA. THIS "BEST BAND" SELECTION (BBS) METHOD RELIES SOLELY ON THE DETERMINISTIC DISTANCE MEASURES OF MINIMUM EUCLIDEAN DISTANCE AND SPECTRAL ANGLE MAPPER. THE RESULTS OF THIS RESEARCH WERE ALGORITHMS THAT GAVEENHANCED CLASS SEPARATION USING A REDUCED NUMBER OF SPECTRAL COLOR BANDS. OUR CURRENT RESEARCH EXTENDS THE OPTIMUM BAND SELECTION TECHNIQUES IN TWO SEPARATE DIRECTIONS. THE FIRST IS TO EXTEND THE BBS RESULTS TO STOCHASTIC DISTANCE METRICS SUCH AS HIDDEN MARKOV AND LEIBLER-KULLBACK MEASURES. STUDIES HAVE SHOWN THAT THE STOCHASTIC DISTANCE MEASURES CAN RESULT IN IMPROVED CLASSIFICATION PERFORMANCE RELATIVE TO DETERMINISTIC METRICS. TO DATE, THE PROBLEM OF BEST BAND SELECTION USING STOCHASTIC METRICS HAS NOT BEEN ADDRESSED IN THE LITERATURE. THE ISSUE OF STOCHASTIC MEASURES FOR BBS WILL BE THE PRIMARY FOCUS OF THE PROPOSED RESEARCH. THE SECOND DIRECTION FOR EXTENDING BEST BAND SELECTION IS IN INCORPORATING SENSOR MODELS OF HSI DATA COLLECTION INTO THE BBS ALGORITHM. WE WILL SPECIFICALLY EXTEND THE BBS METHOD USING DERIVED ANALYTICAL MODELS OF SPECTRAL PROFILES.

Description: PLANETS AND SATELLITES SOUTHWEST RESEARCH INSTITUTE THIS PROPOSAL CONTAINS FOUR TASKS CONCERNING THE EARLY EVOLUTION OF THE OUTER SOLAR SYSTEM. TASK 1 EXAMINES THE EVOLUTION OF A PROTOSATELLITE DISK ORBITING A GROWING GAS PLANET, IN PARTICULAR ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR THE CONFIGURATIONS, MASSES AND COMPOSITIONS OF RESULTING REGULAR SATELLITE SYSTEM. THE OBJECTIVE IS TO MODEL THE FORMATION OF JUPITER'S GALILEAN SATELLITES FROM A GAS-STRAVED CIRCUMPLANETARY ACCRETION DISK WITHIN THE CONTEXT OF THE EARLIEST EVOLUTION OF THE PLANET ITSELF, AND TO ASSESS THE POSSIBILITY THAT EARLIER GENERATIONS OF SATELLITES MAY HAVE FORMED BUT BEEN LOST THROUGH DISK INTERACTIONS. TASK 2 ADDRESSES SEVERAL ASPECTS OF THE SATURNIAN SATELLITE SYSTEM AND THE DOMINANCE OF THIS SYSTEMS TOTAL MASS BY A SINGLE SATELLITE, TITAN. WE PROPOSE TO EVALUTE THE POTENTIAL FOR TITAN TO BE LEFT AS A SOLE LARGE SATELLITE DUE TO ITS ABILITY TO OPEN A GAP IN ITS PROTOSATELLITE DISK, AND TO INVESTIGATE WHETHER RELATED DISK INTERACTIONS COULD ACCOUNT FOR TITAN'S CURRENT ECCENTRICITY AND THE LARGE INCLINATION OF LAPETUS. Description: THERMOMECHANICAL PROCESSING AND MODELING OF HIGH TEMPERATURE SMA'S FOR MULTIFUNCTIONAL ENGINE COMPONENTS Project Description We propose to fabricate Ti49.2Pt20Ni30.8 and Ti49.2Pd30Ni20.8 HTSMAs and process them by at least two different processing techniques, which include Equal Channel Angular Extrusion (ECAE) and rolling/drawing. Superior material behavior can be obtained by varying the percentage of reduction and the temperature of rolling. ECAE is a severe plastic deformation (SPD) technique and can permit application of a large amount of uniform strain without reducing the cross section of the material.  This processing technique combined with post processing techniques such as marforming, aging and other thermomechanical treatment techniques have been shown to provide superior thermomechanical response in SMAs. The proposed processing techniques will be aimed at improving the thermomechanical performance of the material specifically focusing on (1) texturing and texture strengthening using ECAE, (2) minimizing high temperature creep effects by grain refinement/strengthening by deformation twinning in austenite/compound twinning in martensite (3) eliminating large precipitates and, by using Nirich compositions for smaller precipitates, induce precipitation hardening for suppressing plastic deformation and grain growth. Calorimetric effects, microstructure and thermomechanical response will be initially analyzed. The phase diagram ofthe material will be generated by a series of tension and compression tests. The material will also be tested under fixed temperature 'and stress to document the visco-plastic behavior of the material. The visco-plastic behavior of the material due to microstructural thermally activated dislocation motion, atomic diffusion, grain sliding and grain growth may be captured in terms of macroscopic parameters of stress, strain, temperature and time. The need to develop a rate dependent model is motivated by experimental evidence suggesting the presence of significant rate/time effects observed in moderate to high composition palladium and platinum based alloys. The existing phenomenological SMA model capable of predicting complex loading paths will be extended to incorporate the time dependent behavior observed in high temperature SMAs.  Viscosity coefficient and strain rate will be input parameters coupled with the transformation temperatures, maximum transformation strain and the stress influence coefficients to effectively capture the visco-plastic behavior in the material. In summary, the objectives of the proposed research are to, (1) investigate the effect processing techniques on the visco-plastic behavior of High Temperature Shape Memory Alloys (HTSMAs) (2) develop a constitutive SMA model incorporating visco-plasticity to capture the high temperature creep behavior (3) use the model predictions to the effectively predict the thermomechanical response of the HTSMA fabricated by different processing techniques. The key outcomes from the proposed research are identified as, (1) developing a deeper understanding on the effects of different processing techniques on the visco-plastie behavior and the overall thermomechanical behavior of HTSMAs, (2) developing the first thermomechanical constitutive SMA model capturing the high temperature creep effects to predict the HTSMA behavior, (3) implementing the model in a 3-D environment for FEA of smart structures with HTSMAs. (4) strengthening the partnership between NASA and Texas A&M University. The proposed phenomenological SMA model is designed with the purposes of developing an improved prediction tools for obtaining accurate predictions capturing the unique behavior observed in high temperature SMAs and thereby aid in the development of smart structures incorporating HTSMAs for various aerospace applications.

Description: FORMATION OF SATELLITES  Satellite formation appears to be a natural byproduct of planet formation, given the multitude of satellites in our solar system. Here we propose to develop models for the origin of Jupiter's Galilean satellites, including volcanic lo, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto (Task I). Galileo results suggest that all three of the outer satellites may possess liquid water subsurface oceans (e.g., Schubert et al. 2004), with intriguing astrobiological implications in the case of Europa. We also propose to model the origin of the large Uranian satellites (Task 2). This satellite system resembles the Galilean system, but it orbits a planet with a 90 degree obliquity and so may have originated differently. Many of the outer satellites are high-priority targets for planetary exploration, and the conditions of their origin have important implications for the satellites' compositional, thermal, and interior properties. The satellites may also provide clues to conditions in the early outer solar system, and to giant planet formation processes. In Task 1, we propose to improve multiple aspects of the Canup & Ward (2001, 2002, 2006) "slow-inflow" model for the origin of the Galilean satellites and assess its implications for Callistojs state. We will 1) develop a thermal model for the gas disk that is self-consistently coupled to our N-body accretion simulations; 2) incorporate a model for the time-dependent inflow of gas and solids to the protosatellite disk based on models of giant planet formation; 3) consider the contribution of capture processes to the protosatellite disk solid component; and 4) calculate accretional temperature profiles for Callisto using realistic impact histories and heat transfer processes to determine the implications of our model for Callisto's partially differentiated interior. In Task 2, we propose to 1) simulate Uranus tipping impacts, 2) develop a numerical model for the viscous evolution of an initially hot impact-generated disk as it spreads and cools, and 3) model satellite rowth in the resulting gas-free environment.

Description: LUNAR RADIATION ENVIRONMENT AND REGOLITH SHIELDING EXPERIMENT The Lunar Regolith Shielding Experiment (LRSE) is a Lunar Sortie Investigation designed to address 2 of the 3 goal categories of the initial short duration lunar sortie missions, as identified in the NASA Exploration Systems Architecture Study (ESAS) Report. LRSE will perform high priority `emplacement' science by collecting long-term measurements of the lunar radiation environment (GCR, SEP, and albedo neutrons) and monitoring its changes as well as directly measure the shielding properties in-situ of the lunar regolith. The LRSE will also provide unique and important opportunities to perform In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) technology demonstrations by drilling, digging and manipulating samples of lunar regolith to construct simple lunar radiation storm shelters. The LRSE lunar Sortie concept consists of placing two identical, autonomous radiation detectors on the lunar surface, one buried underneath a blanket of regolith simulating a radiation storm shelter, and one sitting exposed on the surface as a `control' detector and to measure and monitor the unshielded long term radiation environment. The radiation detectors would be near `build-to-print' copies of the RAD (Radiation Assessment Detector) instrument, which is currently being developed for ESMD to characterize the radiation environment on the surface of Mars as part of the 2009 Mars Science Laboratory (MSL). RAD is small, lightweight (1.6 kg) and designed to operate completely autonomously to measure the GCR, SEP and back-scattered albedo neutron radiation environment on the surface.

Description: PREDICTION OF FOIL BEARING PERFORMANCE: A COMPUTATIONAL MODEL ANCHORED TO TEST DATATHE STATIC LOAD CAPACITY AND DYNAMIC FORCED PERFORMANCE OF GAS FOIL BEARINGS (GFBS) DEPEND LARGELY ON THE MATERIAL PROPERTIES OF THE SUPPORT ELASTIC STRUCTURE, I.E. A SMOOTH FOIL ON TOP OF BUMP STRIPS. CONVENTIONAL MODELS INCLUDE ONLY THE BUMPS AS AN EQUIVALENT STIFFNESS UNIFORMLY DISTRIBUTED AROUND THE BEARING CIRCUMFERENCE. MORE COMPLEX MODELS COUPLE DIRECTLY THE ELASTIC DEFORMATIONS OF THE TOP FOIL TO THE BUMP UNDERLYING STRUCTURE AS WELL AS TO THE HYDRODYNAMICS OF THE GAS FILM. THE MORE ELABORATE MODELS, ALTHOUGH AIDING TO IMPROVE PREDICTIONS OF GFB PERFORMANCE AS COMPARED TO TEST DATA, DEMAND OF EXCESSIVE COMPUTATIONAL TIMES. ALL COMPUTATIONAL MODELS RELY ON A NUMBER OF ASSUMED PARAMETERS, I.E. OPERATING CLEARANCE, AND EMPIRICAL PARAMETERS, SUCH AS STRUCTURE DRY-FRICTION OR STRUCTURAL DAMPING LOSS COEFFICIENT, FOR RELIABLE PREDICTION OF GFB FORCED PERFORMANCE. A TWO-YEAR RESEARCH PROGRAM, COMPUTATIONAL AND EXPERIMENTAL, IS PROPOSED TO ADVANCE COMPUTATIONAL MODELS FOR DESIGN AND PERFORMANCE PREDICTION OF GAS FOIL BEARINGS OPERATING IN HIGH TEMPERATURE ENVIRONMENTS. THE ANALYSIS WILL COUPLE A GAS FILM THERMOHYDRODYNAMIC MODEL TO A FE MODEL OF THE TOP FOIL AND UNDERSPRING SUPPORT, WITH A LUMPED PARAMETER MODEL FOR THERMAL ENERGY TRANSPORT WITH SIDE COOLING FLOW INDUCED BY EXTERNAL PRESSURIZATION. THE MODEL WILL ACCOUNT FOR THERMOELASTIC DEFORMATION OF THE ROTOR, TOP FOIL AND UNDERSPRING SUPPORT, INCLUDING STRUCTURAL ENERGY DISSIPATION DUE TO DRY FRICTION BETWEEN UNDERSPRING AND BEARING IN LOCAL CONTACT ZONES. THE RESEARCH WILL ALSO FOCUS ON ACQUIRING RELIABLE TEST DATA FOR COMMERCIALLY PROCURED GFBS AND FOR BENCHMARKING THE PREDICTIVE TOOLS. A TEST FACILITY TO PERFORM EXPERIMENTS IN ROTOR-GFB SYSTEMS WITH EXTREME THERMAL GRADIENTS, SUCH AS IN A GAS TURBINE, IS PROBABLY OUT OF THE FINANCIAL RESOURCES OF THE SPONSOR. THUS, THE PI PROPOSES TO CONDUCT EXPERIMENTS USING TWO EXISTING TEST RIGS REVAMPED FOR HIGH TEMPERATURE OPERATION.USING THE FIRST RIG, FOIL BEARING STRUCTURAL PARAMETERS (STIFFNESS AND ENERGY DISSIPATION) WILL BE IDENTIFIED FROM DYNAMIC LOAD TESTS AT INCREASING SHAFT TEMPERATURES OVER A RANGE OF EXCITATION FREQUENCIES. WITH THE SECOND RIG, MEASUREMENTS OF DYNAMIC RESPONSE OF A TEST ROTOR SUPPORTED ON GFBS WILL SHOW ROTOR LIFT OFF AND TOUCH DOWN SPEEDS, LOAD CAPACITY AND DRAG POWER, AND ALLOW FOR IDENTIFICATION OF SYNCHRONOUS SPEED FORCE COEFFICIENTS AND REGIMES OF STABILITY AND LIMIT CYCLE OPERATION FOR ROTOR TEMPERATURES TO 400C (752 F). THE PROPOSED RESEARCH WILL EXTEND WORK FUNDED BY NSF (ENDS MAY 2007), TAMU TURBOMACHINERY RESEARCH CONSORTIUM AND CAPSTONE TURBINE CORP.

Description: Mars Pit Chains: Analysis and Implications for Mechanical Stratigraphy, Subsurface Dilation and Fluid Movement The current state of knowledge of Martian subsurface processes is based primarily on remotely sensed data augmented by limited surface data. The presence and shape of pit craters and pit chains provide important clues to subsurface processes. Unlike impact craters, pit craters provide views of the relatively pristine upper crust, and are some of the youngest features, representing an important indicator of Martian geologic activity. A range of formation mechanisms for pit chains have been proposed, including dike intrusion, Assuring, and dilational faulting, each with its own implications for understanding the tectonic and volcanic history of Mars. Importantly, these processes also strongly influence other processes such as groundwater flow, mineralization, and localization of life. To achieve the goals of (1) understanding the character and distribution of pit chains on Mars, (2) the mechanism(s) of their formation, and (3) relevance to Martian crustal processes, we propose an integrated approach that includes detailed characterization of pit chains on Mars, quantitative field investigations on Earth, physical analog modeling experiments, and numerical modeling. This approach addresses fundamental questions regarding mechanisms for pit chain formation on Mars and implications for other dependent crustal processes. Specifically, we will: (1) use Mars data to constrain pit chain characteristics; (2) conduct quantitative field investigations of pit chains and extensional deformation in Iceland and Hawaii to test the interrelationships of dike intrusion, extensional faulting, fault dilation, and pit chain formation; and (3) perform physical analog and numerical modeling to test the role of mechanical layering and regolith thickness on pit chain formation and the range of proposed mechanisms for pit chain formation. These new analyses will refine our understanding of pit chains, the processes that lead to their development and the implications for mechanical properties, permeability, water content, and mineralization of the Martian brittle upper crust These results have broader implications for understanding processes on other bodies in the solar system where pit chains have also been interpreted. These research activities support NASA's Strategic Objective 2: "Conduct robotic exploration of Mars to search for evidence of life, to understand the history of the solar system, and to prepare for future human exploration" by providing information regarding near surface crustal properties of Mars, its tectonic and volcanic evolution, and potential sites of in situ resources. This investigation also addresses MEPAG (2004) Goal III, specifically, the role of volcanism and tectonism in the formation of pit chains, geologic mapping combined with experiments to constrain mechanical properties necessary to produce observed pit chain characteristics, and analyzing the role of subsurface voids on processes such as groundwater flow and mineralization.

Description: STUDY OF CONJUGATE POLAR IONOSPHERIC STORM RESPONSE DURING TYPICAL AND EXTREME SOLAR WIND CONDITIONS USING ACE AND DMSP SATELLITE OBSERVATIONS  IT IS WELL KNOWN THAT SOLAR WIND CONDITIONS (THE IMF AND THE RAM PRESSURE) ARE, THROUGH THE MAGNETOSPHERE, THE PRIMARY DRIVERS OF THE IONOSPHERIC PHENOMENON IN THE POLAR REGION (CROSS POLAR CAP POTENTIAL DROP, CONVECTION PATTERNS, TRIGGERING OF STORMS, ETC.). WHAT IS NOT AS WELL UNDERSTOOD ARE THE DIFFERENCES IN THESE PHENOMENA BETWEEN THE TWO POLAR IONOSPHERES AS THEY REACT TO THE SAME DRIVERS. TO FIRST ORDER IT WOULD APPEAR THAT THE PHENOMENON IN THE TWO HEMISPHERES SHOULD BE THE SAME (SUCH AS THE POTENTIAL DROP) OR MIRROR IMAGES (SUCH AS THE CONVECTION PATTERN). HOWEVER THIS NEGLECTS THE FEEDBACK ROLE THE IONOSPHERE ITSELF PLAYS. DURING SOLSTICES THERE IS A MARKED DIFFERENCE IN THE CONDUCTANCE BETWEEN THE SUNLIT SUMMER POLE AND THE DARKENED WINTER POLE, SO THERE SHOULD BE A SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCE IN THE CURRENTS, THE POTENTIAL DISTRIBUTION, AND THE POTENTIAL DROP BETWEEN THE TWO HEMISPHERES. TO DATE THERE HAVE BEEN ONLY A FEW LIMITED OBSERVATIONS THAT HAVE ADDRESSED WHETHER THIS ASYMMETRY IN THE POTENTIAL AND POTENTIAL DISTRIBUTION EXISTS OR NOT, SO THE QUESTION IS STILL OPEN. BUT WITH THE OBSERVATIONS FROM THE PLASMA INSTRUMENTS ON MULTIPLE DMSP SPACECRAFT IN POLAR ORBIT IT IS POSSIBLE TO SELECT PERIODS WHERE WE HAVE SIMULTANEOUS OBSERVATIONS IN BOTH HEMISPHERES. THE UPCOMING LAUNCH OF DMSP-F17 IN FALL 2006 COMBINED WITH THE ONGOING MISSION OF DMSP-F13 WILL GIVE US, FOR THE FIRST TIME, A LONG-TERM DATASET OF SIMULTANEOUS DAWN-DUSK POLAR PASSES IN OPPOSITE HEMISPHERES. WE PROPOSE TO IDENTIFY THESE PERIODS THEN COMPARE THE DMSP OBSERVATIONS OF THE POTENTIAL DISTRIBUTION, POTENTIAL DROP, POLAR CAP SIZE, FIELD-ALIGNED CURRENT, LOCATION OF THE AURORAL BOUNDARY, ETC. WITH THE SOLAR WIND DRIVERS (IMF MAGNITUDE AND ORIENTATION, RAM PRESSURE, ETC.) MEASURED BY THE NASA SPACECRAFT ACE. THE RESULTS WILL DEFINITELY ANSWER WHETHER OR NOT THERE IS A DIFFERENCE IN THE TWO POLAR IONOSPHERIC REGIONS' RESPONSES TO THE SOLAR WIND DRIVERS UNDER BOTH NOMINAL AND STORM TIME CONDITIONS AND, IF THERE IS A DIFFERENCE, HOW THEY ARE MEDIATED BY THE MAGNETOSPHERE AND IONOSPHERE. THIS PROPOSAL TO THE INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION COMPONENT OF THE LIVING WITH A STAR TR&T PROGRAM WILL SUPPORT THE LWS GOALS BY FURTHERING THE UNDERSTANDING OF THE SOLAR WIND-MAGNETOSPHERE-IONOSPHERIC COUPLING AND THE STORM-TIME RESPONSE OF THE IONOSPHERE TO THE SOLAR WIND DRIVERS. IN ADDITION THIS WORK WILL MAKE USE OF THE NASA FUNDED ON-LINE DATABASES OF THE ACE AND DMSP DATA.

Description: INFLUENCE OF CENTER OF GRAVITY LOCATION ON STABILITY DURING EXTRA VEHICULAR ACTIVITY  Due to recent aspirations to return to the Moon and extend space exploration to Mars, NASA has revitalized an interest in reduced gravity functional movement and locomotion for considerations in the next generation of space suits. This new suit, to be worn by the astronauts during extravehicular tasks (EVA), must protect them from the surrounding environment without inhibiting their ability to perform exploration tasks on the surface of the Moon or Mars. Furthermore, the ability to efficiently perform tasks is a major contributor to the mission's success. Therefore, in an effort to improve mobility and efficiency in the next generation of space suits, it is important to understand how the suit design can influence the astronauts ability to function while performing exploration responsibilities. One advantage todays researchers have in generating a suit for optimal EVA performance compared to researchers prior to the Apollo missions is that we have a record of activity performed on the moon. Evaluation of the video from the Apollo missions allows researchers to see issues that influenced the performance of the astronauts during their EVAs. One clear issue was the location of the life support system (PLSS). It appears, through visual inspection of the video, that the PLSS location shifted the Apollo Astronauts center of gravity (CG) in a manner that made maneuverability and stability a challenge. Here we proposed to further investigate the stability challenges while wearing a space suit. The purpose of this proposal is three-fold: 1) To determine the influence CG location has on locomotion stability during simulated lunar gravity, 2) To determine the influence CG location has on locomotion stability during simulated Martian gravity and 3) To determine the influence of suit weight on locomotion stability in simulated Martian gravity. This information gained from these experiments can be used to further validate the Cooper Harper Ratings and may influence astronaut training and new space suit design.

Description: Numerical Investigations of the electrodynamics of Mars Dust Disturbances Solar Energetic Particle (SEP) events are the most powerful explosions in the solar system, able to create high radiation levels at Earth with little warning. In the large events, particles are known to be accelerated both in the solar flare itself and by the shock driven by the associated Coronal Mass-Ejection (CME). The flare SEPs are known to have a distinct compositional signature including enhancements in electrons, the rare isotope 3He, and the relative abundance of Fe compared to O. Recent observations have shown that these energetic particle signatures of flare particles are often present in events with powerful CMEs along with shock-accelerated particles. This raises the question what are the basic mechanisms responsible for the most intense SEP events? For example: are the SEPs from the flare directly? or are they pre-accelerated at the flare and further energized by the shock? or are remnant suprathermals from previous flares supplying a critical component of the seed population? The investigation proposed here probes these questions using the heavy ion signature of flare material, namely enhanced Fe/O ratios and their variation with time and energy. We have recently found new evidence that interplanetary scattering plays a critical role in a majority of large western hemisphere SEP events. We describe how to use these observations to provide an observational basis for developing our theoretical understanding of the important role played by particle scattering during large SEP events. Specifically, the observations along with detailed modeling will enable us to place limits on the contributions of particle transport processes to the observed timing and composition in large SEP events. Our proposed study will therefore provide a sound framework for other modelers and TR&T teams to better understand the primary causes of the variability and the temporal evolution of the heavy ion abundances, such as the Fe/O ratio. This, in turn, will allow us to assess the relative contributions of flare particles (either indirectly in the form of seed particles or directly in the form of high-energy particles) to large gradual SEP events observed at 1 AU.

Description: COMTRAINED TWO-LEVEL CORRECTIONS FOR AUTONOMOUS ONBOARD TARGETING This study focuses on the adaptation of a constrained asymmetric two-level corrections process as an onboard targeting algorithm to optimize the Trans-Earth Injection (TEI) maneuver sequence for the lunar return of the CEV. Presently, this sequence includes three maneuvers, the first two of which are designed to minimize the third maneuver. However, entry point constraints depend only on the final maneuver of the sequence and the spacecraft state. The entry point constraints include flight path angle, longitude, radius, and azimuth. At a preliminary analysis level, the proposed approach considers the problem in the context of an end-to-end constrained trajectory design. This entails the minimization of all three maneuvers while satisfying all end-state constraints via a two-level corrections process. The study also considers (a) methods of adapting the algorithm for onboard autonomous targeting, given only the current spacecraft trajectory, and (b) algorithms for automating patch state selection based on the current spacecraft path geometry.

Description: GEOCHEMICAL MODELING OF THE FORMATION AND DIAGENESIS OF SULPHATES AND CLAYS ON MARS  Massive sedimentary sulfates have been observed at Meridiani Planum by the Opportunity Rover. They have apparently experienced a complex history of deposition and diagenesis, involving ground and probably surface waters of varying composition, pH, and oxidation state. Sulfates and phyllosilicates have been observed by the OMEGA instrument at diverse locations on Mars, and phyllosilicates may also co-exist with sulfates at Meridiani, There is an urgent need to model the geochemistry of these formations in order to understand the history of water and climate on Mars. The chemistry and sedimentary history of Meridiani, as revealed by Opportunity, is complex enough, and the data are abundant enough, that sophisticated geochemical modeling, coupled with fluid mixing models are necessary to understand the sequence of events that led to their formation and diagenesis. We will use a variety of geochemical and hydrological software tools, along with constraints from our laboratory experiments on Mars brines and evaporites (funded for the past decade by the Planetary Geology and Geophysics Program) to model the unique geochemistry and history of water that led to the current chemical conditions that we see on Mars today. The project has three major tasks: (1) Geochemical modeling of the formation of primary alteration products and salts at Meridiani, and of their further alteration to produce cements, hematite and other concretions, and crystal molds. (2) Hydrologic modeling of subsurface water flow in Meridiani coupled with reaction path modeling of ion species in groundwater, and (3) Modeling brine-to-evaporite chemistry of laboratory-produced Mars analogs and comparison of synthetic Mars evaporite and clay spectra with Mini-TES, TES, and OMEGA data. Mars had a rich aqueous history, but it remains to be seen how warm and wet it might have been. With a faint young Sun, it is difficult for climate models to predict a warm Mars 3.8 billion years ago. However, precipitation of some kind had to have occurred for subsurface waters to be recharged. Acidic waters on Mars may only have frozen at temperatures below 255 K, and large changes in obliquity may well have offered parts of the surface these conditions on average. This project will shed light on the complex geochemistry of Meridiani, allowing inferences to be made on the nature of Mars' early atmosphere, climate, and surface. The results will point the way to future landed on experiments on Mars that can more directly ascertain whether in fact Mars was habitable and for how long.

Description: The Impact of HZE Particles on Adult Neural Stem Cells and Neurogenesis Astronauts in deep-space missions are exposed galactic cosmic radiation, which consists of HZE particles. Both theI996 National Academy of Science report of interplanetary mission crew hazards and the NASA Radiation Health Bioastronautics Roadmap emphasize that estimating radiation risks to the central nervous system is a high research priority. One CNS cell population that warrants careful analysis for their response to radiation is adult neural stem cells, since these pluripotent cells may play an important role in recovery after radiation-induced brain injury. Studies from radiation biology and tumor biology have generated mixed information whether adult neural stem cells are radiosensitive or not. Understanding how adult neural stem cells respond to radiation and identification of the characteristics of the radioresistant neural stem cells will be pivotal in crafting future strategies to harness stem cells for repair ofthe injured brain. In this proposed study, We will perform a comprehensive analysis of the response and potential recovery of adult neural stem cells after HZE radiation using two mouse models: I) the nestinGFP transgenic mouse, which allows visualization of the neural stem cell population within the adult brain at any point in time; and 2) our unique nestin-CreERT2/R26R-YFP transgenic mouse, which allows inducible and permanent YFP labeling of adult neural stem cells and their progeny for the remainder of the cells life. These complementary models allow us to track the proliferation, differentiation, and survival of neural stem cells and their progeny in vivo after HZE radiation. We hypothesize that adult neural stem cells maintain some ability to repopulate the injured brain after radiation, and that this ability improves with time. We further hypothesize that these invulnerable stem cells will provide clues to radioresistance, which may involve the multiple strategies that neural stem cells employ to repair damaged DNA.

Description: Structural Chromosome Aberrations Formed in Response to Changes in Proton Energy and Dose Rate From the perspective of NASA, risk uncertainties related to radiation exposure during space exploration are unacceptably large. These include the effects of sporadic solar particle events (SPEs) which can produce relatively high levels of radiation, principally from protons. The resultant dose to personnel from an SPE can be high enough to warrant concerns of cancer induction. Because human epidemiological data in this area are not available, reduction in risk uncertainties will require data from meaningful surrogate endpoints, such as chromosome damage. A reasonable and widely held notion is that dose rate effects from protons will be the same as for x- and gamma rays. There is, however, not much direct experimental evidence to support this contention, which adds additional uncertainty to risk projections. We propose to simulate an SPE using proton emissions from a particle accelerator at Loma Linda University. Owing to differences in ionization density that may translate to differences in biological effect, proton energies of 50 MeV and 250 MeV will be studied. These will be delivered at both high and low dose rates. Results will then be compared to those obtained for gamma rays from a 137-Cesium source. Much is known about chromosomal response to other types of radiation, such as x- and gamma rays, including how the level of damage is influenced by the rate at which radiation is delivered. We have chosen structural damage to chromosomes of human cells in culture as a surrogate endpoint for cell death and cancer. We first propose to construct quantitative dose responses for the induction of chromosome aberrations found in cells when they arrive at the first mitosis following exposure. For this and other objectives, multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) will be used, which effectively paints each of the 23 pairs of human chromosomes a unique color. This allows even very complicated rearrangements among all chromosomes to be visualized simultaneously. The second set of objectives involves analysis of chromosome damage in clonal descendents of single cells that survive exposure to radiation. Several such clones will be expanded in culture and examined by mFISH for transmissible chromosome aberrations. A subset of these clones will be further examined for structural aberrations that are too small to be seen under the microscope, by employing comparative genomic hybridization applied to DNA microarrays (aCGH). It is argued that genetic damage in cells surviving radiation may be diagnostic of the type of radiation encountered, and that such damage has more direct relevance to carcinogenesis.

Description: TEXAS ENGINEERING EXPERIMENT STATION RANS AND VARIABLE-RESOLUTION PANS MODELS FOR SEPARATED FLOWS The complexity of the separation problem and its crucial role in aeronautics applications dictates a two-tier research approach. For applications involving steady separation, a sophisticated Reynolds averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) model may be adequate. For applications with unsteady separation - e.g., high-lift airfoils operating close to the boundaries of the flight envelope -- a higher fidelity approach will be necessary. Our proposal is to develop a physics-based integrated closure model suite that provides the best possible closure at any level of scale resolution from RANS to direct numerical simulations (DNS). The proposed approach similar to hybrid methods -- is based on accuracy-on-demand paradigm. It is called the partiallyaveraged Navier-Stokes (PANS) method and presents the user the option of choosing a computational effort level that is in commensurate with the flow physics and desired accuracy. The starting point ofthe research is the RANS stress transport equation (STE) model as it is the lowest level of closure at which the key physical effects can be introduced in a scientifically rigorous manner. RANS algebraic stress model (RANS-ASM) and PANS-ASM closures will then be formally extracted from RANS-STE closures leading to an integrated model. suite. For research planning and execution, the proposed work is divided into six tasks: (l) RANS-STE model development; (2) RANS-ASM closure extraction; (3) RANS validation and testing; (4) PANS-ASM development; (4) PANS improvement to minimize commutation error; and (6) , PANS-ASM testing and validation. Each task represents an important piece of progress in the proposed research. Apart from the PI, two full-time graduate students and one full-time postdoctoral fellow will be involved. The proposed work will directly support NASA research in the sub-topic area A.2.3.2. Other sub-areas that will benefit from the proposed research are highfidelity numerical simulations for unsteady flow fields (A.2.U), physics-based flow modeling for turbulence-chemistry interactions (A.2.2.1) and noise prediction tools (A,2.1.3). Description: PHYSICAL STUDIES OF LARGE SCALE COLLISIONS AND ZODIACAL CLOUD Important insights into the physics of large-scale collisions may be obtained by studying the asteroid belt where disruptive collisions produced the asteroid families and zodiacal dust bands. One such collision produced asteroid (832) Karin and a cluster of fragments nowadays seen at 2.866 AU. Dynamical studies show that this collision occurred 5.8 (+/-0.2) million years ago. This discovery marks the first time that an asteroid breakup has been precisely dated. The relative youth and known age of the Karin cluster (and other young asteroid families reported to date) open several exciting research directions: (1) By using state-of-art computer models of catastrophic collisions, and by comparing their results with the orbital and size-frequency distribution of the Karin cluster members, we propose to improve our understanding of impact physics and asteroid interiors. These studies will be also useful to validate the computer models of large-scale collisions. (2) Observations made by the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS) in 1984 revealed the existence of several Solar System dust bands. Because the dust is dynamically and collisionally short-lived, the observed dust bands are believed to originate in recent disruption events among main belt asteroids. The Karin cluster, and similar young collision groups in the asteroid belt, are important source regions of asteroidal dust. We propose to systematically search for recent asteroid breakups in the main belt and link them with the IRAS dust bands. We will model the detection of the thermal emission from asteroid and cometary particle distributions by IRAS and other infrared space-borne telescopes to explain the origin of the zodiacal cloud.

Description: QUANTIFICATION OF FAULT NETWORK PROPERTIES ON MARS Faults on Mars have acted as conduits for water, and have controlled channel morphology and surface topography, and they provide important information regarding the stress history of the Martian crust.  Because of their influence on fluid flow and storage, faults are key exploration targets.  In this project, we propose to examine the link between large-displacement faults and networks of smaller-displacement faults using a combination of data from Mars exploration: Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, Mars Orbiter Camera, Thermal Emission Imaging System, and High Resolution Stereo Camera data, augmented where necessary by visual imagery from Viking.  The combined data sets will be used to map faults in areas with good data coverage on the flanks of Alba Patera.  We will create and analyze maps of fault displacement, fault-accommodated strain, fault density, and fault displacement spectra.  This work will address three fundamental questions of Martian fault systems: (i) do displacement gradients on large faults control localization of small-scale faulting?  (ii) Do displacement deficits along large-scale faults enhance localized small-scale faulting? (iii) Is there a sytematic relationship between fault displacement distributions and strain?  Understanding the relationship between large- and small-displacement faults, and establishing criteria for quantifying networks of small faults associated with larger displacement faults is important because: (i) fault networks are and have been flow determinants for ground water and other fluids; (ii) faults are potential reservoirs for surviving groundwater (ice) resources; (iii) networks of small faults are more feasible exploration targets than large faults because of their less rugged topography; and (iv) quantifying permeability-determining characteristics of the Martian crust is a necessary step in the development of more refined martian hydrological models.  This proposed research will improve our understanding of normal fault systems on Mars, and will provide important information for efforts to populate hydrologic models of Mars with permeability-determining structures.  The proposed research activities support NASA Strategic goals (2006 NASA Strategic Plan) by providing key information regarding the near surface crustal properties of Mars, its tectonic evolution, and potential sites of in situ resources such as ground water/ice and gas hydrates.  Results of the work proposed here will also contribute to the interpretation of data from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.  By identifying and characterizing areas that are likely to have influenced fluid flow and storage, and which combine low topographic relief with high fault density, this investigation also addresses goals outlined in the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group Report.  Specifically, we will address questions regarding the distribution of water, the evolution of crust and the identification of high-value exploration targets on Mars.

Description: IONOSPHERIC DYNAMICS ASSOCIATED WITH LARGE-SCALE DENSITY GRADIENTS  We propose to utilize satellite observations, ground TEC measurements, and simple computational modeling to investigate the role of ExB drifts and neutral winds in the generation and evolution of electron density gradients at middle to low latitudes in the F region. The appearance of significant density gradients in the region produce large signal fades and loss of control tracking loops in GPS systems and thus the importance of recognizing under what conditions such degradation might appear is of great value. At middle latitudes the interaction between magnetospheric energy inputs, solar radiative inputs, and planetary rotation critically determines the dynamics of the plasma and large-scale spatial gradients in the ion density can result from vastly different dynamic histories of the plasma in neighboring regions. Thus the relevance of this investigation extends beyond the societal impacts of compromised communication and navigation systems to the more fundamental of NASA's strategic goals to understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and specifically how the near space environment responds to changes in the interplanetary medium produced by the Sun. We will identify electron density gradients using two different techniques. Examination of a global distribution of total electron content derived from ground-based TEC measurements will provide a global perspective within the wide and variable spatial and universal time ranges of the available data. Latitude and longitude (local time) profiles of the ionospheric electron density, from the DMSP and ROCSAT satellites respectively, will provide a much higher spatial resolution but in a more limited spatial and universal time range. Together these two data sources provide many opportunities to identify plasma density gradients. In addition, the satellite data provide a detailed description of the dynamics of the plasma associated with the density gradients. From this data set we will establish the differences in the dynamics associated with regions of low and high density and how the transitions between the regions behave. An ionospheric model, driven by ExB drift and neutral wind inputs can be used to conduct parameter studies to establish the relationships between these drivers and field-aligned plasma motions. Since these field-aligned perpendicular motions can be directly measured it is possible to infer the differences in neutral winds and ExB drifts that are associated with regions of low and high density. In this way the conditions for formation of large-scale gradients can be specified.

Description: THE RELATIONSHIP OF THE PLASMASPHERE AND THE RADIATION BELTS (William R. Johnston) The plasmapause separates cold dense plasma in the inner magnetoscope plasma.  This boundary is very dynamic in respone to changes in magnetoscope convection and other stormtime phenomena.  The outer radiation belt during stormtime in terms of both radial location and energentic particle population.  It has been proposed that outer radiation belt particles are variously depleted and energized due to wave-particle interactions associated witht he plasmapause location.  This hypothesis may be tested by simulataneous plasmasphere and radiation belt observations.  We plan to accomplish this by comparing DMSP indenticfications of the plasmapase signature in the ionosphere (specifically the light ion Through)  to radiation belt observations.  By using the continous multiyear coverage by multiple DMSP satellites overlapping radiation belt observation by SAMPEX, this can improve the available observational coverage.  We will develop methods to semi-automatically identify the light ion trough in DMSP Retard Potential Analyzer observations of light ion densities.  The location derived from ths ionospheric signature of the plasmapause will be mapped along field lines using combined internal/external field model, giving a location for the plasmapause.  This method will be compared to plasmapause identifications from IMAGE EUV observations.  We will perform case studies comparing the DMSP-derived plasaapause and SAMPEX radiation belt observations.  These methods will eventually be applied to extract plasmapause locations form the full ulti-year DMSP database.  The resulting database of plasmapause locations will be statistically analyzed with respect to SAMPEX observations of outer radiation belt particle distributions, as well as SAMPEX observations of precipitating particle microbursts.  We will quantify the relationship between light ion trough and the plasmapause, and we will improve physical models for the relationship between the plasmapause location and the outer radiation belt.  This research is important to understanding dynamics of the outer rediation belt and the consequences of the radiation environment on space operations, and thus addresses areas H2 and J1 in NASA's 2005 Heliophysics Roadmap.

Description: Using Satellite Observations and a Fully Coupled Land-Atmosphere-Chemistry Model to Study the Coupling between Vegetation and the Hydrologic Cycle through Biogenic Emissions Pathways Vegetation plays a key role in modulating the Earth's hydrologic cycle and climate. Vegetation not only affects precipitation by changing heat fluxes near the surface, but it also influences climate and the hydrologic cycle by indirectly altering the concentration of atmospheric aerosols. Biogenic volatile organic compounds (BVOCs) emitted by vegetation play an important role in the formation of secondary organic aerosols (SOA), which influence the formation of clouds and which may redistribute the pattern of precipitation. The objectives of the proposed research are to: 1) Quantify the contribution of BVOCs to atmospheric aerosol concentration and cloud formation with the aid of in-situ observations, satellite data, and a coupled numerical model; 2) Assess the effects of SOA produced by the oxidation of BVOCs on precipitation by using satellite-derived aerosol and cloud data; 3) Examine the strength of the coupling between vegetation and the hydrologic cycle through biogenic emissions pathways. To achieve the goals, I will combine satellite data, ground-based observations and modeling together as a means to investigate this coupling. The interaction between vegetation and SOA is given particular attention in this study because vegetation is controlling the emissions of biogenic compounds. Assessment of the uncertainties related to satellite data products and modeling is also a key consideration for the research. This research will make significant contributions to our current understanding of the links between biogenic emissions, SOA, and the hydrologic cycle. The proposed research is related to NASA's strategic plan to develop a scientific understanding of Earth's system and its response to natural or human-induced changes and to improve prediction of climate, weather, and natural hazards. It is also relevant to the Earth Science Division focus areas including ecosystems, biogeochemistry, and water cycle.

Description: Mechanisms of the Repair of HZE Induced DNA Double-Strand Breaks in Human Cells SUMMARY: Complex DNA double-strand breaks along the dense ionizing track induced by HZE particles are difficult to repair and, in some instances, irreparable. These unrepaired and/or misrepaired DNA lesions may contribute to the observed higher relative biological effect (RBE) for cell killing, chromosomal aberrations, mutagenesis, and carcinogenesis in cells irradiated with HZE particle. While the types of DNA lesions induced by high LET radiation have been well studied in vitro, it is still unclear why HZE particles induced DNA lesions are difficult to repair or why the current pathways of DSB repair cannot handle these lesions properly. The goals of this proposal are two fold: 1) to develop new approaches to determine the types of DNA lesions formed and their spatial relationship along the dense ionizing track induced by different HZE particles in human cells, while trying to discern the cellular capability to repair these DNA lesions in situ; and 2) to identify the molecular pathways (nonhomologous end joining and homologous recombination) or factors (Artemis and/or WRN) that may be able to manage HZE particle-induced DNA lesions including DNA DSBs in human cells. In order to achieve these goals, we propose: 1) to verify that multiple types of DNA lesions formed in close vicinity along the dense ionizing tracks induced by HZE particles in situ; 2) to test the hypothesis that Artemis (a specific exo-/endonuclease) may be involved in the repair of complex DNA DSBs induced by HZE particle through the nonhomologous end joining pathway; 3) to test the hypothesis that WRN, a human multifunctional protein with exonucfease and helicase activities, may be involved in managing the repair of HZE induced DNA DSBs; and 4) to determine the role of HR in the repair of complex DSBs induced by HZE particles. Determining the biochemical nature of the DNA damages induced by HZE particles and identifying the factors that are required for the repairing of these DNA Lesions will provide tools to assess individual radiation susceptibility and to validate risk assessment for human exposure to HZE particles. Ultimately, our research would lead to developing counter-measures to enhance astronautsi ability to sustain HZE particles and radiation exposures in space.

Description: There is a significant need within the aerospace industry for analytical tools which can analyze the effects of aging degradation on the ballistic impact performance of advanced composites for jet engine fan containment cases. In the proposed research, advanced constitutive models will be developed to analyze the strain rate dependent response of polymeric matrix materials and polymeric foams, with the effects of aging accounted for. Analytical methods will also be developed to enable the prediction of damage and failure mechanisms such as matrix cracking and fiber/matrix debonding. Homogenization methods will be devised which will permit the analysis of the effective response of polymer composite fan case structures. The analytical methods will be developed in a manner such that they will be able to be utilized within a transient dynamic finite element code. The proposed project will greatly improve the ability of designers to analyze the impact and aging response of composite structures.

Description: Structural Chromosome Aberrations Formed in Response to Changes in Proton Energy and Dose Rate From the perspective of NASA, risk uncertainties related to radiation exposure during space exploration are unacceptably large. These include the effects of sporadic solar particle events (SPEs) which can produce relatively high levels of radiation, principally from protons. The resultant dose to personnel from an SPE can be high enough to warrant concerns of cancer induction. Because human epidemiological data in this area are not available, reduction in risk uncertainties will require data from meaningful surrogate endpoints, such as chromosome damage. A reasonable and widely held notion is that dose rate effects from protons will be the same as for x- and gamma rays. There is, however, not much direct experimental evidence to support this contention, which adds additional uncertainty to risk projections. We propose to simulate an SPE using proton emissions from a particle accelerator at Loma Linda University. Owing to differences in ionization density that may translate to differences in biological effect, proton energies of 50 MeV and 250 MeV will be studied. These will be delivered at both high and low dose rates. Results will then be compared to those obtained for gamma rays from a 137-Cesium source. Much is known about chromosomal response to other types of radiation, such as x- and gamma rays, including how the level of damage is influenced by the rate at which radiation is delivered. We have chosen structural damage to chromosomes of human cells in culture as a surrogate endpoint for cell death and cancer. We first propose to construct quantitative dose responses for the induction of chromosome aberrations found in cells when they arrive at the first mitosis following exposure. For this and other objectives, multiplex fluorescence in situ hybridization (mFISH) will be used, which effectively paints each of the 23 pairs of human chromosomes a unique color. This allows even very complicated rearrangements among all chromosomes to be visualized simultaneously. The second set of objectives involves analysis of chromosome damage in clonal descendents of single cells that survive exposure to radiation. Several such clones will be expanded in culture and examined by mFISH for transmissible chromosome aberrations. A subset of these clones will be further examined for structural aberrations that are too small to be seen under the microscope, by employing comparative genomic hybridization applied to DNA microarrays (aCGH). It is argued that genetic damage in cells surviving radiation may be diagnostic of the type of radiation encountered, and that such damage has more direct relevance to carcinogenesis.

Description: The proposed research program aims at developing a variable-fidelity software tool set for aeroservothermoelastic-propulsive (ASTE-P) modeling that can be routinely applied to the design of aerospace vehicles. The tool set can be applied to conventional vehicle types as well as hypersonic vehicles. The major issues involved in ASTE-P modeling and simulation will be significantly and extensively investigated in this project, which include full coupling between fluid/structure/control dynamics, the aeroservothermoelastic-propulsive instability, the viscous/turbulent effects, shock and shock-boundary layer interaction, as well as the large unsteady and highly nonlinear aerothermal dynamic loading on structure of vehicles. The interface of the structure/control surface dynamic vibration modes with flows will be modeled using particle-based material point method (MPM) in an integrated dynamic fluid-structure interaction environment. The MPM is essentially a particle-based method which avoids dealing with the time-varying mesh distortions and boundary variations due to structure/control surface deformations and/or motions (i.e. wing flutters, FCS/structural mode interaction, PSD turbulence response), thus being significantly more robust and computationally efficient than the traditional finite element methods that must utilize moving-boundary and mesh-regeneration. Phase I will build and demonstrate the initial capability; the end software in Phase II will be fully capable of ASTE-P analysis and evaluation for aerospace vehicles.

Description: The proposed research program aims at developing a variable-fidelity software tool set for aeroservothermoelastic-propulsive (ASTE-P) modeling that can be routinely applied to the design of aerospace vehicles. The tool set can be applied to conventional vehicle types as well as hypersonic vehicles. The major issues involved in ASTE-P modeling and simulation will be significantly and extensively investigated in this project, which include full coupling between fluid/structure/control dynamics, the aeroservothermoelastic-propulsive instability, the viscous/turbulent effects, shock and shock-boundary layer interaction, as well as the large unsteady and highly nonlinear aerothermal dynamic loading on structure of vehicles. The interface of the structure/control surface dynamic vibration modes with flows will be modeled using particle-based material point method (MPM) in an integrated dynamic fluid-structure interaction environment. The MPM is essentially a particle-based method which avoids dealing with the time-varying mesh distortions and boundary variations due to structure/control surface deformations and/or motions (i.e. wing flutters, FCS/structural mode interaction, PSD turbulence response), thus being significantly more robust and computationally efficient than the traditional finite element methods that must utilize moving-boundary and mesh-regeneration. Phase I will build and demonstrate the initial capability; the end software in Phase II will be fully capable of ASTE-P analysis and evaluation for aerospace vehicles.

Description: MDAP: OBSERVATIONS OF CRATER INTERIORS AS A RECORD OF ANCIENT CLIMATE CHANGE Mars polar processes are a sensitive measure of the planet's climate history. Layered terrains and circumpolar dunes record short-term changes in Mars' current climate (Howard, 2000), and changes of polar features over the long-term provide a record of Mars' past climate (Laskar et a]., 2002). In particular, near-polar craters (defined as craters near the pole, covered with seasonal C02 ice, but located well away from the permanent ice cap) provide an opportunity to examine the polar processes in detail. Near-polar craters have novel morphologies, due in large part to their interaction with the seasonal polar caps (Garvin et al., 2000). The first step in understanding these interactions is gathering information on the nature of the crater floor deposits. Circumpolar winds can deposit dust and sand visible in inter-crater dune formations (Christensen, 1983) and C02 ice is seasonally deposited in nearly all polar craters. However, the interaction these craters have with water ice deposits is largely unexplored. Observations of transient patches of water frost in the Northern polar cap (Christensen et a]., 2003) and exposures of water ice near the south pole (Titus et al., 2003) suggests that water ice deposits may play an important role in geological processes near the poles. TES temperature measurements of Korolev crater in the northern polar region show evidence of seasonal water ice and CO--2 ice deposition within the crater (Kieffer and Titus, 2001). In addition, thermal variations revealed by THEMIS IR imagery show distinct thermo-physical regions that correlate with topography, and THEMIS visible imagery shows evidence for layering within the crater (Armstrong et al., 2004b; Armstrong et al., 2004~). In this study, we propose to examine the thermal properties of the interiors of other large near-polar craters, and look for properties that may correlate with elevation and location, as well as differences between craters in the northern and southern polar regions. In addition, we propose to survey a selection of craters at lower latitudes to determine if the morphology imprinted by near-polar phenomena can be seen in I he geological record as an indicator of recent climate change. This study has the following goals: 1. Determine the latitude distribution of the subsurface ice table - Near-polar craters act as a probe for subsurface volatile deposits. By studying near-polar craters, we can measure the geographical edge of the ice table to greater precision, adding value to Gamma Ray Spectrometer (GSR) measurements of the ice able. 2. Characterize surface deposits in polar regions - This study will characterize surface and subsurface deposits in the same latitude band as the upcoming Phoenix Lander, providing addition context for the mission. 3. Probe the link between crater morphology, near-surface volatiles, and climate change - We will compare he latitude dependence of crater morphology with models of recent climate change. Description: STORM TIME IONOSPHERIC ELECTRIC FIELDS We propose to use a very extensive database of plasma drift observations made on-board the Republic of China satellite (ROCSAT-1), Dynamics Explorer (DE-2), and Atmosphere Explorers E and C (AE-E and AE-C) satellites, as well as detailed ground-based magnetic field observations to study the storm-time, latitude-, and longitude-dependent response of mid- and low-latitude Ionospheric electric fields to solar wind and magnetospheric disturbances. We plan to complement our experimental studies with numerical simulations using recent and future upgraded versions of the Rice Convection Model (RCM). The first basic objective of this proposal Is to use this extensive combined satellite database of perturbation electric fields (obtained by removing quiet-time values along satellite orbits) to develop a detailed understanding of the local and storm-time, season, solar cycle dependent response of prompt penetration electric fields (mostly at low latitudes) to various solar wind-magnetosphere-ionosphere driving processes for different storm and solar cycle phases and seasons. These driving processes include the interplanetary electric field, IMF clock angle, and solar wind dynamic pressure. The second objective is the study of the longitudinal and latitudinal variations of the prompt penetration and disturbance dynamo electric fields under different geophysical storm conditions. This includes the study of the longitude-dependent relationship of low-latitude prompt penetration electric fields and subauroral polarization streams (SAPS). The third objective is the use of our experimental results for detailed testing of longitude-dependent predictions from global convection models, particularly during large magnetic storms. These studies should significantly improve the understanding of global characteristics of storm-time ionospheric electric fields and made a major contribution to future NASA missions, particularly to multi-spacecraft Ionospheric missions.

Description: INVESTIGATION OF NITRIC OXIDE INFRARED EMISSIONS AND SPIN-ORBIT POPULATIONS IN THE THERMOSPHERE Infrared emission by NO is an important cooling mechanism in the upper atmosphere. NO emission near 5.3 microns is produced by collisional excitation of NO(v=O) by atomic oxygen. The reactions of N atoms with 02 also produce vibrationally excited NO, and these reactions are enhanced during auroral activity. Recent analysis of NASA SABER data from the April 2002 solar storm has determined that NO emission is the primary pathway for the release of storm energy below 200 km [Mlynczak et al., 2005]. To model the impact of NO emissions on the atmospheric energy budget, it is necessary to quantify the sources of vibrationally excited NO and determine the nascent distributions of energy. The MIPAS satellite instrument measures earthlimb emissions with unapodized resolution of 0.035 cm-1. The high spectral resolution permits detailed investigation of the vibrational, rotational an6 spin-orbit populations of NO. In an initial study of quiescent MIPAS data, we determined that there is a diurnal variation in the spin-orbit ratio of NO in the thermosphere, and our results indicate that the spin-orbit ratio may be a long-lived signature of the NO formation mechanism. We propose to analyze newly available MIPAS data, including data recorded during a recent solar storm, to determine the distribution of energy in NO and to investigate if the spin-orbit ratio can be used to identify and quantify the NO production mechanisms. The MIPAS data will be compared with SABER NO data to further research the production mechanisms, variability, and contribution of NO emissions to the atmospheric energy budget. The MIPAS data will also be used to validate the SABER bandpass filter correction factors that are needed to interpret the SABER NO data. The results of the MIPAS and SABER data analysis will be compared with a non-LTE model of NO infrared emissions in the thermosphere.
