Description: The Open Storage Ring: A Mass-Mobility Spectrometer for in situ Characterization of Planetary Atmospheres and Evolved Gases Objectives. We propose to develop a new type of ion trap which would be used either as a standalone mass-mobility spectrometer or as part ofa hybrid instrument (i.e., a GC-MS-IMS) for composition analysis of planetary atmospheres. Called the Open Storage Ring, this device consists of two flat ceramic plates, each imprinted with a series of concentric metal rings. Radio-frequency voltages are applied to each ring to produce a quadrupolar trapping field with overall toroidal geometry. Unlike traditional hyperbolic or cylindrical ion traps, the toroidal trapping volume dramatically increases ion storage capacity. This design can be miniaturized, allowing operation at relatively high pressure, without sacrificing sensitivity or sample inlet access. In addition, the use of numerous quasi-independent concentric rings can produce an arbitrary field, allowing separate optimization of fields for trapping and mass analysis. With appropriate pressure control, this configuration may allow limited field-asymmetric ion mobility spectrometry of trapped species, which can be used to selectively isolate isobars, such as CO and N2. The combination of mass analysis and mobility analysis in one device, combined with the advantages of toroidal trapping geometry, will result in a very small, low power analyzer. Methods. As the electric fields and electronics of this device are substantially different from other ion traps, much of the proposed effort will focus on theoretical and experimental exploration and optimization the properties ofthe device. Instrument development will involve designing, building, and testing the trap, associated electronics, sampling systems, and detectors. Under this proposal we plan to produce a fully-functional laboratory prototype at TRL 4. Significance. This device would enable significant reductions in mass and power of ion trap mass spectrometers, a class of instruments used in several past and present planetary missions. The proposed design will maintain high resolution and sensitivity, both of which are reduced in traditional miniaturization schemes. At the same time, the instrument would add capabilities not possible with current mass spectrometers, including ion mobility analysis and a higher dynamic range. An instrument based on this new technology would be useful for characterization of major and trace components and isotopes ofthe atmospheres of Mars and Titan, and might be applicable for studies ofthe challenging atmospheres of Venus and Jupiter. The instrument could also be used for other types of samples, such as evolved gases or liquids, enabling high performance surface analysis

Description: DIFFERENCES AND SIMILARITIES OF TROPICAL CYCLONE RAINFALL OVER LAND AND SEA USING MULTISATELLITE ANALYSES: IMPLICATIONS FOR INLAND FLOODING PREDICTION The central goal of this proposal is to quantify differences and similarities of tropical cyclone rainfall distribution over land and sea and understand the relationship between hurricane landfall flooding and its over ocean rainfall potential. Environmental factors influencing the magnitude and distribution of tropical cyclone landfall precipitation will also be examined. A 7-yr landfalling Atlantic tropical cyclone database of rainfall from Tropical Rainfall Measurement Mission (TRMM)-based NASA Goddard multi-satellite precipitation analysis (TMM 3B42) has been collected. Categorizations have been made regarding to the storm intensity and location, e.g. over-land or over-ocean. Preliminary studies based on this database have shown that there are indeed major distinctions of cyclone rainfall distribution between over-land and over-ocean stages. However, connecting a storm ' s rainfall over ocean to its landfall rain provides implications on landfall flooding prediction. It also has been demonstrated that tropical cyclone ' s rainfall potential in one day prior to landfall can be used to discriminate among flooding vs. nonflooding storms. The first objective of this proposal is to expand and update the landfalling tropical cyclone database from the Atlantic basin only to global, from 7 years to 8, and to include environmental parameters from the Navy Operational Global Atmospheric Prediction System (NOGAPS) analysis. The second objective is to continue quantifying differences and similarities of tropical cyclone rainfall distribution over land and oceans for different basins, and developing and verifying the 'rain potentiaL' prediction index for landfall flooding of global tropical cyclones. Additionally we will investigate the complicated landfall scenarios in which the rain production is significantly enhanced by terrain interactions and extratropical transition. The third objective is to evaluate TRMM-based rainfall accumulation estimates for extreme events, e.g. tropical cyclones by using ground-based radar and gauge measurements. This will be done mainly for landfall periods. We will not only quantify the relative biases but examine advantages and disadvantages of these satellite estimates and the underlying physical reasons.

Description: MEASURING THE GLOBAL TROPOPAUSE BY SATELLITE: UNCERTAINTIES, STRUCTURE, AND VARIABILITY. ABSTRACT MEASURING THE GLOBAL TROPOPAUSE BY SATELLITE: UNCERTAINTIES, STRUCTURE, AND VARIABILITY. PAUL STATEN, UNIVERSITY OF UTAH OBJECTIVES: THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVES OF THE PROPOSED WORK ARE (1) TO DEMONSTRATE THE CAPABILITY OF NASA-SPONSORED SATELLITE MISSIONS IN OBSERVING THE TROPOPAUSE ON A GLOBAL SCALE USING RADIO OCCULTATION; (2) TO DETERMINE, FOR THE FIRST TIME, THE QUALITY OF ATMOSPHERIC REANALYSES OVER REMOTE REGIONS USING THIS NEW SATELLITE DATA; AND (3) TO CHARACTERIZE THE STRUCTURE AND VARIABILITY OF THE TROPOPAUSE AND HOW IT RELATES TO LARGE SCALE ATMOSPHERIC PROCESSES AND CLIMATE CHANGE. MOTIVATION: THE TROPOPAUSE IS A FUNDAMENTAL FEATURE OF THE ATMOSPHERE, MARKING THE BOUNDARY BETWEEN THE TROPOSPHERE AND THE STRATOSPHERE. AN UNDERSTANDING OF TROPOPAUSE STRUCTURE IS KEY TO MANY AREAS IN THE STUDY OF CLIMATE AND WEATHER. HOWEVER, IT IS DIFFICULT TO PRECISELY ANALYZE THE GLOBAL TROPOPAUSE USING CONVENTIONAL OBSERVATIONS. SEVERAL NASA SPONSORED MISSIONS ARE LIKELY TO CHANGE THAT. THESE MISSIONS USE RADIO OCCULTATION TO PRODUCE WORLDWIDE ATMOSPHERIC TEMPERATURE PROFILES. IN PARTICULAR, THE NEW COSMIC CONSTELLATION OF SATELLITES WILL BE ABLE TO MONITOR TROPOPAUSE STRUCTURE IN NEAR REAL TIME AND WITH SUPERIOR SPATIAL COVERAGE. WE INTEND TO DEMONSTRATE THE QUALITY OF THIS NEW DATA AND USE IT TO FURTHER OUR UNDERSTANDING OF LARGE SCALE ATMOSPHERIC PROCESSES AND CLIMATE. METHODS: THIS WORK WILL UTILIZE DATA FROM RADIOSONDES, FOUR REANALYSIS PRODUCTS, AND FOUR SATELLITE MISSIONS. USING THE THERMAL TROPOPAUSE DEFINITION, WE WILL DERIVE GLOBAL GRIDDED TROPOPAUSE FIELDS FROM EACH DATA SOURCE. WE WILL USE THESE FIELDS AND STANDARD STATISTICAL TECHNIQUES (1) TO VERIFY REMOTELY SENSED MEASUREMENTS AGAINST NEARBY RADIOSONDE DATA; (2) TO QUANTIFY REANALYSES QUALITY OVER DATA-SPARSE REGIONS WITH INDEPENDENT SATELLITE DATA; AND (3) TO ANALYZE THE SATELLITE DATA TO CONFIRM AND CLARIFY TROPOPAUSE FEATURES SEEN IN CONVENTIONAL DATA. SIGNIFICANCE: THIS RESEARCH WILL ENCOURAGE THE USE OF NEW NASA SPONSORED SATELLITE DATA IN ATMOSPHERIC SCIENCE. IT DIRECTLY ADDRESSES THE GOALS AND OBJECTIVES OF NASA S EARTH SCIENCE DIVISION AND TWO OF ITS FOCUS AREAS: CLIMATE VARIABILITY AND CHANGE, BY DEMONSTRATING THE QUALITY AND APPLICABILITY OF THE OCCULTATION TECHNIQUE, BY CLARIFYING REANALYSIS UNCERTAINTIES, AND BY INVESTIGATING LONG TERM STRUCTURAL CHANGES IN THE TROPOPAUSE; WATER AND ENERGY CYCLE, BY USING NEW, INNOVATIVE METHODS TO MEASURE TROPOPAUSE STRUCTURE AND THEREBY THE LATITUDINAL EXTENT OF THE HADLEY CELL, A CRUCIAL DRIVER OF THE GLOBAL ENERGY AND WATER CYCLE.

Description: "STUDY OF TIBETAN PLATEAU WITH MODIS, TRMM DATA" The Tibetan Plateau plays important roles in determining the formation and varation of regional weather and climate in east and south Asia, as well as atmospheric circulation in the Northern Hemisphere in general.  However, the study of climatic impact of Tibetan Plateau has been relatively limited in the past.  This is partly due to lack of the remotely sensed observational data over the Tibetan Plateau, and also because of the difficulties in exchanging the data between Chinese and western scholars.  With this fellowship proposal, we plan to undertake a first research effort to integrate multi-year (2000-present)NASA MODIS snow cover and TRMM rainfall data with in situ Chineses station data, including the snow data from 60 Chineses ground-observing snow stations over the Tibetan Plateau and 2200 ground-based meteorological stations over Chinese continent, to achieve the following research components:  1) Evaluate the MODIS snow cover estimates and in situ Chinese ground-based snow stations over the Tibetan Plateau.  2)  Incorporate MODIS snow cover estimates and in situ Chinese ground-based snow station data to obtain a database with multi-year winter snow cover and depth over the Tibetan Plateau.  3)  Integrate the obtained multi-year winter snow database with TRMM precipitation estimates (cover global tropics and sub-tropics) and 2200 ground-based Chinese meteorological station data to study the relationship between the Tibetan winter (November to February) snow cover and Asian summer (June to August) precipitation.  4)  Assimilate the snow data into state-of-the-art Community Climate System model (CCSM) to further study the impact of winter Tibetan snow cover on Asian summer precipitation.  Specific attention will be paid to general circulation associated with Asian monsoon activities.  In addition, we will further explore impact of Tibetan snow cover on the global atmospheric circulation in general.  The possible relationship between Tibetan snow cover on Northern American atmospheric circulation will be specifically investigated.  It is anticipated the study from this proposed activities could fill gaps of our knowledge regarding to the weather and climate impact from the Tibetan Plateau.

Description: DIFFERENCES AND SIMILARITIES OF TROPICAL CYCLONE RAINFALL OVER LAND AND SEA USING MULTISATELLITE ANALYSES: IMPLICATIONS FOR INLAND FLOODING PREDICTION The central goal of this proposal is to quantify differences and similarities of tropical cyclone rainfall distribution over land and sea and understand the relationship between hurricane landfall flooding and its over ocean rainfall potential. Environmental factors influencing the magnitude and distribution of tropical cyclone landfall precipitation will also be examined. A 7-yr landfalling Atlantic tropical cyclone database of rainfall from Tropical Rainfall Measurement Mission (TRMM)-based NASA Goddard multi-satellite precipitation analysis (TMM 3B42) has been collected. Categorizations have been made regarding to the storm intensity and location, e.g. over-land or over-ocean. Preliminary studies based on this database have shown that there are indeed major distinctions of cyclone rainfall distribution between over-land and over-ocean stages. However, connecting a storm ' s rainfall over ocean to its landfall rain provides implications on landfall flooding prediction. It also has been demonstrated that tropical cyclone ' s rainfall potential in one day prior to landfall can be used to discriminate among flooding vs. nonflooding storms. The first objective of this proposal is to expand and update the landfalling tropical cyclone database from the Atlantic basin only to global, from 7 years to 8, and to include environmental parameters from the Navy Operational Global Atmospheric Prediction System (NOGAPS) analysis. The second objective is to continue quantifying differences and similarities of tropical cyclone rainfall distribution over land and oceans for different basins, and developing and verifying the 'rain potentiaL' prediction index for landfall flooding of global tropical cyclones. Additionally we will investigate the complicated landfall scenarios in which the rain production is significantly enhanced by terrain interactions and extratropical transition. The third objective is to evaluate TRMM-based rainfall accumulation estimates for extreme events, e.g. tropical cyclones by using ground-based radar and gauge measurements. This will be done mainly for landfall periods. We will not only quantify the relative biases but examine advantages and disadvantages of these satellite estimates and the underlying physical reasons.

Description: A MULTI-SCALE OBSERVATIONAL AND MODELING STUDY OF CIRRUS CLOUDS USING A-TRAIN DATA Our present state of understanding of the relationship between upper tropospheric clouds and the climate system is insufficient due primarily to a lack of detailed measurements that span the contiuum of cloud genre and dynamical forcing.  This shortcoming will be addressed soon with the A-Train satellite constellation that will include the CALIPSO satellite, CloudSat, and Aqua.  With the primary goal of developing understanding of the physical processes that maintain cirrus, we propose to exploit the natural synergy of the A-Train measurements to investigate how cirrus are coupled to and evolve within the large scale atmosphere.  The basic steps to accomplish this task are as follows:  1. Using the A-Train products compiled by the CloudSat science team, identify cirrus events, and extract from the operational data streams the set of measurements that will allow for determination of the macroscale and microphysical cloud properties;  2. Apply a suite of new cloud property retrieval algorithms to the cirrus event profiles.  Using a common set of assumptions, forward model equations, empirical relationships, and inversion framework, these algorithms have been developed specifically for cirrus measured by the A-Train instruments; 3. Using geostationary satellite imagery, construct forward and backward trajectories of the cirrus fields observed by the A-Train and examine the temporal tendencies in the microphysical properties of the cloud field using algorithms applied to multispectral geostationary data along the forward and backward trajectories; 4. Using available analysis data sets, combine the cirrus events with the large scale dynamics and build a global database of cirrus events from which dynamical and microphysical composites can be constructed.  These composites will then be used as the basis for modeling studies that will seek to understand the physical processes that govern the maintenance of cirrus through their lifeycle.  Ultimately, this understanding will be used in the critical evaluation of cirrus parameterizations in global models.  A second objective of this proposal is the use of A-Train clouds in the evaluation of GCM-predicted clouds from the NCAR CAM3 GCM.  The CAM3 is initialized every 24 hours by the U.S. DOE Climate Change Prediction Program (CCPP) ARM Parameterization Testbed (CAPT) so that model-predicted clouds can be evaluated against observations.  We will extract the model output at grid cells along the A-Train track.  This will allow development of both case studies and statistics over climatically important regions.  This work merging modeling at various scales with analysis of a unique global dataset will allow for greater understanding that will influence climate models through improved physically-based parameterizations.

Description: MITIGATION OF WEATHER IMPACTS IN DENSE TERMINAL AIRSPACE.  INVESTIGATE SCHEDULING AND RATIONING ALGORITHMS FOR WEATHER IMPACTED NAS RESOURCES. AIR TRAFFIC OPERATIONS ARE SEVERELY RESTRICTED WHEN OFF NOMINAL OR CONVECTIVE WEATHER CONDITIONS ARE FORECAST FOR DENSE TERMINAL AIRSPACE.  AS PART OF THE TRAFFIC FLOW MANAGEMENT FUNCTION, DEMAND IS BALANCED WITH A PREDICTED REDUCED CAPACITY; WHEN INCLEMENT WEATHER DOES NOT MATERIALIZE, AVAILABLE CAPACITY IS LOST.  WHERE FORECASTS FAIL TO PREDICT INCLEMENT WEATHER (AND IT MATERIALIZES), RESPONSE TO THE WEATHER EVENT IS MANAGED TACTICALLY, AND IS OFTEN CHAOTIC AND INEFFICIENT. TO A LARGE EXTENT WEATHER IMPACT IS DRIVEN BY SAFETY CONCERNS (GIVEN THE LEVEL OF UNCERTAINTY IN WEATHER FORECASTING).  IF SIGNIFICANT GROWTH IN TERMINAL THROUGHPUT IS TO BE REALIZED OVER THE NEXT TWO DECADES, IMPROVEMENTS IN SCHEDULING AND RESOURCE UTILIZATION THAT REDUCE WEATHER-RELATED DELAYS ARE REQUIRED.  THE JOINT PLANNING AND DEVELOPMENT OFFICE (JPDO) ENVISIONS INCREASED THROUGHPUT AT THE BUSIEST (HUB) AIRPORTS AND AT UNDERUTILIZED AIRPORTS IN THE SURROUNDING REGION.  A SIGNIFICANT INCREASE IN PASSENGER AND CARGO THROUGHPUT WILL PLACE ADDED STRAIN ON NATIONAL AIR SPACE (NAS) RESOURCES AND AMPLIFY THE EFFECTS OF HIGHLY UNCERTAIN WEATHER FORECASTS UNDER THE CURRENT PARADIGM.  THROUGH COOPERATION WITH WEATHER FORECASTING AUTHORITIES, THE JPDO WEATHER INTEGRATED PRODUCT TEAMS (IPT) HOPES TO DEFINE WEATHER PRODUCTS THAT ARE MORE APPROPRIATE FOR THE AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM THAN THOSE AVAILABLE TODAY. NEW WEATHER FORECAST PRODUCTS WILL ENABLE IMPROVED RESOLUTION OF WEATHER DATA IN THE TERMINAL DOMAIN, ENHANCED ACCESS TO WEATHER PRODUCTS, AND PRODUCTS TAILORED SPECIFICALLY TO THE NEXT GENERATION AIR TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM (NGATS).  HOWEVER, A SUBSTANTIAL IMPROVEMENT IN THE ACCURACY OF WEATHER FORECASTING IS NOT EXPECTED, AND UNCERTAINTY OF WEATHER FORECASTS WILL REMAIN A KEY DETERMINANT OF AVIATION SYSTEM THROUGHPUT.  THIS TOPIC AREA IS FOCUSED ON DEVELOPING TERMINAL AREA SCHEDULING AND RESOURCE UTILIZATION CONCEPTS AND MODELS THAT WILL LEAD TO MITIGATING THE IMPACT OF THIS FORECAST UNCERTAINTY AS NEXT GENERATION AIR TRAFFIC SYSTEM- RELEVANT WEATHER PRODUCTS BECOME AVAILABLE. (SAP PURCHASE REQUISITION: 4200192933 - THIS CONTRACT REPLACES NNA07BA84C DUE TO PROBLEMS WITH CMM AND SAP.  THE CONTRACT REMAINS UNCHANGED EXCEPT FOR THE CONTRACT NUMBER AND PR NUMBER.)

Description: The purpose of this cooperative agreement is to conduct a shared resource project that will lead to the development of a high-sensitivity heat flux gage for calibrated heat transfer measurements. The proposed effort is described in detail in the Tao Systems Proposal No. 06-HYP-06-0104 submitted to NRA NNH06ZEA001N-HYP. This cooperative agreement will advance the technology developments and research that have been performed on advanced test and diagnostic techniques for ground test and basic hypersonic research. The specific objective is to improve the reliability and performance of heat flux gages. This work will culminate in a fast response, high-temperature heat flux gage for obtaining high-resolution, calibrated heat transfer measurements. Specifically, the heat flux gage will provide higher frequency response and an order of magnitude higher resolution than existing gages using multiple thermoresisteive gage pairs in an Active Sensor Circuit (ASC) configuration. The effort will require optimal selection of suitable high-temperature device materials, design of appropriate gage configuration for reliable heat transfer signal, and absolute calibration of the fabricated ASC-based heat flux gage. The approach integrates state-of-the-art dynamic impedance measurement technology with advanced, customizable microsensor fabrication techniques. The multi-element heat flux gage will be fabricated by Virginia Tech, while the measurement circuit for the heat flux gage elements is provided by ASC, a novel measurement circuit topology pioneered by Tao Systems. In this way, a collaborative partnership is formed that is ideally suited to develop the high-resolution, high-temperature heat flux gage. This collaborative research project will enable reliable and repeatable heat transfer measurements for assessing the aerothermodynamic effects of flow phenomena in hypersonics and other high-speed/high-temperature regimes.

Description: Routine installation and use of high-temperature optical sensors for characterization of advanced materials critical to NASA hypersonic programs are difficult due to the fundamental difficulties of integrating very diverse materials into a reliable, manufacturable sensor. Sensors based on high-temperature optical fibers (including sapphire fibers) have been developed through extensive research; however, little advancement has been made with regard to achieving cost-effective sensors that can be employed in large numbers. Currently, the materials of the mounting site, the materials of the sensor coupon, the fiber itself, sensor assembly methods and the optical interrogation methods have limited compatibility, resulting in each application becoming a custom installation. Recent demonstrations at Virginia Tech, under NASA hypersonic program funding, of advanced Fracture-Release coupon structures, novel connectorization techniques, and improved assembly methods have enabled more rapid fabrication of high-temperature sapphire fiber sensors well-suited to instrumentation of advance materials in hypersonic research. Prime Research, teaming with Virginia Tech, proposes to leverage these previous demonstrations to improve the manufacturability and ease-of-use of sapphire fiber strain gages, and to modify the assembly methods to permit their use with Prime Research's patented spinel-clad sapphire fibers, which have improved optical properties over unclad sapphire fibers.

Description: Metron Aviation will develop optimization algorithms and an automated tool for performing dynamic airspace configuration under different operational scenarios. The Dynamic Airspace Configuration Tool (DACT) takes as an input the regularly updated projections of aggregated demand and weather forecasts and produces optimum airspace boundaries that balance the airspace complexity under various global and regional constraints for time horizons as short as four hours. The optimality criteria are defined separately for different levels of automation in Air Traffic Control (ATC) procedures. DACT enables the ATC managers to initiate high volume operational corridors and other classes of airspace to best serve the user demand for airspace resources. Additionally, when fully developed, DACT provides a capability for airspace managers to dynamically manage the allocation of Special Use Airspace (SUA) and Military Operation Airspace (MOA) to ensure security of the airspace system. DACT enables a more efficient utilization of airspace capacity and reduces the operational cost for air traffic control services by dynamically re-aligning the airspace boundaries to comply with the monthly, daily, and hourly alterations in user aggregated demand, route structures, and changes in weather patterns. DACT address one of the main components of NASA's NGATS Airspace effort in developing an operational framework for DAC concept that provides the air traffic service providers with a new degree of freedom to accommodate the user demand for airspace capacity, balanced against needs of national interest (e.g. security). The proposed effort will combine state of the art mathematical optimization techniques with ATC functional requirements necessary for development of the DAC concept.

Description: The Airspace Flow Program (AFP) is a new Traffic Flow Management (TFM) control technique that has entered operation in 2006. AFPs use two existing technologies, Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Flow Constrained Areas (FCAs), to reduce demand on constrained areas of the airspace by issuing delays to be applied pre-departure. The operational use of AFPs during the 2006 severe weather season was received positively by the TFM community. However, there are significant aspects of AFP operational characteristics that differ from the previous airport-based GDPs. NASA's FACET model has already contributed significantly to the research and evaluation of TFM concepts. As the JPDO continues to refine its vision for the Next Generation Air Transportation System, additional capabilities in FACET will support its use as a critical tool for further NASA research. The development of an AFP model for FACET is an essential addition to support research and analysis of both current and future TFM operations. Mosaic ATM proposes to conduct detailed analysis of AFP operations and to develop an AFP model for FACET.

Description: The core planning algorithms to support the NGATS concepts will need accurate predictions of airport configuration over planning horizons of six hours or more. Such predictions are not currently feasible because the configuration often is not completely determined by factors such as weather forecasts, future demand, and noise restrictions that might be input to an automated predictor. When this is the case, the air traffic control tower personnel choose between the feasible configurations based on factors such as staffing issues and individual controller preferences. Furthermore, the primary meteorological forecasts currently available to the tower are not adequate to enable accurate runway usage prediction. In fact, they often fail to predict required changes in flow direction, causing reactive rather than proactive airport configuration management. In this SBIR, Metron Aviation and WSI Corporation will jointly develop an airport configuration planner incorporating optimized weather forecasts to assist tower controllers in planning runway usage more accurately at longer time horizons than currently possible and to communicate the plan to appropriate National Airspace System (NAS) stakeholders and planning systems. The optimization algorithms in this decision support tool will improve resource allocation not only at individual airports but also over all airports in a metropolitan area.

Description: Aurora Flight Sciences proposes to develop specialized algorithms and software decision-aiding tools for four-dimensional (4D) vehicle-centric, tactical trajectory management (TTM), derived from algorithms developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) to perform similar functions in military scenarios. These algorithms, based on the concept of receding horizon mixed-integer linear programming (RH-MILP), will be specifically tailored to the problem of optimizing the trades between multiple 4D trajectories (4DTs) in the dynamic airspace environment. In particular, the innovation that Aurora proposes is to model and address the stochastic nature of weather and associated airspace and resource restrictions in the flight path, respecting the fact that the time horizon over which sufficiently accurate weather estimates are available may be short compared to the overall TTM request-assign-update cycle (as envisioned by planners of the Next Generation Air Transportation System). The general problem of increasing uncertainty as planning horizons increase will be a central focus of algorithm development. This innovation addresses the needs for rapidly accommodating dynamic changes in aircraft tactical situations and responding to detected external hazards, for introducing any-time planning algorithms, and for generation and specification of 4D trajectories. Currently algorithms that directly address these needs in the context of the NGATS concept of operations (CONOPS) are in the early development stages; technology transition from related military approaches as described herein will therefore greatly benefit the state of the art in national airspace system (NA) operational tools.

Description: Real-time dosimetry is needed to provide immediate feedback, so astronauts can minimize their exposure to ionizing radiation during periods of high solar activity. Advanced optical radiation monitors are also less prone to the radiation induced degradation that plagues diode dosimeters.

Description: Aurora Flight Sciences proposes to develop specialized algorithms and software decision-aiding tools for four-dimensional (4D) vehicle-centric, tactical trajectory management (TTM), derived from algorithms developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) to perform similar functions in military scenarios. These algorithms, based on the concept of receding horizon mixed-integer linear programming (RH-MILP), will be specifically tailored to the problem of optimizing the trades between multiple 4D trajectories (4DTs) in the dynamic airspace environment. In particular, the innovation that Aurora proposes is to model and address the stochastic nature of weather and associated airspace and resource restrictions in the flight path, respecting the fact that the time horizon over which sufficiently accurate weather estimates are available may be short compared to the overall TTM request-assign-update cycle (as envisioned by planners of the Next Generation Air Transportation System). The general problem of increasing uncertainty as planning horizons increase will be a central focus of algorithm development. This innovation addresses the needs for rapidly accommodating dynamic changes in aircraft tactical situations and responding to detected external hazards, for introducing any-time planning algorithms, and for generation and specification of 4D trajectories. Currently algorithms that directly address these needs in the context of the NGATS concept of operations (CONOPS) are in the early development stages; technology transition from related military approaches as described herein will therefore greatly benefit the state of the art in national airspace system (NA) operational tools.

Description: Development of Integrated Algorithms for High-Fidelity Rotorcraft Aeromechanics Predictions within CFD/CSD-Coupled Frameworks (Reference: ROA-2006, NRA NNH06ZEA001N) The objective of this effort is to advance the capabilities of NASA's state-of-the-art prediction tools for rotorcraft aeromechanics of the complete vehicle. This effort will identify, develop and validate algorithms that improve efficiency, accuracy and fidelity of rotorcraft aeromechanics predictions (i.e. performance, dynamic response, loads, vibrations and noise). Deliverable algorithms will be integrated into existing Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) / Computational Structural Dynamics (CSD) coupled frameworks that employ comprehensive aero elastic codes for CSD. The enhancements focus on evolution of the rotor wake, CFD/CSD coupling robustness, and CSD modeling accuracy and efficiency. The resulting methodology from this research will improve accuracy and efficiency for current NASA computational capabilities, help researchers better understand physical phenomena associated with rotorcraft aeromechanics and interaction between multiple disciplines, and allow NASA to adequately analyze future concepts under development. Flexibility of the CFD/CSD coupled framework also accommodates and facilitates the implementation of future technology (e.g. trailing-edge flap, active twist rotor, and active flow control) into the analysis. The approach is to model uniquely identifiable aerodynamic domains appropriately in accordance with the key physical characteristics of each domain, develop algorithms that reflect the physics, and implement the algorithms to be compatible with the existing flow solvers. The following technology topics shall be investigated and results reported: a.Further develop the fully coupled approach using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) in the vicinity of rotor blades to capture the generation of the vortices, and Particle Vortex Transport Method (PVTM) for resolving the evolution of the vortices in the remainder of the flow field. b.Advance the understanding of the field velocity approach, which accounts for the influence of the PVTM wake on various CFD domains. c.Advance the understanding of the methods and processes by which the field velocity approach captures the rotor tip vortices as well as the vortex sheet emanating from each blade, with a good correlation on blade loading between the computations and flight test data.

Description: Development of a Multidisciplinary Computational Tool for Accurate and Efficient Rotorcraft Noise Prediction (MUTE) (Reference: ROA-2006, NRA NNH06ZEA001N). This Statement of Work (SOW) is the result of a proposal submitted by the National Institute of Aerospace, which was selected for award under the NASA Headquarters Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate (ARMD) NRA titled Research Opportunities in Aeronautics (ROA)2006. MUTE is an aggregation of multidisciplinary computational tools that accurately and efficiently model the physics of the source of rotorcraft noise and predict the noise at far-field observer locations. MUTE uses systematic coupling approaches among multiple disciplines including Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Computational Structural Dynamics (CSD), and high-fidelity Acoustics. The objective is to accurately model the physics of the noise source and to understand the basis of the noise generation from rotorcraft in a wide range of flight regimes. Within MUTE, CFD tools are used around the rotor blade to predict the transonic flow (shock wave) effects, which generate the high-speed impulsive noise. Predictions of the blade-vortex interaction noise in low speed flight are also improved by using the Particle Vortex Transport Method (PVTM), which preserves the wake flow details required for blade/wake and fuselage/wake interactions. The accuracy of the source noise prediction is further improved by utilizing a coupling approach between CFD and CSD, so that the effects of key structural dynamics, elastic blade deformations, and trim solutions are correctly represented in the analysis. This effort significantly improves the computational efficiency of MUTE with the implementation of multi-grid algorithms. MUTE can be used to expeditiously evaluate a range of future rotorcraft configurations of all types (helicopters, compounds and tilt rotors) designed especially to be responsive to a variety of environmental concerns. Other important objectives of this effort are to develop an efficient interface with the current state-of-the-art noise propagation analysis and to validate each analysis tool in MUTE (as well as the entire methodology) by comparing them with flight and wind-tunnel test data available from recent publications.

Description: Metron Aviation will develop optimization algorithms and an automated tool for performing dynamic airspace configuration under different operational scenarios. The Dynamic Airspace Configuration Tool (DACT) takes as an input the regularly updated projections of aggregated demand and weather forecasts and produces optimum airspace boundaries that balance the airspace complexity under various global and regional constraints for time horizons as short as four hours. The optimality criteria are defined separately for different levels of automation in Air Traffic Control (ATC) procedures. DACT enables the ATC managers to initiate high volume operational corridors and other classes of airspace to best serve the user demand for airspace resources. Additionally, when fully developed, DACT provides a capability for airspace managers to dynamically manage the allocation of Special Use Airspace (SUA) and Military Operation Airspace (MOA) to ensure security of the airspace system. DACT enables a more efficient utilization of airspace capacity and reduces the operational cost for air traffic control services by dynamically re-aligning the airspace boundaries to comply with the monthly, daily, and hourly alterations in user aggregated demand, route structures, and changes in weather patterns. DACT address one of the main components of NASA's NGATS Airspace effort in developing an operational framework for DAC concept that provides the air traffic service providers with a new degree of freedom to accommodate the user demand for airspace capacity, balanced against needs of national interest (e.g. security). The proposed effort will combine state of the art mathematical optimization techniques with ATC functional requirements necessary for development of the DAC concept.

Description: The core planning algorithms to support the NGATS concepts will need accurate predictions of airport configuration over planning horizons of six hours or more. Such predictions are not currently feasible because the configuration often is not completely determined by factors such as weather forecasts, future demand, and noise restrictions that might be input to an automated predictor. When this is the case, the air traffic control tower personnel choose between the feasible configurations based on factors such as staffing issues and individual controller preferences. Furthermore, the primary meteorological forecasts currently available to the tower are not adequate to enable accurate runway usage prediction. In fact, they often fail to predict required changes in flow direction, causing reactive rather than proactive airport configuration management. In this SBIR, Metron Aviation and WSI Corporation will jointly develop an airport configuration planner incorporating optimized weather forecasts to assist tower controllers in planning runway usage more accurately at longer time horizons than currently possible and to communicate the plan to appropriate National Airspace System (NAS) stakeholders and planning systems. The optimization algorithms in this decision support tool will improve resource allocation not only at individual airports but also over all airports in a metropolitan area.

Description: Purpose, Objective, and Background of Work to be Performed: Next-Generation operations seek to facilitate higher aircraft flow capacity while maintaining, or improving, current safety levels. To achieve this, a number of elements come into play, including infrastructure, technology, procedures, and culture. To accomplish higher capacity aircraft flow in the future, aircraft must have the ability to operate safely under reduced separation standards. These new operational modes will naturally introduce new safety hazards. The purpose of this research is to develop a logic-evolved model to evaluate the Air Traffic Management (ATM) safety impact resulting from new ATM concepts (including both new technology and procedural system modifications) emerging from the NASA NGATS ATM-Airspace Project of the ASP.  This proof-of-concept development phase shall direct the systems modeling focus on a subset of airspace operations for demonstrating the capability. Subsequent option years will address broadening the tool toward providing a full NAS-wide, gate-to-gate assessment capability eventually. Between 2003 and 2006, NASA's (former) Aviation Safety and Security Program (AvSSP) dedicated a significant effort to modeling the Air Transportation System (ATS) with respect to security-related operations. This experience positioned the NASA team with a substantial lead on understanding modeling of the ATS relative to the more general condition of safety and airspace related operations. Given that security attacks against the ATS result in aircraft mishaps, airframe losses, and loss of life, safety and security are analogous. However, aviation safety is the more general aspect of flight operations, extending an overarching umbrella over all aspects of the system, from flight operations, to air traffic control, and airport functions and operations. To understand the safety risks, either from a baseline perspective or relating to changes in risk with current or future changes to the system, a generalized, logical, possibility-based approach, considering probabilities where applicable and available, must be used. This represents a substantial effort and has applications across numerous disciplines for structuring this important modeling effort that has system-wide ramifications. For these reasons, it is in the best interest of NASA to use the Logic Evolved Decision (LED) Support Capability and associated methodologies/tools to perform this work. Additionally, it would be advantageous for NASA to use the LED methodology in this work since the learning curve will be minimized and previously accomplished work for the AvSSP will be leveraged in this new task.

Description: PULSAR WIND NEBULAE AND COMPACT OBJECTS IN SUPERNOVAE Recent X-ray observations of compact objects and pulsar nebulae in young supernova remnants have revolutionized our knowledge of these objects and have demonstrated the variety of possible outcomes in the core collapse of massive stars. The proposed research is aimed at elucidating the physical processes relevant to the central compact ohjects and their interactions with their surroundings in the minutes to years after formation. There are 2 main areas of investigation: 1) Fallback of supernova ejecta to the central object and possible subsequent outflow. Realistic estimates of the angular momentum of supernova ejecta will he used to estimate the early evolution of fallback, including an estimate of the critical accretion rate at which neutrino losses can no longer carry away the gravitational energy. The effects of the opacity of the accreting gas will be taken into account. There is a possible early nonradiative accretion phase that might lead to mass loss, as well as a later a later phase where mass loss might driven by the propeller mechanism. The effect of this mass outflow on the freely expanding ejecta will he estimated using semi-analytic techniques. In particular, the possibility that the "jet" feature in Cas A is formed by a collimated outflow expanding into freely expanding ejecta will be investigated. 2) Structure and spectra of young pulsar nebulae. The standard model for the Crab Nebula involves a shocked, MHD relativistic pulsar wind, with a toroidal structure. However, this model has problems in reproducing the properties of other pulsar nebulae, and alternate models, including a convection-diffusion model, will be investigated. Synchrotron emission spectra will be calculated for evolutionary models with and without strong pulsar spindown, for which there are observational examples. Constraints on possible early magnetic field evolution of pulsars will be obtained from evolutionary models of pulsar nebulae with the corresponding variation in power input.

The Precipitation Processing System (PPS) is the data system that will generate the standard precipitation products for both Version 7 TRMM and precipitation missions in the GPM era. The role of the data system in the testing of retrieval algorithms, generation of standard products and quality control of both is clear. An additional capability ofthe data system is the generation of analysis products (zona Is, time-series, statistical analyses, sensitivity tests, etc.) for the sole purpose of improving retrieval algorithms. The work proposed here goes beyond the mechanics of generating these various analysis products and is focused on the integration of the knowledge gained back into the retrieval algorithms through the Precipitation Measuring Missions (PMM) Science Team. Our group is in a unique position to assist in evaluating and improving precipitation retrieval algorithms, not only having been involved in the development and prototyping ofPPS but having been involved with the TRMM data system and the developers of the retrieval algorithms since before launch.

Description: The Program to Advance Inflatable Decelerators for Atmospheric Entry (PAI-DAE) will conduct a set of ground tests (wind-tunnel and ballistic range), materials development studies, and system trade studies to advance various aspects of the inflatable decelerator technology. The PAI-DAE program is jointly funded by the Innovative Partnership Program, Aeronautics Mission Directorate, and the Exploration Technology Development Program to conduct research and development necessary to demonstrate the inflatable aerodynamic decelerator (IAD) technology as both an entry systems technology and a supersonic decelerator technology. This task is to provide trajectory analysis and entry systems expertise for PAI-DAE testing and trade studies. 3.Description of the Work to be Performed: The contractor shall perform the following task requirements: 3.1The contractor shall conduct trajectory studies for seven IAD flight conditions. The contractor shall perform feasibility studies of IAD technology with respect to multiple mission applications. The contractor shall conduct a parametric study for each flight condition and determine trajectory parameters (altitude vs. time, maximum heat rate, total heat load, and total flight duration) for each ballistic coefficient that results in a trajectory that satisfactorily meets specified criteria per specified initial conditions. 3.1.1The contractor shall document the trajectory studies in data tables. 3.1.2The data tables or associated documentation shall include initial conditions for each trajectory. 3.1.3The data tables or associated documentation shall include any assumptions for each trajectory. 3.1.4The data tables shall include the following parameters: ballistic coefficient, stagnation point heat rate, stagnation point heat load, dynamic pressure, and flight duration. 3.1.5The data tables shall indicate if a trajectory meets specified criteria. 3.2The contractor shall design a sub-scale IAD deployment test wind-tunnel experiment using the NASA Glenn Research Center 10x10 Unitary Wind Tunnel Facility. The contractor shall design a wind-tunnel experiment including test matrix, IAD sizing, and fixturing concepts. The wind-tunnel experiment shall document time histories of IAD angle of attack with respect to time since initial inflation. The test shall cover deployments at a range of Mach numbers from 2 to 3. 3.2.1The contractor shall document the experiment design as a test plan. 3.2.2The test plan shall include the number of wind-tunnel test runs to be completed in a two-week entry into the wind-tunnel, assuming one-day for set-up and one-day for removal. 3.2.3The test plan shall include the experiment variables to be changed per wind-tunnel test run (i.e. wind-tunnel Mach Number, wind-tunnel dynamic pressure, IAD inflation pressure, IAD angle-of-attack). 3.2.4The test plan shall include the specific data to be collected during testing. 3.2.5The test plan shall include the type of instrumentation that will be required on the IAD test article during testing. 3.2.6The test plan shall include the instrumentation required, if any, for the test that will not be available as part of normal operations of the GRC 10x10 Unitary Wind-Tunnel. 3.2.7The test plan shall include a dimensioned drawing of a dynamically scaled IAD required for testing. 3.2.8The test plan shall include a design [dimensioned drawing(s)] of a mechanism for mounting the IAD in the wind-tunnel during testing.PR: 4200188558

Description: AN INVESTIGATION OF THE PERFORMANCE OF MICROWAVE RADAR INSTRUMENT CONCEPTS FOR REMOTE SENSING OF ATMOSPHERIC PRESSURESURFACE AIR PRESSURE IS ONE OF THE MOST IMPORTANT ATMOSPHERIC PARAMETERS THAT ARE REGULARLY MEASURED AT GROUND BASED SURFACE METEOROLOGICAL STATIONS. OVER OCEANS, SEA SURFACE AIR BAROMETRIC PRESSURES ARE USUALLY MEASURED BY A LIMITED NUMBER OF IN-SITUOBSERVATIONS CONDUCTED BY BUOY STATIONS AND OIL PLATFORMS. THE SPATIAL COVERAGE OF THESE OBSERVATIONS IS VERY POOR, ESPECIALLY GIVEN THE TEMPORAL AND SPATIAL VARIABILITY AND THEIMPORTANCE OF THESE VARIATIONS TO WEATHER FORECAST MODELS. FOR EXAMPLE, ALONG THE EAST COAST OF THE UNITED STATES AND GULF OF MEXICO, ONLY ABOUT 40 BUOYS ARE AVAILABLE UNDER THE NOAA OCEAN OBSERVING SYSTEM (NCOS) OF THE NOAA NATIONAL DATA BUOY CENTER(NDBC; BTTP://WWW,NDBC.NOAA.GOV/). THE TROPICAL ATMOSPHERE OCEAN (TAO) PROGRAM ONLY HAS 10 SITES FROM WHICH THE BAROMETRIC PRESSURE IS MEASURED. FOR SEVERE WEATHER CONDITIONS, SUCH AS TROPICAL STORMS AND HURRICANES, TBESE NOOS AND TAO BUOY SYSTEMSUSUALLY CANNOT PROVIDE SPATIALLY DESIRABLE IN-SITU MEASUREMENTS DUE TO EITHER THE LACK OF BUOY STATIONS ON THE TRACK OF STORMS OR MALFUNCTIONS OF BUOYS CAUSED BY THE SEVERE WEATHER ITSELFUNDER TROPICAL CYCLONE CONDITIONS, INCLUDING TROPICAL DEPRESSION, TROPICAL STORM, HURRICANE, AND SUPER-TYPHOON CASES; THE SURFACE BAROMETRIC PRESSURE IS ONE OF THE MOST HIMPORTANT METEOROLOGICAL PARAMETERS IN THE PREDICTION AND FORECAST OF THE INTENSITY AND S TRACK OF TROPICAL STORMS AND HURRICANES. THE CLASSIFICATION OF TROPICAL STORMS ANDHURRICANES ON THE SAFFIR-SIMPSON HURRICANE SCALE (SSHS) IS BASED ON THE MAXIMUM JJ SUSTAINED SURFACE WIND SPEED THAT IS A DIRECT RESULT OF THE INTERACTION BETWEEN THE CENTRAL AIR PRESSURE AND THE PRESSURE FIELDS SURROUNDING TROPICAL STORMS. THUS, THE MEASUREMENT OF CENTRAL PRESSURE AND PRESSURE FIELD ARE IMPORTANT FOR PREDICTIONS AND FORECASTS OF O HURRICANE AND TROPICAL STORM INTENSITY AND STORM TRACK. THE ONLY METHOD CURRENTLY 0 AVAILABLE TO PROVIDE USEFUL SPATIAL SAMPLING IS THE USE OF A MANNED AIRCRAFT DEPLOYING X DROPSONDES. HOWEVER, EACH DROPSONDE SUPPLIES ONLY ONE SPATIAL POINT MEASUREMENT. SO EVEN THIS HIGH COST APPROACH PROVIDES ONLY LIMITED DATA AND LEAVES MOST OF THE STORM AREA UNMEASURED. - TO IMPROVE PREDICTIONS AND FORECASTS OF THE INTENSITY AND TRACK OF TROPICAL STORMS, LARGE SPATIAL COVERAGE AND FREQUENT SAMPLING OF SEA SURFACE BAROMETRY ARE CRITICALLY NEEDED FOR USE IN NUMERICAL WEATHER MODELS. THESE NEEDED MEASUREMENTS OF SEA SURFACE BAROMETRIC PRESSURE CANNOT BE REALIZED BY IN-SITU BUOY AND AIRCRAFT DROPSONDE TECHNIQUES. THE ONLY HOPE OF THE BAROMETRY FOR LARGE SPATIAL AND TEMPORAL SCALES OVER OCEANS IS FROM REMOTE SENSING TECHNIQUES SUCH AS; MANNED AIRCRAFT, UNMANNED AERIAL VEHICLES (UAVS), AND SATELLITE PLATFORMS.

Description: SBIR PHASE II AWARD FOR EFFORT ENTITLED: PASSIVE MICROWAVE HIGH RELIABILITY OSCILLATORS FOR TERAHERTZ SYSTEMS. THE CONTRACTOR WILL DEVELOP A THOROUGH UNDERSTANDING OF THE COMPLEX INTERACTIONS THAT OCCUR WITHIN A CHAIN OF NON-LINEAR FREQUENCY MULTIPLES. THESE NON-LINEAR INTERACTIONS CAN CAUSE RAPID VARIATIONS IN POWER AS THE FREQUENCY OR INPUT POWER ARE TUNED, INCLUDING NULLS AND POWER SURGES THAT CAN DAMAGE INDIVIDUAL COMPONENTS. TODAY, THESE PROBLEMS ARE MITIGATED IN 3 WAYS: MECHANICAL TUNING OR BIAS ADJUSTMENTS, LABORIOUS TWEAKING OF EACH COMPONENT IN THE CHAIN UNTIL ACCEPTABLE SYSTEM PERFORMANCE IS ACHIEVED, AND REDUCTION OF THE SYSTEM BANDWIDTH AND/OR POWER SPECIFICATIONS TO AVOID THE MOST DRAMATIC EFFECTS. HOWEVER, EACH OF THESE "SOLUTIONS" EITHER FUNDAMENTALLY LIMITS THE ELECTRICAL PERFORMANCE OF THE TERAHERTZ SOURCE OR DRAMATICALLY REDUCES THE EASE-OF-USE OF THE SYSTEM. THIS PROPOSED EFFORT REPRESENTS THE FIRST SYSTEMATIC STUDY OF THE COMPLEX INTERACTIONS BETWEEN CASCADED NON-LINEAR MULTIPLIER STAGES, WITH THE GOAL OF DEVELOPING NEW MULTIPLIER AND SYSTEM DESIGNS THAT WILL REDUCE THESE UNWANTED EFFECTS. THE RESULTING TERAHERTZ SOURCES WILL ACHIEVE GREATER RELIABILITY, EFFICIENCY, BANDWIDTH, AND EASE-OF-USE. IN ADDITION, THE KNOWLEDGE GAINED THROUGH THIS RESEARCH WILL BE USED TO ACHIEVE VASTLY IMPROVED TERAHERTZ SOURCES FOR NASA'S ATMOSPHERIC AND RADIO ASTRONOMY MISSIONS; AS WELL AS A WIDE RANGE OF EMERGING COMMERCIAL APPLICATIONS SUCH AS IMAGING SYSTEMS FOR SECURITY SCREENING AND INDUSTRIAL PROCESS CONTROL.

Description: The proposed project presents a remotely-sensed data-driven modeling initiative aimed at evaluating the long-term habitat availability for a critically endangered large carnivorous species in the Russian Far East i the Amur tiger and the Amur leopard. Russian forests are a stronghold for large carnivore preservation efforts because they provide large interconnected areas of suitable habitat necessary to support a minimum viable population of a given species. The projected increase in the occurrence and spatial extent of natural forest disturbances (primarily fire) in a changing climate and an ongoing expansion of logging activities under the prevailing resource-oriented economic model will lead to destruction, degradation, and fragmentation of available habitat. Additionally, climate induced changes in post-disturbance recovery and species composition are likely to force a shift in the carnivorous species distribution to other areas. While the existence of suitable habitat in the future is expected, a need exists for a spatially explicit analysis of habitat change in a temporally dynamic framework to ensure the connectivity of the current and potential future suitable habitats, which will facilitate the successful migration of the carnivores and their prey species. This project is designed to continue the ongoing NASA-sponsored research projects in the area and build upon their results. It will model habitat distribution using the FAREAST forest succession model. This model will utilize inputs on forest cover and disturbances provided by the decision-tree based fusion of remotely sensed data products from passive optical (MODIS, MISR, MSS, TM, ETM+, ASTER), radar (ENVISAT ASAR, ALOS PALSAR) and lidar (ICESAT) sensors. This project will make a significant contribution to the Northern Eurasia Earth Science Partnership Initiative (NEESPI) program by assessing disturbance-driven forest change in the NEESPI area. Additionally, it will strongly contribute to Amur tiger and leopard conservation efforts.

Proposed Effort: The primary objective of this effort is the development of a highly integrated, field-portable multi-parameter distributed fiber-optic instrumentation system which will enable high-spatial resolution interrogation of FBG arrays for non-destructive evaluation, structural health monitoring, wing shape monitoring, and other applications. Key to the miniaturization effort is the adoption of a compact laser source, integration of the existing optical network into a PIC, and electronic design for signal conditioning, sampling, memory, and an FPGA-based CPU to control the various subsystems and perform high-speed data processing.   During the Phase I, Luna demonstrated the viability of a miniaturized, high-speed interrogator through the development of numerous relevant subsystems. The Phase I culminated in a demonstration of 30 Hz sensing with 60 FBGs, and a recommended design concept for Phase II. During the Phase II effort, the development will proceed along the outlined design path. The Phase II effort will culminate in a complete integration of the laser source, PIC, and sampling/processing electronics into a fully integrated interrogator. Phase III will result in technology maturation and transition to manufacture of the instrumentation system. Through its previous commercialization success with distributed fiber-optic instrumentation systems, Luna Innovations has ready access to production facilities and an established sales force and distribution network for the instrument.  To meet the requirements of this effort, Luna will leverage its considerable experience with OFDR system design to accomplish the following technical objectives:  1 Objective 1: Develop a highly integrated OFDR unit  2 Objective 2: Demonstrate 1 kHz sensing  3 Objective 3: Assess performance of sensors in terms of the application environment.  The key advancements arising from the Phase II development include: 1) the development of the hardware, software, and firmware that achieves the performance, size, and weight targets of the effort; 2) a substantial reduction in the cost to manufacture the instrumentation, opening significant commercial markets; and 3) the development of detailed experimental data that confirms the performance of the sensors in the expected application environments.

Description: MEASURING STAR FORMATION RATES IN CLUSTERS OF GALAXIES WITH GALEX Recent UV and optical observations have revealed that a fairly high percentage of clusters of galaxies with short cooling times in the X-ray emitting gas (cooling flow clusters) show evidence for large amounts of star formation, but that there is little evidence for star formation in non-cooling flow clusters. Thus the origin of this star formation is likely to be related to the presence of short cooling times in the X-ray gas. We have obtained XMM Optical Monitor UV imaging data in one color band for 15 clusters and find that the ratio of UV light to inferred X-ray cooling rate shows a range of 100, with some clusters having an implied star formation rate consistent with the X-ray cooling rate and others showing no evidence for 'excess' UV light. We propose to use GALEX data to: 1) confirm the presence of 'excess' UV light in cluster centers which is not related to the old stellar population; 2) use GALEX FUV and NUV colors to age date this population; and 3) use the higher signal to noise GALEX data to derive a surface brightness distribution for the UV light and directly compare it to the optical light and the X-ray inferred cooling flow profile.

Description: INVESTIGATIONS OF RAREFIED/CONTINUUM FLOWFIELDS Abstract  A complex fluid mechanical phenomena is the interaction of a continuum jet injecting into a rarefied free stream.  For spacecraft traveling through the rarefied regime, such as high altitude entry into an atmosphere, understanding this phenomena is essential in modeling and designing trajectory control systems.  This study examines interactions in which a supersonic continuum jet is injected into a rarefied free stream in two directions from a blunt spacecraft model: directly opposing the free stream flow and transversely to the flow.  The first interaction has application to cooling and supersonic propulsive deceleration.  The second interaction has application in reaction control jets, such as those to be used on the Mars Science Laboratory. In order to investigate these interactions, a method called Planar Laser Induced Iodine Fluorescence (PLIIF) is utilized.  The well established technique involves seeding a supersonic flow with iodine and then fluorescing the gas mixture by sending an argon laser sheet across the flow.  This fluorescence allows for planar visualization of the flow as well as quantitative planar measurements of velocity, mole fraction and temperature. With the PLIIF measurements, greater comprehension of these complex continuum/rarefied interactions can be obtained for the two applications mentioned above.  These measurements will be compared with hybrid continuum/rarefied codes under development in the Aerothermodynamics Branch at the NASA Langley Research Center.

Description: This research proposal focuses on verification of satellite instantaneous precipitation products over a variety of climatic regimes for the purpose of assessing TRMM algorithm performance. As main part of this effort, we will evaluate the potential use of the existing U.S. national network of radars and rain gauges for statistical verification of TRMM and future GPM estimates. The distribution of rain rate (R) is of great interest in many fields. For example, hydrological applications such as flood forecasting depend on an accurate representation of the excess rainfall--driven by rain rate-that does not infiltrate the soil. Probability distribution functions (pdf) of R can now be obtained from satellite observations (e.g., the TRMM satellite). How accurate are they? Evaluating the accuracy of the satellite based pdfs is very important also since it allows for indirect evaluation of other rainfall products from space-based observations. The advantage of comparing space-based pdfs with pdfs derived from co-located ground-based observations is that such comparisons are free of the large uncertainties associated with pixel-by-pixel comparisons of the instantaneous products, and also of the satellite temporal sampling errors associated with the accumulated rainfall products. Recent efforts to evaluate the pdfs from TRMM Precipitation Radar (PR) by comparing them to pdfs based on co-located data from gauge adjusted ground radar in central Florida reveals large discrepancies. These discrepancies vary with rain type. To better identify and resolve such significant discrepancies, we propose to utilize the new NOAA/NSSL Next Generation QPE experimental products consisting of high temporal and spatial resolution 3-D radar reflectivity and gauge-adjusted rain rate mosaics (1 km, 5-min) over the entire continental U.S. Utilizing these new products will significantly increase our sample size of ground reference data available for verification of satellite instantaneous rainfall estimates. It will also permit classification by topography, geographic region, season, climate regime, weather extremes, and rain type. Our key objective is to identify and understand the sources of large discrepancies between surface-based and satellite estimates of rain rate in order to evaluate and improve satellite algorithms and products, and to predict algorithm performance in different meteorological regimes. We will develop and apply a new framework for statistical and physical verification of satellite estimates of rainfall based on comparing space- and ground-based pdf of R before and after classifying the pdfs by rain type and other parameters. We will apply this framework to data from the TRMM Ground Validation (GV) site in Central Florida and from the National Network. The National Network-satellite pdf comparison will not be limited to spaceborne radar but will include passive microwave rainfall products. In addition, the PI proposes to continue his efforts of improving the TRMM GV "operational" algorithm and products (TRMM version 6 and beyond). Special emphasis will be given to instantaneous GV rain products and improved GV pdfs for comparison with the satellite pdfs. The proposed objectives will be achieved through collaboration with scientists at NOAA and the work of a Ph.D. student from Universitat Politecnica de Catalunya (UPC) Barcelona at no cost to NASA. The PI, a former member of the TRMM Science Team, has considerable experience addressing validation issues from his work at NASA GSFC in the research, development and application of methodologies for quantitative precipitation estimation, and verification and improvement of TRMM GV rainfall products. He is currently serving on the GPM GV Working Group tasked with formulating the GPM GV program requirements

Description: TAS::80 0120::TAS PURPOSE, OBJECTIVE, AND BACKGROUND OF WORK TO BE PERFORMED:UNDER THE SUPERSONICS ELEMENT OF THE FUNDAMENTAL AERO PROGRAM, NASA LARC HAS BEEN DEVELOPING AND VALIDATING PROGRESSIVE FAILURE METHODS.  MUCH OF THE PRELIMINARY WORK INVOLVES TENSILE LOADED COMPOSITE COUPONS WITH CENTER NOTCHES.  THE CONVENTIONAL METHOD OF MACHINING THE NOTCHES MAY BE LEADING TO MICRO CRACKS THAT ARE AFFECTING THE FAILURE MECHANISMS AND MAKING IT DIFFICULT TO CORRELATE EXPERIMENTS WITH ANALYSIS.  NASA DESIRES TO COMPARE CONVENTIONAL NOTCHED COUPONS WITH THOSE NOTCHED BY LASER CUTTING IN ORDER TO DETERMINE IF THIS IS CAUSING THE OBSERVED PROBLEMS WITH CORRELATION.3.DESCRIPTION OF THE WORK TO BE PERFORMED:  THE CONTRACTOR SHALL PROVIDE ALL THE RESOURCES, INCLUDING LAB RESOURCES, NECESSARY TO PERFORM THE FOLLOWING TASK REQUIREMENTS:3.1. INITIALLY DEMONSTRATE LASER NOTCH CUTTING CAPABILITY BY CUTTING 3-5 NOTCHES IN COMPOSITE LAMINATE SAMPLE MATERIAL SUPPLIED BY NASA LARC.  NOTCHES SHALL BE THROUGH NOTCHES 0.75 INCHES LONG WITH A HEIGHT OF 0.015 INCHES.  THE CONTRACTOR SHALL TAKE CARE TO AVOID CHARRING OR DISCOLORATION AROUND NOTCH BOUNDARIES.  A METHODOLOGY SHALL BE DEVELOPED TO MINIMIZE THIS PHENOMENON.3.2.  HAVING DEMONSTRATED BASIC TECHNOLOGY ON SAMPLE MATERIAL, THE CONTRACTOR SHALL PROCEED BY CUTTING THREE NOTCHES IN A NASA SUPPLIED THREE INCH WIDE COUPON.  NOTCH DIMENSIONS SHALL BE AS FOLLOWS:  ONE NOTCH AT 0.75 INCHES BY 0.015 INCHES, ONE NOTCH AT 0.75 INCHES BY 0.03 INCHES AND ONE NOTCH AT 0.75 INCHES BY 0.09375 INCHES. 3.3.  PREPARE A SERIES OF NASA SUPPLIED SPECIMENS, EACH WITH A SINGLE CENTRAL NOTCH WITH DIMENSIONS MAINTAINING A NOTCH TO WIDTH RATIO OF 0.25.  SPECIMENS OF DIFFERENT LENGTHS WILL BE SUPPLIED BY NASA.  THE NOTCH HEIGHTS WILL EITHER BE 0.015 INCHES, 0.03 INCHES, OR 0.09375 INCHES, TO BE DETERMINED BY NASA.3.4. DEPENDING ON THE SUCCESS OF TESTING SUCH COUPONS, THE GOVERNMENT WILL SUPPLY UP TO 24 ADDITIONAL COUPONS TO BE NOTCHED UTILIZING THE TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPED IN 3.1 THROUGH 3.3 ABOVE.  3.5  THE CONTRACTOR SHALL DEVELOP A PROCEDURE FOR THE LASER CUTTING OF NOTCHES WITH MINIMAL CHARRING EFFECTS.  THE PROCEDURE SHALL BE NO MORE THAN 5 PAGES.

Purpose, Objective, and Background of Work to be Performed: The Fundamental Aero Program (FAP), Subsonic Fixed Wing (SFW) Project, is performing foundational research in the area of nonlinear aerodynamic modeling. Military and civilian requirements for performance and safety improvements have focused international research on improving the fidelity of aerodynamic modeling especially in portions of the flight envelope where nonlinear unsteady behaviors occur. A key aspect of the SFW modeling effort is to produce a comprehensive methodology for obtaining appropriate aerodynamic math models over an extended flight envelope. The methodology includes development of ground and flight test techniques and identification algorithms for obtaining the math models from measured data. This SFW effort, to date, has lacked the modern Design of Experiment (DOE) and Response Surface Modeling (RSM) technologies that can improve accuracy and efficiency of the experimental process. The long term goal of this task is to incorporate DOE/RSM technology into the development of ground-based dynamic test techniques. To support advanced dynamic testing, NASA LaRC is developing appropriate wind tunnel models and a new dynamic test rig (DR) for the LaRC 12-Foot Wind Tunnel (LaRC 12-FT) that will allow a broad spectrum of test techniques including DOE/RSM technology.  3. The proposed research program will include three parts: (1) Dynamic rig control software, (2) Dynamic rig validation, and (3) DOE/RSM dynamic test methods. The contractor shall assist the NASA engineer in developing control software for the mini-rig to later be transferred to the LaRC 12-FT DR. Description: CHARACTERIZING PRECIPITATION AND LATENT HEATING FROM TRMM SATELLITE MEASUREMENTS Precipitation is one of the most important meteorological variables in the global water and energy cycle. One of the salient features of precipitation is its diurnal variability. Various recent studies from the Tropical P~infal1 'Measuring Mission (TfUAM) precipitation datasets indicate that rainfall diurnal variability is a qbmplex global phenomenon with multiple phases that cannot be explained by general causal f41qtors. TRMM studies indicate that there are a host of mechanisms at work in producing diurnal scale rainfall processes. It has been well established that diabatic heating in the tropics is dominated by net latent heat release. It is also accepted that space-time variations in latent heating' (LH) have tremendous impacts on planetary scale tropical zonal and meridional mass OVCrtu1.:nillgs, tropical intraseasonal waves, monsoons, and tropical and midlatitude stormcirculations.1:Moreover, the planetary~scale tropical circulations, various interactions between the tropics and,midlatitudes, and the tropical Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) are greatly influenced by variants in the LH vertical structure. Thus. generation of LH products has been one of the most important TRMM activities. Howev eT~ to date, there has not been a systematic study of the data 'quality of the experimental TRMM LH products, nor an indepth examination of the quantitative error characteristics ofthese experimental products. The proposed study will focus on the ensemble spatial-temporal features of rainfall diurnal . variability based on a long term satellite microwave measurements, specifically from TRMM, and on quantifying the error characteristics of TRMM's CUlTent 4-dimensional LH products based on systematic intercomparisons and validation checks against independently acquired diagnostic LH products. The mainstn~arn validation products are calculated using the classical apparent heating source (Q) and apparent moisture sink (Q]) diagnostic procedures for eight available TRMM-related f'ield campaign radiosonde datasets. These campaign sites are located over a sufficient range ofocean and continental environments to produce a wide spectrum of LH conditions. A secondal] source of diagnostic products ",'ill be Qi approximations for fouf sites which have produced dual-Doppler radar measurements. LH estimates from this variety of sites can support instantaneous comparisons at relatively high spatial resolutions consistent with various of the TRMM level 2 LH products. Since TRMM-related field campaign site datasets and ancillary dual-Doppler radar sitEl datasets are such  valuable commodities for validation research, emphasis will be given to evaluating how much of the spectrum of LH conditions are represented by these sites. In addition, a systematic analysis of TRMM LH products for wellknown and distinct weather systems ,including the MJO, the El Nifio - Southern Oscillation (ENSO), and. the 'South-East Asian (SEA) Monsoon will provide additional information related to LH error characteristics. There are four main scientific objectives of the proposed research: (I) provide scientific explanations of the ensemble characteristics of the global rainfall diurnal cycle, (2) establish foremost amplitude and. vertical structure properties of  standard TRMM LH products at different space-time scales, (3) conduct validation and error analyses of standard TRMM LH products at various space-time scales guided by independent LH estimates tron'! radiosonde networks, duaJDoppler radar wind sites with supporting radiosonde site(s), and heuristic analyses associated with various well known and distinct weather-climate processes, (4) analyze 4-dlmensional vertical LH structures and their evolution processes for different climate regimes and weather systems at various space-time scales.

Description: IMPACT CHEMISTRY IN ICY SATELLITES The Galileo and Cassini missions made spectacular observations of the satellites and rings around Jupiter and Saturn and provided substantial information of surface composition through infrared spectra. Many questions remain about the causes of the different chemical species found on the surfaces. Have they all been generated by interactions with the magnetosphere, and if so how? What is the effect of the solar ultraviolet radiation in determining the lifetime of surface molecules? Here, new laboratory measurements are proposed to address some of the most pressing questions and increase the scientific return from NASA is missions to the outer solar system. The topics include: 1) The analysis of near infrared spectra obtained by Galileo, Cassini and ground based telescopes requires comparison with the spectra of pure ice that has been irradiated. That information does not exist and will be obtained in this project. 2) How can we predict the creation of hydrogen peroxide in ice by the different types of radiation present at Jupiters satellite Europa? More generally, can one obtain general scaling relations for the effect of radiation of electrons, light and heavy ions that, combined with their known energy distributions, would allow reliable models of changes of chemical composition of surface ices? 3) What is the stability of hydrogen peroxide, ammonia, and their compounds with water on icy surfaces of the outer solar system? How does photo-destruction of ammonia by solar ultraviolet light affect the surface properties of Enceladus, Charon, and other objects in the outer solar system? The studies will be done in ultrahigh vacuum using state-of-the-art surface science techniques, mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy, in collaboration with Dr. Robert Carlson, of JPL, of extensive experience in the Galileo mission.

Description: Purpose, Objective, and Background of Work to be Performed: Next-Generation operations seek to facilitate higher aircraft flow capacity while maintaining, or improving, current safety levels. To achieve this, a number of elements come into play, including infrastructure, technology, procedures, and culture. To accomplish higher capacity aircraft flow in the future, aircraft must have the ability to operate safely under reduced separation standards. These new operational modes will naturally introduce new safety hazards. The purpose of this research is to develop a logic-evolved model to evaluate the Air Traffic Management (ATM) safety impact resulting from new ATM concepts (including both new technology and procedural system modifications) emerging from the NASA NGATS ATM-Airspace Project of the ASP.  This proof-of-concept development phase shall direct the systems modeling focus on a subset of airspace operations for demonstrating the capability. Subsequent option years will address broadening the tool toward providing a full NAS-wide, gate-to-gate assessment capability eventually. Between 2003 and 2006, NASA's (former) Aviation Safety and Security Program (AvSSP) dedicated a significant effort to modeling the Air Transportation System (ATS) with respect to security-related operations. This experience positioned the NASA team with a substantial lead on understanding modeling of the ATS relative to the more general condition of safety and airspace related operations. Given that security attacks against the ATS result in aircraft mishaps, airframe losses, and loss of life, safety and security are analogous. However, aviation safety is the more general aspect of flight operations, extending an overarching umbrella over all aspects of the system, from flight operations, to air traffic control, and airport functions and operations. To understand the safety risks, either from a baseline perspective or relating to changes in risk with current or future changes to the system, a generalized, logical, possibility-based approach, considering probabilities where applicable and available, must be used. This represents a substantial effort and has applications across numerous disciplines for structuring this important modeling effort that has system-wide ramifications. For these reasons, it is in the best interest of NASA to use the Logic Evolved Decision (LED) Support Capability and associated methodologies/tools to perform this work. Additionally, it would be advantageous for NASA to use the LED methodology in this work since the learning curve will be minimized and previously accomplished work for the AvSSP will be leveraged in this new task.

Description: PARALLEL UNSTRUCTURED GRID GENERATION BY THE ADVANCING FRONT FOR COMPELX REAL-WORLD COMPUTATIONAL AERODYNAMIC SIMULATIONS In this project we are working with NASA Langley Research Center on a parallel unstructured grid generator based on the advancing front technique targeting in particular CFD (computational fluid dynamic) simulations of complex real-world aerodynamic problems. The parallel unstructured grid generator extends NASA's state-of-the-art sequential advancing front mesher Vgrid. Vgrid was developed at NASA Langley and is an integral component of the TetrUSS software package which serves NASA's computational aerodynamic needs. The desire to perform improved quality and more accurate simulations along with: (1) the widespread availability of parallel machine architectures and (2) the ability of numerical solvers to take advantage of parallel architectures, such as the Usm3D solver used within the TetrUSS software package, impose a much greater and more difficult requirement for the mesh generator. For improved quality and high-accuracy simulations a large-scale, high resolution mesh is required. Generating such a mesh on single machine is a challenging task due to both CPU and memory limitations. A parallel mesher, with distributed memory, is more suitable for this task. In this report we present the current state of the project, the two methods that we have developed for parallel mesh generation, some preliminary data derived on the Sciclone cluster at the college of William and Mary and the Tiger cluster at NASA Langley Research center, and report on the future goals and direction of this work.

Description: INVESTIGATIONS OF RAREFIED/CONTINUUM FLOWFIELDS Abstract  A complex fluid mechanical phenomena is the interaction of a continuum jet injecting into a rarefied free stream.  For spacecraft traveling through the rarefied regime, such as high altitude entry into an atmosphere, understanding this phenomena is essential in modeling and designing trajectory control systems.  This study examines interactions in which a supersonic continuum jet is injected into a rarefied free stream in two directions from a blunt spacecraft model: directly opposing the free stream flow and transversely to the flow.  The first interaction has application to cooling and supersonic propulsive deceleration.  The second interaction has application in reaction control jets, such as those to be used on the Mars Science Laboratory. In order to investigate these interactions, a method called Planar Laser Induced Iodine Fluorescence (PLIIF) is utilized.  The well established technique involves seeding a supersonic flow with iodine and then fluorescing the gas mixture by sending an argon laser sheet across the flow.  This fluorescence allows for planar visualization of the flow as well as quantitative planar measurements of velocity, mole fraction and temperature. With the PLIIF measurements, greater comprehension of these complex continuum/rarefied interactions can be obtained for the two applications mentioned above.  These measurements will be compared with hybrid continuum/rarefied codes under development in the Aerothermodynamics Branch at the NASA Langley Research Center.

Description: Purpose, Objective, and Background of Work to be Performed: Aircraft structural health monitoring systems, currently under development, can detect an acoustic emission (AE) such as an impact or structural fracture or tear that can potentially damage wing or fuselage structure, but not the location and nature of the event generating the AE. This could enable real time in-flight decisions about the continued airworthiness of the aircraft and would be a significant advance in structural health monitoring. The purpose of this task is to utilize the work done in determining the strain and displacement response to an internal breakage in an isotropic plate to determine the nature and location of the breakage by matching measured and calculated responses. It will enable real-time determination of damage on an aircraft from the monitoring of acoustic emission signals via an array of fuselage or wing mounted sensors and recording devices. It will also be a necessary intermediate building block to addressing the same problem for a composite structure in the future.
