Description: INVESTIGATION OF KEY PROBLEM IN IONOSPHERIC PHOTOCHEMISTRY The purpose of this proposed research is to improve our basic understanding of the fundamental photochemistry ofthe ionosphere in support of future NASA missions. This objective will be achieved by detailed examination of Atmosphere Explorer (AE) measurements of ionospheric densities and temperatures with the aid of ionosonde measurements and the Field Line Interhemispheric Plasma (FLIP) model. These studies will take advantage of new understanding of reaction rates, cross sections, and solar EUV fluxes that was not available in the studies that were conducted with the AE data over 20 years ago. The primary outcome will be a better knowledge ofthe basic sources and sinks of ionospheric ions and neutrals. This will in tum lead to improved model calculations of charged particle densities. A good knowledge of ionospheric chemistry will be important for the Geospace Electrodynamic Connections (GEC) and Ionosphere Thermosphere Storm Probes (ITSP) missions. Models will play an important part in these missions because it is unlikely that either mission will be able to measure all the relevant parameters. One ofthe prime objectives ofthe GEC mission is to study the boundary layer region below 200 km altitude where coupling between the ionosphere, thermosphere, and magnetosphere is strongest and where the auroral currents close. Knowledge ofthe relative ion composition is important for determining the magnitude ofthe electrical conductivities. Thus it is important to determine how well we understand the chemistry of this region. The Atmosphere Explorer (AE) database is the only comprehensive database that exists for testing our models ofthe ionosphere and thermosphere. An important collateral benefit of this research is that it will help train the next generation of aeronomers in the analysis of in-situ spacecraft measurements. These people will be essential for the design and implementation ofthe future ionospheric missions.

Description: MONTHLY OCEANIC RAIN RATE FROM MICROWAVE EMMISSION BRIGHTNESS TEMPERATURE HISTOGRAMS (METH) We propose to develop the next generation (TRMM Version 7 or GPM Version 1) of the emission based microwave oceanic monthly rainfall product (3A11, currently V6) to include bias correction due to TRMM boost and to produce this product at 1" latitude by 1" longitude resolution compatible with ground base gauge analysis. The algorithm is based on the Microwave Emission brightness Temperature Histogram (METH) technique developed by Wilheit, Chang and Chiu (1991) and has been applied to SSM/I data to produce the GPCP-PSPDC monthly oceanic rain rate which is an input to the WCRPGPCP merged product. Comparison of V6 3A11 with F13 SSM/I showed a jump between the pre and post boost TRMM data. We will 1) examine the optimal combination channel for the retrieval, 2) incorporate the effect of TRMM boost that i) increases the earth incidence angle, ii) changes the footprint size, hence the so-called beam-filling correction, and iii) increases the freezing level. After these corrections are applied, the difference between the pre and post boost time series will be tested using statistical t-tests. New products will include oceanic rain rate products at 1" by 1" and 2.5" x2.5" boxes. These products will be integrated into the PPS at the direction of Project Director, evaluated and compared with the low resolution (V6 5") products, other satellite oceanic rain products (SSM/1, TMI, PR) for quality control and monitoring.

Description: Institute for Blobal Environment Strategies NASA ESSEA IPY The Earth System Science Education Alliance (ESSEA) is supporting colleges and universities in teacher preparation and professional development for pre-service and in-service middle-high school teachers. This NSF-funded program builds and expands on the successful ESSEA program that was initiated and funded by NASA and implemented by the IGES from 2000-2005. This presents an excellent opportunity to support NASA's IPY objectives. Through a new award from the National Science Foundation (November 2006-October 2009), IGES is enhancing ESSEA by: 1) Using the existing ESSEA online courses as a model to introduce newly upgraded Earth system science undergraduate and graduate courses for middle-high school teachers; 2) Introducing extensive use of data, models and existing Earth system educational materials to support the teacher courses; 3) Disseminating model teaching practices and program success through annual conferences, continuing support, and presentations at geoscience and education conferences; and 4) Expanding the number of participating institutions to 40. Over 1,700 teachers from across the U.S. completed a semester or quarter long ESSEA course from one of the participating ESSEA institutions. Pre- and post-course surveys, follow-up surveys, and case studies with course participants show that the courses have had a significant impact on teachers Earth system content knowledge and beliefs about teaching and learning (Myers et al, 2003). Using the NSF ESSEA program as a forum for dissemination of the IPY, IGES will meet two objectives of the NASA IPY program by: 1. engaging, informing and inspiring pre- and in-service teachers of IPY through a nation-wide teacher professional development program; 1a. extending the ESSEA program with the addition of IPY modules related to polar research. 1b. disseminating NASA IPY information through Web seminars and teleconferences to ESSEA participants, to audiences at national science conferences, and to participants at the annual ESSEA conference. 2. extending polar exploration to the poles of the Moon and Mars through classroom activities. IGES proposes to enhance the ESSEA professional development program with modules and resources that directly support NASA's IPY effort. NASA ROSES/IPY funding will allow IGES to: 1. Develop, add, and pilot eight new polar science modules to the ESSEA middle and high school courses. 2. Revise the K-4 ESSEA course to incorporate NASA IPY-related education resources. It is very important to note that the NSF-funded ESSEA program will focus on middle-high school teacher education; support is not being provided to maintain or update the K-4 course. NASA funding will allow IGES to keep the K-4 teacher course current and incorporate polar science. 3. Description: DEVELOPING TOOLS OF AUTOMATIC CORONAL MASS EJECTION DETECTION AND CHARACTERIZATION  The objective of this proposal is to develop a software package to automatically detect, characterize and catalog corona mass ejections (CMEs) using coronagraph imaging observations. The package provides the following specific functionalities: (1) CME initial detection, using image processing methods based on thresholding, histogram analysis and morphological analysis. (2) CME tracking and characterization based on a continuous sequence of images, taking advantage of the coherent nature of CME movement. (3) CME event classification using various existing data mining methods based on the large number of parameters generated. (4) generation of an accurate and complete CME catalog. (5) developing a near-real time detection and warning module for space weather forecasting. The automated method is far more efficient than the human manual inspection method. The automated method also extracts a large number of meaningful parameters for scientific research, free of human bias. The proposed software package will be developed based on ongoing SOHO/LASCO C2 data, and will be applied to the upcoming STEREO/SECCHI data. We will test and validate the tool package with the manual-based CDAW catalog and the existing CACTUS automated catalog. Comparing with the existing catalogs, our catalog will be much more comprehensive in terms of number and accuracy of the parameters. The proposed near-real-time module will be timely, which is critical for space weather applications. The package will be developed with the IDL programming language. CMEs are the main drivers of particle storms, geomagnetic storms and other severe space weather phenomena. The timely detection and complete catalog of CMEs serve many purposes of the LWS programs. The amount of data available becomes overwhelming. There is a strong need to automate the event detection and classification processes. The proposed methodology helps convert NASA mission data into scientific information quicker and better, or otherwise can not be obtained. Hidden scientific facts could be found through mining the large parameter space produced by automatic means. Therefore, this project will increase the scientific productivity of the SMD research endeavors from present and future NASA missions. This project will be carried out through an inter-discipline effort among experts in computer science and solar physics at George Mason University, through collaboration with the Naval Research Lab. A large part of the funding will be used to support a graduate student working toward his Ph.D. dissertation. This project directly addresses the NASA strategic sub-goal3B and is highly relevant to the strategic sub-goals 3C. If awarded, we plan to organize a summer school addressing the LWS data environment as an E/PO effort.

Description: Rocket Observations of Nitric Oxide in the Polar Night by Stellar  Occultation This is a collaborating Co-I institution proposal in support of 'Rocket Observations of Nitric Oxide in the Polar Night by Stellar Occultation' led by Dr. Scott M. Bailey at Virginia Tech. Technological hurdles have limited our ability to measure the highly variable abundance of NO to sunlit conditions. The objective of our work is to obtain the first ever observations of mesospheric-thermospheric NO in the polar night and confirm the feasibility of the stellar occultation technique. There is strong evidence that NO, created by energetic precipitating particles, is transported to the lower atmosphere during winter where it may have strong, potentially long-term effects on stratospheric ozone distributions. However, the predicted large buildup of NO has never been quantified experimentally. Since the proposed work would make the first nighttime NO observations and demonstrate technology required for future measurements from orbiting spacecraft, it is highly relevant to NASA strategic objectives because Sun Solar System Science and Technology Roadmap 2005-2035 identifies a mission to explore Sun-Earth Coupling by Energetic Particles (SECEP) that includes nighttime NO measurement capability as a top priority. Specifically, we propose to fly a 40-cm diameter Cassegrain telescope, equipped with a high-resolution spectrograph (resolving power 20,000) from Poker Flat near Fairbanks, Ak. The Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics (LASP) will contribute the telescope and spectrograph detector, which will be refurbished equipment from previous NASA sounding rocket programs. LASP will also provide the personnel necessary to prepare the telescope and detector for flight and deliver them to the Va. Tech for integration, perform the optical design of the spectrograph and analyze its performance, participate in the evaluation of the performance of the spectrograph, which will be designed and fabricated at Va. Tech, participate in rocket integration, test, and launch, and contribute to the analysis of the flight data.

Description: IRI SUPPORT FOR "EMPIRICAL IONOSPHERIC E-REGION SOLAR-GEOMAGNETIC STORM CORRECTION TO THE IRI MODEL USING TIMED/SABER DATA We propose to develop an empirical ionospheric E-region storm-time correction to the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) model. Observations from the Sounding of the Atmosphere using Broadband Emission Radiometry (SABER) Instrument onboard the Thermosphere-Ionosphere-Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics (TIMED) satellite will be used to correct the E-region IRI NO+ and electron densities for solar-geomagnetic activity. The objective of this proposal will be achieved in two steps: (1) derive a parameterization of the E-region response to solar-geomagnetic storms as a function of integral ap-index, and (2) validate the proposed storm model by comparisons with SABER-derived NO+ (v) volume emission rates (VER), Incoherent scatter radar measurements, and results from the Ionospheric Model for Auroral Zone (IMAZ). The proxy used to develop the storm model is SABER-derived profiles of NO+ (v) VER. NO+ (v) VER during all magnetically disturbed periods contained in the SABER database from 2002-2006, for example the April 2002 and October-November 2003 storm periods, will be used to develop the storm model parameterization using linear impulse-response theory. The NO+ (v) VER will be retrieved from SABER 4.3 um limb emission measurements by (1) removing the background contribution from C02 infrared emission, and (2) by performing a standard Abel inversion on the residual radiance to obtain the vertical profiles of NCH-(v) VER. The latitude range of the storm model extends from the polar region to mid- to low-latitudes. The magnetic local time coverage is in the dawn to dusk sector. The altitude range is roughly 90 km to 180 km. The empirical storm model is independent of NO+ or electron density profile shapes, and independent of chemistry, kinetics, or spectroscopic parameters. Our storm model will help accurately specify the lower ionosphere during solar-geomagnetic disturbances for all space technologies that use radio wave propagation through the ionosphere. This work is proposed in support of the LWS Tools and Methods component of the Targeted Investigations Program", which also supports NASA' s Strategic Objective (15).

Description: The identification of regional sources and sinks of CO2 is a central issue for the Carbon Science community and a major impediment to reliable forecasts of future atmospheric concentrations of CO2 (see US Carbon Cycle Science Program, Integrated Global Carbon Observing Strategy (IGOS): Carbon Theme Report, International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP), and US Climate Change Science Program (CCSP) below). Measurements using MFLL technology may enable global, day/night measurements under both clear and broken cloud conditions that will enable the carbon science community to account for the growth rate and interannual variations of atmospheric CO2 concentrations and to localize in space and time important carbon sources and sinks. Under consideration by LaRC is an active remote sensing mission that would include a continuous-wave (CW) laser-based instrument, operating in the wavelength region of 1.57 um for column measurements of atmospheric CO2, in the region of ~1.27 for O2, and laser-based range measurement, from a satellite orbiting the Earth at 350 to 450 km down to the surface and cloud tops. The instrument must have a small laser footprint and concentrated laser intensity sufficient that CO2, O2 and range measurements can be made to the surface between clouds and to cloud tops in both day and night. A CW laser instrument using fiber laser technology, modulation techniques, and producing several simultaneous laser wavelengths across the CO2 and O2 absorption line should provide a measure of total column absorption of CO2 and O2 at line center and a weighted column absorption in the lower troposphere on the side of the line. Due to measurement biases from spatial, temporal, clear sky and diurnal effects that are on the order of several tenths of a part per million (ppm), the instrument must have a measurement accuracy for the CO2 mixing ratio of about 0.3%, or about 1 ppm. To satisfy the goals of the NASA Missions measurements and technologies proposed must be at a high technical readiness level (TRL), and support a mission concept appropriate for launch by 2012.

Description: "Sensor-Analysis-Model Interoperability Technology Suite" This proposal addresses NASA's requirements for enabling model interactions in sensor webs using service oriented architecture principles and geospatial interoperability standards. Sensor webs provide a new type of dynamic and real-time resource for earth science data analysis and modeling. The future interaction between sensors and models is expected to be bi-directional: sensors provide input data to models; model output provides information for planning where, when and what sensors will measure next. Today?s earth science models are not capable of routinely assimilating sensor web observations and less capable of driving sensor measurements. The proposed project will use and extend geospatial interoperability and emerging sensor web standards, such as the Open Geospatial Consortium Sensor Web Enablement specifications, to bridge the gap between sensors and models. The proposed project will develop a Sensor-Analysis-Model Interoperability Technology Suite (SAMITS) that provides a package of standards, technologies, methods, use cases, and guidance for implementing networked interaction between sensor webs and models. SAMITS will foster seamless two-way data and control flow between active sensors and data analysis/modeling tools. SAMITS will be tested through use case applications that tie together atmospheric, air quality, and fire sensors with weather and smoke forecasting models. A tenant of the proposed approach is to reuse and extend existing technologies and development efforts. NASA?s return on investment will be maximized and the time to implement two-way interaction between sensors and models minimized if the new technology development reuses existing distributed and interoperable information system components that are already available to assist in information flow between observation databases and models. Technology Readiness Level (TRL): Entry=2/3; Exit=6 Period of performance: 36 months.

Description: Global Characterization and Analysis of Tectonism on Mercury The proposal describes a program of study using data returned by instruments on the MESSENGER spacecraft. MESSENGER will provide the first opportunity to examine the global distribution of tectonic features on Mercury. As a MESSENGER participating scientist, my primary objective will be to take a lead role in the identification, characterization, and mapping of all tectonic landforms on Mercury using images obtained from the Mercury Dual Imaging System (MDIS) cameras, and topographic data obtained from the Mercury Laser Altimeter (MLA) and from stereo imaging. A comprehensive database of Mercury;,s tectonic features that includes location, orientation, and length will be compiled using MDIS regional and global mosaics. From studies of the hemisphere imaged by Mariner 10, deformation on Mercury can be broadly described as either distributed or basin-localized. Known tectonic landforms include lobate scarps, wrinkle ridges, high-relief ridges, and extensional troughs; these are the surface expressions of crustal shortening and extension. The scientific objectives include: 1) determining spatial and temporal distribution of tectonic features, 2) constraining kinematic and mechanical models for their formation, 3) determining the regional and global strain, 4) constraining the mechanical and thermal structure of the lithosphere at the time lobate scarps formed, 5) searching for other expressions of crustal deformation that may account for the deficit between the observed and predicted strain, and 6) determining the tectonic evolution of the Caloris basin and other large, possibly mascon-Iike, basins. Topographic and gravity data will be used to characterize and model basin-localized stresses. This will include the search for evidence of buried impact basins that may have influenced the formation of tectonic features. The ultimate goal of these efforts will be to better understand: 1) the tectonic history of Mercury and the evolution of tectonic stresses with time, 2) the thermal and mechanical structure of Mercury;,s lithosphere, 3) the origin of tectonic stresses and their relationship to the thermal evolution of Mercury. MLA will only obtain altimetry data for the northern hemisphere of Mercury. Topographic data for the southern hemisphere, with the exception of limited radio occultation data, will be obtained from stereo images. As a MESSENGER participating scientist, I will take a lead role in generating stereo-derived topography. The ultimate goal will be to combine stereo, MLA and radio occultation data to obtain a global topographic map for Mercury. I will also contribute to many aspects of the geologic and geophysical analysis of Mercury, and directly contribute to the flight calibration of MDIS images and planning of MDIS flyby and orbital operations.

Description: METROPLEX OPERATIONS The concept of operations for the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen) is predicated on minimizing separation distance between aircraft merging in complex traffic patterns. This proposal includes two approaches to increase the capacity of Metroplex airspace: (1) Increase Capacity Through Optimization of Flow and Airspace Utilization: This proposal will develop concept of operations identified by NASA and JPDO to increase vehicle throughput and maximize use of airspace: (i) optimize boundaries of airspace, (ii) RNP routes for inter-woven flows, and (iii) 4-D trajectories with possibly spatial overlap but no temporal conflicts. Concepts of operations will be developed and detailed procedures will be evaluated via simulation (e.g. FACET, ACES). The outcomes of the research are: (i) procedures for improved Metroplex airspace, and (ii) new definitions of airspace configuration (2) Itinerary Optimization and Cross-linking to Maximize Passenger Throughput of Metroplex:P revious research has focused on the maximization of traffic flow in and out of Metroplex airspace without consideration of airline itinerary changes due to Metroplex congestion, passenger demand dynamics, and inter-airport relationships within a region. The objective of this proposed research is to increase the jeffective capacitj of the Metroplex airspace through improvements in airspace flow in the presence of demandlitinerary dynamics and passenger and crew cross-linking. The research approach, based on the methodology developed by Le/HoffmanlDonohue (2006), shall optimize passenger throughput by itinerary and fleet mix manipulation while maintaining airline profit and network objectiws. The outcomes of this research are: (i) a parametric analjsis of a scheduling, airport coordination, and traffic flow options that will increase the effective capacity of the Metroplex airspace (ii) demand and itinerary simulation and analysis capabilities that can be incorporated into NASA tools (e.g. FACET and ACES). Description: 2. Purpose, Objective, and Background of Work to be Performed: Control Moment Gyroscopes (CMGs) are devices for producing transient reaction torques for vehicle control. At its simplest, a CMG consists of a spinning flywheel mounted in a frame, which is itself fastened to a fix base via a pivot that permits the frame or "gimbal" to rotate about a fixed axis that is orthogonal to the flywheel's spin axis. The reaction torque is produced by rotating the gimbal while the flywheel is spinning, and its magnitude is the product of the the flywheel moment of inertia, the spin rate of the flywheel, and the rotation rate of the gimbal. CMG systems that are intended to produce torques in three axes for free-flying vehicles are frequently built up from a set of four gimballed flywheels, arranged so that the gimbals' four rotation axes redundantly span three dimensions. The purpose of this task is to develop a prototype CMG suitable for controlling small aeronautical vehicles for flight control research, including thrust-levitated vehicles capable of vertical takeoff or landing (VTOL) and fixed-wing aircraft. There are decades of experience in the design and application of CMGs for spacecraft; however, the use of CMGs for controlling aeronautical vehicles imposes a unique performance issue unaddressed in the spacecraft-based state of the art: The vehicle has to continuously expend energy throughout flight in order to lift the CMG against gravity. This makes it critical that the CMG system comprise only the smallest practical fraction of the vehicle's overall mass budget. Although the ideal aeronautical CMG would be capable of supplying any desired reaction torque time history with negligible system mass, such a system would be very technically challenging. The CMGs that arise from this effort are to be used in small, high-risk, flight experiments, they shall relatively inexpensive to build, relying on Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components to reduce cost. Finding the right design compromises between performance and cost is critical in this effort, and it is complicated by the fact that the behavior of the CMG's torques is closely coupled to the motion of the airframe on which it operates. Because of this, the control strategy to be used in the airframe/CMG system is, in turn, closely coupled to the CMG characteristics and - in turn - contributes to defining the CMG performance requirements. The control issues arising in atmospheric flight using CMGs have been investigated in detail over the past several years in the Dynamical Systems and Control Branch at Langley Research Center (LaRC.)

Description: CHARACTERIZING THE COMPOSITION OF LARGE MID-LATITUDE TOPSIDE-IONOSPHERIC/PLASMASPHERIC GRADIENTS The overall goal ofthe 3-year project "Characterizing the Composition of Large Midlatitude Topside-Ionospheric/Plasmaspheric Gradients" is to characterize the latitude and altitude dependence of large midlatitude ionospheric electron and ion density gradients associated with outer plasmaspheric structures using and correlating a number of older data sets including ion mass spectrometer measurements from DME-A, ISIS-2, and OGO-5 and topside sounder data from Alouette 1, 2 and ISIS 1,2. IRI is an empirical model widely used for LWS science, engineering, and educational applications. Based on ground and space measurements, it provides a standard representation of ionospheric Ne, ion densities (0+, H+, He+, N+, 02+, N0+), electron temperature, ion temperature, and ion drift. Dr. Bilitza is one ofthe principal authors ofthe IRI model. As a co-Investigator on this project, Dr. Bilitza will be responsible for all IRI-related tasks including comparisons ofthe data with the IRI model and studying ways to improve the representation of large gradient stmctures in IRI. Dr. Bilitza is also the Task Leader for the Data Acquisition and Archiving activities at the National Space Science Data Center (NSSDC) and Space Physics Data Facility (SPDF) and will help with all project tasks related to the access to the older data sets and their conversion into an easy interpretable format.

Description: The Vibration and Acoustics Labs (VAL) and the Department of Building Construction at Virginia Tech propose an analytical/numerical and experimental program to investigate the development of a model for the prediction of noise inside buildings due to low intensity sonic boom. The main objective of this work is the compilation, integration, improvement, and validation of current available tools to investigate the vibration of the exposed structure to sonic boom and the resulting interior acoustic response. The pressure loading will be assumed as a traveling wave with an arbitrary time history not necessarily constrained to the ideal N-shape observed for high intensity sonic booms. The model will have the capability of considering any arbitrary exterior excitation pressure time history and spatial distribution, e.g. not limited to plane wave fronts used in previous work. The wave diffractions by the buildings are also to be considered in order to assess the pressure loading on the shadow sides of the structure. The in-vacuo structural response to the pressure loading due to the sonic boom will be computed using analytical closed form solutions and finite element methods. The sound transmission inside the rooms will then be investigated using the structure's vibration as the noise source.  Different techniques will be applied for finding the total response of the room, according to the range of validity of each method. The initial transient response, when the sound field is dominated by multiple wall reflections, will be formulated using series solutions in terms of acoustic modes (Green#s functions). The later part of the response, when the sound field becomes rather diffuse, will be investigated using statistical energy analysis (SEA), including the dissipation due to the room absorption. The effect of structural interior walls and coupling of room cavities will be investigated. The model will be validated by testing a simulated building at an outdoors facility excited by a simulated pressure pulse (such as the one generated by controlled explosives). Several arrangements and types of structures will be tested. The experiments will include extensive noise and vibration measurements to monitor the excitationpressure front to accurately determine the input excitation (in time and space), the structure's vibration, and the sound field inside the building. VAL has extensive capabilities in terms of instrumentation (microphones and accelerometers) and data acquisition systems. To facilitate the use of the model, the model modules will be integrated into a visual environment.

Description: We propose to use a Differential Global Positioning System (DGPS) to obtain precision topography across both depositional and erosional landforms within enclosed basins in the western United States. Previous DGPS surveys made by us have provided a series of high precision (2 cm horizontal and 4 cm vertical) transects across glacial-age shorelines in Nevada (through an earlier MFRP grant), and these data have proved valuable for evaluating MOLA data across hypothesized shorelines in the northern lowlands of Mars. Here we plan to obtain similar precision topographic transects across both depositional and erosional features, as well as wave-cut erosional benches and platforms, within glacial lakes that were present within individual basins of the Basin and Range province. The precision topography will be used in combination with commercial Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) to generalize the field transect data for each paleolake. Three field trips are planned for collecting the DGPS data (along with field documentation keyed to the DGPS points) at locations in southern Oregon and northern Nevada, where brief previous visits and photo-interpretation of aerial photographs confirm both the preservation and the accessability of erosional and depositional pluvial features. Focus on individual glacial lakes (each much smaller than the well-studied Bonneville and Lahontan lakes) is motivated by their potential as analogs to hypothesized paleolakes within impact craters on Mars, interest in which has been stimulated by the MER Spirit investigations in Gusev crater. The new DGPS topography would provide a well-documented referent for interpreting how well pluvial features can be resolved in topographic data, and also the spatial resolution required to make pluvial inferences from coarser DEM data. This work is directly relevant to NASA and MEP objectives to support the interpretation of existing data resources to identify and better understand locations on Mars thought to have strong potential for preserving evidence of past life. The work also will provide quantitative information about landform topography and surface sediment characteristics for specific pluvial features that may be analogous to ones that could eventually be explored by robots (or humans) on Mars

Description: The purpose of this cooperative agreement is to conduct a shared resource project that will lead to the development of a high-sensitivity heat flux gage for calibrated heat transfer measurements. The proposed effort is described in detail in the Tao Systems Proposal No. 06-HYP-06-0104 submitted to NRA NNH06ZEA001N-HYP. This cooperative agreement will advance the technology developments and research that have been performed on advanced test and diagnostic techniques for ground test and basic hypersonic research. The specific objective is to improve the reliability and performance of heat flux gages. This work will culminate in a fast response, high-temperature heat flux gage for obtaining high-resolution, calibrated heat transfer measurements. Specifically, the heat flux gage will provide higher frequency response and an order of magnitude higher resolution than existing gages using multiple thermoresisteive gage pairs in an Active Sensor Circuit (ASC) configuration. The effort will require optimal selection of suitable high-temperature device materials, design of appropriate gage configuration for reliable heat transfer signal, and absolute calibration of the fabricated ASC-based heat flux gage. The approach integrates state-of-the-art dynamic impedance measurement technology with advanced, customizable microsensor fabrication techniques. The multi-element heat flux gage will be fabricated by Virginia Tech, while the measurement circuit for the heat flux gage elements is provided by ASC, a novel measurement circuit topology pioneered by Tao Systems. In this way, a collaborative partnership is formed that is ideally suited to develop the high-resolution, high-temperature heat flux gage. This collaborative research project will enable reliable and repeatable heat transfer measurements for assessing the aerothermodynamic effects of flow phenomena in hypersonics and other high-speed/high-temperature regimes.

Description: The identification of regional sources and sinks of CO2 is a central issue for the Carbon Science community and a major impediment to reliable forecasts of future atmospheric concentrations of CO2 (see US Carbon Cycle Science Program, Integrated Global Carbon Observing Strategy (IGOS): Carbon Theme Report, International Geosphere-Biosphere Programme (IGBP), and US Climate Change Science Program (CCSP) below).  Measurements using MFLL technology may enable global, day/night measurements under both clear and broken cloud conditions that will enable the carbon science community to account for the growth rate and interannual variations of atmospheric CO2 concentrations and to localize in space and time important carbon sources and sinks.  Under consideration by LaRC is an active remote sensing mission that would include a continuous-wave (CW) laser-based instrument, operating in the wavelength region of 1.57, for column measurements of atmospheric CO2 from a satellite orbiting the Earth at 350 to 450 km down to the surface or cloud tops.  The instrument must have a small laser footprint and concentrated laser intensity sufficient that CO2 measurements can be made to the surface between clouds and to cloud tops in both day and night.  A CW laser instrument using fiber laser technology, modulation techniques, and producing several simultaneous laser wavelengths across the CO2 absorption line should provide a measure of total column absorption of CO2 at line center and a weighted column absorption in the lower troposphere on the side of the line.  Due to measurement biases from spatial, temporal, clear sky and diurnal effects that are on the order of several tenths of a part per million (ppm), the instrument must have a measurement accuracy for the CO2 mixing ratio of about 0.3%, or about 1 ppm.  To satisfy the goals of the ESSP Program, measurements and technologies proposed must be at a high technical readiness level (TRL), and support a mission concept appropriate for launch by 2013.  A successful proposal to ESSP must document and prove the readiness of the measurement concept and supporting technologies to meet ESSP Program goals with acceptable risk.

Description: NEW PATHWAYS FOR THE FORMATION OF COMPLEX ORGANICS AND PREBIOTIC SYNTHESIS IN THE GAS PHASE, IN NANO CLUSTERS, AND ON DUST GRAIN SURFACES The proposed research is focused on the physical and chemical processes that can lead to the formation of bio-forming polyatomic molecules through gas phase ion-molecule reactions, intracluster reactions, and surface reactions catalyzed by dust grains. The overall objective is to understand the general physical and chemical principles underlying the origin and early evolution of life. To understand how life can begin on a habitable planet such as the Earth, it is essential to know what organic compounds were likely to have been available. Among the key questions we plan to address in this proposal are: (1) how are simple organic compounds assembled into more complex molecular systems and (2) what are the essential processes and pathways by which complex systems can develop those basic properties that are critical to lifEs origins The proposed project involves the study of the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) that are present in interstellar clouds as evidenced by spectroscopy and meteorites. The PAH molecules are readily ionized and their large surfaces provide strong bonding for interstellar species such alkynes (acetylene and polyacetylenes) and polar molecules (formaldehyde, formic acid, HCN, cyanoacetylenes). The PAH surfaces can serve as catalysts for the formation of complex prebiotic organics. The thermochemistry, kinetics, and temperature effects of the gas phase and cluster reactions will be investigated using the mass-selected ion mobility technique. In the nano clusters regime, we will study the photochemical reactions of the PAHs within clusters of interstellar molecules including water clusters. As to reactions on grain surfaces, we will use the LVCC method (Laser Vaporization/Controlled Condensation) to generate highly porous dust-like nanoparticles that model cosmic dust, and study their catalytic and photocatalytic reactions. Building blocks of amino acids such as HCN, ammonia, ketones and aldehydes will be adsorbed on the nanoparticle grains covered with water ice. The porosity and large surface areas of the grains create little nanovessels in which the organic molecules can pool. In the presence of ultraviolet photons, the organics can be polymerized to form more complex molecules. We will study the effects of UV radiation on the catalytic properties of the grains, and the resultant product distribution. Reaction products will be detected using temperature-programmed desorption and mass spectrometry (TPD/MS) from surface-adsorbed gas targets that have been exposed to the UV radiation. The results of proposed work will allow one to assess the relative importance of gas phase, clusters, and grain catalyzed reactions in the formation of complex organics and in prebiotic synthesis under interstellar conditions. This will contribute to the development of new models that provide more accurate predictions of  interstellar molecular abundances. This proposal is directly related to the goals of the NASA Astrobiology Program concerning the formation of complex organic molecules in space and their delivery to planetary surfaces, and investigating models of early environments in which organic chemical synthesis could occur.

Description: MARS - UNDERSTANDING A WORLD   The National Air and Space Museum hosts 8-10 million visitors each year at its National Mall facility.  One of the major galleries in the museum is "Exploring the Planets," which addresses both the technical approaches to planetary exploration and the resulting scientific understanding of our solar system.  Installed in 1976, this gallery has been upgraded several times to incorporate new information, most recently by the addition of flat-panel "What's New" displays.  The Mars section of the gallery reflects a post-Viking view, with little new information gained from the MGS, Odyssey, Pathfinder, and MER missions.  The physical space is also limited by a number of dividing walls. We propose a complete redesign of this exhibit area, including expansion of the space available, new artifact displays, and scientifitc information that captures our much deeper understanding of Mars as a world.

Description: Microstructures for Validation of Nonlinear Ultrasonic Fatigue Measurements and Analytical Models NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) researchers have shown that the use of non-linear ultrasonics, particularly, measurement of the nonlinearity parameter, beta, is a sensitive method for determining the state of fatigue in metallic microstructures. These researchers have developed the fundamental science necessary to make these measurements and continued development in this area has the potential to transition the science into tools needed to evaluate material aging. In the proposed three-year research program, we plan to characterize dislocation substructures and internal elastic stresses formed in metallic single crystals during cyclic loading in order to verify quantitative relationships between non-linear ultrasonic measurements and the fatigue damage microstructure in structural metallic materials. Fatigue testing will be performed on single and polycrystalline copper samples under conditions of uniaxial tension-compression and constant plastic strain amplitude. A wide range of dislocation structures will be produced by varying the crystal orientation, strain amplitude, and number of cycles. After fatigue testing, velocity of sound and ultrasonic non-linearity parameter, beta, measurements will be made using a RITEC study of nonlinear acoustic phenomena (SNAP) system provided by NASA. Detailed microstructural characterization of the same samples by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) will include quantitative determination of the monopole and dipole dislocation densities in veins and persistent slip bands formed, measurements of the loop lengths and dipole heights, densities of secondary dislocations, and the volume fractions of veins and persistent slip bands at various levels of fatigue damage. An assessment of the magnitude of the stress fields generated by these dislocation sub structures will be attempted using convergent-beam electron diffraction in the TEM. These combined ultrasonic and TEM measurements on the same fatigued samples are required to validate the underlying theory and enable transition of this technology into a quantitative metallic fatigue sensor.

Description: IRI SUPPORT FOR "EMPIRICAL IONOSPHERIC E-REGION SOLAR-GEOMAGNETIC STORM CORRECTION TO THE IRI MODEL USING TIMED/SABER DATA We propose to develop an empirical ionospheric E-region storm-time correction to the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) model. Observations from the Sounding of the Atmosphere using Broadband Emission Radiometry (SABER) Instrument onboard the Thermosphere-Ionosphere-Mesosphere Energetics and Dynamics (TIMED) satellite will be used to correct the E-region IRI NO+ and electron densities for solar-geomagnetic activity. The objective of this proposal will be achieved in two steps: (1) derive a parameterization of the E-region response to solar-geomagnetic storms as a function of integral ap-index, and (2) validate the proposed storm model by comparisons with SABER-derived NO+ (v) volume emission rates (VER), Incoherent scatter radar measurements, and results from the Ionospheric Model for Auroral Zone (IMAZ). The proxy used to develop the storm model is SABER-derived profiles of NO+ (v) VER. NO+ (v) VER during all magnetically disturbed periods contained in the SABER database from 2002-2006, for example the April 2002 and October-November 2003 storm periods, will be used to develop the storm model parameterization using linear impulse-response theory. The NO+ (v) VER will be retrieved from SABER 4.3 um limb emission measurements by (1) removing the background contribution from C02 infrared emission, and (2) by performing a standard Abel inversion on the residual radiance to obtain the vertical profiles of NCH-(v) VER. The latitude range of the storm model extends from the polar region to mid- to low-latitudes. The magnetic local time coverage is in the dawn to dusk sector. The altitude range is roughly 90 km to 180 km. The empirical storm model is independent of NO+ or electron density profile shapes, and independent of chemistry, kinetics, or spectroscopic parameters. Our storm model will help accurately specify the lower ionosphere during solar-geomagnetic disturbances for all space technologies that use radio wave propagation through the ionosphere. This work is proposed in support of the LWS Tools and Methods component of the Targeted Investigations Program", which also supports NASA' s Strategic Objective (15).

Description: LIMB SCATTERING RESEARCH WITH SAGE III, PREPARATION FOR THE OMPS PROGRAM Several years ago, the relatively new limb scattering (LS) ozone retrieval technique was selected as the primary source of ozone profile information for the OMPS mission. Since that time, the LS radiative transfer models and ozone retrieval techniques have grown much more mature. Successful ozone retrievals have been obtained from several satellite sensors (including SOLSE/LORE, SAGE III, Odin/OSIRJS and Sciamachy). Intensive efforts to improve the tangent height registration and stray light mitigation for SAGE III LS radiance measurements have borne fruit, improving the quality of the retrieved ozone profiles. This improvement is evident from ongoing validation studies, which show that SAGE III LS ozone profiles have achieved both accuracy and precision of 5-10 percent. We intend to use SAGE III LS data to address outstanding questions about the LS retrieval technique, and to apply the lessons leamed from work with SAGE III LS data to improve the OMPS limb profiler (LP) ozone retrieval algorithm. This is consistent with NASA's strategic objective to "conduct a program of research and technology development to advance Earth observation from space, improve scientific understanding, and demonstrate new technologies with the potential to improve future operational systems". We therefore propose to: Study the existing SAGE III LS data set to quantify the impact of inhomogeneous scenes, stray light mitigation strategies, retrieval of aerosols and other interfering species, and tangent height registration techniques on the retrieved ozone profile. Design future SAGE III LS measurement campaigns to address these outstanding questions about the LS retrieval process Improve the speed of the retrieval algorithm (forward model) Use SAGE III LS radiance data to create a proxy data set to test the OMPS LP ozone retrieval algorithm Suggest improvements to the OMPS LP ozone retrieval algorithm based on experience with the SAGE III LS data.

Description: Development of a Multidisciplinary Computational Tool for Accurate and Efficient Rotorcraft Noise Prediction (MUTE) (Reference: ROA-2006, NRA NNH06ZEA001N). This Statement of Work (SOW) is the result of a proposal submitted by the National Institute of Aerospace, which was selected for award under the NASA Headquarters Aeronautics Research Mission Directorate (ARMD) NRA titled Research Opportunities in Aeronautics (ROA)2006. MUTE is an aggregation of multidisciplinary computational tools that accurately and efficiently model the physics of the source of rotorcraft noise and predict the noise at far-field observer locations. MUTE uses systematic coupling approaches among multiple disciplines including Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), Computational Structural Dynamics (CSD), and high-fidelity Acoustics. The objective is to accurately model the physics of the noise source and to understand the basis of the noise generation from rotorcraft in a wide range of flight regimes. Within MUTE, CFD tools are used around the rotor blade to predict the transonic flow (shock wave) effects, which generate the high-speed impulsive noise. Predictions of the blade-vortex interaction noise in low speed flight are also improved by using the Particle Vortex Transport Method (PVTM), which preserves the wake flow details required for blade/wake and fuselage/wake interactions. The accuracy of the source noise prediction is further improved by utilizing a coupling approach between CFD and CSD, so that the effects of key structural dynamics, elastic blade deformations, and trim solutions are correctly represented in the analysis. This effort significantly improves the computational efficiency of MUTE with the implementation of multi-grid algorithms. MUTE can be used to expeditiously evaluate a range of future rotorcraft configurations of all types (helicopters, compounds and tilt rotors) designed especially to be responsive to a variety of environmental concerns. Other important objectives of this effort are to develop an efficient interface with the current state-of-the-art noise propagation analysis and to validate each analysis tool in MUTE (as well as the entire methodology) by comparing them with flight and wind-tunnel test data available from recent publications.

Description: The use of the bistatic reflection of GPS signals to estimate surface wind speed over the ocean, as well as other geophysical parameters, has been successfully demonstrated and the subject of active research for several years. The technique utilizes the relationship between surface roughness and the shape of the correlation between the direct and reflected GPS signal to estimate surface wind speed over water. It may be possible to utilize other signals of opportunity for similar remote sensing applications. One potential signal that could be utilized for remote sensing is the Direst Broadcast Satellite (DBS) Television signal. The DBS system satellites are located in geostationary orbits and provide a relatively high Effective Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) over much of US costal regions. Recently LaRC researchers have been investigating the possibility of developing techniques to use the correlation between direct and reflected DBS signals in a similar way as the GPS signals were used for remote sensing. NASA LaRC is plarming an experiment to measure the reflected DBS signal from water for various surface roughness conditions. The object of this experiment is to develop a receiver using a DBS antenna, Low Noise Block (LNB), and test receiver to develop an experimental DBS Test Receiver. This receiver will then be used to measure direct DBS signals and the signals reflected from the surface ofthe bay under various wind conditions. These data will be used to study the potential use of bistatic DBS measurements for remote sensing measurements.

Description: "PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF TITAN'S SURFACE FROM MODELING OF CASSINI RADAR DATA" - We propose to study the surface properties of Titan using Cassini RADAR scatterometry, altimetry and SAR data. Mapping changes in composition (via radar-derived dielectric constants) and roughness across different terrain types will help in understanding how the surface is shaped by different physical processes. We will compare the quasi-specular echo component recorded by the scatterometer and altimeter to near-nadir scattering models (e.g. Hagfors, exponential and Gaussian models) in order to map dielectric constants and roughness parameters. We will also fit a fractal scattering model, which will yield dielectric constants and RMS slopes as well as a value for H, the Hurst exponent. The derived H values can be directly compared to those measured in the field for terrestrial surfaces, in order to better understand what Titan would look like to an observer on the surface. Our derived dielectric constants and roughness parameters will be compared to publicly released Cassini near-infrared maps as weU as the Arecibo 12.6 cm wavelength data to investigate how the composition and roughness change as the spacecraft tracks across different geologic features. We will search for any areas that might be responsible for the strong specular reflections observed in the Arecibo data. We also propose to develop a new empirical scattering law for backscatter cross section using terrestrial AIRSAR and field data. Previous analyses have used a Dubois model to derive physical properties from the Cassini radar images, but this model is not ideal for the short-wavelength Cassini radar observations because it breaks down in situations where there is significant surface roughness at the wavelength scale. We wiU use our newly derived scattering law with the Cassini SAR images to characterize the surface roughness across radar bright and dark terrains, as well as impact crater ejecta and possible sites of cyrovolcanism.

Description: Development of Integrated Algorithms for High-Fidelity Rotorcraft Aeromechanics Predictions within CFD/CSD-Coupled Frameworks (Reference: ROA-2006, NRA NNH06ZEA001N) The objective of this effort is to advance the capabilities of NASA's state-of-the-art prediction tools for rotorcraft aeromechanics of the complete vehicle. This effort will identify, develop and validate algorithms that improve efficiency, accuracy and fidelity of rotorcraft aeromechanics predictions (i.e. performance, dynamic response, loads, vibrations and noise). Deliverable algorithms will be integrated into existing Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) / Computational Structural Dynamics (CSD) coupled frameworks that employ comprehensive aero elastic codes for CSD. The enhancements focus on evolution of the rotor wake, CFD/CSD coupling robustness, and CSD modeling accuracy and efficiency. The resulting methodology from this research will improve accuracy and efficiency for current NASA computational capabilities, help researchers better understand physical phenomena associated with rotorcraft aeromechanics and interaction between multiple disciplines, and allow NASA to adequately analyze future concepts under development. Flexibility of the CFD/CSD coupled framework also accommodates and facilitates the implementation of future technology (e.g. trailing-edge flap, active twist rotor, and active flow control) into the analysis. The approach is to model uniquely identifiable aerodynamic domains appropriately in accordance with the key physical characteristics of each domain, develop algorithms that reflect the physics, and implement the algorithms to be compatible with the existing flow solvers. The following technology topics shall be investigated and results reported: a.Further develop the fully coupled approach using Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) in the vicinity of rotor blades to capture the generation of the vortices, and Particle Vortex Transport Method (PVTM) for resolving the evolution of the vortices in the remainder of the flow field. b.Advance the understanding of the field velocity approach, which accounts for the influence of the PVTM wake on various CFD domains. c.Advance the understanding of the methods and processes by which the field velocity approach captures the rotor tip vortices as well as the vortex sheet emanating from each blade, with a good correlation on blade loading between the computations and flight test data.

Description: VERMONT - A PROPOSAL FOR EPSCOR PHASE III RESEARCH INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FUNDING Vermont is in many ways the stereotype of an EPSCoR state. It is small, predominantly rural, and has a population of only slightly more than six hundred thousand people. The University of Vermont (DVM) is the state's only comprehensive university offering graduate programs leading to advanced degrees in STEM disciplines. Baccalaureate degrees in STEM disciplines are offered at Norwich University, St. Michael's College, and the State College System. However, with few exceptions active academic researchers in Vermont are faculty at UVM, which is the state's only Research University. Even at UVM, beyond the College of Medicine, the pool of Vermont academic researchers is relatively small making it hard to create the critical mass of researchers and research support systems needed to compete successfully for Federal research funding. Adding to the difficulty of developing potential collaborations with colleagues at NASA is the fact that Vermont is geographically remote from all NASA Centers. Despite these obstacles, Vermont's NASA EPSCoR program has had considerable success in creating an interest in NASA research priorities among Vermont's academic researchers, in establishing and strengthening connections to collaborators at NASA Centers, in making Vermont's academic researchers more competitive for non-EPSCoR external funding on the National level, and in building Vermont's NASA-related research infrastructure. During Phase II of NASA EPSCoR, research funding awarded by Vermont's program has significantly increased the number of research proposals on topics that are NASA research priorities submitted by Vermont academic researchers to NASA and other Federal agencies through regular (non-EPSCoR) channels. Several of these proposals have led to significant research grants awarded in National funding competitions. Description: It is presumed that most galaxies have a large Black Hole at their center. As galaxies merge in the standard hierarchical scenario of galaxy formation, these Black Holes also can merge and grow. Furthermore the violent dynamics of the merger will deliver a significant amount of gas and stars to the central regions of the merging galaxy further growing the central Black Hole and fueling an Active Galactic Nucleus. We will perform state-of-the-art numerical simulations of this merging process using N-body simulations and gas dynamics. These simulations will resolve the dynamics in the central kiloparsec of the merging galaxies and will be able to follow the sinking of the Black Holes to the center via dynamical friction up to the formation of binary Black Holes. We will also follow the delivery of gas to the central regions to make predictions about the fueling of the AGN. Several missions of the Beyond Einstein program will be attempting to understand the physics of central Black Holes in galaxies. LISA hopes to detect the gravitational radiation as the Black Holes merge, and therefore will need estimates of merger rates. Con-X will be observing the X-ray emission from these objects, and these observations will need to be put into a framework that includes the very dynamic nature of the galactic merging process in order to be fully understood.

ANDREWS SPACE, INC. PROPOSES AN INNOVATIVE TRANSPIRATION COOLED AEROBRAKE TPS DESIGN THAT IS THERMALLY PROTECTIVE, STRUCTURALLY FLEXIBLE, AND LIGHTWEIGHT. THIS INNOVATIVE DESIGN WILL ALSO MEET LAUNCH VOLUME CONSTRAINTS AND SATISFY TERMINAL AEROBRAKING REQUIREMENTS. THE APPROACH WILL FOCUS ON TRANSPIRATION COOLING OF A FLEXIBLE MATERIAL AND WILL CONSIDER ABLATIVE AND INSULATIVE TECHNOLOGIES AS KEY FEATURES OF THE TPS DESIGN. THE APPLICATION OF AEROBRAKING TO REDUCE VELOCITY FOR PLANETARY CAPTURE AND LANDING HAS LONG BEEN ASSUMED FOR USE ON MARS MISSIONS AND HAS BEEN SUGGESTED FOR EARTH REENTRY. THE MAJOR HURDLE TO INFLATABLE AEROBRAKES BECOMING REALITY IS THE DEVELOPMENT OF A LIGHTWEIGHT AND STRUCTURALLY FLEXIBLE THERMAL PROTECTION SYSTEM (TPS). BY COMBINING WELL UNDERSTOOD INSULATIVE AND ABLATIVE TPS WITH AN INNOVATIVE FLEXIBLE TRANSPIRATION COOLED TPS, A REALIZABLE INFLATABLE AEROBRAKE SYSTEM CAN BE DEVELOPED. THE PRIMARY CONCERN IN ATMOSPHERIC ENTRY IS SUFFICIENTLY PROTECTING THE PAYLOAD FROM EXTREME THERMAL LOADS. TO OPTIMIZE PACKING VOLUME DURING LAUNCH, THE MOST EFFICIENT OPTION IS TO CREATE A NON-RIGID STRUCTURE WHICH COULD BE STORED UNTIL ENTRY OCCURS. Description: ANALYSES OF THE DEEP IMPACT EVENT AT COMET TEMPEL 1 This is a proposal to use theory, modeling, experiments and computers to study and interpret the outcome of the Deep Impact event in the comet Tempe1 1. The research will be performed under the auspices of the University of Washington, with experimental work performed under a subcontract to the Boeing Company. It includes five primary components: 1. We will gather all published data to date on high speed impact cratering, including measurements on ejecta masses and velocities. We will formulate the ejecta scaling in a general way, and will make it available to the community by publishing a modern update to the Housen et al. 1983 paper on ejecta scaling. 2. We will apply those scaling results to a study of the dependence on the target material on cratering for the Deep Impact conditions. We will construct results showing the nature, the extent, the distribution, the brightness and the temporal evolution of an ejecta plume for different material assumptions. We will compare those results to the DI observations. 3. The first two tasks are expected to uncover certain holes in our complete understanding of cratering, especially in the transition in a very low gravity environment from gravity to strength effects. In order to address these deficiencies, we will design and conduct impact experiments in appropriate materials with tailored strengths. In all cases we will make measurements of the material strengths using common geological material techniques. We will record high-speed digital movies especially designed to look at the question of the lift-off of the ejecta plume from the target surface, in order to quantify that important aspect. 4. We will explore the possibilities of conducting experiments with target materials with sufficient volatiles to affect the cratering processes. We will investigate the possibilities of using embedded dry ice or pressurized micro-sphere targets. We will conduct theoretical studies of the acceleration of dust particles by expanding vapor clouds. We will study the results of previous researchers, particularly those concerned with comet outburst mechanisms. We will conduct computer studies to model those mechanisms. We will use our collective expertise in these areas, and the data that has been collected during and after the mission to address the fundamental questions about the nature of the comet material: the raison d'etre for the mission. We expect that the application of modern scaling theories and data, the interpretation of existing and planned experiments, and the modeling and code calculations of identified important physical factors will make significant contributions to the science return for that important event.

Description: RESEARCH EFFORT ENTITLED "NEUTRAL AND PLASMA RESPONSES TO GRAVITY WAVE DISSIPATION IN THE THERMOSPHERE AND IONOSPHERE" DATED JULY 12, 2006. The key, central objective of this proposal is to understand the neutral and plasma responses that result in the thermosphere and ionosphere as a consequence of intermittent and spatially variable body forces which arise from the dissipation of GWs from the lower atmosphere. Our objective is to understand these processes locally and globally as a function of solar cycle, local time, and latitude. Convection generates GWs, some of which can penetrate to very high altitudes in the thermosphere. These GWs dissipate in the thermosphere, and create large horizontal body forces at 180-190 km altitude which are 1000km x 1500km x 100-250 km, depending on solar conditions. The resulting accelerations are very large, up to 1 m/s/s. It is likely that these body forces generate large-scale neutral horizontal winds, electric fields, plasma drifts, and secondary GWs. A full investigation of the response of the thermosphere and ionosphere to these body forces involves starting with GW spectra modeled after tropospheric convection, ray tracing these GWs into the thermosphere under varying solar conditions, calculating the temporal and spatial variability of the body forces, running these body forces in the TIME-GCM, examining the neutral and plasma responses to these body forces, and calculating the neutral wind and secondary GW scales and amplitudes not resolvable by the TIME-GCM theoretically. Our methodology involves our convection model which efficiently generates temporally and spatially variable GW spectra from individual convective cells, our ray-tracing code which propagates these spectra through realistic wind and temperature environments (obtained from the TIME-GCM) into the thermosphere, and our TIME-GCM which includes the neutral and plasma dynamics with 2.5 degree resolution. This research is important to the understanding of the thermosphere and ionosphere because it will investigate, for the first time, the potentially important dynamical neutral and plasma processes which occur in Earth's neutral/plasma space environment that result from the dissipation of GWs which propagate upwards from the lower atmosphere. This research is of direct relevance to NASA's Heliophysics Research Program with strategic goal ``3.2: Understand the Sun and its effects on Earth and the solar system" because it will investigate the effects of the solar cycle and solar heating on the neutral and plasma responses to these thermospheric body forces. Because this proposed research will also investigate the horizontal winds and electric fields generated by dissipating GWs as well as the dominant GW scales present at the bottomside of the F layer at equatorial latitudes, it is also of direct relevance to NASA's Coupled Ionized and Neutral Dynamics Instrumentation (CINDI). CINDI will be launched aboard C/NOFS, and will investigate the interactions between neutrals and plasma in the ionosphere.

Description: RESEARCH EFFORT ENTITLED "MULTI-PLATFORM STUDIES OF INTERMEDIATE-SCALE WAVE AND TIDES" DATED JULY 19, 2006. It has long been recognized by the MLT community that the combination of data from satellite instruments in different orbits has the potential to better resolve fast propagating and transient waves and tides. We propose to combine data from the SABER instrument aboard the TIMED satellite and the MLS instrument aboard the EOS-AURA satellite. Our scientific focus will be on waves that are poorly resolved from a single satellite platform, such as the semidiurnal tide at high latitudes, and intermediate-scale quasi-diurnal motions at equatorial latitudes. The first step in our study will be to cross validate the temperatures and geopotential fields in the two datasets, identifying any biases, and correcting these biases to the extent possible. A variety of complementary analysis techniques will be employed. These include binning and compositing (for waves whose period is locked to a diurnal cycle, such as the semidiurnal tide), scending/descending node differencing (for diurnal motions), Kalman filtering, and asynoptic mapping. The waves studied play important roles in atmospheric circulations like the semmiannual oscillation (SAO). The 2006 NASA Strategic Plan describes ....constellations of smart satellites as parts of an integrated, interactive sensor web observing system.... Although combining pairs (or clusters) of space-based instruments to achieve science goals is an obvious strategy, it has been little utilized in the case of studies of middle atmosphere dynamics. As an illustration, we consider the Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite (UARS) mission. During the years 1991.1997 this mission supported two instruments dedicated primarily to measuring mesospheric and lower thermospheric (MLT) winds and temperatures: the high resolution Doppler imager (HRDI), and the wind imaging interferometer (WINDII). The similarities in the measured parameters of HRDI and WINDII sampling imply a high potential for synergistic studies of MLT dynamics. Yet only a handful of investigators have considered both datasets, or integrated the two for scientific studies (McLandress et al., 1996a; Fleming et al., 1996; Yudin et al., 1997; Forbes et al., 2002; Forbes et al., 2003). The proposed investigation would contribute to the long term goal of combining multiple instruments for scientific study by combining data from the SABER instrument aboard the TIMED satellite with data from the MLS instrument aboard the EOS Aura satellite for the study of atmospheric waves and tides. TIMED has more of an upper atmosphere focus than EOS/Aura, but both SABER and EOS/MLS temperature retrievals extend over the entire stratosphere and mesosphere and thus can be exploited for our project. The goal of this proposal is to combine data from two orbiting satellite platforms to maximize their space-time information content for scientific study of waves in the mesosphere. Combination of data from these two satellites leads to significant improvements in spatio-temporal resolution over what can be obtained from an individual dataset. The exercise of combining EOS-Aura and TIMED data also provides an excellent platform for developing electronic tools for data assimilation and combination. Although the EOS-Aura and TIMED missions are highlighted in this proposal, other missions stand to benefit.

Description: NASA/LaRC has a requirement to conduct arcjet testing of an ablative thermal protection system (TPS) material. The Mars Science Laboratory Entry, Descent and Landing Instrumentation (MEDLI) project has been approved to incorporate an atmospheric data system into the Mars Science Laboratory heatshield, for collecting valuable environmental data during the Mars entry. This data system includes a series of pressure ports, through the TPS, which feed to pressure transducers mounted inside the aeroshell. The MEDLI project is on a very aggressive schedule, and an early determination of the proper port configuration is critical to successful integration with the MSL schedule. A matrix of arcjet tests is necessary to find the port diameter that can be sustained under pyrolysis and ablation, providing a good pressure measurement without compromising heatshield integrity. A series of 14 test runs were performed at the Boeing Large Core Arc Tunnel (LCAT) from February 19 to March 1, 2007, to evaluate various size pressure ports in the Super Lightweight Ablator (SLA) 561V heat shield material at MSL-relevant entry heating levels. During this test series, some of the data requirements were compromised because of the small model size (2 inches), chosen to meet the test conditions. The test results showed a need to perform further testing to improve the data fidelity by using a larger model size (3 to 4 inches). Boeing performed a series of exploratory calibration runs from March 26 to March 30, 2007, to assess the potential of the LCAT facility to meet the required conditions with a larger nozzle, to accommodate 3 to 4 inch samples. This calibration series confirmed that the conditions can be met in the LCAT facility, on samples of 3 to 4 inch diameter. The next test series at LCAT is required, to recover data compromised in the previous test effort due to the small model size, and to acquire additional data to evaluate pressure port size effectiveness. For the next test series, expected conditions at the pressure port locations range between 100 and 140 W/cm2 in hot wall heat rate, and 0.15 to 0.25 atmospheres in pressure. The test matrix consists of 9 points spanning these conditions, with 2 port diameters to be compared at each condition. These tests will require up to eight thermocouple and four pressure transducer accommodations per sample.

Description: HIGH RESOLUTION MULTI-FLUID SIMULATIONS AND CASSINI DATA COMPARISONS OF THE INDUCED MAGNETOSPHERE AT TITAN This proposal seeks to use advanced 3D multi-fluid model in conjunction with Cassini data to quantify the plasma interaction between Titans ionosphere and Saturns magnetospheric plasma, and the resultant mass loss rate from Titan. The proposed work seeks use Cassini data from the magnetometer (MAG) and Cassini plasma spectrometer (CAPS) to provide quantitatively validate the modeling which can then be used to develop a full 3-D perspective of Titans induced magnetosphere and mass loss under varying conditions within Saturns magnetosphere. The multi-fluid model incorporates ion cyclotron and multi-ion species effects similar to hybrid codes but the fluid treatment enables grid refinement down to as small as 10 km (or nearly an order of magnitude better hybrid codes) can be achieved. This high resolution is unique to the multi-fluid modeling, and provides an unprecedented view of the magnetic pile up boundary which determines the energy and mass transport through induced magnetosphere. The multi-fluid treatment is also able to incorporate the mixing of the different ions species seen by CAPS. These capabilities are unique to the proposed work and through the proposed data/model comparisons we develop a global picture of the Titan/Saturn interaction that would address four critical features: (1) the overall geometry of the cavity and wake region, specifically studying the asymmetries of the tail for different incident Saturnian magnetospheric plasma (SMP) conditions, (2) quantify and describe the loss of mass from Titan into Saturns magnetosphere for different SMP conditions and solar zenith angles, (3) quantify the magnetic pile-up boundary and ionopause at high resolution where ion cyclotron and heavy ion effects are crucial to the structure of the region and (4) the composition, energy, density, and velocity of ions in Titans ionosphere, magnetotail, and the near Saturn environment.

Description: INTEGRATED ICE SHEET CHANGE ANALYSIS USING RADARSAT AND ICESAT Numerous studies have shown that between 2000 and 2005, glaciers throughout Greenland were losing mass to the ocean at a dramatic and accelerating rate. Because most of these studies have limited temporal and spatial coverage, however, the glaciological mechanisms leading to this mass loss are presently unclear. Some mechanisms, such as ice loss from downstream fjords are likely to produce one-time accelerations of flow speed, that last a few years, while others, such as basin-wide climatic shifts, are likely to produce long-term changes in glacier mass balance. We propose to combine continent-scale mosaics of velocity data measured by RADARSAT with high-resolution measurements of surface elevation change from ICESat to determine the spatial and temporal extent of mass balance changes for each glacier basin in Greenland. Our analysis will determine whether velocity changes are confined to areas close to the grounding line, or whether they are pervasive across the basins. Velocity changes concentrated near the grounding line suggest impulsive dynamic forcings, while widespread changes reflect long-term changes. Further, we will determine whether the elevation changes and the flow changes together reflect steady or unsteady ice flow by determining whether elevation changes have been widespread or localized, and whether they accelerated or decelerated over the three years of the ICESat mission.

Description: INTERPRETATION OF MARTIAN POLAR STRATIGRAPHY USING ICE FLOW INVERSE MODELING How flow and mass balance shape the Martian ice caps, and whether subglacial melting ever occurs, are fundamental questions for exploring and understanding Mars. These questions can be addressed directly and quantitatively by using inverse modeling to interpret observed ice cap stratigraphy and topography. Inverse modeling estimates ice cap variables and climatic forcing by assimilating observations with a rigorous, though judiciously limited, physical model. (Forward modeling, by contrast, specifies parameters in a comprehensive physical model and is driven by specified climate forcing to predict ice cap characteristics.) Data interpretation using inverse modeling has yielded, for example, the discovery of high basal melt rates beneath the Greenland ice cap, where no melting at all had been expected. Such interpretation has yet to be applied to the Martian polar layered deposits (PLD), but it is now timely to do so: Topographic data and imagery to map exposed strata now densely cover the PLD, and we are about to get our first look at basal topography and stratigraphy inside the ice from orbital sounding radars. The University of Washington glaciology group has longstanding expertise in combining observations with ice flow inverse modeling to probe terrestrial ice caps. We propose to combine this expertise with Caltech's long specialization in Mars polar studies, to discriminate mass balance from flow processes on Mars, and to probe for evidence of basal melting that might be recorded within the Martian PLD. Specifically, we aim to address the following questions: (1) Does stratigraphy in the north or south PLD display unambiguous evidence for equilibration by large-scale ice flow, now or in the past? (2) Is there evidence for basal sliding, and thus possible subglacial water? In particular, does ice near complex features such as chasmae show evidence of local flow or basal melting, in the past if not now? (3) What are the regional- to large-scale spatial patterns of accumulation and ablation? By basing our data interpretation on the physical models inherent in the flow inverse method, we will make optimal use of partial or fragmentary observations. The imminent observations of basal topography and internal layering from the MARSIS radar will thus, via this method, provide exceptional insight into past and present ice dynamics on Mars.
