Description: STARDUST SAMPLE ANALYSIS Selected comet Wild 2 samples returned by the Stardust mission will be analyzed by electron microscopy and a variety of other methods to determine both mineralogy and organic contents. The goal of this work will be to determine the nature and origin of the 'rock' and organic components that existed in the Kuiper belt region of the solar nebula and were accreted into Wild 2 during its formation. Much of this work will be done with our new Tecnai F20 field emission transmission electron microscope and, to maximize the science value from the samples, we will also continue existing collaborations with other groups for a variety of coordinated studies on the samples. This will include coordinated TEM, isotopic, XANES, Raman and IR analyses. Using phase identifications, phase associations as well as minor element compositions of minerals such as enstatite and forsterite, we will determine if the silicate components of Wild 2 rocks are consistent with highly processed inner solar system materials that are found in primitive meteorites, components such as chondrules, calcium aluminum inclusions and amoeboid olivine aggregates or if they have other origins. Work done in 2006 has suggested that a significant fraction of the Wild 2 components that are larger than a few microns may be related to such highly processed nebular materials and are products of the inner solar system. We will do spatially resolved work on organic components to determine their origin and similarity to organic components in IDPs and primitive meteorites. We will do this work on specially prepared samples where the organic components are preserved in their original as-captured locations. The work will be done on microtome sections that preserve the spatial relationships between organic and silicate components within the aerogel that they were captured in. A key aspect of this work is the way we process the comet samples. Using unique methods that we developed, we flatten the tracks and imbed the entire track with acrylic. This provides perfect ability of optically examine the 1 to 15 micron fragments that are preserved in the lower half of tracks. Some tracks contain over twenty such fragments and we believe that the methodology that we have developed is the only presently method that leads to the analysis of all of the silicate, sulfide and carbonaceous components still preserved in their aerogel capture matrix. The embedding medium is removed with solvents and work in 2006 has shown that this methods preserves carbonaceous components in the micron and submicron range- still in their original locations in comet dust. We believe that the results of the this work will provide fundamental insights into the origin of comets, large scale mixing in the solar nebular and the origin of crystalline materials around stars.

Description: "AIR-ICE SURFACE ENERGY EXCHANGE AND SEA ICE-MASS REDISTRIBUTION IN THE ARCTIC" SUMMARY: MEASUREMENTS OF THE ARCTIC SEA ICE COVER FROM BUOYS, SUBMARINES, AND SATELLITES INDICATE THE THICKNESS AND THE TEMPORAL AND SPATIAL DISTRIBUTION OF THE ICE HAVE CHANGED OVER THE LAST 30 YEARS.  THESE CHANGES IN THE ARCTIC ICE APPEAR TO BE DRIVEN BY CHANGES IN BOTH THERMODYNAMIC AND DYNAMIC FORCING, AND NUMERICAL MODELING STUDIES HAVE PROVIDED A RANGE OF EXPLANATIONS WHICH DEPEND ON EACH MODEL S SENSITIVITY TO SIMILAR ATMOSPHERIC FORCING.  CHANGES IN ICE MASS ARE CLOSELY LINKED TO THE DYNAMIC RESPONSE TO ATMOSPHERIC FORCING THROUGH THE PROCESSES OF ICE DEFORMATION, LEAD OPENING, AND NEW ICE GROWTH.  HIGH-QUALITY OBSERVATIONAL DATA ON AIR-ICE SURFACE FLUXES AND THE STRESS/STRAIN RELATIONSHIP IN SEA ICE HAVE BECOME AVAILABLE, AND CAN BE USED TO CONSTRAIN THE FORMULATIONS OF AIR-ICE TURBULENT TRANSFER AND ICE RHEOLOGY.  THE SPECIFIC OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY ARE: (I) TO ANALYZE RECENT STRESS/STRAIN AND SURFACE FLUX DATA FOR THE PURPOSE OF DEVELOPING PARAMETERIZATIONS FOR ICE AND CLIMATE MODELS, (II) TO SIMULATE THE ARCTIC SEA ICE COVER OVER RECENT DECADES AND COMPARE THE IMPACT OF CONSTRAINING THE PARAMETERIZATIONS WITH OBSERVATIONS, AND (III) COMPARE MODEL SIMULATIONS WITH ICE THICKNESS OBSERVATIONS AND DETERMINE THE CONTRIBUTIONS OF DYNAMICS AND THERMODYNAMICS TO THE OBSERVED CHANGES. Description: Miles Logsdon/University of Washington THE INTERACTION BETWEEN ANTARCTIC POLYNYAS AND THE REGIONAL OCEANOGRAPHY-PHASE II In the Ross Sea, we are completing a multiyear study of annual ice production calculated using our SSM/I 37Ghz and AMSR-E 36GhzV/H algorithms for the Ross Sea polynya and the smaller Terra Nova Bay and McMurdo Sound polynyas. For the SSM/I, we have calculated the winter production for 1992-2005; for the AMSR-E, we have calculated it for the period 2003-2005. We plan to add the 2006 data as soon as the SSM/I polar gridded brightness temperature data is available (estimate from NSIDC: mid-May). This will provide 4 years of concurrent data to compare SSM/I and AMSR-E results. From the work completed so far and consistent with the higher resolution, we expect larger ice production estimates from AMSR-E compared with the SSM/I. We also see a generally increasing trend in total annual production since 1992. Possible additional goals will be to correlate our results to the Antarctic Oscillation Index (AOI) or other meteorological indices, and to look at monthly ice production values. In the Weddell Sea, we have begun a study to estimate annual and monthly ice production in the major Weddell Sea coastal polynyas using our algorithm based on daily AMSR-E 36Ghz V/H brightness temperature ratios. The process will parallel our work in the Ross Sea, and will cover the period 2003-2006. We will use l-km resolution MODIS imagery to construct an accurate land/shelf/berg mask at the 12.5-km AMSR resolution. Unlike the Ross Sea, there are no large non-stationary icebergs in the Weddell so that berg tracking is not necessary. In the next few months, our goals will be to identify the active polynya sites, construct masks and measurement regions, compile and process daily AMSR and met data, and obtain the ice production estimates. We will then compare the polynya ice production to ice export, where from historical data, we expect the ratio of production to export to be much smaller in the Weddell than in the Ross.

Description: Capabilities for use on Future NASA Aircraft Missions Mercury (Hg) is an important trace constituent of the global atmosphere. Its atmospheric cycling plays an important role in distributing mercury widely throughout the environment. In the Arctic, HgO oxidation by halogen radicals is thought to be a key control on the cycling and deposition of mercury. At the same time, HgO is an excellent tracer of airmasses that contain coal combustion by-products (Jaffe et aI.,2005). There are multiple forms of mercury, including gaseous HgO, gaseous Hg(lI) compounds and particulate-bound Hg. Unfortunately, the cycling of mercury between these forms is very poorly understood and there are virtually no measurements of mercury in the remote free troposphere. Models of the global mercury cycle predict significant concentrations of Hg(lI) in the upper troposphere and stratosphere due to oxidation, yet there are no measurements available, at present, that can be used to evaluate these models. The paucity of airborne Hg measurements reflects the difficulty in making these obser'Jations. lVe propose to develop and evaluate a method for making speciated Hg measurements on a NASA research aircraft. For HgO, our method will rely on the use of cold vapor atomic fluorescence spectroscopy (CVAFS), which has proven to be the most sensitive and reliable method available, based on ground based observations. We will modify a CVAFS instrument from Tekran, Inc. to get better time response and greater flow for use on a NASA aircraft. We will also modify the instrument to get constant sensitivity as a function of pressure and develop a method for in-flight calibrations. Development of a method for gaseous Hg(lI) compounds will be even more challenging. For this, we will evaluate two different methods for airborne use. The first method will utilize KCI-coated denuders to collect Hg(ll) compounds for post-flight analysis. The second method we will evaluate will be a difference method, whereby gaseous mercury is measured in two airstreams simultaneously, one of which has had Hg(lI) compounds removed prior to measurement. The difference in signal yields the Hg(ll) concentration. This method will yield a much faster time response for Hg(II), but has several challenges that will need to be overcome prior to implementation. We expect to have a fully functional system to be ready for the 2008 NASA ARCTAS mission, based on one of these methods.

Description: JRI-N-BODY SIMULATIONS OF GROWTH FROM 1 KM PLANETESIMALS We propose to perform direct N-body computer simulations of terrestrial planets growth beginning with 1 km radius bodies. We will begin with small shearing patches containing 100,000 particles at 0.4, 1.0 and 2.5 AU from a one solar mass single star. As accretion reduces the number of particles per unit area, larger and larger patches will be followed. The patches will be replaced by annuli to appropriately follow the dynamics once a dominant runaway body emerges. Our calculations should realistically investigate the initiation of planetesimal growth. They will yield estimates of the size distribution of planetary embryos and amount of small debris present for the later stages of planetary growth. Damping of non-circular motions by this debris may be a crucial factor in resolving the difference between near circular orbits of the terrestrial planets in our Solar System and the much more dynamically excited systems produced by conventional numerical simulations. Description: Advanced Computer Modeling of the Lunar Plasma Environment in the Dynamic Terrestrial Magnetosphere This proposal seeks to use an advanced 3D multi-fluid model in conjunction with Lunar Prospector data to quantify the plasma environment when the Moon is in the Earth's magnetotail from quiet to storm conditions. The proposed work seeks use Lunar Prospector data from the magnetometer/electron reflectometer (MAG/ER) to first quantitatively validate the modeling and then develop a full 3D perspective of the Moon's near space environment under varying conditions within the Earth's magnetosphere. The multi-fluid model incorporates ion cyclotron and multi-ion species effects similar to hybrid codes but the fluid treatment enables grid refinement down to as small as 10 km can be achieved (or nearly an order of magnitude better hybrid codes). This high resolution is unique to the multi-fluid modeling, and will allow for incorporation of the lunar magnetic anomalies to determine how they modify plasma transport and acceleration on the back side of the Moon. The multi-fluid treatment is able to generate electron spectrogram to enhance comparison with data and is also able to incorporate the mixing of the different ions species, observations that Lunar Prospector was unable to make. These capabilities are unique to the proposed work and through the proposed data/model synthesis, we can develop a global 3D picture of the Moon/Earth interaction out of 1D satellite traces that will address three critical questions: 1. What are the the composition, energy, density, and velocity of ions near the Moon for (a) quiet conditions and (b) sub-storm/storm conditions? 2. What is the overall geometry of the cavity and wake region of the Moon, specifically what are the asymmetries of the wake for different incident terrestrial magnetospheric plasma conditions? 3. What role, if any, do the magnetic anomalies play in modifying the above? This work addresses Strategic Sub-goal 3B by developing an understanding of the space environment around the Moon and the plasma acceleration processes that can lead to energetic particle populations in this region. The work also addresses Strategic Sub-goal 3C by quantifying potential radiation hazards with regard to human habitation on the Moon.

Description: It is presumed that most galaxies have a large Black Hole at their center. As galaxies merge in the standard hierarchical scenario of galaxy formation, these Black Holes also can merge and grow. Furthermore the violent dynamics of the merger will deliver a significant amount of gas and stars to the central regions of the merging galaxy further growing the central Black Hole and fueling an Active Galactic Nucleus. We will perform state-of-the-art numerical simulations of this merging process using N-body simulations and gas dynamics. These simulations will resolve the dynamics in the central kiloparsec of the merging galaxies and will be able to follow the sinking of the Black Holes to the center via dynamical friction up to the formation of binary Black Holes. We will also follow the delivery of gas to the central regions to make predictions about the fueling of the AGN. Several missions of the Beyond Einstein program will be attempting to understand the physics of central Black Holes in galaxies. LISA hopes to detect the gravitational radiation as the Black Holes merge, and therefore will need estimates of merger rates. Con-X will be observing the X-ray emission from these objects, and these observations will need to be put into a framework that includes the very dynamic nature of the galactic merging process in order to be fully understood.

Description: ASSESSMENT OF SEA ICE THICKNESS ESTIMATES OBTAINED FROM SATELLITES USING SUBMARINES, AND OTHER IN SITU OBSERVATIONS Research on the variability of Arctic sea ice requires reliable observational data on sea-ice extent and thickness. While sea-ice extent can be readily obtained from satellites, we are only now developing our capability to remotely monitor thickness. The most promising satellite technique is altimetry to measure freeboard and estimate thickness from freeboard. The sea-ice thickness estimates obtained from satellite altimetry require careful validation, very little of which has been done to date. We plan to compare sea-ice freeboard and estimated thickness from satellites (ICESat in combination with RADARSAT, e.g. Kwok et al. 2004) with in-situ observations. The sources of in-situ data will include (a) spatial profiles of ice draft measured during submarine cruises under the sea ice, (b) time series of draft from moored upward looking sonar, (c) ice thickness surveys from electromagnetic instruments flown over the sea ice, (d) ice and snow measurements during a field camp in 2007, and (e) snow and ice thickness plus thermal and dynamic history of the ice pack from drifting buoys. Many of these datasets will be provided through collaborations with other institutions. The submarine draft measurements are derived from classified data and are a unique product which only our research group is currently capable of producing. Primary goals of this research are to: 1. Extend the public record of sea-ice draft measurements from submarines through 2007 (currently only available to 2000); 2. Compare in situ observations with satellite derived sea-ice freeboard and thickness obtained from ICESat to assess sources and degree of uncertainty in the satellite estimate; 3. Assess methods of improving the satellite estimate of thickness; 4. Study the variability of Arctic sea-ice thickness. Specifically, how do new submarine measurements of ice thickness compare to the longer record in light of moderate/low AO conditions during the past few years?

In summary, our plan is to determine the productivity ofthe Weddell polynyas, then examine the linkage between their productivity and the large-scale atmospheric modes. Description: EVALUATING CLOUDS AND PRECIPITATION IN A MULTISCALE GLOBAL CLIMATE MODEL WITH CLOUDSAT Recently, a new computational approach that couples cloud-scale dynamics with large-scale dynamics in global climate models (GCMs) has been proposed and implemented. In this approach, called a Multiscale Modeling Framework (MMF) or superparameterization, all the cloud-related parameterizations are removed from a traditional GCM and, in each GCM grid column, replaced with a 2D or a small 3D cloud resolving model (CRM). We propose to  compare MMF (and parent GCM) simulations of the vertical profiles of cloud condensate and precipitation against CloudSat cloud-radar observations and retrievals. The proposed comparison and analysis of observations and model output will be conducted in two ways; one based on traditional aggregation of observations and model output on seasonal to annual scales, and one based on an atmospheric classification approach. We plan to use both CloudSat retrievals and reflectivity observations directly. CloudSat reflectivity observations can be compared to model output using a CloudSat-satellite-simulator. By this we mean that we will calculate from the high-resolution CRM, run as part of the MMF, the reflectivity Field that would be observed by CloudSat and compare the statistical properties of the model-simulated vertical reflectivity distribution to the observed distribution. We believe the proposed combination of instrument-simulator and classification techniques will prove capable of uncovering model shortcomings and provide insights to developing new ideas and ultimately, a better model. Regardless of how the model output and data are aggregated (traditional or classification), and whether we use an instrument simulator or satellite retrieved parameters in the comparison, or both, we will use robust statistical tests to evaluate our results. Ultimately our intent is not only to evaluate the current model, but to use this framework to evaluate a number of currently planned and future model improvements.

Description: EARLY DETECTION OF INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE AND THE SUBSEQUENT HEALTH OUTCOMES DUE TO HIGH LET PARTICLE RADIATION: AN INTEGRATED METABOLOMICS STUDY Our new studies reveal that NMR-detectable metabolites (e.g., the concentrations of alanine, acetate, glutamate, creatine, choline, phosphocholine, inositol and myo-inositol, etc.) are increased significantly after rats were exposed to whole body high linear energy transfer (LET) iron ions at doses as low as 0.16 Gy. Dramatic changes were also detected in metabolites in various excised organs from mice exposed to gamma-rays at doses of 3.0 and 7.8 Gy. We hypothesize that metabolite biomarkers sensitive to both high LET particle radiation and low LET gamma-rays will be detectable and quantifiable using both established, and unique, high resolution and high sensitivity NMR and LC-MS metabolomics. We also propose that low doses (0.5Gy) of high LET radiation causes a low grade inflammatory response and triggers a cascade of molecular events detectable with our novel approach. We will perform an integrated NMR and LC-MS metabolomics study of the impact of exposing mice and rats to 0,0.5, and 3 Gy using both high LET proton and iron ion radiation. The metabolic perturbations in global physiology and the subsequent health outcomes will be investigated from 1 day to 1 year post irradiation using key body fluids and excised tissues. In parallel, we will investigate the impact of exposing mice and rats to gamma-rays at low and high doses to determine the differences in dose-dependent effects between proton, iron ions and gamma-rays. Furthermore, histopathologic analysis and basic-translational cell and molecular investigations will be used to link metabolic signatures and disease pathogenesis. The ultimate goal is to elucidate the detailed molecular mechanisms of high LET radiation, with emphasis on understanding the molecular basis of radiation through the discovery of metabolic signatures. This new knowledge will be translated to benefit human health in space exploration.

Description: ICE CLOUD GENERATION BY MESOSCALE CONVECTIVE SYSTEM AND IMPLICATIONS FOR LARGE-SCALE HEATING  This study will assess the structure and radiative heating processes in large, long lasting cirriform clouds produced by mesoscale convective cloud systems (MCSs) and the impacts of this heating on the larger-scale circulation. The A-Train satellites CloudSat and CALIPSO will be the primary data sources for the study. Objective 1 is case-by-case analysis of the cirriform clouds of MCSs. MCSs in the path of the A-train satellites will be identified through analysis of data from Aqua and other satellites. The cloud radar and lidar data from CloudSat and CALIPSO will be ingested into the Zebra visualization tool to analyze the horizontal dimensions, anvil base and top heights, and the distribution of radar reflectivity and lidar backscattering within the cirriform clouds of MCSs, including both precipitating clouds and non-precipitating anvils. Objective 2 is statistical compilation of the MCS ice-cloud characteristics obtained under Objective 1. The results will be grouped by region, season, and type of MCS in the form of frequency distributions representing the spatial dimensions and ice water content of the anvils. The cloud radar and cloud lidar data will be converted to ice water content by the best available algorithms. Objective 3 is to compute the radiative heating by the non-precipitating and precipitating ice clouds of MCSs. The Fu-Liou radiative transfer code will be applied to the observed cirriform cloud structures analyzed under Objectives 1 and 2 to obtain a set of radiative heating proflles that apply generally to MCSs, including their non-precipitating anvils. Objective 4 is to assess the global circulation's response to the radiative heating in cirriform clouds produced by MCSs. The heating profiles derived under Objective 3 will be applied in a simplified climate model to determine the response of the large-scale circulation to the radiative heating occurring in non-precipitating MCS anvils. The response of the large-scale circulation to the non-precipitating anvils will be compared to the large-scale response to latent heating and cooling and radiation in the raining parts of MCSs. Relevance: This research directly addresses the goals of the NASA A-Train satellite program, which aims to evaluate quantitatively the representation of clouds and cloud processes in global atmospheric circulation models, especially in terms of the radiative heating by clouds. Quantifying these processes is essential to the progress of NASA earth system research.

Description: ASSESSING THE EFFECTS OF COMET BOMBARDMENT ON EARTH (GRADUATE STUDENT: NATHAN ANDREW KAIB) We will use direct numerical simulations to model comet showers from the Oort Cloud. Description: Major hydrologic changes have been observed over much of the Eurasian Arctic over the last half century. These include widespread increases in permafrost active layer depth, changes in the extent of lakes and wetlands, and increased river discharge, especially in winter. A number of causes have been suggested for these trends, including thawing of permafrost, construction of dams, land cover change, and melting of land ice. In most cases, coincident changes in precipitation have not been observed. These changes motivate the overarching science question for this proposal:: ?To what extent are changes in permafrost characteristics, as compared with seasonal patterns of snow cover extent, reservoir storage, and land cover change responsible for observed changes in the discharge of major Arctic rivers over the second half of the Twentieth Century?? We intend to address this question through intensive use of IPY permafrost data to be collected as part of IPY project #125, Thermal state of permafrost, with which we will coordinate closely. We will use land surface modeling, incorporating new in situand remote sensing data sets to be acquired as part of IPY activities, as well as recent advances in representation of the hydrologic effects of permafrost, improved modeling of snow cover dynamics over large areas, land cover change, and water management. We will further utilize our land surface model in cooperation with TSP PI (NSF funded project) Vladimir Romanovsky to help identify portions of the pan-arctic domain where additional permafrost borehole measurements will be most useful. Through representation of these potential change agents in long term (50-75 year) simulations of streamflow for the major Eurasian Arctic river basins and their largest tributaries, and comparison with observed streamflow records, we expect to understand the relative effects of these various changes, as well as the direct effects (e.g., through earlier onset of spring snowmelt) of climate change over the last half to three-quarter century.  Our overall approach will be as follows. We will perform retrospective simulations with the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) macroscale hydrology model and a suite of other land surface models in our multi-model hydrologic simulation system over the Eurasian Arctic study domain. Via examination of simulated river discharge in comparison with observations, we will infer the relative magnitudes of long-term (last 50-75 years) changes attributable to each of the proposed change agents  specifically, permafrost active layer depth, climate and hydrologic response (e.g., changes in amount, timing, and location of precipitation and snowmelt), vegetation changes, and the effect of reservoirs.  The proposed project will contribute directly to one of the central questions posed by the NAS 2001 report Enhancing NASA contributions to polar science?, specifically under responses to change, we will address the question posed by the NAS report How will land surface hydrology and energy exchanges be influenced by the climate-induced changes to vegetation structure and distribution across the polar regions This proposal further responds to the second element of the NRA requesting proposals for Integrated regional modeling of the polar regions  that takes advantage of synergies between the enhanced international observational capabilities that will be available during the IPY time frame and NASA satellites?.  This proposal is a slight variation of a proposal by the same PI and co-PI submitted to the NASA NEWS call in December, 2004. We are submitting this proposal to the IPY call at the recommendation of the NASA Terrestrial Hydrology Program Manager, Jared Entin.  This proposal focuses more directly on issues specified in the IPY call (notably permafrost, and a connection with the IPY Thermal State of Permafrost project) than does the NEWS submission.

Description: THE FLUX OF SEA ICE IN AND OUT OF THE WEDDELL SEA:  ITS INTERACTION WITH POLYNYAS, ICEBERGS AND LARGE SCALE ATMOSPHERIC MODES The proposal will examine the flux of sea ice in and out ofthe Weddell Sea, and the augmentation ofthe outward flux by the addition of ice growth in the polynyas adjacent both to the ice shelves and to large icebergs. These bergs calve from the Filchner/Ronne Ice Shelves, then either drift north, or ground on Berkner Bank. Because polynyas form downwind of the bergs, the polynyas must be considered in the overall productivity.  For these polynyas, we will calculate their productivity and impact on the production of the dense shelf water that is related to the Antarctic Bottom Water, and examine the linkage between their annual and monthly productivity and the large-scale atmospheric modes, including the Antarctic Oscillation, the Southern Oscillation and the related Antarctic Dipole.  In summary, our plan is to determine the productivity ofthe Weddell polynyas, then examine the linkage between their productivity and the large-scale atmospheric modes.  For the Weddell, the results will contribute to an understanding ofthe linkage between the large-scale atmospheric modes and the production of dense shelf water, and examine how iceberg calving modifies this dependence.

Description: EARLY DETECTION OF INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE AND THE SUBSEQUENT HEALTH OUTCOMES DUE TO HIGH LET PARTICLE RADIATION: AN INTEGRATED METABOLOMICS STUDY Our new studies reveal that NMR-detectable metabolites (e.g., the concentrations of alanine, acetate, glutamate, creatine, choline, phosphocholine, inositol and myo-inositol, etc.) are increased significantly after rats were exposed to whole body high linear energy transfer (LET) iron ions at doses as low as 0.16 Gy. Dramatic changes were also detected in metabolites in various excised organs from mice exposed to gamma-rays at doses of 3.0 and 7.8 Gy. We hypothesize that metabolite biomarkers sensitive to both high LET particle radiation and low LET gamma-rays will be detectable and quantifiable using both established, and unique, high resolution and high sensitivity NMR and LC-MS metabolomics. We also propose that low doses (0.5Gy) of high LET radiation causes a low grade inflammatory response and triggers a cascade of molecular events detectable with our novel approach. We will perform an integrated NMR and LC-MS metabolomics study of the impact of exposing mice and rats to 0,0.5, and 3 Gy using both high LET proton and iron ion radiation. The metabolic perturbations in global physiology and the subsequent health outcomes will be investigated from 1 day to 1 year post irradiation using key body fluids and excised tissues. In parallel, we will investigate the impact of exposing mice and rats to gamma-rays at low and high doses to determine the differences in dose-dependent effects between proton, iron ions and gamma-rays. Furthermore, histopathologic analysis and basic-translational cell and molecular investigations will be used to link metabolic signatures and disease pathogenesis. The ultimate goal is to elucidate the detailed molecular mechanisms of high LET radiation, with emphasis on understanding the molecular basis of radiation through the discovery of metabolic signatures. This new knowledge will be translated to benefit human health in space exploration.

Description: The goal of this proposed research is to explore a new method for using HRSC and THEMIS visible image data to obtain quantitative, high-resolution estimates of sub-pixel surface roughness and to use them to address key issues in the study of Mars and its future exploration. The approach utilizes the ratio between co-registered pixels in stereo or repeat image pairs to measure the deviation of the Martian surface from Lambertian reflection due to unresolved shadows at the pixel scale of orbiting imagers. Relative differences between these ratios primarily reflect differences in the effective amount of shadows  by the sensor in the two measurements, and are thus used as a relative proxy for sub-pixel surface roughness (SR). In-scene atmospheric corrections enable simple application of this approach, which facilitates robust SR mapping at spatial resolutions comparable to the image data. Relative SR estimates can be translated to physical SR parameters through empirical calibration using rover-based measurements or through model-based radiosity models for synthetic surfaces or hyper-resolution (~mm scale) DEM of Earth analog sites. This new approach complements the other methods currently in use for estimating sub-pixel roughness on Mars and will ad to our abilities to characterize future landing sites and the surface of Mars in general.

Description: LOWENERGY PLANTETARY EXCAVATOR (LPE) SBIR PHASE II LOW-ENERGY PLANETARY EXCAVATOR (LPE) PROTOTYPE SBIR CONTRACT  ORBITEC PROPOSES TO DEVELOP AN INNOVATIVE LOW-ENERGY PLANETARY EXCAVATOR (LPE) TO EXCAVATE IN SITU REGOLITH, ICEREGOLITH MIXTURES, AND A VARIETY OF OTHER GEOLOGIC MATERIALS TO SUPPORT FUTURE ACTIVITIES ON THE MOON AND MARS. THE LPE UTILIZES AN INNOVATIVE CUTTERHEAD TO EFFICIENTLY EXCAVATE A WIDE RANGE OF DIFFERENT PLANETARY SURFACE MATERIALS. CURRENT MECHANICAL EXCAVATORS OPERATES EFFICIENTLY ONLY IN A NARROW RANGE OF MATERIAL CONDITIONS. THE LPE WILL SENSE GEOLOGIC CHANGES AND RESPOND WITH CHANGES IN THE CUTTERHEAD TO ACHIEVE THE LOWEST CUTTING ENERGY POSSIBLE. THE RESULT IS A FLEXIBLE MACHINE WITH REDUCED POWER AND MASS REQUIREMENTS. THE PHASE II LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT IS DESIGNED TO BE A TESTBED TO EVALUATE THE PERFORMANCE OF THE VARIABLE GEOMETRY CUTTERHEAD IN SIMULATED LUNAR ICE-REGOLITH MATERIAL. IT IS NOT DESIGNED TO BE A FULLY-FUNCTIONAL EXCAVATOR. THE CUTTERHEAD IS THE KEY DESIGN DRIVER FOR THE REST OF THE EXCAVATOR. THE REST OF THE EXCAVATOR MUST SUPPLY THE THRUST AND TORQUE REQUIRED TO CAUSE FAILURES IN THE TARGET MATERIAL. THE MAJOR COMPONENTS OF THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT ARE THE CUTTERHEAD ASSEMBLY, THE TRANSLATION STAGE, AND THE SUPPORT FRAME. THE CUTTERHEAD ASSEMBLY CONTAINS ELECTRIC DRIVE MOTORS THAT ROTATE THE CUTTERHEAD, LINEAR ACTUATORS THAT CONTROL THE SUMPING DEPTH (DISTANCE OF THE CUTTERHEAD INTO THE EXCAVATED MATERIAL), LINEAR ACTUATORS THAT CONTROL THE CUTTERHEAD GEOMETRY, AND A MOUNTING BLOCK. THE TRANSLATION STAGE CONSISTS OF A LEAD SCREW AND AN ELECTRIC LEAD SCREW DRIVE MOTOR. THE SUPPORT FRAME CONSISTS OF TWO HORIZONTAL GUIDE RAILS AND THE SUPPORT STANDS.  DURING OPERATION, THE LEAD SCREW MOVES THE CUTTERHEAD ASSEMBLY ALONG THE GUIDE RAILS AND PROVIDES THE FORWARD THRUST ON THE CUTTERHEAD. NOTE THAT THE SUPPORT STANDS WOULD NEED TO BE ATTACHED TO THE FLOOR BEFORE OPERATION. TECHNICAL OBJECTIVES THE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE OF THE PHASE II EFFORT WILL BE TO DESIGN, BUILD, TEST, AND DELIVER AN OPERATIONAL LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT TO NASA.  THE SPECIFIC TECHNICAL OBJECTIVES OF THE PHASE II EFFORT WOULD INCLUDE:   REFINE THE SYSTEM REQUIREMENTS FOR THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT, A PHASE III TECHNOLOGY DEMONSTRATION UNIT, AND A LPE PRODUCTION UNIT;   DETERMINE THE RANGE OF POTENTIAL ICE-REGOLITH MECHANICAL PROPERTIES EXPECTED ON THE MOON;   IDENTIFY AND DEVELOP EFFECTIVE MECHANICAL SIMULANTS THAT ARE AS CLOSE TO TRUE LUNAR CONDITIONS AS POSSIBLE;   DESIGN AND ANALYZE A LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT;   CONSTRUCT A COMPUTERIZED PERFORMANCE PREDICTION MODEL FOR THE CUTTERHEAD AND EXCAVATION MACHINE;   BUILD AND TEST THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT;   DELIVER THE LPE PROTOTYPE UNIT TO NASA AND DEMONSTRATE ITS OPERATION;   DEVELOP CONCEPTUAL DESIGNS FOR A PHASE III LPE TECHNOLOGY DEMONSTRATION UNIT AND A LPE PRODUCTION UNIT. Description: CONSTRAINING PHYSICALLY MOTIVATED GRAVITATIONAL EQUILIBRIA OF DARK MATTER HALOS Our knowledge of structure formation in the universe has grown considerably over the past decade. On the largest scales, computer simulations of dark matter produce webs and filaments that form the matrix for galaxy formation, mimicking observations. On the scale of galaxy clusters and individual galaxies, computer N-body simulations predict 'universal' density, velocity dispersion, and velocity anisotropy behaviors, suggesting that dark matter halo formation follows a well defined path. However, because the simulations are rather complex, neither this path nor the properties of the final virialized state of halos are understood at the level that the structure of stars is appreciated, in terms of gravity and thermodynamical properties. Our objective is to achieve a similar level of basic understanding of collisionless dark matter halos and to describe the relevant physical mechanisms that govern halo formation. To achieve this objective, we will investigate two physically motivated analytical hypotheses that make predictions about the equilibrium states of self-gravitating collisionless systems. The first hypothesis assumes that the "equation of state" of collisionless matter is a power-law in radius, an assumption motivated by the results ofN-body simulations and a semi-analytical halo formation scheme. The second hypothesis is based on a nonextensive thermodynamics where the final state ofthe system is obtained as a maximum of an appropriately defined nonextensive entropy. We will examine and constrain these two hypotheses by comparing their predictions to the results of N-body simulations and to high-resolution visible and X-ray data of galaxies, clusters of galaxies, and globular clusters. Such comparisons will be done using tools we have already developed and will develop as a part of the proposed work. These diagnostic tools will be able to discriminate between various hypotheses and models of dark matter halos, without relying on kinematic data, which is observationally difficult to obtain, and theoretically difficult to translate into unambiguous dynamical information. The requirements necessary to refine and extend these comparison tools will provide useful guidance for future X-ray missions. The theoretical and diagnostic products of this work will further NASA's goal to understand how dark matter and gravity shape galaxies and systems of galaxies.

Description: IMPROVED MODELS OF JOVIAN CLOUD STRUCTURE We propose to derive improved models of Jovian cloud structure using a combination of Cassini and Galileo imaging and spectral observations acquired during the Cassini flyby of Jupiter. Weak, strong, and intermediate methane band and continuum images with the Cassini ISS, combined with center-to-limb variations and phase angle variations, will provide important new constraints at CCD wavelengths, which will be further enhanced by VIMS CCD spatially resolved spectral observations. We will also use Cassini ISS polarization observations to constrain cloud-top altitudes. Near-IW observations by Gaiileo NIMS and Cassini VPMS in the 1-5 micron range wiii taite advantage of recentiy improved modeis of methane absorption (Irwin et al. 2006, Icarus 181,309-313; Sromovsky et al. 2006, Icarus, in Press) to provide better cloud height discrimination that is less affected by Rayleigh scattering and methane absorption coefficient uncertainties. By combining analysis of near-IR and visible imaging, spectroscopy, with center-to-limb and phase angle variations, aided spectrally variable absorptions by methane, ammonia, and hydrogen, and assisted by polarimetry, we hope to resolve the current controversy over the vertical location of the main variable cloud level in Jupiter's atmosphere, which appears to be in the 1-2 bar region from some analyses (Irwin et al. 2001, Icarus 49,397-415; Sromovsky and Fry, 2002, Icarus 157,373-400) and at the ammonia condensation level in others (Banfield, 2001, Proceedings of th Jupiter conference, 25-30 June 2001; Simon-Miller, Icarus 154,459-474). The proposed research will advance the main objective of the Cassini Data Analysis Program by enhancing the return of the Cassini Mission, take advantage of joint Cassini and Galileo observations during the Cassini Flyby and will increase our understanding of the Jupiter system. The proposed effort contributes to the OSS theme of "Exploring the Solar System" and to OSS Science Goal 6, "Understand the nature and history of our Solar System, and what makes Earth similar to and different from its planetary neighbors".

Description: Connections Between Regional Processes and Intercontinental Transport of Air Pollution How do regional processes affect hemispheric pollution transport? This question will be addressed through an integrated analysis with global satellite observations of atmospheric constituents, surface measurements, a regional chemical transport model (Community Multi-scale Air Quality model, CMAQ), and a global chemical transport model (Model of Ozone and Related Tracers, MOZART). We focus on the exchange of species between the atmospheric boundary layer and the free troposphere, especially the exchange processes associated with thermal convection, frontal activity, and topographical circulation patterns. This project complements the goals of the NASA Aura satellite in connecting regional air quality management with global chemistry and transport. The study will focus on three regions with the potential to be important sources and receptors of intercontinental air pollution transport: the Great Lakes Region of North America, the Rocky Mountain Range through Colorado and Arizona, and East Asia, especially northeast China, the Korean Peninsula, and Japan. In each region the study will focus on particular objectives through which regional and large-scale processes are linked. We will first identify the conditions under which satellite and surface observations are well correlated and poorly correlated. The models will then be employed to characterize the mechanisms responsible for rapid exchange between the surface and the free troposphere, and the mechanisms responsible for capping the boundary layer to inhibit vertical mixing. This study will advance NASA's ability to employ global observations from space in monitoring of long-range air pollution transport, in forecasting air quality, and in linking air pollution and global climate change. Only through space-based observing platforms can episodes of global pollution transport be directly observed. These observations aid in understanding the episodic variability of hemispheric transport, and they contribute invaluably to the ongoing growth of a U.S. operational air quality forecast system. We focus on O3, aerosols, and associated precursors, which have well established links to global climate change in terms of radiative forcing and, for aerosols, precipitation effects. By characterizing the regional chemical and meteorological mechanisms that affect the export of emissions from the surface, and import of transported species to the surface, our study will increase the utility of space-based platforms for tackling atmospheric chemistry problems directly related to human health, welfare, and economic activity.

Description: Collaborative Research with the Marshall Spaceflight Center at the National Space and Technology Center replacing the original coooperative agreement NNM06AA04A The NASA Short-term Prediction Research and Transition (SPoRT) Center at MSFC accelerates the transition of unique observing, modeling, and data assimilation capabilities developed under the auspices of the NASA Science Mission Directorate (SMD) to National Weather Service Forecast Offices (NWSFO's) and decision makers. The SPoRT Center conducts both discovery and product-driven research associated with advanced algorithm development, land/atmosphere interactions, satellite data assimilation, convective initiation and evolution, lightning/severe storm kinematics, and quantitative precipitation estimation and forecasting.  Observations from a number of NASA satellite missions and state-of-the-art community-based mesoscale prediction/assimilation systems are used. The SPoRT Center currently provides a number of products from MODIS, AIRS, and AMSR-E, supplemental numerical guidance from the WRF models, and total lightning from the Lightning Mapper Array (LMA) to six NWSFOs in the NWS Southern Region. Description: "Scanning HIS Participation in TC4 2007 for Validation of A-Train Products" Abstract: The Scanning High-resolution Interferometer Sounder (S-HIS) will be flown in the TC4 aircraft campaign for the validation of A-Train observations. Our participation will provide; (1) Further characterization of Tropospheric Emission Spectrometer (TES) radiometric performance, hopefully leading to improved product accuracy, (2) Assessment of tropospheric ozone retrievals from the Aura spacecraft using down-looking remote sensing that only views the troposphere, (3) Cloud properties from high spectral and spatial (~2 km) resolution IR for CALIPSO and CloudSat comparisons, and (4) Temperature and water vapor profile fields below the aircraft. In a more general context this effort is part of a larger endeavor to achieve both consistency and accuracy among the IR observations used for Earth systems science and operations. High spectral resolution infrared spaceborne instruments like TES on Aura and the Atmospheric InfraRed Sounder (AIRS) on Aqua, combined with checks from high altitude aircraft observations that are periodically compared to ground-based NIST transfer standards, provide a significant step toward establishing the valid record of observations needed for detecting climate change, improving weather forecasts, and monitoring atmospheric composition. The primary tool for this effort is the Scanning High-resolution Interferometer Sounder (S-HIS), developed and maintained by the University of Wisconsin-Madison Space Science and Engineering Center. The S-HIS covers the entire spectral region from 580-3000 cm-1 with a resolution of 0.5 cm-1 and performs cross-track scans with ~2 km footprints giving good spectral and spatial overlap with nadir-viewing instruments like TES, CALIPSO, and CloudSat. The S-HIS is a well-proven instrument that has been flown since 1998 on the NASA DC8 and high altitude aircraft, including the NASA ER-2, the Scaled Composites Proteus, and the NASA WB57. The S-HIS has consistently demonstrated its value in satellite validation campaigns, including several for AIRS on Aqua and for the AURA Validation Experiments of 2004, 2005, and 2006. Abstract:

Description: EFFECTS OF FIRE, EXTREME WEATHER, AND ANTHROPOGENIC DISTURBANCE ON AVIAN BIODIVERSITY IN THE UNITED STATES Three primary determinants of biodiversity include habitat structure, climatic stability, and productivity. Natural and anthropogenic disturbances alter all of these determinants and may therefore playa large role in influencing patterns of biodiversity. We propose to measure and predict the effects of disturbance on biodiversity in the conterminous U.S. through remote sensing techniques and long-term, broad-scale datasets. Our analysis will encompass three broad disturbance types (extreme weather, fire, and anthropogenic disturbance) and their effects on aspects of avian biodiversity (species richness, similarity ofthe avian community, and abundance of selected species). The Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) provides historic, annual data on avian biodiversity across the U.S. We will examine avian communities before and after disturbance, and will pair BBS routes that experienced disturbance with BBS routes that remained undisturbed. To quantify the magnitude of fire, heat, and drought disturbance events, we will use MODIS fire, surface temperature, and LAIINPP products. We will also use Landsat TM/ETM+ derived forest disturbance data (LEDAPS) to develop algorithms that quantify the magnitude of disturbance caused by storms, c1earcuts, fragmentation, and housing development. To relate disturbance to biodiversity, we will develop new statistical procedures that not only answer our research questions, but also represent a major advance in statistics by testing several new model selection approaches, some of which (Bayesian hierarchical modeling) have never been applied in biodiversity or remote sensing studies. Understanding determinants of biodiversity pattern is a major scientific challenge of our times. This project has the potential to substantially contribute to the understanding of processes underlying biodiversity pattern, to the nascent of field of remote sensing of biodiversity, and to society at large struggling to protect biodiversity in the face of increasing human land use and land cover change. Description: Against the Grain: The Effects of Widespread, Intensifying Agriculture on tlie Biosphere and Climate System This proposal aims to improve our understanding of how the expansion and intensification of agriculture - including shifting cropping and deforestation practices, plus changing levels of agricultural inputs from fertilizers and irrigation - have affected terrestrial ecosystems across the world and their biogeochemical and biophysical coupling to the climate system. The study has four major objectives: Objective #1 - Documenting Shifting Patterns of Global Agriculture. In order to examine the environmental consequences of agricultural land use, it is important to not only understand the patterns of agricultural land cover (e.g., cropland, pasture), but also of land-use practices (e.g., crop selection, fertilizer use, irrigation, tillage). Using a combination of satellite-based measurements and detailed agricultural census databases, we will derive new spatially explicit, global datasets of agricultural land cover (for croplands, pastures) and land use practices (crop selection and yield, fertilizer inputs, irrigation and tillage). Objective #2 - Documenting Shifting Deforestation Practices in the Tropics. Until recently, characterizing deforestation has largely focused on estimating the changing areas of "forest" and "non-forest" pixels over time. However, tropical landscapes are highly dynamic and complex: they experience cycles of clearing, cultivation, grazing and secondary forest re-growth, resulting in a complex mosaic of intact rainforest, agricultural lands under varying management regimes, and recovering secondary forests. Using a new "hybrid" technique - blending coarse-resolution remote sensing products, fine-resolution satellite data and detailed ground-based surveys - we will examine and document the pan-tropical patterns of gross forest clearing, agricultural land use, and subsequent abandonment and forest re-growth. Furthermore, we will determine characteristic land-cover transition rates following deforestation across the tropics, so that these data may be used in next-generation carbon cycle and coupled carbon-climate models. Objective #3 - Examining Impacts of Changing Agricultural Practices on Terrestrial Ecosystems. We will use a highly integrated, off-line terrestrial ecosystem model (PEGASUS), in conjunction with datasets derived in Objectives #1 and #2, to explore how global ecological and hydrological systems are responding to changes in agricultural land use and management practices (i.e. changing crop selections, increasing fertilizer use and irrigation, shifting fallow cycles, differing modes of deforestation and abandonment). We will use this off-line model, which is far more computationally efficient than our coupled CCSM-IBIS climate-biosphere model, for key hypothesis testing, parameter estimation, algorithm testing, and model validation studies. We will specifically consider global-scale changes in productivity, carbon storage, soil nutrient balance, and continental-scale river discharge. Objective #4 - Exploring Impacts of Agriculture on Coupled Climate-Biosphere System. Finally, we will use a next-generation coupled climate-biosphere model (CCSM-IBIS), with new, detailed treatments of global agricultural lands (including detailed treatments of sub-grid processes, multiple crop types, management systems, fertilizer inputs, and irrigation) to examine the coupling between terrestrial ecosystems and the atmosphere. Using this model, we will consider how agricultural land use practices affect both the biophysical (through energy / water balance) and biogeochemical (through C02) linkages between terrestrial ecosystems and the atmosphere, paying particular attention to the tropics. We will also work to redefine the notion of "radiative forcing" and "global climatic sensitivity" ofthe climate system, which overlooks the impacts of land-cover change.

Description: A LABORATORY SEARCH FOR CARRIER MOLECULES OF THE DIFFUSE INTERSTELLAR BANDS-GRADUATE STUDENT MARK STOCKETT I propose a laboratory search for the carriers of the Diffuse Interstellar Bands (DIBs), a set of over 300 mostly weak absorption features of the interstellar medium (ISM) scattered throughout the visible and infrared. Though large Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) have long been suspected to be the source the DIBs, no definitive matches have been made to laboratory spectra. My research advisor (J E Lawler) has developed a new very broad band high resolution Spatial Heterodyne Spectrometer (SHS) for use on the white light beamline at the Synchrotron Radiation Center near Madison, Wisconsin. The SHS is a new kind of Fourier transform spectrometer with no moving parts. This new instrument in combination with synchrotron radiation will yield a signal to noise ratio of 100,000 in one minute of integration over the visible and near IR. The instrument's wavelength coverage (200-1100 nm) encompasses all know DIBs. The sensitivity of the new SHS will allow us to perform long-awaited gas phase absorption spectroscopy on a broad range of PAHs with simple evaporation and glow-discharge ionization techniques. This combination of facilities, equipment and expertise is available only at the University of Wisconsin, Madison. In particular, the unique UV capabilities of our new SHS will help answer questions about the mixture of ionization states of PAHs in the ISM. The final identification of the DIB carriers will reveal interesting and important things about the ISM and about the formation of polyatomic species in space. Complex organic molecules like PAHs are the building blocks of life as we know it. Understanding their formation and abundance in space may shed light on the origins of life here on Earth. This will further NASA's Originsi programis Research Area Two: Emerging Modern Universe. The variability of relative DIB intensities along different sight lines could he used to understand variations in the environment and radiation field of the ISM, but only once the carrier is known.

Description: COMPARISON OF A-TRAIN CLOUD RETRIEVALS AND MULTI-INSTRUMENT ALGORITHM STUDIES With the addition of CloudSat and CALIPSO, the A-Train constellation of satellites will provide a unique cloud observing capability through a variety of passive and active instruments. We propose to use our experience In developing MODIS operational cloudproducts to compare the various A-Traln cloud products and explore their inter-sensor consistency. The comparisons will be used to evaluate and Improve existing MODIS algorithms and thereby extend information from the A-Train active observations to the imager swath. We will also pursue strategies for combining measurements from different sensors, specifically the MODIS, CALIPSO lidar and AIRS, to Improve the retrievals of existing cloud products as well as retrieve new cloud information (e.g. asymmetry parameter of cirrus clouds). While improved understanding ofthe biases and uncertainties inherent to passive cloud property retrievals is important for a broad range of science Investigations, our focus will be on the radiative and physical properties of cirrus clouds, particularly thin cirrus (defined as an optical depth of less then 2). Specifically, the investigation will Include: 1. Product comparisons: Collocation and comparison of operational MODIS Aqua cloud products with those from AIRS, POLDER (PARASOL), and the active Instruments on CloudSat and CALIPSO. Products of primary interest include cloud detection, thermodynamic phase, cloud-top properties, multilayer cloud detection, liquid and ice water path, optical thickness, and effective particle size. Analysis will include a variety of cloud types, regions, and seasons. The analysis will be used to better understand the limitations of passive retrievals as well as provide a means for Improving passive techniques, and extending these Improvements to historical satellite data sets. 2. Multi-instrument algorithms: In addition to comparing and characterizing the relative consistency of A-Traln cloud products, we will initiate several studies to develop improved cloud products by combining passive and active observations. These studies will benefit from our experience in the development of research-level cloud retrieval algorithms. Cloud boundary Information from tbe active sensors, particularly CALIPSO, will be ujed as a constraint in AIRS and MODIS retrievals. As a next step, we will develop fundamentally new products by combining the multi-Instrument A-Traln observations Into a single  retrieval using Bayesian or optimal estimation approaches. In addition to retrieving a spectrally unified optical depth, the retrieval approach estimates the asymmetry parameter of cirrus clouds. In the coming decades, passive satellite sensors will continue to be a staple for cloud climatology studies, global cloud process Investigations, as well as forecast and climate model validation, parameterization development, and assimilation. The proposed Investigation will provide an Improved understanding of past, current and future operational passive cloud property retrievals and provide a pathway for algorithm Improvements.

Description: This study proposes the use of CALIPSO and CloudSat to Investigate the interaction between aerosols and mixed-phase Arctic stratus clouds during the International Polar Year (IPY). It is hypothesized that large-scale variability in Arctic aerosols influences significantly the formation and longevity of Arctic stratus through the modification of cloud microphysical properties. The objective of this proposal is to investigate this interaction using a highly unique combination of measurement and analysis tools. This Investigation will consist of analysis of measurements and atmospheric simulation. The revolutionary CALIPSO and CloudSat instruments allow for the continuous collection of aerosol and cloud microphysical data at polar latitudes. In addition to the satellite-based sensors, this study will utilize a powerful contingent of ground-based instrumentation. The University ofWisconsin Arctic High-Spectral Resolution Lidar will be in Eureka, Canada as part ofthe Study of Environmental Arctic Change (SEARCH). This instrument is extremely rare in that it overcomes a major drawback of traditional lidar systems by removing the effects of molecular attenuation from Its returns through the use ofa molecular reference channel. This allows for the retrieval of absolutely calibrated measurements of Aerosol backscatter cross-section, optical depth and depolarization. Additionally, it is one of very few lidar systems located in the Arctic providing continual measurements. Other instruments in Eureka for the SEARCH campaign will include a millimeter cloud radar, particle counters, daily rawinsondes, radiometers, and an in cloud aerosol mass spectrometer. The radar-lidar combination Is especially powerful, with the ability to retrieve particle size and morphology information. The mass spectrometer measures aerosol composition and size information. Together with CALIPSO and CloudSat, this instrumentation suite provides an unprecedented wealth of aerosol and cloud microphysical information, and a solid data collection for this investigation. The model to be utilized in this analysis is the University of Wisconsin Non-Hydrostatic Modeling System (UW-NMS). This fully scalable, state ofthe science cloud/mesoscale model will be utilized to simulate both large-scale Arctic aerosol transport and small-scale cloud processes. This model Is unique in its Spectral Habitat Ice Prediction System (SHIPS) microphysics scheme. Unlike traditional "binned" microphysics, SHIPS allows for an evolutionary hydrometeor size spectrum. This is particularly useful for simulating the ice evolution occurring in these mixed-phase clouds. Validation for the UW-NMS simulations will be obtained from measurements obtained by CALIPSO, CloudSat, and SEARCH instrumentation. This research is in direct support the CALIPSO, CloudSat and SEARCH programs, all of which are sponsored through NASA. Data from these programs will be analyzed, integrated Into a single focus and investigated using the UW-NMS. This addresses precisely the call in this NRA for "investigations in support of modeling and analysis of CALIPSO and CloudSat data toward a goal of improved understanding of clouds and aerosols in the Earth System." Additionally, this project addresses directly several science objectives presented by NASA, including the 5th NASA nationai objective ("Studying the Earth System from space") through the use of CALIPSO and CloudSat derived data, several CALIPSO science data analysis objectives (cloud properties, cloud-aerosol interaction, air quality and pollutant transport, properties of mixed phase clouds, use of modeling to interpret CALIPSO observations), and CloudSat science objective ("Improve our understanding ofthe indirect effect of aerosols on clouds by investigating (in cooperation with other satellite platforms) the effect of aerosols on cloud formation and cloud processes").

Description: A NOVAL BIODOSIMETRY METHOD  Exposure of astronauts to space radiation during extended space missions may cause serious health problems. Accurate methods for measuring the biological effects of radiation exposure are, therefore, critical for estimating an individual' s health risks. Biodosimetry measurements reflect variation in radiation sensitivity and consequently result in highly individualized estimates of dose and risk. Our novel biodosimetry approach is based on the hypothesis that non-coding repetitive DNA sequences are sensitive to radiation-induced mutations and that these mutations are not harmful to a cell. Therefore, mutations in non-coding repetitive DNA sequences can accumulate and provide a stable molecular record of genetic damage that can be used to determine cumulative radiation exposure and health risk. In our previous NASA grant, we demonstrated the feasibility of using radiation-induced mutations in non-coding repetitive DNA sequences to estimate radiation dose. Our initial data indicate that radiation-induced mutations in non-coding repetitive DNA markers are stable over time and additive over multiple exposures. In this successor proposal, we plan to extend our previous work by developing optimized multiplex marker panels for human and mouse biodosimetry, validate our approach by comparing our assay to current gold standard cytological methods and then utilize the novel system to assess risks from space radiation and improve our understanding of how these risks are affected by variations in dose rate, dose fractionation and genome stability. The main contribution of the proposed research to manned space exploration is the validation of a novel biodosimetry method for estimating dose and risks from exposure to space radiation. Completion of this research should provide new insights into the effects of space radiation on DNA mutagenesis and establishes panels of human and mouse biomarkers with broad utility for future studies in radiation biology, toxicology and cancer research.

Description: Using Intelligent Agents to Form a Sensor Web for Autonomous Mission Operations ABSTRACT: Our team proposes to develop an architecture which shifts sensor web control to a distributed set of intelligent agents versus a centrally controlled architecture. Constellation missions introduce levels of complexity that are not easily maintained by a central management activity. A network of intelligent agents reduces management requirements by making use of model based system prediction, and autonomic model/agent collaboration. The proposed architecture incorporates agents distributed throughout the operational environment that monitor and manage spacecraft systems and self-manage the sensor web system via peer-to-peer collaboration. The intelligent agents are mobile and thus will be able to traverse between on-orbit and ground based systems. This network of intelligent mobile agents will be capable of modeling the future behavior of the subsystems and components that they are assigned to. Using situational awareness, the agents will be able.to negotiate activities to self-optimize their subsystems or component. Furthermore, presented with a set of system goals, the network of agents will collaborate within the system to arbitrate the best set of proposed three (3) year effort to an end result proof of concept demonstration, at TRL 7. The demonstration will exercise the architectural features and prove applicability across a broad spectrum of Earth Science missions. Building on the team's experience with EO-1 and ST-5, the new demonstration will take steps towards increased levels of autonomy in mission operations.

Description: IN SITU PLANETARY ATMOSPHERIC MEASUREMENT TECHNOLOGIES. SBIR PHASE I. THE OBJECTIVE OF THIS PHASE I PROGRAM IS TO FURTHER DEMONSTRATE THE FEASIBILITY INCORPORATING CURVED TMC PANELS INTO A HEMISPHERICAL PRESSURE VESSEL. FMW PROPOSES TO PERFORM DESIGN AND MANUFACTURING TRADE STUDIES, EXECUTE RISK ANALYSES AND MANUFACTURE A CURVED TMC PANEL WITH AN INTEGRALLY BONDED MONOLITHIC STRUCTURAL ATTACHMENT POINT. THE ANTICIPATED PRESSURE VESSEL DESIGN REQUIREMENTS ARE NOTED BELOW: - NOMINAL OUTSIDE DIAMETER IS 90 cm (35.43 in) - SHELL MUST WITHSTAND 90 ATMOSPHERES (~1,500 psi) EXTERNAL PRESSURE AND 486'C (~900'F) EXTERNAL TEMPERATURE - PRESSURE VESSEL MUST BE HERMETICALLY SEALED AND RESISTANT TO A SULFURIC ACID ENVIRONMENT - MUST ACCOMMODATE SMALL CAMERA WINDOWS, LIFTING LUGS, STRUCTURAL ATTACHMENT POINTS ON INSIDE AND OUTSIDE OF SHELL, ELECTRICAL FEED-THROUGH - MAY BE SECTIONED IN TWO OR THREE PIECES CURRENT STATE-OF-THE-ART MANUFACTURING PROCESSES ALLOW THE FABRICATION OF FLAT OR SIMPLE CURVATURE PANEL STRUCTURES WITH MULTIPLE FIBER DIRECTIONS AND TUBULAR PARTS WITH FIBERS ALIGNED ALONG THE AXIS AND AROUND THE DIAMETER. COMPOUND CURVED PARTS, SUCH AS THE HEMISPHERE REQUIRED FOR THE VENUS LANDER PRESSURE VESSEL, REQUIRE FURTHER DEVELOPMENT. GEOMETRIC CONSTRAINTS DO NOT ALLOW THE DIRECT LAYUP AND CONSOLIDATION OF A HEMISPHERE USING CONTINUOUS FLAT SHEET TMC PREFORM USED IN MANUFACTURING TUBES OF FLAT STRUCTURE. ADDITIONALLY, BECAUSE TMC IS NOT READILY MACHINED AND IS NOT WELDABLE, METHODS OF INCORPORATING INTEGRAL ATTACHMENTS AND FEED-THROUGHS MUST BE DEVELOPED. THE PRIMARY APPROACH TO MITIGATE LAYUP AND CONSOLIDATION ISSUES IS TO MANUFACTURE INDIVIDUAL PANEL;S THAT ARE SUBSEQUENTLY JOINED IN A SECONDARY DIFFUSION BONDING P[ERATION. tHIS APPROACH BUILDS ON FMW'S CURRENT CAPABILITY TO FABRICATE FLAT OR SIMPLE CURVED PANELS, WHILE KEEPING THE CURVATURE OF THE INDIVIDUAL PANEL SMALL ENOUGH TO ALLOW LAYUP AND CONTROL OF THE FIBERS AND MATRIX (AS DEMONSTRATED IN JPL SUBCONTRACT #1281410). THE JOINING PROCESS COULD EITHER UTILIZE A METHOD OF SANDWICHING CONSOLIDATED TMC PANELS WITH MONOLITHIC EDGES BETWEEN MONOLITHIC TITANIUM SHEETS, OR LAYING UP "GREEN" TMC PANELS INTO A SINGLE HEMISPHERICAL TOOL AND CONSOLIDATING.

Description: NASA SPONSORED CLASSROOM OF THE FUTURE During the last decade the Center for Educational Technologies' project, CLASSROOM OF THE FUTURE, has worked closely with NASA Education to explore and develop new tools to improve science teaching and learning with technology. In 2006 COTF proposes to build on recently successful activities and to develop innovations for continual advancements in technology applied to education. The main tasks are (1) convert the Virtual Design Center, evaluations and various web design skills into an educational curriculum development service; (2) Inspiration research to continue understanding the measurement and enhancement of inspiration; (3) Earthispace educator professional development to satisfy a need for increased for training for NASA and other informal educators; (4) LunarWorld: education, research and SIM to develop educational tools to accompany humanity's second foray beyond Earth orbit; (5) NASA's career central to consolidate dispersed career information; (6) Educational technology exploration lab to continue COTF's mandate to be on the leading edge of applications of new technology to education; (7) NASA educational television to assist NASA in program scheduling and planning; and (8) Educational Outreach to continue to represent NASA to teachers through the upper Ohio valley. All of these efforts build on NASA's current and developing exploration and education interests, including the generational movement to the Moon, and development of educational uses for new technologies such as video podcasting.

Description: GENETIC ANALYSIS OF RADIATION EFFECT ON DNA REPAIR MECHANISMS IN P. AERUGINOSA (GRADUATE STUDENT: FREDRICK HEATH DAMRON) SUMMARY: Space radiation is a major hazard of space exploration because it can cause DNA damage that can lead to deleterious or lethal mutations. Here a ubiquitous bacterium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA), will be used to investigate the effect of ultraviolet light radiation on DNA repair. PA has been acknowledged as a challenging microbe to be eradicated from space exploration vehicles. High throughput genetic systems will be applied to study the global gene responses of PA after exposure to UV radiation.  IAlso, the effect on mutation rate due to increased global gene expression will be examined to better understand the downstream effects that infidelity of DNA repair systems can cause. These data will both benefit basic knowledge of DNA repair and in the future be used for design of mechanisms to attenuate he harmful effects of radiation in higher organisms. Our goal is to discover novel DNA repair mechanisms of Pseudomonas aeruqinosa and understand how harsh environments can influence mutation rate.

Description: Using Intelligent Agents to Form a Sensor Web for Autonomous Mission Operations ABSTRACT: Our team proposes to develop an architecture which shifts sensor web control to a distributed set of intelligent agents versus a centrally controlled architecture. Constellation missions introduce levels of complexity that are not easily maintained by a central management activity. A network of intelligent agents reduces management requirements by making use of model based system prediction, and autonomic model/agent collaboration. The proposed architecture incorporates agents distributed throughout the operational environment that monitor and manage spacecraft systems and self-manage the sensor web system via peer-to-peer collaboration. The intelligent agents are mobile and thus will be able to traverse between on-orbit and ground based systems. This network of intelligent mobile agents will be capable of modeling the future behavior of the subsystems and components that they are assigned to. Using situational awareness, the agents will be able.to negotiate activities to self-optimize their subsystems or component. Furthermore, presented with a set of system goals, the network of agents will collaborate within the system to arbitrate the best set of proposed three (3) year effort to an end result proof of concept demonstration, at TRL 7. The demonstration will exercise the architectural features and prove applicability across a broad spectrum of Earth Science missions. Building on the team's experience with EO-1 and ST-5, the new demonstration will take steps towards increased levels of autonomy in mission operations.

Description: Molecular and Cellular Mechanisms Underlying Skeletal Muscle and Cardiovascular Adaptation to Simulated Microgravity Microgravity-induced dysfunctions of the skeletal muscle and cardiovascular system are major impediments to prolonged space travel and countermeasures are essential if NASA is to fulfill thcir long-term objectives. Using rodent hindlimb unweighting (HLU) as a model of microgravity, we seek to: (1.) Explore two novel mechanisms that respond to microgravity, namely, changes in transcription factor signaling (causative) and modulation of circulating adult stem cells (restorative), and (2.) To identify countermeasures that attenuate these deleterious changes in order to improve the function oftarget tissues during and after spaceflight. The central hypothesis, based on strong preliminary data, is that signal transduction, chromatin structure, and restorative adult stem cells are affected by HLU (microgravity). The specific aims are: (1.) To evaluate how HLU-induced changes in Akt and nuclear factor-kappaB (NF- B) activity are related to alterations in muscle mass, ubiquitin ligase activity and muscle protein ubiquitination, (2) To evaluate the number and phenotype of adult stem cells in HLU animals and (3) To develop interventional protocols to reverse HLU-mediated skeletal muscle and cardiovascular dysfunction. Additional NASA priorities in the form of Administrative Aims wiII also be pursued and are: to support NASA,:s educational mission by providing a rich environment for training; to develop a partnership with West Virginia State University to cultivate educational diversity; and to enhance the applicant,:s competitiveness for extramural funding. This proposal outlines an integrated approach to investigate the mechanisms of these events and the use of novel interventions. Educational and outreach activities wiII provide,:value added,: effect and wiII result in the formation of an investigative group whose research wiII be centered on foci important to the mission of NASA. Information gleaned from these studies wiII have applicability to other disease conditions associated with muscle atrophy including cancer cachexia, aging, AIDS and diabetes.

Description: STUDY OF GLOBAL ICE CLOUD AND ARCTIC MIXED-PHASE CLOUD MICROPHYSICAL PROPERTIES BY COMBINING CLOUDSAT RADAR, CALIPSO LIDAR, AND MODIS MEASUREMENTS The NASA A-Train satellites provide a unique combination of active and passive measurement that will advance our understanding of clouds globally.  We propose to study arctic mixed-phase and ice cloudsw microphysical properties by combining CloudSat radar, Calipso lidar and MODIS measurements. Several recent global coupled atmospheric oceanic model simulations suggest that the Arctic is one of the most sensitive areas to climate change with large uncertainties due in part  to our poor understanding of arctic cloud systems.  Because of differences in detection sensitivity and cloud attenuation, CloudSat radar and CALIPSO libar measurements provide different information to characterize mixed-phase clouds and ice-clouds.  We will develop an algorithm to retrieve microphysical properties of artic mixed-phase clouds by combining radar, lidar and MODIS measurements from the A=train.  Applying the proposed mixed-phase cloud algortihm to the A-Train data will cloud microphysical properties on different scales to better characterize mixed-phase cloud systems which occur frequently in the artic.  The microphysical properties retreieved using our algorithim, combined with surface-based retrievals and atmospheric thermodynamic and dynamic data, will be used to study artic mixed-phase cloud processes and to improve their representation in GCMs. We will also generate an ice cloud microphysical propert database over Artic region combining the radar and liadar measurements which will be more physically consistent thatn would be obtained by simply combining separate CLoudSat and CALIPSO ice cloud products.  Although the main goal of the data base is to develop and avaluate a mainly radar-based method to provide reliable ice phase cloud properties for Artic mixed-phase cloud study, the data base is also important to characterize artic clouds.  After sucessfully developing and evaluating the mixed-phase cloud retrieval algorithm over artic, we will imporve it for mixed-phase cloud study over other regions.
